Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Dīghanikāye

In the Dīgha Nikāya

Sīlakkhandhavaggaṭṭhakathā

Commentary on the Sīlakkhandha Section

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ[P 1.0001][V 1.0001][M 1.0001], paññāpajjotavihatamohatamaṃ;

Sanarāmaralokagaruṃ, vande sugataṃ gativimuttaṃ.

I venerate the Sugata, freed from the five destinies, whose heart is cooled by compassion, who has dispelled the darkness of delusion with the light of wisdom, and who is revered by the world with its humans, devas, and brahmās.

Buddhopi buddhabhāvaṃ, bhāvetvā ceva sacchikatvā ca;

Yaṃ upagato gatamalaṃ, vande tamanuttaraṃ dhammaṃ.

I venerate that unsurpassed and stainless Dhamma, by developing and realizing which even the Buddha attained the state of Buddhahood.

Sugatassa orasānaṃ, puttānaṃ mārasenamathanānaṃ;

Aṭṭhannampi samūhaṃ, sirasā vande ariyasaṅghaṃ.

With my head, I venerate the Noble Sangha, the assembly of the eight sons of the Sugata, who are his true-born offspring, the crushers of Māra's army.

Iti [V 1.0002] me pasannamatino, ratanattayavandanāmayaṃ puññaṃ;

Yaṃ suvihatantarāyo, hutvā tassānubhāvena.

By the power of this merit of mine, of one with a clear and joyful mind, which consists of venerating the Triple Gem, having become one whose obstacles are completely removed...

Dīghassa dīghasuttaṅkitassa, nipuṇassa āgamavarassa;

Buddhānubuddhasaṃvaṇṇitassa, saddhāvahaguṇassa.

Of the Long Collection, marked by its long discourses, a subtle and excellent scripture, extolled by the Buddha and those awakened in his wake, endowed with qualities that inspire faith.

Atthappakāsanatthaṃ, aṭṭhakathā ādito vasisatehi;

Pañcahi yā saṅgītā, anusaṅgītā ca pacchāpi.

For the purpose of clarifying the meaning, the commentary which was first recited by five hundred Arahants, and also subsequently recited later.

Sīhaḷadīpaṃ pana ābhatātha, vasinā mahāmahindena;

Ṭhapitā sīhaḷabhāsāya, dīpavāsīnamatthāya.

Then, however, it was brought to the island of Sīhaḷa by the master, Mahāmahindā, and established in the Sīhaḷa language for the benefit of the island's inhabitants.

Apanetvāna [M 1.0002] tatohaṃ, sīhaḷabhāsaṃ manoramaṃ bhāsaṃ;

Tantinayānucchavikaṃ, āropento vigatadosaṃ.

Having removed the Sīhaḷa language from it, I, rendering it into a delightful language that is free from faults and in keeping with the textual method,

Samayaṃ avilomento, therānaṃ theravaṃsapadīpānaṃ;

Sunipuṇavinicchayānaṃ, mahāvihāre nivāsīnaṃ.

Not contradicting the doctrine of the Elders who reside in the Mahāvihāra, who are lamps unto the lineage of the Elders and possess exceedingly subtle judgment,

Hitvā punappunāgatamatthaṃ, atthaṃ pakāsayissāmi;

Sujanassa ca tuṭṭhatthaṃ, ciraṭṭhitatthañca dhammassa.

Having omitted repetitive explanations, I shall clarify the meaning for the satisfaction of good people and for the long endurance of the Dhamma.

Sīlakathā dhutadhammā, kammaṭṭhānāni ceva sabbāni;

Cariyāvidhānasahito, jhānasamāpattivitthāro.

The discourse on virtue, the ascetic practices, and all meditation subjects; together with the arrangement of temperaments, and the detailed exposition of the jhānas and attainments.

Sabbā ca abhiññāyo, paññāsaṅkalananicchayo ceva;

Khandhadhātāyatanindriyāni, ariyāni ceva cattāri.

And all the higher knowledges, and the determination by summarizing wisdom; the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, faculties, and the four noble...

Saccāni [P 1.0002] paccayākāradesanā, suparisuddhanipuṇanayā;

Avimuttatantimaggā, vipassanā bhāvanā ceva.

Truths; the exposition of the conditional relations, with its exceedingly pure and subtle method; and the development of insight, the path of the unbroken textual lineage.

Iti [V 1.0003] pana sabbaṃ yasmā, visuddhimagge mayā suparisuddhaṃ;

Vuttaṃ tasmā bhiyyo, na taṃ idha vicārayissāmi.

Since all this has been explained by me in an exceedingly pure manner in the Visuddhimagga, therefore, I will not treat of it further here.

“Majjhe visuddhimaggo, esa catunnampi āgamānañhi;

Ṭhatvā pakāsayissati, tattha yathā bhāsitaṃ atthaṃ”.

“This Visuddhimagga, standing in the midst of all four Āgamas, will indeed reveal the meaning therein, just as it was spoken.”

Icceva kato tasmā, tampi gahetvāna saddhimetāya;

Aṭṭhakathāya vijānatha, dīghāgamanissitaṃ atthanti.

It was with this very intention that it was composed. Therefore, taking that [Visuddhimagga] also, together with this commentary, you should understand the meaning that is based on the Long Collection.

Nidānakathā

The Introductory Discourse

Tattha dīghāgamo nāma sīlakkhandhavaggo, mahāvaggo, pāthikavaggoti vaggato tivaggo hoti; suttato catuttiṃsasuttasaṅgaho. Tassa vaggesu sīlakkhandhavaggo ādi, suttesu brahmajālaṃ. Brahmajālassāpi “evaṃ [M 1.0003] me suta”ntiādikaṃ āyasmatā ānandena paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle vuttaṃ nidānamādi.

Therein, that which is called the Long Collection has three divisions by way of sections: the Division of the Aggregate of Virtue, the Great Division, and the Pāthika Division; by way of discourses, it is a collection of thirty-four suttas. Among its divisions, the Division of the Aggregate of Virtue is first; among the suttas, the Brahmajāla is first. Of the Brahmajāla also, the introduction beginning “Thus have I heard,” spoken by the venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council, is the beginning.

Paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā

The Account of the First Great Council

Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti nāma cesā kiñcāpi vinayapiṭake tantimārūḷhā, nidānakosallatthaṃ pana idhāpi evaṃ veditabbā. Dhammacakkappavattanañhi ādiṃ katvā yāva subhaddaparibbājakavinayanā katabuddhakicce, kusinārāyaṃ upavattane mallānaṃ sālavane yamakasālānamantare visākhapuṇṇamadivase paccūsasamaye anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbute bhagavati lokanāthe, bhagavato dhātubhājanadivase sannipatitānaṃ sattannaṃ bhikkhusatasahassānaṃ saṅghatthero āyasmā mahākassapo sattāhaparinibbute bhagavati subhaddena vuḍḍhapabbajitena – “alaṃ, āvuso, mā socittha, mā paridevittha, sumuttā mayaṃ tena mahāsamaṇena, upaddutā ca homa – ‘idaṃ vo kappati, idaṃ vo na kappatī’ti, idāni pana mayaṃ yaṃ icchissāma, taṃ karissāma, yaṃ na icchissāma na taṃ karissāmā”ti (cūḷava. 437) vuttavacanamanussaranto, īdisassa ca saṅghasannipātassa puna dullabhabhāvaṃ maññamāno, “ṭhānaṃ [V 1.0004] kho panetaṃ vijjati, yaṃ pāpabhikkhū ‘atītasatthukaṃ pāvacana’nti maññamānā [P 1.0003] pakkhaṃ labhitvā nacirasseva saddhammaṃ antaradhāpeyyuṃ, yāva ca dhammavinayo tiṭṭhati, tāva anatītasatthukameva pāvacanaṃ hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Although this, which is called the First Great Council, has been included in the text of the Vinaya Piṭaka, for the purpose of skill in the introduction, it should be understood here also in this way. For when the Blessed One, the Protector of the World, having completed the Buddha's duties from the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma up to the taming of the wanderer Subhadda, had passed into final Nibbāna with the Nibbāna-element that has no remainder of aggregates in Kusinārā, at the Upavattana Sāla grove of the Mallas, between the twin Sāla trees, on the full-moon day of Visākha, at the time of dawn; on the day of the distribution of the Blessed One's relics, the Venerable Mahākassapa, the Elder of the Saṅgha of the seven hundred thousand monks who had assembled, recalling the words spoken seven days after the Blessed One's final Nibbāna by Subhadda, who had gone forth in old age—'Enough, friends, do not grieve, do not lament. We are well freed from that great ascetic. We were oppressed by his saying, “This is allowable for you, this is not allowable for you.” But now we will do what we wish, and we will not do what we do not wish'—and considering the future rarity of such a gathering of the Saṅgha, thought: 'This possibility indeed exists, that evil monks, thinking “the teaching's Teacher has passed away,” might gain a faction and before long cause the true Dhamma to disappear. And as long as the Dhamma and Vinaya endure, the teaching is one whose Teacher has not passed away. For this was said by the Blessed One—'

‘Yo vo, ānanda, mayā dhammo ca vinayo ca desito paññatto, so vo mamaccayena satthā’ti (dī. ni. 2.216).

'Ānanda, that Dhamma and Vinaya which I have taught and laid down for you, that will be your Teacher after my passing.'

‘Yaṃnūnāhaṃ dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyeyyaṃ, yathayidaṃ sāsanaṃ addhaniyaṃ assa ciraṭṭhitikaṃ’.

'Let me now chant the Dhamma and the Vinaya together, so that this Dispensation might be long-lasting and endure for a long time.'

Yañcāhaṃ bhagavatā –

And I was favored by the Blessed One:

‘Dhāressasi pana me tvaṃ, kassapa, sāṇāni paṃsukūlāni nibbasanānī’ti (saṃ. ni. 2.154) vatvā cīvare sādhāraṇaparibhogena.

by the shared use of his robe, after he said, 'Kassapa, will you wear my worn-out hempen rag-robes?';

‘Ahaṃ, bhikkhave, yāvadeva ākaṅkhāmi vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ [M 1.0004] jhānaṃ upasampajja viharāmi; kassapopi, bhikkhave, yāvadeva, ākaṅkhati vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharatī’ti (saṃ. ni. 2.152).

'Monks, whenever I wish, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. Monks, Kassapa too, whenever he wishes, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.'

Evamādinā nayena navānupubbavihārachaḷabhiññāppabhede uttarimanussadhamme attanā samasamaṭṭhapanena ca anuggahito, tathā ākāse pāṇiṃ cāletvā alaggacittatāya ceva candopamapaṭipadāya ca pasaṃsito, tassa kimaññaṃ āṇaṇyaṃ bhavissati. Nanu maṃ bhagavā rājā viya sakakavacaissariyānuppadānena attano kulavaṃsappatiṭṭhāpakaṃ puttaṃ ‘saddhammavaṃsappatiṭṭhāpako me ayaṃ bhavissatī’ti, mantvā iminā asādhāraṇena anuggahena anuggahesi, imāya ca uḷārāya pasaṃsāya pasaṃsīti cintayanto dhammavinayasaṅgāyanatthaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ussāhaṃ janesi. Yathāha –

By this method beginning thus, I was favored by being placed on an equal level with himself in the superhuman states, which are divided into the nine successive attainments and the six supernormal knowledges; and furthermore, having moved his hand in the air, I was praised for having an unattached mind and for the practice comparable to the moon. For me, such a one, what other freedom from debt could there be? Thinking: 'Did not the Blessed One, like a king bestowing his own armor and sovereignty upon a son who would establish his family lineage, thinking, “This one will be the establisher of my true Dhamma lineage,” favor me with this uncommon support and praise me with this lofty acclaim?' he inspired the monks to strive for the communal recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya. As it is said—

“Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘ekamidāhaṃ, āvuso, samayaṃ [V 1.0005] pāvāya kusināraṃ addhānamaggappaṭipanno mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehī”ti (cūḷava. 437) sabbaṃ subhaddakaṇḍaṃ vitthārato veditabbaṃ. Atthaṃ panassa mahāparinibbānāvasāne āgataṭṭhāneyeva kathayissāma.

'Then the Venerable Mahākassapa addressed the monks: “Once, friends, I was traveling the long road from Pāvā to Kusinārā with a great Saṅgha of monks, with five hundred monks.”' The entire Subhadda section should be understood in detail. But we will explain its meaning only at the place where it appears, at the end of the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta.

Tato paraṃ āha –

After that, he said further:

“Handa mayaṃ, āvuso, dhammañca vinayañca [P 1.0004] saṅgāyāma, pure adhammo dippati, dhammo paṭibāhiyyati; pure avinayo dippati, vinayo paṭibāhiyyati; pure adhammavādino balavanto honti, dhammavādino dubbalā honti, pure avinayavādino balavanto honti, vinayavādino dubbalā hontī”ti (cūḷava. 437).

'Come now, friends, let us chant the Dhamma and the Vinaya together, before the non-Dhamma shines forth and the Dhamma is obstructed; before the non-Vinaya shines forth and the Vinaya is obstructed; before those who speak non-Dhamma become strong and those who speak Dhamma become weak; before those who speak non-Vinaya become strong and those who speak Vinaya become weak.'

Bhikkhū āhaṃsu – “tena hi, bhante, thero bhikkhū uccinatū”ti. Thero pana sakalanavaṅgasatthusāsanapariyattidhare puthujjanasotāpannasakadāgāmianāgāmi sukkhavipassaka khīṇāsavabhikkhū anekasate, anekasahasse ca [M 1.0005] vajjetvā tipiṭakasabbapariyattippabhedadhare paṭisambhidāppatte mahānubhāve yebhuyyena bhagavato etadaggaṃ āropite tevijjādibhede khīṇāsavabhikkhūyeva ekūnapañcasate pariggahesi. Ye sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ – “atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo ekenūnāni pañca arahantasatāni uccinī”ti (cūḷava. 437).

The monks said: 'Well then, venerable sir, let the Elder select the monks.' The Elder, however, having excluded the many hundreds and thousands of worldlings, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, dry-insight practitioners, and Arahant monks who were bearers of the entire nine-limbed teaching of the Teacher, selected only four hundred and ninety-nine Arahant monks who were bearers of the divisions of the entire scriptural teaching of the three Piṭakas, had attained the analytical knowledges, were of great power, and were for the most part those whom the Blessed One had placed in the foremost position with distinctions such as the three knowledges. Regarding them, it was said: 'Then the Venerable Mahākassapa selected four hundred and ninety-nine Arahants.'

Kissa pana thero ekenūnamakāsīti? Āyasmato ānandattherassa okāsakaraṇatthaṃ. Tenahāyasmatā sahāpi, vināpi, na sakkā dhammasaṅgītiṃ kātuṃ. So hāyasmā sekkho sakaraṇīyo, tasmā sahāpi na sakkā. Yasmā panassa kiñci dasabaladesitaṃ suttageyyādikaṃ appaccakkhaṃ nāma natthi. Yathāha –

But why did the Elder make it one less? For the purpose of making an opportunity for the Venerable Elder Ānanda. For with that venerable one, and also without him, it was not possible to hold the Dhamma chanting. For that venerable one was a trainee, with a task yet to be done; therefore, with him it was not possible. Because, however, for him there was nothing at all taught by the Ten-Powered One—such as suttas, geyyas, and so forth—that was not directly witnessed. As he said:

“Dvāsīti buddhato gaṇhiṃ, dve sahassāni bhikkhuto;

Caturāsīti sahassāni, ye me dhammā pavattino”ti. (theragā. 1027);

'Eighty-two thousand I learned from the Buddha, two thousand from the monks; eighty-four thousand are the teachings that are current for me.'

Tasmā vināpi na sakkā.

Therefore, without him also it was not possible.

Yadi evaṃ sekkhopi samāno dhammasaṅgītiyā bahukārattā therena uccinitabbo assa, atha kasmā na uccinitoti? Parūpavādavivajjanato. Thero hi āyasmante ānande ativiya [V 1.0006] vissattho ahosi, tathā hi naṃ sirasmiṃ palitesu jātesupi ‘na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsī’ti, (saṃ. ni. 2.154) kumārakavādena ovadati. Sakyakulappasuto cāyasmā tathāgatassa bhātā cūḷapituputto. Tattha keci bhikkhū chandāgamanaṃ viya maññamānā – “bahū asekkhapaṭisambhidāppatte bhikkhū ṭhapetvā [P 1.0005] ānandaṃ sekkhapaṭisambhidāppattaṃ thero uccinī”ti upavadeyyuṃ. Taṃ parūpavādaṃ parivajjento, ‘ānandaṃ vinā dhammasaṅgītiṃ na sakkā kātuṃ, bhikkhūnaṃyeva naṃ anumatiyā gahessāmī’ti na uccini.

If that is so, then even though he was a learner, because he was of great service to the Dhamma recitation, he was worthy of being selected by the Elder. So why was he not selected? To avoid the accusations of others. For the Elder was extremely familiar with the Venerable Ānanda; indeed, even when grey hairs appeared on his head, he would admonish him with the term ‘young man,’ saying, “This young man does not know his own measure.” And the Venerable Ānanda was born into the Sakyan clan and was the Tathāgata’s brother, the son of his paternal uncle. In that case, some monks, thinking it was like acting out of favoritism, might accuse him thus: “The Elder, having set aside many non-learners who had attained the analytical knowledges, selected Ānanda, a learner who had attained the analytical knowledges.” Avoiding that accusation from others, and thinking, “It is not possible to hold the Dhamma recitation without Ānanda; I will accept him only with the consent of the monks,” he did not select him.

Atha sayameva bhikkhū ānandassatthāya theraṃ yāciṃsu. Yathāha –

Then the monks themselves requested the Elder on Ānanda's behalf. As it is said:

“Bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ mahākassapaṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘ayaṃ, bhante, āyasmā ānando kiñcāpi sekkho abhabbo chandā dosā mohā bhayā agatiṃ gantuṃ, bahu cānena bhagavato santike dhammo ca vinayo ca pariyatto, tena hi, bhante, thero āyasmantampi [M 1.0006] ānandaṃ uccinatū’ti. Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo āyasmantampi ānandaṃ uccinī”ti (cūḷava. 437).

The monks said this to the Venerable Mahākassapa: “Venerable sir, although this Venerable Ānanda is a learner, he is incapable of following an improper course through desire, hatred, delusion, or fear. And much of the Dhamma and Vinaya has been learned by him in the Blessed One's presence. Therefore, venerable sir, let the Elder also select the Venerable Ānanda.” Then the Venerable Mahākassapa also selected the Venerable Ānanda.

Evaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anumatiyā uccinitena tenāyasmatā saddhiṃ pañcatherasatāni ahesuṃ.

Thus, with that venerable one who had been selected with the monks' consent, there were five hundred elders.

Atha kho therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ etadahosi – “kattha nu kho mayaṃ dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyeyyāmā”ti? Atha kho therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ etadahosi – “rājagahaṃ kho mahāgocaraṃ pahūtasenāsanaṃ, yaṃnūna mayaṃ rājagahe vassaṃ vasantā dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyeyyāma, na aññe bhikkhū rājagahe vassaṃ upagaccheyyu”nti (cūḷava. 437).

Then this thought occurred to the elder monks: “Where, indeed, should we chant the Dhamma and the Vinaya?” Then this thought occurred to the elder monks: “Rājagaha has a wide area for alms-rounds and has abundant lodgings. What if we were to spend the rainy season in Rājagaha and chant the Dhamma and the Vinaya, and no other monks were to enter the rains-residence in Rājagaha?”

Kasmā pana nesaṃ etadahosi? “Idaṃ pana amhākaṃ thāvarakammaṃ, koci visabhāgapuggalo saṅghamajjhaṃ pavisitvā ukkoṭeyyā”ti. Athāyasmā mahākassapo ñattidutiyena kammena sāvesi –

But why did this thought occur to them? “This work of ours is a lasting one; let no unsuitable individual, having entered the midst of the Saṅgha, disrupt it.” Then the Venerable Mahākassapa made it known by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation:

“Suṇātu [V 1.0007] me, āvuso saṅgho, yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ saṅgho imāni pañca bhikkhusatāni sammanneyya rājagahe vassaṃ vasantāni dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyituṃ, na aññehi bhikkhūhi rājagahe vassaṃ vasitabba”nti. Esā ñatti.

“Venerables, may the Saṅgha hear me. If the time is right for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should authorize these five hundred monks to chant the Dhamma and the Vinaya while dwelling in Rājagaha for the rainy season. No other monks are to dwell in Rājagaha for the rainy season.” This is the motion.

“Suṇātu me, āvuso saṅgho, saṅgho imāni pañcabhikkhusatāni sammanna”ti ‘rājagahe vassaṃ vasantāni dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyituṃ, na aññehi bhikkhūhi rājagahe vassaṃ vasitabbanti. Yassāyasmato khamati imesaṃ pañcannaṃ [P 1.0006] bhikkhusatānaṃ sammuti’ rājagahe vassaṃ vasantānaṃ dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyituṃ, na aññehi bhikkhūhi rājagahe vassaṃ vasitabbanti, so tuṇhassa; yassa nakkhamati, so bhāseyya.

“Venerables, may the Saṅgha hear me. The Saṅgha authorizes these five hundred monks to chant the Dhamma and the Vinaya while dwelling in Rājagaha for the rainy season; no other monks are to dwell in Rājagaha for the rainy season. Let the venerable one to whom the authorization of these five hundred monks to chant the Dhamma and the Vinaya while dwelling in Rājagaha for the rainy season—and that no other monks are to dwell in Rājagaha for the rainy season—is agreeable, remain silent. He to whom it is not agreeable should speak.”

“Sammatāni saṅghena imāni pañcabhikkhusatāni rājagahe vassaṃ vasantāni dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyituṃ, na aññehi bhikkhūhi rājagahe vassaṃ vasitabbanti, khamati saṅghassa, tasmā tuṇhī, evametaṃ dhārayāmī”ti (cūḷava. 438).

“These five hundred monks have been authorized by the Saṅgha to chant the Dhamma and the Vinaya while dwelling in Rājagaha for the rainy season, and no other monks are to dwell in Rājagaha for the rainy season. This is agreeable to the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent. Thus I bear this in mind.”

Ayaṃ [M 1.0007] pana kammavācā tathāgatassa parinibbānato ekavīsatime divase katā. Bhagavā hi visākhapuṇṇamāyaṃ paccūsasamaye parinibbuto, athassa sattāhaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sarīraṃ gandhamālādīhi pūjayiṃsu. Evaṃ sattāhaṃ sādhukīḷanadivasā nāma ahesuṃ. Tato sattāhaṃ citakāya agginā jhāyi, sattāhaṃ sattipañjaraṃ katvā sandhāgārasālāyaṃ dhātupūjaṃ kariṃsūti, ekavīsati divasā gatā. Jeṭṭhamūlasukkapakkhapañcamiyaṃyeva dhātuyo bhājayiṃsu. Etasmiṃ dhātubhājanadivase sannipatitassa mahābhikkhusaṅghassa subhaddena vuḍḍhapabbajitena kataṃ anācāraṃ ārocetvā vuttanayeneva ca bhikkhū uccinitvā ayaṃ kammavācā katā.

This formal act, however, was performed on the twenty-first day after the Tathāgata’s Parinibbāna. For the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna at dawn on the Visākhā full-moon day. Then, for seven days, they honored his golden-hued body with perfumes, garlands, and so forth. Thus, for seven days, there were what are called 'days of pious celebration.' Then, for seven days, the body was burned by fire on the pyre. For another seven days, having made an enclosure of spears, they performed the veneration of the relics in the assembly hall. Thus, twenty-one days passed. On the fifth day of the waxing moon of the month of Jeṭṭhamūla, they distributed the relics. On this day of the distribution of relics, having announced to the great Saṅgha of monks who had assembled the improper conduct committed by Subhadda, who had gone forth in old age, and having selected the monks in the manner already stated, this formal act was performed.

Imañca pana kammavācaṃ katvā thero bhikkhū āmantesi – “āvuso, idāni tumhākaṃ cattālīsa divasā okāso kato, tato paraṃ ‘ayaṃ nāma no palibodho atthī’ti, vattuṃ na labbhā, tasmā etthantare yassa rogapalibodho vā ācariyupajjhāyapalibodho vā mātāpitupalibodho vā atthi, pattaṃ vā pana pacitabbaṃ, cīvaraṃ vā kātabbaṃ, so taṃ palibodhaṃ chinditvā taṃ karaṇīyaṃ karotū”ti.

And having performed this formal act, the Elder addressed the monks: “Friends, an opportunity of forty days has now been made for you. After that, it will not be allowable to say, ‘We have such-and-such an impediment.’ Therefore, within this period, whoever has an impediment due to illness, or an impediment concerning a teacher or preceptor, or an impediment concerning mother and father, or has a bowl to be fired, or a robe to be made, let him, having severed that impediment, do what needs to be done.”

Evañca pana vatvā thero attano pañcasatāya parisāya parivuto rājagahaṃ gato. Aññepi mahātherā attano attano parivāre gahetvā sokasallasamappitaṃ mahājanaṃ assāsetukāmā taṃ taṃ disaṃ pakkantā. Puṇṇatthero pana sattasatabhikkhuparivāro ‘tathāgatassa parinibbānaṭṭhānaṃ āgatāgataṃ mahājanaṃ assāsessāmī’ti kusinārāyaṃyeva aṭṭhāsi.

And having spoken thus, the Elder, surrounded by his retinue of five hundred, went to Rājagaha. Other great elders also, taking their own retinues, departed to various directions, desiring to console the great populace pierced by the dart of sorrow. But the Elder Puṇṇa, with a retinue of seven hundred monks, remained right in Kusinārā, thinking, “I will console the great populace who come and go to the place of the Tathāgata’s Parinibbāna.”

Āyasmā ānando yathā pubbe aparinibbutassa, evaṃ parinibbutassāpi bhagavato sayameva [V 1.0008] pattacīvaramādāya pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ yena sāvatthi tena cārikaṃ pakkāmi. Gacchato gacchato panassa parivārā bhikkhū gaṇanapathaṃ vītivattā. Tenāyasmatā gatagataṭṭhāne mahāparidevo ahosi[P 1.0007]. Anupubbena pana sāvatthimanuppatte there sāvatthivāsino manussā “thero kira āgato”ti sutvā gandhamālādihatthā paccuggantvā – “bhante, ānanda, pubbe bhagavatā saddhiṃ āgacchatha, ajja kuhiṃ bhagavantaṃ [M 1.0008] ṭhapetvā āgatatthā”tiādīni vadamānā parodiṃsu. Buddhassa bhagavato parinibbānadivase viya mahāparidevo ahosi.

Venerable Ānanda, just as before, when the Blessed One had not yet attained Parinibbāna, so too after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, he himself took the Blessed One's bowl and robe and set out on a journey towards Sāvatthī with five hundred monks. Furthermore, as he went on and on, the monks in his retinue surpassed counting. For that venerable one, in whatever place he went, great lamentation arose. In due course, when the elder arrived at Sāvatthī, the inhabitants of Sāvatthī, having heard, 'The elder, it is said, has come,' and taking perfumes, garlands, and so forth in their hands, went out to meet him. Saying such things as, 'Venerable Ānanda, formerly you came together with the Blessed One. Today, where have you left the Blessed One and come?' they lamented intensely. Great lamentation arose, as on the day of the Parinibbāna of the Buddha, the Blessed One.

Tatra sudaṃ āyasmā ānando aniccatādipaṭisaṃyuttāya dhammiyākathāya taṃ mahājanaṃ saññāpetvā jetavanaṃ pavisitvā dasabalena vasitagandhakuṭiṃ vanditvā dvāraṃ vivaritvā mañcapīṭhaṃ nīharitvā papphoṭetvā gandhakuṭiṃ sammajjitvā milātamālākacavaraṃ chaḍḍetvā mañcapīṭhaṃ atiharitvā puna yathāṭhāne ṭhapetvā bhagavato ṭhitakāle karaṇīyaṃ vattaṃ sabbamakāsi. Kurumāno ca nhānakoṭṭhakasammajjanaudakupaṭṭhāpanādikālesu gandhakuṭiṃ vanditvā – “nanu bhagavā, ayaṃ tumhākaṃ nhānakālo, ayaṃ dhammadesanākālo, ayaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ovādadānakālo, ayaṃ sīhaseyyakappanakālo, ayaṃ mukhadhovanakālo”tiādinā nayena paridevamānova akāsi, yathā taṃ bhagavato guṇagaṇāmatarasaññutāya patiṭṭhitapemo ceva akhīṇāsavo ca anekesu ca jātisatasahassesu aññamaññassūpakārasañjanitacittamaddavo. Tamenaṃ aññatarā devatā – “bhante, ānanda, tumhe evaṃ paridevamānā kathaṃ aññe assāsessathā”ti saṃvejesi. So tassā vacanena saṃviggahadayo santhambhitvā tathāgatassa parinibbānato pabhuti ṭhānanisajjabahulattā ussannadhātukaṃ kāyaṃ samassāsetuṃ dutiyadivase khīravirecanaṃ pivitvā vihāreyeva nisīdi. Yaṃ sandhāya subhena māṇavena pahitaṃ māṇavakaṃ etadavoca –

There, Venerable Ānanda, having comforted that great assembly with a Dhamma talk connected with impermanence and so forth, entered Jetavana. He paid homage to the Fragrant Cell where the One of Ten Powers had resided, opened the door, took out the bed and bench, dusted them off, swept the Fragrant Cell, discarded the withered garlands and rubbish, brought back the bed and bench, and placed them again in their proper places. He performed all the duties that were to be done when the Blessed One was present. And while doing so, at times such as sweeping the bathing chamber and preparing water, he would pay homage to the Fragrant Cell and lament in this manner: 'Blessed One, is this not your time for bathing? Is this not your time for teaching the Dhamma? Is this not your time for giving exhortation to the monks? Is this not your time for taking the lion's repose? Is this not your time for washing your face?' He did so while lamenting intensely, as is befitting for one whose love was firmly established due to knowing the deathless flavour of the Blessed One's collection of virtues, whose cankers were not yet destroyed, and whose heart was tender from the accumulation of mutual help over many hundreds of thousands of births. A certain deity stirred him, saying: 'Venerable Ānanda, if you lament in this way, how will you console others?' He, with his heart stirred by her words, composed himself. And in order to relieve his body, whose elements had become excessive due to much standing and sitting since the Tathāgata's Parinibbāna, on the second day he drank a milk purge and sat down in the monastery itself. It was with reference to this that he said the following to the young man sent by the youth Subha:

“Akālo, kho māṇavaka, atthi me ajja bhesajjamattā pītā, appeva nāma svepi upasaṅkameyyāmā”ti (dī. ni. 1.447).

“It is not the right time, young man. Today I have drunk a medicinal dose. Perhaps tomorrow we may approach.”

Dutiyadivase cetakattherena pacchāsamaṇena gantvā subhena māṇavena puṭṭho imasmiṃ dīghanikāye subhasuttaṃ nāma dasamaṃ suttaṃ abhāsi.

On the second day, having gone with the Elder Cetaka as his attendant monk, when questioned by the youth Subha, he spoke the tenth discourse in this Dīgha Nikāya, named the Subha Sutta.

Atha ānandatthero jetavanamahāvihāre khaṇḍaphullappaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ [P 1.0008] kārāpetvā upakaṭṭhāya vassūpanāyikāya bhikkhusaṅghaṃ ohāya rājagahaṃ gato [M 1.0009] tathā aññepi dhammasaṅgāhakā bhikkhūti. Evañhi gate, te sandhāya ca idaṃ vuttaṃ – “atha kho therā bhikkhū rājagahaṃ agamaṃsu, dhammañca vinayañca [V 1.0009] saṅgāyitu”nti (cūḷava. 438). Te āsaḷhīpuṇṇamāyaṃ uposathaṃ katvā pāṭipadadivase sannipatitvā vassaṃ upagacchiṃsu.

Then, the Elder Ānanda, having arranged for the repair of the broken and dilapidated parts in the Jetavana Great Monastery, when the rains-residence was approaching, left the Saṅgha of monks and went to Rājagaha; likewise did the other monks who were compilers of the Dhamma. Indeed, it was with reference to their having gone in this way that this was said: 'Then the elder monks went to Rājagaha to rehearse the Dhamma and the Vinaya.' They, having performed the Uposatha on the full-moon day of Āsāḷhī, assembled on the following day and entered the rains-residence.

Tena kho pana samayena rājagahaṃ parivāretvā aṭṭhārasa mahāvihārā honti, te sabbepi chaḍḍitapatitauklāpā ahesuṃ. Bhagavato hi parinibbāne sabbepi bhikkhū attano attano pattacīvaramādāya vihāre ca pariveṇe ca chaḍḍetvā agamaṃsu. Tattha katikavattaṃ kurumānā therā bhagavato vacanapūjanatthaṃ titthiyavādaparimocanatthañca – ‘paṭhamaṃ māsaṃ khaṇḍaphullappaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ karomā’ti cintesuṃ. Titthiyā hi evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – “samaṇassa gotamassa sāvakā satthari ṭhiteyeva vihāre paṭijaggiṃsu, parinibbute chaḍḍesuṃ, kulānaṃ mahādhanapariccāgo vinassatī”ti. Tesañca vādaparimocanatthaṃ cintesunti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ cintayitvā ca pana katikavattaṃ kariṃsu. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

Now at that time, there were eighteen great monasteries surrounding Rājagaha, all of which had been abandoned, were dilapidated, and were filled with rubbish. For, on account of the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, all the monks, taking their own bowls and robes, had abandoned the monasteries and their precincts and departed. There, the elders, wishing to establish an agreement in order to honour the Blessed One's word and to be free from the accusations of the sectarians, considered: 'Let us spend the first month repairing what is broken and dilapidated.' For the sectarians might say: 'The disciples of the ascetic Gotama looked after the monasteries only while their Teacher was alive; when he attained Parinibbāna, they abandoned them. The great donation of wealth by the families is being destroyed.' And it is said that they considered this for the sake of freedom from their accusations. Having considered thus, they made an agreement. It is with reference to this that it was said:

“Atha kho therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ etadahosi – bhagavatā, kho āvuso, khaṇḍaphullappaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ vaṇṇitaṃ, handa mayaṃ, āvuso, paṭhamaṃ māsaṃ khaṇḍaphullappaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ karoma, majjhimaṃ māsaṃ sannipatitvā dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyissāmā”ti (cūḷava. 438).

“Then this thought occurred to the elder monks: ‘Friends, the Blessed One has praised the repairing of what is broken and dilapidated. Come now, friends, let us spend the first month repairing what is broken and dilapidated. In the middle month, let us assemble and rehearse the Dhamma and the Vinaya.’”

Te dutiyadivase gantvā rājadvāre aṭṭhaṃsu. Rājā āgantvā vanditvā – “kiṃ bhante, āgatatthā”ti attanā kattabbakiccaṃ pucchi. Therā aṭṭhārasa mahāvihārapaṭisaṅkharaṇatthāya hatthakammaṃ paṭivedesuṃ. Rājā hatthakammakārake manusse adāsi. Therā paṭhamaṃ māsaṃ sabbavihāre paṭisaṅkharāpetvā rañño ārocesuṃ – “niṭṭhitaṃ, mahārāja, vihārapaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ, idāni dhammavinayasaṅgahaṃ karomā”ti. “Sādhu bhante visaṭṭhā karotha, mayhaṃ āṇācakkaṃ[P 1.0009], tumhākañca dhammacakkaṃ hotu, āṇāpetha, bhante, kiṃ karomī”ti. “Saṅgahaṃ karontānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sannisajjaṭṭhānaṃ mahārājā”ti. “Kattha karomi, bhante”ti? “Vebhārapabbatapasse sattapaṇṇi guhādvāre kātuṃ yuttaṃ mahārājā”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti kho rājā ajātasattu vissakammunā [M 1.0010] nimmitasadisaṃ suvibhattabhittithambhasopānaṃ, nānāvidhamālākammalatākammavicittaṃ, abhibhavantamiva rājabhavanavibhūtiṃ, avahasantamiva devavimānasiriṃ, siriyā niketanamiva ekanipātatitthamiva ca devamanussanayanavihaṃgānaṃ, lokarāmaṇeyyakamiva sampiṇḍitaṃ daṭṭhabbasāramaṇḍaṃ maṇḍapaṃ kārāpetvā vividhakusumadāmolambakaviniggalantacāruvitānaṃ nānāratanavicittamaṇikoṭṭimatalamiva ca, naṃ nānāpupphūpahāravicittasupariniṭṭhitabhūmikammaṃ brahmavimānasadisaṃ alaṅkaritvā, tasmiṃ mahāmaṇḍape [V 1.0010] pañcasatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anagghāni pañca kappiyapaccattharaṇasatāni paññapetvā, dakkhiṇabhāgaṃ nissāya uttarābhimukhaṃ therāsanaṃ, maṇḍapamajjhe puratthābhimukhaṃ buddhassa bhagavato āsanārahaṃ dhammāsanaṃ paññapetvā, dantakhacitaṃ bījaniñcettha ṭhapetvā, bhikkhusaṅghassa ārocāpesi – “niṭṭhitaṃ, bhante, mama kicca”nti.

On the second day, they went and stood at the king’s gate. The king came, paid homage, and asked, “Venerable sirs, for what reason have you come?”—thus inquiring about the duty he should perform. The elders informed him of the need for manual labor to restore the eighteen great monasteries. The king provided men for the manual labor. The elders, having had all the monasteries restored during the first month, informed the king: “Great king, the restoration of the monasteries is complete. Now we shall hold a council of the Dhamma and Vinaya.” “Very well, venerable sirs, proceed with confidence. Let mine be the wheel of authority, and yours the wheel of Dhamma. Command me, venerable sirs, what shall I do?” “Great king, a place is needed for the monks holding the council to assemble and sit.” “Where shall I prepare it, venerable sirs?” “Great king, it is suitable to prepare it at the entrance of the Sattapaṇṇi Cave on the slope of Vebhāra Mountain.” “Very well, venerable sirs.” Then King Ajātasattu had a pavilion built that resembled a creation by Vissakamma, the divine architect. It had well-proportioned walls, pillars, and staircases, and was made beautiful with various kinds of garland-work and creeper-work. It seemed to surpass the splendor of a royal palace, to mock the glory of a celestial mansion, to be a very abode of splendor, a single alighting place for the bird-like eyes of gods and humans, and like the loveliness of the world gathered together, an essence of all that is worth seeing. Having had this pavilion built, he had it adorned to resemble a Brahma’s mansion. It had beautiful canopies from which various flower garlands hung, and its ground-work was exquisitely finished and variegated with offerings of various flowers, like a floor paved with gems of many kinds. In that great pavilion, he had five hundred priceless, suitable coverings prepared for the five hundred monks. Against the southern side, he had the elder’s seat placed facing north, and in the middle of the pavilion, a Dhamma seat worthy of the Blessed One, the Buddha, placed facing east. He also placed an ivory-inlaid fan there. Then he had it announced to the Saṅgha of monks: “Venerable sirs, my task is complete.”

Tasmiñca pana divase ekacce bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ sandhāya evamāhaṃsu – “imasmiṃ bhikkhusaṅghe eko bhikkhu vissagandhaṃ vāyanto vicaratī”ti. Thero taṃ sutvā imasmiṃ bhikkhusaṅghe añño vissagandhaṃ vāyanto vicaraṇakabhikkhu nāma natthi. Addhā ete maṃ sandhāya vadantīti saṃvegaṃ āpajji. Ekacce naṃ āhaṃsuyeva – “sve āvuso, ānanda, sannipāto, tvañca sekkho sakaraṇīyo, tena te na yuttaṃ sannipātaṃ gantuṃ, appamatto hohī”ti.

On that day, some monks, referring to Venerable Ānanda, said, "In this community of monks, one monk wanders about emitting a raw, fleshy odor." Hearing this, the elder thought, "In this community of monks, there is no other monk who wanders about emitting a raw, fleshy odor. Surely, they are speaking about me." He was struck with spiritual agitation. Some even said to him directly, "Friend Ānanda, tomorrow there is an assembly. You are still a trainee with duties to perform, so it is not fitting for you to attend the assembly. Be heedful."

Atha kho āyasmā ānando – ‘sve sannipāto, na kho metaṃ patirūpaṃ yvāhaṃ sekkho samāno sannipātaṃ gaccheyya’nti, bahudeva rattiṃ kāyagatāya satiyā vītināmetvā [P 1.0010] rattiyā paccūsasamaye caṅkamā orohitvā vihāraṃ pavisitvā “nipajjissāmī”ti kāyaṃ āvajjesi, dve pādā bhūmito muttā, apattañca sīsaṃ bimbohanaṃ, etasmiṃ antare anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimucci. Ayañhi āyasmā caṅkamena bahi vītināmetvā visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ asakkonto cintesi – “nanu maṃ bhagavā etadavoca – ‘katapuññosi tvaṃ, ānanda, padhānamanuyuñja, khippaṃ hohisi anāsavo’ti (dī. ni. 2.207). Buddhānañca kathādoso nāma natthi, mama pana accāraddhaṃ vīriyaṃ, tena me cittaṃ uddhaccāya saṃvattati. Handāhaṃ vīriyasamataṃ yojemī”ti, caṅkamā orohitvā pādadhovanaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā pāde dhovitvā [M 1.0011] vihāraṃ pavisitvā mañcake nisīditvā, “thokaṃ vissamissāmī”ti kāyaṃ mañcake apanāmesi. Dve pādā bhūmito muttā, sīsaṃ bimbohanamappattaṃ, etasmiṃ antare anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimuttaṃ, catuiriyāpathavirahitaṃ therassa arahattaṃ. Tena “imasmiṃ sāsane anipanno anisinno aṭṭhito acaṅkamanto ko bhikkhu arahattaṃ patto”ti vutte “ānandatthero”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

Then the Venerable Ānanda thought: ‘Tomorrow there is an assembly of the taintless ones, and it is not fitting for me, a trainee, to attend that assembly.’ Having spent much of the night with mindfulness directed to the body, in the early morning he descended from his walking path, entered his dwelling, and inclined his body, thinking, ‘I will lie down.’ His two feet were lifted from the ground, and his head had not yet reached the pillow. In that interval, his mind was liberated from the taints without clinging. For this venerable one, having spent time walking outside, yet unable to achieve a special attainment, reflected: ‘Did not the Blessed One say this to me: “Ānanda, you have made merit; apply yourself to the striving, and you will quickly be without taints”? And there is no fault in the words of the Buddhas. But my energy was excessive, and because of that, my mind tended toward agitation. Come now, let me apply balanced energy.’ Descending from his walking path, standing at the place for washing feet, he washed his feet, entered his dwelling, and sat on the bed. Then, thinking, ‘I will rest a little,’ he reclined his body on the bed. His two feet were lifted from the ground, and his head had not yet reached the pillow. In that interval, his mind was liberated from the taints without clinging. The elder’s attainment of arahantship was free from the four postures. Therefore, when it is asked, ‘In this Dispensation, which monk attained arahantship while not lying down, not sitting, not standing, and not walking?’ it is proper to say, ‘The Elder Ānanda.’

Atha therā bhikkhū dutiyadivase pañcamiyaṃ kāḷapakkhassa katabhattakiccā pattacīvaraṃ paṭisāmetvā dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatiṃsu. Atha kho āyasmā ānando arahā samāno sannipātaṃ agamāsi. Kathaṃ agamāsi? “Idānimhi sannipātamajjhaṃ pavisanāraho”ti haṭṭhatuṭṭhacitto ekaṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ katvā bandhanā muttatālapakkaṃ viya, paṇḍukambale nikkhittajātimaṇi viya, vigatavalāhake nabhe samuggatapuṇṇacando viya, bālātapasamphassavikasitareṇupiñjaragabbhaṃ padumaṃ viya [V 1.0011] ca, parisuddhena pariyodātena sappabhena sassirīkena ca mukhavarena attano arahattappattiṃ ārocayamāno viya agamāsi. Atha naṃ disvā āyasmato mahākassapassa etadahosi – “sobhati vata bho arahattappatto ānando, sace satthā dhareyya, addhā ajjānandassa sādhukāraṃ dadeyya, handa[P 1.0011], dānissāhaṃ satthārā dātabbaṃ sādhukāraṃ dadāmī”ti, tikkhattuṃ sādhukāramadāsi.

Then, on the second day, the fifth of the dark fortnight, the elder monks, having completed their meal duties and put away their bowls and robes, gathered in the Dhamma hall. Then the Venerable Ānanda, being an arahant, went to the assembly. How did he go? Thinking, ‘Now I am worthy to enter the midst of the assembly,’ with a joyful and elated mind, he arranged his robe over one shoulder and went as if announcing his attainment of arahantship with a face that was pure, bright, radiant, and glorious—like a ripe palm fruit freed from its stalk, like a precious gem placed on a pale woolen cloth, like the full moon risen in a cloudless sky, and like a lotus with its golden, pollen-filled core opened by the touch of the morning sun. Seeing him, this thought occurred to the Venerable Mahākassapa: ‘Indeed, the Venerable Ānanda shines, having attained arahantship! If the Teacher were present, he would surely give his acclamation to Ānanda today. Come now, I shall give him the acclamation that the Teacher would have given.’ And he gave his acclamation three times.

Majjhimabhāṇakā pana vadanti – “ānandatthero attano arahattappattiṃ ñāpetukāmo bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ nāgato, bhikkhū yathāvuḍḍhaṃ attano attano pattāsane nisīdantā ānandattherassa āsanaṃ ṭhapetvā nisinnā. Tattha keci evamāhaṃsu – ‘etaṃ āsanaṃ kassā’ti? ‘Ānandassā’ti. ‘Ānando pana kuhiṃ gato’ti? Tasmiṃ samaye thero cintesi – ‘idāni mayhaṃ gamanakālo’ti. Tato attano ānubhāvaṃ dassento pathaviyaṃ nimujjitvā attano āsaneyeva attānaṃ dassesī”ti, ākāsena gantvā nisīdītipi eke. Yathā vā tathā vā hotu. Sabbathāpi taṃ disvā āyasmato mahākassapassa sādhukāradānaṃ yuttameva.

The reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya, however, say: ‘The Elder Ānanda, wishing to make known his attainment of arahantship, did not come with the monks. The monks, sitting according to seniority in their respective seats, left a seat for the Elder Ānanda and sat down. There, some asked, “Whose seat is this?” “It is Ānanda’s.” “But where has Ānanda gone?” At that moment, the Elder thought, “Now is the time for me to go.” Then, displaying his supernormal power, he submerged into the earth and revealed himself on his own seat.’ Some also say he went through the air and sat down. However it may have been, in any case, seeing him, the Venerable Mahākassapa’s giving of acclamation was indeed fitting.

Evaṃ āgate pana tasmiṃ āyasmante mahākassapatthero bhikkhū āmantesi – “āvuso, kiṃ paṭhamaṃ saṅgāyāma, dhammaṃ vā vinayaṃ vā”ti? Bhikkhū [M 1.0012] āhaṃsu – “bhante, mahākassapa, vinayo nāma buddhasāsanassa āyu. Vinaye ṭhite sāsanaṃ ṭhitaṃ nāma hoti. Tasmā paṭhamaṃ vinayaṃ saṅgāyāmā”ti. “Kaṃ dhuraṃ katvā”ti? “Āyasmantaṃ upāli”nti. “Kiṃ ānando nappahotī”ti? “No nappahoti”. Api ca kho pana sammāsambuddho dharamānoyeva vinayapariyattiṃ nissāya āyasmantaṃ upāliṃ etadagge ṭhapesi – “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vinayadharānaṃ yadidaṃ upālī”ti (a. ni. 1.228). ‘Tasmā upālittheraṃ pucchitvā vinayaṃ saṅgāyāmā’ti.

When he had thus arrived, the Elder Mahākassapa addressed the monks: “Friends, what should we rehearse first, the Dhamma or the Vinaya?” The monks replied: “Venerable sir, the Vinaya is the life of the Buddha’s Dispensation. When the Vinaya is established, the Dispensation is said to be established. Therefore, let us rehearse the Vinaya first.” “Having made whom the authority?” “The Venerable Upāli.” “Is Ānanda not capable?” “It is not that he is not capable. However, the Perfectly Enlightened One, while still living, with reference to the Vinaya scriptures, placed the Venerable Upāli in the foremost position, saying: ‘Foremost, monks, among my monk disciples who are masters of the Vinaya is this one, that is, Upāli.’ Therefore, let us question the Elder Upāli and rehearse the Vinaya.”

Tato thero vinayaṃ pucchanatthāya attanāva attānaṃ sammanni. Upālittheropi vissajjanatthāya sammanni. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi – atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo saṅghaṃ ñāpesi –

Then the Elder appointed himself for the purpose of questioning on the Vinaya. The Elder Upāli also appointed himself for the purpose of answering. Herein, this is the Pāli text: Then the Venerable Mahākassapa informed the Saṅgha:

“Suṇātu me, āvuso, saṅgho, yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ,

Ahaṃ upāliṃ vinayaṃ puccheyya”nti.

“Friends, let the Saṅgha hear me. If it is timely for the Saṅgha, I shall question Upāli on the Vinaya.”

Āyasmāpi upāli saṅghaṃ ñāpesi –

The Venerable Upāli also informed the Saṅgha:

“Suṇātu [V 1.0012] me, bhante, saṅgho, yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ,

Ahaṃ āyasmatā mahākassapena vinayaṃ puṭṭho vissajjeyya”nti. (cūḷava. 439);

“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. If it is timely for the Saṅgha, I, being questioned on the Vinaya by the Venerable Mahākassapa, shall answer.”

Evaṃ attānaṃ sammannitvā āyasmā upāli uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ [P 1.0012] katvā there bhikkhū vanditvā dhammāsane nisīdi dantakhacitaṃ bījaniṃ gahetvā, tato mahākassapatthero therāsane nisīditvā āyasmantaṃ upāliṃ vinayaṃ pucchi. “Paṭhamaṃ āvuso, upāli, pārājikaṃ kattha paññatta”nti? “Vesāliyaṃ, bhante”ti. “Kaṃ ārabbhā”ti? “Sudinnaṃ kalandaputtaṃ ārabbhā”ti. “Kismiṃ vatthusmi”nti? “Methunadhamme”ti.

Having thus appointed themselves, the Venerable Upāli rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, paid homage to the elder monks, and, taking an ivory-inlaid fan, sat down on the Dhamma-seat. Then the Elder Mahākassapa, having seated himself on the elder’s seat, questioned the Venerable Upāli on the Vinaya: “Friend Upāli, where was the first Pārājika laid down?” “In Vesālī, venerable sir.” “Concerning whom?” “Concerning Sudinna, the son of Kalandaka.” “In what matter?” “In the matter of sexual intercourse.”

“Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo āyasmantaṃ upāliṃ paṭhamassa pārājikassa vatthumpi pucchi, nidānampi pucchi, puggalampi pucchi, paññattimpi pucchi, anupaññattimpi pucchi, āpattimpi pucchi, anāpattimpi pucchi” (cūḷava. 439). Puṭṭho puṭṭho āyasmā upāli vissajjesi.

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa questioned the Venerable Upāli on the matter of the first Pārājika; he questioned on the origin, he questioned on the individual, he questioned on the primary regulation, he questioned on the supplementary regulation, he questioned on what is an offense, and he questioned on what is not an offense. Each time he was questioned, the Venerable Upāli answered.

Kiṃ panettha paṭhamapārājike kiñci apanetabbaṃ vā pakkhipitabbaṃ vā atthi natthīti? Apanetabbaṃ natthi. Buddhassa hi bhagavato bhāsite apanetabbaṃ nāma natthi. Na hi tathāgatā ekabyañjanampi niratthakaṃ vadanti. Sāvakānaṃ pana devatānaṃ [M 1.0013] vā bhāsite apanetabbampi hoti, taṃ dhammasaṅgāhakattherā apanayiṃsu. Pakkhipitabbaṃ pana sabbatthāpi atthi, tasmā yaṃ yattha pakkhipituṃ yuttaṃ, taṃ pakkhipiṃsuyeva. Kiṃ pana tanti? ‘Tena samayenā’ti vā, ‘tena kho pana samayenā’ti vā, ‘atha khoti vā’, ‘evaṃ vutteti’ vā, ‘etadavocā’ti vā, evamādikaṃ sambandhavacanamattaṃ. Evaṃ pakkhipitabbayuttaṃ pakkhipitvā pana – “idaṃ paṭhamapārājika”nti ṭhapesuṃ. Paṭhamapārājike saṅgahamārūḷhe pañca arahantasatāni saṅgahaṃ āropitanayeneva gaṇasajjhāyamakaṃsu – “tena samayena buddho bhagavā verañjāyaṃ viharatī”ti. Tesaṃ sajjhāyāraddhakāleyeva sādhukāraṃ dadamānā viya mahāpathavī udakapariyantaṃ katvā akampittha.

Now, is there anything in this first Pārājika to be removed or to be added? There is nothing to be removed. For in what was spoken by the Buddha, the Blessed One, there is nothing to be removed. Indeed, the Tathāgatas do not utter even a single syllable that is meaningless. However, in what was spoken by disciples or deities, there can be something to be removed, and that the Elder-compilers of the Dhamma removed. But something to be added exists in all cases; therefore, whatever was suitable to add in any given place, that they added. What is that? It is merely connecting words, such as ‘Tena samayena,’ or ‘Tena kho pana samayena,’ or ‘Atha kho,’ or ‘Evaṃ vutte,’ or ‘Etadavoca,’ and so on. Having thus added what was suitable to be added, they established it, saying: “This is the first Pārājika.” When the first Pārājika was included in the collection, the five hundred Arahants, by the very method by which it was included in the collection, performed a group recitation: “Tena samayena buddho bhagavā verañjāyaṃ viharati…” As soon as they began their recitation, the great earth, as if giving its approval, quaked up to its water-boundary.

Eteneva nayena sesāni tīṇi pārājikāni saṅgahaṃ āropetvā “idaṃ pārājikakaṇḍa”nti ṭhapesuṃ. Terasa saṅghādisesāni “terasaka”nti ṭhapesuṃ. Dve sikkhāpadāni “aniyatānī”ti ṭhapesuṃ. Tiṃsa sikkhāpadāni “nissaggiyāni pācittiyānī”ti ṭhapesuṃ[P 1.0013]. Dvenavuti sikkhāpadāni “pācittiyānī”ti ṭhapesuṃ. Cattāri sikkhāpadāni “pāṭidesanīyānī”ti [V 1.0013] ṭhapesuṃ. Pañcasattati sikkhāpadāni “sekhiyānī”ti ṭhapesuṃ. Satta dhamme “adhikaraṇasamathā”ti ṭhapesuṃ. Evaṃ sattavīsādhikāni dve sikkhāpadasatāni “mahāvibhaṅgo”ti kittetvā ṭhapesuṃ. Mahāvibhaṅgāvasānepi purimanayeneva mahāpathavī akampittha.

By this same method, having included the remaining three Pārājikas in the collection, they established them, saying: “This is the Pārājika Section.” They established the thirteen Saṅghādisesas, saying: “This is the Section of Thirteen.” They established the two training rules, saying: “These are the Undetermined.” They established the thirty training rules, saying: “These are the Nissaggiya Pācittiyas.” They established the ninety-two training rules, saying: “These are the Pācittiyas.” They established the four training rules, saying: “These are the Pāṭidesanīyas.” They established the seventy-five training rules, saying: “These are the Sekhiyas.” They established the seven principles, saying: “These are the Adhikaraṇasamathas.” Thus, having proclaimed the two hundred and twenty-seven training rules, they established them, saying: “This is the Mahāvibhaṅga.” At the conclusion of the Mahāvibhaṅga, the great earth quaked in the same manner as before.

Tato bhikkhunīvibhaṅge aṭṭha sikkhāpadāni “pārājikakaṇḍaṃ nāma ida”nti ṭhapesuṃ. Sattarasa sikkhāpadāni “sattarasaka”nti ṭhapesuṃ. Tiṃsa sikkhāpadāni “nissaggiyāni pācittiyānī”ti ṭhapesuṃ. Chasaṭṭhisatasikkhāpadāni “pācittiyānī”ti ṭhapesuṃ. Aṭṭha sikkhāpadāni “pāṭidesanīyānī”ti ṭhapesuṃ. Pañcasattati sikkhāpadāni “sekhiyānī”ti ṭhapesuṃ. Satta dhamme “adhikaraṇasamathā”ti ṭhapesuṃ. Evaṃ tīṇi sikkhāpadasatāni cattāri ca sikkhāpadāni “bhikkhunīvibhaṅgo”ti kittetvā – “ayaṃ ubhato vibhaṅgo nāma catusaṭṭhibhāṇavāro”ti ṭhapesuṃ. Ubhatovibhaṅgāvasānepi vuttanayeneva mahāpathavikampo ahosi.

Thereafter, in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga, they established eight training rules, saying: 'This is the Pārājika Section.' They established seventeen training rules, saying: 'This is the Section of Seventeen.' They established thirty training rules, saying: 'These are the Nissaggiya Pācittiyas.' They established one hundred and sixty-six training rules, saying: 'These are the Pācittiyas.' They established eight training rules, saying: 'These are the Pāṭidesanīyas.' They established seventy-five training rules, saying: 'These are the Sekhiyas.' They established seven principles, saying: 'These are the Adhikaraṇasamathas.' Thus, having declared the three hundred and four training rules as 'the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga,' they established it, saying: 'This Ubhatovibhaṅga is named the sixty-four recitation sections.' At the conclusion of the Ubhatovibhaṅga, too, the great earth shook in the same manner as stated before.

Etenevupāyena asītibhāṇavāraparimāṇaṃ khandhakaṃ, pañcavīsatibhāṇavāraparimāṇaṃ parivārañca saṅgahaṃ āropetvā “idaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ nāmā”ti ṭhapesuṃ[M 1.0014]. Vinayapiṭakāvasānepi vuttanayeneva mahāpathavikampo ahosi. Taṃ āyasmantaṃ upāliṃ paṭicchāpesuṃ – “āvuso, imaṃ tuyhaṃ nissitake vācehī”ti. Vinayapiṭakasaṅgahāvasāne upālitthero dantakhacitaṃ bījaniṃ nikkhipitvā dhammāsanā orohitvā there bhikkhū vanditvā attano pattāsane nisīdi.

By this same method, having brought into the compilation the Khandhaka, which is eighty recitation sections in measure, and the Parivāra, which is twenty-five recitation sections in measure, they established them, saying: 'This is called the Vinaya Piṭaka.' At the conclusion of the Vinaya Piṭaka, too, the great earth shook in the same manner as stated before. They entrusted it to the Venerable Upāli, saying: 'Friend, teach this to your disciples.' At the conclusion of the compilation of the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Elder Upāli, having laid down his ivory-inlaid fan, descended from the Dhamma seat, paid homage to the elder monks, and sat down in his own appointed seat.

Vinayaṃ saṅgāyitvā dhammaṃ saṅgāyitukāmo āyasmā mahākassapo bhikkhū pucchi – “dhammaṃ saṅgāyante hi kaṃ puggalaṃ dhuraṃ katvā dhammo saṅgāyitabbo”ti? Bhikkhū – “ānandattheraṃ dhuraṃ katvā”ti āhaṃsu.

Having compiled the Vinaya, the Venerable Mahākassapa, wishing to compile the Dhamma, asked the monks: 'When we are to compile the Dhamma, which person should be appointed as the leader?' The monks replied: 'The Elder Ānanda should be appointed as the leader.'

Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo saṅghaṃ ñāpesi –

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa informed the Saṅgha:

“Suṇātu me, āvuso, saṅgho, yadi saṅghassa [P 1.0014] pattakallaṃ,

Ahaṃ ānandaṃ dhammaṃ puccheyya”nti;

'Let the Saṅgha hear me, friends. If it is the proper time for the Saṅgha, I would question Ānanda about the Dhamma.'

Atha kho āyasmā ānando saṅghaṃ ñāpesi –

Then the Venerable Ānanda informed the Saṅgha:

“Suṇātu [V 1.0014] me, bhante, saṅgho, yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ,

Ahaṃ āyasmatā mahākassapena dhammaṃ puṭṭho vissajjeyya”nti;

'Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. If it is the proper time for the Saṅgha, I, being questioned about the Dhamma by the Venerable Mahākassapa, would answer.'

Atha kho āyasmā ānando uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ katvā there bhikkhū vanditvā dhammāsane nisīdi dantakhacitaṃ bījaniṃ gahetvā. Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo bhikkhū pucchi – “kataraṃ, āvuso, piṭakaṃ paṭhamaṃ saṅgāyāmā”ti? “Suttantapiṭakaṃ, bhante”ti. “Suttantapiṭake catasso saṅgītiyo, tāsu paṭhamaṃ kataraṃ saṅgīti”nti? “Dīghasaṅgītiṃ, bhante”ti. “Dīghasaṅgītiyaṃ catutiṃsa suttāni, tayo vaggā, tesu paṭhamaṃ kataraṃ vagga”nti? “Sīlakkhandhavaggaṃ, bhante”ti. “Sīlakkhandhavagge terasa suttantā, tesu paṭhamaṃ kataraṃ sutta”nti? “Brahmajālasuttaṃ nāma bhante, tividhasīlālaṅkataṃ, nānāvidhamicchājīvakuha lapanādividdhaṃsanaṃ, dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhijālaviniveṭhanaṃ, dasasahassilokadhātukampanaṃ, taṃ paṭhamaṃ saṅgāyāmā”ti.

Then the Venerable Ānanda, having risen from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, paid homage to the elder monks, and, taking an ivory-inlaid fan, sat down on the Dhamma seat. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa asked the monks: 'Friends, which Piṭaka shall we recite first?' 'The Suttanta Piṭaka, venerable sir.' 'In the Suttanta Piṭaka there are four collections; of these, which collection shall we recite first?' 'The Dīgha collection, venerable sir.' 'In the Dīgha collection there are thirty-four suttas and three sections; of these, which section first?' 'The Sīlakkhandhavagga, venerable sir.' 'In the Sīlakkhandhavagga there are thirteen suttas; of these, which sutta first?' 'Venerable sir, the Brahmajāla Sutta, which is adorned with the threefold morality, which destroys various wrong livelihoods such as deceit and flattery, which unravels the net of sixty-two views, and which causes the ten-thousandfold world-system to shake. That is what we shall recite first.'

Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ etadavoca, “brahmajālaṃ, āvuso ānanda, kattha bhāsita”nti? “Antarā ca, bhante, rājagahaṃ antarā ca nāḷandaṃ rājāgārake ambalaṭṭhikāya”nti. “Kaṃ ārabbhā”ti[M 1.0015]? “Suppiyañca paribbājakaṃ, brahmadattañca māṇava”nti. “Kismiṃ vatthusmi”nti? “Vaṇṇāvaṇṇe”ti. Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ brahmajālassa nidānampi pucchi, puggalampi pucchi, vatthumpi pucchi (cūḷava. 440). Āyasmā ānando vissajjesi. Vissajjanāvasāne pañca arahantasatāni gaṇasajjhāyamakaṃsu. Vuttanayeneva ca pathavikampo ahosi.

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa said this to the Venerable Ānanda: 'Friend Ānanda, where was the Brahmajāla spoken?' 'Venerable sir, between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā, in the royal rest house at Ambalaṭṭhikā.' 'In reference to whom?' 'In reference to Suppiya the wanderer and Brahmadatta the young man.' 'In what context?' 'In the context of praise and dispraise.' Then the Venerable Mahākassapa asked the Venerable Ānanda about the origin of the Brahmajāla, the persons involved, and the subject matter. The Venerable Ānanda answered. At the conclusion of his answer, the five hundred Arahants performed a group recitation. And the earth shook in the same manner as stated before.

Evaṃ brahmajālaṃ saṅgāyitvā tato paraṃ “sāmaññaphalaṃ, panāvuso ānanda, kattha bhāsita”ntiādinā nayena pucchāvissajjanānukkamena saddhiṃ brahmajālena sabbepi terasa suttante saṅgāyitvā – “ayaṃ sīlakkhandhavaggo nāmā”ti kittetvā ṭhapesuṃ.

Having thus recited the Brahmajāla, and thereafter, by the method of the sequence of questions and answers beginning with, 'But friend Ānanda, where was the Sāmaññaphala spoken?', they recited all thirteen suttas together with the Brahmajāla. Having proclaimed, 'This is called the Sīlakkhandhavagga,' they established it.

Tadanantaraṃ mahāvaggaṃ, tadanantaraṃ pāthikavagganti, evaṃ tivaggasaṅgahaṃ catutiṃsasuttapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ [P 1.0015] catusaṭṭhibhāṇavāraparimāṇaṃ tantiṃ saṅgāyitvā “ayaṃ dīghanikāyo nāmā”ti vatvā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ paṭicchāpesuṃ – “āvuso, imaṃ tuyhaṃ nissitake vācehī”ti.

Immediately after that, the Mahāvagga, and immediately after that, the Pāthikavagga—thus having recited the sacred text which is a collection of three sections, is adorned with thirty-four suttas, and is sixty-four recitation sections in measure, they declared, 'This is called the Dīgha Nikāya,' and entrusted it to the Venerable Ānanda, saying: 'Friend, teach this to your disciples.'

Tato [V 1.0015] anantaraṃ asītibhāṇavāraparimāṇaṃ majjhimanikāyaṃ saṅgāyitvā dhammasenāpatisāriputtattherassa nissitake paṭicchāpesuṃ – “imaṃ tumhe pariharathā”ti.

Immediately after that, having recited the Majjhima Nikāya, which is eighty recitation sections in measure, they entrusted it to the disciples of the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, saying: 'You all should preserve this.'

Tato anantaraṃ satabhāṇavāraparimāṇaṃ saṃyuttanikāyaṃ saṅgāyitvā mahākassapattheraṃ paṭicchāpesuṃ – “bhante, imaṃ tumhākaṃ nissitake vācethā”ti.

Immediately after that, having recited the Saṃyutta Nikāya, which is one hundred recitation sections in measure, they entrusted it to the Elder Mahākassapa, saying: 'Venerable sir, please teach this to your disciples.'

Tato anantaraṃ vīsatibhāṇavārasataparimāṇaṃ aṅguttaranikāyaṃ saṅgāyitvā anuruddhattheraṃ paṭicchāpesuṃ – “imaṃ tumhākaṃ nissitake vācethā”ti.

Immediately after that, having recited the Aṅguttara Nikāya, which is one hundred and twenty recitation sections in measure, they entrusted it to the Elder Anuruddha, saying: 'Please teach this to your disciples.'

Tato anantaraṃ dhammasaṅgahavibhaṅgadhātukathāpuggalapaññattikathāvatthuyamakapaṭṭhānaṃ abhidhammoti vuccati. Evaṃ saṃvaṇṇitaṃ sukhumañāṇagocaraṃ tantiṃ saṅgāyitvā – “idaṃ abhidhammapiṭakaṃ nāmā”ti vatvā pañca arahantasatāni sajjhāyamakaṃsu. Vuttanayeneva pathavikampo ahosīti.

Immediately after that, the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, Yamaka, and Paṭṭhāna are called the Abhidhamma. Having recited the sacred text thus described as the domain of subtle knowledge, and having said, 'This is named the Abhidhamma Piṭaka,' the five hundred arahants made a choral recitation. In the very same way as was stated, an earthquake occurred.

Tato paraṃ jātakaṃ, niddeso, paṭisambhidāmaggo, apadānaṃ, suttanipāto, khuddakapāṭho, dhammapadaṃ, udānaṃ, itivuttakaṃ, vimānavatthu, petavatthu, theragāthā[M 1.0016], therīgāthāti imaṃ tantiṃ saṅgāyitvā “khuddakagantho nāmāya”nti ca vatvā “abhidhammapiṭakasmiṃyeva saṅgahaṃ āropayiṃsū”ti dīghabhāṇakā vadanti. Majjhimabhāṇakā pana “cariyāpiṭakabuddhavaṃsehi saddhiṃ sabbampetaṃ khuddakaganthaṃ nāma suttantapiṭake pariyāpanna”nti vadanti.

After that, having recited this sacred text—the Jātaka, Niddesa, Paṭisambhidāmagga, Apadāna, Suttanipāta, Khuddakapāṭha, Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Vimānavatthu, Petavatthu, Theragāthā, and Therīgāthā—and having said, 'This is named the Khuddaka Collection,' the Dīghabhāṇakas say, 'They included it in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka itself.' The Majjhimabhāṇakas, however, say, 'All this, named the Khuddaka Collection, together with the Cariyāpiṭaka and Buddhavaṃsa, is included in the Suttanta Piṭaka.'

Evametaṃ sabbampi buddhavacanaṃ rasavasena ekavidhaṃ, dhammavinayavasena duvidhaṃ, paṭhamamajjhimapacchimavasena tividhaṃ. Tathā piṭakavasena. Nikāyavasena pañcavidhaṃ, aṅgavasena navavidhaṃ, dhammakkhandhavasena caturāsītisahassavidhanti veditabbaṃ.

Thus, all this word of the Buddha should be known as: onefold by way of flavor, twofold by way of Dhamma and Vinaya, threefold by way of the first, middle, and last. Likewise, it is threefold by way of the Piṭakas. It is fivefold by way of the Nikāyas, ninefold by way of the Aṅgas, and eighty-four thousandfold by way of the Dhamma aggregates.

Kathaṃ rasavasena ekavidhaṃ? Yañhi bhagavatā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhitvā yāva anupādisesāya [P 1.0016] nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyati, etthantare pañcacattālīsavassāni devamanussanāgayakkhādayo anusāsantena vā paccavekkhantena vā vuttaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ ekarasaṃ vimuttirasameva hoti. Evaṃ rasavasena ekavidhaṃ.

How is it onefold by way of flavor? Indeed, whatever was spoken by the Blessed One—while instructing or reflecting upon devas, humans, nāgas, yakkhas, and others for forty-five years in the interval from having awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment until passing into the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining—all of that has only one flavor: the flavor of liberation. Thus, it is onefold by way of flavor.

Kathaṃ dhammavinayavasena duvidhaṃ? Sabbameva cetaṃ dhammo ceva vinayo cāti saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Tattha vinayapiṭakaṃ vinayo, avasesaṃ buddhavacanaṃ dhammo. Tenevāha “yannūna mayaṃ dhammañca [V 1.0016] vinayañca saṅgāyeyyāmā”ti (cūḷava. 437). “Ahaṃ upāliṃ vinayaṃ puccheyyaṃ, ānandaṃ dhammaṃ puccheyya”nti ca. Evaṃ dhammavinayavasena duvidhaṃ.

How is it twofold by way of Dhamma and Vinaya? For all of this comes to be designated as 'Dhamma' and 'Vinaya.' Therein, the Vinaya Piṭaka is the Vinaya; the remaining word of the Buddha is the Dhamma. For that very reason, he said: 'What if we were to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya?' and, 'I would question Upāli on the Vinaya and Ānanda on the Dhamma.' Thus, it is twofold by way of Dhamma and Vinaya.

Kathaṃ paṭhamamajjhimapacchimavasena tividhaṃ? Sabbameva hidaṃ paṭhamabuddhavacanaṃ, majjhimabuddhavacanaṃ, pacchimabuddhavacananti tippabhedaṃ hoti. Tattha –

How is it threefold by way of the first, middle, and last? Indeed, all of this is of three kinds: the first word of the Buddha, the middle word of the Buddha, and the last word of the Buddha. Therein—

“Anekajātisaṃsāraṃ, sandhāvissaṃ anibbisaṃ;

Gahakāraṃ gavesanto, dukkhā jāti punappunaṃ.

Gahakāraka diṭṭhosi, puna gehaṃ na kāhasi;

Sabbā te phāsukā bhaggā, gahakūṭaṃ visaṅkhataṃ;

Visaṅkhāragataṃ cittaṃ, taṇhānaṃ khayamajjhagā”ti. (dha. pa. 153-54);

Through many a birth in saṃsāra have I run, seeking but not finding the builder of this house. Painful is birth again and again. O house-builder, you are seen! You shall not build a house again. All your rafters are broken; the ridge-pole is shattered. My mind has gone to the unconditioned; I have reached the destruction of cravings.

Idaṃ paṭhamabuddhavacanaṃ. Keci “yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā”ti (mahāva. 1) khandhake udānagāthaṃ vadanti. Esā pana pāṭipadadivase sabbaññubhāvappattassa somanassamayañāṇena paccayākāraṃ paccavekkhantassa uppannā udānagāthāti veditabbā.

This is the first word of the Buddha. Some say the udāna-gāthā in the Khandhaka, 'When, indeed, phenomena become manifest,' is the first. However, this should be known as the udāna-gāthā that arose for him who had attained the state of omniscience on the day after the full moon, while he was reflecting on the mode of conditionality with knowledge accompanied by joy.

Yaṃ [M 1.0017] pana parinibbānakāle abhāsi – “handa dāni, bhikkhave, āmantayāmi vo, vayadhammā saṅkhārā, appamādena sampādethā”ti (dī. ni. 2.218) idaṃ pacchimabuddhavacanaṃ. Ubhinnamantare yaṃ vuttaṃ, etaṃ majjhimabuddhavacanaṃ nāma. Evaṃ paṭhamamajjhimapacchimabuddhavacanavasena tividhaṃ.

But as for what was spoken at the time of the Parinibbāna—'Now then, monks, I address you: formations are subject to decay; strive on with heedfulness'—this is the last word of the Buddha. Whatever was spoken between the two is named the middle word of the Buddha. Thus, it is threefold by way of the first, middle, and last words of the Buddha.

Kathaṃ piṭakavasena tividhaṃ? Sabbampi cetaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ suttantapiṭakaṃ abhidhammapiṭakanti tippabhedameva [P 1.0017] hoti. Tattha paṭhamasaṅgītiyaṃ saṅgītañca asaṅgītañca sabbampi samodhānetvā ubhayāni pātimokkhāni, dve vibhaṅgā, dvāvīsati khandhakā, soḷasaparivārāti – idaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ nāma. Brahmajālādicatuttiṃsasuttasaṅgaho dīghanikāyo, mūlapariyāyasuttādidiyaḍḍhasatadvesuttasaṅgaho majjhimanikāyo, oghataraṇasuttādisattasuttasahassasattasatadvāsaṭṭhisuttasaṅgaho saṃyuttanikāyo, cittapariyādānasuttādinavasuttasahassapañcasatasattapaññāsasuttasaṅgaho aṅguttaranikāyo, khuddakapāṭha-dhammapada-udāna-itivuttaka-suttanipāta-vimānavatthu-petavatthu-theragāthā-therīgāthā-jātaka-niddesa-paṭisambhidāmagga-apadāna-buddhavaṃsa-cariyāpiṭakavasena pannarasappabhedo khuddakanikāyoti [V 1.0017] idaṃ suttantapiṭakaṃ nāma. Dhammasaṅgaho, vibhaṅgo, dhātukathā, puggalapaññatti, kathāvatthu, yamakaṃ, paṭṭhānanti – idaṃ abhidhammapiṭakaṃ nāma. Tattha –

How is it threefold by way of the Piṭakas? All of this is indeed of three kinds: the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Suttanta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Therein, having compiled everything at the First Council—both what was recited and what was not recited—the two Pātimokkhas, the two Vibhaṅgas, the twenty-two Khandhakas, and the sixteen Parivāras: this is named the Vinaya Piṭaka. The Dīgha Nikāya, a collection of thirty-four suttas beginning with the Brahmajāla; the Majjhima Nikāya, a collection of one hundred fifty-two suttas beginning with the Mūlapariyāya Sutta; the Saṃyutta Nikāya, a collection of seven thousand seven hundred sixty-two suttas beginning with the Oghataraṇa Sutta; the Aṅguttara Nikāya, a collection of nine thousand five hundred fifty-seven suttas beginning with the Cittapariyādāna Sutta; and the Khuddaka Nikāya, of fifteen divisions by way of the Khuddakapāṭha, Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Suttanipāta, Vimānavatthu, Petavatthu, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, Jātaka, Niddesa, Paṭisambhidāmagga, Apadāna, Buddhavaṃsa, and Cariyāpiṭaka: this is named the Suttanta Piṭaka. The Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, Yamaka, and Paṭṭhāna: this is named the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Therein—

“Vividhavisesanayattā, vinayanato ceva kāyavācānaṃ;

Vinayatthavidūhi ayaṃ, vinayo vinayoti akkhāto”.

Because of its diverse and distinguished methods, and because it disciplines body and speech, this Discipline is called 'Vinaya' by those skilled in the Discipline.

Vividhā hi ettha pañcavidhapātimokkhuddesapārājikādi satta āpattikkhandhamātikā vibhaṅgādippabhedā nayā. Visesabhūtā ca daḷhīkammasithilakaraṇappayojanā anupaññattinayā. Kāyikavācasikaajjhācāranisedhanato cesa kāyaṃ vācañca vineti, tasmā vividhanayattā visesanayattā kāyavācānaṃ vinayanato ceva vinayoti akkhāto. Tenetametassa vacanatthakosallatthaṃ vuttaṃ –

For herein are various methods, with divisions such as the fivefold Pātimokkha recitation, the seven groups of offenses beginning with Pārājika, the Mātikā, and the Vibhaṅga. And there are special methods: the supplementary regulations for the purpose of strengthening and relaxing. And because it prohibits transgression by body and speech, it disciplines the body and speech. Therefore, because it has various methods, special methods, and because it disciplines the body and speech, it is called 'Vinaya.' For that reason, this was said for the sake of skill in its etymological meaning:

“Vividhavisesanayattā, vinayanato ceva kāyavācānaṃ;

Vinayatthavidūhi ayaṃ, vinayo vinayoti akkhāto”ti.

Because of its diverse and distinguished methods, and because it disciplines body and speech, this Discipline is called 'Vinaya' by those skilled in the Discipline.

Itaraṃ [M 1.0018] pana –

As for the other, however:

“Atthānaṃ sūcanato suvuttato, savanatotha sūdanato;

Suttāṇā suttasabhāgato ca, suttanti akkhātaṃ.

Because it indicates meanings, because it is well-spoken, because it yields, and because it pours forth; because it protects well, and because it is similar to a thread, it is called 'Sutta'.

Tañhi attatthaparatthādibhede atthe sūceti. Suvuttā cettha atthā, veneyyajjhāsayānulomena vuttattā. Savati cetaṃ atthe sassamiva phalaṃ, pasavatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sūdati cetaṃ dhenu viya khīraṃ, paggharāpetīti vuttaṃ hoti. Suṭṭhu [P 1.0018] ca ne tāyati, rakkhatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Suttasabhāgañcetaṃ, yathā hi tacchakānaṃ suttaṃ pamāṇaṃ hoti, evametampi viññūnaṃ. Yathā ca suttena saṅgahitāni pupphāni na vikirīyanti, na viddhaṃsīyanti, evameva tena saṅgahitā atthā. Tenetametassa vacanatthakosallatthaṃ vuttaṃ –

For it indicates meanings, distinguishing self-benefit, others' benefit, and so forth. And the meanings here are well-spoken, having been spoken in accordance with the dispositions of those to be trained. And it yields meanings like a crop yields fruit; it is said to produce. And it pours forth meanings like a cow her milk; it is said to cause to stream forth. And it thoroughly protects them; it is said to guard. And it is similar to a thread, for just as a thread serves as a measure for carpenters, so too this for the wise. And just as flowers gathered on a thread are not scattered or destroyed, so too are the meanings gathered by it. Therefore, this has been stated for the sake of skill in the etymological meaning of this word:

“Atthānaṃ sūcanato, suvuttato savanatotha sūdanato;

Suttāṇā suttasabhāgato ca, suttanti akkhāta”nti.

Because it indicates meanings, because it is well-spoken, because it yields, and because it pours forth; because it protects well, and because it is similar to a thread, it is called 'Sutta'.

Itaro [V 1.0018] pana –

As for the other, however:

“Yaṃ ettha vuḍḍhimanto, salakkhaṇā pūjitā paricchinnā;

Vuttādhikā ca dhammā, abhidhammo tena akkhāto”.

That wherein are doctrines possessing growth, with characteristics, honored, and defined; and superior doctrines are stated—by that it is called 'Abhidhamma'.

Ayañhi abhisaddo vuḍḍhilakkhaṇapūjitaparicchinnādhikesu dissati. Tathā hesa “bāḷhā me dukkhā vedanā abhikkamanti, no paṭikkamantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.389) vuḍḍhiyaṃ āgato. “Yā tā rattiyo abhiññātā abhilakkhitā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.49) salakkhaṇe. “Rājābhirājā manujindo”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.399) pūjite. “Paṭibalo vinetuṃ abhidhamme abhivinaye”tiādīsu (mahāva. 85) paricchinne. Aññamaññasaṅkaravirahite dhamme ca vinaye cāti vuttaṃ hoti. “Abhikkantena vaṇṇenā”tiādīsu (vi. va. 819) adhike.

For this prefix 'abhi' is seen in the senses of growth, characteristic, honored, defined, and superior. Thus, it occurs in contexts like, 'Severe painful feelings are increasing in me, not decreasing,' where it conveys growth. In phrases like, 'Those nights that are well-known and well-marked,' it conveys characteristic. In expressions like, 'The king of kings, the lord of men,' it conveys honored. In statements like, 'Capable of guiding in the Abhidhamma and the Abhivinaya,' it conveys defined—meaning the Dhamma and Vinaya are free from mutual confusion. And in phrases like, 'With surpassing beauty,' it conveys superior.

Ettha ca “rūpūpapattiyā maggaṃ bhāveti” (dha. sa. 251), “mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharatī”tiādinā (vibha. 642) nayena vuḍḍhimantopi dhammā vuttā. “Rūpārammaṇaṃ vā saddārammaṇaṃ vā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1) nayena ārammaṇādīhi lakkhaṇīyattā [M 1.0019] salakkhaṇāpi. “Sekkhā dhammā, asekkhā dhammā, lokuttarā dhammā”tiādinā (dha. sa. tikamātikā 11, dukamātikā 12) nayena pūjitāpi, pūjārahāti adhippāyo. “Phasso hoti, vedanā hotī”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1) nayena sabhāvaparicchinnattā paricchinnāpi. “Mahaggatā dhammā, appamāṇā dhammā (dha. sa. tikamātikā 11), anuttarā dhammā”tiādinā (dha. sa. dukamātikā 11) nayena adhikāpi dhammā vuttā. Tenetametassa vacanatthakosallatthaṃ vuttaṃ –

Here, too, doctrines possessing growth are stated, according to the method such as, 'One develops the path for attainment in form' (Dhs. 251), or 'Dwelling, one pervades one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness' (Vibh. 642). And doctrines with characteristics are stated, being characterizable by their objects and so forth, according to the method such as, 'With form as object or sound as object' (Dhs. 1). And doctrines that are honored are stated, in the sense of being worthy of honor, according to the method such as, 'The factors of training, the factors of no-training, the supramundane factors' (Dhs. Tika-mātikā 11, Duka-mātikā 12). And doctrines that are defined are stated, being defined by their intrinsic nature, according to the method such as, 'Contact occurs, feeling occurs' (Dhs. 1). And superior doctrines are stated, according to the method such as, 'Great factors, immeasurable factors, unsurpassed factors' (Dhs. Tika-mātikā 11, Duka-mātikā 11). Therefore, this was stated for the sake of skill in the etymological meaning of this word:

“Yaṃ ettha vuḍḍhimanto, salakkhaṇā pūjitā paricchinnā;

Vuttādhikā ca dhammā, abhidhammo tena akkhāto”ti.

That wherein are doctrines possessing growth, with characteristics, honored, and defined; and superior doctrines are stated—by that it is called 'Abhidhamma'.

Yaṃ panettha avisiṭṭhaṃ, taṃ –

As for that which is common among these:

“Piṭakaṃ piṭakatthavidū, pariyattibbhājanatthato āhu;

Tena samodhānetvā, tayopi vinayādayo ñeyyā”.

Those skilled in the Piṭaka say that 'Piṭaka' has the meaning of 'learning' and 'receptacle'. By combining it with that, the three, beginning with the Vinaya, should be understood.

Pariyattipi [V 1.0019] hi “mā piṭakasampadānenā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.66) piṭakanti vuccati. “Atha puriso āgaccheyya kudālapiṭakamādāyā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.70) yaṃ kiñci bhājanampi. Tasmā ‘piṭakaṃ piṭakatthavidū pariyattibhājanatthato āhu.

For the learning itself is called 'Piṭaka' in passages such as, 'Not by the full attainment of the Piṭaka...' (AN 3.66); and any container is also referred to as such, as in, 'Then a man might come carrying a spade and basket' (AN 3.70). Therefore, those skilled in the Piṭaka say that 'Piṭaka' has the meaning of 'learning' and 'receptacle'.

Idāni ‘tena samodhānetvā [P 1.0019] tayopi vinayādayo ñeyyā’ti, tena evaṃ duvidhatthena piṭakasaddena saha samāsaṃ katvā vinayo ca so piṭakañca pariyattibhāvato, tassa tassa atthassa bhājanato cāti vinayapiṭakaṃ, yathāvutteneva nayena suttantañca taṃ piṭakañcāti suttantapiṭakaṃ, abhidhammo ca so piṭakañcāti abhidhammapiṭakanti. Evamete tayopi vinayādayo ñeyyā.

Now, as for 'by combining it with that, the three, beginning with the Vinaya, should be understood'—by making a compound with the word 'piṭaka' in this twofold sense, the Vinaya, being also a Piṭaka both because it is learning and because it is a receptacle for its respective meaning, is the Vinayapiṭaka. In just the way that was said, the Suttanta, being also a Piṭaka, is the Suttantapiṭaka; and the Abhidhamma, being also a Piṭaka, is the Abhidhammapiṭaka. Thus, these three, beginning with the Vinaya, should be understood.

Evaṃ ñatvā ca punapi tesuyeva piṭakesu nānappakārakosallatthaṃ –

Having known thus, again in those very Piṭakas, for the sake of skill in various ways—

“Desanāsāsanakathābhedaṃ tesu yathārahaṃ;

Sikkhāppahānagambhīrabhāvañca paridīpaye.

Pariyattibhedaṃ sampattiṃ, vipattiñcāpi yaṃ yahiṃ;

Pāpuṇāti yathā bhikkhu, tampi sabbaṃ vibhāvaye”.

Let one elucidate the distinction of teaching, instruction, and discourse in them, as appropriate, and training, abandoning, and profundity. Let one also explain all the distinctions in learning, and the success and failure that a monk attains in each, and how.

Tatrāyaṃ paridīpanā vibhāvanā ca. Etāni hi tīṇi piṭakāni yathākkamaṃ āṇāvohāraparamatthadesanā, yathāparādhayathānulomayathādhammasāsanāni, saṃvarāsaṃvaradiṭṭhiviniveṭhananāmarūpaparicchedakathāti ca vuccanti. Ettha [M 1.0020] hi vinayapiṭakaṃ āṇārahena bhagavatā āṇābāhullato desitattā āṇādesanā, suttantapiṭakaṃ vohārakusalena bhagavatā vohārabāhullato desitattā vohāradesanā, abhidhammapiṭakaṃ paramatthakusalena bhagavatā paramatthabāhullato desitattā paramatthadesanāti vuccati.

Herein is this elucidation and explanation. For these three Piṭakas are called, respectively, the teaching of command, of convention, and of ultimate reality; the instructions according to offense, according to suitability, and according to Dhamma; and the discourses on minor and major restraint, the disentangling of views, and the discernment of name-and-form. Here, the Vinayapiṭaka is called the teaching of command because it was taught by the Blessed One, who is worthy of command, predominantly with commands. The Suttantapiṭaka is called the teaching of convention because it was taught by the Blessed One, who is skilled in convention, predominantly with conventions. The Abhidhammapiṭaka is called the teaching of ultimate reality because it was taught by the Blessed One, who is skilled in ultimate reality, predominantly with ultimate reality.

Tathā paṭhamaṃ – ‘ye te pacurāparādhā sattā, te yathāparādhaṃ ettha sāsitā’ti yathāparādhasāsanaṃ, dutiyaṃ – ‘anekajjhāsayānusayacariyādhimuttikā sattā yathānulomaṃ ettha sāsitā’ti yathānulomasāsanaṃ, tatiyaṃ – ‘dhammapuñjamatte “ahaṃ mamā”ti saññino sattā yathādhammaṃ ettha sāsitā’ti yathādhammasāsananti vuccati.

Similarly, the first is called the instruction according to offense because 'those beings who have many offenses are instructed herein according to their offense.' The second is called the instruction according to suitability because 'beings with diverse dispositions, underlying tendencies, conduct, and inclinations are instructed herein according to suitability.' The third is called the instruction according to Dhamma because 'beings who perceive "I" and "mine" in a mere heap of phenomena are instructed herein according to the Dhamma.'

Tathā paṭhamaṃ – ajjhācārapaṭipakkhabhūto saṃvarāsaṃvaro ettha kathitoti saṃvarāsaṃvarakathā. Saṃvarāsaṃvaroti [V 1.0020] khuddako ceva mahanto ca saṃvaro, kammākammaṃ viya, phalāphalaṃ viya ca, dutiyaṃ – “dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhipaṭipakkhabhūtā diṭṭhiviniveṭhanā ettha kathitā”ti diṭṭhiviniveṭhanakathā, tatiyaṃ – “rāgādipaṭipakkhabhūto nāmarūpaparicchedo ettha kathito”ti nāmarūpaparicchedakathāti vuccati.

Furthermore, regarding the first [Piṭaka], it is called the discourse on minor and major restraint because minor and major restraint, being the counter-aspect to transgression, is taught herein. Minor and major restraint means minor restraint and major restraint, like minor action and major action, and like minor fruit and major fruit. Regarding the second, it is called the discourse on the disentangling of views because the disentangling of views, being the counter-aspect to the sixty-two wrong views, is taught herein.
