Regarding the third, it is called the discourse on the discernment of name-and-form because the discernment of name-and-form, being the counter-aspect to lust and so on, is taught herein.

Tīsupi cetesu tisso sikkhā, tīṇi pahānāni, catubbidho ca gambhīrabhāvo veditabbo. Tathā hi vinayapiṭake visesena adhisīlasikkhā vuttā, suttantapiṭake adhicittasikkhā, abhidhammapiṭake adhipaññāsikkhā.

And in all three of these [Piṭakas], the three trainings, the three abandonments, and the fourfold profundity should be understood. Indeed, in the Vinaya Piṭaka, the training in higher virtue is taught in particular; in the Suttanta Piṭaka, the training in higher mind; and in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the training in higher wisdom.

Vinayapiṭake ca vītikkamappahānaṃ[P 1.0020], kilesānaṃ vītikkamapaṭipakkhattā sīlassa. Suttantapiṭake pariyuṭṭhānappahānaṃ, pariyuṭṭhānapaṭipakkhattā samādhissa. Abhidhammapiṭake anusayappahānaṃ, anusayapaṭipakkhattā paññāya. Paṭhame ca tadaṅgappahānaṃ, itaresu vikkhambhanasamucchedappahānāni. Paṭhame ca duccaritasaṃkilesappahānaṃ, itaresu taṇhādiṭṭhisaṃkilesappahānaṃ.

And in the Vinaya Piṭaka, there is the abandonment of transgression, because virtue is the counter-aspect to the transgression of defilements. In the Suttanta Piṭaka, there is the abandonment of obsession, because concentration is the counter-aspect to obsession. In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, there is the abandonment of latency, because wisdom is the counter-aspect to latency. And in the first, there is abandonment by substitution of opposites; in the others, abandonment by suppression and abandonment by cutting off. And in the first, there is the abandonment of the defilement of misconduct; in the others, the abandonment of the defilements of craving and wrong view.

Ekamekasmiñcettha catubbidhopi dhammatthadesanā paṭivedhagambhīrabhāvo veditabbo. Tattha dhammoti tanti. Atthoti tassāyeva attho. Desanāti tassā manasā vavatthāpitāya tantiyā desanā. Paṭivedhoti tantiyā tantiatthassa ca yathābhūtāvabodho. Tīsupi cetesu ete dhammatthadesanāpaṭivedhā. Yasmā sasādīhi viya mahāsamuddo [M 1.0021] mandabuddhīhi dukkhogāḷhā alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhā ca, tasmā gambhīrā. Evaṃ ekamekasmiṃ ettha catubbidhopi gambhīrabhāvo veditabbo.

And in each one of these [Piṭakas], the fourfold profundity of Dhamma, meaning, exposition, and penetration should be understood. Therein, 'Dhamma' is the Pali text. 'Meaning' is the meaning of that very text. 'Exposition' is the verbal teaching of that text which has been determined by mind. 'Penetration' is the knowledge that correctly penetrates the Pali text and its meaning. And in all three of these [Piṭakas], these—Dhamma, meaning, exposition, and penetration—are profound because, just as the great ocean is for small creatures such as hares, so too for those of dull wisdom they are difficult to enter and a footing cannot be obtained in them. Thus, in each one of these, the fourfold profundity should be understood.

Aparo nayo, dhammoti hetu. Vuttañhetaṃ – “hetumhi ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā”ti. Atthoti hetuphalaṃ, vuttañhetaṃ – “hetuphale ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 720). Desanāti paññatti, yathā dhammaṃ dhammābhilāpoti adhippāyo. Anulomapaṭilomasaṅkhepavitthārādivasena vā kathanaṃ. Paṭivedhoti abhisamayo, so ca lokiyalokuttaro visayato asammohato ca, atthānurūpaṃ dhammesu, dhammānurūpaṃ atthesu, paññattipathānurūpaṃ paññattīsu avabodho. Tesaṃ tesaṃ vā tattha tattha vuttadhammānaṃ paṭivijjhitabbo salakkhaṇasaṅkhāto aviparītasabhāvo.

Another method: 'Dhamma' is cause. For this is stated: 'Knowledge in the cause is the analytical knowledge of Dhamma.' 'Meaning' is the result of the cause. For this is stated: 'Knowledge in the result of the cause is the analytical knowledge of meaning.' 'Exposition' is designation; the intended meaning is the utterance concerning the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma. Or it is the discourse by way of forward order, reverse order, condensation, expansion, and so on. 'Penetration' is realization. And that, being mundane and supramundane, is, with respect to its object and its freedom from delusion, the penetrating knowledge of causes in conformity with their results, of results in conformity with their causes, and of designations in conformity with the way of designation. Or, it is the undistorted nature, known as the intrinsic characteristic, of those various dhammas taught here and there, which is to be penetrated.

Idāni [V 1.0021] yasmā etesu piṭakesu yaṃ yaṃ dhammajātaṃ vā atthajātaṃ vā, yā cāyaṃ yathā yathā ñāpetabbo attho sotūnaṃ ñāṇassa abhimukho hoti, tathā tathā tadatthajotikā desanā, yo cettha aviparītāvabodhasaṅkhāto paṭivedho, tesaṃ tesaṃ vā dhammānaṃ paṭivijjhitabbo salakkhaṇasaṅkhāto aviparītasabhāvo. Sabbampetaṃ anupacitakusalasambhārehi duppaññehi sasādīhi viya mahāsamuddo dukkhogāḷhaṃ alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhañca, tasmā gambhīraṃ. Evampi ekamekasmiṃ ettha catubbidhopi gambhīrabhāvo veditabbo.

Now, because in these Piṭakas there is this: whatever collection of causes or collection of results; and this exposition which illuminates that meaning in whatever way the meaning to be made known becomes manifest to the knowledge of the listeners; and this penetration herein, known as undistorted comprehension, or the undistorted nature of those various dhammas, known as their intrinsic characteristic, which is to be penetrated—all this, for those of dull wisdom who have not accumulated the provisions of the wholesome, is, like the great ocean for small creatures such as hares, difficult to enter and a footing cannot be obtained in it; therefore, it is profound. In this way also, the fourfold profundity in each one of these [Piṭakas] should be understood.

Ettāvatā ca –

And by this much:

“Desanāsāsanakathā, bhedaṃ tesu yathārahaṃ;

Sikkhāppahānagambhīra, bhāvañca paridīpaye”ti [P 1.0021] –

“One should illuminate the exposition, instruction, and discourse, their distinction in these [Piṭakas] as is appropriate, and the profound nature of the trainings and abandonments.”

Ayaṃ gāthā vuttatthāva hoti.

This verse has its meaning already explained.

“Pariyattibhedaṃ sampattiṃ, vipattiñcāpi yaṃ yahiṃ;

Pāpuṇāti yathā bhikkhu, tampi sabbaṃ vibhāvaye”ti –

“One should also clarify all of this: the distinction of learning, its accomplishment and its failure, and what a monk attains, wherein, and how.”

Ettha pana tīsu piṭakesu tividho pariyattibhedo daṭṭhabbo. Tisso hi pariyattiyo – alagaddūpamā, nissaraṇatthā, bhaṇḍāgārikapariyattīti.

Here, in the three Piṭakas, a threefold distinction of learning is to be understood. For there are three kinds of learning: that which is like the water-snake, that for the purpose of escape, and the treasurer's learning.

Tattha yā duggahitā, upārambhādihetu pariyāpuṭā, ayaṃ alagaddūpamā. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso alagaddatthiko alagaddagavesī [M 1.0022] alagaddapariyesanaṃ caramāno, so passeyya mahantaṃ alagaddaṃ, tamenaṃ bhoge vā naṅguṭṭhe vā gaṇheyya, tassa so alagaddo paṭiparivattitvā hatthe vā bāhāyaṃ vā aññatarasmiṃ vā aṅgapaccaṅge ḍaṃseyya, so tato nidānaṃ maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyya, maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkhaṃ. Taṃ kissa hetu? Duggahitattā, bhikkhave, alagaddassa. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, idhekacce moghapurisā dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti, suttaṃ…pe… vedallaṃ, te taṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā tesaṃ dhammānaṃ paññāya atthaṃ na upaparikkhanti, tesaṃ te dhammā paññāya atthaṃ anupaparikkhataṃ na nijjhānaṃ khamanti, te upārambhānisaṃsā ceva dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti, itivādappamokkhānisaṃsā ca, yassa catthāya dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti, tañcassa atthaṃ [V 1.0022] nānubhonti, tesaṃ te dhammā duggahitā dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Duggahitattā, bhikkhave, dhammāna”nti (ma. ni. 1.238).

Therein, that which is wrongly grasped, which is studied for the sake of finding fault and the like, is that which is like the water-snake. With reference to this it was said: 'Suppose, monks, a man needing a venomous snake, looking for a venomous snake, wandering in search of a venomous snake, were to see a large venomous snake. He might seize it by its coils or by its tail. That venomous snake, turning back on him, might bite him on the hand, on the arm, or on some other limb. From that cause, he would come to death or deadly suffering. For what reason? Because of the venomous snake being wrongly grasped, monks. So too, monks, some worthless men here study the Dhamma: Sutta...pe... Vedalla. Having studied that Dhamma, they do not investigate the meaning of those teachings with wisdom. For them, those teachings, not being investigated with wisdom, do not lead to reflective acceptance. They study the Dhamma for the benefit of finding fault and for the benefit of release from refutation in debate, and they do not experience the purpose for which one studies the Dhamma. For them, those teachings, being wrongly grasped, conduce to their harm and suffering for a long time. For what reason? Because of the teachings being wrongly grasped, monks.'

Yā pana suggahitā sīlakkhandhādipāripūriṃyeva ākaṅkhamānena pariyāpuṭā, na upārambhādihetu, ayaṃ nissaraṇatthā. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “tesaṃ te dhammā suggahitā dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya saṃvattanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Suggahitattā, bhikkhave, dhammāna”nti (ma. ni. 1.239).

But that learning which is well-grasped and thoroughly learned by one desiring only the complete fulfillment of the aggregate of virtue and so forth, and not for the sake of contention and the like, this is for the purpose of liberation. With reference to this it was said: “For them, those teachings, being well-grasped, conduce to their welfare and happiness for a long time. For what reason is that? Because, monks, of the teachings being well-grasped.”

Yaṃ pana pariññātakkhandho pahīnakileso bhāvitamaggo paṭividdhākuppo sacchikatanirodho khīṇāsavo kevalaṃ paveṇīpālanatthāya vaṃsānurakkhaṇatthāya pariyāpuṇāti, ayaṃ bhaṇḍāgārikapariyattīti.

Moreover, when one whose aggregates are fully comprehended, whose defilements are abandoned, who has cultivated the path, penetrated the unshakeable, realized cessation, and is an arahant with taints destroyed learns merely for the sake of preserving the tradition and maintaining the lineage, this is the storekeeper’s learning.

Vinaye pana suppaṭipanno bhikkhu sīlasampadaṃ nissāya tisso vijjā pāpuṇāti, tāsaṃyeva ca tattha pabhedavacanato. Sutte suppaṭipanno samādhisampadaṃ nissāya cha abhiññā pāpuṇāti, tāsaṃyeva ca tattha pabhedavacanato. Abhidhamme suppaṭipanno paññāsampadaṃ [P 1.0022] nissāya catasso paṭisambhidā pāpuṇāti, tāsañca tattheva pabhedavacanato, evametesu suppaṭipanno yathākkamena imaṃ vijjāttayachaḷabhiññācatuppaṭisambhidābhedaṃ sampattiṃ pāpuṇāti.

In the Vinaya, a monk who is well-practiced, relying on the accomplishment of virtue, attains the three knowledges, because of the detailed exposition of those very knowledges therein. In the Suttas, one who is well-practiced, relying on the accomplishment of concentration, attains the six superknowledges, because of the detailed exposition of those very superknowledges therein. In the Abhidhamma, one who is well-practiced, relying on the accomplishment of wisdom, attains the four analytical knowledges, because of the detailed exposition of those very analytical knowledges therein. Thus, one who is well-practiced in these attains, in respective order, this accomplishment distinguished as the three knowledges, the six superknowledges, and the four analytical knowledges.

Vinaye pana duppaṭipanno anuññātasukhasamphassaattharaṇapāvuraṇādiphassasāmaññato paṭikkhittesu upādinnakaphassādīsu anavajjasaññī hoti. Vuttampi [M 1.0023] hetaṃ – “tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi, yathā ye me antarāyikā dhammā antarāyikā vuttā bhagavatā, te paṭisevato nālaṃ antarāyāyā”ti (ma. ni. 1.234). Tato dussīlabhāvaṃ pāpuṇāti. Sutte duppaṭipanno – “cattāro me, bhikkhave, puggalā santo saṃvijjamānā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.5) adhippāyaṃ ajānanto duggahitaṃ gaṇhāti, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “attanā duggahitena amhe ceva abbhācikkhati, attānañca khaṇati, bahuñca apuññaṃ pasavatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.236). Tato micchādiṭṭhitaṃ pāpuṇāti. Abhidhamme duppaṭipanno dhammacintaṃ atidhāvanto acinteyyānipi cinteti. Tato cittakkhepaṃ pāpuṇāti, vuttañhetaṃ – “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, acinteyyāni, na cintetabbāni, yāni cintento ummādassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”ti (a. ni. 4.77). Evametesu duppaṭipanno yathākkamena imaṃ dussīlabhāva micchādiṭṭhitā cittakkhepabhedaṃ vipattiṃ pāpuṇātī”ti.

In the Vinaya, one who is ill-practiced, due to the similarity with the touch of permitted pleasant things such as floor-coverings and blankets, perceives no fault in forbidden contacts, such as with a living being. As it is said: “Thus do I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: that those things called obstructions by the Blessed One are not sufficient to be an obstruction for one who indulges in them.” From this, he attains a state of immorality. In the Suttas, one who is ill-practiced—not understanding the intention in passages such as, “Monks, these four persons are found existing…”—grasps wrongly. With reference to this, it is said: “By what is wrongly grasped by himself, he both misrepresents us and digs himself up, and he generates much demerit.” From this, he attains a state of wrong view. In the Abhidhamma, one who is ill-practiced, overstepping the contemplation of phenomena, thinks even about the unthinkable. From this, he attains mental distraction, as it is said: “Monks, these four things are unthinkable, not to be thought about; one who thinks about them would partake of madness or vexation.” Thus, one who is ill-practiced in these attains, in respective order, this ruin distinguished as immorality, wrong view, and mental distraction.

Ettāvatā [V 1.0023] ca –

And by this much:

“Pariyattibhedaṃ sampattiṃ, vipattiñcāpi yaṃ yahiṃ;

Pāpuṇāti yathā bhikkhu, tampi sabbaṃ vibhāvaye”ti –

“The distinction of learning, the accomplishment, and also the ruin; which a monk attains, wherein and how—all that too should be clarified.”

Ayampi gāthā vuttatthāva hoti. Evaṃ nānappakārato piṭakāni ñatvā tesaṃ vasenetaṃ buddhavacanaṃ tividhanti ñātabbaṃ.

This verse also has its meaning already explained. Thus, having known the Piṭakas in their various ways, this word of the Buddha should be known as threefold by way of them.

Kathaṃ nikāyavasena pañcavidhaṃ? Sabbameva cetaṃ dīghanikāyo, majjhimanikāyo, saṃyuttanikāyo, aṅguttaranikāyo, khuddakanikāyoti pañcappabhedaṃ hoti. Tattha katamo dīghanikāyo? Tivaggasaṅgahāni brahmajālādīni catuttiṃsa suttāni.

How is it fivefold by way of the Nikāyas? All of this has five divisions: the Dīgha Nikāya, the Majjhima Nikāya, the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the Aṅguttara Nikāya, and the Khuddaka Nikāya. Therein, what is the Dīgha Nikāya? The thirty-four suttas beginning with the Brahmajāla, which are collected in three groups.

“Catuttiṃseva suttantā, tivaggo yassa saṅgaho;

Esa dīghanikāyoti, paṭhamo anulomiko”ti.

“There are just thirty-four suttas, whose collection is of three groups; this is the Dīgha Nikāya, the first, with a fitting name.”

Kasmā [P 1.0023] panesa dīghanikāyoti vuccati? Dīghappamāṇānaṃ suttānaṃ samūhato nivāsato ca. Samūhanivāsā hi nikāyoti vuccanti. “Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekanikāyampi samanupassāmi evaṃ cittaṃ, yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave[M 1.0024], tiracchānagatā pāṇā” (saṃ. ni. 2.100). Poṇikanikāyo cikkhallikanikāyoti evamādīni cettha sādhakāni sāsanato lokato ca. Evaṃ sesānampi nikāyabhāve vacanattho veditabbo.

But why is this called the Dīgha Nikāya? Because it is a collection (samūha) and a residence (nivāsa) of suttas of long measure. For collections and residences are indeed called ‘nikāya.’ “Monks, I do not see any other single group (ekanikāya) so diverse as these animals that have gone to the animal realm.” The terms ‘Poṇikanikāya’ (the host of Poṇika) and ‘Cikkhallikanikāya’ (the host of Cikkhallika) and so forth are corroborating examples here from both the Teaching and from the world. In this way, the meaning of the word in the case of the remaining Nikāyas should also be understood.

Katamo majjhimanikāyo? Majjhimappamāṇāni pañcadasavaggasaṅgahāni mūlapariyāyasuttādīni diyaḍḍhasataṃ dve ca suttāni.

What is the Majjhima Nikāya? The one hundred and fifty-two suttas of middle length, beginning with the Mūlapariyāya Sutta, which are collected in fifteen groups.

“Diyaḍḍhasatasuttantā, dve ca suttāni yattha so;

Nikāyo majjhimo pañca, dasavaggapariggaho”ti.

“Wherein there are one hundred and fifty suttas and two suttas more, that Nikāya, encompassed by fifteen groups, is the Majjhima.”

Katamo saṃyuttanikāyo? Devatāsaṃyuttādivasena kathitāni oghataraṇādīni satta suttasahassāni satta ca suttasatāni dvāsaṭṭhi ca suttāni.

What is the Saṃyutta Nikāya? The seven thousand, seven hundred, and sixty-two suttas, beginning with the Oghataraṇa Sutta, which were taught by way of the Connected Discourses on Deities and so forth.

“Sattasuttasahassāni[V 1.0024], sattasuttasatāni ca;

Dvāsaṭṭhi ceva suttantā, eso saṃyuttasaṅgaho”ti.

“Seven thousand suttas, and seven hundred suttas, and sixty-two suttas as well; this is the collection of the Saṃyutta.”

Katamo aṅguttaranikāyo? Ekekaaṅgātirekavasena kathitāni cittapariyādānādīni nava suttasahassāni pañca suttasatāni sattapaññāsañca suttāni.

What is the Aṅguttara Nikāya? The nine thousand, five hundred, and fifty-seven suttas, beginning with the Cittapariyādāna Sutta, which were taught by way of exceeding by one factor at a time.

“Nava suttasahassāni, pañca suttasatāni ca;

Sattapaññāsa suttāni, saṅkhyā aṅguttare aya”nti.

“Nine thousand suttas, and five hundred suttas, and fifty-seven suttas; this is the count in the Aṅguttara.”

Katamo khuddakanikāyo? Sakalaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ, abhidhammapiṭakaṃ, khuddakapāṭhādayo ca pubbe dassitā pañcadasappabhedā, ṭhapetvā cattāro nikāye avasesaṃ buddhavacanaṃ.

What is the Khuddaka Nikāya? The entire Vinaya Piṭaka, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the fifteen divisions beginning with the Khuddakapāṭha that were shown previously, and the remaining word of the Buddha after setting aside the four Nikāyas.

“Ṭhapetvā caturopete, nikāye dīghaādike;

Tadaññaṃ buddhavacanaṃ, nikāyo khuddako mato”ti.

“Having set aside these four Nikāyas, beginning with the Dīgha, the other word of the Buddha is considered the Khuddaka Nikāya.”

Evaṃ nikāyavasena pañcavidhaṃ.

Thus, it is fivefold by way of the Nikāyas.

Kathaṃ aṅgavasena navavidhaṃ? Sabbameva hidaṃ suttaṃ, geyyaṃ, veyyākaraṇaṃ, gāthā, udānaṃ, itivuttakaṃ, jātakaṃ, abbhutadhammaṃ, vedallanti navappabhedaṃ hoti. Tattha ubhatovibhaṅganiddesakhandhakaparivārā, suttanipāte maṅgalasuttaratanasuttanālakasuttatuvaṭṭakasuttāni ca aññampi ca suttanāmakaṃ tathāgatavacanaṃ [M 1.0025] suttanti veditabbaṃ. Sabbampi sagāthakaṃ suttaṃ geyyanti [P 1.0024] veditabbaṃ. Visesena saṃyuttake sakalopi sagāthavaggo, sakalampi abhidhammapiṭakaṃ, niggāthakaṃ suttaṃ, yañca aññampi aṭṭhahi aṅgehi asaṅgahitaṃ buddhavacanaṃ, taṃ veyyākaraṇanti veditabbaṃ. Dhammapadaṃ, theragāthā, therīgāthā, suttanipāte nosuttanāmikā suddhikagāthā ca gāthāti veditabbā. Somanassaññāṇamayikagāthā paṭisaṃyuttā dveasīti suttantā udānanti veditabbaṃ. “Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā”tiādinayappavattā dasuttarasatasuttantā itivuttakanti veditabbaṃ. Apaṇṇakajātakādīni paññāsādhikāni pañcajātakasatāni ‘jātaka’nti veditabbaṃ. “Cattārome, bhikkhave, acchariyā abbhutā dhammā ānande”tiādinayappavattā (dī. ni. 2.209) sabbepi acchariyabbhutadhammapaṭisaṃyuttasuttantā abbhutadhammanti veditabbaṃ. Cūḷavedalla-mahāvedalla-sammādiṭṭhi-sakkapañha-saṅkhārabhājaniya-mahāpuṇṇamasuttādayo [V 1.0025] sabbepi vedañca tuṭṭhiñca laddhā laddhā pucchitasuttantā vedallanti veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ aṅgavasena navavidhaṃ.

How is it ninefold by way of its constituents? Indeed, all this Word of the Buddha is of nine kinds: Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla. Therein, the Ubhatovibhaṅga, the Niddesa, the Khandhakas, and the Parivāra; in the Suttanipāta, the Maṅgala Sutta, Ratana Sutta, Nālaka Sutta, and Tuvaṭṭaka Sutta; and any other word of the Tathāgata named 'sutta' are to be understood as 'Sutta.' All suttas containing verses are to be understood as 'Geyya.' Specifically, the entire Sagāthavagga in the Saṃyutta Nikāya is also included. The entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka, suttas without verses, and any other Word of the Buddha not included in the other eight constituents are to be understood as 'Veyyākaraṇa.' The Dhammapada, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, and the pure verses in the Suttanipāta not named 'sutta' are to be understood as 'Gāthā.' The eighty-two suttantas connected with verses born of joy and knowledge are to be understood as 'Udāna.' The one hundred and ten suttantas that proceed in the manner of “Thus was it said by the Blessed One…” are to be understood as 'Itivuttaka.' The five hundred and fifty Jātakas, starting with the Apaṇṇaka Jātaka, are to be understood as 'Jātaka.' All suttantas connected with marvelous and wonderful phenomena, such as those that proceed in the manner of, “Monks, there are these four wonderful and amazing qualities in Ānanda,” are to be understood as 'Abbhutadhamma.' The Cūḷavedalla Sutta, Mahāvedalla Sutta, Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta, Sakkapañha Sutta, Saṅkhārabhājaniya Sutta, Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta, and all other suttantas that were asked after repeatedly gaining knowledge and satisfaction are to be understood as 'Vedalla.' Thus, by way of its constituents, it is ninefold.

Kathaṃ dhammakkhandhavasena caturāsītisahassavidhaṃ? Sabbameva cetaṃ buddhavacanaṃ –

How is it eighty-four thousandfold by way of Dhamma aggregates? All this Word of the Buddha is—

“Dvāsīti buddhato gaṇhiṃ, dve sahassāni bhikkhuto;

Caturāsīti sahassāni, ye me dhammā pavattino”ti.

“Eighty-two thousand I received from the Buddha, and two thousand from the monks; these eighty-four thousand teachings are those that are current for me.”

Evaṃ paridīpitadhammakkhandhavasena caturāsītisahassappabhedaṃ hoti. Tattha ekānusandhikaṃ suttaṃ eko dhammakkhandho. Yaṃ anekānusandhikaṃ, tattha anusandhivasena dhammakkhandhagaṇanā. Gāthābandhesu pañhāpucchanaṃ eko dhammakkhandho, vissajjanaṃ eko. Abhidhamme ekamekaṃ tikadukabhājanaṃ, ekamekañca cittavārabhājanaṃ, ekameko dhammakkhandho. Vinaye atthi vatthu, atthi mātikā, atthi padabhājanīyaṃ, atthi antarāpatti, atthi āpatti, atthi anāpatti, atthi tikacchedo. Tattha ekameko koṭṭhāso ekameko dhammakkhandhoti veditabbo. Evaṃ dhammakkhandhavasena caturāsītisahassavidhaṃ.

Thus, by way of the Dhamma aggregates as expounded, it is of eighty-four thousand kinds. Herein, a sutta with a single continuity is one Dhamma aggregate. Where there are multiple continuities, the Dhamma aggregates are counted according to the continuities. In verse compositions, the question is one Dhamma aggregate, and the answer is one. In the Abhidhamma, each analysis of triads and dyads, and each analysis of a consciousness-round, is one Dhamma aggregate. In the Vinaya, there is the backstory, there is the matrix, there is the word-analysis, there is the intermediate offense, there is the offense, there is the non-offense, and there is the triad-division. Herein, each individual part should be understood as one Dhamma aggregate. Thus, by way of Dhamma aggregates, it is eighty-four thousandfold.

Evametaṃ abhedato rasavasena ekavidhaṃ, bhedato dhammavinayādivasena [P 1.0025] duvidhādibhedaṃ buddhavacanaṃ saṅgāyantena mahākassapappamukhena vasīgaṇena “ayaṃ [M 1.0026] dhammo, ayaṃ vinayo, idaṃ paṭhamabuddhavacanaṃ, idaṃ majjhimabuddhavacanaṃ, idaṃ pacchimabuddhavacanaṃ, idaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ, idaṃ suttantapiṭakaṃ, idaṃ abhidhammapiṭakaṃ, ayaṃ dīghanikāyo…pe… ayaṃ khuddakanikāyo, imāni suttādīni navaṅgāni, imāni caturāsīti dhammakkhandhasahassānī”ti, imaṃ pabhedaṃ vavatthapetvāva saṅgītaṃ. Na kevalañca imameva, aññampi uddānasaṅgaha-vaggasaṅgaha-peyyālasaṅgaha-ekakanipāta-dukanipātādinipātasaṅgaha-saṃyuttasaṅgaha-paṇṇāsasaṅgahādi-anekavidhaṃ tīsu piṭakesu sandissamānaṃ saṅgahappabhedaṃ vavatthapetvā eva sattahi māsehi saṅgītaṃ.

Thus, this Word of the Buddha—which is of one kind without division by way of its single essence, and of two or more kinds with division by way of the Dhamma, Vinaya, and so forth—was chanted by the assembly of masters headed by Mahākassapa only after having established this classification: ‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya; this is the first Word of the Buddha, this is the middle Word of the Buddha, this is the last Word of the Buddha; this is the Vinaya Piṭaka, this is the Suttanta Piṭaka, this is the Abhidhamma Piṭaka; this is the Dīgha Nikāya… this is the Khuddaka Nikāya; these are the nine constituents beginning with Sutta; these are the eighty-four thousand Dhamma aggregates.’ And not only this classification, but also the many other kinds of summary classifications found in the three Piṭakas—such as the summary by verses, summary by chapters, summary by repetition series, summary by numerical collection beginning with the ones and twos, summary by connection, and summary by fifties—were also established before it was chanted over seven months.

Saṅgītipariyosāne cassa – “idaṃ mahākassapattherena dasabalassa sāsanaṃ pañcavassasahassaparimāṇakālaṃ pavattanasamatthaṃ kata”nti sañjātappamodā sādhukāraṃ viya dadamānā ayaṃ mahāpathavī udakapariyantaṃ katvā anekappakāraṃ kampi saṅkampi sampakampi sampavedhi, anekāni ca acchariyāni pāturahesunti, ayaṃ paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti nāma. Yā loke –

And at the conclusion of its chanting, with great joy arising at the thought, “The Venerable Mahākassapa has made this Dispensation of the Ten-Powered One capable of lasting for a period of five thousand years,” this great earth, as if giving its approval, trembled, shook, quaked, and shuddered in many ways to its water boundary, and many wonders appeared. This is called the First Great Council. Which in the world—

“Satehi [V 1.0026] pañcahi katā, tena pañcasatāti ca;

Thereheva katattā ca, therikāti pavuccatī”ti.

“Because it was done by five hundred, it is called the ‘Council of Five Hundred’; and because it was done by the Elders, it is called the ‘Council of the Elders’.”

1. Brahmajālasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta

Paribbājakakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse Concerning Wanderers

Imissā [P 1.0026][V 1.0027][M 1.0027] paṭhamamahāsaṅgītiyā vattamānāya vinayasaṅgahāvasāne suttantapiṭake ādinikāyassa ādisuttaṃ brahmajālaṃ pucchantena āyasmatā mahākassapena – “brahmajālaṃ, āvuso ānanda, kattha bhāsita”nti, evamādivuttavacanapariyosāne yattha ca bhāsitaṃ, yañcārabbha bhāsitaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ pakāsento āyasmā ānando evaṃ me sutantiādimāha. Tena vuttaṃ “brahmajālassāpi evaṃ me sutantiādikaṃ āyasmatā ānandena paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle vuttaṃ nidānamādī”ti.

While this First Great Council was in progress, at the conclusion of the compilation of the Vinaya, in the Suttanta Piṭaka, the Venerable Mahākassapa, questioning about the Brahmajāla, the first sutta of the first collection, said: “Friend Ānanda, where was the Brahmajāla spoken?” At the conclusion of these words, the Venerable Ānanda, making clear where it was spoken and in reference to what it was spoken, said the passage beginning with “Thus have I heard.” Therefore it was said: “The introduction to the Brahmajāla, beginning with ‘Thus have I heard,’ was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council as its beginning.”

1. Tattha evanti nipātapadaṃ. Metiādīni nāmapadāni. Paṭipanno hotīti ettha paṭīti upasaggapadaṃ, hotīti ākhyātapadanti. Iminā tāva nayena padavibhāgo veditabbo.

1. Herein, 'evaṃ' is a particle. 'Me' and so forth are nouns. In 'paṭipanno hoti,' 'paṭi' is a prefix, and 'hoti' is a verb. In this way, first, the classification of words should be understood.

Atthato pana evaṃ-saddo tāva upamūpadesasampahaṃsanagarahaṇavacanasampaṭiggahākāranidassanāvadhāraṇādianekatthappabhedo. Tathāhesa – “evaṃ jātena maccena, kattabbaṃ kusalaṃ bahu”nti (dha. pa. 53) evamādīsu upamāyaṃ āgato. “Evaṃ te abhikkamitabbaṃ, evaṃ te paṭikkamitabba”ntiādīsu (a. ni. 4.122) upadese. “Evametaṃ bhagavā, evametaṃ sugatā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.66) sampahaṃsane. “Evamevaṃ panāyaṃ vasalī yasmiṃ vā tasmiṃ vā tassa muṇḍakassa [P 1.0027] samaṇakassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.187) garahaṇe. “Evaṃ, bhanteti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosu”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.1) vacanasampaṭiggahe. “Evaṃ byā kho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.398) ākāre. “Ehi tvaṃ, māṇavaka, yena samaṇo ānando tenupasaṅkama, upasaṅkamitvā mama vacanena samaṇaṃ ānandaṃ appābādhaṃ [V 1.0028] appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ puccha. “Subho māṇavo todeyyaputto bhavantaṃ ānandaṃ appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ pucchatī”ti. “Evañca vadehi, sādhu kira bhavaṃ ānando yena subhassa [M 1.0028] māṇavassa todeyyaputtassa nivesanaṃ, tenupasaṅkamatu anukampaṃ upādāyā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.445) nidassane. “Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, kālāmā, ime dhammā kusalā vā akusalā vāti? Akusalā, bhante. Sāvajjā vā anavajjā vāti? Sāvajjā, bhante. Viññugarahitā vā viññuppasatthā vāti? Viññugarahitā, bhante. Samattā samādinnā ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanti no vā, kathaṃ vo ettha hotīti? Samattā, bhante, samādinnā ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanti, evaṃ no ettha hotī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.66) avadhāraṇe. Svāyamidha ākāranidassanāvadhāraṇesu daṭṭhabbo.

As to meaning, however, the word 'evaṃ' has many different applications, such as simile, instruction, praise, reproach, acceptance of a statement, manner, demonstration, and determination. For instance, in passages such as, “Thus for a mortal who is born, much that is wholesome should be done,” it is used in the sense of a simile. In passages such as, “Thus you should advance, thus you should retreat,” it is used for instruction. In passages such as, “So it is, Blessed One, so it is, Well-farer,” it is used for praise. In passages such as, “In this very way this wretch praises that shaveling monkling wherever she may be,” it is used for reproach. In passages such as, “‘Even so, venerable sir,’ those monks responded to the Blessed One,” it is used for acceptance of a statement. In passages such as, “In this manner, venerable sir, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One,” it is used for manner. In passages such as, “Come, young man, go to the monk Ānanda, and having approached him, on my authority ask after the monk Ānanda’s freedom from illness and affliction, his good health, strength, and comfortable abiding, saying: ‘The young man Subha, son of Todeyya, asks after the venerable Ānanda’s freedom from illness and affliction, his good health, strength, and comfortable abiding.’ And say this also: ‘It would be good, sir, if the venerable Ānanda would visit the residence of the young man Subha, son of Todeyya, out of compassion,’” it is used for demonstration. In passages such as, “‘What do you think, Kālāmas? Are these things wholesome or unwholesome?’ ‘Unwholesome, venerable sir.’ ‘Blameworthy or blameless?’ ‘Blameworthy, venerable sir.’ ‘Censured by the wise or praised by the wise?’ ‘Censured by the wise, venerable sir.’ ‘When undertaken and fulfilled, do they lead to harm and suffering, or not? What is your view on this matter?’ ‘When undertaken and fulfilled, venerable sir, they lead to harm and suffering. Thus is our view on this matter,’” it is used for determination. This word, here, should be understood in the senses of manner, demonstration, and determination.

Tattha ākāratthena evaṃ-saddena etamatthaṃ dīpeti, nānānayanipuṇamanekajjhāsayasamuṭṭhānaṃ, atthabyañjanasampannaṃ, vividhapāṭihāriyaṃ, dhammatthadesanāpaṭivedhagambhīraṃ, sabbasattānaṃ sakasakabhāsānurūpato sotapathamāgacchantaṃ tassa bhagavato vacanaṃ sabbappakārena ko samattho viññātuṃ, sabbathāmena pana sotukāmataṃ janetvāpi ‘evaṃ me sutaṃ’ mayāpi ekenākārena sutanti.

Herein, with the word 'evaṃ' in the sense of manner, this meaning is shown: The word of that Blessed One—subtle with various methods, arising from numerous dispositions, endowed with meaning and expression, possessing various marvels, profound in Dhamma, meaning, teaching, and penetration, reaching the ear-path of all beings according to their respective languages—who is able to understand it in every way? However, having generated the desire to listen with all one's strength, 'Thus have I heard' means 'by me also it was heard in one manner.'

Nidassanatthena – “nāhaṃ sayambhū, na mayā idaṃ sacchikata”nti attānaṃ parimocento – ‘evaṃ me sutaṃ’, ‘mayāpi evaṃ suta’nti idāni vattabbaṃ sakalaṃ suttaṃ nidasseti.

In the sense of demonstration: freeing himself by stating, “I am not self-arisen, nor was this realized by me,” he demonstrates the entire sutta that is now to be recited with the words, “Thus have I heard,” meaning, “by me also it was thus heard.”

Avadhāraṇatthena – “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahussutānaṃ yadidaṃ ānando, gatimantānaṃ, satimantānaṃ, dhitimantānaṃ, upaṭṭhākānaṃ yadidaṃ [P 1.0028] ānando”ti (a. ni. 1.223). Evaṃ bhagavatā – “āyasmā ānando atthakusalo, dhammakusalo, byañjanakusalo, niruttikusalo, pubbāparakusalo”ti (a. ni. 5.169). Evaṃ dhammasenāpatinā ca pasatthabhāvānurūpaṃ attano dhāraṇabalaṃ dassento sattānaṃ sotukāmataṃ janeti – ‘evaṃ me sutaṃ’, tañca kho atthato vā byañjanato vā anūnamanadhikaṃ, evameva na aññathā daṭṭhabba”nti.

In the sense of determination: In accordance with how he was praised by the Blessed One—“Monks, foremost among my monk disciples who are very learned is Ānanda… who are of ready intelligence… who are mindful… who are resolute… who are attendants, is Ānanda”—and by the General of the Dhamma—“The Venerable Ānanda is skilled in the meaning, skilled in the Dhamma, skilled in the phrasing, skilled in the etymology, and skilled in what comes before and after”—he demonstrates his own power of retention, generating in beings the desire to listen, by saying: “‘Thus have I heard,’ and this should be understood as being neither deficient nor excessive in either meaning or phrasing, but as being exactly so and not otherwise.”

Me-saddo tīsu atthesu dissati. Tathā hissa – “gāthābhigītaṃ me abhojaneyya”ntiādīsu (su. ni. 81) mayāti attho. “Sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṅkhittena dhammaṃ desetū”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.88) mayhanti attho. “Dhammadāyādā me, bhikkhave[V 1.0029][M 1.0029], bhavathā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.29) mamāti attho. Idha pana mayā sutanti ca, mama sutanti ca atthadvaye yujjati.

The word 'me' is seen in three meanings. For instance, in passages such as, “Food obtained by chanting verses is not to be eaten by me,” it has the meaning of 'mayā' (by me). In passages such as, “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief,” it has the meaning of 'mayhaṃ' (to me). In passages such as, “Monks, be my heirs in the Dhamma,” it has the meaning of 'mama' (of me/my). Here, however, it is suitable in both meanings: 'heard by me' and 'my hearing.'

Sutanti ayaṃ suta-saddo saupasaggo ca anupasaggo ca – gamanavissutakilinna-upacitānuyoga-sotaviññeyya-sotadvārānusāra-viññātādianekatthappabhedo, tathā hissa “senāya pasuto”tiādīsu gacchantoti attho. “Sutadhammassa passato”tiādīsu (udā. 11) vissutadhammassāti attho. “Avassutā avassutassā”tiādīsu (pāci. 657) kilinnākilinnassāti attho. “Tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappaka”ntiādīsu (khu. pā. 7.12) upacitanti attho. “Ye jhānapasutā dhīrā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 181) jhānānuyuttāti attho. ‘Diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ muta’ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.241) sotaviññeyyanti attho. “Sutadharo sutasannicayo”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.339) sotadvārānusāraviññātadharoti attho. Idha panassa sotadvārānusārena upadhāritanti vā upadhāraṇanti vāti attho. ‘Me’ saddassa hi ‘mayā’ti atthe sati ‘evaṃ mayā sutaṃ’ sotadvārānusārena upadhāritanti yujjati. ‘Mamā’ti atthe sati evaṃ mama sutaṃ sotadvārānusārena upadhāraṇanti yujjati.

Regarding 'sutaṃ', this word 'suta', both with and without a prefix, has many different meanings, such as: going, renowned, moistened, accumulated, exertion, cognizable by ear-consciousness, and known by following in sequence upon the ear-door. Indeed, in passages such as 'senāya pasuto', its meaning is 'going'. In passages such as 'Sutadhammassa passato', the meaning is 'of one with a renowned Dhamma'. In passages such as 'Avassutā avassutassā', the meaning is 'moistened... of one who is moistened'. In passages such as 'Tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappakaṃ', the meaning is 'accumulated'. In passages such as 'Ye jhānapasutā dhīrā', the meaning is 'devoted to jhāna'. In passages such as 'Diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ', the meaning is 'cognizable by ear-consciousness'. In passages such as 'Sutadharo sutasannicayo', the meaning is 'one who bears what is known by following in sequence upon the ear-door'. Here, however, its meaning is either 'ascertained by following in sequence upon the ear-door' or 'the act of ascertaining'. For, when the word 'me' has the meaning of 'mayā' (by me), it is suitable as: 'Thus by me it was heard' means 'it was ascertained by following in sequence upon the ear-door'. When it has the meaning of 'mama' (of me), it is suitable as: 'Thus my hearing' means 'the ascertainment by following in sequence upon the ear-door'.

Evametesu tīsu padesu evanti sotaviññāṇādiviññāṇakiccanidassanaṃ. Meti vuttaviññāṇasamaṅgipuggalanidassanaṃ. Sutanti assavanabhāvapaṭikkhepato anūnādhikāviparītaggahaṇanidassanaṃ. Tathā evanti tassā sotadvārānusārena pavattāya viññāṇavīthiyā nānappakārena ārammaṇe pavattibhāvappakāsanaṃ. Meti attappakāsanaṃ. Sutanti dhammappakāsanaṃ. Ayañhettha saṅkhepo [P 1.0029] – “nānappakārena ārammaṇe pavattāya viññāṇavīthiyā mayā na aññaṃ kataṃ, idaṃ pana kataṃ, ayaṃ dhammo suto”ti.

Thus, in these three terms: `evaṃ` is an indication of the function of consciousness, such as ear-consciousness. `Me` is an indication of the person endowed with the aforesaid consciousness. `Sutaṃ`, by rejecting the state of not-hearing, is an indication of grasping without deficiency, excess, or distortion. Furthermore, `evaṃ` is a clarification of the state of proceeding in various ways with regard to the object by that cognitive series which proceeds following the ear-door. `Me` is a clarification of the self. `Sutaṃ` is a clarification of the Dhamma. This is the summary here: 'By me, through the cognitive series that proceeded in various ways with regard to the object, nothing else was done, but this was done: this Dhamma was heard.'

Tathā evanti niddisitabbadhammappakāsanaṃ. Meti puggalappakāsanaṃ. Sutanti puggalakiccappakāsanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti. “Yaṃ suttaṃ niddisissāmi, taṃ mayā evaṃ suta”nti.

Furthermore, `evaṃ` is a clarification of the Dhamma to be pointed out. `Me` is a clarification of the person. `Sutaṃ` is a clarification of the person's function. This is what is said: 'Whatever Sutta I shall point out, that was thus heard by me.'

Tathā evanti yassa cittasantānassa nānākārappavattiyā nānatthabyañjanaggahaṇaṃ hoti, tassa nānākāraniddeso. Evanti hi ayamākārapaññatti. Meti kattuniddeso. Sutanti visayaniddeso. Ettāvatā nānākārappavattena [M 1.0030] cittasantānena taṃ samaṅgino kattu visayaggahaṇasanniṭṭhānaṃ kataṃ hoti.

Furthermore, `evaṃ` is an indication of the various modes of that mental continuum, through the proceeding of which in various modes there is the grasping of various meanings and expressions. For `evaṃ` is a concept of mode. `Me` is an indication of the agent. `Sutaṃ` is an indication of the object. By this much, the determination of the grasping of the object by the agent endowed with that mental continuum proceeding in various modes is made.

Athavā [V 1.0030] evanti puggalakiccaniddeso. Sutanti viññāṇakiccaniddeso. Meti ubhayakiccayuttapuggalaniddeso. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo, “mayā savanakiccaviññāṇasamaṅginā puggalena viññāṇavasena laddhasavanakiccavohārena suta”nti.

Alternatively, `evaṃ` is an indication of the person's function. `Sutaṃ` is an indication of consciousness's function. `Me` is an indication of the person connected with both functions. This is the summary here: 'It was heard by me, the person endowed with consciousness whose function is hearing, by means of consciousness which has obtained the designation of having the function of hearing.'

Tattha evanti ca meti ca saccikaṭṭhaparamatthavasena avijjamānapaññatti. Kiñhettha taṃ paramatthato atthi, yaṃ evanti vā meti vā niddesaṃ labhetha? Sutanti vijjamānapaññatti. Yañhi taṃ ettha sotena upaladdhaṃ, taṃ paramatthato vijjamānanti. Tathā ‘eva’nti ca, meti ca, taṃ taṃ upādāya vattabbato upādāpaññatti. ‘Suta’nti diṭṭhādīni upanidhāya vattabbato upanidhāpaññatti. Ettha ca evanti vacanena asammohaṃ dīpeti. Na hi sammūḷho nānappakārapaṭivedhasamattho hoti. ‘Suta’nti vacanena sutassa asammosaṃ dīpeti. Yassa hi sutaṃ sammuṭṭhaṃ hoti, na so kālantarena mayā sutanti paṭijānāti. Iccassa asammohena paññāsiddhi, asammosena pana satisiddhi. Tattha paññāpubbaṅgamāya satiyā byañjanāvadhāraṇasamatthatā, satipubbaṅgamāya paññāya atthapaṭivedhasamatthatā. Tadubhayasamatthatāyogena atthabyañjanasampannassa dhammakosassa anupālanasamatthato dhammabhaṇḍāgārikattasiddhi.

Therein, both `evaṃ` and `me` are non-existent concepts in the sense of true and ultimate meaning. For what is there here in an ultimate sense that could receive the designation `evaṃ` or `me`? `Sutaṃ` is an existent concept. For that which is apprehended here by the ear is ultimately existent. Furthermore, both `evaṃ` and `me` are concepts of dependence, because they are spoken in dependence on this or that. `Sutaṃ` is a concept of comparison, because it is spoken in comparison to things seen, and so forth. And here, by the word `evaṃ`, he indicates non-delusion. For one who is deluded is not capable of penetrating in various ways. By the word `sutaṃ`, he indicates non-forgetfulness of what was heard. For one whose hearing is forgotten does not, after a time, acknowledge, 'It was heard by me.' Thus, for him, through non-delusion, there is the accomplishment of wisdom, and through non-forgetfulness, the accomplishment of mindfulness. Therein, with mindfulness preceded by wisdom, there is the capability to ascertain the letter; with wisdom preceded by mindfulness, there is the capability to penetrate the meaning. Through the connection with the capability for both, because of the ability to protect the treasury of the Dhamma which is complete in meaning and letter, there is the accomplishment of the state of being the Treasurer of the Dhamma.

Aparo nayo, evanti vacanena yoniso manasikāraṃ dīpeti. Ayoniso manasikaroto hi nānappakārapaṭivedhābhāvato. Sutanti vacanena avikkhepaṃ dīpeti, vikkhittacittassa savanābhāvato. Tathā hi vikkhittacitto puggalo sabbasampattiyā vuccamānopi [P 1.0030] “na mayā sutaṃ, puna bhaṇathā”ti bhaṇati. Yoniso manasikārena cettha attasammāpaṇidhiṃ pubbe ca katapuññataṃ sādheti, sammā appaṇihitattassa pubbe akatapuññassa vā tadabhāvato. Avikkhepena saddhammassavanaṃ sappurisūpanissayañca sādheti. Na hi vikkhittacitto sotuṃ sakkoti, na ca sappurise anupassayamānassa savanaṃ atthīti.

Another method: by the word `evaṃ`, he indicates wise attention, because for one who attends unwisely, there is an absence of penetration in various ways. By the word `sutaṃ`, he indicates non-distraction, because for one with a distracted mind, there is an absence of hearing. Indeed, a person with a distracted mind, even when spoken to with all completeness, says, 'It was not heard by me, speak again.' And here, through wise attention, he accomplishes right direction of the self and merit made in the past, because of the absence of that for one whose self is not rightly directed or for one who has not made merit in the past. Through non-distraction, he accomplishes the hearing of the good Dhamma and association with good persons. For one with a distracted mind is not able to hear, and for one not associating with good persons, there is no hearing.

Aparo [M 1.0031] nayo, yasmā evanti yassa cittasantānassa nānākārappavattiyā nānatthabyañjanaggahaṇaṃ hoti, tassa nānākāraniddesoti vuttaṃ, so ca evaṃ bhaddako ākāro na sammāappaṇihitattano pubbe akatapuññassa vā hoti, tasmā evanti iminā bhaddakenākārena pacchimacakkadvayasampattimattano dīpeti. Sutanti savanayogena purimacakkadvayasampattiṃ. Na hi appatirūpadese vasato sappurisūpanissayavirahitassa vā savanaṃ atthi. Iccassa pacchimacakkadvayasiddhiyā āsayasuddhisiddhā hoti, purimacakkadvayasiddhiyā payogasuddhi, tāya ca āsayasuddhiyā adhigamabyattisiddhi, payogasuddhiyā āgamabyattisiddhi. Iti [V 1.0031] payogāsayasuddhassa āgamādhigamasampannassa vacanaṃ aruṇuggaṃ viya sūriyassa udayato yoniso manasikāro viya ca kusalakammassa arahati bhagavato vacanassa pubbaṅgamaṃ bhavitunti ṭhāne nidānaṃ ṭhapento – “evaṃ me suta”ntiādimāha.

Another way: Because `evaṃ` was said to be 'an indication of the various modes of that mental continuum by whose proceeding in various modes there is the grasping of various meanings and expressions', and since such an excellent mode does not arise for one whose self is not well-directed or who has not made merit previously, therefore, by `evaṃ`, with this excellent mode, he reveals his own accomplishment of the latter two wheels. By `sutaṃ`, through the connection with listening, he reveals the accomplishment of the former two wheels. Indeed, there is no listening for one dwelling in an unsuitable place or for one lacking reliance on good persons. Thus, for him, through the completion of the latter two wheels, purity of disposition is accomplished; through the completion of the former two wheels, purity of endeavor is accomplished. And by that purity of disposition, the accomplishment of proficiency in realization is achieved; by the purity of endeavor, the accomplishment of proficiency in the textual tradition is achieved. Thus, the words of one whose endeavor and disposition are pure, and who is endowed with the textual tradition and realization, are fit to be the forerunner of the Blessed One's words, just as the sunrise is for the rising sun, and just as wise attention is for wholesome kamma. Therefore, placing the introduction in its proper place, he said, 'Thus have I heard,' and so on.

Aparo nayo, ‘eva’nti iminā nānappakārapaṭivedhadīpakena vacanena attano atthapaṭibhānapaṭisambhidāsampattisabbhāvaṃ dīpeti. ‘Suta’nti iminā sotabbappabhedapaṭivedhadīpakena dhammaniruttipaṭisambhidāsampattisabbhāvaṃ. ‘Eva’nti ca idaṃ yoniso manasikāradīpakaṃ vacanaṃ bhāsamāno – “ete mayā dhammā manasānupekkhitā, diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhā”ti dīpeti. ‘Suta’nti idaṃ savanayogadīpakaṃ vacanaṃ bhāsamāno – “bahū mayā dhammā sutā dhātā vacasā paricitā”ti dīpeti. Tadubhayenāpi atthabyañjanapāripūriṃ dīpento savane ādaraṃ janeti. Atthabyañjanaparipuṇṇañhi dhammaṃ ādarena assuṇanto mahatā hitā paribāhiro hotīti, tasmā ādaraṃ janetvā sakkaccaṃ ayaṃ dhammo sotabboti.

Another way: By this word 'thus,' which indicates the penetration of various kinds, he reveals the actual existence of his accomplishment in the analytical knowledge of meaning and the analytical knowledge of ready wit. By this word 'heard,' which indicates the penetration of the distinctions of what is to be heard, he reveals the actual existence of his accomplishment in the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma and the analytical knowledge of language. And in saying this word 'thus,' which indicates wise attention, he reveals: "These teachings have been repeatedly contemplated by me with the mind and well penetrated by wisdom." In saying this word 'heard,' which indicates the connection with listening, he reveals: "Many teachings have been heard by me, borne in mind, and repeatedly practiced by way of recitation." By both of these, in indicating the completeness of meaning and phrasing, he generates reverence for listening. Indeed, one who does not listen with reverence to a Dhamma complete in meaning and phrasing becomes external to great benefit. Therefore, having generated reverence, this Dhamma should be listened to carefully.

“Evaṃ [P 1.0031] me suta”nti iminā pana sakalena vacanena āyasmā ānando tathāgatappaveditaṃ dhammaṃ attano adahanto asappurisabhūmiṃ atikkamati. Sāvakattaṃ paṭijānanto sappurisabhūmiṃ okkamati. Tathā asaddhammā cittaṃ vuṭṭhāpeti, saddhamme cittaṃ patiṭṭhāpeti. “Kevalaṃ sutamevetaṃ mayā, tasseva bhagavato vacana”nti dīpento attānaṃ parimoceti, satthāraṃ apadisati, jinavacanaṃ appeti, dhammanettiṃ patiṭṭhāpeti.

Furthermore, by this entire statement "Thus have I heard," the Venerable Ānanda, not taking the Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata as his own, transcends the domain of the ignoble. Acknowledging his state as a disciple, he enters the domain of the noble. Thus, he raises the mind from the false Dhamma and establishes the mind in the true Dhamma. By indicating, "This was merely heard by me, the very words of that Blessed One," he frees himself, points to the Teacher, attributes the Victor's words, and establishes the guideline of the Dhamma.

Apica [M 1.0032] “evaṃ me suta”nti attanā uppāditabhāvaṃ appaṭijānanto purimavacanaṃ vivaranto – “sammukhā paṭiggahitamidaṃ mayā tassa bhagavato catuvesārajjavisāradassa dasabaladharassa āsabhaṭṭhānaṭṭhāyino sīhanādanādino sabbasattuttamassa dhammissarassa dhammarājassa dhammādhipatino dhammadīpassa dhammasaraṇassa saddhammavaracakkavattino sammāsambuddhassa vacanaṃ, na ettha atthe vā dhamme vā pade vā byañjane vā kaṅkhā vā vimati vā kātabbā”ti sabbesaṃ devamanussānaṃ imasmiṃ dhamme assaddhiyaṃ vināseti, saddhāsampadaṃ uppādeti. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Moreover, by saying, "Thus have I heard," not acknowledging it as his own production and explaining the pre-existing words, he says: "This word I received in person from that Blessed One—who is fearless with the four kinds of fearlessness, the bearer of the ten powers, who stands in the noble position, who utters the lion's roar, the supreme among all beings, the lord of the Dhamma, the king of the Dhamma, the sovereign of the Dhamma, the lamp of the Dhamma, the refuge of the Dhamma, the turner of the noble wheel of the true Dhamma, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Herein, no doubt or hesitation should be made regarding the meaning, the teaching, the phrase, or the expression." Thus, he destroys the faithlessness in this Dhamma for all devas and humans and generates the accomplishment of faith. Therefore, it is said:

“Vināsayati assaddhaṃ, saddhaṃ vaḍḍheti sāsane;

Evaṃ me sutamiccevaṃ, vadaṃ gotamasāvako”ti.

"He destroys faithlessness, he increases faith in the Dispensation; 'Thus have I heard'—so speaking, a disciple of Gotama."

Ekanti [V 1.0032] gaṇanaparicchedaniddeso. Samayanti paricchinnaniddeso. Ekaṃ samayanti aniyamitaparidīpanaṃ. Tattha samayasaddo –

'One' is a designation indicating demarcation by number. 'Time' is a designation of what is demarcated. 'At one time' is an expression indicating an unspecified time. Therein, the word 'samaya'—

“Samavāye khaṇe kāle, samūhe hetudiṭṭhisu;

Paṭilābhe pahāne ca, paṭivedhe ca dissati”.

"Is seen in the sense of conjunction, opportunity, time, collection, cause, and views, in attainment, abandonment, and in penetration."

Tathā hissa – “appevanāma svepi upasaṅkameyyāma kālañca samayañca upādāyā”ti evamādīsu (dī. ni. 1.447) samavāyo attho. “Ekova kho bhikkhave, khaṇo ca samayo ca brahmacariyavāsāyā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 8.29) khaṇo. “Uṇhasamayo pariḷāhasamayo”tiādīsu (pāci. 358) kālo. “Mahāsamayo pavanasmi”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.332) samūho. “Samayopi kho te, bhaddāli, appaṭividdho ahosi, bhagavā kho [P 1.0032] sāvatthiyaṃ viharati, bhagavāpi maṃ jānissati, bhaddāli nāma bhikkhu satthusāsane sikkhāya aparipūrakārī’ti. Ayampi kho, te bhaddāli, samayo appaṭividdho ahosī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.135) hetu. “Tena kho pana samayena uggahamāno paribbājako samaṇamuṇḍikāputto samayappavādake tindukācīre ekasālake mallikāya ārāme paṭivasatī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.260) diṭṭhi.

Indeed, for this word: In passages such as, “Perhaps tomorrow we might approach, taking into account the time and the conjunction of causes,” the meaning is ‘conjunction.’ In passages such as, “Monks, there is only one opportunity and occasion for living the holy life,” the meaning is ‘opportunity.’ In passages such as, “A time of heat, a time of scorching,” the meaning is ‘time.’ In passages such as, “A great assembly in the great forest,” the meaning is ‘collection.’ In passages such as, “You, Bhaddāli, did not penetrate this reason: ‘The Blessed One is dwelling at Sāvatthī, and the Blessed One will know of me: “The monk named Bhaddāli is one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.”’ This reason, Bhaddāli, was also not penetrated by you,” the meaning is ‘cause.’ In passages such as, “At that time, the wanderer Uggahamāna, son of the ascetic Muṇḍikā, was dwelling in Mallikā’s park, in the single-hall sanctuary with a row of Tinduka trees, a place for debating views,” the meaning is ‘view.’

“Diṭṭhe dhamme ca yo attho, yo cattho samparāyiko;

Atthābhisamayā dhīro, paṇḍitoti pavuccatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.128) –

"The benefit that is in this visible life, and the benefit that pertains to the future life—through the attainment of this benefit, the wise one is called a sage.” –

Ādīsu [M 1.0033] paṭilābho. “Sammā mānābhisamayā antamakāsi dukkhassā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 7.9) pahānaṃ. “Dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho saṅkhataṭṭho santāpaṭṭho vipariṇāmaṭṭho abhisamayaṭṭho”tiādīsu (paṭi. 108) paṭivedho. Idha panassa kālo attho. Tena saṃvaccharautumāsaḍḍhamāsarattidivapubbaṇhamajjhanhikasāyanhapaṭhamamajjhi-mapacchimayāmamuhuttādīsu kālappabhedabhūtesu samayesu ekaṃ samayanti dīpeti.

In such passages, the meaning is ‘attainment.’ In passages such as, “Through the right overcoming of conceit, he made an end of suffering,” the meaning is ‘abandonment.’ In passages such as, “Of suffering, the meaning is oppression, the meaning is the conditioned, the meaning is burning, the meaning is change, the meaning is that which is to be penetrated,” the meaning is ‘that which is to be penetrated.’ Here, however, its meaning is ‘time.’ By this, it indicates ‘at one time’ among the times that are the various divisions of time, such as year, season, month, half-month, night, day, forenoon, midday, afternoon, first, middle, and last watches of the night, moment, and so forth.

Tattha kiñcāpi etesu saṃvaccharādīsu samayesu yaṃ yaṃ suttaṃ yasmiṃ yasmiṃ saṃvacchare utumhi māse pakkhe rattibhāge vā divasabhāge vā vuttaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ therassa suviditaṃ suvavatthāpitaṃ paññāya. Yasmā pana – “evaṃ me sutaṃ” asukasaṃvacchare asukautumhi asukamāse asukapakkhe asukarattibhāge asukadivasabhāge vāti evaṃ vutte na sakkā sukhena [V 1.0033] dhāretuṃ vā uddisituṃ vā uddisāpetuṃ vā, bahu ca vattabbaṃ hoti, tasmā ekeneva padena tamatthaṃ samodhānetvā “ekaṃ samaya”nti āha. Ye vā ime gabbhokkantisamayo, jātisamayo, saṃvegasamayo, abhinikkhamanasamayo, dukkarakārikasamayo, māravijayasamayo, abhisambodhisamayo diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārasamayo, desanāsamayo, parinibbānasamayoti, evamādayo bhagavato devamanussesu ativiya pakāsā anekakālappabhedā eva samayā. Tesu samayesu desanāsamayasaṅkhātaṃ ekaṃ samayanti dīpeti. Yo cāyaṃ ñāṇakaruṇākiccasamayesu karuṇākiccasamayo, attahitaparahitapaṭipattisamayesu parahitapaṭipattisamayo, sannipatitānaṃ karaṇīyadvayasamayesu dhammikathāsamayo desanāpaṭipattisamayesu [P 1.0033] desanāsamayo, tesupi samayesu aññataraṃ samayaṃ sandhāya “ekaṃ samaya”nti āha.

Herein, although whatever discourse was spoken in whatever year, season, month, fortnight, or part of the night or day among these periods such as the year and so forth, all of that was well-known and well-determined by the Elder through wisdom. However, since if it were said, “Thus have I heard in such and such a year, such and such a season, such and such a month, such and such a fortnight, such and such a part of the night, or such and such a part of the day,” it would not be possible to easily bear it in mind, or to recite it, or to have it recited, and much would have to be said; therefore, having combined that meaning with a single phrase, he said, “at one time.” Or, these are the occasions: the occasion of conception, the occasion of birth, the occasion of spiritual urgency, the occasion of renunciation, the occasion of practicing austerities, the occasion of conquering Māra, the occasion of perfect enlightenment, the occasion of dwelling in bliss in the present life, the occasion of teaching, the occasion of final Nibbāna—such and other occasions of the Blessed One, which are indeed the many different divisions of time, were exceedingly manifest among gods and humans. Among these occasions, he indicates one occasion reckoned as the occasion of teaching. And this, among the occasions for the tasks of knowledge and compassion, is the occasion for the task of compassion; among the occasions for the practice for one’s own welfare and the welfare of others, it is the occasion for the practice for the welfare of others; among the occasions of the two duties for those who have assembled, it is the occasion for a Dhamma talk; among the occasions of teaching and practice, it is the occasion of teaching—referring to one or another among these occasions also, he said, “at one time.”

Kasmā panettha yathā abhidhamme “yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacara”nti (dha. sa. 1) ca, ito aññesu ca suttapadesu – “yasmiṃ samaye, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehī”ti ca bhummavacananiddeso kato, vinaye ca – “tena samayena buddho bhagavā”ti karaṇavacanena, tathā akatvā “ekaṃ samaya”nti upayogavacananiddeso katoti? Tattha tathā idha ca aññathā atthasambhavato. Tattha hi abhidhamme ito aññesu suttapadesu ca adhikaraṇattho [M 1.0034] bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇattho ca sambhavati. Adhikaraṇañhi kālattho, samūhattho ca samayo, tattha tattha vuttānaṃ phassādidhammānaṃ khaṇasamavāyahetusaṅkhātassa ca samayassa bhāvena tesaṃ bhāvo lakkhīyati, tasmā tadatthajotanatthaṃ tattha bhummavacananiddeso kato.

Why here was the indication made with the accusative case as “ekaṃ samayaṃ,” and not as it was done elsewhere: with the locative case in the Abhidhamma, as in “yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ,” and in other sutta passages, as in “yasmiṃ samaye, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehī,” and with the instrumental case in the Vinaya, as in “tena samayena buddho bhagavā”? It is because the meaning is possible in that way there, and in another way here. For there, in the Abhidhamma and in other sutta passages, the meaning of locus and the meaning of a state being the characteristic of another state are possible. For “samaya” has the meaning of time and the meaning of collection, which are the locus for the dhammas such as contact, etc., spoken of there. And by the state of the “samaya”—reckoned as moment, conjunction, and cause—the state of those dhammas is characterized. Therefore, to illuminate that meaning, the indication was made there with the locative case.

Vinaye ca hetuattho karaṇattho ca sambhavati. Yo hi so sikkhāpadapaññattisamayo sāriputtādīhipi dubbiññeyyo, tena samayena hetubhūtena karaṇabhūtena ca sikkhāpadāni paññāpayanto sikkhāpadapaññattihetuñca apekkhamāno bhagavā tattha tattha vihāsi, tasmā tadatthajotanatthaṃ tattha karaṇavacanena niddeso kato.

And in the Vinaya, the meaning of cause and the meaning of instrument are possible. For that time of laying down the training rules was difficult to be known even by Sāriputta and others. The Blessed One, while laying down the training rules and having regard for the cause of laying down the training rules by means of that time, which had become the cause and the instrument, dwelt here and there. Therefore, to illuminate that meaning, the indication was made there with the instrumental case.

Idha pana aññasmiñca evaṃ jātike accantasaṃyogattho sambhavati. Yañhi samayaṃ bhagavā imaṃ aññaṃ vā suttantaṃ desesi, accantameva taṃ samayaṃ karuṇāvihārena vihāsi, tasmā tadatthajotanatthaṃ idha upayogavacananiddeso katoti.

Here, however, and in other instances of this kind, the meaning of continuous connection is possible. For throughout whatever time the Blessed One taught this or another Suttanta, he dwelt uninterruptedly throughout that time with the abiding of compassion. Therefore, to illuminate that meaning, the indication is given here with the accusative case.

Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Therefore it is said:

“Taṃ [V 1.0034] taṃ atthamapekkhitvā, bhummena karaṇena ca;

Aññatra samayo vutto, upayogena so idhā”ti.

“Having had regard for this and that meaning, elsewhere ‘samayo’ is stated by the locative and by the instrumental; here it is by the accusative.”

Porāṇā pana vaṇṇayanti – “tasmiṃ samaye”ti vā, “tena samayenā”ti vā, “ekaṃ samaya”nti vā, abhilāpamattabhedo esa, sabbattha bhummamevatthoti. Tasmā “ekaṃ samaya”nti vuttepi “ekasmiṃ samaye”ti attho veditabbo.

The ancients, however, explain: Whether it is “tasmiṃ samaye,” or “tena samayena,” or “ekaṃ samayaṃ,” this is a difference only in expression; in all cases the meaning is only the locative. Therefore, even when “ekaṃ samayaṃ” is said, the meaning should be understood as “ekasmiṃ samaye.”

Bhagavāti garu. Garuñhi loke bhagavāti vadanti. Ayañca [P 1.0034] sabbaguṇavisiṭṭhatāya sabbasattānaṃ garu, tasmā bhagavāti veditabbo. Porāṇehipi vuttaṃ –

“Bhagavā” means one who is venerable. For in the world, they call a venerable person “bhagavā.” And this one, because of being distinguished by all virtues, is venerable to all beings; therefore, he should be known as “Bhagavā.” It was also said by the ancients:

“Bhagavāti vacanaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, bhagavāti vacanamuttamaṃ;

Garu gāravayutto so, bhagavā tena vuccatī”ti.

“The word ‘Bhagavā’ is excellent, the word ‘Bhagavā’ is supreme; he is venerable, endowed with reverence, therefore he is called ‘Bhagavā’.”

Api ca –

Furthermore:

“Bhāgyavā bhaggavā yutto, bhagehi ca vibhattavā;

Bhattavā vantagamano, bhavesu bhagavā tato”ti.

“He was possessed of fortune, he had broken, and was endowed with glories, he had analyzed; he had cultivated, and had abandoned journeying in existences; therefore, he is Bhagavā.”

Imissā [M 1.0035] gāthāya vasenassa padassa vitthāraattho veditabbo. So ca visuddhimagge buddhānussatiniddese vuttoyeva.

By means of this verse, the detailed meaning of this word should be understood. And that has indeed been stated in the Visuddhimagga, in the exposition of the recollection of the Buddha.

Ettāvatā cettha evaṃ me sutanti vacanena yathāsutaṃ dhammaṃ dassento bhagavato dhammakāyaṃ paccakkhaṃ karoti. Tena “nayidaṃ atikkantasatthukaṃ pāvacanaṃ, ayaṃ vo satthā”ti satthu adassanena ukkaṇṭhitaṃ janaṃ samassāseti.

And to this extent, herein, by the words “Thus have I heard,” showing the Dhamma as it was heard, he makes the Dhamma-body of the Blessed One directly perceptible. By that, he reassures the people who are weary because of not seeing the Teacher, thinking: “This teaching is not one whose teacher has passed away; this is your teacher.”

Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavāti vacanena tasmiṃ samaye bhagavato avijjamānabhāvaṃ dassento rūpakāyaparinibbānaṃ sādheti. Tena “evaṃvidhassa nāma ariyadhammassa desako dasabaladharo vajirasaṅghāta samānakāyo sopi bhagavā parinibbuto, kena aññena jīvite āsā janetabbā”ti jīvitamadamattaṃ janaṃ saṃvejeti, saddhamme cassa ussāhaṃ janeti.

By the words “at one time the Blessed One,” showing the state of the Blessed One’s non-existence at that time, he establishes the final Nibbāna of the physical body. By that, he stirs up spiritual urgency in people intoxicated by the pride of life, thinking: “Even that Blessed One—the teacher of such a noble Dhamma, the bearer of the ten powers, whose body was like a solid diamond—has attained final Nibbāna. By what other person should hope in life be generated?” And he generates enthusiasm for the true Dhamma in them.

Evanti [V 1.0035] ca bhaṇanto desanāsampattiṃ niddisati. Me sutanti sāvakasampattiṃ. Ekaṃ samayanti kālasampattiṃ. Bhagavāti desakasampattiṃ.

And by saying “Thus,” he indicates the accomplishment of the teaching. By “heard by me,” the accomplishment of the hearer. By “at one time,” the accomplishment of the time. By “the Blessed One,” the accomplishment of the teacher.

Antarā ca rājagahaṃ antarā ca nāḷandanti antarā-saddo kāraṇakhaṇacittavemajjhavivarādīsu dissati. “Tadantaraṃ ko jāneyya aññatra tathāgatā”ti (a. ni. 6.44) ca, “janā saṅgamma mantenti mañca tañca kimantara”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.228) ca ādīsu hi kāraṇe antarā-saddo. “Addasa maṃ, bhante, aññatarā itthī vijjantarikāya bhājanaṃ dhovantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.149) khaṇe. “Yassantarato na santi kopā”tiādīsu (udā. 20) citte. “Antarā vosānamāpādī”tiādīsu [P 1.0035] (cūḷava. 350) vemajjhe. “Api cāyaṃ, bhikkhave, tapodā dvinnaṃ mahānirayānaṃ antarikāya āgacchatī”tiādīsu (pārā. 231) vivare. Svāyamidha vivare vattati, tasmā rājagahassa ca nāḷandāya ca vivareti evametthattho veditabbo. Antarā-saddena pana yuttattā upayogavacanaṃ kataṃ. Īdisesu ca ṭhānesu akkharacintakā “antarā gāmañca nadiñca yātī”ti evaṃ ekameva antarāsaddaṃ payujjanti, so dutiyapadenapi yojetabbo hoti, ayojiyamāne upayogavacanaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Idha pana yojetvāyeva vuttoti.

Between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā: The word 'antarā' is found in such meanings as cause, moment, mind, the middle, and gap. For instance, in 'Who could know that cause, other than the Tathāgata?' (A.N. 6.44) and 'People gather and confer, “What is the cause between me and you?”' (S.N. 1.228), the word 'antarā' is indeed used for cause. In 'Venerable sir, a certain woman saw me washing a vessel in the moment of a lightning flash' (M.N. 2.149), it is used for moment. In 'For whom there are no internal defilements' (Ud. 20), it is used for mind. In 'In the middle, he reached the end' (Cūḷava. 350), it is used for the middle. In 'Moreover, bhikkhus, this Tapodā river flows in the gap between two great hells' (Pārā. 231), it is used for gap. Here, in this text, it is used in the sense of a gap; therefore, the meaning should be understood as 'in the gap between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā.' However, because it is connected with the word 'antarā', the accusative case is used. And in such places, grammarians use the word 'antarā' only once, as in 'he goes between the village and the river,' but it should also be connected with the second noun. If it is not connected, the accusative case is not attained. Here, however, it is stated as having been explicitly connected.

Addhānamaggappaṭipanno [M 1.0036] hotīti addhānasaṅkhātaṃ maggaṃ paṭipanno hoti, “dīghamagga”nti attho. Addhānagamanasamayassa hi vibhaṅge “aḍḍhayojanaṃ gacchissāmīti bhuñjitabba”ntiādivacanato (pāci. 218) aḍḍhayojanampi addhānamaggo hoti. Rājagahato pana nāḷandā yojanameva.

He had set out on a long journey: He had entered upon a road known as a long journey; the meaning is 'a long road.' For in the Vibhaṅga on the occasion of undertaking a journey, from the statement, 'Thinking, “I will go half a yojana,” one may eat' (Pāci. 218), it is understood that even half a yojana is a long journey. From Rājagaha to Nāḷandā, however, is just one yojana.

Mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhinti ‘mahatā’ti guṇamahattenapi mahatā, saṅkhyāmahattenapi mahatā. So hi bhikkhusaṅgho guṇehipi mahā ahosi, appicchatādiguṇasamannāgatattā. Saṅkhyāyapi mahā, pañcasatasaṅkhyattā. Bhikkhūnaṃ saṅgho ‘bhikkhusaṅgho’, tena bhikkhusaṅghena. Diṭṭhisīlasāmaññasaṅghātasaṅkhātena samaṇagaṇenāti attho. Saddhinti ekato.

Together with a great community of bhikkhus: 'Great' means great in terms of virtue and also great in terms of number. For that community of bhikkhus was great in virtues, being endowed with qualities such as having few desires. It was also great in number, having a count of five hundred. A community of bhikkhus is a 'bhikkhusaṅgha'; thus, with that community of bhikkhus. The meaning is: with the group of ascetics, designated as a community by commonality of view and virtue. 'Saddhiṃ' means together.

Pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehīti pañcamattā etesanti pañcamattāni. Mattāti pamāṇaṃ vuccati, tasmā yathā “bhojane mattaññū”ti vutte “bhojane mattaṃ jānāti, pamāṇaṃ jānātī”ti attho hoti, evamidhāpi – “tesaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ pañcamattā pañcapamāṇa”nti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Bhikkhūnaṃ satāni bhikkhusatāni, tehi pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi.

With five-measured hundreds of bhikkhus: 'Their measure is five,' thus they are 'pañcamattāni' (of five measures). 'Mattā' is said to mean measure. Therefore, just as when it is said, 'one who knows the measure in food,' the meaning is 'he knows the measure in food, he knows the proper amount,' so too here the meaning should be understood thus: 'Of those hundreds of bhikkhus, their measure is five, their number is five.' Hundreds of bhikkhus are 'bhikkhusatāni'; with those five-measured hundreds of bhikkhus.

Suppiyopi [V 1.0036] kho paribbājakoti suppiyoti tassa nāmaṃ. Pi-kāro maggappaṭipannasabhāgatāya puggalasampiṇḍanattho. Kho-kāro padasandhikaro, byañjanasiliṭṭhatāvasena vutto. Paribbājakoti sañjayassa antevāsī channaparibbājako. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “yadā bhagavā taṃ addhānamaggaṃ [P 1.0036] paṭipanno, tadā suppiyopi paribbājako paṭipanno ahosī”ti. Atītakālattho hettha hoti-saddo.

Suppiya the wanderer also: 'Suppiya' is his name. The particle 'pi' has the meaning of aggregating persons due to the shared state of being travelers on the road. The particle 'kho' is a conjunct, spoken for the sake of euphonic smoothness of the syllables. 'Paribbājako' means a 'channa' wanderer (i.e., one who is covered), who was a disciple of Sañjaya. This is what is said: 'When the Blessed One had set out on that long journey, then Suppiya the wanderer had also set out.' Here the word 'hoti' has the meaning of the past tense.

Saddhiṃ antevāsinā brahmadattena māṇavenāti – ettha ante vasatīti antevāsī. Samīpacāro santikāvacaro sissoti attho. Brahmadattoti tassa nāmaṃ. Māṇavoti sattopi coropi taruṇopi vuccati.

Together with his pupil Brahmadatta, the young man: Here, 'one who lives near' is an 'antevāsī' (pupil). The meaning is a disciple who moves about nearby, who attends closely. 'Brahmadatta' is his name. 'Māṇava' can refer to a being, a thief, or a youth.

“Coditā devadūtehi, ye pamajjanti māṇavā;

Te dīgharattaṃ socanti, hīnakāyūpagā narā”ti. (ma. ni. 3.271) –

Urged by the divine messengers, those beings who are heedless, those people, having gone to an inferior existence, grieve for a long time. (M.N. 3.271)

Ādīsu [M 1.0037] hi satto māṇavoti vutto. “Māṇavehipi samāgacchanti katakammehipi akatakammehipī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.149) coro. “Ambaṭṭho māṇavo, aṅgako māṇavo”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.316) taruṇo ‘māṇavo’ti vutto. Idhāpi ayamevattho. Idañhi vuttaṃ hoti – brahmadattena nāma taruṇantevāsinā saddhinti.

In these and other texts, a being is called a 'māṇava'. In 'They associate with māṇavas, both those who have committed deeds and those who have not,' and so on (M.N. 2.149), it means a thief. In 'Ambaṭṭha the māṇava, Aṅgaka the māṇava,' and so on (D.N. 1.316), a youth is called a 'māṇava'. Here too, this same meaning applies. For this is what is said: 'together with the young pupil named Brahmadatta.'

Tatrāti tasmiṃ addhānamagge, tesu vā dvīsu janesu. Sudanti nipātamattaṃ. Anekapariyāyenāti pariyāya-saddo tāva vāradesanākāraṇesu vattati. “Kassa nu kho, ānanda, ajja pariyāyo bhikkhuniyo ovaditu”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.398) hi vāre pariyāyasaddo vattati. “Madhupiṇḍikapariyāyotveva naṃ dhārehī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.205) desanāyaṃ. “Imināpi kho, te rājañña, pariyāyena evaṃ hotū”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.411) kāraṇe. Svāyamidhāpi kāraṇe vattati, tasmā ayamettha attho – “anekavidhena kāraṇenā”ti, “bahūhi kāraṇehī”ti vuttaṃ hoti.

'Tatra' means on that long journey, or among those two persons. 'Sudaṃ' is merely a particle. 'Anekapariyāyena'—first, the word 'pariyāya' is used in the senses of turn, teaching, and reason. For instance, in 'Whose turn is it today, Ānanda, to advise the bhikkhunīs?' (M.N. 3.398), the word 'pariyāya' is indeed used in the sense of a turn. In 'You should remember it as the "Discourse of the Honey-ball,"' (M.N. 1.205), it is used for a teaching. In 'By this reason too, O noble, let it be so for you,' (D.N. 2.411), it is used for a reason. Here too, it is used in the sense of reason. Therefore, this is the meaning here: 'by reason of many kinds,' which is to say, 'by many reasons.'

Buddhassa avaṇṇaṃ bhāsatīti avaṇṇavirahitassa aparimāṇavaṇṇasamannāgatassāpi buddhassa bhagavato – “yaṃ loke jātivuḍḍhesu kattabbaṃ abhivādanādisāmīcikammaṃ ‘sāmaggiraso’ti vuccati, taṃ samaṇassa gotamassa natthi tasmā arasarūpo samaṇo gotamo, nibbhogo, akiriyavādo, ucchedavādo, jegucchī, venayiko, tapassī, apagabbho. Natthi samaṇassa gotamassa [V 1.0037] uttarimanussadhammo alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso. Takkapariyāhataṃ samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti, vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ, sayaṃpaṭibhānaṃ. Samaṇo gotamo na sabbaññū, na lokavidū, na anuttaro, na aggapuggalo”ti. Evaṃ taṃ taṃ akāraṇameva kāraṇanti vatvā [P 1.0037] tathā tathā avaṇṇaṃ dosaṃ nindaṃ bhāsati.

He speaks dispraise of the Buddha: Of the Blessed One, the Buddha, who is devoid of dispraise and endowed with limitless praise, he says: 'That respectful conduct, such as paying homage, which should be performed in the world towards those senior in birth, is called “the flavor of concord.” The ascetic Gotama does not have this. Therefore, the ascetic Gotama is of a nature without savor, one who does not partake, a proponent of non-action, a proponent of cutting off tradition, a disdainful one, a subverter of discipline, a tormentor, one barren of a good rebirth. The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman state, no special, noble knowledge and vision. The ascetic Gotama teaches a Dhamma hammered out by reasoning, followed by investigation, apprehended by his own intelligence. The ascetic Gotama is not all-knowing, not a world-knower, not unsurpassed, not the foremost person.' Thus, having said that this or that non-reason is a reason, he speaks dispraise, fault, and blame in such and such a way.

Yathā ca buddhassa, evaṃ dhammassāpi taṃ taṃ akāraṇameva kāraṇato vatvā – “samaṇassa gotamassa dhammo durakkhāto, duppaṭivedito, aniyyāniko, anupasamasaṃvattaniko”ti tathā tathā avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati.

And just as with the Buddha, so too with the Dhamma, having stated one non-reason or another as a reason, he speaks dispraise in various ways, saying: 'The Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama is poorly proclaimed, poorly taught for penetration, not leading to liberation, and not conducive to peace.'

Yathā [M 1.0038] ca dhammassa, evaṃ saṅghassāpi yaṃ vā taṃ vā akāraṇameva kāraṇato vatvā – “micchāpaṭipanno samaṇassa gotamassa sāvakasaṅgho, kuṭilapaṭipanno, paccanīkapaṭipadaṃ ananulomapaṭipadaṃ adhammānulomapaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno”ti tathā tathā avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati.

And just as with the Dhamma, so too with the Saṅgha, having stated whatever baseless reason as a reason, he speaks dispraise in various ways, saying: 'The Saṅgha of disciples of the ascetic Gotama is of wrong practice and of crooked practice; it has undertaken the contrary practice, the non-conforming practice, and the practice that conforms to what is not the Dhamma.'

Antevāsī panassa – “amhākaṃ ācariyo aparāmasitabbaṃ parāmasati, anakkamitabbaṃ akkamati, svāyaṃ aggiṃ gilanto viya, hatthena asidhāraṃ parāmasanto viya, muṭṭhinā sineruṃ padāletukāmo viya, kakacadantapantiyaṃ kīḷamāno viya, pabhinnamadaṃ caṇḍahatthiṃ hatthena gaṇhanto viya ca vaṇṇārahasseva ratanattayassa avaṇṇaṃ bhāsamāno anayabyasanaṃ pāpuṇissati. Ācariye kho pana gūthaṃ vā aggiṃ vā kaṇṭakaṃ vā kaṇhasappaṃ vā akkamante, sūlaṃ vā abhirūhante, halāhalaṃ vā visaṃ khādante, khārodakaṃ vā pakkhalante, narakapapātaṃ vā papatante, na antevāsinā taṃ sabbamanukātabbaṃ hoti. Kammassakā hi sattā attano kammānurūpameva gatiṃ gacchanti. Neva pitā puttassa kammena gacchati, na putto pitu kammena, na mātā puttassa, na putto mātuyā, na bhātā bhaginiyā, na bhaginī bhātu, na ācariyo antevāsino, na antevāsī ācariyassa kammena gacchati. Mayhañca ācariyo tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, mahāsāvajjo kho panāriyūpavādoti. Evaṃ yoniso ummujjitvā ācariyavādaṃ maddamāno sammākāraṇameva kāraṇato apadisanto anekapariyāyena tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ vaṇṇaṃ bhāsitumāraddho, yathā taṃ paṇḍitajātiko kulaputto”. Tena vuttaṃ – “suppiyassa pana paribbājakassa antevāsī brahmadatto māṇavo anekapariyāyena buddhassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, dhammassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, saṅghassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatī”ti.

But his pupil thought: 'Our teacher handles what should not be handled and treads on what should not be trodden on. Like one swallowing fire, like one handling a sword's edge with his hand, like one wishing to split Mount Sineru with his fist, like one playing with a row of saw-teeth, and like one seizing a fierce elephant in musth with his hand, by speaking dispraise of the Triple Gem, which is indeed worthy of praise, he will come to ruin and disaster. Furthermore, when a teacher treads on dung, or fire, or a thorn, or a black serpent, or climbs onto a stake, or eats deadly poison, or stumbles into a harsh current, or falls into the precipice of hell, it is not for the pupil to imitate all that. For beings are owners of their kamma; they go to a destination only in accordance with their own kamma. A father does not go by his son's kamma, nor a son by his father's kamma; not a mother by her son's, nor a son by his mother's; not a brother by his sister's, nor a sister by her brother's; not a teacher by his pupil's, nor a pupil by his teacher's kamma. And my teacher speaks dispraise of the Three Jewels—but reviling the Noble Ones is indeed a grave offense.' Thus wisely extricating himself, refuting his teacher's doctrine, pointing out only a right reason as the reason, he began to speak the praise of the Three Jewels in many ways, as would a clansman of wise nature. Therefore it is said: 'But the pupil of the wanderer Suppiya, the young man Brahmadatta, in many ways spoke the praise of the Buddha, spoke the praise of the Dhamma, and spoke the praise of the Saṅgha.'

Tattha vaṇṇanti vaṇṇa-saddo saṇṭhāna-jāti-rūpāyatana-kāraṇa-pamāṇa-guṇa-pasaṃsādīsu dissati[V 1.0038]. Tattha “mahantaṃ sapparājavaṇṇaṃ [P 1.0038] abhinimminitvā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.142) saṇṭhānaṃ vuccati. “Brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.402) jāti. “Paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgato”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.303) rūpāyatanaṃ.

Herein, the word 'vaṇṇa' is seen in such meanings as form, caste, visible form, reason, measure, quality, and praise. Among these, in passages such as 'having created the great form of a serpent-king,' it is said to mean form. In passages such as 'The brahmin is the excellent caste; any other caste is inferior,' it means caste. In passages such as 'endowed with the supreme excellence of complexion,' it means visible form.

“Na [M 1.0039] harāmi na bhañjāmi, ārā siṅghāmi vārijaṃ;

Atha kena nu vaṇṇena, gandhatthenoti vuccatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.234) –

I do not take it, I do not break it; I only smell the water-born lotus from afar. Then for what reason am I called a 'scent-thief'?

Ādīsu kāraṇaṃ. “Tayo pattassa vaṇṇā”tiādīsu (pārā. 602) pamāṇaṃ. “Kadā saññūḷhā pana, te gahapati, ime samaṇassa gotamassa vaṇṇā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.77) guṇo. “Vaṇṇārahassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 2.135) pasaṃsā. Idha guṇopi pasaṃsāpi. Ayaṃ kira taṃ taṃ bhūtameva kāraṇaṃ apadisanto anekapariyāyena ratanattayassa guṇūpasañhitaṃ pasaṃsaṃ abhāsi. Tattha – “itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”tiādinā (pārā. 1) nayena, “ye bhikkhave, buddhe pasannā agge te pasannā”tiādinā “ekapuggalo, bhikkhave, loke uppajjamāno uppajjati…pe… asamo asamasamo”tiādinā (a. ni. 1.174) ca nayena buddhassa vaṇṇo veditabbo. “Svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo”ti (dī. ni. 2.159) ca “ālayasamugghāto vaṭṭupacchedo”ti (iti. 90, a. ni. 4.34) ca, “ye bhikkhave, ariye aṭṭhaṅgike magge pasannā, agge te pasannā”ti ca evamādīhi nayehi dhammassa vaṇṇo veditabbo. “Suppaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho”ti (dī. ni. 2.159) ca, “ye, bhikkhave, saṅghe pasannā, agge te pasannā”ti (a. ni. 4.34) ca evamādīhi pana nayehi saṅghassa vaṇṇo veditabbo. Pahontena pana dhammakathikena pañcanikāye navaṅgaṃ satthusāsanaṃ caturāsītidhammakkhandhasahassāni ogāhitvā buddhādīnaṃ vaṇṇo pakāsetabbo.
