Imasmiñhi ṭhāne buddhādīnaṃ guṇe pakāsento atitthena pakkhando dhammakathikoti na sakkā vattuṃ. Īdisesu hi ṭhānesu dhammakathikassa thāmo veditabbo. Brahmadatto pana māṇavo anussavādimattasambandhitena attano thāmena ratanattayassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati.

In such passages, it means reason. In passages such as 'There are three measures of the bowl,' it means measure. In passages such as 'When, householder, were these qualities of the ascetic Gotama composed by you?,' it means quality. In passages such as 'he speaks the praise of one worthy of praise,' it means praise. Here, it means both quality and praise. It is said that this young man, pointing out this or that true reason, spoke in many ways the praise connected with the qualities of the Triple Gem. Therein, the praise of the Buddha is to be understood by such methods as: 'Thus is the Blessed One an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One...'; and 'Bhikkhus, those who are confident in the Buddha are confident in the supreme...'; and 'Bhikkhus, one person, when arising in the world, arises... without an equal, with none like him...'. The praise of the Dhamma is to be understood by such methods as: 'The Dhamma is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One...'; and 'it uproots clinging, it cuts off the round of existence...'; and 'Bhikkhus, those who are confident in the Noble Eightfold Path are confident in the supreme...'. And the praise of the Saṅgha is to be understood by such methods as: 'The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples has practiced the good way...'; and 'Bhikkhus, those who are confident in the Saṅgha are confident in the supreme...'. However, a capable Dhamma-preacher should proclaim the praise of the Buddha and the others after having penetrated with wisdom the five Nikāyas, the nine-limbed Teaching of the Master, and the eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma. For in this situation, it is not possible to say that a Dhamma-preacher who proclaims the qualities of the Buddha and the others is 'one who plunges in at an improper ford.' For in such situations, the capacity of the Dhamma-preacher is to be understood. But the young man Brahmadatta speaks the praise of the Triple Gem with his own capacity, which is connected merely with what has been heard through tradition and so on.

Itiha te ubho ācariyantevāsīti evaṃ te dve ācariyantevāsikā. Aññamaññassāti añño aññassa. Ujuvipaccanīkavādāti īsakampi apariharitvā ujumeva vividhapaccanīkavādā, anekavāraṃ viruddhavādā eva hutvāti [P 1.0039] attho. Ācariyena hi ratanattayassa [V 1.0039] avaṇṇe bhāsite antevāsī vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, puna itaro avaṇṇaṃ, itaro vaṇṇanti evaṃ ācariyo sāraphalake visarukkhaāṇiṃ ākoṭayamāno viya [M 1.0040] punappunaṃ ratanattayassa avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati. Antevāsī pana suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimayāya āṇiyā taṃ āṇiṃ paṭibāhayamāno viya punappunaṃ ratanattayassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati. Tena vuttaṃ – “ujuvipaccanīkavādā”ti.

Thus, those two were teacher and pupil. ‘Of each other’ means one to the other. ‘Opposing each other directly in speech’ means: without avoiding even a little, holding various opposing views directly; having repeatedly held contradictory views—this is the meaning. For when the teacher spoke in dispraise of the Triple Gem, the pupil spoke in praise; then again, the former spoke in dispraise, and the latter in praise. In this way, the teacher, like one striking a peg of a poison-tree into a sound plank, repeatedly spoke in dispraise of the Triple Gem. The pupil, however, like one resisting that peg with a peg made of gold, silver, and jewels, repeatedly spoke in praise of the Triple Gem. Therefore, it was said: ‘opposing each other directly in speech.’

Bhagavantaṃ piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhā honti bhikkhusaṅghañcāti bhagavantañca bhikkhusaṅghañca pacchato pacchato dassanaṃ avijahantā iriyāpathānubandhanena anubandhā honti, sīsānulokino hutvā anugatā hontīti attho.

‘They follow the Blessed One from behind, from behind, and the community of monks’ means that, not losing sight of the Blessed One and the community of monks from behind, they follow by means of following their posture, and they follow looking along with their heads—this is the meaning.

Kasmā pana bhagavā taṃ addhānaṃ paṭipanno? Kasmā ca suppiyo anubandho? Kasmā ca so ratanattayassa avaṇṇaṃ bhāsatīti? Bhagavā tāva tasmiṃ kāle rājagahaparivattakesu aṭṭhārasasu mahāvihāresu aññatarasmiṃ vasitvā pātova sarīrappaṭijagganaṃ katvā bhikkhācāravelāyaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto rājagahe piṇḍāya carati. So taṃ divasaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa sulabhapiṇḍapātaṃ katvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pattacīvaraṃ gāhāpetvā – “nāḷandaṃ gamissāmī”ti, rājagahato nikkhamitvā taṃ addhānaṃ paṭipanno. Suppiyopi kho tasmiṃ kāle rājagahaparivattake aññatarasmiṃ paribbājakārāme vasitvā paribbājakaparivuto rājagahe bhikkhāya carati. Sopi taṃ divasaṃ paribbājakaparisāya sulabhabhikkhaṃ katvā bhuttapātarāso paribbājake paribbājakaparikkhāraṃ gāhāpetvā – nāḷandaṃ gamissāmicceva bhagavato taṃ maggaṃ paṭipannabhāvaṃ ajānantova anubandho. Sace pana jāneyya nānubandheyya. So ajānitvāva gacchanto gīvaṃ ukkhipitvā olokayamāno bhagavantaṃ addasa buddhasiriyā sobhamānaṃ rattakambalaparikkhittamiva jaṅgamakanakagirisikharaṃ.

Why, then, did the Blessed One travel that road? Why did Suppiya follow? And why did he speak in dispraise of the Triple Gem? First, the Blessed One, at that time, having stayed at one of the eighteen great monasteries in the vicinity of Rājagaha, attended to his bodily needs early in the morning. Having returned from the almsround after the meal, he had the community of monks take up their bowls and robes and, thinking, ‘I will go to Nāḷanda,’ he departed from Rājagaha and set out on that road. Suppiya, too, at that time was staying in one of the wanderers' parks in the vicinity of Rājagaha. Surrounded by wanderers, he went for alms in Rājagaha. That day, having made alms easily available to the assembly of wanderers and having eaten his morning meal, he had the wanderers take up their requisites and, thinking, ‘I will go to Nāḷanda,’ he followed, not knowing that the Blessed One had set out on that road. If he had known, he would not have followed. Unaware, as he walked along, he lifted his neck and looked around—and there he saw the Blessed One, radiant with the splendor of a Buddha, like a moving golden mountain peak wrapped in a red blanket.

Tasmiṃ kira samaye dasabalassa sarīrato nikkhamitvā chabbaṇṇarasmiyo samantā asītihatthappamāṇe padese ādhāvanti vidhāvanti ratanāveḷaratanadāmaratanacuṇṇavippakiṇṇaṃ [P 1.0040] viya, pasāritaratanacittakañcanapaṭamiva, rattasuvaṇṇarasanisiñcamānamiva, ukkāsatanipātasamākulamiva, nirantaravippakiṇṇakaṇikārapupphamiva vāyuvegakkhittacīnapiṭṭhacuṇṇamiva, indadhanuvijjulatātārāgaṇappabhāvisaravipphuritaviccharitamiva ca taṃ vanantaraṃ hoti.

At that time, it is said, six-colored rays, having emerged from the body of the Ten-Powered One, darted towards and about in all directions within an area eighty cubits in extent. That forest-interior became as if strewn with gem-diadems, gem-garlands, and scattered gem-powder; like a spread-out golden cloth variegated with gems; as if being sprinkled with the liquid of red gold; as if filled with the falling of hundreds of meteors; like kaṇikāra flowers scattered without interval; like fine flour thrown by the force of the wind; and as if diffused and sparkling with the spreading radiance of rainbows, lightning, and the host of stars.

Asīti [M 1.0041] anubyañjanānurañjitañca pana bhagavato sarīraṃ vikasitakamaluppalamiva, saraṃ sabbapāliphullamiva [V 1.0040] pāricchattakaṃ, tārāmarīcivikasitamiva, gaganatalaṃ siriyā avahasantamiva, byāmappabhāparikkhepavilāsinī cassa dvattiṃsavaralakkhaṇamālā ganthetvā ṭhapitadvattiṃsacandamālāya dvattiṃsasūriyamālāya paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapitadvattiṃsacakkavattidvattiṃsasakkadevarājadvattiṃsamahābrahmānaṃ siriṃ siriyā abhibhavantimiva. Tañca pana bhagavantaṃ parivāretvā ṭhitā bhikkhū sabbeva appicchā santuṭṭhā pavivittā asaṃsaṭṭhā codakā pāpagarahino vattāro vacanakkhamā sīlasampannā samādhipaññāvimuttivimuttiññāṇadassanasampannā. Tesaṃ majjhe bhagavā rattakambalapākāraparikkhitto viya kañcanathambho, rattapadumasaṇḍamajjhagatā viya suvaṇṇanāvā, pavāḷavedikāparikkhitto viya aggikkhandho, tārāgaṇaparivārito viya puṇṇacando migapakkhīnampi cakkhūni pīṇayati, pageva devamanussānaṃ. Tasmiñca pana divase yebhuyyena asītimahātherā meghavaṇṇaṃ paṃsukūlaṃ ekaṃsaṃ karitvā kattaradaṇḍaṃ ādāya suvammavammitā viya gandhahatthino vigatadosā vantadosā bhinnakilesā vijaṭitajaṭā chinnabandhanā bhagavantaṃ parivārayiṃsu. So sayaṃ vītarāgo vītarāgehi, sayaṃ vītadoso vītadosehi, sayaṃ vītamoho vītamohehi, sayaṃ vītataṇho vītataṇhehi, sayaṃ nikkileso nikkilesehi, sayaṃ buddho anubuddhehi parivārito; pattaparivāritaṃ viya kesaraṃ, kesaraparivāritā viya kaṇṇikā, aṭṭhanāgasahassaparivārito viya chaddanto nāgarājā, navutihaṃsasahassaparivārito viya dhataraṭṭho haṃsarājā, senaṅgaparivārito viya cakkavattirājā, devagaṇaparivārito viya sakko devarājā, brahmagaṇaparivārito viya hārito mahābrahmā, aparimitakālasañcitapuññabalanibbattāya acinteyyāya anopamāya buddhalīlāya [P 1.0041] cando viya gaganatalaṃ taṃ maggaṃ paṭipanno hoti.

Furthermore, the Blessed One's body, adorned with the eighty minor characteristics, was as if mocking with its splendor: a lake with blooming lotuses and water lilies; a Pāricchattaka tree in full bloom; and the surface of the sky, opened with the rays of the stars. And his garland of thirty-two excellent marks, resplendent with a surrounding aura of a fathom's length, was as if overwhelming with its splendor the glory of a garland of thirty-two moons and a garland of thirty-two suns, strung and placed, and the glory of thirty-two wheel-turning monarchs, thirty-two Sakka lords of devas, and thirty-two Great Brahmas, placed in order. Furthermore, the bhikkhus standing surrounding that Blessed One were all of few wishes, content, secluded, unentangled, admonishers, reprovers of evil, speakers, patient with speech, accomplished in virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. In their midst, the Blessed One was like a golden pillar surrounded by a wall of red blankets, like a golden boat in the midst of a cluster of red lotuses, like a mass of fire encircled by a coral railing, like the full moon surrounded by a host of stars—delighting the eyes of even beasts and birds, how much more so those of devas and humans. And on that day, for the most part, eighty great elders, having arranged a cloud-colored refuse-rag robe over one shoulder and taking up a staff, surrounded the Blessed One like well-armored gandha elephants—their faults departed, their faults vomited forth, their defilements shattered, their tangles untangled, their bonds broken. He, himself free from lust, was surrounded by those free from lust; himself free from hatred, by those free from hatred; himself free from delusion, by those free from delusion; himself free from craving, by those free from craving; himself without defilements, by those without defilements; himself the Buddha, by those who had awakened after him. He was like the filament surrounded by petals, like the pericarp surrounded by filaments, like the elephant king Chaddanta surrounded by eight thousand elephants, like the swan king Dhataraṭṭha surrounded by ninety thousand swans, like a wheel-turning king surrounded by the constituents of his army, like Sakka, king of devas, surrounded by the host of devas, like the Great Brahmā Hārita surrounded by the host of brahmās. With the inconceivable, incomparable Buddha's grace, produced by the power of merit accumulated over a limitless time, he traveled that road like the moon traversing the surface of the sky.

Athevaṃ bhagavantaṃ anopamāya buddhalīlāya gacchantaṃ bhikkhū ca okkhittacakkhū santindriye santamānase uparinabhe ṭhitaṃ puṇṇacandaṃ viya bhagavantaṃyeva namassamāne disvāva paribbājako attano parisaṃ avalokesi. Sā hoti kājadaṇḍake olambetvā gahitoluggaviluggapiṭṭhakatidaṇḍamorapiñchamattikāpattapasibbakakuṇḍikādianekaparikkhārabhārabharitā[M 1.0042]. “Asukassa hatthā sobhaṇā, asukassa pādā”ti evamādiniratthakavacanā mukharā vikiṇṇavācā adassanīyā apāsādikā. Tassa taṃ disvā vippaṭisāro udapādi.

Then, upon seeing the Blessed One walking with incomparable Buddha's graceful bearing, and the bhikkhus with eyes cast down, their faculties tranquil, their minds serene, worshipping only the Blessed One who was like the full moon standing in the sky above, the wanderer glanced at his own assembly. It was laden with the burden of many requisites hanging from carrying poles: worn-out and dilapidated small mats, three-legged stools, bundles of peacock feathers, clay bowls, small bags, water strainers, and so on. They were of harsh speech and scattered words, saying such meaningless things as, 'So-and-so's hands are beautiful; so-and-so's feet are lovely.' They were unpleasant to behold and uninspiring. Seeing this, displeasure arose in him.

Idāni tena bhagavato vaṇṇo vattabbo bhaveyya. Yasmā panesa lābhasakkārahāniyā ceva pakkhahāniyā ca niccampi bhagavantaṃ usūyati. Aññatitthiyānañhi yāva buddho loke nuppajjati, tāvadeva lābhasakkārā nibbattanti, buddhuppādato pana paṭṭhāya parihīnalābhasakkārā honti[V 1.0041], sūriyuggamane khajjopanakā viya nissirīkataṃ āpajjanti. Upatissakolitānañca sañjayassa santike pabbajitakāleyeva paribbājakā mahāparisā ahesuṃ, tesu pana pakkantesu sāpi tesaṃ parisā bhinnā. Iti imehi dvīhi kāraṇehi ayaṃ paribbājako yasmā niccampi bhagavantaṃ usūyati, tasmā taṃ usūyavisuggāraṃ uggiranto ratanattayassa avaṇṇameva bhāsatīti veditabbo.

Now, it would have been fitting for him to speak of the Blessed One's virtue. But because this wanderer, due to the decline of gain and honor and the decline of his following, is always envious of the Blessed One. For indeed, as long as a Buddha does not arise in the world, the gain and honor of other sectarians flourish; but from the time of a Buddha's arising, their gain and honor decline, and they become bereft of splendor, like fireflies at sunrise. Also, when Upatissa and Kolita went forth in the presence of Sañjaya, the wanderers had a large following; but when they departed, that following of his also broke up. Thus, for these two reasons, this wanderer is always envious of the Blessed One. Therefore, it should be understood that, while vomiting forth the vomit of the poison of envy, he speaks only dispraise of the Three Jewels.

2. Atha kho bhagavā ambalaṭṭhikāyaṃ rājāgārake ekarattivāsaṃ upagacchi saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghenāti bhagavā tāya buddhalīlāya gacchamāno anupubbena ambalaṭṭhikādvāraṃ pāpuṇitvā sūriyaṃ oloketvā – “akālo dāni gantuṃ, atthasamīpaṃ gato sūriyo”ti ambalaṭṭhikāyaṃ rājāgārake ekarattivāsaṃ upagacchi.

2. The text states: 'Then the Blessed One approached the royal house in Ambalaṭṭhikā for a one-night stay, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.' The meaning is: The Blessed One, journeying with that Buddha's graceful bearing, gradually reached the gate of Ambalaṭṭhikā and, looking at the sun, reflected, 'It is now not the time to go on; the sun has neared its setting.' Thus, he approached the royal house in Ambalaṭṭhikā for a one-night stay.

Tattha ambalaṭṭhikāti rañño uyyānaṃ. Tassa kira dvārasamīpe taruṇaambarukkho atthi, taṃ “ambalaṭṭhikā”ti vadanti. Tassa avidūre bhavattā uyyānampi ambalaṭṭhikā tveva saṅkhyaṃ gataṃ. Taṃ chāyūdakasampannaṃ [P 1.0042] pākāraparikkhittaṃ suyojitadvāraṃ mañjusā viya suguttaṃ. Tattha rañño kīḷanatthaṃ paṭibhānacittavicittaṃ agāraṃ akaṃsu. Taṃ “rājāgāraka”nti vuccati.

Therein, 'Ambalaṭṭhikā' is the king's park. It is said that near its gate there was a young mango tree, which they call 'Ambalaṭṭhikā'. Because of its proximity, the park also came to be known as 'Ambalaṭṭhikā'. It was endowed with shade and water, enclosed by a wall, had a well-fitted gate, and was as well-guarded as a casket. There, for the king's amusement, they had built a house that was wonderfully and variously designed with artistic ingenuity. It is called the 'rājāgāraka' (royal house).

Suppiyopi khoti suppiyopi tasmiṃ ṭhāne sūriyaṃ oloketvā – “akālo dāni gantuṃ, bahū khuddakamahallakā paribbājakā, bahuparissayo ca ayaṃ maggo corehipi vāḷayakkhehipi vāḷamigehipi. Ayaṃ kho pana samaṇo gotamo uyyānaṃ paviṭṭho, samaṇassa ca gotamassa vasanaṭṭhāne [M 1.0043] devatā ārakkhaṃ gaṇhanti, handāhampi idha ekarattivāsaṃ upagantvā sveva gamissāmī”ti tadevuyyānaṃ pāvisi. Tato bhikkhusaṅgho bhagavato vattaṃ dassetvā attano attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ sallakkhesi. Paribbājakopi uyyānassa ekapasse paribbājakaparikkhāre otāretvā vāsaṃ upagacchi saddhiṃ attano parisāya. Pāḷiyamārūḷhavaseneva pana – “saddhiṃ attano antevāsinā brahmadattena māṇavenā”ti vuttaṃ.

Suppiya the wanderer also, looking at the sun in that place, considered: 'It is now not the time to go. There are many wanderers, both young and old, and this road has many dangers from thieves, fierce yakkhas, and fierce wild beasts. This ascetic Gotama has entered the park, and deities take up guard in the dwelling place of the ascetic Gotama. Well then, I too will stay here for one night and go only tomorrow.' Thus, he entered that very park. Thereupon, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, having performed their duties for the Blessed One, marked out their respective dwelling places. The wanderer, too, having had the wanderers' requisites set down in one part of the park, took up residence with his assembly. However, by the force of the wording that has come down in the Pāli text, it is said: 'with his own disciple, the young man Brahmadatta.'

Evaṃ vāsaṃ upagato pana so paribbājako rattibhāge dasabalaṃ olokesi. Tasmiñca samaye samantā vippakiṇṇatārakā viya padīpā jalanti, majjhe bhagavā nisinno hoti, bhikkhusaṅgho ca bhagavantaṃ parivāretvā. Tattha ekabhikkhussapi hatthakukkuccaṃ vā pādakukkuccaṃ vā ukkāsitasaddo vā khipitasaddo vā natthi. Sā hi parisā attano ca sikkhitasikkhatāya satthari ca gāravenāti dvīhi kāraṇehi nivāte padīpasikhā viya niccalā [V 1.0042] sannisinnāva ahosi. Paribbājako taṃ vibhūtiṃ disvā attano parisaṃ olokesi. Tattha keci hatthaṃ khipanti, keci pādaṃ, keci vippalapanti, keci nillālitajivhā paggharitakheḷā, dante khādantā kākacchamānā gharugharupassāsino sayanti. So ratanattayassa guṇavaṇṇe vattabbepi issāvasena puna avaṇṇameva ārabhi. Brahmadatto pana vuttanayeneva vaṇṇaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “tatrāpi sudaṃ suppiyo paribbājako”ti sabbaṃ vattabbaṃ. Tattha tatrāpīti tasmimpi, ambalaṭṭhikāyaṃ uyyāneti attho.

Having thus taken up residence, that wanderer looked upon the One of Ten Powers during the night. At that time, lamps were burning all around like scattered stars, with the Blessed One seated in the middle, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. There, not a single bhikkhu showed any fidgeting of hand or foot, nor was there any sound of coughing or sneezing. For that assembly, due to two reasons—their own accomplished training and their reverence for the Teacher—was seated perfectly still, motionless like the flame of a lamp in a windless place. Seeing this splendor, the wanderer looked at his own assembly. There, some were flinging their hands about, some their feet; some were muttering deliriously; some lay with lolling tongues and dripping saliva, grinding their teeth, making crow-like noises, and breathing heavily as they slept. Although he should have spoken of the virtuous qualities of the Three Jewels, he, through the power of envy, again began to speak only dispraise. But Brahmadatta, in the way already described, spoke praise. Therefore it is said: 'There, too, Suppiya the wanderer...'—all of this should be stated. Therein, 'there too' means 'in that very place, that is, in the park at Ambalaṭṭhikā'.

3. Sambahulānanti bahukānaṃ. Tattha vinayapariyāyena tayo janā “sambahulā”ti vuccanti. Tato paraṃ saṅgho. Suttantapariyāyena [P 1.0043] pana tayo tayova tato paṭṭhāya sambahulā. Idha suttantapariyāyena “sambahulā”ti veditabbā. Maṇḍalamāḷeti katthaci dve kaṇṇikā gahetvā haṃsavaṭṭakacchannena katā kūṭāgārasālāpi “maṇḍalamāḷo”ti vuccati, katthaci ekaṃ kaṇṇikaṃ gahetvā thambhapantiṃ parikkhipitvā katā upaṭṭhānasālāpi “maṇḍalamāḷo”ti vuccati. Idha pana nisīdanasālā “maṇḍalamāḷo”ti veditabbo. Sannisinnānanti nisajjanavasena. Sannipatitānanti samodhānavasena. Ayaṃ saṅkhiyadhammoti saṅkhiyā vuccati kathā[M 1.0044], kathādhammoti attho. Udapādīti uppanno. Katamo pana soti? Acchariyaṃ āvusoti evamādi. Tattha andhassa pabbatārohaṇaṃ viya niccaṃ na hotīti acchariyaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva saddanayo. Ayaṃ pana aṭṭhakathānayo – accharāyogganti acchariyaṃ. Accharaṃ paharituṃ yuttanti attho. Abhūtapubbaṃ bhūtanti abbhutaṃ. Ubhayaṃ petaṃ vimhayassevādhivacanaṃ. Yāvañcidanti yāva ca idaṃ tena suppaṭividitatāya appameyyattaṃ dasseti.

3. “Sambahulānaṃ” means ‘of many.’ Therein, according to the Vinaya method, three persons are called “sambahulā.” Beyond that is the Saṅgha. According to the Suttanta method, however, three are just three, and starting from that number they are called “sambahulā.” Here, it should be understood as “sambahulā” according to the Suttanta method. “Maṇḍalamāḷa” (circular hall): in some places, a gabled hall made with two pinnacles and a roofing like a hamsa's wing is called a “maṇḍalamāḷa”; in other places, an assembly hall made with one pinnacle and surrounded by a row of pillars is also called a “maṇḍalamāḷa.” Here, however, a sitting hall should be understood as a “maṇḍalamāḷa.” “Sannisinnānaṃ” (of those sitting) is by way of sitting. “Sannipatitānaṃ” (of those assembled) is by way of coming together. Regarding “Ayaṃ saṅkhiyadhammo” (this topic of discussion): “saṅkhiyā” is called talk; the meaning is “the nature of the talk.” “Udapādi” (it arose) means it has arisen. What, then, is it? It is the speech beginning with “Wonderful, friend…” Therein, “acchariyaṃ” (wonderful) is so called because it does not always happen, like a blind person's climbing of a mountain. This, firstly, is the grammatical method. This, however, is the commentary's method: “acchariyaṃ” means “worthy of a finger-snap.” The meaning is: it is fit for snapping one's fingers. “Abbhutaṃ” (unprecedented) means: having not been before, it has now come to be. Both these terms are designations for a cause of wonder. “Yāvañcidaṃ” is “yāva ca idaṃ,” and by this it shows the immeasurability of his state of having thoroughly penetrated it.

Tena bhagavatā jānatā…pe… suppaṭividitāti etthāyaṃ saṅkhepattho. Yo so bhagavā samatiṃsa pāramiyo pūretvā sabbakilese bhañjitvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho, tena bhagavatā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ āsayānusayaṃ jānatā, hatthatale ṭhapitaṃ āmalakaṃ viya sabbañeyyadhammaṃ passatā.

“By that Blessed One, who knows... well penetrated”—herein is the concise meaning. That Blessed One who, having fulfilled the thirty perfections, having destroyed all defilements, and having fully awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect self-enlightenment; by that Blessed One, knowing the dispositions and underlying tendencies of those various beings, and seeing all knowable things as clearly as a myrobalan fruit placed on the palm of the hand.

Api ca pubbenivāsādīhi jānatā, dibbena cakkhunā passatā. Tīhi vijjāhi chahi vā pana abhiññāhi jānatā, sabbattha appaṭihatena samantacakkhunā passatā. Sabbadhammajānanasamatthāya vā paññāya jānatā, sabbasattānaṃ cakkhuvisayātītāni tirokuṭṭādigatānipi rūpāni ativisuddhena maṃsacakkhunā passatā. Attahitasādhikāya vā samādhipadaṭṭhānāya [V 1.0043] paṭivedhapaññāya jānatā, parahitasādhikāya karuṇāpadaṭṭhānāya desanāpaññāya passatā.

Furthermore, by one knowing through the knowledge of former existences and so on, seeing with the divine eye. Or, by one knowing through the three true knowledges or the six supernormal knowledges, seeing with the all-seeing eye that is unobstructed in every respect. Or, by one knowing with the wisdom capable of knowing all dhammas, seeing even forms that are beyond the range of vision of all beings—such as those that have gone behind a wall—with the exceedingly pure physical eye. Or, by one knowing with the wisdom of penetration which has concentration as its proximate cause and accomplishes one's own welfare, and seeing with the wisdom of teaching which has compassion as its proximate cause and accomplishes the welfare of others.

Arīnaṃ hatattā paccayādīnañca arahattā arahatā. Sammā sāmañca sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattā sammāsambuddhena antarāyikadhamme [P 1.0044] vā jānatā, niyyānikadhamme passatā, kilesārīnaṃ hatattā arahatā. Sammā sāmañca sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattā sammāsambuddhenāti. Evaṃ catūvesārajjavasena catūhākārehi thomitena sattānaṃ nānādhimuttikatā nānajjhāsayatā suppaṭividitā yāva ca suṭṭhu paṭividitā.

Because of having destroyed the enemies, the defilements, and because of being worthy of requisites and so on, he is an Arahant. Because of having rightly and by himself awakened to all dhammas, he is a Sammāsambuddha. Alternatively, knowing the obstructive dhammas, seeing the dhammas leading to escape, and because of having destroyed the enemies that are the defilements, he is an Arahant. Because of having rightly and by himself awakened to all dhammas, he is a Sammāsambuddha. Thus, by him, the Blessed One, praised in these four ways by means of the four grounds of self-confidence, the diversity of beings' dispositions and the diversity of their inclinations are thoroughly penetrated, indeed, exceedingly well penetrated.

Idānissa suppaṭividitabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ ayañhītiādimāha. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti yā ca ayaṃ bhagavatā “dhātuso, bhikkhave, sattā saṃsandanti samenti, hīnādhimuttikā hīnādhimuttikehi saddhiṃ saṃsandanti samenti, kalyāṇādhimuttikā kalyāṇādhimuttikehi saddhiṃ saṃsandanti samenti. Atītampi kho, bhikkhave, addhānaṃ dhātusova sattā saṃsandiṃsu samiṃsu, hīnādhimuttikā [M 1.0045] hīnādhimuttikehi…pe… kalyāṇādhimuttikā kalyāṇādhimuttikehi saddhiṃ saṃsandiṃsu samiṃsu, anāgatampi kho, bhikkhave, addhānaṃ…pe… saṃsandissanti samessanti, etarahipi kho, bhikkhave, paccuppannaṃ addhānaṃ dhātusova sattā saṃsandanti samenti, hīnādhimuttikā hīnādhimuttikehi…pe… kalyāṇādhimuttikā kalyāṇādhimuttikehi saddhiṃ saṃsandanti samentī”ti evaṃ sattānaṃ nānādhimuttikatā, nānajjhāsayatā, nānādiṭṭhikatā, nānākhantitā, nānārucitā, nāḷiyā minantena viya tulāya tulayantena viya ca nānādhimuttikatāñāṇena sabbaññutaññāṇena viditā, sā yāva suppaṭividitā. Dvepi nāma sattā ekajjhāsayā dullabhā lokasmiṃ. Ekasmiṃ gantukāme eko ṭhātukāmo hoti, ekasmiṃ pivitukāme eko bhuñjitukāmo. Imesu cāpi dvīsu ācariyantevāsīsu ayañhi “suppiyo paribbājako…pe… bhagavantaṃ piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhā honti bhikkhusaṅghañcā”ti. Tattha itihameti itiha ime, evaṃ imeti attho. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Now, to show the fact of this being thoroughly penetrated, the passage beginning with “ayañhi” was spoken. This is what was said by the Blessed One: “Monks, beings associate and come together according to element. Those with inferior dispositions associate and come together with those of inferior dispositions; those with noble dispositions associate and come together with those of noble dispositions. In the past, too, monks, beings associated and came together according to element... In the future, too, monks... they will associate and come together... And now, too, in the present, monks, beings associate and come together according to element...” Thus, this diversity of beings' dispositions, inclinations, views, tolerances, and preferences is known by the knowledge of omniscience, which is the knowledge of the diversity of dispositions, as if by one measuring with a measuring tube or weighing with a scale; it is indeed thoroughly penetrated. Indeed, two beings of the same inclination are hard to find in the world. When one wishes to go, another wishes to stay; when one wishes to drink, another wishes to eat. And even among these two, the teacher and the student, it is said: “this Suppiya the wanderer... follows closely behind the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks.” Therein, “itihame” is “iti ha ime.” The meaning is “thus these are.” The rest is as has been explained.

4. Atha kho bhagavā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ imaṃ saṅkhiyadhammaṃ viditvāti ettha viditvāti sabbaññutaññāṇena jānitvā. Bhagavā hi katthaci maṃsacakkhunā disvā jānāti – “addasā kho bhagavā mahantaṃ dārukkhandhaṃ gaṅgāya nadiyā sotena vuyhamāna”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.241) viya. Katthaci dibbacakkhunā disvā jānāti – “addasā kho bhagavā dibbena cakkhunā [P 1.0045] visuddhena atikkantamānusakena tā devatāyo sahassasseva pāṭaligāme vatthūni parigaṇhantiyo”tiādīsu [V 1.0044] (dī. ni. 2.152) viya. Katthaci pakatisotena sutvā jānāti – “assosi kho bhagavā āyasmato ānandassa subhaddena paribbājakena saddhiṃ imaṃ kathāsallāpa”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.213) viya. Katthaci dibbasotena sutvā jānāti – “assosi kho bhagavā dibbāya sotadhātuyā visuddhāya atikkantamānusikāya sandhānassa gahapatissa nigrodhena paribbājakena saddhiṃ imaṃ kathāsallāpa”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.54) viya. Idha pana sabbaññutaññāṇena sutvā aññāsi. Kiṃ karonto aññāsi? Pacchimayāmakiccaṃ, kiccañca nāmetaṃ sātthakaṃ, niratthakanti duvidhaṃ hoti. Tattha niratthakakiccaṃ bhagavatā bodhipallaṅkeyeva arahattamaggena samugghātaṃ kataṃ. Sātthakaṃyeva pana [M 1.0046] bhagavato kiccaṃ hoti. Taṃ pañcavidhaṃ – purebhattakiccaṃ, pacchābhattakiccaṃ, purimayāmakiccaṃ, majjhimayāmakiccaṃ, pacchimayāmakiccanti.

4. Then the Blessed One, having known this discourse on analysis regarding those monks—here, `viditvā` (having known) means knowing with the knowledge of omniscience. For the Blessed One indeed knows in some instances by seeing with the physical eye, as in the instance: “Indeed, the Blessed One saw a large log being carried along by the current of the Ganges river.” In some instances, He knows by seeing with the divine eye, as in the instance: “Indeed, the Blessed One saw with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, those deities, a thousand in all, taking possession of dwellings in Pāṭaligāma.” In some instances, He knows by hearing with the ordinary ear, as in the instance: “The Blessed One heard this conversation of the Venerable Ānanda with the wanderer Subhadda.” In some instances, He knows by hearing with the divine ear, as in the instance: “The Blessed One heard with the divine element of hearing, purified and surpassing the human, this conversation of the householder Sandhāna with the wanderer Nigrodha.” Here, however, He knew by perceiving with the knowledge of omniscience. While performing what duty did He know? The duty of the last watch of the night. And this, known as duty, is twofold: purposeful and pointless. Therein, the pointless duty was completely eradicated by the Blessed One right at the seat of enlightenment through the path of Arahantship. Furthermore, for the Blessed One, there is only purposeful duty. That is fivefold: the duty before the meal, the duty after the meal, the duty of the first watch, the duty of the middle watch, and the duty of the last watch.

Tatridaṃ purebhattakiccaṃ –

Among these, this is the duty before the meal:

Bhagavā hi pātova uṭṭhāya upaṭṭhākānuggahatthaṃ sarīraphāsukatthañca mukhadhovanādisarīraparikammaṃ katvā yāva bhikkhācāravelā tāva vivittāsane vītināmetvā, bhikkhācāravelāyaṃ nivāsetvā kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā cīvaraṃ pārupitvā pattamādāya kadāci ekako, kadāci bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto, gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya pavisati; kadāci pakatiyā, kadāci anekehi pāṭihāriyehi vattamānehi. Seyyathidaṃ, piṇḍāya pavisato lokanāthassa purato purato gantvā mudugatavātā pathaviṃ sodhenti, valāhakā udakaphusitāni muñcantā magge reṇuṃ vūpasametvā upari vitānaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhanti, apare vātā pupphāni upasaṃharitvā magge okiranti, unnatā bhūmippadesā onamanti, onatā unnamanti, pādanikkhepasamaye samāva bhūmi hoti, sukhasamphassāni padumapupphāni vā pāde sampaṭicchanti. Indakhīlassa anto ṭhapitamatte dakkhiṇapāde sarīrato chabbaṇṇarasmiyo nikkhamitvā suvaṇṇarasapiñjarāni viya citrapaṭaparikkhittāni viya ca pāsādakūṭāgārādīni alaṅkarontiyo ito cito [P 1.0046] ca dhāvanti, hatthiassavihaṅgādayo sakasakaṭṭhānesu ṭhitāyeva madhurenākārena saddaṃ karonti, tathā bherivīṇādīni tūriyāni manussānañca kāyūpagāni ābharaṇāni. Tena saññāṇena manussā jānanti – “ajja bhagavā idha piṇḍāya paviṭṭho”ti. Te sunivatthā supārutā gandhapupphādīni ādāya gharā nikkhamitvā antaravīthiṃ paṭipajjitvā bhagavantaṃ gandhapupphādīhi sakkaccaṃ pūjetvā vanditvā – “amhākaṃ, bhante, dasa bhikkhū, amhākaṃ vīsati, paññāsaṃ…pe… sataṃ dethā”ti yācitvā bhagavatopi pattaṃ gahetvā āsanaṃ [V 1.0045] paññapetvā sakkaccaṃ piṇḍapātena paṭimānenti. Bhagavā katabhattakicco tesaṃ sattānaṃ cittasantānāni oloketvā tathā dhammaṃ deseti, yathā keci saraṇagamanesu patiṭṭhahanti, keci pañcasu sīlesu, keci sotāpattisakadāgāmianāgāmiphalānaṃ aññatarasmiṃ; keci pabbajitvā aggaphale arahatteti. Evaṃ mahājanaṃ anuggahetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ gacchati. Tattha [M 1.0047] gantvā maṇḍalamāḷe paññattavarabuddhāsane nisīdati, bhikkhūnaṃ bhattakiccapariyosānaṃ āgamayamāno. Tato bhikkhūnaṃ bhattakiccapariyosāne upaṭṭhāko bhagavato nivedeti. Atha bhagavā gandhakuṭiṃ pavisati. Idaṃ tāva purebhattakiccaṃ.

For the Blessed One, rising early in the morning, in order to benefit his attendants and for the comfort of his body, after performing bodily duties such as washing his face, and so forth, spends the time in a secluded seat until the time for the almsround. At the time for the almsround, he puts on his lower robe, fastens his waistband, drapes his outer robe, takes his bowl, and enters a village or town for alms—sometimes alone, sometimes accompanied by the community of monks. Sometimes he goes in the usual manner, sometimes with many miracles occurring. For instance, when the Protector of the World enters for alms, gentle winds go ahead and sweep the ground clean; clouds, releasing drops of water, settle the dust on the path and stand above as a canopy. Other winds gather flowers and scatter them on the path. High ground becomes low, low ground becomes high, and the ground becomes level at the moment of his footfall; or lotus flowers with a pleasant touch receive his feet. When his right foot is placed just inside the threshold-post, six-colored rays emerge from his body, adorning palaces, pinnacled houses, and so forth, as if they were made tawny with liquid gold or draped with variegated cloths, and they dart here and there. Elephants, horses, birds, and so forth, while standing in their own places, make sounds in a sweet manner, as do drums, lutes, and other musical instruments, and the ornaments worn on the bodies of humans. By these signs, people know: “Today the Blessed One has entered here for alms.” Well-dressed and well-robed, they come out of their homes carrying perfumes and flowers, proceed to the main street, reverently honor the Blessed One with perfumes and flowers, pay homage, and request: “Venerable sir, give us ten monks, give us twenty, fifty… a hundred!” They take the Blessed One’s bowl, prepare a seat, and respectfully honor him with almsfood. Having finished his meal, the Blessed One observes the mental continuities of those beings and teaches the Dhamma in such a way that some establish themselves in the refuges, some in the five precepts, some in one of the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, or non-returning; and some, having gone forth, establish themselves in the supreme fruit, Arahantship. Thus, having benefited the great multitude, he rises from his seat and goes to the monastery. Having gone there, he sits on the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the circular hall, awaiting the completion of the monks’ meal-duty. Then, upon the completion of the monks’ meal-duty, the attendant informs the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One enters the Perfumed Chamber. This, for now, is the duty before the meal.

Atha bhagavā evaṃ katapurebhattakicco gandhakuṭiyā upaṭṭhāne nisīditvā pāde pakkhāletvā pādapīṭhe ṭhatvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ ovadati – “bhikkhave, appamādena sampādetha, dullabho buddhuppādo lokasmiṃ, dullabho manussattapaṭilābho, dullabhā sampatti, dullabhā pabbajjā, dullabhaṃ saddhammassavana”nti. Tattha keci bhagavantaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ pucchanti. Bhagavāpi tesaṃ cariyānurūpaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ deti. Tato sabbepi bhagavantaṃ vanditvā attano attano rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānāni gacchanti. Keci araññaṃ, keci rukkhamūlaṃ, keci pabbatādīnaṃ aññataraṃ, keci cātumahārājikabhavanaṃ…pe… keci vasavattibhavananti. Tato bhagavā gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā sace ākaṅkhati, dakkhiṇena [P 1.0047] passena sato sampajāno muhuttaṃ sīhaseyyaṃ kappeti. Atha samassāsitakāyo vuṭṭhahitvā dutiyabhāge lokaṃ voloketi. Tatiyabhāge yaṃ gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā upanissāya viharati tattha mahājano purebhattaṃ dānaṃ datvā pacchābhattaṃ sunivattho supāruto gandhapupphādīni ādāya vihāre sannipatati. Tato bhagavā sampattaparisāya anurūpena pāṭihāriyena gantvā dhammasabhāyaṃ paññattavarabuddhāsane nisajja dhammaṃ deseti kālayuttaṃ samayayuttaṃ, atha kālaṃ viditvā parisaṃ uyyojeti, manussā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā pakkamanti. Idaṃ pacchābhattakiccaṃ.

Then the Blessed One, having thus completed his forenoon duties, sat down in the vicinity of the Perfumed Chamber. Having washed his feet and stood on the foot-washing stool, he admonished the community of monks: “Monks, strive with heedfulness! The arising of a Buddha in the world is difficult to obtain; the attainment of a human state is difficult to obtain; good fortune is difficult to obtain; the going forth is difficult to obtain; the hearing of the True Dhamma is difficult to obtain.” There, some monks asked the Blessed One for a meditation subject. The Blessed One gave them a meditation subject suitable to their temperaments. Then, all of them, having paid homage to the Blessed One, went to their respective places for the night and places for the day. Some went to the forest, some to the foot of a tree, some to another place among mountains and so on, some to the realm of the Four Great Kings... and so on... some to the realm of Vasavatti. Then the Blessed One, having entered the Perfumed Chamber, if he so wishes, mindful and clearly comprehending, for a moment adopts the lion's posture on his right side. Then, with his body well-refreshed, having arisen, in the second part he surveys the world. In the third part, in whatever village or town he is dwelling near, the great populace, having given alms in the forenoon, assembles at the monastery in the afternoon, well-dressed and well-robed, taking perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. Then the Blessed One, having gone with a miracle suitable for the assembled congregation, sits on the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the Dhamma hall and teaches the Dhamma that is suitable for the time and suitable for the occasion. Then, knowing the time, he dismisses the congregation. The people, having paid homage to the Blessed One, depart. This is the after-meal duty.

So evaṃ niṭṭhitapacchābhattakicco sace gattāni osiñcitukāmo hoti, buddhāsanā vuṭṭhāya nhānakoṭṭhakaṃ pavisitvā upaṭṭhākena paṭiyāditaudakena gattāni utuṃ gaṇhāpeti. Upaṭṭhākopi buddhāsanaṃ ānetvā gandhakuṭipariveṇe paññapeti. Bhagavā surattadupaṭṭaṃ nivāsetvā kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā uttarāsaṅgaṃ ekaṃsaṃ karitvā tattha gantvā nisīdati ekakova muhuttaṃ paṭisallīno, atha bhikkhū tato tato āgamma bhagavato upaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchanti. Tattha ekacce pañhaṃ pucchanti, ekacce kammaṭṭhānaṃ, ekacce [M 1.0048] dhammassavanaṃ yācanti. Bhagavā tesaṃ adhippāyaṃ sampādento purimayāmaṃ vītināmeti. Idaṃ purimayāmakiccaṃ.

That Blessed One, having thus completed the after-meal duties, if he wishes to have water poured on his limbs, arises from the Buddha-seat and, with water prepared by an attendant, bathes his limbs. The attendant also, having brought the Buddha-seat, prepares it in the enclosure of the Perfumed Chamber. The Blessed One, having put on the well-dyed, two-layered lower garment, having fastened the waistband, and having placed the upper robe over one shoulder, goes there and sits alone for a moment in seclusion. Then monks, having come from here and there, come to attend upon the Blessed One. There, some ask questions, some a meditation subject, and some request the hearing of the Dhamma. The Blessed One, fulfilling their intentions, passes the first watch of the night. This is the duty of the first watch.

Purimayāmakiccapariyosāne [V 1.0046] pana bhikkhūsu bhagavantaṃ vanditvā pakkantesu sakaladasasahassilokadhātudevatāyo okāsaṃ labhamānā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pañhaṃ pucchanti, yathābhisaṅkhataṃ antamaso caturakkharampi. Bhagavā tāsaṃ devatānaṃ pañhaṃ vissajjento majjhimayāmaṃ vītināmeti. Idaṃ majjhimayāmakiccaṃ.

Furthermore, at the end of the duty of the first watch, when the monks, having paid homage to the Blessed One, have departed, the deities of the entire ten-thousand world-systems, obtaining the opportunity, approach the Blessed One and ask questions as they had arranged, even down to one of four syllables. The Blessed One, answering the questions of those deities, passes the middle watch of the night. This is the duty of the middle watch.

Pacchimayāmaṃ pana tayo koṭṭhāse katvā purebhattato paṭṭhāya nisajjāya pīḷitassa sarīrassa kilāsubhāvamocanatthaṃ ekaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ caṅkamena vītināmeti. Dutiyakoṭṭhāse gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā dakkhiṇena passena sato sampajāno sīhaseyyaṃ kappeti. Tatiyakoṭṭhāse paccuṭṭhāya nisīditvā purimabuddhānaṃ santike dānasīlādivasena katādhikārapuggaladassanatthaṃ [P 1.0048] buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ voloketi. Idaṃ pacchimayāmakiccaṃ.

Furthermore, dividing the last watch of the night into three parts, he spends one part in walking meditation to release the weariness of his body, which has been afflicted by sitting since before the meal. In the second part, entering the Perfumed Chamber, he adopts the lion's posture on his right side, mindful and clearly comprehending. In the third part, having arisen again and sat down, he surveys the world with the Buddha-eye to see persons who have made their aspiration through giving, virtue, and so on, in the presence of former Buddhas. This is the duty of the last watch.

Tasmiṃ pana divase bhagavā purebhattakiccaṃ rājagahe pariyosāpetvā pacchābhatte maggaṃ āgato, purimayāme bhikkhūnaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā, majjhimayāme devatānaṃ pañhaṃ vissajjetvā, pacchimayāme caṅkamaṃ āruyha caṅkamamāno pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ imaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ ārabbha pavattaṃ kathaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇeneva sutvā aññāsīti. Tena vuttaṃ – “pacchimayāmakiccaṃ karonto aññāsī”ti.

On that day, however, the Blessed One, having completed his forenoon duties in Rājagaha, came along the road in the after-meal time. In the first watch, having taught a meditation subject to the monks; in the middle watch, having answered the questions of the deities; and in the last watch, having ascended the walking path and while walking, he heard with his knowledge of omniscience itself this talk of the five hundred monks that had arisen concerning the knowledge of omniscience, and he knew. Therefore, it was said: “While performing the duties of the last watch, he knew.”

Ñatvā ca panassa etadahosi – “ime bhikkhū mayhaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ ārabbha guṇaṃ kathenti, etesañca sabbaññutaññāṇakiccaṃ na pākaṭaṃ, mayhameva pākaṭaṃ. Mayi pana gate ete attano kathaṃ nirantaraṃ ārocessanti, tato nesaṃ ahaṃ taṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā tividhaṃ sīlaṃ vibhajanto, dvāsaṭṭhiyā ṭhānesu appaṭivattiyaṃ sīhanādaṃ nadanto, paccayākāraṃ samodhānetvā buddhaguṇe pākaṭe katvā, sineruṃ ukkhipento viya suvaṇṇakūṭena nabhaṃ paharanto viya ca dasasahassilokadhātukampanaṃ brahmajālasuttantaṃ arahattanikūṭena niṭṭhāpento desessāmi, sā me desanā parinibbutassāpi pañcavassasahassāni sattānaṃ amatamahānibbānaṃ sampāpikā bhavissatī”ti. Evaṃ cintetvā yena maṇḍalamāḷo tenupasaṅkamīti[M 1.0049]. Yenāti yena disābhāgena, so upasaṅkamitabbo. Bhummatthe vā etaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ, yasmiṃ padese so maṇḍalamāḷo, tattha gatoti ayamettha attho.

And having known this, this thought occurred to him: “These monks speak of the quality concerning my knowledge of omniscience, but for them the function of the knowledge of omniscience is not manifest; it is manifest only to me. But when I have gone, these monks will continuously bring up their talk. Then, for them, having made that the occasion for the discourse, analyzing the threefold virtue, roaring the irreversible lion's roar in sixty-two instances, connecting the causal conditionality, having made the qualities of a Buddha manifest, like one lifting Mount Sineru and like one striking the sky with a golden hammer, I will teach the Brahmajāla Suttanta, which causes the ten-thousand world-systems to tremble, concluding it with the pinnacle which is Arahantship. That teaching of mine, even after I have attained Parinibbāna, for five thousand years, will be one that leads beings to the deathless, great Nibbāna.” Having thought thus, he approached the place where the circular hall was. Herein, ‘yena’ means by which direction he was to be approached. Or, this is an instrumental word in the locative sense, meaning: in which place that circular hall was, there he went. This is the meaning here.

Paññatte āsane nisīdīti buddhakāle kira yattha yattha ekopi bhikkhu viharati sabbattha buddhāsanaṃ paññattameva hoti. Kasmā? Bhagavā kira attano santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā phāsukaṭṭhāne [V 1.0047] viharante manasi karoti – “asuko mayhaṃ santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā gato, sakkhissati nu kho visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ no vā”ti. Atha naṃ passati kammaṭṭhānaṃ vissajjetvā akusalavitakkaṃ vitakkayamānaṃ, tato “kathañhi nāma mādisassa satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā [P 1.0049] viharantaṃ imaṃ kulaputtaṃ akusalavitakkā abhibhavitvā anamatagge vaṭṭadukkhe saṃsāressantī”ti tassa anuggahatthaṃ tattheva attānaṃ dassetvā taṃ kulaputtaṃ ovaditvā ākāsaṃ uppatitvā puna attano vasanaṭṭhānameva gacchati. Athevaṃ ovadiyamānā te bhikkhū cintayiṃsu – “satthā amhākaṃ manaṃ jānitvā āgantvā amhākaṃ samīpe ṭhitaṃyeva attānaṃ dasseti”. Tasmiṃ khaṇe – “bhante, idha nisīdatha, idha nisīdathā”ti āsanapariyesanaṃ nāma bhāroti. Te āsanaṃ paññapetvāva viharanti. Yassa pīṭhaṃ atthi, so taṃ paññapeti. Yassa natthi, so mañcaṃ vā phalakaṃ vā kaṭṭhaṃ vā pāsāṇaṃ vā vālukapuñjaṃ vā paññapeti. Taṃ alabhamānā purāṇapaṇṇānipi saṅkaḍḍhitvā tattha paṃsukūlaṃ pattharitvā ṭhapenti. Idha pana rañño nisīdanāsanameva atthi, taṃ papphoṭetvā paññapetvā parivāretvā te bhikkhū bhagavato adhimuttikañāṇamārabbha guṇaṃ thomayamānā nisīdiṃsu. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “paññatte āsane nisīdī”ti.

Regarding 'He sat down on the prepared seat': It is said that in the Buddha's time, wherever even a single monk resided, a Buddha-seat was always prepared. Why? The Blessed One, it seems, would direct his mind toward monks who, having received a meditation subject in his presence, were dwelling in a comfortable place, thinking: 'Such-and-such a monk took a meditation subject from me and departed; will he be able to bring about a special attainment, or not?' Then, he might see that monk, having abandoned the meditation subject, thinking unwholesome thoughts. Thereupon, thinking, 'How indeed could unwholesome thoughts, having overpowered this clansman who is dwelling after receiving a meditation subject in the presence of a teacher like me, cause him to sink into the suffering of the round of existence which has no known beginning?', for that clansman's benefit, he would manifest himself right there, advise that clansman, soar into the sky, and then return to his own dwelling place. Being thus advised, those monks would reflect: 'The Teacher, knowing our minds, comes and shows himself standing right near us.' At that moment, the search for a seat—'Venerable sir, please sit here, please sit here!'—is a burden. Therefore, they would dwell only after having prepared a seat. Whoever had a stool would prepare it. Whoever did not would prepare a bed, a plank of wood, a piece of timber, a stone slab, or a pile of sand. If they could not obtain these, they would gather even old leaves, spread a rag-robe over them, and set it in place. Here, however, there was the king's own sitting seat. Having shaken it, prepared it, and surrounded it, those monks sat down, praising the virtue of the Blessed One's knowledge of dispositions. With reference to this, it was said: 'He sat down on the prepared seat.'

Evaṃ nisinno pana jānantoyeva kathāsamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ bhikkhū pucchi. Te cassa sabbaṃ kathayiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “nisajja kho bhagavā”tiādi. Tattha kāya nutthāti katamāya nu kathāya sannisinnā bhavathāti attho. Kāya netthātipi pāḷi, tassā katamāya nu etthāti attho kāya notthātipi pāḷi. Tassāpi purimoyeva attho.

Then, having thus sat down, knowing full well, he asked the monks for the purpose of raising a topic of conversation. And they told him everything. Therefore, it was said: 'The Blessed One, having sat down,' and so on. Therein, 'kāya nutthā' means 'With what discussion, indeed, were you seated together?' The Pāḷi also has 'kāya netthā,' and its meaning is 'With what, indeed, here?' The Pāḷi also has 'kāya notthā,' and its meaning is also the same as the first one.

Antarākathāti[M 1.0050], kammaṭṭhānamanasikārauddesaparipucchādīnaṃ antarā aññā ekā kathā. Vippakatāti, mama āgamanapaccayā apariniṭṭhitā sikhaṃ appattā. Tena kiṃ dasseti? “Nāhaṃ tumhākaṃ kathābhaṅgatthaṃ āgato, ahaṃ pana sabbaññutāya tumhākaṃ kathaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā matthakappattaṃ katvā dassāmīti āgato”ti nisajjeva sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ pavāreti. Ayaṃ kho no, bhante, antarākathā vippakatā[P 1.0050], atha bhagavā anuppattoti etthāpi ayamadhippāyo. Ayaṃ bhante amhākaṃ bhagavato sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ ārabbha guṇakathā vippakatā, na rājakathādikā tiracchānakathā, atha bhagavā anuppatto; taṃ no idāni niṭṭhāpetvā desethāti.

'Interim talk' means another, different kind of talk in between the contemplation of the meditation subject, recitation, repeated questioning, and so on. 'Unfinished' means that on account of my arrival, it was not concluded, it had not reached its peak. What does he show by this? 'I have not come for the purpose of interrupting your talk. Rather, I have come to finish your talk through my omniscience, bring it to its culmination, and teach.' Thus, just by sitting down, he makes the invitation of an omniscient one. In the passage, 'This, venerable sir, was our interim talk that was unfinished, and then the Blessed One arrived,' this is also the intention: 'Venerable sir, this unfinished talk of ours was a talk on the virtues concerning the Blessed One's knowledge of omniscience, not base talk such as talk of kings. And then the Blessed One arrived. Now, having finished it for us, please teach.'

Ettāvatā ca yaṃ āyasmatā ānandena kamalakuvalayujjalavimalasādhurasasalilāya pokkharaṇiyā sukhāvataraṇatthaṃ nimmalasilātalaracanavilāsasobhitaratanasopānaṃ, vippakiṇṇamuttātalasadisavālukākiṇṇapaṇḍarabhūmibhāgaṃ [V 1.0048] titthaṃ viya suvibhattabhittivicitravedikāparikkhittassa nakkhattapathaṃ phusitukāmatāya viya, vijambhitasamussayassa pāsādavarassa sukhārohaṇatthaṃ dantamayasaṇhamuduphalakakañcanalatāvinaddhamaṇigaṇappabhāsamudayujjalasobhaṃ sopānaṃ viya, suvaṇṇavalayanūpurādisaṅghaṭṭanasaddasammissitakathitahasitamadhurassaragehajanavicaritassa uḷārissarivibhavasobhitassa mahāgharassa sukhappavesanatthaṃ suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimuttapavāḷādijutivissaravijjotitasuppatiṭṭhitavisāladvārabāhaṃ mahādvāraṃ viya ca atthabyañjanasampannassa buddhaguṇānubhāvasaṃsūcakassa imassa suttassa sukhāvagahaṇatthaṃ kāladesadesakavatthuparisāpadesapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ nidānaṃ bhāsitaṃ, tassatthavaṇṇanā samattāti.

And thus, the explanation of the meaning of the introduction—which was spoken by the venerable Ānanda, adorned with indications of the time, place, speaker, subject, and assembly, for the easy comprehension of this sutta which is complete in meaning and letter and indicative of the power of the Buddha's virtues—is completed. This introduction is like a jeweled staircase, beautified by the elegance of its flawless stone construction, for easy descent into a pond with water that is radiant with lotuses and water lilies, pure, and of a pleasant taste, and like a landing place with a ground of white sand resembling a surface of scattered pearls; and like a staircase, radiant with the splendor of a mass of light from a collection of gems entwined with golden vines on smooth, soft ivory planks, for the easy ascent to a supreme palace with a towering structure that seems to stretch out as if desiring to touch the path of the stars, surrounded by well-portioned walls and ornate railings; and also like a great gateway, with well-established, wide doorposts illuminated by the diffusion of light from gold, silver, gems, pearls, coral, and so on, for the easy entry into a great mansion, beautified by the glory of noble sovereignty and wealth, where the people of the house move about with the sweet sounds of conversation and laughter mingled with the sounds of the clashing of gold bracelets, anklets, and other ornaments.

5. Idāni – “mamaṃ vā, bhikkhave, pare avaṇṇaṃ bhāseyyu”ntiādinā nayena bhagavatā nikkhittassa suttassa vaṇṇanāya okāso anuppatto. Sā panesā suttavaṇṇanā. Yasmā suttanikkhepaṃ vicāretvā vuccamānā pākaṭā hoti, tasmā suttanikkhepaṃ tāva vicārayissāma. Cattāro hi suttanikkhepā – attajjhāsayo, parajjhāsayo, pucchāvasiko, aṭṭhuppattikoti.

5. Now, the opportunity has arrived for the commentary on the sutta laid down by the Blessed One with the method beginning, 'Monks, should others speak in dispraise of me...' And this commentary on the sutta, because it becomes clear when it is explained after having examined the exposition of the sutta, we shall therefore first examine the exposition of the sutta. For there are four expositions of a sutta: that based on one's own disposition, that based on another's disposition, that based on a question, and that based on an occasion.

Tattha [M 1.0051] yāni suttāni bhagavā parehi anajjhiṭṭho kevalaṃ attano ajjhāsayeneva kathesi; seyyathidaṃ, ākaṅkheyyasuttaṃ, vatthasuttaṃ, mahāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ, mahāsaḷāyatanavibhaṅgasuttaṃ, ariyavaṃsasuttaṃ, sammappadhānasuttantahārako, iddhipādaindriyabalabojjhaṅgamaggaṅgasuttantahārakoti evamādīni; tesaṃ attajjhāsayo nikkhepo.

Therein, those suttas which the Blessed One taught unrequested by others, solely from his own disposition—namely, the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta, the Vattha Sutta, the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, the Mahāsaḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta, the Ariyavaṃsa Sutta, the collection of suttas on the Right Exertions, the collection of suttas on the Bases of Spiritual Power, the Spiritual Faculties, the Powers, the Factors of Enlightenment, and the Path Factors, and others such as these—their exposition is based on his own disposition.

Yāni pana “paripakkā kho rāhulassa vimuttiparipācaniyā dhammā; yaṃnūnāhaṃ rāhulaṃ uttariṃ [P 1.0051] āsavānaṃ khaye vineyya”nti; (saṃ. ni. 4.121) evaṃ paresaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ khantiṃ manaṃ abhinīhāraṃ bujjhanabhāvañca avekkhitvā parajjhāsayavasena kathitāni; seyyathidaṃ, cūḷarāhulovādasuttaṃ, mahārāhulovādasuttaṃ, dhammacakkappavattanaṃ, dhātuvibhaṅgasuttanti evamādīni; tesaṃ parajjhāsayo nikkhepo.

Furthermore, those discourses taught in accordance with the inclination of others, after having considered their disposition, preference, mentality, aspiration, and capacity for understanding—as in the thought, 'The qualities in Rāhula that lead to the ripening of liberation are now mature; let me now train Rāhula further for the destruction of the taints'—such as the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta, the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, and the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, and others of this kind; for these, the mode of exposition is that of another's inclination.

Bhagavantaṃ pana upasaṅkamitvā catasso parisā, cattāro vaṇṇā, nāgā, supaṇṇā, gandhabbā, asurā, yakkhā, mahārājāno, tāvatiṃsādayo devā, mahābrahmāti evamādayo – “bojjhaṅgā bojjhaṅgā”ti, bhante, vuccanti. “Nīvaraṇā nīvaraṇā”ti, bhante, vuccanti; “ime nu kho, bhante, pañcupādānakkhandhā”. “Kiṃ sūdha vittaṃ purisassa seṭṭha”ntiādinā nayena pañhaṃ [V 1.0049] pucchanti. Evaṃ puṭṭhena bhagavatā yāni kathitāni bojjhaṅgasaṃyuttādīni, yāni vā panaññānipi devatāsaṃyutta-mārasaṃyutta-brahmasaṃyutta-sakkapañha-cūḷavedalla-mahāvedalla-sāmaññaphala-āḷavaka-sūciloma-kharalomasuttādīni; tesaṃ pucchāvasiko nikkhepo.

Furthermore, having approached the Blessed One, the four assemblies, the four castes, nāgas, supaṇṇas, gandhabbas, asuras, yakkhas, great kings, the Tāvatiṃsa devas and the like, and Mahābrahmā—these and others ask questions in this manner: 'Venerable Sir, it is said, “factors of enlightenment, factors of enlightenment.”' 'Venerable Sir, it is said, “hindrances, hindrances.”' 'Venerable Sir, are these the five aggregates subject to clinging?' 'What here is the best wealth for a person?' and so on. For those discourses spoken by the Blessed One when thus questioned—such as the Connected Discourses on the Factors of Enlightenment and others, or any other discourses like the Connected Discourses with Devas, Māra, and Brahmā, the Questions of Sakka, the Shorter and Greater Vedalla Suttas, the Sutta on the Fruits of the Ascetic Life, and the Āḷavaka, Sūciloma, and Kharaloma Suttas—their mode of exposition is that which is prompted by a question.

Yāni pana tāni uppannaṃ kāraṇaṃ paṭicca kathitāni, seyyathidaṃ – dhammadāyādaṃ, cūḷasīhanādaṃ, candūpamaṃ, puttamaṃsūpamaṃ, dārukkhandhūpamaṃ, aggikkhandhūpamaṃ, pheṇapiṇḍūpamaṃ, pāricchattakūpamanti evamādīni; tesaṃ aṭṭhuppattiko nikkhepo.

Furthermore, as for those discourses that have been spoken in connection with an arisen occasion—such as the Dhammadāyāda Sutta, the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta, the Candūpama Sutta, the Puttamaṃsūpama Sutta, the Dārukkhandhūpama Sutta, the Aggikkhandhūpama Sutta, the Pheṇapiṇḍūpama Sutta, and the Pāricchattakūpama Sutta, and others of this kind—for these, the mode of exposition is that of an arisen occasion.

Evametesu catūsu nikkhepesu imassa suttassa aṭṭhuppattiko nikkhepo. Aṭṭhuppattiyā hi idaṃ bhagavatā nikkhittaṃ. Katarāya aṭṭhuppattiyā? Vaṇṇāvaṇṇe. Ācariyo ratanattayassa avaṇṇaṃ abhāsi, antevāsī vaṇṇaṃ. Iti imaṃ vaṇṇāvaṇṇaṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā desanākusalo bhagavā – “mamaṃ vā, bhikkhave, pare avaṇṇaṃ bhāseyyu”nti desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha mamanti[M 1.0052], sāmivacanaṃ, mamāti attho. Vāsaddo vikappanattho. Pareti, paṭiviruddhā sattā. Tatrāti ye avaṇṇaṃ vadanti tesu.

Thus, among these four modes of exposition, the mode of exposition for this discourse is that of an arisen occasion. For this was set forth by the Blessed One on account of an arisen occasion. On account of what arisen occasion? That of praise and dispraise. The teacher spoke dispraise of the Triple Gem; the student spoke praise. Thus, having made this praise and dispraise the occasion for its arising, the Blessed One, skilled in teaching, began the discourse, saying: 'Monks, should others speak dispraise of me...' Herein, 'mamaṃ' is a genitive term, meaning 'of me.' The word 'vā' has the meaning of alternation. 'Others' refers to opposing beings. 'Therein' refers to those who speak dispraise.

Na āghātotiādīhi kiñcāpi tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ āghātoyeva natthi, atha kho āyatiṃ kulaputtānaṃ īdisesupi ṭhānesu akusaluppattiṃ paṭisedhento dhammanettiṃ [P 1.0052] ṭhapeti. Tattha āhanati cittanti ‘āghāto’; kopassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Appatītā honti tena atuṭṭhā asomanassikāti appaccayo; domanassassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Neva attano na paresaṃ hitaṃ abhirādhayatīti anabhiraddhi; kopassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Evamettha dvīhi padehi saṅkhārakkhandho, ekena vedanākkhandhoti dve khandhā vuttā. Tesaṃ vasena sesānampi sampayuttadhammānaṃ kāraṇaṃ paṭikkhittameva.

With the words 'no ill will,' and so on: although those monks indeed had no ill will, the Blessed One nevertheless establishes this guideline of the Dhamma in order to prevent the arising of unwholesome states for future clansmen in such situations. Herein, 'āghāta' (ill will) is so called because 'it strikes (āhanati) the mind'; this is a synonym for anger (kopa). 'Appaccayo' (displeasure) is so called because through it 'they are not pleased (appatītā), not satisfied (atuṭṭhā), not mentally happy (asomanassikā)'; this is a synonym for sorrow (domanassa). 'Anabhiraddhi' (discontent) is so called because 'it accomplishes (abhirādhayati) the welfare of neither oneself nor others'; this is a synonym for anger (kopa). Thus, herein, by two terms the aggregate of formations is stated, and by one the aggregate of feeling; in this way, two aggregates are stated. By means of these, the generation of the remaining associated mental states is also rejected.

Evaṃ paṭhamena nayena manopadosaṃ nivāretvā, dutiyena nayena tattha ādīnavaṃ dassento āha – “tatra ce tumhe assatha kupitā vā anattamanā vā, tumhaṃ yevassa tena antarāyo”ti. Tattha ‘tatra ce tumhe assathā’ti tesu avaṇṇabhāsakesu, tasmiṃ vā avaṇṇe tumhe bhaveyyātha ce; yadi bhaveyyāthāti attho. ‘Kupitā’ kopena, anattamanā domanassena. ‘Tumhaṃ yevassa tena antarāyo’ti tumhākaṃyeva tena kopena, tāya ca anattamanatāya paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ antarāyo bhaveyya.

Thus, having prevented the corruption of the mind by the first method, he then showed the danger in it by the second method, saying: 'If you were to become angry or displeased there, that would be an obstacle for you alone.' Herein, 'if you were to be there' means: among those who speak dispraise, or in the face of that dispraise, if you were to become so; that is the meaning. 'Angry' means with anger; 'displeased' means with sorrow. 'That would be an obstacle for you alone' means: that very anger and that very displeasure would become an obstacle for you alone, hindering the attainment of the first jhāna and so forth.

Evaṃ [V 1.0050] dutiyena nayena ādīnavaṃ dassetvā, tatiyena nayena vacanatthasallakkhaṇamattepi asamatthataṃ dassento – “api nu tumhe paresa”ntiādimāha. Tattha paresanti yesaṃ kesaṃ ci. Kupito hi neva buddhapaccekabuddhaariyasāvakānaṃ, na mātāpitūnaṃ, na paccatthikānaṃ subhāsitadubbhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānāti. Yathāha –

Thus, having shown the danger by the second method, by a third method he demonstrates the inability even to merely discern the meaning of words, saying, 'And would you [understand] what others say...?' Herein, 'others' refers to anyone at all. For an angry person does not clearly understand the meaning of what is well-spoken or ill-spoken, whether by Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, noble disciples, mother and father, or by enemies. As it is said:

“Kuddho atthaṃ na jānāti, kuddho dhammaṃ na passati;

Andhaṃ tamaṃ tadā hoti, yaṃ kodho sahate naraṃ.

An angry person does not know the meaning, an angry person does not see the Dhamma. Then there is a blinding darkness when anger overwhelms a person.

Anatthajanano kodho, kodho cittappakopano;

Bhayamantarato jātaṃ, taṃ jano nāvabujjhatī”ti. (a. ni. 7.64);

Anger is a generator of harm, anger is a corrupter of the mind; Fear is born from within, that a person does not comprehend.

Evaṃ [M 1.0053] sabbathāpi avaṇṇe manopadosaṃ nisedhetvā idāni paṭipajjitabbākāraṃ dassento – “tatra tumhehi abhūtaṃ abhūtato”tiādimāha.

Thus, having in every way forbidden corruption of the mind on account of dispraise, now, showing the manner in which one should conduct oneself, he says the words beginning: 'Therein, by you, what is untrue should be recognized as untrue...'

Tattha tatra tumhehīti, tasmiṃ avaṇṇe tumhehi. Abhūtaṃ abhūtato nibbeṭhetabbanti yaṃ abhūtaṃ, taṃ abhūtabhāveneva [P 1.0053] apanetabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Itipetaṃ abhūtantiādinā nayena. Tatrāyaṃ yojanā – “tumhākaṃ satthā na sabbaññū, dhammo durakkhāto, saṅgho duppaṭipanno”tiādīni sutvā na tuṇhī bhavitabbaṃ. Evaṃ pana vattabbaṃ – “iti petaṃ abhūtaṃ, yaṃ tumhehi vuttaṃ, taṃ imināpi kāraṇena abhūtaṃ, imināpi kāraṇena atacchaṃ, ‘natthi cetaṃ amhesu’, ‘na ca panetaṃ amhesu saṃvijjati’, sabbaññūyeva amhākaṃ satthā, svākkhāto dhammo, suppaṭipanno saṅgho, tatra idañcidañca kāraṇa”nti. Ettha ca dutiyaṃ padaṃ paṭhamassa, catutthañca tatiyassa vevacananti veditabbaṃ. Idañca avaṇṇeyeva nibbeṭhanaṃ kātabbaṃ, na sabbattha. Yadi hi “tvaṃ dussīlo, tavācariyo dussīlo, idañcidañca tayā kataṃ, tavācariyena kata”nti vutte tuṇhībhūto adhivāseti, āsaṅkanīyo hoti. Tasmā manopadosaṃ akatvā avaṇṇo nibbeṭhetabbo. “Oṭṭhosi, goṇosī”tiādinā pana nayena dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosantaṃ puggalaṃ ajjhupekkhitvā adhivāsanakhantiyeva tattha kātabbā.

Herein, 'in that case, by you' means, in that dispraise, by you. 'What is untrue should be refuted as untrue' means that what is untrue should be dispelled by its very nature of being untrue. How? By the method of saying, 'For this reason, this is untrue,' and so on. Herein, this is the application: Having heard statements such as 'Your teacher is not all-knowing, the Dhamma is poorly expounded, the Saṅgha is practicing wrongly,' one should not remain silent. Instead, one should say: 'For this reason, this is untrue; what you have said is untrue for this reason, and false for this reason; ‘This does not exist among us,’ and ‘This is not found among us’; our teacher is indeed all-knowing; the Dhamma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha is practicing rightly; and in that matter, this and that is the reason.' Here, it should be understood that the second term is a synonym for the first, and the fourth for the third. And this refutation should be made only in the case of dispraise, not in all cases. For if, when it is said, 'You are immoral, your teacher is immoral, this and that was done by you, and by your teacher,' one remains silent and endures it, one becomes suspect. Therefore, without creating ill-will of the mind, the dispraise should be refuted. However, toward a person who insults with the ten grounds for abuse by the method of saying, 'You are a camel, you are an ox,' and so on, having regarded them with equanimity, only the patience of endurance should be practiced.

6. Evaṃ avaṇṇabhūmiyaṃ tādilakkhaṇaṃ dassetvā idāni vaṇṇabhūmiyaṃ dassetuṃ “mamaṃ vā, bhikkhave, pare vaṇṇaṃ bhāseyyu”ntiādimāha. Tattha pareti ye keci pasannā devamanussā. Ānandanti etenāti ānando, pītiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sumanassa bhāvo somanassaṃ, cetasikasukhassetaṃ [V 1.0051] adhivacanaṃ. Uppilāvino bhāvo uppilāvitattaṃ. Kassa uppilāvitattanti? Cetasoti. Uddhaccāvahāya uppilāpanapītiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Idhāpi dvīhi padehi saṅkhārakkhandho, ekena vedanākkhandho vutto.

6. Having thus shown the characteristic of one who is 'such' in the domain of dispraise, now, in order to show it in the domain of praise, he says, 'Monks, if others should speak in praise of me...' and so on. Therein, 'others' refers to any devoted devas or humans. 'They rejoice because of this,' thus it is 'ānanda' (joy); this is a designation for pīti (rapture). The state of a good mind is 'somanassa' (gladness); this is a designation for mental happiness. The state of being buoyant is 'uppilāvitattaṃ'. 'Whose uppilāvitattaṃ?' 'Of the mind.' This is a designation for the uplifting rapture that brings about restlessness. Here too, by two terms the aggregate of formations is stated, and by one, the aggregate of feeling.

Evaṃ paṭhamanayena uppilāvitattaṃ nivāretvā, dutiyena tattha ādīnavaṃ dassento – “tatra ce tumhe assathā”tiādimāha. Idhāpi tumhaṃ yevassa tena antarāyoti tena uppilāvitattena tumhākaṃyeva paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ [M 1.0054] antarāyo bhaveyyāti attho veditabbo. Kasmā [P 1.0054] panetaṃ vuttaṃ? Nanu bhagavatā –

Thus, having prevented elation by the first method, and by the second method showing the danger in it, he said, 'And if you were to be...' and so on. Here too, 'it would be an obstacle for you alone' should be understood to mean: because of that elation, there would be an obstacle for you alone to the first jhāna and so forth. But why was this said? Is it not that the Blessed One has praised...

“Buddhoti kittayantassa, kāye bhavati yā pīti;

Varameva hi sā pīti, kasiṇenāpi jambudīpassa.

For one who proclaims 'Buddha,' whatever rapture arises in the body, that rapture is indeed more excellent than the whole of Jambudīpa.

Dhammoti kittayantassa, kāye bhavati yā pīti;

Varameva hi sā pīti, kasiṇenāpi jambudīpassa.

For one who proclaims 'Dhamma,' whatever rapture arises in the body, that rapture is indeed more excellent than the whole of Jambudīpa.

Saṅghoti kittayantassa, kāye bhavati yā pīti;

Varameva hi sā pīti, kasiṇenāpi jambudīpassā”ti ca.

For one who proclaims 'Saṅgha,' whatever rapture arises in the body, that rapture is indeed more excellent than the whole of Jambudīpa.

“Ye, bhikkhave, buddhe pasannā, agge te pasannā”ti ca evamādīhi anekasatehi suttehi ratanattaye pītisomanassameva vaṇṇitanti. Saccaṃ vaṇṇitaṃ, taṃ pana nekkhammanissitaṃ. Idha – “amhākaṃ buddho, amhākaṃ dhammo”tiādinā nayena āyasmato channassa uppannasadisaṃ gehassitaṃ pītisomanassaṃ adhippetaṃ. Idañhi jhānādipaṭilābhāya antarāyakaraṃ hoti. Tenevāyasmā channopi yāva buddho na parinibbāyi, tāva visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhi, parinibbānakāle paññattena pana brahmadaṇḍena tajjito taṃ pītisomanassaṃ pahāya visesaṃ nibbattesi. Tasmā antarāyakaraṃyeva sandhāya idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Ayañhi lobhasahagatā pīti. Lobho ca kodhasadisova. Yathāha –

And by hundreds of suttas such as, 'Monks, those who have confidence in the Buddha have confidence in the foremost,' joy and gladness in the Three Jewels have been praised, have they not? Truly, it is praised. However, that is based on renunciation. Here, joy and gladness associated with the household life, similar to what arose in the Venerable Channa by way of thinking 'Our Buddha, our Dhamma,' etc., is intended. For this is an obstacle to the attainment of jhāna and so on. For that very reason, the Venerable Channa, for as long as the Buddha had not attained Parinibbāna, was unable to bring about a special attainment. But at the time of the Parinibbāna, being threatened by the imposed brahma-penalty, he abandoned that joy and gladness and brought about a special attainment. Therefore, it should be understood that this was said referring only to that which is an obstacle. For this is rapture accompanied by greed. And greed is just like anger. As it was said:

“Luddho atthaṃ na jānāti, luddho dhammaṃ na passati;

Andhaṃ tamaṃ tadā hoti, yaṃ lobho sahate naraṃ.

A greedy person does not know the meaning, a greedy person does not see the Dhamma; blinding darkness there is then, when greed overcomes a person.

Anatthajanano [V 1.0052] lobho, lobho cittappakopano;

Bhayamantarato jātaṃ, taṃ jano nāvabujjhatī”ti. (itivu. 88);

Greed is a generator of harm, greed is a corrupter of the mind; fear is born from within, that, people do not understand.

Tatiyavāro pana idha anāgatopi atthato āgato yevāti veditabbo. Yatheva hi kuddho, evaṃ luddhopi atthaṃ na jānātīti.

However, the third section, though not directly present here, should be understood as having arrived in terms of meaning. For just as an angry person, so too a greedy person does not know the meaning.

Paṭipajjitabbākāradassanavāre panāyaṃ yojanā – “tumhākaṃ satthā sabbaññū arahaṃ sammāsambuddho, dhammo svākkhāto, saṅgho suppaṭipanno”tiādīni sutvā na tuṇhī bhavitabbaṃ. Evaṃ pana paṭijānitabbaṃ – “itipetaṃ bhūtaṃ[M 1.0055], yaṃ tumhehi vuttaṃ, taṃ imināpi kāraṇena bhūtaṃ, imināpi kāraṇena tacchaṃ. So hi bhagavā itipi arahaṃ, itipi sammāsambuddho; dhammo itipi svākkhāto, itipi sandiṭṭhiko[P 1.0055]; saṅgho itipi suppaṭipanno, itipi ujuppaṭipanno”ti. “Tvaṃ sīlavā”ti pucchitenāpi sace sīlavā, “sīlavāhamasmī”ti paṭijānitabbameva. “Tvaṃ paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhī…pe… arahā”ti puṭṭhenāpi sabhāgānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃyeva paṭijānitabbaṃ. Evañhi pāpicchatā ceva parivajjitā hoti, sāsanassa ca amoghatā dīpitā hotīti. Sesaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Now, in the section showing the manner in which one should practice, this is the application: Having heard such things as, 'Your teacher is all-knowing, an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One; the Dhamma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha is practicing well,' one should not be silent. Rather, it should be acknowledged thus: 'For this reason, this is true. What you have said, for this reason it is true, for this reason it is factual. For that Blessed One is an Arahant for this reason, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One for this reason; the Dhamma is well-expounded for this reason, directly visible for this reason; the Saṅgha is practicing well for this reason, practicing uprightly for this reason.' Even when asked, 'Are you virtuous?', if one is virtuous, one should indeed acknowledge, 'I am virtuous.' When asked, 'Are you an attainer of the first jhāna… an Arahant?', one should acknowledge it only to monks of a similar standing. For in this way, having evil wishes is avoided, and the non-futility of the Dispensation is shown. The remainder should be understood in the way already stated.

Cūḷasīlavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Minor Morality

7. Appamattakaṃ kho panetaṃ, bhikkhaveti ko anusandhi? Idaṃ suttaṃ dvīhi padehi ābaddhaṃ vaṇṇena ca avaṇṇena ca. Tattha avaṇṇo – “iti petaṃ abhūtaṃ iti petaṃ ataccha”nti, ettheva udakantaṃ patvā aggiviya nivatto. Vaṇṇo pana bhūtaṃ bhūtato paṭijānitabbaṃ – “iti petaṃ bhūta”nti evaṃ anuvattatiyeva. So pana duvidho brahmadattena bhāsitavaṇṇo ca bhikkhusaṅghena acchariyaṃ āvusotiādinā nayena āraddhavaṇṇo ca. Tesu bhikkhusaṅghena vuttavaṇṇassa upari suññatāpakāsane anusandhiṃ dassessati. Idha pana brahmadattena vuttavaṇṇassa anusandhiṃ dassetuṃ “appamattakaṃ kho panetaṃ, bhikkhave”ti desanā āraddhā.

7. With regard to the passage, “But this, bhikkhus, is a small matter,” what is the connection? This discourse is bound by two aspects: praise and dispraise. Therein, dispraise—expressed as, “This is false, this is untrue”—comes to a stop right there, like a fire that has receded upon reaching the water’s edge. Praise, however, acknowledging what is true as true—“This is true”—continues on. This praise is twofold: the praise spoken by Brahmadatta and the praise initiated by the Sangha of bhikkhus with the words, “Wonderful, venerable sirs!” and so on. Of these, the connection to the praise spoken by the Sangha of bhikkhus will be shown later in the section that clarifies emptiness. Here, however, to show the connection to the praise spoken by Brahmadatta, the discourse was begun with, “But this, bhikkhus, is a small matter.”

Tattha appamattakanti parittassa nāmaṃ. Oramattakanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Mattāti vuccati pamāṇaṃ. Appaṃ mattā etassāti appamattakaṃ. Oraṃ mattā etassāti oramattakaṃ. Sīlameva sīlamattakaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ‘appamattakaṃ kho, panetaṃ bhikkhave, oramattakaṃ sīlamattakaṃ’ nāma [V 1.0053] yena “tathāgatassa vaṇṇaṃ vadāmī”ti ussāhaṃ katvāpi vaṇṇaṃ vadamāno puthujjano vadeyyāti. Tattha siyā – nanu idaṃ sīlaṃ nāma yogino aggavibhūsanaṃ? Yathāhu porāṇā –

Therein, ‘a small matter’ (appamattaka) is a name for what is minor. ‘An inferior matter’ (oramattaka) is a synonym for it. The word `mattā` means measure (`pamāṇa`). Its measure is small (appā mattā etassa), thus it is ‘a small matter’ (appamattaka). Its measure is inferior (oraṃ mattā etassa), thus it is ‘an inferior matter’ (oramattaka). Virtue itself is ‘a matter of mere virtue’ (sīlamattaka). This is what is meant: ‘Indeed, bhikkhus, this is called a small matter, an inferior matter, a matter of mere virtue,’ by which an ordinary person, even after making an effort, might speak praise, saying, “I will speak in praise of the Tathāgata.” Therein, it might be objected: Is not this, which is called virtue, the supreme adornment of a yogī? As the ancients have said:

“Sīlaṃ yogissa’laṅkāro, sīlaṃ yogissa maṇḍanaṃ;

Sīlehi’laṅkato yogī, maṇḍane aggataṃ gato”ti.

“Virtue is the yogī’s ornament, virtue is the yogī’s adornment; adorned with virtues, the yogī, through this adornment, has reached supremacy.”

Bhagavatāpi [M 1.0056] ca anekesu suttasatesu sīlaṃ mahantameva katvā kathitaṃ. Yathāha – “ākaṅkheyya ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu [P 1.0056] ‘sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyo cassaṃ manāpo ca garu ca bhāvanīyo cā’ti, sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī”ti (ma. ni. 1.65) ca.

And by the Blessed One, too, in many hundreds of suttas, virtue has been taught as something great. As he said: “If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should wish, ‘May I be dear and agreeable to my companions in the holy life, respected and esteemed,’ he should be one who fulfills the virtues.”

“Kikīva aṇḍaṃ, camarīva vāladhiṃ;

Piyaṃva puttaṃ, nayanaṃva ekakaṃ.

Tatheva sīlaṃ, anurakkhamānā;

Supesalā hotha, sadā sagāravā”ti ca.

“Just as the hen guards her egg, or the yak her tail; as a mother her beloved son, or a man his only eye; in that same way, guarding virtue, may you be of excellent conduct, always respectful.”

“Na pupphagandho paṭivātameti;

Na candanaṃ taggaramallikā vā.

Satañca gandho paṭivātameti;

Sabbā disā sappuriso pavāyati.

“The scent of flowers does not travel against the wind, nor that of sandalwood, tagara, or jasmine. But the scent of the virtuous travels against the wind; the good person pervades all directions.”

Candanaṃ tagaraṃ vāpi, uppalaṃ atha vassikī;

Etesaṃ gandhajātānaṃ, sīlagandho anuttaro.

“Sandalwood or tagara, lotus or jasmine—among these kinds of fragrances, the fragrance of virtue is supreme.”

Appamatto ayaṃ gandho, yvāyaṃ tagaracandanaṃ;

Yo ca sīlavataṃ gandho, vāti devesu uttamo.

“Insignificant is this fragrance of tagara and sandalwood; but the fragrance of the virtuous, wafting among the gods, is supreme.”

Tesaṃ sampannasīlānaṃ, appamādavihārinaṃ;

Sammadaññā vimuttānaṃ, māro maggaṃ na vindatī”ti ca. (dha. pa. 57);

“Of those possessed of perfect virtue, who dwell heedfully, liberated through right understanding, Māra does not find the path.”

“Sīle [V 1.0054] patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño, cittaṃ paññañca bhāvayaṃ;

Ātāpī nipako bhikkhu, so imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭa”nti ca. (saṃ. ni. 1.23);

“Established in virtue, a wise person, developing mind and wisdom, ardent and discerning—that bhikkhu can untangle this tangle.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, ye keci bījagāmabhūtagāmā vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjanti, sabbe te pathaviṃ nissāya, pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāya; evamete bījagāmabhūtagāmā vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjanti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sīlaṃ nissāya sīle patiṭṭhāya sattabojjhaṅge bhāvento sattabojjhaṅge bahulīkaronto vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ pāpuṇāti dhammesū”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.150) ca. Evaṃ aññānipi anekāni suttāni daṭṭhabbāni. Evamanekesu suttasatesu sīlaṃ mahantameva katvā kathitaṃ. Taṃ “kasmā [M 1.0057] imasmiṃ ṭhāne appamattaka”nti āhāti? Upari [P 1.0057] guṇe upanidhāya. Sīlañhi samādhiṃ na pāpuṇāti, samādhi paññaṃ na pāpuṇāti, tasmā uparimaṃ upanidhāya heṭṭhimaṃ oramattakaṃ nāma hoti. Kathaṃ sīlaṃ samādhiṃ na pāpuṇāti? Bhagavā hi abhisambodhito sattame saṃvacchare sāvatthinagara – dvāre kaṇḍambarukkhamūle dvādasayojane ratanamaṇḍape yojanappamāṇe ratanapallaṅke nisīditvā tiyojanike dibbasetacchatte dhāriyamāne dvādasayojanāya parisāya attādānaparidīpanaṃ titthiyamaddanaṃ – “uparimakāyato aggikkhandho pavattati, heṭṭhimakāyato udakadhārā pavattati…pe… ekekalomakūpato aggikkhandho pavattati, ekekalomakūpato udakadhārā pavattati, channaṃ vaṇṇāna”ntiādinayappavattaṃ yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ dasseti. Tassa suvaṇṇavaṇṇasarīrato suvaṇṇavaṇṇā rasmiyo uggantvā yāva bhavaggā gacchanti, sakaladasasahassacakkavāḷassa alaṅkaraṇakālo viya hoti, dutiyā dutiyā rasmiyo purimāya purimāya yamakayamakā viya ekakkhaṇe viya pavattanti.

“Just as, bhikkhus, whatever seed-based and plant-based life attains growth, increase, and fullness, all of them do so by relying on the earth, by being established on the earth; in this way, this seed-based and plant-based life attains growth, increase, and fullness. So too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, by relying on virtue, by being established in virtue, developing the seven factors of enlightenment, cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment, attains growth, increase, and fullness in the teachings.” In this way, many other suttas should also be seen. Thus, in many hundreds of suttas, virtue has been taught as something great. Why, then, in this place, did he say it is “a small matter”? By comparison with the higher qualities. For virtue does not reach concentration, and concentration does not reach wisdom. Therefore, by comparison with what is higher, what is lower is called ‘an inferior matter.’ How is it that virtue does not reach concentration?
