In the seventh year after his full enlightenment, the Blessed One, at the gate of Sāvatthī, at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree, sitting on a jewel throne one yojana in size within a jewel pavilion of twelve yojanas, while a divine white canopy of three yojanas was being held over him, displayed the Twin Miracle to an assembly of twelve yojanas—a demonstration of his own power and a subjugation of the sectarians—which proceeded in this way: “From the upper part of his body a mass of fire issued forth, from the lower part of his body a stream of water issued forth… from each and every hair-pore a mass of fire issued forth, from each and every hair-pore a stream of water issued forth, of six colors.” From his golden-hued body, golden-hued rays arose and went as far as the peak of existence. It was as if it were a time of adornment for the entire ten-thousandfold world system. The succeeding rays followed the preceding ones like pairs, appearing as if in a single moment.

Dvinnañca cittānaṃ ekakkhaṇe pavatti nāma natthi. Buddhānaṃ pana bhagavantānaṃ bhavaṅgaparivāsassa lahukatāya pañcahākārehi āciṇṇavasitāya ca, tā ekakkhaṇe viya pavattanti. Tassā tassā pana rasmiyā āvajjanaparikammādhiṭṭhānāni visuṃ visuṃyeva.

And there is no such thing as the arising of two minds in a single moment. But for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, due to the swiftness of the bhavaṅga’s process and their mastery perfected in five ways, those rays arise as if in a single moment. For each and every ray, however, the adverting, preliminary action, and determination are indeed distinct.

Nīlarasmiatthāya hi bhagavā nīlakasiṇaṃ samāpajjati, pītarasmiatthāya pītakasiṇaṃ, lohitaodātarasmiatthāya lohitaodātakasiṇaṃ, aggikkhandhatthāya tejokasiṇaṃ, udakadhāratthāya āpokasiṇaṃ samāpajjati. Satthā caṅkamati, nimmito tiṭṭhati vā nisīdati vā seyyaṃ vā kappetīti [V 1.0055] sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Ettha ekampi sīlassa kiccaṃ natthi, sabbaṃ samādhikiccameva. Evaṃ sīlaṃ samādhiṃ na pāpuṇāti.

Indeed, for the sake of the blue radiance, the Blessed One attains the absorption on the blue kasiṇa; for the sake of the golden radiance, the absorption on the yellow kasiṇa; for the sake of the red and white radiances, the absorptions on the red and white kasiṇas; for the sake of a mass of fire, the absorption on the fire kasiṇa; for the sake of a stream of water, he attains the absorption on the water kasiṇa. The Teacher walks, while the created image stands, or sits, or assumes a reclining posture—all this should be elaborated. Herein, there is not even one function of virtue; all is solely the function of concentration. Thus, virtue does not attain to concentration.

Yaṃ pana bhagavā kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni pāramiyo pūretvā, ekūnatiṃsavassakāle cakkavattisirīnivāsabhūtā bhavanā nikkhamma anomānadītīre [P 1.0058] pabbajitvā, chabbassāni padhānayogaṃ katvā, visākhapuṇṇamāyaṃ uruvelagāme sujātāya dinnaṃ pakkhittadibbojaṃ madhupāyāsaṃ paribhuñjitvā, sāyanhasamaye dakkhiṇuttarena bodhimaṇḍaṃ pavisitvā [M 1.0058] assatthadumarājānaṃ tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā, pubbuttarabhāge ṭhito tiṇasanthāraṃ santharitvā, tisandhipallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā, caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ mettākammaṭṭhānaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā, vīriyādhiṭṭhānaṃ adhiṭṭhāya, cuddasahatthapallaṅkavaragato suvaṇṇapīṭhe ṭhapitaṃ rajatakkhandhaṃ viya paññāsahatthaṃ bodhikkhandhaṃ piṭṭhito katvā, upari maṇichattena viya bodhisākhāya dhāriyamāno, suvaṇṇavaṇṇe cīvare pavāḷasadisesu bodhiaṅkuresu patamānesu, sūriye atthaṃ upagacchante mārabalaṃ vidhamitvā, paṭhamayāme pubbenivāsaṃ anussaritvā, majjhimayāme dibbacakkhuṃ visodhetvā, paccūsakāle sabbabuddhānamāciṇṇe paccayākāre ñāṇaṃ otāretvā, ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā, tadeva pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā, maggapaṭipāṭiyā adhigatena catutthamaggena sabbakilese khepetvā sabbabuddhaguṇe paṭivijjhi, idamassa paññākiccaṃ. Evaṃ samādhi paññaṃ na pāpuṇāti.

But the Blessed One, having fulfilled the perfections for four incalculables and over one hundred thousand eons; at the age of twenty-nine, having gone forth from the palace that was the abode of the majesty of a universal monarch and taken ordination on the bank of the Anomā river; having practiced the noble striving for six years; on the full moon day of Visākha, in the village of Uruvelā, having partaken of the milk-rice with divine essence added, offered by Sujātā; in the evening, having entered the Bodhimaṇḍa by the south-north path, having circumambulated the king of Assattha trees three times; standing in the north-eastern quarter, having spread the grass mat; having formed the cross-legged posture with three joints; having made the loving-kindness meditation, endowed with four factors, the forerunner; having made the resolution of energy; seated on the excellent throne of fourteen cubits, having placed the fifty-cubit Bodhi trunk behind him like a silver trunk placed on a golden seat; being sheltered by the Bodhi branch above as if by a jeweled parasol; while the coral-like Bodhi shoots were falling upon his golden-hued robe; as the sun was setting, having dispersed the force of Māra; in the first watch, having recollected past existences; in the middle watch, having purified the divine eye; at dawn, having directed his knowledge to the mode of conditions practiced by all Buddhas; having produced the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing, and making just that the basis, having developed insight; by means of the fourth path attained in due succession of the paths, having exhausted all defilements, he penetrated all the qualities of a Buddha—this is his function of wisdom. Thus, concentration does not attain to wisdom.

Tattha yathā hatthe udakaṃ pātiyaṃ udakaṃ na pāpuṇāti, pātiyaṃ udakaṃ ghaṭe udakaṃ na pāpuṇāti, ghaṭe udakaṃ kolambe udakaṃ na pāpuṇāti, kolambe udakaṃ cāṭiyaṃ udakaṃ na pāpuṇāti, cāṭiyaṃ udakaṃ mahākumbhiyaṃ udakaṃ na pāpuṇāti, mahākumbhiyaṃ udakaṃ kusobbhe udakaṃ na pāpuṇāti, kusobbhe udakaṃ kandare udakaṃ na pāpuṇāti, kandare udakaṃ kunnadiyaṃ udakaṃ na pāpuṇāti, kunnadiyaṃ udakaṃ pañcamahānadiyaṃ udakaṃ na pāpuṇāti, pañcamahānadiyaṃ udakaṃ cakkavāḷamahāsamudde [P 1.0059] udakaṃ na pāpuṇāti, cakkavāḷamahāsamudde udakaṃ sinerupādake mahāsamudde udakaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Pātiyaṃ udakaṃ upanidhāya hatthe udakaṃ parittaṃ…pe… sinerupādakamahāsamudde udakaṃ upanidhāya cakkavāḷamahāsamudde udakaṃ parittaṃ. Iti uparūpari udakaṃ bahukaṃ upādāya heṭṭhā heṭṭhā udakaṃ parittaṃ hoti.

Herein, it is as when the water in the hand does not attain to the water in a drinking bowl; the water in a drinking bowl does not attain to the water in a water pot; the water in a water pot does not attain to the water in a cooking pot; the water in a cooking pot does not attain to the water in a large jar; the water in a large jar does not attain to the water in a large water-storage jar; the water in a large water-storage jar does not attain to the water in a pond; the water in a pond does not attain to the water in a mountain gorge; the water in a mountain gorge does not attain to the water in a small river; the water in a small river does not attain to the water of the five great rivers; the water of the five great rivers does not attain to the water in the Cakkavāḷa great ocean; the water in the Cakkavāḷa great ocean does not attain to the water in the great ocean at the foot of Sineru. Compared to the water in a drinking bowl, the water in the hand is little… (and so on until) … Compared to the water in the great ocean at the foot of Sineru, the water in the Cakkavāḷa great ocean is little. Thus, by considering the water in each higher level as abundant, the water in each lower level is little.

Evameva upari upari guṇe upādāya heṭṭhā heṭṭhā sīlaṃ appamattakaṃ oramattakanti veditabbaṃ. Tenāha – “appamattakaṃ kho panetaṃ, bhikkhave, oramattakaṃ sīlamattaka”nti.

In this very same way, by considering the higher and higher qualities, virtue at the lower and lower levels should be understood as of small measure and of inferior measure. Therefore, he said: ‘Monks, this is of small measure, of inferior measure, a mere matter of virtue.’

Yena [V 1.0056] puthujjanoti, ettha –

Regarding the phrase ‘yena puthujjanoti’ (by which an ordinary person):

“Duve puthujjanā vuttā, buddhenādiccabandhunā;

Andho puthujjano eko, kalyāṇeko puthujjano”ti.

‘Two ordinary persons are spoken of by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun: one is the blind ordinary person, the other is the good ordinary person.’

Tattha [M 1.0059] yassa khandhadhātuāyatanādīsu uggahaparipucchāsavanadhāraṇapaccavekkhaṇāni natthi, ayaṃ andhaputhujjano. Yassa tāni atthi, so kalyāṇaputhujjano. Duvidhopi panesa –

Among these, the one for whom there is no learning, repeated questioning, hearing, retaining, or reflecting upon the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and so forth, this is the blind ordinary person. The one for whom these exist, that is the good ordinary person. Furthermore, both kinds of these:

“Puthūnaṃ jananādīhi, kāraṇehi puthujjano;

Puthujjanantogadhattā, puthuvāyaṃ jano iti”.

‘One is an ordinary person (puthujjano) because of causes such as generating (janana) many (puthu) things; because of being included among the multitude of ordinary people; or because this person (jano) is separate (puthu).’

So hi puthūnaṃ nānappakārānaṃ kilesādīnaṃ jananādīhi kāraṇehi puthujjano. Yathāha –

For that person is an ordinary person because of causes such as generating many various kinds of defilements and so on. As it is said:

“Puthu kilese janentīti puthujjanā, puthu avihatasakkāyadiṭṭhikāti puthujjanā, puthu satthārānaṃ mukhullokikāti puthujjanā, puthu sabbagatīhi avuṭṭhitāti puthujjanā, puthu nānābhisaṅkhāre abhisaṅkharontīti puthujjanā, puthu nānāoghehi vuyhanti, puthu santāpehi santappanti, puthu pariḷāhehi pariḍayhanti, puthu pañcasu kāmaguṇesu rattā giddhā gathitā mucchitā ajjhopannā laggā laggitā palibuddhāti puthujjanā, puthu pañcahi nīvaraṇehi āvutā nivutā ovutā pihitā paṭicchannā paṭikujjitāti puthujjanā”ti. Puthūnaṃ gaṇanapathamatītānaṃ ariyadhammaparammukhānaṃ nīcadhammasamācārānaṃ janānaṃ antogadhattāpi puthujjano, puthuvāyaṃ visuṃyeva saṅkhyaṃ gato visaṃsaṭṭho sīlasutādiguṇayuttehi ariyehi janehīti puthujjanoti.

‘They are called ordinary persons (puthujjanā) because they generate many (puthu) defilements. They are ordinary persons because they have many unabandoned personality views. They are ordinary persons because they look up to the faces of many teachers. They are ordinary persons because they have not risen out of all destinations. They are ordinary persons because they form many and various formations. They are swept away by many and various floods; they are tormented by many and various fevers; they are consumed by many and various blazes. They are ordinary persons because, regarding the five cords of sensual pleasure, they are impassioned, greedy, tied, infatuated, engulfed, clinging, stuck, and ensnared. They are ordinary persons because they are obstructed, hindered, enmeshed, shut in, covered over, and overturned by the five hindrances.’ Or, one is an ordinary person because of being included among the many people who are beyond the path of reckoning, who have turned their faces from the noble Dhamma, and who practice low conduct. Or, this person is called an ordinary person because he is counted as separate (puthu), distinct, and unmixed with the noble people who are endowed with the qualities of virtue, learning, and so on.

Tathāgatassāti aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi bhagavā tathāgato. Tathā āgatoti tathāgato, tathā gatoti tathāgato, tathalakkhaṇaṃ [P 1.0060] āgatoti tathāgato, tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddhoti tathāgato, tathadassitāya tathāgato, tathavāditāya tathāgato, tathākāritāya tathāgato, abhibhavanaṭṭhena tathāgatoti.

Regarding ‘Tathāgatassa’: The Blessed One is the Tathāgata for eight reasons. He has ‘come thus’ (tathā āgato); he has ‘gone thus’ (tathā gato); he has ‘arrived at the true characteristic’ (tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgato); he has ‘fully understood the true dhammas as they really are’ (tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddho); because of ‘seeing what is true’ (tathadassitāya); because of ‘speaking what is true’ (tathavāditāya); because of ‘doing what is true’ (tathākāritāya); and in the sense of ‘overcoming’ (abhibhavanaṭṭhena).

Kathaṃ bhagavā tathā āgatoti tathāgato? Yathā sabbalokahitāya ussukkamāpannā purimakā sammāsambuddhā āgatā, yathā vipassī bhagavā āgato, yathā sikhī bhagavā, yathā vessabhū bhagavā, yathā kakusandho bhagavā, yathā koṇāgamano bhagavā, yathā kassapo bhagavā āgato[V 1.0057]. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yena abhinīhārena ete [M 1.0060] bhagavanto āgatā, teneva amhākampi bhagavā āgato. Atha vā yathā vipassī bhagavā…pe… yathā kassapo bhagavā dānapāramiṃ pūretvā, sīlanekkhammapaññāvīriyakhantisaccaadhiṭṭhānamettāupekkhāpāramiṃ pūretvā, imā dasa pāramiyo, dasa upapāramiyo, dasa paramatthapāramiyoti samatiṃsapāramiyo pūretvā aṅgapariccāgaṃ, nayanadhanarajjaputtadārapariccāganti ime pañca mahāpariccāge pariccajitvā pubbayogapubbacariyadhammakkhānañātatthacariyādayo pūretvā buddhicariyāya koṭiṃ patvā āgato; tathā amhākampi bhagavā āgato. Atha vā yathā vipassī bhagavā…pe… kassapo bhagavā cattāro satipaṭṭhāne, cattāro sammappadhāne, cattāro iddhipāde, pañcindriyāni, pañca balāni, satta bojjhaṅge, ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bhāvetvā brūhetvā āgato, tathā amhākampi bhagavā āgato. Evaṃ tathā āgatoti tathāgato.

How is the Blessed One a Tathāgata, one who has thus come? Just as the former Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones, who had undertaken exertion for the welfare of the entire world, came; just as the Blessed One Vipassī came, as the Blessed One Sikhī, as the Blessed One Vessabhū, as the Blessed One Kakusandha, as the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, as the Blessed One Kassapa came. What is meant by this? By whichever aspiration those Blessed Ones came, by that very same aspiration our Blessed One also came. Or else, just as the Blessed One Vipassī… up to the Blessed One Kassapa, having fulfilled the perfection of generosity, having fulfilled the perfections of morality, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity—these ten perfections, ten secondary perfections, and ten ultimate perfections, thus fulfilling thirty perfections; having made the five great relinquishments: the relinquishment of limbs, of eyes, wealth, kingdom, and children and wife; having fulfilled prior striving, prior conduct, the expounding of the Dhamma, conduct for the welfare of relatives, and so forth, and having reached the culmination of the conduct of a Buddha, he came; in that same way, our Blessed One also came. Or else, just as the Blessed One Vipassī… up to the Blessed One Kassapa, having developed and cultivated the four establishments of mindfulness, the four right strivings, the four bases of spiritual power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path, came; in that same way, our Blessed One also came. Thus, having thus come, he is the Tathāgata.

“Yatheva lokamhi vipassiādayo,

Sabbaññubhāvaṃ munayo idhāgatā;

Tathā ayaṃ sakyamunīpi āgato,

Tathāgato vuccati tena cakkhumā”ti.

Just as in this world Vipassī and other sages arrived at the state of omniscience; in that same way this Sakyan sage has also arrived. Therefore, the One with Vision is called Tathāgata.

Evaṃ tathā āgatoti tathāgato.

Thus, having thus come, he is the Tathāgata.

Kathaṃ tathā gatoti tathāgato? Yathā sampatijāto vipassī bhagavā gato…pe… kassapo bhagavā gato.

How, having thus gone, is he the Tathāgata? Just as the Blessed One Vipassī, immediately upon birth, went… up to… as the Blessed One Kassapa went.

Kathañca so bhagavā gato[P 1.0061]? So hi sampati jātova samehi pādehi pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāya uttarābhimukho sattapadavītihārena gato. Yathāha – “sampatijāto kho, ānanda, bodhisatto samehi pādehi patiṭṭhahitvā uttarābhimukho sattapadavītihārena gacchati, setamhi chatte anudhāriyamāne sabbā ca disā anuviloketi, āsabhiṃ vācaṃ bhāsati – ‘aggohamasmi lokassa, jeṭṭhohamasmi lokassa, seṭṭhohamasmi lokassa, ayamantimā jāti, natthidāni punabbhavo’ti” (dī. ni. 2.31).

And in what manner did that Blessed One go? For he, immediately upon birth, having stood on the earth with even feet, facing north, went with a stride of seven steps. As it is said: ‘Ānanda, immediately upon birth, the Bodhisatta, having stood with even feet, goes with a stride of seven steps facing north, while a white parasol is being held over him. He surveys all the directions and utters a bull-like utterance: “I am the foremost of the world, I am the eldest of the world, I am the supreme of the world. This is the last birth. Now there is no renewed existence.”’

Tañcassa [M 1.0061] gamanaṃ tathaṃ ahosi? Avitathaṃ anekesaṃ visesādhigamānaṃ pubbanimittabhāvena. Yañhi [V 1.0058] so sampatijātova samehi pādehi patiṭṭhahi. Idamassa caturiddhipādapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ.

And that going of his was true and not false, by being a forerunner to the attainment of many distinctions. For that he stood with even feet immediately upon birth, this was a forerunner of his attainment of the four bases of spiritual power.

Uttarābhimukhabhāvo pana sabbalokuttarabhāvassa pubbanimittaṃ.

The state of facing north, however, was a forerunner of the state of being supreme over the entire world.

Sattapadavītihāro, sattabojjhaṅgaratanapaṭilābhassa.

The stride of seven steps was a forerunner of the attainment of the seven jewel-like factors of enlightenment.

“Suvaṇṇadaṇḍā vītipatanti cāmarā”ti, ettha vuttacāmarukkhepo pana sabbatitthiyanimmaddanassa.

In the phrase, ‘Chowries with golden handles are waved to and fro,’ the waving of the chowries mentioned therein was a forerunner of the subduing of all sectarians.

Setacchattadhāraṇaṃ, arahattavimuttivaravimalasetacchattapaṭilābhassa.

The holding of the white parasol was a forerunner of the attainment of the supreme, stainless white parasol of the liberation of Arahantship.

Sattamapadūpari ṭhatvā sabbadisānuvilokanaṃ, sabbaññutānāvaraṇañāṇapaṭilābhassa.

Standing upon the seventh step and surveying all directions was a forerunner of the attainment of the unobstructed knowledge that is omniscience.

Āsabhivācābhāsanaṃ appaṭivattiyavaradhammacakkappavattanassa pubbanimittaṃ.

The uttering of the bull-like speech was a forerunner of the setting in motion of the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, which cannot be turned back.

Tathā ayaṃ bhagavāpi gato, tañcassa gamanaṃ tathaṃ ahosi, avitathaṃ, tesaṃyeva visesādhigamānaṃ pubbanimittabhāvena.

In that manner, this Blessed One also went, and that going of his was true, not false, by being a forerunner of the attainment of those very same distinctions.

Tenāhu porāṇā –

Therefore the ancients have said:

“Muhuttajātova gavampatī yathā,

Samehi pādehi phusī vasundharaṃ;

So vikkamī satta padāni gotamo,

Setañca chattaṃ anudhārayuṃ marū.

‘Just as a lord of cattle, immediately upon birth, touches the earth with even feet; so Gotama strode seven steps, and the gods held up a white parasol over him.

Gantvāna so satta padāni gotamo,

Disā vilokesi samā samantato;

Aṭṭhaṅgupetaṃ giramabbhudīrayi,

Sīho yathā pabbatamuddhaniṭṭhito”ti.

Having gone seven steps, that Gotama surveyed the directions all around; he uttered speech endowed with eight factors, just as a lion standing on a mountain peak.’

Evaṃ [V 1.0059] tathā gatoti tathāgato.

Thus, having thus gone, he is the Tathāgata.

Atha vā yathā vipassī bhagavā…pe… yathā kassapo bhagavā, ayampi bhagavā tatheva nekkhammena kāmacchandaṃ pahāya gato[P 1.0062], abyāpādena byāpādaṃ, ālokasaññāya thinamiddhaṃ, avikkhepena uddhaccakukkuccaṃ, dhammavavatthānena vicikicchaṃ pahāya ñāṇena avijjaṃ padāletvā, pāmojjena [M 1.0062] aratiṃ vinodetvā, paṭhamajjhānena nīvaraṇakavāṭaṃ ugghāṭetvā, dutiyajjhānena vitakkavicāraṃ vūpasametvā, tatiyajjhānena pītiṃ virājetvā, catutthajjhānena sukhadukkhaṃ pahāya, ākāsānañcāyatanasamāpattiyā rūpasaññāpaṭighasaññānānattasaññāyo samatikkamitvā, viññāṇañcāyatanasamāpattiyā ākāsānañcāyatanasaññaṃ, ākiñcaññāyatanasamāpattiyā viññāṇañcāyatanasaññaṃ, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiyā ākiñcaññāyatanasaññaṃ samatikkamitvā gato.

Or else, just as the Blessed One Vipassī… up to… just as the Blessed One Kassapa, this Blessed One also, in that very same way, by means of renunciation, having abandoned sensual desire, has gone; by non-ill will, having abandoned ill will; by the perception of light, having abandoned sloth and torpor; by non-distraction, having abandoned restlessness and remorse; by the determination of phenomena, having abandoned doubt; by knowledge, having broken through ignorance; by gladness, having dispelled discontent; by the first jhāna, having opened the door-leaf of the hindrances; by the second jhāna, having stilled applied and sustained thought; by the third jhāna, having become dispassionate towards rapture; by the fourth jhāna, having abandoned pleasure and pain; by the attainment of the base of infinite space, having transcended perceptions of form, perceptions of resistance, and perceptions of diversity; by the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness, having transcended the perception of the base of infinite space; by the attainment of the base of nothingness, having transcended the perception of the base of infinite consciousness; by the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, having transcended the perception of the base of nothingness, he has gone.

Aniccānupassanāya niccasaññaṃ pahāya, dukkhānupassanāya sukhasaññaṃ, anattānupassanāya attasaññaṃ, nibbidānupassanāya nandiṃ, virāgānupassanāya rāgaṃ, nirodhānupassanāya samudayaṃ, paṭinissaggānupassanāya ādānaṃ, khayānupassanāya ghanasaññaṃ, vayānupassanāya āyūhanaṃ, vipariṇāmānupassanāya dhuvasaññaṃ, animittānupassanāya nimittaṃ, appaṇihitānupassanāya paṇidhiṃ, suññatānupassanāya abhinivesaṃ, adhipaññādhammavipassanāya sārādānābhinivesaṃ, yathābhūtañāṇadassanena sammohābhinivesaṃ, ādīnavānupassanāya ālayābhinivesaṃ, paṭisaṅkhānupassanāya appaṭisaṅkhaṃ, vivaṭṭānupassanāya saṃyogābhinivesaṃ, sotāpattimaggena diṭṭhekaṭṭhe kilese bhañjitvā, sakadāgāmimaggena oḷārike kilese pahāya, anāgāmimaggena aṇusahagate kilese samugghāṭetvā, arahattamaggena sabbakilese samucchinditvā gato. Evampi tathā gatoti tathāgato.

By contemplation of impermanence, having abandoned the perception of permanence; by contemplation of suffering, the perception of pleasure; by contemplation of not-self, the perception of self; by contemplation of weariness, delight; by contemplation of dispassion, passion; by contemplation of cessation, arising; by contemplation of relinquishment, grasping; by contemplation of destruction, the perception of compactness; by contemplation of passing away, accumulation; by contemplation of alteration, the perception of stability; by contemplation of the signless, the sign; by contemplation of the desireless, longing; by contemplation of emptiness, tenacious adherence; by insight into phenomena with higher wisdom, tenacious adherence to grasping the essenceless as essential; by the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are, tenacious adherence born of delusion; by contemplation of danger, tenacious adherence to things as a resort; by contemplation with reflection, the absence of reflection; by contemplation of turning away, tenacious adherence to connections; by the path of stream-entry, having destroyed the defilements that are of a single lot with wrong view; by the path of once-returning, having abandoned the gross defilements; by the path of non-returning, having uprooted the subtle defilements; by the path of Arahantship, having cut off all defilements, he has gone. In this way too, because he has ‘Thus Gone,’ he is the Tathāgata.

Kathaṃ tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgatoti tathāgato?Pathavīdhātuyā kakkhaḷattalakkhaṇaṃ tathaṃ avitathaṃ. Āpodhātuyā paggharaṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Tejodhātuyā uṇhattalakkhaṇaṃ. Vāyodhātuyā vitthambhanalakkhaṇaṃ. Ākāsadhātuyā asamphuṭṭhalakkhaṇaṃ. Viññāṇadhātuyā vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ.

How is it that because he has come to the true characteristic, he is the Tathāgata? The characteristic of the earth element, which is the state of hardness, is true, not untrue. The characteristic of the water element is flowing. The characteristic of the fire element is the state of heat. The characteristic of the wind element is stiffening. The characteristic of the space element is the state of being untouched. The characteristic of the consciousness element is cognizing.

Rūpassa [P 1.0063] ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ. Vedanāya vedayitalakkhaṇaṃ. Saññāya sañjānanalakkhaṇaṃ. Saṅkhārānaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Viññāṇassa vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ.

The characteristic of form is alteration. The characteristic of feeling is experiencing. The characteristic of formations is constructing. The characteristic of consciousness is cognizing.

Vitakkassa [V 1.0060][M 1.0063] abhiniropanalakkhaṇaṃ. Vicārassa anumajjanalakkhaṇaṃ pītiyā pharaṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Sukhassa sātalakkhaṇaṃ. Cittekaggatāya avikkhepalakkhaṇaṃ. Phassassa phusanalakkhaṇaṃ.

The characteristic of applied thought is directing towards the object. The characteristic of sustained thought is repeatedly examining the object. The characteristic of rapture is pervading. The characteristic of pleasure is pleasantness. The characteristic of one-pointedness of mind is non-distraction. The characteristic of contact is touching.

Saddhindriyassa adhimokkhalakkhaṇaṃ. Vīriyindriyassa paggahalakkhaṇaṃ. Satindriyassa upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ. Samādhindriyassa avikkhepalakkhaṇaṃ. Paññindriyassa pajānanalakkhaṇaṃ.

The characteristic of the faith faculty is resolving. The characteristic of the energy faculty is uplifting. The characteristic of the mindfulness faculty is establishing. The characteristic of the concentration faculty is non-distraction. The characteristic of the wisdom faculty is knowing distinctly.

Saddhābalassa assaddhiye akampiyalakkhaṇaṃ. Vīriyabalassa kosajje, satibalassa muṭṭhassacce. Samādhibalassa uddhacce, paññābalassa avijjāya akampiyalakkhaṇaṃ.

The power of faith has the characteristic of being unshakable by faithlessness. The power of energy, by laziness. The power of mindfulness, by forgetfulness. The power of concentration, by restlessness. The power of wisdom has the characteristic of being unshakable by ignorance.

Satisambojjhaṅgassa upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ. Dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa pavicayalakkhaṇaṃ. Vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa paggahalakkhaṇaṃ. Pītisambojjhaṅgassa pharaṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa vūpasamalakkhaṇaṃ. Samādhisambojjhaṅgassa avikkhepalakkhaṇaṃ. Upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa paṭisaṅkhānalakkhaṇaṃ.

The enlightenment factor of mindfulness has the characteristic of establishing. The enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena has the characteristic of detailed investigation. The enlightenment factor of energy has the characteristic of uplifting. The enlightenment factor of rapture has the characteristic of pervading. The enlightenment factor of tranquility has the characteristic of calming. The enlightenment factor of concentration has the characteristic of non-distraction. The enlightenment factor of equanimity has the characteristic of reflecting.

Sammādiṭṭhiyā dassanalakkhaṇaṃ. Sammāsaṅkappassa abhiniropanalakkhaṇaṃ. Sammāvācāya pariggahalakkhaṇaṃ. Sammākammantassa samuṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ. Sammāājīvassa vodānalakkhaṇaṃ. Sammāvāyāmassa [P 1.0064] paggahalakkhaṇaṃ. Sammāsatiyā upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ. Sammāsamādhissa avikkhepalakkhaṇaṃ.

Right view has the characteristic of seeing. Right thought has the characteristic of directing towards. Right speech has the characteristic of embracing. Right action has the characteristic of originating. Right livelihood has the characteristic of cleansing. Right effort has the characteristic of uplifting. Right mindfulness has the characteristic of establishing. Right concentration has the characteristic of non-distraction.

Avijjāya aññāṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Saṅkhārānaṃ cetanālakkhaṇaṃ. Viññāṇassa vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ. Nāmassa namanalakkhaṇaṃ. Rūpassa ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ. Saḷāyatanassa āyatanalakkhaṇaṃ. Phassassa phusanalakkhaṇaṃ. Vedanāya vedayitalakkhaṇaṃ. Taṇhāya hetulakkhaṇaṃ. Upādānassa gahaṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Bhavassa āyūhanalakkhaṇaṃ. Jātiyā nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ. Jarāya jīraṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Maraṇassa cutilakkhaṇaṃ.

Ignorance has the characteristic of not-knowing. Formations have the characteristic of volition. Consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing. Name has the characteristic of bending. Form has the characteristic of alteration. The six sense bases have the characteristic of being spheres of arising. Contact has the characteristic of touching. Feeling has the characteristic of experiencing. Craving has the characteristic of being a cause. Clinging has the characteristic of grasping. Becoming has the characteristic of striving. Birth has the characteristic of arising. Aging has the characteristic of decaying. Death has the characteristic of passing away.

Dhātūnaṃ suññatālakkhaṇaṃ. Āyatanānaṃ āyatanalakkhaṇaṃ. Satipaṭṭhānānaṃ upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ. Sammappadhānānaṃ padahanalakkhaṇaṃ. Iddhipādānaṃ ijjhanalakkhaṇaṃ. Indriyānaṃ adhipatilakkhaṇaṃ. Balānaṃ akampiyalakkhaṇaṃ. Bojjhaṅgānaṃ niyyānalakkhaṇaṃ. Maggassa hetulakkhaṇaṃ.

The elements have the characteristic of being void. The sense bases have the characteristic of being spheres of arising. The foundations of mindfulness have the characteristic of establishing. The right strivings have the characteristic of striving. The bases of power have the characteristic of accomplishment. The faculties have the characteristic of sovereignty. The powers have the characteristic of being unshakable. The enlightenment factors have the characteristic of leading out. The path has the characteristic of being a cause.

Saccānaṃ [V 1.0061][M 1.0064] tathalakkhaṇaṃ. Samathassa avikkhepalakkhaṇaṃ. Vipassanāya anupassanālakkhaṇaṃ. Samathavipassanānaṃ ekarasalakkhaṇaṃ. Yuganaddhānaṃ anativattanalakkhaṇaṃ.

The truths have the characteristic of being true. Serenity has the characteristic of non-distraction. Insight has the characteristic of repeated contemplation. Serenity and insight have the characteristic of having a single function. The yoked pair has the characteristic of not overstepping one another.

Sīlavisuddhiyā saṃvaralakkhaṇaṃ. Cittavisuddhiyā avikkhepalakkhaṇaṃ. Diṭṭhivisuddhiyā dassanalakkhaṇaṃ.

The purification of virtue has the characteristic of restraint. The purification of mind has the characteristic of non-distraction.

Khaye ñāṇassa samucchedanalakkhaṇaṃ. Anuppāde ñāṇassa passaddhilakkhaṇaṃ.

The knowledge in destruction has the characteristic of cutting off. The knowledge in non-arising has the characteristic of calming.

Chandassa [P 1.0065] mūlalakkhaṇaṃ. Manasikārassa samuṭṭhāpanalakkhaṇaṃ. Phassassa samodhānalakkhaṇaṃ. Vedanāya samosaraṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Samādhissa pamukhalakkhaṇaṃ. Satiyā ādhipateyyalakkhaṇaṃ. Paññāya tatuttariyalakkhaṇaṃ. Vimuttiyā sāralakkhaṇaṃ… amatogadhassa nibbānassa pariyosānalakkhaṇaṃ tathaṃ avitathaṃ. Evaṃ tathalakkhaṇaṃ ñāṇagatiyā āgato avirajjhitvā patto anuppattoti tathāgato. Evaṃ tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgatoti tathāgato.

Desire has the characteristic of being a root. Attention has the characteristic of arousing. Contact has the characteristic of coming together. Feeling has the characteristic of being a meeting place. Concentration has the characteristic of being foremost. Mindfulness has the characteristic of sovereignty. Wisdom has the characteristic of being superior to those. Liberation has the characteristic of being the essence. Of Nibbāna, which is the Deathless destination, the characteristic is culmination; this is true, not untrue. Thus, because he has come by the passage of knowledge to this true characteristic, having reached and attained it without error, he is the Tathāgata. Thus, because he has come to the true characteristic, he is the Tathāgata.

Kathaṃ tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddhoti tathāgato? Tathadhammā nāma cattāri ariyasaccāni. Yathāha – “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, tathāni avitathāni anaññathāni. Katamāni cattāri? ‘Idaṃ dukkha’nti bhikkhave, tathametaṃ avitathametaṃ anaññathameta”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.1090) vitthāro. Tāni ca bhagavā abhisambuddho, tasmā tathānaṃ dhammānaṃ abhisambuddhattā tathāgatoti vuccati. Abhisambuddhattho hettha gatasaddo.

How is the Tathāgata one who has fully awakened to true phenomena as they really are? True phenomena are the Four Noble Truths. As it is said: 'Monks, these four are true, not unreal, not otherwise. What four? Monks, "This is suffering." This is true, this is not unreal, this is not otherwise' (Saṃ. Ni. 5.1090) and so on in detail. And the Blessed One has fully awakened to these; therefore, because of having fully awakened to these true phenomena, he is called the Tathāgata. Herein, the word 'gata' has the meaning of 'fully awakened'.

Api ca jarāmaraṇassa jātipaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho tatho avitatho anaññatho…pe…, saṅkhārānaṃ avijjāpaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho tatho avitatho anaññatho…pe…, tathā avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ paccayaṭṭho, saṅkhārānaṃ viññāṇassa paccayaṭṭho…pe…, jātiyā jarāmaraṇassa paccayaṭṭho tatho avitatho anaññatho. Taṃ sabbaṃ bhagavā abhisambuddho, tasmāpi tathānaṃ dhammānaṃ abhisambuddhattā tathāgatoti vuccati. Evaṃ tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddhoti tathāgato.

Furthermore, the characteristic of aging and death—being well-produced from birth as its condition and arising accordingly—is true, not unreal, not otherwise… and so on… the characteristic of formations—being well-produced from ignorance as its condition and arising accordingly—is true, not unreal, not otherwise… and so on… Likewise, the characteristic of ignorance as a condition for formations, the characteristic of formations as a condition for consciousness… and so on… the characteristic of birth as a condition for aging and death is true, not unreal, not otherwise. The Blessed One has fully awakened to all of that. Therefore also, because of having fully awakened to these true phenomena, he is called the Tathāgata. Thus, because he has fully awakened to true phenomena as they really are, he is the Tathāgata.

Kathaṃ tathadassitāya tathāgato? Bhagavā yaṃ sadevake loke…pe…, sadevamanussāya pajāya aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu aparimāṇānaṃ [M 1.0065] sattānaṃ cakkhudvāre āpāthamāgacchantaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ nāma atthi, taṃ sabbākārato jānāti passati. Evaṃ jānatā passatā ca, tena taṃ [V 1.0062] iṭṭhāniṭṭhādivasena vā diṭṭhasutamutaviññātesu labbhamānakapadavasena vā. “Katamaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ? Yaṃ [P 1.0066] rūpaṃ catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya vaṇṇanibhā sanidassanaṃ sappaṭighaṃ nīlaṃ pītaka”ntiādinā (dha. sa. 616) nayena anekehi nāmehi terasahi vārehi dvepaññāsāya nayehi vibhajjamānaṃ tathameva hoti, vitathaṃ natthi. Esa nayo sotadvārādīsupi āpāthaṃ āgacchantesu saddādīsu. Vuttañcetaṃ bhagavatā – “yaṃ bhikkhave, sadevakassa lokassa…pe… sadevamanussāya pajāya diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ viññātaṃ pattaṃ pariyesitaṃ anuvicaritaṃ manasā, tamahaṃ jānāmi. Tamahaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, taṃ tathāgatassa viditaṃ, taṃ tathāgato na upaṭṭhāsī”ti (a. ni. 4.24). Evaṃ tathadassitāya tathāgato. Tattha tathadassī atthe tathāgatoti padasambhavo veditabbo.

How is the Tathāgata so called because of seeing what is true? The Blessed One knows and sees in all its aspects whatever form-object there is that comes into the range of the eye-door of countless beings in countless world-systems, in this world with its devas… for the generation with its devas and humans. When that form-object is analyzed by him who knows and sees thus—whether by way of the desirable, undesirable, and so on, or by way of terms obtainable among the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, such as in the method beginning: 'What is that form, the form-base? That form which, derived from the four great elements, is color, visible and impinging, blue, yellow…' (Dhs. § 616), and by many names, thirteen sections, and fifty-two methods—it is just so, it is not unreal. This same method applies to sounds and other objects that come into the range of the ear-door and so on. And this was stated by the Blessed One: 'Monks, whatever in the world with its devas… for the generation with its devas and humans is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and traversed by the mind—that I know. That I have directly known. That is known to the Tathāgata, but the Tathāgata did not attend to it' (A. Ni. 4.24). Thus, he is the Tathāgata because of seeing what is true. Herein, the derivation of the term 'Tathāgata' should be understood in the sense of 'one who sees thus' (tathadassī).

Kathaṃ [P 1.0067] tathavāditāya tathāgato? Yaṃ rattiṃ bhagavā bodhimaṇḍe aparājitapallaṅke nisinno tiṇṇaṃ mārānaṃ matthakaṃ madditvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho, yañca rattiṃ yamakasālānamantare anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyi, etthantare pañcacattālīsavassaparimāṇe kāle paṭhamabodhiyāpi majjhimabodhiyāpi pacchimabodhiyāpi yaṃ bhagavatā bhāsitaṃ – suttaṃ, geyyaṃ…pe… vedallaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ atthato ca byañjanato ca anupavajjaṃ, anūnamanadhikaṃ, sabbākāraparipuṇṇaṃ, rāgamadanimmadanaṃ, dosamohamadanimmadanaṃ. Natthi tattha vālaggamattampi avakkhalitaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ ekamuddikāya lañchitaṃ viya, ekanāḷiyā mitaṃ viya, ekatulāya tulitaṃ viya ca, tathameva hoti avitathaṃ anaññathaṃ. Tenāha – “yañca, cunda, rattiṃ tathāgato anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhati, yañca rattiṃ anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyati, yaṃ etasmiṃ antare bhāsati lapati niddisati, sabbaṃ taṃ tatheva hoti, no aññathā. Tasmā ‘tathāgato’ti vuccatī”ti (a. ni. 4.23). Gadattho hettha gatasaddo. Evaṃ tathavāditāya tathāgato.

How is the Tathāgata so called because of speaking what is true? On the night the Blessed One, sitting on the unconquered seat at the site of Awakening, crushed the heads of the three Māras and fully awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; and on the night he attained parinibbāna with the Nibbāna-element that has no residue remaining, between the twin sāl trees—whatever the Blessed One spoke in the intervening period of forty-five years, be it Sutta, Geyya… or Vedalla, all of it is irreproachable in both meaning and phrasing, not deficient and not excessive, complete in all aspects, subduing the intoxication of lust, and subduing the intoxication of hatred and delusion. There is not even a hair's tip of error therein. All of it is just so, not unreal, not otherwise, as if stamped with a single seal, measured with a single measure, and weighed with a single scale. Therefore, he said: 'Cunda, on the night the Tathāgata fully awakens to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and on the night he attains parinibbāna with the Nibbāna-element that has no residue remaining—whatever he speaks, utters, and indicates in between, all of it is just so, not otherwise. Therefore, he is called "Tathāgata"' (A. Ni. 4.23). Herein, the word 'gata' has the meaning of 'spoken'. Thus, he is the Tathāgata because of speaking what is true.

Api [M 1.0066] ca āgadanaṃ āgado, vacananti attho. Tayo aviparīto āgado assāti, da-kārassa ta-kāraṃ katvā tathāgatoti evametasmiṃ atthe padasiddhi veditabbā.

Furthermore, 'proclamation' (āgadanaṃ) is 'āgado'; the meaning is 'speech' (vacanaṃ). Because his (assa) proclamation (āgado) is true (tatho) and undistorted (aviparīto), the term 'Tathāgata' is formed by changing the letter 'd' to 't'. Thus, the formation of the word should be understood in this sense.

Kathaṃ tathākāritāya tathāgato? Bhagavato hi vācāya kāyo anulometi, kāyassapi vācā, tasmā yathāvādī tathākārī, yathākārī tathāvādī ca hoti. Evaṃbhūtassa cassa yathāvācā, kāyopi tathā gato pavattoti attho. Yathā ca kāyo, vācāpi tathā gatā pavattāti tathāgato. Tenevāha – “yathāvādī, bhikkhave, tathāgato tathākārī, yathākārī tathāvādī[V 1.0063]. Iti yathāvādī tathākārī yathākārī tathāvādī. Tasmā ‘tathāgato’ti vuccatī”ti (a. ni. 4.23). Evaṃ tathākāritāya tathāgato.

How is the Tathāgata so called because of acting accordingly? For the Blessed One, the body conforms to the speech, and the speech to the body. Therefore, as he speaks, so he acts; and as he acts, so he speaks. For him who is thus, the meaning is: as his speech has gone, so too his body has gone, has proceeded. And as his body has gone, so too his speech has gone, has proceeded; therefore, he is the Tathāgata. For that reason, he said: 'Monks, as the Tathāgata speaks, so he acts; as he acts, so he speaks. Thus, because he acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts, he is called "Tathāgata"' (A. Ni. 4.23). In this way, he is the Tathāgata because of acting accordingly.

Kathaṃ abhibhavanaṭṭhena tathāgato? Upari bhavaggaṃ heṭṭhā avīciṃ pariyantaṃ katvā tiriyaṃ aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu sabbasatte abhibhavati sīlenapi samādhināpi paññāyapi vimuttiyāpi, vimuttiñāṇadassanenapi na tassa tulā vā pamāṇaṃ vā atthi; atulo appameyyo anuttaro rājātirājā devadevo sakkānaṃ atisakko brahmānaṃ atibrahmā. Tenāha – “sadevake, bhikkhave, loke…pe… sadevamanussāya pajāya tathāgato abhibhū anabhibhūto aññadatthudaso vasavattī, tasmā ‘tathāgato’ti vuccatī”ti.

How is the Tathāgata so called in the sense of overcoming? Having made the peak of existence above and the Avīci hell below the limit, he overcomes all beings across the immeasurable world-systems by means of virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. There is no equivalent or measure for him; he is incomparable, immeasurable, unsurpassed, a king over kings, a deva over devas, a supreme Sakka over Sakkas, a supreme Brahmā over Brahmās. Therefore, he said: 'Monks, in the world with its devas… for the generation with its devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the overcomer, the unovercome, the one who sees all, the wielder of power. Therefore, he is called "Tathāgata".'

Tatrevaṃ padasiddhi veditabbā. Agado viya agado. Ko panesa? Desanāvilāsamayo ceva puññussayo ca. Tena hesa mahānubhāvo bhisakko dibbāgadena sappe viya sabbaparappavādino sadevakañca lokaṃ abhibhavati. Iti sabbālokābhibhavane tatho aviparīto desanāvilāsamayo ceva puññussayo ca agado assāti. Da-kārassa ta-kāraṃ katvā tathāgatoti veditabbo. Evaṃ abhibhavanaṭṭhena tathāgato.

Herein, the accomplishment of the term should be understood in this way. Like a divine medicine (`agada`), he is `Agada`. What, then, is this [divine medicine]? It is both the gracefulness of his teaching and his abundance of merit. For by this, this physician of great power overwhelms all who hold opposing views and the world with its devas, just as [a physician] with a divine medicine overwhelms snakes. Thus, because in overwhelming the entire world, the gracefulness of his teaching and his abundance of merit is for him a true and unfailing divine medicine (`agada`), by changing the letter 'da' to 'ta', he should be known as 'Tathāgata'. In this way, he is the Tathāgata in the sense of overwhelming.

Api ca tathāya gatotipi tathāgato, tathaṃ gatotipi tathāgato. Gatoti avagato, atīto patto paṭipannoti attho.

Furthermore, he is the Tathāgata also because of the etymology `tathāya gato`, and he is the Tathāgata also because of the etymology `tathaṃ gato`. The meaning of `gato` is: 'has penetrated and known' (`avagato`), 'has transcended' (`atīto`), 'has reached' (`patto`), 'has practiced' (`paṭipanno').

Tattha [M 1.0067] sakalalokaṃ tīraṇapariññāya tathāya gato avagatoti tathāgato. Lokasamudayaṃ pahānapariññāya tathāya gato atītoti tathāgato. Lokanirodhaṃ sacchikiriyāya tathāya gato pattoti tathāgato. Lokanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ tathaṃ gato paṭipannoti tathāgato. Tena [P 1.0068] vuttaṃ bhagavatā –

Therein, because he has gone (`gato`), that is, has penetrated and known (`avagato`), the entire world truly (`tathāya`) by means of the full understanding of scrutinizing (`tīraṇapariññā`), he is the Tathāgata. Because he has gone (`gato`), that is, has transcended (`atīto`), the origin of the world truly (`tathāya`) by means of the full understanding of abandoning (`pahānapariññā`), he is the Tathāgata. Because he has gone (`gato`), that is, has reached (`patto`), the cessation of the world truly (`tathāya`) by means of realization (`sacchikiriyā`), he is the Tathāgata. Because he has gone (`gato`), that is, has practiced (`paṭipanno`), the true (`tathaṃ`) path leading to the cessation of the world, he is the Tathāgata. Thus it was said by the Blessed One:

“Loko, bhikkhave, tathāgatena abhisambuddho, lokasmā tathāgato visaṃyutto. Lokasamudayo, bhikkhave, tathāgatena abhisambuddho, lokasamudayo tathāgatassa pahīno. Lokanirodho, bhikkhave, tathāgatena abhisambuddho, lokanirodho tathāgatassa sacchikato. Lokanirodhagāminī paṭipadā, bhikkhave, tathāgatena abhisambuddhā, lokanirodhagāminī paṭipadā tathāgatassa bhāvitā. Yaṃ bhikkhave, sadevakassa lokassa…pe… sabbaṃ taṃ tathāgatena abhisambuddhaṃ. Tasmā, tathāgatoti vuccatī”ti (a. ni. 4.23).

“Monks, the world has been thoroughly understood by the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is disjoined from the world. Monks, the origin of the world has been thoroughly understood by the Tathāgata; the origin of the world has been abandoned by the Tathāgata. Monks, the cessation of the world has been thoroughly understood by the Tathāgata; the cessation of the world has been realized by the Tathāgata. Monks, the path leading to the cessation of the world has been thoroughly understood by the Tathāgata; the path leading to the cessation of the world has been developed by the Tathāgata. Whatever, monks, in the world with its devas… all that has been thoroughly understood by the Tathāgata. Therefore, he is called ‘Tathāgata.’”

Tassapi [V 1.0064] evaṃ attho veditabbo. Idampi ca tathāgatassa tathāgatabhāvadīpane mukhamattameva. Sabbākārena pana tathāgatova tathāgatassa tathāgatabhāvaṃ vaṇṇeyya.

The meaning of that [speech] should also be understood in this way. And this is merely an introduction in revealing the Tathāgata's state of being a Tathāgata. Indeed, only a Tathāgata could describe a Tathāgata's state of being a Tathāgata in all its aspects.

Katamañca taṃ bhikkhaveti yena appamattakena oramattakena sīlamattakena puthujjano tathāgatassa vaṇṇaṃ vadamāno vadeyya, taṃ katamanti pucchati? Tattha pucchā nāma adiṭṭhajotanā pucchā, diṭṭhasaṃsandanā pucchā, vimaticchedanā pucchā, anumatipucchā, kathetukamyatā pucchāti pañcavidhā hoti.

He asks: 'And what, monks, is that mere morality, of small measure, of inferior measure, by which an ordinary person, speaking the praise of the Tathāgata, might speak? What is that?' Therein, what is called a question is of five kinds: a question that illuminates the unseen, a question for comparing the seen, a question that cuts off doubt, a question for approval, and a question from the desire to speak.

Tattha katamā adiṭṭhajotanā pucchā? Pakatiyā lakkhaṇaṃ aññātaṃ hoti, adiṭṭhaṃ atulitaṃ atīritaṃ avibhūtaṃ avibhāvitaṃ, tassa ñāṇāya dassanāya tulanāya tīraṇāya vibhāvanāya pañhaṃ pucchati, ayaṃ adiṭṭhajotanā pucchā.

Therein, which is the question that illuminates the unseen? By nature, a characteristic is not yet known, not seen, not weighed, not determined, not manifest, not made manifest. One asks a question for the sake of knowing it, seeing it, weighing it, determining it, and making it manifest. This is the question that illuminates the unseen.

Katamā diṭṭhasaṃsandanā pucchā? Pakatiyā lakkhaṇaṃ ñātaṃ hoti, diṭṭhaṃ tulitaṃ tīritaṃ vibhūtaṃ vibhāvitaṃ, tassa aññehi paṇḍitehi saddhiṃ saṃsandanatthāya pañhaṃ pucchati, ayaṃ diṭṭhasaṃsandanā pucchā.

Which is the question for comparing the seen? By nature, a characteristic is known, seen, weighed, determined, manifest, and made manifest. One asks a question for the purpose of comparing it with other wise persons. This is the question for comparing the seen.

Katamā [M 1.0068] vimaticchedanā pucchā? Pakatiyā saṃsayapakkhando hoti, vimatipakkhando, dveḷhakajāto, “evaṃ nu kho, na nu kho, kinnu kho, kathaṃ nu kho”ti. So vimaticchedanatthāya pañhaṃ pucchati. Ayaṃ vimaticchedanā pucchā.

Which is the question that cuts off doubt? By nature, one is inclined to doubt, inclined to uncertainty, having become of two minds, [thinking]: 'Is it so? Is it not so? What can it be? How can it be?' That person asks a question for the purpose of cutting off uncertainty. This is the question that cuts off doubt.

Katamā anumatipucchā? Bhagavā bhikkhūnaṃ anumatiyā pañhaṃ pucchati – “taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti. Aniccaṃ, bhante. Yaṃ panāniccaṃ[P 1.0069], dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vāti? Dukkhaṃ bhanteti (mahāva. 21) sabbaṃ vattabbaṃ, ayaṃ anumatipucchā.

Which is the question for approval? The Blessed One asks a question for the monks' approval: 'What do you think of this, monks, is form permanent or impermanent?' 'Impermanent, venerable sir.' 'Now, that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?' 'It is suffering, venerable sir.' All [of the sutta] should be stated. This is the question for approval.

Katamā kathetukamyatā pucchā? Bhagavā bhikkhūnaṃ kathetukamyatāya pañhaṃ pucchati. Cattārome, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānā. Katame cattāro?…Pe… aṭṭhime bhikkhave maggaṅgā. Katame aṭṭhāti, ayaṃ kathetukamyatā pucchā.

Which is the question from the desire to speak? The Blessed One asks the monks a question out of a desire to explain. 'There are these four establishments of mindfulness, monks. Which four? ... There are these eight path factors, monks. Which eight?' This is the question from the desire to speak.

Iti imāsu pañcasu pucchāsu adiṭṭhassa tāva kassaci dhammassa abhāvato tathāgatassa adiṭṭhajotanā [V 1.0065] pucchā natthi. “Idaṃ nāma aññehi paṇḍitehi samaṇabrāhmaṇehi saddhiṃ saṃsanditvā desessāmī”ti samannāhārasseva anuppajjanato diṭṭhasaṃsandanā pucchāpi natthi. Yasmā pana buddhānaṃ ekadhammepi āsappanā parisappanā natthi, bodhimaṇḍeyeva sabbā kaṅkhā chinnā; tasmā vimaticchedanā pucchāpi natthiyeva. Avasesā pana dve pucchā buddhānaṃ atthi, tāsu ayaṃ kathetukamyatā pucchā nāma.

Thus, among these five questions, firstly, because there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is unseen by the Tathāgata, for him there is no question that illuminates the unseen. Because the thought itself, 'Having compared this with other wise ascetics and brahmins, I will teach it,' does not arise, there is also no question for comparing the seen. Furthermore, because for the Buddhas there is no wavering towards or wavering around even a single phenomenon—all doubts having been cut off at the very seat of Awakening—therefore, there is also no question that cuts off doubt. However, the remaining two questions do exist for the Buddhas. Among them, this one is called the question from the desire to speak.

8. Idāni taṃ kathetukamyatāya pucchāya pucchitamatthaṃ kathetuṃ “pāṇātipātaṃ pahāyā”tiādimāha.

8. Now, in order to explain the meaning asked by the question from the desire to speak, he spoke the passage beginning with 'Having abandoned the taking of life...'

Tattha pāṇassa atipāto pāṇātipāto, pāṇavadho, pāṇaghātoti vuttaṃ hoti. Pāṇoti cettha vohārato satto, paramatthato jīvitindriyaṃ, tasmiṃ pana pāṇe pāṇasaññino jīvitindriyupacchedakaupakkamasamuṭṭhāpikā kāyavacīdvārānaṃ aññataradvārappavattā vadhakacetanā pāṇātipāto. So guṇavirahitesu tiracchānagatādīsu pāṇesu khuddake pāṇe appasāvajjo, mahāsarīre mahāsāvajjo, kasmā? Payogamahantatāya. Payogasamattepi vatthumahantatāya. Guṇavantesu manussādīsu appaguṇe pāṇe appasāvajjo, mahāguṇe mahāsāvajjo. Sarīraguṇānaṃ pana samabhāve sati kilesānaṃ upakkamānañca mudutāya appasāvajjo, tibbatāya mahāsāvajjoti veditabbo.

Therein, the striking down (`atipāto`) of a living being (`pāṇassa`) is `pāṇātipāta`; it means the killing of a living being, the slaughter of a living being. Herein, `pāṇa` is conventionally a being; in the ultimate sense, it is the life faculty. With regard to that being, `pāṇātipāta` is the volition of one who kills, which proceeds through one of the doors of body or speech, which causes the arising of an effort that cuts off the life faculty, and which belongs to one who is percipient of it as a living being. That [act] is of small fault in the case of a small being among those devoid of qualities, such as animals, and of great fault in the case of one with a large body. Why? Because of the greatness of the effort. Even when the effort is equal, [it is] because of the greatness of the object. Among those with qualities, such as humans, it is of small fault in the case of a being with few qualities, and of great fault in the case of one with great qualities. But when the body and qualities are equal, it is of small fault because of the mildness of the defilements and the efforts, and of great fault because of their intensity. Thus it should be understood.

Tassa [M 1.0069] pañca sambhārā honti – pāṇo, pāṇasaññitā, vadhakacittaṃ, upakkamo, tena maraṇanti[P 1.0070]. Cha payogā – sāhatthiko, āṇattiko, nissaggiyo, thāvaro, vijjāmayo, iddhimayoti. Imasmiṃ panatthe vitthāriyamāne ativiya papañco hoti, tasmā taṃ na vitthārayāma, aññañca evarūpaṃ. Atthikehi pana samantapāsādikaṃ vinayaṭṭhakathaṃ oloketvā gahetabbaṃ.

Of that, there are five components: a living being, the perception that it is a living being, the intention to kill, the effort, and death resulting from it. There are six modes of application: by one's own hand, by command, by projectile, by a fixed device, by incantation, and by psychic power. However, when this subject is elaborated upon, it becomes an exceedingly extensive discourse; therefore, we do not elaborate on it, nor on anything similar. But by those who desire it, the meaning should be grasped by consulting the Samantapāsādikā, the commentary on the Vinaya.

Pahāyāti imaṃ pāṇātipātacetanāsaṅkhātaṃ dussīlyaṃ pajahitvā. Paṭiviratoti pahīnakālato paṭṭhāya tato dussīlyato orato viratova. Natthi tassa vītikkamissāmīti cakkhusotaviññeyyā dhammā pageva kāyikāti imināva nayena aññesupi evarūpesu padesu attho veditabbo.

'Having abandoned' means having abandoned this immoral volition known as the destruction of life. 'Abstaining' means that from the time of its abandonment, one is indeed abstinent from that immorality. For him, there are no unwholesome states cognizable by eye-consciousness or ear-consciousness that arise with the thought, 'I will transgress'; how much more so for bodily transgressions. By this very method, the meaning should be understood in other similar passages as well.

Samaṇoti bhagavā samitapāpatāya laddhavohāro. Gotamoti gottavasena. Na kevalañca bhagavāyeva [V 1.0066] pāṇātipātā paṭivirato, bhikkhusaṅghopi paṭivirato, desanā pana ādito paṭṭhāya evaṃ āgatā, atthaṃ pana dīpentena bhikkhusaṅghavasenāpi dīpetuṃ vaṭṭati.

'Samaṇa' means the Blessed One has acquired this designation because he has pacified evil. 'Gotama' is by way of his clan name. And it is not only the Blessed One who abstains from the destruction of life; the community of monks also abstains. However, the teaching has come down in this way from the beginning. But for one explaining the meaning, it is also proper to explain it by way of the community of monks.

Nihitadaṇḍo nihitasatthoti parūpaghātatthāya daṇḍaṃ vā satthaṃ vā ādāya avattanato nikkhittadaṇḍo ceva nikkhittasattho cāti attho. Ettha ca ṭhapetvā daṇḍaṃ sabbampi avasesaṃ upakaraṇaṃ sattānaṃ viheṭhanabhāvato satthanti veditabbaṃ. Yaṃ pana bhikkhū kattaradaṇḍaṃ vā dantakaṭṭhaṃ vā vāsiṃ pipphalikaṃ vā gahetvā vicaranti, na taṃ parūpaghātatthāya. Tasmā nihitadaṇḍo nihitasattho tveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati.

'He has laid down the rod, he has laid down the weapon' means that because he does not take up and wield a rod or a weapon for the purpose of harming others, he has laid down the rod and laid down the weapon. And here, setting aside the rod, every remaining implement should be understood as a 'weapon' due to its nature of harming beings. However, whatever walking stick, tooth-stick, knife for cutting a tooth-stick, or small nail-clipping knife the monks take and wander with, that is not for the purpose of harming others. Therefore, they are indeed reckoned as 'one who has laid down the rod, one who has laid down the weapon'.

Lajjīti pāpajigucchanalakkhaṇāya lajjāya samannāgato. Dayāpannoti dayaṃ mettacittataṃ āpanno. Sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampīti; sabbe pāṇabhūte hitena anukampako. Tāya dayāpannatāya sabbesaṃ pāṇabhūtānaṃ hitacittakoti attho. Viharatīti iriyati yapeti yāpeti pāleti[M 1.0070]. Iti vā hi, bhikkhaveti evaṃ vā bhikkhave. Vā saddo upari “adinnādānaṃ [P 1.0071] pahāyā”tiādīni apekkhitvā vikappattho vutto, evaṃ sabbattha purimaṃ vā pacchimaṃ vā apekkhitvā vikappabhāvo veditabbo.

'Conscientious' means one is endowed with conscientiousness, which has the characteristic of revulsion for evil. 'Compassionate' means one has attained compassion, a mind of loving-kindness. 'Sympathetic for the welfare of all living beings' means one is sympathetic toward all living beings for their welfare. The meaning is that because of having attained that compassion, one has a mind directed toward the welfare of all living beings. 'Dwells' means one moves, maintains oneself, carries on, or protects. 'Or thus, O monks' means 'or in this way, O monks.' The word 'or' is spoken with the meaning of alternation, with reference to what follows, such as 'having abandoned taking what is not given.' Thus, everywhere, the state of alternation should be understood with reference to either the preceding or the succeeding.

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo – bhikkhave, puthujjano tathāgatassa vaṇṇaṃ vadamāno evaṃ vadeyya – “samaṇo gotamo pāṇaṃ na hanati, na ghāteti, na tattha samanuñño hoti, virato imasmā dussīlyā; aho, vata re buddhaguṇā mahantā”ti, iti mahantaṃ ussāhaṃ katvā vaṇṇaṃ vattukāmopi appamattakaṃ oramattakaṃ ācārasīlamattakameva vakkhati. Upari asādhāraṇabhāvaṃ nissāya vaṇṇaṃ vattuṃ na sakkhissati. Na kevalañca puthujjanova sotāpannasakadāgāmianāgāmiarahantopi paccekabuddhāpi na sakkontiyeva; tathāgatoyeva pana sakkoti, taṃ vo upari vakkhāmīti, ayamettha sādhippāyā atthavaṇṇanā. Ito paraṃ pana apubbapadameva vaṇṇayissāma.

This is the summary here: Monks, an ordinary person, speaking in praise of the Tathāgata, might say thus: 'The ascetic Gotama does not kill a living being, does not cause others to kill, and does not consent to it; he abstains from this immorality. Oh, how great are the virtues of the Buddha!' Thus, even though desiring to speak his praise and having made a great effort, he will speak only of a small, inferior, mere matter of virtuous conduct. He will not be able to speak in praise by relying on the unique state that is higher. And it is not only an ordinary person; even stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arahants, and Paccekabuddhas are indeed unable to do so. But only the Tathāgata himself is able. I will explain that to you later. This is the explanation of the meaning with its intention here. But from this point on, we will explain only terms not previously explained.

Adinnādānaṃ pahāyāti ettha adinnassa ādānaṃ adinnādānaṃ, parasaṃharaṇaṃ, theyyaṃ, corikāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha adinnanti parapariggahitaṃ, yattha paro yathākāmakāritaṃ āpajjanto adaṇḍāraho anupavajjo ca hoti. Tasmiṃ parapariggahite parapariggahitasaññino, tadādāyakaupakkamasamuṭṭhāpikā theyyacetanā adinnādānaṃ. Taṃ hīne parasantake appasāvajjaṃ, paṇīte mahāsāvajjaṃ, kasmā? Vatthupaṇītatāya. Vatthusamatte sati guṇādhikānaṃ santake vatthusmiṃ mahāsāvajjaṃ[V 1.0067]. Taṃ taṃ guṇādhikaṃ upādāya tato tato hīnaguṇassa santake vatthusmiṃ appasāvajjaṃ.

In the phrase 'having abandoned taking what is not given,' the taking of what is not given is called `adinnādāna`; it is said to be the carrying away of another's property, theft, or thievery. Therein, 'what is not given' means what is possessed by another, with which that other person, being able to do as they wish, is not liable to punishment and is blameless. With regard to that which is possessed by another, the thievish volition of one who perceives it as possessed by another, which gives rise to the effort to take it, is `adinnādāna`. That act, concerning the inferior property of another, is of small blame; concerning excellent property, it is of great blame. Why? Because of the excellence of the object. When the objects are equal, the act concerning the property of those with superior virtue is of great blame. Taking into account this or that person of superior virtue, the act concerning the property of one with virtue inferior to that is of small blame.

Tassa pañca sambhārā honti – parapariggahitaṃ, parapariggahitasaññitā, theyyacittaṃ, upakkamo, tena haraṇanti. Cha payogā – sāhatthikādayova. Te ca kho yathānurūpaṃ theyyāvahāro, pasayhāvahāro, paṭicchannāvahāro, parikappāvahāro, kusāvahāroti imesaṃ avahārānaṃ vasena pavattā, ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana samantapāsādikāyaṃ vutto.

Of that, there are five components: that which is possessed by another, the perception that it is possessed by another, a thievish mind, the effort, and the carrying away of it by that effort. There are six modes of application, beginning with 'by one's own hand.' And these occur, as is appropriate, by way of these types of appropriation: appropriation by stealth, appropriation by force, appropriation of concealed goods, appropriation by scheming, and appropriation by manipulating lots. This is the summary here. The detailed explanation, however, is given in the Samantapāsādikā.

Dinnameva [P 1.0072][M 1.0071] ādiyatīti dinnādāyī. Cittenapi dinnameva paṭikaṅkhatīti dinnapāṭikaṅkhī. Thenetīti theno. Na thenena athenena. Athenattāyeva sucibhūtena. Attanāti attabhāvena. Athenaṃ sucibhūtaṃ attānaṃ katvā viharatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ paṭhamasikkhāpade vuttanayeneva yojetabbaṃ. Yathā ca idha, evaṃ sabbattha.

Because he takes only what is given, he is a 'taker of what is given' (`dinnādāyī`). Because he expects only what is given even in his mind, he is an 'expecter of what is given' (`dinnapāṭikaṅkhī`). One who steals is a 'thief' (`theno`). 'Not by a thief' (`na thenena`) means by a non-thief (`athenena`). 'By being purified' (`sucibhūtena`) is precisely through non-thievishness. 'By oneself' (`attanā`) means by one's own being (`attabhāvena`). It is said that he dwells having made his own being non-thievish and purified. The remainder should be connected by the same method as stated in the first training rule. And as it is here, so it is everywhere.

Abrahmacariyanti aseṭṭhacariyaṃ. Brahmaṃ seṭṭhaṃ ācāraṃ caratīti brahmacārī. Ārācārīti abrahmacariyato dūracārī. Methunāti rāgapariyuṭṭhānavasena sadisattā methunakāti laddhavohārehi paṭisevitabbato methunāti saṅkhyaṃ gatā asaddhammā. Gāmadhammāti gāmavāsīnaṃ dhammā.

'Unchastity' (`abrahmacariya`) means ignoble conduct. Because one practices the supreme, noble conduct (`brahmaṃ seṭṭhaṃ ācāraṃ`), one is a `brahmacārī`. 'Practicing afar' (`ārācārī`) means one practices far from unchastity. 'Sexual intercourse' (`methuna`) refers to the ignoble practice that has come to be called 'sexual intercourse' because it is to be engaged in by those who have acquired the designation 'sexual partners' (`mithunā`) due to their similarity in being overcome by lust. 'Village-practice' (`gāmadhamma`) means the practice of village-dwellers.

9. Musāvādaṃ pahāyāti ettha musāti visaṃvādanapurekkhārassa atthabhañjanako vacīpayogo kāyapayogo, vā visaṃvādanādhippāyena panassa paravisaṃvādakakāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā musāvādo.

9. In the phrase 'having abandoned false speech,' 'false' (`musā`) refers to the verbal or bodily effort of a person who has the intention to deceive, an effort which destroys the benefit. However, the volition (`cetanā`) of that person, with the intention to deceive, which gives rise to the bodily or verbal effort that deceives another, is 'false speech' (`musāvādo`).

Aparo nayo, ‘musā’ti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ vatthu. ‘Vādo’ti tassa bhūtato tacchato viññāpanaṃ. Lakkhaṇato pana atathaṃ vatthuṃ tathato paraṃ viññāpetukāmassa tathāviññattisamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā musāvādo. So yamatthaṃ bhañjati, tassa appatāya appasāvajjo, mahantatāya mahāsāvajjo.

Another way: 'musā' (falsehood) is a non-existent, untrue matter. 'Vādo' (speech) is the making known of that matter as if it were existent and true. Alternatively, it is the volition that is the cause of making it known. Furthermore, by way of characteristic, for one who desires to make another know an untrue matter as true, the volition that, in that manner, gives rise to bodily or verbal intimation is 'musāvādo' (false speech). As to whatever benefit it destroys, due to that benefit being small, it is of minor fault; due to it being great, it is of major fault.

Api ca gahaṭṭhānaṃ attano santakaṃ adātukāmatāya natthītiādinayappavatto appasāvajjo, sakkhinā hutvā atthabhañjanatthaṃ vutto mahāsāvajjo, pabbajitānaṃ appakampi telaṃ vā sappiṃ vā labhitvā hasādhippāyena – “ajja gāme telaṃ nadī maññe sandatī”ti pūraṇakathānayena [V 1.0068] pavatto appasāvajjo, adiṭṭhaṃyeva pana diṭṭhantiādinā nayena vadantānaṃ mahāsāvajjo.

Furthermore, for householders, false speech that occurs in the manner of 'There is none,' etc., due to the state of not wishing to give one's own property, is of minor fault. False speech spoken for the purpose of destroying a benefit, having become a witness, is of major fault. For renunciants, having received even a small amount of oil or ghee, false speech that occurs with humorous intent in the manner of an exaggerated statement, such as, 'Today in the village, oil flows like a river,' is of minor fault. However, for those who speak in the manner of 'I have seen' what was not seen, etc., it is of major fault.

Tassa cattāro sambhārā honti – atathaṃ vatthu, visaṃvādanacittaṃ, tajjo vāyāmo, parassa tadatthavijānananti. Eko payogo sāhatthikova. So kāyena vā kāyapaṭibaddhena vā vācāya [P 1.0073] vā paravisaṃvādanakiriyākaraṇena daṭṭhabbo. Tāya ce kiriyāya paro tamatthaṃ jānāti, ayaṃ kiriyasamuṭṭhāpikacetanākkhaṇeyeva musāvādakammunā bajjhati.

Of that false speech, there are four components: an untrue matter; a mind to deceive; the effort arising in accordance with that mind; and the other's understanding of that intended meaning. The one effort is only that done by oneself. And that should be understood as the performance of an act of deceiving another, whether by body, by something connected to the body, or by speech. If, by that action, the other person understands that meaning, this person is bound by the kamma of false speech at the very moment of the volition that gives rise to the action.

Yasmā [M 1.0072] pana yathā kāyakāyapaṭibaddhavācāhi paraṃ visaṃvādeti, tathā “idamassa bhaṇāhī”ti āṇāpentopi paṇṇaṃ likhitvā purato nissajjantopi, “ayamattho evaṃ daṭṭhabbo”ti kuḍḍādīsu likhitvā ṭhapentopi. Tasmā ettha āṇattikanissaggiyathāvarāpi payogā yujjanti, aṭṭhakathāsu pana anāgatattā vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbā.

Furthermore, because just as one can deceive another by body, by something connected to the body, and by speech, so too can one deceive by commanding, 'Tell this to him'; or by writing a letter and placing it before someone; or by writing on walls and so on, 'This meaning should be understood thus,' and leaving it there. Therefore, in this matter of false speech, the efforts of command, of depositing, and of a permanent fixture are also suitable. However, because they have not come down in the commentaries, they should be accepted after investigation.

Saccaṃ vadatīti saccavādī. Saccena saccaṃ sandahati ghaṭetīti saccasandho. Na antarantarā musā vadatīti attho. Yo hi puriso kadāci musā vadati, kadāci saccaṃ, tassa musāvādena antaritattā saccaṃ saccena na ghaṭīyati; tasmā so na saccasandho. Ayaṃ pana na tādiso, jīvitahetupi musā avatvā saccena saccaṃ sandahati yevāti saccasandho.

Because He speaks truth, He is called `saccavādī` (a speaker of truth). Because He connects a later truth with a former truth, He is called `saccasandho` (one who joins truth to truth). The meaning is: He does not speak falsehood in between. Indeed, for a person who sometimes speaks falsehood and sometimes speaks truth, because it is interrupted by false speech, truth is not joined with truth. Therefore, he is not `saccasandho`. But this Blessed One is not such a person. Even for the sake of His life, not speaking falsehood, He connects a later truth with a former truth indeed. Therefore, He is called `saccasandho`.

Thetoti thiro thirakathoti attho. Eko hi puggalo haliddirāgo viya, thusarāsimhi nikhātakhāṇu viya, assapiṭṭhe ṭhapitakumbhaṇḍamiva ca na thirakatho hoti, eko pāsāṇalekhā viya, indakhīlo viya ca thirakatho hoti, asinā sīsaṃ chindantepi dve kathā na katheti, ayaṃ vuccati theto.

'Theto' (steadfast) means firm, having firm speech. Indeed, a certain person—like the color of turmeric dye, like a post driven into a heap of chaff, and like a gourd placed on a horse's back—is not one of firm speech. A certain person—like writing on stone and like a city-gate post—is one of firm speech. Even while his head is being cut off with a sword, he does not speak two kinds of speech. This person is called 'theto'.

Paccayikoti pattiyāyitabbako, saddhāyitabbakoti attho. Ekacco hi puggalo na paccayiko hoti, “idaṃ kena vuttaṃ, asukenā”ti vutte “mā tassa vacanaṃ saddahathā”ti vattabbataṃ āpajjati. Eko paccayiko hoti, “idaṃ kena vuttaṃ, asukenā”ti vutte “yadi tena vuttaṃ, idameva pamāṇaṃ, idāni upaparikkhitabbaṃ natthi, evameva ida”nti vattabbataṃ āpajjati, ayaṃ vuccati paccayiko. Avisaṃvādako lokassāti tāya saccavāditāya lokaṃ na visaṃvādetīti attho.

'Paccayiko' (trustworthy) means one who is to be approached with confidence, one who is a basis for faith. Indeed, a certain person is not trustworthy. When asked, 'By whom was this said?' and it is said, 'By so-and-so,' he becomes one of whom it should be said, 'Do not believe that person's word.' A certain person is trustworthy. When asked, 'By whom was this said?' and it is said, 'By so-and-so,' he becomes one of whom it should be said, 'If it was said by him, this itself is the authority. Now there is nothing to be investigated. This is just so.' This person is called 'paccayiko'. 'Avisaṃvādako lokassa' (not a deceiver of the world) means: due to that state of being a speaker of truth, He does not deceive the world.

Pisuṇaṃ [V 1.0069] vācaṃ pahāyātiādīsu yāya vācāya yassa taṃ vācaṃ [P 1.0074] bhāsati, tassa hadaye attano piyabhāvaṃ, parassa ca suññabhāvaṃ karoti, sā pisuṇā vācā.

In the phrases beginning with 'having abandoned divisive speech': that speech by which, when one speaks it to a person, one creates in that person's heart the state of being dear for oneself and the state of being devoid of affection for the other—that is divisive speech.

Yāya pana attānampi parampi pharusaṃ karoti, yā vācā sayampi pharusā, neva kaṇṇasukhā na hadayaṅgamā, ayaṃ pharusā vācā.

Furthermore, that speech by which one makes both oneself and the other harsh, that speech which is itself harsh, is neither pleasant to the ear nor goes to the heart—this is harsh speech.

Yena [M 1.0073] samphaṃ palapati niratthakaṃ, so samphappalāpo.

That by which one speaks variously of what is destructive of benefit and is meaningless—that is idle chatter.

Tesaṃ mūlabhūtā cetanāpi pisuṇavācādināmeva labhati, sā eva ca idhādhippetāti.

The volition that is the root of these—divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter—also receives the very name 'divisive speech', and so on. And here in the Cūḷasīla, that very volition is intended.

Tattha saṃkiliṭṭhacittassa paresaṃ vā bhedāya attano piyakamyatāya vā kāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā pisuṇavācā. Sā yassa bhedaṃ karoti, tassa appaguṇatāya appasāvajjā, mahāguṇatāya mahāsāvajjā.

Therein, for one with a defiled mind, the volition that gives rise to bodily and verbal effort, either for the division of others or for the sake of one's own desire to be dear, is divisive speech. As for the person whose division it creates, due to that person's state of having few virtues, it is of minor fault; due to the state of having great virtues, it is of major fault.

Tassā cattāro sambhārā – bhinditabbo paro, “iti ime nānā bhavissanti, vinā bhavissantī”ti bhedapurekkhāratā vā, “iti ahaṃ piyo bhavissāmi vissāsiko”ti piyakamyatā vā, tajjo vāyāmo, tassa tadatthavijānananti. Imesaṃ bhedāyāti, yesaṃ itoti vuttānaṃ santike sutaṃ tesaṃ bhedāya.

Of that divisive speech, there are four components: another who is to be divided; either the state of having the division as one's aim, thinking, 'Thus they will become separate, they will be divided,' or the state of desiring to be dear, thinking, 'Thus I will become dear and trusted'; the effort arising in accordance with that; and that person's understanding of that meaning. The phrase 'for their division' means: for division from those from whom one has heard.

Bhinnānaṃ vā sandhātāti dvinnaṃ mittānaṃ vā samānupajjhāyakādīnaṃ vā kenacideva kāraṇena bhinnānaṃ ekamekaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “tumhākaṃ īdise kule jātānaṃ evaṃ bahussutānaṃ idaṃ na yutta”ntiādīni vatvā sandhānaṃ kattā anukattā. Anuppadātāti sandhānānuppadātā. Dve jane samagge disvā – “tumhākaṃ evarūpe kule jātānaṃ evarūpehi guṇehi samannāgatānaṃ anucchavikameta”ntiādīni vatvā daḷhīkammaṃ kattāti attho. Samaggo ārāmo assāti samaggārāmo. Yattha samaggā natthi, tattha vasitumpi na icchatīti attho. Samaggarāmotipi pāḷi, ayamevettha attho. Samaggaratoti samaggesu rato, te pahāya aññattha gantumpi na icchatīti attho. Samagge disvāpi sutvāpi nandatīti samagganandī, samaggakaraṇiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitāti yā vācā satte samaggeyeva karoti[P 1.0075], taṃ sāmaggiguṇaparidīpikameva vācaṃ bhāsati, na itaranti.

'A reconciler of the divided' means: when two friends, or those with the same preceptor, etc., have become divided for some reason, He approaches each one and, saying such things as, 'For you who are born in such a family and are so learned, this is not fitting,' He is a maker and a suitable maker of reconciliation. 'A giver of support' means a giver of support for reconciliation. Seeing two people in harmony, and saying such things as, 'For you who are born in such a family and are endowed with such virtues, this is appropriate,' He is a maker of strengthening the bond; this is the meaning. 'Harmony is His resort' (`ārāma`), thus He is `samaggārāmo`. The meaning is: where there are no harmonious people, He does not wish even to dwell. `Samaggarāmo` is also a Pali reading, and this is its meaning here. 'Delighting in harmony' (`samaggarato`) means He delights in the harmonious; He does not wish to go elsewhere, abandoning them; this is the meaning. 'Rejoicing in harmony' (`samagganandī`) means He rejoices upon seeing or hearing of the harmonious. 'He speaks speech that creates harmony' means: that speech which makes beings harmonious indeed, He speaks that speech which indeed illuminates the virtue of harmony, and not the other.

Parassa [V 1.0070] mammacchedakakāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā ekantapharusacetanā pharusāvācā. Tassā āvibhāvatthamidaṃ vatthu – eko kira dārako mātuvacanaṃ anādiyitvā araññaṃ gacchati, taṃ mātā nivattetumasakkontī – “caṇḍā taṃ mahiṃsī anubandhatū”ti akkosi. Athassa tatheva araññe mahiṃsī [M 1.0074] uṭṭhāsi. Dārako “yaṃ mama mātā mukhena kathesi, taṃ mā hotu, yaṃ cittena cintesi taṃ hotū”ti, saccakiriyamakāsi. Mahiṃsī tattheva baddhā viya aṭṭhāsi. Evaṃ mammacchedakopi payogo cittasaṇhatāya na pharusā vācā hoti. Mātāpitaro hi kadāci puttake evaṃ vadanti – “corā vo khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ karontū”ti, uppalapattampi ca nesaṃ upari patantaṃ na icchanti. Ācariyupajjhāyā ca kadāci nissitake evaṃ vadanti – “kiṃ ime ahirīkā anottappino caranti, niddhamatha ne”ti, atha ca nesaṃ āgamādhigamasampattiṃ icchanti. Yathā ca cittasaṇhatāya pharusā vācā na hoti, evaṃ vacanasaṇhatāya apharusā vācā na hoti. Na hi mārāpetukāmassa – “imaṃ sukhaṃ sayāpethā”ti vacanaṃ apharusā vācā hoti, cittapharusatāya panesā pharusā vācāva. Sā yaṃ sandhāya pavattitā, tassa appaguṇatāya appasāvajjā, mahāguṇatāya mahāsāvajjā. Tassā tayo sambhārā – akkositabbo paro, kupitacittaṃ, akkosanāti.

Harsh speech is an exclusively harsh intention that gives rise to bodily and verbal effort that cuts at the vitals of another. Here is a story to illustrate this: It is said that a certain child, not heeding his mother’s words, went into the forest. Unable to make him return, the mother cursed him, saying, 'May a fierce she-buffalo follow you!' Then, just as she had said, a she-buffalo arose in the forest. The child made an act of truth: 'May what my mother spoke with her mouth not come to pass, but may what she intended in her mind come to pass!' The she-buffalo stood right there as if bound. Thus, even an effort that cuts at the vitals is not harsh speech due to the gentleness of the mind. For parents sometimes say to their children, 'May thieves cut you into pieces!' yet they do not wish for even a lotus petal to fall upon them. And teachers and preceptors sometimes say to their dependents, 'Why do these ones wander about without shame and fear of wrongdoing? Expel them!' and yet they desire for them the accomplishment of learning and attainment. And just as speech is not harsh due to a gentle mind, so speech is not non-harsh due to gentle words. Indeed, for one who desires to have someone killed, the statement, 'Have this one lie down comfortably,' is not non-harsh speech; rather, due to the harshness of the mind, this is truly harsh speech. That speech, with reference to whomever it is uttered, is of little fault if that person is of little virtue, and of great fault if that person is of great virtue. Its requisites are three: another person to be abused, an angry mind, and the act of abusing.

Nelāti elaṃ vuccati doso, nāssā elanti nelā, niddosāti attho. “Nelaṅgo setapacchādo”ti, (udā. 65) ettha vuttanelaṃ viya. Kaṇṇasukhāti byañjanamadhuratāya kaṇṇānaṃ sukhā, sūcivijjhanaṃ viya kaṇṇasūlaṃ na janeti. Atthamadhuratāya sakalasarīre kopaṃ ajanetvā pemaṃ janetīti pemanīyā. Hadayaṃ gacchati, appaṭihaññamānā sukhena cittaṃ pavisatīti hadayaṅgamā. Guṇaparipuṇṇatāya pure bhavāti porī pure saṃvaḍḍhanārī [P 1.0076] viya sukumārātipi porī. Purassa esātipi porī. Nagaravāsīnaṃ kathāti attho. Nagaravāsino hi yuttakathā honti. Pitimattaṃ pitāti vadanti, bhātimattaṃ bhātāti vadanti, mātimattaṃ mātāti vadanti. Evarūpī kathā bahuno janassa kantā hotīti bahujanakantā. Kantabhāveneva bahuno janassa manāpā cittavuḍḍhikarāti bahujanamanāpā.

Regarding `nelā`: a fault is called `elaṃ`. `N'assā elaṃ` means 'it has no fault'; therefore, it is `nelā`. The meaning is 'faultless', like the word `nela` spoken in the verse, 'Faultless in limb, clad in white...' (Ud 6.2). 'Pleasing to the ear' (`kaṇṇasukhā`): because of the sweetness of its syllables, it is pleasant to the ears; it does not cause an ear-ache like being pierced by a needle. 'Endearing' (`pemanīyā`): because of the sweetness of its meaning, it does not give rise to anger in the whole body but gives rise to affection. 'Reaching the heart' (`hadayaṅgamā`): it goes to the heart; unresisted, it enters the mind with ease. 'Civic' (`porī`): because it is complete with virtues, it is `porī`, meaning 'urbane' (literally, 'of the city'). Also, because it is refined like a well-bred woman in a city, it is `porī`. Also, because it is 'of the city', it is `porī`. The meaning is 'the speech of city-dwellers'. Indeed, city-dwellers have suitable speech. They call one of a father's stature 'father', one of a brother's stature 'brother', and one of a mother's stature 'mother'. 'Dear to many people' (`bahujanakantā`): such speech is dear to many people. 'Pleasing to many people' (`bahujanamanāpā`): precisely because it is dear, it is pleasing to many people, causing the mind to grow.

Anatthaviññāpikā kāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā akusalacetanā samphappalāpo. So āsevanamandatāya appasāvajjo, āsevanamahantatāya mahāsāvajjo, tassa dve sambhārā – bhāratayuddhasītāharaṇādiniratthakakathāpurekkhāratā, tathārūpī kathā kathanañca.

Frivolous speech is an unwholesome intention that gives rise to bodily and verbal effort, making known what is meaningless or unbeneficial.
