Due to the infrequency of its practice, it is of little fault; due to the frequency of its practice, it is of great fault. Its requisites are two: being intent on meaningless talk such as the war of the Bhāratas, the abduction of Sītā, and so on; and the uttering of such talk.

Kālena [M 1.0075] vadatīti kālavādī vattabbayuttakālaṃ sallakkhetvā vadatīti attho. Bhūtaṃ tathaṃ tacchaṃ [V 1.0071] sabhāvameva vadatīti bhūtavādī. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikatthasannissitameva katvā vadatīti atthavādī. Navalokuttaradhammasannissitaṃ katvā vadatīti dhammavādī saṃvaravinayapahānavinayasannissitaṃ katvā vadatīti vinayavādī.

Because he speaks at the right time, he is a speaker in season (`kālavādī`); the meaning is that he speaks after having marked the suitable time for what should be said. Because he speaks what is factual, real, and true, he is a speaker of fact (`bhūtavādī`). Because he speaks based only on what is connected with benefit in the present life and in the future, he is a speaker of benefit (`atthavādī`). Because he speaks based on what is connected with the nine supramundane Dhammas, he is a speaker of Dhamma (`dhammavādī`). Because he speaks based on what is connected with the discipline of restraint and the discipline of abandoning, he is a speaker of Discipline (`vinayavādī`).

Nidhānaṃ vuccati ṭhapanokāso, nidhānamassā atthīti nidhānavatī. Hadaye nidhātabbayuttakaṃ vācaṃ bhāsitāti attho. Kālenāti evarūpiṃ bhāsamānopi ca – “ahaṃ nidhānavatiṃ vācaṃ bhāsissāmī”ti na akālena bhāsati, yuttakālaṃ pana apekkhitvāva bhāsatīti attho. Sāpadesanti saupamaṃ, sakāraṇanti attho. Pariyantavatinti paricchedaṃ dassetvā yathāssā paricchedo paññāyati, evaṃ bhāsatīti attho. Atthasaṃhitanti [P 1.0077] anekehipi nayehi vibhajantena pariyādātuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya atthasampannaṃ bhāsati. Yaṃ vā so atthavādī atthaṃ vadati, tena atthena sahitattā atthasaṃhitaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati, na aññaṃ nikkhipitvā aññaṃ bhāsatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

A place for storing is called a `nidhāna`; because it has a `nidhāna`, it is called `nidhānavatī` (containing a treasure). The meaning is that he speaks speech fit to be stored in the heart. By `kālena` (at the right time): even when speaking such speech, he does not speak at an unsuitable time, thinking, 'I will speak speech worthy of being stored'; rather, he speaks only after considering the suitable time. This is the meaning. By `sāpadesaṃ` (with demonstration): with simile, with reason. This is the meaning. By `pariyantavatiṃ` (with a limit): having shown the limit, he speaks in such a way that its limit is made known. This is the meaning. By `atthasaṃhitaṃ` (connected with benefit): he speaks speech that is so complete with meaning that it cannot be fully comprehended even by one analyzing it through many methods. Or alternatively: that speaker of benefit speaks speech that is connected with the very benefit he is speaking of; he does not set aside one meaning and speak of another. This is what is said.

10. Bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhāti mūlabījaṃ khandhabījaṃ phaḷubījaṃ aggabījaṃ bījabījanti pañcavidhassa bījagāmassa ceva, yassa kassaci nīlatiṇarukkhādikassa bhūtagāmassa ca samārambhā, chedanabhedanapacanādibhāvena vikopanā paṭiviratoti attho.

10. Regarding the destruction of seed-life and plant-life (`bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhā`): the meaning is that he refrains from ruining (`samārambhā`)—by way of cutting, breaking, burning, and so on—the five kinds of seed-life (`bījagāma`), namely, root-seed, stem-seed, joint-seed, bud-seed, and seed-seed, and also any plant-life (`bhūtagāma`) such as green grass, trees, and so on.

Ekabhattikoti pātarāsabhattaṃ sāyamāsabhattanti dve bhattāni, tesu pātarāsabhattaṃ antomajjhanhikena paricchinnaṃ, itaraṃ majjhanhikato uddhaṃ anto aruṇena. Tasmā antomajjhanhike dasakkhattuṃ bhuñjamānopi ekabhattikova hoti. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “ekabhattiko”ti.

Regarding `ekabhattiko` (one who eats a single meal): there are two meal periods, the morning meal period (`pātarāsabhatta`) and the evening meal period (`sāyamāsabhatta`). Of these, the morning meal period is delimited by the time before midday, and the other is from after midday until dawn. Therefore, even if one eats ten times within the time before midday, one is still an `ekabhattiko`. It is with reference to this that `ekabhattiko` is said.

Rattiyā bhojanaṃ ratti, tato uparatoti rattūparato. Atikkante majjhanhike yāva sūriyatthaṅgamanā bhojanaṃ vikālabhojanaṃ nāma. Tato viratattā virato vikālabhojanā. Kadā virato? Anomānadītīre pabbajitadivasato paṭṭhāya.

Eating at night is `ratti`; because he has ceased (`uparato`) from that, he is `rattūparato` (one who has ceased from eating at night). When midday has passed, eating until sunset is called `vikālabhojana` (eating at the wrong time). Because he has refrained (`virato`) from that, he is `virato vikālabhojanā` (one who refrains from eating at the wrong time). When did he refrain? From the day he went forth on the bank of the river Anomā.

Sāsanassa ananulomattā visūkaṃ paṭāṇībhūtaṃ dassananti visūkadassanaṃ. Attanā naccananaccāpanādivasena naccā ca gītā ca vāditā ca antamaso [M 1.0076] mayūranaccādivasenapi pavattānaṃ naccādīnaṃ visūkabhūtā dassanā cāti naccagītavāditavisūkadassanā. Naccādīni hi attanā [V 1.0072] payojetuṃ vā parehi payojāpetuṃ vā payuttāni passituṃ vā neva bhikkhūnaṃ na bhikkhunīnañca vaṭṭanti.

Because it is unsuitable for the Dispensation, a sight that is contrary and like a stake is called a 'distracting spectacle'. By way of dancing oneself, causing others to dance, and so on, there is dancing, singing, and playing instruments; and even by way of, at the very least, the dancing of peacocks and so on, there is seeing or listening to such dancing and the like which has become a distracting spectacle. Thus, it is 'dancing, singing, instrumental music, and distracting spectacles'. Indeed, for monks and for nuns, it is not allowable to engage in dancing and the like themselves, to cause others to engage in them, or to watch or listen to them when they are performed.

Mālādīsu mālāti yaṃ kiñci pupphaṃ. Gandhanti yaṃ kiñci gandhajātaṃ. Vilepananti chavirāgakaraṇaṃ. Tattha piḷandhanto dhāreti nāma, ūnaṭṭhānaṃ pūrento maṇḍeti nāma, gandhavasena chavirāgavasena ca sādiyanto vibhūseti nāma. Ṭhānaṃ vuccati kāraṇaṃ. Tasmā yāya [P 1.0078] dussīlyacetanāya tāni mālādhāraṇādīni mahājano karoti, tato paṭiviratoti attho.

Among garlands and the like, 'garland' means any flower whatsoever. 'Scent' means any kind of fragrant substance. 'Ointment' means that which causes attachment to the skin's complexion. Therein, one who wears flowers is said 'to wear'; one who fills a deficient place is said 'to adorn'; one who delights by means of fragrance and by means of causing attachment to the skin's complexion is said 'to embellish'. The word `ṭhāna` is said to mean 'cause'. Therefore, the meaning is: he abstains from that immoral volition by which the great populace performs those acts of wearing garlands and so on.

Uccāsayanaṃ vuccati pamāṇātikkantaṃ. Mahāsayananti akappiyapaccattharaṇaṃ. Tato viratoti attho.

A 'high seat or bed' is said to be that which exceeds the standard measure. A 'great seat or bed' is an unallowable spread. The meaning is: he abstains from that high and great seat or bed.

Jātarūpanti suvaṇṇaṃ. Rajatanti kahāpaṇo, lohamāsako, jatumāsako, dārumāsakoti ye vohāraṃ gacchanti. Tassa ubhayassāpi paṭiggahaṇā paṭivirato, neva naṃ uggaṇhāti, na uggaṇhāpeti, na upanikkhittaṃ sādiyatīti attho.

'Jātarūpa' is gold. 'Rajata' is whatever is used in commerce, such as the kahāpaṇa, the copper māsaka, the lac māsaka, or the wooden māsaka. He abstains from accepting both of these. The meaning is: he neither accepts it himself, nor does he cause others to accept it, nor does he consent to it when it is placed or deposited nearby.

Āmakadhaññapaṭiggahaṇāti, sālivīhiyavagodhūmakaṅguvarakakudrūsakasaṅkhātassa sattavidhassāpi āmakadhaññassa paṭiggahaṇā. Na kevalañca etesaṃ paṭiggahaṇameva, āmasanampi bhikkhūnaṃ na vaṭṭatiyeva. Āmakamaṃsapaṭiggahaṇāti ettha aññatra odissa anuññātā āmakamaṃsamacchānaṃ paṭiggahaṇameva bhikkhūnaṃ na vaṭṭati, no āmasanaṃ.

From 'acceptance of raw grain' means from the acceptance of the seven kinds of raw grain, namely: `sāli` rice, `vīhi` paddy, barley, wheat, millet, `varaka`, and `kudrūsaka`. And not only is the acceptance of these unallowable for monks, but even touching them is not allowable. Regarding 'acceptance of raw meat', herein, apart from what is specifically permitted, only the acceptance of raw meat and fish is not allowable for monks; touching them is not unallowable, that is, it is allowable.

Itthikumārikapaṭiggahaṇāti ettha itthīti purisantaragatā, itarā kumārikā nāma, tāsaṃ paṭiggahaṇampi āmasanampi akappiyameva.

Regarding 'acceptance of women and young girls', herein, a 'woman' is one who has gone to another man; the other is called a 'young girl'. Both accepting them and touching them is indeed unallowable.

Dāsidāsapaṭiggahaṇāti ettha dāsidāsavaseneva tesaṃ paṭiggahaṇaṃ na vaṭṭati. “Kappiyakārakaṃ dammi, ārāmikaṃ dammī”ti evaṃ vutte pana vaṭṭati.

Regarding 'acceptance of female and male slaves', herein, accepting them specifically as female and male slaves is not allowable. However, when it is said, 'I give a `kappiyakāraka` (an attendant who makes things allowable),' or 'I give a monastery attendant,' then it is allowable.

Ajeḷakādīsu khettavatthupariyosānesu kappiyākappiyanayo vinayavasena upaparikkhitabbo. Tattha khettaṃ nāma yasmiṃ pubbaṇṇaṃ ruhati. Vatthu nāma yasmiṃ aparaṇṇaṃ ruhati. Yattha vā ubhayampi ruhati, taṃ khettaṃ. Tadatthāya [M 1.0077] akatabhūmibhāgo vatthu. Khettavatthusīsena cettha vāpitaḷākādīnipi saṅgahitāneva.

Regarding goats, sheep, and so on, up to the end of the list with fields and sites, the method of what is allowable and unallowable should be investigated according to the Vinaya. Therein, a 'field' (`khetta`) is where early grain grows. A 'site' (`vatthu`) is where later grain grows. Or where both grow, that is a 'field'. An unprepared portion of land for that purpose is a 'site'. And here, under the heading of 'fields and sites', reservoirs, tanks, and the like are also included.

Dūteyyaṃ [V 1.0073] vuccati dūtakammaṃ, gihīnaṃ pahitaṃ paṇṇaṃ vā sāsanaṃ vā gahetvā tattha tattha gamanaṃ. Pahiṇagamanaṃ vuccati gharā gharaṃ pesitassa khuddakagamanaṃ. Anuyogo nāma tadubhayakaraṇaṃ. Tasmā dūteyyapahiṇagamanānaṃ anuyogāti. Evamettha attho veditabbo.

'Messenger duty' (`dūteyya`) is said to be the work of a messenger: taking a letter or a verbal message sent by householders and going from place to place. 'Going on an errand' (`pahiṇagamana`) is said to be the short journey of one who is sent from house to house. 'Engagement' (`anuyoga`) is the doing of both of these. Therefore, it is 'from engagement in messenger duties and going on errands'. This is how the meaning should be understood here.

Kayavikkayāti kayā ca vikkayā ca. Tulākūṭādīsu [P 1.0079] kūṭanti vañcanaṃ. Tattha tulākūṭaṃ nāma rūpakūṭaṃ aṅgakūṭaṃ, gahaṇakūṭaṃ, paṭicchannakūṭanti catubbidhaṃ hoti. Tattha rūpakūṭaṃ nāma dve tulā samarūpā katvā gaṇhanto mahatiyā gaṇhāti, dadanto khuddikāya deti. Aṅgakūṭaṃ nāma gaṇhanto pacchābhāge hatthena tulaṃ akkamati, dadanto pubbabhāge. Gahaṇakūṭaṃ nāma gaṇhanto mūle rajjuṃ gaṇhāti, dadanto agge. Paṭicchannakūṭaṃ nāma tulaṃ susiraṃ katvā anto ayacuṇṇaṃ pakkhipitvā gaṇhanto taṃ pacchābhāge karoti, dadanto aggabhāge.

'Buying and selling' means from buying and from selling. Regarding 'cheating with scales' and so on, 'cheating' (`kūṭa`) means deception. Therein, 'cheating with scales' is of four kinds: cheating by form, cheating by limb, cheating by holding, and cheating by concealment. Therein, 'cheating by form' is when, having made two scales of similar appearance, one takes with the large one when receiving and gives with the small one when giving. 'Cheating by limb' is when one presses down on the back part of the scale with the hand when receiving, and on the front part when giving. 'Cheating by holding' is when one holds the cord at the base when receiving, and at the tip when giving. 'Cheating by concealment' is when, having made the scale-beam hollow and put iron powder inside, one causes it to be in the back part when receiving, and in the front part when giving.

Kaṃso vuccati suvaṇṇapāti, tāya vañcanaṃ kaṃsakūṭaṃ. Kathaṃ? Ekaṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ katvā aññā dve tisso lohapātiyo suvaṇṇavaṇṇe karoti, tato janapadaṃ gantvā kiñcideva aḍḍhaṃ kulaṃ pavisitvā – “suvaṇṇabhājanāni kiṇathā”ti vatvā agghe pucchite samagghataraṃ dātukāmā honti. Tato tehi – “kathaṃ imesaṃ suvaṇṇabhāvo jānitabbo”ti vutte, “vīmaṃsitvā gaṇhathā”ti suvaṇṇapātiṃ pāsāṇe ghaṃsitvā sabbā pātiyo datvā gacchati.

A 'golden bowl' (`suvaṇṇapāti`) is called `kaṃsa`; deception with it is `kaṃsakūṭa`. How? Having made one golden bowl, one makes two or three other bronze bowls to have the color of gold. Then, going to the countryside and entering some wealthy household, one says, 'Buy these golden vessels.' When asked the price, one says, 'I wish to sell them for a very cheap price.' Then, when asked by them, 'How are we to know that these are gold?', one replies, 'Examine them and then take them.' Then, having rubbed the golden bowl on a touchstone, one gives them all the bowls and departs.

Mānakūṭaṃ nāma hadayabhedasikhābhedarajjubhedavasena tividhaṃ hoti. Tattha hadayabhedo sappitelādiminanakāle labbhati. Tāni hi gaṇhanto heṭṭhāchiddena mānena – “saṇikaṃ āsiñcā”ti vatvā antobhājane bahuṃ paggharāpetvā gaṇhāti, dadanto chiddaṃ pidhāya sīghaṃ pūretvā deti.

'Cheating with measures' (`mānakūṭa`) is of three kinds: by way of breaking the center, breaking the peak, and breaking the rope. Therein, 'breaking the center' is found when measuring ghee, oil, and so on. For when receiving these things, using a measure with a hole at the bottom, one says, 'Pour slowly,' and causing much to flow out into one's own vessel, one takes it. When giving, one covers the hole and, filling it quickly, gives it.

Sikhābhedo tilataṇḍulādiminanakāle labbhati. Tāni hi gaṇhanto saṇikaṃ sikhaṃ ussāpetvā gaṇhāti, dadanto vegena pūretvā sikhaṃ chindanto deti.

'Breaking the peak' is found when measuring sesame, rice, and so on. For when receiving these things, one slowly raises up the peak and takes it. When giving, one fills the measure with force and, cutting off the peak, gives it.

Rajjubhedo [M 1.0078] khettavatthuminanakāle labbhati. Lañjaṃ alabhantā hi khettaṃ amahantampi mahantaṃ katvā minanti.

'Breaking the rope' is found when measuring fields and sites. For those who do not receive a bribe measure a field that is not large as if it were large.

Ukkoṭanādīsu ukkoṭananti assāmike sāmike kātuṃ lañjaggahaṇaṃ. Vañcananti tehi tehi upāyehi paresaṃ vañcanaṃ. Tatridamekaṃ vatthu – eko kira luddako migañca migapotakañca gahetvā [V 1.0074] āgacchati[P 1.0080], tameko dhutto – “kiṃ bho, migo agghati, kiṃ migapotako”ti āha. “Migo dve kahāpaṇe, migapotako eka”nti ca vutte ekaṃ kahāpaṇaṃ datvā migapotakaṃ gahetvā thokaṃ gantvā nivatto – “na me bho, migapotakena attho, migaṃ me dehī”ti āha. Tena hi – dve kahāpaṇe dehīti. So āha – “nanu te bho, mayā paṭhamaṃ eko kahāpaṇo dinno”ti? “Āma, dinno”ti. “Idaṃ migapotakaṃ gaṇha, evaṃ so ca kahāpaṇo, ayañca kahāpaṇagghanako migapotakoti dve kahāpaṇā bhavissantī”ti. So “kāraṇaṃ vadatī”ti sallakkhetvā migapotakaṃ gahetvā migaṃ adāsīti. Nikatīti yogavasena vā māyāvasena vā apāmaṅgaṃ pāmaṅganti, amaṇiṃ maṇinti, asuvaṇṇaṃ suvaṇṇanti katvā patirūpakena vañcanaṃ. Sāciyogoti kuṭilayogo, etesaṃyeva ukkoṭanādīnametaṃ nāmaṃ. Tasmā – ukkoṭanasāciyogo, vañcanasāciyogo, nikatisāciyogoti, evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Keci aññaṃ dassetvā aññassa parivattanaṃ sāciyogoti vadanti. Taṃ pana vañcaneneva saṅgahitaṃ.

Among the practices of extortion, etc., 'extortion' (ukkoṭana) means taking a bribe to make non-owners into owners. 'Deception' (vañcana) means deceiving others by various counterfeit means. Here is one example: A hunter, they say, caught a deer and a fawn and was coming along when a rogue said to him, 'Hey, how much is the deer worth, and how much the fawn?' When told, 'The deer is worth two kahāpaṇas, the fawn one,' he gave one kahāpaṇa, took the fawn, went a short distance, then turned back and said, 'Hey, I have no use for the fawn; give me the deer.' 'In that case, give two kahāpaṇas,' was the reply. He said, 'Hey, did I not already give you one kahāpaṇa?' 'Yes, you did.' 'Take this fawn; thus, that kahāpaṇa and this fawn, worth one kahāpaṇa, will become two kahāpaṇas.' Perceiving that he spoke a valid reason, the hunter took the fawn and gave him the deer. 'Fraud' (nikati) means deceiving by means of a counterfeit—making what is not a proper emblem into a proper emblem, what is not a gem into a gem, what is not gold into gold—either by the power of spells or by the power of illusion. 'Crooked dealing' (sāciyoga) means crooked practice; this is another name for these very practices of extortion, etc. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as 'crooked dealing in extortion,' 'crooked dealing in deception,' and 'crooked dealing in fraud.' Some say that 'crooked dealing' is showing one thing and substituting another. But that is included under deception.

Chedanādīsu chedananti hatthacchedanādi. Vadhoti māraṇaṃ. Bandhoti rajjubandhanādīhi bandhanaṃ. Viparāmosoti himaviparāmoso, gumbaviparāmosoti duvidho. Yaṃ himapātasamaye himena paṭicchannā hutvā maggappaṭipannaṃ janaṃ musanti, ayaṃ himaviparāmoso. Yaṃ gumbādīhi paṭicchannā musanti, ayaṃ gumbaviparāmoso. Ālopo vuccati gāmanigamādīnaṃ vilopakaraṇaṃ. Sahasākāroti sāhasikakiriyā. Gehaṃ pavisitvā manussānaṃ ure satthaṃ ṭhapetvā icchitabhaṇḍānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Evametasmā chedana…pe… sahasākārā paṭivirato samaṇo gotamoti. Iti vā hi, bhikkhave, puthujjano tathāgatassa vaṇṇaṃ vadamāno vadeyyāti.

Among the violent acts, 'cutting' (chedana) means cutting off hands, etc. 'Tormenting' (vadha) means causing affliction. 'Binding' (bandha) means binding with ropes, etc. 'Robbery' (viparāmosa) is of two kinds: robbery by snow and robbery by thickets. When, at the time of snowfall, they rob a person traveling on the road while concealed by snow, this is robbery by snow. When they rob while concealed by thickets, etc., this is robbery by thickets. 'Pillage' (ālopa) is said to be the plundering of villages, towns, etc. 'Violence' (sahasākāra) means a violent action: entering a house, placing a weapon on a person's chest, and taking desired goods. Thus, the recluse Gotama abstains from this cutting... and so on... up to violence. For in this way, bhikkhus, a worldling might speak when praising the Tathāgata.

Ettāvatā cūḷasīlaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ hoti.

With this much, the Minor Morality is concluded.

Majjhimasīlavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Middle Morality

11. Idāni [P 1.0081][M 1.0079] majjhimasīlaṃ vitthārento “yathā vā paneke bhonto”tiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ anuttānapadavaṇṇanā. Saddhādeyyānīti kammañca phalañca idhalokañca paralokañca saddahitvā dinnāni. ‘Ayaṃ me ñātī’ti vā, ‘mitto’ti vā, idaṃ paṭikarissati, idaṃ vā tena katapubbanti vā, evaṃ na dinnānīti attho. Evaṃ dinnāni hi na saddhādeyyāni nāma honti[V 1.0075]. Bhojanānīti desanāsīsamattametaṃ, atthato pana saddhādeyyāni bhojanāni bhuñjitvā cīvarāni pārupitvā senāsanāni sevamānā gilānabhesajjaṃ paribhuñjamānāti sabbametaṃ vuttameva hoti.

11. Now, elaborating on the Middle Morality, he begins with 'Just as some venerables,' etc. Here is the explanation of the terms whose meaning is not obvious. 'Offerings of faith' (saddhādeyyāni) means things given with faith in kamma and its result, and in this world and the next world. The meaning is that they are not given with thoughts such as, 'This is my relative,' or 'This is my friend,' or 'They will repay this,' or 'This was done by them before.' For things given in such a way are not called 'offerings of faith.' 'Foods' (bhojanāni) here is merely the heading of the discourse; but in terms of meaning, it is indeed said of all this: consuming foods given out of faith, wearing robes, using lodgings, and partaking of medicines for the sick.

Seyyathidanti nipāto. Tassattho katamo so bījagāmabhūtagāmo, yassa samārambhaṃ anuyuttā viharantīti. Tato taṃ dassento mūlabījantiādimāha. Tattha mūlabījaṃ nāma haliddi, siṅgiveraṃ, vacā, vacattaṃ, ativisā, kaṭukarohiṇī, usīraṃ, bhaddamuttakanti evamādi. Khandhabījaṃ nāma assattho, nigrodho, pilakkho, udumbaro, kacchako, kapitthanoti evamādi. Phaḷubījaṃ nāma ucchu, naḷo, veḷūti evamādi. Aggabījaṃ nāma ajjakaṃ, phaṇijjakaṃ, hiriveranti evamādi. Bījabījaṃ nāma pubbaṇṇaṃ aparaṇṇanti evamādi. Sabbañhetaṃ rukkhato viyojitaṃ viruhanasamatthameva “bījagāmo”ti vuccati. Rukkhato pana aviyojitaṃ asukkhaṃ “bhūtagāmo”ti vuccati. Tattha bhūtagāmasamārambho pācittiyavatthu, bījagāmasamārambho dukkaṭavatthūti veditabbo.

'Such as' (seyyathidaṃ) is a particle. Its meaning is: What is that seed-group and plant-group, to the destruction of which they dwell committed? To explain this, he begins with 'root-seed,' etc. Here, 'root-seed' refers to turmeric, ginger, orris root, sweet flag, ativisa, kaṭukarohiṇī, usīra root, bhaddamuttaka, and so on. 'Stem-seed' refers to the assattha tree, banyan tree, pilakkha tree, udumbara tree, kacchaka, kapitthana, and so on. 'Joint-seed' refers to sugarcane, reeds, bamboo, and so on. 'Tip-seed' refers to ajjaka, phaṇijjaka, hirivera, and so on. 'Seed-as-seed' refers to early-ripening grain, late-ripening grain, and so on. All this, when separated from the plant yet capable of sprouting, is called a 'seed-group' (bījagāma). But when not separated from the plant and not dried out, it is called a 'plant-group' (bhūtagāma). Herein, it should be understood that the destruction of a plant-group is an offense of expiation (pācittiya), while the destruction of a seed-group is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

12. Sannidhikāraparibhoganti sannidhikatassa paribhogaṃ. Tattha duvidhā kathā, vinayavasena ca sallekhavasena ca. Vinayavasena tāva yaṃ kiñci annaṃ ajja paṭiggahitaṃ aparajju sannidhikārakaṃ hoti, tassa paribhoge pācittiyaṃ[P 1.0082]. Attanā laddhaṃ pana sāmaṇerānaṃ datvā, tehi laddhaṃ ṭhapāpetvā dutiyadivase bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, sallekho pana na hoti.

12. 'Consumption of stored things' (sannidhikāraparibhoga) means the consumption of what has been stored. Here, the discussion is twofold: from the perspective of the Vinaya and from the perspective of the practice of effacement. From the perspective of the Vinaya, any food received today becomes a stored item for the next day; its consumption entails an offense of expiation (pācittiya). However, it is permissible to give what one has received to novices, have them store what they have received, and then eat it on the second day; but this is not the practice of effacement.

Pānasannidhimhipi eseva nayo. Tattha pānaṃ nāma ambapānādīni aṭṭha pānāni, yāni ca tesaṃ anulomāni. Tesaṃ vinicchayo samantapāsādikāyaṃ vutto.

In the case of stored drinks, this same principle applies. Here, 'drink' (pāna) refers to the eight kinds of drinks beginning with mango drink, and those that are in accordance with them. The determination of these is stated in the Samantapāsādikā.

Vatthasannidhimhi [M 1.0080] anadhiṭṭhitaṃ avikappitaṃ sannidhi ca hoti, sallekhañca kopeti, ayaṃ pariyāyakathā. Nippariyāyato pana ticīvarasantuṭṭhena bhavitabbaṃ, catutthaṃ labhitvā aññassa dātabbaṃ. Sace yassa kassaci dātuṃ na sakkoti, yassa pana dātukāmo hoti, so uddesatthāya vā paripucchatthāya vā gato, āgatamatte dātabbaṃ, adātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Cīvare pana appahonte satiyā paccāsāya anuññātakālaṃ ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sūcisuttacīvarakārakānaṃ alābhena tato parampi vinayakammaṃ katvā ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. “Imasmiṃ jiṇṇe puna īdisaṃ kuto labhissāmī”ti pana ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭati, sannidhi ca hoti, sallekhañca kopeti.

Regarding the storing of cloth: cloth that is neither determined nor shared is stored, and it corrupts the practice of effacement. This is an indirect statement. Directly, however, one should be content with the three robes. Having obtained a fourth, it should be given to another. If one is not able to give it to just anyone, but wishes to give it to someone who has gone away for the purpose of recitation or inquiry, it should be given as soon as he has returned. It is not proper not to give it. However, if the robe-cloth is insufficient, it is proper to keep it for the permitted time with expectation. Due to the unavailability of a needle, thread, and robe-makers, it is proper to keep it even beyond that time after having performed a Vinaya act. However, it is not proper to keep it thinking, 'When this is worn out, from where will I get another like it again?' This is storing, and it corrupts the practice of effacement.

Yānasannidhimhi [V 1.0076] yānaṃ nāma vayhaṃ, ratho, sakaṭaṃ, sandamānikā, sivikā, pāṭaṅkīti; netaṃ pabbajitassa yānaṃ. Upāhanā pana pabbajitassa yānaṃyeva. Ekabhikkhussa hi eko araññatthāya, eko dhotapādakatthāyāti, ukkaṃsato dve upāhanasaṅghāṭā vaṭṭanti. Tatiyaṃ labhitvā aññassa dātabbo. “Imasmiṃ jiṇṇe aññaṃ kuto labhissāmī”ti hi ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭati, sannidhi ca hoti, sallekhañca kopeti.

Regarding the storing of vehicles: a vehicle means a covered carriage, a chariot, a cart, a sandamānikā litter, a sivikā litter, or a cloth palanquin. This is not a vehicle for one who has gone forth. Footwear, however, is indeed a vehicle for one who has gone forth. Indeed, for a single monk, one pair for the forest and one for protecting washed feet—thus, at most, two pairs of footwear are proper. Having obtained a third pair, it should be given to another. Indeed, it is not proper to keep it thinking, 'When this pair is worn out, from where will I get another?' This is storing, and it corrupts the practice of effacement.

Sayanasannidhimhi sayananti mañco. Ekassa bhikkhuno eko gabbhe, eko divāṭhāneti ukkaṃsato dve mañcā vaṭṭanti. Tato uttari labhitvā aññassa bhikkhuno vā gaṇassa vā dātabbo; adātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sannidhi ca hoti, sallekhañca kopeti.

Regarding the storing of beds: 'sayana' means a couch. For one monk, one in his cell and one in his day-quarters—thus, at most, two couches are proper. Having obtained more than that, it should be given to another monk or to the community. It is not proper not to give it. This is storing, and it corrupts the practice of effacement.

Gandhasannidhimhi bhikkhuno kaṇḍukacchuchavidosādiābādhe [P 1.0083] sati gandhā vaṭṭanti. Te gandhe āharāpetvā tasmiṃ roge vūpasante aññesaṃ vā ābādhikānaṃ dātabbā, dvāre pañcaṅguligharadhūpanādīsu vā upanetabbā. “Puna roge sati bhavissantī”ti pana ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭati, sannidhi ca hoti, sallekhañca kopeti.

Regarding the storing of perfumes: if a monk has an illness such as itching, scabies, or skin disease, perfumes are proper. Having had those perfumes brought, when that illness has subsided, they should be given to other sick persons, or they should be applied at the door, for making a five-finger mark, fumigating the dwelling, and so on. However, it is not proper to keep them thinking, 'They will be there if the illness occurs again.' This is storing, and it corrupts the practice of effacement.

Āmisanti vuttāvasesaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ, idhekacco bhikkhu – “tathārūpe kāle upakārāya bhavissatī”ti tilataṇḍulamuggamāsanāḷikeraloṇamacchamaṃsavallūrasappitelaguḷabhājanādīni āharāpetvā ṭhapeti. So vassakāle kālasseva sāmaṇerehi yāguṃ pacāpetvā paribhuñjitvā “sāmaṇera, udakakaddame dukkhaṃ gāmaṃ pavisituṃ, gaccha asukaṃ kulaṃ [M 1.0081] gantvā mayhaṃ vihāre nisinnabhāvaṃ ārocehi; asukakulato dadhiādīni āharā”ti peseti. Bhikkhūhi – “kiṃ, bhante, gāmaṃ pavisissathā”ti vuttepi, “duppaveso, āvuso, idāni gāmo”ti vadati. Te – “hotu, bhante, acchatha tumhe, mayaṃ bhikkhaṃ pariyesitvā āharissāmā”ti gacchanti. Atha sāmaṇeropi dadhiādīni āharitvā bhattañca byañjanañca sampādetvā upaneti, taṃ bhuñjantasseva upaṭṭhākā bhattaṃ pahiṇanti, tatopi manāpaṃ manāpaṃ bhuñjati. Atha bhikkhū piṇḍapātaṃ gahetvā āgacchanti, tatopi manāpaṃ manāpaṃ gīvāyāmakaṃ bhuñjatiyeva. Evaṃ catumāsampi vītināmeti. Ayaṃ vuccati – “bhikkhu muṇḍakuṭumbikajīvikaṃ jīvati, na samaṇajīvika”nti. Evarūpo āmisasannidhi nāma hoti.

What remains after what has been said should be understood as material things. It is as follows: here, a certain monk, thinking, 'It will be of use at such a time,' has sesame, rice, green gram, black gram, coconut oil, salt, fish, meat, dried meat, and pots of ghee, oil, and molasses, etc., brought and stores them. During the rainy season, that monk, having had gruel cooked by the novices very early and having consumed it, sends a novice, saying, 'Novice, it is difficult to enter the village in the mud and water. Go to such-and-such a family, inform them that I am sitting in my monastery, and bring yogurt and so on from such-and-such a family.' Even when asked by the other monks, 'Venerable sir, will you enter the village?' he says, 'Friends, the village is difficult to enter now.' They go, saying, 'So be it, venerable sir. You stay. We will search for almsfood and bring it back.' Then the novice, having brought the yogurt and so on, prepares rice and curry and offers it. Even while he is eating that, his supporters send food. From that too, he eats whatever is choice. Then the monks return, having collected almsfood. From that too, he eats whatever is choice, stretching his neck. In this way, he passes the four months. Of this monk it is said: 'He lives the life of a shaven-headed householder, not the life of a recluse.' Such a thing is called the storing of material things.

Bhikkhuno pana vasanaṭṭhāne ekā taṇḍulanāḷi, eko guḷapiṇḍo, catubhāgamattaṃ sappīti ettakaṃ nidhetuṃ vaṭṭati, akāle sampattacorānaṃ atthāya. Te hi ettakampi āmisapaṭisanthāraṃ alabhantā [V 1.0077] jīvitāpi voropeyyuṃ, tasmā sace ettakaṃ natthi, āharāpetvāpi [P 1.0084] ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Aphāsukakāle ca yadettha kappiyaṃ, taṃ attanāpi paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Kappiyakuṭiyaṃ pana bahuṃ ṭhapentassāpi sannidhi nāma natthi. Tathāgatassa pana taṇḍulanāḷiādīsu vā yaṃ kiñci caturatanamattaṃ vā pilotikakhaṇḍaṃ “idaṃ me ajja vā sve vā bhavissatī”ti ṭhapitaṃ nāma natthi.

However, for a monk, in his dwelling place, it is proper to store this much: one nāḷi of rice, one lump of molasses, and a quarter-measure of ghee, for the sake of thieves who arrive at an unsuitable time. For if they, not receiving even this much material hospitality, might even take a life. Therefore, if this much is not there, it is proper even to have it brought and stored. And in a time of illness, whatever among this is allowable, it is proper for him to consume that himself. However, for one who stores much in an allowable storehouse, there is no 'storing.' For the Tathāgata, there is no such thing as storing anything among things like a nāḷi of rice, or a piece of cloth worth four ratanas, thinking, 'This will be for me today or tomorrow.'

13. Visūkadassanesu naccaṃ nāma yaṃ kiñci naccaṃ, taṃ maggaṃ gacchantenāpi gīvaṃ pasāretvā daṭṭhuṃ na vaṭṭati. Vitthāravinicchayo panettha samantapāsādikāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Yathā cettha, evaṃ sabbesu sikkhāpadapaṭisaṃyuttesu suttapadesu. Ito parañhi ettakampi avatvā tattha tattha payojanamattameva vaṇṇayissāmāti.

13. Among the shows, 'dancing' is any dancing whatsoever. It is not proper even for one going along a road to stretch one's neck to watch it. The detailed explanation here should be understood according to the method stated in the Samantapāsādikā. And as it is here, so it is in all Sutta passages connected with the training rules. For from now on, without saying even this much, we will explain only the essential meaning in each respective case.

Pekkhanti naṭasamajjaṃ. Akkhānanti bhāratayujjhanādikaṃ. Yasmiṃ ṭhāne kathīyati, tattha gantumpi na vaṭṭati. Pāṇissaranti kaṃsatāḷaṃ, pāṇitāḷantipi vadanti. Vetāḷanti ghanatāḷaṃ, mantena matasarīruṭṭhāpanantipi eke. Kumbhathūṇanti caturassaambaṇakatāḷaṃ, kumbhasaddantipi eke. Sobhanakanti naṭānaṃ [M 1.0082] abbhokkiraṇaṃ, sobhanakaraṃ vā, paṭibhānacittanti vuttaṃ hoti. Caṇḍālanti ayoguḷakīḷā, caṇḍālānaṃ sāṇadhovanakīḷātipi vadanti. Vaṃsanti veḷuṃ ussāpetvā kīḷanaṃ.

They watch a festival of dancers (naṭasamajjaṃ). Akkhāna means recitations of things like the Bhārata war; it is not proper even to go to a place where this is recited. Pāṇissara means the sound of bronze cymbals; some say it is hand-clapping. Vetāḷa means a solid percussion instrument; some say it is the raising of a dead body by means of a spell. Kumbhathūṇa means the sound of a square ambaṇaka drum; some say it is the sound of a pot-drum. Sobhanaka means making offerings on behalf of dancers, or making things beautiful, which is to say, pictorial art born of inspiration. Caṇḍāla means the iron-ball game; some say it is the caṇḍālas' game of washing hemp. Vaṃsa means playing by setting up a bamboo pole.

Dhovananti aṭṭhidhovanaṃ, ekaccesu kira janapadesu kālaṅkate ñātake na jhāpenti, nikhaṇitvā ṭhapenti. Atha nesaṃ pūtibhūtaṃ kāyaṃ ñatvā nīharitvā aṭṭhīni dhovitvā gandhehi makkhetvā ṭhapenti. Te nakkhattakāle ekasmiṃ ṭhāne aṭṭhīni ṭhapetvā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne surādīni ṭhapetvā rodantā paridevantā suraṃ pivanti. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “atthi, bhikkhave[P 1.0085], dakkhiṇesu janapadesu aṭṭhidhovanaṃ nāma, tattha hoti annampi pānampi khajjampi bhojjampi leyyampi peyyampi naccampi gītampi vāditampi. Atthetaṃ, bhikkhave, dhovanaṃ, netaṃ natthīti vadāmī”ti (a. ni. 10.107). Ekacce pana indajālena aṭṭhidhovanaṃ dhovanantipi vadanti.

Dhovananti means the bone-washing festival. It is said that in some regions, they do not cremate deceased relatives; having buried them, they keep them. Then, knowing their body has become putrid, they take it out, wash the bones, anoint them with perfumes, and keep them. At the time of a star festival, they place the bones in one place and liquor and so on in another place, and weeping and lamenting, they drink liquor. And this was also said: 'Bhikkhus, in the southern regions, there is what is called the bone-washing festival. Therein, there is food, drink, hard food, soft food, things to be licked, things to be drunk, dancing, singing, and music. This bone-washing exists, bhikkhus; I do not say it does not exist' (A 10.107). Some, however, say that dhovanaṃ means bone-washing or displaying the bones by means of magic like Indra's net.

Hatthiyuddhādīsu bhikkhuno neva hatthiādīhi saddhiṃ yujjhituṃ, na te yujjhāpetuṃ, na yujjhante daṭṭhuṃ vaṭṭati. Nibbuddhanti mallayuddhaṃ. Uyyodhikanti yattha sampahāro dissati. Balagganti balagaṇanaṭṭhānaṃ. Senābyūhanti senāniveso, sakaṭabyūhādivasena senāya nivesanaṃ. Anīkadassananti – “tayo hatthī pacchimaṃ hatthānīka”ntiādinā (pāci. 324) nayena vuttassa anīkassa dassanaṃ.

Regarding elephant fights and so on: it is not proper for a bhikkhu to fight with elephants and so on, nor to cause them to fight, nor to watch them fighting. Nibbuddhanti means a wrestling match. Uyyodhikanti means where a fierce striking is seen. Balagganti means the place for counting troops. Senābyūhanti means the encampment of an army, or the disposition of an army by means of formations such as the cart-formation. Anīkadassananti means the viewing of a military division spoken of by the method of 'three elephants are the rearmost elephant division,' and so on (Pācittiya 324).

14. Pamādo [V 1.0078] ettha tiṭṭhatīti pamādaṭṭhānaṃ. Jūtañca taṃ pamādaṭṭhānañcāti jūtappamādaṭṭhānaṃ. Ekekāya pantiyā aṭṭha aṭṭha padāni assāti aṭṭhapadaṃ dasapadepi eseva nayo. Ākāsanti aṭṭhapadadasapadesu viya ākāseyeva kīḷanaṃ. Parihārapathanti bhūmiyaṃ nānāpathamaṇḍalaṃ katvā tattha tattha pariharitabbaṃ, pathaṃ pariharantānaṃ kīḷanaṃ. Santikanti santikakīḷanaṃ. Ekajjhaṃ ṭhapitā sāriyo vā sakkharāyo vā acālentā nakheneva apanenti ca upanenti ca, sace tattha kāci calati, parājayo hoti, evarūpāya kīḷāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Khalikanti jūtaphalake pāsakakīḷanaṃ. Ghaṭikā vuccati dīghadaṇḍakena rassadaṇḍakaṃ paharaṇakīḷanaṃ. Salākahatthanti lākhāya vā mañjiṭṭhikāya vā piṭṭhodakena vā salākahatthaṃ [P 1.0086] temetvā – “kiṃ [M 1.0083] hotū”ti bhūmiyaṃ vā bhittiyaṃ vā taṃ paharitvā hatthiassādirūpadassanakīḷanaṃ. Akkhanti guḷakīḷā. Paṅgacīraṃ vuccati paṇṇanāḷikaṃ, taṃ dhamantā kīḷanti. Vaṅkakanti gāmadārakānaṃ kīḷanakaṃ khuddakanaṅgalaṃ. Mokkhacikā vuccati samparivattanakīḷā, ākāse vā daṇḍakaṃ gahetvā bhūmiyaṃ vā sīsaṃ ṭhapetvā heṭṭhupariyabhāvena parivattanakīḷāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ciṅgulikaṃ vuccati tālapaṇṇādīhi kataṃ vātappahārena paribbhamanacakkaṃ. Pattāḷhakaṃ vuccati paṇṇanāḷikā. Tāya vālukādīni minantā kīḷanti. Rathakanti khuddakarathaṃ. Dhanukanti khuddakadhanumeva. Akkharikā vuccati ākāse vā piṭṭhiyaṃ vā akkharajānanakīḷā. Manesikā nāma manasā cintitajānanakīḷā. Yathāvajjaṃ nāma kāṇakuṇikhujjādīnaṃ yaṃ yaṃ vajjaṃ, taṃ taṃ payojetvā dassanakīḷā.

14. Heedlessness stands here, thus it is a basis for heedlessness. It is both gambling and a basis for heedlessness, thus it is the gambling-basis for heedlessness. Because it has eight squares in each row, it is called aṭṭhapada; the same method applies to dasapada. Ākāsa means playing in the open air, just as on an aṭṭhapada or dasapada board. Parihārapatha is the game of those who avoid the paths, having made various circular paths on the ground to be avoided here and there. Santika is the game of santika. Counters or pebbles are placed together, and one removes or brings them near with only the nail without shaking them; if any of them moves, it is a loss. This is the term for such a game. Khalika is playing with dice on a gambling board. Ghaṭikā is the name for the game of striking a short stick with a long stick. Salākahattha is the game of showing figures of elephants, horses, and so on, by moistening a bundle of palm fibers with lac, madder, or rice-flour water, asking 'What shall it be?', and striking it on the ground or a wall. Akkha is the game of playing with marbles. Paṅgacīra is the name for a small leaf-pipe; they play by blowing it. Vaṅkaka is a small toy plow for village children. Mokkhacikā is the name for the game of turning somersaults; it is said to be the game of revolving with an up-and-down motion, either by grasping a pole in the air or by placing the head on the ground. Ciṅgulika is the name for a wheel made of palm leaves or the like that spins by the force of the wind. Pattāḷhaka is the name for a small measuring basket made of leaves; they play by measuring sand and so on with it. Rathaka means a small chariot. Dhanuka means just a small bow. Akkharikā is the name for the game of identifying letters in the air or on one's back. Manesikā is the name for the game of knowing a thought conceived in the mind.

15. Āsandinti pamāṇātikkantāsanaṃ. Anuyuttā viharantīti idaṃ apekkhitvā pana sabbapadesu upayogavacanaṃ kataṃ. Pallaṅkoti pādesu vāḷarūpāni ṭhapetvā kato. Gonakoti dīghalomako mahākojavo, caturaṅgulādhikāni kira tassa lomāni. Cittakanti vānavicittaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇaṃ. Paṭikāti uṇṇāmayo setattharaṇo. Paṭalikāti [P 1.0087] ghanapupphako uṇṇāmayattharaṇo. Yo āmalakapattotipi vuccati. Tūlikāti tiṇṇaṃ tūlānaṃ aññatarapuṇṇā tūlikā. Vikatikāti sīhabyagghādirūpavicitro uṇṇāmayattharaṇo. Uddalomīti ubhayatodasaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇaṃ, keci “ekatouggatapuppha”nti vadanti. Ekantalomīti ekatodasaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇaṃ. Keci “ubhatouggatapuppha”nti vadanti. Kaṭṭissanti ratanaparisibbitaṃ koseyyakaṭṭissamayapaccattharaṇaṃ. Koseyyanti ratanaparisibbitameva kosiyasuttamayapaccattharaṇaṃ. Suddhakoseyyaṃ pana vaṭṭatīti vinaye vuttaṃ. Dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “ṭhapetvā tūlikaṃ sabbāneva gonakādīni ratanaparisibbitāni na vaṭṭantī”ti vuttaṃ.

15. Āsandī means a seat that exceeds the standard measure. However, with reference to the phrase 'they dwell engaged in,' the accusative case has been used in all these instances. Pallaṅka is a couch made by placing figures of fierce animals on its legs. Gonaka is a large rug with long fleece; it is said its fleece is more than four finger-breadths long. Cittaka is a woolen spread with variegated weaving. Paṭikā is a white woolen spread. Paṭalikā is a woolen spread with thick flower patterns, which is also called 'myrobalan-leaf-patterned.' Tūlikā is a mattress filled with one of the three kinds of cotton. Vikatikā is a woolen spread variegated with figures of lions, tigers, and so on. Uddalomī is a woolen spread with a fringe on both sides; some say it has raised flowers on one side. Ekantalomī is a woolen spread with a fringe on one side; some say it has raised flowers on both sides. Kaṭṭissa is a coverlet made of coarse silk, interwoven with jewels. Koseyya is a coverlet made of silk thread, also interwoven with jewels. But in the Vinaya it is said that plain silk is allowable. In the Dīghanikāya commentary, however, it is said: 'Except for the tūlikā, all the others, from gonaka onwards, if interwoven with jewels, are not allowable.'

Kuttakanti soḷasannaṃ nāṭakitthīnaṃ ṭhatvā naccanayoggaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇaṃ. Hatthattharaṃ assattharanti [V 1.0079] hatthiassapiṭṭhīsu attharaṇaattharakāyeva. Rathattharepi eseva nayo. Ajinappaveṇīti ajinacammehi mañcappamāṇena sibbitvā katā [M 1.0084] paveṇī. Kadalīmigapavarapaccattharaṇanti kadalīmigacammaṃ nāma atthi, tena kataṃ pavarapaccattharaṇaṃ; uttamapaccattharaṇanti attho. Taṃ kira setavatthassa upari kadalīmigacammaṃ pattharitvā sibbetvā karonti. Sauttaracchadanti saha uttaracchadena, uparibaddhena rattavitānena saddhinti attho. Setavitānampi heṭṭhā akappiyapaccattharaṇe sati na vaṭṭati, asati pana vaṭṭati. Ubhatolohitakūpadhānanti sīsūpadhānañca pādūpadhānañcāti [P 1.0088] mañcassa ubhatolohitakaṃ upadhānaṃ, etaṃ na kappati. Yaṃ pana ekameva upadhānaṃ ubhosu passesu rattaṃ vā hoti padumavaṇṇaṃ vā vicitraṃ vā, sace pamāṇayuttaṃ, vaṭṭati. Mahāupadhānaṃ pana paṭikkhittaṃ. Alohitakāni dvepi vaṭṭantiyeva. Tato uttari labhitvā aññesaṃ dātabbāni. Dātuṃ asakkonto mañce tiriyaṃ attharitvā upari paccattharaṇaṃ datvā nipajjitumpi labhati. Āsandīādīsu pana vuttanayeneva paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, āsandiyā pāde chinditvā paribhuñjituṃ, pallaṅkassa vāḷe bhinditvā paribhuñjituṃ, tūlikaṃ vijaṭetvā bimbohanaṃ kātuṃ, avasesaṃ bhummattharaṇaṃ kātu”nti (cūḷava. 297).

Kuttaka is a woolen covering suitable for sixteen dancing girls to stand on and dance. Hatthatthara and assatthara are coverings to be spread on the backs of elephants and horses respectively. The same method applies also to a chariot cover. Ajinappaveṇī is a layered covering made by sewing together black antelope skins to the size of a bed. Kadalīmigapavarapaccattharaṇa is an excellent upper covering made from what is called a kadalīmiga hide; this means a superior upper covering. It is said that they make it by spreading and sewing the kadalīmiga hide over a white cloth. Sauttaracchada means 'together with an upper canopy'; that is, along with a red canopy attached above. A white canopy is also not allowable if there is an unallowable upper covering beneath it, but if there is not, it is allowable. Ubhatolohitakūpadhāna means a head-cushion and a foot-cushion, thus a red cushion at both ends of the bed; this is not allowable. However, a single cushion that is red, lotus-colored, or variegated on both its sides is allowable if it is of proper size. A large cushion, however, is rejected. Two non-red cushions are indeed allowable. Having obtained more than that, they should be given to others. One who is unable to give them away may spread them crosswise on the bed, place an upper covering on top, and lie down. Furthermore, regarding the āsandī and so forth, one should act only in the manner that has been stated. For it has been said: 'Bhikkhus, I allow you to cut off the legs of a high seat (āsandī) and use it, to break off the animal figures of a couch (pallaṅka) and use it, to undo a cotton-filled mattress and make a pillow, and to make a ground-covering of the remainder.' (Cūḷavagga 297)

16. Ucchādanādīsu mātukucchito nikkhantadārakānaṃ sarīragandho dvādasavassapattakāle nassati, tesaṃ sarīraduggandhaharaṇatthāya gandhacuṇṇādīhi ucchādenti, evarūpaṃ ucchādanaṃ na vaṭṭati. Puññavante pana dārake ūrūsu nipajjāpetvā telena makkhetvā hatthapādaūrunābhiādīnaṃ saṇṭhānasampādanatthaṃ parimaddanti, evarūpaṃ parimaddanaṃ na vaṭṭati.

16. Regarding ucchādana and so forth: For children who have come out from their mother's womb, their body odor disappears when they reach the age of twelve. For the purpose of removing their bad body odor, they are rubbed with scented powders and so forth; such rubbing is not allowable. However, in the case of fortunate children, after making them lie on the thighs and smearing them with oil, they are massaged for the purpose of perfecting the form of their hands, feet, thighs, navel, and so on; such massaging is not allowable.

Nhāpananti tesaṃyeva dārakānaṃ gandhādīhi nhāpanaṃ. Sambāhananti mahāmallānaṃ viya hatthapāde muggarādīhi paharitvā bāhuvaḍḍhanaṃ. Ādāsanti yaṃ kiñci ādāsaṃ pariharituṃ na vaṭṭati. Añjananti alaṅkārañjanameva. Mālāti baddhamālā vā abaddhamālā vā. Vilepananti yaṃ kiñci chavirāgakaraṇaṃ. Mukhacuṇṇaṃ mukhalepananti mukhe kāḷapīḷakādīnaṃ haraṇatthāya mattikakakkaṃ denti, tena lohite calite sāsapakakkaṃ denti, tena dose khādite tilakakkaṃ denti, tena lohite sannisinne haliddikakkaṃ denti, tena chavivaṇṇe ārūḷhe mukhacuṇṇakena mukhaṃ cuṇṇenti, taṃ sabbaṃ na vaṭṭati.

Nhāpana means bathing those same children with scented water and so forth. Sambāhana means developing the arms by striking the hands and feet with clubs and so forth, like great wrestlers do. Ādāsa: It is not allowable to keep any kind of mirror as one's own possession. Añjana means only collyrium used for adornment. Mālā means either bound flowers (i.e., garlands) or unbound flowers. Vilepana means anything that beautifies the skin's complexion and causes attachment. Mukhacuṇṇa and mukhalepana: For the purpose of removing black boils and the like from the face, they apply a medicinal clay paste. When the bad blood is agitated by that, they apply a mustard paste. When the affliction of blood is consumed by that, they apply a sesame paste. When the blood is settled by that, they apply a turmeric paste. When the skin's complexion has improved due to that, they powder the face with face powder. All of this is not allowable.

Hatthabandhādīsu [P 1.0089][M 1.0085] hatthe vicitrasaṅkhakapālādīni bandhitvā vicaranti, taṃ vā aññaṃ vā sabbampi hatthābharaṇaṃ na vaṭṭati, apare sikhaṃ bandhitvā vicaranti. Suvaṇṇacīrakamuttalatādīhi ca [V 1.0080] taṃ parikkhipanti; taṃ sabbaṃ na vaṭṭati. Apare catuhatthadaṇḍaṃ vā aññaṃ vā pana alaṅkatadaṇḍakaṃ gahetvā vicaranti, tathā itthipurisarūpādivicittaṃ bhesajjanāḷikaṃ suparikkhittaṃ vāmapasse olaggitaṃ; apare kaṇṇikaratanaparikkhittakosaṃ atitikhiṇaṃ asiṃ, pañcavaṇṇasuttasibbitaṃ makaradantakādivicittaṃ chattaṃ, suvaṇṇarajatādivicitrā morapiñchādiparikkhittā upāhanā, keci ratanamattāyāmaṃ caturaṅgulavitthataṃ kesantaparicchedaṃ dassetvā meghamukhe vijjulataṃ viya nalāṭe uṇhīsapaṭṭaṃ bandhanti, cūḷāmaṇiṃ dhārenti, cāmaravālabījaniṃ dhārenti, taṃ sabbaṃ na vaṭṭati.

Regarding hatthabandha and so forth: They wander about having bound variegated ornaments like conch-shell cups on their hands; that or any other hand ornament whatsoever is not allowable. Others tie their hair in a topknot and wander about. They also encircle it with golden hair ornaments, strings of pearls, and the like; all of that is not allowable. Others wander about carrying a staff four cubits long or another decorated staff, and likewise a well-protected medicine tube, variegated with figures of men and women, etc., hung on the left side. Others carry an extremely sharp sword in a sheath surrounded by pinnacle-gems; a parasol stitched with five-colored thread and variegated with makara-tooth patterns, etc.; and sandals variegated with gold, silver, etc., and surrounded by peacock feathers, etc. Some, showing a hairline one ratana in length and four fingers in breadth, tie a forehead-plate on the forehead like a flash of lightning at the edge of a cloud. They wear a crest-jewel. They carry a yak-tail whisk. All of that is not allowable.

17. Aniyyānikattā saggamokkhamaggānaṃ tiracchānabhūtā kathāti tiracchānakathā. Tattha rājānaṃ ārabbha mahāsammato mandhātā dhammāsoko evaṃ mahānubhāvotiādinā nayena pavattā kathā rājakathā. Esa nayo corakathādīsu. Tesu asuko rājā abhirūpo dassanīyotiādinā nayena gehassitakathāva tiracchānakathā hoti. Sopi nāma evaṃ mahānubhāvo khayaṃ gatoti evaṃ pavattā pana kammaṭṭhānabhāve tiṭṭhati. Coresu mūladevo evaṃ mahānubhāvo, meghamālo evaṃ mahānubhāvoti tesaṃ kammaṃ paṭicca aho sūrāti gehassitakathāva tiracchānakathā. Yuddhepi bhāratayuddhādīsu asukena asuko evaṃ mārito, evaṃ viddhoti kāmassādavaseneva kathā tiracchānakathā. Tepi nāma khayaṃ gatāti evaṃ pavattā pana sabbattha kammaṭṭhānameva hoti. Api ca annādīsu evaṃ vaṇṇavantaṃ gandhavantaṃ rasavantaṃ phassasampannaṃ khādimha bhuñjimhāti kāmassādavasena kathetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sātthakaṃ [P 1.0090] pana katvā pubbe evaṃ vaṇṇādisampannaṃ annaṃ pānaṃ vatthaṃ sayanaṃ mālaṃ gandhaṃ sīlavantānaṃ adamha, cetiye pūjaṃ karimhāti kathetuṃ vaṭṭati. Ñātikathādīsu pana “amhākaṃ ñātakā sūrā samatthā”ti vā “pubbe mayaṃ evaṃ vicitrehi yānehi vicarimhā”ti vā assādavasena vattuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sātthakaṃ pana katvā “tepi no ñātakā khayaṃ gatā”ti vā “pubbe mayaṃ evarūpā upāhanā saṅghassa adamhā”ti vā kathetuṃ vaṭṭati. Gāmakathāpi suniviṭṭhadunniviṭṭhasubhikkhadubbhikkhādivasena vā “asukagāmavāsino sūrā samatthā”ti [M 1.0086] vā evaṃ assādavasena na vaṭṭati. Sātthakaṃ pana katvā “saddhā pasannā”ti vā “khayavayaṃ gatā”ti vā vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Nigamanagarajanapadakathādīsupi eseva nayo.

17. Because it is non-conducive to release, being an obstruction to the paths to heaven and liberation, such talk is called 'animal-level talk'. Herein, talk about kings—such as 'Mahāsammata, Mandhātā, and Dhammāsoka were of great power'—narrated in this manner, is called talk about kings. This same principle applies to talk about thieves and so on. Among these, statements like 'Such-and-such a king was handsome and pleasing to behold,' and similar talk connected with worldly life, is animal-level talk. However, if such talk proceeds with 'Even one so mighty has passed on to destruction,' it then stands as a basis for meditation. Regarding thieves, tales like 'Mūladeva was of such great power,' or 'Meghamāla was of such great power,' and then, based on their deeds, exclaiming 'Oh, how brave!'—this too, is talk connected with worldly life and is animal-level talk. In battle as well, such as in the Bhārata war and others, talk like 'By so-and-so, such-and-such a person was killed thus, was pierced thus,' spoken only with sensual delight, is animal-level talk. However, if such talk proceeds with 'They too have passed on to destruction,' it becomes solely a basis for meditation in all cases. Furthermore, regarding food and so on, it is not proper to speak with sensual delight, saying, 'We have chewed and eaten such food, endowed with color, fragrance, taste, and pleasant texture.' Instead, making the talk meaningful, it is proper to say, 'In the past, we gave such food, drink, clothing, lodging, garlands, and perfumes, endowed with color and so on, to the virtuous.' Regarding talk about relatives and so on, it is not proper to speak with delight, saying, 'Our relatives are brave and capable,' or 'In the past, we traveled in such splendid vehicles.' Instead, making the talk meaningful, it is proper to say, 'Even those relatives of ours have passed on to destruction,' or 'In the past, we gave such footwear to the Sangha.' Talk about villages is also not proper when spoken with delight, whether by way of being well-established or poorly-established, of abundance or famine, or saying, 'The inhabitants of such-and-such a village are brave and capable.' Instead, making the talk meaningful, it is proper to say, 'They have faith and are devout,' or 'They have passed on to destruction and decay.' This same principle applies to talk about market towns, cities, countries, and so on.

Itthikathāpi vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādīni paṭicca assādavasena na vaṭṭati, saddhā pasannā khayavayaṃ gatāti evameva vaṭṭati. Sūrakathāpi ‘nandimitto nāma yodho sūro ahosī’ti assādavasena na vaṭṭati. Saddho ahosi khayaṃ gatoti evameva vaṭṭati. Visikhākathāpi “asukā [V 1.0081] visikhā suniviṭṭhā dunniviṭṭhā sūrā samatthā”ti assādavasena na vaṭṭati. Saddhā pasannā khayavayaṃ gatāti evameva vaṭṭati.

Talk about women is also not proper if, based on their complexion, figure, and so on, it is spoken with delight; it is proper only in this way: 'She has faith, is devout,' or 'She has passed on to destruction and decay.' Talk about heroes is also not proper if spoken with delight, saying, 'A warrior named Nandimitta was brave.' It is proper only in this way: 'He was faithful,' or 'He has passed on to destruction.' Talk about streets is also not proper if spoken with delight, saying, 'Such-and-such a street is well-established or poorly-established,' or 'Its residents are brave and capable.' It is proper only in this way: 'They have faith, are devout,' or 'They have passed on to destruction and decay.'

Kumbhaṭṭhānakathāti udakaṭṭhānakathā, udakatitthakathātipi vuccati, kumbhadāsikathā vā, sāpi “pāsādikā naccituṃ gāyituṃ chekā”ti assādavasena na vaṭṭati; saddhā pasannātiādinā nayeneva vaṭṭati. Pubbapetakathāti atītañātikathā. Tattha vattamānañātikathāsadiso vinicchayo.

Talk about `kumbhaṭṭhāna` (water-pot stands) is talk about places for water—also called talk about watering places—or it is talk about a potter's slave-girl (`kumbhadāsī`). That too is not proper if spoken with delight, saying, 'She is charming, and skilled in dancing and singing'; it is proper only in the manner of 'She has faith, is devout,' and so on. Talk about past departed ones (`pubbapeta`) is talk about relatives who have passed away. Therein, the judgment is similar to that for talk about present relatives.

Nānattakathāti purimapacchimakathāhi vimuttā avasesā nānāsabhāvā niratthakakathā. Lokakkhāyikāti ayaṃ loko kena nimmito, asukena nāma [P 1.0091] nimmito. Kāko seto, aṭṭhīnaṃ setattā; balākā rattā. Lohitassa rattattāti evamādikā lokāyatavitaṇḍasallāpakathā.

Talk about diversity (`nānattakathā`) is the remaining meaningless talk of various natures, which is separate from the preceding and succeeding topics. Talk about world-speculation (`lokakkhāyikā`) is worldly speculation and sophistry (`lokāyatavitaṇḍasallāpa`) such as: 'By whom was this world created?' 'It was created by so-and-so'; 'A crow is white because of the whiteness of its bones; a crane is red because of the redness of its blood,' and so on.

Samuddakkhāyikā nāma kasmā samuddo sāgaro? Sāgaradevena khato, tasmā sāgaro. Khato meti hatthamuddāya sayaṃ niveditattā “samuddo”ti evamādikā niratthakā samuddakkhāyanakathā. Bhavoti vuḍḍhi. Abhavoti hāni. Iti bhavo, iti abhavoti yaṃ vā taṃ vā niratthakakāraṇaṃ vatvā pavattitakathā itibhavābhavakathā.

Talk called `samuddakkhāyikā` (ocean-speculation) is meaningless talk explaining the ocean, such as: 'Why is the ocean called `sāgara`? Because it was dug by the deva Sāgara, therefore it is called `sāgara`.' Or, 'Because he himself made it known with a hand gesture, saying, "It was dug by me," it is called `samudda`.' `Bhava` is prosperity; `abhava` is decline. Talk of 'thus there is prosperity, thus there is decline,' which proceeds by stating some or other meaningless reason, is called talk of prosperity and decline (`itibhavābhavakathā`).

18. Viggāhikakathāti viggahakathā, sārambhakathā. Tattha sahitaṃ meti mayhaṃ vacanaṃ sahitaṃ siliṭṭhaṃ atthayuttaṃ kāraṇayuttanti attho. Asahitaṃ teti tuyhaṃ vacanaṃ asahitaṃ asiliṭṭhaṃ. Adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvattanti yaṃ tuyhaṃ dīgharattāciṇṇavasena suppaguṇaṃ, taṃ mayhaṃ ekavacaneneva viparāvattaṃ parivattitvā ṭhitaṃ, na kiñci jānāsīti attho.

18. Contentious talk (`viggāhikakathā`) is talk of dispute, talk of heated argument. Therein, 'My statement is coherent' means: 'My statement is coherent, polished, meaningful, and logical.' 'Your statement is incoherent' means: 'Your statement is incoherent and unpolished.' 'What you have long practiced has been overturned' means: 'That which was well-mastered by you through long practice has been overturned and stands reversed by my single statement; you know nothing.'

Āropito [M 1.0087] te vādoti mayā tava doso āropito. Cara vādappamokkhāyāti dosamocanatthaṃ cara, vicara; tattha tattha gantvā sikkhāti attho. Nibbeṭhehi vā sace pahosīti atha sayaṃ pahosi, idānimeva nibbeṭhehīti.

'A charge has been brought against you' means: 'I have imputed a fault to you.' 'Go for release from the charge' means: 'For the sake of release from the fault, go, wander about; go to various teachers and learn.' 'Or refute it, if you are able,' means: 'If you yourself are able, then refute it right now.'

19. Dūteyyakathāyaṃ idha gacchāti ito asukaṃ nāma ṭhānaṃ gaccha. Amutrāgacchāti tato asukaṃ nāma ṭhānaṃ āgaccha. Idaṃ harāti ito idaṃ nāma hara. Amutra idaṃ āharāti asukaṭṭhānato [V 1.0082] idaṃ nāma idha āhara. Saṅkhepato pana idaṃ dūteyyaṃ nāma ṭhapetvā pañca sahadhammike ratanattayassa upakārapaṭisaṃyuttañca gihīsāsanaṃ aññesaṃ na vaṭṭati.

19. In talk of messages (`dūteyyakathā`): 'Go here' means: 'Go from this place to such-and-such a place.' 'Come there' means: 'Come from that place to such-and-such a place.' 'Take this' means: 'Take this thing from this place.' 'Bring this from there' means: 'Bring this thing from such-and-such a place to this place.' In brief, this act of being a messenger is not proper, except for the five fellow practitioners of the Dhamma and for a message from laypeople that is connected with what is beneficial to the Triple Gem.

20. Kuhakātiādīsu tividhena kuhanavatthunā lokaṃ kuhayanti, vimhāpayantīti kuhakā. Lābhasakkāratthikā hutvā lapantīti lapakā. Nimittaṃ sīlametesanti nemittikā. Nippeso sīlametesanti nippesikā. Lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanti [P 1.0092] magganti pariyesantīti lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsitāro. Kuhanā, lapanā, nemittikatā, nippesikatā, lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatāti etāhi samannāgatānaṃ puggalānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārena panetā kuhanādikā visuddhimagge sīlaniddeseyeva pāḷiñca aṭṭhakathañca āharitvā pakāsitāti.

20. In 'deceivers' and so on: because they cause the world to be astonished by means of the three kinds of bases for deception, they are called deceivers (`kuhakā`). Being desirous of gain and honor, they flatter; thus they are called flatterers (`lapakā`). The practice of making signs is their habit; thus they are called hinters (`nemittikā`). The practice of belittling is their habit; thus they are called belittlers (`nippesikā`). They seek and search for a large gain by means of a small gain; thus they are called 'those who pursue gain with gain' (`lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsitāro`). Deception, flattery, the state of being a hinter, the state of being a belittler, and the state of pursuing gain with gain—this is the designation for individuals endowed with these qualities. This is the summary here. In detail, however, these—deception and so on—have been explained in the Visuddhimagga, in the Exposition of Virtue itself, by citing both the Pāḷi and the commentary.

Ettāvatā majjhimasīlaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ hoti.

Thus far, the intermediate section on virtue is concluded.

Mahāsīlavaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Great Virtue

21. Ito paraṃ mahāsīlaṃ hoti. Aṅganti hatthapādādīsu yena kenaci evarūpena aṅgena samannāgato dīghāyu yasavā hotītiādinayappavattaṃ aṅgasatthaṃ. Nimittanti nimittasatthaṃ. Paṇḍurājā kira tisso muttāyo muṭṭhiyaṃ katvā nemittikaṃ pucchi – “kiṃ me hatthe”ti? So ito cito ca vilokesi, tasmiñca samaye gharagolikāya makkhikā gayhantī muttā, so “muttā”ti āha. Puna “katī”ti puṭṭho kukkuṭassa tikkhattuṃ ravantassa saddaṃ sutvā “tisso”ti āha. Evaṃ taṃ taṃ ādisitvā nimittamanuyuttā viharanti.

21. Hereafter is the Great Virtue. 'Limb' (`aṅga`) means the science of limbs (`aṅgasatthaṃ`), which proceeds according to the method: 'A person endowed with any such limb among hands, feet, and so on, becomes long-lived and famous,' and so on. 'Sign' (`nimitta`) means the science of signs (`nimittasatthaṃ`). It is said that King Paṇḍu, having placed three pearls in his fist, asked a sign-reader, 'What is in my hand?' He looked here and there, and at that moment, a fly being caught by a house lizard was released (`muttā`). So he said, 'Pearls' (`muttā`). When asked again, 'How many?' he heard the sound of a rooster crowing three times and said, 'Three.' Thus, indicating this and that sign, they dwell devoted to signs.

Uppātanti [M 1.0088] asanipātādīnaṃ mahantānaṃ uppatitaṃ, tañhi disvā “idaṃ bhavissati, evaṃ bhavissatī”ti ādisanti. Supinanti yo pubbaṇhasamaye supinaṃ passati, evaṃ vipāko hoti; yo idaṃ nāma passati, tassa idaṃ nāma hotītiādinā nayena supinakaṃ anuyuttā viharanti. Lakkhaṇanti iminā lakkhaṇena samannāgato rājā hoti, iminā uparājātiādikaṃ. Mūsikacchinnanti undūrakhāyitaṃ. Tenāpi hi ahate vā vatthe anahate vā vatthe ito paṭṭhāya evaṃ chinne idaṃ nāma hotīti ādisanti. Aggihomanti [P 1.0093] evarūpena dārunā evaṃ [V 1.0083] hute idaṃ nāma hotīti aggijuhanaṃ. Dabbihomādīnipi aggihomāneva, evarūpāya dabbiyā īdisehi kaṇādīhi hute idaṃ nāma hotīti evaṃ pavattivasena pana visuṃ vuttāni.

'Portent' (`uppāta`) means the occurrence of great signs such as the striking of lightning; for, having seen that, they declare, 'This will happen,' or 'It will happen thus.' 'Dream' (`supina`) means they live devoted to the science of dreams according to the method: 'Whoever sees a dream in the early morning, such is the result'; 'Whoever sees such-and-such, for them such-and-such will be the result,' and so on. 'Characteristic' (`lakkhaṇa`) refers to such things as: 'One endowed with this characteristic becomes a king; with this, a viceroy.' 'Rat-gnawed' (`mūsikacchinna`) means gnawed by a rat. For, based on that, they declare, 'If a new cloth or a used cloth is gnawed in such a way from this point, such-and-such will be the result.' 'Fire offering' (`aggihoma`) is the offering to fire, according to: 'When an offering is made in such a way with such-and-such wood, such-and-such will be the result.' 'Ladle offering' (`dabbihoma`) and so on are also fire offerings; however, they are mentioned separately on account of their proceeding thus: 'When an offering is made with such-and-such a ladle, with such things as broken rice, such-and-such will be the result.'

Tattha kaṇoti kuṇḍako. Taṇḍulāti sāliādīnañceva tiṇajātīnañca taṇḍulā. Sappīti gosappiādikaṃ. Telanti tilatelādikaṃ. Sāsapādīni pana mukhena gahetvā aggimhi pakkhipanaṃ, vijjaṃ parijappitvā juhanaṃ vā mukhahomaṃ. Dakkhiṇakkhakajaṇṇulohitādīhi juhanaṃ lohitahomaṃ. Aṅgavijjāti pubbe aṅgameva disvā byākaraṇavasena aṅgaṃ vuttaṃ, idha aṅgulaṭṭhiṃ disvā vijjaṃ parijappitvā ayaṃ kulaputto vā no vā, sirīsampanno vā no vātiādibyākaraṇavasena aṅgavijjā vuttā. Vatthuvijjāti gharavatthuārāmavatthādīnaṃ guṇadosasallakkhaṇavijjā. Mattikādivisesaṃ disvāpi hi vijjaṃ parijappitvā heṭṭhā pathaviyaṃ tiṃsaratanamatte, ākāse ca asītiratanamatte padese guṇadosaṃ passanti. Khattavijjāti abbheyyamāsurakkharājasatthādisatthaṃ. Sivavijjāti susāne pavisitvā santikaraṇavijjā, siṅgālarutavijjātipi vadanti. Bhūtavijjāti bhūtavejjamanto. Bhūrivijjāti bhūrighare vasantena uggahetabbamanto. Ahivijjāti sappadaṭṭhatikicchanavijjā ceva sappāvhāyanavijjā ca. Visavijjāti yāya, purāṇavisaṃ vā rakkhanti, navavisaṃ vā karonti visavantameva vā. Vicchikavijjāti vicchikadaṭṭhatikicchanavijjā. Mūsikavijjāyapi [M 1.0089] eseva nayo. Sakuṇavijjāti sapakkhakaapakkhakadvipadacatuppadānaṃ rutagatādivasena sakuṇañāṇaṃ. Vāyasavijjāti kākarutañāṇaṃ, taṃ visuññeva satthaṃ, tasmā [P 1.0094] visuṃ vuttaṃ.

Therein, `kaṇa` is broken rice. `Taṇḍulā` are the grains of fine rice and so on, and of grass species. `Sappi` is ghee from a cow and so on. `Tela` is sesame oil and so on. Taking mustard seeds and the like in the mouth and placing them in the fire, or muttering a spell and making an offering, is a mouth-offering (`mukhahoma`). Offering with blood from the right collarbone, the knee, and so on, is a blood-offering (`lohitahoma`). Regarding the science of limbs (`aṅgavijjā`): previously, `aṅga` was mentioned in the sense of making a prediction after seeing a limb itself; here, the science of limbs (`aṅgavijjā`) is mentioned in the sense of making a prediction—after seeing a finger-bone and muttering a spell—as to whether 'this is a son of good family or not,' 'is endowed with fortune or not,' and so on. The science of sites (`vatthuvijjā`) is the science of discerning the merits and faults of sites for houses, parks, and so on. For, having seen the specific nature of the soil and so on and having muttered a spell, they see the merits and faults in a place thirty cubits below the earth and eighty cubits in the sky. The science of statecraft (`khattavijjā`) is the science of treatises such as the Abbheyya, Māsurakkha, and Rājasattha. The science of ghouls (`sivavijjā`) is the science of pacification performed after entering a charnel ground; some also say it is the science of jackal cries. The science of spirits (`bhūtavijjā`) is the spell for controlling spirits. The science of earth-dwellings (`bhūrivijjā`) is a spell to be learned while living in an earth-house. The science of snakes (`ahivijjā`) is both the science of treating snakebites and the science of summoning snakes. The science of poison (`visavijjā`) is that by which they either preserve old poison, or make new poison, or make the poison itself emit. The science of scorpions (`vicchikavijjā`) is the science of treating scorpion stings. For the science of rats (`mūsikavijjā`), the method is the same. The science of bird omens (`sakuṇavijjā`) is the knowledge of omens based on the cries, movements, and so on of winged and wingless creatures, bipeds, and quadrupeds. The science of crows (`vāyasavijjā`) is the knowledge of crow cries; that is a separate science, therefore it is mentioned separately.

Pakkajjhānanti paripākagatacintā. Idāni “ayaṃ ettakaṃ jīvissati, ayaṃ ettaka”nti evaṃ pavattaṃ ādiṭṭhañāṇanti attho. Saraparittāṇanti sararakkhaṇaṃ, yathā attano upari na āgacchati, evaṃ karaṇavijjā. Migacakkanti idaṃ sabbasaṅgāhikaṃ sabbasakuṇacatuppadānaṃ rutañāṇavasena vuttaṃ.

'Divining lifespan' (`pakkajjhāna`) means mature thought. The meaning is: it is the knowledge of prediction that proceeds thus, 'This person will live for this long; this person for that long.' 'Arrow-warding' (`saraparittāṇa`) is protection from arrows; it is the science of acting in such a way that an arrow does not come upon oneself. 'The animal cycle' (`migacakka`) is mentioned as an all-encompassing science, in the sense of knowledge of the cries of all birds and quadrupeds.

22. Maṇilakkhaṇādīsu evarūpo maṇi pasattho, evarūpo apasattho, sāmino ārogyaissariyādīnaṃ hetu hoti, na hotīti, evaṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādivasena maṇiādīnaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ anuyuttā viharantīti attho. Tattha āvudhanti ṭhapetvā asiādīni avasesaṃ āvudhaṃ. Itthilakkhaṇādīnipi yamhi kule te itthipurisādayo vasanti, tassa vuḍḍhihānivaseneva veditabbāni. Ajalakkhaṇādīsu pana evarūpānaṃ ajādīnaṃ maṃsaṃ khāditabbaṃ, evarūpānaṃ na khāditabbanti ayaṃ viseso veditabbo.

22. In 'characteristics of gems' and so on, the meaning is that they live devoted to the characteristics of gems and so on based on color, shape, and the like, determining: 'Such a gem is auspicious; such a gem is inauspicious'; 'It is a cause for the owner's health, sovereignty, and so on,' or 'It is not.' Therein, 'weapon' (`āvudha`) means the remaining weapons, having set aside swords and so on. The characteristics of women and so on should also be known simply by way of the growth or decline of the family in which those women, men, and so on dwell. In 'characteristics of goats' and so on, however, this distinction should be known: 'The meat of such-and-such goats and so on is to be eaten; of such-and-such, it is not to be eaten.'

Api [V 1.0084] cettha godhāya lakkhaṇe cittakammapiḷandhanādīsupi evarūpāya godhāya sati idaṃ nāma hotīti ayaṃ viseso veditabbo. Idañcettha vatthu – ekasmiṃ kira vihāre cittakamme godhaṃ aggiṃ dhamamānaṃ akaṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya bhikkhūnaṃ mahāvivādo jāto. Eko āgantukabhikkhu taṃ disvā makkhesi. Tato paṭṭhāya vivādo mandībhūto hoti. Kaṇṇikalakkhaṇaṃ piḷandhanakaṇṇikāyapi gehakaṇṇikāyapi vasena veditabbaṃ. Kacchapalakkhaṇaṃ godhālakkhaṇasadisameva. Migalakkhaṇaṃ sabbasaṅgāhikaṃ sabbacatuppadānaṃ lakkhaṇavasena vuttaṃ.

Furthermore, here, regarding the characteristics of a monitor lizard, it should be understood that even in elaborate paintings, sculptures, ornaments, and so on, if there is a monitor lizard image of this sort, such and such a result occurs—this distinction should be known. And this is the story here: It is said that in a certain monastery, in an elaborate painting or sculpture, they made an image of a monitor lizard blowing on a fire. From that time onwards, a great dispute arose among the monks. A certain visiting monk, upon seeing it, erased it. From that time onwards, the dispute subsided. The characteristic of a 'kaṇṇika' should be understood by way of both the 'kaṇṇika' of an ornament and the 'kaṇṇika' of a house. The characteristic of a turtle is just like the characteristic of a monitor lizard. The characteristic of a wild animal, being all-encompassing, was spoken by way of the characteristics of all quadrupeds.

23. Raññaṃ niyyānaṃ bhavissatīti asukadivase asukanakkhattena asukassa nāma rañño niggamanaṃ bhavissatīti evaṃ rājūnaṃ pavāsagamanaṃ byākaroti. Esa nayo sabbattha. Kevalaṃ panettha aniyyānanti vippavutthānaṃ puna āgamanaṃ. Abbhantarānaṃ raññaṃ upayānaṃ bhavissati[P 1.0095], bāhirānaṃ raññaṃ apayānanti antonagare amhākaṃ rājā paṭiviruddhaṃ bahirājānaṃ upasaṅkamissati, tato tassa paṭikkamanaṃ bhavissatīti evaṃ raññaṃ upayānāpayānaṃ [M 1.0090] byākaroti. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Jayaparājayā pākaṭāyeva.

23. ‘There will be a departure of kings’ means: he predicts the departure of kings for a foreign land, saying, ‘On such-and-such a day, under such-and-such a constellation, the departure for battle of the king named so-and-so will occur.’ This is the method everywhere. Here, however, ‘non-departure’ means the return of those who are away from their country. ‘There will be an advance for the internal kings and a retreat for the external kings’ means: he predicts the advance and retreat of kings, saying, ‘Our king in the inner city will approach the opposing external king, and consequently, the latter’s retreat will occur.’ In the second phrase as well, this is the same method. Victory and defeat are self-evident.

24. Candaggāhādayo asukadivase rāhu candaṃ gahessatīti byākaraṇavaseneva veditabbā. Api ca nakkhattassa aṅgārakādigāhasamāyogopi nakkhattagāhoyeva. Ukkāpātoti ākāsato ukkānaṃ patanaṃ. Disāḍāhoti disākālusiyaṃ aggisikhadhūmasikhādīhi ākulabhāvo viya. Devadudrabhīti sukkhavalāhakagajjanaṃ. Uggamananti udayanaṃ. Okkamananti atthaṅgamanaṃ. Saṃkilesanti avisuddhatā. Vodānanti visuddhatā. Evaṃ vipākoti lokassa evaṃ vividhasukhadukkhāvaho.

24. Lunar eclipses and the like should be known simply by way of prediction, such as: ‘On such-and-such a day, Rāhu will seize the moon.’ Furthermore, the conjunction of a constellation with planets such as Mars is itself a ‘seizure of the constellation.’ ‘A fall of firebrands’ is the falling of torch-like lights from the sky. ‘A burning of the directions’ is a gloominess in the directions, like a state of agitation by flames, plumes of smoke, and the like. ‘A celestial drum’ is the rumbling of dry clouds. ‘Ascent’ is rising. ‘Descent’ is setting. ‘Defilement’ is impurity. ‘Purification’ is purity. ‘Such is the result’ means bringing various kinds of happiness and suffering to the world.

25. Suvuṭṭhikāti devassa sammādhārānuppavecchanaṃ. Dubbuṭṭhikāti avaggāho, vassavibandhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Muddāti hatthamuddā. Gaṇanā vuccati acchiddakagaṇanā. Saṅkhānanti saṅkalanasaṭuppādanādivasena piṇḍagaṇanā. Yassa sā paguṇā hoti, so rukkhampi disvā ettakāni ettha paṇṇānīti jānāti. Kāveyyanti “cattārome, bhikkhave, kavī. Katame cattāro? Cintākavi, sutakavi, atthakavi, paṭibhānakavī”ti (a. ni. 4.231). Imesaṃ catunnaṃ kavīnaṃ attano cintāvasena vā; “vessantaro nāma rājā ahosī”tiādīni sutvā sutavasena vā; imassa ayaṃ attho, evaṃ taṃ yojessāmīti evaṃ atthavasena vā; kiñcideva disvā tappaṭibhāgaṃ kattabbaṃ karissāmīti evaṃ ṭhānuppattikapaṭibhānavasena vā; jīvikatthāya kabyakaraṇaṃ. Lokāyataṃ [P 1.0096] vuttameva.

25. ‘Good rainfall’ is the proper, uninterrupted flow of streams of water from the rain-deity. ‘Poor rainfall’ is a poor downpour, which is to say, an obstruction of rain. ‘Muddā’ is hand-reckoning. ‘Gaṇanā’ is called unbroken counting. ‘Saṅkhāna’ is aggregate counting by way of addition, separation, and so on. One for whom this is fluent, upon seeing even a tree, knows, ‘There are this many leaves on it.’ ‘Kāveyya’ is the composition of poetry for the sake of a livelihood by these four kinds of poets mentioned in the Aṅguttara Nikāya—‘Monks, there are these four kinds of poets. What four? The poet of thought, the poet of learning, the poet of meaning, and the poet of inspiration’—either by way of one’s own thought; or by way of what is heard, after hearing things such as, ‘There was a king named Vessantara’; or by way of meaning, thinking, ‘This is the meaning of this phrase; thus I will apply it’; or by way of spontaneous, situational inspiration, thinking, ‘Having seen something, I will compose a suitable response to it.’ ‘Lokāyata’ has already been explained.

26. Āvāhanaṃ [V 1.0085] nāma imassa dārakassa asukakulato asukanakkhattena dārikaṃ ānethāti āvāhakaraṇaṃ. Vivāhananti imaṃ dārikaṃ asukassa nāma dārakassa asukanakkhattena detha, evamassā vuḍḍhi bhavissatīti vivāhakaraṇaṃ. Saṃvaraṇanti saṃvaraṇaṃ nāma ‘ajja nakkhattaṃ sundaraṃ, ajjeva samaggā hotha, iti vo viyogo na bhavissatī’ti evaṃ samaggakaraṇaṃ. Vivaraṇaṃ nāma ‘sace viyujjitukāmattha, ajjeva viyujjatha[M 1.0091], iti vo puna saṃyogo na bhavissatī’ti evaṃ visaṃyogakaraṇaṃ. Saṅkiraṇanti ‘uṭṭhānaṃ vā iṇaṃ vā dinnaṃ dhanaṃ ajja saṅkaḍḍhatha, ajja saṅkaḍḍhitañhi taṃ thāvaraṃ hotī’ti evaṃ dhanapiṇḍāpanaṃ. Vikiraṇanti ‘sace payogauddhārādivasena dhanaṃ payojitukāmattha, ajja payojitaṃ diguṇacatugguṇaṃ hotī’ti evaṃ dhanapayojāpanaṃ. Subhagakaraṇanti piyamanāpakaraṇaṃ vā sassirīkakaraṇaṃ vā. Dubbhagakaraṇanti tabbiparītaṃ. Viruddhagabbhakaraṇanti viruddhassa vilīnassa aṭṭhitassa matassa gabbhassa karaṇaṃ. Puna avināsāya bhesajjadānanti attho. Gabbho hi vātena, pāṇakehi, kammunā cāti tīhi kāraṇehi vinassati. Tattha vātena vinassante nibbāpanīyaṃ sītalaṃ bhesajjaṃ deti, pāṇakehi vinassante pāṇakānaṃ paṭikammaṃ karoti, kammunā vinassante pana buddhāpi paṭibāhituṃ na sakkonti.

26. ‘Āvāhana’ is the act of bringing a bride, saying, ‘Bring a girl from such-and-such a family under such-and-such a constellation for this boy,’ or it is the art of selecting an auspicious day for bringing a bride. ‘Vivāhana’ is the act of giving a bride in marriage, saying, ‘Give this girl to the boy named so-and-so under such-and-such a constellation; thus she will prosper,’ or it is the art of selecting an auspicious day for giving a daughter in marriage. ‘Saṃvaraṇa’ is the act of creating harmony, saying, ‘Today the constellation is favorable; today you should reconcile, so that separation will not occur between you,’ or it is the art of selecting an auspicious day for creating harmony. ‘Vivaraṇa’ is the act of causing separation, saying, ‘If you wish to part, do so today, so that reunion will not happen again between you,’ or it is the art of selecting an auspicious day for causing separation. ‘Saṅkiraṇa’ is causing wealth to be amassed, saying, ‘Today, collect the revenue or the wealth given as a loan, for what is collected today becomes stable,’ or it is the art of selecting an auspicious day for causing wealth to be amassed. ‘Vikiraṇa’ is causing wealth to be invested, saying, ‘If you wish to invest wealth by way of trade, lending, and so on, what is invested today can become double or quadruple,’ or it is the art of selecting an auspicious day for causing wealth to be invested. ‘Subhagakaraṇa’ is the act of making one beloved and agreeable or making one glorious, or it is the art of teaching the method for doing so. ‘Dubbhagakaraṇa’ is the opposite of that. ‘Viruddhagabbhakaraṇa’ is the treatment of a fetus that is contrary, dissolved, unstable, or dead. The meaning is the giving of medicine so that it does not perish again. For a fetus is destroyed by three causes: by wind, by small creatures, and by kamma. Among these, if it is being destroyed by wind, one gives a cooling, calming medicine. If it is being destroyed by small creatures, one performs a counter-treatment for the small creatures. But if it is being destroyed by kamma, not even the Buddhas are able to prevent it.

Jivhānibandhananti mantena jivhāya bandhakaraṇaṃ. Hanusaṃhanananti [P 1.0097] mukhabandhamantena yathā hanukaṃ cāletuṃ na sakkonti, evaṃ bandhakaraṇaṃ. Hatthābhijappananti hatthānaṃ parivattanatthaṃ mantajappanaṃ. Tasmiṃ kira mante sattapadantare ṭhatvā jappite itaro hatthe parivattetvā khipati. Kaṇṇajappananti kaṇṇehi saddaṃ assavanatthāya vijjāya jappanaṃ. Taṃ kira jappitvā vinicchayaṭṭhāne yaṃ icchati, taṃ bhaṇati, paccatthiko taṃ na suṇāti, tato paṭivacanaṃ sampādetuṃ na sakkoti. Ādāsapañhanti ādāse devataṃ otāretvā pañhapucchanaṃ. Kumārikapañhanti kumārikāya sarīre devataṃ otāretvā pañhapucchanaṃ. Devapañhanti dāsiyā sarīre devataṃ otāretvā pañhapucchanaṃ. Ādiccupaṭṭhānanti jīvikatthāya ādiccapāricariyā. Mahatupaṭṭhānanti tatheva mahābrahmapāricariyā. Abbhujjalananti mantena mukhato aggijālānīharaṇaṃ. Sirivhāyananti “ehi siri, mayhaṃ sire patiṭṭhāhī”ti evaṃ sirena siriyā avhāyanaṃ.

Jivhānibandhana, 'binding of the tongue,' is the act of binding the tongue by means of a spell. Hanusaṃhanana, 'locking of the jaws,' is the act of binding by means of a mouth-binding spell in such a way that they cannot move the jaw. Hatthābhijappana, 'hand-charming,' is the recitation of a spell for the purpose of turning back the hands. It is said that when this spell is recited while one stands within seven steps, the other person turns back their hands and throws them down. Kaṇṇajappana, 'ear-charming,' is the recitation of a charm for the purpose of not hearing a sound with the ears. It is said that having recited it, one speaks what one wishes in a place of judgment, the opponent does not hear it, and therefore cannot formulate a reply. Ādāsapañha, 'mirror-questioning,' is causing a deity to descend into a mirror and asking a question. Kumārikapañha, 'maiden-questioning,' is causing a deity to descend into the body of a young girl and asking a question. Devapañha, 'deity-questioning,' is causing a deity to descend into the body of a female servant and asking a question. Ādiccupaṭṭhāna, 'worship of the sun,' is the service of the sun for the sake of a livelihood. Mahatupaṭṭhāna, 'worship of the great one,' is likewise the service of Mahābrahmā. Abbhujjalana, 'flame-belching,' is bringing forth a flame of fire from the mouth by means of a spell. Sirivhāyana, 'the summoning of fortune,' is the summoning of Siri, the goddess of fortune, with the head, saying: 'Come, O Siri, establish yourself upon my head!'

27. Santikammanti devaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā sace me idaṃ nāma samijjhissati, tumhākaṃ iminā ca iminā ca upahāraṃ karissāmīti samiddhikāle kattabbaṃ santipaṭissavakammaṃ. Tasmiṃ pana samiddhe tassa karaṇaṃ paṇidhikammaṃ nāma. Bhūrikammanti bhūrighare vasitvā gahitamantassa payogakaraṇaṃ. Vassakammaṃ vossakammanti ettha vassoti puriso, vossoti paṇḍako[V 1.0086]. Iti vossassa [M 1.0092] vassakaraṇaṃ vassakammaṃ, vassassa vossakaraṇaṃ vossakammaṃ. Taṃ pana karonto acchandikabhāvamattaṃ pāpeti, na liṅgaṃ antaradhāpetuṃ sakkoti.
