Vatthukammanti [P 1.0098] akatavatthusmiṃ gehapatiṭṭhāpanaṃ. Vatthuparikammanti “idañcidañcāharathā”ti vatvā vatthubalikammakaraṇaṃ. Ācamananti udakena mukhasuddhikaraṇaṃ. Nhāpananti aññesaṃ nhāpanaṃ. Juhananti tesaṃ atthāya aggijuhanaṃ. Vamananti yogaṃ datvā vamanakaraṇaṃ. Virecanepi eseva nayo. Uddhaṃvirecananti uddhaṃ dosānaṃ nīharaṇaṃ. Adhovirecananti adho dosānaṃ nīharaṇaṃ. Sīsavirecananti sirovirecanaṃ. Kaṇṇatelanti kaṇṇānaṃ bandhanatthaṃ vā vaṇaharaṇatthaṃ vā bhesajjatelapacanaṃ. Nettatappananti akkhitappanatelaṃ. Natthukammanti telena yojetvā natthukaraṇaṃ. Añjananti dve vā tīṇi vā paṭalāni nīharaṇasamatthaṃ khārañjanaṃ. Paccañjananti nibbāpanīyaṃ sītalabhesajjañjanaṃ. Sālākiyanti salākavejjakammaṃ. Sallakattiyanti sallakattavejjakammaṃ. Dārakatikicchā vuccati komārabhaccavejjakammaṃ. Mūlabhesajjānaṃ anuppādananti iminā kāyatikicchanaṃ dasseti. Osadhīnaṃ paṭimokkhoti khārādīni datvā tadanurūpe vaṇe gate tesaṃ apanayanaṃ.

27. Santikamma, a 'propitiatory rite,' is going to a deity’s abode and performing the act of vowing an offering to be made at the time of success, saying: 'If this particular thing succeeds for me, I will make an offering to you with this and that.' Then, when that has succeeded, the performance of it is called paṇidhikamma, the 'act of fulfilling a vow.' Bhūrikamma, an 'earth-rite,' is residing in an earth-house and performing the application of a learned spell. Regarding Vassakamma, the 'art of masculinization,' and Vossakamma, the 'art of emasculation': here, 'vassa' is a man, and 'vossa' is a eunuch. Thus, making a eunuch into a man is vassakamma; making a man into a eunuch is vossakamma. But one who does this only brings about a state of no sexual desire; one is not able to make the sexual organ disappear. Vatthukamma, a 'site-rite,' is establishing a house on a site where one has not been built. Vatthuparikamma, 'site-preparation,' is saying, 'Bring this and that,' and performing the ritual offering for the site. Ācamana, 'rinsing,' is cleansing the mouth with water. Nhāpana, 'bathing,' is bathing others. Juhana, 'offering,' is making a fire offering for their benefit. Vamana, 'inducing emesis,' is giving a preparation and causing vomiting. The same method applies to Virecana, 'purgation.' Uddhaṃvirecana, 'upward purgation,' is the upward expulsion of humors. Adhovirecana, 'downward purgation,' is the downward expulsion of humors. Sīsavirecana, 'head-purgation,' is purging the head. Kaṇṇatela, 'ear-oil,' is the cooking of medicinal oil for the purpose of reattaching ears or for removing a wound. Nettatappana, 'eye-soothing,' is oil for soothing the eyes. Natthukamma, 'nasal application,' is applying medication through the nose, having mixed it with oil. Añjana, 'eye-salve,' is a caustic eye-salve capable of removing two or three films from the eyes. Paccañjana, 'cooling eye-salve,' is a cooling medicinal eye-salve that extinguishes heat. Sālākiya is the medical practice with a probe. Sallakattiya is the medical practice of a surgeon. The medical practice of a pediatrician, komārabhacca, is called dārakatikicchā, the 'treatment of children.' The phrase 'the administering of root-medicines' indicates the treatment of the body. Osadhīnaṃ paṭimokkha, 'release from medicines,' is, having applied caustics and so on, their removal when a suitable wound has formed.

Ettāvatā mahāsīlaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ hoti.

Thus far, the great morality is concluded.

Pubbantakappikasassatavādavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Eternalist Views Regarding the Past

28. Evaṃ brahmadattena vuttavaṇṇassa anusandhivasena tividhaṃ sīlaṃ vitthāretvā idāni bhikkhusaṅghena vuttavaṇṇassa [P 1.0099] anusandhivasena – “atthi, bhikkhave, aññeva dhammā gambhīrā duddasā”tiādinā nayena suññatāpakāsanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha dhammāti guṇe, desanāyaṃ, pariyattiyaṃ, nissatteti evamādīsu dhammasaddo vattati.

28. Thus, having elaborated the threefold morality by way of connection with the praise spoken by Brahmadatta, the Teacher now began the exposition of emptiness by way of connection with the praise spoken by the community of monks, using the method that begins: 'There are, O monks, other things that are profound, difficult to see...' Herein, the word 'dhamma' is used in such senses as: qualities, teachings, scripture, non-sentient reality, and so on.

“Na hi dhammo adhammo ca, ubho samavipākino;

Adhammo nirayaṃ neti, dhammo pāpeti suggati”nti. (theragā. 304);

For Dhamma and non-Dhamma do not both have the same result; non-Dhamma leads to hell, while Dhamma leads to a good destination.

Ādīsu hi guṇe dhammasaddo. “Dhammaṃ, vo bhikkhave, desessāmi ādikalyāṇa”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.420) desanāyaṃ. “Idha bhikkhu dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇāti suttaṃ[V 1.0087][M 1.0093], geyya”ntiādīsu (a. ni. 5.73) pariyattiyaṃ. “Tasmiṃ kho pana samaye dhammā honti, khandhā hontī”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 121) nissatte. Idha pana guṇe vattati. Tasmā atthi, bhikkhave, aññeva tathāgatassa guṇāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

For in such texts as the preceding, the word 'dhamma' is used in the sense of 'quality.' In such texts as, 'Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma, good in the beginning...,' it is in the sense of 'teaching.' In such texts as, 'Here, a monk learns the Dhamma: suttas, geyyas...,' it is in the sense of 'scripture.' In such texts as, 'But at that time there are dhammas, there are aggregates...,' it is in the sense of 'non-sentient realities.' Here, however, it is used in the sense of 'quality.' Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: 'There are, O monks, other qualities of the Tathāgata.'

Gambhīrāti mahāsamuddo viya makasatuṇḍasūciyā aññatra tathāgatā aññesaṃ ñāṇena alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhā, gambhīrattāyeva duddasā. Duddasattāyeva duranubodhā. Nibbutasabbapariḷāhattā santā, santārammaṇesu pavattanatopi santā. Atittikaraṇaṭṭhena paṇītā, sādurasabhojanaṃ viya. Uttamañāṇavisayattā na takkena avacaritabbāti atakkāvacarā. Nipuṇāti saṇhasukhumasabhāvattā. Bālānaṃ avisayattā, paṇḍitehiyeva veditabbāti paṇḍitavedanīyā.

Profound: Like the great ocean, their foundation is unattainable by the knowledge of others—apart from the Tathāgata—as if with the needle-like beak of a mosquito. Precisely because of their profundity, they are difficult to see. Precisely because they are difficult to see, they are difficult to comprehend. They are tranquil because all fevers have been extinguished; they are also tranquil because they proceed amidst tranquil objects. They are sublime in the sense of not causing satiety, like a delicious meal. Because they are the domain of supreme knowledge, they are not to be fathomed by reasoning; thus they are 'beyond the sphere of reasoning.' Subtle: This is because of their fine and subtle nature. Because they are not the domain of fools and are to be known only by the wise, they are 'to be known by the wise.'

Ye tathāgato sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedetīti ye dhamme tathāgato anaññaneyyo hutvā sayameva abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇena paccakkhaṃ katvā pavedeti, dīpeti, katheti, pakāsetīti attho. Yehīti yehi guṇadhammehi. Yathābhuccanti yathābhūtaṃ. Vaṇṇaṃ sammā vadamānā vadeyyunti tathāgatassa vaṇṇaṃ vattukāmā sammā vadeyyuṃ, ahāpetvā vattuṃ sakkuṇeyyunti attho. Katame ca pana te dhammā bhagavatā evaṃ thomitāti? Sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ. Yadi evaṃ, kasmā bahuvacananiddeso [P 1.0100] katoti? Puthucittasamāyogato ceva, puthuārammaṇato ca. Tañhi catūsu ñāṇasampayuttamahākiriyacittesu labbhati, na cassa koci dhammo ārammaṇaṃ nāma na hoti. Yathāha – “atītaṃ sabbaṃ jānātīti sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, tattha āvaraṇaṃ natthīti anāvaraṇañāṇa”ntiādi (paṭi. ma. 1.120). Iti puthucittasamāyogato punappunaṃ uppattivasena puthuārammaṇato ca bahuvacananiddeso katoti.

`Which the Tathāgata, having directly known and personally realized them, makes known`: the meaning is, those qualities which the Tathāgata, being one not taught by others, having made them directly evident for himself alone with his special knowledge, makes known in detail, shows, tells, and clarifies. `By which` means: by which qualitative states. `As they truly are` means: as they have come to be. `Speaking rightly of his praise, they would speak` means: those who desire to speak the praise of the Tathāgata would be able to speak rightly, without diminishing it. And what, then, are those qualities so praised by the Blessed One? The knowledge of omniscience. If so, why is the plural designation made? Both because of its association with many minds and because of its many objects. For it is obtained in the four great functional consciousnesses associated with knowledge, and there is no quality whatsoever that is not its object. As it is said: 'He knows all that is past... this is the knowledge of omniscience; there is no obstruction to it—this is unobstructed knowledge,' and so on. Thus, because of its association with many minds—by way of arising again and again—and because of its many objects, the plural designation is made.

“Aññevā”ti idaṃ panettha vavatthāpanavacanaṃ, “aññeva, na pāṇātipātā veramaṇiādayo. Gambhīrāva na uttānā”ti evaṃ sabbapadehi yojetabbaṃ. Sāvakapāramīñāṇañhi gambhīraṃ, paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ pana tato gambhīrataranti tattha vavatthānaṃ natthi, sabbaññutaññāṇañca tatopi gambhīrataranti tatthāpi vavatthānaṃ natthi, ito panaññaṃ gambhīrataraṃ natthi; tasmā gambhīrā vāti vavatthānaṃ labbhati. Tathā duddasāva duranubodhā vāti sabbaṃ veditabbaṃ.

`Others indeed`—this here is a word of determination. It should be connected with all the words thus: 'Others indeed, not abstinence from killing living beings and so on. Deep indeed, not shallow.' For the knowledge of a disciple's perfection is deep, but the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha is deeper still—yet no determination is made in that case. And the knowledge of omniscience is even deeper than that—yet no determination is made in that case either. But other than this, there is nothing deeper; therefore, the determination 'deep indeed' is obtained. Similarly, all should be understood regarding 'hard to see indeed' and 'difficult to understand indeed'.

Katame [M 1.0094] ca te bhikkhaveti ayaṃ pana tesaṃ dhammānaṃ kathetukamyatā pucchā. Santi, bhikkhave, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇātiādi pucchāvissajjanaṃ. Kasmā panetaṃ evaṃ āraddhanti ce? Buddhānañhi cattāri ṭhānāni patvā gajjitaṃ mahantaṃ hoti, ñāṇaṃ anupavisati, buddhañāṇassa mahantabhāvo [V 1.0088] paññāyati, desanā gambhīrā hoti, tilakkhaṇāhatā, suññatāpaṭisaṃyuttā. Katamāni cattāri? Vinayapaññattiṃ, bhūmantaraṃ, paccayākāraṃ, samayantaranti. Tasmā – “idaṃ lahukaṃ, idaṃ garukaṃ, idaṃ satekicchaṃ, idaṃ atekicchaṃ, ayaṃ āpatti, ayaṃ anāpatti, ayaṃ chejjagāminī, ayaṃ vuṭṭhānagāminī, ayaṃ desanāgāminī, ayaṃ lokavajjā, ayaṃ paṇṇattivajjā, imasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ idaṃ paññapetabba”nti yaṃ evaṃ otiṇṇe vatthusmiṃ [P 1.0101] sikkhāpadapaññāpanaṃ nāma, tattha aññesaṃ thāmo vā balaṃ vā natthi; avisayo esa aññesaṃ, tathāgatasseva visayo. Iti vinayapaññattiṃ patvā buddhānaṃ gajjitaṃ mahantaṃ hoti, ñāṇaṃ anupavisati…pe… suññatāpaṭisaṃyuttāti.

`And what, monks, are they?` This is a question due to the desire to speak of those qualities. The passage beginning `There are, monks, some ascetics and brahmins` is the answer to the question. If it is asked, 'But why is this undertaken thus?' For when the Buddhas have reached four occasions, their roar is great, knowledge penetrates, the greatness of the Buddha’s knowledge becomes apparent, the teaching becomes profound, stamped with the three characteristics, and connected with emptiness. What are the four? The laying down of the Vinaya, the distinction of planes, the mode of conditionality, and the distinction of views. Therefore—‘This is light, this is heavy, this is with remedy, this is without remedy, this is an offense, this is not an offense, this leads to expulsion, this leads to restoration, this leads to confession, this is a worldly fault, this is an enacted fault, in this matter this should be enacted’—regarding what is called the laying down of a training rule when a matter has arisen, therein others have no strength or power; this is not the domain of others, it is the domain of the Tathāgata alone. Thus, having reached the laying down of the Vinaya, the Buddhas’ roar is great, knowledge penetrates… connected with emptiness.

Tathā ime cattāro satipaṭṭhānā nāma…pe… ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo nāma, pañca khandhā nāma, dvādasa āyatanāni nāma, aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo nāma, cattāri ariyasaccāni nāma, bāvīsatindriyāni nāma, nava hetū nāma, cattāro āhārā nāma, satta phassā nāma, satta vedanā nāma, satta saññā nāma, satta cetanā nāma, satta cittāni nāma. Etesu ettakā kāmāvacarā dhammā nāma, ettakā rūpāvacaraarūpāvacarapariyāpannā dhammā nāma, ettakā lokiyā dhammā nāma, ettakā lokuttarā dhammā nāmāti catuvīsatisamantapaṭṭhānaṃ anantanayaṃ abhidhammapiṭakaṃ vibhajitvā kathetuṃ aññesaṃ thāmo vā balaṃ vā natthi, avisayo esa aññesaṃ, tathāgatasseva visayo. Iti bhūmantaraparicchedaṃ patvā buddhānaṃ gajjitaṃ mahantaṃ hoti, ñāṇaṃ anupavisati…pe… suññatāpaṭisaṃyuttāti.

Similarly, these are called the four foundations of mindfulness… the noble eightfold path, the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, the eighteen elements, the four noble truths, the twenty-two faculties, the nine causes, the four kinds of nutriment, the seven contacts, the seven kinds of feeling, the seven kinds of perception, the seven kinds of volition, the seven kinds of consciousness. Among these, this many are called sense-sphere qualities, this many are called form-sphere qualities, this many are called formless-sphere qualities, this many are called included qualities, this many are called worldly qualities, this many are called supramundane qualities. To analyze and teach the Abhidhamma Piṭaka—with its Paṭṭhāna of twenty-four universal relations and its endless methods—is a matter wherein others have no strength or power; this is not the domain of others, it is the domain of the Tathāgata alone. Thus, having reached the analysis of the distinction of planes, the Buddhas’ roar is great, knowledge penetrates… connected with emptiness.

Tathā ayaṃ avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ navahākārehi paccayo hoti, uppādo hutvā paccayo hoti, pavattaṃ hutvā, nimittaṃ, āyūhanaṃ, saṃyogo, palibodho, samudayo, hetu, paccayo hutvā paccayo hoti, tathā saṅkhārādayo viññāṇādīnaṃ. Yathāha – “kathaṃ paccayapariggahe paññā dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ? Avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ uppādaṭṭhiti ca pavattaṭṭhiti ca, nimittaṭṭhiti [M 1.0095] ca, āyūhanaṭṭhiti ca, saṃyogaṭṭhiti ca, palibodhaṭṭhiti ca, samudayaṭṭhiti ca, hetuṭṭhiti ca, paccayaṭṭhiti ca, imehi navahākārehi avijjā paccayo, saṅkhārā paccayasamuppannā, ubhopete dhammā paccayasamuppannāti paccayapariggahe paññā dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ. Atītampi addhānaṃ, anāgatampi addhānaṃ avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ uppādaṭṭhiti ca…pe… [P 1.0102] jāti jarāmaraṇassa uppādaṭṭhiti ca…pe… paccayaṭṭhiti ca, imehi navahākārehi jāti paccayo, jarāmaraṇaṃ paccayasamuppannaṃ, ubhopete dhammā paccayasamuppannāti paccayapariggahe paññā dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.45). Evamimaṃ tassa tassa dhammassa tathā tathā paccayabhāvena pavattaṃ tivaṭṭaṃ tiyaddhaṃ [V 1.0089] tisandhiṃ catusaṅkhepaṃ vīsatākāraṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṃ vibhajitvā kathetuṃ aññesaṃ thāmo vā balaṃ vā natthi, avisayo esa aññesaṃ, tathāgatasseva visayo, iti paccayākāraṃ patvā buddhānaṃ gajjitaṃ mahantaṃ hoti, ñāṇaṃ anupavisati…pe… suññatāpaṭisaṃyuttāti.

Furthermore, this ignorance is a condition for formations in nine aspects: as arising, as continuance, as a sign, as exertion, as conjunction, as an obstruction, as an origin, as a root-cause, and as a supporting condition. Similarly, formations and so on are conditions for consciousness and the rest. As it is said: “How is wisdom in the grasping of conditions the knowledge of the stability of things? Ignorance is a condition for formations in terms of its being a basis for arising, a basis for continuance, a basis for a sign, a basis for exertion, a basis for conjunction, a basis for obstruction, a basis for origin, a basis for a root-cause, and a basis for a supporting condition. In these nine aspects, ignorance is the condition, and formations are conditionally arisen; both these phenomena are conditionally arisen. Thus, wisdom in the grasping of conditions is the knowledge of the stability of things. In the past period as well… and in the future period as well, ignorance is a condition for formations in terms of its being a basis for arising… and so on… birth is a condition for aging and death in terms of its being a basis for arising… and so on… a basis for a supporting condition. In these nine aspects, birth is the condition, and aging and death are conditionally arisen; both these phenomena are conditionally arisen. Thus, wisdom in the grasping of conditions is the knowledge of the stability of things” (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.45). Thus, to analyze and teach this dependent origination—which proceeds according to the conditionality of each and every phenomenon, having three rounds, three periods of time, three connections, four summaries, and twenty aspects—others have neither the strength of wisdom nor the strength of energy. This is not the domain of others; it is the domain of the Tathāgata alone. Thus, having arrived at the mode of conditionality, the roar of the Buddhas becomes great, knowledge penetrates… it is associated with emptiness.

Tathā cattāro janā sassatavādā nāma, cattāro ekaccasassatavādā, cattāro antānantikā, cattāro amarāvikkhepikā, dve adhiccasamuppannikā, soḷasa saññīvādā, aṭṭha asaññīvādā, aṭṭha nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā, satta ucchedavādā, pañca diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā nāma. Te idaṃ nissāya idaṃ gaṇhantīti dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhigatāni bhinditvā nijjaṭaṃ niggumbaṃ katvā kathetuṃ aññesaṃ thāmo vā balaṃ vā natthi, avisayo esa aññesaṃ, tathāgatasseva visayo. Iti samayantaraṃ patvā buddhānaṃ gajjitaṃ mahantaṃ hoti, ñāṇaṃ anupavisati, buddhañāṇassa mahantatā paññāyati, desanā gambhīrā hoti, tilakkhaṇāhatā, suññatāpaṭisaṃyuttāti.

Furthermore, there are four kinds of people who are eternalists, four who are partial-eternalists, four who are finitists and infinitists, four who are eel-wrigglers, two who are fortuitous-originists, sixteen who are perceptionists, eight who are non-perceptionists, eight who are neither-perceptionists-nor-non-perceptionists, seven who are annihilationists, and five who are proponents of Nibbāna in this very life. Relying on this, they grasp at that. Thus, to analyze and refute the sixty-two kinds of wrong views, making them untangled and free of thickets, and then to teach—others have neither the strength of wisdom nor the strength of energy. This is not the domain of others; it is the domain of the Tathāgata alone. Thus, having arrived at the topic of other doctrines, the roar of the Buddhas becomes great, knowledge penetrates, the greatness of the Buddha’s knowledge is made known, the teaching becomes profound, stamped with the three characteristics, and associated with emptiness.

Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne samayantaraṃ labbhati, tasmā sabbaññutaññāṇassa mahantabhāvadassanatthaṃ desanāya ca suññatāpakāsanavibhāvanatthaṃ samayantaraṃ anupavisanto dhammarājā – “santi, bhikkhave, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā”ti evaṃ pucchāvissajjanaṃ ārabhi.

However, at this point, the topic of other doctrines is found. Therefore, for the purpose of demonstrating the greatness of the knowledge of omniscience and of clearly revealing the exposition of emptiness in the teaching, the King of Dhamma, entering into the topic of other doctrines, began the passage of question and answer thus: “Monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins.”

29. Tattha santīti atthi saṃvijjanti upalabbhanti. Bhikkhaveti ālapanavacanaṃ. Eketi ekacce. Samaṇabrāhmaṇāti pabbajjūpagatabhāvena samaṇā, jātiyā brāhmaṇā. Lokena vā samaṇāti ca brāhmaṇāti ca evaṃ sammatā. Pubbantaṃ [P 1.0103] kappetvā vikappetvā gaṇhantīti pubbantakappikā. Pubbantakappo vā [M 1.0096] etesaṃ atthīti pubbantakappikā. Tattha antoti ayaṃ saddo antaabbhantaramariyādalāmakaparabhāgakoṭṭhāsesu dissati. “Antapūro udarapūro”tiādīsu hi ante antasaddo. “Caranti loke parivārachannā anto asuddhā bahi sobhamānā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.122) abbhantare. “Kāyabandhanassa anto jīrati (cūḷava. 278). “Sā haritantaṃ vā panthantaṃ vā selantaṃ vā udakantaṃ vā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.304) mariyādāyaṃ. “Antamidaṃ, bhikkhave, jīvikānaṃ yadidaṃ piṇḍolya”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.80) lāmake. “Esevanto dukkhassā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.51) parabhāge. Sabbapaccayasaṅkhayo hi dukkhassa parabhāgo koṭīti vuccati. “Sakkāyo kho, āvuso, eko anto”tiādīsu (a. ni. 6.61) koṭṭhāse. Svāyaṃ idhāpi koṭṭhāse vattati.

29. Therein, 'there are' (santi) means they exist (atthi), they are evidently present (saṃvijjanti), they are found (upalabbhanti). 'Monks' (bhikkhave) is a term of address. 'Some' (eke) means certain ones. 'Ascetics and brahmins' (samaṇabrāhmaṇā): they are ascetics by virtue of having gone forth, and brahmins by birth. Or, they are those designated by the world as 'ascetics' and 'brahmins'. They are called 'speculators on the past' (pubbantakappikā) because they conceive (kappetvā), specially conceive (vikappetvā), and grasp (gaṇhanti) the past. Or, they are called 'speculators on the past' because they possess speculation on the past (pubbantakappo). Therein, this word 'anta' is seen in the senses of intestine, interior, boundary, inferior, the further part, and section. For in passages such as, “full of intestines (antapūro), full of what is in the stomach (udarapūro),” the word 'anta' is seen in the sense of intestine. In passages such as, “They wander in the world, concealed by their retinue, impure within (anto), appearing beautiful without,” it is in the sense of interior. In passages such as, “The end (anto) of the waistband is worn out,” and “It, having reached the boundary of green grass (haritantaṃ), or the boundary of a path (panthantaṃ), or the boundary of a rock (selantaṃ), or the boundary of water (udakantaṃ)...,” it is in the sense of boundary. In passages such as, “This, monks, is an inferior (antaṃ) livelihood, that is, collecting alms,” it is in the sense of inferior. In passages such as, “This is the end (anto) of suffering,” it is in the sense of the further part. For the cessation of all conditions is called the further part, the extremity of suffering. In passages such as, “The personal identity, friend, is one section (anto),” it is in the sense of section. Here too, this word is used in the sense of section.

Kappasaddopi – [V 1.0090] “tiṭṭhatu, bhante bhagavā kappaṃ” (dī. ni. 2.167), “atthi kappo nipajjituṃ” (a. ni. 8.80), “kappakatena akappakataṃ saṃsibbitaṃ hotī”ti, (pāci. 371) evaṃ āyukappalesakappavinayakappādīsu sambahulesu atthesu vattati. Idha taṇhādiṭṭhīsu vattatīti veditabbo. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “kappāti dve kappā, taṇhākappo ca diṭṭhikappo cā”ti (mahāni. 28). Tasmā taṇhādiṭṭhivasena atītaṃ khandhakoṭṭhāsaṃ kappetvā pakappetvā ṭhitāti pubbantakappikāti evamettha attho veditabbo. Tesaṃ evaṃ pubbantaṃ kappetvā ṭhitānaṃ punappunaṃ uppajjanavasena pubbantameva anugatā diṭṭhīti pubbantānudiṭṭhino. Te evaṃdiṭṭhino taṃ pubbantaṃ ārabbha āgamma paṭicca aññampi janaṃ diṭṭhigatikaṃ karontā anekavihitāni adhimuttipadāni abhivadanti aṭṭhārasahi vatthūhi.

The word 'kappa' also occurs in many senses, such as in “May the Blessed One, sir, remain for the lifespan-eon (kappaṃ),” “There is a slight reason (kappo) to lie down,” and “An unmarked cloth (akappakataṃ) is sewn together with a marked one (kappakatena)”; thus it occurs in many meanings such as lifespan-eon (āyukappa), a slight matter (lesakappa), and the Vinaya procedure (vinayakappa). Here, it should be understood as occurring in the sense of craving and view. And this has been said: “'Kappa' means two kappas: the craving-kappa and the view-kappa.” Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: they are called 'speculators on the past' (pubbantakappikā) because they stand having conceived and specially conceived the past portion of the aggregates by means of craving and view. Of those who stand thus conceiving the past, because their view follows the past by way of arising again and again, they are called 'those whose views follow the past' (pubbantānudiṭṭhino). Those with such views, taking that past as their object, resorting to it, and depending on it, while causing other people to adopt wrong views, proclaim various expressions of their convictions on eighteen grounds.

Tattha anekavihitānīti anekavidhāni. Adhimuttipadānīti adhivacanapadāni. Atha vā bhūtaṃ atthaṃ [P 1.0104] abhibhavitvā yathāsabhāvato aggahetvā pavattanato adhimuttiyoti diṭṭhiyo vuccanti. Adhimuttīnaṃ padāni adhimuttipadāni, diṭṭhidīpakāni vacanānīti attho. Aṭṭhārasahi vatthūhīti aṭṭhārasahi kāraṇehi.

Herein, anekavihitāni means of many kinds. Adhimuttipadāni means terms of designation. Alternatively, because they arise from overpowering the real meaning and not grasping it according to its true nature, views (diṭṭhiyo) are called assertions (adhimutti). The terms of assertions (adhimuttīnaṃ padāni) are adhimuttipadāni; the meaning is: expressions that illuminate views. Aṭṭhārasahi vatthūhi means by eighteen reasons.

30. Idāni [M 1.0097] yehi aṭṭhārasahi vatthūhi abhivadanti, tesaṃ kathetukamyatāya pucchāya “te ca kho bhonto”tiādinā nayena pucchitvā tāni vatthūni vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “santi, bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Tattha vadanti etenāti vādo, diṭṭhigatassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sassato vādo etesanti sassatavādā, sassatadiṭṭhinoti attho. Eteneva nayena ito paresampi evarūpānaṃ padānaṃ attho veditabbo. Sassataṃ attānañca lokañcāti rūpādīsu aññataraṃ attāti ca lokoti ca gahetvā taṃ sassataṃ amaraṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ paññapenti. Yathāha – “rūpaṃ attā ceva loko ca sassato cāti attānañca lokañca paññapenti tathā vedanaṃ, saññaṃ, saṅkhāre, viññāṇaṃ attā ceva loko ca sassato cāti attānañca lokañca paññapentī”ti.

30. Now, desiring to explain the eighteen grounds by which they assert their views, having asked according to the method beginning, 'But, venerable sirs...', in order to show those grounds by analyzing them, He said the passage beginning, 'There are, O bhikkhus...'. Herein, 'that by which they assert' is a doctrine (vādo); this is a designation for a wrong view. 'Their doctrine is eternal'; thus they are eternalists (sassatavādā). The meaning is: those who hold the eternalist view. By this same method, the meaning of the other similar terms that follow should be understood. 'The self and the world as eternal' means: having taken one or another of the aggregates, such as form, to be the self and the world, they declare it to be eternal, deathless, permanent, and constant. As it was said: 'They declare form to be the self and the world, and to be eternal; thus they declare the self and the world. Likewise, they declare feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness to be the self and the world, and to be eternal; thus they declare the self and the world.'

31. Ātappamanvāyātiādīsu vīriyaṃ kilesānaṃ ātāpanabhāvena ātappanti vuttaṃ. Tadeva padahanavasena padhānaṃ. Punappunaṃ yuttavasena anuyogoti. Evaṃ tippabhedaṃ vīriyaṃ anvāya āgamma paṭiccāti attho. Appamādo vuccati satiyā avippavāso. Sammā manasikāroti upāyamanasikāro, pathamanasikāro, atthato ñāṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Yasmiñhi manasikāre ṭhitassa pubbenivāsānussati ñāṇaṃ ijjhati, ayaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne manasikāroti adhippeto. Tasmā vīriyañca satiñca ñāṇañca āgammāti ayamettha saṅkhepattho. Tathārūpanti tathājātikaṃ. Cetosamādhinti [V 1.0091] cittasamādhiṃ. Phusatīti vindati paṭilabhati. Yathā samāhite citteti yena samādhinā sammā āhite suṭṭhu ṭhapite cittamhi anekavihitaṃ [P 1.0105] pubbenivāsantiādīnaṃ attho visuddhimagge vutto.

31. In the phrases beginning ātappamanvāya, energy (vīriyaṃ) is called 'ardor' (ātappa) because of its nature of suppressing the defilements. That same energy, by way of striving, is 'striving' (padhāna). By way of repeated application, it is 'application' (anuyoga). Thus, the meaning is: having followed, come to, and relied upon this threefold energy. Heedfulness (appamādo) is called non-separation from mindfulness. 'Right attention' (sammā manasikāro) means skillful attention (upāyamanasikāro), methodical attention (pathamanasikāro); in essence, it is said to be knowledge (ñāṇa). For when one is established in that attention, the knowledge of recollecting past lives succeeds; this is the 'attention' intended in this context. Therefore, 'having come to energy, mindfulness, and knowledge'—this is the summary meaning here. Tathārūpaṃ means of that nature. Cetosamādhiṃ means concentration of the mind. Phusati means finds, obtains. As for yathā samāhite citte, the meaning of the passage beginning anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ, which occurs when the mind is rightly established and well-placed by that concentration, has been stated by me in the Visuddhimagga.

So evamāhāti so evaṃ jhānānubhāvasampanno hutvā diṭṭhigatiko evaṃ vadati. Vañjhoti vañjhapasuvañjhatālādayo viya aphalo kassaci ajanakoti. Etena “attā”ti ca “loko”ti ca gahitānaṃ jhānādīnaṃ rūpādijanakabhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati. Pabbatakūṭaṃ viya ṭhitoti kūṭaṭṭho. Esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhitoti esikaṭṭhāyī viya hutvā ṭhitoti esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhito. Yathā sunikhāto esikatthambho niccalo tiṭṭhati, evaṃ ṭhitoti attho. Ubhayenapi lokassa vināsābhāvaṃ dīpeti. Keci pana īsikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhitoti pāḷiṃ vatvā muñje īsikā viya ṭhitoti vadanti[M 1.0098]. Tatrāyamadhippāyo – yadidaṃ jāyatīti vuccati, taṃ muñjato īsikā viya vijjamānameva nikkhamati. Yasmā ca īsikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhito, tasmā teva sattā sandhāvanti, ito aññattha gacchantīti attho.

'He speaks thus' (so evamāha) means: that person, being an adherent of wrong views endowed with the power of jhāna, speaks thus. 'Barren' (vañjho) means fruitless, like a barren animal or a barren palm tree, not generating anything. By this, he rejects the capacity of jhāna, etc.—which are grasped as 'self' and 'world'—to generate form, etc. 'Standing like a mountain peak' is kūṭaṭṭho. 'Standing firm like a door-post' is esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhito. Just as a well-embedded door-post stands immovable, so does it stand; this is the meaning. By both terms, he indicates the non-perishing of the world. Some, however, reciting the Pāḷi as īsikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhito, say it means 'standing like the pith within muñja grass'. Therein, this is the intended meaning: that which is said to 'arise' emerges already existing, like the pith from the muñja grass. And because it stands like the pith of the grass, therefore those very beings transmigrate (sandhāvanti), meaning they go from here to another place.

Saṃsarantīti aparāparaṃ sañcaranti. Cavantīti evaṃ saṅkhyaṃ gacchanti. Tathā upapajjantīti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana pubbe “sassato attā ca loko cā”ti vatvā idāni te ca sattā sandhāvantītiādinā vacanena ayaṃ diṭṭhigatiko attanāyeva attano vādaṃ bhindati, diṭṭhigatikassa dassanaṃ nāma na nibaddhaṃ, thusarāsimhi nikhātakhāṇu viya cañcalaṃ, ummattakapacchiyaṃ pūvakhaṇḍagūthagomayādīni viya cettha sundarampi asundarampi hoti yevāti vuttaṃ. Atthitveva sassatisamanti ettha sassatīti niccaṃ vijjamānatāya mahāpathaviṃva maññati, tathā sinerupabbatacandimasūriye. Tato tehi samaṃ attānaṃ maññamānā atthi tveva sassatisamanti vadanti.

Saṃsaranti means they wander from one existence to another. Cavantīti means they come to be designated thus. Similarly for upapajjanti. In the Commentary, however, it is said: having previously stated, 'The self and the world are eternal,' now, with the statement beginning, 'Those beings transmigrate,' this adherent of wrong views breaks his own doctrine by himself. The seeing of an adherent of wrong views is not fixed; it is unsteady like a post planted in a heap of chaff. And in this view, like in a madman's basket where there are cake fragments, excrement, and cow-dung, there are both fine and foul things. Regarding atthitveva sassatisamaṃ: here, sassati refers to what is perpetually existing, which he conceives to be like the great earth, and similarly, Mount Sineru, the moon, and the sun. Then, conceiving the self to be equal to these, they declare, 'It exists indeed, on a par with the eternal.'

Idāni sassato attā ca loko cātiādikāya paṭiññāya sādhanatthaṃ hetuṃ dassento “taṃ kissa hetu? Ahañhi ātappamanvāyā”tiādimāha. Tattha [P 1.0106] imināmahaṃ etaṃ jānāmīti iminā visesādhigamena ahaṃ etaṃ paccakkhato jānāmi, na kevalaṃ saddhāmattakeneva vadāmīti dasseti, makāro panettha padasandhikaraṇatthaṃ vutto. Idaṃ, bhikkhave, paṭhamaṃ ṭhānanti catūhi vatthūhīti vatthusaddena vuttesu catūsu ṭhānesu idaṃ paṭhamaṃ ṭhānaṃ, idaṃ jātisatasahassamattānussaraṇaṃ paṭhamaṃ kāraṇanti attho.

Now, showing the reason to establish the declaration beginning, 'The self and the world are eternal,' he said the passage beginning, 'For what reason? For I, by means of ardor...'. Herein, by the phrase iminā’haṃ etaṃ jānāmi, he shows: 'By this special attainment, I know this directly; I do not speak merely from faith alone.' The letter 'm' here is stated for the purpose of euphonic conjunction between words. Idaṃ, bhikkhave, paṭhamaṃ ṭhānaṃ means: among the four grounds spoken of with the word 'ground', this is the first ground. The meaning is: this recollection of about a hundred thousand births is the first reason (kāraṇaṃ).

32-33. Upari [V 1.0092] vāradvayepi eseva nayo. Kevalañhi ayaṃ vāro anekajātisatasahassānussaraṇavasena vutto. Itare dasacattālīsasaṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappānussaraṇavasena. Mandapañño hi titthiyo anekajātisatasahassamattaṃ anussarati, majjhimapañño dasasaṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappāni, tikkhapañño cattālīsaṃ, na tato uddhaṃ.

32-33. In the subsequent two sections as well, this is the same method. The only difference is that this first section is stated by way of recollecting many hundreds of thousands of births, whereas the others are stated by way of recollecting ten, and forty, eons of contraction and expansion. Indeed, a sectarian with dull wisdom recollects up to many hundreds of thousands of births; one with medium wisdom recollects ten eons of contraction and expansion; and one with sharp wisdom recollects forty, but not beyond that.

34. Catutthavāre takkayatīti takkī, takko vā assa atthīti takkī. Takketvā vitakketvā diṭṭhigāhino etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vīmaṃsāya samannāgatoti vīmaṃsī. Vīmaṃsā nāma tulanā ruccanā khamanā. Yathā hi puriso yaṭṭhiyā udakaṃ vīmaṃsitvā otarati, evameva yo tulayitvā ruccitvā [M 1.0099] khamāpetvā diṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti, so “vīmaṃsī”ti veditabbo. Takkapariyāhatanti takkena pariyāhataṃ, tena tena pariyāyena takketvāti attho. Vīmaṃsānucaritanti tāya vuttappakārāya vīmaṃsāya anucaritaṃ. Sayaṃpaṭibhānanti attano paṭibhānamattasañjātaṃ. Evamāhāti sassatadiṭṭhiṃ gahetvā evaṃ vadati.

34. In the fourth section: 'one who speculates' is a speculator (takkī), or 'one who has speculation' is a speculator (takkī). This is a designation for one who grasps views after speculating and pondering. 'Endowed with investigation' means an investigator (vīmaṃsī). Investigation means weighing, liking, and approving. Just as a man tests the water with a stick before entering, so too, one who, having weighed, liked, and approved, grasps a view, is to be understood as an 'investigator.' 'Struck by speculation' means struck by speculation; the meaning is, having speculated in various ways. 'Followed by investigation' means followed by that investigation of the kind described. 'Self-inspired' means arisen from one's own spontaneous insight alone. 'Thus he declares' means having grasped the eternalist view, he speaks thus.

Tattha catubbidho takkī – anussutiko, jātissaro, lābhī, suddhatakkikoti. Tattha yo “vessantaro nāma rājā ahosī”tiādīni sutvā “tena hi yadi vessantarova bhagavā, sassato [P 1.0107] attā”ti takkayanto diṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti, ayaṃ anussutiko nāma. Dve tisso jātiyo saritvā – “ahameva pubbe asukasmiṃ nāma ahosiṃ, tasmā sassato attā”ti takkayanto jātissaratakkiko nāma. Yo pana lābhitāya “yathā me idāni attā sukhī hoti, atītepi evaṃ ahosi, anāgatepi bhavissatī”ti takkayitvā diṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti, ayaṃ lābhītakkiko nāma. “Evaṃ sati idaṃ hotī”ti takkamatteneva gaṇhanto pana suddhatakkiko nāma.

Here, the speculator is of four kinds: one who relies on hearsay, one who remembers past lives, one who has attainment, and one who is a pure reasoner. Among them, one who hears statements like, 'There was once a king named Vessantara,' and then reasons, 'If Vessantara was the Blessed One, then the self is eternal,' and grasps such a view—this is called one who relies on hearsay. One who remembers two or three past lives and reasons, 'I myself existed before in such-and-such an existence, therefore the self is eternal,' is called a speculator who remembers past lives. One who, due to their attainment, reasons, 'Just as my self is happy now, so it was in the past, and so it will be in the future,' and grasps such a view—this is called a speculator who has attainment. One who grasps a view merely by reasoning, thinking, 'If it is thus, this occurs,' is called a pure reasoner.

35. Etesaṃ vā aññatarenāti etesaṃyeva catunnaṃ vatthūnaṃ aññatarena ekena vā dvīhi vā tīhi vā. Natthi ito bahiddhāti imehi pana vatthūhi bahi aññaṃ ekaṃ kāraṇampi sassatapaññattiyā natthīti appaṭivattiyaṃ sīhanādaṃ nadati.

35. 'Or by any one of these' means by any one, or two, or three of these four grounds themselves. 'There is nothing beyond this' means that outside these grounds, there is not even a single other reason for the eternalist assertion. Thus, he utters an unassailable lion's roar.

36. Tayidaṃ, bhikkhave, tathāgato pajānātīti bhikkhave, taṃ idaṃ catubbidhampi diṭṭhigataṃ tathāgato nānappakārato jānāti. Tato taṃ pajānanākāraṃ dassento ime diṭṭhiṭṭhānātiādimāha. Tattha diṭṭhiyova diṭṭhiṭṭhānā nāma. Api ca diṭṭhīnaṃ kāraṇampi diṭṭhiṭṭhānameva. Yathāha “katamāni aṭṭha diṭṭhiṭṭhānāni? Khandhāpi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ, avijjāpi, phassopi[V 1.0093], saññāpi, vitakkopi, ayonisomanasikāropi, pāpamittopi, paratoghosopi diṭṭhiṭṭhāna”nti. “Khandhā hetu, khandhā paccayo diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ upādāya samuṭṭhānaṭṭhena, evaṃ khandhāpi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ. Avijjā hetu…pe… pāpamitto hetu. Paratoghoso hetu, paratoghoso paccayo diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ upādāya samuṭṭhānaṭṭhena, evaṃ paratoghosopi diṭṭhiṭṭhāna”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.124). Evaṃgahitāti diṭṭhisaṅkhātā tāva [M 1.0100] diṭṭhiṭṭhānā – “sassato attā ca loko cā”ti evaṃgahitā ādinnā, pavattitāti attho. Evaṃparāmaṭṭhāti nirāsaṅkacittatāya punappunaṃ āmaṭṭhā parāmaṭṭhā, ‘idameva saccaṃ, moghamañña’nti pariniṭṭhāpitā[P 1.0108]. Kāraṇasaṅkhātā pana diṭṭhiṭṭhānā yathā gayhamānā diṭṭhiyo samuṭṭhāpenti, evaṃ ārammaṇavasena ca pavattanavasena ca āsevanavasena ca gahitā. Anādīnavadassitāya punappunaṃ gahaṇavasena parāmaṭṭhā. Evaṃgatikāti evaṃ nirayatiracchānapettivisayagatikānaṃ aññataragatikā. Evaṃ abhisamparāyāti idaṃ purimapadasseva vevacanaṃ, evaṃvidhaparalokāti vuttaṃ hoti.

36. "This, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata understands." Thus, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata knows this fourfold group of views in various ways. Then, showing the manner of understanding them, he says, "These are the grounds of views," and so on. Here, the grounds of views are simply the views themselves. Moreover, the causes of views are also the grounds of views. As it is said: "What are the eight grounds of views? The aggregates are a ground of views, ignorance is a ground of views, contact is a ground of views, perception is a ground of views, thought is a ground of views, unwise attention is a ground of views, a bad friend is a ground of views, and the voice of another is a ground of views." "The aggregates are the cause, the aggregates are the condition for the grounds of views in the sense of being the basis for their arising; thus, the aggregates are a ground of views. Ignorance is the cause… a bad friend is the cause. The voice of another is the cause, the voice of another is the condition for the grounds of views in the sense of being the basis for their arising; thus, the voice of another is also a ground of views." "Thus grasped" refers first to the grounds of views that are themselves views—"The self and the world are eternal," and so on—thus grasped, adopted, which means set in motion. "Thus adhered to" means repeatedly considered and adhered to without doubt, firmly concluding, "This alone is true, all else is false." The grounds of views as causes, however, are grasped in terms of being their object, their occurrence, and their cultivation, in such a way that, being grasped, they give rise to views. They are adhered to repeatedly by way of grasping, due to not seeing their drawbacks. "Having such a destination" means having one of these destinations—hell, the animal realm, or the realm of ghosts. "Having such a future life" is a synonym for the previous phrase, meaning "having such a future world."

Tañca tathāgato pajānātīti na kevalañca tathāgato sakāraṇaṃ sagatikaṃ diṭṭhigatameva pajānāti, atha kho tañca sabbaṃ pajānāti, tato ca uttaritaraṃ sīlañceva samādhiñca sabbaññutaññāṇañca pajānāti. Tañca pajānanaṃ na parāmasatīti tañca evaṃvidhaṃ anuttaraṃ visesaṃ pajānantopi ahaṃ pajānāmīti taṇhādiṭṭhimānaparāmāsavasena tañca na parāmasati. Aparāmasato cassa paccattaññeva nibbuti viditāti evaṃ aparāmasato cassa aparāmāsapaccayā sayameva attanāyeva tesaṃ parāmāsakilesānaṃ nibbuti viditā. Pākaṭaṃ, bhikkhave, tathāgatassa nibbānanti dasseti.

"And this the Tathāgata understands." Not only does the Tathāgata understand the view with its cause and destination, but he understands all of it, and beyond that, he understands virtue, concentration, and the knowledge of omniscience. And understanding it, he does not misapprehend: even while understanding such an unsurpassed distinction, he does not misapprehend it by way of craving, view, and conceit, thinking, 'I understand.' For one who does not misapprehend, quenching is personally known; thus, for one who does not misapprehend, due to not misapprehending, the quenching of those defilements of misapprehension is known by himself, within himself. This shows the meaning: 'The Nibbāna of the Tathāgata, O bhikkhus, is manifest.'

Idāni yathāpaṭipannena tathāgatena sā nibbuti adhigatā, taṃ paṭipattiṃ dassetuṃ yāsu vedanāsu rattā titthiyā “idha sukhino bhavissāma, ettha sukhino bhavissāmā”ti diṭṭhigahanaṃ pavisanti, tāsaṃyeva vedanānaṃ vasena kammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhanto vedanānaṃ samudayañcātiādimāha. Tattha yathābhūtaṃ viditvāti “avijjāsamudayā vedanāsamudayoti paccayasamudayaṭṭhena vedanākkhandhassa udayaṃ passati, taṇhāsamudayā vedanāsamudayoti paccayasamudayaṭṭhena vedanākkhandhassa udayaṃ passati, kammasamudayā vedanāsamudayoti paccayasamudayaṭṭhena vedanākkhandhassa udayaṃ passati, phassasamudayā vedanāsamudayoti paccayasamudayaṭṭhena vedanākkhandhassa udayaṃ passati (paṭi. ma. 1.50). Nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ passantopi vedanākkhandhassa udayaṃ passatī”ti imesaṃ pañcannaṃ lakkhaṇānaṃ vasena vedanānaṃ samudayaṃ yathābhūtaṃ viditvā; “avijjānirodhā vedanānirodhoti paccayanirodhaṭṭhena vedanākkhandhassa [P 1.0109] vayaṃ passati, taṇhānirodhā [V 1.0094] vedanānirodhoti paccayanirodhaṭṭhena vedanākkhandhassa vayaṃ passati[M 1.0101], kammanirodhā vedanānirodhoti paccayanirodhaṭṭhena vedanākkhandhassa vayaṃ passati, phassanirodhā vedanānirodhoti paccayanirodhaṭṭhena vedanākkhandhassa vayaṃ passati. Vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ passantopi vedanākkhandhassa vayaṃ passatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.50) imesaṃ pañcannaṃ lakkhaṇānaṃ vasena vedanānaṃ atthaṅgamaṃ yathābhūtaṃ viditvā, “yaṃ vedanaṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ, ayaṃ vedanāya assādo”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.26) evaṃ assādañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā, “yaṃ vedanā aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā, ayaṃ vedanāya ādīnavo”ti evaṃ ādīnavañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā, “yo vedanāya chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṃ, idaṃ vedanāya nissaraṇa”nti evaṃ nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā vigatachandarāgatāya anupādāno anupādāvimutto, bhikkhave, tathāgato; yasmiṃ upādāne sati kiñci upādiyeyya, upādinnattā ca khandho bhaveyya, tassa abhāvā kiñci dhammaṃ anupādiyitvāva vimutto bhikkhave tathāgatoti.

Now, to show the practice by which the Tathāgata attained that extinguishment, he spoke the passage beginning with 'the arising of feelings,' teaching the meditation subject by means of those very feelings to which sectarians are attached—thinking, 'Here we shall be happy, here we shall be happy,' and thus entering the thicket of views. Therein, 'having known as it really is' means: having known as it really is the arising of feelings by means of these five characteristics—seeing the arising of the feeling aggregate in terms of the arising of conditions, namely, 'with the arising of ignorance... with the arising of craving... with the arising of kamma... with the arising of contact, there is the arising of feelings'; and seeing the characteristic of production. And, having known as it really is the passing away of feelings by means of these five characteristics—seeing the passing away of the feeling aggregate in terms of the cessation of conditions, namely, 'with the cessation of ignorance... with the cessation of craving... with the cessation of kamma... with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feelings'; and seeing the characteristic of change. And, having known as it really is the gratification thus: 'Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on a feeling, this is the gratification in feeling.' And, having known as it really is the danger thus: 'That feelings are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, this is the danger in feelings.' And, having known as it really is the escape thus: 'Whatever is the removal of desire and lust, the abandoning of desire and lust for feelings, this is the escape from feelings.' Because of being devoid of desire and lust, the Tathāgata, bhikkhus, is without clinging, liberated through non-clinging. If there were any clinging whereby he might cling to something, and because of that clinging a new aggregate of existence would arise, due to the absence of that, the Tathāgata, bhikkhus, is liberated without clinging to anything whatsoever.

37. Ime kho te, bhikkhaveti ye te ahaṃ – “katame, ca te, bhikkhave, dhammā gambhīrā”ti apucchiṃ, “ime kho te, bhikkhave, tañca tathāgato pajānāti tato ca uttaritaraṃ pajānātī”ti evaṃ niddiṭṭhā sabbaññutaññāṇadhammā gambhīrā duddasā…pe… paṇḍitavedanīyāti veditabbā. Yehi tathāgatassa neva puthujjano, na sotāpannādīsu aññataro vaṇṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ vattuṃ sakkoti, atha kho tathāgatova yathābhūtaṃ vaṇṇaṃ sammā vadamāno vadeyyāti evaṃ pucchamānenāpi sabbaññutaññāṇameva puṭṭhaṃ, niyyātentenāpi tadeva niyyātitaṃ, antarā pana diṭṭhiyo vibhattāti.

37. The phrase 'These indeed, bhikkhus, are those things' refers to this: Those qualities of the knowledge of omniscience about which I asked, 'And what, bhikkhus, are those profound things?' and which were pointed out thus, 'These indeed, bhikkhus, are those things which the Tathāgata knows, and he knows what is even beyond that,' should be known as profound, difficult to see... to be experienced by the wise. By these qualities, neither an ordinary person nor any of the noble ones from the stream-enterer onwards can speak the Tathāgata’s praise as it really is. Rather, only the Tathāgata himself, speaking rightly, could declare his praise as it really is. Thus, by the one asking, it was the knowledge of omniscience that was asked about; and by the one concluding, it was that very knowledge that was concluded upon. In between the question and answer, however, the views were analyzed.

Paṭhamabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the first recitation section is concluded.

Ekaccasassatavādavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Partial Eternalist View

38. Ekaccasassatikāti ekaccasassatavādā. Te duvidhā honti – sattekaccasassatikā, saṅkhārekaccasassatikāti. Duvidhāpi idha gahitāyeva.

38. ‘Partial eternalists’ means those who are proponents of partial eternalism. They are of two kinds: those who are partial eternalists regarding beings, and those who are partial eternalists regarding conditioned things. Both kinds are included here.

39. Yanti [P 1.0110] nipātamattaṃ. Kadācīti kismiñci kāle. Karahacīti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Dīghassa [V 1.0095] addhunoti dīghassa kālassa. Accayenāti atikkamena[M 1.0102]. Saṃvaṭṭatīti vinassati. Yebhuyyenāti ye uparibrahmalokesu vā arūpesu vā nibbattanti, tadavasese sandhāya vuttaṃ. Jhānamanena nibbattattā manomayā. Pīti tesaṃ bhakkho āhāroti pītibhakkhā. Attanova tesaṃ pabhāti sayaṃpabhā. Antalikkhe carantīti antalikkhacarā. Subhesu uyyānavimānakapparukkhādīsu tiṭṭhantīti, subhaṭṭhāyino subhā vā manorammavatthābharaṇā hutvā tiṭṭhantīti subhaṭṭhāyino. Ciraṃ dīghamaddhānanti ukkaṃsena aṭṭha kappe.

39. The word yaṃ is merely a particle. Kadāci means 'at some time.' Karahaci is a synonym for that. Dīghassa addhuno means 'of a long time.' Accayena means 'by the passing.' Saṃvaṭṭati means 'it perishes.' Yebhuyyena ('for the most part'): this is said with reference to the remaining beings, excluding those who are reborn in the higher Brahmā worlds or the formless realms. Manomayā ('mind-made') because they are born from the jhāna-mind. Pītibhakkhā ('rapture-eaters') because rapture is their food, their nourishment. Sayaṃpabhā ('self-luminous') because they have their own radiance. Antalikkhacarā ('sky-farers') because they travel in the sky. Subhaṭṭhāyino ('abiding in splendor') because they abide in splendid parks, celestial mansions, wish-fulfilling trees, and so on; or, they abide being splendid, having delightful clothes and ornaments. Ciraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ ('for a long, long time') means for at most eight great aeons.

40. Vivaṭṭatīti saṇṭhāti. Suññaṃ brahmavimānanti pakatiyā nibbattasattānaṃ natthitāya suññaṃ, brahmakāyikabhūmi nibbattatīti attho. Tassa kattā vā kāretā vā natthi, visuddhimagge vuttanayena pana kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhānā ratanabhūmi nibbattati. Pakatinibbattiṭṭhānesuyeva cettha uyyānakapparukkhādayo nibbattanti. Atha sattānaṃ pakatiyā vasitaṭṭhāne nikanti uppajjati, te paṭhamajjhānaṃ bhāvetvā tato otaranti, tasmā atha kho aññataro sattotiādimāha. Āyukkhayā vā puññakkhayā vāti ye uḷāraṃ puññakammaṃ katvā yattha katthaci appāyuke devaloke nibbattanti, te attano puññabalena ṭhātuṃ [P 1.0111] na sakkonti, tassa pana devalokassa āyuppamāṇeneva cavantīti āyukkhayā cavantīti vuccanti. Ye pana parittaṃ puññakammaṃ katvā dīghāyukadevaloke nibbattanti, te yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhātuṃ na sakkonti, antarāva cavantīti puññakkhayā cavantīti vuccanti. Dīghamaddhānaṃ tiṭṭhatīti kappaṃ vā upaḍḍhakappaṃ vā.

40. Vivaṭṭati means it is established. Suññaṃ brahmavimānaṃ: The Brahmā mansion is empty because of the non-existence of beings born there by nature. The meaning is that the Brahmakāyika realm comes into being. There is no maker or one who causes it to be made, but according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga, a jeweled ground arises, having kamma as its supporting condition and temperature as its origin. And here, in these very places of natural origination, parks, wish-fulfilling trees, and so on, arise. Then, for beings, attachment arises in the place where they had naturally dwelt. Having developed the first jhāna, they descend from there. Therefore, it is said, “Then a certain being…” and so on. Āyukkhayā vā puññakkhayā vā: This refers to those who, having performed abundant meritorious deeds, are reborn in any short-lived deva realm. Unable to remain there by the power of their merit, they pass away only at the lifespan of that deva realm—this is called “passing away due to the exhaustion of lifespan.” Others, having performed limited meritorious deeds, are reborn in long-lived deva realms but cannot remain for their full lifespan, passing away midway—this is called “passing away due to the exhaustion of merit.” Dīghamaddhānaṃ tiṭṭhati: This means it lasts for an eon or half an eon.

41. Anabhiratīti aparassāpi sattassa āgamanapatthanā. Yā pana paṭighasampayuttā ukkaṇṭhitā, sā brahmaloke natthi. Paritassanāti ubbijjanā phandanā, sā panesā tāsatassanā, taṇhātassanā, diṭṭhitassanā, ñāṇatassanāti catubbidhā hoti. Tattha “jātiṃ paṭicca bhayaṃ bhayānakaṃ chambhitattaṃ lomahaṃso cetaso utrāso. Jaraṃ… byādhiṃ… maraṇaṃ paṭicca…pe… utrāso”ti (vibha. 921) ayaṃ tāsatassanā nāma. “Aho vata aññepi sattā itthattaṃ āgaccheyyu”nti (dī. ni. 3.38) ayaṃ taṇhātassanā nāma. “Paritassitavipphanditamevā”ti ayaṃ diṭṭhitassanā nāma. “Tepi tathāgatassa dhammadesanaṃ [M 1.0103] sutvā yebhuyyena bhayaṃ saṃvegaṃ santāsaṃ āpajjantī”ti (a. ni. 4.33) ayaṃ ñāṇatassanā nāma. Idha pana taṇhātassanāpi diṭṭhitassanāpi vaṭṭati. Brahmavimānanti idha pana paṭhamābhinibbattassa atthitāya suññanti na vuttaṃ. Upapajjantīti upapattivasena upagacchanti. Sahabyatanti sahabhāvaṃ.

41. Anabhirati: This means wishing for the arrival of another being. But that discontent which is associated with repugnance does not exist in the Brahma world. Paritassanā: This means agitation, trembling; and it is of four kinds: anxiety due to fear, anxiety due to craving, anxiety due to views, and anxiety due to knowledge. Therein, anxiety due to fear is this: “Dependent on birth arise fear, dread, terror, trembling, and horripilation. Dependent on aging… sickness… death… arise… terror.” Anxiety due to craving is this: “Oh, that other beings also would come to this state!” Anxiety due to views is this: “It is simply the trembling through craving and wrong view.” Anxiety due to knowledge is this: “Having heard the Tathāgata’s teaching, for the most part they experience fear, agitation, and terror.” But here, both anxiety due to craving and anxiety due to views are applicable. Brahmavimānaṃ: But here it is not said to be empty because of the existence of the one first born. Upapajjanti: They approach by way of rebirth. Sahabyataṃ: This means the state of being together.

42. Abhibhūti [V 1.0096] abhibhavitvā ṭhito jeṭṭhakohamasmīti. Anabhibhūtoti aññehi anabhibhūto. Aññadatthūti ekaṃsavacane nipāto. Dassanavasena daso, sabbaṃ passāmīti attho. Vasavattīti sabbaṃ janaṃ vase vattemi. Issaro kattā nimmātāti ahaṃ loke issaro, ahaṃ lokassa kattā ca nimmātā ca, pathavī – himavanta-sineru-cakkavāḷa-mahāsamudda-candima-sūriyā mayā nimmitāti. Seṭṭho sajitāti ahaṃ lokassa uttamo ca sajitā ca, “tvaṃ khattiyo nāma hohi, tvaṃ brāhmaṇo, vesso, suddo, gahaṭṭho, pabbajito nāma. Antamaso [P 1.0112] tvaṃ oṭṭho hohi, goṇo hohī”ti “evaṃ sattānaṃ saṃvisajetā aha”nti maññati. Vasī pitā bhūtabhabyānanti (dī. ni. 1.17) ahamasmi ciṇṇavasitāya vasī, ahaṃ pitā bhūtānañca bhabyānañcāti maññati. Tattha aṇḍajajalābujā sattā antoaṇḍakose ceva antovatthimhi ca bhabyā nāma, bahi nikkhantakālato paṭṭhāya bhūtā nāma. Saṃsedajā paṭhamacittakkhaṇe bhabyā, dutiyato paṭṭhāya bhūtā. Opapātikā paṭhamairiyāpathe bhabyā, dutiyato paṭṭhāya bhūtāti veditabbā. Te sabbepi mayhaṃ puttāti saññāya “ahaṃ pitā bhūtabhabyāna”nti maññati.

42. Abhibhū: This means, having overcome, I stand; I am the most senior. Anabhibhūta: This means not overcome by others. Aññadatthu: This is a particle used in a definitive sense. Dasa: By way of seeing; the meaning is “I see all.” Vasavattī: This means “I make all people proceed according to my will.” Issaro kattā nimmātā: This means “I am the lord in the world, I am the maker and creator of the world—the earth, Himalayas, Sineru, the world-sphere, the great ocean, the moon, and the sun were created by me.” Seṭṭho sajitā: This means “I am supreme in the world and the ordainer—‘You shall be a noble, you a brahmin, a merchant, a worker, a householder, or a renunciant. Even you shall be a camel, an ox.’ Thus, I am the one who divides beings,” he thinks. Vasī pitā bhūtabhabyānaṃ: He thinks, “I am a master because of having practiced mastery, I am the father of those who have been and those who are to be.” Herein, egg-born and womb-born beings are called “to be” while still inside the egg-shell or womb; from the time they emerge, they are called “have been.” Moisture-born beings are called “to be” at the first moment of consciousness; from the second moment onward, they are called “have been.” Spontaneously-born beings are called “to be” in their first posture; from the second onward, they are called “have been.” With the perception “All these are my children,” he thinks, “I am the father of those who have been and those who are to be.”

Idāni kāraṇato sādhetukāmo – “mayā ime sattā nimmitā”ti paṭiññaṃ katvā “taṃ kissa hetū”tiādimāha. Itthattanti itthabhāvaṃ, brahmabhāvanti attho. Iminā mayanti attano kammavasena cutāpi upapannāpi ca kevalaṃ maññanāmatteneva “iminā mayaṃ nimmitā”ti maññamānā vaṅkacchidde vaṅkaāṇī viya onamitvā tasseva pādamūlaṃ gacchantīti.

Now, wishing to establish it by reason, having made the declaration, “These beings were created by me,” he says the passage beginning with, “For what reason is that?” Itthattaṃ: This means this state, the state of a Brahmā. Iminā mayaṃ: Although they have passed away and been reborn due to their own kamma, merely through wrong thinking, they think, “We were created by this one.” Like a crooked peg in a crooked hole, they bend down and go to his feet.

43. Vaṇṇavantataro cāti vaṇṇavantataro, abhirūpo pāsādikoti attho. Mahesakkhataroti issariyaparivāravasena mahāyasataro.

43. Vaṇṇavantataro ca: This means more beautiful, exceedingly beautiful, and inspiring confidence. Mahesakkhataro: This means more greatly renowned by way of dominion and retinue.

44. Ṭhānaṃ [M 1.0104] kho panetanti kāraṇaṃ kho panetaṃ. So tato cavitvā aññatra na gacchati, idheva āgacchati, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Agārasmāti gehā. Anagāriyanti pabbajjaṃ. Pabbajjā hi yasmā agārassa hi taṃ kasigorakkhādikammaṃ tattha natthi, tasmā anagāriyanti vuccati. Pabbajatīti upagacchati. Tato paraṃ nānussaratīti tato pubbenivāsā paraṃ na sarati, sarituṃ asakkonto tattha ṭhatvā diṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti.

44. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ: This is the reason. This was said in reference to one who, having passed away from there, does not go elsewhere but comes right here. Agārasmā: This means from the house. Anagāriyaṃ: This refers to the going forth. Because the work that is for the welfare of the house, such as farming and cattle-herding, does not exist in the going forth, it is called homelessness. Pabbajati: This means he approaches. Tato paraṃ nānussarati: This means beyond that previous existence, he does not remember; being unable to remember, he stands there and grasps a view.

Niccotiādīsu tassa upapattiṃ apassanto niccoti vadati, maraṇaṃ apassanto dhuvoti, sadābhāvato sassatoti, jarāvasenāpi [P 1.0113] vipariṇāmassa abhāvato avipariṇāmadhammoti. Sesamettha paṭhamavāre uttānamevāti.

In passages beginning with Nicco: Not seeing his arising, he says “permanent”; not seeing his death, he says “stable”; because of its constant existence, he says “eternal”; because of the absence of change even through aging, he says “of an unchanging nature.” The rest here in this first section is clear.

45-46. Dutiyavāre [V 1.0097] khiḍḍāya padussanti vinassantīti khiḍḍāpadosikā, padūsikātipi pāḷiṃ likhanti, sā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ natthi. Ativelanti atikālaṃ, aticiranti attho. Hassakhiḍḍāratidhammasamāpannāti hassarati dhammañceva khiḍḍāratidhammañca samāpannā anuyuttā, keḷihassasukhañceva kāyikavācasikakīḷāsukhañca anuyuttā, vuttappakāraratidhammasamaṅgino hutvā viharantīti attho.

45-46. In the second instance: Because they are corrupted and perish through play, they are called 'those corrupted by play' (khiḍḍāpadosikā). Some also write the Pāḷi as 'padūsikā,' but that is not found in the commentary. 'Ativelaṃ' means 'for an excessive time,' 'for a very long time.' 'Hassakhiḍḍāratidhammasamāpannā' means: having well attained and being repeatedly engaged in both the nature of delight in sexual union and the nature of delight in play; being repeatedly engaged in the pleasure arising from the joy of amorous sport and the pleasure of physical and verbal play; they dwell, having become endowed with the nature of delight of the aforesaid kinds—this is the meaning.

Sati sammussatīti khādanīyabhojanīyesu sati sammussati. Te kira puññavisesādhigatena mahantena attano sirivibhavena nakkhattaṃ kīḷantā tāya sampattimahantatāya – “āhāraṃ paribhuñjimha, na paribhuñjimhā”tipi na jānanti. Atha ekāhārātikkamanato paṭṭhāya nirantaraṃ khādantāpi pivantāpi cavantiyeva, na tiṭṭhanti. Kasmā? Kammajatejassa balavatāya, karajakāyassa mandatāya, manussānañhi kammajatejo mando, karajakāyo balavā. Tesaṃ tejassa mandatāya karajakāyassa balavatāya sattāhampi atikkamitvā uṇhodakaacchayāguādīhi sakkā vatthuṃ upatthambhetuṃ. Devānaṃ pana tejo balavā hoti, karajaṃ mandaṃ. Te ekaṃ āhāravelaṃ atikkamitvāva saṇṭhātuṃ na sakkonti. Yathā nāma gimhānaṃ majjhanhike tattapāsāṇe ṭhapitaṃ padumaṃ vā uppalaṃ vā sāyanhasamaye ghaṭasatenāpi siñciyamānaṃ pākatikaṃ na hoti, vinassatiyeva. Evameva pacchā nirantaraṃ khādantāpi pivantāpi cavantiyeva, na [M 1.0105] tiṭṭhanti. Tenāha “satiyā sammosā te devā tamhā kāyā cavantī”ti. Katame [P 1.0114] pana te devāti? Ime devāti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vicāraṇā natthi, “devānaṃ kammajatejo balavā hoti, karajaṃ manda”nti avisesena vuttattā pana ye keci kabaḷīkārāhārūpajīvino devā evaṃ karonti, teyeva cavantīti veditabbā. Keci panāhu – “nimmānaratiparanimmitavasavattino te devā”ti. Khiḍḍāpadussanamatteneva hete khiḍḍāpadosikāti vuttā. Sesamettha purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Regarding 'memory is lost': memory concerning hard and soft foods is lost. It is said that those devas, while playing at a festival with the great splendor and prosperity attained through their special merit, do not even know, due to the greatness of that fortune, 'Have we consumed our food, or have we not consumed it?' Then, starting from the time of missing one meal, even while eating and drinking continuously, they just pass away; they do not endure. Why? Because of the strength of their kamma-born heat and the weakness of their physical body. For humans, indeed, the kamma-born heat is weak, and the physical body is strong. Due to the weakness of their heat and the strength of their physical body, it is possible to support the body even after seven days have passed with things like hot water and clear rice gruel. For devas, however, their heat is strong, and their physical body is weak. They are unable to endure after transgressing even a single mealtime. Just as a lotus or a water lily placed on a hot stone at midday in summer, even if sprinkled with a hundred pots of water in the evening, does not become natural again but just perishes; in the very same way, afterwards, even while eating and drinking continuously, they just pass away; they do not endure. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Due to loss of memory, those devas fall from that body.' But which devas are they? There is no investigation in the commentary as to which devas these are. However, since it is stated without distinction, 'For devas, the kamma-born heat is strong, and the physical body is weak,' it should be known that whichever devas subsisting on solid food act in this way, they are the very ones who pass away. But some say: 'Those devas are the Nimmānaratī and the Paranimmitavasavattī.' Indeed, they are called 'khiḍḍāpadosikā' merely because of being corrupted by play. The remainder here should be understood in the same way as before.

47-48. Tatiyavāre manena padussanti vinassantīti manopadosikā, ete cātumahārājikā. Tesu kira eko devaputto – nakkhattaṃ kīḷissāmīti saparivāro rathena vīthiṃ paṭipajjati, athañño nikkhamanto taṃ purato gacchantaṃ disvā – ‘bho ayaṃ kapaṇo’, adiṭṭhapubbaṃ viya etaṃ disvā – “pītiyā uddhumāto viya bhijjamāno viya ca gacchatī”ti kujjhati. Purato gacchantopi nivattitvā taṃ kuddhaṃ disvā – kuddhā nāma suviditā hontīti kuddhabhāvamassa ñatvā – “tvaṃ kuddho, mayhaṃ kiṃ karissasi, ayaṃ sampatti mayā dānasīlādīnaṃ vasena laddhā, na tuyhaṃ vasenā”ti paṭikujjhati. Ekasmiñhi kuddhe itaro akuddho [V 1.0098] rakkhati, ubhosu pana kuddhesu ekassa kodho itarassa paccayo hoti. Tassapi kodho itarassa paccayo hotīti ubho kandantānaṃyeva orodhānaṃ cavanti. Ayamettha dhammatā. Sesaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

47-48. In the third instance: Because they are corrupted and perish through the mind, they are called 'those corrupted by mind' (manopadosikā). These are the Cātumahārājikā devas. It is said that among them, one devaputta, thinking, 'I will play at the festival,' proceeds along the road in a chariot with his retinue. Then another, coming out and seeing him going ahead, becomes angry, thinking: 'Sirs, this wretch, seeing this fortune as if never seen before, goes about as if puffed up with joy, as if bursting with it!' The one going ahead, turning back and seeing him angry—for angry ones are easily known—and thus knowing his state of anger, becomes angry in return, saying: 'You are angry, but what can you do to me? This fortune was obtained by me through the power of giving, virtue, and so on, not through your power.' Indeed, when one is angry, the other, not being angry, protects from passing away. But when both are angry, the anger of one becomes a condition for the other, and his anger, in turn, becomes a condition for the first. Thus, both pass away even while their consorts are wailing. This is the natural law here. The remainder should be understood in the way already stated.

49-52. Takkīvāde ayaṃ cakkhādīnaṃ bhedaṃ passati, cittaṃ pana yasmā purimaṃ purimaṃ pacchimassa pacchimassa paccayaṃ datvāva nirujjhati, tasmā cakkhādīnaṃ bhedato balavatarampi cittassa bhedaṃ na passati. So taṃ apassanto yathā nāma sakuṇo ekaṃ rukkhaṃ jahitvā aññasmiṃ nilīyati, evameva imasmiṃ attabhāve bhinne cittaṃ aññatra gacchatīti gahetvā evamāha. Sesamettha vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

49-52. In the case of the reasoner: This one sees the breaking up of the eye and other physical phenomena. But because the mind ceases only after each preceding moment has given a condition to its succeeding moment, he therefore does not see the breaking up of the mind, which is even more powerful than the breaking up of the eye and other physical phenomena. He, not seeing that, holds the view that 'Just as a bird, having abandoned one tree, settles on another, in the very same way, when this personality-group is broken, the mind goes to another,' and speaks thus. The remainder here should be understood in the way already stated.

Antānantavādavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Doctrine of the Finite and Infinite.

53. Antānantikāti [P 1.0115] antānantavādā, antaṃ vā anantaṃ vā antānantaṃ vā nevantānānantaṃ vā ārabbha pavattavādāti attho.

53. ‘Antānantikā’ means those who hold the view of the finite and infinite; that is, their view has arisen in dependence on the finite, or the infinite, or both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite. This is the meaning.

54-60. Antasaññī [M 1.0106] lokasmiṃ viharatīti paṭibhāganimittaṃ cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ avaḍḍhetvā taṃ – “loko”ti gahetvā antasaññī lokasmiṃ viharati, cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ katvā vaḍḍhitakasiṇo pana anantasaññī hoti, uddhamadho avaḍḍhetvā pana tiriyaṃ vaḍḍhetvā uddhamadho antasaññī, tiriyaṃ anantasaññī. Takkīvādo vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Ime cattāropi attanā diṭṭhapubbānusāreneva diṭṭhiyā gahitattā pubbantakappikesu paviṭṭhā.

54-60. ‘One who has a perception of the finite dwells in the world’ means that, not having expanded the counterpart sign up to the boundary of the world-sphere, one takes it as ‘the world’ and dwells in the world with a perception of the finite. However, a person who has expanded the kasiṇa up to the boundary of the world-sphere becomes one with a perception of the infinite. Furthermore, not having expanded it upwards and downwards but having expanded it horizontally, one has a perception of the finite upwards and downwards, and a perception of the infinite horizontally. The case of the reasoner should be understood by the method already stated. These four, because they have been grasped by a view that is only in accordance with what was previously seen by themselves, are included among those who speculate on the past.

Amarāvikkhepavādavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Doctrine of Endless Evasion.

61. Na maratīti amarā. Kā sā? Evantipi me notiādinā nayena pariyantarahitā diṭṭhigatikassa diṭṭhi ceva vācā ca. Vividho khepoti vikkhepo, amarāya diṭṭhiyā vācāya ca vikkhepoti amarāvikkhepo, so etesaṃ atthīti amarāvikkhepikā, aparo nayo – amarā nāma ekā macchajāti, sā ummujjananimujjanādivasena udake sandhāvamānā gahetuṃ na sakkāti, evameva ayampi vādo itocito ca sandhāvati, gāhaṃ na upagacchatīti amarāvikkhepoti vuccati. So etesaṃ atthīti amarāvikkhepikā.

61. Because it does not end (na marati), it is called inconclusive (amarā). What is that? It is the endless view and speech of one who holds a wrong view, in accordance with the method beginning with ‘Even so, it is not for me.’ Vikkhepa means various (vividho) rejections (khepo). Amarāvikkhepa is the evasion (vikkhepa) by means of the inconclusive (amarāya) view and speech. Because this exists for them, they are called amarāvikkhepikā (evasive equivocators). Another method: Amarā is the name of a species of fish. That fish, darting about in the water by way of emerging and submerging, cannot be caught. In the same way, this doctrine also darts from here and there and does not come into one's grasp. Therefore, it is called amarāvikkhepa (eel-wriggling). Because this exists for them, they are called amarāvikkhepikā (eel-wrigglers).

62. “Idaṃ [V 1.0099] kusala”nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātīti dasa kusalakammapathe yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātīti attho. Akusalepi dasa akusalakammapathāva adhippetā. So mamassa vighātoti “musā mayā bhaṇita”nti vippaṭisāruppattiyā mama vighāto assa, dukkhaṃ bhaveyyāti attho. So mamassa antarāyoti so mama saggassa ceva maggassa ca antarāyo assa. Musāvādabhayā musāvādaparijegucchāti musāvāde ottappena ceva hiriyā ca. Vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjatīti vācāya vikkhepaṃ āpajjati. Kīdisaṃ? Amarāvikkhepaṃ, apariyantavikkhepanti attho.

62. ‘One does not know as it really is, “This is wholesome”’ means one does not know the ten wholesome courses of action as they really are. This is the meaning. In the case of the unwholesome, the ten unwholesome courses of action are also intended. ‘That would be a vexation for me’ means: ‘A falsehood has been spoken by me’; due to the arising of remorse, there would be vexation for me, there would be suffering. This is the meaning. ‘That would be an obstacle for me’ means: that would be an obstacle for me to heaven and to the path. ‘From fear of false speech, from disgust with false speech’ means: due to moral dread and moral shame regarding false speech. ‘Resorts to verbal evasion’ means one resorts to evasion by means of speech. What kind? Inconclusive evasion, endless evasion. This is the meaning.

Evantipi me notiādīsu evantipi me noti aniyamitavikkhepo[P 1.0116]. Tathātipi me noti “sassato attā ca loko cā”ti vuttaṃ sassatavādaṃ paṭikkhipati. Aññathātipi me noti sassatato aññathā vuttaṃ ekaccasassataṃ paṭikkhipati. Notipi me noti – “na [M 1.0107] hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā”ti vuttaṃ ucchedaṃ paṭikkhipati. No notipi me noti “neva hoti na na hotī”ti vuttaṃ takkīvādaṃ paṭikkhipati. Sayaṃ pana “idaṃ kusala”nti vā “akusala”nti vā puṭṭho na kiñci byākaroti. “Idaṃ kusala”nti puṭṭho “evantipi me no”ti vadati. Tato “kiṃ akusala”nti vutte “tathātipi me no”ti vadati. “Kiṃ ubhayato aññathā”ti vutte “aññathātipi me no”ti vadati. Tato “tividhenāpi na hoti, kiṃ te laddhī”ti vutte “notipi me no”ti vadati. Tato “kiṃ no noti te laddhī”ti vutte “no notipi me no”ti evaṃ vikkhepameva āpajjati, ekasmimpi pakkhe na tiṭṭhati.

In the phrases beginning with ‘Even so, it is not for me’: ‘Even so, it is not for me’ is the evasion of an undetermined doctrine. ‘Thus, it is not for me’ rejects the doctrine of eternalism, which states, ‘The self and the world are eternal.’ ‘Otherwise, it is not for me’ rejects the doctrine of partial-eternalism, which is stated as being otherwise than eternalism. ‘It is not, for me’ rejects annihilationism, which states, ‘The Tathāgata is not after death.’ ‘It is not not, for me’ rejects the doctrine of the sophist, which states, ‘He neither is nor is not.’ He himself, however, when asked, ‘Is this wholesome?’ or ‘Is this unwholesome?’ does not declare anything. When asked, ‘Is this wholesome?’ he says, ‘My view is not “even so”.’ Then, when it is said, ‘Is it unwholesome?’ he says, ‘My view is not “thus” either.’ When it is said, ‘Is it otherwise than both?’ he says, ‘My view is not “otherwise” either.’ Then, when it is said, ‘Is it not in any of the three ways? What is your view?’ he says, ‘My view is not “it is not” either.’ Then, when it is said, ‘Is your view “not not”?’ he says, ‘My view is not “not not” either.’ In this way, he resorts only to evasion and does not stand on any single position.

63. Chando vā rāgo vāti ajānantopi sahasā kusalameva “kusala”nti vatvā akusalameva “akusala”nti vatvā mayā asukassa nāma evaṃ byākataṃ, kiṃ taṃ subyākatanti aññe paṇḍite pucchitvā tehi – “subyākataṃ, bhadramukha, kusalameva tayā kusalaṃ, akusalameva akusalanti byākata”nti vutte natthi mayā sadiso paṇḍitoti evaṃ me tattha chando vā rāgo vā assāti attho. Ettha ca chando dubbalarāgo, rāgo balavarāgo. Doso vā paṭigho vāti kusalaṃ pana “akusala”nti, akusalaṃ vā “kusala”nti vatvā aññe paṇḍite pucchitvā tehi – “dubyākataṃ tayā”ti vutte ettakampi nāma na jānāmīti tattha me assa doso vā paṭigho vāti attho. Idhāpi doso dubbalakodho, paṭigho balavakodho.

63. ‘Desire or lust’ means: even without knowing, having hastily declared what is wholesome as ‘wholesome’ and what is unwholesome as ‘unwholesome’, and having asked other wise persons, ‘I have declared thus to so-and-so; was that well-declared?’, if they should say, ‘It was well-declared, good sir. You have declared what is wholesome as wholesome, and what is unwholesome as unwholesome,’ then thinking, ‘There is no wise person equal to me,’ in that case there would be desire or lust for me. This is the meaning. And here, desire (chanda) is weak lust, and lust (rāga) is strong lust. ‘Aversion or animosity’ means: however, having declared what is wholesome as ‘unwholesome’, or what is unwholesome as ‘wholesome’, and having asked other wise persons, if they should say, ‘You have declared it badly,’ then thinking, ‘Do I not even know this much?’, in that case there would be aversion or animosity for me. This is the meaning. Here too, aversion (dosa) is weak anger, and animosity (paṭigha) is strong anger.

Taṃ [V 1.0100] mamassa upādānaṃ, so mamassa vighātoti taṃ chandarāgadvayaṃ mama upādānaṃ assa, dosapaṭighadvayaṃ vighāto. Ubhayampi vā daḷhaggahaṇavasena upādānaṃ[P 1.0117], vihananavasena vighāto. Rāgo hi amuñcitukāmatāya ārammaṇaṃ gaṇhāti jalūkā viya. Doso vināsetukāmatāya āsīviso viya. Ubhopi cete santāpakaṭṭhena vihananti yevāti “upādāna”nti ca “vighāto”ti ca vuttā. Sesaṃ paṭhamavārasadisameva.

‘That would be clinging for me, that would be a vexation for me’ means: that pair of desire and lust would be clinging for me; the pair of aversion and animosity would be a vexation. Or, both are called ‘clinging’ by way of firm grasping, and ‘vexation’ by way of oppressing. Indeed, lust, due to its desire not to let go, grasps its object like a leech. Aversion, due to its desire to destroy, grasps its object like a venomous snake. And both of these indeed oppress by their nature of burning; therefore they are called ‘clinging’ and ‘vexation’. The remainder is just like the first case.

64. Paṇḍitāti [M 1.0108] paṇḍiccena samannāgatā. Nipuṇāti saṇhasukhumabuddhino sukhumaatthantaraṃ paṭivijjhanasamatthā. Kataparappavādāti viññātaparappavādā ceva parehi saddhiṃ katavādaparicayā ca. Vālavedhirūpāti vālavedhidhanuggahasadisā. Te bhindantā maññeti vālavedhi viya vālaṃ sukhumānipi paresaṃ diṭṭhigatāni attano paññāgatena bhindantā viya carantīti attho. Te maṃ tatthāti te samaṇabrāhmaṇā maṃ tesu kusalākusalesu. Samanuyuñjeyyunti “kiṃ kusalaṃ, kiṃ akusalanti attano laddhiṃ vadā”ti laddhiṃ puccheyyuṃ. Samanugāheyyunti “idaṃ nāmā”ti vutte “kena kāraṇena etamatthaṃ gāheyyu”nti kāraṇaṃ puccheyyuṃ. Samanubhāseyyunti “iminā nāma kāraṇenā”ti vutte kāraṇe dosaṃ dassetvā “na tvaṃ idaṃ jānāsi, idaṃ pana gaṇha, idaṃ vissajjehī”ti evaṃ samanuyuñjeyyuṃ. Na sampāyeyyanti na sampādeyyaṃ, sampādetvā kathetuṃ na sakkuṇeyyanti attho. So mamassa vighātoti yaṃ taṃ punappunaṃ vatvāpi asampāyanaṃ nāma, so mama vighāto assa, oṭṭhatālujivhāgalasosanadukkhameva assāti attho. Sesametthāpi paṭhamavārasadisameva.

64. “Wise” means endowed with the wisdom characteristic of a wise person. “Skillful” means having a delicate and subtle intellect, capable of penetrating subtle and various meanings. “Having refuted others’ doctrines” means they are those who have understood the doctrines of others and are practiced in debate with others. “Like a hair-splitter” means similar to an archer who can shoot a hair-tip. The meaning of “They shatter” is: just as a hair-splitting archer splits a hair, so they go about as if shattering even the subtle views of others with their own particular wisdom. “They would question me there” means those ascetics and brahmins would question me regarding those wholesome and unwholesome matters. “They would question” means they would ask about my doctrine, saying, “What is wholesome? What is unwholesome? State your doctrine.” “They would cross-examine” means when I have replied, “It is this,” they would ask the reason, saying, “For what reason do you accept this meaning?” “They would press further” means when I have said, “For this particular reason we accept this meaning,” they, having pointed out a fault in the reason, would instruct and urge me thus: “You do not know this. Instead, accept this; reject that.” “I would not satisfy them” means I would not be able to bring it to completion; the meaning is that I would not be able to bring it to completion and explain. “That would be a vexation for me” means: that which is called the inability to bring to completion even after speaking again and again, that would be a vexation for me; the meaning is, it would be only the suffering of dryness of the lips, palate, tongue, and throat. Here too, the remainder is just like the first case.

65-66. Mandoti mandapañño apaññassevetaṃ nāmaṃ. Momūhoti atisammūḷho. Hoti [P 1.0118] tathāgatotiādīsu satto “tathāgato”ti adhippeto. Sesamettha uttānameva. Imepi cattāro pubbe pavattadhammānusāreneva diṭṭhiyā gahitattā pubbantakappikesu paviṭṭhā.

65-66. “Dull” means of dull wisdom; this is a name for one without wisdom. “Bewildered” means extremely deluded. In such phrases as “the Tathāgata exists,” a being is intended by “Tathāgata.” The remainder here is self-evident. These four also, because they have grasped a wrong view in accordance with a doctrine that arose in the past, are included among those who speculate on the past.

Adhiccasamuppannavādavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Doctrine of Fortuitous Origination

67. “Adhiccasamuppanno attā ca loko cā”ti dassanaṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ. Taṃ etesaṃ atthīti adhiccasamuppannikā. Adhiccasamuppannanti akāraṇasamuppannaṃ.

67. The wrong view that “the self and the world have arisen fortuitously” is called ‘fortuitous origination.’ Because this view exists for them, they are called ‘adherents of fortuitous origination.’ ‘Fortuitous origination’ means arisen without a cause.

68-73. Asaññasattāti desanāsīsametaṃ, acittuppādā rūpamattakaattabhāvāti attho. Tesaṃ evaṃ uppatti veditabbā – ekacco hi titthāyatane pabbajitvā vāyokasiṇe parikammaṃ katvā [V 1.0101] catutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā jhānā vuṭṭhāya – “citte dosaṃ passati, citte sati hatthacchedādidukkhañceva [M 1.0109] sabbabhayāni ca honti, alaṃ iminā cittena, acittakabhāvova santo”ti, evaṃ citte dosaṃ passitvā aparihīnajjhāno kālaṃ katvā asaññasattesu nibbattati, cittamassa cuticittanirodhena idheva nivattati, rūpakkhandhamattameva tattha pātubhavati. Te tattha yathā nāma jiyāvegakkhitto saro yattako jiyāvego, tattakameva ākāse gacchati. Evameva jhānavegakkhittā upapajjitvā yattako jhānavego, tattakameva kālaṃ tiṭṭhanti, jhānavege pana parihīne tattha rūpakkhandho antaradhāyati, idha pana paṭisandhisaññā uppajjati. Yasmā pana tāya idha uppannasaññāya tesaṃ tattha cuti paññāyati, tasmā “saññuppādā ca pana te devā tamhā kāyā cavantī”ti vuttaṃ. Santatāyāti santabhāvāya. Sesamettha uttānameva. Takkīvādopi vuttanayeneva veditabboti.
