68-73. “Non-percipient beings” is the heading of this discourse; the meaning is: beings whose existence consists only of form, without the arising of consciousness. Their arising should be understood thus: Indeed, a certain person, having gone forth in a heretical sect, having performed the preliminary work on the air kasiṇa and produced the fourth jhāna, emerges from that jhāna and sees a fault in consciousness, thinking: “When there is consciousness, there is suffering such as the cutting off of hands, and all fears arise. Enough with this consciousness! The state without consciousness is peaceful.” Thus, having seen a fault in consciousness, being one whose jhāna has not declined, he dies and is reborn among the non-percipient beings. His consciousness ceases right here with the cessation of the death-consciousness; only the form aggregate manifests there. There, just as an arrow shot by the force of a bowstring travels in the air only for as long as the bowstring’s force lasts, in the same way, they, having been propelled by the force of jhāna and taken rebirth, remain for only as long as the jhāna’s force lasts. When, however, the jhāna’s force has waned, the form aggregate there disappears, and here rebirth-perception arises. And because their passing away from there is discerned by means of that perception which has arisen here, therefore it was said: “And with the arising of perception, those devas pass away from that group.” “For continuity” (santatāya) means for the sake of existence (santabhāvāya). The remainder here is self-evident. The doctrine of the logicians should also be understood in the way that has been stated.

Aparantakappikavaṇṇanā

Explanation of Speculations About the Future

74. Evaṃ aṭṭhārasa pubbantakappike dassetvā idāni catucattārīsaṃ aparantakappike dassetuṃ – “santi, bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Tattha anāgatakoṭṭhāsasaṅkhātaṃ aparantaṃ kappetvā gaṇhantīti aparantakappikā, aparantakappo vā etesaṃ [P 1.0119] atthīti aparantakappikā. Evaṃ sesampi pubbe vuttappakāranayeneva veditabbaṃ.

74. Having thus shown the eighteen speculators about the past, now, in order to show the forty-four speculators about the future, the Blessed One said, beginning with, “There are, bhikkhus…” Herein, those who conceive and grasp the future, which is reckoned as the future portion, are called ‘speculators about the future’ (aparantakappikā); or, those for whom speculation about the future exists are ‘speculators about the future.’ Thus, the remainder should also be understood by the very method stated previously.

Saññīvādavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Doctrine of Percipience

75. Uddhamāghātanikāti āghātanaṃ vuccati maraṇaṃ, uddhamāghātanā attānaṃ vadantīti uddhamāghātanikā. Saññīti pavatto vādo, saññīvādo, so etesaṃ atthīti saññīvādā.

75. Regarding `Uddhamāghātanikā`: `āghātana` is said to be death. Because they speak of the self as existing after death, they are called `uddhamāghātanikā`. The doctrine that has arisen as '[the self] is percipient' is `saññīvāda`; because this doctrine is theirs, they are called `saññīvādā`.

76-77. Rūpī attātiādīsu kasiṇarūpaṃ “attā”ti tattha pavattasaññañcassa “saññā”ti gahetvā vā ājīvakādayo viya takkamatteneva vā “rūpī attā hoti, arogo paraṃ maraṇā saññī”ti naṃ paññapenti. Tattha arogoti nicco. Arūpasamāpattinimittaṃ pana “attā”ti samāpattisaññañcassa “saññā”ti gahetvā vā nigaṇṭhādayo viya takkamatteneva vā “arūpī attā hoti, arogo paraṃ maraṇā saññī”ti naṃ paññapenti. Tatiyā pana missakagāhavasena pavattā diṭṭhi. Catutthā takkagāheneva. Dutiyacatukkaṃ [M 1.0110] antānantikavāde vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Tatiyacatukke samāpannakavasena ekattasaññī[V 1.0102], asamāpannakavasena nānattasaññī, parittakasiṇavasena parittasaññī, vipulakasiṇavasena appamāṇasaññīti veditabbā. Catutthacatukke pana dibbena cakkhunā tikacatukkajjhānabhūmiyaṃ nibbattamānaṃ disvā “ekantasukhī”ti gaṇhāti. Niraye nibbattamānaṃ disvā “ekantadukkhī”ti. Manussesu nibbattamānaṃ disvā “sukhadukkhī”ti. Vehapphaladevesu nibbattamānaṃ disvā “adukkhamasukhī”ti gaṇhāti. Visesato hi pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇalābhino pubbantakappikā honti, dibbacakkhukā aparantakappikāti.

76-77. In statements such as “The self is material,” some, like the Ājīvakas, taking a kasiṇa-form as “self” and the perception arising in connection with it as “its perception,” or merely through conjecture, assert, “The self is material, unimpaired after death, and percipient.” Here, “unimpaired” means eternal. Others, like the Nigaṇṭhas, taking the object of the formless attainments as “self” and the attainment-perception as “its perception,” or merely through conjecture, assert, “The self is immaterial, unimpaired after death, and percipient.” The third, however, is a view that arises by way of grasping a mixture. The fourth is by way of grasping through conjecture alone. The second tetrad should be understood by the very method explained in the section on the doctrines of the finite and the infinite. In the third tetrad, it should be understood that by way of one in attainment, the self has a unified perception; by way of one not in attainment, the self has a diversified perception; by way of a limited kasiṇa, the self has a limited perception; by way of an extensive kasiṇa, the self has a boundless perception. In the fourth tetrad, however, seeing with the divine eye a being reborn in the realm of the third and fourth jhānas, one holds that “the self is exclusively happy.” Seeing a being reborn in hell, one holds that it is “exclusively miserable.” Seeing a being reborn among humans, one holds that it is “both happy and miserable.” Seeing a being reborn among the Vehapphala devas, one holds that it is “neither-miserable-nor-happy.” For it is specifically those who have gained the knowledge of recollection of past lives who become speculators about the past, and those with the divine eye who become speculators about the future.

Asaññīvādavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Doctrine of Non-Percipience

78-83. Asaññīvādo saññīvāde ādimhi vuttānaṃ dvinnaṃ catukkānaṃ vasena veditabbo. Tathā nevasaññīnāsaññīvādo. Kevalañhi tattha “saññī attā”ti gaṇhantānaṃ tā diṭṭhiyo, idha “asaññī”ti ca “nevasaññīnāsaññī”ti ca. Tattha na ekantena kāraṇaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ. Diṭṭhigatikassa hi gāho ummattakapacchisadisoti vuttametaṃ.

78–83. The doctrine of non-percipience should be understood by way of the two tetrads stated at the beginning of the doctrine of percipience. Likewise, the doctrine of neither-percipience-nor-non-percipience. For, in the former case, those views belong to those who hold that 'the self is percipient,' whereas in the latter case, they belong to those who hold that 'the self is non-percipient' and that 'the self is neither percipient nor non-percipient.' In this matter, a specific reason should not be sought. For it has been said: 'The grasping of one who is given to views is like the basket of a madman.'

Ucchedavādavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Annihilationist Doctrine

84. Ucchedavāde satoti vijjamānassa. Ucchedanti upacchedaṃ[P 1.0120]. Vināsanti adassanaṃ. Vibhavanti bhāvavigamaṃ. Sabbānetāni aññamaññavevacanāneva. Tattha dve janā ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhanti, lābhī ca alābhī ca. Lābhī arahato dibbena cakkhunā cutiṃ disvā upapattiṃ apassanto, yo vā cutimattameva daṭṭhuṃ sakkoti, na upapātaṃ; so ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti. Alābhī ca “ko paralokaṃ na jānātī”ti kāmasukhagiddhatāya vā. “Yathā rukkhato paṇṇāni patitāni na puna viruhanti, evameva sattā”tiādinā takkena vā ucchedaṃ gaṇhāti. Idha pana taṇhādiṭṭhīnaṃ vasena tathā ca aññathā ca vikappetvāva imā satta diṭṭhiyo uppannāti veditabbā.

84. In the annihilationist doctrine, `sato` means 'of an existing being.' `Ucchedam` means 'cutting off.' `Vināsam` means 'disappearance.' `Vibhavam` means 'cessation of being.' All these are simply synonyms for one another. Therein, two kinds of persons take up the annihilationist view: one who has attained and one who has not. The one who has attained, having seen with the divine eye the passing away of an Arahant but not seeing the rebirth—or one who is able to see only the passing away, not the arising—takes up the annihilationist view. The one who has not attained takes up the annihilationist view, thinking, 'Who knows the next world?'; or due to greed for sensual pleasures; or through such reasoning as: 'Just as leaves that have fallen from a tree do not grow again, so too beings do not.' Here, however, it should be understood that these seven views have arisen only by speculating in this way and in other ways, by the power of craving and views.

85. Tattha rūpīti rūpavā. Cātumahābhūtikoti catumahābhūtamayo. Mātāpitūnaṃ etanti mātāpettikaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Sukkasoṇitaṃ. Mātāpettike [M 1.0111] sambhūto jātoti mātāpettikasambhavo. Iti rūpakāyasīsena manussattabhāvaṃ “attā”ti vadati. Ittheketi itthaṃ eke evameketi attho.

85. Therein, `rūpī` means 'possessing form.' `Cātumahābhūtiko` means 'composed of the four great elements.' `Mātāpettikaṃ` is so called because 'this belongs to the mother and father.' What is that? Semen and blood. `Mātāpettikasambhavo` is so called because one is 'produced and born from what belongs to the mother and father.' Thus, with the material body as the principal part, one speaks of the human state of being as 'self.' `Ittheke` means 'thus some' or 'in this way, some.'

86. Dutiyo [V 1.0103] taṃ paṭikkhipitvā dibbattabhāvaṃ vadati. Dibboti devaloke sambhūto. Kāmāvacaroti cha kāmāvacaradevapariyāpanno. Kabaḷīkāraṃ āhāraṃ bhakkhatīti kabaḷīkārāhārabhakkho.

86. The second, having rejected that, speaks of a divine state of being. `Dibbo` means 'born in the deva world.' `Kāmāvacaro` means 'included among the six sense-sphere devas.' `Kabaḷīkārāhārabhakkho` is so called because one 'eats edible food.'

87. Manomayoti jhānamanena nibbatto. Sabbaṅgapaccaṅgīti sabbaṅgapaccaṅgayutto. Ahīnindriyoti paripuṇṇindriyo. Yāni brahmaloke atthi, tesaṃ vasena itaresañca saṇṭhānavasenetaṃ vuttaṃ.

87. `Manomayo` means 'produced by the jhāna-mind.' `Sabbaṅgapaccaṅgī` means 'endowed with all major and minor limbs.' `Ahīnindriyo` means 'possessing complete faculties.' This is said by way of those faculties that exist in the Brahma world, and by way of the form of the other faculties.

88-92. Sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamātiādīnaṃ attho visuddhimagge vutto. Ākāsānañcāyatanūpagotiādīsu pana ākāsānañcāyatanabhavaṃ upagatoti, evamattho veditabbo. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.

88–92. The meaning of the phrases beginning with 'by completely transcending perceptions of form' has been stated in the Visuddhimagga. However, in the phrases beginning with 'one who has reached the base of infinite space,' the meaning should be understood thus: 'one who has reached the existence of the base of infinite space.' The rest here is self-evident.

Diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Doctrine of Nibbāna in the Visible World

93. Diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāde [P 1.0121] diṭṭhadhammoti paccakkhadhammo vuccati, tattha tattha paṭiladdhattabhāvassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Diṭṭhadhamme nibbānaṃ diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ, imasmiṃyeva attabhāve dukkhavūpasamananti attho. Taṃ vadantīti diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā. Paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānanti paramaṃ diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ uttamanti attho.

93. In the doctrine of Nibbāna in the visible world, 'the visible world' (diṭṭhadhammo) is said to be the present existence (paccakkhadhammo). This is a designation for the existence obtained in any given realm. Nibbāna in the visible world (diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ) is the quenching of suffering in the visible world; the meaning is the calming of suffering in this very existence. Because they declare this, they are proponents of the doctrine of Nibbāna in the visible world (diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā). As for 'supreme Nibbāna in the visible world' (paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ), the meaning is the supreme (paramaṃ), the highest (uttamaṃ) Nibbāna in the visible world.

94. Pañcahi kāmaguṇehīti manāpiyarūpādīhi pañcahi kāmakoṭṭhāsehi bandhanehi vā. Samappitoti suṭṭhu appito allīno hutvā. Samaṅgībhūtoti samannāgato. Paricāretīti tesu kāmaguṇesu yathāsukhaṃ indriyāni cāreti sañcāreti itocito ca upaneti. Atha vā laḷati ramati kīḷati. Ettha ca duvidhā kāmaguṇā – mānusakā ceva dibbā ca. Mānusakā mandhātukāmaguṇasadisā daṭṭhabbā, dibbā paranimmitavasavattidevarājassa kāmaguṇasadisāti. Evarūpe kāme upagatānañhi te diṭṭhadhammanibbānasampattiṃ paññapenti.

94. ‘By the five strands of sensual pleasure’ (pañcahi kāmaguṇehi) means by the five portions of sensuality (kāmakoṭṭhāsehi), such as agreeable forms, or by the bonds (bandhanehi) of sensuality. ‘Endowed’ (samappito) means being well-applied (suṭṭhu appito), having clung (allīno). ‘Possessed’ (samaṅgībhūto) means furnished with (samannāgato). ‘Indulges’ (paricāreti) means that in those strands of sensual pleasure, he causes his senses to wander (cāreti) as he pleases (yathāsukhaṃ), he causes them to wander about (sañcāreti), and he brings them (upaneti) to this object and that (itocito). Alternatively, he adorns himself (laḷati), delights (ramati), and plays (kīḷati). And here, sensual pleasures are of two kinds: human and divine. Human sensual pleasures should be understood as similar to the sensual pleasures of King Mandhātu; divine sensual pleasures should be understood as similar to the sensual pleasures of the king of the Paranimmitavasavattī devas. Indeed, for those who have approached such sensual pleasures, they (the proponents) declare the accomplishment of Nibbāna in the visible world.

95. Dutiyavāre [M 1.0112] hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccā paṭipīḷanaṭṭhena dukkhā, pakatijahanaṭṭhena vipariṇāmadhammāti veditabbā. Tesaṃ vipariṇāmaññathābhāvāti tesaṃ kāmānaṃ vipariṇāmasaṅkhātā aññathābhāvā, yampi me ahosi, tampi me natthīti vuttanayena uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā. Tattha antonijjhāyanalakkhaṇo soko, tannissitalālappanalakkhaṇo [V 1.0104] paridevo, kāyappaṭipīḷanalakkhaṇaṃ dukkhaṃ, manovighātalakkhaṇaṃ domanassaṃ, visādalakkhaṇo upāyāso, vivicceva kāmehītiādīnamattho visuddhimagge vutto.

95. In the second case, they should be known as impermanent (aniccā) in the sense of non-existence after having been; as suffering (dukkhā) in the sense of oppression; and as subject to change (vipariṇāmadhammā) in the sense of abandoning their natural state. ‘Because of their change and otherness’ (tesaṃ vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā) means: because of the otherness of those sensual pleasures, which is called change, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in the manner spoken: ‘That which was mine, that too is no more for me.’ Therein, sorrow (soko) has the characteristic of inner burning; lamentation (paridevo) has the characteristic of wailing dependent on that; pain (dukkhaṃ) has the characteristic of bodily oppression; grief (domanassaṃ) has the characteristic of mental affliction; despair (upāyāso) has the characteristic of dejection. The meaning of ‘secluded from sensual pleasures’ (vivicceva kāmehi) and so on has been stated by me in the Visuddhimagga.

96. Vitakkitanti abhiniropanavasena pavatto vitakko. Vicāritanti [P 1.0122] anumajjanavasena pavatto vicāro. Etenetanti etena vitakkitena ca vicāritena ca etaṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ oḷārikaṃ sakaṇḍakaṃ viya khāyati.

96. ‘Thought’ (vitakkitaṃ) is the applied thought (vitakko) that proceeds by way of directing the mind onto an object. ‘Examination’ (vicāritaṃ) is the sustained thought (vicāro) that proceeds by way of repeatedly exploring the object. ‘By this’ (etena) means that by this thought and examination, this first jhāna appears coarse (oḷārikaṃ), as if with thorns (sakaṇṭakaṃ).

97-98. Pītigatanti pītiyeva. Cetaso uppilāvitattanti cittassa uppilabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Cetaso ābhogoti jhānā vuṭṭhāya tasmiṃ sukhe punappunaṃ cittassa ābhogo manasikāro samannāhāroti. Sesamettha diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāde uttānameva.

97–98. ‘Filled with rapture’ (pītigataṃ) is just rapture (pīti). ‘Buoyancy of mind’ (cetaso uppilāvitattaṃ) means that which makes the mind buoyant. ‘Inclination of mind’ (cetaso ābhogo) means that, having arisen from the jhāna, there is repeated inclination (ābhogo), attention (manasikāro), or application (samannāhāro) of the mind towards that bliss. The remainder here in the doctrine of Nibbāna in the visible world is self-evident.

Ettāvatā sabbāpi dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhiyo kathitā honti. Yāsaṃ satteva ucchedadiṭṭhiyo, sesā sassatadiṭṭhiyo.

By this much, all sixty-two views have been explained. Of these, seven are annihilationist views; the remaining fifty-five are eternalist views.

100-104. Idāni – “imehi kho te, bhikkhave”ti iminā vārena sabbepi te aparantakappike ekajjhaṃ niyyātetvā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ vissajjeti. Puna – “imehi, kho te bhikkhave”tiādinā vārena sabbepi te pubbantāparantakappike ekajjhaṃ niyyātetvā tadeva ñāṇaṃ vissajjeti. Iti “katame ca te, bhikkhave, dhammā”tiādimhi pucchamānopi sabbaññutaññāṇameva pucchitvā vissajjamānopi sattānaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ tulāya tulayanto viya sinerupādato vālukaṃ uddharanto viya dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhigatāni uddharitvā sabbaññutaññāṇameva vissajjeti. Evamayaṃ yathānusandhivasena desanā āgatā.

100–104. Now, with this section beginning ‘These, bhikkhus…’ (imehi kho te, bhikkhave), having brought all those speculators on the future to a conclusion together, he expounds the knowledge of omniscience. Again, with the section beginning ‘These, bhikkhus…’ (imehi kho te, bhikkhave), having brought all those speculators on the past and future to a conclusion together, he expounds that very same knowledge. Thus, in the passage beginning ‘And what, bhikkhus, are those things?’ (katame ca te, bhikkhave, dhammā), when asking, he asked about the knowledge of omniscience itself; and when answering, as if weighing the dispositions of beings with a scale, as if extracting sand from the foot of Mount Sineru, having extracted the sixty-two wrong views, he expounds the knowledge of omniscience itself. In this way, this discourse has proceeded in accordance with its connections.

Tayo hi suttassa anusandhī – pucchānusandhi, ajjhāsayānusandhi, yathānusandhīti. Tattha “evaṃ vutte aññataro bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – kiṃ nu [M 1.0113] kho, bhante, orimaṃ tīraṃ, kiṃ pārimaṃ tīraṃ, ko majjhe saṃsīdo, ko thale ussādo, ko manussaggāho, ko amanussaggāho, ko āvaṭṭaggāho, ko antopūtibhāvo”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.241) evaṃ pucchantānaṃ bhagavatā vissajjitasuttavasena pucchānusandhi veditabbo.

Indeed, there are three connections of a sutta: the connection by way of a question (pucchānusandhi), the connection by way of disposition (ajjhāsayānusandhi), and the connection as it occurs (yathānusandhi). Therein, the connection by way of a question should be understood in terms of a sutta expounded by the Blessed One in response to those who ask, such as: ‘When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One: “What, venerable sir, is the near shore? What is the far shore? What is sinking in the middle? What is being cast up on high ground? What is seizure by humans? What is seizure by non-humans? What is seizure by a whirlpool? What is being inwardly putrid?”’

Atha kho aññatarassa bhikkhuno evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi – “iti kira bho rūpaṃ anattā…, vedanā…, saññā…, saṅkhārā [P 1.0123]…, viññāṇaṃ anattā, anattakatāni kira kammāni [V 1.0105] kamattānaṃ phusissantī”ti. Atha kho bhagavā tassa bhikkhuno cetasā ceto parivitakkamaññāya bhikkhū āmantesi – “ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, bhikkhave, vijjati, yaṃ idhekacco moghapuriso avidvā avijjāgato taṇhādhipateyyena cetasā satthusāsanaṃ atidhāvitabbaṃ maññeyya – “iti kira bho rūpaṃ anattā…pe… phusissantī”ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti (ma. ni. 3.10). Evaṃ paresaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ viditvā bhagavatā vuttasuttavasena ajjhāsayānusandhi veditabbo.

Then a thought arose in the mind of a certain bhikkhu: ‘It seems, sirs, that form is not-self… feeling… perception… formations… consciousness is not-self. It seems that actions done by what is not-self—what self will they touch?’ Then the Blessed One, having known with his own mind the thought in that bhikkhu’s mind, addressed the bhikkhus: ‘Bhikkhus, this situation exists, wherein some worthless person here, being ignorant, fallen into ignorance, with a mind dominated by craving, might think the Teacher’s instruction should be over-run, thinking: “It seems, sirs, that form is not-self… what self will they touch?” What do you think, bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent?’ Thus, the connection by way of disposition should be understood in terms of a sutta spoken by the Blessed One after having known the disposition of others.

Yena pana dhammena ādimhi desanā uṭṭhitā, tassa dhammassa anurūpadhammavasena vā paṭipakkhavasena vā yesu suttesu upari desanā āgacchati, tesaṃ vasena yathānusandhi veditabbo. Seyyathidaṃ, ākaṅkheyyasutte heṭṭhā sīlena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari cha abhiññā āgatā. Vatthasutte heṭṭhā kilesena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari brahmavihārā āgatā. Kosambakasutte heṭṭhā bhaṇḍanena uṭṭhitā, upari sāraṇīyadhammā āgatā. Kakacūpame heṭṭhā akkhantiyā uṭṭhitā, upari kakacūpamā āgatā. Imasmimpi brahmajāle heṭṭhā diṭṭhivasena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari suññatāpakāsanaṃ āgataṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “evamayaṃ yathānusandhivasena desanā āgatā”ti.

Moreover, by whichever principle a teaching has arisen in the beginning, the sequential connection should be understood by way of those suttas in which a subsequent teaching appears, either through a principle conforming to that original principle or through an opposing principle. That is to say: in the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta, the teaching arises below with virtue, and above, the six direct knowledges appear. In the Vattha Sutta, the teaching arises below with defilement, and above, the divine abodes appear. In the Kosambaka Sutta, the teaching arises below with quarreling, and above, the principles of cordiality appear. In the Kakacūpama Sutta, the teaching arises below with impatience, and above, the simile of the saw appears. In this Brahmajāla Sutta as well, the teaching arises below by way of views, and above, the exposition of emptiness appears. Therefore, it was said: 'Thus this teaching has come by way of sequential connection.'

Paritassitavipphanditavāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on Agitation and Trembling

105-117. Idāni mariyādavibhāgadassanatthaṃ – “tatra bhikkhave”tiādikā desanā āraddhā. Tadapi tesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ ajānataṃ apassataṃ vedayitaṃ taṇhāgatānaṃ paritassitavipphanditamevāti yena diṭṭhiassādena [M 1.0114] diṭṭhisukhena diṭṭhivedayitena te somanassajātā sassataṃ attānañca lokañca paññapenti catūhi vatthūhi, tadapi tesaṃ bhavantānaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ dhammānaṃ sabhāvaṃ ajānantānaṃ apassantānaṃ vedayitaṃ taṇhāgatānaṃ kevalaṃ taṇhāgatānaṃyeva taṃ [P 1.0124] vedayitaṃ, tañca kho panetaṃ paritassitavipphanditameva. Diṭṭhisaṅkhātena ceva taṇhāsaṅkhātena ca paritassitena vipphanditameva calitameva kampitameva thusarāsimhi nikhātakhāṇusadisaṃ, na sotāpannassa dassanamiva niccalanti dasseti. Esa nayo ekaccasassatavādādīsupi.

Now, for the purpose of showing the distinct boundary, the teaching beginning with 'There, bhikkhus...' was undertaken. By the passage 'That feeling of those venerable ascetics and brahmins—who do not know, do not see, and are overcome by craving—is simply agitation and trembling,' He shows the following meaning: By whatever relish of views, pleasure of views, and feeling of views they, having become mentally joyful, posit the self and the world as eternal on four grounds—that feeling of those venerable ascetics and brahmins, who do not know and do not see the true nature of phenomena, is a feeling of those overcome by craving. It is simply of those overcome by craving. And that feeling is simply agitation and trembling. It is simply trembled, simply moved, simply shaken by that agitation which is designated as 'view' and designated as 'craving,' like a post planted in a heap of chaff; it is not unmoving like the vision of a stream-enterer. This is the method also in the cases of the partial-eternalists and others.

Phassapaccayavāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on 'Conditioned by Contact'

118-130. Puna – “tatra, bhikkhave, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā sassatavādā”tiādi paramparapaccayadassanatthaṃ āraddhaṃ[V 1.0106]. Tattha tadapi phassapaccayāti yena diṭṭhiassādena diṭṭhisukhena diṭṭhivedayitena te somanassajātā sassataṃ attānañca lokañca paññapenti catūhi vatthūhi, tadapi taṇhādiṭṭhipariphanditaṃ vedayitaṃ phassapaccayāti dasseti. Esa nayo sabbattha.

Again, the passage beginning, 'There, bhikkhus, those ascetics and brahmins who are eternalists...' was undertaken for the purpose of showing the successive conditions. Therein, by the phrase 'That too is conditioned by contact,' He shows the following: By whatever relish of views, pleasure of views, and feeling of views those ascetics and brahmins, having become mentally joyful, posit the self and the world as eternal on four grounds—that feeling, agitated by craving and views, also arises from contact as its condition. This is the method in all such doctrines.

131-143. Idāni tassa paccayassa diṭṭhivedayite balavabhāvadassanatthaṃ puna – “tatra, bhikkhave, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā sassatavādā”tiādimāha. Tattha te vata aññatra phassāti te vata samaṇabrāhmaṇā taṃ vedayitaṃ vinā phassena paṭisaṃvedissantīti kāraṇametaṃ natthīti. Yathā hi patato gehassa upatthambhanatthāya thūṇā nāma balavapaccayo hoti, na taṃ thūṇāya anupatthambhitaṃ ṭhātuṃ sakkoti, evameva phassopi vedanāya balavapaccayo, taṃ vinā idaṃ diṭṭhivedayitaṃ natthīti dasseti. Esa nayo sabbattha.

Now, for the purpose of showing the powerful nature of that condition in relation to the feeling based on views, He again stated the passage beginning, 'There, bhikkhus, those ascetics and brahmins who are eternalists...' Therein, by the phrase 'They, indeed, apart from contact,' He shows this meaning: 'That those ascetics and brahmins will experience that feeling without contact—this cause does not exist.' For just as a pillar is a powerful condition for supporting a collapsing house, and that house cannot stand unsupported by the pillar, even so is contact a powerful condition for feeling. He shows that without it, this feeling based on views does not exist. This is the method in all doctrines.

Diṭṭhigatikādhiṭṭhānavaṭṭakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Round Based on Adherence to Views

144. Idāni tatra bhikkhave, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā sassatavādā sassataṃ attānañca lokañca paññapenti catūhi vatthūhi, yepi te samaṇabrāhmaṇā ekaccasassatikātiādinā nayena sabbadiṭṭhivedayitāni sampiṇḍeti. Kasmā? Upari phasse pakkhipanatthāya. Kathaṃ? Sabbe te chahi phassāyatanehi phussa phussa paṭisaṃvedentīti. Tattha cha phassāyatanāni nāma – cakkhuphassāyatanaṃ, sotaphassāyatanaṃ, ghānaphassāyatanaṃ, jivhāphassāyatanaṃ, kāyaphassāyatanaṃ, manophassāyatananti imāni cha. Sañjāti-samosaraṇa-kāraṇa-paṇṇattimattatthesu hi ayaṃ [M 1.0115] āyatanasaddo pavattati. Tattha – “kambojo assānaṃ āyatanaṃ, gunnaṃ dakkhiṇāpatho”ti [P 1.0125] sañjātiyaṃ pavattati, sañjātiṭṭhāneti attho. “Manorame āyatane, sevanti naṃ vihaṅgamā”ti (a. ni. 5.38) samosaraṇe. “Sati satiāyatane”ti (a. ni. 3.102) kāraṇe. “Araññāyatane paṇṇakuṭīsu sammantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.255) paṇṇattimatte. Svāyamidha sañjātiādiatthattayepi yujjati. Cakkhādīsu hi phassapañcamakā dhammā sañjāyanti samosaranti, tāni ca tesaṃ kāraṇanti āyatanāni. Idha pana “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.43) iminā nayena phassasīseneva desanaṃ āropetvā phassaṃ ādiṃ katvā paccayaparamparaṃ dassetuṃ phassāyatanādīni vuttāni.

144. Now, by the method beginning, 'There, bhikkhus, those ascetics and brahmins who are eternalists and proclaim the self and the world as eternal based on four grounds, and also those ascetics and brahmins who are partial-eternalists...', He summarizes all feelings based on views. Why? For the purpose of including them in contact subsequently. How? 'All of them experience by repeatedly contacting through the six contact-bases.' Herein, the six contact-bases are: the eye-contact-base, the ear-contact-base, the nose-contact-base, the tongue-contact-base, the body-contact-base, and the mind-contact-base. Indeed, this word ‘base’ (āyatana) functions in the senses of origination, confluence, cause, and mere designation. Therein: ‘Kamboja is a breeding ground for horses, the southern region for cattle’ is used in the sense of origination, meaning a place of origination. ‘In a delightful resort, birds frequent it’ is used in the sense of confluence. ‘When there is a cause...’ is used in the sense of cause. ‘In the forest domain, they dwell peacefully in leaf huts’ is used in the sense of mere designation. This word ‘āyatana’ here is suitable in the three meanings beginning with origination. For in the eye, etc., phenomena that have contact as the fifth originate and come together, and those faculties are their cause; therefore, they are called bases. Here, however, following the method: ‘Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact,’ the teaching is presented with contact as the head, and making contact the starting point to show the sequence of conditions, the contact-bases and so forth were spoken of.

Phussa phussa paṭisaṃvedentīti phusitvā phusitvā paṭisaṃvedenti. Ettha ca kiñcāpi āyatanānaṃ [V 1.0107] phusanakiccaṃ viya vuttaṃ, tathāpi na tesaṃ phusanakiccatā veditabbā. Na hi āyatanāni phusanti, phassova taṃ taṃ ārammaṇaṃ phusati, āyatanāni pana phasse upanikkhipitvā dassitāni; tasmā sabbe te cha phassāyatanasambhavena phassena rūpādīni ārammaṇāni phusitvā taṃ diṭṭhivedanaṃ paṭisaṃvedayantīti evamettha attho veditabbo.

‘By repeatedly contacting, they experience’ means they experience by repeatedly contacting. And here, although the function of contacting is spoken of as if belonging to the bases, nevertheless, their state of having the function of contacting should not be understood. For the bases do not contact; it is contact itself that touches the respective object. The bases, however, are presented by being included under contact. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: all those ascetics and brahmins, by means of contact arising from the six contact-bases, having contacted objects such as forms, experience that feeling based on views.

Tesaṃ vedanāpaccayā taṇhātiādīsu vedanāti cha phassāyatanasambhavā vedanā. Sā rūpataṇhādibhedāya taṇhāya upanissayakoṭiyā paccayo hoti. Tena vuttaṃ – “tesaṃ vedanāpaccayā taṇhā”ti. Sā pana catubbidhassa upādānassa upanissayakoṭiyā ceva sahajātakoṭiyā ca paccayo hoti. Tathā upādānaṃ bhavassa. Bhavo jātiyā upanissayakoṭiyā paccayo hoti.

In the passage beginning 'For them, with feeling as condition, there is craving,' 'feeling' means the feeling arising from the six contact-bases. That feeling is a condition for craving—which is differentiated as craving for forms, etc.—by way of the category of decisive support. Therefore it was said: 'For them, with feeling as condition, there is craving.' That feeling, moreover, is a condition for the four kinds of clinging by way of the category of decisive support and by way of the category of co-nascence. Likewise, clinging is a condition for existence. Existence is a condition for birth by way of the category of decisive support.

Jātīti panettha savikārā pañcakkhandhā daṭṭhabbā, jāti jarāmaraṇassa ceva sokādīnañca upanissayakoṭiyā paccayo hoti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato pana paṭiccasamuppādakathā visuddhimagge vuttā. Idha panassa payojanamattameva veditabbaṃ. Bhagavā [P 1.0126] hi vaṭṭakathaṃ kathento – “purimā, bhikkhave, koṭi na paññāyati avijjāya, ‘ito pubbe avijjā nāhosi, atha pacchā samabhavī’ti evañcetaṃ, bhikkhave, vuccati, atha ca pana paññāyati “idappaccayā avijjā”ti (a. ni. 10.61) evaṃ avijjāsīsena vā, purimā, bhikkhave, koṭi [M 1.0116] na paññāyati bhavataṇhāya…pe… “idappaccayā bhavataṇhā”ti (a. ni. 10.62) evaṃ taṇhāsīsena vā, purimā, bhikkhave, koṭi na paññāyati bhavadiṭṭhiyā…pe… “idappaccayā bhavadiṭṭhī”ti evaṃ diṭṭhisīsena vā kathesi”. Idha pana diṭṭhisīsena kathento vedanārāgena uppajjamānā diṭṭhiyo kathetvā vedanāmūlakaṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṃ kathesi. Tena idaṃ dasseti – “evamete diṭṭhigatikā, idaṃ dassanaṃ gahetvā tīsu bhavesu catūsu yonīsu pañcasu gatīsu sattasu viññāṇaṭṭhitīsu navasu sattāvāsesu ito ettha etto idhāti sandhāvantā saṃsarantā yante yuttagoṇo viya, thambhe upanibaddhakukkuro viya, vātena vippannaṭṭhanāvā viya ca vaṭṭadukkhameva anuparivattanti, vaṭṭadukkhato sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ na sakkontī”ti.

Here, 'birth' should be understood as the five aggregates together with their alterations. Birth is a condition for aging-and-death, as well as for sorrow and so on, by way of the category of decisive support. This is the summary here; for the detailed account, the discourse on dependent origination has been spoken of in the Visuddhimagga. Here, however, only its application should be understood. For the Blessed One, when giving a discourse on the round of existence, taught with ignorance as the head, saying: 'Bhikkhus, the prior limit of ignorance is not discerned... Yet it is discerned: “With this as condition, ignorance comes to be”' (AN 10.61); and similarly with craving for existence as the head (AN 10.62); and with the view of existence as the head. Here, however, teaching with views as the head, having spoken of the views that arise through lust for feeling, He taught the dependent origination that is rooted in feeling. By this, He shows the following: 'Thus these who are given to views, having grasped this doctrine, run on and transmigrate through the three kinds of existence, the four modes of generation, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings, from here to there, and from there to here. Like an ox yoked to a mill, like a dog tied to a post, or like a ship wrecked by the wind, they keep revolving only in the suffering of the round; they are unable to lift their heads out of the suffering of the round.'

Vivaṭṭakathādivaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on the Unraveling of the Round

145. Evaṃ diṭṭhigatikādhiṭṭhānaṃ vaṭṭaṃ kathetvā idāni yuttayogabhikkhuadhiṭṭhānaṃ katvā vivaṭṭaṃ dassento – “yato kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhū”tiādimāha. Tattha yatoti yadā. Channaṃ phassāyatanānanti [V 1.0108] yehi chahi phassāyatanehi phusitvā paṭisaṃvedayamānānaṃ diṭṭhigatikānaṃ vaṭṭaṃ vattati, tesaṃyeva channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ. Samudayantiādīsu avijjāsamudayā cakkhusamudayotiādinā vedanākammaṭṭhāne vuttanayena phassāyatanānaṃ samudayādayo veditabbā. Yathā pana tattha “phassasamudayā phassanirodhā”ti vuttaṃ, evamidha, taṃ cakkhādīsu – “āhārasamudayā āhāranirodhā”ti veditabbaṃ. Manāyatane “nāmarūpasamudayā nāmarūpanirodhā”ti.

145. Having thus explained the round of existence which is the basis for those with wrong views, now, making the basis the monk who is engaged in the practice and demonstrating that which is the opposite of the round, He spoke the passage beginning with: “When, O monks, a monk…” Therein, `yato` means `yadā` (when). As for `channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ` (of the six contact-bases): it refers to those very six contact-bases through which, for those with wrong views who experience by making contact, the round of existence proceeds. In the words beginning with `samudaya` (arising), the arising, etc., of the contact-bases should be known by the method explained in the meditation subject on feeling, beginning with “from the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of the eye.” However, just as it was said there, “from the arising of contact, there is the cessation of contact,” so here, in regard to the eye, etc., it should be known as “from the arising of nutriment, there is the cessation of nutriment.” In the case of the mind base, it should be known as “from the arising of name-and-form, there is the cessation of name-and-form.”

Uttaritaraṃ pajānātīti diṭṭhigatiko diṭṭhimeva jānāti. Ayaṃ pana diṭṭhiñca diṭṭhito ca uttaritaraṃ sīlasamādhipaññāvimuttinti [P 1.0127] yāva arahattā jānāti. Ko evaṃ jānātīti? Khīṇāsavo jānāti, anāgāmī, sakadāgāmī, sotāpanno, bahussuto, ganthadharo bhikkhu jānāti, āraddhavipassako jānāti. Desanā pana arahattanikūṭeneva niṭṭhāpitāti.

As for `uttaritaraṃ pajānāti` (he knows what is more excellent): a person with wrong views knows only the wrong view. But this monk knows both the wrong view and that which is more excellent than the wrong view—virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation—up to the fruit of Arahantship. Who knows thus? The one whose cankers are destroyed knows; the Non-returner, the Once-returner, and the Stream-enterer know; the monk of great learning who bears the scriptures knows; the one who has undertaken insight meditation knows. However, the discourse is concluded only with the pinnacle which is Arahantship.

146. Evaṃ [M 1.0117] vivaṭṭaṃ kathetvā idāni “desanājālavimutto diṭṭhigatiko nāma natthī”ti dassanatthaṃ puna – “ye hi keci, bhikkhave”ti ārabhi. Tattha antojālīkatāti imassa mayhaṃ desanājālassa antoyeva katā. Ettha sitā vāti etasmiṃ mama desanājāle sitā nissitā avasitāva. Ummujjamānā ummujjantīti kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Te adho osīdantāpi uddhaṃ uggacchantāpi mama desanājāle sitāva hutvā osīdanti ca uggacchanti ca. Ettha pariyāpannāti ettha mayhaṃ desanājāle pariyāpannā, etena ābaddhā antojālīkatā ca hutvā ummujjamānā ummujjanti, na hettha asaṅgahito diṭṭhigatiko nāma atthīti.

146. Having thus explained that which is the opposite of the round, now, for the purpose of showing that “there is no person with wrong views who is freed from the net of the discourse,” He began again with: “For whatever, O monks…” Therein, `antojālīkatā` (made to be inside the net) means they are made to be only inside this net of my discourse. As for `ettha sitā vā` (they are attached here), it means they are attached to, dependent on, and settled in this net of my discourse. As for `ummujjamānā ummujjanti` (emerging, they emerge), what is the meaning stated? Those persons, whether sinking down below or rising up above, being attached to the net of my discourse, both sink and rise. As for `ettha pariyāpannā` (they are included here), it means they are included in this net of my discourse. Being bound by this and made to be inside the net, when emerging, they emerge. Indeed, herein, there is no person with wrong views who is not gathered in.

Sukhumacchikenāti saṇhaacchikena sukhumacchiddenāti attho. Kevaṭṭo viya hi bhagavā, jālaṃ viya desanā, parittaudakaṃ viya dasasahassilokadhātu, oḷārikā pāṇā viya dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatikā. Tassa tīre ṭhatvā olokentassa oḷārikānaṃ pāṇānaṃ antojālīkatabhāvadassanaṃ viya bhagavato sabbadiṭṭhigatānaṃ desanājālassa antokatabhāvadassananti evamettha opammasaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

As for `sukhumacchikena` (with a fine-meshed net): it means with fine meshes, with fine holes. For the Blessed One is like a fisherman; the discourse, like a net; the ten-thousandfold world-system, like a small body of water; and the sixty-two persons with wrong views, like large aquatic creatures. Just as a fisherman standing on the shore and looking sees the large creatures made to be inside the net, so too the Blessed One sees all those with wrong views made to be inside the net of the discourse. Thus, herein, the connection of the simile should be known.

147. Evaṃ imāhi dvāsaṭṭhiyā diṭṭhīhi sabbadiṭṭhīnaṃ saṅgahitattā sabbesaṃ diṭṭhigatikānaṃ etasmiṃ desanājāle pariyāpannabhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni attano katthaci apariyāpannabhāvaṃ dassento – “ucchinnabhavanettiko, bhikkhave, tathāgatassa kāyo”tiādimāha. Tattha nayanti etāyāti netti. Nayantīti gīvāya bandhitvā ākaḍḍhanti, rajjuyā etaṃ nāmaṃ. Idha pana nettisadisatāya [P 1.0128][V 1.0109] bhavataṇhā nettīti adhippetā. Sā hi mahājanaṃ gīvāya bandhitvā taṃ taṃ bhavaṃ neti upanetīti bhavanetti. Arahattamaggasatthena ucchinnā bhavanetti assāti ucchinnabhavanettiko.

147. Thus, having shown that because all wrong views are gathered in by means of these sixty-two wrong views, all persons with wrong views are included in this net of the discourse, now, wishing to show His own state of not being included anywhere, He spoke the passage beginning with: “O monks, for the Tathāgata, the guide to existence is cut off…” Therein, `netti` means ‘that by which they lead.’ As for `nayanti` (they lead), it means they bind at the neck and drag; this is a name for a rope. Here, however, because of its similarity to a rope, craving for existence is intended by `netti`. Indeed, that craving, binding the great mass of beings at the neck, leads them and brings them near to this and that existence; therefore, it is called `bhavanetti` (the guide to existence). He is `ucchinnabhavanettiko` (one for whom the guide to existence is cut off) because for him the guide to existence has been cut by the sword of the Arahant path.

Kāyassa bhedā uddhanti kāyassa bhedato uddhaṃ. Jīvitapariyādānāti jīvitassa sabbaso pariyādinnattā parikkhīṇattā, puna appaṭisandhikabhāvāti attho. Na taṃ dakkhantīti taṃ tathāgataṃ. Devā vā manussā vā na dakkhissanti, apaṇṇattikabhāvaṃ gamissatīti attho.

As for kāyassa bhedā uddhaṃ: this means upward from the breakup of the body. As for jīvitapariyādānā: the meaning is because the life faculty has been completely taken up and exhausted, because of the state of there being no more rebirth-linking. As for na taṃ dakkhanti: this refers to the Tathāgata. Neither gods nor humans will see him; the meaning is that he will arrive at a state beyond designation.

Seyyathāpi[M 1.0118], bhikkhaveti, upamāyaṃ pana idaṃ saṃsandanaṃ. Ambarukkho viya hi tathāgatassa kāyo, rukkhe jātamahāvaṇṭo viya taṃ nissāya pubbe pavattataṇhā. Tasmiṃ vaṇṭe upanibaddhā pañcapakkadvādasapakkaaṭṭhārasapakkaparimāṇā ambapiṇḍī viya taṇhāya sati taṇhūpanibandhanā hutvā āyatiṃ nibbattanakā pañcakkhandhā dvādasāyatanāni aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo. Yathā pana tasmiṃ vaṇṭe chinne sabbāni tāni ambāni tadanvayāni honti, taṃyeva vaṇṭaṃ anugatāni, vaṇṭacchedā chinnāni yevāti attho; evameva ye bhavanettivaṇṭassa anupacchinnattā āyatiṃ uppajjeyyuṃ pañcakkhandhā dvādasāyatanāni aṭṭhārasadhātuyo, sabbe te dhammā tadanvayā honti bhavanettiṃ anugatā, tāya chinnāya chinnā yevāti attho.

Now, in the simile beginning with Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, this is the connection. The Tathāgata’s body is indeed like a mango tree; the craving that previously arose depending on him is like a great stalk that grew on the tree. Like a cluster of mangoes bound to that stalk, numbering five, twelve, or eighteen ripe fruits, so are the five aggregates, twelve sense bases, and eighteen elements which, when craving exists, being bound by craving, will come to be in the future. Now, just as when that stalk is cut, all those mangoes follow it, they go along with that very stalk—the meaning is, with the cutting of the stalk, they are indeed cut; so too, those five aggregates, twelve sense bases, and eighteen elements that would arise in the future because the stalk which is the guide to existence has not been cut—all those phenomena follow it, they go along with the guide to existence. When that is cut, they are indeed cut; this is the meaning.

Yathā pana tasmimpi rukkhe maṇḍūkakaṇṭakavisasamphassaṃ āgamma anupubbena sussitvā mate – “imasmiṃ ṭhāne evarūpo nāma rukkho ahosī”ti vohāramattameva hoti, na taṃ rukkhaṃ koci passati, evaṃ ariyamaggasamphassaṃ āgamma taṇhāsinehassa pariyādinnattā anupubbena sussitvā viya bhinne imasmiṃ kāye, kāyassa bhedā uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā na taṃ dakkhanti, tathāgatampi devamanussā na dakkhissanti, evarūpassa nāma kira satthuno idaṃ sāsananti vohāramattameva bhavissatīti anupādisesanibbānadhātuṃ pāpetvā desanaṃ niṭṭhapesi.

And just as, when that tree, on account of contact with the poison of a frog’s thorn, gradually dries up and dies—so that it becomes a mere matter of speech, ‘In this place, there was once such a tree,’ and no one sees that tree—so too, on account of contact with the Noble Path, with the sap of craving exhausted, when this body breaks up as if having gradually dried up, then after the breakup of the body, with the exhaustion of life, they will not see him. Gods and humans will not see the Tathāgata. It will become a mere matter of speech: ‘This, it seems, was the teaching of such a Teacher.’ Thus, having brought the discourse to the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining, he concluded it.

148. Evaṃ [P 1.0129] vutte āyasmā ānandoti evaṃ bhagavatā imasmiṃ sutte vutte thero ādito paṭṭhāya sabbaṃ suttaṃ samannāharitvā evaṃ buddhabalaṃ dīpetvā kathitasuttassa na bhagavatā nāmaṃ gahitaṃ, handassa nāmaṃ gaṇhāpessāmīti cintetvā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca.

148. As for Evaṃ vutte āyasmā Ānando: When this discourse had been spoken thus by the Blessed One, the Elder, having brought the entire discourse to mind from the beginning, and considering how the Buddha's power was thus demonstrated, thought: 'The Blessed One has not given a name to this discourse that has been taught. Well then, I shall have a name given to it.' Having thought thus, he said this to the Blessed One.

Tasmātiha tvantiādīsu ayamatthayojanā – ānanda, yasmā imasmiṃ dhammapariyāye idhatthopi paratthopi vibhatto, tasmātiha tvaṃ imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ “atthajāla”ntipi naṃ dhārehi; yasmā panettha bahū tantidhammā kathitā, tasmā “dhammajāla”ntipi naṃ dhārehi; yasmā ca ettha seṭṭhaṭṭhena [V 1.0110] brahmaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ vibhattaṃ, tasmā “brahmajāla”ntipi naṃ dhārehi; yasmā ettha dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhiyo vibhattā, tasmā “diṭṭhijāla”ntipi naṃ dhārehi; yasmā pana imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ sutvā devaputtamārampi khandhamārampi maccumārampi kilesamārampi [M 1.0119] sakkā maddituṃ, tasmā “anuttaro saṅgāmavijayotipi naṃ dhārehī”ti.

In the passage beginning Tasmātiha tvaṃ, this is the application of the meaning: Ānanda, because in this exposition of the Dhamma both the benefit in this life and the benefit in the next life have been analyzed in detail, therefore you should bear in mind this exposition of the Dhamma as the 'Net of Benefits.' Because many scriptural teachings have been taught herein, therefore you should bear it in mind as the 'Net of the Dhamma.' And because herein the supreme knowledge of omniscience has been analyzed in detail in the sense of 'supreme' (brahma), therefore you should bear it in mind as the 'Supreme Net.' Because the sixty-two views have been analyzed in detail herein, therefore you should bear it in mind as the 'Net of Views.' Furthermore, because by hearing this exposition of the Dhamma it is possible to crush Māra the son of a deva, Māra as the aggregates, Māra as death, Māra as the defilements, and Māra as volitional formations, therefore you should bear it in mind as the 'Unsurpassed Victory in Battle.'

Idamavoca bhagavāti idaṃ nidānāvasānato pabhuti yāva “anuttaro saṅgāmavijayotipi naṃ dhārehī”ti sakalaṃ suttantaṃ bhagavā paresaṃ paññāya alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhaṃ paramagambhīraṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pakāsento sūriyo viya andhakāraṃ diṭṭhigatamahandhakāraṃ vidhamanto avoca.

As for Idamavoca bhagavā: The Blessed One spoke this entire discourse—from the end of the introduction up to '...bear it in mind as the Unsurpassed Victory in Battle'—revealing the supremely profound knowledge of omniscience, which has a foundation unattainable by the wisdom of others, and dispelling the great darkness of wrong views just as the sun dispels darkness.

149. Attamanā te bhikkhūti te bhikkhū attamanā sakamanā, buddhagatāya pītiyā udaggacittā hutvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhagavato bhāsitanti evaṃ vicitranayadesanāvilāsayuttaṃ idaṃ suttaṃ karavīkarutamañjunā kaṇṇasukhena paṇḍitajanahadayānaṃ amatābhisekasadisena brahmassarena bhāsamānassa bhagavato vacanaṃ. Abhinandunti anumodiṃsu ceva sampaṭicchiṃsu ca. Ayañhi abhinandasaddo – “abhinandati abhivadatī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.5) taṇhāyampi āgato. “Annamevābhinandanti, ubhaye devamānusā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.43) upagamanepi.

149. As for Attamanā te bhikkhū: those monks were delighted, pleased in their own minds, having become uplifted in mind with joy directed towards the Buddha. Thus it is said. As for Bhagavato bhāsitaṃ: this is the utterance of the Blessed One, who spoke this discourse—which is endowed with the grace of a teaching of various methods—with a voice like Brahmā's, a voice lovely like the call of the karavīka bird, pleasant to the ear, and like an anointing with ambrosia for the hearts of the wise. As for Abhinanduṃ: they both repeatedly rejoiced and accepted it. Indeed, this word abhinandati also occurs in the sense of craving, as in passages such as 'one rejoices, one speaks in praise of.' It also occurs in the sense of approaching, as in passages such as 'Both gods and humans approach food.'

“Cirappavāsiṃ [P 1.0130] purisaṃ, dūrato sotthimāgataṃ;

Ñātimittā suhajjā ca, abhinandanti āgata”nti. (dha. pa. 219);

A man long absent, come safely from afar; his kinsmen, friends, and well-wishers welcome him on his arrival.

Ādīsu sampaṭicchanepi. “Abhinanditvā anumoditvā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.205) anumodanepi. Svāyamidha anumodanasampaṭicchanesu yujjati. Tena vuttaṃ – “abhinandunti anumodiṃsu ceva sampaṭicchiṃsu cā”ti.

In such passages, it is also used in the sense of accepting. In passages such as 'having rejoiced, having approved,' it is also used in the sense of repeatedly rejoicing. Here, this word is suitable in the meanings of repeatedly rejoicing and accepting. Therefore I have said: 'abhinanduṃ means they both repeatedly rejoiced and accepted it.'

Subhāsitaṃ sulapitaṃ, “sādhu sādhū”ti tādino;

Anumodamānā sirasā, sampaṭicchiṃsu bhikkhavoti.

The monks, repeatedly rejoicing in what was well-spoken and well-uttered by the Such-One, saying 'Excellent! Excellent!', accepted it with bowed heads.

Imasmiñca pana veyyākaraṇasminti imasmiṃ niggāthakasutte. Niggāthakattā hi idaṃ veyyākaraṇanti vuttaṃ.

As for Imasmiñca pana veyyākaraṇasmiṃ: this means in this discourse without verses. For because it is without verses, it was called an 'exposition' by the compilers of the canon.

Dasasahassī [V 1.0111] lokadhātūti dasasahassacakkavāḷaparimāṇā lokadhātu. Akampitthāti na suttapariyosāneyeva akampitthāti veditabbā. Bhaññamāneti hi vuttaṃ. Tasmā dvāsaṭṭhiyā diṭṭhigatesu viniveṭhetvā desiyamānesu [M 1.0120] tassa tassa diṭṭhigatassa pariyosāne pariyosāneti dvāsaṭṭhiyā ṭhānesu akampitthāti veditabbā.

As for dasasahassī lokadhātu: this means the world-system the size of ten thousand universes. As for akampittha: it should not be understood that it quaked only at the very end of the discourse. For it was said, 'while it was being spoken.' Therefore, it should be understood that it quaked in sixty-two instances: at the very end of the explanation of each and every wrong view, as the sixty-two wrong views were being taught and disentangled.

Tattha aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi pathavīkampo veditabbo – dhātukkhobhena, iddhimato ānubhāvena, bodhisattassa gabbhokkantiyā, mātukucchito nikkhamanena, sambodhippattiyā, dhammacakkappavattanena, āyusaṅkhārossajjanena, parinibbānenāti. Tesaṃ vinicchayaṃ – “aṭṭha kho ime, ānanda, hetū aṭṭha paccayā mahato bhūmicālassa pātubhāvāyā”ti evaṃ mahāparinibbāne āgatāya tantiyā vaṇṇanākāle vakkhāma. Ayaṃ pana mahāpathavī aparesupi aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu akampittha – mahābhinikkhamane, bodhimaṇḍūpasaṅkamane, paṃsukūlaggahaṇe, paṃsukūladhovane, kāḷakārāmasutte, gotamakasutte, vessantarajātake, imasmiṃ brahmajāleti. Tattha mahābhinikkhamanabodhimaṇḍūpasaṅkamanesu vīriyabalena akampittha. Paṃsukūlaggahaṇe [P 1.0131] dvisahassadīpaparivāre cattāro mahādīpe pahāya pabbajitvā susānaṃ gantvā paṃsukūlaṃ gaṇhantena dukkaraṃ bhagavatā katanti acchariyavegābhihatā akampittha. Paṃsukūladhovanavessantarajātakesu akālakampanena akampittha. Kāḷakārāmagotamakasuttesu – “ahaṃ sakkhī bhagavā”ti sakkhibhāvena akampittha. Imasmiṃ pana brahmajāle dvāsaṭṭhiyā diṭṭhigatesu vijaṭetvā niggumbaṃ katvā desiyamānesu sādhukāradānavasena akampitthāti veditabbā.

In this context, an earthquake is to be understood as occurring for eight reasons: due to a disturbance of the elements; by the power of one possessing psychic potency; at the Bodhisatta's conception; at his emergence from his mother's womb; at his attainment of full enlightenment; at the setting in motion of the Wheel of the Dhamma; at the relinquishing of the life-formation; and at his final Nibbāna. We will explain the analysis of these—as stated in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, 'Ānanda, there are these eight causes, these eight conditions for the manifestation of a great earthquake'—when we comment on that passage. However, this great earth also quaked on eight other occasions: at the Great Renunciation; when approaching the seat of enlightenment; when taking up the rag-robe; when washing the rag-robe; during the Kāḷakārāma Sutta; during the Gotamaka Sutta; during the Vessantara Jātaka; and during this Brahmajāla Sutta. Among these, at the Great Renunciation and when approaching the seat of enlightenment, it quaked by the power of his energy. When he was taking up the rag-robe—having gone forth, renouncing the four great continents with their two thousand surrounding islands, and having gone to a charnel ground to take up a rag-robe—it quaked, struck by the force of astonishment, thinking, 'A difficult deed has been done by the Blessed One!' During the washing of the rag-robe and the Vessantara Jātaka, it quaked with an untimely quaking. During the Kāḷakārāma and Gotamaka Suttas, it quaked in its capacity as a witness, as if to say, 'I am your witness, Blessed One!' And in this Brahmajāla Sutta, it should be understood that it quaked by way of giving cries of 'Excellent!' as the sixty-two wrong views were being taught, having been unraveled and made free of tangles.

Na kevalañca etesu ṭhānesuyeva pathavī akampittha, atha kho tīsu saṅgahesupi mahāmahindattherassa imaṃ dīpaṃ āgantvā jotivane nisīditvā dhammaṃ desitadivasepi akampittha. Kalyāṇiyavihāre ca piṇḍapātiyattherassa cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ sammajjitvā tattheva nisīditvā buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ gahetvā imaṃ suttantaṃ āraddhassa suttapariyosāne udakapariyantaṃ katvā akampittha. Lohapāsādassa pācīnaambalaṭṭhikaṭṭhānaṃ nāma ahosi. Tattha nisīditvā dīghabhāṇakattherā brahmajālasuttaṃ ārabhiṃsu, tesaṃ sajjhāyapariyosānepi udakapariyantameva katvā pathavī akampitthāti.

And not only in these places did the earth shake, but indeed it also shook at the three Councils, and on the day when the great elder Mahinda, having come to this island and sat in Jotivana, taught the Dhamma. And at Kalyāṇiya monastery, when the Elder Piṇḍapātiya, having swept the cetiya courtyard and sat right there, took up joy with the Buddha as its object, at the conclusion of this sutta which he had begun, the earth shook down to its water-boundary. There was a place called the Eastern Ambalaṭṭhika of the Lohapāsāda. Sitting there, the elders who were reciters of the Dīgha Nikāya began the Brahmajāla Sutta; at the end of their recitation too, the earth shook down to its very water-boundary.

Evaṃ [M 1.0121] yassānubhāvena, akampittha anekaso;

Medanī suttaseṭṭhassa, desitassa sayambhunā.

Thus, by the power of this excellent sutta taught by the Self-become One, the earth shook many times.

Brahmajālassa [V 1.0112] tassīdha, dhammaṃ atthañca paṇḍitā;

Sakkaccaṃ uggahetvāna, paṭipajjantu yonisoti.

Here, may the wise, having respectfully learned the text and the meaning of that Brahmajāla, practice with wise attention.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Thus in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya,

Brahmajālasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Brahmajāla Sutta is concluded.

2. Sāmaññaphalasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Exposition of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta

Rājāmaccakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Discourse concerning the King and his Ministers

150. Evaṃ [P 1.0132][V 1.0113][M 1.0122] me sutaṃ…pe… rājagaheti sāmaññaphalasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ apubbapadavaṇṇanā – rājagaheti evaṃnāmake nagare. Tañhi mandhātumahāgovindādīhi pariggahitattā rājagahanti vuccati. Aññepi ettha pakāre vaṇṇayanti, kiṃ tehi? Nāmamattametaṃ tassa nagarassa. Taṃ panetaṃ buddhakāle ca cakkavattikāle ca nagaraṃ hoti, sesakāle suññaṃ hoti yakkhapariggahitaṃ, tesaṃ vasanavanaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati. Viharatīti avisesena iriyāpathadibbabrahmaariyavihāresu aññataravihārasamaṅgiparidīpanametaṃ. Idha pana ṭhānagamananisajjasayanappabhedesu iriyāpathesu aññatarairiyāpathasamāyogaparidīpanaṃ. Tena ṭhitopi gacchantopi nisinnopi sayānopi bhagavā viharati ceva veditabbo. So hi ekaṃ iriyāpathabādhanaṃ aññena iriyāpathena vicchinditvā aparipatantaṃ attabhāvaṃ harati pavatteti, tasmā viharatīti vuccati.

150. “Thus have I heard… at Rājagaha”—this is the Sāmaññaphala Sutta. Therein, this is the exposition of the initial words. “At Rājagaha” means in the city of that name. Indeed, it is called Rājagaha because it was occupied by Mandhātu, Mahāgovinda, and others. Others also explain it in various ways, but what is the use of those? This is merely the name of that city. Now, this becomes a city in the time of a Buddha and in the time of a Wheel-turning Monarch; at other times it is empty. Having become occupied by yakkhas, it stands as their dwelling-forest. “He was dwelling” (viharati), without distinction, indicates being endowed with one of the abidings among the postures, the divine abiding, the brahma-abiding, and the noble abiding. Here, however, it indicates engagement in one of the postures, which are divided into standing, going, sitting, and lying down. Therefore, it should be understood that the Blessed One “dwells” whether he is standing, going, sitting, or lying down. For he, having cut off the affliction of one posture with another posture, carries on and maintains his being, which does not perish. Therefore, it is said, “he dwells”.

Jīvakassa komārabhaccassa ambavaneti idamassa yaṃ gocaragāmaṃ upanissāya viharati, tassa samīpanivāsanaṭṭhānaparidīpanaṃ. Tasmā – rājagahe viharati jīvakassa komārabhaccassa ambavaneti rājagahasamīpe jīvakassa komārabhaccassa ambavane viharatīti evamettha attho veditabbo. Samīpatthe hetaṃ bhummavacanaṃ. Tattha [P 1.0133] jīvatīti jīvako, kumārena bhatoti komārabhacco. Yathāha – “kiṃ bhaṇe, etaṃ kākehi samparikiṇṇanti? Dārako devāti. Jīvati bhaṇeti? Jīvati, devāti. Tena hi, bhaṇe taṃ dārakaṃ amhākaṃ antepuraṃ netvā dhātīnaṃ detha posetunti. Tassa jīvatīti jīvakoti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Kumārena posāpitoti komārabhaccoti nāmaṃ akaṃsū”ti (mahāva. 328) ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārena pana jīvakavatthukhandhake āgatameva. Vinicchayakathāpissa samantapāsādikāya vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttā.

“In Jīvaka Komārabhacca’s mango grove”—this phrase indicates the nearby dwelling place relative to the alms-resort village which he depends upon while dwelling. Therefore, in the passage “he dwells at Rājagaha, in Jīvaka Komārabhacca’s mango grove,” the meaning should be understood thus: “he dwells in the mango grove of Jīvaka Komārabhacca, near Rājagaha.” For this is a locative expression in the sense of proximity. Therein, because “he lives” (jīvati), he is called Jīvaka; because “he was nourished by the prince” (kumārena bhato), he is called Komārabhacca. As it is said: “Sirs, what is this, swarmed over by crows?” “It is a child, your highness.” “Sirs, does he live?” “He lives, your highness.” “Well then, sirs, take that child to our inner palace and give him to the nurses to be raised.” Because of the question “Does he live?” (jīvati), they gave him the name Jīvaka. Because he was caused to be raised by the prince, they gave him the name Komārabhacca. This here is the summary. But the story of Jīvaka has come down in detail in the Khandhaka. The judicial account of him has also been stated by me in the Samantapāsādikā, the Vinaya commentary.

Ayaṃ [V 1.0114][M 1.0123] pana jīvako ekasmiṃ samaye bhagavato dosābhisannaṃ kāyaṃ virecetvā siveyyakaṃ dussayugaṃ datvā vatthānumodanāpariyosāne sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya cintesi – “mayā divasassa dvattikkhattuṃ buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ gantabbaṃ, idañca veḷuvanaṃ atidūre, mayhaṃ pana ambavanaṃ uyyānaṃ āsannataraṃ, yaṃnūnāhaṃ ettha bhagavato vihāraṃ kāreyya”nti. So tasmiṃ ambavane rattiṭṭhānadivāṭhānaleṇakuṭimaṇḍapādīni sampādetvā bhagavato anucchavikaṃ gandhakuṭiṃ kārāpetvā ambavanaṃ aṭṭhārasahatthubbedhena tambapaṭṭavaṇṇena pākārena parikkhipāpetvā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sacīvarabhattena santappetvā dakkhiṇodakaṃ pātetvā vihāraṃ niyyātesi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “jīvakassa komārabhaccassa ambavane”ti.

Now this Jīvaka, on one occasion, having administered a purge to the Blessed One’s body, which was afflicted by an imbalance of the humors, and having given a pair of Siveyyaka cloths, became established in the fruit of stream-entry at the conclusion of the thanksgiving for the cloths. He thought: “I should go to attend upon the Buddha two or three times a day, but this Veḷuvana is very far. My mango grove park, however, is much nearer. What if I were to have a dwelling for the Blessed One built here?” So, in that mango grove, having prepared buildings such as night-quarters, day-quarters, caves, huts, and pavilions, and having had a suitable fragrant chamber built for the Blessed One, and having had the mango grove enclosed with a wall eighteen cubits high, the color of a copper sheet, he satisfied the community of monks with the Buddha at its head with food together with robes, and letting fall the water of dedication, he dedicated the monastery. It was said referring to this: “in Jīvaka Komārabhacca’s mango grove.”

Aḍḍhateḷasehi bhikkhusatehīti aḍḍhasatena ūnehi terasahi bhikkhusatehi. Rājātiādīsu rājati attano issariyasampattiyā catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi mahājanaṃ rañjeti vaḍḍhetīti rājā. Magadhānaṃ issaroti māgadho. Ajātoyeva rañño sattu bhavissatīti nemittakehi niddiṭṭhoti ajātasattu.

“With twelve hundred and fifty monks” (aḍḍhateḷasehi bhikkhusatehi) means with thirteen hundred monks less half a hundred. In the case of “rājā” (king) and so on: because he shines (rājati) by his own sovereign accomplishment, he is called “rājā.” Or, because he delights (rañjeti) and causes the great populace to prosper with the four bases of sympathy, he is called “rājā.” Because he is the lord of the Magadhans, he is called “Māgadho.” Because he was pointed out by soothsayers with the words, “While yet unborn (ajāto), he will be an enemy (sattu) to the king,” he is called “Ajātasattu.”

Tasmiṃ kira kucchigate deviyā evarūpo dohaḷo uppajji – “aho [P 1.0134] vatāhaṃ rañño dakkhiṇabāhulohitaṃ piveyya”nti, sā “bhāriye ṭhāne dohaḷo uppanno, na sakkā kassaci ārocetu”nti taṃ kathetuṃ asakkontī kisā dubbaṇṇā ahosi. Taṃ rājā pucchi – “bhadde, tuyhaṃ attabhāvo na pakativaṇṇo, kiṃ kāraṇa”nti? “Mā puccha, mahārājāti”. “Bhadde, tvaṃ attano ajjhāsayaṃ mayhaṃ akathentī kassa kathessasī”ti tathā tathā nibandhitvā kathāpesi. Sutvā ca – “bāle, kiṃ ettha tuyhaṃ bhāriyasaññā ahosī”ti vejjaṃ pakkosāpetvā suvaṇṇasatthakena bāhuṃ phālāpetvā suvaṇṇasarakena lohitaṃ gahetvā udakena sambhinditvā pāyesi. Nemittakā taṃ sutvā – “esa gabbho rañño sattu bhavissati, iminā rājā haññissatī”ti byākariṃsu. Devī sutvā – “mayhaṃ kira kucchito nikkhanto rājānaṃ māressatī”ti gabbhaṃ pātetukāmā uyyānaṃ gantvā kucchiṃ maddāpesi, gabbho na patati. Sā punappunaṃ gantvā tatheva kāresi. Rājā kimatthaṃ ayaṃ [M 1.0124] abhiṇhaṃ uyyānaṃ gacchatīti parivīmaṃsanto taṃ kāraṇaṃ sutvā – “bhadde, tava kucchiyaṃ puttoti vā dhītāti vā na paññāyati, attano nibbattadārakaṃ evamakāsīti mahā aguṇarāsipi no jambudīpatale āvibhavissati, mā tvaṃ evaṃ karohī”ti nivāretvā ārakkhaṃ adāsi. Sā gabbhavuṭṭhānakāle “māressāmī”ti cintesi. Tadāpi ārakkhamanussā dārakaṃ apanayiṃsu. Athāparena samayena vuḍḍhippattaṃ [V 1.0115] kumāraṃ deviyā dassesuṃ. Sā taṃ disvāva puttasinehaṃ uppādesi, tena naṃ māretuṃ nāsakkhi. Rājāpi anukkamena puttassa oparajjamadāsi.

It is said that when he was in the womb, such a craving arose in the queen: 'Oh, it would be wonderful if I could drink the blood from the king's right arm!' She, thinking, 'A craving has arisen in me concerning a weighty matter; it is not possible to tell anyone,' and being unable to speak of it, became thin and of poor complexion. The king asked her, 'My dear, your physical appearance is not its natural color. What is the reason?' 'Do not ask, great king.' 'My dear, if you do not tell me your inclination, to whom will you tell it?' Thus, pressing her in various ways, he made her speak. And having heard, he said, 'Foolish one, did you perceive this as a weighty matter?' Summoning a physician, he had his arm lanced with a small golden knife, and having collected the blood in a small golden cup and mixed it with water, he had her drink it. The soothsayers, having heard of this, declared: 'This fetus will be the king's enemy; by him the king will be killed.' The queen, having heard this, thought, 'It is said that the one who comes forth from my womb will kill the king,' and desiring to cause an abortion, she went to the park and had her belly pressed, but the fetus did not fall. She went again and again and had the same thing done. The king, investigating why she went to the park so frequently, heard the reason and said: 'My dear, it is not yet apparent whether it is a son or a daughter in your womb. If you do this to the child born of you, a great mass of fault will become manifest for us on the surface of Jambudīpa. Do not do this.' Having forbidden her, he provided a guard. At the time of birth, she thought, 'I will kill him.' At that time also, the guardsmen removed the child. Then, at a later time, they showed the prince, who had reached maturity, to the queen. Upon seeing him, motherly affection arose in her; therefore, she was not able to kill him. The king also, in due course, gave his son the position of viceroy.

Athekasmiṃ [P 1.0135] samaye devadatto rahogato cintesi – “sāriputtassa parisā mahāmoggallānassa parisā mahākassapassa parisāti, evamime visuṃ visuṃ dhurā, ahampi ekaṃ dhuraṃ nīharāmī”ti. So “na sakkā vinā lābhena parisaṃ uppādetuṃ, handāhaṃ lābhaṃ nibbattemī”ti cintetvā khandhake āgatanayena ajātasattuṃ kumāraṃ iddhipāṭihāriyena pasādetvā sāyaṃ pātaṃ pañcahi rathasatehi upaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchantaṃ ativissatthaṃ ñatvā ekadivasaṃ upasaṅkamitvā etadavoca – “pubbe kho, kumāra, manussā dīghāyukā, etarahi appāyukā, tena hi tvaṃ kumāra, pitaraṃ hantvā rājā hohi, ahaṃ bhagavantaṃ hantvā buddho bhavissāmī”ti kumāraṃ pituvadhe uyyojeti.

Then at a certain time, Devadatta, having gone into seclusion, reflected: 'Sāriputta has a following, Mahāmoggallāna has a following, Mahākassapa has a following; thus, these are each leaders in their own right. I too shall take up a leading role.' He reflected, 'It is not possible to create a following without gain; come now, I shall produce gain.' Having reflected thus, according to the method described in the Khandhaka, he impressed Prince Ajātasattu with a display of psychic power. Knowing that the prince, who came to attend upon him in the evening and the morning with five hundred chariots, had become very familiar, he approached him one day and said this: 'Formerly, Prince, humans were long-lived; nowadays, humans are short-lived. Therefore, Prince, you should kill your father and become king. I shall kill the Blessed One and become a Buddha.' Thus he incited the prince to patricide.

So – “ayyo devadatto mahānubhāvo, etassa aviditaṃ nāma natthī”ti ūruyā potthaniyaṃ bandhitvā divā divassa bhīto ubbiggo ussaṅkī utrasto antepuraṃ pavisitvā vuttappakāraṃ vippakāraṃ akāsi. Atha naṃ amaccā gahetvā anuyuñjitvā – “kumāro ca hantabbo, devadatto ca, sabbe ca bhikkhū hantabbā”ti sammantayitvā rañño āṇāvasena karissāmāti rañño ārocesuṃ.

He, thinking, 'The Venerable Devadatta is of great power; there is nothing unknown to him,' bound a small dagger to his thigh. In broad daylight, being frightened, agitated, apprehensive, and terrified, he entered the inner palace and committed the treacherous act as spoken of. Then, the ministers, having seized and interrogated him, consulted together, saying, 'The prince should be killed, Devadatta should be killed, and all the monks should be killed.' Thinking, 'We shall act by the power of the king's command,' they reported to the king.

Rājā ye amaccā māretukāmā ahesuṃ, tesaṃ ṭhānantarāni acchinditvā, ye na māretukāmā, te uccesu ṭhānesu ṭhapetvā kumāraṃ pucchi – “kissa pana tvaṃ, kumāra, maṃ māretukāmosī”ti? “Rajjenamhi, deva, atthiko”ti. Rājā tassa rajjaṃ adāsi.

The king, having removed from their posts those ministers who were desirous of executing them, and having established in high positions those who were not desirous of executing them, asked the prince: 'But for what reason, Prince, were you desirous of killing me?' 'Your Majesty, I have need of the kingdom.' The king gave him the kingdom.

So [M 1.0125] mayhaṃ manoratho nipphannoti devadattassa ārocesi. Tato naṃ so āha – “tvaṃ siṅgālaṃ antokatvā bheripariyonaddhapuriso [P 1.0136] viya sukiccakārimhīti maññasi, katipāheneva te pitā tayā kataṃ avamānaṃ cintetvā sayameva rājā bhavissatī”ti. Atha, bhante, kiṃ karomīti? Mūlaghaccaṃ ghātehīti. Nanu, bhante, mayhaṃ pitā na satthavajjhoti? Āhārupacchedena naṃ mārehīti. So pitaraṃ tāpanagehe pakkhipāpesi, tāpanagehaṃ nāma kammakaraṇatthāya kataṃ dhūmagharaṃ. “Mama mātaraṃ ṭhapetvā aññassa daṭṭhuṃ mā dethā”ti āha. Devī suvaṇṇasarake bhattaṃ pakkhipitvā ucchaṅgenādāya pavisati. Rājā taṃ bhuñjitvā yāpeti. So – “mayhaṃ pitā kathaṃ yāpetī”ti pucchitvā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā – “mayhaṃ mātu ucchaṅgaṃ katvā [V 1.0116] pavisituṃ mā dethā”ti āha. Tato paṭṭhāya devī moḷiyaṃ pakkhipitvā pavisati. Tampi sutvā “moḷiṃ bandhitvā pavisituṃ mā dethā”ti. Tato suvaṇṇapādukāsu bhattaṃ ṭhapetvā pidahitvā pādukā āruyha pavisati. Rājā tena yāpeti. Puna “kathaṃ yāpetī”ti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā “pādukā āruyha pavisitumpi mā dethā”ti āha. Tato paṭṭhāya devī gandhodakena nhāyitvā sarīraṃ catumadhurena makkhetvā pārupitvā pavisati. Rājā tassā sarīraṃ lehitvā yāpeti. Puna pucchitvā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā “ito paṭṭhāya mayhaṃ mātu pavesanaṃ nivārethā”ti āha. Devī dvāramūle ṭhatvā “sāmi, bimbisāra, etaṃ daharakāle māretuṃ na adāsi, attano sattuṃ attanāva posesi, idaṃ pana dāni te pacchimadassanaṃ, nāhaṃ ito paṭṭhāya tumhe passituṃ labhāmi, sace mayhaṃ doso atthi, khamatha devā”ti roditvā kanditvā nivatti.

He informed Devadatta, 'My wish has been fulfilled.' Then Devadatta said to him: 'Do you think, "I have done a good deed," like a man who has stretched a drum with a jackal inside? In just a few days, your father, reflecting on the disrespect you have shown, will himself become king.' 'Then, venerable sir, what should I do?' 'Kill him, destroying him root and all.' 'But, venerable sir, is my father not one who should not be slain by a weapon?' 'Kill him by cutting off his food supply.' So he had his father put in a heating-house; a heating-house is a smoke-house built for the purpose of inflicting punishment. He said, 'Except for my mother, do not allow anyone else to see him.' The queen would put food in a golden bowl, carry it in her lap, and enter. The king ate it and sustained himself. He asked, 'How does my father sustain himself?' and upon hearing the account, he said, 'Do not allow my mother to enter carrying anything in her lap.' From then on, the queen would put the food in her top-knot and enter. Hearing of that too, he said, 'Do not allow her to enter with her hair tied in a top-knot.' Then she placed the food in golden slippers, covered them, and entered wearing the slippers. The king sustained himself with that. Again he asked, 'How does he sustain himself?' and upon hearing the matter, he said, 'Do not allow her to enter even wearing slippers.' From then on, the queen would bathe with scented water, anoint her body with the four sweets, cover herself, and enter. The king would lick her body and sustain himself. Again he asked, and upon hearing the account, he said, 'From this day forward, prevent my mother's entry.' The queen stood at the doorway and said, 'My lord, Bimbisāra, you did not allow this one to be killed when he was a child; you yourself have nourished your own enemy. Now this is the last sight of you. From this day forward, I shall not be able to see you. If there is any fault in me, please forgive me, my lord.' Weeping and wailing, she turned back.

Tato [P 1.0137] paṭṭhāya rañño āhāro natthi. Rājā maggaphalasukhena caṅkamena yāpeti. Ativiya assa attabhāvo virocati. So – “kathaṃ, me bhaṇe, pitā yāpetī”ti pucchitvā “caṅkamena, deva, yāpeti; ativiya cassa attabhāvo virocatī”ti sutvā ‘caṅkamaṃ dānissa hāressāmī’ti cintetvā – “mayhaṃ pitu pāde khurena phāletvā loṇatelena makkhetvā khadiraṅgārehi vītaccitehi pacathā”ti nhāpite pesesi. Rājā te disvā – “nūna mayhaṃ putto kenaci saññatto bhavissati, ime mama massukaraṇatthāyāgatā”ti [M 1.0126] cintesi. Te gantvā vanditvā aṭṭhaṃsu. ‘Kasmā āgatatthā’ti ca puṭṭhā taṃ sāsanaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Tumhākaṃ rañño manaṃ karothā”ti ca vuttā ‘nisīda, devā’ti vatvā ca rājānaṃ vanditvā – “deva, mayaṃ rañño āṇaṃ karoma, mā amhākaṃ kujjhittha, nayidaṃ tumhādisānaṃ dhammarājūnaṃ anucchavika”nti vatvā vāmahatthena gopphake gahetvā dakkhiṇahatthena khuraṃ gahetvā pādatalāni phāletvā loṇatelena makkhetvā khadiraṅgārehi vītaccitehi paciṃsu. Rājā kira pubbe cetiyaṅgaṇe saupāhano agamāsi, nisajjanatthāya paññattakaṭasārakañca adhotehi pādehi akkami, tassāyaṃ nissandoti vadanti. Rañño balavavedanā uppannā. So – “aho buddho, aho dhammo, aho saṅgho”ti anussarantoyeva cetiyaṅgaṇe khittamālā viya milāyitvā cātumahārājikadevaloke vessavaṇassa paricārako janavasabho nāma yakkho hutvā nibbatti.

From that time onward, the king had no food. The king sustained himself by walking with the bliss of the path and its fruition. His person became exceedingly radiant. He asked, 'My good men, how does my father sustain himself?' and upon hearing, 'He sustains himself by walking, lord, and his person is exceedingly radiant,' he thought, 'Now I will take away his walking.' He sent barbers with the order: 'Split my father’s feet with a razor, smear them with salt and oil, and roast them over flameless acacia embers.' Seeing them, the king thought, 'Surely my son has been persuaded by someone; these men must have come to tend to my beard.' They approached, paid homage, and stood there. When asked, 'Why have you come?' they delivered the message. And when they were told, 'Do your king's will,' they said, 'Be seated, lord.' Then, paying homage to the king, they said, 'Lord, we are carrying out the king’s command. Do not be angry with us; this is not befitting for righteous kings such as yourself.' Then, holding his ankles with their left hand and taking a razor in their right, they split the soles of his feet, smeared them with salt and oil, and roasted them over flameless acacia embers. It is said that in the past, the king had walked in the courtyard of the cetiya wearing shoes, and had stepped with unwashed feet on a mat spread for sitting. This, they say, was the result of that. Intense pain arose in the king. Continuously recollecting, 'Oh, the Buddha! Oh, the Dhamma! Oh, the Sangha!' he withered like a garland cast aside in the cetiya courtyard and was reborn as a yakkha named Janavasabha, an attendant of Vessavaṇa in the Cātumahārājika deva world.

Taṃ divasameva ajātasattussa putto jāto, puttassa jātabhāvañca pitumatabhāvañca nivedetuṃ dve lekhā ekakkhaṇeyeva āgatā. Amaccā – “paṭhamaṃ puttassa jātabhāvaṃ ārocessāmā”ti taṃ lekhaṃ rañño hatthe ṭhapesuṃ. Rañño taṅkhaṇeyeva puttasineho uppajjitvā sakalasarīraṃ [P 1.0138][V 1.0117] khobhetvā aṭṭhimiñjaṃ āhacca aṭṭhāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe pituguṇamaññāsi – “mayi jātepi mayhaṃ pitu evameva sineho uppanno”ti. So – “gacchatha, bhaṇe, mayhaṃ pitaraṃ vissajjethā”ti āha. “Kiṃ vissajjāpetha, devā”ti itaraṃ lekhaṃ hatthe ṭhapayiṃsu.

On that very day, a son was born to Ajātasattu, and two letters arrived at the very same moment to announce the birth of his son and the death of his father. The ministers decided, 'First, we shall announce the birth of his son,' and placed that letter in the king's hand. At that very moment, paternal love arose in the king, pervaded his entire body, and striking to the very marrow of his bones, it became established. In that moment, he understood his father's goodness, thinking, 'When I was born, this same love must have arisen in my father.' He said, 'Go, my good men, release my father.' 'Why would you have him released, lord?' they asked, placing the other letter in his hand.

So taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā rodamāno mātusamīpaṃ gantvā – “ahosi nu, kho, amma, mayhaṃ pitu mayi jāte sineho”ti? Sā āha – “bālaputta, kiṃ vadesi, tava daharakāle aṅguliyā pīḷakā uṭṭhahi. Atha taṃ rodamānaṃ saññāpetuṃ asakkontā taṃ gahetvā vinicchayaṭṭhāne nisinnassa tava pitu santikaṃ agamaṃsu. Pitā te aṅguliṃ mukhe ṭhapesi. Pīḷakā mukheyeva bhijji. Atha kho pitā tava sinehena taṃ lohitamissakaṃ pubbaṃ aniṭṭhubhitvāva ajjhohari. Evarūpo te pitu sineho”ti. So roditvā paridevitvā pitu sarīrakiccaṃ akāsi.

Hearing that account, he went weeping to his mother and asked, 'Mother, was there truly love in my father for me when I was born?' She replied, 'Foolish son, what are you saying? When you were a child, a boil arose on your finger. Then, unable to soothe you as you were crying, they took you to your father, who was sitting in the place of judgment. Your father placed your finger in his mouth. The boil burst right there in his mouth. Then, out of love for you, your father swallowed that pus mixed with blood without spitting it out. Such was your father's love for you.' Weeping and lamenting, he performed the funeral rites for his father’s body.

Devadattopi [M 1.0127] ajātasattuṃ upasaṅkamitvā – “purise, mahārāja, āṇāpehi, ye samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ jīvitā voropessantī”ti vatvā tena dinne purise pesetvā sayaṃ gijjhakūṭaṃ āruyha yantena silaṃ pavijjhitvā nāḷāgirihatthiṃ muñcāpetvāpi kenaci upāyena bhagavantaṃ māretuṃ asakkonto parihīnalābhasakkāro pañca vatthūni yācitvā tāni alabhamāno tehi janaṃ saññāpessāmīti saṅghabhedaṃ katvā sāriputtamoggallānesu parisaṃ ādāya pakkantesu uṇhalohitaṃ mukhena chaḍḍetvā navamāse gilānamañce nipajjitvā vippaṭisārajāto – “kuhiṃ etarahi satthā vasatī”ti pucchitvā “jetavane”ti vutte mañcakena maṃ āharitvā satthāraṃ dassethāti vatvā āhariyamāno bhagavato [P 1.0139] dassanārahassa kammassa akatattā jetavane pokkharaṇīsamīpeyeva dvedhā bhinnaṃ pathaviṃ pavisitvā mahāniraye patiṭṭhitoti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārakathānayo khandhake āgato. Āgatattā pana sabbaṃ na vuttanti. Evaṃ ajātoyeva rañño sattu bhavissatīti nemittakehi niddiṭṭhoti ajātasattu.

Devadatta approached Ajātasattu and said, "Great King, command men who will deprive the ascetic Gotama of life." Having said this, he sent the men given by him, climbed Gijjhakūṭa mountain himself, rolled down a stone with a machine, and even had the elephant Nālāgiri released—yet being unable to kill the Blessed One by any means, his gain and honor diminished. He requested five articles, and not obtaining them, he thought, "I will make the people understand with these." He created a schism in the Sangha; but when Sāriputta and Moggallāna departed, taking the assembly with them, he vomited hot blood from his mouth, lay on a sickbed for nine months, and became remorseful. He asked, "Where does the Teacher reside now?" When it was said, "At Jetavana," he said, "Bring me on a small bed and show me the Teacher." But as he was being brought, because he had not done a kamma worthy of seeing the Blessed One, he entered the earth that had split in two right near the lotus pond at Jetavana and was established in the great hell. This is the summary here. The detailed narrative is found in the Khandhaka. However, since it is found there, not everything is stated here. Thus, "Even while unborn, he will be an enemy to the king," was pointed out by the soothsayers; therefore, he is called Ajātasattu.

Vedehiputtoti ayaṃ kosalarañño dhītāya putto, na videharañño. Vedehīti pana paṇḍitādhivacanametaṃ. Yathāha – “vedehikā gahapatānī (ma. ni. 1.226), ayyo ānando vedehamunī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.154). Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – vidanti etenāti vedo, ñāṇassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vedena īhati ghaṭati vāyamatīti vedehī. Vedehiyā putto vedehiputto.
