"Son of Vedehī" (Vedehiputta): This one is the son of the daughter of the Kosala king, not of the Videha king. "Vedehī," however, is a term for a wise woman. As it is said: "Vedehikā, the householder's wife," and "the venerable Ānanda, the Vedeha sage." Herein, this is the meaning of the word: "They know by means of this," thus it is 'veda'; this is a term for wisdom. "She strives, exerts, and endeavors with wisdom," thus she is 'Vedehī'. The son of Vedehī is Vedehiputta.

Tadahūti tasmiṃ ahu, tasmiṃ divaseti attho. Upavasanti etthāti uposatho, upavasantīti [V 1.0118] sīlena vā anasanena vā upetā hutvā vasantīti attho. Ayaṃ panettha atthuddhāro – “āyāmāvuso, kappina, uposathaṃ gamissāmā”tiādīsu pātimokkhuddeso uposatho. “Evaṃ aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgato kho, visākhe, uposatho upavuttho”tiādīsu (a. ni. 8.43) sīlaṃ. “Suddhassa ve sadā phaggu, suddhassuposatho sadā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.79) upavāso. “Uposatho nāma nāgarājā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.246) paññatti[M 1.0128]. “Na, bhikkhave, tadahuposathe sabhikkhukā āvāsā”tiādīsu (mahāva. 181) upavasitabbadivaso. Idhāpi soyeva adhippeto. So panesa aṭṭhamī cātuddasī pannarasībhedena tividho. Tasmā sesadvayanivāraṇatthaṃ pannaraseti vuttaṃ. Teneva vuttaṃ – “upavasanti etthāti uposatho”ti.

Tadahu means 'on that day'; the meaning is 'on that day'. "They observe on this day" (upavasanti ettha), thus it is uposatha. The meaning of upavasanti is that they dwell (vasanti) having become endowed (upetā) with either virtue (sīla) or fasting (anasana). This is the extraction of meanings here: in passages such as, "Come, friend Kappina, let us go to the uposatha," uposatha is the recital of the Pātimokkha. In passages such as, "Thus, Visākhā, the uposatha observed is endowed with eight factors," it is virtue. In passages such as, "For the pure one, it is always an auspicious day; for the pure one, it is always an uposatha," it is the observance of fasting. In passages such as, "Uposatha is the name of a nāga king," it is a designation. In passages such as, "Bhikkhus, on that uposatha day, one should not go from a residence with bhikkhus..." it is the day on which the observance should be undertaken. Here, too, that very one is intended. Now, this uposatha is threefold, distinguished as the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth day. Therefore, to preclude the other two, "on the fifteenth" was stated. For that very reason, it was said: "They observe on this day, thus it is uposatha."

Komudiyāti kumudavatiyā. Tadā kira kumudāni supupphitāni honti, tāni ettha santīti komudī. Cātumāsiniyāti cātumāsiyā, sā hi catunnaṃ māsānaṃ pariyosānabhūtāti cātumāsī. Idha pana cātumāsinīti vuccati. Māsapuṇṇatāya [P 1.0140] utupuṇṇatāya saṃvaccharapuṇṇatāya puṇṇā sampuṇṇāti puṇṇā. Mā iti cando vuccati, so ettha puṇṇoti puṇṇamā. Evaṃ puṇṇāya puṇṇamāyāti imasmiṃ padadvaye ca attho veditabbo.

Komudī means abounding in water lilies. For at that time, the water lilies are well-blossomed. Because they are present on this night, it is called komudī. Cātumāsinī means belonging to the four months. For that night is the end of the four months, thus it is cātumāsī. Here, however, it is called cātumāsinī. Because of the fullness of the month, the fullness of the season, and the fullness of the year, it is full (puṇṇā), completely full (sampunnā); thus, it is called puṇṇā. The moon is called mā. It is full on this night; thus, it is puṇṇamā. In this way, the meaning in this pair of words, puṇṇāya puṇṇamāya, should also be understood.

Rājāmaccaparivutoti evarūpāya rajataghaṭaviniggatāhi khīradhārāhi dhoviyamānadisābhāgāya viya, rajatavimānaviccutehi muttāvaḷisumanakusumadāmasetadukūlakumudavisarehi samparikiṇṇāya viya ca, caturupakkilesavimuttapuṇṇacandappabhāsamudayobhāsitāya rattiyā rājāmaccehi parivutoti attho. Uparipāsādavaragatoti pāsādavarassa uparigato. Mahārahe samussitasetacchatte kañcanāsane nisinno hoti. Kasmā nisinno? Niddāvinodanatthaṃ. Ayañhi rājā pitari upakkantadivasato paṭṭhāya – “niddaṃ okkamissāmī”ti nimīlitamattesuyeva akkhīsu sattisataabbhāhato viya kandamānoyeva pabujjhi. Kimetanti ca vutte, na kiñcīti vadati. Tenassa amanāpā niddā, iti niddāvinodanatthaṃ nisinno. Api ca tasmiṃ divase nakkhattaṃ saṅghuṭṭhaṃ hoti. Sabbaṃ nagaraṃ sittasammaṭṭhaṃ vippakiṇṇavālukaṃ pañcavaṇṇakusumalājapuṇṇaghaṭapaṭimaṇḍitagharadvāraṃ samussitadhajapaṭākavicitrasamujjalitadīpamālālaṅkatasabbadisābhāgaṃ vīthisabhāgena racchāsabhāgena nakkhattakīḷaṃ anubhavamānena mahājanena samākiṇṇaṃ hoti. Iti nakkhattadivasatāyapi nisinnoti vadanti. Evaṃ pana vatvāpi – “rājakulassa nāma sadāpi nakkhattameva, niddāvinodanatthaṃyeva panesa nisinno”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ kataṃ.

The meaning of rājāmaccaparivuto (surrounded by royal ministers) is: surrounded by royal ministers on a night illuminated by the rising splendor of the full moon, which is free from the four blemishes—a night that was as if the quarters of the sky were being washed by streams of milk flowing from a silver pot, and as if strewn all around with strings of pearls, garlands of jasmine flowers, white cloths, and masses of water lilies that had emerged from a silver celestial mansion. Uparipāsādavaragato (gone to the top of the excellent palace) means he had gone to the top of the excellent palace. He was seated on a golden seat, worthy of a great person, under a raised white parasol. Why was he seated? To dispel sleepiness. For this king, starting from the day he transgressed against his father, as soon as he closed his eyes, thinking, "I will fall asleep," he would awaken, crying out as if struck by a hundred spears. And when asked, "What is this?" he would say, "Nothing." Therefore, sleep was unpleasant for him; thus, he was seated to dispel sleepiness. Furthermore, on that day a festival of constellations was proclaimed. The whole city was sprinkled and swept, with sand scattered about; the doorways of the houses were adorned with five-colored flowers, parched grain, and full water pots; all the quarters were decorated with raised flags and banners and variegated, brightly lit rows of lamps; and it was crowded with a great multitude experiencing the festival of constellations in the main streets and side streets. Thus, they say he was seated also because it was the day of the festival of constellations. However, even after saying this, the conclusion was made: "For a royal family, it is always a festival. Indeed, this one was seated only to dispel sleepiness."

Udānaṃ [V 1.0119][M 1.0129] udānesīti udāhāraṃ udāhari, yathā hi yaṃ telaṃ mānaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti, vissanditvā gacchati, taṃ avasekoti [P 1.0141] vuccati. Yañca jalaṃ taḷākaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti, ajjhottharitvā gacchati, taṃ oghoti vuccati; evameva yaṃ pītivacanaṃ hadayaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti, adhikaṃ hutvā anto asaṇṭhahitvā bahinikkhamati, taṃ udānanti vuccati. Evarūpaṃ pītimayaṃ vacanaṃ nicchāresīti attho.

Udānaṃ udānesi means he uttered an inspired utterance. For just as oil that a measuring vessel cannot hold flows out and is called 'overflow,' and just as water that a lake cannot hold overflows and is called a 'flood,' in the very same way, a joyous utterance that the heart cannot hold, becoming excessive and not staying inside, comes out—that is called an udāna. The meaning is that he sent forth such a speech born of joy.

Dosināti dosāpagatā, abbhā, mahikā, dhūmo, rajo, rāhūti imehi pañcahi upakkilesehi virahitāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tasmā ramaṇīyātiādīni pañca thomanavacanāni. Sā hi mahājanassa manaṃ ramayatīti ramaṇīyā. Vuttadosavimuttāya candappabhāya obhāsitattā ativiya surūpāti abhirūpā. Dassituṃ yuttāti dassanīyā. Cittaṃ pasādetīti pāsādikā. Divasamāsādīnaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ bhavituṃ yuttāti lakkhaññā.

Dosinā means free from faults; that is, it is said to be free from these five blemishes: clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu. Therefore, the five words beginning with 'delightful' are words of praise. Indeed, that night delights the minds of the great multitude, thus it is delightful (ramaṇīyā). Because it is illuminated by the moonlight that is free from the aforementioned faults, it is exceedingly beautiful, thus it is resplendent (abhirūpā). It is fit to be seen, thus it is fair to see (dassanīyā). It clarifies the mind, thus it is serene (pāsādikā). It is fit to be a sign for the day, month, and so on, thus it is auspicious (lakkhaññā).

Kaṃ nu khvajjāti kaṃ nu kho ajja. Samaṇaṃ vā brāhmaṇaṃ vāti samitapāpatāya samaṇaṃ. Bāhitapāpatāya brāhmaṇaṃ. Yaṃ no payirupāsatoti vacanabyattayo esa, yaṃ amhākaṃ pañhapucchanavasena payirupāsantānaṃ madhuraṃ dhammaṃ sutvā cittaṃ pasīdeyyāti attho. Iti rājā iminā sabbenapi vacanena obhāsanimittakammaṃ akāsi. Kassa akāsīti? Jīvakassa. Kimatthaṃ? Bhagavato dassanatthaṃ. Kiṃ bhagavantaṃ sayaṃ dassanāya upagantuṃ na sakkotīti? Āma, na sakkoti. Kasmā? Mahāparādhatāya.

'Kaṃ nu khvajjā' means 'Whom indeed today...'. As for 'a recluse or a brahmin': 'recluse' (samaṇa) because of having pacified evil; 'brahmin' (brāhmaṇa) because of having cast out evil. The phrase 'yaṃ no payirupāsato' is an irregularity of case. The meaning is: 'Whom, if we were to attend upon him by way of asking questions, our minds would become clear upon hearing the sweet Dhamma.' Thus, with all these words, the king made a hint by allusion. For whom did he do it? For Jīvaka. For what purpose? For the purpose of seeing the Blessed One. Is it that he is not able to go himself to see the Blessed One? Yes, he is not able. Why? Because of his great offense.

Tena hi bhagavato upaṭṭhāko ariyasāvako attano pitā mārito, devadatto ca tameva nissāya bhagavato bahuṃ anatthamakāsi, iti mahāparādho esa, tāya mahāparādhatāya sayaṃ gantuṃ na sakkoti. Jīvako pana bhagavato upaṭṭhāko, tassa piṭṭhichāyāya bhagavantaṃ passissāmīti obhāsanimittakammaṃ akāsi. Kiṃ jīvako pana – “mayhaṃ idaṃ obhāsanimittakamma”nti jānātīti? Āma jānāti. Atha kasmā tuṇhī ahosīti? Vikkhepapacchedanatthaṃ.

Indeed, by that king, his own father—a noble disciple and attendant of the Blessed One—was killed. And Devadatta, relying on that very king, caused much harm to the Blessed One. Thus, this one has a great offense; because of that great offense, he is not able to go himself. Jīvaka, however, is an attendant of the Blessed One. Thinking, 'I will see the Blessed One under his protection,' he made the hint by allusion. But does Jīvaka know, 'He made this hint by allusion for me'? Yes, he knows. Then why was he silent? For the purpose of cutting off interruption.

Tassañhi parisati channaṃ satthārānaṃ upaṭṭhākā bahū [P 1.0142] sannipatitā, te asikkhitānaṃ payirupāsanena sayampi asikkhitāva. Te mayi bhagavato guṇakathaṃ [M 1.0130] āraddhe antarantarā uṭṭhāyuṭṭhāya attano satthārānaṃ guṇaṃ kathessanti, evaṃ me satthu guṇakathā pariyosānaṃ na gamissati. Rājā pana imesaṃ kulūpake upasaṅkamitvā gahitāsāratāya tesaṃ guṇakathāya anattamano [V 1.0120] hutvā maṃ paṭipucchissati, athāhaṃ nibbikkhepaṃ satthu guṇaṃ kathetvā rājānaṃ satthu santikaṃ gahetvā gamissāmīti jānantova vikkhepapacchedanatthaṃ tuṇhī ahosīti.

For in that assembly, many attendants of the six teachers were gathered. They, by attending upon the undisciplined, are themselves also undisciplined. 'When I have begun a talk on the qualities of the Blessed One, they will, from time to time, stand up and speak of the qualities of their own teachers. In this way, my talk on the qualities of the Teacher will not reach its conclusion. The king, however, having approached these family advisors and grasped their lack of substance, will be displeased with the talk on their qualities and will question me in turn. Then I, having spoken of the Teacher's qualities without interruption, will take the king and go to the Teacher's presence.' Thus, knowing this, he was silent for the purpose of cutting off interruption.

Tepi amaccā evaṃ cintesuṃ – “ajja rājā pañcahi padehi rattiṃ thometi, addhā kiñci samaṇaṃ vā brāhmaṇaṃ vā upasaṅkamitvā pañhaṃ pucchitvā dhammaṃ sotukāmo, yassa cesa dhammaṃ sutvā pasīdissati, tassa ca mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ karissati, yassa pana kulūpako samaṇo rājakulūpako hoti, bhaddaṃ tassā”ti.

Those ministers also thought thus: 'Today the king praises the night with five phrases. Surely, he desires to hear the Dhamma after approaching some recluse or brahmin and asking a question. And he in whom he gains confidence after hearing his Dhamma, to him he will give great honor. Moreover, for whichever minister's family-advisor recluse becomes the king's family advisor, it will be a good thing for him.'

151-152. Te evaṃ cintetvā – “ahaṃ attano kulūpakasamaṇassa vaṇṇaṃ vatvā rājānaṃ gahetvā gamissāmi, ahaṃ gamissāmī”ti attano attano kulūpakānaṃ vaṇṇaṃ kathetuṃ āraddhā. Tenāha – “evaṃ vutte aññataro rājāmacco”tiādi. Tattha pūraṇoti tassa satthupaṭiññassa nāmaṃ. Kassapoti gottaṃ. So kira aññatarassa kulassa ekūnadāsasataṃ pūrayamāno jāto, tenassa pūraṇoti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Maṅgaladāsattā cassa “dukkaṭa”nti vattā natthi, akataṃ vā na katanti. So “kimahaṃ ettha vasāmī”ti palāyi. Athassa corā vatthāni acchindiṃsu, so paṇṇena vā tiṇena vā paṭicchādetumpi ajānanto jātarūpeneva ekaṃ gāmaṃ pāvisi. Manussā taṃ disvā “ayaṃ samaṇo arahā appiccho, natthi iminā sadiso”ti pūvabhattādīni gahetvā upasaṅkamanti. So – “mayhaṃ sāṭakaṃ anivatthabhāvena idaṃ uppanna”nti tato paṭṭhāya sāṭakaṃ labhitvāpi na nivāsesi, tadeva pabbajjaṃ aggahesi, tassa santike [P 1.0143] aññepi aññepīti pañcasatamanussā pabbajiṃsu. Taṃ sandhāyāha – “pūraṇo kassapo”ti.

They, having thought thus—'I will speak of the virtues of my family-advisor recluse, take the king, and go. I will go!'—began to speak of the virtues of their respective family advisors. Therefore, it was said: 'When this was said, a certain royal minister...' and so on. Therein, 'Pūraṇa' is the name of that one who claimed to be a teacher. 'Kassapa' is his clan name. It is said that he was born completing the hundredth slave for a certain family; therefore, they gave him the name 'Pūraṇa'. And because he was an auspicious slave, there was no one to say 'wrongly done' of what he had done, nor 'it is not done' of what was undone. He, thinking, 'Why should I live here?' fled. Then thieves stole his clothes. He, not knowing how to cover himself even with a leaf or with grass, entered a village in his birth-form. People, seeing him and thinking, 'This is a recluse, an arahant, of few wishes; there is no one like him,' approached him, taking cakes, rice, and other foods. He thought, 'This has arisen for me because of my not wearing a cloth.' From then on, even upon receiving a cloth, he did not wear it. He took up that very state as his renunciation. In his presence, others and still others, five hundred men in all, went forth. Referring to him, it was said, 'Pūraṇa Kassapa.'

Pabbajitasamūhasaṅkhāto saṅgho assa atthīti saṅghī. Sveva gaṇo assa atthīti gaṇī. Ācārasikkhāpanavasena tassa gaṇassa ācariyoti gaṇācariyo. Ñātoti paññāto pākaṭo. “Appiccho [M 1.0131] santuṭṭho. Appicchatāya vatthampi na nivāsetī”ti evaṃ samuggato yaso assa atthīti yasassī. Titthakaroti laddhikaro. Sādhusammatoti ayaṃ sādhu, sundaro, sappurisoti evaṃ sammato. Bahujanassāti assutavato andhabālaputhujjanassa. Pabbajitato paṭṭhāya atikkantā bahū rattiyo jānātīti rattaññū. Ciraṃ pabbajitassa assāti cirapabbajito, acirapabbajitassa hi kathā okappanīyā na hoti, tenāha “cirapabbajito”ti. Addhagatoti addhānaṃ gato, dve tayo rājaparivaṭṭe atītoti adhippāyo. Vayoanuppattoti pacchimavayaṃ anuppatto. Idaṃ ubhayampi – “daharassa kathā okappanīyā na hotī”ti etaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

He has a saṅgha, which is termed an assembly of renunciants, thus he is saṅghī. That same group is his gaṇa, thus he is gaṇī. By way of teaching his conduct, he is the teacher (ācariyo) of that group, thus he is gaṇācariyo. Ñāta means known, manifest. He has fame that has arisen thus: 'He has few wishes, is content. Because of having few wishes, he does not even wear a cloth,' thus he is yasassī. Titthakaro means a maker of a doctrine. Sādhusammato means he is esteemed thus: 'This one is good, excellent, a virtuous person.' Bahujanassa (of many people) means of the uninstructed, blind, foolish worldling. He knows many nights that have passed since his renunciation, thus he is rattaññū. He has been a renunciate for a long time, thus he is cirapabbajito; indeed, the talk of one who has not been a renunciate for long is not trustworthy, therefore it is said cirapabbajito. Addhagato means one who has gone a long way; the intention is that he has passed through two or three changes of kings. Vayoanuppatto means one who has reached the last stage of life. Both of these are said with reference to this: 'The talk of a young person is not trustworthy.'

Tuṇhī [V 1.0121] ahosīti suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ madhurarasaṃ ambapakkaṃ khāditukāmo puriso āharitvā hatthe ṭhapitaṃ kājarapakkaṃ disvā viya jhānābhiññādiguṇayuttaṃ tilakkhaṇabbhāhataṃ madhuraṃ dhammakathaṃ sotukāmo pubbe pūraṇassa dassanenāpi anattamano idāni guṇakathāya suṭṭhutaraṃ anattamano hutvā tuṇhī ahosi. Anattamano samānopi pana “sacāhaṃ etaṃ tajjetvā gīvāyaṃ gahetvā nīharāpessāmi, ‘yo yo kathesi, taṃ taṃ rājā evaṃ karotī’ti bhīto aññopi koci kiñci na kathessatī”ti amanāpampi taṃ kathaṃ adhivāsetvā tuṇhī eva ahosi. Athañño – “ahaṃ attano kulūpakassa vaṇṇaṃ kathessāmī”ti cintetvā vattuṃ ārabhi. Tena vuttaṃ – aññataropi khotiādi. Taṃ sabbaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

"He remained silent"—like a man desiring to eat a golden-colored, sweet mango, who, upon seeing a ripe kājara fruit placed in his hand, becomes displeased. Similarly, though he wished to hear the sweet Dhamma talk endowed with the qualities of jhānas and supernormal knowledge, and struck by the three characteristics, having been displeased even by the sight of Pūraṇa before, he now became even more displeased by the talk of his qualities and remained silent. Although displeased, he thought: 'If I were to threaten this man, seize him by the neck, and have him expelled, then others, fearing that 'the king does this to whoever speaks,' would not speak anything at all.' Thus, enduring that unpleasant talk, he remained silent. Then another, thinking, 'I will speak of the good qualities of my own teacher,' began to speak. Therefore, it is said, 'And another one...' etc. All this should be understood in the very way that has been stated.

Ettha pana makkhalīti tassa nāmaṃ. Gosālāya jātattā gosāloti dutiyaṃ nāmaṃ. Taṃ kira sakaddamāya bhūmiyā telaghaṭaṃ [P 1.0144] gahetvā gacchantaṃ – “tāta, mā khalī”ti sāmiko āha. So pamādena khalitvā patitvā sāmikassa bhayena palāyituṃ āraddho. Sāmiko upadhāvitvā dussakaṇṇe aggahesi. So sāṭakaṃ chaḍḍetvā acelako hutvā palāyi. Sesaṃ pūraṇasadisameva.

Here, Makkhalī is his name. Gosāla is his second name because he was born in a cowshed. It is said that while he was walking on muddy ground carrying a pot of oil, his master said, "My dear, do not slip!" He, through negligence, slipped and fell. Fearing his master, he began to run away. The master ran up to him and grabbed the edge of his cloth. He, having discarded his outer garment, became clothless and fled. The rest is just like that of Pūraṇa.

153. Ajitoti tassa nāmaṃ. Kesakambalaṃ dhāretīti kesakambalo. Iti nāmadvayaṃ saṃsanditvā ajito kesakambaloti vuccati[M 1.0132]. Tattha kesakambalo nāma manussakesehi katakambalo. Tato paṭikiṭṭhataraṃ vatthaṃ nāma natthi. Yathāha – “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, yāni kānici tantāvutānaṃ vatthānaṃ, kesakambalo tesaṃ paṭikiṭṭho akkhāyati. Kesakambalo, bhikkhave, sīte sīto, uṇhe uṇho, dubbaṇṇo duggandho dukkhasamphasso”ti (a. ni. 3.138).

153. Ajita is his name. He is called 'Kesakambala' because he wears a hair blanket. Thus, combining the two names, he is called Ajita Kesakambala. Here, 'kesakambala' means a blanket made of human hair. There is no cloth more inferior than this. As it is said: "Monks, just as among all woven cloths, a hair blanket is said to be the most inferior. A hair blanket, monks, is cold in the cold, hot in the heat, has a bad color, a bad smell, and is unpleasant to touch" (A. i. 286).

154. Pakudhoti tassa nāmaṃ. Kaccāyanoti gottaṃ. Iti nāmagottaṃ saṃsanditvā pakudho kaccāyanoti vuccati. Sītudakapaṭikkhittako esa, vaccaṃ katvāpi udakakiccaṃ na karoti, uṇhodakaṃ vā kañjiyaṃ vā labhitvā karoti, nadiṃ vā maggodakaṃ vā atikkamma – “sīlaṃ me bhinna”nti vālikathūpaṃ katvā sīlaṃ adhiṭṭhāya gacchati. Evarūpo nissirīkaladdhiko esa.

154. Pakudha is his name. Kaccāyana is his clan name. Thus, combining the name and clan name, he is called Pakudha Kaccāyana. He was one who rejected cold water; even after defecating, he would not perform the water duty. He would do it only after obtaining hot water or sour gruel. Or, after crossing a river or water on the road, thinking, 'My virtue is broken,' he would make a sand stupa and then proceed after undertaking the virtue. Such was this man, who held a wretched doctrine.

155. Sañcayoti tassa nāmaṃ. Belaṭṭhassa puttoti belaṭṭhaputto.

155. Sañcaya is his name. Because he was the son of Belaṭṭha, he was Belaṭṭhaputta.

156. Amhākaṃ gaṇṭhanakileso palibandhanakileso natthi, kilesagaṇṭharahitā mayanti evaṃvāditāya laddhanāmavasena nigaṇṭho. Nāṭassa putto nāṭaputto.

156. He is Nigaṇṭha by way of the name obtained through his custom of stating: 'For us, there is no knot-making defilement, no binding defilement; we are free from the knot of defilements.' The son of Nāṭa is Nāṭaputta.

Komārabhaccajīvakakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of Jīvaka Komārabhacca.

157. Atha [V 1.0122] kho rājāti rājā kira tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā cintesi – “ahaṃ yassa yassa vacanaṃ na sotukāmo, so so eva [P 1.0145] kathesi. Yassa panamhi vacanaṃ sotukāmo, esa nāgavasaṃ pivitvā ṭhito supaṇṇo viya tuṇhībhūto, anattho vata me”ti. Athassa etadahosi – “jīvako upasantassa buddhassa bhagavato upaṭṭhāko, sayampi upasanto, tasmā vattasampanno bhikkhu viya tuṇhībhūtova nisinno, na esa mayi akathente kathessati, hatthimhi kho pana maddante hatthisseva pādo gahetabbo”ti tena saddhiṃ sayaṃ mantetumāraddho. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho rājā”ti. Tattha kiṃ tuṇhīti kena kāraṇena tuṇhī. Imesaṃ amaccānaṃ attano attano kulūpakasamaṇassa vaṇṇaṃ kathentānaṃ mukhaṃ nappahoti[M 1.0133]. Kiṃ yathā etesaṃ, evaṃ tava kulūpakasamaṇo natthi, kiṃ tvaṃ daliddo, na te mama pitarā issariyaṃ dinnaṃ, udāhu assaddhoti pucchati.

157. Then the king, it is said, having heard their words, thought: 'Whosever words I do not wish to hear, that very person spoke. But the one whose words I wish to hear, like a garuḍa standing after having drunk the poison of a nāga, is silent. Alas, what a disadvantage for me!' Then this thought occurred to him: 'Jīvaka is the attendant of the peaceful Buddha, the Blessed One. He himself is also peaceful. Therefore, like a monk accomplished in his duties, he is seated, being silent. He will not speak if I do not speak first. Indeed, when an elephant is trampling, it is the elephant's own foot that should be seized.' Thus, he began to consult with him himself. Therefore, it was said: 'Then the king...' Therein, 'Why are you silent?' means 'For what reason are you silent?' While these ministers are speaking of the virtues of their own respective family ascetics, is your mouth not capable? Is it that you do not have a family ascetic like they do? Are you poor? Was sovereignty not given to you by my father? Or are you without faith?'—thus he asks.

Tato jīvakassa etadahosi – “ayaṃ rājā maṃ kulūpakasamaṇassa guṇaṃ kathāpeti, na dāni me tuṇhībhāvassa kālo, yathā kho panime rājānaṃ vanditvā nisinnāva attano kulūpakasamaṇānaṃ guṇaṃ kathayiṃsu, na mayhaṃ evaṃ satthuguṇe kathetuṃ yutta”nti uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavato vihārābhimukho pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā dasanakhasamodhānasamujjalaṃ añjaliṃ sirasi paggahetvā – “mahārāja, mā maṃ evaṃ cintayittha, ‘ayaṃ yaṃ vā taṃ vā samaṇaṃ upasaṅkamatī’ti, mama satthuno hi mātukucchiokkamane, mātukucchito nikkhamane, mahābhinikkhamane, sambodhiyaṃ, dhammacakkappavattane ca, dasasahassilokadhātu kampittha, evaṃ yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ akāsi, evaṃ devorohaṇaṃ, ahaṃ satthuno guṇe kathayissāmi, ekaggacitto suṇa, mahārājā”ti vatvā – “ayaṃ deva, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”tiādimāha. Tattha [P 1.0146] taṃ kho pana bhagavantanti itthambhūtākhyānatthe upayogavacanaṃ, tassa kho pana bhagavatoti attho. Kalyāṇoti kalyāṇaguṇasamannāgato, seṭṭhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Kittisaddoti kittiyeva. Thutighoso vā. Abbhuggatoti sadevakaṃ lokaṃ ajjhottharitvā uggato. Kinti? “Itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho…pe… bhagavā”ti.

Then this thought occurred to Jīvaka: 'This king wants to make me speak of the virtues of my family ascetic. Now is not the time for my silence. However, just as these ministers, having paid homage to the king and while seated, spoke of the virtues of their own family ascetics, it is not proper for me to speak of my Teacher's virtues in such a way.' Rising from his seat, facing the Blessed One's monastery, having paid homage with the five-point prostration, and having raised to his head his añjali, resplendent with the collection of his ten fingernails, he said: 'Great King, do not think of me thus: "This one approaches just any ascetic whatsoever." Indeed, at the time of my Teacher's descent into his mother's womb, his emergence from his mother's womb, his great renunciation, his full awakening, and the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the ten-thousandfold world-system trembled. In such a way he performed the twin miracle, in such a way the descent from the deva realm. I shall speak of the Teacher's virtues. Listen with a concentrated mind, Great King.' Having said this, he spoke the words beginning with, 'This, Sire, is the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.' Therein, the phrase `taṃ kho pana bhagavantaṃ` is a term in the accusative case used in the sense of describing one of such a nature; the meaning is 'of that Blessed One' (`tassa kho pana bhagavato`). `Kalyāṇa` means endowed with excellent qualities; it is said to mean 'supreme'. `Kittisadda` is fame itself, or the sound of praise. `Abbhuggata` means having arisen, having overwhelmed the world with its devas. How so? 'For this reason, too, that Blessed One is an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One... the Blessed One.'

Tatrāyaṃ padasambandho – so bhagavā itipi arahaṃ itipi sammāsambuddho…pe… itipi bhagavāti. Iminā ca iminā ca kāraṇenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha ārakattā arīnaṃ, arānañca hatattā, paccayādīnaṃ arahattā, pāpakaraṇe rahābhāvāti, imehi tāva kāraṇehi so bhagavā [V 1.0123] arahanti veditabbotiādinā nayena mātikaṃ nikkhipitvā sabbāneva cetāni padāni visuddhimagge buddhānussatiniddese vitthāritānīti tato nesaṃ vitthāro gahetabbo.

Herein, this is the connection of the words: That Blessed One, for this reason too, is an Arahant; for this reason too, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One... for this reason too, a Bhagavā. ‘For this reason and for that reason’ is what is meant. Therein, because of being far from defilements, because of having destroyed the enemies, the defilements, and the spokes of the wheel of existence, because of being worthy of requisites and so on, and because of the absence of a secret place for doing evil—for these reasons, first of all, that Blessed One should be known as ‘Arahant’. Having laid down the matrix in this way, and so forth, and since all these terms have been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga, in the Exposition on the Recollection of the Buddha, their detailed explanation should be taken from there.

Jīvako pana ekamekassa padassa atthaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā – “evaṃ, mahārāja, arahaṃ mayhaṃ satthā, evaṃ sammāsambuddho…pe… evaṃ bhagavā”ti vatvā – “taṃ, devo, bhagavantaṃ payirupāsatu, appeva nāma devassa taṃ bhagavantaṃ payirupāsato cittaṃ pasīdeyyā”ti āha. Ettha ca taṃ devo payirupāsatūti vadanto “mahārāja, tumhādisānañhi satenapi sahassenapi satasahassenapi puṭṭhassa [M 1.0134] mayhaṃ satthuno sabbesaṃ cittaṃ gahetvā kathetuṃ thāmo ca balañca atthi, vissattho upasaṅkamitvā puccheyyāsi mahārājā”ti āha.

But Jīvaka, having brought to conclusion the meaning of each and every term, said, ‘For this reason, Great King, my Teacher is an Arahant; for this reason, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One... for this reason, a Bhagavā.’ Having said this, he spoke: ‘Let Your Majesty attend upon that Blessed One. It may well be that Your Majesty's mind will become serene by attending upon that Blessed One.’ And herein, in saying, ‘Let Your Majesty attend upon him,’ he meant: ‘Great King, my Teacher, when questioned by a hundred, a thousand, or even a hundred thousand such as you, has the strength and the power to grasp the minds of all and to answer. You may approach with confidence and ask, Great King.’

Raññopi bhagavato guṇakathaṃ suṇantassa sakalasarīraṃ pañcavaṇṇāya pītiyā nirantaraṃ phuṭaṃ ahosi. So taṅkhaṇaññeva gantukāmo hutvā – “imāya kho pana velāya mayhaṃ dasabalassa santikaṃ gacchato na añño koci khippaṃ yānāni yojetuṃ sakkhissati aññatra jīvakā”ti cintetvā – “tena hi, samma jīvaka, hatthiyānāni kappāpehī”ti āha.

As for the king, while listening to the discourse on the Blessed One's virtues, his entire body became uninterruptedly pervaded with joy of five kinds. Desiring to go at that very moment, he thought: ‘But at this time, as I am going to the presence of the one with Ten Powers, no one other than Jīvaka will be able to prepare the vehicles quickly.’ Having thought thus, he said: ‘Well then, friend Jīvaka, have the elephant-vehicles made ready.’

158. Tattha tena hīti uyyojanatthe nipāto. Gaccha, samma jīvakāti [P 1.0147] vuttaṃ hoti. Hatthiyānānīti anekesu assarathādīsu yānesu vijjamānesupi hatthiyānaṃ uttamaṃ; uttamassa santikaṃ uttamayāneneva gantabbanti ca, assayānarathayānāni sasaddāni, dūratova tesaṃ saddo suyyati, hatthiyānassa padānupadaṃ gacchantāpi saddaṃ na suṇanti. Nibbutassa pana kho bhagavato santike nibbuteheva yānehi gantabbanti ca cintayitvā hatthiyānānīti āha.

158. Therein, `tena hi` is a particle in the sense of urging. It means, ‘Go, friend Jīvaka.’ As for ‘elephant-vehicles’: although many vehicles such as horse-vehicles and chariots exist, the elephant-vehicle is the most excellent. And because one should go to the presence of the most excellent one only by the most excellent vehicle; and because horse-vehicles and chariots are noisy and their sound is heard from afar, while even those following step-by-step in the tracks of an elephant-vehicle do not hear a sound; and moreover, because one should go to the presence of the Blessed One, who is extinguished, only by extinguished, that is, quiet, vehicles—having considered thus, he said ‘elephant-vehicles’.

Pañcamattāni hatthinikāsatānīti pañca kareṇusatāni. Kappāpetvāti ārohaṇasajjāni kāretvā. Ārohaṇīyanti ārohaṇayoggaṃ, opaguyhanti attho. Kiṃ panesa raññā vuttaṃ akāsi avuttanti? Avuttaṃ. Kasmā? Paṇḍitatāya. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – rājā imāya velāya gacchāmīti vadati, rājāno ca nāma bahupaccatthikā. Sace antarāmagge koci antarāyo hoti, mampi garahissanti – “jīvako rājā me kathaṃ gaṇhātīti akālepi rājānaṃ gahetvā nikkhamatī”ti. Bhagavantampi garahissanti “samaṇo gotamo, ‘mayhaṃ kathā vattatī’ti kālaṃ asallakkhetvāva dhammaṃ kathetī”ti. Tasmā yathā neva mayhaṃ, na bhagavato, garahā uppajjati; rañño ca rakkhā susaṃvihitā hoti, tathā karissāmī”ti.

‘Five hundred female elephants’ means five hundred she-elephants. ‘Having had them made ready’ means having them prepared for mounting. `Ārohaṇīyaṃ` means suitable for mounting, capable of concealing; this is the meaning. Now then, did he do what was said by the king, or what was not said? He did what was not said. Why? Due to his wisdom. It is said, this thought occurred to him: ‘The king says, “I will go at this time,” and kings, indeed, have many enemies. If some danger occurs on the way, they will blame me too, saying: “Jīvaka, thinking, ‘The king heeds my word,’ takes the king and departs even at an unsuitable time.” They will also blame the Blessed One, saying: “The ascetic Gotama, thinking, ‘My teaching prevails,’ teaches the Dhamma without considering the time.” Therefore, I will act in such a way that blame arises neither for me nor for the Blessed One, and that the king's protection is well-arranged.’

Tato [P 1.0148][V 1.0124] itthiyo nissāya purisānaṃ bhayaṃ nāma natthi, ‘sukhaṃ itthiparivuto gamissāmī’ti pañca hatthinikāsatāni kappāpetvā pañca itthisatāni purisavesaṃ gāhāpetvā – “asitomarahatthā rājānaṃ parivāreyyāthā”ti vatvā puna cintesi – “imassa rañño imasmiṃ attabhāve maggaphalānaṃ [M 1.0135] upanissayo natthi, buddhā ca nāma upanissayaṃ disvāva dhammaṃ kathenti. Handāhaṃ, mahājanaṃ sannipātāpemi, evañhi sati satthā kassacideva upanissayena dhammaṃ desessati, sā mahājanassa upakārāya bhavissatī”ti. So tattha tattha sāsanaṃ pesesi, bheriṃ carāpesi – “ajja rājā bhagavato santikaṃ gacchati, sabbe attano vibhavānurūpena rañño ārakkhaṃ gaṇhantū”ti.

Therefore, thinking, ‘Relying on women, there is no such thing as danger from men; I will go comfortably, surrounded by women,’ he had five hundred female elephants made ready and had five hundred women assume the guise of men. After saying, ‘With swords and spears in hand, you should surround the king,’ he thought again: ‘For this king, in this existence, there is no strong supporting condition for the paths and fruits. And Buddhas, indeed, teach the Dhamma only after seeing a strong supporting condition. Well now, I shall have a great crowd assemble. For when this is so, the Teacher, on account of the strong supporting condition of someone or other, will teach the Dhamma. That teaching will be for the benefit of the great crowd.’ So he sent a message here and there and had a drum beaten, announcing: ‘Today the king is going to the presence of the Blessed One. Let everyone, according to their own means, take up protection for the king.’

Tato mahājano cintesi – “rājā kira satthudassanatthaṃ gacchati, kīdisī vata bho dhammadesanā bhavissati, kiṃ no nakkhattakīḷāya, tattheva gamissāmā”ti. Sabbe gandhamālādīni gahetvā rañño āgamanaṃ ākaṅkhamānā magge aṭṭhaṃsu. Jīvakopi rañño paṭivedesi – “kappitāni kho te, deva, hatthiyānāni, yassa dāni kālaṃ maññasī”ti. Tattha yassa dāni kālaṃ maññasīti upacāravacanametaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “yaṃ tayā āṇattaṃ, taṃ mayā kataṃ, idāni tvaṃ yassa gamanassa vā agamanassa vā kālaṃ maññasi, tadeva attano ruciyā karohī”ti.

Then the great crowd thought: ‘It is said the king is going for the purpose of seeing the Teacher. Oh, what kind of Dhamma discourse will it be! What use is the star festival to us? We shall go right there.’ All of them, taking perfumes, garlands, and so on, stood on the road, awaiting the king's arrival. Jīvaka also informed the king: ‘Indeed, Your Majesty, the elephant-vehicles have been prepared. Now you may act as you deem the time is right.’ Therein, the phrase ‘for which you now deem the time’ is a conventional expression. This is what is meant: ‘What was commanded by you, that has been done by me. Now, whether you deem it the time for going or for not going, do just that according to your own wish.’

159. Paccekā itthiyoti pāṭiyekkā itthiyo, ekekissā hatthiniyā ekekaṃ itthinti vuttaṃ hoti. Ukkāsu dhāriyamānāsūti daṇḍadīpikāsu dhāriyamānāsu. Mahacca rājānubhāvenāti mahatā rājānubhāvena. Mahaccātipi pāḷi, mahatiyāti attho, liṅgavipariyāyo esa. Rājānubhāvo vuccati rājiddhi. Kā panassa rājiddhi? Tiyojanasatānaṃ dvinnaṃ mahāraṭṭhānaṃ issariyasirī. Tassa hi asukadivasaṃ rājā tathāgataṃ upasaṅkamissatīti paṭhamataraṃ saṃvidahane asatipi taṅkhaṇaññeva pañca itthisatāni purisavesaṃ gahetvā paṭimukkaveṭhanāni aṃse āsattakhaggāni maṇidaṇḍatomare gahetvā nikkhamiṃsu. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “paccekā itthiyo āropetvā”ti.

159. 'Each woman' means individual women; it is said, one woman for each female elephant. 'While torches were being held' means while staff-torches were being held. 'With great royal power' means by great royal power. There is also the Pāli reading mahaccā; the meaning is mahatiyā (great); this is an instance of gender change. Royal majesty is called royal power. What, then, was his royal majesty? The glory of sovereignty over two great kingdoms of three hundred yojanas. For, although there was no prior arrangement that 'on such-and-such a day the king will approach the Tathāgata,' at that very moment five hundred women, having assumed the guise of men, with turbans fastened, swords slung on their shoulders, and holding jewel-staffed lances, went forth. It is with reference to this that it was said: 'having mounted each woman.'

Aparāpi soḷasasahassakhattiyanāṭakitthiyo rājānaṃ parivāresuṃ. Tāsaṃ pariyante khujjavāmanakakirātādayo. Tāsaṃ pariyante antepurapālakā vissāsikapurisā. Tesaṃ pariyante vicitravesavilāsino saṭṭhisahassamattā mahāmattā. Tesaṃ pariyante vividhālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā nānappakāraāvudhahatthā [M 1.0136] vijjādharataruṇā viya navutisahassamattā raṭṭhiyaputtā. Tesaṃ pariyante satagghanikāni [P 1.0149][V 1.0125] nivāsetvā pañcasatagghanikāni ekaṃsaṃ katvā sunhātā suvilittā kañcanamālādinānābharaṇasobhitā dasasahassamattā brāhmaṇā dakkhiṇahatthaṃ ussāpetvā jayasaddaṃ ghosantā gacchanti. Tesaṃ pariyante pañcaṅgikāni tūriyāni. Tesaṃ pariyante dhanupantiparikkhepo. Tassa pariyante hatthighaṭā. Hatthīnaṃ pariyante gīvāya gīvaṃ paharamānā assapanti. Assapariyante aññamaññaṃ saṅghaṭṭanarathā. Rathapariyante bāhāya bāhaṃ paharayamānā yodhā. Tesaṃ pariyante attano attano anurūpāya ābharaṇasampattiyā virocamānā aṭṭhārasa seniyo. Iti yathā pariyante ṭhatvā khitto saro rājānaṃ na pāpuṇāti, evaṃ jīvako komārabhacco rañño parisaṃ saṃvidahitvā attanā rañño avidūreneva gacchati – “sace koci upaddavo hoti, paṭhamatara rañño jīvitadānaṃ dassāmī”ti. Ukkānaṃ pana ettakāni satāni vā sahassāni vāti paricchedo natthīti evarūpiṃ rājiddhiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “mahaccarājānubhāvena yena jīvakassa komārabhaccassa ambavanaṃ, tena pāyāsī”ti.

Also, sixteen thousand women, dancing girls of the Khattiya caste, surrounded the king. At their edge were hunchbacked women, dwarfish women, Kirāta women, and so on. At their edge were the trusted men who guarded the inner palace. At their edge were sixty thousand chief ministers, charming with their varied attire. At their edge were ninety thousand sons of provincial rulers, adorned with various ornaments, with various kinds of weapons in hand, like young Vidyādharas. At their edge, ten thousand brahmins proceed, having worn garments worth a hundred, having arranged garments worth five hundred over one shoulder, well-bathed, well-anointed, resplendent with golden garlands and other various ornaments, raising their right arms and proclaiming shouts of victory. At their edge, the five-fold musical ensemble proceeds. At their edge is a perimeter of a row of archers. At its edge is a troop of elephants. At the elephants' edge is a row of horses, as if striking neck against neck. At the horses' edge are chariots colliding with one another. At the chariots' edge are warriors, as if striking arm against arm. At their edge are eighteen guilds, shining with the splendor of their own respective ornaments. Thus, Jīvaka Komārabhacca, having arranged the king's retinue in such a way that an arrow shot from the edge would not reach the king, himself went not far from the king, thinking, 'If any misfortune should occur, I will be the first to give the gift of life to the king.' Furthermore, as for the torches, there was no limit as to whether there were so many hundreds or so many thousands. It was with reference to such royal majesty that it was said: 'With great royal power, he departed for Jīvaka Komārabhacca’s mango grove.'

Ahudeva bhayanti ettha cittutrāsabhayaṃ, ñāṇabhayaṃ, ārammaṇabhayaṃ, ottappabhayanti catubbidhaṃ bhayaṃ, tattha “jātiṃ paṭicca bhayaṃ bhayānaka”ntiādinā nayena vuttaṃ cittutrāsabhayaṃ nāma. “Tepi tathāgatassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā yebhuyyena bhayaṃ saṃvegaṃ santāsaṃ āpajjantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.78) evamāgataṃ ñāṇabhayaṃ nāma. “Etaṃ nūna taṃ bhayabheravaṃ āgacchatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.49) ettha vuttaṃ ārammaṇabhayaṃ nāma.

Herein, in the passage “there was fear,” fear is of four kinds: fear as mental terror (cittutrāsabhaya), fear as knowledge (ñāṇabhaya), fear as a fearful object (ārammaṇabhaya), and fear as moral dread (ottappabhaya). Among these, that which is spoken of in the manner beginning with “Conditioned by birth, there is fear, a fearful thing,” is called fear as mental terror. That which comes in the passage, “Having heard the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, they for the most part fall into fear, a sense of urgency, and terror,” is called fear as knowledge. That which is spoken of in the passage, “Surely this is that fear and dread coming,” is called fear as a fearful object.

“Bhīruṃ pasaṃsanti, na hi tattha sūraṃ;

Bhayā hi santo, na karonti pāpa”nti [P 1.0150]. (saṃ. ni. 1.33);

“They praise the one who is fearful; indeed, not the brave one there. For the good, out of fear, do not commit evil.”

Idaṃ ottappabhayaṃ nāma. Tesu idha cittutrāsabhayaṃ, ahu ahosīti attho. Chambhitattanti chambhitassa bhāvo. Sakalasarīracalananti attho. Lomahaṃsoti lomahaṃsanaṃ, uddhaṃ ṭhitalomatāti attho. So panāyaṃ lomahaṃso dhammassavanādīsu pītiuppattikāle pītiyāpi hoti[M 1.0137]. Bhīrukajātikānaṃ sampahārapisācādidassanesu bhayenāpi. Idha bhayalomahaṃsoti veditabbo.

This is called fear as moral dread. Among these types of fear, here it was the fear as mental terror that occurred. Ahu means ‘it occurred’ (ahosi). ‘Being paralyzed’ (chambhitatta) is the state of being stiff; it means the trembling of the entire body. ‘Bristling of the hairs’ (lomahaṃso) means the hair standing up, that is, the state of having hairs standing on end. This bristling of the hairs can also occur due to joy at the time of the arising of joy when hearing the Dhamma and so forth. For those of a timid nature, it can also occur due to fear upon seeing battles, ghouls, and the like. Here, it should be understood as the bristling of the hairs due to fear.

Kasmā panesa bhītoti? Andhakārenāti eke vadanti. Rājagahe kira dvattiṃsa mahādvārāni, catusaṭṭhi khuddakadvārāni. Jīvakassa ambavanaṃ pākārassa ca gijjhakūṭassa ca antarā hoti. So pācīnadvārena nikkhamitvā pabbatacchāyāya pāvisi, tattha pabbatakūṭena cando [V 1.0126] chādito, pabbatacchāyāya ca rukkhacchāyāya ca andhakāraṃ ahosīti, tampi akāraṇaṃ. Tadā hi ukkānaṃ satasahassānampi paricchedo natthi.

But why was he afraid? Some say it was because of the darkness. It is said that in Rājagaha there were thirty-two great gates and sixty-four small gates. Jīvaka’s mango grove is between the city wall and Gijjhakūṭa. He left by the eastern gate and entered by way of the mountain’s shadow. There, the moon was covered by a mountain peak, and due to the mountain’s shadow and the trees’ shadow, it became dark. But that too is not the reason. For at that time, there was no limit even to hundreds of thousands of torches.

Ayaṃ pana appasaddataṃ nissāya jīvake āsaṅkāya bhīto. Jīvako kirassa uparipāsādeyeva ārocesi – “mahārāja appasaddakāmo bhagavā, appasaddeneva upasaṅkamitabbo”ti. Tasmā rājā tūriyasaddaṃ nivāresi. Tūriyāni kevalaṃ gahitamattāneva honti, vācampi uccaṃ anicchārayamānā accharāsaññāya gacchanti. Ambavanepi kassaci khipitasaddopi na suyyati. Rājāno ca nāma saddābhiratā honti. So taṃ appasaddataṃ nissāya ukkaṇṭhito jīvakepi āsaṅkaṃ uppādesi. “Ayaṃ jīvako mayhaṃ ambavane aḍḍhateḷasāni bhikkhusatānī”ti āha. Ettha ca khipitasaddamattampi na suyyati, abhūtaṃ maññe, esa vañcetvā maṃ nagarato nīharitvā purato balakāyaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā maṃ gaṇhitvā attanā chattaṃ ussāpetukāmo. Ayañhi pañcannaṃ hatthīnaṃ balaṃ dhāreti. Mama ca avidūreneva [P 1.0151] gacchati, santike ca me āvudhahattho ekapurisopi natthi. Aho vata me anattho”ti. Evaṃ bhāyitvā ca pana abhīto viya sandhāretumpi nāsakkhi. Attano bhītabhāvaṃ tassa āvi akāsi. Tena vuttaṃ. “Atha kho rājā…pe… na nigghoso”ti. Tattha sammāti vayassābhilāpo esa, kacci maṃ vayassāti vuttaṃ hoti. Na palambhesīti yaṃ natthi taṃ atthīti vatvā kacci maṃ na vippalambhayasi. Nigghosoti kathāsallāpanigghoso.

Now, this king was afraid on account of the quietness, due to his suspicion of Jīvaka. It is said that Jīvaka had already informed him while on the upper level of the palace: 'Great king, the Blessed One desires quiet; he should be approached with quietness.' Therefore, the king silenced the sound of the musical instruments. The instruments were merely held, and not wishing to raise their voices, they proceeded by the signal of a finger-snap. In the mango grove, not even the sound of a sneeze from anyone could be heard. And kings, by nature, delight in sound. He, being distressed by that quietness, developed suspicion toward Jīvaka. He thought: 'This Jīvaka told me there are twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus in my mango grove. Yet here, not even the sound of a sneeze is heard. I think this is untrue. Deceiving me, he has led me out of the city, stationed a force ahead, and intends to seize me and raise the royal umbrella himself. For this man possesses the strength of five elephants. And he walks not far from me, while near me there is not even a single man with a weapon in hand. Alas, my ruin is at hand!' Having thus become afraid, he was unable to compose himself as if unafraid. He made his state of fear apparent to Jīvaka. Therefore it was said: 'Then the king… no loud sound.' Therein, `samma` is a term of address for a peer; it is as if 'Friend' was said. `Na palambhesi` means: 'Surely you are not deceiving me by saying that what does not exist, exists?' `Nigghoso` means the loud sound of conversation.

Mā bhāyi, mahārājāti jīvako – “ayaṃ rājā maṃ na jānāti ‘nāyaṃ paraṃ jīvitā voropetī’ti; sace kho pana naṃ na assāsessāmi, vinasseyyā”ti [M 1.0138] cintayitvā daḷhaṃ katvā samassāsento “mā bhāyi mahārājā”ti vatvā “na taṃ devā”tiādimāha. Abhikkamāti abhimukho kama gaccha, pavisāti attho. Sakiṃ vutte pana daḷhaṃ na hotīti taramānova dvikkhattuṃ āha. Ete maṇḍalamāḷe dīpā jhāyantīti mahārāja, corabalaṃ nāma na dīpe jāletvā tiṭṭhati, ete ca maṇḍalamāḷe dīpā jalanti. Etāya dīpasaññāya yāhi mahārājāti vadati.

Jīvaka, thinking: 'This king does not know of me that “This man does not deprive another of life.” But if I do not reassure him, he might perish,' and wanting to reassure him firmly, said, 'Do not fear, great king!' and then spoke the words beginning, 'It is not so, sire.' `Abhikkama` means: 'Go forward, proceed, enter.' And since it would not be firm if said only once, he spoke twice, hurrying. When he says, 'These lamps are burning in the circular pavilion,' he means: 'Great king, a company of thieves does not stand around having lit lamps, and yet these lamps are burning in the circular pavilion. Go by this sign of the lamps, great king!'

Sāmaññaphalapucchāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Question of the Fruits of Recluseship

160. Nāgassa bhūmīti yattha sakkā hatthiṃ abhirūḷhena gantuṃ, ayaṃ nāgassa bhūmi nāma. Nāgā paccorohitvāti vihārassa bahidvārakoṭṭhake hatthito orohitvā. Bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhitasamakālameva [V 1.0127] pana bhagavato tejo rañño sarīraṃ phari. Athassa tāvadeva sakalasarīrato sedā mucciṃsu, sāṭakā pīḷetvā apanetabbā viya ahesuṃ. Attano aparādhaṃ saritvā mahābhayaṃ uppajji. So ujukaṃ bhagavato santikaṃ gantuṃ asakkonto jīvakaṃ hatthe gahetvā ārāmacārikaṃ caramāno viya “idaṃ te samma jīvaka suṭṭhu kāritaṃ idaṃ suṭṭhu kārita”nti vihārassa [P 1.0152] vaṇṇaṃ bhaṇamāno anukkamena yena maṇḍalamāḷassa dvāraṃ tenupasaṅkami, sampattoti attho.

160. The ground for an elephant is a place where one can go mounted on an elephant; this is what is called 'the ground for an elephant.' 'Having descended from the elephant' means having dismounted from the elephant at the outer gatehouse of the monastery. Then, at the very moment he stood on the ground, the Blessed One's power pervaded the king's body. At that very moment, sweat poured from his entire body, and his garments were as if they needed to be wrung out and removed. Remembering his own offense, great fear arose. He, being unable to go directly into the Blessed One's presence, took Jīvaka by the hand and, as if strolling through the monastery park, speaking in praise of the monastery, saying, “Friend Jīvaka, this has been well made by you, this has been well made,” he gradually approached the door of the circular pavilion. The meaning is that he arrived.

Kahaṃ pana sammāti kasmā pucchīti. Eke tāva “ajānanto”ti vadanti. Iminā kira daharakāle pitarā saddhiṃ āgamma bhagavā diṭṭhapubbo, pacchā pana pāpamittasaṃsaggena pitughātaṃ katvā abhimāre pesetvā dhanapālaṃ muñcāpetvā mahāparādho hutvā bhagavato sammukhībhāvaṃ na upagatapubboti asañjānanto pucchatīti. Taṃ akāraṇaṃ, bhagavā hi ākiṇṇavaralakkhaṇo anubyañjanapaṭimaṇḍito chabbaṇṇāhi rasmīhi sakalaṃ ārāmaṃ obhāsetvā tārāgaṇaparivuto viya puṇṇacando bhikkhugaṇaparivuto maṇḍalamāḷamajjhe nisinno, taṃ ko na jāneyya. Ayaṃ pana attano issariyalīlāya pucchati. Pakati hesā rājakulānaṃ, yaṃ jānantāpi ajānantā viya pucchanti. Jīvako pana taṃ sutvā – ‘ayaṃ rājā pathaviyaṃ ṭhatvā kuhiṃ pathavīti, nabhaṃ ulloketvā kuhiṃ candimasūriyāti, sinerumūle ṭhatvā [M 1.0139] kuhiṃ sinerūti vadamāno viya dasabalassa purato ṭhatvā kuhiṃ bhagavā’ti pucchati. “Handassa bhagavantaṃ dassessāmī”ti cintetvā yena bhagavā tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā “eso mahārājā”tiādimāha. Purakkhatoti parivāretvā nisinnassa purato nisinno.

‘But where, friend?’—why did he ask? Some, to begin with, say, ‘Because he did not know.’ It is said that this king had seen the Blessed One before when he came with his father in his youth, but later, due to association with evil friends, having committed the murder of his father, having sent assassins, and having had Dhanapāla released, he became one of great offense and had never before come into the Blessed One's presence; therefore, not recognizing him, he asks. That is not a valid reason. For the Blessed One, possessing the excellent major marks and adorned with the minor characteristics, illuminating the entire monastery with six-colored rays, seated in the middle of the circular pavilion surrounded by the assembly of monks like the full moon surrounded by a host of stars—who would not know him? Rather, this king asks with the majestic air of a sovereign. Indeed, this is the nature of royal families, that even when they know, they ask as if not knowing. Then Jīvaka, having heard that, thought: ‘This king, standing on the earth, asks, “Where is the earth?”; looking up at the sky, he asks, “Where are the moon and sun?”; standing at the foot of Mount Sineru, he asks, “Where is Sineru?”; in the same way, standing before the one with Ten Powers, he asks, “Where is the Blessed One?”’ Thinking, ‘Come, I will show the Blessed One to him,’ he extended his joined hands in the direction of the Blessed One and said, ‘Here he is, great king,’ and so on. `Purakkhato` means seated in front of the assembly that sat surrounding him.

161. Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti yattha bhagavā tattha gato, bhagavato santikaṃ upagatoti attho. Ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsīti bhagavantaṃ vā bhikkhusaṃghaṃ vā asaṅghaṭṭayamāno attano ṭhātuṃ anucchavike ekasmiṃ padese bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekova aṭṭhāsi. Tuṇhībhūtaṃ tuṇhībhūtanti yato yato anuviloketi, tato tato tuṇhībhūtamevāti attho. Tattha hi ekabhikkhussapi hatthakukkuccaṃ vā pādakukkuccaṃ vā khipitasaddo vā natthi, sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ [P 1.0153] nāṭakaparivāraṃ bhagavato abhimukhe ṭhitaṃ rājānaṃ vā rājaparisaṃ vā ekabhikkhupi na olokesi. Sabbe bhagavantaṃyeva olokayamānā nisīdiṃsu.

161. 'He approached where the Blessed One was' means he went to where the Blessed One was, he drew near to the Blessed One's presence; this is the meaning. 'He stood to one side' means, without bumping against either the Blessed One or the assembly of monks, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood alone in a suitable place. 'The assembly was silent, silent' means that wherever he looked around, it was simply silent. For there, not even a single monk was fidgeting with his hands or feet, nor was there the sound of a sneeze or a cough. Not even one monk looked at the king or the king's retinue, who stood before the Blessed One adorned with all ornaments and with an entourage like a troupe of dancers. All sat looking only at the Blessed One.

Rājā tesaṃ upasame pasīditvā vigatapaṅkatāya vippasannarahadamiva upasantindriyaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ punappunaṃ anuviloketvā udānaṃ udānesi. Tattha imināti yena kāyikena ca vācasikena [V 1.0128] ca mānasikena ca sīlūpasamena bhikkhusaṅgho upasanto, iminā upasamenāti dīpeti. Tattha “aho vata me putto pabbajitvā ime bhikkhū viya upasanto bhaveyyā”ti nayidaṃ sandhāya esa evamāha. Ayaṃ pana bhikkhusaṅghaṃ disvā pasanno puttaṃ anussari. Dullabhañhi laddhā acchariyaṃ vā disvā piyānaṃ ñātimittādīnaṃ anussaraṇaṃ nāma lokassa pakatiyeva. Iti bhikkhusaṅghaṃ disvā puttaṃ anussaramāno esa evamāha.

The king, pleased with their tranquility, repeatedly gazed upon the assembly of monks, whose faculties were tranquil like a clear lake free from mud, and uttered an inspired utterance. Therein, iminā (‘by this’) shows: by which bodily, verbal, and mental tranquility of virtue the assembly of monks is tranquil, by this tranquility. He did not say this with the intention, “Oh, would that my son, having gone forth, might become tranquil like these monks.” Rather, this king, pleased on seeing the assembly of monks, remembered his son. Indeed, upon obtaining something difficult to get or seeing something wonderful, it is the very nature of the world to remember dear relatives, friends, and others. Thus, remembering his son upon seeing the assembly of monks, he spoke thus.

Api ca putte āsaṅkāya tassa upasamaṃ icchamāno pesa evamāha. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi, putto me pucchissati – “mayhaṃ pitā daharo. Ayyako me kuhi”nti. So “pitarā te ghātito”ti sutvā “ahampi pitaraṃ ghātetvā rajjaṃ kāressāmī”ti maññissati. Iti putte āsaṅkāya tassa upasamaṃ icchamāno pesa evamāha. Kiñcāpi hi esa evamāha. Atha kho naṃ putto ghātessatiyeva. Tasmiñhi vaṃse pituvadho pañcaparivaṭṭe gato. Ajātasattu bimbisāraṃ ghātesi, udayo ajātasattuṃ[M 1.0140]. Tassa putto mahāmuṇḍiko nāma udayaṃ. Tassa putto anuruddho nāma mahāmuṇḍikaṃ. Tassa putto nāgadāso nāma anuruddhaṃ. Nāgadāsaṃ pana – “vaṃsacchedakarājāno ime, kiṃ imehī”ti raṭṭhavāsino kupitā ghātesuṃ.

Furthermore, it was because of suspicion regarding his son and wishing for his tranquility that he spoke thus. It is said that this occurred to him: ‘My son will ask, “My father is young. Where is my grandfather?” Hearing, “He was killed by your father,” he will think, “I too will kill my father and take the kingdom.”’ Thus, because of suspicion regarding his son and wishing for his tranquility, he spoke thus. And although he spoke thus, his son did indeed kill him. For in that lineage, patricide continued for five generations. Ajātasattu killed Bimbisāra; Udaya killed Ajātasattu; his son, named Mahāmuṇḍika, killed Udaya; his son, named Anuruddha, killed Mahāmuṇḍika; his son, named Nāgadāsa, killed Anuruddha. But as for Nāgadāsa, the inhabitants of the country, being enraged, killed him, thinking, ‘These are kings who destroy their lineage! What is the use of them?’

Agamā kho tvanti kasmā evamāha? Bhagavā kira rañño vacībhede akateyeva cintesi – “ayaṃ rājā āgantvā tuṇhī niravo ṭhito, kiṃ nu kho cintesī”ti. Athassa cittaṃ ñatvā – “ayaṃ mayā saddhiṃ sallapituṃ asakkonto bhikkhusaṅghaṃ [P 1.0154] anuviloketvā puttaṃ anussari, na kho panāyaṃ mayi anālapante kiñci kathetuṃ sakkhissati, karomi tena saddhiṃ kathāsallāpa”nti. Tasmā rañño vacanānantaraṃ “agamā kho tvaṃ, mahārāja, yathāpema”nti āha. Tassattho – mahārāja, yathā nāma unname vuṭṭhaṃ udakaṃ yena ninnaṃ tena gacchati, evameva tvaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ anuviloketvā yena pemaṃ tena gatoti.

Why did he say, 'You have indeed gone?' Because the Blessed One, even before the king broke his silence, thought: 'This king has come and stands silent and soundless. What could he be thinking?' Then, knowing his mind, he thought: 'This one, being unable to converse with me, is looking over the assembly of monks and has remembered his son. Furthermore, he will not be able to say anything if I do not speak. I shall initiate a conversation with him.' Therefore, immediately after the king's utterance, he said, 'You have indeed gone, great king, according to your affection.' The meaning of this is: Great king, just as rainwater that has fallen on high ground flows to wherever is low, in the very same way you, having looked over the assembly of monks, have gone to where your affection lies.

Atha rañño etadahosi – “aho acchariyā buddhaguṇā, mayā sadiso bhagavato aparādhakārako nāma natthi, mayā hissa aggupaṭṭhāko ghātito, devadattassa ca kathaṃ gahetvā abhimārā pesitā, nāḷāgiri mutto, maṃ nissāya devadattena silā paviddhā, evaṃ mahāparādhaṃ nāma maṃ ālapato dasabalassa mukhaṃ nappahoti; aho bhagavā pañcahākārehi tādilakkhaṇe suppatiṭṭhito. Evarūpaṃ nāma satthāraṃ pahāya bahiddhā na pariyesissāmā”ti so somanassajāto bhagavantaṃ ālapanto “piyo me, bhante”tiādimāha.

Then this thought occurred to the king: 'Oh, how wonderful are the virtues of the Buddha! There is no one who has offended the Blessed One as I have. For by me his chief attendant was killed; and having taken Devadatta's word, assassins were sent; Nāḷāgiri was released; on account of me, the rock was hurled by Devadatta. The mouth of the Ten-Powered One is more than sufficient to address me, who has committed such great offenses. Oh, the Blessed One is well-established in the characteristic of 'suchness' in five ways. Having abandoned such a teacher, I will not seek one outside the Dispensation.' He, with joy arisen, addressing the Blessed One, said: 'Beloved to me, Venerable Sir,' and so on.

162. Bhikkhusaṅghassa [V 1.0129] añjaliṃ paṇāmetvāti evaṃ kirassa ahosi bhagavantaṃ vanditvā itocito ca gantvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ vandantena ca bhagavā piṭṭhito kātabbo hoti, garukāropi cesa na hoti. Rājānaṃ vanditvā uparājānaṃ vandantenapi hi rañño agāravo kato hoti. Tasmā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā ṭhitaṭṭhāneyeva bhikkhusaṅghassa añjaliṃ paṇāmetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Kañcideva desanti kañci okāsaṃ.

162. Regarding 'having paid homage to the assembly of bhikkhus with hands in añjali': it seems this thought occurred to him—that by one who, after venerating the Blessed One, goes here and there to venerate the assembly of bhikkhus, the Blessed One would be placed at one's back, and this would not be showing due respect. For even when one venerates the king and then venerates the viceroy, disrespect is shown to the king. Therefore, having venerated the Blessed One, right in the place where he stood, he paid homage to the assembly of bhikkhus with hands in añjali and sat down to one side. 'Some place' means 'some space'.

Athassa [M 1.0141] bhagavā pañhapucchane ussāhaṃ janento āha – “puccha, mahārāja, yadākaṅkhasī”ti. Tassattho – “puccha yadi ākaṅkhasi, na me pañhavissajjane bhāro atthi”. Atha vā “puccha, yaṃ ākaṅkhasi, sabbaṃ te vissajjessāmī”ti sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ pavāresi, asādhāraṇaṃ paccekabuddhaaggasāvakamahāsāvakehi. Te hi yadākaṅkhasīti na vadanti, sutvā vedissāmāti vadanti. Buddhā [P 1.0155] pana – “puccha, āvuso, yadākaṅkhasī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.237), vā “puccha, mahārāja, yadākaṅkhasī”ti vā,

Then the Blessed One, generating enthusiasm in him for asking questions, said: 'Ask, great king, what you wish.' The meaning of this is: 'Ask if you wish; for me there is no burden in answering questions.' Or else: 'Ask what you wish; I will answer everything for you.' Thus he extended the invitation of an omniscient one, an invitation not shared with Paccekabuddhas, chief disciples, and great disciples. For they do not say, 'Ask what you wish'; they say, 'Having heard, we shall know.' But Buddhas say, 'Ask, friend, what you wish,' or 'Ask, great king, what you wish,' or,

“Puccha, vāsava, maṃ pañhaṃ, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasi;

Tassa tasseva pañhassa, ahaṃ antaṃ karomi te”ti. (dī. ni. 2.356) vā;

‘Ask me a question, Vāsava, whatever you desire in your mind; of that very question, I will make an end for you.’ (Dī. Ni. 2.356) or;

Tena hi tvaṃ, bhikkhu, sake āsane nisīditvā puccha, yadākaṅkhasīti vā,

‘Then, bhikkhu, having sat on your own seat, ask if you wish;’ or,

“Bāvarissa ca tuyhaṃ vā, sabbesaṃ sabbasaṃsayaṃ;

Katāvakāsā pucchavho, yaṃ kiñci manasicchathā”ti. (su. ni. 1036) vā;

‘For Bāvari and for you, and for all, regarding every doubt, the opportunity has been granted; ask whatever you desire in your minds.’ (Su. Ni. 1036) or;

“Puccha maṃ, sabhiya, pañhaṃ, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasi;

Tassa tasseva pañhassa, ahaṃ antaṃ karomi te”ti. (su. ni. 517) vā;

‘Ask me a question, Sabhiya, whatever you desire in your mind; of that very question, I will make an end for you.’ (Su. Ni. 517) or;

Tesaṃ tesaṃ yakkhanarindadevasamaṇabrāhmaṇaparibbājakānaṃ sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ pavārenti. Anacchariyañcetaṃ, yaṃ bhagavā buddhabhūmiṃ patvā etaṃ pavāraṇaṃ pavāreyya. Yo bodhisattabhūmiyaṃ padesañāṇe ṭhito –

To those various yakkhas, human kings, devas, samaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and paribbājakas, they extend the invitation of an omniscient one. And it is not wonderful that the Blessed One, having reached the Buddha-stage, should extend this invitation. He who, while standing in the Bodhisatta-stage, with partial knowledge—

“Koṇḍañña[V 1.0130], pañhāni viyākarohi;

Yācanti taṃ isayo sādhurūpā.

Koṇḍañña, eso manujesu dhammo;

Yaṃ vuddhamāgacchati esa bhāro”ti. (jā. 2.17.60);

‘Koṇḍañña, answer the questions; the sages of good character entreat you. Koṇḍañña, this is the custom among humans: that this responsibility falls to the elder.’ (Jā. 2.17.60);

Evaṃ sakkādīnaṃ atthāya isīhi yācito –

Thus, being requested by the sages for the benefit of Sakka and others—

“Katāvakāsā pucchantu bhonto,

Yaṃ kiñci pañhaṃ manasābhipatthitaṃ;

Ahañhi taṃ taṃ vo viyākarissaṃ,

Ñatvā sayaṃ lokamimaṃ parañcā”ti. (jā. 2.17.61);

‘Sirs, the opportunity has been granted; please ask whatever question is desired in your minds. For I shall explain each of them to you, having myself known this world and the next.’ (Jā. 2.17.61);

Evaṃ [M 1.0142] sarabhaṅgakāle. Sambhavajātake ca sakalajambudīpaṃ tikkhattuṃ vicaritvā pañhānaṃ antakaraṃ adisvā suciratena brāhmaṇena, pañhaṃ puṭṭhuṃ okāse kārite jātiyā sattavassiko rathikāya paṃsuṃ kīḷanto pallaṅkamābhujitvā antaravīthiyaṃ nisinnova –

Thus it was at the time of Sarabhaṅga. And in the Sambhava Jātaka, having wandered throughout all of Jambudīpa three times and not seeing one who could make an end of questions, when an opportunity to ask a question was made by the brahmin Sucirata, the Sambhava-prince, being seven years of age by birth, while playing with dust on a chariot road, sat right in the middle of the street with his legs crossed—

“Taggha [P 1.0156] te ahamakkhissaṃ, yathāpi kusalo tathā;

Rājā ca kho taṃ jānāti, yadi kāhati vā na vā”ti. (jā. 1.16.172);

‘Indeed, I will tell you, just as a skilled one would. And the king indeed knows you, whether he will act or not.’ (Jā. 1.16.172);

Sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ pavāresi.

He extended the invitation of an omniscient one.

163. Evaṃ bhagavatā sabbaññupavāraṇāya pavāritāya attamano rājā pañhaṃ pucchanto – “yathā nu kho imāni, bhante”tiādimāha. Tattha sippameva sippāyatanaṃ. Puthusippāyatanānīti bahūni sippāni. Seyyathidanti katame pana te. Hatthārohātiādīhi ye taṃ taṃ sippaṃ nissāya jīvanti, te dasseti. Ayañhi assādhippāyo – “yathā imesaṃ sippūpajīvīnaṃ taṃ taṃ sippaṃ nissāya sandiṭṭhikaṃ sippaphalaṃ paññāyati. Sakkā nu kho evaṃ sandiṭṭhikaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ paññāpetu”nti. Tasmā sippāyatanāni āharitvā sippūpajīvino dasseti.

163. Thus, when the invitation of an omniscient one had been extended by the Blessed One, the king, pleased in mind, while asking a question, said, 'Venerable sir, just as there are these...' and so on. Therein, 'basis of craft' (sippāyatana) is craft itself. 'Many bases of craft' means many crafts. 'That is to say' (seyyathidaṃ) means: but what are they? By 'elephant-trainers' and so on, he indicates those who live by relying on this or that craft. For this is his intention: 'Just as for these who live by crafts, a visible fruit of the craft is made known by relying on this or that craft, is it possible in the same way to make known a visible fruit of the contemplative life?' Therefore, having brought forward the bases of craft, he indicates those who live by crafts.

Tattha hatthārohāti sabbepi hatthācariyahatthivejjahatthimeṇḍādayo dasseti. Assārohāti sabbepi [V 1.0131] assācariyaassavejjaassameṇḍādayo. Rathikāti sabbepi rathācariyarathayodharatharakkhādayo. Dhanuggahāti dhanuācariyā issāsā. Celakāti ye yuddhe jayadhajaṃ gahetvā purato gacchanti. Calakāti idha rañño ṭhānaṃ hotu, idha asukamahāmattassāti evaṃ senābyūhakārakā. Piṇḍadāyakāti sāhasikamahāyodhā. Te kira parasenaṃ pavisitvā parasīsaṃ piṇḍamiva chetvā chetvā dayanti, uppatitvā uppatitvā niggacchantīti attho. Ye vā saṅgāmamajjhe yodhānaṃ bhattapātiṃ gahetvā parivisanti, tesampetaṃ nāmaṃ. Uggā [P 1.0157] rājaputtāti uggatuggatā saṅgāmāvacarā rājaputtā. Pakkhandinoti ye “kassa sīsaṃ vā āvudhaṃ vā āharāmā”ti [M 1.0143] “vatvā asukassā”ti vuttā saṅgāmaṃ pakkhanditvā tadeva āharanti, ime pakkhandantīti pakkhandino. Mahānāgāti mahānāgā viya mahānāgā, hatthiādīsupi abhimukhaṃ āgacchantesu anivattitayodhānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sūrāti ekantasūrā, ye sajālikāpi sacammikāpi samuddaṃ tarituṃ sakkonti. Cammayodhinoti ye cammakañcukaṃ vā pavisitvā saraparittāṇacammaṃ vā gahetvā yujjhanti. Dāsikaputtāti balavasinehā gharadāsayodhā. Āḷārikāti pūvikā. Kappakāti nhāpikā. Nhāpakāti ye nhāpenti. Sūdāti bhattakārakā. Mālākārādayo pākaṭāyeva. Gaṇakāti acchiddakapāṭhakā. Muddikāti hatthamuddāya gaṇanaṃ nissāya jīvino. Yāni vā panaññānipīti ayakāradantakāracittakārādīni. Evaṃgatānīti evaṃ pavattāni. Te diṭṭheva dhammeti te hatthārohādayo tāni puthusippāyatanāni dassetvā rājakulato mahāsampattiṃ labhamānā sandiṭṭhikameva sippaphalaṃ upajīvanti. Sukhentīti sukhitaṃ karonti. Pīṇentīti pīṇitaṃ thāmabalūpetaṃ karonti. Uddhaggikādīsu upari phalanibbattanato uddhaṃ aggamassā [P 1.0158] atthīti uddhaggikā. Saggaṃ arahatīti sovaggikā. Sukho vipāko assāti sukhavipākā. Suṭṭhu agge rūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbaāyuvaṇṇasukhayasaādhipateyyasaṅkhāte dasa dhamme saṃvatteti nibbattetīti saggasaṃvattanikā. Taṃ evarūpaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ dānaṃ patiṭṭhapentīti attho. Sāmaññaphalanti ettha paramatthato maggo sāmaññaṃ. Ariyaphalaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ. Yathāha – “katamañca, bhikkhave, sāmaññaṃ? Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo. Seyyathidaṃ, sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sāmaññaṃ. Katamāni ca, bhikkhave, sāmaññaphalāni? Sotāpattiphalaṃ…pe… arahattaphala”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.35). Taṃ esa rājā na jānāti. Upari āgataṃ pana dāsakassakopamaṃ sandhāya pucchati.

Herein, by `hatthārohā` (elephant-riders), it indicates all such as elephant masters, elephant-riding warriors, elephant doctors, and elephant keepers. By `assārohā` (horse-riders), it indicates all such as horse masters, horse-riding warriors, horse doctors, and horse keepers. By `rathikā` (charioteers), it indicates all such as chariot masters, chariot warriors, and chariot guards. By `dhanuggahā` (archers), it means bow masters and archers. `Celakā` are those who, taking the victory banner in battle, go to the front. `Calakā` are the arrangers of the army formation, saying thus: 'Let the king's position be here; let such-and-such a great minister's position be here.' `Piṇḍadāyakā` (lump-givers) are bold, great warriors. It is said that they, having entered the enemy's army and having repeatedly cut off an enemy's head like a lump of food, leap and escape. Or, it is also the name for those who, in the midst of battle, take the food bowls of the warriors and serve them. `Uggā rājaputtā` (eminent princes) are eminent and distinguished princes who frequent the battlefield. `Pakkhandino` (chargers) are those who, having said, 'Whose head or whose weapon shall we bring?' and being told, 'Bring so-and-so's,' charge into battle and bring that very thing. Because they charge (`pakkhandanti`), they are called `pakkhandino`. `Mahānāgā` (great nāgas) are like great elephants; this is an epithet for warriors who do not retreat even when elephants and others are coming towards them. `Sūrā` (heroes) are the supremely brave, those who are able to cross the ocean even with nets or with leather shields. `Cammayodhino` (leather-clad warriors) are those who fight having entered into a leather coat or having taken up a leather shield for protection from arrows. `Dāsikaputtā` (sons of female slaves) are warriors who are household slaves with strong affection for their master. `Āḷārikā` are cake-makers. `Kappakā` are barbers. `Nhāpakā` are those who give baths. `Sūdā` are cooks. Florists and the like are well-known. `Gaṇakā` (calculators) are those who recite the science of calculation without interruption. `Muddikā` (counters by hand signs) are those who make a living relying on calculation by hand signs. By `yāni vā panaññānipi` (and whatever other...), it refers to blacksmiths, ivory-workers, painters, and so on. `Evaṃgatāni` (of such a kind) means 'thus occurred.' By `te diṭṭheva dhamme` (by them in this very life), it means: those elephant-riders and others, by displaying those various crafts and skills, having obtained great wealth from the royal family, live on the immediately visible fruit of their craft. `Sukhenti` (they make happy) means they make one happy. `Pīṇenti` (they satisfy) means they make one satisfied, endowed with strength and power. Among the terms beginning with `uddhaggikā`, the meaning should be understood thus: because its fruit is produced in a higher realm, it has a high (`uddhaṃ`) and supreme (`aggaṃ`) result; therefore, it is called `uddhaggikā`. Because it is worthy of heaven (`saggaṃ`), it is called `sovaggikā`. Because it has a happy (`sukho`) result (`vipāko`), it is called `sukhavipākā`. Because it brings about the ten things known as form, sound, smell, taste, touch, lifespan, beauty, happiness, fame, and sovereignty, which are excellent and supreme, it is called `saggasaṃvattanikā`. The meaning is that they establish such a worthy offering. Regarding `sāmaññaphalaṃ` (the fruit of the contemplative life), herein, in the ultimate sense, the path is `sāmaññaṃ` (the contemplative life), and the noble fruit is `sāmaññaphalaṃ`. As it was said: 'And what, monks, is the contemplative life? It is this very Noble Eightfold Path, that is: right view... right concentration. This, monks, is called the contemplative life. And what, monks, are the fruits of the contemplative life? The fruit of stream-entry... the fruit of arahantship.' This, that king does not know. But he asks with reference to the simile of the slave and the farmer that comes later.

Atha bhagavā pañhaṃ avissajjetvāva cintesi – “ime bahū aññatitthiyasāvakā rājāmaccā idhāgatā, te kaṇhapakkhañca sukkapakkhañca dīpetvā kathīyamāne amhākaṃ rājā mahantena [V 1.0132] ussāhena idhāgato, tassāgatakālato paṭṭhāya samaṇo gotamo samaṇakolāhalaṃ samaṇabhaṇḍanameva [M 1.0144] kathetīti ujjhāyissanti, na sakkaccaṃ dhammaṃ sossanti, raññā pana kathīyamāne ujjhāyituṃ na sakkhissanti, rājānameva anuvattissanti. Issarānuvattako hi loko. ‘Handāhaṃ raññova bhāraṃ karomī’ti rañño bhāraṃ karonto “abhijānāsi no tva”ntiādimāha.

Then the Blessed One, without yet answering the question, considered: “These many disciples of other sectarians and royal ministers have come here. If, while the Dhamma is being taught by explaining both the dark side and the bright side, they will complain, saying: ‘Our king came here with great effort, and from the time of his arrival, the recluse Gotama speaks only of the clamor of recluses and the disputes of recluses.’ They will not listen to the Dhamma respectfully. But if it is spoken by the king, they will not be able to complain; they will just follow the king. For the world follows the one in authority. ‘Well now, I shall make it the king’s responsibility.’ Thus, making it the king’s responsibility, he said, ‘Do you recall...’ and so on.

164. Tattha abhijānāsi no tvanti abhijānāsi nu tvaṃ. Ayañca no-saddo parato pucchitāti padena yojetabbo. Idañhi vuttaṃ hoti – “mahārāja, tvaṃ imaṃ pañhaṃ aññe samaṇabrāhmaṇe pucchitā nu, abhijānāsi ca naṃ puṭṭhabhāvaṃ, na te sammuṭṭha”nti. Sace te agarūti sace tuyhaṃ yathā [P 1.0159] te byākariṃsu, tathā idha bhāsituṃ bhāriyaṃ na hoti, yadi na koci aphāsukabhāvo atthi, bhāsassūti attho. Na kho me bhanteti kiṃ sandhāyāha? Paṇḍitapatirūpakānañhi santike kathetuṃ dukkhaṃ hoti, te pade pade akkhare akkhare dosameva vadanti. Ekantapaṇḍitā pana kathaṃ sutvā sukathitaṃ pasaṃsanti, dukkathitesu pāḷipadaatthabyañjanesu yaṃ yaṃ virujjhati, taṃ taṃ ujukaṃ katvā denti. Bhagavatā ca sadiso ekantapaṇḍito nāma natthi. Tenāha – “na kho me, bhante, garu; yatthassa bhagavā nisinno bhagavantarūpo vā”ti.

164. Herein, `abhijānāsi no tvaṃ` means `abhijānāsi nu tvaṃ` (Do you recall?). And this word `no` should be connected with the word `pucchitā` that follows. For this is what is said: ‘Great King, have you asked this question of other recluses and brahmins? And do you recall the fact of having asked? It is not forgotten by you, is it?’ Regarding `sace te agarū` (if it is not a burden for you), the meaning is: ‘If it is not a heavy burden for you to speak here in the way that they answered, if there is no discomfort whatsoever, then please speak.’ With reference to what did he say, `na kho me bhante` (Indeed, it is no burden for me, venerable sir)? For it is difficult to speak in the presence of counterfeit wise men; they speak of faults at every word, at every syllable. The truly wise, however, having heard the talk, praise what is well-spoken. And in what is poorly spoken—among the Pali words, their meanings, and phrases—whatever is incorrect, they make it straight and present it. And there is no one called 'truly wise' who is equal to the Blessed One. Therefore, he said: ‘Indeed, it is no burden for me, venerable sir, where the Blessed One is seated, or one like the Blessed One.’

Pūraṇakassapavādavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Doctrine of Pūraṇa Kassapa

165. Ekamidāhanti ekaṃ idha ahaṃ. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvāti sammodajanakaṃ saritabbayuttakaṃ kathaṃ pariyosāpetvā.

165. `Ekamidāhaṃ` means `ekaṃ idha ahaṃ`. `Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā` (having exchanged pleasant and memorable greetings) means 'having concluded a conversation that generates joy and is fit to be recollected'.

166. “Karoto kho, mahārāja, kārayato”tiādīsu karototi sahatthā karontassa. Kārayatoti āṇattiyā kārentassa. Chindatoti paresaṃ hatthādīni chindantassa. Pacatoti pare daṇḍena pīḷentassa. Socayatoti parassa bhaṇḍaharaṇādīhi socayato. Socāpayatoti sokaṃ sayaṃ karontassapi parehi kārāpentassapi[M 1.0145]. Kilamatoti āhārupacchedabandhanāgārappavesanādīhi sayaṃ kilamantassapi parehi kilamāpentassapi. Phandato phandāpayatoti paraṃ phandantaṃ phandanakāle sayampi phandato parampi phandāpayato. Pāṇamatipātāpayatoti pāṇaṃ hanantassapi hanāpentassapi. Evaṃ sabbattha karaṇakāraṇavaseneva attho veditabbo.

166. In 'For one who acts, O great king, or causes to act,' etc., `karoto` means for one who acts with one's own hand. `Kārayato` means for one who causes others to act by command. `Chindato` means for one who cuts off the hands, etc., of others. `Pacato` means for one who oppresses others with a rod. `Socayato` means for one who causes grief to another by stealing their goods, etc. `Socāpayato` means for one who causes sorrow oneself, or causes others to do so. Regarding `kilamato` and `kilamāpayato`, this means for one who endures hardship oneself through deprivation of food, confinement in prison, etc., or for one who causes others to endure hardship. `Phandato phandāpayato` means for one who, when another is trembling, also trembles oneself, or causes another to tremble. Regarding `pāṇamatipātāpayato`, this means for one who kills a living being or causes it to be killed. Thus, in all cases, the meaning should be understood according to the principle of acting oneself and causing another to act.

Sandhinti [V 1.0133] gharasandhiṃ. Nillopanti mahāvilopaṃ. Ekāgārikanti ekameva gharaṃ parivāretvā viluppanaṃ. Paripantheti āgatāgatānaṃ acchindanatthaṃ magge tiṭṭhato. Karoto na karīyati pāpanti yaṃ kiñci pāpaṃ karomīti saññāya karotopi pāpaṃ na karīyati, natthi pāpaṃ. Sattā pana pāpaṃ karomāti evaṃsaññino hontīti dīpeti. Khurapariyantenāti [P 1.0160] khuraneminā, khuradhārasadisapariyantena vā. Ekaṃ maṃsakhalanti ekaṃ maṃsarāsiṃ. Puñjanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Tatonidānanti ekamaṃsakhalakaraṇanidānaṃ.

`Sandhi` means a house-joint. `Nillopa` means a great plundering. `Ekāgārika` means the plundering of a single house after surrounding it. `Paripantha` refers to one who stands on the road for the purpose of robbing those who come and go. Regarding 'For one who acts, no evil is done': even for one who acts with the perception 'I am doing some evil,' no evil is done; there is no evil. It shows, however, that beings have the perception, 'We are doing evil.' `Khurapariyantena` means with a razor-rim, or with an edge similar to a razor's blade. `Ekaṃ maṃsakhalaṃ` means a single heap of flesh. `Puñja` is a synonym for that very word. `Tatonidānaṃ` means having the making of a single heap of flesh as its cause.

Dakkhiṇanti dakkhiṇatīre manussā kakkhaḷā dāruṇā, te sandhāya “hananto”tiādimāha. Uttaratīre sattā saddhā honti pasannā buddhamāmakā dhammamāmakā saṅghamāmakā, te sandhāya dadantotiādimāha. Tattha yajantoti mahāyāgaṃ karonto. Damenāti indriyadamena uposathakammena vā. Saṃyamenāti sīlasaṃyamena. Saccavajjenāti saccavacanena. Āgamoti āgamanaṃ, pavattīti attho. Sabbathāpi pāpapuññānaṃ kiriyameva paṭikkhipati.

`Dakkhiṇa` (southern) refers to the people on the southern bank, who are harsh and cruel; with reference to them, he spoke the words beginning with 'killing.' On the northern bank, beings are faithful, serene, devoted to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha; with reference to them, he spoke the words beginning with 'giving.' Therein, `yajanto` (sacrificing) means performing a great sacrifice. `Damena` (by restraint) means by restraint of the sense faculties or by the Uposatha observance. `Saṃyamena` (by self-control) means by restraint of moral virtue. `Saccavajjena` (by truthful speech) means by truthful speech. `Āgamo` means arrival; the meaning is 'occurrence.' In every way, it rejects only the very doing of evil and merit.

Ambaṃ puṭṭho labujaṃ byākaroti nāma, yo kīdiso ambo kīdisāni vā ambassa khandhapaṇṇapupphaphalānīti vutte ediso labujo edisāni vā labujassa khandhapaṇṇapupphaphalānīti byākaroti. Vijiteti āṇāpavattidese. Apasādetabbanti viheṭhetabbaṃ. Anabhinanditvāti “sādhu sādhū”ti evaṃ pasaṃsaṃ akatvā. Appaṭikkositvāti bāladubbhāsitaṃ tayā bhāsitanti evaṃ appaṭibāhitvā. Anuggaṇhantoti sārato aggaṇhanto. Anikkujjantoti sāravaseneva idaṃ nissaraṇaṃ, ayaṃ paramatthoti hadaye aṭṭhapento. Byañjanaṃ pana tena uggahitañceva nikkujjitañca.

The saying 'Being asked about a mango, he explains a breadfruit' refers to one who, when asked, 'What is a mango like? Or what are the mango's trunk, leaves, flowers, and fruits like?' answers, 'A breadfruit is like this, or the breadfruit's trunk, leaves, flowers, and fruits are like this.' `Vijite` means in a region where one's authority prevails. `Apasādetabbaṃ` means it should be harassed. `Anabhinanditvā` means not having praised thus, 'Good, good!' `Appaṭikkositvā` means not having forbidden it thus, 'Fool! What you have said is ill-spoken!' `Anuggaṇhanto` means not grasping its essence. `Anikkujjanto` means not establishing in one's heart that 'By its very essence, this is the escape; this is the ultimate meaning.' The phrasing, however, was both grasped and established by him.

Makkhaligosālavādavaṇṇanā

An Exposition on the Doctrine of Makkhali Gosāla

167-169. Makkhalivāde [M 1.0146] paccayoti hetuvevacanameva, ubhayenāpi vijjamānameva kāyaduccaritādīnaṃ saṃkilesapaccayaṃ, kāyasucaritādīnañca visuddhipaccayaṃ paṭikkhipati. Attakāreti attakāro. Yena attanā katakammena ime sattā [P 1.0161] devattampi mārattampi brahmattampi sāvakabodhimpi paccekabodhimpi sabbaññutampi pāpuṇanti, tampi paṭikkhipati.
