Dutiyapadena yaṃ parakāraṃ parassa ovādānusāsaniṃ nissāya ṭhapetvā mahāsattaṃ avaseso jano manussasobhagyataṃ ādiṃ katvā yāva arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, taṃ parakāraṃ paṭikkhipati. Evamayaṃ bālo jinacakke pahāraṃ deti nāma. Natthi purisakāreti yena purisakārena sattā vuttappakārā sampattiyo pāpuṇanti[V 1.0134], tampi paṭikkhipati. Natthi balanti yamhi attano bale patiṭṭhitā sattā vīriyaṃ katvā tā sampattiyo pāpuṇanti, taṃ balaṃ paṭikkhipati. Natthi vīriyantiādīni sabbāni purisakāravevacanāneva. “Idaṃ no vīriyena idaṃ purisathāmena, idaṃ purisaparakkamena pavatta”nti evaṃ pavattavacanapaṭikkhepakaraṇavasena panetāni visuṃ ādiyanti.

In the doctrine of Makkhali, the word 'condition' is merely a synonym for 'cause'. By both, he denies the actually existing cause of defilement for bodily misconduct and so on, and the cause of purification for good bodily conduct and so on. By `attakāre` (self-action) is meant one's own action. He also denies that kamma by which, done by oneself, these beings attain the state of a deva, the state of Māra, the state of a Brahmā, the enlightenment of a disciple, the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha, and omniscience. By the second term, he denies that action of another (`parakāra`), namely the advice and instruction of another, relying on which—setting aside the great being—the remaining people attain human good fortune and so on, up to Arahantship. In this way, this fool is said to deliver a blow to the wheel of the Conqueror. By 'there is no human agency' (`natthi purisakāro`), he denies that human agency by which beings attain the aforementioned kinds of success. By 'there is no strength' (`natthi balaṃ`), he denies that strength of one's own, established in which beings, having made an effort, attain those successes. 'There is no energy' (`natthi vīriyaṃ`) and so on are all merely synonyms for human agency. However, these are taken up separately for the purpose of rejecting such statements as: 'This arose from our energy,' 'This from human stamina,' 'This from human exertion.'

Sabbe sattāti oṭṭhagoṇagadrabhādayo anavasese pariggaṇhāti. Sabbe pāṇāti ekindriyo pāṇo, dvindriyo pāṇotiādivasena vadati. Sabbe bhūtāti aṇḍakosavatthikosesu bhūte sandhāya vadati. Sabbe jīvāti sāliyavagodhumādayo sandhāya vadati. Tesu hi so virūhanabhāvena jīvasaññī. Avasā abalā avīriyāti tesaṃ attano vaso vā balaṃ vā vīriyaṃ vā natthi. Niyatisaṅgatibhāvapariṇatāti ettha niyatīti niyatā. Saṅgatīti channaṃ abhijātīnaṃ tattha tattha gamanaṃ. Bhāvoti sabhāvoyeva. Evaṃ niyatiyā ca saṅgatiyā ca bhāvena ca pariṇatā nānappakārataṃ pattā. Yena hi yathā bhavitabbaṃ, so tatheva bhavati. Yena na bhavitabbaṃ, so na bhavatīti dasseti. Chasvevābhijātīsūti chasu eva abhijātīsu ṭhatvā sukhañca dukkhañca paṭisaṃvedenti. Aññā sukhadukkhabhūmi natthīti dasseti.

By 'all beings' (sabbe sattā), he includes all without remainder, such as camels, cattle, and donkeys. By 'all living things' (sabbe pāṇā), he speaks with reference to beings with one sense faculty, beings with two sense faculties, and so on. By 'all creatures' (sabbe bhūtā), he speaks with reference to beings that have come to be in egg-shells and wombs. By 'all that has life' (sabbe jīvā), he speaks with reference to rice, barley, wheat, and so on. For he perceives them as having life due to their characteristic of growth. By 'without power, without strength, without energy' (avasā abalā avīriyā), it means they have no power, strength, or energy of their own. Regarding 'matured by destiny, association, and nature' (niyatisaṅgatibhāvapariṇatā): here, 'destiny' (niyati) means fixedness. 'Association' (saṅgati) means the going to this or that among the six classes of birth. 'Nature' (bhāvo) is just inherent nature. Thus, matured by destiny, association, and nature, they have attained great variety. For he shows that however one is meant to be, so one becomes; however one is not meant to be, so one does not become. By 'in the six classes of birth alone' (chasvevābhijātīsu), he shows that it is only by being established in the six classes of birth that they experience pleasure and pain, and that there is no other plane for experiencing pleasure and pain.

Yonipamukhasatasahassānīti pamukhayonīnaṃ uttamayonīnaṃ [P 1.0162] cuddasasatasahassāni aññāni ca saṭṭhisatāni aññāni ca chasatāni. Pañca ca kammuno [M 1.0147] satānīti pañcakammasatāni ca. Kevalaṃ takkamattakena niratthakaṃ diṭṭhiṃ dīpeti. Pañca ca kammāni tīṇi ca kammānītiādīsupi eseva nayo. Keci panāhu – “pañca ca kammānīti pañcindriyavasena bhaṇati. Tīṇīti kāyakammādivasenā”ti. Kamme ca upaḍḍhakamme cāti ettha panassa kāyakammañca vacīkammañca kammanti laddhi, manokammaṃ upaḍḍhakammanti. Dvaṭṭhipaṭipadāti dvāsaṭṭhi paṭipadāti vadati. Dvaṭṭhantarakappāti ekasmiṃ kappe catusaṭṭhi antarakappā nāma honti. Ayaṃ pana aññe dve ajānanto evamāha.

By 'one million four hundred and six thousand six hundred principal wombs' (yonipamukhasatasahassāni etc.) is meant: fourteen hundred thousand principal, excellent wombs; another six thousand; and another six hundred. By 'and five hundred kammas' is meant five hundred kammas. He is merely setting forth a meaningless view based on conjecture alone. This same method applies to 'five kammas and three kammas' and so on. Some, however, say: 'He says "five kammas" with reference to the five faculties. He says "three" with reference to bodily kamma and so on.' Furthermore, regarding 'a kamma and a half-kamma', his doctrine is that bodily kamma and verbal kamma are 'kamma', while mental kamma is a 'half-kamma'. By 'sixty-two paths' (dvaṭṭhipaṭipadā), he speaks of sixty-two paths. By 'sixty-two intermediate eons' (dvaṭṭhantarakappā): in one eon there are sixty-four intermediate eons, but this one, not knowing the other two, spoke thus.

Chaḷābhijātiyoti kaṇhābhijāti, nīlābhijāti, lohitābhijāti, haliddābhijāti, sukkābhijāti, paramasukkābhijātīti imā cha abhijātiyo vadati. Tattha orabbhikā, sākuṇikā, māgavikā, sūkarikā, luddā, macchaghātakā corā, coraghātakā, bandhanāgārikā, ye vā panaññepi keci kurūrakammantā, ayaṃ kaṇhābhijātīti (a. ni. 6.57) vadati. Bhikkhū nīlābhijātīti vadati, te kira catūsu paccayesu kaṇṭake pakkhipitvā khādanti. “Bhikkhū kaṇṭakavuttikā”ti (a. ni. 6.57) ayañhissa pāḷiyeva. Atha vā [V 1.0135] kaṇṭakavuttikā eva nāma eke pabbajitāti vadati. Lohitābhijāti nāma nigaṇṭhā ekasāṭakāti vadati. Ime kira purimehi dvīhi paṇḍaratarā. Gihī odātavasanā acelakasāvakā haliddābhijātīti vadati. Evaṃ attano paccayadāyake nigaṇṭhehipi jeṭṭhakatare karoti. Ājīvakā ājīvakiniyo sukkābhijātīti vadati. Te kira purimehi catūhi paṇḍaratarā. Nando, vaccho, kiso, saṅkiccho, makkhaligosālo, paramasukkābhijātīti (a. ni. 6.57) vadati. Te kira sabbehi paṇḍaratarā.

By 'six classes of birth' (chaḷābhijātiyo), he speaks of these six classes: the black class, the blue class, the red class, the yellow class, the white class, and the supremely white class. Therein, sheep-butchers, fowlers, deer-stalkers, pig-butchers, hunters, fishermen, thieves, executioners, jailers, or any others who have cruel occupations—this, he says, is the black class. Monks, he says, are the blue class; for it is said they consume the four requisites after inserting thorns into them. 'Monks have a thorny livelihood' is his own Pāli text. Alternatively, he says there are certain ascetics who are just called 'those of thorny practice'. The Nigaṇṭhas who wear a single garment, he says, are the red class; it is said they are purer than the previous two. The lay disciples of the naked ascetics who wear white clothes, he says, are the yellow class. Thus he makes his own donors of requisites out to be more senior than even the Nigaṇṭhas. Male and female Ājīvakas, he says, are the white class; it is said they are purer than the previous four. Nanda, Vaccha, Kisa, Saṅkiccha, and Makkhali Gosāla, he says, are the supremely white class; it is said they are the purest of all.

Aṭṭha purisabhūmiyoti mandabhūmi, khiḍḍābhūmi, padavīmaṃsabhūmi, ujugatabhūmi, sekkhabhūmi, samaṇabhūmi[P 1.0163], jinabhūmi, pannabhūmīti imā aṭṭha purisabhūmiyoti vadati. Tattha jātadivasato paṭṭhāya sattadivase sambādhaṭṭhānato nikkhantattā sattā mandā honti momūhā, ayaṃ mandabhūmīti vadati. Ye pana duggatito āgatā honti, te abhiṇhaṃ rodanti ceva viravanti ca, sugatito āgatā taṃ anussaritvā hasanti, ayaṃ khiḍḍābhūmi nāma. Mātāpitūnaṃ hatthaṃ vā pādaṃ vā mañcaṃ vā pīṭhaṃ vā gahetvā bhūmiyaṃ padanikkhipanaṃ padavīmaṃsabhūmi nāma. Padasā gantuṃ samatthakāle ujugatabhūmi nāma. Sippāni sikkhitakāle [M 1.0148] sekkhabhūmi nāma. Gharā nikkhamma pabbajitakāle samaṇabhūmi nāma. Ācariyaṃ sevitvā jānanakāle jinabhūmi nāma. Bhikkhu ca pannako jino na kiñci āhāti evaṃ alābhiṃ samaṇaṃ pannabhūmīti vadati.

Regarding the ‘eight stages of a man’: he speaks of these eight stages of a man: the dull stage, the playful stage, the foot-exploration stage, the upright stage, the learner stage, the ascetic stage, the conqueror stage, and the fallen stage. Therein, from the day of birth for seven days, because beings have come out from a confined place, they are dull and bewildered; this he calls the dull stage. Those who have come from a woeful state constantly weep and wail, while those who have come from a happy state, remembering it, smile; this is called the playful stage. Taking hold of the mother's or father's hand or foot, or a bed or chair, and placing a foot on the ground is called the foot-exploration stage. The time when one is able to walk on one's feet is called the upright stage. The time when one learns the arts is called the learner stage. The time when one goes forth from home into homelessness is called the ascetic stage. The time when, having served a teacher, one comes to know, is called the conqueror stage. And he calls an ascetic who receives no alms—like an old, fallen conqueror about whom it is said, 'the bhikkhu says nothing'—the fallen stage.

Ekūnapaññāsa ājīvakasateti ekūnapaññāsaājīvakavuttisatāni. Paribbājakasateti paribbājakapabbajjāsatāni. Nāgāvāsasateti nāgamaṇḍalasatāni. Vīse indriyasateti vīsatindriyasatāni. Tiṃse nirayasateti tiṃsa nirayasatāni. Rajodhātuyoti rajaokiraṇaṭṭhānāni, hatthapiṭṭhipādapiṭṭhādīni sandhāya vadati. Satta saññīgabbhāti oṭṭhagoṇagadrabhaajapasumigamahiṃse sandhāya vadati. Satta asaññīgabbhāti sālivīhiyavagodhūmakaṅguvarakakudrūsake sandhāya vadati. Nigaṇṭhigabbhāti gaṇṭhimhi jātagabbhā, ucchuveḷunaḷādayo sandhāya vadati. Satta devāti bahū devā. So pana sattāti vadati. Manussāpi anantā, so sattāti vadati. Satta [P 1.0164] pisācāti pisācā mahantamahantā sattāti vadati. Sarāti mahāsarā, kaṇṇamuṇḍarathakāraanotattasīhappapātachaddantamandākinīkuṇāladahe gahetvā vadati.

‘Forty-nine hundred livelihoods’ means forty-nine hundred modes of livelihood. ‘Hundreds of wanderers’ means hundreds of wanderer ordinations. ‘Hundreds of Nāga abodes’ means hundreds of Nāga realms. ‘Twenty hundred faculties’ means twenty hundred faculties. ‘Thirty hundred hells’ means thirty hundred hells. ‘Elements of dust’ refers to places where dust is scattered, meaning the backs of the hands, the backs of the feet, and so on. ‘Seven conscious embryonic states’ refers to the camel, ox, donkey, goat, sheep, deer, and buffalo. ‘Seven non-conscious embryonic states’ refers to fine rice, paddy, barley, wheat, millet, varaka-grain, and kudrūsaka-grain. ‘Knot-embryonic states’ refers to those whose embryos are born in knots, meaning sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, and so on. ‘Seven gods’: there are many gods, but he speaks of seven. Humans are also infinite, but he speaks of seven. ‘Seven pisācas’: pisācas are exceedingly numerous, but he speaks of seven. ‘Lakes’ refers to great lakes; taking the Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Rathakāra, Anotatta, Sīhappapāta, Chaddanta, Mandākinī, and Kuṇāla lakes, he speaks of them.

Pavuṭāti gaṇṭhikā. Papātāti mahāpapātā. Papātasatānīti khuddakapapātasatāni. Supināti mahāsupinā. Supinasatānīti khuddakasupinasatāni. Mahākappinoti mahākappānaṃ. Tattha [V 1.0136] ekamhā mahāsarā vassasate vassasate kusaggena ekaṃ udakabinduṃ nīharitvā sattakkhattuṃ tamhi sare nirudake kate eko mahākappoti vadati. Evarūpānaṃ mahākappānaṃ caturāsītisatasahassāni khepetvā bāle ca paṇḍite ca dukkhassantaṃ karontīti ayamassa laddhi. Paṇḍitopi kira antarā visujjhituṃ na sakkoti. Bālopi tato uddhaṃ na gacchati.

‘Knots’ refers to things with joints. ‘Precipices’ refers to great precipices. ‘Hundreds of precipices’ refers to seven hundred small precipices. ‘Dreams’ refers to great dreams. ‘Hundreds of dreams’ refers to seven hundred small dreams. ‘Great eons’ refers to the great eons. Therein, he says that one great eon is when, from a great lake, once every hundred years, one drop of water is removed with the tip of a blade of kusa grass, and in this way that lake is made devoid of water seven times. This is his doctrine: after passing through eighty-four hundred thousand such great eons, both fools and the wise make an end of suffering. It is said that even the wise cannot attain purification in the interim. And the fool does not go beyond that time.

Sīlenāti acelakasīlena vā aññena vā yena kenaci. Vatenāti tādiseneva vatena. Tapenāti tapokammena. Aparipakkaṃ paripāceti nāma, yo “ahaṃ paṇḍito”ti antarā visujjhati. Paripakkaṃ phussa phussa byantiṃ karoti nāma yo “ahaṃ bālo”ti vuttaparimāṇaṃ kālaṃ atikkamitvā yāti. Hevaṃ natthīti evaṃ natthi. Tañhi ubhayampi na sakkā [M 1.0149] kātunti dīpeti. Doṇamiteti doṇena mitaṃ viya. Sukhadukkheti sukhadukkhaṃ. Pariyantakateti vuttaparimāṇena kālena katapariyante. Natthi [P 1.0165] hāyanavaḍḍhaneti natthi hāyanavaḍḍhanāni. Na saṃsāro paṇḍitassa hāyati, na bālassa vaḍḍhatīti attho. Ukkaṃsāvakaṃseti ukkaṃsāvakaṃsā. Hāyanavaḍḍhanānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

By ‘morality’ is meant the morality of a naked ascetic or any other kind whatsoever. By ‘vow’ is meant a vow of that same sort. By ‘austerity’ is meant the practice of asceticism. ‘He ripens the unripe’ refers to one who, thinking ‘I am wise,’ purifies himself in the interim. ‘Having repeatedly attained the ripe, he makes it endless’ refers to one who, thinking ‘I am a fool,’ transgresses the stated measure of time and continues on. ‘This is not so’ indicates that this is not so; for it shows that neither of the two can be done. ‘Measured by a doṇa’ means as if measured with a doṇa-basket. ‘Pleasure and pain’ means pleasure and pain are measured as if by a doṇa. ‘Its limit is made’ means its limit is made by the stated measure of time. ‘There is no decrease or increase’ means there are no decreases or increases. The meaning is: saṃsāra does not decrease for the wise, nor does it increase for the fool. ‘Exaltation and diminution’ means excesses and deficiencies. This is a synonym for decrease and increase.

Idāni tamatthaṃ upamāya sādhento “seyyathāpi nāmā”tiādimāha. Tattha suttaguḷeti veṭhetvā katasuttaguḷe. Nibbeṭhiyamānameva paletīti pabbate vā rukkhagge vā ṭhatvā khittaṃ suttappamāṇena nibbeṭhiyamānameva gacchati, sutte khīṇe tattheva tiṭṭhati, na gacchati. Evameva vuttakālato uddhaṃ na gacchatīti dasseti.

Now, establishing that meaning with a simile, he said, ‘Just as…’ and so on. Therein, ‘a ball of thread’ refers to a ball of thread made by winding. ‘It runs out only as it is being unwound’ means that when thrown from a mountain or a treetop, it goes only as far as the length of the thread as it is being unwound; when the thread is exhausted, it stops right there and does not go further. In the same way, he shows that one does not go beyond the stated time.

Ajitakesakambalavādavaṇṇanā

An Exposition of the Doctrine of Ajita Kesakambala

170-172. Ajitavāde natthi dinnanti dinnaphalābhāvaṃ sandhāya vadati. Yiṭṭhaṃ vuccati mahāyāgo. Hutanti paheṇakasakkāro adhippeto. Tampi ubhayaṃ phalābhāvameva sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Sukatadukkaṭānanti sukatadukkaṭānaṃ, kusalākusalānanti attho. Phalaṃ vipākoti yaṃ phalanti vā vipākoti vā vuccati, taṃ natthīti vadati. Natthi ayaṃ lokoti paraloke ṭhitassa ayaṃ loko natthi, natthi paro lokoti idha loke ṭhitassāpi paro loko natthi, sabbe tattha tattheva ucchijjantīti dasseti. Natthi mātā natthi pitāti tesu sammāpaṭipattimicchāpaṭipattīnaṃ phalābhāvavasena vadati. Natthi sattā opapātikāti cavitvā upapajjanakā sattā nāma natthīti vadati.

In Ajita's doctrine, when it is said 'there is no gift,' it is said with reference to the non-existence of the fruit of giving. 'Yiṭṭha' is called a great sacrifice. 'Huta' is intended to mean the honor shown to guests. He rejects both of these as well, with reference to the non-existence of their fruit. 'Of good and bad deeds' means of well-done and ill-done deeds, that is, of wholesome and unwholesome actions. 'Fruit and result': he says that what is called 'fruit' or 'result' does not exist. 'There is no this world' means that for one established in the other world, this world does not exist. 'There is no other world' means that even for one established in this world, the other world does not exist; he shows that all beings are annihilated right there in their respective worlds. 'There is no mother, there is no father': he says this by way of the non-existence of fruit for right and wrong conduct towards them. 'There are no spontaneously arisen beings': he says that beings who, having passed away, are reborn, do not exist.

Cātumahābhūtikoti [V 1.0137] catumahābhūtamayo. Pathavī pathavikāyanti ajjhattikapathavīdhātu bāhirapathavīdhātuṃ. Anupetīti anuyāyati. Anupagacchatīti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Anugacchatītipi attho. Ubhayenāpi upeti, upagacchatīti dasseti. Āpādīsupi eseva nayo. Indriyānīti [P 1.0166] manacchaṭṭhāni indriyāni ākāsaṃ pakkhandanti. Āsandipañcamāti nipannamañcena pañcamā, mañco ceva cattāro mañcapāde gahetvā ṭhitā cattāro purisā cāti attho. Yāvāḷāhanāti yāva susānā. Padānīti ‘ayaṃ evaṃ sīlavā [M 1.0150] ahosi, evaṃ dussīlo’tiādinā nayena pavattāni guṇāguṇapadāni, sarīrameva vā ettha padānīti adhippetaṃ. Kāpotakānīti kapotavaṇṇāni, pārāvatapakkhavaṇṇānīti attho. Bhassantāti bhasmantā, ayameva vā pāḷi. Āhutiyoti yaṃ paheṇakasakkārādibhedaṃ dinnadānaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ chārikāvasānameva hoti, na tato paraṃ phaladāyakaṃ hutvā gacchatīti attho. Dattupaññattanti dattūhi bālamanussehi paññattaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ‘bālehi abuddhīhi paññattamidaṃ dānaṃ, na paṇḍitehi. Bālā denti, paṇḍitā gaṇhantī’ti dasseti.

'Composed of the four great elements' means made of the four great elements. Regarding 'earth goes to the earth-body,' this means the internal earth element goes towards the external earth element. 'Anupeti' means it follows. 'Anupagacchati' is a synonym for that very word. The meaning is also 'it follows along.' By both terms, it shows that 'it approaches, it goes towards.' This same method applies to the water element and so on. 'The faculties' means the faculties with the mind as the sixth leap into space. 'With the bier as the fifth': the meaning is the bier and the four men standing holding the four legs of the bier. 'As far as the charnel ground' means up to the charnel ground. 'Traces' refers to the collections of virtues and faults that have occurred in the manner of 'this one was virtuous thus, this one was immoral thus,' etc. Alternatively, here 'padāni' is intended to mean the body itself. 'Pigeon-colored' means having the color of a pigeon, the color of a dove's wings. 'Ending in ashes' means having ashes as the end. Or, this very word, bhasmantā, is the original Pali reading. 'Offerings': whatever gift is given, of various kinds such as honor shown to guests, all of it ends in ashes; it does not go beyond that to become fruit-bearing. This is the meaning. 'A precept of fools' means it was laid down by fools, by foolish people. This is what is said: 'This giving was laid down by fools, by the unwise, not by the wise.' It shows: 'Fools give, the wise take.'

Tattha pūraṇo “karoto na karīyati pāpa”nti vadanto kammaṃ paṭibāhati. Ajito “kāyassa bhedā ucchijjatī”ti vadanto vipākaṃ paṭibāhati. Makkhali “natthi hetū”ti vadanto ubhayaṃ paṭibāhati. Tattha kammaṃ paṭibāhantenāpi vipāko paṭibāhito hoti, vipākaṃ paṭibāhantenāpi kammaṃ paṭibāhitaṃ hoti. Iti sabbepete atthato ubhayappaṭibāhakā ahetukavādā ceva akiriyavādā ca natthikavādā ca honti.

Therein, Pūraṇa, saying, 'For one who acts, evil is not done,' obstructs kamma. Ajita, saying, 'At the breakup of the body, one is annihilated,' obstructs the result. Makkhali, saying, 'There is no cause,' obstructs both. Therein, even by one who obstructs kamma, the result is obstructed; and even by one who obstructs the result, kamma is obstructed. Thus, all these, in essence, are obstructors of both, proponents of causelessness, proponents of inaction, and proponents of nihilism.

Ye vā pana tesaṃ laddhiṃ gahetvā rattiṭṭhāne divāṭhāne nisinnā sajjhāyanti vīmaṃsanti, tesaṃ “karoto na karīyati pāpaṃ, natthi hetu, natthi paccayo, mato ucchijjatī”ti tasmiṃ ārammaṇe micchāsati santiṭṭhati, cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, javanāni javanti, paṭhamajavane satekicchā honti, tathā dutiyādīsu, sattame buddhānampi atekicchā anivattino ariṭṭhakaṇṭakasadisā. Tattha koci ekaṃ dassanaṃ okkamati, koci dve, koci tīṇipi, ekasmiṃ okkantepi, dvīsu [P 1.0167] tīsu okkantesupi, niyatamicchādiṭṭhikova hoti; patto saggamaggāvaraṇañceva mokkhamaggāvaraṇañca, abhabbo tassattabhāvassa anantaraṃ saggampi gantuṃ, pageva mokkhaṃ. Vaṭṭakhāṇu nāmesa satto pathavigopako, yebhuyyena evarūpassa bhavato vuṭṭhānaṃ natthi.

Furthermore, for those who, having taken up their doctrine, sit reciting and investigating by night or by day, wrong mindfulness is established in that object: 'For one who acts, evil is not done; there is no cause, no condition; upon death, one is annihilated.' The mind becomes one-pointed, the impulsive moments of consciousness run their course. In the first impulsive moment, they are curable; likewise in the second and so on. In the seventh, they are incurable even by the Buddhas, irreversible, like Ariṭṭha and Kaṇṭaka. Therein, some enter upon one view, some two, some even three. Having entered upon one, two, or three, one becomes of fixed wrong view. One has reached what is an obstruction to the path to heaven and an obstruction to the path to liberation. Immediately after that existence, one is incapable of going even to heaven, much less to liberation. This being is called a 'stake in the round of rebirths,' a guardian of the earth. For the most part, for one of such a nature, there is no rising up from that state of existence.

“Tasmā [V 1.0138] akalyāṇajanaṃ, āsīvisamivoragaṃ;

Ārakā parivajjeyya, bhūtikāmo vicakkhaṇo”ti.

Therefore, a discerning person who desires well-being should avoid an unvirtuous person from afar, like a venomous snake.

Pakudhakaccāyanavādavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Doctrine of Pakudha Kaccāyana

173-175. Pakudhavāde [M 1.0151] akaṭāti akatā. Akaṭavidhāti akatavidhānā. Evaṃ karohīti kenaci kārāpitāpi na hontīti attho. Animmitāti iddhiyāpi na nimmitā. Animmātāti animmāpitā, keci animmāpetabbāti padaṃ vadanti, taṃ neva pāḷiyaṃ, na aṭṭhakathāyaṃ dissati. Vañjhādipadattayaṃ vuttatthameva. Na iñjantīti esikatthambho viya ṭhitattā na calanti. Na vipariṇamantīti pakatiṃ na jahanti. Na aññamaññaṃ byābādhentīti na aññamaññaṃ upahananti. Nālanti na samatthā. Pathavikāyotiādīsu pathavīyeva pathavikāyo, pathavisamūho vā. Tatthāti tesu jīvasattamesu kāyesu. Sattannaṃ tveva kāyānanti yathā muggarāsiādīsu pahataṃ satthaṃ muggādīnaṃ antarena pavisati, evaṃ sattannaṃ kāyānaṃ antarena chiddena vivarena satthaṃ pavisati. Tattha ahaṃ imaṃ jīvitā voropemīti kevalaṃ saññāmattameva hotīti dasseti.

In the doctrine of Pakudha, akaṭā means not made. Akaṭavidhā means having no arrangement for being made. The meaning is that even when caused to be made by someone saying, 'Do thus!', they do not come to be. Animmitā means not fashioned, even by psychic power. Animmātā means not caused to be fashioned. Some say the word is animmāpetabbā, but that word is not seen in the Pāḷi, nor in the commentary. The group of three words beginning with 'barren' has the meaning already stated. Na iñjanti (they do not move) means that because they are established like a door-post, they do not move. Na vipariṇamanti (they do not change) means they do not abandon their own nature. Na aññamaññaṃ byābādhenti (they do not harm one another) means they do not oppress one another. Nālaṃ means they are not able. In the words beginning with pathavikāyo (earth-body), the earth element itself is the earth-body, or a collection of the earth element is. Tattha (therein) means in those bodies which have life as the seventh. By the text sattannaṃ tveva kāyānaṃ (of the seven bodies), it is shown that just as a weapon that is struck enters through the space between beans, etc., in a heap of beans, etc., in the same way, a weapon enters through the space, through the opening, through the cavity, between the seven bodies. In that case, the thought, 'I deprive this one of the life faculty,' is merely a perception.

Nigaṇṭhanāṭaputtavādavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Doctrine of Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta

176-178. Nāṭaputtavāde cātuyāmasaṃvarasaṃvutoti catukoṭṭhāsena saṃvarena saṃvuto. Sabbavārivārito [P 1.0168] cāti vāritasabbaudako paṭikkhittasabbasītodakoti attho. So kira sītodake sattasaññī hoti, tasmā na taṃ vaḷañjeti. Sabbavāriyuttoti sabbena pāpavāraṇena yutto. Sabbavāridhutoti sabbena pāpavāraṇena dhutapāpo. Sabbavāriphuṭoti sabbena pāpavāraṇena phuṭṭho. Gatattoti koṭippattacitto. Yatattoti saṃyatacitto. Ṭhitattoti suppatiṭṭhitacitto. Etassa vāde kiñci sāsanānulomampi atthi, asuddhaladdhitāya pana sabbā diṭṭhiyeva jātā.

In the doctrine of Nāṭaputta, cātuyāmasaṃvarasaṃvuto (restrained by the fourfold restraint) means he is restrained by the restraint in four parts. Sabbavārivārito ca (and restrained from all water) means he is one for whom all water is prevented, one for whom all cold water is rejected; this is the meaning. It is said that he has the perception of beings in cold water; therefore, he does not use it. Sabbavāriyutto (endowed with all restraints) means endowed with the prevention of all evil. Sabbavāridhuto (having shaken off all restraints) means he is one whose evil has been shaken off by means of preventing all evil. Sabbavāriphuṭṭho (touched by all restraints) means he is touched by the prevention of all evil. Gatatto (one who has reached the self) is said to be one whose mind has reached the summit. Yatatto (one who is restrained in self) is said to be one whose mind is restrained. Ṭhitatto (one who is firm in self) is said to be one whose mind is well-established. In his doctrine, there is something that is in accordance with the Dispensation, but because of having an impure doctrine, all of it has become wrong view only.

Sañcayabelaṭṭhaputtavādavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Doctrine of Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta

179-181. Sañcayavādo amarāvikkhepe vuttanayo eva.

The doctrine of Sañcaya has the same method as that stated in the section on the Amarāvikkhepa.

Paṭhamasandiṭṭhikasāmaññaphalavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the First Visible Fruit of the Ascetic Life

182. Sohaṃ[V 1.0139][M 1.0152], bhanteti so ahaṃ bhante, vālukaṃ pīḷetvā telaṃ alabhamāno viya titthiyavādesu sāraṃ alabhanto bhagavantaṃ pucchāmīti attho.

182. The meaning of sohaṃ, bhante (I, venerable sir) is: 'I, venerable sir, like one who, having pressed sand, does not obtain oil, not obtaining the essence in the doctrines of the sectarians, ask the Blessed One.'

183. Yathā te khameyyāti yathā te rucceyya. Dāsoti antojātadhanakkītakaramarānītasāmaṃdāsabyopagatānaṃ aññataro. Kammakāroti analaso kammakaraṇasīloyeva. Dūrato disvā paṭhamameva uṭṭhahatīti pubbuṭṭhāyī. Evaṃ uṭṭhito sāmino āsanaṃ paññapetvā pādadhovanādikattabbakiccaṃ katvā pacchā nipatati nisīdatīti pacchānipātī. Sāmikamhi vā sayanato avuṭṭhite pubbeyeva vuṭṭhātīti pubbuṭṭhāyī. Paccūsakālato paṭṭhāya yāva sāmino rattiṃ niddokkamanaṃ, tāva sabbakiccāni katvā pacchā nipatati, seyyaṃ kappetīti pacchānipātī. Kiṃ karomi, kiṃ karomīti evaṃ kiṃkārameva paṭisuṇanto vicaratīti kiṃ kārapaṭissāvī. Manāpameva kiriyaṃ karotīti manāpacārī. Piyameva vadatīti piyavādī. Sāmino tuṭṭhapahaṭṭhaṃ mukhaṃ ullokayamāno vicaratīti mukhullokako.

183. “As it pleases you” means as it is agreeable to you. “A slave” refers to one among these: one born in the household, one purchased with wealth, one brought as a captive of war, or one who has become a slave of his own accord. “A worker” means one who is not lazy and is accustomed to doing work. He is called pubbuṭṭhāyī (one who rises first) because, seeing his master from afar, he rises first of all. Having thus risen, he prepares a seat for his master, performs the necessary duties such as washing his feet, and afterwards lies down or sits down; therefore, he is called pacchānipātī (one who lies down last). Alternatively, he is called pubbuṭṭhāyī because he rises before his master has risen from bed. He is called pacchānipātī because, from dawn until his master goes to sleep at night, he performs all duties and only then lies down and prepares his bed. He is called kiṃkārapaṭissāvī (one who is responsive to what is to be done) because he goes about hearkening for what to do, saying, “What shall I do? What shall I do?” He is called manāpacārī (one who acts agreeably) because he performs only agreeable actions. He is called piyavādī (one who speaks endearingly) because he speaks only endearing words. He is called mukhullokiko (one who looks up to the face) because he goes about looking up to his master's pleased and delighted face.

Devo maññeti devo viya. So [P 1.0169] vatassāhaṃ puññāni kareyyanti so vata ahaṃ evarūpo assaṃ, yadi puññāni kareyyanti attho. “So vatassa’ssa”ntipi pāṭho, ayamevattho. Yaṃnūnāhanti sace dānaṃ dassāmi, yaṃ rājā ekadivasaṃ deti, tato satabhāgampi yāvajīvaṃ na sakkhissāmi dātunti pabbajjāyaṃ ussāhaṃ katvā evaṃ cintanabhāvaṃ dasseti.

Devo maññe (he considers him a god) means like a god. The meaning of so vatassāhaṃ puññāni kareyyaṃ (Oh, that I might perform meritorious deeds!) is: 'Oh, that I might become of such a nature like that one, if I were to perform meritorious deeds!' There is also the reading so vatassa’ssaṃ; this has the very same meaning. By the text yaṃnūnāhaṃ (what if I...), it shows the state of thinking thus, having made an effort towards the going forth: 'If I were to give alms, I would not be able to give for my whole life even a hundredth part of what the king gives in a single day. I shall go forth!'

Kāyena saṃvutoti kāyena pihito hutvā akusalassa pavesanadvāraṃ thaketvāti attho. Eseva nayo sesapadadvayepi. Ghāsacchādanaparamatāyāti ghāsacchādanena paramatāya uttamatāya, etadatthampi anesanaṃ pahāya aggasallekhena santuṭṭhoti attho. Abhirato paviveketi “kāyaviveko ca vivekaṭṭhakāyānaṃ, cittaviveko ca nekkhammābhiratānaṃ, paramavodānappattānaṃ upadhiviveko ca nirupadhīnaṃ puggalānaṃ visaṅkhāragatāna”nti evaṃ vutte tividhepi viveke rato; gaṇasaṅgaṇikaṃ [M 1.0153] pahāya kāyena eko viharati, cittakilesasaṅgaṇikaṃ pahāya aṭṭhasamāpattivasena eko viharati, phalasamāpattiṃ vā nirodhasamāpattiṃ vā pavisitvā nibbānaṃ patvā viharatīti attho. Yaggheti codanatthe nipāto.

Kāyena saṃvuto (restrained in body) means: having been closed off by the body, having shut the entrance for the unwholesome; this is the meaning. This is the same method for the remaining two terms. Ghāsacchādanaparamatāya (with food and clothing as the highest) means: he is content through the supreme practice of effacement, having abandoned improper seeking even for the sake of this food and clothing, which is the highest, the supreme; this is the meaning. Abhirato paviveke (delighting in seclusion) means: he delights in the three kinds of seclusion spoken of thus: 'There is bodily seclusion for those whose bodies are secluded; there is mental seclusion for those who delight in renunciation, who have reached supreme purity; and there is seclusion from the substrata of existence for those who are without substrata, for individuals who have gone beyond formations.' The meaning is: having abandoned socializing with a group, he dwells alone in body; having abandoned the socializing of mental defilements, he dwells alone by means of the eight attainments; or, having entered the fruition attainment or the cessation attainment, he dwells having reached Nibbāna. Yagghe is a particle that occurs in the sense of urging.

184. Āsanenapi [V 1.0140] nimanteyyāmāti nisinnāsanaṃ papphoṭetvā idha nisīdathāti vadeyyāma. Abhinimanteyyāmapi nanti abhiharitvāpi naṃ nimanteyyāma. Tattha duvidho abhihāro – vācāya ceva kāyena ca. Tumhākaṃ icchiticchitakkhaṇe amhākaṃ cīvarādīhi vadeyyātha yenatthoti vadanto hi vācāya abhiharitvā nimanteti nāma. Cīvarādivekallaṃ sallakkhetvā idaṃ gaṇhāthāti tāni dento pana kāyena abhiharitvā nimanteti nāma. Tadubhayampi sandhāya abhinimanteyyāmapi [P 1.0170] nanti āha. Ettha ca gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāroti yaṃ kiñci gilānassa sappāyaṃ osadhaṃ. Vacanattho pana visuddhimagge vutto. Rakkhāvaraṇaguttinti rakkhāsaṅkhātañceva āvaraṇasaṅkhātañca guttiṃ. Sā panesā na āvudhahatthe purise ṭhapentena dhammikā nāma saṃvidahitā hoti. Yathā pana avelāya kaṭṭhahārikapaṇṇahārikādayo vihāraṃ na pavisanti, migaluddakādayo vihārasīmāya mige vā macche vā na gaṇhanti, evaṃ saṃvidahantena dhammikā nāma rakkhā saṃvihitā hoti, taṃ sandhāyāha – “dhammika”nti.

184. ‘We would invite even with a seat’ means that, having shaken out the seat one is sitting on, we would say, ‘Sit here.’ ‘We would also invite him by bringing forward’ means we would invite him by bringing something forward. Herein, bringing forward is twofold: by speech and by body. Indeed, one who says, ‘At any moment you wish, I will provide for your use requisites such as robes; please state what is needed,’ invites by bringing forward with speech. On the other hand, one who, having noticed a lack of robes or other requisites, gives them, saying, ‘Please accept this,’ invites by bringing forward with the body. It was with reference to both of these that he said, ‘We would also invite him by bringing forward.’ And here, ‘requisites of medicine for the sick’ means any medicine whatsoever that is suitable for the sick. The word-meaning, however, has been stated by me in the Visuddhimagga. ‘Protection, safeguard, and security’ means the security which is designated as protection and as a safeguard. This righteous security, however, is not arranged by one who stations men with weapons in hand. But when it is arranged so that, for instance, women gathering firewood or leaves do not enter the monastery at an improper time, and hunters and the like do not catch deer or fish within the monastery boundary, then a righteous protection is arranged. It was with reference to this that he said, ‘righteous.’

185. Yadi evaṃ santeti yadi tava dāso tuyhaṃ santikā abhivādanādīni labheyya. Evaṃ sante. Addhāti ekaṃsavacanametaṃ. Paṭhamanti bhaṇanto aññassāpi atthitaṃ dīpeti. Teneva ca rājā sakkā pana, bhante, aññampītiādimāha.

185. ‘If it were so’ means: if your slave were to obtain from you benefits such as respectful salutation, this being so... ‘Indeed’ (addhā) is a word expressing certainty. In saying ‘the first,’ He reveals the existence of another as well. For that very reason, the king said, ‘But, venerable sir, is it possible for another...?’ and so on.

Dutiyasandiṭṭhikasāmaññaphalavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Second Visible Fruit of Recluseship

186-188. Kasatīti kassako. Gehassa pati, ekagehamatte jeṭṭhakoti gahapatiko. Balisaṅkhātaṃ karaṃ karotīti karakārako. Dhaññarāsiṃ dhanarāsiñca vaḍḍhetīti rāsivaḍḍhako.

‘He ploughs’ (kasati), therefore he is a farmer (kassako). He is the ‘master of a house’ (gehassa pati), the chief in a single house, therefore he is a householder (gahapatiko). ‘He produces the tax’ (karaṃ karoti) designated as a levy, therefore he is a tax-payer (karakārako). ‘He increases the heap’ (rāsiṃ vaḍḍheti) of grain and the heap of wealth, therefore he is an increaser of heaps (rāsivaḍḍhako).

Appaṃ [M 1.0154] vāti parittakaṃ vā antamaso taṇḍulanāḷimattakampi. Bhogakkhandhanti bhogarāsiṃ. Mahantaṃ vāti vipulaṃ vā. Yathā hi mahantaṃ pahāya pabbajituṃ dukkaraṃ, evaṃ appampīti dassanatthaṃ ubhayamāha. Dāsavāre pana yasmā dāso attanopi anissaro, pageva bhogānaṃ. Yañhi tassa dhanaṃ, taṃ sāmikānaññeva hoti, tasmā bhogaggahaṇaṃ na kataṃ. Ñātiyeva ñātiparivaṭṭo.

‘Or a little’ means a small amount, or at the very least, as much as a nāḷi measure of rice. ‘A mass of wealth’ means a heap of wealth. ‘Or great’ means extensive. Indeed, just as it is difficult to go forth having abandoned a great mass of wealth, so too is it difficult having abandoned even a small amount. To show this, he spoke of both. In the section on the slave, however, since a slave is not master even of himself, how much less of wealth? For whatever wealth he has belongs to his masters alone. Therefore, the mention of wealth was not made. Kinsfolk themselves are the circle of kinsfolk.

Paṇītatarasāmaññaphalavaṇṇanā

An Exposition of the More Sublime Fruit of Recluseship

189. Sakkā pana, bhante, aññampi diṭṭheva dhammeti idha evamevāti na vuttaṃ. Taṃ kasmāti [V 1.0141] ce, evamevāti hi vuccamāne pahoti bhagavā sakalampi rattindivaṃ tato vā bhiyyopi evarūpāhi upamāhi sāmaññaphalaṃ dīpetuṃ. Tattha kiñcāpi etassa bhagavato vacanasavane pariyantaṃ nāma natthi, tathāpi attho tādisoyeva bhavissatīti cintetvā [P 1.0171] upari visesaṃ pucchanto evamevāti avatvā – “abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañcā”ti āha. Tattha abhikkantataranti abhimanāpataraṃ atiseṭṭhataranti attho. Paṇītataranti uttamataraṃ. Tena hīti uyyojanatthe nipāto. Savane uyyojento hi naṃ evamāha. Suṇohīti abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca sāmaññaphalaṃ suṇāti.

189. In the passage, ‘But, venerable sir, is it possible to point out another fruit of recluseship visible in this very life?’, the words ‘It is just so’ were not spoken. If it is asked, ‘Why is that?’, the answer is: if ‘It is just so’ were said, the Blessed One would be able to explain the fruit of recluseship with such similes for a whole day and night, or even longer. In that case, although there is indeed no limit to hearing the words of this Blessed One, the king, thinking, ‘Nevertheless, the meaning will be just the same,’ and wishing to ask about a further distinction, did not say, ‘It is just so,’ but said, ‘more excellent and more sublime.’ Therein, abhikkantatara means more pleasing, more excellent. Paṇītatara means more supreme. Tena hi is a particle in the sense of urging. Indeed, wishing to urge him to listen, He said this to him. Suṇohi means: ‘Listen to the fruit of recluseship that is more excellent and more sublime.’

Sādhukaṃ manasikarohīti ettha pana sādhukaṃ sādhūti ekatthametaṃ. Ayañhi sādhu-saddo āyācanasampaṭicchanasampahaṃsanasundara daḷhīkammādīsu dissati. “Sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṅkhittena dhammaṃ desetū”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.95) hi āyācane dissati. “Sādhu, bhanteti kho so bhikkhu bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.86) sampaṭicchane. “Sādhu sādhu, sāriputtā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.349) sampahaṃsane.

Now, in the phrase ‘attend well,’ sādhukaṃ and sādhu have the same meaning. For this word sādhu is seen in the senses of requesting, accepting, rejoicing, ‘good,’ strengthening, and so on. For instance, in passages such as, ‘Good, venerable sir, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief,’ it is seen in the sense of requesting. In passages such as, ‘“Good, venerable sir,” that bhikkhu, having delighted in and rejoiced at the Blessed One’s statement...,’ it is seen in the sense of accepting. In passages such as, ‘Good, good, Sāriputta,’ it is seen in the sense of rejoicing.

“Sādhu dhammaruci rājā, sādhu paññāṇavā naro;

Sādhu mittānamaddubbho, pāpassākaraṇaṃ sukha”nti. (jā. 2.17.101);

‘Good is a king who delights in the Dhamma; good is a person endowed with wisdom; good is one who is not treacherous to friends; the non-commission of evil is happiness.’

Ādīsu sundare. “Tena hi, brāhmaṇa, suṇohi sādhukaṃ manasi karohī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 5.192) sādhukasaddoyeva daḷhīkamme, āṇattiyantipi vuccati[M 1.0155]. Idhāpi assa ettheva daḷhīkamme ca āṇattiyañca veditabbo. Sundarepi vaṭṭati. Daḷhīkammatthena hi daḷhamimaṃ dhammaṃ suṇāhi, suggahitaṃ gaṇhanto. Āṇattiatthena mama āṇattiyā suṇāhi, sundaratthena sundaramimaṃ bhaddakaṃ dhammaṃ suṇāhīti evaṃ dīpitaṃ hoti.

In the preceding and other passages, it is seen in the sense of ‘good.’ In passages such as, ‘Well then, brahmin, listen and attend well,’ the word sādhuka itself is also said to be in the sense of strengthening and command. Here too, this word sādhuka should be understood in this very sense of strengthening and command. It is also suitable in the sense of ‘good.’ For, by the meaning of strengthening, it is explained thus: ‘Listen to this Dhamma steadfastly, grasping it well.’ By the meaning of command: ‘Listen by my command.’ By the meaning of ‘good’: ‘Listen to this good, excellent Dhamma.’

Manasi karohīti āvajja, samannāharāti attho, avikkhittacitto hutvā nisāmehi, citte karohīti adhippāyo. Api cettha suṇohīti sotindriyavikkhepanivāraṇametaṃ. Sādhukaṃ manasi karohīti manasikāre daḷhīkammaniyojanena manindriyavikkhepanivāraṇaṃ. Purimañcettha byañjanavipallāsaggāhavāraṇaṃ, pacchimaṃ atthavipallāsaggāhavāraṇaṃ. Purimena ca dhammassavane niyojeti, pacchimena sutānaṃ dhammānaṃ dhāraṇūpaparikkhādīsu. Purimena ca sabyañjano ayaṃ dhammo, tasmā savanīyoti dīpeti[P 1.0172]. Pacchimena sattho, tasmā sādhukaṃ manasi kātabboti. Sādhukapadaṃ [V 1.0142] vā ubhayapadehi yojetvā yasmā ayaṃ dhammo dhammagambhīro ceva desanāgambhīro ca, tasmā suṇāhi sādhukaṃ, yasmā atthagambhīro ca paṭivedhagambhīro ca, tasmā sādhukaṃ manasi karohīti evaṃ yojanā veditabbā. Bhāsissāmīti sakkā mahārājāti evaṃ paṭiññātaṃ sāmaññaphaladesanaṃ vitthārato bhāsissāmi. “Desessāmī”ti hi saṅkhittadīpanaṃ hoti. Bhāsissāmīti vitthāradīpanaṃ. Tenāha vaṅgīsatthero –

Manasi karohi means 'reflect,' 'bring well to mind'; this is the meaning. The intention is: 'having become one with an undistracted mind, listen intently,' 'place it in the mind.' Furthermore, herein, suṇohi is for preventing the distraction of the ear-faculty. Sādhukaṃ manasi karohi is for preventing the distraction of the mind-faculty by way of enjoining the strengthening of attention. And herein, the former term is for preventing the perverse grasping of the phrasing, while the latter is for preventing the perverse grasping of the meaning. And by the former, He enjoins the hearing of the Dhamma; by the latter, He enjoins the retention, examination, and so on, of the teachings that have been heard. And by the former, He shows: 'This Dhamma is endowed with phrasing, therefore it should be heard.' By the latter: 'It is endowed with meaning, therefore it should be well attended to in the mind.' Or, the word sādhukaṃ can be connected with both phrases, and the construction should be understood thus: 'Because this Dhamma is profound in its teaching and profound in its exposition, therefore listen well. Because it is profound in its meaning and profound in its penetration, therefore attend well in the mind.' Bhāsissāmi means: 'I will speak in detail on the teaching of the fruit of recluseship that was promised thus, "It is possible, great king."' For desessāmi is an explanation in brief, whereas bhāsissāmi is an explanation in detail. Therefore, the Elder Vaṅgīsa said:

“Saṅkhittenapi deseti, vitthārenapi bhāsati;

Sāḷikāyiva nigghoso, paṭibhānaṃ udīrayī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.214);

“He teaches concisely and speaks at length; like the call of the Sāḷikā bird, he utters inspired speech.”

Evaṃ vutte ussāhajāto hutvā – “evaṃ, bhante”ti kho rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto bhagavato paccassosi bhagavato vacanaṃ sampaṭicchi, paṭiggahesīti vuttaṃ hoti.

When this was said, King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Videha queen, having become filled with enthusiasm, replied to the Blessed One, “So be it, venerable sir.” This means that he listened back to the Blessed One; he accepted the Blessed One's word; he received it.

190. Athassa bhagavā etadavoca, etaṃ avoca, idāni vattabbaṃ “idha mahārājā”tiādiṃ sakalaṃ suttaṃ avocāti attho. Tattha idhāti desāpadese nipāto, svāyaṃ katthaci lokaṃ upādāya vuccati. Yathāha – “idha tathāgato loke uppajjatī”ti. Katthaci sāsanaṃ yathāha [M 1.0156] – “idheva, bhikkhave, paṭhamo samaṇo, idha dutiyo samaṇo”ti (a. ni. 4.241). Katthaci okāsaṃ. Yathāha –

190. Then the Blessed One said this to him. “He said this” means: He spoke the entire sutta that should now be spoken, beginning with “Here, great king.” Therein, idha is a particle used in the sense of indicating a place. It is sometimes spoken with reference to the world, as was said: “Here, a Tathāgata arises in the world.” Sometimes it is spoken with reference to the Dispensation, as was said: “Here, monks, is the first recluse; here, the second recluse...” Sometimes it is spoken with reference to a location, as was said:

“Idheva tiṭṭhamānassa, devabhūtassa me sato;

Punarāyu ca me laddho, evaṃ jānāhi mārisā”ti. (dī. ni. 2.369);

“While I was standing right here, having become a deva and being mindful, a renewed life-span was obtained by me. Know this, good sirs.”

Katthaci padapūraṇamattameva. Yathāha “idhāhaṃ, bhikkhave, bhuttāvī assaṃ pavārito”ti (ma. ni. 1.30). Idha pana lokaṃ upādāya vuttoti veditabbo. Mahārājāti yathā paṭiññātaṃ desanaṃ desetuṃ puna mahārājāti ālapati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “mahārāja imasmiṃ loke [P 1.0173] tathāgato uppajjati arahaṃ…pe… buddho bhagavā”ti. Tattha tathāgatasaddo brahmajāle vutto. Arahantiādayo visuddhimagge vitthāritā. Loke uppajjatīti ettha pana lokoti – okāsaloko sattaloko saṅkhāralokoti tividho. Idha pana sattaloko adhippeto. Sattaloke uppajjamānopi ca tathāgato na devaloke, na brahmaloke, manussalokeva uppajjati. Manussalokepi na aññasmiṃ cakkavāḷe, imasmiṃyeva cakkavāḷe. Tatrāpi na sabbaṭṭhānesu, “puratthimāya disāya gajaṅgalaṃ nāma nigamo tassāparena mahāsālo, tato parā paccantimā janapadā [V 1.0143] orato majjhe, puratthimadakkhiṇāya disāya salaḷavatī nāma nadī. Tato parā paccantimā janapadā, orato majjhe, dakkhiṇāya disāya setakaṇṇikaṃ nāma nigamo, tato parā paccantimā janapadā, orato majjhe, pacchimāya disāya thūṇaṃ nāma brāhmaṇagāmo, tato parā paccantimā janapadā, orato majjhe, uttarāya disāya usiraddhajo nāma pabbato, tato parā paccantimā janapadā orato majjhe”ti evaṃ paricchinne āyāmato tiyojanasate, vitthārato aḍḍhateyyayojanasate, parikkhepato navayojanasate majjhimapadese uppajjati. Na kevalañca tathāgato, paccekabuddhā, aggasāvakā, asītimahātherā, buddhamātā, buddhapitā, cakkavattī rājā aññe ca sārappattā brāhmaṇagahapatikā etthevuppajjanti.

In some places, it is merely for the purpose of filling out the words. As it is said: “Here, monks, I, having eaten, would be satisfied” (MN 1.30). Here, however, it should be understood as spoken with reference to the world. “Great king”—in order to teach the discourse as was promised, he again addresses him as “great king.” This is what is said: “Great king, in this world, a Tathāgata arises, an Arahant… the Buddha, the Bhagavā.” Therein, the term “Tathāgata” is explained in the Brahmajāla Sutta. The terms “Arahant” and so on are elaborated upon in the Visuddhimagga. As for ‘arises in the world’—here, ‘world’ (loka) is threefold: the world of space (okāsaloka), the world of beings (sattaloka), and the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka). Here, however, the world of beings is intended. And although arising in the world of beings, the Tathāgata does not arise in the world of devas, nor in the world of brahmās; he arises only in the human world. Even in the human world, he does not arise in another universe, but only in this very universe. Nor does he arise in all places within it, but only in the central region defined thus: “To the east is a market town named Gajaṅgala, beyond it the great Sāla forest, then the borderlands—within the middle region; to the southeast is a river named Salaḷavatī, beyond it the borderlands—within the middle region; to the south is a market town named Setakaṇṇika, beyond it the borderlands—within the middle region; to the west is a brahmin village named Thūṇa, beyond it the borderlands—within the middle region; to the north is a mountain named Usiraddhaja, beyond it the borderlands—within the middle region.” This region is three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty yojanas in width, and nine hundred yojanas in circumference. And not only the Tathāgata, but also Paccekabuddhas, the chief disciples, the eighty great elders, the Buddha’s mother, the Buddha’s father, a wheel-turning monarch, and other brahmins and householders who have attained the essence arise only here.

Tattha [M 1.0157] tathāgato sujātāya dinnamadhupāyāsabhojanato yāva arahattamaggo, tāva uppajjati nāma, arahattaphale uppanno nāma. Mahābhinikkhamanato vā yāva arahattamaggo. Tusitabhavanato vā yāva arahattamaggo. Dīpaṅkarapādamūlato vā yāva arahattamaggo, tāva uppajjati nāma, arahattaphale [P 1.0174] uppanno nāma. Idha sabbapaṭhamaṃ uppannabhāvaṃ sandhāya uppajjatīti vuttaṃ. Tathāgato loke uppanno hotīti ayañhettha attho.

Therein, the Tathāgata is called 'arising' from the time of eating the milk-rice offered by Sujātā up until the path of Arahantship; at the fruit of Arahantship, he is called 'arisen'. Or, from the Great Renunciation up until the path of Arahantship. Or, from the Tusita realm up until the path of Arahantship. Or, from the time at the feet of Dīpaṅkara up until the path of Arahantship, he is called 'arising'; at the fruit of Arahantship, he is called 'arisen'. Here, 'he arises' is said with reference to the very first state of having arisen. The meaning here is this: The Tathāgata has arisen in the world.

So imaṃ lokanti so bhagavā imaṃ lokaṃ. Idāni vattabbaṃ nidasseti. Sadevakanti saha devehi sadevakaṃ. Evaṃ saha mārena samārakaṃ, saha brahmunā sabrahmakaṃ, saha samaṇabrāhmaṇehi sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ. Pajātattā pajā, taṃ pajaṃ. Saha devamanussehi sadevamanussaṃ. Tattha sadevakavacanena pañca kāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Samāraka – vacanena chaṭṭhakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ. Sabrahmakavacanena brahmakāyikādibrahmaggahaṇaṃ. Sassamaṇabrāhmaṇīvacanena sāsanassa paccatthikapaccāmittasamaṇabrāhmaṇaggahaṇaṃ, samitapāpabāhitapāpasamaṇabrāhmaṇaggahaṇañca. Pajāvacanena sattalokaggahaṇaṃ. Sadevamanussavacanena sammutidevaavasesamanussaggahaṇaṃ. Evamettha tīhi padehi okāsalokena saddhiṃ sattaloko. Dvīhi pajāvasena sattalokova gahitoti veditabbo.

‘He, this world’ means: that Blessed One points out this world which is now to be spoken of. ‘With its devas’ means ‘together with the devas.’ Similarly, ‘with its Māra’ means ‘together with Māra’; ‘with its Brahmā’ means ‘together with Brahmā’; ‘with its ascetics and brahmins’ means ‘together with ascetics and brahmins.’ Because of being born, they are called ‘progeny’; this refers to that progeny. ‘With its devas and humans’ means ‘together with devas and humans.’ Therein, by the word ‘with its devas,’ the inclusion of the devas of the five sense-sphere realms should be understood. By the word ‘with its Māra,’ the inclusion of the devas of the sixth sense-sphere realm. By the word ‘with its Brahmā,’ the inclusion of the brahmās beginning with the Brahmakāyika group. By the word ‘with its ascetics and brahmins,’ the inclusion of ascetics and brahmins who are opponents and adversaries of the Teaching, and also of ascetics with pacified evil and brahmins with banished evil. By the word ‘progeny,’ the inclusion of the world of beings. By the word ‘with its devas and humans,’ the inclusion of conventional devas and the remaining humans. Thus, herein, by three terms, the world of space is included; by two terms, by way of ‘progeny,’ the world of beings is included. Thus it should be understood.

Aparo nayo, sadevakaggahaṇena arūpāvacaradevaloko gahito. Samārakaggahaṇena cha kāmāvacaradevaloko. Sabrahmakaggahaṇena rūpī brahmaloko. Sassamaṇabrāhmaṇādiggahaṇena catuparisavasena sammutidevehi vā saha manussaloko, avasesasabbasattaloko vā.

Another method: by the term ‘with its devas,’ the formless-sphere deva-world is included. By the term ‘with its Māra,’ the six sense-sphere deva-worlds are included. By the term ‘with its Brahmā,’ the form-sphere brahmā-world is included. By the term ‘with its ascetics and brahmins, etc.,’ the human world is included by way of the four assemblies; or the human world together with conventional devas; or all the remaining world of beings.

Api cettha sadevakavacanena ukkaṭṭhaparicchedato sabbassa lokassa sacchikatabhāvamāha. Tato [V 1.0144] yesaṃ ahosi – “māro mahānubhāvo cha kāmāvacarissaro vasavattī, kiṃ sopi etena sacchikato”ti, tesaṃ [P 1.0175] vimatiṃ vidhamanto “samāraka”nti āha. Yesaṃ pana ahosi – “brahmā mahānubhāvo ekaṅguliyā ekasmiṃ cakkavāḷasahasse ālokaṃ pharati, dvīhi [M 1.0158] …pe… dasahi aṅgulīhi dasasu cakkavāḷasahassesu ālokaṃ pharati. Anuttarañca jhānasamāpattisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti, kiṃ sopi sacchikato”ti, tesaṃ vimatiṃ vidhamanto sabrahmakanti āha. Tato ye cintesuṃ – “puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇā sāsanassa paccatthikā, kiṃ tepi sacchikatā”ti, tesaṃ vimatiṃ vidhamanto sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ pajanti āha. Evaṃ ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭhānaṃ sacchikatabhāvaṃ pakāsetvā atha sammutideve avasesamanusse ca upādāya ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavasena sesasattalokassa sacchikatabhāvaṃ pakāsento sadevamanussanti āha. Ayamettha bhāvānukkamo.

Furthermore, herein, by the word ‘with its devas,’ by way of the highest determination, he stated the direct realization of the entire world. Then, for those who had the doubt, “Māra is of great power, the lord of the six sense-sphere realms, the wielder of power—has he too been directly realized by this one?”—dispelling their doubt, he said, ‘with its Māra.’ For those who had the doubt, “Brahmā is of great power; with one finger he illuminates a thousand world-systems… with ten fingers he illuminates ten thousand world-systems. He experiences the unsurpassed bliss of jhāna-attainment—has he too been directly realized?”—dispelling their doubt, he said, ‘with its Brahmā.’ Then, for those who thought, “There are many ascetics and brahmins who are opponents of the Teaching—have they too been directly realized?”—dispelling their doubt, he said, ‘with its ascetics and brahmins, the progeny.’ Thus, having declared the direct realization of the most excellent ones, he then, taking into account conventional devas and the remaining humans, declared the direct realization of the remaining world of beings by way of the highest determination, saying ‘with its devas and humans.’ This, herein, is the sequence of meaning according to the view of others.

Porāṇā panāhu sadevakanti devehi saddhiṃ avasesalokaṃ. Samārakanti mārena saddhiṃ avasesalokaṃ. Sabrahmakanti brahmehi saddhiṃ avasesalokaṃ. Evaṃ sabbepi tibhavūpage satte tīhākārehi tīsu padesu pakkhipitvā puna dvīhi padehi pariyādiyanto sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ pajaṃ sadevamanussanti āha. Evaṃ pañcahipi padehi tena tenākārena tedhātukameva pariyādinnanti.

The ancient teachers, however, have said: ‘With its devas’ means the remaining world together with the devas of the formless sphere. ‘With its Māra’ means the remaining world together with Māra. ‘With its Brahmā’ means the remaining world together with the brahmās of the form sphere. Thus, having included all beings who have reached the three realms of existence by these three modes in these three terms, and wishing to encompass them again with two terms, he said, ‘the progeny with its ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans.’ In this way, by these five terms, only the three realms have been fully encompassed in their respective ways. Thus they have said.

Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedetīti ettha pana sayanti sāmaṃ aparaneyyo hutvā. Abhiññāti abhiññāya, adhikena ñāṇena ñatvāti attho. Sacchikatvāti paccakkhaṃ katvā, etena anumānādipaṭikkhepo kato hoti. Pavedetīti bodheti viññāpeti pakāseti.

Regarding the phrase 'Having directly known and realized it for himself, he declares it' (sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedeti), here, 'for himself' (sayaṃ) means by himself, not being led by another. 'Having directly known' (abhiññā) means with higher knowledge (abhiññāya), that is, having known with superior knowledge (adhikena ñāṇena). 'Having realized' (sacchikatvā) means having made it directly perceptible (paccakkhaṃ katvā); by this, inference and the like are rejected. 'Declares' (pavedeti) means causes to understand (bodheti), makes known (viññāpeti), and reveals (pakāseti).

So dhammaṃ deseti ādikalyāṇaṃ…pe… pariyosānakalyāṇanti so bhagavā sattesu kāruññataṃ paṭicca hitvāpi anuttaraṃ vivekasukhaṃ dhammaṃ deseti. Tañca kho appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā desento ādikalyāṇādippakārameva deseti. Ādimhipi, kalyāṇaṃ bhaddakaṃ anavajjameva katvā deseti, majjhepi, pariyosānepi, kalyāṇaṃ bhaddakaṃ anavajjameva katvā desetīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha atthi desanāya ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ, atthi sāsanassa. Desanāya tāva catuppadikāyapi gāthāya paṭhamapādo ādi nāma, tato dve majjhaṃ nāma, ante eko pariyosānaṃ nāma. Ekānusandhikassa suttassa nidānaṃ ādi, idamavocāti pariyosānaṃ, ubhinnamantarā [M 1.0159] majjhaṃ. Anekānusandhikassa [P 1.0176] suttassa paṭhamānusandhi ādi, ante anusandhi pariyosānaṃ, majjhe eko vā dve vā bahū vā majjhameva.

‘He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning… good in the end.’ That Blessed One teaches the Dhamma out of compassion for beings, even having relinquished the unsurpassed bliss of seclusion. And whether teaching a little or a lot, he teaches it in a way that is good in the beginning and so forth. In the beginning also, he teaches, having made it good, excellent, and only what is blameless; in the middle also, and in the end also, he teaches, having made it good, excellent, and only what is blameless—thus it is said. In this context, there is a beginning, middle, and end to the teaching of the scriptures, and there is a beginning, middle, and end to the Dispensation of practice. First, the beginning, middle, and end of the teaching of the scriptures should be understood thus: even in a four-lined verse, the first line is called the beginning; the two after that are called the middle; the one at the end is called the end. For a sutta with a single connection, the introduction is the beginning, the phrase ‘Thus he spoke’ is the end, and the text between the two is the middle. For a sutta with many connections, the first connection is the beginning, the connection at the end is the end, and in the middle, whether there is one, two, or many connections, it is just the middle.

Sāsanassa pana sīlasamādhivipassanā ādi nāma. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “ko cādi kusalānaṃ [V 1.0145] dhammānaṃ? Sīlañca suvisuddhaṃ diṭṭhi ca ujukā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.369). “Atthi, bhikkhave, majjhimā paṭipadā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā”ti evaṃ vutto pana ariyamaggo majjhaṃ nāma. Phalañceva nibbānañca pariyosānaṃ nāma. “Etadatthamidaṃ, brāhmaṇa, brahmacariyaṃ, etaṃ sāraṃ, etaṃ pariyosāna”nti (ma. ni. 1.324) hi ettha phalaṃ pariyosānanti vuttaṃ. “Nibbānogadhaṃ hi, āvuso visākha, brahmacariyaṃ vussati, nibbānaparāyanaṃ nibbānapariyosāna”nti (ma. ni. 1.466) ettha nibbānaṃ pariyosānanti vuttaṃ. Idha desanāya ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ adhippetaṃ. Bhagavā hi dhammaṃ desento ādimhi sīlaṃ dassetvā majjhe maggaṃ pariyosāne nibbānaṃ dasseti. Tena vuttaṃ – “so dhammaṃ deseti ādikalyāṇaṃ majjhekalyāṇaṃ pariyosānakalyāṇa”nti. Tasmā aññopi dhammakathiko dhammaṃ kathento –

On the other hand, for the Dispensation of practice, virtue, concentration, and insight are called the beginning. And this has been said: 'What is the beginning of wholesome qualities? Virtue that is well-purified and a view that is straight.' Furthermore, the Noble Path, spoken of thus, 'There is, monks, a middle way realized by the Tathāgata,' is called the middle. Both the fruit and Nibbāna are called the end. Indeed, in the passage, 'For this purpose, brahmin, is the holy life; this is its essence, this is its end,' the fruit is spoken of as the end. In the passage, 'The holy life, friend Visākha, is lived with Nibbāna as its foundation, Nibbāna as its destination, Nibbāna as its final end,' Nibbāna is spoken of as the end. Here, the beginning, middle, and end of the teaching are intended. Indeed, when the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma, having shown virtue in the beginning, he shows the path in the middle and Nibbāna at the end. Therefore it was said: 'He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end.' Therefore, any other Dhamma-expounder, when teaching the Dhamma—

“Ādimhi sīlaṃ dasseyya, majjhe maggaṃ vibhāvaye;

Pariyosānamhi nibbānaṃ, esā kathikasaṇṭhitī”ti.

In the beginning, one should show virtue; in the middle, one should make clear the path; and at the end, one should make clear Nibbāna. This is the proper practice of a Dhamma-expounder.

Sātthaṃ sabyañjananti yassa hi yāgubhattaitthipurisādivaṇṇanānissitā desanā hoti, na so sātthaṃ deseti. Bhagavā pana tathārūpaṃ desanaṃ pahāya catusatipaṭṭhānādinissitaṃ desanaṃ deseti. Tasmā sātthaṃ desetīti vuccati. Yassa pana desanā ekabyañjanādiyuttā vā sabbaniroṭṭhabyañjanā vā sabbavissaṭṭhasabbaniggahītabyañjanā vā, tassa damiḷakirātasavarādimilakkhūnaṃ bhāsā viya byañjanapāripūriyā abhāvato abyañjanā nāma desanā hoti. Bhagavā pana –

Regarding 'with meaning, with expression': Indeed, one whose teaching relies on the elaboration of things such as porridge, rice, women, and men, does not teach 'with meaning.' The Blessed One, on the other hand, having abandoned such a teaching, teaches that which is based on the four foundations of mindfulness and so on. Therefore, it is said that he teaches 'with meaning.' Furthermore, one whose teaching is endowed with a single type of letter, or has letters that are all non-labial, or has letters that are all released or all nasalized, their teaching—like the language of barbarians such as the Damiḷas, Kirātas, and Savaras—is called a teaching 'without expression' due to the absence of completeness of the letters. The Blessed One, however—

“Sithilaṃ [P 1.0177] dhanitañca dīgharassaṃ, garukaṃ lahukañca niggahītaṃ;

Sambandhavavatthitaṃ vimuttaṃ, dasadhā byañjanabuddhiyā pabhedo”ti.

Lax and tense, long and short, heavy and light, nasalized, connected, separated, and released: thus is the tenfold division of the consciousness that produces the letters.

Evaṃ [M 1.0160] vuttaṃ dasavidhaṃ byañjanaṃ amakkhetvā paripuṇṇabyañjanameva katvā dhammaṃ deseti, tasmā sabyañjanaṃ dhammaṃ desetīti vuccati. Kevalaparipuṇṇanti ettha kevalanti sakalādhivacanaṃ. Paripuṇṇanti anūnādhikavacanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti sakalaparipuṇṇameva deseti, ekadesanāpi aparipuṇṇā natthīti. Upanetabbaapanetabbassa abhāvato kevalaparipuṇṇanti veditabbaṃ. Parisuddhanti nirupakkilesaṃ. Yo hi imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ nissāya lābhaṃ vā sakkāraṃ vā labhissāmīti deseti, tassa aparisuddhā desanā hoti. Bhagavā pana lokāmisanirapekkho hitapharaṇena [V 1.0146] mettābhāvanāya muduhadayo ullumpanasabhāvasaṇṭhitena cittena deseti. Tasmā parisuddhaṃ dhammaṃ desetīti vuccati.

Without effacing the tenfold letters thus spoken of, he teaches the Dhamma, making it one of perfectly complete letters; therefore, it is said that he teaches the Dhamma 'with expression.' Regarding 'wholly complete,' here 'kevala' is a term for 'all' or 'entire.' 'Paripuṇṇa' is a term for the state of being without deficiency or excess. This is what is said: he teaches what is entirely and perfectly complete; not even one part of the teaching is incomplete. It should be understood as 'wholly complete' due to the absence of anything to be added or removed. 'Perfectly pure' means without defilement. For one who teaches thinking, 'By means of this Dhamma teaching I will obtain gain or honor,' their teaching is impure. The Blessed One, on the other hand, being unconcerned with worldly gain, teaches with a tender heart through the development of loving-kindness that pervades with benefit, and with a mind well-established in the nature of rescuing. Therefore, it is said that he teaches the Dhamma 'perfectly pure.'

Brahmacariyaṃ pakāsetīti ettha panāyaṃ brahmacariya-saddo dāne veyyāvacce pañcasikkhāpadasīle appamaññāsu methunaviratiyaṃ sadārasantose vīriye uposathaṅgesu ariyamagge sāsaneti imesvatthesu dissati.

Regarding the phrase 'He proclaims the holy life': here, this term 'brahmacariya' is seen in these meanings: giving, service, the virtue of the five training precepts, the immeasurables, abstinence from sexual intercourse, contentment with one's own wife, energy, the Uposatha factors, the Noble Path, and the Dispensation.

“Kiṃ te vataṃ kiṃ pana brahmacariyaṃ,

Kissa suciṇṇassa ayaṃ vipāko;

Iddhī jutī balavīriyūpapatti,

Idañca te nāga, mahāvimānaṃ.

What is your observance, what then is your holy life? Of what well-practiced deed is this the result—the attainment of psychic power, splendor, strength, and energy, and this great mansion of yours, O Nāga?

Ahañca bhariyā ca manussaloke,

Saddhā ubho dānapatī ahumhā;

Opānabhūtaṃ me gharaṃ tadāsi,

Santappitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca.

My wife and I, in the human world, were both faithful, generous patrons. My home was then like a public well, and ascetics and brahmins were satisfied.

Taṃ [P 1.0178] me vataṃ taṃ pana brahmacariyaṃ,

Tassa suciṇṇassa ayaṃ vipāko;

Iddhī jutī balavīriyūpapatti,

Idañca me dhīra mahāvimāna”nti. (jā. 2.17.1595);

That was my observance, that was my holy life; of that well-practiced deed this is the result—the attainment of psychic power, splendor, strength, and energy, and this great mansion of mine, O wise one.

Imasmiñhi puṇṇakajātake dānaṃ brahmacariyanti vuttaṃ.

For in this Puṇṇaka Jātaka, giving is said to be the holy life.

“Kena pāṇi kāmadado, kena pāṇi madhussavo;

Kena te brahmacariyena, puññaṃ pāṇimhi ijjhati.

By what is your hand a giver of desires, by what is it a source of sweetness? By what holy life of yours is merit accomplished in your hand?

Tena [M 1.0161] pāṇi kāmadado, tena pāṇi madhussavo;

Tena me brahmacariyena, puññaṃ pāṇimhi ijjhatī”ti. (pe. va. 275,277);

By that is my hand a giver of desires, by that is it a source of sweetness; by that holy life of mine, merit is accomplished in my hand.

Imasmiṃ [V 1.0147] aṅkurapetavatthumhi veyyāvaccaṃ brahmacariyanti vuttaṃ. “Evaṃ, kho taṃ bhikkhave, tittiriyaṃ nāma brahmacariyaṃ ahosī”ti (cūḷava. 311) imasmiṃ tittirajātake pañcasikkhāpadasīlaṃ brahmacariyanti vuttaṃ. “Taṃ kho pana me, pañcasikha, brahmacariyaṃ neva nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya…pe… yāvadeva brahmalokūpapattiyā”ti (dī. ni. 2.329) imasmiṃ mahāgovindasutte catasso appamaññāyo brahmacariyanti vuttā. “Pare abrahmacārī bhavissanti, mayamettha brahmacārī bhavissāmā”ti (ma. ni. 1.83) imasmiṃ sallekhasutte methunavirati brahmacariyanti vuttā.

In this Aṅkura Petavatthu, service is said to be the holy life. In this Tittira Jātaka, with the words, “Thus, monks, that was the holy life of the partridge,” the virtue of the five training precepts is said to be the holy life. In this Mahāgovinda Sutta, with the words, “That holy life of mine, Pañcasikha, did not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation… but only as far as rebirth in the Brahma world,” the four immeasurables are said to be the holy life. In this Sallekha Sutta, with the words, “Others will not live the holy life, but we here will live the holy life,” abstinence from sexual intercourse is said to be the holy life.

“Mayañca bhariyā nātikkamāma,

Amhe ca bhariyā nātikkamanti;

Aññatra tāhi brahmacariyaṃ carāma,

Tasmā hi amhaṃ daharā na mīyare”ti. (jā. 1.4.97);

We do not transgress against our wives, and our wives do not transgress against us; apart from them, we live the holy life. Therefore, our young ones do not die.

Mahādhammapālajātake sadārasantoso brahmacariyanti vutto. “Abhijānāmi [P 1.0179] kho panāhaṃ, sāriputta, caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ brahmacariyaṃ caritā, tapassī sudaṃ homī”ti (ma. ni. 1.155) lomahaṃsanasutte vīriyaṃ brahmacariyanti vuttaṃ.

In the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka, contentment with one's own wife is said to be the holy life. In the Lomahaṃsana Sutta, with the words, “I recall, Sāriputta, having lived the holy life endowed with four factors; I was an ascetic indeed,” energy is said to be the holy life.

“Hīnena brahmacariyena, khattiye upapajjati;

Majjhimena ca devattaṃ, uttamena visujjhatī”ti. (jā. 1.8.75);

By an inferior holy life, one is reborn among the nobles; by a middling one, to the state of a god; by the highest, one is purified.

Evaṃ nimijātake attadamanavasena kato aṭṭhaṅgiko uposatho brahmacariyanti vutto. “Idaṃ kho pana me, pañcasikha, brahmacariyaṃ ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya…pe… ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo”ti (dī. ni. 2.329) mahāgovindasuttasmiṃyeva ariyamaggo brahmacariyanti vutto. “Tayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ iddhañceva phītañca vitthārikaṃ bāhujaññaṃ puthubhūtaṃ yāva devamanussehi suppakāsita”nti (dī. ni. 3.174) pāsādikasutte sikkhattayasaṅgahitaṃ sakalasāsanaṃ brahmacariyanti vuttaṃ. Imasmimpi ṭhāne idameva brahmacariyanti adhippetaṃ. Tasmā brahmacariyaṃ pakāsetīti so dhammaṃ deseti ādikalyāṇaṃ…pe… parisuddhaṃ. Evaṃ desento ca sikkhattayasaṅgahitaṃ sakalasāsanaṃ brahmacariyaṃ pakāsetīti [M 1.0162] evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Brahmacariyanti seṭṭhaṭṭhena brahmabhūtaṃ cariyaṃ. Brahmabhūtānaṃ vā buddhādīnaṃ cariyanti vuttaṃ hoti.

Thus, in the Nimi Jātaka, the eight-factored Uposatha undertaken by way of self-taming is said to be the holy life. “This holy life of mine, Pañcasikha, leads exclusively to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation… this is that same Noble Eightfold Path.” In the Mahāgovinda Sutta itself, the Noble Path is said to be the holy life. “This holy life is successful and prosperous, widespread, known to many, widely diffused, well-proclaimed among gods and humans.” In the Pāsādika Sutta, the entire Dispensation as comprised in the threefold training is said to be the holy life. In this place too, this very same thing is intended as the holy life. Therefore, when it says, “he makes known the holy life,” it means he teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning… and perfectly pure. And in teaching thus, he makes known the entire Dispensation as comprised in the threefold training, which is the holy life. This is how the meaning should be understood here. The term “brahmacariya” means noble conduct (brahmabhūtaṃ cariyaṃ) in the sense of being the best. Or else it is said to be the conduct of those who have become noble (brahmabhūtānaṃ), such as the Buddhas and others.

191. Taṃ dhammanti [V 1.0148] taṃ vuttappakārasampadaṃ dhammaṃ. Suṇāti gahapati vāti kasmā paṭhamaṃ gahapatiṃ niddisati? Nihatamānattā, ussannattā ca. Yebhuyyena hi khattiyakulato pabbajitā jātiṃ nissāya mānaṃ karonti. Brāhmaṇakulā pabbajitā mante nissāya mānaṃ karonti. Hīnajaccakulā pabbajitā attano attano vijātitāya patiṭṭhātuṃ na sakkonti. Gahapatidārakā pana kacchehi sedaṃ muñcantehi piṭṭhiyā loṇaṃ pupphamānāya bhūmiṃ kasitvā tādisassa mānassa abhāvato nihatamānadappā honti. Te pabbajitvā [P 1.0180] mānaṃ vā dappaṃ vā akatvā yathābalaṃ sakalabuddhavacanaṃ uggahetvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karontā sakkonti arahatte patiṭṭhātuṃ. Itarehi ca kulehi nikkhamitvā pabbajitā nāma na bahukā, gahapatikāva bahukā. Iti nihatamānattā ussannattā ca paṭhamaṃ gahapatiṃ niddisatīti.

191. “That Dhamma” means that Dhamma endowed with the qualities of the kind already mentioned. Why is the householder indicated first when it says, “a householder… listens”? Because of having humbled pride, and because of being numerous. For the most part, those who have gone forth from a Khattiya family, relying on their birth, produce pride. Those who have gone forth from a Brahmin family, relying on their sacred verses, produce pride. Those who have gone forth from families of low birth are unable to establish themselves because of their own respective inferior birth. But the sons of householders, who have plowed the earth with sweat pouring from their armpits and salt efflorescing on their backs, are of humbled pride and arrogance due to the absence of such pride. Having gone forth, not producing pride or arrogance, having learned the entire word of the Buddha according to their ability, and undertaking the practice of insight meditation, they are able to become established in Arahantship. Furthermore, those who have gone forth from other families are not many; it is householders who are many. Thus, because of having humbled pride and because of being numerous, he indicates the householder first.

Aññatarasmiṃ vāti itaresaṃ vā kulānaṃ aññatarasmiṃ. Paccājātoti patijāto. Tathāgate saddhaṃ paṭilabhatīti parisuddhaṃ dhammaṃ sutvā dhammassāmimhi tathāgate – “sammāsambuddho vata so bhagavā”ti saddhaṃ paṭilabhati. Iti paṭisañcikkhatīti evaṃ paccavekkhati. Sambādho gharāvāsoti sacepi saṭṭhihatthe ghare yojanasatantarepi vā dve jāyampatikā vasanti, tathāpi nesaṃ sakiñcanasapalibodhaṭṭhena gharāvāso sambādhoyeva. Rajopathoti rāgarajādīnaṃ uṭṭhānaṭṭhānanti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Āgamanapathotipi vadanti. Alagganaṭṭhena abbhokāso viyāti abbhokāso. Pabbajito hi kūṭāgāraratanapāsādadevavimānādīsu pihitadvāravātapānesu paṭicchannesu vasantopi neva laggati, na sajjati, na bajjhati. Tena vuttaṃ – “abbhokāso pabbajjā”ti. Api ca sambādho gharāvāso kusalakiriyāya okāsābhāvato. Rajopatho asaṃvutasaṅkāraṭṭhānaṃ viya rajānaṃ kilesarajānaṃ sannipātaṭṭhānato. Abbhokāso pabbajjā kusalakiriyāya yathāsukhaṃ okāsasabbhāvato.

“In some other [family]” means in one of the other families. “Is born into” means one who is born into a family. “He gains faith in the Tathāgata” means, having heard the perfectly pure Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata, the master of the Dhamma, thinking, “Indeed, the Blessed One is a fully and perfectly enlightened Buddha.” “He reflects thus” means he considers in this way. “The household life is confining” means that even if a married couple lives in a house of sixty cubits or in a place a hundred yojanas apart, still for them, because it involves possessions and obstacles, the household life is indeed confining. “A path of dust” means a place for the arising of the dust of passion and so on—so it is said in the great commentary. Others say it is a path of arrival. “Open space” is so called because, like an open space, it is free of attachment. For one who has gone forth, even when dwelling in gabled mansions, jeweled palaces, celestial abodes, and the like, with doors and windows closed and concealed, does not cling, is not attached, is not bound. Therefore it was said: “Going forth is an open space.” Furthermore, the household life is confining because there is no opportunity for performing wholesome actions. The path of dust, being a gathering place for the dust of the defilements, is like an uncovered rubbish heap for dust. Going forth is an open space because there is ample opportunity for performing wholesome actions as one wishes.

Nayidaṃ [M 1.0163] sukaraṃ…pe… pabbajeyyanti etthāyaṃ saṅkhepakathā, yadetaṃ sikkhattayabrahmacariyaṃ ekampi divasaṃ akhaṇḍaṃ katvā carimakacittaṃ pāpetabbatāya ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ, caritabbaṃ ekadivasampi ca kilesamalena amalīnaṃ katvā carimakacittaṃ pāpetabbatāya ekantaparisuddhaṃ[P 1.0181]. Saṅkhalikhitanti likhitasaṅkhasadisaṃ dhotasaṅkhasappaṭibhāgaṃ caritabbaṃ. Idaṃ na sukaraṃ agāraṃ ajjhāvasatā agāramajjhe vasantena ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ…pe… carituṃ, yaṃnūnāhaṃ kese ca massuñca ohāretvā kasāyarasapītatāya kāsāyāni brahmacariyaṃ carantānaṃ anucchavikāni vatthāni acchādetvā paridahitvā agārasmā nikkhamitvā anagāriyaṃ pabbajeyyanti. Ettha ca yasmā [V 1.0149] agārassa hitaṃ kasivāṇijjādikammaṃ agāriyanti vuccati, tañca pabbajjāya natthi, tasmā pabbajjā anagāriyanti ñātabbā, taṃ anagāriyaṃ. Pabbajeyyanti paṭipajjeyyaṃ.

This is not easy... I would go forth. Here is the summary: This holy life of the threefold training should be practiced, even for a single day, having made it unbroken, because it ought to be brought to the final consciousness, as utterly complete. And even for a single day, it should be practiced, having made it unstained by the stain of defilements, because it ought to be brought to the final consciousness, as utterly pure. The term saṅkhalikhitaṃ (like a polished conch shell) means it should be practiced to be like a polished conch shell, comparable to a washed conch shell. This is not easy for one living at home, dwelling in the midst of a house, to practice as utterly complete... What if I, having shaved off my hair and beard, having covered and put on the ochre robes that are suitable for those practicing the holy life, having gone out from the home, were to go forth into the state without household affairs? And here, because work such as agriculture and commerce, which is for the welfare of the household, is called 'that which pertains to the household' (agāriya), and that does not exist in the going-forth, therefore the going-forth should be known as 'that which does not pertain to the household' (anagāriya). That state without household affairs. 'I would go forth' means 'I would undertake'.

192-193. Appaṃ vāti sahassato heṭṭhā bhogakkhandho appo nāma hoti, sahassato paṭṭhāya mahā. Ābandhanaṭṭhena ñātiyeva ñātiparivaṭṭo. Sopi vīsatiyā heṭṭhā appo nāma hoti, vīsatiyā paṭṭhāya mahā. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutoti pātimokkhasaṃvarena samannāgato. Ācāragocarasampannoti ācārena ceva gocarena ca sampanno. Aṇumattesūti appamattakesu. Vajjesūti akusaladhammesu. Bhayadassāvīti bhayadassī. Samādāyāti sammā ādiyitvā. Sikkhati sikkhāpadesūti sikkhāpadesu taṃ taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyitvā sikkhati. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimagge vutto.

192-193. As for 'a little': an aggregate of wealth below a thousand is called 'little'; from a thousand upwards, it is 'large'. In the sense of binding, relatives themselves are the 'circle of relatives'. That too, below twenty, is called 'little'; from twenty upwards, it is 'large'. 'Restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint' means endowed with the Pātimokkha restraint. 'Accomplished in conduct and resort' means accomplished in conduct and in resort. 'In minute matters' means in those of small measure. 'In faults' means in unwholesome states. 'Seeing danger' means one who sees danger. 'Having undertaken' means having rightly taken up. 'He trains in the training rules' means: having undertaken each and every training rule among the training rules, he trains. This is the summary here; but the detailed account has been stated by me in the Visuddhimagga.

Kāyakammavacīkammena samannāgato kusalena parisuddhājīvoti ettha ācāragocaraggahaṇeneva ca kusale kāyakammavacīkamme gahitepi yasmā idaṃ ājīvapārisuddhisīlaṃ nāma na ākāse vā rukkhaggādīsu vā uppajjati, kāyavacīdvāresuyeva pana uppajjati; tasmā tassa uppattidvāradassanatthaṃ kāyakammavacīkammena samannāgato kusalenāti vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana tena samannāgato, tasmā parisuddhājīvo. Samaṇamuṇḍikaputtasuttantavasena [P 1.0182] (ma. ni. 2.260) vā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha hi “katame ca, thapati, kusalā sīlā? Kusalaṃ [M 1.0164] kāyakammaṃ, kusalaṃ vacīkammaṃ, parisuddhaṃ ājīvampi kho ahaṃ thapati sīlasmiṃ vadāmī”ti vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana tena samannāgato, tasmā parisuddhājīvoti veditabbo.

In the phrase 'endowed with wholesome bodily and verbal action, of pure livelihood': Here, although wholesome bodily and verbal action are included by the taking up of 'conduct and resort', because this virtue of purity of livelihood does not arise in the sky or on the tops of trees, etc., but arises only at the bodily and verbal doors, therefore, for the purpose of showing its doors of arising, it is said, 'endowed with wholesome bodily and verbal action.' And because one is endowed with that, therefore one is of pure livelihood. Or, it is said thus in accordance with the Samaṇamuṇḍikaputta Sutta, for there it is said: 'And what, master builder, are the wholesome virtues? Wholesome bodily action, wholesome verbal action; and purified livelihood too, master builder, I declare to be in the category of virtue.' And because one is endowed with that, one should be known as being of pure livelihood.
