Sīlasampannoti brahmajāle vuttena tividhena sīlena samannāgato hoti. Indriyesu guttadvāroti manacchaṭṭhesu indriyesu pihitadvāro hoti. Satisampajaññena samannāgatoti abhikkante paṭikkantetiādīsu sattasu ṭhānesu satiyā ceva sampajaññena ca samannāgato hoti. Santuṭṭhoti catūsu paccayesu tividhena santosena santuṭṭho hoti.

'Endowed with virtue' means one is endowed with the threefold virtue spoken of in the Brahmajāla Sutta. 'With guarded doors in the sense faculties' means one's doors are closed in the sense faculties which have mind as the sixth. 'Endowed with mindfulness and full awareness' means one is endowed with mindfulness and with full awareness in the seven instances beginning with 'in going forward, in returning'. 'Content' means one is content with the four requisites by means of the threefold contentment.

Cūḷasīlavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Minor Virtue

194-211. Evaṃ mātikaṃ nikkhipitvā anupubbena bhājento “kathañca, mahārāja, bhikkhu sīlasampanno hotī”tiādimāha. Tattha idampissa hoti sīlasminti idampi assa bhikkhuno pāṇātipātā veramaṇi sīlasmiṃ ekaṃ sīlaṃ hotīti attho. Paccattavacanatthe vā etaṃ [V 1.0150] bhummaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyañhi idampi tassa samaṇassa sīlanti ayameva attho vutto. Sesaṃ brahmajāle vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Idamassa hoti sīlasminti idaṃ assa sīlaṃ hotīti attho.

194-211. Having thus laid down the matrix and explaining it sequentially, he said, “And how, great king, is a bhikkhu accomplished in virtue?” and so on. Therein, idampissa hoti sīlasmiṃ (this too is in his virtue) means: this abstinence from taking life is one virtue of that bhikkhu within the collection of virtues. Alternatively, this locative case is used in the sense of the nominative. Indeed, in the Great Commentary, this very meaning has been stated: “This too is the virtue of that ascetic.” The remainder should be understood in the same way as stated in the Brahmajāla Sutta. Idamassa hoti sīlasmiṃ (this is in his virtue) means: this is his virtue.

212. Na kutoci bhayaṃ samanupassati, yadidaṃ sīlasaṃvaratoti yāni asaṃvaramūlakāni bhayāni uppajjanti, tesu yaṃ idaṃ bhayaṃ sīlasaṃvarato bhaveyya, taṃ kutoci ekasaṃvaratopi na samanupassati. Kasmā? Saṃvarato asaṃvaramūlakassa bhayassa abhāvā. Muddhābhisittoti yathāvidhānavihitena khattiyābhisekena muddhani avasitto. Yadidaṃ paccatthikatoti yaṃ kutoci ekapaccatthikatopi bhayaṃ bhaveyya, taṃ na samanupassati. Kasmā? Yasmā nihatapaccāmitto. Ajjhattanti [P 1.0183] niyakajjhattaṃ, attano santāneti attho. Anavajjasukhanti anavajjaṃ aninditaṃ kusalaṃ sīlapadaṭṭhānehi avippaṭisārapāmojjapītipassaddhidhammehi pariggahitaṃ kāyikacetasikasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti. Evaṃ kho, mahārāja, bhikkhu sīlasampanno hotīti evaṃ nirantaraṃ vitthāretvā dassitena tividhena sīlena samannāgato bhikkhu sīlasampanno nāma hotīti sīlakathaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

212. He perceives no danger from any quarter, that is, from the restraint of virtue: As for the dangers that arise rooted in non-restraint, he does not perceive any danger that might arise from restraint in virtue, from any single aspect of restraint. Why? Because due to restraint, there is no danger rooted in non-restraint. Anointed on the head: anointed on the head with the consecration of a noble warrior, performed according to established custom. That is, from any single adversary: he does not perceive any danger that might arise from any single adversary. Why? Because his enemies are defeated. Internally: one’s own internal state, that is, in one’s own continuum. He experiences blameless happiness: he experiences bodily and mental happiness that is blameless, irreproachable, wholesome, founded on virtuous states, encompassed by the states of non-remorse, gladness, joy, and tranquility. Thus, great king, a bhikkhu is endowed with virtue: Having thus explained in detail without interruption, he concludes the discourse on virtue by stating that a bhikkhu endowed with the threefold virtue, as demonstrated, is called “endowed with virtue.”

Indriyasaṃvarakathā

Discourse on Restraint of the Sense Faculties

213. Indriyesu [M 1.0165] guttadvārabhājanīye cakkhunā rūpanti ayaṃ cakkhusaddo katthaci buddhacakkhumhi vattati, yathāha – “buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokesī”ti (mahāva. 9). Katthaci sabbaññutaññāṇasaṅkhāte samantacakkhumhi, yathāha – “tathūpamaṃ dhammamayaṃ, sumedha, pāsādamāruyha samantacakkhū”ti (mahāva. 8). Katthaci dhammacakkhumhi “virajaṃ vītamalaṃ dhammacakkhuṃ udapādī”ti (mahāva. 16) hi ettha ariyamaggattayapaññā. “Cakkhuṃ udapādi ñāṇaṃ udapādī”ti (mahāva. 15) ettha pubbenivāsādiñāṇaṃ paññācakkhūti vuccati. “Dibbena cakkhunā”ti (ma. ni. 1.284) āgataṭṭhānesu dibbacakkhumhi vattati. “Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe cā”ti ettha pasādacakkhumhi vattati. Idha panāyaṃ pasādacakkhuvohārena cakkhuviññāṇe vattati, tasmā cakkhuviññāṇena rūpaṃ disvāti ayametthattho. Sesapadesu yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ visuddhimagge vuttaṃ. Abyāsekasukhanti kilesabyāsekavirahitattā abyāsekaṃ asammissaṃ parisuddhaṃ adhicittasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedetīti.

213. In the section on guarding the sense doors, regarding “by the eye, a form”: this word “eye” in some passages occurs in the sense of the Buddha-eye, as it is said: “He surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye.” In some passages, it occurs in the sense of the all-seeing eye, which is called the knowledge of omniscience, as it is said: “Having ascended the palace made of Dhamma, O wise one, with the all-seeing eye.” In some passages, it occurs in the sense of the Dhamma-eye; indeed, in the passage, “The dust-free, stainless Dhamma-eye arose,” the wisdom in the three lower noble paths is called the Dhamma-eye. In the passage, “The eye arose, knowledge arose,” the knowledge of previous existences and so on is called the wisdom-eye. In the passages where “with the divine eye” occurs, it occurs in the sense of the divine eye. In the passage, “Dependent on the eye and also on forms,” it occurs in the sense of the sensitive eye. Here, however, this word, by the convention of the sensitive eye, occurs in the sense of eye-consciousness. Therefore, the meaning here is: “having seen a form with eye-consciousness.” Regarding the remaining terms, whatever should be said has all been stated in the Visuddhimagga. Unadulterated happiness means: because it is free from the admixture of defilements, one experiences unadulterated, unmixed, utterly pure happiness of the higher mind.

Satisampajaññakathā

Discourse on Mindfulness and Clear Comprehension

214. Satisampajaññabhājanīyamhi [V 1.0151] abhikkante paṭikkanteti ettha tāva abhikkantaṃ vuccati gamanaṃ, paṭikkantaṃ nivattanaṃ, tadubhayampi catūsu iriyāpathesu labbhati. Gamane tāva purato kāyaṃ abhiharanto abhikkamati nāma[P 1.0184]. Paṭinivattanto paṭikkamati nāma. Ṭhānepi ṭhitakova kāyaṃ purato onāmento abhikkamati nāma, pacchato apanāmento paṭikkamati nāma. Nisajjāya nisinnakova āsanassa purimaaṅgābhimukho saṃsaranto abhikkamati nāma, pacchimaaṅgapadesaṃ paccāsaṃsaranto paṭikkamati nāma. Nipajjanepi eseva nayo.

214. In the exposition of mindfulness and clear comprehension, regarding 'advancing' (abhikkanta) and 'retreating' (paṭikkanta): here, 'advancing' is said to be going forward, and 'retreating' is returning. Both are found in the four postures. In walking, when one moves the body forward, it is called advancing. When one turns back, it is called retreating. Even when standing, if one inclines the body forward while standing, it is called advancing; if one moves it back, it is called retreating. In sitting, while seated, if one shifts towards the front part of the seat, it is called advancing; if one shifts back towards the rear part of the seat, it is called retreating. The same principle applies to lying down.

Sampajānakārī hotīti sampajaññena sabbakiccakārī. Sampajaññameva vā kārī. So hi abhikkantādīsu sampajaññaṃ karoteva. Na katthaci sampajaññavirahito hoti. Tattha sātthakasampajaññaṃ, sappāyasampajaññaṃ, gocarasampajaññaṃ asammohasampajaññanti catubbidhaṃ sampajaññaṃ. Tattha abhikkamanacitte uppanne cittavaseneva agantvā – “kinnu me ettha gatena attho atthi natthī”ti atthānatthaṃ pariggahetvā atthapariggaṇhanaṃ sātthakasampajaññaṃ. Tattha [M 1.0166] ca atthoti cetiyadassanabodhisaṅghatheraasubhadassanādivasena dhammato vuḍḍhi. Cetiyaṃ vā bodhiṃ vā disvāpi hi buddhārammaṇaṃ, saṅghadassanena saṅghārammaṇaṃ, pītiṃ uppādetvā tadeva khayavayato sammasanto arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. There disvā tesaṃ ovāde patiṭṭhāya, asubhaṃ disvā tattha paṭhamajjhānaṃ uppādetvā tadeva khayavayato sammasanto arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tasmā etesaṃ dassanaṃ sātthakanti vuttaṃ. Keci pana āmisatopi vuḍḍhi atthoyeva, taṃ nissāya brahmacariyānuggahāya paṭipannattāti vadanti.

‘He acts with clear comprehension’ means he performs all duties with clear comprehension, or he is simply one who acts with clear comprehension. For he indeed practices clear comprehension in going forward and so on. He is never devoid of clear comprehension in any matter. Herein, clear comprehension is fourfold: clear comprehension of purpose, clear comprehension of suitability, clear comprehension of the domain, and clear comprehension of non-delusion. Among these, when the thought of going forward arises, instead of going merely by the mind's inclination, one discerns the benefit and non-benefit by thinking, 'Is there a benefit for me in going there, or is there not?' The grasping of the benefit is the clear comprehension of purpose. Herein, 'benefit' refers to growth in the Dhamma by way of seeing shrines, Bodhi trees, the Sangha, elders, or contemplating the unattractive, and so on. For after seeing a shrine or a Bodhi tree and arousing joy with the Buddha as the object, or after seeing the Sangha and arousing joy with the Sangha as the object, by contemplating that very joy by way of its decay and vanishing, one can attain arahantship. After seeing elders and establishing oneself in their advice, or after seeing an unattractive object and producing the first jhāna, by contemplating that very jhāna by way of its decay and vanishing, one attains arahantship. Therefore, seeing these things is said to be purposeful. Some, however, say that growth by way of material requisites is also a benefit, because one practices for the support of the holy life by relying on them.

Tasmiṃ pana gamane sappāyāsappāyaṃ pariggahetvā sappāyapariggaṇhanaṃ sappāyasampajaññaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – cetiyadassanaṃ tāva sātthakaṃ, sace pana cetiyassa mahāpūjāya dasadvādasayojanantare parisā sannipatanti, attano vibhavānurūpā itthiyopi purisāpi alaṅkatapaṭiyattā cittakammarūpakāni [P 1.0185] viya sañcaranti. Tatra cassa iṭṭhe ārammaṇe lobho hoti, aniṭṭhe paṭigho, asamapekkhane moho uppajjati, kāyasaṃsaggāpattiṃ vā āpajjati. Jīvitabrahmacariyānaṃ vā antarāyo hoti, evaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ asappāyaṃ hoti. Vuttappakāraantarāyābhāve sappāyaṃ. Bodhidassanepi eseva nayo. Saṅghadassanampi sātthaṃ. Sace pana antogāme mahāmaṇḍapaṃ kāretvā sabbarattiṃ dhammassavanaṃ karontesu manussesu vuttappakāreneva janasannipāto [V 1.0152] ceva antarāyo ca hoti, evaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ asappāyaṃ hoti. Antarāyābhāve sappāyaṃ. Mahāparisaparivārānaṃ therānaṃ dassanepi eseva nayo.

Furthermore, in that going, having discerned what is suitable and unsuitable, the grasping of what is suitable is the clear comprehension of suitability. This is as follows: seeing a shrine is, in the first place, purposeful. However, if for a great ceremony at the shrine, crowds gather within a ten or twelve yojana radius, and women and men, adorned according to their wealth, move about like painted and sculpted figures, then for that monk, greed can arise towards a desirable object, aversion towards an undesirable one, or delusion can arise through improper consideration. Or he may fall into an offense of bodily contact, or there may be a danger to his life and holy life. In such a case, that place is unsuitable. In the absence of the dangers described, it is suitable. This same principle applies to seeing the Bodhi tree. Seeing the Sangha is also purposeful. However, if people have a great pavilion built inside a village and listen to the Dhamma all night, and if a gathering of people and danger arise in the way described, in such a case, that place is unsuitable. In the absence of danger, it is suitable. This same principle applies to seeing elders who are surrounded by a great assembly.

Asubhadassanampi sātthaṃ, tadatthadīpanatthañca idaṃ vatthu – eko kira daharabhikkhu sāmaṇeraṃ gahetvā dantakaṭṭhatthāya gato. Sāmaṇero maggā okkamitvā purato gacchanto asubhaṃ disvā paṭhamajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā tadeva pādakaṃ katvā saṅkhāre sammasanto tīṇi phalāni sacchikatvā uparimaggatthāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariggahetvā aṭṭhāsi. Daharo taṃ apassanto sāmaṇerāti pakkosi. So ‘mayā pabbajitadivasato paṭṭhāya bhikkhunā saddhiṃ dve kathā nāma na kathitapubbā. Aññasmimpi divase upari visesaṃ nibbattessāmī’ti cintetvā kiṃ, bhanteti paṭivacanamadāsi. ‘Ehī’ti ca vutte ekavacaneneva āgantvā, ‘bhante, iminā tāva maggeneva gantvā mayā ṭhitokāse muhuttaṃ [M 1.0167] puratthābhimukho ṭhatvā olokethā’ti āha. So tathā katvā tena pattavisesameva pāpuṇi. Evaṃ ekaṃ asubhaṃ dvinnaṃ janānaṃ atthāya jātaṃ. Evaṃ sātthampi panetaṃ purisassa mātugāmāsubhaṃ asappāyaṃ, mātugāmassa ca purisāsubhaṃ asappāyaṃ, sabhāgameva sappāyanti evaṃ sappāyapariggaṇhanaṃ sappāyasampajaññaṃ nāma.

The contemplation of the unattractive is also purposeful, and to clarify this purpose, this story is told: A young monk, it is said, took a novice with him to get a tooth-stick. The novice, walking ahead after leaving the path, saw an unattractive object and produced the first jhāna. Making that his foundation, he contemplated the formations and realized three fruits. Then, having taken up the meditation subject for the higher path, he stood still. The young monk, not seeing him, called out, 'Novice!' The novice thought, 'Since the day I went forth, I have not had what could be called a conversation with a monk. I shall attain a higher distinction on another day.' Thinking thus, he replied, 'What is it, venerable sir?' And when told, 'Come,' he came, speaking only a single word. Then he said, 'Venerable sir, please go by this path, and when you reach the place where I was standing, stand for a moment facing east and look.' The monk did so and attained the very same special attainment as he had. Thus, one unattractive object was for the benefit of two people. However, even though it is purposeful in this way, for a man, the unattractiveness of a woman is unsuitable, and for a woman, the unattractiveness of a man is unsuitable. Only an object of the same nature is suitable. In this way, the grasping of what is suitable is called the clear comprehension of suitability.

Evaṃ pariggahitasātthakasappāyassa pana aṭṭhatiṃsāya kammaṭṭhānesu attano cittaruciyaṃ kammaṭṭhānasaṅkhātaṃ [P 1.0186] gocaraṃ uggahetvā bhikkhācāragocare taṃ gahetvāva gamanaṃ gocarasampajaññaṃ nāma. Tassāvibhāvanatthaṃ idaṃ catukkaṃ veditabbaṃ –

Furthermore, for one who has thus discerned what is purposeful and suitable, the clear comprehension of the domain is as follows: having learned from among the thirty-eight meditation subjects a meditation subject, known as a ‘domain,’ which is agreeable to one’s own mind, one goes on the alms-round domain while holding to that very subject. To make this clear, this tetrad should be understood:

Idhekacco bhikkhu harati, na paccāharati; ekacco paccāharati, na harati; ekacco pana neva harati, na paccāharati; ekacco harati ca, paccāharati cāti. Tattha yo bhikkhu divasaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāya ca āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodhetvā tathā rattiyā paṭhamayāme, majjhimayāme seyyaṃ kappetvā pacchimayāmepi nisajjacaṅkamehi vītināmetvā pageva cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇavattaṃ katvā bodhirukkhe udakaṃ āsiñcitvā, pānīyaṃ paribhojanīyaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā ācariyupajjhāyavattādīni sabbāni khandhakavattāni samādāya vattati. So sarīraparikammaṃ katvā senāsanaṃ pavisitvā dve tayo pallaṅke usumaṃ gāhāpento kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjitvā bhikkhācāravelāyaṃ uṭṭhahitvā kammaṭṭhānasīseneva pattacīvaramādāya senāsanato nikkhamitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontova cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ gantvā, sace buddhānussatikammaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, taṃ avissajjetvāva cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ pavisati. Aññaṃ ce kammaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, sopānamūle ṭhatvā hatthena gahitabhaṇḍaṃ viya taṃ ṭhapetvā buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ gahetvā cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ āruyha, mahantaṃ cetiyaṃ [V 1.0153] ce, tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā catūsu ṭhānesu vanditabbaṃ. Khuddakaṃ cetiyaṃ ce, tatheva padakkhiṇaṃ katvā aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu vanditabbaṃ. Cetiyaṃ vanditvā bodhiyaṅgaṇaṃ pattenāpi buddhassa bhagavato sammukhā viya nipaccākāraṃ dassetvā bodhi vanditabbā. So evaṃ cetiyañca bodhiñca vanditvā paṭisāmitaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā paṭisāmitabhaṇḍakaṃ hatthena gaṇhanto viya nikkhittakammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā gāmasamīpe kammaṭṭhānasīseneva cīvaraṃ pārupitvā gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisati. Atha naṃ manussā disvā ayyo no āgatoti paccuggantvā [P 1.0187] pattaṃ gahetvā āsanasālāya vā gehe vā [M 1.0168] nisīdāpetvā yāguṃ datvā yāva bhattaṃ na niṭṭhāti, tāva pāde dhovitvā telena makkhetvā purato te nisīditvā pañhaṃ vā pucchanti, dhammaṃ vā sotukāmā honti. Sacepi na kathāpenti, janasaṅgahatthaṃ dhammakathā nāma kātabbā yevāti aṭṭhakathācariyā vadanti. Dhammakathā hi kammaṭṭhānavinimuttā nāma natthi, tasmā kammaṭṭhānasīseneva dhammakathaṃ kathetvā kammaṭṭhānasīseneva āhāraṃ paribhuñjitvā anumodanaṃ katvā nivattiyamānehipi manussehi anugatova gāmato nikkhamitvā tattha te nivattetvā maggaṃ paṭipajjati.

Here, in this Dispensation, a certain bhikkhu carries [the meditation subject] on the way there, but does not carry [it] on the way back; a certain one carries [it] on the way back, but does not carry [it] on the way there; a certain one, however, neither carries [it] on the way there nor carries [it] on the way back; a certain one both carries [it] on the way there and carries [it] on the way back. Among them, the bhikkhu who, having thoroughly cleansed his mind from the hindering states by walking and sitting during the day, and likewise in the first watch of the night, having lain down to sleep in the middle watch, and having also passed the last watch with sitting and walking; and who, early in the morning, having performed the duties of the cetiya-courtyard and the Bodhi-courtyard, having poured water on the Bodhi tree, having set up drinking water and water for use, undertakes and practices all the duties found in the Khandhakas, such as the duties towards teachers and preceptors. That bhikkhu, having attended to his body, enters his dwelling, and for the duration of two or three cross-legged sittings, while letting his body warm up, applies himself to his meditation subject. At the time for the alms-round, having risen, taking his bowl and robe with the meditation subject as primary, he leaves his dwelling. While continuing to attend to his meditation subject, he goes to the cetiya-courtyard. If his meditation subject is the recollection of the Buddha, he enters the cetiya-courtyard without abandoning it. If it is another meditation subject, standing at the foot of the stairs, he sets it aside like an object carried in the hand, and taking up joy with the Buddha as its object, he ascends to the cetiya-courtyard. If it is a large cetiya, he should circumambulate it three times and pay homage at the four places. If it is a small cetiya, he should likewise circumambulate it and pay homage at the eight places. Having paid homage to the cetiya, upon reaching the Bodhi-courtyard, showing reverence as if in the presence of the Buddha, the Blessed One, the Bodhi tree should be venerated. Thus, having paid homage to the cetiya and the Bodhi tree, he goes to the place where he had set it aside, and like one picking up a stored item with the hand, he takes up the meditation subject that he had set down. Near the village, with the meditation subject as primary, he puts on his robe and enters the village for alms. Then people, seeing him, say, 'Our noble one has come!' and go out to meet him. Taking his bowl, they have him sit in a rest hall or in a house. Having given him gruel, while the meal is not yet ready, they wash his feet, anoint them with oil, and sitting before him, they ask a question or are desirous of hearing the Dhamma. Even if they do not ask him to speak, the commentary teachers say, 'For the sake of gathering the people, a Dhamma talk should certainly be given.' Indeed, there is no such thing as a Dhamma talk separate from a meditation subject. Therefore, having given a Dhamma talk with the meditation subject as primary, and having consumed the food with the meditation subject as primary, he gives the anumodanā (blessing). While returning, he is followed by the people. Leaving the village, he sends them back there and proceeds on his way.

Atha naṃ puretaraṃ nikkhamitvā bahigāme katabhattakiccā sāmaṇeradaharabhikkhū disvā paccuggantvā pattacīvaramassa gaṇhanti. Porāṇakabhikkhū kira amhākaṃ upajjhāyo ācariyoti na mukhaṃ oloketvā vattaṃ karonti, sampattaparicchedeneva karonti. Te taṃ pucchanti – “bhante, ete manussā tumhākaṃ kiṃ honti, mātipakkhato sambandhā pitipakkhato”ti? Kiṃ disvā pucchathāti? Tumhesu etesaṃ pemaṃ bahumānanti. Āvuso, yaṃ mātāpitūhipi dukkaraṃ, taṃ ete amhākaṃ karonti, pattacīvarampi no etesaṃ santakameva, etesaṃ ānubhāvena neva bhaye bhayaṃ, na chātake chātakaṃ jānāma. Īdisā nāma amhākaṃ upakārino natthīti tesaṃ guṇe kathento gacchati. Ayaṃ vuccati harati na paccāharatīti.

Then, novices and junior bhikkhus, who had gone out earlier and finished their meal duties outside the village, see him, go out to meet him, and take his bowl and robe. It is said that the bhikkhus of old did not perform their duties by looking at the face to see if it was 'our preceptor' or 'our teacher'; they performed them simply based on the seniority of those who had arrived. They ask him: 'Venerable sir, what are these people to you? Are they related on your mother's side or on your father's side?' 'Seeing what do you ask?' 'Seeing their affection and great respect for you.' 'Friends, what is difficult to be done even by one's mother and father, that these people do for us. Our bowl and robe are their property indeed. Through their power, we do not know fear in times of danger, nor hunger in times of famine. There are no such benefactors for us as these.' Thus, speaking of their virtues, he goes on his way. This one is called: 'He carries [it] on the way there, but does not carry [it] on the way back.'

Yassa pana pageva vuttappakāraṃ vattapaṭipattiṃ karontassa kammajatejodhātu pajjalati, anupādinnakaṃ muñcitvā upādinnakaṃ gaṇhāti, sarīrato sedā muñcanti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ vīthiṃ nārohati, so pageva pattacīvaramādāya vegasā cetiyaṃ vanditvā gorūpānaṃ nikkhamanavelāyameva gāmaṃ yāgubhikkhāya pavisitvā yāguṃ labhitvā āsanasālaṃ gantvā pivati, athassa dvattikkhattuṃ [P 1.0188] ajjhoharaṇamatteneva kammajatejodhātu upādinnakaṃ muñcitvā anupādinnakaṃ gaṇhāti, ghaṭasatena nhāto viya tejodhātu pariḷāhanibbānaṃ patvā kammaṭṭhānasīsena yāguṃ paribhuñjitvā pattañca mukhañca dhovitvā antarābhatte kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikatvā avasesaṭṭhāne piṇḍāya caritvā kammaṭṭhānasīsena āhārañca paribhuñjitvā tato paṭṭhāya poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ upaṭṭhahamānaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā [V 1.0154] āgacchati, ayaṃ vuccati paccāharati [M 1.0169] na haratīti. Edisā ca bhikkhū yāguṃ pivitvā vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā buddhasāsane arahattappattā nāma gaṇanapathaṃ vītivattā. Sīhaḷadīpeyeva tesu tesu gāmesu āsanasālāyaṃ vā na taṃ āsanamatthi, yattha yāguṃ pivitvā arahattappattā bhikkhū natthīti.

Furthermore, for the bhikkhu who, while practicing the duties in the aforementioned way early in the morning, the fire element born of kamma flares up, it releases the un-grasped [food] and seizes the grasped [bodily fluids]; sweat is released from his body, and the meditation subject does not enter the path of consciousness. That bhikkhu, early in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, quickly pays homage to the cetiya, and at the very time the cattle are coming out, he enters the village for gruel. Having received the gruel, he goes to a rest hall and drinks it. Then, for him, merely by swallowing two or three times, the fire element born of kamma releases the grasped [bodily fluids] and seizes the un-grasped [food]. Like one bathed with a hundred pots of water, having reached the cooling of the burning of the fire element, he consumes the gruel with the meditation subject as primary. Having washed his bowl and mouth, he attends to the meditation subject in the interval before the main meal. Having wandered for alms in the remaining places, he consumes the food with the meditation subject as primary. From then on, taking up the meditation subject as it arises in uninterrupted succession, he returns. This one is called: 'He carries [it] on the way back, but does not carry [it] on the way there.' And such bhikkhus, having drunk gruel and undertaken insight meditation, who have attained Arahantship in the Buddha's Dispensation are beyond counting. In the island of Sīhaḷa alone, in such and such villages or in a rest hall, there is no seat where there are no bhikkhus who attained Arahantship after drinking gruel.

Yo pana pamādavihārī hoti, nikkhittadhuro sabbavattāni bhinditvā pañcavidhacetokhīlavinibandhacitto viharanto – “kammaṭṭhānaṃ nāma atthī”ti saññampi akatvā gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisitvā ananulomikena gihisaṃsaggena saṃsaṭṭho caritvā ca bhuñjitvā ca tuccho nikkhamati, ayaṃ vuccati neva harati na paccāharatīti.

On the other hand, a certain monk who dwells heedlessly, having laid down the burden of practice, having broken all observances, dwells with a mind fettered by the five kinds of mental barrenness and the five kinds of mental bondage. Without even forming the perception, “There is such a thing as a meditation subject,” he enters a village for alms-food. Having mingled in unsuitable association with householders, and having wandered about and eaten, he departs empty of a meditation subject. This one is called, ‘He neither carries it away nor brings it back.’”

Yo panāyaṃ – “harati ca paccāharati cā”ti vutto, so gatapaccāgatavattavaseneva veditabbo. Attakāmā hi kulaputtā sāsane pabbajitvā dasapi vīsampi tiṃsampi cattālīsampi paññāsampi satampi ekato vasantā katikavattaṃ katvā viharanti, “āvuso, tumhe na iṇaṭṭā, na bhayaṭṭā, na jīvikāpakatā pabbajitā, dukkhā muccitukāmā panettha pabbajitā, tasmā gamane uppannakilesaṃ gamaneyeva niggaṇhatha, tathā ṭhāne, nisajjāya, sayane uppannakilesaṃ sayaneva niggaṇhathā”ti.

But as for this one who is said to be, ‘He carries it away and brings it back,’ he should be understood by way of the observance of going and returning. For indeed, clansmen desiring their own welfare, having gone forth in the Dispensation, dwelling together in groups of ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or even a hundred, make an agreement and abide by it, saying: ‘Venerable sirs, you have not gone forth because you were oppressed by debt, nor oppressed by fear, nor because your livelihood failed. Rather, you have gone forth in this Dispensation desiring to be freed from suffering. Therefore, a defilement that has arisen in the posture of going, you must restrain right in the posture of going. Likewise, for a defilement that has arisen in the posture of standing, sitting, or lying down, you must restrain it right in that very posture.’”

Te evaṃ katikavattaṃ katvā bhikkhācāraṃ [P 1.0189] gacchantā aḍḍhausabhausabhaaḍḍhagāvutagāvutantaresu pāsāṇā honti, tāya saññāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontāva gacchanti. Sace kassaci gamane kileso uppajjati, tattheva naṃ niggaṇhāti. Tathā asakkonto tiṭṭhati, athassa pacchato āgacchantopi tiṭṭhati. So “ayaṃ bhikkhu tuyhaṃ uppannavitakkaṃ jānāti, ananucchavikaṃ te eta”nti attānaṃ paṭicodetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā tattheva ariyabhūmiṃ okkamati; tathā asakkonto nisīdati. Athassa pacchato āgacchantopi nisīdatīti soyeva nayo. Ariyabhūmiṃ okkamituṃ asakkontopi taṃ kilesaṃ vikkhambhetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontova gacchati, na kammaṭṭhānavippayuttena cittena pādaṃ uddharati, uddharati ce, paṭinivattitvā purimapadesaṃyeva eti. Ālindakavāsī mahāphussadevatthero viya.

Having made such an agreement, while going on their alms-round, there are stones at intervals of half an usabha, an usabha, half a gāvuta, and a gāvuta. Using those as markers, they go while attending to their meditation subject. If a defilement arises in any one of them while walking, he restrains it right there. Being unable to do so, he stands still. Then the one coming behind him also stands still. He, having admonished himself, thinking, ‘This monk knows the thought that has arisen in you; this is unsuitable for you,’ develops insight and right there enters the noble ground. Being unable to do so, he sits down. Then the one coming behind him also sits down—this is the same method. Even if unable to enter the noble ground, having suppressed that defilement, he goes on while attending to the meditation subject. He does not lift a foot with a mind disconnected from the meditation subject; and if he does lift it, he turns back and returns to the very same previous spot, like the Elder Mahāphussadeva, the resident of Ālindaka.

So [M 1.0170] kira ekūnavīsativassāni gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūrento eva vihāsi, manussāpi addasaṃsu antarāmagge kasantā ca vapantā ca maddantā ca kammāni ca karontā theraṃ tathāgacchantaṃ disvā – “ayaṃ thero punappunaṃ nivattitvā gacchati, kinnu kho maggamūḷho, udāhu [V 1.0155] kiñci pamuṭṭho”ti samullapanti. So taṃ anādiyitvā kammaṭṭhānayuttacitteneva samaṇadhammaṃ karonto vīsativassabbhantare arahattaṃ pāpuṇi, arahattappattadivase cassa caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ adhivatthā devatā aṅgulīhi dīpaṃ ujjāletvā aṭṭhāsi. Cattāropi mahārājāno sakko ca devānamindo brahmā ca sahampati upaṭṭhānaṃ agamaṃsu. Tañca obhāsaṃ disvā vanavāsī mahātissatthero taṃ dutiyadivase pucchi – “rattibhāge āyasmato santike obhāso ahosi, kiṃ so obhāso”ti? Thero vikkhepaṃ karonto obhāso nāma dīpobhāsopi hoti, maṇiobhāsopīti evamādimāha. Tato ‘paṭicchādetha tumhe’ti nibaddho ‘āmā’ti paṭijānitvā [P 1.0190] ārocesi. Kāḷavallimaṇḍapavāsī mahānāgatthero viya ca.

It is said that he dwelt for nineteen years fulfilling only the observance of going and returning. People, while plowing, sowing, threshing, and doing their work along the way, saw the Elder going in that manner and discussed among themselves, saying: ‘This elder goes on, turning back again and again. Is he perhaps lost on the path, or has he forgotten something?’ He, paying them no heed, practicing the ascetic's duties with a mind connected only to the meditation subject, attained Arahantship within twenty years. On the very day he attained Arahantship, the deity dwelling at the end of his walking path stood there, causing a light to shine with her fingers. The Four Great Kings, Sakka, lord of the devas, and Brahmā Sahampati also came to attend on him. Seeing that radiance, the Elder Mahātissa, a forest-dweller, asked him on the second day: ‘Venerable sir, during the night there was a radiance in your presence. What was that radiance?’ The Elder, wishing to evade the question, said things such as, ‘Radiance can be the radiance of a lamp, or the radiance of a gem.’ Then, being pressed with the words, ‘You are concealing it, venerable sir,’ he admitted, ‘Yes,’ and revealed the matter. And also like the Elder Mahānāga, the resident of the Kāḷavalli Pavilion.

Sopi kira gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūrento – paṭhamaṃ tāva bhagavato mahāpadhānaṃ pūjessāmīti sattavassāni ṭhānacaṅkamameva adhiṭṭhāsi. Puna soḷasavassāni gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūretvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. So kammaṭṭhānayutteneva cittena pādaṃ uddharanto, viyuttena uddhaṭe paṭinivattento gāmasamīpaṃ gantvā “gāvī nu pabbajito nū”ti āsaṅkanīyapadese ṭhatvā cīvaraṃ pārupitvā kacchakantarato udakena pattaṃ dhovitvā udakagaṇḍūsaṃ karoti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Mā me bhikkhaṃ dātuṃ vā vandituṃ vā āgate manusse ‘dīghāyukā hothā’ti vacanamattenāpi kammaṭṭhānavikkhepo ahosīti. “Ajja, bhante, katimī”ti divasaṃ vā bhikkhugaṇanaṃ vā pañhaṃ vā pucchito pana udakaṃ gilitvā āroceti. Sace divasādīni pucchakā na honti, nikkhamanavelāya gāmadvāre niṭṭhubhitvāva yāti.

It is said that he too, while fulfilling the observance of going and returning, first thinking, ‘I will pay homage to the Blessed One’s Great Striving,’ undertook only standing and walking meditation for seven years. Again, for sixteen years, he fulfilled the observance of going and returning and attained Arahantship. He would lift his foot only with a mind connected to the meditation subject; when it was lifted with a disconnected mind, he would turn back. Having gone near a village, he would stand in a place where one might doubt, ‘Is it a cow or a monk?’, put on his robe, wash his bowl with water from a container carried under his armpit, and take a mouthful of water. For what reason? So that there would be no distraction to his meditation subject even by the mere words, ‘May you be long-lived,’ spoken to people who had come to give him alms-food or to pay homage. But when asked about the day, such as, ‘Venerable sir, what is the date today?’, or about the number of monks, or some other question, he would swallow the water and answer. If there were no people asking about the day and so on, at the time of departure, he would spit it out at the village gate and then go.

Kalambatitthavihāre vassūpagatā paññāsabhikkhū viya ca. Te kira āsaḷhipuṇṇamāyaṃ katikavattaṃ akaṃsu – “arahattaṃ appatvā aññamaññaṃ nālapissāmā”ti, gāmañca piṇḍāya pavisantā udakagaṇḍūsaṃ katvā pavisiṃsu. Divasādīsu pucchitesu vuttanayeneva paṭipajjiṃsu. Tattha manussā niṭṭhubhanaṃ [M 1.0171] disvā jāniṃsu – “ajjeko āgato, ajja dve”ti. Evañca cintesuṃ – “kinnu kho ete amhehiyeva saddhiṃ na sallapanti, udāhu aññamaññampi. Sace aññamaññampi na sallapanti, addhā vivādajātā bhavissanti. Etha ne aññamaññaṃ khamāpessāmā”ti, sabbe vihāraṃ gantvā paññāsāya bhikkhūsu dvepi bhikkhū ekokāse nāddasaṃsu. Tato yo tesu cakkhumā puriso, so āha – “na bho kalahakārakānaṃ [P 1.0191] vasanokāso īdiso hoti, susammaṭṭhaṃ cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇaṃ, sunikkhittā sammajjaniyo, sūpaṭṭhapitaṃ pānīyaṃ paribhojanīya”nti, te tatova nivattā. Tepi bhikkhū anto temāseyeva arahattaṃ patvā mahāpavāraṇāya visuddhipavāraṇaṃ pavāresuṃ.

And like the fifty monks who had entered the rains-retreat at the Kalambatittha Monastery. It is said that they, on the full moon day of Āsāḷhī, made a pact: 'Until we attain Arahantship, we will not speak to one another.' And when entering the village for alms, they took a mouthful of water and entered. When asked about the day and other such things, they acted in the manner already described. There, the people, seeing the spitting, knew: 'Today one has come, today two.' And they thought thus: 'Why is it that these monks do not speak with us? Or is it that they do not speak even with one another? If they do not speak even with one another, surely they have come to be in a dispute. Come, let us have them ask forgiveness of one another.' All of them went to the monastery, but among the fifty monks, they did not see even two monks in one place. Then, the man among them who had the eye of wisdom said: 'Sirs, the dwelling place of quarrelers is not like this. The cetiya-courtyard and the Bodhi-courtyard are well-swept, the brooms are well-placed, and drinking water and water for use are well-prepared.' They turned back from that very place. Those monks, within the three months, attained Arahantship and on the day of the Great Pavāraṇā, they performed the Pavāraṇā of purity.

Evaṃ [V 1.0156] kāḷavallimaṇḍapavāsī mahānāgatthero viya, kalambatitthavihāre vassūpagatabhikkhū viya ca kammaṭṭhānayutteneva cittena pādaṃ uddharanto gāmasamīpaṃ gantvā udakagaṇḍūsaṃ katvā vīthiyo sallakkhetvā, yattha surāsoṇḍadhuttādayo kalahakārakā caṇḍahatthiassādayo vā natthi, taṃ vīthiṃ paṭipajjati. Tattha ca piṇḍāya caramāno na turitaturito viya javena gacchati. Na hi javena piṇḍapātiyadhutaṅgaṃ nāma kiñci atthi. Visamabhūmibhāgappattaṃ pana udakasakaṭaṃ viya niccalo hutvā gacchati. Anugharaṃ paviṭṭho ca dātukāmaṃ vā adātukāmaṃ vā sallakkhetvā tadanurūpaṃ kālaṃ āgamento bhikkhaṃ paṭilabhitvā ādāya antogāme vā bahigāme vā vihārameva vā āgantvā yathā phāsuke patirūpe okāse nisīditvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikaronto āhāre paṭikūlasaññaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā akkhabbhañjana – vaṇalepanaputtamaṃsūpamavasena paccavekkhanto aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ āhāraṃ āhāreti, neva davāya na madāya na maṇḍanāya na vibhūsanāya…pe… bhuttāvī ca udakakiccaṃ katvā muhuttaṃ bhattakilamathaṃ paṭippassambhetvā yathā purebhattaṃ, evaṃ pacchābhattaṃ purimayāmaṃ pacchimayāmañca kammaṭṭhānameva manasi karoti, ayaṃ vuccati harati ca paccāharati cāti.

Thus, like the great elder Mahānāga who dwelt in the Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa, and like the monks who had entered the rains-retreat at the Kalambatittha Monastery, with a mind connected only with the meditation subject, he lifts his foot. Having gone near the village and taken a mouthful of water, he observes the streets and proceeds along a street where there are no drunkards, womanizers, and other quarrelers, nor fierce elephants, horses, and other such animals. And while walking there for alms, he does not go with speed as if in a great hurry. For there is no such thing as an ascetic practice of the alms-round that is done with speed. But, like a water-cart that has reached an uneven part of the ground, he goes on having become steady. And having entered the houses in succession, observing those who wish to give and those who do not, and waiting for a suitable time, he receives the almsfood. Having received it, he returns either to a place inside the village, or outside the village, or to the monastery itself. Having sat down in a suitable, comfortable place, while attending to the meditation subject, he establishes the perception of repulsiveness in regard to the food. Reflecting by way of the similes of anointing an axle, applying ointment to a wound, and the flesh of one's son, he partakes of the food endowed with eight factors: not for sport, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for beautification. And having eaten, having done what is to be done with water, and having for a moment allayed the fatigue from the meal, just as before the meal, so too after the meal, in the first watch and the last watch, he attends only to the meditation subject. This one is called 'he who carries and carries back'.

Idaṃ pana haraṇapaccāharaṇasaṅkhātaṃ gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūrento yadi upanissayasampanno hoti, paṭhamavaye eva arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. No ce paṭhamavaye pāpuṇāti, atha [P 1.0192] majjhimavaye; no ce majjhimavaye pāpuṇāti, atha maraṇasamaye; no ce maraṇasamaye pāpuṇāti, atha [M 1.0172] devaputto hutvā; no ce devaputto hutvā pāpuṇāti, anuppanne buddhe nibbatto paccekabodhiṃ sacchikaroti. No ce paccekabodhiṃ sacchikaroti, atha buddhānaṃ sammukhībhāve khippābhiñño hoti; seyyathāpi thero bāhiyo dārucīriyo mahāpañño vā, seyyathāpi thero sāriputto mahiddhiko vā, seyyathāpi thero mahāmoggallāno dhutavādo vā, seyyathāpi thero mahākassapo dibbacakkhuko vā, seyyathāpi thero anuruddho vinayadharo vā, seyyathāpi thero upāli dhammakathiko vā, seyyathāpi thero puṇṇo mantāṇiputto āraññiko vā, seyyathāpi thero revato bahussuto vā, seyyathāpi thero ānando bhikkhākāmo vā, seyyathāpi thero rāhulo buddhaputtoti. Iti imasmiṃ catukke yvāyaṃ harati ca paccāharati ca, tassa gocarasampajaññaṃ sikhāpattaṃ hoti.

Furthermore, one who fulfills this duty of going and returning, known as 'carrying and carrying back,' if he is endowed with strong supporting conditions, attains Arahantship in the first age of life. If he does not attain it in the first age, then in the middle age; if he does not attain it in the middle age, then at the time of death; if he does not attain it at the time of death, then having become a devaputta; if he does not attain it having become a devaputta, then being born when a Buddha has not arisen, he realizes Paccekabodhi. If he does not realize Paccekabodhi, then in the presence of the Buddhas he becomes one of swift insight, just like the Elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya; or one of great wisdom, just like the Elder Sāriputta; or one of great psychic power, just like the Elder Mahāmoggallāna; or an exponent of the ascetic practices, just like the Elder Mahākassapa; or one with the divine eye, just like the Elder Anuruddha; or a master of the Vinaya, just like the Elder Upāli; or a preacher of the Dhamma, just like the Elder Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta; or a forest-dweller, just like the Elder Revata; or one of great learning, just like the Elder Ānanda; or one desirous of the training, just like the Elder Rāhula, the Buddha's son. Thus, in this tetrad, for that person who 'carries and carries back,' his clear comprehension of the resort reaches its peak.

Abhikkamādīsu pana asammuyhanaṃ asammohasampajaññaṃ, taṃ evaṃ veditabbaṃ – idha bhikkhu abhikkamanto vā paṭikkamanto vā yathā andhabālaputhujjanā abhikkamādīsu – “attā abhikkamati, attanā abhikkamo nibbattito”ti vā, “ahaṃ abhikkamāmi, mayā abhikkamo [V 1.0157] nibbattito”ti vā sammuyhanti, tathā asammuyhanto “abhikkamāmī”ti citte uppajjamāne teneva cittena saddhiṃ cittasamuṭṭhānā vāyodhātu viññattiṃ janayamānā uppajjati. Iti cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāravasena ayaṃ kāyasammato aṭṭhisaṅghāto abhikkamati. Tassevaṃ abhikkamato ekekapāduddharaṇe pathavīdhātu āpodhātūti dve dhātuyo omattā honti mandā, itarā dve adhimattā honti balavatiyo; tathā atiharaṇavītiharaṇesu. Vossajjane tejodhātu vāyodhātūti dve dhātuyo omattā honti mandā, itarā dve adhimattā balavatiyo, tathā sannikkhepanasannirujjhanesu. Tattha uddharaṇe [P 1.0193] pavattā rūpārūpadhammā atiharaṇaṃ na pāpuṇanti, tathā atiharaṇe pavattā vītiharaṇaṃ, vītiharaṇe pavattā vossajjanaṃ, vossajjane pavattā sannikkhepanaṃ, sannikkhepane pavattā sannirujjhanaṃ na pāpuṇanti. Tattha tattheva pabbaṃ pabbaṃ sandhi sandhi odhi odhi hutvā tattakapāle [M 1.0173] pakkhittatilāni viya paṭapaṭāyantā bhijjanti. Tattha ko eko abhikkamati, kassa vā ekassa abhikkamanaṃ? Paramatthato hi dhātūnaṃyeva gamanaṃ, dhātūnaṃ ṭhānaṃ, dhātūnaṃ nisajjanaṃ, dhātūnaṃ sayanaṃ. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ koṭṭhāse saddhiṃ rūpena.

Furthermore, the non-bewilderment in going forward and so on is the clear comprehension of non-delusion. It should be understood thus: Here, a bhikkhu, when going forward or returning, is not bewildered in the way that blind, foolish worldlings are bewildered in going forward and so on—thinking, “A self goes forward; the going forward is produced by a self,” or, “I go forward; the going forward is produced by me.” Not being bewildered in that way, when the thought, “I will go forward,” arises, together with that very mind, the wind element originating from the mind arises, producing bodily intimation. Thus, by the power of the movement of the wind element due to the mind’s activity, this collection of bones, designated as the body, goes forward. As it thus goes forward, at the time of lifting each foot, the two elements, the earth element and the water element, become of lesser measure and weak; the other two become of greater measure and strong. It is similar in the case of carrying forward and carrying aside. At the time of releasing the foot, the two elements, the fire element and the wind element, become of lesser measure and weak; the other two become of greater measure and strong. It is similar in the case of placing and pressing down. Therein, the material and immaterial phenomena that occurred at the moment of lifting do not reach the moment of carrying forward; similarly, those that occurred at the moment of carrying forward do not reach the moment of carrying aside; those that occurred at the moment of carrying aside do not reach the moment of releasing; those that occurred at the moment of releasing do not reach the moment of placing; and those that occurred at the moment of placing do not reach the moment of pressing down. Therein, in that very place, becoming joint by joint, connection by connection, part by part, they break up, crackling like sesame seeds thrown onto a heated pan. Therein, who is the one that goes forward? Or of which one is the going forward? For, in an ultimate sense, it is only the going of the elements, the standing of the elements, the sitting of the elements, the lying down of the elements. In each and every part, along with materiality.

Aññaṃ uppajjate cittaṃ, aññaṃ cittaṃ nirujjhati;

Avīcimanusambandho, nadīsotova vattatīti.

Another mind arises, another mind ceases; an uninterrupted, continuous succession proceeds like the current of a river.

Evaṃ abhikkamādīsu asammuyhanaṃ asammohasampajaññaṃ nāmāti.

Thus, non-bewilderment in going forward and so on is called the clear comprehension of non-delusion.

Niṭṭhito abhikkante paṭikkante sampajānakārī hotīti padassa attho.

The meaning of the phrase 'he is one who acts with clear comprehension in going forward and returning' is concluded.

Ālokite vilokiteti ettha pana ālokitaṃ nāma purato pekkhaṇaṃ. Vilokitaṃ nāma anudisāpekkhaṇaṃ. Aññānipi heṭṭhā upari pacchato pekkhaṇavasena olokitaullokitāpalokitāni nāma honti, tāni idha na gahitāni. Sāruppavasena pana imāneva dve gahitāni, iminā vā mukhena sabbānipi tāni gahitānevāti.

Now, regarding 'in looking ahead and in looking around': 'looking ahead' means looking forward. 'Looking around' means looking towards a diagonal direction. There are also other ways of looking—downwards, upwards, and backwards—which are called looking down, looking up, and looking back; these are not taken up here. However, on account of their suitability for bhikkhus, only these two are taken up. Alternatively, by means of these two, which are primary, all of those are indeed taken up.

Tattha “ālokessāmī”ti citte uppanne cittavaseneva anoloketvā atthapariggaṇhanaṃ sātthakasampajaññaṃ, taṃ āyasmantaṃ nandaṃ kāyasakkhiṃ katvā veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “sace, bhikkhave, nandassa puratthimā disā āloketabbā hoti, sabbaṃ cetasā samannāharitvā nando puratthimaṃ disaṃ āloketi – ‘evaṃ me puratthimaṃ disaṃ ālokayato na abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssavissantī’ti. Itiha tattha sampajāno [P 1.0194] hoti [V 1.0158] (a. ni. 8.9). Sace, bhikkhave, nandassa pacchimā disā…pe… uttarā disā…pe… dakkhiṇā disā…pe… uddhaṃ…pe… adho…pe… anudisā anuviloketabbā hoti, sabbaṃ cetasā samannāharitvā nando anudisaṃ anuviloketi – ‘evaṃ me anudisaṃ anuvilokayato na abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssavissantī’ti. Itiha tattha sampajāno hotī”ti.

Therein, when the thought, 'I will look ahead,' arises, not looking merely according to the mind's wish, but grasping the purpose, is the clear comprehension of purposefulness. This should be understood by making the Venerable Nanda a personal witness. For this was said by the Blessed One: 'Monks, if the Venerable Nanda has to look towards the eastern direction, having fully attended with his mind, Nanda looks towards the eastern direction, reflecting: “As I am looking towards the eastern direction, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure will not flow in.” Thus, he is clearly comprehending therein. Monks, if the Venerable Nanda has to look around towards the western direction... and so on... the northern direction... and so on... the southern direction... and so on... upwards... and so on... downwards... and so on... a diagonal direction, having fully attended with his mind, Nanda looks around towards the diagonal direction, reflecting: “As I am looking around towards the diagonal direction, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure will not flow in.” Thus, he is clearly comprehending therein.'

Api ca idhāpi pubbe vuttacetiyadassanādivaseneva sātthakatā ca sappāyatā ca veditabbā, kammaṭṭhānassa pana avijahanameva gocarasampajaññaṃ. Tasmā [M 1.0174] ettha khandhadhātuāyatanakammaṭṭhānikehi attano kammaṭṭhānavaseneva, kasiṇādikammaṭṭhānikehi vā pana kammaṭṭhānasīseneva ālokanaṃ vilokanaṃ kātabbaṃ. Abbhantare attā nāma āloketā vā viloketā vā natthi, ‘ālokessāmī’ti pana citte uppajjamāne teneva cittena saddhiṃ cittasamuṭṭhānā vāyodhātu viññattiṃ janayamānā uppajjati. Iti cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāravasena heṭṭhimaṃ akkhidalaṃ adho sīdati, uparimaṃ uddhaṃ laṅgheti. Koci yantakena vivaranto nāma natthi. Tato cakkhuviññāṇaṃ dassanakiccaṃ sādhentaṃ uppajjatīti evaṃ pajānanaṃ panettha asammohasampajaññaṃ nāma. Api ca mūlapariññā āgantukatāva kālikabhāvavasena pettha asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ. Mūlapariññāvasena tāva –

Furthermore, here too, purposefulness and suitability should be understood by way of the previously mentioned seeing of a cetiya and so on. However, the non-abandonment of the meditation subject is itself the clear comprehension of the resort. Therefore, herein, those who practice meditation on the aggregates, elements, and sense bases should perform looking and glancing only by way of their own meditation subject. And those who practice meditation on kasiṇas and so on should do so with the meditation subject as their primary focus. Inside, there is no self that is a looker or a glancer. But when the thought, 'I will look,' arises, together with that very mind, the wind element originating from the mind arises, producing bodily intimation. Thus, by the power of the movement of the wind element due to the mind’s activity, the lower eyelid sinks down and the upper one leaps up. There is no one who opens it with a machine. Then, eye-consciousness arises, accomplishing the function of seeing. Thus, knowing in this way is called the clear comprehension of non-delusion. Furthermore, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood here also by way of comprehending the root, and by way of its nature as adventitious and temporary. First, by way of comprehending the root:

Bhavaṅgāvajjanañceva, dassanaṃ sampaṭicchanaṃ;

Santīraṇaṃ voṭṭhabbanaṃ, javanaṃ bhavati sattamaṃ.

Life-continuum and adverting, seeing, receiving, investigating, determining; impulsion is the seventh.

Tattha bhavaṅgaṃ upapattibhavassa aṅgakiccaṃ sādhayamānaṃ pavattati, taṃ āvaṭṭetvā kiriyamanodhātu āvajjanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā, taṃnirodhā cakkhuviññāṇaṃ dassanakiccaṃ sādhayamānaṃ, taṃnirodhā vipākamanodhātu sampaṭicchanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā, taṃnirodhā vipākamanoviññāṇadhātu santīraṇakiccaṃ sādhayamānā, taṃnirodhā kiriyamanoviññāṇadhātu voṭṭhabbanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā[P 1.0195], taṃnirodhā sattakkhattuṃ javanaṃ javati. Tattha paṭhamajavanepi – “ayaṃ itthī, ayaṃ puriso”ti rajjanadussanamuyhanavasena ālokitavilokitaṃ nāma na hoti. Dutiyajavanepi…pe… sattamajavanepi. Etesu pana yuddhamaṇḍale yodhesu viya heṭṭhupariyavasena bhijjitvā patitesu – “ayaṃ itthī, ayaṃ puriso”ti rajjanādivasena ālokitavilokitaṃ hoti. Evaṃ tāvettha mūlapariññāvasena asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Therein, the life-continuum proceeds, accomplishing the function of the principal component of rebirth-existence. Having turned that away, the functional mind-element proceeds, accomplishing the function of adverting. Upon its cessation, eye-consciousness proceeds, accomplishing the function of seeing. Upon its cessation, the resultant mind-element proceeds, accomplishing the function of receiving. Upon its cessation, the resultant mind-consciousness-element proceeds, accomplishing the function of investigating. Upon its cessation, the functional mind-consciousness-element proceeds, accomplishing the function of determining. Upon its cessation, the impulsion runs seven times. Therein, even during the first impulsion, what is called 'looking and glancing' by way of lust, aversion, and delusion—thinking, 'This is a woman, this is a man'—does not occur. Nor during the second impulsion... and so on... nor during the seventh impulsion. However, with regard to these, when they have been broken and have fallen—like warriors in a battlefield by way of being struck from above and below—then 'looking and glancing' by way of lust and so on, thinking, 'This is a woman, this is a man,' occurs. Thus, firstly, in this context, non-deluded clear comprehension should be understood by way of understanding the root.

Cakkhudvāre [V 1.0159] pana rūpe āpāthamāgate bhavaṅgacalanato uddhaṃ sakakiccanipphādanavasena āvajjanādīsu uppajjitvā niruddhesu avasāne javanaṃ uppajjati, taṃ pubbe uppannānaṃ āvajjanādīnaṃ gehabhūte cakkhudvāre āgantukapuriso viya hoti. Tassa yathā paragehe kiñci yācituṃ paviṭṭhassa āgantukapurisassa gehassāmikesu tuṇhīmāsinesu āṇākaraṇaṃ na yuttaṃ, evaṃ [M 1.0175] āvajjanādīnaṃ gehabhūte cakkhudvāre āvajjanādīsupi arajjantesu adussantesu amuyhantesu ca rajjanadussanamuyhanaṃ ayuttanti evaṃ āgantukabhāvavasena asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, when a visible object has come into the range of the eye-door, after the vibration of the life-continuum, when adverting and the other consciousnesses have arisen and ceased by way of accomplishing their respective functions, at the end, impulsion arises. That impulsion is like a visiting man in the eye-door, which has become the house of the previously arisen adverting and other consciousnesses. Just as it is not proper for a visiting man, who has entered another's house to ask for something, to issue commands while the masters of the house are sitting in silence, so too, in the eye-door which has become the house of adverting and the others, when even adverting and the others are not lustful, not averse, and not deluded, it is improper for the impulsion to be lustful, averse, or deluded. Thus, non-deluded clear comprehension should be understood by way of the state of being a visitor.

Yāni panetāni cakkhudvāre voṭṭhabbanapariyosānāni cittāni uppajjanti, tāni saddhiṃ sampayuttadhammehi tattha tattheva bhijjanti, aññamaññaṃ na passantīti, ittarāni tāvakālikāni honti. Tattha yathā ekasmiṃ ghare sabbesu mānusakesu matesu avasesassa ekassa taṅkhaṇaññeva maraṇadhammassa na yuttā naccagītādīsu abhirati nāma. Evameva ekadvāre sasampayuttesu āvajjanādīsu tattha tattheva matesu avasesassa taṅkhaṇeyeva maraṇadhammassa javanassāpi rajjanadussanamuyhanavasena abhirati nāma na yuttāti. Evaṃ tāvakālikabhāvavasena asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, whatever consciousnesses arise in the eye-door ending with determining, they break up right then and there together with their associated mental states; they do not see one another. Thus, they are trifling and temporary. In this regard, it is like in a certain house where all the people have died; for the one person remaining, who is subject to death at that very moment, delight in dancing, singing, and so on is not fitting. In the very same way, at a single sense-door, when adverting and the other consciousnesses along with their associated states have 'died'—that is, ceased—right then and there, for the remaining impulsion, which is also subject to death at that very moment, delight by way of lust, aversion, and delusion is not fitting. Thus, non-deluded clear comprehension should be understood by way of this temporary nature.

Api ca khandhāyatanadhātupaccayapaccavekkhaṇavasena petaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ettha hi cakkhu ceva rūpā ca rūpakkhandho, dassanaṃ viññāṇakkhandho, taṃsampayuttā [P 1.0196] vedanā vedanākkhandho, saññā saññākkhandho, phassādikā saṅkhārakkhandho. Evametesaṃ pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ samavāye ālokanavilokanaṃ paññāyati. Tattha ko eko āloketi, ko viloketi?

Furthermore, this non-deluded clear comprehension should also be understood by way of reviewing the aggregates, sense bases, elements, and conditions. For herein, the eye and forms are the aggregate of form; seeing is the aggregate of consciousness; the feeling associated with it is the aggregate of feeling; perception is the aggregate of perception; contact and so on are the aggregate of formations. Thus, through the combination of these five aggregates, looking and looking around becomes manifest. In that case, what single one looks? What single one looks around?

Tathā cakkhu cakkhāyatanaṃ, rūpaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ, dassanaṃ manāyatanaṃ, vedanādayo sampayuttadhammā dhammāyatanaṃ. Evametesaṃ catunnaṃ āyatanānaṃ samavāye ālokanavilokanaṃ paññāyati. Tattha ko eko āloketi, ko viloketi?

Likewise, the eye is the eye-base; the visible object is the form-base; seeing is the mind-base; and associated states such as feeling are the phenomenon-base. Thus, through the combination of these four bases, looking and looking around becomes manifest. In that case, what single one looks? What single one looks around?

Tathā cakkhu cakkhudhātu, rūpaṃ rūpadhātu, dassanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇadhātu, taṃsampayuttā vedanādayo dhammā dhammadhātu. Evametāsaṃ catunnaṃ dhātūnaṃ samavāye ālokanavilokanaṃ paññāyati. Tattha ko eko āloketi, ko viloketi?

Likewise, the eye is the eye-element; the visible object is the form-element; seeing is the eye-consciousness-element; and the states associated with it, such as feeling, are the phenomenon-element. Thus, through the combination of these four elements, looking and looking around becomes manifest. In that case, what single one looks? What single one looks around?

Tathā cakkhu nissayapaccayo, rūpā ārammaṇapaccayo, āvajjanaṃ anantarasamanantarūpanissayanatthivigatapaccayo[V 1.0160], āloko upanissayapaccayo, vedanādayo sahajātapaccayo. Evametesaṃ paccayānaṃ samavāye [M 1.0176] ālokanavilokanaṃ paññāyati. Tattha ko eko āloketi, ko viloketīti? Evamettha khandhāyatanadhātupaccayapaccavekkhaṇavasenapi asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Likewise, the eye is a dependence condition; the visible object is an object condition; adverting is an immediate contiguity, contiguity, decisive support, absence, and disappearance condition; light is a supporting condition; and feeling and other states are co-nascence and other conditions. Thus, through the combination of these conditions, looking and looking around becomes manifest. In that case, what single one looks? What single one looks around? In this way, non-deluded clear comprehension should also be understood by way of reviewing the aggregates, sense bases, elements, and conditions.

Samiñjite pasāriteti pabbānaṃ samiñjanapasāraṇe. Tattha cittavaseneva samiñjanapasāraṇaṃ akatvā hatthapādānaṃ samiñjanapasāraṇapaccayā atthānatthaṃ pariggaṇhitvā atthapariggaṇhanaṃ sātthakasampajaññaṃ. Tattha hatthapāde aticiraṃ samiñjetvā vā pasāretvā vā ṭhitassa khaṇe khaṇe vedanā uppajjati, cittaṃ ekaggataṃ na labhati, kammaṭṭhānaṃ paripatati, visesaṃ nādhigacchati. Kāle samiñjentassa kāle pasārentassa pana tā vedanā nuppajjanti, cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ phātiṃ gacchati, visesamadhigacchatīti[P 1.0197], evaṃ atthānatthapariggaṇhanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Regarding 'in bending, in stretching': this refers to the bending and stretching of the limbs. Therein, not bending and stretching by the power of mind alone, but having discerned the benefit and harm on account of bending and stretching the hands and feet—this discerning of the benefit is clear comprehension of purpose. In this regard, for one who remains having bent or stretched the hands and feet for too long, feeling arises from moment to moment, the mind does not obtain one-pointedness, the meditation subject falls away, and one does not attain any special distinction. But for one who bends at the proper time and stretches at the proper time, those feelings do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed, the meditation subject flourishes, and one attains special distinction. Thus, the discernment of benefit and harm should be understood.

Atthe pana satipi sappāyāsappāyaṃ pariggaṇhitvā sappāyapariggaṇhanaṃ sappāyasampajaññaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ nayo –

Furthermore, even when there is a benefit, having discerned what is suitable and unsuitable, the discerning of what is suitable is clear comprehension of suitability. In this regard, this is the method:

Mahācetiyaṅgaṇe kira daharabhikkhū sajjhāyaṃ gaṇhanti, tesaṃ piṭṭhipassesu daharabhikkhuniyo dhammaṃ suṇanti. Tatreko daharo hatthaṃ pasārento kāyasaṃsaggaṃ patvā teneva kāraṇena gihī jāto. Aparo bhikkhu pādaṃ pasārento aggimhi pasāresi, aṭṭhimāhacca pādo jhāyi. Aparo vammike pasāresi, so āsīvisena ḍaṭṭho. Aparo cīvarakuṭidaṇḍake pasāresi, taṃ maṇisappo ḍaṃsi. Tasmā evarūpe asappāye apasāretvā sappāye pasāretabbaṃ. Idamettha sappāyasampajaññaṃ.

It is said that young monks were reciting in the courtyard of the Great Cetiya, and young nuns were listening to the Dhamma behind them. There, one young monk, stretching out his hand, came into physical contact and for that very reason became a layman. Another monk, stretching out his foot, stretched it into a fire; his foot struck a bone and was burned. Another stretched his foot onto an anthill, and he was bitten by a venomous snake. Another stretched his foot onto the pole of a robe-hut, and a Maṇi-snake bit him. Therefore, one should not stretch out in such an unsuitable place, but should stretch out in a suitable place. This, herein, is the clear comprehension of suitability.

Gocarasampajaññaṃ pana mahātheravatthunā dīpetabbaṃ – mahāthero kira divāṭhāne nisinno antevāsikehi saddhiṃ kathayamāno sahasā hatthaṃ samiñjetvā puna yathāṭhāne ṭhapetvā saṇikaṃ samiñjesi. Taṃ antevāsikā pucchiṃsu – “kasmā, bhante, sahasā hatthaṃ samiñjitvā puna yathāṭhāne ṭhapetvā saṇikaṃ samiñjiyitthā”ti? Yato paṭṭhāyāhaṃ, āvuso, kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikātuṃ āraddho, na me kammaṭṭhānaṃ muñcitvā hattho samiñjitapubbo, idāni pana me tumhehi saddhiṃ kathayamānena kammaṭṭhānaṃ muñcitvā samiñjito. Tasmā puna yathāṭhāne ṭhapetvā samiñjesinti. Sādhu[M 1.0177], bhante, bhikkhunā nāma evarūpena bhavitabbanti. Evametthāpi kammaṭṭhānāvijahanameva gocarasampajaññanti veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, clear comprehension of the domain should be illustrated by the story of the great elder. It is said that the great elder, sitting in his daytime dwelling while conversing with his resident pupils, suddenly bent his hand, then placed it back in its original position and bent it slowly. His resident pupils asked him, “Venerable sir, why did you suddenly bend your hand, then place it back in its original position and bend it slowly?” “Friends, from the time I began to apply my mind to a meditation subject, my hand had never before been bent having abandoned the meditation subject. But just now, while conversing with you, it was bent having abandoned the meditation subject. Therefore, I placed it back in its original position and bent it.” “Excellent, venerable sir, a monk should indeed be of such a nature.” Thus, here too, the very non-abandoning of the meditation subject should be understood as clear comprehension of the domain.

Abbhantare [V 1.0161] attā nāma koci samiñjento vā pasārento vā natthi, vuttappakāracittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena pana suttākaḍḍhanavasena dāruyantassa hatthapādalacalanaṃ viya samiñjanapasāraṇaṃ hotīti evaṃ parijānanaṃ panettha asammohasampajaññanti veditabbaṃ.

Internally, there is no 'self' that flexes or stretches; rather, flexing and stretching occur due to the movement of the wind element generated by the activity of the mind in the manner described, like the movement of the hands and feet of a wooden puppet caused by the pulling of strings. Thus, discerning this is to be understood herein as the clear comprehension of non-delusion.

Saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇeti ettha saṅghāṭicīvarānaṃ [P 1.0198] nivāsanapārupanavasena pattassa bhikkhāpaṭiggahaṇādivasena paribhogo dhāraṇaṃ nāma. Tattha saṅghāṭicīvaradhāraṇe tāva nivāsetvā vā pārupitvā vā piṇḍāya carato āmisalābho sītassa paṭighātāyātiādinā nayena bhagavatā vuttappakāroyeva ca attho attho nāma. Tassa vasena sātthakasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

In the phrase 'the wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and robes,' 'wearing' (dhāraṇa) means use: the use of the saṅghāṭī and robes by way of dressing and draping, and the use of the bowl by way of receiving almsfood and so on. Therein, with regard to the wearing of the saṅghāṭī and robes: for one who wanders for alms having dressed or draped himself, the gain of material requisites, and also the benefit of the kind stated by the Blessed One in the manner of 'for the warding off of cold,' etc.—this is what is called 'benefit' (attha). By means of that benefit, clear comprehension of purpose should be understood.

Uṇhapakatikassa pana dubbalassa ca cīvaraṃ sukhumaṃ sappāyaṃ, sītālukassa ghanaṃ dupaṭṭaṃ. Viparītaṃ asappāyaṃ. Yassa kassaci jiṇṇaṃ asappāyameva, aggaḷādidānena hissa taṃ palibodhakaraṃ hoti. Tathā paṭṭuṇṇadukūlādibhedaṃ lobhanīyacīvaraṃ. Tādisañhi araññe ekakassa nivāsantarāyakaraṃ jīvitantarāyakarañcāpi hoti. Nippariyāyena pana yaṃ nimittakammādimicchājīvavasena uppannaṃ, yañcassa sevamānassa akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyanti, taṃ asappāyaṃ. Viparītaṃ sappāyaṃ. Tassa vasenettha sappāyasampajaññaṃ. Kammaṭṭhānāvijahanavaseneva gocarasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, for one who is of a hot constitution and is weak, a fine robe is suitable, while for one sensitive to cold, a thick, double-layered robe is suitable. The opposite is unsuitable. For anyone, a worn-out robe is unsuitable, for having to apply patches and so on to it becomes an obstruction. Likewise, an alluring robe of various kinds such as silk or fine linen is unsuitable. Indeed, for one dwelling alone in the forest, such a robe can become an obstacle to his dwelling and even an obstacle to his life. And absolutely, a robe that is obtained by means of wrong livelihood such as making hints, and any robe which, when used, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline, is unsuitable. The opposite is suitable. By means of that, clear comprehension of suitability is to be understood herein. And by means of the non-abandoning of the meditation subject alone, clear comprehension of the domain should be understood.

Abbhantare attā nāma koci cīvaraṃ pārupento natthi, vuttappakārena cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva pana cīvarapārupanaṃ hoti. Tattha cīvarampi acetanaṃ, kāyopi acetano. Cīvaraṃ na jānāti – “mayā kāyo pārupito”ti. Kāyopi na jānāti – “ahaṃ cīvarena pārupito”ti. Dhātuyova dhātusamūhaṃ paṭicchādenti paṭapilotikāyapotthakarūpapaṭicchādane viya. Tasmā neva sundaraṃ cīvaraṃ labhitvā somanassaṃ kātabbaṃ, na asundaraṃ labhitvā domanassaṃ.

Internally, there is no 'self' that puts on the robe. Rather, the putting on of the robe occurs simply due to the movement of the wind element generated by the activity of the mind, in the manner described. Therein, the robe is insentient, and the body is also insentient. The robe does not know, “I have covered the body,” and the body does not know, “I am covered by the robe.” Elements just cover a collection of elements, like covering a plaster figure with a piece of cloth. Therefore, one should feel neither joy upon obtaining a beautiful robe, nor sorrow upon obtaining an unattractive one.

Nāgavammikacetiyarukkhādīsu [M 1.0178] hi keci mālāgandhadhūmavatthādīhi sakkāraṃ karonti, keci gūthamuttakaddamadaṇḍasatthappahārādīhi asakkāraṃ. Na tehi nāgavammikarukkhādayo somanassaṃ vā domanassaṃ vā karonti. Evameva neva sundaraṃ cīvaraṃ labhitvā somanassaṃ kātabbaṃ[P 1.0199], na asundaraṃ labhitvā domanassanti, evaṃ pavattapaṭisaṅkhānavasenettha asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Indeed, some people pay homage to Nāga-anthills, cetiyas, trees, and so on with garlands, perfumes, incense, cloths, and the like, while others show disrespect with excrement, urine, mud, sticks, weapon blows, and so on. But those Nāga-anthills, trees, and the like feel neither joy nor sorrow because of these actions. In the very same way, one should feel neither joy upon obtaining a beautiful robe, nor sorrow upon obtaining an unattractive one. Thus, by means of such ongoing reflection, clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood herein.

Pattadhāraṇepi [V 1.0162] pattaṃ sahasāva aggahetvā imaṃ gahetvā piṇḍāya caramāno bhikkhaṃ labhissāmīti, evaṃ pattaggahaṇapaccayā paṭilabhitabbaṃ atthavasena sātthakasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

In the case of carrying the bowl also, one should not take up the bowl hastily. Rather, reflecting, “Taking this and wandering for alms, I will receive almsfood,” clear comprehension of purpose should thus be understood by way of the benefit to be obtained that is conditioned by taking the bowl.

Kisadubbalasarīrassa pana garupatto asappāyo, yassa kassaci catupañcagaṇṭhikāhato dubbisodhanīyo asappāyova. Duddhotapattopi na vaṭṭati, taṃ dhovantasseva cassa palibodho hoti. Maṇivaṇṇapatto pana lobhanīyo, cīvare vuttanayeneva asappāyo, nimittakammādivasena laddho pana yañcassa sevamānassa akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyanti, ayaṃ ekantaasappāyova. Viparīto sappāyo. Tassa vasenettha sappāyasampajaññaṃ. Kammaṭṭhānāvijahanavaseneva ca gocarasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, for one with an emaciated and weak body, a heavy bowl is unsuitable. For anyone, a bowl mended in four or five places and difficult to clean is unsuitable. An uncleanly washed bowl is also not allowable, and for the user, cleaning it becomes an obstruction. A bowl with the color of a gemstone is alluring and is unsuitable in the same way as described for the robe. Furthermore, a bowl obtained by means of making hints, etc., and any bowl which, when used, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline—this is entirely unsuitable. The opposite is suitable. By means of that, clear comprehension of suitability is to be understood herein. And by means of the non-abandoning of the meditation subject alone, clear comprehension of the domain should be understood.

Abbhantare attā nāma koci pattaṃ gaṇhanto natthi, vuttappakārena cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāravaseneva pattaggahaṇaṃ nāma hoti. Tattha pattopi acetano, hatthāpi acetanā. Patto na jānāti – “ahaṃ hatthehi gahito”ti. Hatthāpi na jānanti – “amhehi patto gahito”ti. Dhātuyova dhātusamūhaṃ gaṇhanti, saṇḍāsena aggivaṇṇapattaggahaṇe viyāti. Evaṃ pavattapaṭisaṅkhānavasenettha asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Within, there is no so-called self that takes the bowl. The so-called taking of the bowl occurs solely by the power of the vibration of the wind element, which is the activity of the mind as previously described. Therein, the bowl is also insentient, and the hands are also insentient. The bowl does not know, 'I am taken by the hands.' The hands also do not know, 'The bowl is taken by us.' Elements alone grasp a collection of elements, just as in taking a fire-colored bowl with tongs. Thus, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be known here by way of reflection on what is occurring.

Api ca yathā chinnahatthapāde vaṇamukhehi paggharitapubbalohitakimikule nīlamakkhikasamparikiṇṇe anāthasālāyaṃ nipanne anāthamanusse disvā, ye dayālukā purisā, te tesaṃ vaṇamattacoḷakāni ceva kapālādīhi ca bhesajjāni upanāmenti. Tattha coḷakānipi kesañci saṇhāni, kesañci thūlāni pāpuṇanti. Bhesajjakapālakānipi kesañci [M 1.0179] susaṇṭhānāni, kesañci dussaṇṭhānāni pāpuṇanti, na te tattha sumanā vā dummanā vā honti[P 1.0200]. Vaṇapaṭicchādanamatteneva hi coḷakena, bhesajjapaṭiggahaṇamatteneva ca kapālakena tesaṃ attho. Evameva yo bhikkhu vaṇacoḷakaṃ viya cīvaraṃ, bhesajjakapālakaṃ viya ca pattaṃ, kapāle bhesajjamiva ca patte laddhaṃ bhikkhaṃ sallakkheti, ayaṃ saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe asammohasampajaññena uttamasampajānakārīti veditabbo.

Moreover, just as when compassionate men see helpless people with severed hands and feet lying in a shelter for the destitute, their wounds oozing pus and blood and swarming with worms, and surrounded by blue flies, they bring them cloths the size of their wounds and medicines in potsherds and the like. Therein, some receive soft cloths, others coarse ones. Some receive well-formed medicine potsherds, others ill-formed ones—yet they are neither pleased nor displeased thereat. For their need is only for a cloth sufficient to cover the wound, and for a potsherd sufficient to receive the medicine. In the very same way, a monk who regards the robe like a wound-cloth, the bowl like a medicine potsherd, and the almsfood received in the bowl like medicine in a potsherd—this one should be known as a practitioner of the highest clear comprehension, with the clear comprehension of non-delusion, in the wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and robes.

Asitādīsu asiteti piṇḍapātabhojane. Pīteti yāguādipāne. Khāyiteti piṭṭhakhajjādikhādane. Sāyiteti madhuphāṇitādisāyane. Tattha neva davāyātiādinā nayena vutto aṭṭhavidhopi attho attho nāma. Tasseva vasena sātthakasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

In 'eating,' and so forth: 'eating' refers to eating almsfood. 'Drinking' refers to drinking gruel and the like. 'Chewing' refers to chewing flour-based foods and the like. 'Savoring' refers to savoring honey, molasses, and the like. Therein, the eightfold purpose spoken of in the manner beginning 'not for amusement,' and so forth, is called 'purpose.' By way of that very purpose, the clear comprehension of purposefulness should be known.

Lūkhapaṇītatittamadhurarasādīsu [V 1.0163] pana yena bhojanena yassa phāsu na hoti, taṃ tassa asappāyaṃ. Yaṃ pana nimittakammādivasena paṭiladdhaṃ, yañcassa bhuñjato akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyanti, taṃ ekantaasappāyameva, viparītaṃ sappāyaṃ. Tassa vasenettha sappāyasampajaññaṃ. Kammaṭṭhānāvijahanavaseneva ca gocarasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, among foods that are coarse, refined, bitter, sweet-tasting, and so forth, whatever food does not bring comfort to someone, that is unsuitable for them. And that which is obtained by means of making signs and the like, and that which, when one is eating it, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline, that is entirely unsuitable. The opposite is suitable. By way of that, herein is the clear comprehension of suitability. And by way of not abandoning the meditation subject, the clear comprehension of the resort should be known.

Abbhantare attā nāma koci bhuñjako natthi, vuttappakāracittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva pattappaṭiggahaṇaṃ nāma hoti. Cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva hatthassa patte otāraṇaṃ nāma hoti. Cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva ālopakaraṇaṃ ālopauddhāraṇaṃ mukhavivaraṇañca hoti, na koci kuñcikāya yantakena vā hanukaṭṭhīni vivarati. Cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva ālopassa mukhe ṭhapanaṃ, uparidantānaṃ musalakiccasādhanaṃ, heṭṭhimadantānaṃ udukkhalakiccasādhanaṃ, jivhāya hatthakiccasādhanañca hoti. Iti tattha aggajivhāya tanukakheḷo mūlajivhāya bahalakheḷo makkheti. Taṃ heṭṭhādantaudukkhale jivhāhatthaparivattakaṃ kheḷodakena temitaṃ uparidantamusalasañcuṇṇitaṃ koci kaṭacchunā [P 1.0201] vā dabbiyā vā antopavesento nāma natthi, vāyodhātuyāva pavisati. Paviṭṭhaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ koci palālasanthāraṃ katvā dhārento nāma natthi, vāyodhātuvaseneva tiṭṭhati. Ṭhitaṃ ṭhitaṃ koci uddhanaṃ katvā aggiṃ jāletvā pacanto nāma natthi, tejodhātuyāva paccati. Pakkaṃ pakkaṃ koci daṇḍakena vā [M 1.0180] yaṭṭhiyā vā bahi nīhārako nāma natthi, vāyodhātuyeva nīharati. Iti vāyodhātu paṭiharati ca, vītiharati ca, dhāreti ca, parivatteti ca, sañcuṇṇeti ca, visoseti ca, nīharati ca. Pathavīdhātu dhāreti ca, parivatteti ca, sañcuṇṇeti ca, visoseti ca. Āpodhātu sineheti ca, allattañca anupāleti. Tejodhātu antopaviṭṭhaṃ paripāceti. Ākāsadhātu añjaso hoti. Viññāṇadhātu tattha tattha sammāpayogamanvāya ābhujatīti. Evaṃ pavattapaṭisaṅkhānavasenettha asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Within, there is no so-called self that is an eater. The so-called act of receiving the bowl occurs solely by the vibration of the wind element due to the activity of the mind in the manner described. The lowering of the hand into the bowl occurs solely by the vibration of the wind element due to the activity of the mind. The making of a morsel, the lifting of the morsel, and the opening of the mouth also occur solely by the vibration of the wind element due to the activity of the mind—no one opens the jawbones with a key or a machine. The placing of the morsel in the mouth, the accomplishing of the function of a pestle by the upper teeth, the accomplishing of the function of a mortar by the lower teeth, and the accomplishing of the function of a hand by the tongue—all these occur solely by the vibration of the wind element due to the activity of the mind. Thus, therein, the thin saliva at the tip of the tongue and the thick saliva at the root of the tongue smear it. That morsel, turned about by the tongue-hand in the lower-teeth-mortar, moistened with saliva-water, and well-ground by the upper-teeth-pestle—no one causes it to enter inside with a spoon or a ladle; it enters solely by means of the wind element. What has entered, no one holds by spreading a straw mat; it stays solely by the power of the wind element. What stays, no one cooks by setting up a hearth and lighting a fire; it is cooked solely by the fire element. What is cooked, no one removes outside with a stick or a rod; the wind element alone removes it. Thus, the wind element brings forward, distributes, holds, turns, grinds, dries up, and removes. The earth element holds, turns, grinds, and dries up. The water element moistens and maintains moisture. The fire element digests what has entered. The space element provides a path. The consciousness element, depending on the right application in each case, directs the mind. In this way, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be known here by way of reflection on what is occurring.

Api ca gamanato pariyesanato paribhogato āsayato nidhānato aparipakkato paripakkato phalato nissandato sammakkhanatoti, evaṃ dasavidhapaṭikūlabhāvapaccavekkhaṇato pettha asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ. Vitthārakathā panettha visuddhimagge āhārapaṭikūlasaññāniddesato gahetabbā.

Moreover, also by reflecting on the tenfold state of repulsiveness—namely, by way of going, searching, consuming, the receptacle, the storage place, its undigested state, its digested state, its fruit, its discharge, and its being smeared—herein the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be known. The detailed account here should be taken from the Visuddhimagga, from the exposition on the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment.

Uccārapassāvakammeti uccārassa ca passāvassa ca karaṇe. Tattha pattakāle uccārapassāvaṃ akarontassa sakalasarīrato sedā muccanti, akkhīni bhamanti, cittaṃ na ekaggaṃ [V 1.0164] hoti, aññe ca rogā uppajjanti. Karontassa pana sabbaṃ taṃ na hotīti ayamettha attho. Tassa vasena sātthakasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Regarding the act of defecation and urination: this refers to the act of evacuating feces and urine. Therein, for one who does not defecate and urinate at the proper time, sweat is released from the entire body, the eyes spin, the mind is not one-pointed, and other diseases arise. But for one who does so, none of that occurs—this is the purpose here. By way of that purpose, the clear comprehension of purposefulness should be known.

Aṭṭhāne uccārapassāvaṃ karontassa pana āpatti hoti, ayaso vaḍḍhati, jīvitantarāyo hoti, patirūpe ṭhāne karontassa sabbaṃ taṃ na hotīti idamettha sappāyaṃ tassa vasena sappāyasampajaññaṃ. Kammaṭṭhānāvijahanavaseneva ca gocarasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, for one who defecates and urinates in an unsuitable place, an offense is incurred, ill-repute increases, and there can be danger to life. For one who does so in a suitable place, none of that occurs. This is what is suitable here. By way of that suitability, the clear comprehension of suitability should be known. And by way of not abandoning the meditation subject, the clear comprehension of the resort should also be known.

Abbhantare attā nāma uccārapassāvakammaṃ karonto natthi, cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva pana uccārapassāvakammaṃ hoti[P 1.0202]. Yathā vā pana pakke gaṇḍe gaṇḍabhedena pubbalohitaṃ akāmatāya nikkhamati. Yathā ca atibharitā udakabhājanā udakaṃ akāmatāya nikkhamati. Evaṃ pakkāsayamuttavatthīsu sannicitā uccārapassāvā vāyuvegasamuppīḷitā akāmatāyapi nikkhamanti. So panāyaṃ evaṃ nikkhamanto uccārapassāvo neva [M 1.0181] tassa bhikkhuno attano hoti, na parassa, kevalaṃ sarīranissandova hoti. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā udakatumbato purāṇudakaṃ chaḍḍentassa neva taṃ attano hoti, na paresaṃ; kevalaṃ paṭijagganamattameva hoti; evaṃ pavattapaṭisaṅkhānavasenettha asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.
