Inside, there is no being called 'self' that performs the act of defecation and urination; rather, the act of defecation and urination occurs solely through the agitation of the air element by mental activity. Just as, when a boil is ripe, pus and blood issue forth from the bursting of the boil without volition, and just as water issues forth from an overfilled water pot without volition, in the same way, feces and urine accumulated in the stomach and bladder, being compressed by the force of the air element, issue forth even without volition. This feces and urine thus issuing forth is neither the monk's own, nor another's; it is merely a discharge from the body. What is the simile? Just as when one discards old water from a water gourd, that water is neither one's own nor another's; it is merely for the sake of cleaning. In the same way, herein, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood by way of reflecting on what has occurred.

Gatādīsu gateti gamane. Ṭhiteti ṭhāne. Nisinneti nisajjāya. Sutteti sayane. Jāgariteti jāgaraṇe. Bhāsiteti kathane. Tuṇhībhāveti akathane. “Gacchanto vā gacchāmīti pajānāti, ṭhito vā ṭhitomhīti pajānāti, nisinno vā nisinnomhīti pajānāti, sayāno vā sayānomhīti pajānātī”ti imasmiñhi sutte addhānairiyāpathā kathitā. “Abhikkante paṭikkante ālokite vilokite samiñjite pasārite”ti imasmiṃ majjhimā. “Gate ṭhite nisinne sutte jāgarite”ti idha pana khuddakacuṇṇiyairiyāpathā kathitā. Tasmā tesupi vuttanayeneva sampajānakāritā veditabbā.

Regarding 'going' and so forth: 'gate' means in going. 'Ṭhite' means in standing. 'Nisinne' means in sitting. 'Sutte' means in lying down. 'Jāgarite' means in being awake. 'Bhāsite' means in speaking. 'Tuṇhībhāve' means in not speaking. For in this Sutta, where it is said, 'When going, one understands, "I am going"; when standing, one understands, "I am standing"; when sitting, one understands, "I am sitting"; when lying down, one understands, "I am lying down,"' the postures of long duration are taught. In this passage, 'When going forward, returning... bending, stretching,' the medium postures are taught. Here, however, in 'In going, standing, sitting, lying down, being awake,' the minor and fragmentary postures are taught. Therefore, in these cases too, the state of acting with clear comprehension should be understood in the manner already stated.

Tipiṭakamahāsivatthero panāha – yo ciraṃ gantvā vā caṅkamitvā vā aparabhāge ṭhito iti paṭisañcikkhati – “caṅkamanakāle pavattā rūpārūpadhammā ettheva niruddhā”ti[P 1.0203]. Ayaṃ gate sampajānakārī nāma.

However, the Elder Tipiṭaka Mahāsiva said: Whoever, having gone or having paced for a long time, later, while standing, reflects thus: 'The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred at the time of pacing have ceased right there.' This person is called one who acts with clear comprehension in going.

Yo sajjhāyaṃ vā karonto, pañhaṃ vā vissajjento, kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā manasikaronto ciraṃ ṭhatvā [V 1.0165] aparabhāge nisinno iti paṭisañcikkhati – “ṭhitakāle pavattā rūpārūpadhammā ettheva niruddhā”ti. Ayaṃ ṭhite sampajānakārī nāma.

Whoever, while making recitation, or answering a question, or attending to a meditation subject, having stood for a long time, later, while sitting, reflects thus: 'The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred at the time of standing have ceased right there.' This person is called one who acts with clear comprehension in standing.

Yo sajjhāyādikaraṇavaseneva ciraṃ nisīditvā aparabhāge uṭṭhāya iti paṭisañcikkhati – “nisinnakāle pavattā rūpārūpadhammā ettheva niruddhā”ti. Ayaṃ nisinne sampajānakārī nāma.

Whoever, by way of performing recitation and so forth, having sat for a long time, later, having arisen, reflects thus: 'The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred at the time of sitting have ceased right there.' This person is called one who acts with clear comprehension in sitting.

Yo pana nipannako sajjhāyaṃ vā karonto kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā manasikaronto niddaṃ okkamitvā aparabhāge uṭṭhāya iti paṭisañcikkhati – “sayanakāle pavattā rūpārūpadhammā ettheva niruddhā”ti. Ayaṃ sutte jāgarite ca sampajānakārī nāma. Kiriyamayacittānañhi appavattanaṃ soppaṃ nāma, pavattanaṃ jāgaritaṃ nāma.

Furthermore, whoever, being one who is lying down, while making recitation or attending to a meditation subject, falls into sleep, and later, having arisen, reflects thus: 'The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred at the time of lying down have ceased right there.' This person is called one who acts with clear comprehension in sleeping and in being awake. For the non-occurrence of functional consciousnesses is called 'sleep', and their occurrence is called 'wakefulness'.

Yo [M 1.0182] pana bhāsamāno – “ayaṃ saddo nāma oṭṭhe ca paṭicca, dante ca jivhañca tāluñca paṭicca, cittassa ca tadanurūpaṃ payogaṃ paṭicca jāyatī”ti sato sampajānova bhāsati. Ciraṃ vā pana kālaṃ sajjhāyaṃ vā katvā, dhammaṃ vā kathetvā, kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā pavattetvā, pañhaṃ vā vissajjetvā, aparabhāge tuṇhībhūto iti paṭisañcikkhati – “bhāsitakāle uppannā rūpārūpadhammā ettheva niruddhā”ti. Ayaṃ bhāsite sampajānakārī nāma.

Furthermore, whoever, while speaking, speaks mindfully and with clear comprehension thus: 'This thing called sound arises depending on the lips, the teeth, the tongue, and the palate, and depending on the mind's corresponding effort.' Or, having recited for a long time, or having taught the Dhamma, or having brought forth a meditation subject, or having answered a question, and later having become silent, reflects thus: 'The material and immaterial phenomena that arose at the time of speaking have ceased right there.' This person is called one who acts with clear comprehension in speaking.

Yo tuṇhībhūto ciraṃ dhammaṃ vā kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā manasikatvā aparabhāge iti paṭisañcikkhati – “tuṇhībhūtakāle pavattā rūpārūpadhammā ettheva niruddhā”ti. Upādārūpappavattiyañhi sati bhāsati nāma, asati tuṇhī bhavati nāmāti. Ayaṃ tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī nāmāti.

Whoever, being silent, having for a long time attended to the Dhamma or a meditation subject, later reflects thus: 'The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred at the time of being silent have ceased right there.' For when there is the occurrence of derived matter, it is called 'speaking'; when it is not present, it is called 'being silent.' This person is called one who acts with clear comprehension in the state of silence.

Tayidaṃ mahāsivattherena vuttaṃ asammohadhuraṃ mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutte adhippetaṃ. Imasmiṃ pana sāmaññaphale sabbampi catubbidhaṃ sampajaññaṃ labbhati. Tasmā vuttanayeneva cettha catunnaṃ sampajaññānaṃ vasena sampajānakāritā veditabbā. Sampajānakārīti ca sabbapadesu satisampayuttasseva sampajaññassa vasena attho veditabbo. Satisampajaññena samannāgatoti etassa hi padassa ayaṃ vitthāro. Vibhaṅgappakaraṇe pana – “sato sampajāno abhikkamati, sato sampajāno paṭikkamatī”ti evaṃ etāni padāni vibhattāneva. Evaṃ, kho mahārājāti evaṃ [V 1.0166] satisampayuttassa sampajaññassa [P 1.0204] vasena abhikkamādīni pavattento satisampajaññena samannāgato nāma hotīti attho.

This which was stated by the Elder Mahāsiva has non-delusion as its chief point and is what is intended in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta. Here, however, in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, all four kinds of clear comprehension are obtained. Therefore, here too, the state of acting with clear comprehension should be understood by way of the four kinds of clear comprehension in the manner already stated. And in all passages with 'sampajānakārī', the meaning should be understood by way of clear comprehension that is associated with mindfulness. For this is the detailed explanation of the term 'endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension.' However, in the Vibhaṅga, these terms are indeed analyzed thus: 'Mindful and with clear comprehension, one goes forward; mindful and with clear comprehension, one returns.' The meaning is: 'Thus, O great king,' a monk who brings about going forward and so on by way of clear comprehension associated with mindfulness is called one endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension.

Santosakathā

The Discourse on Contentment

215. Idha, mahārāja, bhikkhu santuṭṭho hotīti ettha santuṭṭhoti itarītarapaccayasantosena samannāgato. So panesa santoso dvādasavidho hoti, seyyathidaṃ – cīvare yathālābhasantoso, yathābalasantoso, yathāsāruppasantosoti tividho. Evaṃ piṇḍapātādīsu. Tassāyaṃ pabhedavaṇṇanā –

215. In the text, “Here, O great king, a bhikkhu is content,” the word ‘content’ means being endowed with contentment with requisites of any kind. This contentment is of twelve kinds, namely: with regard to robes, there are three kinds—contentment according to what is obtained, contentment according to one’s strength, and contentment according to suitability. It is the same for almsfood and so on. The detailed explanation of this is as follows:

Idha bhikkhu cīvaraṃ labhati, sundaraṃ vā asundaraṃ vā. So teneva yāpeti, aññaṃ na pattheti, labhantopi na gaṇhati. Ayamassa cīvare yathālābhasantoso. Atha pana pakatidubbalo vā hoti, ābādhajarābhibhūto [M 1.0183] vā, garucīvaraṃ pārupanto kilamati. So sabhāgena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ taṃ parivattetvā lahukena yāpentopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa cīvare yathābalasantoso. Aparo paṇītapaccayalābhī hoti. So pattacīvarādīnaṃ aññataraṃ mahagghapattacīvaraṃ bahūni vā pana pattacīvarāni labhitvā idaṃ therānaṃ cirapabbajitānaṃ, idaṃ bahussutānaṃ anurūpaṃ, idaṃ gilānānaṃ, idaṃ appalābhīnaṃ hotūti datvā tesaṃ purāṇacīvaraṃ vā gahetvā saṅkārakūṭādito vā nantakāni uccinitvā tehi saṅghāṭiṃ katvā dhārentopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa cīvare yathāsāruppasantoso.

Here, a bhikkhu obtains a robe, whether fine or coarse. He subsists on that alone, does not long for another, and does not accept one even if he obtains it. This is his contentment with robes according to what is obtained. Furthermore, he may be naturally weak or overcome by illness or old age, and wearing a heavy robe exhausts him. He exchanges it with a bhikkhu of similar disposition for a lighter one and is still content. This is his contentment with robes according to his strength. Another is accustomed to receiving excellent requisites. Having received a valuable robe of some kind, or many robes, he thinks, "This is suitable for the elders of long standing, this for the very learned, this for the sick, this for those who receive little," and gives them away. Taking their old robes or picking up rags from a rubbish heap and making a double-layered outer robe from them, he wears it and yet remains content. This is his contentment with robes according to suitability.

Idha pana bhikkhu piṇḍapātaṃ labhati lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā, so teneva yāpeti, aññaṃ na pattheti, labhantopi na gaṇhati. Ayamassa piṇḍapāte yathālābhasantoso. Yo pana attano pakativiruddhaṃ vā byādhiviruddhaṃ vā piṇḍapātaṃ labhati, yenassa paribhuttena aphāsu hoti. So sabhāgassa bhikkhuno taṃ datvā tassa hatthato sappāyabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karontopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa piṇḍapāte yathābalasantoso. Aparo bahuṃ paṇītaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ labhati. So taṃ cīvaraṃ viya theracirapabbajitabahussutaappalābhīgilānānaṃ datvā tesaṃ vā sesakaṃ piṇḍāya vā caritvā [P 1.0205] missakāhāraṃ bhuñjantopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa piṇḍapāte yathāsāruppasantoso.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu receives almsfood, whether coarse or fine. He subsists on that alone, does not long for another, and does not accept it even if he obtains it. This is his contentment with almsfood according to what is obtained. Furthermore, one may receive almsfood that is contrary to his constitution or harmful to his illness, and eating it makes him uncomfortable. He gives it to a bhikkhu of similar disposition and, having eaten suitable food from his hand, he remains content even while practicing the monk's duties. This is his contentment with almsfood according to his strength. Another bhikkhu receives much fine almsfood. He gives it away like a robe to the elders, the long-ordained, the very learned, those who gain little, or the sick. Then, eating either their leftovers or, having gone on an alms round, eating mixed food, he still remains content. This is his contentment with almsfood according to suitability.

Idha pana bhikkhu senāsanaṃ labhati, manāpaṃ vā amanāpaṃ vā, so tena neva somanassaṃ, na [V 1.0167] domanassaṃ uppādeti; antamaso tiṇasanthārakenapi yathāladdheneva tussati. Ayamassa senāsane yathālābhasantoso. Yo pana attano pakativiruddhaṃ vā byādhiviruddhaṃ vā senāsanaṃ labhati, yatthassa vasato aphāsu hoti, so taṃ sabhāgassa bhikkhuno datvā tassa santake sappāyasenāsane vasantopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa senāsane yathābalasantoso.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu obtains a dwelling, whether agreeable or disagreeable, and he does not generate either joy or displeasure because of it; at the very least, even with a grass spread, he is content with whatever he has obtained. This is his contentment with dwellings according to what is obtained. Furthermore, if he obtains a dwelling that is contrary to his constitution or harmful to his health, where residing is uncomfortable, he may give it to a bhikkhu of similar disposition and dwell in a suitable dwelling belonging to that bhikkhu, yet he remains content. This is his contentment with dwellings according to his strength.

Aparo mahāpuñño leṇamaṇḍapakūṭāgārādīni bahūni paṇītasenāsanāni labhati. So tāni cīvaraṃ viya theracirapabbajitabahussutaappalābhīgilānānaṃ datvā yattha katthaci vasantopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa [M 1.0184] senāsane yathāsāruppasantoso. Yopi – “uttamasenāsanaṃ nāma pamādaṭṭhānaṃ, tattha nisinnassa thinamiddhaṃ okkamati, niddābhibhūtassa puna paṭibujjhato kāmavitakkā pātubhavantī”ti paṭisañcikkhitvā tādisaṃ senāsanaṃ pattampi na sampaṭicchati. So taṃ paṭikkhipitvā abbhokāsarukkhamūlādīsu vasantopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayampissa senāsane yathāsāruppasantoso.

Another of great merit obtains many excellent dwellings such as caves, pavilions, peaked houses, and so on. He gives these away, like a robe, to the elders, the long-ordained, the very learned, those who gain little, or the sick. Then, even dwelling wherever, he remains content. This is his contentment with dwellings according to suitability. Moreover, one might reflect thus: "A superior dwelling is a basis for heedlessness; for one sitting there, sloth and torpor descend, and for one overcome by sleep, evil thoughts arise again upon reawakening." Having reflected thus, he does not accept such a dwelling even when it is available. Rejecting it, even dwelling in the open air, at the foot of a tree, or in similar places, he remains content. This too is his contentment with dwellings according to suitability.

Idha pana bhikkhu bhesajjaṃ labhati, lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā, so yaṃ labhati, teneva tussati, aññaṃ na pattheti, labhantopi na gaṇhati. Ayamassa gilānapaccaye yathālābhasantoso. Yo pana telena atthiko phāṇitaṃ labhati. So taṃ sabhāgassa bhikkhuno datvā tassa hatthato telaṃ gahetvā aññadeva vā pariyesitvā bhesajjaṃ karontopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa gilānapaccaye yathābalasantoso.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu obtains medicine, whether coarse or fine. Whatever he obtains, he is content with just that, does not long for anything else, and does not accept another even if he obtains it. This is his contentment with requisites for the sick according to what is obtained. Furthermore, if one who needs oil obtains molasses, he gives it to a bhikkhu of similar disposition and, having taken oil from his hand or having sought for other oil, remains content even while preparing the medicine. This is his contentment with requisites for the sick according to his strength.

Aparo mahāpuñño bahuṃ telamadhuphāṇitādipaṇītabhesajjaṃ labhati. So taṃ cīvaraṃ viya theracirapabbajitabahussutaappalābhīgilānānaṃ datvā tesaṃ ābhatena yena kenaci yāpentopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Yo pana ekasmiṃ bhājane muttaharīṭakaṃ [P 1.0206] ṭhapetvā ekasmiṃ catumadhuraṃ – “gaṇhāhi, bhante, yadicchasī”ti vuccamāno sacassa tesu aññatarenapi rogo vūpasammati, atha muttaharīṭakaṃ nāma buddhādīhi vaṇṇitanti catumadhuraṃ paṭikkhipitvā muttaharīṭakeneva bhesajjaṃ karonto paramasantuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa gilānapaccaye yathāsāruppasantoso.

Another of great merit obtains much excellent medicine such as oil, honey, molasses, and the like. Just as with a robe, he gives these to the elders, the long-ordained, the very learned, those who gain little, or the sick, and remains content, even subsisting on whatever is brought by them. Furthermore, there is one who, when myrobalan soaked in urine is placed in one bowl and the four sweets in another, is told, "Take, venerable sir, whatever you wish." If his illness can be allayed by either of them, then, reflecting, "Myrobalan soaked in urine is praised by the Buddhas and others," he rejects the four sweets and prepares the medicine with only the myrobalan soaked in urine, thus remaining supremely content. This is his contentment with requisites for the sick according to suitability.

Iminā pana dvādasavidhena itarītarapaccayasantosena samannāgatassa bhikkhuno aṭṭha parikkhārā vaṭṭanti. Tīṇi cīvarāni, patto, dantakaṭṭhacchedanavāsi, ekā sūci, kāyabandhanaṃ parissāvananti. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Furthermore, for a bhikkhu endowed with this twelvefold contentment regarding requisites of any kind, eight requisites are permissible: three robes, a bowl, an adze for cutting tooth-sticks, a single needle, a waistband, and a water-strainer. And this has been said:

“Ticīvarañca [V 1.0168] patto ca, vāsi sūci ca bandhanaṃ;

Parissāvanena aṭṭhete, yuttayogassa bhikkhuno”ti.

"The three robes and the bowl, the adze, the needle, and the waistband; with the water-strainer, these eight are the requisites of a bhikkhu devoted to the practice."

Te sabbe kāyaparihārikāpi honti kucchiparihārikāpi. Kathaṃ? Ticīvaraṃ tāva nivāsetvā ca pārupitvā ca vicaraṇakāle kāyaṃ pariharati, posetīti kāyaparihārikaṃ hoti. Cīvarakaṇṇena udakaṃ parissāvetvā [M 1.0185] pivanakāle khāditabbaphalāphalagahaṇakāle ca kucchiṃ pariharati; posetīti kucchiparihārikaṃ hoti.

All of those requisites are both for maintaining the body and for maintaining the belly. How so? First, the three robes, having been worn as a lower garment and draped as an upper garment, maintain and nourish the body at the time of wandering; thus, they are for maintaining the body. With the corner of a robe, having filtered water at the time of drinking, and at the time of receiving edible small and large fruits, one maintains and nourishes the belly; thus, they are for maintaining the belly.

Pattopi tena udakaṃ uddharitvā nhānakāle kuṭiparibhaṇḍakaraṇakāle ca kāyaparihāriko hoti. Āhāraṃ gahetvā bhuñjanakāle kucchiparihāriko.

The bowl also, by means of it, having drawn up water at the time of bathing and at the time of cleaning the small dwelling, is for maintaining the body. At the time of taking food and eating, it is for maintaining the belly.

Vāsipi tāya dantakaṭṭhacchedanakāle mañcapīṭhānaṃ aṅgapādacīvarakuṭidaṇḍakasajjanakāle ca kāyaparihārikā hoti. Ucchuchedananāḷikerāditacchanakāle kucchiparihārikā.

The adze also, by means of it, at the time of cutting a tooth-stick, and at the time of preparing the parts and legs of beds and chairs and the small pole for a robe-dwelling, is for maintaining the body. At the time of cutting sugarcane and scraping coconuts and so on, it is for maintaining the belly.

Sūcipi cīvarasibbanakāle kāyaparihārikā hoti. Pūvaṃ vā phalaṃ vā vijjhitvā khādanakāle kucchiparihārikā.

The needle also, at the time of sewing a robe, is for maintaining the body. When piercing a cake or a fruit to eat, it is for maintaining the belly.

Kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā vicaraṇakāle kāyaparihārikaṃ. Ucchuādīni bandhitvā gahaṇakāle kucchiparihārikaṃ.

The waistband, when tied for wandering about, is for maintaining the body. At the time of taking sugarcane and so on by tying them up, it is for maintaining the belly.

Parissāvanaṃ tena udakaṃ parissāvetvā nhānakāle, senāsanaparibhaṇḍakaraṇakāle ca kāyaparihārikaṃ. Pānīyaṃ parissāvanakāle, teneva tilataṇḍulaputhukādīni gahetvā khādanakāle ca kucchiparihāriyaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva aṭṭhaparikkhārikassa parikkhāramattā. Navaparikkhārikassa [P 1.0207] pana seyyaṃ pavisantassa tatraṭṭhakaṃ paccattharaṇaṃ vā kuñcikā vā vaṭṭati. Dasaparikkhārikassa nisīdanaṃ vā cammakhaṇḍaṃ vā vaṭṭati. Ekādasaparikkhārikassa pana kattarayaṭṭhi vā telanāḷikā vā vaṭṭati. Dvādasaparikkhārikassa chattaṃ vā upāhanaṃ vā vaṭṭati. Etesu ca aṭṭhaparikkhārikova santuṭṭho, itare asantuṭṭhā mahicchā mahābhārāti na vattabbā. Etepi hi appicchāva santuṭṭhāva subharāva sallahukavuttinova. Bhagavā pana na yimaṃ suttaṃ tesaṃ vasena kathesi, aṭṭhaparikkhārikassa vasena kathesi. So hi khuddakavāsiñca sūciñca parissāvane pakkhipitvā pattassa anto ṭhapetvā pattaṃ aṃsakūṭe laggetvā ticīvaraṃ kāyapaṭibaddhaṃ katvā yenicchakaṃ [V 1.0169] sukhaṃ pakkamati. Paṭinivattetvā gahetabbaṃ nāmassa na hoti. Iti [M 1.0186] imassa bhikkhuno sallahukavuttitaṃ dassento bhagavā – “santuṭṭho hoti kāyaparihārikena cīvarenā”tiādimāha. Tattha kāyaparihārikenāti kāyapariharaṇamattakena. Kucchiparihārikenāti kucchipariharaṇamattakena. Samādāyeva pakkamatīti aṭṭhaparikkhāramattakaṃ sabbaṃ gahetvāva kāyapaṭibaddhaṃ katvāva gacchati. “Mama vihāro pariveṇaṃ upaṭṭhāko”ti āsaṅgo vā bandho vā na hoti. So jiyā mutto saro viya, yūthā apakkanto madahatthī viya ca icchiticchitaṃ senāsanaṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ vanapabbhāraṃ paribhuñjanto ekova tiṭṭhati, ekova nisīdati. Sabbiriyāpathesu ekova adutiyo.

The water strainer, by means of it, having filtered water at the time of bathing and at the time of cleaning the lodging, is for maintaining the body. At the time of filtering drinking water, and by means of it, at the time of eating after taking sesame, rice, parched grain, and so on, it is for maintaining the belly. This, first of all, is the measure of requisites for one with eight requisites. But for one with nine requisites, when entering a lodging, a ground-covering found there or a key is allowable. For one with ten requisites, a sitting cloth or a piece of hide is allowable. But for one with eleven requisites, a staff or an oil tube is allowable. For one with twelve requisites, an umbrella or footwear is allowable. And among these, it should not be said that only the one with eight requisites is content, and the others are discontent, have great desire, and are a great burden. For indeed, these others are also of few desires, content, easily supported, and of light livelihood. However, the Blessed One did not teach this discourse on account of them; he taught it on account of the one with eight requisites. For he, having placed the small adze and the needle into the water strainer, and having put that inside the bowl, having hung the bowl on the point of his shoulder, and having made the three robes bound to his body, departs happily wherever he wishes. There is nothing for him that must be retrieved by returning. Thus, showing the light livelihood of this bhikkhu, the Blessed One said the passage beginning with, 'He is content with a robe sufficient for maintaining the body...' Therein, 'for maintaining the body' means just enough to maintain the body. 'For maintaining the belly' means just enough to maintain the belly. 'He departs taking them along' means he goes only after taking all that is the measure of the eight requisites and making them bound to his body. There is no attachment or bond such as, 'My monastery, my monastic compound, my attendant.' He, like an arrow released from a bowstring, and like a musth elephant that has departed from the herd, making use of any desired lodging—a forest grove, the foot of a tree, a mountain cleft in the forest—stands alone, sits alone. In all postures, he is alone, without a second.

“Cātuddiso appaṭigho ca hoti,

Santussamāno itarītarena;

Parissayānaṃ sahitā achambhī,

Eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti. (su. ni. 42);

Having the four directions as his domain and being unopposed, content with one requisite or another, an endurer of dangers and unafraid—one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

Evaṃ vaṇṇitaṃ khaggavisāṇakappataṃ āpajjati.

He attains the state of being like the horn of a rhinoceros, as described thus.

Idāni [P 1.0208] tamatthaṃ upamāya sādhento – “seyyathāpī”tiādimāha. Tattha pakkhī sakuṇoti pakkhayutto sakuṇo. Ḍetīti uppatati. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – sakuṇā nāma “asukasmiṃ padese rukkho paripakkaphalo”ti ñatvā nānādisāhi āgantvā nakhapattatuṇḍādīhi tassa phalāni vijjhantā vidhunantā khādanti. ‘Idaṃ ajjatanāya, idaṃ svātanāya bhavissatī’ti tesaṃ na hoti. Phale pana khīṇe neva rukkhassa ārakkhaṃ ṭhapenti, na tattha pattaṃ vā nakhaṃ vā tuṇḍaṃ vā ṭhapenti. Atha kho tasmiṃ rukkhe anapekkho hutvā, yo yaṃ disābhāgaṃ icchati, so tena sapattabhārova uppatitvā gacchati. Evameva ayaṃ bhikkhu nissaṅgo nirapekkho yena kāmaṃ pakkamati. Tena vuttaṃ “samādāyeva pakkamatī”ti.

Now, wishing to establish that meaning with a simile, he said the passage beginning with, 'Just as...' Therein, 'a winged bird' means a bird endowed with wings. 'Flies' means it flies up. This is the concise meaning here: Birds, having known, 'In such-and-such a place there is a tree with fully ripe fruit,' come from various directions and eat its fruits, piercing them and shaking them down with their claws, wings, beaks, and so on. They do not have the thought, 'This is for today, this will be for tomorrow.' But when the fruit is exhausted, they neither place a guard for the tree, nor do they leave a feather, a claw, or a beak there. Rather, being unconcerned about that tree, whichever bird desires to go to whichever region, it flies up and goes there with only its wings as its burden. In this very way, this bhikkhu, unattached and unconcerned, departs wherever he pleases. Therefore it was said, 'He departs taking them along.'

Nīvaraṇappahānakathā

Exposition on Abandoning the Hindrances

216. So [M 1.0187] iminā cātiādinā kiṃ dasseti? Araññavāsassa paccayasampattiṃ dasseti. Yassa hi ime cattāro paccayā natthi, tassa araññavāso na ijjhati. Tiracchānagatehi vā vanacarakehi vā saddhiṃ vattabbataṃ āpajjati. Araññe adhivatthā devatā – “kiṃ [V 1.0170] evarūpassa pāpabhikkhuno araññavāsenā”ti bheravasaddaṃ sāventi, hatthehi sīsaṃ paharitvā palāyanākāraṃ karonti. “Asuko bhikkhu araññaṃ pavisitvā idañcidañca pāpakammaṃ akāsī”ti ayaso pattharati. Yassa panete cattāro paccayā atthi, tassa araññavāso ijjhati. So hi attano sīlaṃ paccavekkhanto kiñci kāḷakaṃ vā tilakaṃ vā apassanto pītiṃ uppādetvā taṃ khayavayato sammasanto ariyabhūmiṃ okkamati. Araññe adhivatthā devatā attamanā vaṇṇaṃ bhaṇanti. Itissa udake pakkhittatelabindu viya yaso vitthāriko hoti.

216. By this passage beginning with 'So iminā,' what does He show? He shows the fulfillment of the supporting conditions for dwelling in the forest. Indeed, for any monk who lacks these four supporting conditions, dwelling in the forest does not succeed. He becomes worthy of being spoken of in the same breath as animals or hunters. The devas dwelling in the forest—thinking, 'What is the use of dwelling in the forest for such a wicked monk?'—cause terrifying sounds to be heard, strike their heads with their hands, and make gestures to drive him away. Ill-fame spreads: 'The monk so-and-so entered the forest and committed this and that evil deed.' But for any monk who possesses these four supporting conditions, dwelling in the forest succeeds. Indeed, while reflecting on his own virtue and seeing no coarse fault like a black spot or subtle fault like a mole, he generates rapture, and by contemplating its decay and vanishing, he enters the noble ground. The devas dwelling in the forest, being delighted, speak his praise. Thus, his fame becomes widespread, like a drop of oil dropped on water.

Tattha vivittanti suññaṃ, appasaddaṃ, appanigghosanti attho. Etadeva hi sandhāya vibhaṅge – “vivittanti santike cepi senāsanaṃ hoti, tañca anākiṇṇaṃ gahaṭṭhehi pabbajitehi. Tena taṃ vivitta”nti vuttaṃ. Seti ceva āsati ca etthāti senāsanaṃ mañcapīṭhādīnametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tenāha – “senāsananti mañcopi senāsanaṃ[P 1.0209], pīṭhampi, bhisipi, bimbohanampi, vihāropi, aḍḍhayogopi, pāsādopi, hammiyampi, guhāpi, aṭṭopi, māḷopi leṇampi, veḷugumbopi, rukkhamūlampi, maṇḍapopi, senāsanaṃ, yattha vā pana bhikkhū paṭikkamanti, sabbametaṃ senāsana”nti (vibha. 527).

Therein, 'secluded' means empty of people, with little or no human sound, with little or no noise from towns and villages. Indeed, with reference to this, it is said in the Vibhaṅga: 'Secluded means that even if a lodging is near a town or village, it is not crowded with householders or monastics. For that reason, it is called secluded.' 'One lies down and one sits here,' thus it is a `senāsana` (lodging); this is a designation for couches, chairs, and so on. Therefore, He said: 'A lodging means a couch is a lodging, a chair also, a cushion, a pillow, a monastery, a gabled building, a mansion, an upper storey of a mansion, a cave, a watchtower, a hall, a rock-shelter, a bamboo grove, the foot of a tree, a pavilion is also a lodging; or wherever monks retire—all this is a lodging' (Vibh. 527).

Api ca – “vihāro aḍḍhayogo pāsādo hammiyaṃ guhā”ti idaṃ vihārasenāsanaṃ nāma. “Mañco pīṭhaṃ bhisi bimbohana”nti idaṃ mañcapīṭhasenāsanaṃ nāma. “Cimilikā cammakhaṇḍo tiṇasanthāro paṇṇasanthāro”ti idaṃ santhatasenāsanaṃ nāma. “Yattha vā pana bhikkhū paṭikkamantī”ti idaṃ okāsasenāsanaṃ nāmāti. Evaṃ catubbidhaṃ senāsanaṃ hoti, taṃ sabbaṃ senāsanaggahaṇena saṅgahitameva.

Furthermore: 'A monastery, a gabled building, a mansion, an upper storey, and a cave'—this is called a `vihāra-senāsana` (monastery-lodging). 'A couch, a chair, a cushion, and a pillow'—this is called a `mañcapīṭha-senāsana` (couch-and-chair-lodging). 'A coarse cloth, a piece of hide, a grass mat, and a leaf mat'—this is called a `santhata-senāsana` (spread-lodging). 'Or wherever monks withdraw'—this is called an `okāsa-senāsana` (space-lodging). Thus, a lodging is of four kinds, and all of it is included by the term 'lodging'.

Idha panassa sakuṇasadisassa cātuddisassa bhikkhuno anucchavikasenāsanaṃ dassento araññaṃ rukkhamūlantiādimāha. Tattha araññanti nikkhamitvā [M 1.0188] bahi indakhīlā sabbametaṃ araññanti. Idaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ vasena āgataṃ. “Āraññakaṃ nāma senāsanaṃ pañcadhanusatikaṃ pacchima”nti (pārā. 654) idaṃ pana imassa bhikkhuno anurūpaṃ. Tassa lakkhaṇaṃ visuddhimagge dhutaṅganiddese vuttaṃ. Rukkhamūlanti yaṃ kiñci sandacchāyaṃ vivittarukkhamūlaṃ. Pabbatanti selaṃ. Tattha hi udakasoṇḍīsu udakakiccaṃ katvā sītāya rukkhacchāyāya nisinnassa nānādisāsu khāyamānāsu sītena vātena bījiyamānassa cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti. Kandaranti kaṃ vuccati udakaṃ, tena dāritaṃ, udakena bhinnaṃ pabbatapadesaṃ. Yaṃ nadītumbantipi, nadīkuñjantipi [V 1.0171] vadanti. Tattha hi rajatapaṭṭasadisā vālikā hoti, matthake maṇivitānaṃ viya vanagahaṇaṃ, maṇikhandhasadisaṃ udakaṃ sandati. Evarūpaṃ kandaraṃ oruyha pānīyaṃ pivitvā gattāni sītāni katvā vālikaṃ ussāpetvā [P 1.0210] paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ paññapetvā nisinnassa samaṇadhammaṃ karoto cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti. Giriguhanti dvinnaṃ pabbatānaṃ antare, ekasmiṃyeva vā umaggasadisaṃ mahāvivaraṃ susānalakkhaṇaṃ visuddhimagge vuttaṃ. Vanapatthanti gāmantaṃ atikkamitvā manussānaṃ anupacāraṭṭhānaṃ, yattha na kasanti na vapanti, tenevāha – “vanapatthanti dūrānametaṃ senāsanānaṃ adhivacana”ntiādi. Abbhokāsanti acchannaṃ. Ākaṅkhamāno panettha cīvarakuṭiṃ katvā vasati. Palālapuñjanti palālarāsi. Mahāpalālapuñjato hi palālaṃ nikkaḍḍhitvā pabbhāraleṇasadise ālaye karonti, gacchagumbhādīnampi upari palālaṃ pakkhipitvā heṭṭhā nisinnā samaṇadhammaṃ karonti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

Here, however, wishing to show a suitable lodging for that monk who is like a bird and belongs to the four directions, He spoke the passage beginning with 'the forest, the foot of a tree.' Therein, 'forest' means everything outside the village threshold-post. This definition is given in connection with the bhikkhunīs. But this is suitable for this monk: 'A lodging called `āraññaka` (belonging to the forest) is at a minimum distance of five hundred bow-lengths' (Pārā. 654). Its characteristic has been stated in the Visuddhimagga, in the Exposition of the Ascetic Practices. 'The foot of a tree' means the secluded foot of any tree whatsoever that has pleasant shade. 'A mountain' means a rock. For there, for one who has performed his water-duties in the water pools and is sitting in the cool shade of a tree, while the various directions become clear and he is being fanned by a cool wind, the mind becomes one-pointed. 'A ravine' (`kandara`): `kaṃ` is said to be water; it is a mountain region `dāritaṃ` (split) by that water. It is also called a `nitamba` (mountain slope) or a `nikuñja` (glen). For there, the sand is like a silver sheet; above, the forest thicket is like a jeweled canopy; and water like a mass of jewels flows. For one who has descended into such a ravine, drunk water, cooled his limbs, heaped up the sand, spread his rag-robe, and is sitting while practicing the ascetic's duty, the mind becomes one-pointed. 'A mountain cave' means a cavity between two mountains, or a large, tunnel-like opening in a single mountain. The characteristic of a charnel ground is stated in the Visuddhimagga. 'A woodland thicket' means a place beyond the village boundary, a place not frequented by humans, where they do not plow and do not sow. Therefore He said: 'A woodland thicket—this is a designation for remote lodgings,' and so on. 'In the open air' means an uncovered place. If desiring, one may dwell there having made a robe-hut. 'A heap of straw' means a pile of straw. For, having pulled out straw from a large heap of straw, they make dwellings like a mountain slope or a rock-shelter; or, having thrown straw on top of bushes, thickets, and so on, sitting underneath, they practice the ascetic's duty. With reference to this, it was said.

Pacchābhattanti bhattassa pacchato. Piṇḍapātapaṭikkantoti piṇḍapātapariyesanato paṭikkanto. Pallaṅkanti samantato ūrubaddhāsanaṃ. Ābhujitvāti bandhitvā. Ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāyāti uparimaṃ sarīraṃ ujuṃ ṭhapetvā aṭṭhārasa piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṭṭhike koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭipādetvā. Evañhi nisinnassa cammamaṃsanhārūni na paṇamanti. Athassa yā tesaṃ paṇamanapaccayā khaṇe khaṇe vedanā uppajjeyyuṃ, tā nuppajjanti. Tāsu anuppajjamānāsu cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ na paripatati, vuḍḍhiṃ phātiṃ vepullaṃ upagacchati. Parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvāti kammaṭṭhānābhimukhaṃ satiṃ ṭhapayitvā. Mukhasamīpe [M 1.0189] vā katvāti attho. Teneva vibhaṅge vuttaṃ – “ayaṃ sati upaṭṭhitā hoti sūpaṭṭhitā nāsikagge [P 1.0211] vā mukhanimitte vā, tena vuccati parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā”ti (vibha. 537). Athavā parīti pariggahaṭṭho. Mukhanti niyyānaṭṭho. Satīti upaṭṭhānaṭṭho. Tena vuccati – “parimukhaṃ sati”nti. Evaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ vuttanayenapettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepo – “pariggahitaniyyānasatiṃ katvā”ti.

'After the meal' means after the mealtime. 'Returning from the alms-round' means returning from seeking alms. 'Cross-legged' means sitting with the thighs bound all around. 'Having folded' means 'having bound'. 'Setting the body upright' means keeping the upper body straight and causing the eighteen vertebrae to touch end to end. For, when one is seated thus, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not bend down. Consequently, the feelings that would arise moment by moment due to their bending down do not arise. When those feelings do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed, the meditation subject does not fall away, and it approaches growth, prosperity, and an extensive state. 'Establishing mindfulness in front' means having placed mindfulness facing the meditation subject. Or, it means having placed it near the mouth. For that very reason, it is said in the Vibhaṅga: "This mindfulness is established, well-established, at the tip of the nose or at the sign of the mouth. Therefore, it is called 'establishing mindfulness in front'." Alternatively, 'pari' has the meaning of grasping. 'Mukha' has the meaning of outlet. 'Sati' has the meaning of establishment. Therefore, it is called 'parimukhaṃ sati'. Thus, the meaning here should also be understood according to the method stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. Therein, this is the summary: "having made mindfulness an outlet that is grasped".

217. Abhijjhaṃ loketi ettha lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena pañcupādānakkhandhā loko, tasmā pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu rāgaṃ pahāya kāmacchandaṃ vikkhambhetvāti ayametthattho. Vigatābhijjhenāti vikkhambhanavasena pahīnattā vigatābhijjhena, na cakkhuviññāṇasadisenāti attho. Abhijjhāya cittaṃ parisodhetīti abhijjhāto cittaṃ parimoceti. Yathā taṃ sā muñcati ceva, muñcitvā ca na puna gaṇhati, evaṃ karotīti attho. Byāpādapadosaṃ pahāyātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Byāpajjati iminā cittaṃ pūtikummāsādayo viya purimapakatiṃ vijahatīti byāpādo. Vikārāpattiyā padussati, paraṃ vā padūseti vināsetīti padoso. Ubhayametaṃ kodhassevādhivacanaṃ[V 1.0172]. Thinaṃ cittagelaññaṃ. Middhaṃ cetasikagelaññaṃ, thinañca middhañca thinamiddhaṃ. Ālokasaññīti rattimpi divādiṭṭhālokasañjānanasamatthāya vigatanīvaraṇāya parisuddhāya saññāya samannāgato. Sato sampajānoti satiyā ca ñāṇena ca samannāgato. Idaṃ ubhayaṃ ālokasaññāya upakārattā vuttaṃ. Uddhaccañca kukkuccañca uddhaccakukkuccaṃ. Tiṇṇavicikicchoti vicikicchaṃ taritvā atikkamitvā ṭhito. “Kathamidaṃ kathamida”nti evaṃ nappavattatīti akathaṃkathī. Kusalesu dhammesūti anavajjesu dhammesu. “Ime nu kho kusalā kathamime kusalā”ti evaṃ na vicikicchati. Na kaṅkhatīti attho. Ayamettha [P 1.0212] saṅkhepo. Imesu pana nīvaraṇesu vacanatthalakkhaṇādibhedato yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ visuddhimagge vuttaṃ.

217. Here, in the phrase 'covetousness in the world,' 'the world' refers to the five aggregates of clinging, by reason of their liability to break up and disintegrate. Therefore, the meaning here is this: having abandoned lust for the five aggregates of clinging, one has suppressed sensual desire. 'With covetousness departed' means that because it has been abandoned by way of suppression, it is 'with covetousness departed'; this is not like eye-consciousness—this is the meaning. 'Purifies the mind from covetousness' means one causes the mind to be released from covetousness. The meaning is that one acts in such a way that it (covetousness) releases that (mind), and having released it, does not grasp it again. In the passages beginning with 'having abandoned ill will and malice' also, this is the same method. By this, the mind is corrupted, abandoning its former nature like rotten barley-cakes and so on; thus it is called 'ill will.' It is defiled by reaching a state of distortion, or it defiles and destroys another; thus it is called 'malice.' Both these terms are designations for anger alone. 'Sloth' is sickness of mind. 'Torpor' is sickness of mental factors. Sloth and torpor are 'sloth-and-torpor.' 'Perceiving light' means one is endowed with a perception that is capable of recognizing, even at night, the light seen during the day, a perception that is free from the hindrance and is utterly pure. 'Mindful and fully aware' means endowed with mindfulness and with knowledge. This pair is mentioned because of its helpfulness to the perception of light. Restlessness and remorse are 'restlessness-and-remorse.' 'Having crossed over doubt' means one is established, having crossed over and gone beyond doubt. One who does not proceed thus, "How is this? How is this?" is called 'not questioning how.' 'Regarding wholesome states' means regarding blameless states. One does not doubt thus, "Are these wholesome? How are these wholesome?" The meaning is that one does not waver. This is the summary here. Furthermore, regarding these hindrances, whatever should be said by way of the distinctions of verbal meaning, characteristic, and so on, all that has been said in the Visuddhimagga.

218. Yā panāyaṃ seyyathāpi mahārājāti upamā vuttā. Tattha iṇaṃ ādāyāti vaḍḍhiyā dhanaṃ gahetvā. Byantiṃ kareyyāti vigatantaṃ kareyya[M 1.0190], yathā tesaṃ kākaṇikamattopi pariyanto nāma nāvasissati, evaṃ kareyya; sabbaso paṭiniyyāteyyāti attho. Tato nidānanti āṇaṇyanidānaṃ. So hi “aṇaṇomhī”ti āvajjanto balavapāmojjaṃ labhati, somanassaṃ adhigacchati, tena vuttaṃ – “labhetha pāmojjaṃ, adhigaccheyya somanassa”nti.

218. Furthermore, this simile beginning with "Just as, great king..." has been spoken. Therein, 'having taken a debt' means having taken wealth with interest. 'Would make an end of it' means one would make it be without remainder; one would act in such a way that not even a remainder the size of a kākaṇika of those debts would be left over. The meaning is that one would repay it completely in all respects. 'On that account' means on account of being free from debt. For he, reflecting, "I am free from debt," obtains strong joy and attains gladness. Therefore it was said: "he would obtain joy, he would attain gladness."

219. Visabhāgavedanuppattiyā kakaceneva catuiriyāpathaṃ chindanto ābādhatīti ābādho, svāssa atthīti ābādhiko. Taṃ samuṭṭhānena dukkhena dukkhito. Adhimattagilānoti bāḷhagilāno. Nacchādeyyāti adhimattabyādhiparetatāya na rucceyya. Balamattāti balameva, balañcassa kāye na bhaveyyāti attho. Tatonidānanti ārogyanidānaṃ. Tassa hi – “arogomhī”ti āvajjayato tadubhayaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ – “labhetha pāmojjaṃ, adhigaccheyya somanassa”nti.

219. Because it afflicts by cutting off the four postures as if with a saw through the arising of disagreeable feeling, it is called an 'affliction.' He has that, therefore he is 'afflicted.' He is pained by the suffering originating from that. 'Excessively ill' means gravely ill. 'Food would not appeal' means that because of being overcome by excessive illness, it would not be agreeable. 'And a measure of strength' means just strength; the meaning is that there would be no strength in his body. 'On that account' means on account of health. For to him, reflecting, "I am healthy," that pair of joy and gladness arises. Therefore it was said: "he would obtain joy, he would attain gladness."

220. Na cassa kiñci bhogānaṃ vayoti kākaṇikamattampi bhogānaṃ vayo na bhaveyya. Tatonidānanti bandhanāmokkhanidānaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayeneva sabbapadesu yojetabbaṃ.

220. 'And there would be no loss of any of his wealth' means there would not be a loss of wealth even to the extent of a kākaṇika. 'On that account' means on account of release from bondage. The remainder should be applied in all passages according to the method already stated.

221-222. Anattādhīnoti na attani adhīno, attano ruciyā kiñci kātuṃ na labhati. Parādhīnoti paresu adhīno parasseva ruciyā vattati. Na yena kāmaṃ gamoti yena disābhāgenassa gantukāmatā hoti, icchā uppajjati gamanāya, tena gantuṃ na labhati. Dāsabyāti [P 1.0213] dāsabhāvā. Bhujissoti attano santako. Tatonidānanti bhujissanidānaṃ. Kantāraddhānamagganti [V 1.0173] kantāraṃ addhānamaggaṃ, nirudakaṃ dīghamagganti attho. Tatonidānanti khemantabhūminidānaṃ.

'Not his own master' means not dependent on oneself; one does not get to do anything according to one's own wish. 'Dependent on others' means dependent on others; one acts only according to another's wish. 'Not able to go where he wishes' means he does not get to go in whatever direction he has the desire to go, where the wish to go arises. 'From slavery' means from the state of being a slave. 'A free man' means one who is his own master. 'On that account' means on account of being a free man. 'A long road through a wilderness' means a wilderness, a long road; the meaning is a waterless, long road. 'On that account' means on account of reaching a place of safety.

223. Ime pañca nīvaraṇe appahīneti ettha bhagavā appahīnakāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ iṇasadisaṃ, sesāni rogādisadisāni katvā dasseti. Tatrāyaṃ sadisatā. Yo hi paresaṃ iṇaṃ gahetvā vināseti, so tehi iṇaṃ dehīti vuccamānopi pharusaṃ vuccamānopi bajjhamānopi vadhīyamānopi [M 1.0191] kiñci paṭibāhituṃ na sakkoti, sabbaṃ titikkhati. Titikkhākāraṇaṃ hissa taṃ iṇaṃ hoti. Evameva yo yamhi kāmacchandena rajjati, taṇhāsahagatena taṃ vatthuṃ gaṇhati, so tena pharusaṃ vuccamānopi bajjhamānopi vadhīyamānopi sabbaṃ titikkhati, titikkhākāraṇaṃ hissa so kāmacchando hoti, gharasāmikehi vadhīyamānānaṃ itthīnaṃ viyāti, evaṃ iṇaṃ viya kāmacchando daṭṭhabbo.

223. In the passage 'these five hindrances unabandoned,' the Blessed One shows that the unabandoned hindrance of sensual desire is similar to a debt, and the remaining hindrances are similar to illness and so on. Herein is the similarity: For a man who, having taken a debt from others, squanders it, even when told by them, 'Give the debt!', even when spoken to harshly, even when bound, even when tormented, is not able to prevent anything but endures everything. For that debt is the reason for his endurance. In the same way, a person who is infatuated with some object through sensual desire and grasps that object with craving, even when spoken to harshly on account of it, even when bound, even when tormented, endures everything. For that sensual desire is the reason for his endurance, like women being tormented by their household masters. Thus, sensual desire should be seen as being like a debt.

Yathā pana pittarogāturo madhusakkarādīsupi dinnesu pittarogāturatāya tesaṃ rasaṃ na vindati, “tittakaṃ tittaka”nti uggiratiyeva. Evameva byāpannacitto hitakāmehi ācariyupajjhāyehi appamattakampi ovadiyamāno ovādaṃ na gaṇhati. “Ati viya me tumhe upaddavethā”tiādīni vatvā vibbhamati. Pittarogāturatāya so puriso madhusakkarādīnaṃ viya kodhāturatāya jhānasukhādibhedaṃ sāsanarasaṃ na vindatīti. Evaṃ rogo viya byāpādo daṭṭhabbo.

Furthermore, just as a person who is unwell with a bile disorder, even when given honey, sugar, and so on, does not find their taste due to being unwell with a bile disorder, but just spits it out, saying, 'It is bitter! It is bitter!' In the same way, a monk with a corrupt mind, even when admonished in the slightest by teachers and preceptors who desire his welfare, does not accept the admonition. Having said such things as, 'You torment me too much,' he disrobes. Just as that person, due to being unwell with a bile disorder, does not find the taste of honey, sugar, and so on, so too, due to being unwell with anger, he does not find the taste of the teaching, which has distinctions such as the bliss of jhāna. Thus, ill will should be seen as being like a disease.

Yathā pana nakkhattadivase bandhanāgāre baddho puriso nakkhattassa neva ādiṃ na majjhaṃ na pariyosānaṃ passati. So dutiyadivase mutto aho hiyyo nakkhattaṃ manāpaṃ, aho naccaṃ, aho gītantiādīni sutvāpi paṭivacanaṃ na deti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Nakkhattassa ananubhūtattā. Evameva [P 1.0214] thinamiddhābhibhūto bhikkhu vicittanayepi dhammassavane pavattamāne neva tassa ādiṃ na majjhaṃ na pariyosānaṃ jānāti. Sopi uṭṭhite dhammassavane aho dhammassavanaṃ, aho kāraṇaṃ, aho upamāti dhammassavanassa vaṇṇaṃ bhaṇamānānaṃ sutvāpi paṭivacanaṃ na deti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Thinamiddhavasena dhammakathāya ananubhūtattā. Evaṃ bandhanāgāraṃ viya thinamiddhaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Furthermore, just as a man bound in a prison on a festival day sees neither the beginning, nor the middle, nor the end of the festival. On the second day, when released, even having heard such things as, 'Oh, yesterday's festival was delightful! Oh, the dancing! Oh, the singing!', he does not give a reply. For what reason? Because of not having experienced the festival. In the same way, a monk overcome by sloth and torpor, even when a Dhamma hearing with various methods is proceeding, knows neither its beginning, nor its middle, nor its end. He too, when the Dhamma hearing has concluded, even having heard those who are speaking in praise of the Dhamma hearing, saying, 'Oh, the Dhamma hearing! Oh, the reasoning! Oh, the simile!', does not give a reply. For what reason? Because of not having experienced the Dhamma talk, by the power of sloth and torpor. Thus, sloth and torpor should be seen as being like a prison.

Yathā pana nakkhattaṃ kīḷantopi dāso – “idaṃ nāma accāyikaṃ karaṇīyaṃ atthi, sīghaṃ tattha gacchāhi. No ce gacchasi, hatthapādaṃ vā te chindāmi kaṇṇanāsaṃ vā”ti vutto sīghaṃ gacchatiyeva[V 1.0174]. Nakkhattassa ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ anubhavituṃ na labhati, kasmā? Parādhīnatāya, evameva vinaye apakataññunā vivekatthāya araññaṃ paviṭṭhenāpi kismiñcideva [M 1.0192] antamaso kappiyamaṃsepi akappiyamaṃsasaññāya uppannāya vivekaṃ pahāya sīlavisodhanatthaṃ vinayadharassa santikaṃ gantabbaṃ hoti, vivekasukhaṃ anubhavituṃ na labhati, kasmā? Uddhaccakukkuccābhibhūtatāyāti. Evaṃ dāsabyaṃ viya uddhaccakukkuccaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Furthermore, just as a slave, even while enjoying a festival, when told, 'There is this urgent task to be done; go there quickly. If you do not go, I will cut off your hands and feet, or your ears and nose,' goes quickly indeed. He does not get to experience the beginning, middle, and end of the festival. Why? Because of being dependent on another. In the same way, a monk who is unskilled in the Vinaya, even having entered the forest for the sake of seclusion, when a perception of unallowable meat has arisen in regard to some thing or other—at the very least, even in regard to allowable meat—must abandon seclusion and go to the presence of a Vinaya-holder for the purpose of purifying his morality. He does not get to experience the bliss of seclusion. Why? Because of being overcome by restlessness and remorse. Thus, restlessness and remorse should be seen as being like the state of a slave.

Yathā pana kantāraddhānamaggappaṭipanno puriso corehi manussānaṃ viluttokāsaṃ pahatokāsañca disvā daṇḍakasaddenapi sakuṇasaddenapi “corā āgatā”ti ussaṅkitaparisaṅkitova hoti, gacchatipi tiṭṭhatipi nivattatipi, gataṭṭhānato agataṭṭhānameva bahutaraṃ hoti. So kicchena kasirena khemantabhūmiṃ pāpuṇāti vā na vā pāpuṇāti. Evameva yassa aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu vicikicchā uppannā hoti, so – “buddho nu kho, no nu kho buddho”tiādinā nayena vicikicchanto adhimuccitvā saddhāya gaṇhituṃ na sakkoti. Asakkonto maggaṃ vā phalaṃ vā na pāpuṇātīti. Yathā kantāraddhānamagge – “corā atthi natthī”ti punappunaṃ āsappanaparisappanaṃ apariyogāhanaṃ chambhitattaṃ cittassa [P 1.0215] uppādento khemantapattiyā antarāyaṃ karoti, evaṃ vicikicchāpi – “buddho nu kho, na buddho”tiādinā nayena punappunaṃ āsappanaparisappanaṃ apariyogāhanaṃ chambhitattaṃ cittassa uppādayamānā ariyabhūmippattiyā antarāyaṃ karotīti kantāraddhānamaggo viya vicikicchā daṭṭhabbā.

Furthermore, just as a man who has entered upon a long, difficult wilderness path, having seen a place where people have been robbed by thieves and a place where they have been struck, becomes suspicious and apprehensive even at the sound of a twig or a bird, thinking, 'Thieves have come!' He goes, he stands, he turns back, and the place not yet gone to remains much greater than the place already gone to. He, with difficulty and hardship, may or may not reach the land of safety. In the same way, one in whom doubt has arisen in the eight instances, doubting by way of 'Is he indeed the Buddha, or is he not the Buddha?' and so on, is not able to grasp with faith, having made a firm decision. Being unable, he does not attain the path or the fruit. Just as on the wilderness path, by producing repeated advancing and recoiling, non-penetration, and trembling of the mind, thinking 'Are there thieves or not?', one creates an obstacle to the attainment of safety, in the same way, doubt also, by producing repeated advancing and recoiling, non-penetration, and trembling of the mind by way of 'Is he indeed the Buddha, or is he not the Buddha?' and so on, creates an obstacle to the attainment of the noble ground. Thus, doubt should be seen as being like a long, difficult wilderness path.

224. Idāni – “seyyathāpi, mahārāja, āṇaṇya”nti ettha bhagavā pahīnakāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ āṇaṇyasadisaṃ, sesāni ārogyādisadisāni katvā dasseti. Tatrāyaṃ sadisatā, yathā hi puriso iṇaṃ ādāya kammante payojetvā samiddhataṃ patto – “idaṃ iṇaṃ nāma palibodhamūla”nti cintetvā savaḍḍhikaṃ iṇaṃ niyyātetvā paṇṇaṃ phālāpeyya. Athassa tato paṭṭhāya neva koci dūtaṃ peseti, na paṇṇaṃ. So iṇasāmike disvāpi sace icchati, āsanā uṭṭhahati, no ce na uṭṭhahati, kasmā? Tehi saddhiṃ nillepatāya alaggatāya. Evameva bhikkhu – “ayaṃ kāmacchando nāma palibodhamūla”nti cintetvā cha dhamme bhāvetvā kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ pajahati. Te pana cha dhamme mahāsatipaṭṭhāne vaṇṇayissāma. Tassevaṃ pahīnakāmacchandassa [M 1.0193] yathā iṇamuttassa purisassa iṇassāmike disvā neva bhayaṃ na chambhitattaṃ hoti. Evameva paravatthumhi neva saṅgo na baddho hoti. Dibbānipi rūpāni passato kileso na samudācarati. Tasmā bhagavā āṇaṇyamiva kāmacchandappahānaṃ āha.

224. Now, in the passage, “Just as, great king, being without debt,” the Blessed One shows the abandoned hindrance of sensual desire as being similar to being without debt, and the remaining hindrances as being similar to health and so forth. Herein, this is the similarity: just as a man, having taken a loan and invested it in his work, attains prosperity and, thinking, “This thing called debt is the root of trouble,” repays the loan with its interest and has the promissory note torn up. Then, from that time onwards, no one sends him a messenger, nor a note. That man, even upon seeing his creditors, if he wishes, he rises from his seat; if he does not wish, he does not rise. Why? Because of his non-adherence and non-attachment with them. In the very same way, a monk, thinking, “This thing called sensual desire is the root of trouble,” develops six states and abandons the hindrance of sensual desire. We will explain those six states in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta. For that monk who has thus abandoned sensual desire, just as for a man freed from debt, upon seeing his creditors, there is neither fear nor trembling. In the very same way, regarding an external object, there is neither clinging nor bondage. Even when seeing divine forms, defilement does not arise. Therefore, the Blessed One said the abandoning of sensual desire is like being without debt.

Yathā [V 1.0175] pana so pittarogāturo puriso bhesajjakiriyāya taṃ rogaṃ vūpasametvā tato paṭṭhāya madhusakkarādīnaṃ rasaṃ vindati. Evameva bhikkhu “ayaṃ byāpādo nāma mahā anatthakaro”ti cha dhamme bhāvetvā byāpādanīvaraṇaṃ pajahati. Sabbanīvaraṇesu cha dhamme mahāsatipaṭṭhāneyeva vaṇṇayissāma. Na kevalañca teyeva, yepi thinamiddhādīnaṃ pahānāya bhāvetabbā, tepi sabbe tattheva vaṇṇayissāma. So evaṃ pahīnabyāpādo yathā pittarogavimutto puriso madhusakkarādīnaṃ rasaṃ sampiyāyamāno paṭisevati, evameva ācārapaṇṇattiādīni [P 1.0216] sikkhāpadāni sirasā sampaṭicchitvā sampiyāyamāno sikkhati. Tasmā bhagavā ārogyamiva byāpādappahānaṃ āha.

Furthermore, just as that man afflicted with a bilious disease, having pacified that disease through medical treatment, from that time onwards enjoys the taste of honey, sugar, and so forth; in the very same way, a bhikkhu, thinking, “This thing called ill will is a great cause of harm,” develops six states and abandons the hindrance of ill will. We shall explain the six states for all the hindrances in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta itself. And not only those, but also all the states that should be developed for the abandoning of sloth and torpor and so forth, all of them we shall explain right there. That monk who has thus abandoned ill will, just as the man freed from the bilious disease partakes of the taste of honey, sugar, and so forth, greatly cherishing it, in the very same way, having accepted with his head the training rules concerning conduct, precepts, and so forth, he trains, greatly cherishing them. Therefore, the Blessed One said the abandoning of ill will is like health.

Yathā so nakkhattadivase bandhanāgāraṃ pavesito puriso aparasmiṃ nakkhattadivase – “pubbepi ahaṃ pamādadosena baddho, tena nakkhattaṃ nānubhaviṃ. Idāni appamatto bhavissāmī”ti yathāssa paccatthikā okāsaṃ na labhanti, evaṃ appamatto hutvā nakkhattaṃ anubhavitvā – ‘aho nakkhattaṃ, aho nakkhatta’nti udānaṃ udānesi, evameva bhikkhu – “idaṃ thinamiddhaṃ nāma mahāanatthakara”nti cha dhamme bhāvetvā thinamiddhanīvaraṇaṃ pajahati, so evaṃ pahīnathinamiddho yathā bandhanā mutto puriso sattāhampi nakkhattassa ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ anubhavati, evameva dhammanakkhattassa ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ anubhavanto saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tasmā bhagavā bandhanā mokkhamiva thinamiddhappahānaṃ āha.

Just as a man who was put into prison on a festival day, on another festival day thinks, “Previously, I was bound due to the fault of negligence, and because of that I did not experience the festival. Now I will be diligent,” and being diligent in such a way that his enemies do not get an opportunity, he experiences the festival and utters an inspired utterance, “Oh, what a festival! Oh, what a festival!”; in the very same way, a bhikkhu, thinking, “This thing called sloth and torpor is a great cause of harm,” develops six states and abandons the hindrance of sloth and torpor. That bhikkhu, having thus abandoned sloth and torpor, just as a man freed from bondage experiences the beginning, middle, and end of the festival for a whole seven days, in the very same way, experiencing the beginning, middle, and end of the Dhamma-festival, he attains Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Therefore, the Blessed One said the abandoning of sloth and torpor is like release from bondage.

Yathā pana dāso kiñcideva mittaṃ upanissāya sāmikānaṃ dhanaṃ datvā attānaṃ bhujissaṃ katvā tato paṭṭhāya yaṃ icchati, taṃ karoti. Evameva bhikkhu – “idaṃ uddhaccakukkuccaṃ nāma mahā anatthakara”nti cha dhamme bhāvetvā uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pajahati. So evaṃ pahīnauddhaccakukkucco yathā bhujisso puriso yaṃ icchati, taṃ karoti, na taṃ koci balakkārena tato nivatteti[M 1.0194], evameva yathā sukhaṃ nekkhammapaṭipadaṃ paṭipajjati, na taṃ uddhaccakukkuccaṃ balakkārena tato nivatteti. Tasmā bhagavā bhujissaṃ viya uddhaccakukkuccappahānaṃ āha.

Furthermore, just as a slave, relying on some friend, gives wealth to his masters, makes himself a free man, and from that time onwards does what he wishes; in the very same way, a bhikkhu, thinking, “This thing called restlessness and remorse is a great cause of harm,” develops six states and abandons restlessness and remorse. He, having thus abandoned restlessness and remorse, just as a free man does what he wishes, and no one can forcibly make him turn back from that, in the very same way, he practices the path of renunciation at ease, and restlessness and remorse cannot forcibly make him turn back from that. Therefore, the Blessed One said the abandoning of restlessness and remorse is like being a free man.

Yathā balavā puriso hatthasāraṃ gahetvā sajjāvudho saparivāro kantāraṃ paṭipajjeyya, taṃ corā dūratova disvā palāyeyyuṃ. So sotthinā taṃ kantāraṃ nittharitvā khemantaṃ patto haṭṭhatuṭṭho assa. Evameva bhikkhu “ayaṃ vicikicchā nāma mahā anatthakārikā”ti cha dhamme bhāvetvā vicikicchaṃ pajahati[P 1.0217]. So evaṃ pahīnavicikiccho yathā balavā puriso sajjāvudho saparivāro nibbhayo core tiṇaṃ viya agaṇetvā sotthinā nikkhamitvā khemantabhūmiṃ pāpuṇāti, evameva bhikkhu [V 1.0176] duccaritakantāraṃ nittharitvā paramaṃ khemantabhūmiṃ amataṃ mahānibbānaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tasmā bhagavā khemantabhūmiṃ viya vicikicchāpahānaṃ āha.

Just as a strong man, taking his essential wealth, armed and with a retinue, might travel through a wilderness, and bandits, seeing him from afar, would flee. He, having safely crossed that wilderness and reached a place of security, would be joyful and elated. In the very same way, a bhikkhu, thinking, “This thing called doubt is a great cause of harm,” develops six states and abandons doubt. He, having thus abandoned doubt, just as a strong man, armed, with a retinue, fearless, not regarding the bandits as even grass, having departed safely, reaches a land of security; in the very same way, the bhikkhu, having crossed the wilderness of misconduct, reaches the supreme land of security, the Deathless, the great Nibbāna. Therefore, the Blessed One said the abandoning of doubt is like reaching a land of security.

225. Pāmojjaṃ jāyatīti tuṭṭhākāro jāyati. Pamuditassa pīti jāyatīti tuṭṭhassa sakalasarīraṃ khobhayamānā pīti jāyati. Pītimanassa kāyo passambhatīti pītisampayuttacittassa puggalassa nāmakāyo passambhati, vigatadaratho hoti. Sukhaṃ vedetīti kāyikampi cetasikampi sukhaṃ vedayati. Cittaṃ samādhiyatīti iminā nekkhammasukhena sukhitassa upacāravasenapi appanāvasenapi cittaṃ samādhiyati.

225. ‘Gladness arises’ means a state of delight arises. ‘For one who is gladdened, rapture arises’ means for one who is delighted, rapture arises, capable of agitating the entire body. ‘For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil’ means for a person whose mind is associated with rapture, the mental body becomes tranquil; he becomes one whose fever of defilements is gone. ‘He feels happiness’ means he experiences both bodily and mental happiness. ‘The mind becomes concentrated’ means for one who is made happy by this happiness of renunciation, the mind becomes concentrated both by way of access concentration and by way of absorption concentration.

Paṭhamajjhānakathā

Discourse on the First Jhāna

226. So vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharatītiādi pana upacārasamādhinā samāhite citte uparivisesadassanatthaṃ appanāsamādhinā samāhite citte tassa samādhino pabhedadassanatthaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Imameva kāyanti imaṃ karajakāyaṃ. Abhisandetīti temeti sneheti, sabbattha pavattapītisukhaṃ karoti. Parisandetīti samantato sandeti. Paripūretīti vāyunā bhastaṃ viya pūreti. Parippharatīti samantato phusati. Sabbāvato kāyassāti assa bhikkhuno sabbakoṭṭhāsavato kāyassa kiñci upādinnakasantatipavattiṭṭhāne chavimaṃsalohitānugataṃ [M 1.0195] aṇumattampi ṭhānaṃ paṭhamajjhānasukhena aphuṭaṃ nāma na hoti.

226. Furthermore, it should be known that the passage beginning, 'He, secluded from sensual pleasures...pe... enters and abides in the first jhāna,' was spoken for the purpose of showing the higher distinction when the mind is concentrated by access concentration, and for the purpose of showing the divisions of that concentration when the mind is concentrated by absorption concentration. 'This very body' means this physical body. 'Drenches' means it moistens, it saturates; it produces rapture and happiness that occurs everywhere. 'Suffuses' means it moistens all around. 'Fills' means it fills, like filling a bellows with air. 'Pervades' means it spreads all around. 'Of his entire body': Of this bhikkhu's physical body, which has all its parts, in the place where the continuity of kamma-born matter occurs, which is followed by skin, flesh, and blood, there is no place whatsoever, even the size of an atom, that is not pervaded by the happiness of the first jhāna.

227. Dakkhoti cheko paṭibalo nhānīyacuṇṇāni kātuñceva payojetuñca sannetuñca. Kaṃsathāleti yena kenaci lohena katabhājane. Mattikabhājanaṃ pana thiraṃ na hoti. Sannentassa bhijjati. Tasmā taṃ na dasseti. Paripphosakaṃ [P 1.0218] paripphosakanti siñcitvā siñcitvā. Sanneyyāti vāmahatthena kaṃsathālaṃ gahetvā dakkhiṇahatthena pamāṇayuttaṃ udakaṃ siñcitvā siñcitvā parimaddanto piṇḍaṃ kareyya. Snehānugatāti udakasinehena anugatā. Snehaparetāti udakasinehena pariggahitā. Santarabāhirāti saddhiṃ antopadesena ceva bahipadesena ca sabbatthakameva udakasinehena phuṭāti attho. Na ca paggharaṇīti na ca bindu bindu udakaṃ paggharati, sakkā hoti hatthenapi dvīhipi tīhipi aṅgulīhi gahetuṃ ovaṭṭikāyapi kātunti attho.

227. ‘Dakkho’ means skilled, competent, and able to prepare, use, and mix bath powders. ‘In a bronze bowl’ means in a vessel made of any kind of metal. An earthen vessel, however, is not firm; it is liable to break while being mixed. Therefore, that is not shown. ‘Sprinkling again and again’ means having sprinkled repeatedly. ‘One should mix’ means: taking the bronze bowl with the left hand, and with the right hand sprinkling a suitable amount of water again and again, while kneading it, one should make a ball. ‘Permeated with moisture’ means followed by the moisture of water. ‘Saturated with moisture’ means surrounded by the moisture of water. ‘Inside and out’ means: pervaded by the moisture of water together with the internal part and the external part, that is, everywhere. ‘And not oozing’ means: and it does not ooze water drop by drop; it is possible to take it with the hand, or with two or three fingers; it is even possible to place it in the fold of one's lower garment. This is the meaning.

Dutiyajjhānakathā

Discourse on the Second Jhāna

228-229. Dutiyajjhānasukhūpamāyaṃ [V 1.0177] ubbhidodakoti ubbhinnaudako, na heṭṭhā ubbhijjitvā uggacchanakaudako. Antoyeva pana ubbhijjanakaudakoti attho. Āyamukhanti āgamanamaggo. Devoti megho. Kālena kālanti kāle kāle, anvaddhamāsaṃ vā anudasāhaṃ vāti attho. Dhāranti vuṭṭhiṃ. Na anuppaveccheyyāti na ca paveseyya, na vasseyyāti attho. Sītā vāridhārā ubbhijjitvāti sītaṃ dhāraṃ uggantvā rahadaṃ pūrayamānaṃ ubbhijjitvā. Heṭṭhā uggacchanaudakañhi uggantvā uggantvā bhijjantaṃ udakaṃ khobheti, catūhi disāhi pavisanaudakaṃ purāṇapaṇṇatiṇakaṭṭhadaṇḍakādīhi udakaṃ khobheti, vuṭṭhiudakaṃ dhārānipātapubbuḷakehi udakaṃ khobheti. Sannisinnameva pana hutvā iddhinimmitamiva uppajjamānaṃ udakaṃ imaṃ padesaṃ pharati, imaṃ padesaṃ na pharatīti natthi, tena aphuṭokāso nāma na hotīti. Tattha rahado viya karajakāyo. Udakaṃ viya dutiyajjhānasukhaṃ. Sesaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

229. In the simile of the happiness of the second jhāna: 'with water welling up' means having water that has welled up; not having water that, having burst forth from below, rises up. Rather, the meaning is: having water that wells up only from within the lake itself. 'Inlet' means the path of entry. 'Deva' means a cloud. 'From time to time' means at the right times; the meaning is every half-month or every ten days. 'Stream' means rain. 'Should not convey' means it should not let in, it should not rain; this is the meaning. 'Cool streams of water having welled up' means a cool stream, having welled up, fills the lake. For water rising from below, as it rises up again and again and breaks forth, agitates the water. Water entering from the four directions agitates the water with old leaves, grass, sticks, and so on. Rainwater agitates the water with the falling of its streams and the resulting bubbles. But the water that wells up, being calm, as if created by psychic power, there is no such thing as 'it pervades this area, it does not pervade that area.' Therefore, there is no place whatsoever that is not pervaded. Therein, the physical body is like the lake. The happiness of the second jhāna is like the water. The rest should be understood in the same way as before.

Tatiyajjhānakathā

The Account of the Third Jhāna

230-231. Tatiyajjhānasukhūpamāyaṃ [P 1.0219][M 1.0196] uppalāni ettha santīti uppalinī. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Ettha ca setarattanīlesu yaṃ kiñci uppalaṃ uppalameva. Ūnakasatapattaṃ puṇḍarīkaṃ, satapattaṃ padumaṃ. Pattaniyamaṃ vā vināpi setaṃ padumaṃ, rattaṃ puṇḍarīkanti ayamettha vinicchayo. Udakānuggatānīti udakato na uggatāni. Anto nimuggaposīnīti udakatalassa anto nimuggāniyeva hutvā posīni, vaḍḍhīnīti attho. Sesaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

231. In the simile of the happiness of the third jhāna: because there are lotuses (uppalāni) here, it is called a lotus pond (uppalinī). The same method applies to the remaining two terms. And here, among the white, red, and blue lotuses, any one is simply an uppala. A puṇḍarīka has fewer than a hundred petals; a paduma has a hundred or more petals. Alternatively, without a fixed rule regarding the petals, a white lotus is a paduma, and a red one is a puṇḍarīka—this is the determination here. 'Not having emerged from the water' means not having risen up from the water. 'Nourished while submerged within' means they grow and are nourished while being entirely submerged within the water; that is the meaning. The rest should be understood in the same way as before.

Catutthajjhānakathā

The Account of the Fourth Jhāna

232-233. Catutthajjhānasukhūpamāyaṃ parisuddhena cetasā pariyodātenāti ettha nirupakkilesaṭṭhena parisuddhaṃ, pabhassaraṭṭhena pariyodātanti veditabbaṃ. Odātena vatthenāti idaṃ utupharaṇatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiliṭṭhavatthena hi utupharaṇaṃ na hoti, taṅkhaṇadhotaparisuddhena utupharaṇaṃ balavaṃ hoti. Imissāya hi upamāya vatthaṃ viya karajakāyo, utupharaṇaṃ viya catutthajjhānasukhaṃ. Tasmā yathā sunhātassa purisassa parisuddhaṃ vatthaṃ sasīsaṃ pārupitvā nisinnassa sarīrato utu sabbameva vatthaṃ pharati. Na koci vatthassa aphuṭokāso hoti. Evaṃ catutthajjhānasukhena bhikkhuno [V 1.0178] karajakāyassa na koci okāso aphuṭo hotīti. Evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Imesaṃ pana catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ anupadavaṇṇanā ca bhāvanānayo ca visuddhimagge vuttoti idha na vitthārito.

232–233. In the simile of the happiness of the fourth jhāna, regarding the phrase 'with a mind purified and bright,' it should be understood that 'purified' is in the sense of being without defilements, and 'bright' is in the sense of being radiant. The phrase 'with a white cloth' is stated to illustrate the pervasion of warmth. For with a soiled cloth, the pervasion of warmth does not occur, but with a cloth just washed and purified, the pervasion of warmth is strong. Indeed, in this simile, the kamma-born body is like the cloth, and the happiness of the fourth jhāna is like the pervasion of warmth. Therefore, just as when a man who has bathed well sits wrapped in a clean cloth, including his head, the warmth from his body pervades the entire cloth, and there is no part of the cloth that remains unpervaded; in the same way, for a bhikkhu, there is no part of the kamma-born body that is not pervaded by the happiness of the fourth jhāna. This is how the meaning should be understood here. Furthermore, the sequential word-by-word explanation of these four jhānas and the method of cultivation have been stated in the Visuddhimagga, and so are not elaborated upon here.

Ettāvatā cesa rūpajjhānalābhīyeva, na arūpajjhānalābhīti na veditabbo. Na hi aṭṭhasu samāpattīsu cuddasahākārehi ciṇṇavasībhāvaṃ vinā upari abhiññādhigamo hoti. Pāḷiyaṃ pana rūpajjhānāniyeva āgatāni. Arūpajjhānāni āharitvā kathetabbāni.

And by this much, it should not be understood that this person is one who has attained only the form jhānas and not the formless jhānas. For without having achieved the state of practiced mastery in the eight attainments through fourteen aspects, the attainment of the higher knowledges beyond does not occur. In the Pāli text, however, only the form jhānas are mentioned. The formless jhānas should be brought in and spoken of.

Vipassanāñāṇakathā

The Account of Insight Knowledge

234. So evaṃ samāhite citte…pe… āneñjappatteti so cuddasahākārehi aṭṭhasu samāpattīsu ciṇṇavasībhāvo bhikkhūti [P 1.0220] dasseti[M 1.0197]. Sesamettha visuddhimagge vuttanayena veditabbaṃ. Ñāṇadassanāya cittaṃ abhinīharatīti ettha ñāṇadassananti maggañāṇampi, vuccati phalañāṇampi, sabbaññutaññāṇampi, paccavekkhaṇañāṇampi, vipassanāñāṇampi. “Kiṃ nu kho, āvuso, ñāṇadassanavisuddhatthaṃ bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussatī”ti (mahāni. 1.257) ettha hi maggañāṇaṃ ñāṇadassananti vuttaṃ. “Ayamañño uttarimanussadhammo alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso adhigato phāsuvihāro”ti (ma. ni. 1.328) ettha phalañāṇaṃ. “Bhagavatopi kho ñāṇadassanaṃ udapādi sattāhakālaṅkato āḷāro kālāmo”ti (mahāva. 10) ettha sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ. “Ñāṇañca pana me dassanaṃ udapādi akuppā me vimutti, ayamantimā jātī”ti (mahāva. 16) ettha paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ idha pana ñāṇadassanāya cittanti idaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ ñāṇadassananti vuttanti.

234. 234. ‘He, with a mind thus concentrated… up to… having attained the imperturbable’—this shows that the bhikkhu is one who has practiced mastery in the eight attainments through the fourteen aspects. The rest here should be understood in the manner stated in the Visuddhimagga. In the phrase ‘directs the mind to knowledge and vision,’ the term ‘knowledge and vision’ can refer to path-knowledge, fruition-knowledge, omniscience-knowledge, reviewing-knowledge, and insight-knowledge. For in the passage, ‘For what purpose, friend, is the holy life lived under the Blessed One? For the purification of knowledge and vision?’, it is path-knowledge that is called ‘knowledge and vision.’ In ‘This is another superhuman state, a distinction in noble knowledge and vision attained, a pleasant abiding,’ it is fruition-knowledge. In ‘Knowledge and vision arose in the Blessed One: “Āḷāra Kālāma died seven days ago,”’ it is omniscience-knowledge. In ‘And knowledge and vision arose in me: “Unshakeable is my liberation; this is the final birth,”’ it is reviewing-knowledge. Here, however, in the phrase ‘directs the mind to knowledge and vision,’ it is this insight-knowledge that is called ‘knowledge and vision.’

Abhinīharatīti vipassanāñāṇassa nibbattanatthāya tanninnaṃ tappoṇaṃ tappabbhāraṃ karoti. Rūpīti ādīnamattho vuttoyeva. Odanakummāsūpacayoti odanena ceva kummāsena ca upacito vaḍḍhito. Aniccucchādanaparimaddanabhedanaviddhaṃsanadhammoti hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccadhammo. Duggandhavighātatthāya tanuvilepanena ucchādanadhammo. Aṅgapaccaṅgābādhavinodanatthāya khuddakasambāhanena parimaddanadhammo. Daharakāle vā ūrūsu sayāpetvā gabbhāvāsena dussaṇṭhitānaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ aṅgānaṃ saṇṭhānasampādanatthaṃ añchanapīḷanādivasena parimaddanadhammo. Evaṃ pariharitopi bhedanaviddhaṃsanadhammo bhijjati ceva vikirati ca, evaṃ sabhāvoti attho. Tattha [P 1.0221] rūpī cātumahābhūtikotiādīsu chahi [V 1.0179] padehi samudayo kathito. Aniccapadena saddhiṃ pacchimehi dvīhi atthaṅgamo. Ettha sitaṃ ettha paṭibaddhanti ettha cātumahābhūtike kāye nissitañca paṭibaddhañca.

‘He directs’ (abhinīharati) means that for the purpose of the arising of insight-knowledge, he makes the mind inclined towards it, bent towards it, and sloped towards it. The meaning of ‘form’ (rūpī), etc., has already been stated. ‘An accumulation of rice and barley-meal’ (odanakummāsūpacayo) means accumulated and increased by both rice and barley-meal. ‘Of a nature to be impermanent, to be anointed, to be massaged, to break up, and to be scattered’ (aniccucchādanaparimaddanabhedanaviddhaṃsanadhammo) means: it has the nature of impermanence (aniccadhammo) in the sense of ceasing to be after having come into being. It has the nature of being anointed (ucchādanadhammo) by way of fine ointments for the purpose of dispelling bad odors. It has the nature of being massaged (parimaddanadhammo) by way of gentle rubbing for the purpose of dispelling aches in the major and minor limbs. Or, it has the nature of being massaged by means of stretching, pressing, etc., for the purpose of perfecting the shape of various limbs that are ill-formed due to having been in the mother's womb, after having been made to sleep on the thighs in childhood. Even when so maintained, it has the nature of breaking up and being scattered (bhedanaviddhaṃsanadhammo); it both breaks up and is scattered—such is its nature. Therein, among the terms beginning with ‘form, composed of the four great elements,’ arising is taught with six terms. With the term ‘impermanent,’ together with the last two terms, cessation is taught. ‘Herein based, herein bound’ (ettha sitaṃ ettha paṭibaddhaṃ) means based on and bound to this body composed of the four great elements.

235. Subhoti sundaro. Jātimāti parisuddhākarasamuṭṭhito. Suparikammakatoti suṭṭhu kataparikammo apanītapāsāṇasakkharo. Acchoti tanucchavi. Vippasannoti suṭṭhu pasanno. Sabbākārasampannoti dhovanavedhanādīhi sabbehi ākārehi sampanno. Nīlantiādīhi vaṇṇasampattiṃ dasseti. Tādisañhi āvutaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti. Evameva khoti ettha evaṃ upamāsaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Maṇi viya hi karajakāyo. Āvutasuttaṃ [M 1.0198] viya vipassanāñāṇaṃ. Cakkhumā puriso viya vipassanālābhī bhikkhu, hatthe karitvā paccavekkhato ayaṃ kho maṇīti maṇino āvibhūtakālo viya vipassanāñāṇaṃ, abhinīharitvā nisinnassa bhikkhuno cātumahābhūtikakāyassa āvibhūtakālo, tatridaṃ suttaṃ āvutanti suttassāvibhūtakālo viya vipassanāñāṇaṃ, abhinīharitvā nisinnassa bhikkhuno tadārammaṇānaṃ phassapañcamakānaṃ vā sabbacittacetasikānaṃ vā vipassanāñāṇasseva vā āvibhūtakāloti.

235. ‘Excellent’ (subha) means beautiful. ‘Of good stock’ (jātimā) means arisen from a perfectly pure mine. ‘Well-wrought’ (suparikammakato) means well-prepared, with stones and gravel removed. ‘Clear’ (accha) means having a fine surface. ‘Very limpid’ (vippasanna) means exceedingly clear. ‘Complete in all aspects’ (sabbākārasampanno) means endowed with all aspects, such as washing, piercing, etc. With the terms beginning with ‘blue,’ he shows the perfection of color. For a thread of such a kind, when strung through, becomes manifest. In the phrase ‘Just so,’ the correlation of the simile should be understood in this way: Indeed, the kamma-born body is like the gem. Insight-knowledge is like the thread strung through it. The bhikkhu who has attained insight is like the man with good eyes. Just as for the man examining it in his hand, saying, ‘This is indeed a gem,’ there is a time when the gem becomes manifest, so too for the bhikkhu seated after directing his mind, there is a time when the body composed of the four great elements becomes manifest. And just as in the phrase ‘and herein this thread is strung through,’ there is a time when the thread becomes manifest, so too for the bhikkhu seated after directing his mind, there is a time when the mental states that have that kamma-born body as their object—be they the pentad with contact as the fifth, or all mind and mental factors, or even just insight-knowledge itself—become manifest.

Idañca vipassanāñāṇaṃ maggañāṇānantaraṃ. Evaṃ santepi yasmā abhiññāvāre āraddhe etassa antarāvāro natthi tasmā idheva dassitaṃ. Yasmā ca aniccādivasena akatasammasanassa dibbāya sotadhātuyā bheravaṃ saddaṃ suṇato, pubbenivāsānussatiyā bherave khandhe anussarato, dibbena cakkhunā bheravampi rūpaṃ passato bhayasantāso uppajjati, na aniccādivasena katasammasanassa tasmā abhiññaṃ pattassa bhayavinodanahetusampādanatthampi idaṃ idheva dassitaṃ. Api ca yasmā vipassanāsukhaṃ nāmetaṃ maggaphalasukhasampādakaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ sandiṭṭhikaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ [P 1.0222] tasmāpi āditova idaṃ idha dassitanti veditabbaṃ.

And this insight-knowledge is the proximate condition for path-knowledge. Even so, because when the section on the higher knowledges is commenced there is no intermediate turn for this insight-knowledge, it is shown right here. And because for one who has not performed comprehension by way of impermanence, etc., fear and dread arise when hearing a terrifying sound with the divine ear element, when recollecting terrifying aggregates with the recollection of past lives, or when seeing a terrifying form with the divine eye—but not for one who has performed comprehension by way of impermanence, etc.—therefore, also for the purpose of accomplishing the cause for dispelling fear for one who has attained the higher knowledges, this is shown right here. Furthermore, because this so-called happiness of insight is a distinct, directly visible fruit of recluseship that accomplishes the happiness of the path and fruition, therefore also, this is shown right at the beginning. Thus it should be understood.

Manomayiddhiñāṇakathā

Discourse on the Knowledge of Mind-Made Psychic Power

236-237. Manomayanti manena nibbattitaṃ. Sabbaṅgapaccaṅginti sabbehi aṅgehi ca paccaṅgehi ca samannāgataṃ. Ahīnindriyanti saṇṭhānavasena avikalindriyaṃ. Iddhimatā nimmitarūpañhi sace iddhimā odāto tampi odātaṃ. Sace aviddhakaṇṇo tampi aviddhakaṇṇanti evaṃ sabbākārehi tena sadisameva hoti. Muñjamhā īsikantiādi upamāttayampi hi sadisabhāvadassanatthameva vuttaṃ. Muñjasadisā eva hi tassa anto īsikā hoti. Kosisadisoyeva asi, vaṭṭāya kosiyā vaṭṭaṃ asimeva pakkhipanti, patthaṭāya patthaṭaṃ[V 1.0180]. Karaṇḍāti idampi ahikañcukassa nāmaṃ, na vilīvakaraṇḍakassa. Ahikañcuko hi ahinā sadisova hoti. Tattha kiñcāpi “puriso ahiṃ karaṇḍā uddhareyyā”ti hatthena uddharamāno viya dassito, atha kho cittenevassa uddharaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.
