Ayañhi ahi nāma sajātiyaṃ ṭhito, kaṭṭhantaraṃ vā rukkhantaraṃ vā nissāya, tacato sarīraṃ nikkaḍḍhanappayogasaṅkhātena [M 1.0199] thāmena, sarīraṃ khādayamānaṃ viya purāṇatacaṃ jigucchantoti imehi catūhi kāraṇehi sayameva kañcukaṃ pajahati, na sakkā tato aññena uddharituṃ, tasmā cittena uddharaṇaṃ sandhāya idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Iti muñjādisadisaṃ imassa bhikkhuno sarīraṃ, īsikādisadisaṃ nimmitarūpanti. Idamettha opammasaṃsandanaṃ. Nimmānavidhānaṃ panettha parato ca iddhividhādipañcaabhiññākathā sabbākārena visuddhimagge vitthāritāti tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Upamāmattameva hi idha adhikaṃ.

236-237. ‘Mind-made’ means produced by the mind. ‘With all limbs and minor limbs’ means endowed with all major limbs and minor limbs. ‘With intact faculties’ means having unimpaired faculties by way of physical form. For indeed, the form created by one with psychic power, if the one with psychic power is fair, it too is fair. If he has unpierced ears, it too has unpierced ears. Thus, in all aspects, it is just the same as him. The three similes, such as ‘a reed from muñja grass,’ were spoken only for the purpose of showing the similarity. For the reed inside it is just like the muñja grass. The sword is just like the scabbard; into a round scabbard they insert a round sword, into a flat one, a flat one. This term ‘karaṇḍa’ is a name for a snake’s slough, not for a woven basket. For a snake’s slough is just like the snake. Therein, although it is shown as if ‘a man were to draw a snake from a slough’—as if drawing it with his hand—yet its drawing out should be understood as being done by the mind alone. For this snake, being among its own kind, relying on the space between logs or trees, by the strength described as the effort of drawing its body from its skin, and being disgusted with its old skin as if it were devouring its body—for these four reasons, it sheds its slough by itself. It cannot be drawn out from there by another. Therefore, it should be understood that this was said referring to the drawing out by the mind. Thus, this monk’s body is like the muñja grass, etc., and the created form is like the reed, etc. This, herein, is the connection of the simile. The method of creation and, further, the discourse on the five higher knowledges beginning with the psychic powers, are explained in all aspects in the Visuddhimagga, so they should be understood in the way stated there. For here, only the simile is additional.

Iddhividhañāṇādikathā

Discourse on the Knowledge of Psychic Powers, etc.

238-239. Tattha chekakumbhakārādayo viya iddhividhañāṇalābhī [P 1.0223] bhikkhu daṭṭhabbo. Suparikammakatamattikādayo viya iddhividhañāṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Icchiticchitabhājanavikatiādikaraṇaṃ viya tassa bhikkhuno vikubbanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

238-239. Therein, a monk who has obtained the knowledge of psychic powers should be seen like a skilled potter and so on. The knowledge of psychic powers should be seen like well-prepared clay and so on. That monk's performing of transformations should be seen like the making of whatever kind of vessel is desired.

240-241. Dibbasotadhātuupamāyaṃ yasmā kantāraddhānamaggo sāsaṅko hoti sappaṭibhayo. Tattha ussaṅkitaparisaṅkitena ‘ayaṃ bherisaddo’, ‘ayaṃ mudiṅgasaddo’ti na sakkā vavatthapetuṃ, tasmā kantāraggahaṇaṃ akatvā khemamaggaṃ dassento addhānamaggappaṭipannoti āha. Appaṭibhayañhi khemamaggaṃ sīse sāṭakaṃ katvā saṇikaṃ paṭipanno vuttappakāre sadde sukhaṃ vavatthapeti. Tassa savanena tesaṃ tesaṃ saddānaṃ āvibhūtakālo viya yogino dūrasantikabhedānaṃ dibbānañceva mānussakānañca saddānaṃ āvibhūtakālo veditabbo.

240-241. In the simile of the divine ear element, because a long-distance wilderness path is perilous and fraught with danger, one who is suspicious and apprehensive there cannot determine, ‘This is the sound of a great drum,’ or, ‘This is the sound of a small drum.’ Therefore, not taking up the term ‘wilderness,’ and wishing to show a safe path, he said, ‘one who has set out on a long-distance path.’ For one who has set out slowly on a safe, fearless path, having placed a cloth on his head, can easily determine the various kinds of sounds mentioned. Just as for that man, by hearing, the time of the manifestation of those various sounds is to be known, so too for the yogi, the time of the manifestation of sounds, both divine and human, distinguished as distant and near, is to be known.

242-243. Cetopariyañāṇūpamāyaṃ daharoti taruṇo. Yuvāti yobbannena samannāgato. Maṇḍanakajātikoti yuvāpi samāno na ālasiyo na kiliṭṭhavatthasarīro, atha kho maṇḍanapakatiko, divasassa dve tayo vāre nhāyitvā suddhavatthaparidahanaalaṅkārakaraṇasīloti attho. Sakaṇikanti kāḷatilakavaṅgamukhadūsipīḷakādīnaṃ aññatarena sadosaṃ. Tattha yathā tassa mukhanimittaṃ paccavekkhato mukhe doso pākaṭo hoti, evaṃ cetopariyañāṇāya cittaṃ abhinīharitvā nisinnassa bhikkhuno paresaṃ soḷasavidhaṃ cittaṃ pākaṭaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ.

242-243. In the simile of the knowledge of others’ minds, ‘young’ (daharo) means youthful (taruṇo). ‘A youth’ (yuvā) means one endowed with youthfulness. ‘Of an ornamental nature’ (maṇḍanakajātiko) means that although a youth, he is not lazy, nor does he have soiled clothes and body, but rather his nature is to adorn himself; he is accustomed to bathing two or three times a day, wearing clean clothes, and putting on ornaments—this is the meaning. ‘With a blemish’ (sakaṇikaṃ) means with a fault, through one or another defect such as a black mole, a disfigurement, a face-spoiling pimple, and so on. Therein, just as for him, when he reflects on the image of his face, a fault on the face becomes manifest, so too, it should be known that for a monk who sits having directed his mind towards the knowledge of others' minds, the sixteen-fold mind of others becomes manifest.

244-245. Pubbenivāsañāṇūpamāyaṃ [V 1.0181][M 1.0200] taṃ divasaṃ katakiriyā pākaṭā hotīti taṃ divasaṃ gatagāmattayameva gahitaṃ. Tattha gāmattayagatapuriso viya pubbenivāsañāṇalābhī daṭṭhabbo, tayo gāmā viya tayo bhavā daṭṭhabbā, tassa purisassa tīsu gāmesu taṃ divasaṃ katakiriyāya āvibhāvo viya pubbenivāsāya cittaṃ abhinīharitvā nisinnassa bhikkhuno tīsu bhavesu katakiriyāya pākaṭabhāvo daṭṭhabbo.

244-245. In the simile of the knowledge of past lives, because the actions done on that day become manifest, only the three villages gone to on that day are taken. Therein, the man who has gone to the three villages should be seen as the monk who has obtained the knowledge of past lives; the three villages should be seen as the three existences; and just as for that man there is the manifestation of the actions done on that day in the three villages, so for the monk who sits having directed his mind towards past lives, the state of manifestation of the actions done in the three existences should be seen.

246-247. Dibbacakkhūpamāyaṃ [P 1.0224] vīthiṃ sañcaranteti aparāparaṃ sañcarante. Vīthiṃ carantetipi pāṭho. Ayamevattho. Tattha nagaramajjhe siṅghāṭakamhi pāsādo viya imassa bhikkhuno karajakāyo daṭṭhabbo, pāsāde ṭhito cakkhumā puriso viya ayameva dibbacakkhuṃ patvā ṭhito bhikkhu, gehaṃ pavisantā viya paṭisandhivasena mātukucchiyaṃ pavisantā, gehā nikkhamantā viya mātukucchito nikkhamantā, rathikāya vīthiṃ sañcarantā viya aparāparaṃ sañcaraṇakasattā, purato abbhokāsaṭṭhāne majjhe siṅghāṭake nisinnā viya tīsu bhavesu tattha tattha nibbattasattā, pāsādatale ṭhitapurisassa tesaṃ manussānaṃ āvibhūtakālo viya dibbacakkhuñāṇāya cittaṃ abhinīharitvā nisinnassa bhikkhuno tīsu bhavesu nibbattasattānaṃ āvibhūtakālo daṭṭhabbo. Idañca desanāsukhatthameva vuttaṃ. Āruppe pana dibbacakkhussa gocaro natthīti.

246-247. In the simile of the divine eye, 'moving along the road' means moving from one to another. There is also the reading 'traveling the road'; the meaning is the same. Herein, this monk's physical body should be seen as like a palace at a crossroads in the middle of a city; this very monk who stands having attained the divine eye is like a man with vision standing in the palace; like those entering a house are beings entering a mother's womb by way of rebirth-linking; like those leaving a house are beings emerging from the mother's womb; like those moving from one street to another are beings who wander from one existence to another; like those sitting in front in an open space in the middle at a crossroads are beings born here and there in the three existences. Just as the time when those people become manifest to the man standing on the upper floor of the palace, so too should be understood the time when beings born in the three existences become manifest to the monk who, having directed his mind to the divine-eye knowledge, is seated. And this is said merely for the sake of ease in teaching. For in the formless realm, the divine eye has no sphere.

Āsavakkhayañāṇakathā

Discourse on the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints

248. So evaṃ samāhite citteti idha vipassanāpādakaṃ catutthajjhānacittaṃ veditabbaṃ. Āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāyāti āsavānaṃ khayañāṇanibbattanatthāya. Ettha ca āsavānaṃ khayo nāma maggopi phalampi nibbānampi bhaṅgopi vuccati. “Khaye ñāṇaṃ, anuppāde ñāṇa”nti ettha hi maggo āsavānaṃ khayoti vutto. “Āsavānaṃ khayā samaṇo hotī”ti (ma. ni. 1.438) ettha phalaṃ.

248. 248. 'With his mind thus concentrated'—herein, the fourth jhāna consciousness, which is the basis for insight, should be understood. 'For the knowledge of the destruction of the taints' means for the purpose of bringing about the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. And here, 'the destruction of the taints' is said to refer to the path, the fruit, Nibbāna, and dissolution. Indeed, in the phrase 'knowledge in destruction, knowledge in non-arising,' the path is called the destruction of the taints. In 'Through the destruction of the taints, one becomes a recluse,' the fruit is meant.

“Paravajjānupassissa, niccaṃ ujjhānasaññino;

Āsavā tassa vaḍḍhanti, ārā so āsavakkhayā”ti. (dha. pa. 253);

For one who looks to the faults of others and is ever of a mind to criticize, his taints increase; he is far from the destruction of the taints.

Ettha [M 1.0201] nibbānaṃ. “Āsavānaṃ khayo vayo bhedo aniccatā antaradhāna”nti ettha bhaṅgo. Idha pana nibbānaṃ adhippetaṃ. Arahattamaggopi vaṭṭatiyeva.

Herein, Nibbāna is meant. In 'The destruction, wearing away, dissolution, impermanence, and disappearance of the taints,' dissolution is meant. Here, however, Nibbāna is intended. The path of Arahantship is also applicable.

Cittaṃ [V 1.0182] abhinīharatīti vipassanā cittaṃ tanninnaṃ tappoṇaṃ tappabbhāraṃ karoti. So idaṃ dukkhantiādīsu “ettakaṃ dukkhaṃ, na ito bhiyyo”ti [P 1.0225] sabbampi dukkhasaccaṃ sarasalakkhaṇapaṭivedhena yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti attho. Tassa ca dukkhassa nibbattikaṃ taṇhaṃ “ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo”ti. Tadubhayampi yaṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā nirujjhati, taṃ tesaṃ appavattiṃ nibbānaṃ “ayaṃ dukkhanirodho”ti; tassa ca sampāpakaṃ ariyamaggaṃ “ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā”ti sarasalakkhaṇapaṭivedhena yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti attho.

'He directs the mind' means he makes the insight-mind incline towards it, tend towards it, and be directed towards it. In the passages beginning with 'This is suffering,' the meaning is that he distinctly knows the entire truth of suffering as it really is by penetrating its own characteristic, thinking, 'Suffering is only this much; there is no more than this.' And the craving that brings about that suffering, he knows, 'This is the origin of suffering.' Having reached which state both of these cease, that Nibbāna, which is their non-occurrence, he knows as, 'This is the cessation of suffering'; and the noble path that leads to that cessation, he knows as, 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.' The meaning is that he knows this as it really is by penetrating its own characteristic.

Evaṃ sarūpato saccāni dassetvā puna kilesavasena pariyāyato dassento “ime āsavā”tiādimāha. Tassa evaṃ jānato evaṃ passatoti tassa bhikkhuno evaṃ jānantassa evaṃ passantassa, saha vipassanāya koṭippattaṃ maggaṃ kathesi. Kāmāsavāti kāmāsavato. Vimuccatīti iminā maggakkhaṇaṃ dasseti. Vimuttasminti iminā phalakkhaṇaṃ. Vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hotīti iminā paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ. Khīṇā jātītiādīhi tassa bhūmiṃ. Tena hi ñāṇena khīṇāsavo paccavekkhanto khīṇā jātītiādīni pajānāti.

Having thus shown the truths according to their individual nature, and again showing them discursively in connection with the defilements, he said, 'These are the taints,' and so on. 'For one who knows thus and sees thus': for that monk who knows thus and sees thus, he taught the path that has reached its culmination together with insight. 'From the taint of sensual desire.' With 'is freed,' he shows the moment of the path. With 'in the liberated,' he shows the moment of the fruit. With 'the knowledge "It is freed" arises,' he shows the reviewing knowledge. With the words beginning 'Destroyed is birth,' he shows its basis. Indeed, with that knowledge, the one whose taints are destroyed, while reviewing, distinctly knows the matters beginning with 'Destroyed is birth.'

Katamā panassa jāti khīṇā? Kathañca naṃ pajānātīti? Na tāvassa atītā jāti khīṇā, pubbeva khīṇattā. Na anāgatā, anāgate vāyāmābhāvato. Na paccuppannā, vijjamānattā. Yā pana maggassa abhāvitattā uppajjeyya ekacatupañcavokārabhavesu ekacatupañcakkhandhappabhedā jāti, sā maggassa bhāvitattā āyatiṃ anuppādadhammataṃ āpajjanena khīṇā. Taṃ so maggabhāvanāya pahīnakilese paccavekkhitvā “kilesābhāve vijjamānampi kammaṃ āyatiṃ appaṭisandhikaṃva hotī”ti jānanto pajānāti.

But which birth of his is destroyed? And how does he know it? His past birth is not destroyed, because it was already destroyed before. Not the future birth, because there is no exertion regarding the future. Not the present birth, because it still exists. But that birth which would have arisen in one-, four-, or five-constituent existences—differentiated as one, four, or five aggregates—due to the path not having been developed, that birth is destroyed due to the path having been developed, by its reaching the state of having the nature of non-arising in the future. He knows this by reviewing the defilements abandoned through the development of the path, knowing: 'In the absence of defilements, even existing kamma becomes incapable of producing a future rebirth-linking.'

Vusitanti vutthaṃ parivutthaṃ. Brahmacariyanti maggabrahmacariyaṃ. Puthujjanakalyāṇakena hi saddhiṃ satta sekkhā brahmacariyavāsaṃ vasanti nāma, khīṇāsavo vutthavāso, tasmā so attano brahmacariyavāsaṃ paccavekkhanto vusitaṃ brahmacariyanti pajānāti. Kataṃ [P 1.0226] karaṇīyanti catūsu saccesu catūhi maggehi pariññāpahānasacchikiriyābhāvanāvasena [M 1.0202] soḷasavidhaṃ kiccaṃ niṭṭhāpitaṃ. Tena tena maggena pahātabbakilesā pahīnā, dukkhamūlaṃ samucchinnanti attho. Puthujjanakalyāṇakādayo hi taṃ kiccaṃ karonti, khīṇāsavo katakaraṇīyo. Tasmā so attano karaṇīyaṃ paccavekkhanto kataṃ karaṇīyanti pajānāti. Nāparaṃ itthattāyāti idāni puna itthabhāvāya evaṃ soḷasakiccabhāvāya kilesakkhayabhāvāya vā kattabbaṃ [V 1.0183] maggabhāvanākiccaṃ me natthīti pajānāti. Atha vā itthattāyāti itthabhāvato imasmā evaṃ pakārā. Idāni vattamānakhandhasantānā aparaṃ khandhasantānaṃ mayhaṃ natthi. Ime pana pañcakkhandhā pariññātā tiṭṭhanti chinnamūlakā rukkhā viya, te carimakacittanirodhena anupādāno viya jātavedo nibbāyissanti apaṇṇattikabhāvañca gamissantīti pajānāti.

'Lived' means lived, completely lived. 'The holy life' means the holy life of the path. Indeed, the seven trainees together with the virtuous worldling are said to be dwelling the holy life, whereas the one whose taints are destroyed is one who has completed the dwelling. Therefore, reflecting on his own dwelling in the holy life, he knows, 'The holy life has been lived.' 'What had to be done has been done' means the sixteenfold task regarding the four truths by means of the four paths—in terms of full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing—has been accomplished. Indeed, virtuous worldlings and others are doing that task, whereas the one whose taints are destroyed is one who has done what was to be done. Therefore, reflecting on his own task, he knows, 'What had to be done has been done.' 'There is nothing further for this state of being' means he knows: 'Now, there is no further task of developing the path to be done by me for the sake of this state, for the sake of such a sixteenfold task, or for the sake of the destruction of defilements.' Or alternatively, 'for this state of being' means from this state of being, of this kind. 'Now, apart from this present continuum of aggregates, there is no other continuum of aggregates for me. But these five aggregates, having been fully understood, stand like trees with their roots cut. With the cessation of the final consciousness, they will be extinguished like a fire without fuel and will go to a state beyond designation.' Thus he knows.

249. Pabbatasaṅkhepeti pabbatamatthake. Anāviloti nikkaddamo. Sippiyo ca sambukā ca sippisambukaṃ. Sakkharā ca kathalāni ca sakkharakathalaṃ. Macchānaṃ gumbā ghaṭāti macchagumbaṃ. Tiṭṭhantampi carantampīti ettha sakkharakathalaṃ tiṭṭhatiyeva, itarāni carantipi tiṭṭhantipi. Yathā pana antarantarā ṭhitāsupi nisinnāsupi vijjamānāsupi “etā gāvo carantī”ti carantiyo upādāya itarāpi carantīti vuccanti. Evaṃ tiṭṭhantameva sakkharakathalaṃ upādāya itarampi dvayaṃ tiṭṭhantanti vuttaṃ. Itarañca dvayaṃ [P 1.0227] carantaṃ upādāya sakkharakathalampi carantanti vuttaṃ. Tattha cakkhumato purisassa tīre ṭhatvā passato sippikasambukādīnaṃ vibhūtakālo viya āsavānaṃ khayāya cittaṃ abhinīharitvā nisinnassa bhikkhuno catunnaṃ saccānaṃ vibhūtakālo daṭṭhabboti.

249. “Pabbatasaṅkhepe” means on the summit of a mountain. “Anāvilo” means free from mud. “Sippiyo ca sambukā ca” is sippisambukaṃ (shells and oysters). “Sakkharā ca kathalāni ca” is sakkharakathalaṃ (gravel and potsherds). “Macchānaṃ gumbā ghaṭāti” is macchagumbaṃ (a school of fish). Regarding “tiṭṭhantampi carantampi,” here the gravel and potsherds only stand still, while the others both move and stand still. Just as, although there are cows standing and sitting here and there, by taking into account the moving ones, the others are also said to be moving. Similarly, by taking into account the gravel and potsherds which only stand still, the other two groups are also said to be standing still. And by taking into account the other two moving groups, the gravel and potsherds are also said to be moving. In that context, just as for a man with good eyesight standing on the bank and looking, it is the time when the shells, oysters, and so on become distinct, so for a monk who is seated, having directed his mind towards the destruction of the taints, the time when the four truths become distinct should be understood.

Ettāvatā vipassanāñāṇaṃ, manomayañāṇaṃ, iddhividhañāṇaṃ, dibbasotañāṇaṃ, cetopariyañāṇaṃ, pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ, dibbacakkhuvasena nipphannaṃ anāgataṃsañāṇayathākammūpagañāṇadvayaṃ, dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ, āsavakkhayañāṇanti dasa ñāṇāni niddiṭṭhāni honti. Tesaṃ ārammaṇavibhāgo jānitabbo – tattha vipassanāñāṇaṃ parittamahaggataatītānāgatapaccuppannaajjhattabahiddhāvasena sattavidhārammaṇaṃ. Manomayañāṇaṃ nimmitabbarūpāyatanamattameva ārammaṇaṃ karotīti [M 1.0203] parittapaccuppannabahiddhārammaṇaṃ. Āsavakkhayañāṇaṃ appamāṇabahiddhānavattabbārammaṇaṃ. Avasesānaṃ ārammaṇabhedo visuddhimagge vutto. Uttaritaraṃ vā paṇītataraṃ vāti yena kenaci pariyāyena ito seṭṭhataraṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ nāma natthīti bhagavā arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

By this much, ten knowledges have been specified: insight knowledge, mind-made knowledge, knowledge of psychic powers, divine ear knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of past lives, the pair of knowledges accomplished by means of the divine eye—namely, knowledge of the future and knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their kamma—divine eye knowledge, and knowledge of the destruction of the taints. The distinction of their objects should be known. Therein, insight knowledge has seven kinds of objects, by way of the limited, exalted, past, future, present, internal, and external. Mind-made knowledge takes only the form-object that is to be created as its object; thus, it has a limited, present, external object. The knowledge of the destruction of the taints has an immeasurable, external, and inexpressible object. The distinction of objects for the remaining knowledges has been stated in the Visuddhimagga. Regarding “higher or more refined,” by any means whatsoever, there is no fruit of recluseship more excellent than this. Thus the Blessed One concluded the discourse with the pinnacle which is the fruit of Arahantship.

Ajātasattuupāsakattapaṭivedanākathā

The Discourse on Ajātasattu's Declaration of Being a Lay Follower

250. Rājā tattha tattha sādhukāraṃ pavattento ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ sakkaccaṃ sutvā “ciraṃ vatamhi ime pañhe puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇe pucchanto, thuse koṭṭento viya kiñci sāraṃ nālatthaṃ, aho vata bhagavato guṇasampadā, yo me dīpasahassaṃ jālento viya mahantaṃ ālokaṃ katvā ime pañhe vissajjesi. Suciraṃ vatamhi dasabalassa guṇānubhāvaṃ ajānanto vañcito”ti [V 1.0184] cintetvā buddhaguṇānussaraṇasambhūtāya pañcavidhāya pītiyā phuṭasarīro attano pasādaṃ āvikaronto upāsakattaṃ paṭivedesi. Taṃ dassetuṃ “evaṃ vutte rājā”tiādi āraddhaṃ.

250. The king, giving cries of “Sādhu!” here and there, listened respectfully from beginning to end and thought: “Alas, for a long time I have been asking these questions of many ascetics and brahmins, but like one pounding husks, I obtained no essence. Oh, how wonderful is the perfection of the Blessed One's virtues, who, as if lighting a thousand lamps for me, created a great light and answered these questions! Alas, for a very long time, not knowing the power of the virtues of the Ten-Powered One, I have been deceived.” Having thought thus, his body suffused with the five kinds of joy that arose from recollecting the Buddha's virtues, making his confidence manifest, he declared his state as a lay follower. To show this, the passage beginning “When this was said, the king...” was commenced.

Tattha abhikkantaṃ, bhanteti ayaṃ abhikkantasaddo khayasundarābhirūpaabbhanumodanesu dissati. “Abhikkantā [P 1.0228] bhante, ratti, nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo, ciranisinno bhikkhusaṅgho”tiādīsu (a. ni. 8.20) hi khaye dissati. “Ayaṃ me puggalo khamati, imesaṃ catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.100) sundare.

Herein, the word “abhikkanta” is seen in the senses of passing, beauty, beautiful form, and approval. For instance, in “Venerable sir, the night has passed (abhikkantā), the first watch is over, the community of monks has been seated for a long time,” and so on, it is seen in the sense of passing. In “This person is acceptable to me; he is more excellent (abhikkantataro) and more refined than these four persons,” and so on, it is in the sense of beauty.

“Ko me vandati pādāni, iddhiyā yasasā jalaṃ;

Abhikkantena vaṇṇena, sabbā obhāsayaṃ disā”ti. (vi. va. 857);

“Who is it that worships my feet, blazing with psychic power and fame, with surpassing beauty, illuminating all directions?”

Ādīsu abhirūpe. “Abhikkantaṃ bho, gotamā”tiādīsu (pārā. 15) abbhanumodane. Idhāpi abbhanumodaneyeva. Yasmā ca abbhanumodane, tasmā ‘sādhu sādhu bhante’ti vuttaṃ hotīti veditabbo.

In such verses, it is in the sense of beautiful form. In “Excellent, Master Gotama!” and so on, it is in the sense of approval. Here too, it is in the sense of approval. And because it is in the sense of approval, it should be understood as meaning, “Excellent, excellent, venerable sir!”

Bhaye kodhe pasaṃsāyaṃ, turite kotūhalacchare;

Hāse soke pasāde ca, kare āmeḍitaṃ budhoti.

“In fear, anger, praise, haste, curiosity, and wonder; in laughter, sorrow, and confidence, a wise person uses repetition.”

Iminā [M 1.0204] ca lakkhaṇena idha pasādavasena, pasaṃsāvasena cāyaṃ dvikkhattuṃ vuttoti veditabbo. Athavā abhikkantanti abhikantaṃ atiiṭṭhaṃ atimanāpaṃ atisundaranti vuttaṃ hoti.

And by this principle, it should be understood that here it is spoken twice on account of confidence and praise. Alternatively, “abhikkantaṃ” means exceedingly desired, exceedingly pleasing, and exceedingly beautiful.

Ettha ekena abhikkantasaddena desanaṃ thometi, ekena attano pasādaṃ. Ayañhettha adhippāyo, abhikkantaṃ bhante, yadidaṃ bhagavato dhammadesanā, ‘abhikkantaṃ’ yadidaṃ bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ āgamma mama pasādoti. Bhagavatoyeva vā vacanaṃ dve dve atthe sandhāya thometi. Bhagavato vacanaṃ abhikkantaṃ dosanāsanato, abhikkantaṃ guṇādhigamanato. Tathā saddhājananato, paññājananato, sātthato, sabyañjanato, uttānapadato, gambhīratthato, kaṇṇasukhato, hadayaṅgamato, anattukkaṃsanato[V 1.0185], aparavambhanato, karuṇāsītalato, paññāvadātato, āpātharamaṇīyato, vimaddakkhamato, suyyamānasukhato, vīmaṃsiyamānahitatoti evamādīhi yojetabbaṃ.

Here, with one “abhikkanta” word he praises the teaching; with the other, his own confidence. This is the intention here: “Excellent, venerable sir, is this teaching of the Blessed One,” and “Excellent is the confidence in me that has arisen on account of the Blessed One's teaching.” Alternatively, he praises the Blessed One's speech itself, referring to pairs of meanings. The Blessed One's speech is excellent because it destroys faults, and excellent because it leads to the attainment of virtues. Likewise, it is excellent because it generates faith and because it generates wisdom; because it is meaningful and because it is well-phrased; because its words are plain and because its meaning is profound; because it is pleasant to the ear and because it goes to the heart; because it does not exalt oneself and because it does not disparage others; because it is cool with compassion and because it is purified by wisdom; because it is delightful at first hearing and because it withstands examination; because it is pleasant while being heard and because it is beneficial when being investigated. It should be connected with these and similar meanings.

Tato parampi catūhi upamāhi desanaṃyeva thometi. Tattha nikkujjitanti adhomukhaṭhapitaṃ heṭṭhāmukhajātaṃ vā. Ukkujjeyyāti upari mukhaṃ kareyya. Paṭicchannanti tiṇapaṇṇādichāditaṃ. Vivareyyāti ugghāṭeyya. Mūḷhassa vāti disāmūḷhassa. Maggaṃ ācikkheyyāti hatthe gahetvā “esa maggo”ti vadeyya, andhakāreti kāḷapakkhacātuddasī [P 1.0229] aḍḍharattaghanavanasaṇḍameghapaṭalehi caturaṅge tame. Ayaṃ tāva anuttānapadattho. Ayaṃ pana sādhippāyayojanā. Yathā koci nikkujjitaṃ ukkujjeyya, evaṃ saddhammavimukhaṃ asaddhamme patitaṃ maṃ asaddhammā vuṭṭhāpentana. Yathā paṭicchannaṃ vivareyya, evaṃ kassapassa bhagavato sāsanantaradhānā pabhuti micchādiṭṭhigahanapaṭicchannaṃ sāsanaṃ vivarantena, yathā mūḷhassa maggaṃ ācikkheyya, evaṃ kummaggamicchāmaggappaṭipannassa me saggamokkhamaggaṃ āvikarontena, yathā andhakāre telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya, evaṃ mohandhakāranimuggassa me buddhādiratanarūpāni apassato tappaṭicchādakamohandhakāraviddhaṃsakadesanāpajjotadhārakena mayhaṃ bhagavatā etehi pariyāyehi pakāsitattā anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsitoti.

Furthermore, he praises the teaching with four similes. Therein, 'overturned' (nikkujjitaṃ) means placed face down or having become face down. 'Would turn upright' (ukkujjeyya) means would make it face up. 'Covered' (paṭicchannaṃ) means covered by grass, leaves, and so on. 'Would uncover' (vivareyya) means would open. 'For one who is lost' (mūḷhassa) means for one who is confused about the directions. 'Would point out the path' (maggaṃ ācikkheyya) means, taking one by the hand, one would say, 'This is the path.' 'In the darkness' (andhakāre) means in a fourfold darkness, comprised of the fourteenth day of the waning moon, midnight, a dense forest thicket, and a layer of clouds. This, for now, is the meaning of the unclear words. This, however, is the application of the intended meaning. Just as one might turn upright what is overturned, so has the venerable Gotama raised me—who had turned away from the good Dhamma and was established in the bad Dhamma—from that bad Dhamma. Just as one might uncover what is covered, so has he revealed the teaching, which had been covered by the thicket of wrong view since the disappearance of the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa. Just as one might point out the path to one who is lost, so has he explained to me—who had entered the wrong path, the false path—the path to heaven and liberation. Just as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness, so has he held up the lamp of the teaching that destroys the darkness of delusion for me, who was sunk in the darkness of delusion and unable to see the forms of the gems such as the Buddha, which were covered by that darkness. Because the Dhamma has been clarified for me by the venerable Gotama through these various methods, the Dhamma has been clarified in many ways.

Evaṃ desanaṃ thometvā imāya desanāya ratanattaye pasannacitto pasannākāraṃ karonto esāhantiādimāha. Tattha esāhanti eso ahaṃ[M 1.0205]. Bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmīti bhagavā me saraṇaṃ, parāyanaṃ, aghassa tātā, hitassa ca vidhātāti. Iminā adhippāyena bhagavantaṃ gacchāmi bhajāmi sevāmi payirupāsāmi, evaṃ vā jānāmi bujjhāmīti. Yesañhi dhātūnaṃ gatiattho, buddhipi tesaṃ attho. Tasmā gacchāmīti imassa jānāmi bujjhāmīti ayampi attho vutto. Dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañcāti ettha pana adhigatamagge sacchikatanirodhe yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne catūsu apāyesu apatamāne dhāretīti dhammo, so atthato ariyamaggo ceva nibbānañca. Vuttañcetaṃ – “yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”ti (a. ni. 4.34) vitthāro. Na kevalañca ariyamaggo ceva nibbānañca. Api ca kho ariyaphalehi saddhiṃ pariyattidhammopi[P 1.0230]. Vuttañhetaṃ chattamāṇavakavimāne –

Having thus praised the teaching, with a mind confident in the Triple Gem through this discourse, and wishing to make a gesture of confidence, he said 'esāhaṃ' and so on. Therein, 'esāhaṃ' means 'this I'. 'I go to the Blessed One for refuge' means: the Blessed One is my refuge, my resort, the protector from evil, and the arranger of welfare. With this intention, I go to, attend, serve, and wait upon the Blessed One; or thus I know, I understand. For those verbal roots that have the meaning of 'going', they also have the meaning of 'knowing'. Therefore, for 'I go' (gacchāmi), the meaning 'I know, I understand' is also stated. As for 'and the Dhamma and the Sangha of bhikkhus', herein, that which supports beings who have attained the path, have personally realized cessation, and are practicing as instructed, preventing them from falling into the four states of woe, is the Dhamma. In essence, that is the Noble Path and Nibbāna. And this was said: 'Bhikkhus, inasmuch as there are conditioned things, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared the chief among them.' This is the detailed explanation. And it is not only the Noble Path and Nibbāna. But also, it is the Dhamma of the scriptures along with the noble fruits. For this was said in the Chattamāṇavaka Vimāna—

“Rāgavirāgamanejamasokaṃ, dhammamasaṅkhatamappaṭikūlaṃ;

Madhuramimaṃ paguṇaṃ suvibhattaṃ, dhammamimaṃ saraṇatthamupehī”ti. (vi. va. 887);

“Go for refuge to the Dhamma that is dispassion for lust, unshaken, sorrowless, unconditioned, and unopposed; this sweet, proficient, and well-analyzed Dhamma.”

Ettha [V 1.0186] hi rāgavirāgoti maggo kathito. Anejamasokanti phalaṃ. Dhammamasaṅkhatanti nibbānaṃ. Appaṭikūlaṃ madhuramimaṃ paguṇaṃ suvibhattanti piṭakattayena vibhattā dhammakkhandhāti. Diṭṭhisīlasaṃghātena saṃhatoti saṅgho, so atthato aṭṭha ariyapuggalasamūho. Vuttañhetaṃ tasmiññeva vimāne –

Here, by 'dispassion for lust', the Path is taught. By 'unshaken and sorrowless', the Fruit is taught. By 'the unconditioned Dhamma', Nibbāna is taught. By 'unopposed, sweet, proficient, and well-analyzed', the aggregates of the Dhamma, as divided by the three Piṭakas, are taught. Because they are united by a commonality of view and virtue, they are the 'Saṅgha'. In essence, that is the community of the eight noble individuals. And this was said in that same celestial mansion—

“Yattha ca dinnamahapphalamāhu, catūsu sucīsu purīsayugesu;

Aṭṭha ca puggaladhammadasā te, saṅghamimaṃ saraṇatthamupehī”ti. (vi. va. 888);

“Where giving is said to bear great fruit—to the four pure pairs of persons; and those eight individuals who have seen the Dhamma—to this Saṅgha, go for refuge.”

Bhikkhūnaṃ saṅgho bhikkhusaṅgho. Ettāvatā rājā tīṇi saraṇagamanāni paṭivedesi.

The community of bhikkhus is the Bhikkhusaṅgha. Thus, the brahmin professed the three goings for refuge.

Saraṇagamanakathā

The Discourse on Going for Refuge

Idāni tesu saraṇagamanesu kosallatthaṃ saraṇaṃ, saraṇagamanaṃ, yo ca saraṇaṃ gacchati, saraṇagamanappabhedo, saraṇagamanaphalaṃ, saṅkileso, bhedoti, ayaṃ vidhi veditabbo. Seyyathidaṃ – saraṇatthato tāva hiṃsatīti saraṇaṃ. Saraṇagatānaṃ teneva saraṇagamanena bhayaṃ santāsaṃ dukkhaṃ duggatiparikilesaṃ hanati vināsetīti attho, ratanattayassevetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

Now, in these goings for refuge, for the sake of proficiency, this procedure should be understood: refuge, the going for refuge, the one who goes for refuge, the distinction of going for refuge, the fruit of going for refuge, defilement, and the breach. That is to say: firstly, from the meaning of the word `saraṇa`: because it destroys (hiṃsati), it is called `saraṇa` (refuge). The meaning is that for those who have gone for refuge, by that very going for refuge, it destroys and eliminates fear, terror, suffering, and the defilements of a woeful state. This is a designation for the Triple Gem itself.

Atha [M 1.0206] vā hite pavattanena ahitā ca nivattanena sattānaṃ bhayaṃ hiṃsati buddho. Bhavakantārā uttāraṇena assāsadānena ca dhammo; appakānampi kārānaṃ vipulaphalapaṭilābhakaraṇena saṅgho[P 1.0231]. Tasmā imināpi pariyāyena ratanattayaṃ saraṇaṃ. Tappasādataggarutāhi vihatakileso tapparāyaṇatākārappavatto cittuppādo saraṇagamanaṃ. Taṃ samaṅgīsatto saraṇaṃ gacchati. Vuttappakārena cittuppādena etāni me tīṇi ratanāni saraṇaṃ, etāni parāyaṇanti evaṃ upetīti attho. Evaṃ tāva saraṇaṃ, saraṇagamanaṃ, yo ca saraṇaṃ gacchati, idaṃ tayaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Alternatively, the Buddha destroys the fear of beings by causing them to engage in what is beneficial and to turn away from what is unbeneficial. The Dhamma destroys fear by conveying them across the wilderness of existence and by giving solace. The Saṅgha destroys fear by bringing about the attainment of abundant fruit even from small deeds. Therefore, by this explanation as well, the Triple Gem is a refuge. The going for refuge is a mind-state that has its defilements destroyed through faith in and reverence for them, and that proceeds in the manner of having them as the ultimate resort. A being endowed with this goes for refuge. The meaning is that with a mind-state of the kind described, one approaches thus: 'These three jewels are my refuge; these are my ultimate resort.' Thus, for now, refuge, the going for refuge, and the one who goes for refuge—this triad should be known.

Saraṇagamanappabhede pana duvidhaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ – lokuttaraṃ lokiyañca. Tattha lokuttaraṃ diṭṭhasaccānaṃ maggakkhaṇe saraṇagamanupakkilesasamucchedena ārammaṇato nibbānārammaṇaṃ hutvā kiccato sakalepi ratanattaye ijjhati. Lokiyaṃ puthujjanānaṃ saraṇagamanupakkilesavikkhambhanena ārammaṇato buddhādiguṇārammaṇaṃ hutvā ijjhati. Taṃ atthato buddhādīsu vatthūsu saddhāpaṭilābho saddhāmūlikā [V 1.0187] ca sammādiṭṭhi dasasu puññakiriyavatthūsu diṭṭhijukammanti vuccati. Tayidaṃ catudhā vattati – attasanniyyātanena, tapparāyaṇatāya, sissabhāvūpagamanena, paṇipātenāti.

Now, regarding the distinction of going for refuge, the going for refuge is twofold: supramundane and mundane. Therein, the supramundane, for those who have seen the truths, is accomplished at the moment of the path through the eradication of the corruptions of going for refuge; with respect to its object, it has Nibbāna as its object, and with respect to its function, it is fulfilled in regard to the entire Triple Gem. The mundane, for worldlings, is accomplished through the suppression of the corruptions of going for refuge; with respect to its object, it has the qualities of the Buddha and so on as its object. In essence, this is the acquisition of faith in the objects such as the Buddha, and faith-based right view; among the ten grounds of meritorious action, it is called 'the straightening of view.' This occurs in four ways: by self-dedication, by having them as the ultimate resort, by approaching the state of a disciple, and by prostration.

Tattha attasanniyyātanaṃ nāma – “ajjādiṃ katvā ahaṃ attānaṃ buddhassa niyyātemi, dhammassa, saṅghassā”ti evaṃ buddhādīnaṃ attapariccajanaṃ. Tapparāyaṇatā nāma “ajjādiṃ katvā ‘ahaṃ buddhaparāyaṇo, dhammaparāyaṇo, saṅghaparāyaṇo’ti. Maṃ dhārethā”ti evaṃ tapparāyaṇabhāvo. Sissabhāvūpagamanaṃ nāma – “ajjādiṃ katvā – ‘ahaṃ buddhassa antevāsiko, dhammassa, saṅghassa antevāsiko’ti maṃ dhārethā”ti evaṃ sissabhāvūpagamo. Paṇipāto nāma – “ajjādiṃ katvā ahaṃ abhivādanapaccuṭṭhānaañjalikammasāmīcikammaṃ buddhādīnaṃyeva tiṇṇaṃ vatthūnaṃ karomī’ti maṃ dhārethā”ti evaṃ buddhādīsu paramanipaccākāro. Imesañhi catunnaṃ ākārānaṃ aññatarampi karontena gahitaṃyeva hoti saraṇaṃ.

Therein, self-dedication means the relinquishing of oneself to the Buddha and so on, thus: 'From today onwards, I dedicate myself to the Buddha, to the Dhamma, to the Saṅgha.' Having them as the ultimate resort means the state of having them as the ultimate resort, thus: 'From today onwards, may you hold me as one who has the Buddha as the ultimate resort, the Dhamma as the ultimate resort, the Saṅgha as the ultimate resort.' Approaching the state of a disciple means the approaching of the state of a disciple, thus: 'From today onwards, may you hold me as a resident disciple of the Buddha, of the Dhamma, of the Saṅgha.' Prostration means the supreme act of reverence towards the Buddha and so on, thus: 'From today onwards, I perform acts of veneration, rising in respect, joining the palms, and proper conduct only for these three objects: the Buddha and so on.' For by one who performs even one of these four modes, refuge is indeed taken.

Api ca bhagavato attānaṃ pariccajāmi, dhammassa, saṅghassa, attānaṃ pariccajāmi, jīvitaṃ pariccajāmi, pariccattoyeva [P 1.0232] me attā, pariccattaṃyeva jīvitaṃ, jīvitapariyantikaṃ buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, buddho me saraṇaṃ leṇaṃ tāṇanti[M 1.0207]; evampi attasanniyyātanaṃ veditabbaṃ. “Satthārañca vatāhaṃ passeyyaṃ, bhagavantameva passeyyaṃ, sugatañca vatāhaṃ passeyyaṃ, bhagavantameva passeyyaṃ, sammāsambuddhañca vatāhaṃ passeyyaṃ, bhagavantameva passeyya”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.154). Evampi mahākassapassa saraṇagamanaṃ viya sissabhāvūpagamanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore: 'I relinquish myself to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, to the Saṅgha. I relinquish myself; I relinquish my life. My self is indeed relinquished; my life is indeed relinquished. For the duration of my life, I go to the Buddha for refuge. The Buddha is my refuge, my shelter, my protection.' In this way too, self-dedication should be understood. 'Oh, that I might see the Teacher! I would see only the Blessed One. Oh, that I might see the Sugata! I would see only the Blessed One. Oh, that I might see the Perfectly Enlightened One! I would see only the Blessed One.' In this way too, like the going for refuge of Mahākassapa, the approaching of the state of a disciple should be understood.

“So ahaṃ vicarissāmi, gāmā gāmaṃ purā puraṃ;

Namassamāno sambuddhaṃ, dhammassa ca sudhammata”nti. (su. ni. 194);

'Thus I shall wander from village to village and from town to town, paying homage to the Perfectly Enlightened One and to the excellence of the Dhamma.'

Evampi āḷavakādīnaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ viya tapparāyaṇatā veditabbā. Atha kho brahmāyu brāhmaṇo uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā bhagavato pādesu sirasā nipatitvā bhagavato pādāni mukhena ca paricumbati, pāṇīhi ca parisambāhati, nāmañca sāveti – “brahmāyu ahaṃ, bho gotama brāhmaṇo, brahmāyu ahaṃ, bho gotama brāhmaṇo”ti (ma. ni. 2.394) evampi paṇipāto daṭṭhabbo.

In this way too, like the going for refuge of Āḷavaka and others, having them as the ultimate resort should be known. Then the brahmin Brahmāyu, having risen from his seat, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, fell at the Blessed One’s feet with his head, and he kisses the Blessed One’s feet with his mouth and massages them with his hands, and announces his name: 'I am Brahmāyu, venerable Gotama, the brahmin; I am Brahmāyu, venerable Gotama, the brahmin.' In this way too, prostration should be seen.

So panesa ñātibhayācariyadakkhiṇeyyavasena catubbidho hoti. Tattha dakkhiṇeyyapaṇipātena saraṇagamanaṃ hoti, na itarehi. Seṭṭhavaseneva hi saraṇaṃ gaṇhāti, seṭṭhavasena [V 1.0188] ca bhijjati. Tasmā yo sākiyo vā koliyo vā – “buddho amhākaṃ ñātako”ti vandati, aggahitameva hoti saraṇaṃ. Yo vā – “samaṇo gotamo rājapūjito mahānubhāvo avandīyamāno anatthampi kareyyā”ti bhayena vandati, aggahitameva hoti saraṇaṃ. Yo vā bodhisattakāle bhagavato santike kiñci uggahitaṃ saramāno buddhakāle vā –

This prostration, moreover, is fourfold: by way of kinship, fear, a teacher, and one worthy of offerings. Therein, the going for refuge occurs through prostration to one worthy of offerings, not through the others. For one takes refuge only by way of the supreme, and it is broken by way of the supreme. Therefore, for whichever Sākiyan or Koliyan who venerates thinking, 'The Buddha is our kinsman,' refuge is not taken. Or for one who venerates out of fear, thinking, 'The ascetic Gotama is honored by kings and of great power; if not venerated, he might even bring harm,' refuge is not taken. Or for one who, remembering something learned in the presence of the Blessed One during the time he was a Bodhisatta, or during the time of the Buddha—

“Catudhā vibhaje bhoge, paṇḍito gharamāvasaṃ;

Ekena bhogaṃ bhuñjeyya, dvīhi kammaṃ payojaye;

Catutthañca nidhāpeyya, āpadāsu bhavissatī”ti. (dī. ni. 3.265);

'A wise person living the household life should divide their wealth into four. With one part, they should enjoy their wealth; with two, they should apply it to their work; and the fourth they should set aside, for it will be there in times of misfortune.'

Evarūpaṃ anusāsaniṃ uggahetvā – “ācariyo me”ti vandati, aggahitameva [P 1.0233] hoti saraṇaṃ. Yo pana – “ayaṃ loke aggadakkhiṇeyyo”ti vandati, teneva gahitaṃ hoti saraṇaṃ.

—having learned such an instruction, venerates thinking, 'He is my teacher,' refuge is not taken. But for one who venerates thinking, 'This one is the foremost in the world worthy of offerings,' by that one is refuge taken.

Evaṃ gahitasaraṇassa ca upāsakassa vā upāsikāya vā aññatitthiyesu pabbajitampi ñātiṃ – “ñātako me aya”nti vandato saraṇagamanaṃ na [M 1.0208] bhijjati, pageva apabbajitaṃ. Tathā rājānaṃ bhayavasena vandato. So hi raṭṭhapūjitattā avandīyamāno anatthampi kareyyāti. Tathā yaṃ kiñci sippaṃ sikkhāpakaṃ titthiyampi – “ācariyo me aya”nti vandatopi na bhijjati, evaṃ saraṇagamanappabhedo veditabbo.

For a male or female lay follower who has thus taken refuge, if they pay homage to a relative who has gone forth among other sectarians, thinking, 'This is my relative,' their going for refuge is not broken; how much more so if the relative is not one who has gone forth. Similarly, for one who pays homage to a king out of fear. For if such a king, being honored by the country, is not paid homage to, he might cause harm. Likewise, even for one who pays homage to a heretic who is a teacher of some art, thinking, 'This is my teacher,' it is not broken. Thus, the distinctions of going for refuge should be understood.

Ettha ca lokuttarassa saraṇagamanassa cattāri sāmaññaphalāni vipākaphalaṃ, sabbadukkhakkhayo ānisaṃsaphalaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Herein, for the supramundane going for refuge, the four fruits of recluseship are the resultant fruit, and the exhaustion of all suffering is the fruit of benefit. For this was stated:

“Yo ca buddhañca dhammañca, saṅghañca saraṇaṃ gato;

Cattāri ariyasaccāni, sammappaññāya passati.

“Whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, sees with right wisdom the Four Noble Truths:

Dukkhaṃ dukkhasamuppādaṃ, dukkhassa ca atikkamaṃ;

Ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ, dukkhūpasamagāminaṃ.

Suffering, the origin of suffering, the overcoming of suffering, and the Noble Eightfold Path that leads to the stilling of suffering.

Etaṃ kho saraṇaṃ khemaṃ, etaṃ saraṇamuttamaṃ;

Etaṃ saraṇamāgamma, sabbadukkhā pamuccatī”ti. (dha. pa. 192);

This indeed is the secure refuge, this is the supreme refuge; having come to this refuge, one is released from all suffering.”

Api [V 1.0189] ca niccādito anupagamanādivasena petassa ānisaṃsaphalaṃ veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – “aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso, yaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo kañci saṅkhāraṃ niccato upagaccheyya…pe… kañci saṅkhāraṃ sukhato…pe… kañci dhammaṃ attato upagaccheyya…pe… mātaraṃ jīvitā voropeyya…pe… pitaraṃ…pe… arahantaṃ…pe… paduṭṭhacitto tathāgatassa lohitaṃ uppādeyya…pe…. saṅghaṃ bhindeyya…pe… aññaṃ satthāraṃ uddiseyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti (a. ni. 1.290). Lokiyassa pana saraṇagamanassa bhavasampadāpi bhogasampadāpi phalameva. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Moreover, the fruit of benefit of this supramundane going for refuge should be understood by way of not approaching formations as permanent, and so on. For it was said: 'It is impossible, it is not possible, that a person accomplished in view would approach any formation as permanent... or approach any formation as pleasant... or approach any phenomenon as self... or would deprive his mother of life... or his father... or an arahant... or with a corrupt mind would cause the Tathāgata's blood to flow... or would split the Saṅgha... or would point to another as teacher; this is not possible.' However, for the worldly going for refuge, accomplishment in existence and accomplishment in wealth are indeed the fruit. For this was stated:

“Ye keci buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gatāse, na te gamissanti apāyabhūmiṃ;

Pahāya mānusaṃ dehaṃ, devakāyaṃ paripūressantī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.37);

“Whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha, they will not go to a plane of misery; having abandoned the human body, they will fill the host of devas.”

Aparampi [P 1.0234] vuttaṃ – “atha kho sakko devānamindo asītiyā devatāsahassehi saddhiṃ yenāyasmā mahāmoggallāno tenupasaṅkami…pe… ekamantaṃ ṭhitaṃ kho sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ āyasmā mahāmoggallāno etadavoca – “sādhu kho, devānaminda, buddhaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ hoti. Buddhaṃ saraṇagamanahetu kho, devānaminda, evamidhekacce sattā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ [M 1.0209] maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjanti…pe… te aññe deve dasahi ṭhānehi adhigaṇhanti – dibbena āyunā, dibbena vaṇṇena, dibbena sukhena, dibbena yasena, dibbena ādhipateyyena, dibbehi rūpehi saddehi gandhehi rasehi phoṭṭhabbehī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.341). Esa nayo dhamme ca saṅghe ca. Api ca velāmasuttādīnaṃ vasenāpi saraṇagamanassa phalaviseso veditabbo. Evaṃ saraṇagamanassa phalaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, it was stated: “Then Sakka, lord of the devas, together with eighty thousand devas, approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna... While Sakka, lord of the devas, was standing to one side, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to him: 'It is good, lord of the devas, to go for refuge to the Buddha. Because of going for refuge to the Buddha, lord of the devas, some beings here, on the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world... They surpass other devas in ten respects: with divine lifespan, with divine beauty, with divine happiness, with divine fame, with divine sovereignty, and with divine forms, sounds, scents, tastes, and tangibles.' This is the method for the Dhamma and the Saṅgha as well. Moreover, the special fruit of going for refuge should be understood by way of the Velāma Sutta and others. Thus, the fruit of going for refuge should be understood.

Tattha ca lokiyasaraṇagamanaṃ tīsu vatthūsu aññāṇasaṃsayamicchāñāṇādīhi saṃkilissati, na mahājutikaṃ hoti, na mahāvipphāraṃ. Lokuttarassa natthi saṃkileso. Lokiyassa ca saraṇagamanassa duvidho bhedo – sāvajjo ca anavajjo ca. Tattha sāvajjo aññasatthārādīsu attasanniyyātanādīhi hoti, so ca aniṭṭhaphalo hoti. Anavajjo kālakiriyāya hoti, so avipākattā aphalo. Lokuttarassa pana nevatthi bhedo. Bhavantarepi hi ariyasāvako aññaṃ satthāraṃ na uddisatīti. Evaṃ saraṇagamanassa saṃkileso ca bhedo ca veditabboti.

Herein, the worldly going for refuge is defiled by ignorance, doubt, wrong knowledge, and so on, regarding the three objects; it is not of great radiance, nor of great pervasion. For the supramundane, there is no defilement. And the worldly going for refuge has a twofold breaking: blameworthy and blameless. Among these, the blameworthy breaking occurs through dedicating oneself to other teachers, and so on, and it has an undesirable fruit. The blameless breaking occurs through death, and that, being without result, is fruitless. But for the supramundane, there is no breaking whatsoever. For even in another existence, a noble disciple does not point to another as teacher. Thus, the defilement and the breaking of the going for refuge should be understood.

Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhante bhagavā dhāretūti maṃ bhagavā “upāsako aya”nti evaṃ dhāretu, jānātūti attho. Upāsakavidhikosallatthaṃ panettha – ko upāsako? Kasmā upāsakoti vuccati[V 1.0190]? Kimassa sīlaṃ? Ko ājīvo? Kā vipatti? Kā sampattīti? Idaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ veditabbaṃ.

“May the Blessed One, venerable sir, remember me as a lay follower” means: “May the Blessed One remember me thus: ‘This is a lay follower,’” that is, “may he know me.” Here, for the sake of skill in the procedure of a lay follower, this miscellaneous collection should be understood: Who is a lay follower? Why is he called a lay follower? What is his virtue? What is his livelihood? What is his failure? What is his accomplishment?

Tattha ko upāsakoti yo koci saraṇagato gahaṭṭho. Vuttañhetaṃ – “yato kho, mahānāma, buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti, dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti, saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti. Ettāvatā kho, mahānāma, upāsako hotī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1033).

Therein, “Who is a lay follower?” Any householder who has gone for refuge. For this was stated: “Mahānāma, when one has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha, to that extent, Mahānāma, one is a lay follower.”

Kasmā upāsakoti ratanattayaṃ upāsanato. So hi buddhaṃ upāsatīti upāsako, tathā dhammaṃ saṃghaṃ.

“Why is he called a lay follower?” Because of attending upon the Triple Gem. For he attends upon the Buddha, thus he is a lay follower; likewise, he attends upon the Dhamma and the Saṅgha.

Kimassa [P 1.0235] sīlanti pañca veramaṇiyo. Yathāha – “yato kho, mahānāma, upāsako pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hoti, adinnādānā… kāmesumicchācārā… musāvādā… surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā paṭivirato hoti, ettāvatā kho, mahānāma, upāsako sīlavā hotī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1033).

“What is his virtue?” The five abstinences. As it was said: “Mahānāma, when a lay follower is one who abstains from taking life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from distilled and fermented intoxicants which are the basis for heedlessness—to that extent, Mahānāma, a lay follower is virtuous.”

Ko [M 1.0210] ājīvoti pañca micchāvaṇijjā pahāya dhammena samena jīvitakappanaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – “pañcimā, bhikkhave, vaṇijjā upāsakena akaraṇīyā. Katamā pañca? Satthavaṇijjā, sattavaṇijjā, maṃsavaṇijjā, majjavaṇijjā, visavaṇijjā. Imā kho, bhikkhave, pañca vaṇijjā upāsakena akaraṇīyā”ti (a. ni. 5.177).

“What is his livelihood?” It is making a living righteously and justly, having abandoned the five wrong trades. For this was stated: “Bhikkhus, these five trades should not be engaged in by a lay follower. Which five? Trading in weapons, trading in living beings, trading in meat, trading in intoxicants, and trading in poisons. These, bhikkhus, are the five trades that should not be engaged in by a lay follower.”

Kā vipattīti yā tasseva sīlassa ca ājīvassa ca vipatti, ayamassa vipatti. Api ca yāya esa caṇḍālo ceva hoti, malañca patikuṭṭho ca, sāpissa vipattīti veditabbā. Te ca atthato assaddhiyādayo pañca dhammā honti. Yathāha – “pañcahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato upāsako upāsakacaṇḍālo ca hoti, upāsakamalañca, upāsakapatikuṭṭho ca. Katamehi pañcahi? Assaddho hoti, dussīlo hoti, kotūhalamaṅgaliko hoti, maṅgalaṃ pacceti, no kammaṃ, ito ca bahiddhā dakkhiṇeyyaṃ pariyesati, tattha ca pubbakāraṃ karotī”ti (a. ni. 5.175).

“What is downfall?” That which is the downfall of that very virtue and livelihood, this is his downfall. Furthermore, that wrong practice by which this lay follower becomes an outcaste, a stain, and a despicable person, that too should be known as a downfall. And in terms of their essential meaning, these are the five qualities beginning with faithlessness. As it is said: ‘Bhikkhus, a lay follower endowed with five qualities is a lay follower-outcaste, a lay follower-stain, and a lay follower-despicable person. With which five? He is faithless, immoral, believes in superstitious omens, trusts in omens and not in kamma, seeks a recipient of offerings outside of this Dispensation, and performs the initial service there.’”

Kā sampattīti yā cassa sīlasampadā ceva ājīvasampadā ca, sā sampatti; ye cassa ratanabhāvādikarā saddhādayo pañca dhammā. Yathāha – “pañcahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato upāsako [V 1.0191] upāsakaratanañca hoti, upāsakapadumañca, upāsakapuṇḍarīkañca. Katamehi pañcahi? Saddho hoti, sīlavā hoti, na kotūhalamaṅgaliko hoti, kammaṃ pacceti, no maṅgalaṃ, na ito bahiddhā dakkhiṇeyyaṃ gavesati, idha ca pubbakāraṃ karotī”ti (a. ni. 5.175).

What is prosperity? That which is his accomplishment in virtue and accomplishment in livelihood, that is prosperity. Furthermore, those five qualities beginning with faith, which cause one to become a jewel and so forth, are also prosperity. As it is said: ‘Bhikkhus, a lay follower endowed with five qualities is a lay follower-jewel, a lay follower-red lotus, and a lay follower-white lotus. With which five? He has faith, is virtuous, does not believe in superstitious omens, trusts in kamma and not in omens, does not seek a recipient of offerings outside of this Dispensation, and performs the initial service here.’”

Ajjataggeti etthāyaṃ aggasaddo ādikoṭikoṭṭhāsaseṭṭhesu dissati. “Ajjatagge, samma dovārika, āvarāmi dvāraṃ nigaṇṭhānaṃ nigaṇṭhīna”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.70) hi ādimhi dissati. “Teneva aṅgulaggena taṃ aṅgulaggaṃ parāmaseyya[P 1.0236]. Ucchaggaṃ veḷagga”ntiādīsu (kathā. 281) koṭiyaṃ. “Ambilaggaṃ vā madhuraggaṃ vā tittakaggaṃ vā vihāraggena vā pariveṇaggena vā bhājetu”ntiādīsu (cūḷava. 317) koṭṭhāse. “Yāvatā, bhikkhave, sattā apadā vā…pe… tathāgato tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.34) seṭṭhe. Idha panāyaṃ ādimhi daṭṭhabbo. Tasmā ajjataggeti ajjataṃ ādiṃ katvāti evametthattho veditabbo. Ajjatanti [M 1.0211] ajjabhāvaṃ. Ajjadaggeti vā pāṭho, dakāro padasandhikaro. Ajja agganti attho.

Regarding 'ajjatagge': Here, the word 'agga' is seen in the senses of beginning, extremity, portion, and excellence. For instance, in ‘From today onwards (ajjatagge), dear gatekeeper, I close the door to the Nigaṇṭhas and Nigaṇṭhīs,’ it is seen in the sense of beginning. In ‘with that very fingertip (aṅgulaggena)... the tip of the sugarcane (ucchaggaṃ), the tip of the bamboo (veḷaggaṃ),’ it is seen in the sense of extremity. In ‘divide the sour portion (ambilaggaṃ), or the sweet portion (madhuraggaṃ), or the bitter portion (tittakaggaṃ)... by monastery portion (vihāraggena) or by precinct portion (pariveṇaggena),’ it is seen in the sense of portion. In ‘Bhikkhus, of all beings... the Tathāgata is declared the foremost (aggaṃ),’ it is seen in the sense of excellence. Here, however, this word should be understood in the sense of beginning. Therefore, in 'ajjatagge,' the meaning should be understood thus: 'having made today the beginning.' 'Ajjataṃ' means the state of being today. Alternatively, the reading is 'ajjadagge,' where the letter 'd' is for euphonic conjunction. The meaning is 'having made today the beginning.'

Pāṇupetanti pāṇehi upetaṃ. Yāva me jīvitaṃ pavattati, tāva upetaṃ anaññasatthukaṃ tīhi saraṇagamanehi saraṇaṃ gataṃ upāsakaṃ kappiyakārakaṃ maṃ bhagavā dhāretu jānātu. Ahañhi sacepi me tikhiṇena asinā sīsaṃ chindeyya, neva buddhaṃ “na buddho”ti vā, dhammaṃ “na dhammo”ti vā, saṅghaṃ “na saṅgho”ti vā vadeyyanti.

Regarding 'pāṇupetaṃ': it means 'endowed with life.' As long as my life continues, for that long may the Blessed One hold me in mind and know me as a lay follower who is endowed with life, has no other teacher, and has gone for refuge by means of the three goings for refuge. For even if they were to cut off my head with a sharp sword, I would never say of the Buddha, ‘He is not the Buddha,’ or of the Dhamma, ‘It is not the Dhamma,’ or of the Saṅgha, ‘It is not the Saṅgha.’”

Evaṃ attasanniyyātanena saraṇaṃ gantvā attanā kataṃ aparādhaṃ pakāsento accayo maṃ, bhantetiādimāha. Tattha accayoti aparādho. Maṃ accagamāti maṃ atikkamma abhibhavitvā pavatto. Dhammikaṃ dhammarājānanti ettha dhammaṃ caratīti dhammiko. Dhammeneva rājā jāto, na pitughātanādinā adhammenāti dhammarājā. Jīvitā voropesinti jīvitā viyojesiṃ. Paṭiggaṇhātūti khamatu. Āyatiṃ saṃvarāyāti anāgate saṃvaratthāya. Puna evarūpassa aparādhassa dosassa khalitassa akaraṇatthāya.

Having thus gone for refuge by means of self-surrender, wishing to declare the offense committed by himself, he said the phrase beginning with, ‘Venerable sir, a transgression has overcome me.’ Therein, ‘transgression’ (accayo) means an offense. ‘Has overcome me’ (accagamā) means it has occurred, having surpassed and overwhelmed me. Regarding ‘a righteous one, a king of righteousness’: one who practices the Dhamma is ‘righteous’ (dhammiko). He became king through righteousness itself, not through unrighteousness such as patricide; therefore he is a ‘king of righteousness’ (dhammarājā). ‘I deprived him of life’ (jīvitāvoropesiṃ) means I caused him to be separated from the life faculty. ‘May you accept’ (paṭiggaṇhātu) means may you forgive. ‘For future restraint’ (āyatiṃ saṃvarāya) means for the purpose of restraint in the future, for the purpose of not again committing such an offense, fault, or lapse.

251. Tagghāti ekaṃse nipāto. Yathā dhammaṃ paṭikarosīti yathā dhammo ṭhito tatheva karosi, khamāpesīti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ te mayaṃ paṭiggaṇhāmāti taṃ tava aparādhaṃ mayaṃ khamāma. Vuḍḍhihesā, mahārāja ariyassa vinayeti esā, mahārāja, ariyassa vinaye buddhassa bhagavato [V 1.0192] sāsane vuḍḍhi nāma. Katamā? Yāyaṃ accayaṃ accayato disvā yathādhammaṃ paṭikaritvā [P 1.0237] āyatiṃ saṃvarāpajjanā, desanaṃ pana puggalādhiṭṭhānaṃ karonto – “yo accayaṃ accayato disvā yathādhammaṃ paṭikaroti, āyatiṃ saṃvaraṃ āpajjatī”ti āha.

251. ‘Taggha’ is a particle that occurs in the sense of certainty. ‘You make amends according to the Dhamma’ means you act in the very way that the Dhamma stands; that is to say, you ask for forgiveness. ‘We accept that from you’ means we forgive that offense of yours. ‘This, O king, is growth in the Noble One’s Discipline’ means this, O king, is called growth in the Discipline of the Noble One, in the Dispensation of the Buddha, the Blessed One. What is called growth? It is this: seeing a transgression as a transgression, making amends according to the Dhamma, and attaining restraint in the future. However, making the teaching based on the individual, he said: ‘Whoever sees a transgression as a transgression, makes amends according to the Dhamma, and attains restraint in the future.’”

252. Evaṃ vutteti evaṃ bhagavatā vutte. Handa ca dāni mayaṃ bhanteti ettha handāti vacasāyatthe nipāto. So hi gamanavacasāyaṃ katvā evamāha. Bahukiccāti balavakiccā. Bahukaraṇīyāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Yassadāni tvanti yassa idāni tvaṃ mahārāja gamanassa kālaṃ maññasi jānāsi, tassa kālaṃ tvameva jānāsīti vuttaṃ hoti. Padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmīti tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā dasanakhasamodhānasamujjalaṃ añjaliṃ [M 1.0212] sirasi patiṭṭhapetvā yāva dassanavisayaṃ bhagavato abhimukhova paṭikkamitvā dassanavijahanaṭṭhānabhūmiyaṃ pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā pakkāmi.

252. ‘When it was thus said’ means when it was thus said by the Blessed One. Regarding ‘Well then, venerable sir, we shall now depart’: here, ‘handa’ is a particle in the sense of concluding a speech. For he, having made a concluding speech for the purpose of departing, spoke thus. ‘We have much to do’ means we have many duties. ‘We have many tasks’ is a synonym for that. Regarding ‘It is now time for you to do as you see fit’: this means, ‘O great king, now, whatever time for departure you consider appropriate, you yourself know that time.’ This is what is meant. Regarding ‘having circumambulated respectfully, he departed’: this means having circumambulated respectfully three times, placing on his head the añjali, resplendent from the joining of the ten fingernails, he retreated while facing the Blessed One as far as the range of vision. At the place where vision was lost, he paid homage with the five-point prostration and departed.

253. Khatāyaṃ, bhikkhave, rājāti khato ayaṃ, bhikkhave, rājā. Upahatāyanti upahato ayaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ayaṃ, bhikkhave, rājā khato upahato bhinnapatiṭṭho jāto, tathānena attanāva attā khato, yathā attano patiṭṭhā na jātāti. Virajanti rāgarajādivirahitaṃ. Rāgamalādīnaṃyeva vigatattā vītamalaṃ. Dhammacakkhunti dhammesu vā cakkhuṃ, dhammamayaṃ vā cakkhuṃ, aññesu ṭhānesu tiṇṇaṃ maggānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Idha pana sotāpattimaggasseva. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sace iminā pitā ghātito nābhavissa, idāni idhevāsane nisinno sotāpattimaggaṃ patto abhavissa, pāpamittasaṃsaggena panassa antarāyo jāto. Evaṃ santepi yasmā ayaṃ tathāgataṃ upasaṅkamitvā ratanattayaṃ saraṇaṃ gato, tasmā mama sāsanamahantatāya yathā nāma koci purisassa vadhaṃ katvā pupphamuṭṭhimattena daṇḍena mucceyya, evameva lohakumbhiyaṃ nibbattitvā [P 1.0238] tiṃsavassasahassāni adho patanto heṭṭhimatalaṃ patvā tiṃsavassasahassāni uddhaṃ gacchanto punapi uparimatalaṃ pāpuṇitvā muccissatīti idampi kira bhagavatā vuttameva, pāḷiyaṃ pana na ārūḷhaṃ.

253. ‘This king, O monks, is undermined’ means ‘this king, O monks, is undermined.’ ‘He is destroyed’ means ‘he is destroyed.’ This is what is meant: ‘This king, O monks, is undermined, destroyed, has become one whose foundation is broken; in such a way has he undermined himself that his own foundation is not established.’ ‘Dust-free’ means free from the dust of lust and so on. Because of the very departure of the stains of lust and so on, it is stainless. ‘The Dhamma-eye’ means the eye regarding the Dhammas, or the eye made of Dhamma; in other places, this is a designation for the three lower paths. Here, however, it is a designation for only the path of stream-entry. This is what is meant: ‘If his father had not been killed by him, now, while sitting in this very seat, he would have attained the path of stream-entry. But due to association with an evil friend, an obstacle has arisen for him.’ Even so, because he approached the Tathāgata and went for refuge to the Triple Gem, and due to the greatness of my Dispensation, just as someone who has committed the murder of a man might be released from the death penalty by a fine of a mere handful of flowers, in the very same way, having arisen in the Lohakumbhī hell, falling downwards for thirty thousand years, and having reached the bottom plane, then rising upwards for thirty thousand years, and again having reached the upper plane, he will be released. This too, it is said, was indeed spoken by the Blessed One, but it was not included in the Pāḷi Canon.

Idaṃ pana suttaṃ sutvā raññā koci ānisaṃso laddhoti? Mahāānisaṃso laddho. Ayañhi pitu māritakālato paṭṭhāya neva rattiṃ na divā niddaṃ labhati, satthāraṃ pana upasaṅkamitvā imāya madhurāya ojavantiyā dhammadesanāya sutakālato paṭṭhāya niddaṃ labhi. Tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ mahāsakkāraṃ akāsi. Pothujjanikāya saddhāya samannāgato nāma iminā raññā sadiso nāhosi. Anāgate pana vijitāvī nāma paccekabuddho hutvā parinibbāyissatīti[V 1.0193]. Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

Now, having heard this discourse, was any benefit obtained by the king? A great benefit was obtained. Indeed, from the time of killing his father, he obtained no sleep either by night or by day. However, having approached the Teacher, from the time of hearing this sweet and nourishing Dhamma discourse, he obtained sleep. He paid great honor to the Three Jewels. There was no one endowed with the faith of a worldling who was equal to this king. Furthermore, in the future, having become a Paccekabuddha named Vijitāvī, he will attain Parinibbāna. The Blessed One said this. Those monks, being delighted, rejoiced in what was spoken by the Blessed One.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Thus, in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya,

Sāmaññaphalasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta is concluded.

3. Ambaṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Ambaṭṭha Sutta Commentary

Addhānagamanavaṇṇanā

The Exposition on Journeying

254. Evaṃ [P 1.0239][V 1.0194][M 1.0213] me sutaṃ…pe… kosalesūti ambaṭṭhasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ apubbapadavaṇṇanā. Kosalesūti kosalā nāma jānapadino rājakumārā. Tesaṃ nivāso ekopi janapado rūḷhīsaddena kosalāti vuccati, tasmiṃ kosalesu janapade. Porāṇā panāhu – yasmā pubbe mahāpanādaṃ rājakumāraṃ nānānāṭakādīni disvā sitamattampi akarontaṃ sutvā rājā āha – “yo mama puttaṃ hasāpeti, sabbālaṅkārena naṃ alaṅkaromī”ti. Tato naṅgalānipi chaḍḍetvā mahājanakāye sannipatite manussā sātirekāni sattavassāni nānākīḷāyo dassetvāpi taṃ hasāpetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, tato sakko devarājā nāṭakaṃ pesesi, so dibbanāṭakaṃ dassetvā hasāpesi. Atha te manussā attano attano vasanokāsābhimukhā pakkamiṃsu. Te paṭipathe mittasuhajjādayo disvā paṭisanthāraṃ karontā – “kacci bho kusalaṃ, kacci bho kusala”nti āhaṃsu. Tasmā taṃ “kusala”nti vacanaṃ upādāya so padeso kosalāti vuccatīti.

This sutta beginning with 'Thus have I heard... in Kosala' is the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. Herein, this is the explanation of terms not previously explained. 'In Kosala': the Kosalas are princes who are rulers of the country. Their residence, even a single country, is called 'Kosala' by conventional usage; it is in that country of Kosala. The ancient commentators, however, said: Because formerly, having heard that the prince Mahāpanāda, even after seeing various kinds of performances, did not so much as smile, the king said: 'Whoever makes my son laugh, I will adorn him with every ornament.' Thereupon, even discarding their plows, when a great crowd of people had gathered, they were unable to make him laugh even after showing various entertainments for more than seven years. Then Sakka, the king of the devas, sent a dancer. He, showing a celestial dance, made him laugh. Then those people departed, heading towards their respective dwelling places. On the way, seeing friends, companions, and others, they exchanged friendly greetings, saying: 'Friend, are you well? Friend, are you well?' Therefore, it is said that by adopting that word 'kusalaṃ', that region is called Kosala.

Cārikaṃ caramānoti addhānagamanaṃ gacchanto. Cārikā ca nāmesā bhagavato duvidhā hoti – turitacārikā ca, aturitacārikā ca. Tattha dūrepi bodhaneyyapuggalaṃ disvā tassa bodhanatthāya sahasā gamanaṃ turitacārikā nāma, sā mahākassapassa paccuggamanādīsu daṭṭhabbā. Bhagavā hi mahākassapattheraṃ paccuggacchanto muhuttena tigāvutaṃ maggaṃ agamāsi. Āḷavakassatthāya tiṃsayojanaṃ, tathā [P 1.0240] aṅgulimālassa. Pakkusātissa pana pañcacattālīsayojanaṃ. Mahākappinassa vīsayojanasataṃ. Dhaniyassatthāya sattayojanasatāni agamāsi. Dhammasenāpatino saddhivihārikassa vanavāsītissasāmaṇerassa tigāvutādhikaṃ vīsayojanasataṃ.

254. ‘Journeying on a tour’ means going on a long journey. This wandering of the Blessed One is of two kinds: a swift wandering and an unhurried wandering. Therein, seeing a person fit to be enlightened even at a distance and going quickly for the purpose of enlightening them is called a swift wandering. This should be seen in instances such as going out to meet Mahākassapa. Indeed, the Blessed One, going out to meet the Elder Mahākassapa, traveled a path of three gāvutas in a moment. For the sake of Āḷavaka, he traveled thirty yojanas; likewise for Aṅgulimāla. For Pakkusāti, however, forty-five yojanas. For Mahākappina, one hundred and twenty yojanas. For the sake of Dhaniya, he traveled seven hundred yojanas. For the sake of the novice Vanavāsī Tissa, the co-resident of the General of the Dhamma, he traveled one hundred and twenty yojanas plus three gāvutas.

Ekadivasaṃ kira thero – “tissasāmaṇerassa santikaṃ, bhante, gacchāmī”ti āha. Bhagavā [V 1.0195] – “ahampi gamissāmī”ti vatvā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ [M 1.0214] āmantesi – “ānanda, vīsatisahassānaṃ chaḷabhiññānaṃ ārocehi, bhagavā kira vanavāsissa tissasāmaṇerassa santikaṃ gamissatī”ti. Tato dutiyadivase vīsatisahassakhīṇāsavaparivāro ākāse uppatitvā vīsatiyojanasatamatthake tassa gocaragāmadvāre otaritvā cīvaraṃ pārupi. Taṃ kammantaṃ gacchamānā manussā disvā – “satthā no āgato, mā kammantaṃ agamitthā”ti vatvā āsanāni paññapetvā yāguṃ datvā pātarāsabhattaṃ karontā – “kuhiṃ, bhante, bhagavā gacchatī”ti daharabhikkhū pucchiṃsu. Upāsakā na bhagavā aññattha gacchati, idheva tissasāmaṇerassa dassanatthāyāgatoti. Te – “amhākaṃ kulūpakassa kira therassa dassanatthāya satthā āgato, no vata no thero oramattako”ti somanassajātā ahesuṃ.

It is said that one day the Elder said, 'Venerable sir, I am going to the novice Tissa.' The Blessed One, saying, 'I too will go,' addressed the Venerable Ānanda: 'Ānanda, inform the twenty thousand who possess the six higher knowledges that the Blessed One, it seems, will go to the forest-dwelling novice Tissa.' Then, on the second day, with a retinue of twenty thousand destroyers of the cankers, he rose into the sky and, above the one hundred and twenty yojanas, descended at the gate of his alms-resort village and put on his robe. People going to work saw him and, saying, 'Our Teacher has come; do not go to work,' prepared seats, gave gruel, and while preparing the morning meal, they asked the junior monks, 'Venerable sirs, where is the Blessed One going?' The junior monks replied, 'Lay devotees, the Blessed One is not going elsewhere; he has come here for the purpose of seeing the novice Tissa.' They became joyful, thinking, 'It seems the Teacher has come for the purpose of seeing the elder who is our family's intimate! Indeed, our elder is of no small measure!'

Atha kho bhagavato bhattakiccapariyosāne sāmaṇero gāme piṇḍāya caritvā – “upāsakā, mahābhikkhusaṅgho”ti pucchi. Athassa te “satthā, bhante, āgato”ti ārocesuṃ. So bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā piṇḍapātena āpucchi. Satthā tassa pattaṃ hatthena gahetvā – “alaṃ, tissa, niṭṭhitaṃ bhattakicca”nti āha. Tato upajjhāyaṃ āpucchitvā attano pattāsane nisīditvā bhattakiccamakāsi. Athassa bhattakiccapariyosāne satthā maṅgalaṃ vatvā nikkhamitvā gāmadvāre ṭhatvā – “kataro te, tissa, vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gatamaggo”ti āha. Ayaṃ bhagavāti. Maggaṃ desayamāno purato yāhi tissāti. Bhagavā kira sadevakassa lokassa maggadesakopi samāno sakale tigāvute magge ‘sāmaṇeraṃ daṭṭhuṃ [P 1.0241] lacchāmī’ti taṃ maggadesakaṃ akāsi.

Then, when the Blessed One's meal was finished, the novice, having gone for alms in the village, asked, 'Lay devotees, the community of monks is so large!' Then they informed him, 'Venerable sir, the Teacher has arrived.' He approached the Blessed One and offered his almsfood. The Teacher, taking his bowl with his hand, said, 'Enough, Tissa, the meal is finished.' Then, having taken leave of his preceptor, he sat in the seat prepared for him and had his meal. When his meal was finished, the Teacher gave the blessing, departed, and standing at the village gate, said, 'Tissa, which is the path that goes to your dwelling place?' Tissa replied, 'This is it, Blessed One.' The Buddha said, 'Tissa, go in front, showing the path.' It is said that the Blessed One, although he is the shower of the path for the world with its devas, made him the path-shower on the entire three-gāvuta path, thinking, 'I shall get to see the novice.'

So attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā bhagavato vattamakāsi. Atha naṃ bhagavā – “kataro te, tissa, caṅkamo”ti pucchitvā tattha gantvā sāmaṇerassa nisīdanapāsāṇe nisīditvā – “tissa, imasmiṃ ṭhāne sukhaṃ vasī”ti pucchi. So āha – “āma, bhante, imasmiṃ ṭhāne vasantassa sīhabyagghahatthimigamorādīnaṃ saddaṃ suṇato araññasaññā uppajjati, tāya sukhaṃ vasāmī”ti. Atha naṃ bhagavā – “tissa, bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātehi, buddhadāyajjaṃ te dassāmī”ti vatvā sannipatite bhikkhusaṅghe upasampādetvā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva agamāsīti. Ayaṃ turitacārikā nāma. Yaṃ [M 1.0215] pana gāmanigamapaṭipāṭiyā devasikaṃ yojanadviyojanavasena piṇḍapātacariyādīhi lokaṃ anuggaṇhantassa gamanaṃ, ayaṃ aturitacārikā nāma.

He went to his dwelling place and performed his duties for the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One asked him, “Tissa, which is your walking path?” and having gone there and sat on the novice’s sitting stone, he asked, “Tissa, do you dwell happily in this place?” He replied, “Yes, venerable sir. Dwelling in this place, hearing the sounds of lions, tigers, elephants, deer, peacocks, and so on, the perception of the forest arises, and with that I dwell happily.” Then the Blessed One said to him, “Tissa, gather the community of monks; I will give you the Buddha's inheritance.” Having said this, when the community of monks had assembled, he had him ordained and then returned to his own dwelling place. This is called the swift wandering. As for the wandering that involves going from village to town in sequence daily, covering one or two yojanas for alms rounds and other activities to benefit the world, this is called the unhurried wandering.

Imaṃ pana cārikaṃ caranto bhagavā mahāmaṇḍalaṃ, majjhimamaṇḍalaṃ, antomaṇḍalanti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ maṇḍalānaṃ aññatarasmiṃ carati. Tattha mahāmaṇḍalaṃ navayojanasatikaṃ, majjhimamaṇḍalaṃ chayojanasatikaṃ[V 1.0196], antomaṇḍalaṃ tiyojanasatikaṃ. Yadā mahāmaṇḍale cārikaṃ caritukāmo hoti, mahāpavāraṇāya pavāretvā pāṭipadadivase mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivāro nikkhamati. Samantā yojanasataṃ ekakolāhalaṃ hoti. Purimaṃ purimaṃ āgatā nimantetuṃ labhanti. Itaresu dvīsu maṇḍalesu sakkāro mahāmaṇḍale osarati. Tattha bhagavā tesu tesu gāmanigamesu ekāhaṃ dvīhaṃ vasanto mahājanaṃ āmisappaṭiggahena anuggaṇhanto dhammadānena cassa vivaṭṭasannissitaṃ kusalaṃ vaḍḍhento navahi māsehi cārikaṃ pariyosāpeti. Sace pana antovasse bhikkhūnaṃ samathavipassanā taruṇā honti, mahāpavāraṇāya apavāretvā pavāraṇāsaṅgahaṃ datvā kattikapuṇṇamāyaṃ pavāretvā migasirassa paṭhamapāṭipadadivase mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivāro nikkhamitvā majjhimamaṇḍale osarati. Aññenapi [P 1.0242] kāraṇena majjhimamaṇḍale cārikaṃ caritukāmo catumāsaṃ vasitvāva nikkhamati. Vuttanayeneva itaresu dvīsu maṇḍalesu sakkāro majjhimamaṇḍale osarati. Bhagavā purimanayeneva lokaṃ anuggaṇhanto aṭṭhahi māsehi cārikaṃ pariyosāpeti. Sace pana catumāsaṃ vutthavassassāpi bhagavato veneyyasattā aparipakkindriyā honti, tesaṃ indriyaparipākaṃ āgamayamāno aparampi ekamāsaṃ vā dviticatumāsaṃ vā tattheva vasitvā mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivāro nikkhamati. Vuttanayeneva itaresu dvīsu maṇḍalesu sakkāro antomaṇḍale osarati. Bhagavā purimanayeneva lokaṃ anuggaṇhanto sattahi vā chahi vā pañcahi vā catūhi vā māsehi cārikaṃ pariyosāpeti. Iti imesu tīsu maṇḍalesu yattha katthaci cārikaṃ caranto na cīvarādihetu carati. Atha kho ye duggatabālajiṇṇabyādhitā, te kadā tathāgataṃ āgantvā passissanti. Mayi pana cārikaṃ carante mahājano tathāgatassa dassanaṃ labhissati. Tattha keci cittāni pasādessanti[M 1.0216], keci mālādīhi pūjessanti, keci kaṭacchubhikkhaṃ dassanti, keci micchādassanaṃ pahāya sammādiṭṭhikā bhavissanti. Taṃ nesaṃ bhavissati dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyāti. Evaṃ lokānukampakāya cārikaṃ carati.

Furthermore, while undertaking this wandering, the Blessed One travels within one of these three regions: the great region, the middle region, or the inner region. Therein, the great region is nine hundred yojanas, the middle region is six hundred yojanas, and the inner region is three hundred yojanas. When he wishes to travel in the great region, having performed the Pavāraṇā on the day of the Great Pavāraṇā, he departs on the first day of the next fortnight, surrounded by a great assembly of bhikkhus. For a hundred yojanas all around, there is a single great commotion. Those who arrive first get the opportunity to invite him. The offerings from the other two regions converge upon the great region. There, in those various villages and market towns, the Blessed One, staying for one or two days, while supporting the great multitude by the acceptance of material offerings and, by the gift of the Dhamma, increasing their wholesome karma that is connected to that which is free from the round of rebirth, completes the wandering in nine months. However, if during the rains-residence the bhikkhus’ serenity and insight are still developing, then not having performed the Pavāraṇā on the Great Pavāraṇā day, but having granted a concession for the Pavāraṇā, and having performed the Pavāraṇā on the full moon day of Kattika, he departs on the first day of the month of Migasira, surrounded by a great assembly of bhikkhus, and enters the middle region. For another reason too, wishing to travel in the middle region, he departs only after staying for four months. In the way already stated, the offerings from the other two regions converge upon the middle region. The Blessed One, supporting the world in the same way as before, completes the wandering in eight months. But if, even after the Blessed One has completed the four-month rains-residence, the beings to be trained have immature faculties, then, while waiting for their faculties to mature, he stays in that very place for another one, two, three, or four months, and then departs surrounded by a great assembly of bhikkhus. In the way already stated, the offerings from the other two regions converge upon the inner region. The Blessed One, supporting the world in the same way as before, completes the wandering in seven, or six, or five, or four months. Thus, when wandering anywhere within these three regions, he does not travel for the sake of robes and so on. Rather, he thinks: 'Those who are unfortunate, foolish, aged, and sick—when will they be able to come and see the Tathāgata? But while I am wandering, the great multitude will get to see the Tathāgata. There, some will make their minds confident, some will make offerings with flowers and so on, some will give a ladleful of alms-food, and some, having abandoned wrong view, will become holders of right view. That will be for their welfare and happiness for a long time.' Thus, he travels out of compassion for the world.

Api ca catūhi kāraṇehi buddhā bhagavanto cārikaṃ caranti, jaṅghavihāravasena sarīraphāsukatthāya, atthuppattikālābhikaṅkhanatthāya, bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāpadapaññāpanatthāya, tattha tattha paripākagatindriye bodhaneyyasatte bodhanatthāyāti. Aparehipi catūhi kāraṇehi buddhā bhagavanto cārikaṃ caranti buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchissantīti vā, dhammaṃ, saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchissantīti vā, mahatā dhammavassena catasso parisā santappessāmīti vā. Aparehipi pañcahi kāraṇehi buddhā bhagavanto cārikaṃ caranti pāṇātipātā viramissantīti vā, adinnādānā[P 1.0243], kāmesumicchācārā, musāvādā, surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā viramissantīti vā. Aparehipi aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi buddhā bhagavanto cārikaṃ caranti – paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ paṭilabhissantīti vā, dutiyaṃ [V 1.0197] jhānaṃ…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiṃ paṭilabhissantīti vā. Aparehipi aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi buddhā bhagavanto cārikaṃ caranti – sotāpattimaggaṃ adhigamissantīti vā, sotāpattiphalaṃ…pe… arahattaphalaṃ sacchikarissantīti vāti.
