Ayaṃ aturitacārikā, idha cārikāti adhippetā. Sā panesā duvidhā hoti – anibaddhacārikā ca nibaddhacārikā ca. Tattha yaṃ gāmanigamanagarapaṭipāṭivasena carati, ayaṃ anibaddhacārikā nāma. Yaṃ panekasseva bodhaneyyasattassatthāya gacchati, ayaṃ nibaddhacārikā nāma. Esā idha adhippetā.

Furthermore, for four reasons the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, undertake a wandering: by way of journeying on foot for the sake of bodily comfort; for the sake of awaiting the time for an occasion to arise; for the sake of laying down training rules for the bhikkhus; and for the sake of awakening, in various places, those beings fit to be awakened whose faculties have reached maturity. And for another four reasons the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, undertake a wandering: thinking, 'They will go for refuge to the Buddha,' or 'They will go for refuge to the Dhamma,' or 'They will go for refuge to the Saṅgha,' or 'I will satisfy the four assemblies with a great rain of the Dhamma.' And for another five reasons the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, undertake a wandering: thinking, 'They will abstain from killing living beings,' '...from taking what is not given,' '...from sexual misconduct,' '...from false speech,' and '...from liquor, intoxicants, and substances that are a basis for heedlessness.' And for another eight reasons the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, undertake a wandering: thinking, 'They will attain the first jhāna,' '...the second jhāna,' and so on up to '...they will attain the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' And for another eight reasons the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, undertake a wandering: thinking, 'They will attain the path of stream-entry,' '...the fruit of stream-entry,' and so on up to '...they will realize the fruit of arahantship.' This is the unhurried wandering, and it is this that is intended here by 'wandering.' Furthermore, this wandering is of two kinds: the unbound wandering and the bound wandering. Among these two, the wandering that proceeds in sequence through villages, market towns, and cities is called the unbound wandering. But the journey undertaken for the sake of one single being who is fit to be awakened is called the bound wandering. It is this latter one that is intended here.

Tadā kira bhagavato pacchimayāmakiccapariyosāne dasasahassilokadhātuyā ñāṇajālaṃ pattharitvā bodhaneyyabandhave olokentassa pokkharasātibrāhmaṇo sabbaññutaññāṇajālassa anto paviṭṭho. Atha bhagavā ayaṃ brāhmaṇo mayhaṃ ñāṇajāle paññāyati, “atthi nu khvassa upanissayo”ti vīmaṃsanto sotāpattimaggassa upanissayaṃ disvā – “eso mayi etaṃ janapadaṃ gate lakkhaṇapariyesanatthaṃ ambaṭṭhaṃ antevāsiṃ pahiṇissati, so mayā saddhiṃ vādapaṭivādaṃ katvā nānappakāraṃ asabbhivākyaṃ vakkhati, tamahaṃ dametvā nibbisevanaṃ karissāmi. So [M 1.0217] ācariyassa kathessati, athassācariyo taṃ kathaṃ sutvā āgamma mama lakkhaṇāni pariyesissati, tassāhaṃ dhammaṃ desessāmi. So desanāpariyosāne sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahissati. Desanā mahājanassa saphalā bhavissatī”ti pañcabhikkhusataparivāro taṃ janapadaṃ paṭipanno. Tena vuttaṃ – “kosalesu cārikaṃ caramāno mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehī”ti.

It is said that at that time, at the conclusion of the Blessed One's duties of the last watch of the night, he spread out the net of knowledge over the ten-thousandfold world-system and surveyed those kinsmen who were ready for awakening. The brahmin Pokkharasāti then entered within the net of omniscient knowledge. Then the Blessed One thought: “This brahmin appears in my net of knowledge. Does he have the supporting condition?” Investigating thus, he saw the supporting condition for the path of stream-entry and thought: “When I go to that country, he will send his resident pupil Ambaṭṭha to search for my marks. That pupil will engage in debate with me and speak various kinds of unseemly words. I will tame him and make him docile. He will then report to his teacher, and his teacher, upon hearing that account, will come and search for my marks. I will teach him the Dhamma. At the end of the discourse, he will be established in the fruit of stream-entry. The discourse will be fruitful for the great assembly.” With a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus, he set out for that country. Therefore it was said: “while wandering on tour in the Kosalan country with a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, with five hundred bhikkhus.”

Yena icchānaṅgalanti yena disābhāgena icchānaṅgalaṃ avasaritabbaṃ. Yasmiṃ vā padese icchānaṅgalaṃ. Ijjhānaṅgalantipi pāṭho. Tadavasarīti [P 1.0244] tena avasari, taṃ vā avasari. Tena disābhāgena gato, taṃ vā padesaṃ gatoti attho. Icchānaṅgale viharati icchānaṅgalavanasaṇḍeti icchānaṅgalaṃ upanissāya icchānaṅgalavanasaṇḍe sīlakhandhāvāraṃ bandhitvā samādhikontaṃ ussāpetvā sabbaññutaññāṇasaraṃ parivattayamāno dhammarājā yathābhirucitena vihārena viharati.

‘Yena Icchānaṅgalaṃ’ means ‘by which direction Icchānaṅgala is to be approached,’ or ‘in which place Icchānaṅgala is.’ The reading ‘Ijjhānaṅgala’ is also found. ‘Tadavasarī’ means ‘he approached by that direction,’ or ‘he approached that place.’ The meaning is: ‘he went by that direction,’ or ‘he went to that place.’ ‘He was dwelling at Icchānaṅgala, in the Icchānaṅgala wood’ means that the King of Dhamma, relying on Icchānaṅgala, having established the camp of virtue in the Icchānaṅgala wood, having raised the spear of concentration, and wielding the arrow of omniscient knowledge, dwelt as he pleased.

Pokkharasātivatthuvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of Pokkharasāti

255. Tena kho pana samayenāti yena samayena bhagavā tattha viharati, tena samayena, tasmiṃ samayeti ayamattho. Brahmaṃ aṇatīti brāhmaṇo, mante sajjhāyatīti attho. Idameva hi jātibrāhmaṇānaṃ niruttivacanaṃ. Ariyā pana bāhitapāpattā brāhmaṇāti vuccanti. Pokkharasātīti [V 1.0198] idaṃ tassa nāmaṃ. Kasmā pokkharasātīti vuccati. Tassa kira kāyo setapokkharasadiso, devanagare ussāpitarajatatoraṇaṃ viya sobhati. Sīsaṃ panassa kāḷavaṇṇaṃ indanīlamaṇimayaṃ viya. Massupi candamaṇḍale kāḷamegharāji viya khāyati. Akkhīni nīluppalasadisāni. Nāsā rajatapanāḷikā viya suvaṭṭitā suparisuddhā. Hatthapādatalāni ceva mukhadvārañca katalākhārasaparikammaṃ viya sobhati, ativiya sobhaggappatto brāhmaṇassa attabhāvo. Arājake ṭhāne rājānaṃ kātuṃ yuttamimaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ. Evamesa sassiriko. Iti naṃ pokkharasadisattā pokkharasātīti sañjānanti.

255. ‘Tena kho pana samayena’ means ‘at that time,’ ‘on that occasion,’ when the Blessed One was dwelling there. This is the meaning. ‘Brāhmaṇa’ (brahmin) is one who recites ‘Brahma’ (the sacred texts); the meaning is one who recites the mantras. This, indeed, is the etymological definition for brahmins by birth. The noble ones, on the other hand, are called brahmins because they have banished evil. ‘Pokkharasāti’ was his name. Why was he called Pokkharasāti? It is said that his body was like a white lotus, beautiful like a silver archway erected in a city of devas. His head, moreover, was black in color, as if made of sapphire. His beard, too, appeared like a streak of dark clouds on the disk of the moon. His eyes were like blue water lilies. His nose was well-rounded and perfectly pure, like a silver pipe. The soles of his hands and feet, and the opening of his mouth, were beautiful as if treated with lac-dye; the brahmin's person had attained a state of extreme beauty. In a place without a king, it would be fitting to make this brahmin king. Thus he was majestic. So, because he was like a lotus (pokkhara), they knew him as Pokkharasāti.

Ayaṃ [M 1.0218] pana kassapasammāsambuddhakāle tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū dasabalassa dānaṃ datvā dhammadesanaṃ sutvā devaloke nibbatti. So tato manussalokamāgacchanto mātukucchivāsaṃ jigucchitvā himavantapadese mahāsare padumagabbhe nibbatti. Tassa ca sarassa avidūre tāpaso paṇṇasālāya vasati. So tīre ṭhito taṃ padumaṃ disvā – “idaṃ padumaṃ avasesapadumehi mahantataraṃ. Pupphitakāle naṃ gahessāmī”ti cintesi. Taṃ sattāhenāpi na pupphati. Tāpaso kasmā nu kho idaṃ sattāhenāpi na pupphati. Handa naṃ gahessāmīti otaritvā gaṇhi. Taṃ tena nāḷato chinnamattaṃyeva [P 1.0245] pupphitaṃ. Athassabbhantare suvaṇṇacuṇṇapiñjaraṃ viya rajatabimbakaṃ padumareṇupiñjaraṃ setavaṇṇaṃ dārakaṃ addasa. So mahāpuñño esa bhavissati. Handa naṃ paṭijaggāmīti paṇṇasālaṃ netvā paṭijaggitvā sattavassakālato paṭṭhāya tayo vede uggaṇhāpesi. Dārako tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāraṃ gantvā paṇḍito byatto jambudīpe aggabrāhmaṇo ahosi. So aparena samayena rañño kosalassa sippaṃ dassesi. Athassa sippe pasanno rājā ukkaṭṭhaṃ nāma mahānagaraṃ brahmadeyyaṃ adāsi. Iti naṃ pokkhare sayitattā pokkharasātīti sañjānanti.

Furthermore, in the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One, Kassapa, this brahmin, being a master of the three Vedas, gave a gift to the Ten-Powered One, and after hearing a Dhamma discourse, was reborn in the deva world. Coming from there to the human world, and being disgusted with dwelling in a mother’s womb, he was reborn in a great lake in the Himalayan region, within a lotus calyx. Not far from that lake, an ascetic lived in a leaf hut. Standing on the shore, he saw that lotus and thought, 'This lotus is much larger than the other lotuses. When it blooms, I will take it.' But even after seven days, it did not bloom. The ascetic thought, 'Why has it not bloomed even in seven days? Come, I will take it.' Descending into the water, he took it. As soon as he cut it from its stem, it bloomed. Then, inside it, he saw a white child, made golden-hued by lotus pollen, like a small silver image made golden with gold dust. He thought, 'This one will have great merit. Come, I will raise him.' Taking him to the leaf hut, he raised him, and from the age of seven, had him learn the three Vedas. The boy, having mastered the three Vedas, became wise and astute, the foremost brahmin in Jambudīpa. At a later time, he demonstrated his skill to the King of Kosala. Then the king, pleased with his skill, gave him the great city named Ukkaṭṭha as a royal grant. Thus, because he had lain (sayita) in a lotus (pokkhara), they knew him as Pokkharasāti.

Ukkaṭṭhaṃ ajjhāvasatīti ukkaṭṭhanāmake nagare vasati. Abhibhavitvā vā āvasati. Tassa nagarassa sāmiko hutvā yāya mariyādāya tattha vasitabbaṃ, tāya mariyādāya vasi. Tassa kira nagarassa vatthuṃ ukkā ṭhapetvā ukkāsu jalamānāsu aggahesuṃ, tasmā taṃ ukkaṭṭhanti vuccati. Okkaṭṭhantipi pāṭho, soyevattho. Upasaggavasena panettha bhummatthe upayogavacanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tassa anupayogattā ca sesapadesu. Tattha lakkhaṇaṃ saddasatthato pariyesitabbaṃ.

‘He dwells in Ukkaṭṭha’ means ‘he resides in the city named Ukkaṭṭha,’ or ‘he dwells there, having taken possession of it.’ Having become the master of that city, he lived there according to the custom by which one ought to reside. It is said that they took the site of that city by placing torches (ukkā) and taking possession while the torches were burning; hence it is called Ukkaṭṭha. The reading ‘Okkaṭṭha’ is also found; it has the same meaning. Here, on account of the prefixes in the verb, the accusative case should be understood in the sense of the locative. And due to its connection with the other words, they too are in the accusative. The grammatical rule for this should be sought from the treatises on grammar.

Sattussadanti sattehi ussadaṃ, ussannaṃ bahujanaṃ ākiṇṇamanussaṃ. Posāvaniyahatthiassamoramigādianekasattasamākiṇṇañcāti [V 1.0199] attho. Yasmā panetaṃ nagaraṃ bahi āvijjhitvā jātena hatthiassādīnaṃ ghāsatiṇena ceva gehacchādanatiṇena ca sampannaṃ. Tathā dārukaṭṭhehi ceva gehasambhārakaṭṭhehi ca. Yasmā cassabbhantare vaṭṭacaturassādisaṇṭhānā bahū pokkharaṇiyo jalajakusumavicittāni ca bahūni anekāni taḷākāni udakassa niccabharitāneva honti, tasmā satiṇakaṭṭhodakanti vuttaṃ. Saha dhaññenāti sadhaññaṃ pubbaṇṇāparaṇṇādibhedaṃ bahudhaññasannicayanti attho[M 1.0219]. Ettāvatā yasmiṃ nagare brāhmaṇo setacchattaṃ ussāpetvā rājalīlāya vasati, tassa samiddhisampatti dīpitā hoti.

‘Sattussadaṃ’ means: teeming with beings, abundant, with many people, crowded with humans. The meaning is also ‘teeming with many beings such as elephants, horses, peacocks, and deer that are to be reared.’ Moreover, because this city was well-supplied with grass for fodder for elephants, horses, and so on, that grew surrounding it on the outside, and with grass for thatching houses. Likewise, it was well-supplied with firewood and with timber for house-building. And because within it there were many ponds of circular, quadrangular, and other shapes, and many and various lakes adorned with water-born flowers, which are always filled with water, therefore it is called ‘possessing grass, timber, and water.’ ‘Saha dhaññena’ means ‘sadhaññaṃ,’ a place for the accumulation of much grain of various kinds, such as early and late crops; this is the meaning. By this much, the opulence and prosperity of the city where the brahmin dwells, having raised a white parasol with royal splendor, is shown.

Rājato laddhaṃ bhoggaṃ rājabhoggaṃ. Kena [P 1.0246] dinnanti ce? Raññā pasenadinā kosalena dinnaṃ. Rājadāyanti rañño dāyabhūtaṃ, dāyajjanti attho. Brahmadeyyanti seṭṭhadeyyaṃ, chattaṃ ussāpetvā rājasaṅkhepena bhuñjitabbanti attho. Atha vā rājabhogganti sabbaṃ chejjabhejjaṃ anusāsantena nadītitthapabbatādīsu suṅkaṃ gaṇhantena setacchattaṃ ussāpetvā raññā hutvā bhuñjitabbaṃ. Raññā pasenadinā kosalena dinnaṃ rājadāyanti ettha taṃ nagaraṃ raññā dinnattā rājadāyaṃ dāyakarājadīpanatthaṃ panassa “raññā pasenadinā kosalena dinna”nti idaṃ vuttaṃ. Brahmadeyyanti seṭṭhadeyyaṃ. Yathā dinnaṃ na puna gahetabbaṃ hoti, nissaṭṭhaṃ pariccattaṃ. Evaṃ dinnanti attho.

‘Rājabhoggaṃ’ is enjoyment obtained from the king. If it is asked, 'By whom was it given?' It was given by King Pasenadi of Kosala. ‘Rājadāyaṃ’ means a gift from the king that has become an inheritance; this is the meaning. ‘Brahmadeyyaṃ’ means a noble gift, to be enjoyed by raising a parasol with the status of a king; this is the meaning. Alternatively, ‘rājabhoggaṃ’ means that which is to be enjoyed by one who has become a king, raising a white parasol, administering all that is to be cut and divided, and collecting taxes at places like river crossings and mountain passes. In the phrase 'a royal gift given by King Pasenadi of Kosala,' here that city is a 'royal gift' because it was given by the king. Furthermore, to show the king who was the giver, this phrase 'given by King Pasenadi of Kosala' was spoken. ‘Brahmadeyyaṃ’ means a noble gift. It is given in such a way that it is not to be taken back again; it is released, relinquished. The meaning is that it is given thus.

Assosīti suṇi upalabhi, sotadvārasampattavacananigghosānusārena aññāsi. Khoti avadhāraṇatthe padapūraṇamatte vā nipāto. Tattha avadhāraṇatthena assosi eva, nāssa koci savanantarāyo ahosīti ayamattho veditabbo. Padapūraṇena pana padabyañjanasiliṭṭhatāmattameva.

‘Assosi’ means: he heard, he received, he knew by following the sound of speech that reached the ear-door. ‘Kho’ is a particle that occurs either in the sense of emphasis or merely as a sentence-filler. In the sense of emphasis, the meaning to be understood is this: he indeed heard; there was no impediment to his hearing. As a sentence-filler, however, it is to be understood as merely for the smoothness of the words and syllables.

Idāni yamatthaṃ brāhmaṇo pokkharasāti assosi, taṃ pakāsento – “samaṇo khalu bho gotamo”tiādimāha. Tattha samitapāpattā samaṇoti veditabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ – “samitāssa honti pāpakā akusalā dhammā”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.434). Bhagavā ca anuttarena ariyamaggena samitapāpo. Tenassa yathābhūtaguṇādhigatametaṃ nāmaṃ, yadidaṃ samaṇoti. Khalūti anussavanatthe nipāto. Bhoti brāhmaṇajātisamudāgataṃ ālapanamattaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “bhovādī nāma so hoti, sace hoti sakiñcano”ti (dha. pa. 55). Gotamoti bhagavantaṃ gottavasena parikitteti. Tasmā samaṇo khalu bho gotamoti ettha samaṇo kira bho gotamagottoti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

Now, showing what the brahmin Pokkharasāti heard, he said, 'The ascetic Gotama, indeed, Master...' and so on. Therein, ‘samaṇa’ is to be understood as one who has stilled evil. For it is said: 'For him, evil, unwholesome states are stilled,' and so on. And the Blessed One has stilled evil by the unsurpassed noble path. Therefore, this name, ‘samaṇa,’ is a name acquired by him through his true qualities. ‘Khalu’ is a particle in the sense of hearsay. ‘Bho’ is merely a term of address that comes from the brahmin caste. For this too was said: 'He is called a 'bho-sayer' if he has impediments.' With ‘gotamo,’ he speaks of the Blessed One by way of his clan name. Therefore, in the phrase ‘samaṇo khalu bho gotamo,’ the meaning should be understood thus: 'Master, the ascetic of the Gotama clan, it is said.'

Sakyaputtoti [V 1.0200] idaṃ pana bhagavato uccākulaparidīpanaṃ[P 1.0247]. Sakyakulā pabbajitoti saddhāpabbajitabhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Kenaci pārijuññena anabhibhūto aparikkhīṇaṃyeva [M 1.0220] taṃ kulaṃ pahāya saddhāya pabbajitoti vuttaṃ hoti. Tato paraṃ vuttatthameva. Taṃ kho panātiādi sāmaññaphale vuttameva. Sādhu kho panāti sundaraṃ kho pana. Atthāvahaṃ sukhāvahanti vuttaṃ hoti. Tathārūpānaṃ arahatanti yathārūpo so bhavaṃ gotamo, evarūpānaṃ yathābhūtaguṇādhigamena loke arahantoti laddhasaddhānaṃ arahataṃ. Dassanaṃ hotīti pasādasommāni akkhīni ummīletvā dassanamattampi sādhu hotīti, evaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ katvā.

‘Sakyaputto’ (Son of the Sakyans) is a term that shows the Blessed One's high clan. ‘Sakyakulā pabbajito’ (having gone forth from the Sakyan clan) is a term that shows the state of having gone forth out of faith. It is said that he went forth out of faith, having left that clan while it was still undiminished, not overcome by any decline. After that, the meaning has already been explained. ‘Taṃ kho pana,’ etc., has been explained in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta. ‘Sādhu kho pana’ means: it is indeed good. It is said to be beneficial and conducive to happiness. ‘Tathārūpānaṃ arahataṃ’ (of such Arahants) refers to those Arahants in the world who have gained faith through the attainment of true qualities, just as the venerable Gotama has. ‘Dassanaṃ hoti’ (there is the seeing) means that even the mere sight, with eyes opened in clarity and serenity, is good; this is said having formed such an intention.

Ambaṭṭhamāṇavakathā

The Account of the Young Man Ambaṭṭha

256. Ajjhāyakoti idaṃ – “na dānime jhāyanti, na dānime jhāyantīti kho, vāseṭṭha, ajjhāyakā ajjhāyakā tveva tatiyaṃ akkharaṃ upanibbatta”nti, evaṃ paṭhamakappikakāle jhānavirahitānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ garahavacanaṃ. Idāni pana taṃ ajjhāyatīti ajjhāyako. Mante parivattetīti iminā atthena pasaṃsāvacanaṃ katvā voharanti. Mante dhāretīti mantadharo.

256. This term ‘Ajjhāyaka’ is explained: 'Now they do not practice jhāna, now they do not practice jhāna.' For this reason, Vāseṭṭha, the third designation, 'ajjhāyakā, ajjhāyakā,' came into being. Thus, in the time of the first cosmic aeon, this was a term of reproach for brahmins who were devoid of jhāna. Now, however, they have made it a term of praise and use it with this meaning: 'He recites (ajjhāyati), therefore he is an ajjhāyaka.' 'He recites the mantras repeatedly (mante parivatteti).' 'He retains the mantras (mante dhāreti), therefore he is a mantadharo (a retainer of the mantras).'

Tiṇṇaṃ vedānanti iruvedayajuvedasāmavedānaṃ. Oṭṭhapahatakaraṇavasena pāraṃ gatoti pāragū. Saha nighaṇḍunā ca keṭubhena ca sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānaṃ. Nighaṇḍūti nighaṇḍurukkhādīnaṃ vevacanapakāsakaṃ satthaṃ. Keṭubhanti kiriyākappavikappo kavīnaṃ upakārāvahaṃ satthaṃ. Saha akkharappabhedena sākkharappabhedānaṃ. Akkharappabhedoti sikkhā ca nirutti ca. Itihāsapañcamānanti āthabbaṇavedaṃ catutthaṃ katvā itiha āsa, itiha āsāti īdisavacanapaṭisaṃyutto purāṇakathāsaṅkhāto itihāso pañcamo etesanti itihāsapañcamā, tesaṃ itihāsapañcamānaṃ vedānaṃ.

‘Of the three Vedas’ means of the Irubeda, Yajubeda, and Sāmaveda. He has gone to the far shore (pāraṃ gato) by means of the act of striking the lips in recitation, therefore he is one who has reached the far shore (pāragū). ‘Of those with the Nighaṇḍu and Keṭubha’ (sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānaṃ). Nighaṇḍu is a treatise that explains the synonyms of trees and so forth. Keṭubha is a treatise beneficial to poets, concerning the composition and variation of expression. ‘Of those with the analysis of letters’ (sākkharappabhedānaṃ). The analysis of letters (Akkharappabhedo) refers to phonetics (sikkhā) and etymology (nirutti). ‘Of those with history as the fifth’ (Itihāsapañcamānaṃ): Having made the Āthabbaṇaveda the fourth, history (itihāsa)—which is designated as ancient lore connected with such sayings as 'Thus it was here' (iti ha āsa), 'Thus it was here' (iti ha āsa)—is the fifth of these Vedas. Therefore, they are said to have history as the fifth. ‘Tesaṃ itihāsapañcamānaṃ vedānaṃ’ means of those Vedas which have history as the fifth.

Padaṃ tadavasesañca byākaraṇaṃ adhīyati vedeti cāti padako veyyākaraṇo. Lokāyataṃ vuccati vitaṇḍavādasatthaṃ. Mahāpurisalakkhaṇanti [P 1.0248] mahāpurisānaṃ buddhādīnaṃ lakkhaṇadīpakaṃ dvādasasahassaganthapamāṇaṃ satthaṃ. Yattha soḷasasahassagāthāparimāṇā buddhamantā nāma ahesuṃ, yesaṃ vasena iminā lakkhaṇena samannāgatā buddhā nāma honti, iminā paccekabuddhā, iminā dve aggasāvakā, asīti mahāsāvakā[M 1.0221], buddhamātā, buddhapitā, aggupaṭṭhāko, aggupaṭṭhāyikā, rājā cakkavattīti ayaṃ viseso paññāyati.

Because he studies and knows the pada and the remaining byākaraṇa, he is a master of etymology and a grammarian. The treatise on sophistry is called Lokāyata. The Marks of a Great Man is a treatise of twelve thousand textual units that illuminates the marks of great beings such as the Buddhas. Therein were what are known as the Buddha-mantras, numbering one thousand and sixteen verses, by virtue of which this distinction is known: those endowed with this mark become Buddhas; with this, Paccekabuddhas; with this, the two chief disciples; the eighty great disciples; the Buddha's mother; the Buddha's father; the chief male attendant; the chief female attendant; or a wheel-turning monarch.

Anavayoti [V 1.0201] imesu lokāyatamahāpurisalakkhaṇesu anūno paripūrakārī, avayo na hotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Avayo nāma yo tāni atthato ca ganthato ca sandhāretuṃ na sakkoti. Anuññātapaṭiññātoti anuññāto ceva paṭiññāto ca. Ācariyenassa “yaṃ ahaṃ jānāmi, taṃ tvaṃ jānāsī”tiādinā anuññāto. “Āma ācariyā”ti attanā tassa paṭivacanadānapaṭiññāya paṭiññātoti attho. Katarasmiṃ adhikāre? Sake ācariyake tevijjake pāvacane. Esa kira brāhmaṇo cintesi “imasmiṃ loke ‘ahaṃ buddho, ahaṃ buddho’ti uggatassa nāmaṃ gahetvā bahū janā vicaranti. Tasmā na me anussavamatteneva upasaṅkamituṃ yuttaṃ. Ekaccañhi upasaṅkamantassa apakkamanampi garu hoti, anatthopi uppajjati. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ mama antevāsikaṃ pesetvā – ‘buddho vā, no vā’ti jānitvāva upasaṅkameyya”nti, tasmā māṇavaṃ āmantetvā ayaṃ tātātiādimāha.

Not deficient means that in regard to these treatises, the Lokāyata and the Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa, he is not lacking; he is one who brings them to completion. It is said that he is not deficient. A deficient person is one who is unable to retain them both in terms of their meaning and their text. Permitted and professed means he is both permitted by his teacher and has professed it himself. He is permitted by his teacher with such words as, 'What I know, you know.' He has professed it by his own affirmative reply to the teacher, 'Yes, teacher.' This is the meaning. In what sphere? In his own traditional teaching of the three Vedas. It is said that this brahmin thought: 'In this world, many people wander about, taking up the name of some eminent figure and claiming, "I am a Buddha, I am a Buddha." Therefore, it is not proper for me to approach him based on mere hearsay. Indeed, for one who approaches a certain person, even to withdraw becomes burdensome, and disadvantage can arise. What if I first send my disciple, and only after finding out whether he is a Buddha or not, I then approach him?' Therefore, he summoned the young man and spoke the words beginning with, 'This, dear one...'

257. Taṃ bhavantanti tassa bhoto gotamassa. Tathā santaṃ yevāti tathā satoyeva. Idhāpi hi itthambhūtākhyānatthavaseneva upayogavacanaṃ.

257. That venerable one means that venerable Gotama. Being truly thus means being one who truly exists as such. For here too, the accusative case is used in the sense of describing a particular state.

258. Yathā kathaṃ panāhaṃ, bho, tanti ettha kathaṃ panāhaṃ bho taṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ jānissāmi, yathā sakkā so ñātuṃ, tathā me ācikkhāhīti attho. Yathāti vā nipātamattamevetaṃ. Kathanti ayaṃ ākārapucchā. Kenākārenāhaṃ taṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ jānissāmīti attho. Evaṃ vutte kira naṃ upajjhāyo “kiṃ tvaṃ, tāta, pathaviyaṃ [P 1.0249] ṭhito, pathaviṃ na passāmīti viya; candimasūriyānaṃ obhāse ṭhito, candimasūriye na passāmīti viya vadasī”tiādīni vatvā jānanākāraṃ dassento āgatāni kho, tātātiādimāha.

258. Regarding the phrase 'But how, O master, shall I...?', the meaning is: 'But how, O master, shall I know that venerable Gotama? Please explain to me the way in which he can be known.' Alternatively, 'yathā' is merely a particle, and 'kathaṃ' is a question about the manner. The meaning is: 'In what manner shall I know that venerable Gotama?' When this was said, it is said that his teacher, wishing to show him the way of knowing, replied: 'Dear boy, why do you speak like one who, while standing on the earth, says, "I do not see the earth," or like one who, while standing in the light of the moon and sun, says, "I do not see the moon and sun"?' and so on. Then he spoke the words beginning with, 'It has come down in our tradition, dear one...'

Tattha mantesūti vedesu. Tathāgato kira uppajjissatīti paṭikacceva suddhāvāsā devā vedesu lakkhaṇāni pakkhipitvā buddhamantā nāmeteti brāhmaṇaveseneva vede vācenti. Tadanusārena mahesakkhā sattā tathāgataṃ jānissantīti. Tena pubbe vedesu mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni [M 1.0222] āgacchanti. Parinibbute pana tathāgate anukkamena antaradhāyanti. Tenetarahi natthīti. Mahāpurisassāti paṇidhisamādānañāṇakaruṇādiguṇamahato purisassa. Dveyeva gatiyoti dveyeva niṭṭhā. Kāmañcāyaṃ gatisaddo “pañca kho imā, sāriputta, gatiyo”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.153) bhavabhede vattati. “Gati migānaṃ pavana”ntiādīsu (pari. 399) nivāsaṭṭhāne. “Evaṃ adhimattagatimanto”tiādīsu paññāyaṃ. “Gatigata”ntiādīsu visaṭabhāve. Idha pana niṭṭhāyaṃ vattatīti veditabbo.

Therein, 'in the mantras' means in the Vedas. The explanation is that, long before the Tathāgata was to arise, the devas of the Pure Abodes inserted the marks into the Vedas, calling them 'Buddha-mantras,' and in the guise of brahmins, they taught the Vedas. They did so thinking, 'In accordance with these, beings of great power will be able to recognize the Tathāgata.' For that reason, the marks of a Great Man formerly appeared in the Vedas. But after the Parinibbāna of the Tathāgata, they gradually disappeared. Therefore, they no longer exist today. 'Of a Great Man' means of a great being, one who is great due to such qualities as aspiration, undertaking, knowledge, and compassion. 'Only two destinies' means only two final outcomes. And although this word 'gati' is used in the sense of a type of existence in passages such as, 'Sāriputta, there are these five destinies'; in the sense of a dwelling place in passages such as, 'The resort of deer is the great forest'; in the sense of wisdom in passages such as, 'Thus they are endowed with supreme wisdom'; and in the sense of pervasiveness in passages such as, 'pervaded'; here, however, it should be understood in the sense of a final outcome.

Tattha [V 1.0202] kiñcāpi yehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgato rājā cakkavattī hoti, na teheva buddho hoti; jātisāmaññato pana tāniyeva tānīti vuccanti. Tena vuttaṃ – “yehi samannāgatassā”ti. Sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasatīti yadi agāre vasati. Rājā hoti cakkavattīti catūhi acchariyadhammehi, saṅgahavatthūhi ca lokaṃ rañjanato rājā, cakkaratanaṃ vatteti, catūhi sampatticakkehi vattati, tehi ca paraṃ vatteti, parahitāya ca iriyāpathacakkānaṃ vatto etasmiṃ atthīti cakkavattī. Ettha ca rājāti sāmaññaṃ. Cakkavattīti visesaṃ. Dhammena caratīti dhammiko. Ñāyena samena vattatīti attho. Dhammena rajjaṃ labhitvā rājā jātoti dhammarājā. Parahitadhammakaraṇena vā dhammiko. Attahitadhammakaraṇena dhammarājā. Caturantāya issaroti cāturanto, catusamuddaantāya, catubbidhadīpavibhūsitāya pathaviyā issaroti attho. Ajjhattaṃ [P 1.0250] kopādipaccatthike bahiddhā ca sabbarājāno vijetīti vijitāvī. Janapadatthāvariyappattoti janapade dhuvabhāvaṃ thāvarabhāvaṃ patto, na sakkā kenaci cāletuṃ. Janapado vā tamhi thāvariyappatto anuyutto sakammanirato acalo asampavedhīti janapadatthāvariyappatto.

Here, although one who is endowed with certain marks becomes a wheel-turning monarch, he does not, with those very same marks, become a Buddha; but due to similarity of type, those very marks are said to be these marks. Therefore it was said: 'with which he is endowed.' 'If he lives in a household' means if he dwells in a home. 'A king becomes a wheel-turning monarch': he is a king (rājā) because he delights the world with the four marvelous qualities and the four means of beneficence; he is a wheel-turner (cakkavattī) because he turns the wheel-treasure, because he proceeds with the four wheels of accomplishment and causes others to proceed with them, and because in him there is the turning of the wheels of postures for the welfare of others. And herein, 'king' is a general term; 'wheel-turner' is a specific term. He is righteous (dhammiko) because he acts according to the Dhamma; the meaning is that he proceeds rightly and equitably. He is a king of Dhamma (dhammarājā) because he becomes a king having obtained the kingdom righteously. Alternatively, he is righteous by performing righteous deeds for the welfare of others; he is a king of Dhamma by performing righteous deeds for his own welfare. He is sovereign of the four ends (cāturanto) because he is the lord of the four ends; the meaning is that he is the lord of the earth that has the four oceans as its end and is adorned with the four continents. He is a conqueror (vijitāvī) because he has conquered internal enemies such as anger and, externally, all kings. He has attained the stability of the country (janapadatthāvariyappatto) because he has attained a firm and stable state in the country and cannot be shaken by anyone. Alternatively, the country under him has attained stability—devoted, diligent in its own work, unshakable, and untrembling—therefore he has attained the stability of the country.

Seyyathidanti nipāto, tassa cetāni katamānīti attho. Cakkaratanantiādīsu cakkañca, taṃ ratijananaṭṭhena ratanañcāti cakkaratanaṃ. Esa nayo sabbattha. Imesu pana ratanesu ayaṃ cakkavattirājā cakkaratanena ajitaṃ jināti, hatthiassaratanehi vijite yathāsukhaṃ anucarati, pariṇāyakaratanena [M 1.0223] vijitamanurakkhati, avasesehi upabhogasukhamanubhavati. Paṭhamena cassa ussāhasattiyogo, pacchimena mantasattiyogo, hatthiassagahapatiratanehi pabhusattiyogo suparipuṇṇo hoti, itthimaṇiratanehi tividhasattiyogaphalaṃ. So itthimaṇiratanehi bhogasukhamanubhavati, sesehi issariyasukhaṃ. Visesato cassa purimāni tīṇi adosakusalamūlajanitakammānubhāvena sampajjanti, majjhimāni alobhakusalamūlajanitakammānubhāvena, pacchimamekaṃ amohakusalamūlajanitakammānubhāvenāti veditabbaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana bojjhaṅgasaṃyutte ratanasuttassa upadesato gahetabbo.

The word seyyathidaṃ is a particle; its meaning is: 'What are these?' In the passage beginning with cakkaratanaṃ, the meaning should be understood thus: it is a wheel, and it is a treasure in the sense that it generates delight, thus it is a wheel-treasure. This is the method in all cases. Now, among these treasures, this wheel-turning monarch conquers the unconquered with the wheel-treasure; with the elephant and horse treasures, he travels at ease through conquered territory; with the advisor-treasure, he protects what has been conquered; and with the remaining treasures, he experiences the pleasure of enjoyment. Furthermore, through the first treasure, his endowment with the power of energy is fully complete; through the last, his endowment with the power of counsel; through the elephant, horse, and householder treasures, his endowment with the power of sovereignty is fully complete; and through the woman and jewel treasures, the fruit of his endowment with these three powers becomes fully complete. He experiences the pleasure of enjoyment with the woman and jewel treasures, and the pleasure of sovereignty with the rest. Moreover, it should be understood that, specifically, his first three treasures arise through the power of kamma generated by the wholesome root of non-hatred; the middle three arise through the power of kamma generated by the wholesome root of non-greed; and the last one arises through the power of kamma generated by the wholesome root of non-delusion. This is the summary here. The detailed explanation, however, should be taken from the instruction on the Ratana Sutta in the Bojjhaṅga Saṃyutta.

Parosahassanti atirekasahassaṃ. Sūrāti abhīrukajātikā. Vīraṅgarūpāti devaputtasadisakāyā. Evaṃ tāva eke vaṇṇayanti. Ayaṃ panettha sabbhāvo. Vīrāti uttamasūrā vuccanti, vīrānaṃ aṅgaṃ vīraṅgaṃ, vīrakāraṇaṃ vīriyanti vuttaṃ hoti. Vīraṅgarūpaṃ etesanti vīraṅgarūpā, vīriyamayasarīrā viyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Parasenappamaddanāti sace paṭimukhaṃ tiṭṭheyya parasenā taṃ parimaddituṃ samatthāti adhippāyo. Dhammenāti “pāṇo na hantabbo”tiādinā pañcasīladhammena[V 1.0203]. Arahaṃ hoti sammāsambuddho loke vivaṭṭacchadoti ettha rāgadosamohamānadiṭṭhiavijjāduccaritachadanehi [P 1.0251] sattahi paṭicchanne kilesandhakāre loke taṃ chadanaṃ vivaṭṭetvā samantato sañjātāloko hutvā ṭhitoti vivaṭṭacchado. Tattha paṭhamena padena pūjārahatā. Dutiyena tassā hetu, yasmā sammāsambuddhoti, tatiyena buddhattahetubhūtā vivaṭṭacchadatā vuttāti veditabbā. Atha vā vivaṭṭo ca vicchado cāti vivaṭṭacchado, vaṭṭarahito chadanarahito cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tena arahaṃ vaṭṭābhāvena, sammāsambuddho chadanābhāvenāti evaṃ purimapadadvayasseva hetudvayaṃ vuttaṃ hoti, dutiyena vesārajjena cettha purimasiddhi, paṭhamena dutiyasiddhi, tatiyacatutthehi tatiyasiddhi hoti. Purimañca dhammacakkhuṃ, dutiyaṃ buddhacakkhuṃ, tatiyaṃ samantacakkhuṃ sādhetīti veditabbaṃ. Tvaṃ mantānaṃ paṭiggahetāti iminā’ssa mantesu sūrabhāvaṃ janeti.

More than a thousand means exceeding a thousand. Sūrā means those of a fearless nature. Vīraṅgarūpā means having bodies like those of divine beings. Thus some explain it. But this is the true meaning here: vīrā are called supreme heroes; the factor of heroes (vīraṅga) is the cause of heroism, which is to say, energy (vīriya). They have a heroic form, thus they are vīraṅgarūpā; this is to say, their bodies are as if made of energy. Crushers of others' armies means that if an enemy army were to stand before them, they are capable of crushing it. By Dhamma means by the Dhamma of the five precepts, beginning with 'A living being should not be killed.' Regarding the phrase 'He is an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, one with the covering rolled back in the world' (vivaṭṭacchado): in a world covered by the seven coverings—lust, hatred, delusion, pride, views, ignorance, and misconduct—and by the darkness of defilements, he has rolled back that covering and stands, having become one with light arisen all around; thus he is vivaṭṭacchado. Therein, by the first term, his worthiness of offerings is stated. By the second, the cause for that is stated: because he is a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. It should be understood that by the third, the state of having the covering rolled back, which is the cause of Buddhahood, is stated. Alternatively, he is vivaṭṭacchado because he is both without the round of rebirth (vivaṭṭo) and without a covering (vicchado); this is to say, he is free from the round of rebirth and free from the covering. By this, it is said that he is an Arahant due to the absence of the round of rebirth, and a Sammāsambuddha due to the absence of the covering; thus, the two causes for the preceding two terms are stated. And herein, by the second ground of self-confidence, the first accomplishment (Arahantship) is achieved; by the first, the second accomplishment (Perfect Self-Enlightenment) is achieved; and by the third and fourth, the third accomplishment (having the covering rolled back) is achieved. And it should be understood that the first term accomplishes the Dhamma-eye, the second the Buddha-eye, and the third the all-seeing eye. With the words, 'You are a recipient of the mantras,' he generates in him a heroic disposition regarding the mantras.

259. Sopi [M 1.0224] tāya ācariyakathāya lakkhaṇesu vigatasammoho ekobhāsajāte viya buddhamante sampassamāno evaṃ bhoti āha. Tassattho – ‘yathā, bho, tvaṃ vadasi, evaṃ karissāmī’ti. Vaḷavārathamāruyhāti vaḷavāyuttaṃ rathaṃ abhirūhitvā. Brāhmaṇo kira yena rathena sayaṃ vicarati, tameva rathaṃ datvā māṇavaṃ pesesi. Māṇavāpi pokkharasātisseva antevāsikā. So kira tesaṃ – “ambaṭṭhena saddhiṃ gacchathā”ti saññaṃ adāsi.

259. He too, through that speech of his teacher, became free from delusion regarding the marks, and seeing the Buddha-mantras as if a single light had arisen, said, 'So be it, sir.' The meaning of this is: 'Sir, as you say, so I will do.' 'Having mounted the mare-chariot' means having ascended the chariot yoked with mares. It is said that the brahmin, having given the young man the very chariot in which he himself travels, sent him. The other young men were also resident pupils of Pokkharasāti. It is said that he gave them a sign, saying: 'Go with Ambaṭṭha.'

Yāvatikā yānassa bhūmīti yattakaṃ sakkā hoti yānena gantuṃ, ayaṃ yānassa bhūmi nāma. Yānā paccorohitvāti ayānabhūmiṃ, dvārakoṭṭhakasamīpaṃ gantvā yānato paṭiorohitvā.

'As far as is ground for a vehicle' means as far as it is possible to go by vehicle. 'Having dismounted from the vehicle' means having gone to the area not for vehicles, near the gate-tower, and having descended from the vehicle.

Tena kho pana samayenāti yasmiṃ samaye ambaṭṭho ārāmaṃ pāvisi. Tasmiṃ pana samaye, ṭhitamajjhanhikasamaye. Kasmā pana tasmiṃ samaye caṅkamantīti? Paṇītabhojanapaccayassa thinamiddhassa vinodanatthaṃ, divāpadhānikā vā te. Tādisānañhi pacchābhattaṃ caṅkamitvā nhāyitvā [P 1.0252] sarīraṃ utuṃ gāhāpetvā nisajja samaṇadhammaṃ karontānaṃ cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti. Yena te bhikkhūti so kira – “kuhiṃ samaṇo gotamo”ti pariveṇato pariveṇaṃ anāgantvā “pucchitvāva pavisissāmī”ti vilokento araññahatthī viya mahācaṅkame caṅkamamāne paṃsukūlike bhikkhū disvā tesaṃ santikaṃ agamāsi. Taṃ sandhāya yena te bhikkhūtiādi vuttaṃ. Dassanāyāti daṭṭhuṃ, passitukāmā hutvāti attho.

'At that time' means at the time when Ambaṭṭha entered the monastery. At that time, it was high noon. But why were they walking at that time? It was to dispel the sloth and torpor caused by rich food, or perhaps they were monks who strive during the day. For such monks, after the meal, having walked, having bathed, having allowed the body to adjust to the climate, and then sitting and practicing the ascetic's duties, their minds become one-pointed. The phrase 'Where the monks were' is explained thus: It is said that he, thinking, 'Where is the ascetic Gotama?', decided not to go from one enclosure to another, but rather, 'I will enter only after asking.' Looking about, he saw monks wearing rag-robes walking on a great promenade like wild elephants, and he approached them. With reference to this, the words 'Where the monks were,' etc., were spoken. 'For seeing' means in order to see; that is, having become desirous of seeing. This is the meaning.

260. Abhiññātakolaññoti pākaṭakulajo. Tadā kira jambudīpe ambaṭṭhakulaṃ nāma pākaṭakulamahosi[V 1.0204]. Abhiññātassāti rūpajātimantakulāpadesehi pākaṭassa. Agarūti abhāriko. Yo hi ambaṭṭhaṃ ñāpetuṃ na sakkuṇeyya, tassa tena saddhiṃ kathāsallāpo garu bhaveyya. Bhagavato pana tādisānaṃ māṇavānaṃ satenāpi sahassenāpi [M 1.0225] pañhaṃ puṭṭhassa vissajjane dandhāyitattaṃ natthīti maññamānā – “agaru kho panā”ti cintayiṃsu. Vihāroti gandhakuṭiṃ sandhāya āhaṃsu.

260. 'Abhiññātakolañño' means one born into a prominent family. At that time, it is said, in Jambudīpa the Ambaṭṭha clan was a prominent clan. 'Abhiññātassa' means of one who is prominent on account of appearance, birth, sacred texts, and clan. 'Agaru' means not burdensome. Indeed, for whoever would not be able to make Ambaṭṭha understand, conversation with him would be burdensome. However, knowing that for the Blessed One, even when asked a question by a hundred or a thousand of such young men, there is no slowness in answering, they thought, 'Indeed, it is not burdensome.' By 'vihāra,' they spoke referring to the perfumed chamber.

Ataramānoti aturito, saṇikaṃ padappamāṇaṭṭhāne padaṃ nikkhipanto vattaṃ katvā susammaṭṭhaṃ muttādalasinduvārasantharasadisaṃ vālikaṃ avināsentoti attho. Āḷindanti pamukhaṃ. Ukkāsitvāti ukkāsitasaddaṃ katvā. Aggaḷanti dvārakavāṭaṃ. Ākoṭehīti agganakhehi saṇikaṃ kuñcikacchiddasamīpe ākoṭehīti vuttaṃ hoti. Dvāraṃ kira atiupari amanussā, atiheṭṭhā dīghajātikā koṭenti. Tathā anākoṭetvā majjhe chiddasamīpe koṭetabbanti idaṃ dvārākoṭanavattanti dīpentā vadanti.

'Ataramāno' means not hurried; slowly placing the foot in the space of a foot's measure, having performed one's duties, not disturbing the well-swept sand which was like a pearl-strewn surface and a spread of sinduvāra flowers. This is the meaning. 'Āḷindaṃ' means the front porch. 'Ukkāsitvā' means having made the sound of clearing one's throat. 'Aggaḷaṃ' means the door panel. 'Ākoṭehi' means: knock gently with the fingertips near the keyhole. This is what is meant. It is said that non-humans knock on the door very high up, and long-bodied beings knock very low down. Thus, without knocking in that way, one should knock in the middle, near the hole for the latch. Explaining this, they say this is the etiquette of knocking on a door.

261. Vivari bhagavā dvāranti na bhagavā uṭṭhāya dvāraṃ vivari. Vivariyatūti pana hatthaṃ pasāresi. Tato “bhagavā tumhehi [P 1.0253] anekāsu kappakoṭīsu dānaṃ dadamānehi na sahatthā dvāravivaraṇakammaṃ kata”nti sayameva dvāraṃ vivaṭaṃ. Taṃ pana yasmā bhagavato manena vivaṭaṃ, tasmā vivari bhagavā dvāranti vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

261. 'The Blessed One opened the door' means: the Blessed One did not get up and open the door. Rather, thinking, 'Let it be opened,' he extended his hand. Thereupon, as if in recognition that the Blessed One, who had given gifts for countless crores of eons, had never performed the act of opening a door with his own hand, the door opened by itself. However, since that door was opened by the mind of the Blessed One, it is therefore fitting to say, 'The Blessed One opened the door.'

Bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodiṃsūti yathā khamanīyādīni pucchanto bhagavā tehi, evaṃ tepi bhagavatā saddhiṃ samappavattamodā ahesuṃ. Sītodakaṃ viya uṇhodakena sammoditaṃ ekībhāvaṃ agamaṃsu. Yāya ca “kacci, bho gotama, khamanīyaṃ; kacci yāpanīyaṃ, kacci bhoto ca gotamassa sāvakānañca appābādhaṃ, appātaṅkaṃ, lahuṭṭhānaṃ, balaṃ, phāsuvihāro”tiādikāya kathāya sammodiṃsu, taṃ pītipāmojjasaṅkhātasammodajananato sammodituṃ yuttabhāvato ca sammodanīyaṃ, atthabyañjanamadhuratāya sucirampi kālaṃ sāretuṃ nirantaraṃ pavattetuṃ arahabhāvato saritabbabhāvato ca sāraṇīyaṃ. Suyyamānasukhato sammodanīyaṃ, anussariyamānasukhato ca sāraṇīyaṃ. Tathā byañjanaparisuddhatāya sammodanīyaṃ, atthaparisuddhatāya sāraṇīyaṃ. Evaṃ anekehi pariyāyehi sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā pariyosāpetvā niṭṭhapetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu.

They exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Just as the Blessed One inquired about their well-being and so forth, so they too had pleasant conversation with the Blessed One, with mutually flowing joy. Like cool water mixed with warm, they reached a state of unity. The conversation by which they greeted him—"Venerable Gotama, is it well with you? Are you able to continue? Is there little illness, little disease, lightness of body, strength, and comfortable living for you and your disciples?"—was fit to generate joy and delight, and so was a greeting (sammodanīyaṃ). Because of the sweetness of its meaning and phrasing, it was worthy of being remembered for a long time and continuously engaged in, and because it was fit to be recalled, it was something to be recalled (sāraṇīyaṃ). It was a greeting because of the pleasure in hearing it, and something to be recalled because of the pleasure in recollecting it. Due to the purity of its phrasing, it was a greeting (sammodanīyaṃ), and due to the purity of its meaning, it was something to be recalled (sāraṇīyaṃ). Thus, having brought this conversation, which in many ways was a greeting and something to be recalled, to an end, having finished it, and completed it, they sat down to one side.

Ambaṭṭho [M 1.0226] pana māṇavoti so kira bhagavato rūpasampattiyaṃ cittappasādamattampi akatvā “dasabalaṃ [V 1.0205] apasādessāmī”ti udare baddhasāṭakaṃ muñcitvā kaṇṭhe olambetvā ekena hatthena dussakaṇṇaṃ gahetvā caṅkamaṃ abhirūhitvā kālena bāhuṃ, kālena udaraṃ, kālena piṭṭhiṃ dassento, kālena hatthavikāraṃ, kālena bhamukavikāraṃ karonto, “kacci te bho, gotama, dhātusamatā, kacci bhikkhāhārena na kilamatha, akilamathākāroyeva pana te paññāyati; thūlāni hi te aṅgapaccaṅgāni, pāsādikattha gatagataṭṭhāne. ‘te bahujanā rājapabbajitoti ca buddho’ti ca uppannabahumānā paṇītaṃ ojavantamāhāraṃ denti. Passatha, bho, gehaṃ, cittasālā viya, dibbapāsādo viya. Imaṃ mañcaṃ passatha, bimbohanaṃ passatha, kiṃ evarūpe ṭhāne vasantassa samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ dukkara”nti evarūpaṃ uppaṇḍanakathaṃ anācārabhāvasāraṇīyaṃ katheti, tena [P 1.0254] vuttaṃ – “ambaṭṭho pana māṇavo caṅkamantopi nisinnena bhagavatā kiñci kiñci kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāreti, ṭhitopi nisinnena bhagavatā kiñci kiñci kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretī”ti.

'Ambaṭṭho pana māṇavo' means: it is said that Ambaṭṭha, without feeling even a little mental confidence in the Blessed One's perfection of form, thought, 'I will disparage the Ten-Powered One.' Having untied the cloth bound at his waist and let it hang from his neck, having grasped the edge of the cloth with one hand, he ascended the walking path. At times showing his arm, at times his belly, at times his back; at times making gestures with his hand, at times making gestures with his eyebrows, he said: 'I say, Gotama, are your bodily elements in balance? Do you not tire from eating almsfood? Indeed, your appearance shows no weariness. For your major and minor limbs are plump, and you are pleasing wherever you go. Many people, having great esteem, thinking, "He is one gone forth from royalty," and "He is a Buddha," give you exquisite and nutritious food. Look, sirs, at the dwelling, like a decorated hall, like a divine mansion. Look at this couch, look at this pillow. What is difficult about practicing the ascetic's duties for one living in such a place?' He spoke such mocking speech, which is memorable for its incivility. Therefore it was said: 'Ambaṭṭha the young man, while walking, exchanged some memorable conversation with the seated Blessed One; while standing, he exchanged some memorable conversation with the seated Blessed One.'

262. Atha kho bhagavāti atha bhagavā – “ayaṃ māṇavo hatthaṃ pasāretvā bhavaggaṃ gahetukāmo viya, pādaṃ pasāretvā avīciṃ vicaritukāmo viya, mahāsamuddaṃ taritukāmo viya, sineruṃ ārohitukāmo viya ca aṭṭhāne vāyamati, handa, tena saddhiṃ mantemī”ti ambaṭṭhaṃ māṇavaṃ etadavoca. Ācariyapācariyehīti ācariyehi ca tesaṃ ācariyehi ca.

Then the Blessed One, thinking: 'This young man strives in an impossible matter, like one stretching out his hand wishing to grasp the peak of existence, like one stretching out his foot wishing to wander in Avīci, like one wishing to swim across the great ocean, and like one wishing to ascend Mount Sineru. Come now, let me converse with him,' said this to the young man Ambaṭṭha. 'Ācariyapācariyehi' means: with teachers and with their teachers.

Paṭhamaibbhavādavaṇṇanā

262. Explanation of the First 'Ibbha' Statement

263. Gacchanto vāti ettha kāmaṃ tīsu iriyāpathesu brāhmaṇo ācariyabrāhmaṇena saddhiṃ sallapitumarahati. Ayaṃ pana māṇavo mānathaddhatāya kathāsallāpaṃ karonto cattāropi iriyāpathe yojessāmīti “sayāno vā hi, bho gotama, sayānenā”ti āha.

Regarding 'Whether walking': Here, it is indeed proper for a brahmin student to converse with his brahmin teacher in the three postures. This young man, however, due to his stiff pride, while engaging in conversation, thought, 'I will employ all four postures,' and thus said, 'Or lying down, Master Gotama, with one who is lying down...'

Tato [M 1.0227] kira taṃ bhagavā – “ambaṭṭha, gacchantassa vā gacchantena, ṭhitassa vā ṭhitena, nisinnassa vā nisinnenācariyena saddhiṃ kathā nāma sabbācariyesu labbhati. Tvaṃ pana sayāno sayānenācariyena saddhiṃ kathesi, kiṃ te ācariyo gorūpaṃ, udāhu tva”nti āha. So kujjhitvā – “ye ca kho te, bho gotama, muṇḍakā”tiādimāha. Tattha muṇḍe muṇḍāti samaṇe ca samaṇāti vattuṃ vaṭṭeyya. Ayaṃ pana hīḷento muṇḍakā samaṇakāti āha. Ibbhāti gahapatikā. Kaṇhāti kaṇhā, kāḷakāti attho. Bandhupādāpaccāti ettha bandhūti brahmā adhippeto. Tañhi brāhmaṇā pitāmahoti voharanti. Pādānaṃ apaccā pādāpaccā, brahmuno piṭṭhipādato [V 1.0206] jātāti adhippāyo. Tassa kira ayaṃ laddhi – brāhmaṇā brahmuno mukhato nikkhantā, khattiyā urato, vessā nābhito, suddā jāṇuto, samaṇā piṭṭhipādatoti. Evaṃ kathento ca panesa kiñcāpi aniyametvā katheti. Atha kho bhagavantameva vadāmīti katheti.

263. Then, it is said, the Blessed One said to him: 'Ambaṭṭha, conversation is indeed permissible among all teachers for a student who is walking with a teacher who is walking, for a student who is standing with a teacher who is standing, or for a student who is sitting with a teacher who is sitting. But you, lying down, converse with a teacher who is lying down. Is your teacher cow-like, or are you?' Angered, he replied: 'Those, Venerable Gotama, mere shavelings...' and so on. Here, it would be proper to call shaven ones 'shaven,' and ascetics 'ascetics.' But this one, intending to disparage, said 'mere shavelings, petty ascetics.' 'Ibbha' means 'little householders.' 'Kaṇha' means 'black'; the meaning is 'dark ones.' Regarding 'Bandhupādāpacca,' here 'Bandhu' (kinsman) is intended to mean Brahmā. For brahmins refer to him as 'Grandfather.' 'Pādānaṃ apaccā' means 'offspring of the feet'; the intention is 'born from Brahmā's instep.' For this is his doctrine: brahmins issued from Brahmā's mouth, khattiyas from his chest, vessas from his navel, suddas from his knees, and ascetics from his instep. And in speaking thus, although he spoke without specifying anyone, yet he spoke with the intention, 'I am speaking only of the Blessed One.'

Atha kho bhagavā – “ayaṃ ambaṭṭho āgatakālato paṭṭhāya mayā saddhiṃ kathayamāno mānameva nissāya kathesi, āsīvisaṃ [P 1.0255] gīvāyaṃ gaṇhanto viya, aggikkhandhaṃ āliṅganto viya, mattavāraṇaṃ soṇḍāya parāmasanto viya, attano pamāṇaṃ na jānāti. Handa naṃ jānāpessāmī”ti cintetvā “atthikavato kho pana te, ambaṭṭhā”tiādimāha. Tattha āgantvā kattabbakiccasaṅkhāto attho, etassa atthīti atthikaṃ, tassa māṇavassa cittaṃ. Atthikamassa atthīti atthikavā, tassa atthikavato tava idhāgamanaṃ ahosīti attho.

Then the Blessed One thought: 'This Ambaṭṭha, from the time of his arrival, in speaking with me has spoken relying solely on pride, like one grasping a venomous snake by the neck, like one embracing a mass of fire, or like one touching a maddened elephant on its trunk—he does not know his own measure. Well now, I shall make him know his measure.' Having reflected thus, he said, 'But you, Ambaṭṭha, have a purpose...' and so on. Therein, the meaning is as follows: the purpose, known as the duty to be performed upon arrival, exists for this mind, hence it is called `atthikaṃ`—the mind of that young man. He has this purposeful mind, hence he is `atthikavā`. Therefore, the meaning is: 'Your coming here was that of one with a purpose.'

Kho panāti nipātamattaṃ. Yāyeva kho panatthāyāti yeneva kho panatthena. Āgaccheyyāthāti mama vā aññesaṃ vā santikaṃ yadā kadāci āgaccheyyātha. Tameva atthanti idaṃ purisaliṅgavaseneva vuttaṃ. Manasi kareyyāthāti citte kareyyātha. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tvaṃ ācariyena attano karaṇīyena pesito, na amhākaṃ paribhavanatthāya, tasmā tameva kiccaṃ manasi karohīti. Evamassa aññesaṃ santikaṃ āgatānaṃ vattaṃ dassetvā mānaniggaṇhanatthaṃ “avusitavāyeva kho panā”tiādimāha. Tassattho passatha bho ayaṃ ambaṭṭho māṇavo ācariyakule avusitavā [M 1.0228] asikkhito appassutova samāno. Vusitamānīti “ahaṃ vusitavā sikkhito bahussuto”ti attānaṃ maññati. Etassa hi evaṃ pharusavacanasamudācāre kāraṇaṃ kimaññatra avusitattāti ācariyakule asaṃvuddhā asikkhitā appassutāyeva hi evaṃ vadantīti.

'Kho pana' is merely a particle. 'Yāyeva kho panatthāya' means 'for whatever purpose.' 'Āgaccheyyātha' means 'whenever you might come into my presence or that of others.' 'Tameva atthaṃ' is spoken in the masculine gender. 'Manasi kareyyātha' means 'you should place it in your mind.' This is what is said: 'You were sent by your teacher for his own task, not for the purpose of insulting us; therefore, you should attend only to that task in your mind.' Thus, having shown him the proper conduct for those who have come into the presence of others, in order to crush his pride, the Blessed One said, 'He has not lived in the teacher's household...' and so on. Its meaning is: 'Behold, sirs, this young man Ambaṭṭha, though not having lived in his teacher's household, is uninstructed and of little learning. Yet he is conceited about having lived there (`vusitamānī`), meaning he considers himself, "I have lived there, I am instructed, I am of great learning." For what other reason could there be for such harsh speech and conduct from him, other than his not having lived there? For indeed, it is only those who are uncultivated, uninstructed, and of little learning in a teacher's household who speak in this way.'

264. Kupitoti kuddho. Anattamanoti asakamano, kiṃ pana bhagavā tassa kujjhanabhāvaṃ ñatvā evamāha udāhu añatvāti? Ñatvā āhāti. Kasmā ñatvā āhāti? Tassa mānanimmadanatthaṃ. Bhagavā hi aññāsi – “ayaṃ mayā evaṃ vutte kujjhitvā mama ñātake akkosissati. Athassāhaṃ yathā nāma kusalo bhisakko dosaṃ uggiletvā nīharati, evameva gottena gottaṃ, kulāpadesena kulāpadesaṃ[P 1.0256], uṭṭhāpetvā bhavaggappamāṇena viya uṭṭhitaṃ mānaddhajaṃ mūle chetvā nipātessāmī”ti. Khuṃsentoti ghaṭṭento. Vambhentoti hīḷento. Pāpito bhavissatīti caṇḍabhāvādidosaṃ pāpito bhavissati.

264. ‘Kupito’ means angry. ‘Anattamano’ means displeased, with a mind not his own. But did the Blessed One speak thus knowing his state of being prone to anger, or without knowing it? He spoke knowing it. Why did he speak knowing it? To crush his pride. For the Blessed One knew beforehand: ‘When I speak thus, this one will get angry and abuse my relatives. Then, just as a skilled physician extracts a malady by causing it to be vomited up, so too will I, by raising up lineage against lineage and clan designation against clan designation, cut down at the root his banner of pride, which has risen as if to the height of the peak of existence, and make it fall.’ ‘Khuṃsento’ means provoking. ‘Vambhento’ means disparaging. ‘Pāpito bhavissati’ means he will be brought to the faulty state of being harsh and so on.

Caṇḍāti [V 1.0207] mānanissitakodhayuttā. Pharusāti kharā. Lahusāti lahukā. Appakeneva tussanti vā dussanti vā udakapiṭṭhe alābukaṭāhaṃ viya appakeneva uplavanti. Bhassāti bahubhāṇino. Sakyānaṃ mukhe vivaṭe aññassa vacanokāso natthīti adhippāyeneva vadati. Samānāti idaṃ santāti purimapadassa vevacanaṃ. Na sakkarontīti na brāhmaṇānaṃ sundarenākārena karonti. Na garuṃ karontīti brāhmaṇesu gāravaṃ na karonti. Na mānentīti na manena piyāyanti. Na pūjentīti mālādīhi nesaṃ pūjaṃ na karonti. Na apacāyantīti abhivādanādīhi nesaṃ apacitikammaṃ nīcavuttiṃ na dassenti tayidanti taṃ idaṃ. Yadime sakyāti yaṃ ime sakyā na brāhmaṇe sakkaronti…pe… na apacāyanti, taṃ tesaṃ asakkārakaraṇādi sabbaṃ na yuttaṃ, nānulomanti attho.

‘Caṇḍā’ means endowed with anger that relies on pride. ‘Pharusā’ means rough. ‘Lahusā’ means fickle. For little reason they are pleased or displeased; like a gourd bowl on the surface of the water, they float up for little reason. ‘Bhassā’ means talkative. The intention is that when the Sakyans' mouths are open, there is no opportunity for another to speak. ‘Samānā’: this is a synonym for the preceding word ‘santā’. ‘They do not honor’ means they do not treat the brahmins in a good manner. ‘They do not esteem’ means they show no reverence toward the brahmins. ‘They do not respect’ means they do not hold them dear in their minds. ‘They do not venerate’ means they do not offer them veneration with garlands and so forth. ‘They do not pay homage’ means they do not show them respectful action and humble conduct through gestures like salutation. ‘Tayidaṃ’ means ‘taṃ idaṃ’ (that is this). The phrase ‘yadime sakyā’ means ‘that these Sakyans do not honor the brahmins… and so on… do not pay homage.’ The meaning is that all such failure to honor and so on is not proper, not fitting.

Dutiyaibbhavādavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Second Accusation concerning Menials.

265. Aparaddhunti aparajjhiṃsu. Ekamidāhanti ettha idanti nipātamattaṃ. Ekaṃ ahanti attho. Sandhāgāranti rajjaanusāsanasālā. Sakyāti abhisittarājāno[M 1.0229]. Sakyakumārāti anabhisittā. Uccesūti yathānurūpesu pallaṅkapīṭhakavettāsanaphalakacittattharaṇādibhedesu. Sañjagghantāti uppaṇḍanavasena mahāhasitaṃ hasantā. Saṃkīḷantāti hasitamatta karaṇaaṅgulisaṅghaṭṭanapāṇippahāradānādīni karontā. Mamaññeva maññeti evamahaṃ maññāmi, mamaññeva anuhasanti, na aññanti.

265. ‘Aparaddhuṃ’ means they transgressed. In ‘ekamidāhaṃ,’ ‘idaṃ’ is merely a particle. The meaning is ‘ekaṃ ahaṃ’ (once, I). ‘Sandhāgāraṃ’ is the hall for instructing on state affairs. ‘Sakyā’ are the consecrated kings. ‘Sakyakumārā’ are the unconsecrated princes. ‘Uccesu’ means on various suitable seats such as couches, stools, wicker chairs, planks, and decorated mats. ‘Sañjagghantā’ means laughing a great laugh by way of mocking. ‘Saṃkīḷantā’ means doing things such as merely smiling, snapping fingers, and clapping hands. ‘Mamaññeva maññe’ means, ‘Thus I think: they are laughing directed only at me, not at anyone else.’

Kasmā pana te evamakaṃsūti? Te [P 1.0257] kira ambaṭṭhassa kulavaṃsaṃ jānanti. Ayañca tasmiṃ samaye yāva pādantā olambetvā nivatthasāṭakassa ekena hatthena dussakaṇṇaṃ gahetvā khandhaṭṭhikaṃ nāmetvā mānamadena matto viya āgacchati. Tato – “passatha bho amhākaṃ dāsassa kaṇhāyanagottassa ambaṭṭhassa āgamanakāraṇa”nti vadantā evamakaṃsu. Sopi attano kulavaṃsaṃ jānāti. Tasmā “mamaññeva maññe”ti takkayittha.

But why did they act thus? It is said that they knew Ambaṭṭha's family lineage. And at that time, he was coming along with his lower garment hanging down to his feet, holding the edge of the cloth with one hand, and raising his shoulder-bone, as if intoxicated with the intoxication of pride. Then, saying, 'Look, sirs, at the manner of arrival of Ambaṭṭha of the Kaṇhāyana clan, our slave,' they acted thus. He too knew his own lineage. Therefore, he reasoned, 'It is surely of me they think.'

Āsanenāti “idamāsanaṃ, ettha nisīdāhī”ti evaṃ āsanena nimantanaṃ nāma hoti, tathā na koci akāsi.

‘By a seat’ means that an invitation by means of a seat is when one says, ‘This is a seat, sit here’; but no one did so.

Tatiyaibbhavādavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Third Accusation concerning Menials.

266. Laṭukikāti [V 1.0208] khettaleḍḍūnaṃ antarenivāsinī khuddakasakuṇikā. Kulāvaketi nivāsanaṭṭhāne. Kāmalāpinīti yadicchakabhāṇinī, yaṃ yaṃ icchati taṃ taṃ lapati, na taṃ koci haṃso vā koñco vā moro vā āgantvā “kiṃ tvaṃ lapasī’ti nisedheti. Abhisajjitunti kodhavasena laggituṃ.

266. ‘Laṭukikā’ is a small female bird that lives between the clods of earth in a field. ‘In its own nest’ means in its dwelling place. ‘Speaking as it pleases’ means one who speaks as she wishes; whatever she wishes to say, that she says, and no goose, crane, or peacock comes and forbids her, saying, ‘What are you saying?’ ‘To get angry’ means to attack out of anger.

Evaṃ vutte māṇavo – “ayaṃ samaṇo gotamo attano ñātake laṭukikasadise katvā amhe haṃsakoñcamorasadise karoti, nimmāno dāni jāto”ti maññamāno uttari cattāro vaṇṇe dasseti.

When this was said, the young man, thinking, 'This ascetic Gotama, by making his own relatives like the laṭukikā bird and making us like geese, cranes, and peacocks, has now become without pride,' further pointed out the four classes.

Dāsiputtavādavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Saying about the Son of a Slave Woman.

267. Nimmādetīti nimmadeti nimmāne karoti. Yaṃnūnāhanti yadi panāhaṃ. “Kaṇhāyanohamasmi, bho gotamā”ti idaṃ kira vacanaṃ ambaṭṭho tikkhattuṃ [M 1.0230] mahāsaddena avoca. Kasmā avoca? Kiṃ asuddhabhāvaṃ na jānātīti? Āma jānāti. Jānantopi bhavapaṭicchannametaṃ kāraṇaṃ, taṃ anena na diṭṭhaṃ. Apassanto mahāsamaṇo kiṃ vakkhatīti maññamāno mānathaddhatāya avoca. Mātāpettikanti mātāpitūnaṃ santakaṃ. Nāmagottanti paṇṇattivasena nāmaṃ, paveṇīvasena gottaṃ. Anussaratoti anussarantassa kulakoṭiṃ sodhentassa. Ayyaputtāti sāmino puttā. Dāsiputtoti gharadāsiyāva putto. Tasmā yathā dāsena sāmino upasaṅkamitabbā, evaṃ anupasaṅkamantaṃ [P 1.0258] taṃ disvā sakyā anujagghiṃsūti dasseti.

267. 'He makes them without pride' means he makes them without conceit. 'What if I were to...' means 'If I were to ask, it would be good.' It is said that Ambaṭṭha loudly repeated this phrase, 'I am of the Kaṇhāyana clan, good Gotama,' three times. Why did he say it? Does he not know the fact of his lineage being impure? Yes, he knows. But even knowing, he thought, 'This reason is concealed by his state of being; it has not been seen by this ascetic. Not seeing it, what will the great ascetic be able to say?' and so he spoke out of the stiffness of pride. 'Belonging to mother and father' means belonging to one's mother and father. 'Name and lineage' means the name by way of designation, and the lineage by way of tradition. 'As he was tracing back' means of one who is tracing back, of one who is purifying the origin of the lineage. 'Sons of the master' means sons of the lord. 'Son of a slave woman' means the son of a house-slave woman. Therefore, it is shown that: 'Because the Sakyans are sons of the master and you are the son of a slave woman, seeing you not approaching in the way a slave should approach his masters, the Sakyans laughed derisively at you.'

Ito paraṃ tassa dāsabhāvaṃ sakyānañca sāmibhāvaṃ pakāsetvā attano ca ambaṭṭhassa ca kulavaṃsaṃ āharanto sakyā kho panātiādimāha. Tattha dahantīti ṭhapenti, okkāko no pubbapurisoti, evaṃ karontīti attho. Tassa kira rañño kathanakāle ukkā viya mukhato pabhā niccharati, tasmā taṃ “okkāko”ti sañjāniṃsūti. Pabbājesīti nīhari.

Hereafter, having revealed his status as a slave and the Sakyans' status as masters, and wishing to bring forth the lineage of both himself and Ambaṭṭha, he spoke the passage beginning 'The Sakyans, indeed...' Therein, 'dahanti' means they establish, they designate; the meaning is, 'they do thus: "Okkāka is our ancestor."' It is said that when that king spoke, a light issued from his mouth like a torch flame; therefore, they recognized him as 'Okkāka.' 'Pabbājesi' means he expelled.

Idāni te nāmavasena dassento – “okkāmukha”ntiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ anupubbī kathā – paṭhamakappikānaṃ kira rañño mahāsammatassa rojo nāma putto ahosi. Rojassa vararojo, vararojassa kalyāṇo, kalyāṇassa varakalyāṇo, varakalyāṇassa mandhātā, mandhātussa varamandhātā[V 1.0209], varamandhātussa uposatho, uposathassa varo, varassa upavaro, upavarassa maghadevo, maghadevassa paramparāya caturāsītikhattiyasahassāni ahesuṃ. Tesaṃ pacchato tayo okkākavaṃsā ahesuṃ. Tesu tatiyaokkākassa pañca mahesiyo ahesuṃ – hatthā, cittā, jantu, jālinī, visākhāti. Ekekissā pañcapañcaitthisataparivārā. Sabbajeṭṭhāya cattāro puttā – okkāmukho, karakaṇḍu, hatthiniko, sinisūroti. Pañca dhītaro – piyā, suppiyā, ānandā, vijitā, vijitasenāti. Iti sā nava putte vijāyitvā kālamakāsi.

Now, wishing to show them by way of name, he spoke the passage beginning 'Okkāmukha...' Therein, this is the sequential story: It is said that among those of the first aeon, King Mahāsammata had a son named Roja. Roja's son was Vararoja; Vararoja's son was Kalyāṇa; Kalyāṇa's son was Varakalyāṇa; Varakalyāṇa's son was Mandhātā; Mandhātā's son was Varamandhātā; Varamandhātā's son was Uposatha; Uposatha's son was Vara; Vara's son was Upavara; Upavara's son was Maghadeva. In Maghadeva's line, there were eighty-four thousand kings. After them, there were three successions of the Okkāka lineage. Among them, the third Okkāka had five chief queens: Hatthā, Cittā, Jantu, Jālinī, and Visākhā. Each had an entourage of five hundred women. The eldest chief queen had four sons: Okkāmukha, Karakaṇḍu, Hatthinika, and Sinisūra; and five daughters: Piyā, Suppiyā, Ānandā, Vijitā, and Vijitasenā. Thus, having given birth to nine children, she passed away.

Atha rājā aññaṃ dahariṃ abhirūpaṃ rājadhītaraṃ ānetvā aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Sā jantuṃ nāma puttaṃ vijāyi. Atha naṃ pañcamadivase alaṅkaritvā [M 1.0231] rañño dassesi. Rājā tuṭṭho tassā varaṃ adāsi. Sā ñātakehi saddhiṃ mantetvā puttassa rajjaṃ yāci. Rājā – “nassa, vasali, mama puttānaṃ antarāyaṃ icchasī”ti tajjesi. Sā punappunaṃ raho rājānaṃ paritosetvā – “mahārāja, musāvādo nāma na vaṭṭatī”tiādīni vatvā yācatiyeva. Atha rājā putte āmantesi – “ahaṃ tātā, tumhākaṃ kaniṭṭhaṃ jantukumāraṃ disvā tassa mātuyā sahasā varaṃ adāsiṃ[P 1.0259], sā puttassa rajjaṃ pariṇāmetuṃ icchati. Tumhe ṭhapetvā maṅgalahatthiṃ maṅgalaassaṃ maṅgalarathañca yattake icchatha, tattake hatthiassarathe gahetvā gacchatha. Mamaccayena āgantvā rajjaṃ kareyyāthā”ti, aṭṭhahi amaccehi saddhiṃ uyyojesi.

Then the king brought another young and beautiful princess and established her in the position of chief queen. She gave birth to a son named Jantu. Then, on the fifth day, having adorned him, she showed him to the king. The king, being pleased, granted her a boon. She, having consulted with her relatives, asked for the kingdom for her son. The king rebuked her, saying, 'Perish, you wretch! You desire harm for my elder sons.' She, again and again, pleasing the king in private and saying things such as, 'Great king, speaking falsehood is not proper,' kept on asking. Then the king addressed his elder sons, saying: 'My dear sons, upon seeing your youngest brother, Jantu, I hastily granted his mother a boon. She wishes to transfer the kingdom to her son. You, leaving aside the state elephant, the state horse, and the state chariot, may take as many elephants, horses, and chariots as you wish and depart. After my passing, you may return and take the kingdom.' And he sent them away together with eight ministers.

Te nānappakāraṃ roditvā kanditvā – “tāta, amhākaṃ dosaṃ khamathā”ti rājānañceva rājorodhe ca khamāpetvā, “mayampi bhātūhi saddhiṃ gacchāmā”ti rājānaṃ āpucchitvā nagarā nikkhantā bhaginiyo ādāya caturaṅginiyā senāya parivutā nagarā nikkhamiṃsu. “Kumārā pituaccayena āgantvā rajjaṃ kāressanti, gacchāma ne upaṭṭhahāmā”ti cintetvā bahū manussā anubandhiṃsu. Paṭhamadivase yojanamattā senā ahosi, dutiye dviyojanamattā, tatiye tiyojanamattā. Kumārā mantayiṃsu – “mahā balakāyo, sace mayaṃ kañci sāmantarājānaṃ madditvā janapadaṃ gaṇheyyāma, sopi no nappasaheyya. Kiṃ paresaṃ pīḷāya katāya, mahā ayaṃ jambudīpo, araññe nagaraṃ māpessāmā”ti himavantābhimukhā gantvā nagaravatthuṃ pariyesiṃsu.

They wept and lamented in various ways, saying, “Father, forgive our fault,” and after causing the king and the royal consorts to forgive them, they took their sisters—who had departed from the city after taking leave of the king, saying, “We too shall go with our brothers”—and went forth from the city, surrounded by a fourfold army. Thinking, “The princes will return after their father’s passing and rule the kingdom; let us go and attend upon them,” many people followed them. On the first day, the army was one yojana in extent; on the second, two yojanas; and on the third, three yojanas. The princes deliberated: “The body of troops is great. If we were to crush a neighboring king and take his country, he would not be able to overcome us. But what is the use of affliction caused to others? This Jambudīpa is vast; let us create a city in the forest.” Facing the Himalayas, they went in search of a site for a city.

Tasmiñca samaye amhākaṃ bodhisatto brāhmaṇamahāsālakule nibbattitvā kapilabrāhmaṇo nāma hutvā nikkhamma isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavantapasse pokkharaṇiyā tīre sākavanasaṇḍe paṇṇasālaṃ māpetvā vasati. So kira bhummajālaṃ nāma vijjaṃ jānāti, yāya uddhaṃ asītihatthe ākāse, heṭṭhā ca bhūmiyampi guṇadosaṃ passati. Etasmiṃ padese tiṇagumbalatā [V 1.0210] dakkhiṇāvaṭṭā pācīnābhimukhā jāyanti. Sīhabyagghādayo migasūkare sappabiḷārā ca maṇḍūkamūsike anubandhamānā taṃ padesaṃ patvā na sakkonti te anubandhituṃ. Tehi te aññadatthu [M 1.0232] santajjitā nivattantiyeva. So – “ayaṃ pathaviyā aggapadeso”ti ñatvā tattha attano paṇṇasālaṃ māpesi.

At that time, our Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of great brahmin wealth, and becoming known as Kapila the Brahmin, he went forth into the ascetic life. He resided in a leaf-hut which he had made in a grove of teak trees on the shore of a pond on the slopes of the Himalayas. It is said that he knew a science called Bhummajāla, by which he could perceive virtues and faults eighty cubits above in the sky, eighty cubits below in the earth, and also upon the earth's surface. In that place, grasses, shrubs, and vines grew curving to the right and facing east. When lions, tigers, and other predators pursued deer and boars, or when snakes and cats pursued frogs and mice, upon reaching that place, they were unable to continue the pursuit. On the contrary, being threatened by their prey, they would simply turn back. Knowing, “This is the foremost place on earth,” he had his leaf-hut made there.

Atha te kumāre nagaravatthuṃ pariyesamāne attano vasanokāsaṃ [P 1.0260] āgate disvā pucchitvā taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā tesu anukampaṃ janetvā avoca – “imasmiṃ paṇṇasālaṭṭhāne māpitaṃ nagaraṃ jambudīpe agganagaraṃ bhavissati. Ettha jātapurisesu ekeko purisasatampi purisasahassampi abhibhavituṃ sakkhissati. Ettha nagaraṃ māpetha, paṇṇasālaṭṭhāne rañño gharaṃ karotha. Imasmiñhi okāse ṭhatvā caṇḍālaputtopi cakkavattibalena atiseyyo”ti. Nanu, bhante, ayyassa vasanokāsoti? “Mama vasanokāso”ti mā cintayittha. Mayhaṃ ekapasse paṇṇasālaṃ katvā nagaraṃ māpetvā kapilavatthunti nāmaṃ karothā”ti. Te tathā katvā tattha nivāsaṃ kappesuṃ.

Then, seeing the princes who were searching for a site for a city arrive at his dwelling place, he inquired, and having learned their story, he generated compassion for them and said: “A city built on the site of this leaf-hut will become the foremost city in Jambudīpa. Of the men born here, a single one will be able to overcome even a hundred or a thousand men. Build a city here, and make the king’s palace on the site of the leaf-hut. For standing in this place, even the son of an outcaste would be superior with the might of a wheel-turning monarch.” “But venerable sir, is this not your dwelling place?” “Do not think, ‘This is my dwelling place.’ Make a leaf-hut for me on one side, build the city, and give it the name Kapilavatthu.” They did so and established their residence there.

Athāmaccā – “ime dārakā vayappattā, sace nesaṃ pitā santike bhaveyya, so āvāhavivāhaṃ kareyya. Idāni pana amhākaṃ bhāro”ti cintetvā kumārehi saddhiṃ mantayiṃsu. Kumārā amhākaṃ sadisā khattiyadhītaro nāma na passāma, nāpi bhaginīnaṃ sadise khattiyakumārake, asadisasaṃyoge ca no uppannā puttā mātito vā pitito vā aparisuddhā jātisambhedaṃ pāpuṇissanti. Tasmā mayaṃ bhaginīhiyeva saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ rocemāti. Te jātisambhedabhayena jeṭṭhakabhaginiṃ mātuṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā avasesāhi saṃvāsaṃ kappesuṃ.

Then the ministers thought, “These young men have come of age. If their father were near, he would arrange their marriages. But now it is our responsibility.” Having thought thus, they consulted with the princes. The princes said, “We do not see any khattiya daughters who are our equals, nor do we see any khattiya princes who are the equals of our sisters. And in an unequal union, the children born to us would be impure from either the mother’s side or the father’s side and would attain a mixing of birth. Therefore, we prefer to cohabit with our sisters alone.” Fearing the mixing of birth, they placed the eldest sister in the position of a mother and cohabited with the remaining sisters.

Tesaṃ puttehi ca dhītāhi ca vaḍḍhamānānaṃ aparena samayena jeṭṭhakabhaginiyā kuṭṭharogo udapādi, koviḷārapupphasadisāni gattāni ahesuṃ. Rājakumārā imāya saddhiṃ ekato nisajjaṭṭhānabhojanādīni karontānampi upari ayaṃ rogo saṅkamatīti cintetvā ekadivasaṃ uyyānakīḷaṃ gacchantā viya taṃ yāne āropetvā araññaṃ pavisitvā bhūmiyaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇāpetvā tattha khādanīyabhojanīyena saddhiṃ taṃ pakkhipitvā gharasaṅkhepena upari padaraṃ paṭicchādetvā paṃsuṃ datvā pakkamiṃsu.

As they were flourishing with sons and daughters, after some time the disease of leprosy arose in the eldest sister; her limbs became like koviḷāra flowers. The princes, thinking, “This disease is contagious even to those who sit, stand, and eat together with her,” one day, as if going for sport in the park, placed her in a vehicle, entered the forest, and had a pond dug in the ground. They placed her in it together with hard and soft food, covered it over with a plank in the manner of a house, put soil on top, and departed.

Tena [M 1.0233] ca samayena rāmo nāma bārāṇasirājā kuṭṭharogo nāṭakitthīhi ca orodhehi ca jigucchiyamāno tena saṃvegena jeṭṭhaputtassa rajjaṃ datvā araññaṃ pavisitvā tattha paṇṇasālaṃ māpetvā [P 1.0261] mūlaphalāni paribhuñjanto nacirasseva arogo suvaṇṇavaṇṇo hutvā ito cito ca vicaranto [V 1.0211] mahantaṃ susirarukkhaṃ disvā tassabbhantare soḷasahatthappamāṇaṃ okāsaṃ sodhetvā dvārañca vātapānañca yojetvā nisseṇiṃ bandhitvā tattha vāsaṃ kappesi. So aṅgārakaṭāhe aggiṃ katvā rattiṃ migasūkarādīnaṃ sadde suṇanto sayati. So – “asukasmiṃ padese sīho saddamakāsi, asukasmiṃ byaggho”ti sallakkhetvā pabhāte tattha gantvā vighāsamaṃsaṃ ādāya pacitvā khādati.

At that time, a king of Bārāṇasī named Rāma, who was afflicted with leprosy, was despised by the dancing girls and the women of the court. Moved by this distress, he handed over the kingdom to his eldest son and entered the forest. There, he had a leaf-hut made and lived on roots and fruits. Before long, he became free from illness and his complexion became golden. Wandering here and there, he saw a large hollow tree. He cleared a space of sixteen cubits inside it, fitted a door and a window, fastened a ladder, and took up residence there. He would make a fire in a charcoal pan and lie down at night, listening to the sounds of deer, boars, and other animals. He would note, “In such-and-such a place a lion made a sound, in such-and-such a place a tiger,” and in the morning, he would go there, take the leftover meat, cook it, and eat.

Athekadivasaṃ tasmiṃ paccūsasamaye aggiṃ jāletvā nisinne rājadhītāya sarīragandhena āgantvā byaggho tasmiṃ padese paṃsuṃ viyūhanto padare vivaramakāsi, tena ca vivarena sā byagghaṃ disvā bhītā vissaramakāsi. So taṃ saddaṃ sutvā – “itthisaddo eso”ti ca sallakkhetvā pātova tattha gantvā – “ko etthā”ti āha. Mātugāmo sāmīti. Kiṃ jātikāsīti? Okkākamahārājassa dhītā sāmīti. Nikkhamāti? Na sakkā sāmīti. Kiṃ kāraṇāti? Chavirogo me atthīti. So sabbaṃ pavattiṃ pucchitvā khattiyamānena anikkhamantiṃ – “ahampi khattiyo”ti attano khattiyabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā nisseṇiṃ datvā uddharitvā attano vasanokāsaṃ netvā sayaṃ paribhuttabhesajjāniyeva datvā nacirasseva arogaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ katvā tāya saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ kappesi. Sā paṭhamasaṃvāseneva gabbhaṃ gaṇhitvā dve putte vijāyi, punapi dveti, evaṃ soḷasakkhattumpi vijāyi. Evaṃ dvattiṃsa bhātaro ahesuṃ. Te anupubbena vuḍḍhippatte pitā sabbasippāni sikkhāpesi.

Then, one day at dawn, while he was sitting, having kindled a fire, a tiger, attracted by the scent of the princess's body, came to that place and, while digging up the earth, made an opening in the plank. Through that opening, she saw the tiger and, becoming frightened, made a distressed cry. He, having heard that sound and noting, 'This is the voice of a woman,' went there early in the morning and asked, 'Who is here?' 'A woman, sir.' 'Of what caste are you?' 'I am the daughter of the great king Okkāka, sir.' 'Come out.' 'It is not possible, sir.' 'For what reason?' 'I have a skin disease.' He, having asked about the entire incident, and as she would not come out due to her Khattiya pride, made known his own Khattiya status by saying, 'I too am a Khattiya.' Then, having given her a ladder, he lifted her out, took her to his own dwelling place, and gave her the very medicines he himself had used. Before long, he made her free from disease and of a golden complexion, and he cohabited with her. She, from the very first cohabitation, conceived and gave birth to two sons. Again, she gave birth to two, and thus she gave birth sixteen times. In this way, there were thirty-two brothers. As they successively reached maturity, their father had them taught all the arts.

Athekadivasaṃ eko rāmarañño nagaravāsī vanacarako pabbate ratanāni gavesanto rājānaṃ disvā sañjānitvā āha – “jānāmahaṃ, deva, tumhe”ti. Tato naṃ rājā sabbaṃ pavattiṃ pucchi. Tasmiṃyeva ca khaṇe te dārakā āgamiṃsu. So te disvā – “ke ime”ti āha. “Puttā me”ti ca vutte tesaṃ mātikavaṃsaṃ [P 1.0262] pucchitvā – “laddhaṃ dāni me [M 1.0234] pābhata”nti nagaraṃ gantvā rañño ārocesi. So ‘pitaraṃ ānayissāmī’ti caturaṅginiyā senāya tattha gantvā pitaraṃ vanditvā – “rajjaṃ, deva, sampaṭicchā”ti yāci. So – “alaṃ, tāta, na tattha gacchāmi, idheva me imaṃ rukkhaṃ apanetvā nagaraṃ māpehī”ti āha. So tathā katvā tassa nagarassa kolarukkhaṃ apanetvā katattā kolanagaranti ca byagghapathe katattā byagghapathanti cāti dve nāmāni āropetvā pitaraṃ vanditvā attano nagaraṃ agamāsi.

Then one day, a certain city-dwelling forest-wanderer of King Rāma, while searching for gems on a mountain, saw the king, recognized him, and said: 'I know you, Your Majesty.' Thereupon, the king asked him about the entire situation. And at that very moment, those boys arrived. The forest-wanderer, seeing them, asked, 'Who are these?' When it was said, 'They are my sons,' he asked about their maternal lineage and, thinking, 'Now I have obtained a gift of news,' he went to the city and informed the king. That king, thinking, 'I will bring my father,' went there with a four-limbed army, paid homage to his father, and pleaded, 'Your Majesty, please accept the kingship.' He replied, 'Enough, dear son, I will not go there. Right here, for my sake, have a city built after removing this Kola tree.' He did so, and because that city was made by removing the Kola tree, it was named Kolanagara, and because it was made on the tiger's path, it was named Byagghapatha. Thus, having established the two names, he paid homage to his father and returned to his own city.

Tato vayappatte kumāre mātā āha – “tātā, tumhākaṃ kapilavatthuvāsino sakyā mātulā santi. Mātuladhītānaṃ pana vo evarūpaṃ nāma kesaggahaṇaṃ hoti, evarūpaṃ dussagahaṇaṃ. Yadā [V 1.0212] tā nhānatitthaṃ āgacchanti, tadā gantvā yassa yā ruccati, so taṃ gaṇhatū”ti. Te tatheva gantvā tāsu nhatvā sīsaṃ sukkhāpayamānāsu yaṃ yaṃ icchiṃsu, taṃ taṃ gahetvā nāmaṃ sāvetvā agamiṃsu. Sakyarājāno sutvā “hotu, bhaṇe, amhākaṃ ñātakā eva te”ti tuṇhī ahesuṃ. Ayaṃ sakyakoliyānaṃ uppatti. Evaṃ tesaṃ sakyakoliyānaṃ aññamaññaṃ āvāhavivāhaṃ karontānaṃ yāva buddhakālā anupacchinnova vaṃso āgato. Tattha bhagavā sakyavaṃsaṃ dassetuṃ – “te raṭṭhasmā pabbājitā himavantapasse pokkharaṇiyā tīre”tiādimāha. Tattha sammantīti vasanti. Sakyā vata bhoti raṭṭhasmā pabbājitā araññe vasantāpi jātisambhedamakatvā kulavaṃsaṃ anurakkhituṃ sakyā, samatthā, paṭibalāti attho. Tadaggeti taṃ aggaṃ katvā, tato paṭṭhāyāti attho.
