So ca nesaṃ pubbapurisoti so okkāko rājā etesaṃ pubbapuriso. Natthi etesaṃ gahapativaṃsena sambhedamattampīti.

Thereupon, when the princes came of age, their mother said: 'Dear sons, you have maternal uncles, the Sakyans, who dwell in Kapilavatthu. For your maternal cousins, there is such-and-such a way of taking the hair and such-and-such a way of taking their garments. When they come to the bathing place, go there, and whichever princess is pleasing to whichever son, let him take her.' They went just as she had said, and while the princesses, having bathed, were drying their hair, they took whichever ones they desired, announced their own names, and came away. The Sakyan kings, having heard this, said, 'So be it, sirs. They are our own kinsmen,' and they became silent. This is the origin of the Sakyans and the Koliyans. Thus, as those Sakyans and Koliyans performed marriages with one another, the lineage came down unbroken until the time of the Buddha. Therein, the Blessed One, to show the Sakyan lineage, said: 'Banished from their country...' and so on. Therein, 'sammanti' means 'they dwell.' 'Sakyā vata bho' means: 'Indeed, they were able! Though banished from the country and living in the forest, they were able, capable, and competent to preserve their family lineage without mixing their caste.' This is the meaning. 'Tadagge' means 'making that the beginning,' that is, 'starting from that.' This is the meaning. 'So ca nesaṃ pubbapuriso' means: That King Okkāka was their ancestor. There was not even a trace of mixing with the lineage of householders.

Evaṃ sakyavaṃsaṃ pakāsetvā idāni ambaṭṭhavaṃsaṃ pakāsento – “rañño kho panā”tiādimāha. Kaṇhaṃ [P 1.0263] nāma janesīti kāḷavaṇṇaṃ antokucchiyaṃyeva sañjātadantaṃ parūḷhamassudāṭhikaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi. Pabyāhāsīti yakkho jātoti bhayena palāyitvā dvāraṃ pidhāya ṭhitesu gharamānusakesu ito cito ca vicaranto dhovatha mantiādīni vadanto uccāsaddamakāsi.

Having thus explained the Sakyan lineage, now, wishing to explain the lineage of Ambaṭṭha, he spoke the words beginning with 'rañño kho pana...' As to 'Kaṇhaṃ nāma janesi,' it means: she gave birth to a black-complexioned son with teeth already grown in the womb and a fully grown beard and canine teeth. As to 'pabyāhāsi,' it means: when the people of the house, saying, 'A yakkha has been born!', fled in fear, shut the door, and stood there, he, wandering here and there and saying things such as, 'Wash me!', made a loud noise.

268. Te [M 1.0235] māṇavakā bhagavantaṃ etadavocunti attano upārambhamocanatthāya – “etaṃ mā bhava”ntiādivacanaṃ avocuṃ. Tesaṃ kira etadahosi – “ambaṭṭho amhākaṃ ācariyassa jeṭṭhantevāsī, sace mayaṃ evarūpe ṭhāne ekadvevacanamattampi na vakkhāma, ayaṃ no ācariyassa santike amhe paribhindissatī”ti upārambhamocanatthaṃ evaṃ avocuṃ. Cittena panassa nimmadabhāvaṃ ākaṅkhanti. Ayaṃ kira mānanissitattā tesampi appiyova. Kalyāṇavākkaraṇoti madhuravacano. Asmiṃ vacaneti attanā uggahite vedattayavacane. Paṭimantetunti pucchitaṃ pañhaṃ paṭikathetuṃ, vissajjetunti attho. Etasmiṃ vā dāsiputtavacane. Paṭimantetunti uttaraṃ kathetuṃ.

268. As to 'Those young men spoke thus to the Blessed One': for the purpose of freeing themselves from blame, they spoke the words beginning with, 'Let this not be so, good sir.' It seems this was their thought: 'Ambaṭṭha is our teacher's senior pupil. If we, in such a situation, do not say even a word or two, he will slander us to our teacher.' Thus, for the purpose of freeing themselves from blame, they spoke in this way. But in their minds, they desired his state of being without pride. It seems that he, because of his reliance on conceit, was indeed disliked by them too. 'Kalyāṇavākkaraṇo' means 'one of sweet speech.' 'Asmiṃ vacane' means 'in the speech of the three Vedas that he had learned.' 'Paṭimantetuṃ' means 'to speak back to a question that was asked,' that is, 'to answer.' Alternatively, in this speech about being a slave-woman's son, 'paṭimantetuṃ' means 'to speak a reply.'

269. Atha kho bhagavāti atha kho bhagavā – “sace ime māṇavakā ettha nisinnā evaṃ uccāsaddaṃ karissanti, ayaṃ kathā pariyosānaṃ na gamissati. Handa, ne nissadde katvā ambaṭṭheneva saddhiṃ kathemī”ti te māṇavake etadavoca. Tattha mantavhoti mantayatha. Mayā saddhiṃ paṭimantetūti mayā saha kathetu. Evaṃ vutte māṇavakā cintayiṃsu – “ambaṭṭho tāva dāsiputtosīti vutte puna sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ nāsakkhi. Ayaṃ kho jāti nāma dujjānā, sace [V 1.0213] aññampi kiñci samaṇo gotamo ‘tvaṃ dāso’ti vakkhati, ko tena saddhiṃ aḍḍaṃ karissati. Ambaṭṭho attanā baddhaṃ puṭakaṃ attanāva mocetū”ti attānaṃ parimocetvā tasseva upari khipantā – “sujāto ca bho gotamā”tiādimāhaṃsu.

269. Then the Blessed One thought: "If these young men, sitting here, make such a loud noise, this discussion will not reach its conclusion. Now, let me make them silent and speak with Ambaṭṭha alone." And he said this to those young men. Therein, `mantavho` means deliberate. `Mayā saddhiṃ paṭimantetu` means let him speak with me. When this was said, the young men thought: "When told, 'Ambaṭṭha, you are the son of a slave woman,' he was unable to lift his head again. This thing called birth is indeed difficult to know. If the ascetic Gotama says to someone else, 'You are a slave,' who will argue with him? Let Ambaṭṭha untie the bundle he himself has tied." Freeing themselves and throwing it upon him, they said, "Well-born is Master Gotama," and so on.

270. Sahadhammikoti sahetuko sakāraṇo. Akāmā byākātabboti attanā anicchantenapi byākaritabbo, avassaṃ vissajjetabboti attho. Aññena [P 1.0264] vā aññaṃ paṭicarissasīti aññena vacanena aññaṃ vacanaṃ paṭicarissasi ajjhottharissasi, paṭicchādessasīti attho. Yo hi “kiṃ gotto tva”nti evaṃ puṭṭho – “ahaṃ tayo vede jānāmī”tiādīni vadati, ayaṃ aññena aññaṃ paṭicarati nāma. Pakkamissasi vāti pucchitaṃ pañhaṃ jānantova akathetukāmatāya uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkamissasi vā.

270. ‘With good reason’ (sahadhammika) means with generative cause, with supporting cause. ‘Should be answered unwillingly’ (akāmā byākātabba) means it should be answered even if one does not wish to; the meaning is, it must certainly be answered. ‘Or you will cover over one thing with another’ (aññena vā aññaṃ paṭicarissasi) means you will cover over one statement with another statement, you will obscure it, you will conceal it. This is the meaning. For one who, when asked, ‘What is your clan?’ says such things as, ‘I know the three Vedas,’ this is called covering over one thing with another. ‘Or will you go away’ (pakkamissasi vā) means, knowing the question that was asked, will you rise from your seat and go away out of an unwillingness to speak?

Tuṇhī [M 1.0236] ahosīti samaṇo gotamo maṃ sāmaṃyeva dāsiputtabhāvaṃ kathāpetukāmo, sāmaṃ kathite ca dāso nāma jātoyeva hoti. Ayaṃ pana dvatikkhattuṃ codetvā tuṇhī bhavissati, tato ahaṃ parivattitvā pakkamissāmīti cintetvā tuṇhī ahosi.

‘He was silent’ (tuṇhī ahosi) means: He thought, ‘The ascetic Gotama desires to make me myself state the fact of being a slave-woman's son, and when it is stated by oneself, one is truly established as a slave. However, this one, after reproaching me twice or three times, will become silent, and then I will turn around and go away.’ Thinking thus, he was silent.

271. Vajiraṃ pāṇimhi assāti vajirapāṇi. Yakkhoti na yo vā so vā yakkho, sakko devarājāti veditabbo. Ādittanti aggivaṇṇaṃ. Sampajjalitanti suṭṭhu pajjalitaṃ. Sajotibhūtanti samantato jotibhūtaṃ, ekaggijālabhūtanti attho. Ṭhito hotīti mahantaṃ sīsaṃ, kandalamakuḷasadisā dāṭhā bhayānakāni akkhināsādīni evaṃ virūparūpaṃ māpetvā ṭhito.

271. ‘Because there is a vajra in his hand’ (vajiraṃ pāṇimhi assa), he is Vajirapāṇi. ‘Yakkha’ (yakkha) is not just any yakkha; it should be known as Sakka, the king of the devas. ‘Blazing’ (āditta) means having the color of fire. ‘Aflame’ (sampajjalita) means well ablaze. ‘Radiant’ (sajotibhūta) means having become radiant all around; the meaning is having become a single mass of flames. ‘He stood’ (ṭhito hoti) means: having created a deformed form—with a great head, fangs like kandala buds, and frightening eyes, nose, and so on—he stood.

Kasmā panesa āgatoti? Diṭṭhivissajjāpanatthaṃ. Api ca – “ahañceva kho pana dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ, pare ca me na ājāneyyu”nti evaṃ dhammadesanāya appossukkabhāvaṃ āpanne bhagavati sakko mahābrahmunā saddhiṃ āgantvā – “bhagavā dhammaṃ desetha, tumhākaṃ āṇāya avattamāne mayaṃ vattāpessāma, tumhākaṃ dhammacakkaṃ hotu, amhākaṃ āṇācakka”nti paṭiññaṃ akāsi. Tasmā – “ajja ambaṭṭhaṃ tāsetvā pañhaṃ vissajjāpessāmī”ti āgato.

But why did he come? To make him relinquish his view. Furthermore, when the Blessed One had reached a state of being unconcerned about teaching the Dhamma, thinking, ‘If I were to teach the Dhamma, others might not understand me,’ Sakka came together with Mahābrahmā and made a promise, saying: ‘Let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma. Those who do not conduct themselves under your authority, we will make them do so. Let there be your Wheel of Dhamma; let there be our wheel of authority.’ Therefore, he came thinking, ‘Today, having frightened Ambaṭṭha, I will make him answer the question.’

Bhagavā ceva passati ambaṭṭho cāti yadi hi taṃ aññepi passeyyuṃ, taṃ kāraṇaṃ agaru assa, “ayaṃ samaṇo gotamo ambaṭṭhaṃ attano vāde anotarantaṃ ñatvā yakkhaṃ āvāhetvā dassesi, tato ambaṭṭho bhayena kathesī”ti vadeyyuṃ. Tasmā bhagavā ceva passati ambaṭṭho ca. Tassa taṃ disvāva sakalasarīrato sedā mucciṃsu. Antokucchi viparivattamānā mahāravaṃ viravi[V 1.0214]. So “aññepi nu kho [P 1.0265] passantī”ti olokento kassaci lomahaṃsamattampi nāddasa. Tato – “idaṃ bhayaṃ mameva uppannaṃ, sacāhaṃ yakkhoti vakkhāmi, ‘kiṃ tavameva akkhīni atthi, tvameva yakkhaṃ passasi, paṭhamaṃ yakkhaṃ adisvā samaṇena gotamena vādasaṅghaṭṭe pakkhittova yakkhaṃ passasī’ti vadeyyu”nti cintetvā “na dāni me [M 1.0237] idha aññaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ atthi, aññatra samaṇā gotamā”ti maññamāno atha kho ambaṭṭho māṇavo…pe… bhagavantaṃ etadavoca.

‘Only the Blessed One sees, and Ambaṭṭha.’ For if others were to see it, that reason would be without weight. They would say, ‘This ascetic Gotama, knowing that Ambaṭṭha was not yielding to his argument, summoned a yakkha by incantation and showed him, and then Ambaṭṭha spoke out of fear.’ Therefore, only the Blessed One sees, and Ambaṭṭha. Upon seeing it, sweat was released from his entire body. His insides, as if turning upside down, cried out with a great sound. He, looking around thinking, ‘Do others see it?’ did not see even the slightest bristling of hair in anyone. Then he thought, ‘This fear has arisen for me alone. If I say, “It is a yakkha,” they would say, “What, do only you have eyes? Do only you see the yakkha? Having not seen a yakkha at first, only after being cornered in the debate by the ascetic Gotama do you see a yakkha?”’ Thinking thus, and knowing, ‘Now there is no other refuge for me here, other than the ascetic Gotama,’ then the young man Ambaṭṭha… said this to the Blessed One.

272. Tāṇaṃ gavesīti tāṇaṃ gavesamāno. Leṇaṃ gavesīti leṇaṃ gavesamāno. Saraṇaṃ gavesīti saraṇaṃ gavesamāno. Ettha ca tāyati rakkhatīti tāṇaṃ. Nilīyanti etthāti leṇaṃ. Saratīti saraṇaṃ, bhayaṃ hiṃsati, viddhaṃsetīti attho. Upanisīditvāti upagamma heṭṭhāsane nisīditvā. Bravitūti vadatu.

272. ‘Seeking a protector’ (tāṇaṃ gavesī) means seeking a protector. ‘Seeking a shelter’ (leṇaṃ gavesī) means seeking a shelter. ‘Seeking a refuge’ (saraṇaṃ gavesī) means seeking a refuge. And here, because he protects (tāyati, rakkhati), he is a protector (tāṇaṃ). Because they hide (nilīyanti) in him (ettha), he is a shelter (leṇaṃ). Because he destroys (sarati), he is a refuge (saraṇaṃ); the meaning is, he harms and demolishes fear. ‘Having sat down near’ (upanisīditvā) means having approached and sat down in a lower seat. ‘Let him speak’ (bravītu) means let him speak.

Ambaṭṭhavaṃsakathā

The Story of Ambaṭṭha's Lineage

273-274. Dakkhiṇajanapadanti dakkhiṇāpathoti pākaṭaṃ. Gaṅgāya dakkhiṇato pākaṭajanapadaṃ. Tadā kira dakkhiṇāpathe bahū brāhmaṇatāpasā honti, so tattha gantvā ekaṃ tāpasaṃ vattapaṭipattiyā ārādhesi. So tassa upakāraṃ disvā āha – “ambho, purisa, mantaṃ te demi, yaṃ icchasi, taṃ mantaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti. So āha – “na me ācariya, aññena mantena, kiccaṃ atthi, yassānubhāvena āvudhaṃ na parivattati, taṃ me mantaṃ dehī”ti. So – “bhadraṃ, bho”ti tassa dhanuagamanīyaṃ ambaṭṭhaṃ nāma vijjaṃ adāsi, so taṃ vijjaṃ gahetvā tattheva vīmaṃsitvā – “idāni me manorathaṃ pūressāmī”ti isivesaṃ gahetvā okkākassa santikaṃ gato. Tena vuttaṃ – “dakkhiṇajanapadaṃ gantvā brahmamante adhīyitvā rājānaṃ okkākaṃ upasaṅkamitvā”ti.

273–274. The southern country is that which is well-known as the southern region, a well-known country south of the Ganges. At that time, it is said, many brahmin ascetics lived in the southern region. He went there and pleased one ascetic with his conduct and practice. Seeing his service, the ascetic said, 'Good man, I will give you a mantra. Take whichever mantra you wish.' He replied, 'Teacher, I have no need for any other mantra. Give me the mantra by whose power a weapon does not turn upon one.' The ascetic said, 'Very well,' and gave him the science named Ambaṭṭha, which prevents the approach of a bow. Having learned that science and tested it right there, he thought, 'Now I shall fulfill my desire.' Taking the guise of an ascetic, he went to King Okkāka. Hence it is said: 'Having gone to the southern country, having studied the sacred verses, he approached King Okkāka...'

Ettha brahmamanteti ānubhāvasampannatāya seṭṭhamante. Ko nevaṃ’re ayaṃ mayhaṃ dāsiputtoti ko nu evaṃ are ayaṃ mama dāsiputto. So [P 1.0266] taṃ khurappanti so rājā taṃ māretukāmatāya sannahitaṃ saraṃ tassa mantānubhāvena neva khipituṃ na apanetuṃ sakkhi, tāvadeva sakalasarīre sañjātasedo bhayena vedhamāno aṭṭhāsi.

Here, 'sacred verses' means excellent verses, due to their power. 'Who is this son of my slave-woman?'—who indeed is this son of my slave-woman? The king, wishing to kill him, nocked that razor-arrow, but by the power of the mantra, he could neither shoot it nor remove it. At that very moment, sweat broke out all over his body, and he stood trembling with fear.

Amaccāti mahāmaccā. Pārisajjāti itare parisāvacarā. Etadavocunti – “daṇḍakīrañño [V 1.0215] kisavacchatāpase aparaddhassa āvudhavuṭṭhiyā sakalaraṭṭhaṃ vinaṭṭhaṃ[M 1.0238]. Nāḷikero pañcasu tāpasasatesu ajjuno ca aṅgīrase aparaddho pathaviṃ bhinditvā nirayaṃ paviṭṭho”ti cintayantā bhayena etaṃ sotthi, bhaddantetiādivacanaṃ avocuṃ.

Ministers means great ministers. Attendants means other members of the assembly. They said this—thinking, “When King Daṇḍakī wronged the ascetic Kisavaccha, a rain of weapons destroyed the entire kingdom. Nāḷikera wronged five hundred ascetics, and Ajjuna, having wronged Aṅgīrasa, split the earth and entered hell,” they spoke out of fear, saying, “Peace, venerable sir!” and so forth.

Sotthi bhavissati raññoti idaṃ vacanaṃ kaṇho ciraṃ tuṇhī hutvā tato anekappakāraṃ yācīyamāno – “tumhākaṃ raññā mādisassa isino khurappaṃ sannayhantena bhāriyaṃ kammaṃ kata”ntiādīni ca vatvā pacchā abhāsi. Undriyissatīti bhijjissati, thusamuṭṭhi viya vippakiriyissatīti. Idaṃ so “janaṃ tāsessāmī”ti musā bhaṇati. Sarasanthambhanamatteyeva hissa vijjāya ānubhāvo, na aññatra. Ito paresupi vacanesu eseva nayo.

‘May there be safety for the king’—this statement Kaṇha spoke only after remaining silent for a long time and then being begged in many ways, saying: ‘Your king has done a grave deed by nocking a razor-arrow against an ascetic like me,’ and so on. ‘It will be split apart’ means it will be broken; it will be scattered like a fistful of chaff. This he speaks falsely, thinking, ‘I will frighten the people.’ For the power of his science is only in immobilizing the arrow, and nothing else. In the statements that follow this, the method is the same.

Pallomoti pannalomo. Lomahaṃsanamattampissa na bhavissati. Idaṃ kira so “sace me rājā taṃ dārikaṃ dassatī”ti paṭiññaṃ kāretvā avaca. Kumāre khurappaṃ patiṭṭhapesīti tena “saro otaratū”ti mante parivatti, te kumārassa nābhiyaṃ patiṭṭhapesi. Dhītaraṃ adāsīti sīsaṃ dhovitvā adāsaṃ bhujissaṃ katvā dhītaraṃ adāsi, uḷāre ca taṃ ṭhāne ṭhapesi. Mā kho tumhe māṇavakāti idaṃ pana bhagavā – “ekena pakkhena ambaṭṭho sakyānaṃ ñāti hotī”ti pakāsento tassa samassāsanatthaṃ āha. Tato ambaṭṭho ghaṭasatena abhisitto viya passaddhadaratho hutvā samassāsetvā samaṇo gotamo maṃ “tosessāmī”ti ekena pakkhena ñātiṃ karoti, khattiyo kirāhamasmī”ti cintesi.

‘His hair will be limp’ means his hair will have fallen; not even the slightest bristling of hair will occur for him. It is said that Kaṇha spoke this after having the king make a promise: ‘If the king will give me that girl...’ ‘He established the razor-arrow on the prince’ means that when he repeatedly recited the mantra, ‘Let the arrow descend,’ he caused it to be established on the prince's navel. ‘He gave his daughter’ means that, having performed the head-washing ceremony and made her a free woman, he gave his daughter. And he placed him [Kaṇha] in a high position. ‘Do not, young man...’—this the Blessed One spoke to reassure Ambaṭṭha, making it clear that ‘on one side, Ambaṭṭha is a relative of the Sakyans.’ Then Ambaṭṭha, as if anointed with a hundred jars of water, his distress calmed, was reassured and thought: ‘The ascetic Gotama, wishing to please me, makes me a relative on one side. It seems I am a khattiya!’

Khattiyaseṭṭhabhāvavaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Supremacy of the Khattiya

275. Atha [P 1.0267] kho bhagavā – “ayaṃ ambaṭṭho khattiyosmī”ti saññaṃ karoti, attano akhattiyabhāvaṃ na jānāti, handa naṃ jānāpessāmīti khattiyavaṃsaṃ dassetuṃ uttaridesanaṃ vaḍḍhento – “taṃ kiṃ maññasi ambaṭṭhā”tiādimāha. Tattha idhāti imasmiṃ loke. Brāhmaṇesūti brāhmaṇānaṃ antare. Āsanaṃ vā udakaṃ vāti aggāsanaṃ vā aggodakaṃ vā. Saddheti matake uddissa katabhatte. Thālipāketi maṅgalādibhatte. Yaññeti yaññabhatte. Pāhuneti pāhunakānaṃ katabhatte paṇṇākārabhatte vā. Api nussāti api nu assa khattiyaputtassa. Āvaṭaṃ vā assa anāvaṭaṃ vāti[M 1.0239], brāhmaṇakaññāsu nivāraṇaṃ bhaveyya vā no vā, brāhmaṇadārikaṃ labheyya vā na vā labheyyāti attho. Anupapannoti khattiyabhāvaṃ apatto, aparisuddhoti attho.

275. Then the Blessed One, thinking, 'This Ambaṭṭha makes the perception, “I am a khattiya,” but does not know his own state of not being a khattiya. Come now, I shall make him know,' and wishing to show the khattiya lineage by elaborating upon the further teaching, spoke the words beginning with, 'What do you think of that, Ambaṭṭha?' Therein, idha means 'in this world.' Brāhmaṇesu means 'among brahmins.' Āsanaṃ vā udakaṃ vā means 'the foremost seat or the foremost water.' Saddhe refers to 'a memorial feast made in dedication to the deceased.' Thālipāke means 'food for auspicious occasions and so on.' Yaññe means 'food for a sacrifice.' Pāhune means 'food made for guests or food as a gift.' Api nussā means 'for that son of a khattiya.' Āvaṭaṃ vā assa anāvaṭaṃ vā means 'would there be a restriction regarding brahmin maidens, or would there not be? Could he obtain a brahmin girl, or could he not?' Anupapanno means 'not having attained the state of a khattiya'; the meaning is 'impure on the mother's side.'

276. Itthiyā [V 1.0216] vā itthiṃ karitvāti itthiyā vā itthiṃ pariyesitvā. Kismiñcideva pakaraṇeti kismiñcideva dose brāhmaṇānaṃ ayutte akattabbakaraṇe. Bhassapuṭenāti bhasmapuṭena, sīse chārikaṃ okiritvāti attho.

276. Itthiyā vā itthiṃ karitvā means 'having sought a wife, or by means of a woman.' Kismiñcideva pakaraṇe means 'due to some fault, due to the brahmins doing an improper act that should not be done.' Bhassapuṭena means 'with a container of ash'; the meaning is 'having scattered ash on the head.'

277. Janetasminti janitasmiṃ, pajāyāti attho. Ye gottapaṭisārinoti ye janetasmiṃ gottaṃ paṭisaranti – “ahaṃ gotamo, ahaṃ kassapo”ti, tesu loke gottapaṭisārīsu khattiyo seṭṭho. Anumatā mayāti mama sabbaññutaññāṇena saddhiṃ saṃsanditvā desitā mayā anuññātā.

277. Janetasmiṃ means 'among the populace'; the meaning is 'among the people.' Ye gottapaṭisārino refers to those who, among the populace, take refuge in their clan—saying, 'I am a Gotama,' 'I am a Kassapa.' Among those in the world who take refuge in their clan, the khattiya is the most excellent. Anumatā mayā means 'taught by me after comparing it with my omniscient knowledge; permitted by me.'

Paṭhamabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the First Recitation Section is concluded.

Vijjācaraṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Discourse on Knowledge and Conduct

278. Imāya pana gāthāya vijjācaraṇasampannoti idaṃ padaṃ sutvā ambaṭṭho cintesi – “vijjā nāma tayo vedā, caraṇaṃ pañca sīlāni, tayidaṃ amhākaṃyeva atthi, vijjācaraṇasampanno [P 1.0268] ce seṭṭho, mayameva seṭṭhā”ti niṭṭhaṃ gantvā vijjācaraṇaṃ pucchanto – “katamaṃ pana taṃ, bho gotama, caraṇaṃ, katamā ca pana sā vijjā”ti āha. Athassa bhagavā taṃ brāhmaṇasamaye siddhaṃ jātivādādipaṭisaṃyuttaṃ vijjācaraṇaṃ paṭikkhipitvā anuttaraṃ vijjācaraṇaṃ dassetukāmo – “na kho ambaṭṭhā”tiādimāha. Tattha jātivādoti jātiṃ ārabbha vādo, brāhmaṇassevidaṃ vaṭṭati, na suddassātiādi vacananti attho. Esa nayo sabbattha. Jātivādavinibaddhāti jātivāde vinibaddhā. Esa nayo sabbattha.

278. Now, upon hearing the phrase 'endowed with knowledge and conduct' in this verse, Ambaṭṭha thought: 'Knowledge means the three Vedas, and conduct means the five precepts. This is something that exists only in our tradition. If one endowed with knowledge and conduct is the most excellent, then in that case, we alone are the excellent ones.' Having come to this conclusion, and wishing to ask about knowledge and conduct, he said: 'But what, Venerable Gotama, is that conduct, and what is that knowledge?' Then the Blessed One, wishing to reject that knowledge and conduct connected with claims of birth and so on—which is established in the doctrine of the brahmins—and to show the unsurpassed knowledge and conduct, spoke the words beginning with: 'Not so, Ambaṭṭha.' Therein, jātivādo means 'a saying or a doctrine based on birth'; the meaning is a statement such as, 'This is proper only for a brahmin, not for a sudda.' This method applies everywhere. Jātivādavinibaddhā means 'bound up in the saying or doctrine based on birth.' This method applies everywhere.

Tato ambaṭṭho – “yattha dāni mayaṃ laggissāmāti cintayimha, tato no samaṇo gotamo mahāvāte thusaṃ dhunanto viya dūrameva avakkhipi. Yattha pana mayaṃ na laggāma, tattha no niyojesi. Ayaṃ no vijjācaraṇasampadā ñātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā puna vijjācaraṇasampadaṃ pucchi. Athassa [M 1.0240] bhagavā samudāgamato pabhuti vijjācaraṇaṃ dassetuṃ – “idha ambaṭṭha tathāgato”tiādimāha.

Then Ambaṭṭha thought: 'We had thought, “Now we are attached to this,” but from that, the ascetic Gotama has cast us far down, like someone shaking off chaff in a great wind. And where we were not attached, there he has urged us on. It is fitting for us to know this perfection of knowledge and conduct.' Having thought thus, he again asked about the perfection of knowledge and conduct. Then, in order to show him the knowledge and conduct from its very arising, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with: 'Here, Ambaṭṭha, a Tathāgata...'

279. Ettha ca bhagavā caraṇapariyāpannampi tividhaṃ sīlaṃ vibhajanto “idamassa hoti caraṇasmi”nti [V 1.0217] aniyyātetvā “idampissa hoti sīlasmi”nti sīlavaseneva niyyātesi. Kasmā? Tassapi hi kiñci kiñci sīlaṃ atthi, tasmā caraṇavasena niyyātiyamāne “mayampi caraṇasampannā”ti tattha tattheva laggeyya. Yaṃ pana tena supinepi na diṭṭhapubbaṃ, tasseva vasena niyyātento paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Idampissa hoti caraṇasmiṃ…pe… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, idampissa hoti caraṇasmintiādimāha. Ettāvatā aṭṭhapi samāpattiyo caraṇanti niyyātitā honti, vipassanā ñāṇato pana paṭṭhāya aṭṭhavidhāpi paññā vijjāti niyyātitā.

279. And here, the Blessed One, while analyzing the threefold virtue which is also included in 'conduct,' did not conclude by saying, 'This of his is in conduct,' but concluded only in terms of virtue, saying, 'This also of his is in virtue.' Why? Because he too has some virtue. Therefore, if it were concluded in terms of 'conduct,' he might cling right there, thinking, 'We too are endowed with conduct.' But, wishing to conclude in terms of that which he had never before seen even in a dream, He said the words beginning with: 'He enters and abides in the first jhāna. This too of his is in conduct... up to... he enters and abides in the fourth jhāna. This too of his is in conduct.' By this much, the eight attainments are concluded as 'conduct.' But beginning from insight-knowledge, the eight kinds of wisdom are concluded as 'knowledge.'

Catuapāyamukhakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Discourse on the Four Causes of Ruin

280. Apāyamukhānīti vināsamukhāni. Anabhisambhuṇamānoti asampāpuṇanto, avisahamāno vā. Khārividhamādāyāti [P 1.0269] ettha khārīti araṇī kamaṇḍalu sujādayo tāpasaparikkhārā. Vidhoti kājo. Tasmā khāribharitaṃ kājamādāyāti attho. Ye pana khārivividhanti paṭhanti, te “khārīti kājassa nāmaṃ, vividhanti bahukamaṇḍaluādiparikkhāra”nti vaṇṇayanti. Pavattaphalabhojanoti patitaphalabhojano. Paricārakoti kappiyakaraṇapattapaṭiggahaṇapādadhovanādivattakaraṇavasena paricārako. Kāmañca guṇādhikopi khīṇāsavasāmaṇero puthujjanabhikkhuno vuttanayena paricārako hoti, ayaṃ pana na tādiso guṇavasenapi veyyāvaccakaraṇavasenapi lāmakoyeva.

280. 'Causes of ruin' (apāyamukhāni) means causes of destruction (vināsamukhāni). 'Not being able to accomplish' (anabhisambhuṇamāno) means not being able to attain properly, or alternatively, not being able to strive. In the phrase 'taking a carrying pole with requisites' (khārividhamādāya), 'requisites' (khārī) refers to the requisites of ascetics, such as a fire-drill and stick, a water pot, a sacrificial ladle, a chowrie, and so on. 'Carrying pole' (vidho) means a carrying pole (kājo). Therefore, the meaning is 'taking a carrying pole filled with the requisites of ascetics'. Alternatively, those who recite it as khārivividhaṃ explain it thus: 'The name khārī is a name for a carrying pole (kāja), and vividhaṃ means many requisites such as water pots.' 'One who eats available fruit' (pavatta­phala­bhojano) means one who eats fallen fruit. 'Attendant' (paricārako) means an attendant by way of performing duties such as making things allowable, taking the bowl, washing the feet, and so on. Indeed, even a novice who is an Arahant, superior in virtue, may be an attendant for a worldling monk in the manner described; however, this ascetic is not like that. He is simply inferior, both by way of virtue and by way of performing services.

Kasmā pana tāpasapabbajjā sāsanassa vināsamukhanti vuttāti? Yasmā gacchantaṃ gacchantaṃ sāsanaṃ tāpasapabbajjāvasena osakkissati. Imasmiñhi sāsane pabbajitvā tisso sikkhā pūretuṃ asakkontaṃ lajjino sikkhākāmā – “natthi tayā saddhiṃ uposatho vā pavāraṇā vā saṅghakammaṃ vā”ti jigucchitvā parivajjenti. So “dukkaraṃ khuradhārūpamaṃ sāsane paṭipattipūraṇaṃ dukkhaṃ, tāpasapabbajjā pana sukarā ceva bahujanasammatā cā”ti vibbhamitvā tāpaso hoti. Aññe taṃ disvā – “kiṃ tayā kata”nti pucchanti. So – “bhāriyaṃ tumhākaṃ sāsane kammaṃ, idha pana sachandacārino maya”nti [M 1.0241] vadati. Sopi, yadi evaṃ ahampi ettheva pabbajāmīti tassa anusikkhanto tāpaso hoti. Evamaññepi aññepīti kamena tāpasāva bahukā honti. Tesaṃ uppannakāle sāsanaṃ osakkitaṃ nāma bhavissati. Loke evarūpo buddho nāma uppajji, tassa īdisaṃ nāma sāsanaṃ ahosīti sutamattameva bhavissati. Idaṃ sandhāya bhagavā tāpasapabbajjaṃ sāsanassa vināsamukhanti āha.

But why was the ascetic's going-forth said to be a cause of the Dispensation's destruction? Because, as time goes on, the Dispensation will decline by way of the ascetic's going-forth. For in this Dispensation, when one who has gone forth is unable to fulfill the three trainings, conscientious monks who are desirous of the training shun him with disgust, saying, 'There is no Uposatha, or Pavāraṇā, or other Saṅgha act with you.' He, thinking, 'The fulfillment of practice in the Dispensation, which is difficult to perform and is like walking on a razor's edge, is suffering; on the other hand, the ascetic's going-forth is easy and approved by many people,' disrobes and becomes an ascetic. Others, seeing him, ask, 'What have you done?' He replies, 'The work in your Dispensation is burdensome, but here we are free to wander according to our own wishes.' That monk too, thinking, 'If so, I too will go forth right here,' follows his example and becomes an ascetic. In this way, other monks also become ascetics, and still others. Thus, in sequence, only ascetics become numerous. At the time of their arising, the Dispensation will be called 'declined'. In the world, it will only be a matter of having heard, 'A Buddha of such a nature, so-named, arose. His Dispensation, of such a kind, so-named, existed.' With reference to this, the Blessed One said that the ascetic's going-forth is a cause of the Dispensation's destruction.

Kudālapiṭakanti [V 1.0218] kandamūlaphalaggahaṇatthaṃ kudālañceva piṭakañca. Gāmasāmantaṃ vāti vijjācaraṇasampadādīni anabhisambhuṇanto, kasikammādīhi ca jīvitaṃ nipphādetuṃ dukkhanti maññamāno bahujanakuhāpanatthaṃ [P 1.0270] gāmasāmante vā nigamasāmante vā aggisālaṃ katvā sappiteladadhimadhuphāṇitatilataṇḍulādīhi ceva nānādārūhi ca homakaraṇavasena aggiṃ paricaranto acchati.

'A hoe and a basket' (`kudālapiṭakaṃ`) means a hoe and a basket for the purpose of taking yams, roots, and fruits. 'Near a village' (`gāmasāmantaṃ vā`) means that, being unable to properly attain accomplishments such as knowledge and conduct, and also thinking, 'It is difficult to make a living through farming and so on,' for the purpose of amazing many people, he builds a fire-hut near a village or near a town, and lives tending the fire by way of making fire-offerings with ghee, oil, curd, honey, molasses, sesame, rice, and so on, and also with various kinds of firewood.

Catudvāraṃ agāraṃ karitvāti catumukhaṃ pānāgāraṃ katvā tassa dvāre maṇḍapaṃ katvā tattha pānīyaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā āgatāgate pānīyena āpucchati. Yampissa addhikā kilantā pānīyaṃ pivitvā parituṭṭhā bhattapuṭaṃ vā taṇḍulādīni vā denti, taṃ sabbaṃ gahetvā ambilayāguādīni katvā bahutaraṃ āmisagahaṇatthaṃ kesañci annaṃ deti, kesañci bhattapacanabhājanādīni. Tehipi dinnaṃ āmisaṃ vā pubbaṇṇādīni vā gaṇhati, tāni vaḍḍhiyā payojeti. Evaṃ vaḍḍhamānavibhavo gomahiṃsadāsīdāsapariggahaṃ karoti, mahantaṃ kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapeti. Imaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ – “catudvāraṃ agāraṃ karitvā acchatī”ti. “Tamahaṃ yathāsatti yathābalaṃ paṭipūjessāmī”ti idaṃ panassa paṭipattimukhaṃ. Iminā hi mukhena so evaṃ paṭipajjatīti. Ettāvatā ca bhagavatā sabbāpi tāpasapabbajjā niddiṭṭhā honti.

'Having made a four-doored dwelling' (`catudvāraṃ agāraṃ karitvā`) means: having made a four-entranced drinking-water shelter, and having made a pavilion at its doorway, and having placed drinking water there, he invites travelers who come and go with drinking water. Whatever travelers, being weary, drink the water and, being pleased, give to him—be it a packet of cooked rice or rice and so on—he takes all of it. Then, making things like sour gruel, for the sake of receiving even more material things, he gives food to some and gives cooking pots and so on to others. From them too, he receives the material things given, such as robes, or grain and so on, and he applies them to increase. In this way, with increasing prosperity, he acquires cattle, buffaloes, female slaves, and male slaves, and establishes a great household. With reference to this practice, this was said: 'Having made a four-doored dwelling... he lives.' Now, this statement, 'I will honor him according to my ability and strength' (`tamahaṃ... paṭipūjessāmi`), is the introduction to his deceitful practice. For with this introduction, he practices in this manner. And by this much, all the goings-forth of ascetics have been pointed out by the Blessed One.

Kathaṃ? Aṭṭhavidhā hi tāpasā – saputtabhariyā, uñchācariyā, anaggipakkikā, asāmapākā, asmamuṭṭhikā, dantavakkalikā, pavattaphalabhojanā, paṇḍupalāsikāti. Tattha ye keṇiyajaṭilo viya kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapetvā vasanti, te saputtabhariyā nāma.

How so? To elaborate, ascetics are of eight kinds: `saputtabhariyā`, `uñchācariyā`, `anaggipakkikā`, `asāmapākā`, `asmamuṭṭhikā`, `dantavakkalikā`, `pavatta­phala­bhojanā`, and `paṇḍupalāsikā`. Among them, those who, like the matted-hair ascetic Keṇiya, establish a household and live, are called `saputtabhariyā` (those with sons and wives).

Ye [M 1.0242] pana “saputtadārabhāvo nāma pabbajitassa ayutto”ti lāyanamaddanaṭṭhānesu vīhimuggamāsatilādīni saṅkaḍḍhitvā pacitvā paribhuñjanti, te uñchācariyā nāma.

On the other hand, those who, thinking, 'The state of being with sons and wives is unsuitable for one who has gone forth,' gather paddy, green gram, cowpeas, sesame, and so on from reaping places and threshing places, cook them, and consume them, are called `uñchācariyā` (those who live by gleaning).

Ye “khalena khalaṃ vicaritvā vīhiṃ āharitvā koṭṭetvā paribhuñjanaṃ nāma ayutta”nti gāmanigamesu taṇḍulabhikkhaṃ gahetvā pacitvā paribhuñjanti, te anaggipakkikā nāma.

Those who, thinking, 'It is unsuitable to go from one threshing floor to another, bring back paddy, pound it, and consume it,' instead take alms of uncooked rice in villages and towns, cook it, and consume it, are called `anaggipakkikā` (those who do not live on food cooked by fire).

Ye pana “kiṃ pabbajitassa sāmapākenā”ti gāmaṃ pavisitvā pakkabhikkhameva gaṇhanti[P 1.0271], te asāmapākā nāma.

On the other hand, those who, thinking, 'What has one who has gone forth to do with cooking for himself?' enter a village and accept only already-cooked almsfood, are called `asāmapākā` (those who do not cook for themselves).

Ye [V 1.0219] “divase divase bhikkhāpariyeṭṭhi nāma dukkhā pabbajitassā”ti muṭṭhipāsāṇena ambāṭakādīnaṃ rukkhānaṃ tacaṃ koṭṭetvā khādanti, te asmamuṭṭhikā nāma.

Those who, thinking, 'This seeking of alms day after day is suffering for one who has gone forth,' pound the bark of trees such as the hog plum with a fist-sized stone and eat it, are called `asmamuṭṭhikā` (stone-pounders).

Ye pana “pāsāṇena tacaṃ koṭṭetvā vicaraṇaṃ nāma dukkha”nti danteheva ubbāṭetvā khādanti, te dantavakkalikā nāma.

On the other hand, those who, thinking, 'This wandering about, pounding bark with a stone, is suffering,' pull it out with their teeth alone and eat it, are called `dantavakkalikā` (bark-eaters).

Ye “dantehi ubbāṭetvā khādanaṃ nāma dukkhaṃ pabbajitassā”ti leḍḍudaṇḍādīhi paharitvā patitāni phalāni paribhuñjanti, te pavattaphalabhojanā nāma.

Those who, thinking, 'This pulling out with the teeth and eating is suffering for one who has gone forth,' strike with clods of earth, sticks, and so on, and consume the fruits that have been made to fall, are called `pavatta­phala­bhojanā` (eaters of fruit made to fall).

Ye pana “leḍḍudaṇḍādīhi pātetvā paribhogo nāma asāruppo pabbajitassā”ti sayaṃ patitāneva pupphaphalapaṇḍupalāsādīni khādantā yāpenti, te paṇḍupalāsikā nāma.

On the other hand, those who, thinking, 'This making things fall with clods of earth, sticks, and so on, and then consuming them is improper for one who has gone forth,' sustain themselves by eating only flowers, fruits, pale yellow leaves, and so on, that have fallen by themselves, are called `paṇḍupalāsikā` (eaters of withered leaves).

Te tividhā – ukkaṭṭhamajjhimamudukavasena. Tattha ye nisinnaṭṭhānato anuṭṭhāya hatthena pāpuṇanaṭṭhāneva patitaṃ gahetvā khādanti, te ukkaṭṭhā. Ye ekarukkhato aññaṃ rukkhaṃ na gacchanti, te majjhimā. Ye taṃ taṃ rukkhamūlaṃ gantvā pariyesitvā khādanti, te mudukā.

They are of three kinds: strict, moderate, and mild. Among them, those who, without rising from their sitting place, take with their hand what has fallen within reach and eat it, are the strict ones. Those who do not go from one tree to another are the moderate ones. Those who go to the base of this or that tree, search, and then eat, are the mild ones.

Imā pana aṭṭhapi tāpasapabbajjā imāhi catūhiyeva saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Kathaṃ? Etāsu hi saputtabhariyā ca uñchācariyā ca agāraṃ bhajanti. Anaggipakkikā ca asāmapākā ca agyāgāraṃ bhajanti. Asmamuṭṭhikā ca dantavakkalikā ca kandamūlaphalabhojanaṃ bhajanti. Pavattaphalabhojanā ca paṇḍupalāsikā ca pavattaphalabhojanaṃ bhajanti. Tena vuttaṃ – “ettāvatā ca bhagavatā sabbāpi tāpasapabbajjā niddiṭṭhā hontī”ti.

Furthermore, these eight kinds of ascetic renunciations are included within just these four. How so? Among them, the `saputtabhariyā` (those with wives and children) and the `uñchācariyā` (gleaners) are included under the `agāra` (household) renunciation. The `anaggipakkikā` (those not eating food cooked on a fire) and the `asāmapākā` (those not cooking for themselves) are included under the `agyāgāra` (fire-house) renunciation. The `asmamuṭṭhikā` (stone-pounders) and the `dantavakkalikā` (bark-eaters) are included under the `kandamūlaphalabhojana` (eating roots, tubers, and fruits) renunciation. The `pavatta­phala­bhojanā` (eaters of fruit made to fall) and the `paṇḍupalāsikā` (eaters of withered leaves) are included under the `pavatta­phala­bhojana` (eating fruit made to fall) renunciation. Therefore it was said: 'To this extent, all ascetic renunciations have been pointed out by the Blessed One.'

281-282. Idāni [M 1.0243] bhagavā sācariyakassa ambaṭṭhassa vijjācaraṇasampadāya apāyamukhampi appattabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ taṃ kiṃ maññasi ambaṭṭhātiādimāha. Taṃ uttānatthameva. Attanā āpāyikopi aparipūramānoti attanā vijjācaraṇasampadāya āpāyikenāpi aparipūramānena.

281-282. Now, in order to show that Ambaṭṭha, together with his teacher, had not even reached the doorway to ruin in the matter of the accomplishment in knowledge and conduct, the Blessed One said, “What do you think, Ambaṭṭha?” and so on. The meaning of that is plain. Attanā āpāyikopi aparipūramāno (‘though being himself a cause of ruin, he does not fulfill it’) means: being himself a cause of ruin with respect to the accomplishment in knowledge and conduct, and not even fulfilling that.

Pubbakaisibhāvānuyogavaṇṇanā

An Exposition on the Practice of the Ancient Seers

283. Dattikanti dinnakaṃ. Sammukhībhāvampi na dadātīti kasmā na dadāti? So kira sammukhā [V 1.0220] āvaṭṭaniṃ nāma vijjaṃ [P 1.0272] jānāti. Yadā rājā mahārahena alaṅkārena alaṅkato hoti, tadā rañño samīpe ṭhatvā tassa alaṅkārassa nāmaṃ gaṇhati. Tassa rājā nāme gahite na demīti vattuṃ na sakkoti. Datvā puna chaṇadivase alaṅkāraṃ āharathāti vatvā, natthi, deva, tumhehi brāhmaṇassa dinnoti vutto, “kasmā me dinno”ti pucchi. Te amaccā ‘so brāhmaṇo sammukhā āvaṭṭanimāyaṃ jānāti. Tāya tumhe āvaṭṭetvā gahetvā gacchatī’ti āhaṃsu. Apare raññā saha tassa atisahāyabhāvaṃ asahantā āhaṃsu – “deva, etassa brāhmaṇassa sarīre saṅkhaphalitakuṭṭhaṃ nāma atthi. Tumhe etaṃ disvāva āliṅgatha parāmasatha, idañca kuṭṭhaṃ nāma kāyasaṃsaggavasena anugacchati, mā evaṃ karothā”ti. Tato paṭṭhāya tassa rājā sammukhībhāvaṃ na deti.

283. Dattikaṃ means ‘what is given.’ As for sammukhībhāvampi na dadāti (‘he does not even grant an audience’): why does he not grant an audience? It is said that he knows a science called sammukhā-āvaṭṭanī (bewitchment in one's presence). Whenever the king is adorned with a magnificent ornament, the brahmin stands near the king and takes the name of that ornament. When its name is taken, the king is unable to say, “I will not give it.” Having given it, when the king later, on a festival day, says, “Bring the ornament,” and is told, “It is not here, Your Majesty, it was given by you to the brahmin,” he asks, “Why was it given by me?” Those ministers replied, “That brahmin knows the magic of bewitchment in one's presence. With that, he bewitches you, takes it, and goes.” Other ministers, unable to tolerate his excessive intimacy with the king, said: “Your Majesty, this brahmin has on his body a disease called ‘conch-shell-like leprosy.’ Upon seeing him, you embrace and touch him, and this leprosy is contagious through bodily contact. Do not do so.” From then on, the king did not grant him an audience.

Yasmā pana so brāhmaṇo paṇḍito khattavijjāya kusalo, tena saha mantetvā katakammaṃ nāma na virujjhati, tasmā sāṇipākārassa anto ṭhatvā bahi ṭhitena tena saddhiṃ manteti. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “tiro dussantena mantetī”ti. Tattha tirodussantenāti tirodussena. Ayameva vā pāṭho. Dhammikanti anavajjaṃ. Payātanti abhiharitvā dinnaṃ. Kathaṃ tassa rājāti yassa rañño brāhmaṇo īdisaṃ bhikkhaṃ paṭiggaṇheyya, kathaṃ tassa brāhmaṇassa so rājā sammukhībhāvampi na dadeyya. Ayaṃ pana adinnakaṃ māyāya gaṇhati, tenassa sammukhībhāvaṃ rājā na detīti niṭṭhamettha gantabbanti ayamettha adhippāyo. “Idaṃ pana kāraṇaṃ ṭhapetvā rājānañceva brāhmaṇañca na añño koci jānāti. Tadetaṃ evaṃ rahassampi paṭicchannampi addhā sabbaññū samaṇo gotamoti niṭṭhaṃ gamissatī”ti bhagavā pakāsesi.

However, since that brahmin is wise and skilled in the political science of the warrior class, a deed done after consulting with him does not go wrong. Therefore, the king stands inside a cloth curtain and consults with the brahmin who stands outside. It is with reference to this that it was said, “He consults from behind a cloth screen.” Here, tirodussantena means tirodussena (from behind a cloth). Or this itself is the reading. Dhammikaṃ means ‘blameless.’ Payataṃ means ‘brought forward and given.’ Kathaṃ tassa rājā (‘How for that king?’): For a king whose brahmin would accept such alms, how could that king not grant that brahmin an audience? But this one takes what is not given by means of magic; therefore the king does not grant him an audience. This is the conclusion to be reached here. This is the intention here: 'Apart from the king and the brahmin, no one else knows this reason. He will come to the conclusion about this matter, so secret and concealed: “Truly, the ascetic Gotama is omniscient!”' Thinking thus, the Blessed One revealed it.

284. Idāni [M 1.0244] ayañca ambaṭṭho, ācariyo cassa mante nissāya atimānino. Tena tesaṃ mantanissitamānanimmadanatthaṃ uttari desanaṃ vaḍḍhento taṃ kiṃ maññasi, ambaṭṭha, idha rājātiādimāha. Tattha [P 1.0273] rathūpatthareti rathamhi rañño ṭhānatthaṃ attharitvā sajjitapadese. Uggehi vāti uggatuggatehi vā amaccehi. Rājaññehīti anabhisittakumārehi. Kiñcideva mantananti asukasmiṃ dese taḷākaṃ vā mātikaṃ vā kātuṃ vaṭṭati, asukasmiṃ gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā nagaraṃ vā nivesetunti evarūpaṃ pākaṭamantanaṃ. Tadeva mantananti yaṃ raññā mantitaṃ tadeva. Tādisehiyeva sīsukkhepabhamukkhepādīhi ākārehi manteyya. Rājabhaṇitanti yathā raññā bhaṇitaṃ, tassatthassa sādhanasamatthaṃ. Sopi tassatthassa sādhanasamatthameva bhaṇitaṃ bhaṇatīti attho.

284. Now, this Ambaṭṭha and his teacher are excessively proud, relying on their sacred texts. Therefore, in order to crush their pride which is based on reliance on these texts, the Blessed One extended the teaching further, saying, “What do you think, Ambaṭṭha? Suppose a king here…” and so on. Here, rathūpatthare (‘on the prepared chariot-floor’) means: in a place on the chariot that has been prepared and spread for the king to stand. Uggehi vā (‘or with eminent men’) means: with ministers who are exceedingly eminent. Rājaññehi means: with unanointed princes. Kiñcideva mantanaṃ (‘some consultation’) means: a public consultation of this kind: ‘It is proper to build a reservoir or a canal in such-and-such a place’; or ‘It is proper to found a village, a market town, or a city in such-and-such a place.’ Tadeva mantanaṃ (‘that very consultation’) means: that which was consulted on by the king. He would consult with just such gestures as raising the head and raising the eyebrows. Rājabhaṇitaṃ (‘what was said by the king’) means: just as the king speaks what is capable of accomplishing that purpose, so too does that person speak what is capable of accomplishing that purpose. This is the meaning.

285. Pavattāroti pavattayitāro. Yesanti yesaṃ santakaṃ. Mantapadanti vedasaṅkhātaṃ mantameva[V 1.0221]. Gītanti aṭṭhakādīhi dasahi porāṇakabrāhmaṇehi sarasampattivasena sajjhāyitaṃ. Pavuttanti aññesaṃ vuttaṃ, vācitanti attho. Samihitanti samupabyūḷhaṃ rāsikataṃ, piṇḍaṃ katvā ṭhapitanti attho. Tadanugāyantīti etarahi brāhmaṇā taṃ tehi pubbe gītaṃ anugāyanti anusajjhāyanti. Tadanubhāsantīti taṃ anubhāsanti, idaṃ purimasseva vevacanaṃ. Bhāsitamanubhāsantīti tehi bhāsitaṃ sajjhāyitaṃ anusajjhāyanti. Vācitamanuvācentīti tehi aññesaṃ vācitaṃ anuvācenti.

285. Pavattāro means ‘promulgators.’ Yesaṃ means ‘of whom it is the possession.’ Mantapadaṃ means the sacred text itself, known as the Veda. Gītaṃ (‘chanted’) means: chanted with perfection of voice by the ten ancient brahmin seers, Aṭṭhaka and others. Pavuttaṃ (‘proclaimed’) means: spoken to others, that is, taught. Samihitaṃ (‘compiled’) means: well compiled, collected into a heap, made into a mass and set down. Tadanugāyanti (‘they sing in accordance with it’) means: the brahmins of today sing after that which was previously sung by them; they chant after them. Tadanubhāsanti (‘they speak in accordance with it’) means: they speak after it; this is a synonym for the previous term. Bhāsitamanubhāsanti (‘they speak in accordance with what was spoken’) means: they chant after what was spoken and chanted by them. Vācitamanuvācenti (‘they teach in accordance with what was taught’) means: they teach what was taught by them to others.

Seyyathidanti te katamehi attho. Aṭṭhakotiādīni tesaṃ nāmāni. Te kira dibbena cakkhunā oloketvā parūpaghātaṃ akatvā kassapasammāsambuddhassa bhagavato pāvacanena saha saṃsanditvā mante ganthiṃsu. Aparāpare pana brāhmaṇā pāṇātipātādīni pakkhipitvā tayo vede bhinditvā buddhavacanena saddhiṃ viruddhe akaṃsu. Netaṃ [P 1.0274] ṭhānaṃ vijjatīti yena tvaṃ isi bhaveyyāsi, etaṃ kāraṇaṃ na vijjati. Idha bhagavā yasmā – “esa pucchiyamānopi, attano avattharaṇabhāvaṃ ñatvā paṭivacanaṃ na dassatī”ti jānāti, tasmā paṭiññaṃ agahetvāva taṃ isibhāvaṃ paṭikkhipi.

The word `seyyathidaṃ` means: who are they? Aṭṭhaka and so on are their names. It is said that they, having looked with the divine eye and without harming others, composed the mantras in harmony with the teaching of the Blessed One, Kassapa the Perfectly Enlightened One. However, later brahmins, having inserted the killing of living beings and so on, corrupted the three Vedas and made them contradictory to the word of the Buddha. As for 'This is not a possible condition': the reason for which you could be a seer does not exist. Here, the Blessed One knows: 'This one, even when questioned, knowing he is about to be overwhelmed, will not give a reply.' Therefore, without taking his admission, He rejected that state of being a seer.

286. Idāni [M 1.0245] yasmā te porāṇā dasa brāhmaṇā nirāmagandhā anitthigandhā rajojalladharā brahmacārino araññāyatane pabbatapādesu vanamūlaphalāhārā vasiṃsu. Yadā katthaci gantukāmā honti, iddhiyā ākāseneva gacchanti, natthi tesaṃ yānena kiccaṃ. Sabbadisāsu ca nesaṃ mettādibrahmavihārabhāvanāva ārakkhā hoti, natthi tesaṃ pākārapurisaguttīhi attho. Iminā ca ambaṭṭhena sutapubbā tesaṃ paṭipatti; tasmā imassa sācariyakassa tesaṃ paṭipattito ārakabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ – “taṃ kiṃ maññasi, ambaṭṭhā”tiādimāha.

286. Now, because those ten ancient brahmin seers—being without the stench of defilements, without the scent of women, bearing coarse and fine dust, and leading the holy life—dwelt in forest abodes at the foothills of mountains, living on the roots and fruits of the forest. When they wished to go anywhere, they went through the sky by psychic power; they had no need for a vehicle. And in all directions, their protection was only the development of the divine abodes such as loving-kindness; they had no need for protection by walls and armed men. And this practice of theirs had been heard before by this Ambaṭṭha; therefore, to show how far removed the practice of this Ambaṭṭha, along with his teacher, was from their practice, He said, 'What do you think, Ambaṭṭha?' and so on.

Tattha vicitakāḷakanti vicinitvā apanītakāḷakaṃ. Veṭhakanatapassāhīti dussapaṭṭadussaveṇi ādīhi veṭhakehi namitaphāsukāhi. Kuttavālehīti sobhākaraṇatthaṃ kappetuṃ, yuttaṭṭhānesu kappitavālehi. Ettha ca vaḷavānaṃyeva vālā kappitā, na rathānaṃ, vaḷavapayuttattā pana rathāpi “kuttavālā”ti vuttā. Ukkiṇṇaparikhāsūti khataparikhāsu. Okkhittapalighāsūti ṭhapitapalighāsu. Nagarūpakārikāsūti ettha upakārikāti paresaṃ ārohanivāraṇatthaṃ samantā nagaraṃ pākārassa adhobhāge katasudhākammaṃ vuccati. Idha pana tāhi upakārikāhi yuttāni nagarāneva “nagarūpakārikāyo”ti adhippetāni. Rakkhāpentīti tādisesu nagaresu vasantāpi attānaṃ rakkhāpenti. Kaṅkhāti “sabbaññū, na sabbaññū”ti evaṃ saṃsayo. Vimatīti tasseva vevacanaṃ, virūpā [V 1.0222] mati, vinicchinituṃ asamatthāti attho. Idaṃ bhagavā “ambaṭṭhassa iminā attabhāvena maggapātubhāvo natthi, kevalaṃ divaso vītivattati, ayaṃ kho pana lakkhaṇapariyesanatthaṃ āgato, tampi [P 1.0275] kiccaṃ nassarati. Handassa satijananatthaṃ nayaṃ demī”ti āha.

Therein, `vicitakāḷakaṃ` means having selected and removed the black parts. `Veṭhakanatapassāhi` means with ribs made to bend by wrappings such as cloth strips and cloth braids. `Kuttavālehi` means with hair cut in appropriate places for the purpose of beautification. And here, only the hair of the mares was cut, not that of the chariots; however, because they were yoked with mares, the chariots are also called `kuttavālā`. `Ukkiṇṇaparikhāsu` means with moats having been dug. `Okkhittapalighāsu` means with gate-bars having been placed. As for `nagarūpakārikāsu`, herein, `upakārikā` refers to the plasterwork done at the lower part of the city wall all around the city to prevent enemies from climbing. But here, the cities themselves endowed with those `upakārikā` are intended by `nagarūpakārikāyo`. `Rakkhāpenti` means that even while living in such cities, they have themselves guarded. `Kaṅkhā` is doubt, thus: 'Is he omniscient, or not omniscient?' `Vimati` is a synonym for that, meaning a different kind of knowing, unable to decide. The Blessed One said this, thinking: 'For Ambaṭṭha, with this present state of being, there is no arising of the path. The day is merely passing by. This one has come to search for the marks, but that task is also being forgotten. Come now, let me give him a method for arousing mindfulness.'

Dvelakkhaṇadassanavaṇṇanā

The Exposition on Seeing the Two Marks

287. Evaṃ vatvā pana yasmā buddhānaṃ nisinnānaṃ vā nipannānaṃ vā koci lakkhaṇaṃ pariyesituṃ na sakkoti, ṭhitānaṃ pana caṅkamantānaṃ vā sakkoti. Āciṇṇañcetaṃ buddhānaṃ lakkhaṇapariyesanatthaṃ āgatabhāvaṃ ñatvā uṭṭhāyāsanā caṅkamādhiṭṭhānaṃ nāma, tena bhagavā uṭṭhāyāsanā bahi nikkhanto. Tasmā atha kho bhagavātiādi vuttaṃ.

287. Having said this, however, since no one is able to search for the marks of Buddhas when they are sitting or lying down, but is able when they are standing or walking; and since it is the custom of Buddhas, knowing that someone has come for the purpose of searching for the marks, to rise from their seat and undertake to walk back and forth, for that reason the Blessed One rose from his seat and went outside. Therefore, 'Then the Blessed One...' and so on was said by the venerable Ānanda.

Samannesīti [M 1.0246] gavesi, ekaṃ dveti vā gaṇayanto samānayi. Yebhuyyenāti pāyena, bahukāni addasa, appāni na addasāti attho. Tato yāni na addasa tesaṃ dīpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ – “ṭhapetvā dve”ti. Kaṅkhatīti “aho vata passeyya”nti patthanaṃ uppādeti. Vicikicchatīti tato tato tāni vicinanto kicchati na sakkoti daṭṭhuṃ. Nādhimuccatīti tāya vicikicchāya sanniṭṭhānaṃ na gacchati. Na sampasīdatīti tato – “paripuṇṇalakkhaṇo aya”nti bhagavati pasādaṃ nāpajjati. Kaṅkhāya vā dubbalā vimati vuttā, vicikicchāya majjhimā, anadhimuccanatāya balavatī, asampasādena tehi tīhi dhammehi cittassa kālusiyabhāvo. Kosohiteti vatthikosena paṭicchanne. Vatthaguyheti aṅgajāte bhagavato hi varavāraṇasseva kosohitaṃ vatthaguyhaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ padumagabbhasamānaṃ. Taṃ so vatthapaṭicchannattā apassanto, antomukhagatāya ca jivhāya pahūtabhāvaṃ asallakkhento tesu dvīsu lakkhaṇesu kaṅkhī ahosi vicikicchī.

`Samannesi` means he investigated; or, counting 'one, two,' he collated them. `Yebhuyyena` means for the most part; he saw many, but did not see a few—that is the meaning. Then, to explain those he did not see, it was said: 'except for two.' `Kaṅkhati` means he gives rise to the wish, 'Oh, that I might see!' `Vicikicchati` means that, searching for them here and there, he struggles and is unable to see. `Nādhimuccati` means that due to that hesitation, he does not reach a conclusion. `Na sampasīdati` means that because of this, he does not arrive at faith in the Blessed One, thinking, 'This one has the complete marks.' Alternatively, by `kaṅkhā` a weak uncertainty is meant; by `vicikicchā`, a middling one; and by `anadhimuccanatā`, a strong one. By `asampasādena` is meant the sullied state of the mind due to those three things. `Kosohite` means concealed in a sheath. `Vatthaguyhe` means in the generative organ. Indeed, the Blessed One's generative organ, concealed in a sheath, is like that of a noble elephant, golden in color, and like the pericarp of a lotus. Not seeing it because it was concealed by his robe, and not perceiving the vastness of his tongue which had gone into his mouth, he was doubtful and hesitant regarding those two marks.

288. Tathārūpanti taṃ rūpaṃ. Kimettha aññena vattabbaṃ? Vuttametaṃ nāgasenatthereneva milindaraññā puṭṭhena – “dukkaraṃ, bhante, nāgasena, bhagavatā katanti. Kiṃ mahārājāti? Mahājanena hirikaraṇokāsaṃ brahmāyu brāhmaṇassa ca antevāsi uttarassa ca, bāvarissa antevāsīnaṃ soḷasabrāhmaṇānañca[P 1.0276], selassa brāhmaṇassa ca antevāsīnaṃ tisatamāṇavānañca dassesi, bhanteti. Na, mahārāja, bhagavā guyhaṃ dassesi. Chāyaṃ bhagavā dassesi. Iddhiyā abhisaṅkharitvā nivāsananivatthaṃ kāyabandhanabaddhaṃ cīvarapārutaṃ chāyārūpakamattaṃ dassesi mahārājāti. Chāyaṃ diṭṭhe sati diṭṭhaṃyeva nanu, bhanteti? Tiṭṭhatetaṃ, mahārāja, hadayarūpaṃ disvā [V 1.0223] bujjhanakasatto bhaveyya, hadayamaṃsaṃ nīharitvā dasseyya sammāsambuddhoti. Kallosi, bhante, nāgasenā”ti.

288. `Tathārūpaṃ` means that form. What more is there to be said here by another? This was said by the Elder Nāgasena when asked by King Milinda: 'Venerable Nāgasena, a difficult thing was done by the Blessed One.' 'What, great king?' 'Venerable sir, he showed the place that causes shame to a great assembly of people: to the brahmin Brahmāyu and his pupil Uttara, to Bāvarī's sixteen brahmin pupils, and to the brahmin Sela and his three hundred young pupils.' 'No, great king, the Blessed One did not show the private part. The Blessed One showed a likeness. Having fashioned it by psychic power, he showed merely the likeness of a form, wearing a lower garment, bound with a waistband, and covered with an outer robe, great king.' 'But, venerable sir, when a likeness is seen, is it not in fact seen?' 'Let that be, great king. If there were a being who could attain awakening by seeing the form of the heart, a Perfectly Enlightened One would take out his heart-flesh and show it.' 'You are skilled, venerable Nāgasena.'

Ninnāmetvāti nīharitvā. Anumasīti kathinasūciṃ viya katvā anumajji, tathākaraṇena cettha mudubhāvo, kaṇṇasotānumasanena dīghabhāvo, nāsikasotānumasanena tanubhāvo, nalāṭacchādanena puthulabhāvo pakāsitoti veditabbo.

`Ninnāmetvāti` means having drawn it out. `Anumasīti` means having made it like a hard needle, he stroked it. And by this action, its softness was revealed; by stroking the ear canals, its length; by stroking the nostrils, its thinness; and by covering the forehead, its breadth was made manifest. Thus it should be understood.

289. Paṭimānentoti [M 1.0247] āgamento, āgamanamassa patthento udikkhantoti attho.

289. `Paṭimānento` means awaiting, desiring his coming, looking out for him; this is the meaning.

290. Kathāsallāpoti kathā ca sallāpo ca, kathanaṃ paṭikathananti attho.

290. `Kathāsallāpo` means both an initial statement (`kathā`) and a reply (`sallāpo`); that is, speaking and speaking in return. This is the meaning.

291. Aho vatāti garahavacanametaṃ. Reti idaṃ hīḷanavasena āmantanaṃ. Paṇḍitakāti tameva jigucchanto āha. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Evarūpena kira bho puriso atthacarakenāti idaṃ yādiso tvaṃ, edise atthacarake hitakārake sati puriso nirayaṃyeva gaccheyya, na aññatrāti imamatthaṃ sandhāya vadati. Āsajja āsajjāti ghaṭṭetvā ghaṭṭetvā. Amhepi evaṃ upaneyya upaneyyāti brāhmaṇo kho pana ambaṭṭha pokkharasātītiādīni vatvā evaṃ upanetvā upanetvā paṭicchannaṃ kāraṇaṃ āvikaritvā suṭṭhu dāsādibhāvaṃ āropetvā avaca, tayā amhe akkosāpitāti adhippāyo. Padasāyeva pavattesīti pādena paharitvā bhūmiyaṃ pātesi. Yañca so pubbe ācariyena saddhiṃ rathaṃ āruhitvā sārathi hutvā agamāsi[P 1.0277], tampissa ṭhānaṃ acchinditvā rathassa purato padasā yevassa gamanaṃ akāsi.

291. “Aho vata” is a term of reproach. “Re” is a term of address used with contempt. He said “Paṇḍitaka” while being disgusted with that very person. The same method applies to the remaining two phrases. Regarding “Evarūpena kira bho puriso atthacarakenāti,” this is said with the following meaning in mind: “With a beneficial attendant who acts for one's welfare such as you, a man would surely go only to hell, not to another destination.” “Āsajja āsajja” means having provoked again and again. Regarding “Amhepi evaṃ upaneyya upaneyyāti,” having said the words beginning with “The brahmin Pokkharasāti, Ambaṭṭha…,” he thus repeatedly brought up the matter, revealed the hidden reason, thoroughly established their state of being slaves, and then spoke. The brahmin's intention was: “You have caused us to be reviled.” “Padasāyeva pavattesīti” means he kicked him with his foot and made him fall to the ground. And whereas previously he had mounted the chariot with his teacher and gone as a charioteer, he now deprived him of that position and made him go on foot in front of the chariot.

Pokkharasātibuddhūpasaṅkamanavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on Pokkharasāti's Approach to the Buddha

292-296. Ativikāloti suṭṭhu vikālo, sammodanīyakathāyapi kālo natthi. Āgamā nu khvidha bhoti āgamā nu kho idha bho. Adhivāsetūti sampaṭicchatu. Ajjatanāyāti yaṃ me tumhesu kāraṃ karoto ajja bhavissati puññañca pītipāmojjañca tadatthāya. Adhivāsesi bhagavā tuṇhībhāvenāti bhagavā kāyaṅgaṃ vā vācaṅgaṃ vā acopetvā abbhantareyeva khantiṃ dhārento tuṇhībhāvena adhivāsesi. Brāhmaṇassa anuggahaṇatthaṃ manasāva sampaṭicchīti vuttaṃ hoti.

“Ativikālo” means it is very much the wrong time; there is no time even for pleasant conversation. “Āgamā nu khvidha bho” means “Has the master indeed come here?” “Adhivāsetūti” means “May he accept.” “Ajjatanāyāti” means for the sake of whatever merit, joy, and gladness will be mine today as I perform this service for you. “Adhivāsesi bhagavā tuṇhībhāvenāti” means the Blessed One, not moving any part of his body or speech, maintaining consent only internally, accepted by means of silence. It is said that he accepted with the mind alone for the sake of benefiting the brahmin.

297. Paṇītenāti [V 1.0224] uttamena. Sahatthāti sahatthena. Santappesīti suṭṭhu tappesi paripuṇṇaṃ suhitaṃ yāvadatthaṃ akāsi. Sampavāresīti [M 1.0248] suṭṭhu pavāresi, alaṃ alanti hatthasaññāya paṭikkhipāpesi. Bhuttāvinti bhuttavantaṃ. Onītapattapāṇinti pattato onītapāṇiṃ, apanītahatthanti vuttaṃ hoti. Onittapattapāṇintipi pāṭho. Tassattho – onittaṃ nānābhūtaṃ vinābhūtaṃ pattaṃ pāṇito assāti onittapattapāṇi, taṃ onittapattapāṇiṃ. Hatthe ca pattañca dhovitvā ekamante pattaṃ nikkhipitvā nisinnanti attho. Ekamantaṃ nisīdīti bhagavantaṃ evaṃ bhūtaṃ ñatvā ekasmiṃ okāse nisīdīti attho.

297. “Paṇītenāti” means with the finest. “Sahatthāti” means with his own hand. “Santappesīti” means he satisfied him well; he made him complete, well-provided for, and fulfilled his every wish. “Sampavāresīti” means he served him to his satisfaction; he had him refuse further food with a hand gesture, indicating “Enough, enough.” “Bhuttāvinti” means one who has finished eating. “Onītapattapāṇinti” means one whose hand has been removed from the bowl; it is said to mean one whose hand has been taken away. There is also the reading “onittapattapāṇi.” Its meaning should be understood thus: he is onittapattapāṇi because he has a bowl that is separated and apart from his hand. It refers to him, the one whose bowl is separated from his hand. The meaning is: having washed his hands and the bowl, and having placed the bowl to one side, he was seated. “Ekamantaṃ nisīdīti” means: knowing the Blessed One to be in this state, he sat down in a suitable place. This is the meaning.

298. Anupubbiṃ kathanti anupaṭipāṭikathaṃ. Ānupubbikathā nāma dānānantaraṃ sīlaṃ, sīlānantaraṃ saggo, saggānantaraṃ maggoti etesaṃ atthānaṃ dīpanakathā. Teneva – “seyyathidaṃ dānakatha”ntiādimāha. Okāranti avakāraṃ lāmakabhāvaṃ. Sāmukkaṃsikāti sāmaṃ ukkaṃsikā, attanāyeva uddharitvā gahitā, sayambhūñāṇena diṭṭhā, asādhāraṇā aññesanti attho. Kā pana sāti? Ariyasaccadesanā. Tenevāha – “dukkhaṃ, samudayaṃ, nirodhaṃ, magga”nti. Dhammacakkhunti [P 1.0278] ettha sotāpattimaggo adhippeto. Tassa uppattiākāradassanatthaṃ – “yaṃ kiñci samudayadhammaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ nirodhadhamma”nti āha. Tañhi nirodhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā kiccavasena evaṃ sabbasaṅkhataṃ paṭivijjhantaṃ uppajjati.

298. “Anupubbiṃ kathaṃ” means a talk in sequential order. An “ānupubbikathā” is a discourse that explains these topics in sequence: after giving, virtue; after virtue, heaven; after heaven, the path. For that reason, he spoke the words beginning with, “that is, the talk on giving.” “Okāraṃ” means degradation, a state of baseness. “Sāmukkaṃsikāti” means that which is personally exalted, discovered and grasped by oneself alone, seen with self-originating knowledge, and not shared with others; this is the meaning. And what is that teaching? It is the exposition of the Noble Truths. For that reason, he said, “suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.” Here, by “dhammacakkhuṃ” (the Dhamma-eye), the path of stream-entry is intended. To show the manner of its arising, he said: “Whatever is of a nature to arise, all that is of a nature to cease.” Indeed, that Dhamma-eye arises by taking cessation as its object and, by way of its function, it penetrates all conditioned things thus.

Pokkharasātiupāsakattapaṭivedanāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of Pokkharasāti's Declaration of Lay Followership

299. Diṭṭho ariyasaccadhammo etenāti diṭṭhadhammo. Esa nayo sesapadesupi. Tiṇṇā vicikicchā anenāti tiṇṇavicikiccho. Vigatā kathaṃkathā assāti vigatakathaṃkatho. Vesārajjappattoti visāradabhāvaṃ patto. Kattha? Satthusāsane. Nāssa paro paccayo, na parassa saddhāya ettha vattatīti aparappaccayo. Sesaṃ sabbattha vuttanayattā uttānatthattā ca pākaṭamevāti.

299. The Dhamma of the Noble Truths has been seen by him, thus he is one who has seen the Dhamma (diṭṭhadhamma). This is the method in the remaining terms as well. Doubt has been crossed over by him, thus he is one who has crossed over doubt (tiṇṇavicikiccha). Perplexity has departed for him, thus he is one for whom perplexity has departed (vigatakathaṃkatha). “Having attained confidence” means he has attained a state of fearlessness. Where? In the Teacher’s Dispensation. For him there is no other condition, nor does he proceed herein by faith in another, thus he is independent (aparappaccaya). The remainder is everywhere evident because of the method already stated and because the meaning is obvious.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Thus, in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya,

Ambaṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ambaṭṭha Sutta is concluded.

4. Soṇadaṇḍasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta

300. Evaṃ [P 1.0279][V 1.0225][M 1.0249] me sutaṃ…pe… aṅgesūti soṇadaṇḍasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ apubbapadavaṇṇanā. Aṅgesūti aṅgā nāma aṅgapāsādikatāya evaṃ laddhavohārā jānapadino rājakumārā, tesaṃ nivāso ekopi janapado rūḷhisaddena aṅgāti vuccati, tasmiṃ aṅgesu janapade. Cārikanti idhāpi aturitacārikā ceva nibaddhacārikā ca adhippetā. Tadā kira bhagavato dasasahassilokadhātuṃ olokentassa soṇadaṇḍo brāhmaṇo ñāṇajālassa anto paññāyittha. Atha bhagavā ayaṃ brāhmaṇo mayhaṃ ñāṇajāle paññāyati. ‘Atthi nu khvassupanissayo’ti vīmaṃsanto addasa. ‘Mayi tattha gate etassa antevāsino dvādasahākārehi brāhmaṇassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsitvā mama santike āgantuṃ na dassanti. So pana tesaṃ vādaṃ bhinditvā ekūnatiṃsa ākārehi mama vaṇṇaṃ bhāsitvā maṃ upasaṅkamitvā pañhaṃ pucchissati. So pañhavissajjanapariyosāne saraṇaṃ gamissatī’ti, disvā pañcasatabhikkhuparivāro taṃ janapadaṃ paṭipanno. Tena vuttaṃ – aṅgesu cārikaṃ caramāno…pe… yena campā tadavasarīti.

300. “Thus have I heard…pe…in Aṅga”—this is the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta. Therein, this is the explanation of words not previously explained. Regarding “in Aṅga”: The Aṅgas are princes of the country who received this designation because of the gracefulness of their limbs. Their dwelling place, though a single country, is called “Aṅga” by conventional usage; in that country of Aṅga. Regarding “wandering”: here too, both unhurried wandering and wandering without a fixed connection are intended. It is said that at that time, as the Blessed One was surveying the ten-thousandfold world-system, the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa appeared within the net of His knowledge. Then the Blessed One considered: “This brahmin appears in my net of knowledge. Does he have a supporting condition?” Investigating, He saw: “When I go there, his resident pupils, having praised the brahmin in twelve ways, will not permit him to come to my presence. He, however, breaking their argument and praising me in twenty-nine ways, will approach me and ask a question. At the conclusion of the answer to the question, he will go for refuge.” Having seen this, with a retinue of five hundred monks, He set out for that country. Therefore it was said by the Venerable Ānanda: “Wandering in Aṅga…pe…he arrived at Campā.”

Gaggarāya pokkharaṇiyā tīreti tassa campānagarassa avidūre gaggarāya nāma rājaggamahesiyā khaṇitattā gaggarāti laddhavohārā pokkharaṇī atthi. Tassā tīre samantato nīlādipañcavaṇṇakusumapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ [P 1.0280] mahantaṃ campakavanaṃ. Tasmiṃ bhagavā kusumagandhasugandhe campakavane viharati. Taṃ sandhāya gaggarāya pokkharaṇiyā tīreti vuttaṃ. Māgadhena seniyena bimbisārenāti ettha so rājā magadhānaṃ issarattā māgadho. Mahatiyā senāya samannāgatattā seniyo. Bimbīti suvaṇṇaṃ. Tasmā sārasuvaṇṇasadisavaṇṇatāya bimbisāroti vuccati.

'On the bank of the Gaggarā pond': Near the city of Campā, there is a pond that received the designation 'Gaggarā' because it was excavated by the king's chief queen, Gaggarā. On its bank, all around, is a great campaka grove, adorned with flowers of five colors, such as blue. The Blessed One dwells in that campaka grove, fragrant with the scent of flowers. Referring to this, it was said: 'on the bank of the Gaggarā pond.' Regarding 'by Seniya Bimbisāra, the Magadhan': that king is called 'Māgadha' because he was lord of the Magadhans. He is called 'Seniya' because he was endowed with a great army. 'Bimbī' means gold. Therefore, because he had a complexion similar to the color of excellent gold, he is called Bimbisāra.

301-302. Bahū bahū hutvā saṃhatāti saṅghā. Ekekissāya disāya saṅgho etesaṃ atthīti saṅghī. Pubbe nagarassa anto agaṇā bahi nikkhamitvā gaṇataṃ pattāti gaṇībhūtā. Khattaṃ [V 1.0226] āmantesīti. Khattā vuccati pucchitapañhe byākaraṇasamattho mahāmatto, taṃ āmantesi āgamentūti muhuttaṃ paṭimānentu, mā gacchantūti vuttaṃ hoti.

Having become many, they are assembled; therefore they are called assemblies (saṅghā). For each and every direction, there is an assembly of them; therefore they are called saṅghī. Previously, inside the city, they were not a group, but having gone outside, they attained the state of being a group; therefore they are called gaṇībhūtā. 'He addressed the chamberlain': A great minister who is capable of explaining questions that are asked is called a chamberlain (khattā). He addressed him. 'Let them wait' means 'Let them wait for a moment; let them not go'; this is what is said.

Soṇadaṇḍaguṇakathā

The Account of Soṇadaṇḍa's Qualities

303. Nānāverajjakānanti [M 1.0250] nānāvidhesu rajjesu, aññesu aññesu kāsikosalādīsu rajjesu jātā, tāni vā tesaṃ nivāsā, tato vā āgatāti nānāverajjakā, tesaṃ nānāverajjakānaṃ. Kenacideva karaṇīyenāti tasmiṃ kira nagare dvīhi karaṇīyehi brāhmaṇā sannipatanti – yaññānubhavanatthaṃ vā mantasajjhāyanatthaṃ vā. Tadā ca tasmiṃ nagare yamaññā natthi. Soṇadaṇḍassa pana santike mantasajjhāyanatthaṃ ete sannipatitā. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “kenacideva karaṇīyenā”ti. Te tassa gamanaṃ sutvā cintesuṃ – “ayaṃ soṇadaṇḍo uggatabrāhmaṇo yebhuyyena ca aññe brāhmaṇā samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gatā, ayameva na gato. Svāyaṃ sace tattha gamissati, addhā samaṇassa gotamassa āvaṭṭaniyā māyāya āvaṭṭito, taṃ saraṇaṃ gamissati. Tato etassāpi gehadvāre brāhmaṇānaṃ sannipāto na bhavissatī”ti. “Handassa gamanantarāyaṃ karomā”ti sammantayitvā tattha agamaṃsu. Taṃ sandhāya – atha kho te brāhmaṇātiādi vuttaṃ.

303. The term 'from various kingdoms' (nānāverajjakānaṃ) means: they were born (jātā) in various kinds of kingdoms (nānāvidhesu rajjesu), in other kingdoms such as Kāsi and Kosala; or (vā) those were their residences (nivāsā); or (vā) they had come from there (tato āgatā). Thus they are called 'those from various kingdoms' (nānāverajjakā). Of those from various kingdoms. The phrase 'for some purpose' (kenacideva karaṇīyena) means: it is said that in that city, brahmins gather for two purposes—either to partake in a sacrifice (yaññānubhavanatthaṃ) or to recite mantras (mantasajjhāyanatthaṃ). And at that time, there was no sacrifice in that city. However, these brahmins had gathered in the presence of Soṇadaṇḍa for the purpose of reciting mantras. It was with reference to this that it was said, 'for some purpose.' Hearing of his going, they thought: 'This Soṇadaṇḍa is an eminent brahmin, and for the most part, other brahmins have gone to the ascetic Gotama for refuge, but this one has not. If he goes there, he will surely be captivated by the ascetic Gotama’s enchanting spell and will go to him for refuge. Then, there will no longer be a gathering of brahmins at his house door.' Thinking, 'Come, let us create an obstacle to his going,' they conferred and went there. It is with reference to this that the passage beginning 'Then those brahmins...' was spoken.

Tattha [P 1.0281] imināpaṅgenāti imināpi kāraṇena. Evaṃ etaṃ kāraṇaṃ vatvā puna – “attano vaṇṇe bhaññamāne atussanakasatto nāma natthi. Handassa vaṇṇaṃ bhaṇanena gamanaṃ nivāressāmā”ti cintetvā bhavañhi soṇadaṇḍo ubhato sujātotiādīni kāraṇāni āhaṃsu.

Therein, the phrase 'by this point' (imināpaṅgena) means: by this reason as well. Having stated this reason, they then thought: 'There is no being who is not pleased when their own praise is spoken. Come, let us, by speaking of his praise, prevent his going.' Having thought thus, they stated the reasons beginning with, 'For the venerable Soṇadaṇḍa is well-born on both sides...'

Ubhatoti dvīhi pakkhehi. Mātito ca pitito cāti bhoto mātā brāhmaṇī, mātumātā brāhmaṇī, tassāpi mātā brāhmaṇī; pitā brāhmaṇo, pitupitā brāhmaṇo, tassāpi pitā brāhmaṇoti, evaṃ bhavaṃ ubhato sujāto mātito ca pitito ca. Saṃsuddhagahaṇikoti saṃsuddhā te mātugahaṇī kucchīti attho. Samavepākiniyā gahaṇiyāti ettha pana kammajatejodhātu “gahaṇī”ti vuccati.

'On both sides' (ubhato) means: from two sides (pakkhehi). 'From the mother's side and from the father's side' (mātito ca pitito ca) means: the venerable one's mother is a brahmin woman, the mother's mother is a brahmin woman, and her mother is also a brahmin woman; the father is a brahmin, the father's father is a brahmin, and his father is also a brahmin. Thus, the venerable one is well-born (sujāto) on both sides, from the mother's side and from the father's side. 'Of pure womb-descent' (saṃsuddhagahaṇiko) means: your mother's womb (gahaṇī, kucchi) is pure. However, in the phrase 'samavepākiniyā gahaṇiyā,' the fire element born of kamma (kammajatejodhātu) is called 'gahaṇī.'

Yāva sattamā pitāmahayugāti ettha pitupitā pitāmaho, pitāmahassa yugaṃ pitāmahayugaṃ. Yuganti āyuppamāṇaṃ vuccati. Abhilāpamattameva cetaṃ. Atthato pana pitāmahoyeva pitāmahayugaṃ. Tato uddhaṃ sabbepi pubbapurisā pitāmahaggahaṇeneva gahitā. Evaṃ yāva sattamo puriso[V 1.0227][M 1.0251], tāva saṃsuddhagahaṇiko. Atha vā akkhitto anupakuṭṭho jātivādenāti dassenti. Akkhittoti – “apanetha etaṃ, kiṃ iminā”ti evaṃ akkhitto anavakkhitto. Anupakuṭṭhoti na upakuṭṭho, na akkosaṃ vā nindaṃ vā laddhapubbo. Kena kāraṇenāti? Jātivādena. Itipi – “hīnajātiko eso”ti evarūpena vacanenāti attho.

Regarding the phrase 'up to the seventh paternal-ancestor generation' (yāva sattamā pitāmahayugā): herein, the father's father is the paternal ancestor (pitāmaho). The generation of the paternal ancestor is the paternal-ancestor generation (pitāmahayugaṃ). 'Generation' (yuga) refers to the measure of a lifespan (āyuppamāṇaṃ). This, however, is merely a conventional expression (abhilāpamatta). In terms of meaning, the paternal ancestor himself is the 'paternal-ancestor generation.' All male ancestors (pubbapurisā) above him are included by this term 'paternal ancestor.' Thus, as far back as the seventh man, he is of pure womb-descent (saṃsuddhagahaṇiko). Alternatively, they show that he is 'unreproached and unreviled on account of birth' (akkhitto anupakuṭṭho jātivādena). 'Unreproached' (akkhitto) means not reproached or cast down with words like, 'Remove this one, what is he good for?' 'Unreviled' (anupakuṭṭho) means not reviled; he has never before received abuse (akkosaṃ) or blame (nindaṃ). For what reason? On account of birth (jātivādena). This means, by a statement of the kind, 'This one is of low birth.'

Aḍḍhoti issaro. Mahaddhanoti mahatā dhanena samannāgato. Bhavato hi gehe pathaviyaṃ paṃsuvālikā viya bahudhanaṃ, samaṇo pana gotamo adhano bhikkhāya udaraṃ pūretvā yāpetīti dassenti. Mahābhogoti pañcakāmaguṇavasena mahāupabhogo. Evaṃ yaṃ yaṃ guṇaṃ vadanti, tassa tassa paṭipakkhavasena bhagavato aguṇaṃyeva dassemāti maññamānā vadanti.

'Wealthy' (aḍḍho) means: he is a master (issaro). 'Of great wealth' (mahaddhano) means: he is endowed with great wealth. They indicate: 'Indeed, in the venerable one's house, there is much wealth, like the dust and sand on the earth; the ascetic Gotama, on the other hand, is without wealth and maintains himself by filling his belly through alms.' 'Of great possessions' (mahābhogo) means: he has great enjoyment (mahāupabhogo) by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure. Thus, they speak, thinking, 'For whatever quality we mention, by way of its opposite, we are showing only the Blessed One's lack of that quality.'

Abhirūpoti aññehi manussehi abhirūpo adhikarūpo. Dassanīyoti divasampi passantānaṃ atittikaraṇato dassanayoggo. Dassaneneva cittapasādajananato pāsādiko. Pokkharatā [P 1.0282] vuccati sundarabhāvo, vaṇṇassa pokkharatā vaṇṇapokkharatā, tāya vaṇṇasampattiyā yuttoti attho. Porāṇā panāhu – “pokkharanti sarīraṃ vadanti, vaṇṇaṃ vaṇṇamevā”ti. Tesaṃ matena vaṇṇañca pokkharañca vaṇṇapokkharāni. Tesaṃ bhāvo vaṇṇapokkharatā. Iti paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāyāti uttamena parisuddhena vaṇṇena ceva sarīrasaṇṭhānasampattiyā cāti attho. Brahmavaṇṇīti seṭṭhavaṇṇī. Parisuddhavaṇṇesupi seṭṭhena suvaṇṇavaṇṇena samannāgatoti attho. Brahmavacchasīti mahābrahmuno sarīrasadiseneva sarīrena samannāgato. Akhuddāvakāso dassanāyāti “bhoto sarīre dassanassa okāso na khuddako mahā, sabbāneva te aṅgapaccaṅgāni dassanīyāneva, tāni cāpi mahantānevā”ti dīpenti.

'Handsome' (abhirūpo) means: he is handsome, of a superior form to other humans. 'Pleasing to see' (dassanīyo) means: he is worthy of being seen, because looking at him even for a whole day does not bring satiety. 'Inspiring' (pāsādiko) means: he inspires confidence, because the mere sight of him generates mental clarity. 'Beauty' (pokkharatā) is said to be the state of being beautiful (sundarabhāvo). The beauty of the complexion is 'vaṇṇapokkharatā'; the meaning is that he is endowed with that perfection of complexion. The ancients (porāṇā), however, said: 'They call the body (sarīraṃ) "pokkhara," and the complexion (vaṇṇaṃ) simply "vaṇṇa."' According to their view, complexion and body are 'vaṇṇapokkharāni,' and their state is 'vaṇṇapokkharatā.' Thus, 'with supreme beauty of complexion and form' (paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya) means: with a supreme, pure complexion and with a supreme perfection of bodily form. 'Of Brahmā-like complexion' (brahmavaṇṇī) means: of the finest complexion (seṭṭhavaṇṇī). The meaning is that even among those with pure complexions, he is endowed with the finest, golden-hued complexion. 'Of Brahmā-like radiance' (brahmavacchasī) means: he is endowed with a bodily radiance just like that of a Mahābrahmā. By 'the opportunity for viewing him is not slight' (akhuddāvakāso dassanāya), they explain: 'The scope (okāso) for viewing the venerable one's body is not small, but great. All your major and minor limbs are indeed pleasing to see, and they are also large.'

Sīlamassa atthīti sīlavā. Vuddhaṃ vaddhitaṃ sīlamassāti vuddhasīlī. Vuddhasīlenāti vuddhena vaddhitena sīlena. Samannāgatoti yutto. Idaṃ vuddhasīlīpadasseva vevacanaṃ. Sabbametaṃ pañcasīlamattameva sandhāya vadanti.

'He is virtuous' (sīlavā) means: he has virtue (sīlaṃ). 'He is of mature virtue' (vuddhasīlī) means: his virtue is mature (vuddhaṃ) and developed (vaddhitaṃ). 'With mature virtue' (vuddhasīlena) means: with virtue that is mature and developed. 'Endowed' (samannāgato) means yutto. This is a synonym (vevacanaṃ) for the word 'vuddhasīlī.' They say all this with reference only to the five precepts.

Kalyāṇavācotiādīsu kalyāṇā sundarā parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanā vācā assāti kalyāṇavāco. Kalyāṇaṃ madhuraṃ vākkaraṇaṃ assāti kalyāṇavākkaraṇo[M 1.0252]. Vākkaraṇanti udāharaṇaghoso. Guṇaparipuṇṇabhāvena pure bhavāti porī. Pure vā bhavattā porī. Poriyā nāgarikitthiyā sukhumālattanena sadisāti porī, tāya poriyā. Vissaṭṭhāyāti apalibuddhāya sandiṭṭhavilambitādidosarahitāya. Anelagalāyāti elagaḷenavirahitāya. Yassa kassaci hi kathentassa [V 1.0228] elā gaḷanti, lālā vā paggharanti, kheḷaphusitāni vā nikkhamanti, tassa vācā elagaḷaṃ nāma hoti, tabbiparitāyāti attho. Atthassa viññāpaniyāti ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā bhāsitatthassa viññāpanasamatthāya.

In the phrases beginning with 'kalyāṇavāco': Because one's speech (vācā) is good (kalyāṇā), beautiful (sundarā), and has well-rounded words and syllables (parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanā), one is called kalyāṇavāco. Because one's manner of speaking (vākkaraṇaṃ) is good (kalyāṇaṃ) and sweet (madhuraṃ), one is called kalyāṇavākkaraṇo. Vākkaraṇaṃ means the sound of utterance. Speech is called porī because it arises in a state of fullness (pure bhavā), being complete with virtues. Or, it is called porī because it occurs in a great city (pure). It is also called porī because it is similar in its subtlety to a city woman (poriyā nāgarikitthiyā); by that porī speech. Vissaṭṭhā means unobstructed, free from faults such as being indistinct and hesitant. Anelagalā means free from elagaḷa. For when anyone speaks, if saliva (elā) flows, or drool (lālā) drips, or drops of spittle (kheḷaphusitāni) come out, that person's speech is called elagaḷa; the meaning here is the opposite of that. Atthassa viññāpaniyā means capable of making the meaning of what is spoken known by making the beginning, middle, and end clear.

Jiṇṇoti [P 1.0283] jarājiṇṇatāya jiṇṇo. Vuddhoti aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ vuddhibhāvamariyādappatto. Mahallakoti jātimahallakatāya samannāgato. Cirakālappasutoti vuttaṃ hoti. Addhagatoti addhānaṃ gato, dve tayo rājaparivaṭṭe atītoti adhippāyo. Vayoanuppattoti pacchimavayaṃ sampatto, pacchimavayo nāma vassasatassa pacchimo tatiyabhāgo.
