Jiṇṇa means aged due to being worn out by old age. Vuddha means one who has reached the limit of growth in his major and minor limbs. Mahallaka means one endowed with the quality of being elderly by birth. This means he has been born a long time ago. Addhagata means one who has gone a long way; the meaning is that he has passed two or three reigns of kings. Vayoanuppatta means one who has reached the final stage of life; the final stage of life is the last third part of a hundred years.

Api ca jiṇṇoti porāṇo, cirakālappavattakulanvayoti vuttaṃ hoti. Vuddhoti sīlācārādiguṇavuddhiyā yutto. Mahallakoti vibhavamahantāya samannāgato. Addhagatoti maggappaṭipanno brāhmaṇānaṃ vatacariyādimariyādaṃ avītikkamma caraṇasīlo. Vayoanuppattoti jātivuddhabhāvampi antimavayaṃ anuppatto.

Moreover, jiṇṇa means ancient, signifying a lineage that has been long established. Vuddha means one endowed with growth in virtues such as morality and conduct. Mahallaka means one endowed with great prosperity. Addhagata means one who has entered the path, whose conduct does not transgress the standard of the brahmins' observances and practices. Vayoanuppatta means one who has reached the final stage of life, having also attained the state of being old by birth.

Buddhaguṇakathā

A Discourse on the Buddha's Virtues

304. Evaṃ vutteti evaṃ tehi brāhmaṇehi vutte. Soṇadaṇḍo – “ime brāhmaṇā jātiādīhi mama vaṇṇaṃ vadanti, na kho pana metaṃ yuttaṃ attano vaṇṇe rajjituṃ. Handāhaṃ etesaṃ vādaṃ bhinditvā samaṇassa gotamassa mahantabhāvaṃ ñāpetvā etesaṃ tattha gamanaṃ karomī”ti cintetvā tena hi – bho mamapi suṇāthātiādimāha. Tattha yepi ubhato sujātoti ādayo attano guṇehi sadisā guṇā tepi[M 1.0253]; “ko cāhaṃ ke ca samaṇassa gotamassa jātisampattiādayo guṇā”ti attano guṇehi uttaritareyeva maññamāno, itare pana ekanteneva bhagavato mahantabhāvadīpanatthaṃ pakāseti.

304. When it was thus said means when it was thus said by those brahmins. Soṇadaṇḍa thought, 'These brahmins speak of my qualities because of birth and so forth, but it is not proper for me to be attached to my own qualities. Now, let me refute their argument, make known the greatness of the ascetic Gotama, and cause them to go to him.' Having thought thus, he said, 'Then, sirs, listen to me as well.' Therein, even regarding those qualities beginning with 'well-born on both sides,' which are similar to his own qualities, he reveals them while considering the ascetic Gotama's qualities, such as perfection of birth, to be far superior to his own. As for the other qualities, he reveals them solely for the purpose of demonstrating the Blessed One's greatness.

Mayameva arahāmāti evaṃ niyāmentovettha idaṃ dīpeti – “yadi guṇamahantatāya upasaṅkamitabbo nāma hoti. Yathā hi sineruṃ upanidhāya sāsapo, mahāsamuddaṃ upanidhāya gopadakaṃ, sattasu mahāsaresu udakaṃ upanidhāya ussāvabindu paritto lāmako. Evameva samaṇassa gotamassa jātisampattiādayopi guṇe upanidhāya amhākaṃ guṇā parittā lāmakā; tasmā mayameva arahāma taṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ dassanāya upasaṅkamitu”nti.

'We alone are worthy.' Thus determining, he explains this here: 'If one is to be approached on account of greatness of virtue, then just as a mustard seed is small and insignificant when compared to Mount Sineru, as the water in a cow's hoof-print is when compared to the great ocean, and as a dewdrop is when compared to the water in the seven great lakes, in the very same way, when compared to the virtues such as the perfection of birth of the ascetic Gotama, our virtues are small and insignificant. Therefore, we alone are worthy to approach the venerable Gotama for an audience.'

Mahantaṃ [V 1.0229] ñātisaṃghaṃ ohāyāti mātipakkhe asītikulasahassāni[P 1.0284], pitipakkhe asītikulasahassānīti evaṃ saṭṭhikulasatasahassaṃ ohāya pabbajito.

Having left behind a great assembly of relatives means: having abandoned eighty thousand families on his mother's side and eighty thousand families on his father's side—thus, one hundred and sixty thousand families in total—he went forth.

Bhūmigatañca vehāsaṭṭhañcāti ettha rājaṅgaṇe ceva uyyāne ca sudhāmaṭṭhapokkharaṇiyo sattaratanānaṃ pūretvā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapitaṃ dhanaṃ bhūmigataṃ nāma. Pāsādaniyūhādayo paripūretvā ṭhapitaṃ vehāsaṭṭhaṃ nāma. Etaṃ tāva kulapariyāyena āgataṃ. Tathāgatassa pana jātadivaseyeva saṅkho, elo, uppalo, puṇḍarīkoti cattāro nidhayo uggatā. Tesu saṅkho gāvutiko, elo aḍḍhayojaniko, uppalo tigāvutiko, puṇḍarīko yojaniko. Tesupi gahitaṃ gahitaṃ pūratiyeva, iti bhagavā pahūtaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ ohāya pabbajitoti veditabbo.

Regarding 'on the ground and in the air': Here, wealth placed on the ground, having filled plastered ponds in the royal courtyard and in the parks with the seven precious things, is called 'wealth on the ground.' Wealth placed having completely filled the projecting eaves of palaces and so forth is called 'wealth in the air.' This much came by way of family lineage. Moreover, on the very day the Tathāgata was born, four treasure troves arose: Saṅkha (Conch), Ela, Uppala (Blue Lotus), and Puṇḍarīka (White Lotus). Among these, Saṅkha was one gāvuta in size, Ela was half a yojana, Uppala was three gāvutas, and Puṇḍarīka was one yojana. Even when treasure was taken from them, they would always be replenished. Thus, it should be understood that the Blessed One went forth, having renounced abundant silver and gold.

Daharova samānoti taruṇova samāno. Susukāḷakesoti suṭṭhu kāḷakeso, añjanavaṇṇasadisakeso hutvā vāti attho. Bhadrenāti bhaddakena. Paṭhamena vayasāti tiṇṇaṃ vayānaṃ paṭhamavayena. Akāmakānanti anicchamānānaṃ. Anādaratthe sāmivacanaṃ. Assūni mukhe etesanti assumukhā, tesaṃ assumukhānaṃ, assūhi kilinnamukhānanti attho. Rudantānanti [M 1.0254] kanditvā rodamānānaṃ. Akhuddāvakāsoti ettha bhagavato aparimāṇoyeva dassanāya okāsoti veditabbo.

Daharova samāno means being youthful. Susukāḷakeso means having very black hair, that is, having hair resembling the color of collyrium. Bhadrena means with what is fine. Paṭhamena vayasā means with the first of the three stages of life. Akāmakānaṃ means of those who are unwilling; the genitive case is used here in the sense of disregard. Assūni mukhe etesaṃ means they are assumukhā (tear-faced); tesaṃ assumukhānaṃ means of those whose faces are wet with tears. Rudantānaṃ means of those who are wailing and weeping. Here, akhuddāvakāso should be understood to mean that the opportunity to see the Blessed One is indeed immeasurable.

Tatridaṃ vatthu – rājagahe kira aññataro brāhmaṇo samaṇassa gotamassa pamāṇaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkotīti sutvā bhagavato piṇḍāya pavisanakāle saṭṭhihatthaṃ veḷuṃ gahetvā nagaradvārassa bahi ṭhatvā sampatte bhagavati veḷuṃ gahetvā samīpe aṭṭhāsi. Veḷu bhagavato jāṇukamattaṃ pāpuṇi. Puna divase dve veḷū ghaṭetvā samīpe aṭṭhāsi. Bhagavāpi dvinnaṃ veḷūnaṃ upari kaṭimattameva paññāyamāno – “brāhmaṇa, kiṃ karosī”ti āha. Tumhākaṃ pamāṇaṃ gaṇhāmīti. “Brāhmaṇa, sacepi tvaṃ sakalacakkavāḷagabbhaṃ pūretvā ṭhite veḷū ghaṭetvā [P 1.0285] āgamissasi, neva me pamāṇaṃ gahetuṃ sakkhissasi. Na hi mayā cattāri asaṅkhyeyāni kappasatasahassañca tathā pāramiyo pūritā, yathā me paro pamāṇaṃ gaṇheyya, atulo, brāhmaṇa, tathāgato appameyyo”ti vatvā dhammapade gāthamāha –

Here is the story: It is said that in Rājagaha, a certain brahmin, having heard that one is not able to take the measure of the ascetic Gotama, took a sixty-cubit bamboo and stood outside the city gate at the time when the Blessed One was entering for alms-food. When the Blessed One arrived, the brahmin took the bamboo and stood nearby. The bamboo reached only to the Blessed One’s knee. On the next day, he joined two bamboos together and stood nearby. The Blessed One, making himself appear only up to his waist above the two bamboos, said, 'Brahmin, what are you doing?' 'I am taking your measure.' 'Brahmin, even if you were to come having joined together bamboos that stand filling the entire Cakkavāḷa-sphere, you would still not be able to take my measure. For the perfections were not fulfilled by me for four incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand world-cycles in such a way that another could take my measure. Incomparable, O brahmin, is the Tathāgata, immeasurable.' Having said this, he spoke a verse in the Dhammapada:

“Te tādise pūjayato, nibbute akutobhaye;

Na sakkā puññaṃ saṅkhātuṃ, imettamapi kenacī”ti. (dha. pa. 36);

For one who pays homage to such ones—who are extinguished and free from fear from any quarter—it is not possible for anyone to calculate the merit, saying, 'It is this much.'

Gāthāpariyosāne [V 1.0230] caturāsītipāṇasahassāni amataṃ piviṃsu.

At the end of the verse, eighty-four thousand beings drank the deathless.

Aparampi vatthu – rāhu kira asurindo cattāri yojanasahassāni aṭṭha ca yojanasatāni ucco. Bāhantaramassa dvādasayojanasatāni. Bahalantarena cha yojanasatāni. Hatthatalapādatalānaṃ puthulato tīṇi yojanasatāni. Aṅgulipabbāni paṇṇāsayojanāni. Bhamukantaraṃ paṇṇāsayojanaṃ. Mukhaṃ dviyojanasataṃ tiyojanasatagambhīraṃ tiyojanasataparimaṇḍalaṃ. Gīvā tiyojanasataṃ. Nalāṭaṃ tiyojanasataṃ. Sīsaṃ navayojanasataṃ. “So ahaṃ uccosmi, satthāraṃ onamitvā oloketuṃ na sakkhissāmī”ti cintetvā nāgacchi. So ekadivasaṃ bhagavato vaṇṇaṃ sutvā – “yathākathañca olokessāmī”ti āgato.

This is another story: It is said that Rāhu, the lord of the asuras, was four thousand and eight hundred yojanas tall. The space between his upper arms was twelve hundred yojanas. The measure of his torso was six hundred yojanas. The width of his palms and soles was three hundred yojanas. His finger and toe joints were fifty yojanas. The space between his eyebrows was fifty yojanas. His mouth was two hundred yojanas wide, three hundred yojanas deep, and three hundred yojanas in circumference. His neck was three hundred yojanas. His forehead was three hundred yojanas. His head was nine hundred yojanas. Thinking, 'I am tall; I will not be able to see the Teacher by bending down,' he did not come. One day, having heard of the Blessed One's virtue, he came, thinking, 'I will see him by some means or other.'

Atha bhagavā tassajjhāsayaṃ viditvā – “catūsu iriyāpathesu katarena dassessāmī”ti cintetvā “ṭhitako nāma nīcopi ucco viya paññāyati. Nipannovassa [M 1.0255] attānaṃ dassessāmī”ti “ānanda, gandhakuṭipariveṇe mañcakaṃ paññāpehī”ti vatvā tattha sīhaseyyaṃ kappesi. Rāhu āgantvā nipannaṃ bhagavantaṃ gīvaṃ unnāmetvā nabhamajjhe puṇṇacandaṃ viya ullokesi. Kimidaṃ asurindāti ca vutte – “bhagavā onamitvā oloketuṃ na sakkhissāmī”ti nāgacchinti. Na mayā, asurinda, adhomukhena pāramiyo pūritā. Uddhaggameva katvā dānaṃ dinnanti. Taṃ divasaṃ rāhu saraṇaṃ agamāsi. Evaṃ bhagavā akhuddāvakāso dassanāya.

Then the Blessed One, knowing his intention, thought, 'In which of the four postures shall I show myself?' and having considered, 'One who is standing, though short, appears as if tall. I shall show myself to him while lying down,' he said, 'Ānanda, prepare a small couch in the perfumed chamber's enclosure.' Having said this, he adopted the lion's posture there. Rāhu, having approached, looked up at the recumbent Blessed One by raising his neck, as one would look at the full moon in the middle of the sky. And when it was said, 'What is this, O lord of asuras?' he replied, 'O Blessed One, I did not come previously, thinking, "I will not be able to see by bending down."' 'O lord of asuras, the perfections were not fulfilled by me with my face downwards. The gift was given only with an upward-facing attitude.' On that day, Rāhu went for refuge. Thus, the Blessed One provides a not-small opportunity for being seen.

Catupārisuddhisīlena [P 1.0286] sīlavā, taṃ pana sīlaṃ ariyaṃ uttamaṃ parisuddhaṃ. Tenāha – “ariyasīlī”ti. Tadetaṃ anavajjaṭṭhena kusalaṃ. Tenāha – “kusalasīlī”ti. Kusalasīlenāti idamassa vevacanaṃ.

He is virtuous by means of the fourfold purity of virtue. And that virtue is noble, supreme, and completely pure. Therefore, he is called 'one of noble virtue.' That same virtue is skillful in the sense of being blameless. Therefore, he is called 'one of skillful virtue.' The phrase 'with skillful virtue' is a synonym for this.

Bahūnaṃ ācariyapācariyoti bhagavato ekekāya dhammadesanāya caturāsītipāṇasahassāni aparimāṇāpi devamanussā maggaphalāmataṃ pivanti, tasmā bahūnaṃ ācariyo. Sāvakaveneyyānaṃ pana pācariyoti.

'Teacher and great teacher of many' means this: at each single Dhamma discourse of the Blessed One, eighty-four thousand beings and also immeasurable gods and humans drink the deathless nectar of the path and fruit. Therefore, he is the teacher of many. Furthermore, he is the principal teacher of the disciples who are to be trained.

Khīṇakāmarāgoti ettha kāmaṃ bhagavato sabbepi kilesā khīṇā. Brāhmaṇo pana te na jānāti. Attano jānanaṭṭhāneyeva guṇaṃ katheti. Vigatacāpalloti – “pattamaṇḍanā cīvaramaṇḍanā [V 1.0231] senāsanamaṇḍanā imassa vā pūtikāyassa…pe… kelanā paṭikelanā”ti (vibha. 854) evaṃ vuttacāpallā virahito.

Regarding the phrase 'one whose sensual passion is destroyed,' indeed, all the defilements of the Blessed One are destroyed. However, because the brahmin does not know those other defilements, he speaks of this virtue only within the sphere of his own knowledge. 'Devoid of fickleness' means he is free from the fickleness described thus: 'adorning the bowl, adorning the robes, adorning the lodging, or of this putrid body... playfulness and repeated playfulness.'

Apāpapurekkhāroti apāpe nava lokuttaradhamme purato katvā vicarati. Brahmaññāya pajāyāti sāriputtamoggallānamahākassapādibhedāya brāhmaṇapajāya, etissāya ca pajāya purekkhāro. Ayañhi pajā samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ purakkhatvā caratīti attho. Api ca apāpapurekkhāroti na pāpaṃ purekkhāro na pāpaṃ purato katvā carati, na pāpaṃ icchatīti attho. Kassa? Brahmaññāya pajāya. Attanā saddhiṃ paṭiviruddhāyapi brāhmaṇapajāya aviruddho hitasukhatthiko yevāti vuttaṃ hoti.

'One who does not put evil foremost' means that he fares having placed the nine supramundane Dhammas, which are free from evil, before him. 'For the brahmin folk' means for the community of brahmins, distinguished as Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Mahākassapa, and others; and for this community, he is placed at the forefront. Indeed, the meaning is that this community fares having placed the ascetic Gotama at its forefront. Furthermore, 'one who does not put evil foremost' means he does not make evil his leader, he does not fare having placed evil before him, he does not desire evil. For whom? For the brahmin folk. It is meant that even toward the community of brahmins who are opposed to him, he is not in opposition, but is one who desires their welfare and happiness.

Tiroraṭṭhāti pararaṭṭhato. Tirojanapadāti parajanapadato. Pañhaṃ pucchituṃ āgacchantīti khattiyapaṇḍitādayo ceva devabrahmanāgagandhabbādayo ca [M 1.0256] – “pañhe abhisaṅkharitvā pucchissāmā”ti āgacchanti. Tattha keci pucchāya vā dosaṃ vissajjanasampaṭicchane vā asamatthataṃ sallakkhetvā apucchitvāva tuṇhī nisīdanti. Keci pucchanti. Kesañci bhagavā pucchāya ussāhaṃ janetvā vissajjeti. Evaṃ sabbesampi tesaṃ vimatiyo tīraṃ patvā mahāsamuddassa ūmiyo viya bhagavantaṃ patvā bhijjanti.

'From across the country' means from another country. 'From across the district' means from another district. 'They come to ask questions' means that Khattiya scholars and others, as well as gods, brahmās, nāgas, gandhabbas, and others, come thinking, 'Having prepared questions, we will ask.' Among them, some, having perceived either a flaw in their own question or their inability to accept the answer, sit in silence without asking. Some ask. For some, the Blessed One, having generated enthusiasm for the question, gives an answer. Thus, the doubts of all of them, upon reaching the Blessed One, are broken apart, just as the waves of the great ocean are broken apart upon reaching the shore.

Ehi [P 1.0287] svāgatavādīti devamanussapabbajitagahaṭṭhesu taṃ taṃ attano santikaṃ āgataṃ – “ehi svāgata”nti evaṃ vadatīti attho. Sakhiloti tattha katamaṃ sākhalyaṃ? “Yā sā vācā nelā kaṇṇasukhā”tiādinā nayena vuttasākhalyena samannāgato, muduvacanoti attho. Sammodakoti paṭisanthārakusalo, āgatāgatānaṃ catunnaṃ parisānaṃ – “kacci, bhikkhave, khamanīyaṃ, kacci yāpanīya”ntiādinā nayena sabbaṃ addhānadarathaṃ vūpasamento viya paṭhamataraṃ sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ kattāti attho. Abbhākuṭikoti yathā ekacce parisaṃ patvā thaddhamukhā saṅkuṭitamukhā honti, na ediso, parisadassanena panassa bālātapasamphassena viya padumaṃ mukhapadumaṃ vikasati puṇṇacandasassirikaṃ hoti. Uttānamukhoti yathā ekacce nikujjitamukhā viya sampattāya parisāya na kiñci kathenti, atidullabhakathā honti, na evarūpo. Samaṇo pana gotamo sulabhakatho. Na tassa santikaṃ āgatāgatānaṃ – “kasmā mayaṃ idhāgatā”ti vippaṭisāro uppajjati dhammaṃ pana sutvā attamanāva hontīti dasseti. Pubbabhāsīti bhāsanto ca paṭhamataraṃ bhāsati, tañca kho kālayuttaṃ pamāṇayuttaṃ atthanissitameva bhāsati, na niratthakakathaṃ.

'Ehi svāgatavādī' (He is welcoming in speech) means that to devas, humans, renunciants, and householders who come to his presence, he is accustomed to saying, 'Come, you are welcome'—this is the meaning. 'Sakhilo' (affable) means he is endowed with the affability spoken of by the method beginning with, 'That speech which is flawless, pleasing to the ear,' etc.—this means he has gentle speech. 'Sammodako' (courteous) means skilled in friendly greetings; to the four assemblies who come, he is accustomed to first making pleasant conversation, such as, 'I hope, monks, you are well, I hope you are getting by,' as if dispelling all the weariness of the journey—this is the meaning. 'Abbhākuṭiko' (with a bright face) means he is not like some who, upon reaching an assembly, have stiff or scowling faces. Rather, upon seeing an assembly, his lotus-like face blossoms like a lotus touched by the morning sun, becoming possessed of the splendor of the full moon. 'Uttānamukho' (with an open countenance) means he is not like some who, like those with an overturned face, say nothing to an assembly that has arrived, being of very difficult speech. But the ascetic Gotama is of easy speech. For those who come to his presence, the regret, 'Why have we come here?' does not arise; rather, having heard the Dhamma, they are indeed pleased in mind—this it shows. 'Pubbabhāsī' (he speaks first) means that when speaking, he speaks first, and that speech is timely, measured, and connected with benefit, not useless talk.

Na [V 1.0232] tasmiṃ gāme vāti yattha kira bhagavā paṭivasati, tattha mahesakkhā devatā ārakkhaṃ gaṇhanti, taṃ nissāya manussānaṃ upaddavo na hoti, paṃsupisācakādayoyeva hi manusse viheṭhenti, te tāsaṃ ānubhāvena dūraṃ apakkamanti. Api ca bhagavato mettābalenapi na amanussā manusse viheṭhenti.

It is said that in whatever place the Blessed One resides, powerful deities undertake protection. Relying on them, there is no danger for humans. Indeed, it is only dust-demons and the like that harass humans, and they, by the power of those deities, go far away. Moreover, also by the power of the Blessed One's loving-kindness, non-humans do not harass humans.

Saṅghītiādīsu anusāsitabbo sayaṃ vā uppādito saṅgho assa atthīti saṅghī. Tādiso cassa gaṇo atthīti gaṇī. Purimapadasseva vā vevacanametaṃ. Ācārasikkhāpanavasena gaṇassa ācariyoti gaṇācariyo[M 1.0257]. Puthutitthakarānanti bahūnaṃ titthakarānaṃ. Yathā [P 1.0288] vā tathā vāti yena vā tena vā acelakādimattakenāpi kāraṇena. Samudāgacchatīti samantato upagacchati abhivaḍḍhati.

Regarding terms like 'Saṅghī' and so forth: He is 'Saṅghī' because he has a Saṅgha (community) that should be instructed, or a Saṅgha produced by himself. He is 'Gaṇī' because he has such a group. Alternatively, this is a synonym for the preceding word. He is 'Gaṇācariyo' because he is a teacher of the group by way of instructing in conduct. 'Puthutitthakarānaṃ' means of many sect-founders. 'Yathā vā tathā vā' (in whatever way) means for any reason whatsoever, even for the mere fact of being a naked ascetic, etc. 'Samudāgacchati' (comes together) means it approaches from all around, it increases.

Atithi no te hontīti te amhākaṃ āgantukā, navakā pāhunakā hontīti attho. Pariyāpuṇāmīti jānāmi. Aparimāṇavaṇṇoti tathārūpeneva sabbaññunāpi appameyyavaṇṇo – “pageva mādisenā”ti dasseti. Vuttampi cettaṃ –

'Atithi no te hontīti' (They are our guests) means they are our visitors, newcomers, and guests—that is the meaning. 'Pariyāpuṇāmīti' (I know) means I know. 'Aparimāṇavaṇṇo' (of immeasurable quality) means that even by an Omniscient One of such a nature, his quality is immeasurable—'how much more so by one like me'—this it shows. And this has been said:

“Buddhopi buddhassa bhaṇeyya vaṇṇaṃ,

Kappampi ce aññamabhāsamāno;

Khīyetha kappo ciradīghamantare,

Vaṇṇo na khīyetha tathāgatassā”ti.

“Even if a Buddha were to speak the quality of a Buddha for a whole eon, speaking of nothing else; in that long, long interval the eon would be exhausted, but the quality of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.”

305. Imaṃ pana satthu guṇakathaṃ sutvā te brāhmaṇā cintayiṃsu – yathā soṇadaṇḍo brāhmaṇo samaṇassa gotamassa vaṇṇe bhaṇati, anomaguṇo so bhavaṃ gotamo; evaṃ tassa guṇe jānamānena kho pana ācariyena aticiraṃ adhivāsitaṃ, handa naṃ anuvattāmāti anuvattiṃsu. Tasmā evaṃ vutte “te brāhmaṇā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha alamevāti yuttameva. Api puṭosenāti puṭosaṃ vuccati pātheyyaṃ, taṃ gahetvāpi upasaṅkamituṃ yuttamevāti attho. Puṭaṃsenātipi pāṭho, tassattho, puṭo aṃse assāti puṭaṃso, tena puṭaṃsena. Aṃsena hi pātheyyapuṭaṃ vahantenāpīti vuttaṃ hoti.

305. But having heard this talk on the Teacher’s qualities, those brahmins thought: 'In the way that the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa speaks of the ascetic Gotama's qualities, the venerable Gotama is of excellent qualities. Indeed, our teacher, knowing his qualities, has held back for a very long time. Come, let us follow him.' And so they followed. Therefore, when this was said, the passage beginning 'those brahmins' was spoken. Therein, 'alameva' means it is indeed fitting. Regarding 'Api puṭosena,' provisions for a journey are called 'puṭosa'; 'even taking them, it is indeed fitting to approach'—this is the meaning. There is also the reading 'Puṭaṃsena'; its meaning is, 'puṭaṃso' is one who has a bundle on his shoulder, and the phrase means by that 'puṭaṃsa.' For it means 'even while carrying the bundle of provisions on the shoulder.'

Soṇadaṇḍaparivitakkavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of Soṇadaṇḍa's Reflections

306-308. Tirovanasaṇḍagatassāti [V 1.0233] antovanasaṇḍe gatassa, vihārabbhantaraṃ paviṭṭhassāti attho. Añjaliṃ paṇāmetvāti ete ubhatopakkhikā, te evaṃ cintayiṃsu – “sace no micchādiṭṭhikā codessanti – ‘kasmā tumhe samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ vanditthā’ti? Tesaṃ – ‘kiṃ añjalimattakaraṇenāpi vandanaṃ nāma hotī’ti vakkhāma. Sace no sammādiṭṭhikā codessanti – ‘kasmā tumhe bhagavantaṃ na vanditthā’ti. ‘Kiṃ sīsena bhūmiyaṃ paharanteneva vandanaṃ nāma hoti, nanu añjalikammampi vandanaṃ evā’ti [M 1.0258] vakkhāmā”ti. Nāmagottanti [P 1.0289] “bho, gotama, ahaṃ asukassa putto datto nāma, mitto nāma, idhāgato”ti vadantā nāmaṃ sāventi nāma. “Bho, gotama, ahaṃ vāseṭṭho nāma, kaccāno nāma, idhāgato”ti vadantā gottaṃ sāventi nāma. Ete kira daliddā jiṇṇā kulaputtā “parisamajjhe nāmagottavasena pākaṭā bhavissāmā”ti evamakaṃsu. Ye pana tuṇhībhūtā nisīdiṃsu, te kerāṭikā ceva andhabālā ca. Tattha kerāṭikā – “ekaṃ dve kathāsallāpepi karonto vissāsiko hoti, atha vissāse sati ekaṃ dve bhikkhā adātuṃ na yutta”nti tato attānaṃ mocetvā tuṇhī nisīdanti. Andhabālā aññāṇatāyeva avakkhittamattikāpiṇḍo viya yattha katthaci tuṇhībhūtā nisīdanti.

'Tirovanasaṇḍagatassa' means one who has gone into the forest grove, that is, one who has entered the monastery. 'Añjaliṃ paṇāmetvā' refers to these who belonged to two factions; they thought thus: 'If those of wrong view should reproach us, saying, “Why did you pay homage to the ascetic Gotama?” we will reply, “Is it called homage merely by the act of raising the hands in reverence?” If those of right view should reproach us, saying, “Why did you not pay homage to the Blessed One?” we will reply, “Is paying homage only done by striking one's head on the ground? Surely the act of raising the hands in reverence is also homage?”' 'Nāmagotta' means announcing one's name and clan. Saying, 'Venerable Gotama, I, named Datta, son of so-and-so, have come here,' or '...named Mitta...', is to announce one's name. Saying, 'Venerable Gotama, I, named Vāseṭṭha, have come here,' or '...named Kaccāna...', is to announce one's clan. It is said that these were poor, aged men of good family who did this thinking, 'We shall become well-known in the midst of the assembly by means of our name and clan.' As for those who sat down in silence, they were either crafty or blind fools. Among them, the crafty, thinking, 'Engaging in even one or two words of conversation makes one familiar, and then, when there is familiarity, it is not proper not to give one or two alms-portions,' thus freeing themselves from that, sat silently. The blind fools, out of sheer ignorance, sat down silently wherever they were, like a lump of clay that has been thrown down.

Brāhmaṇapaññattivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Definition of a Brahmin.

309-310. Cetasā cetoparivitakkanti bhagavā – “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo āgatakālato paṭṭhāya adhomukho thaddhagatto kiṃ cintayamāno nisinno, kiṃ nu kho cintetī”ti āvajjanto attano cetasā tassa cittaṃ aññāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāyā”ti. Vihaññatīti vighātaṃ āpajjati. Anuviloketvā parisanti bhagavato sakasamaye pañhapucchanena udake miyamāno ukkhipitvā thale ṭhapito viya samapassaddhakāyacitto hutvā parisaṃ saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ diṭṭhisañjāneneva “upadhārentu me bhonto vacana”nti vadanto viya anuviloketvā parisaṃ bhagavantaṃ etadavoca.

'Cetasā cetoparivitakkaṃ' means that the Blessed One, reflecting, 'What is this brahmin pondering, sitting with downcast face and rigid body from the moment he arrived? What indeed is he thinking?' thus knew his mind with His own mind. Therefore it was said by the Venerable Ānanda: 'Having known with His mind the other's reflection.' 'Vihaññati' means he comes to mental distress. As for 'Anuviloketvā parisaṃ,' the brahmin, having become calm in body and mind—like one who is drowning in water being lifted out and placed on dry land—due to the Blessed One's asking a question concerning his own doctrine, then for the purpose of winning over the assembly, and just by his thorough knowledge of his own view, as if saying, 'Sirs, may you pay attention to my words,' surveyed the assembly and said this to the Blessed One.

311-313. Sujaṃ paggaṇhantānanti yaññayajanatthāya sujaṃ gaṇhantesu brāhmaṇesu paṭhamo vā dutiyo vāti attho. Sujāya diyyamānaṃ mahāyāgaṃ paṭiggaṇhantānanti porāṇā. Iti brāhmaṇo sakasamayavasena sammadeva pañhaṃ vissajjesi. Bhagavā pana visesato uttamabrāhmaṇassa dassanatthaṃ [V 1.0234] – “imesaṃ panā”tiādimāha. Etadavocunti sace jātivaṇṇamantasampanno brāhmaṇo na hoti, atha ko carahi loke brāhmaṇo [M 1.0259] bhavissati? Nāseti no ayaṃ soṇadaṇḍo, handassa vādaṃ paṭikkhipissāmāti cintetvā etadavocuṃ. Apavadatīti [P 1.0290] paṭikkhipati. Anupakkhandatīti anupavisati. Idaṃ – “sace tvaṃ pasādavasena samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gantukāmo, gaccha; mā brāhmaṇassa samayaṃ bhindī”ti adhippāyena āhaṃsu.

'Sujaṃ paggaṇhantānaṃ' means among the brahmins who take up the sacrificial ladle for the purpose of performing sacrifices, being either the first or the second. The ancients say it means 'among those who receive the great sacrifice given by means of the ladle.' Thus, the brahmin answered the question perfectly well in accordance with his own doctrine. The Blessed One, however, for the purpose of showing the supreme brahmin in a special sense, said the words beginning, 'But among these...' As for 'Etadavocuṃ,' they thought, 'If one endowed with birth, complexion, and mantras is not a brahmin, then who in the world will be a brahmin? This Soṇadaṇḍa is ruining us. Come, let us refute his doctrine,' and so they said this. 'Apavadati' means he refutes. 'Anupakkhandati' means he follows along. This they said with the intention: 'If you wish to go for refuge to the ascetic Gotama out of faith, then go; but do not break the doctrine of the brahmins.'

314. Etadavocāti imesu brāhmaṇesu evaṃ ekappahāreneva viravantesu “ayaṃ kathā pariyosānaṃ na gamissati, handa ne nissadde katvā soṇadaṇḍeneva saddhiṃ kathemī”ti cintetvā – “etaṃ sace kho tumhāka”ntiādikaṃ vacanaṃ avoca.

314. As for 'Etadavoca,' when these brahmins were all clamoring at once, the Blessed One thought, 'This discussion will not reach a conclusion. Come, let me silence them and speak with Soṇadaṇḍa alone.' Having thought thus, he spoke the words beginning, 'If, for you...'

315-316. Sahadhammenāti sakāraṇena. Samasamoti ṭhapetvā ekadesasamattaṃ samabhāvena samo, sabbākārena samoti attho. Ahamassa mātāpitaro jānāmīti bhaginiyā puttassa mātāpitaro kiṃ na jānissati, kulakoṭiparidīpanaṃ sandhāyeva vadati. Musāvādampi bhaṇeyyāti atthabhañjanakaṃ musāvādaṃ katheyya. Kiṃ vaṇṇo karissatīti abbhantare guṇe asati kiṃ karissati? Kimassa brāhmaṇabhāvaṃ rakkhituṃ sakkhissatīti attho. Athāpi siyā puna – “pakatisīle ṭhitassa brāhmaṇabhāvaṃ sādhentī”ti evampi sīlameva sādhessati, tasmiṃ hissa asati brāhmaṇabhāvo nāhosīti sammohamattaṃ vaṇṇādayo. Idaṃ pana sutvā te brāhmaṇā – “sabhāvaṃ ācariyo āha, akāraṇāva mayaṃ ujjhāyimhā”ti tuṇhī ahesuṃ.

'Sahadhammena' means with a valid reason. 'Samasama' means, setting aside partial equality, equal in a state of equality; the meaning is equal in all respects. 'I know his parents' implies, 'How would one not know the parents of one's sister’s son?' He speaks this way intending to highlight the family's lineage. 'Musāvādampi bhaṇeyya' means he might speak a falsehood that destroys one's welfare. 'Kiṃ vaṇṇo karissatī?' means, 'If there are no inner qualities, what can complexion do?' The meaning is, 'How will it be able to preserve his brahminhood?' Or, should you have this thought: 'For one established in natural virtue, complexion and the other factors accomplish brahminhood,' even so, it is virtue alone that will accomplish brahminhood. Why? Because for him, when that virtue was absent, his brahminhood was no more. Therefore, the idea that complexion and so on are factors of brahminhood is mere delusion. Hearing this, the brahmins fell silent, thinking, 'The teacher has spoken the true nature of things; we found fault without cause.'

Sīlapaññākathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Discourse on Virtue and Wisdom.

317. Tato bhagavā ‘kathito brāhmaṇena pañho, kiṃ panettha patiṭṭhātuṃ sakkhissati, na sakkhissatī’ti? Tassa vīmaṃsanatthaṃ – “imesaṃ pana brāhmaṇā”tiādimāha. Sīlaparidhotāti sīlaparisuddhā. Yattha sīlaṃ tattha paññāti yasmiṃ puggale sīlaṃ, tattheva paññā, kuto dussīle paññā? Paññārahite vā jaḷe eḷamūge kuto sīlanti? Sīlapaññāṇanti sīlañca paññāṇañca sīlapaññāṇaṃ. Paññāṇanti paññāyeva. Evametaṃ brāhmaṇāti [M 1.0260] bhagavā brāhmaṇassa vacanaṃ [P 1.0291] anujānanto āha. Tattha sīlaparidhotā paññāti catupārisuddhisīlena dhotā. Kathaṃ pana sīlena paññaṃ dhovatīti? Yassa puthujjanassa sīlaṃ saṭṭhiasītivassāni akhaṇḍaṃ hoti, so maraṇakālepi sabbakilese ghātetvā sīlena paññaṃ dhovitvā arahattaṃ gaṇhāti. Kandarasālapariveṇe mahāsaṭṭhivassatthero viya. There kira maraṇamañce nipajjitvā balavavedanāya nitthunante[V 1.0235], tissamahārājā “theraṃ passissāmī”ti gantvā pariveṇadvāre ṭhito taṃ saddaṃ sutvā pucchi – “kassa saddo aya”nti? Therassa nitthunanasaddoti. “Pabbajjāya saṭṭhivassena vedanāpariggahamattampi na kataṃ, na dāni naṃ vandissāmī”ti nivattitvā mahābodhiṃ vandituṃ gato. Tato upaṭṭhākadaharo theraṃ āha – “kiṃ no, bhante, lajjāpetha, saddhopi rājā vippaṭisārī hutvā na vandissāmī”ti gatoti. Kasmā āvusoti? Tumhākaṃ nitthunanasaddaṃ sutvāti. “Tena hi me okāsaṃ karothā”ti vatvā vedanaṃ vikkhambhitvā arahattaṃ patvā daharassa saññaṃ adāsi – “gacchāvuso, idāni rājānaṃ amhe vandāpehī”ti. Daharo gantvā – “idāni kira theraṃ, vandathā”ti āha. Rājā saṃsumārapatitena theraṃ vandanto – “nāhaṃ ayyassa arahattaṃ vandāmi, puthujjanabhūmiyaṃ pana ṭhatvā rakkhitasīlameva vandāmī”ti āha, evaṃ sīlena paññaṃ dhovati nāma. Yassa pana abbhantare sīlasaṃvaro natthi, ugghāṭitaññutāya pana catuppadikagāthāpariyosāne paññāya sīlaṃ dhovitvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Ayaṃ paññāya sīlaṃ dhovati nāma. Seyyathāpi santatimahāmatto.

317. Then the Blessed One, to examine him, considered: 'The question has been answered by the brahmin, but will he be able to be established in this, or not?' and said, 'But of these, brahmin...' and so on. 'Purified by virtue' means well-purified by virtue. 'Where there is virtue, there is wisdom' means: in whichever person virtue exists, in that very person wisdom exists. In one who is without virtue, whence wisdom? Or, in one devoid of wisdom, who is dull and a drooling idiot, whence virtue? 'Virtue and wisdom' means virtue and also wisdom. 'Wisdom' means wisdom itself. The Blessed One, approving the brahmin's statement, said, 'So it is, brahmin.' Therein, 'wisdom purified by virtue' means cleansed by the fourfold purity of virtue. But how does one cleanse wisdom with virtue? For whichever worldling whose virtue is unbroken for sixty or eighty years, that person, even at the time of death, having destroyed all defilements and having cleansed wisdom with virtue, attains Arahantship. Like the great elder of sixty vassas in the Kandarasāla monastic compound. It is said that while he lay on his deathbed, groaning from severe pain, King Tissa the Great, wanting to see the elder, went and stood at the monastery gate. Hearing the sound, he asked, 'Whose sound is this?' 'The elder's groaning,' they replied. 'After sixty years of monastic life, he has not even accomplished the mere comprehension of feeling—now I will not pay homage to him,' he said and turned back to venerate the Great Bodhi tree. Then the elder's young attendant said, 'Venerable sir, why do you shame us? Even the faithful king, having become regretful, has gone away, saying, "I will not pay homage."' 'Why, friend?' 'Having heard your groaning.' 'Then grant me an opportunity,' he said, and suppressing the pain, he attained Arahantship and gave the young attendant a signal: 'Go, friend, now have the king pay homage to us.' The young man went and said, 'Now, it seems, you should pay homage to the elder.' The king, prostrating before the elder like a crocodile, said, 'I do not pay homage to the venerable one's Arahantship, but to the very virtue protected while he was still in the state of a worldling.' Thus, it is said that one cleanses wisdom with virtue. On the other hand, for one who lacks internal moral restraint, yet through sharp intelligence, at the conclusion of a four-lined verse, cleanses virtue with wisdom and attains Arahantship along with the analytical knowledges—this is called cleansing virtue with wisdom. Like the great minister Santati.

318. Katamaṃ pana taṃ brāhmaṇāti kasmā āha? Bhagavā kira cintesi – “brāhmaṇā brāhmaṇasamaye pañcasīlāni ‘sīla’nti paññāpenti, vedattayauggahaṇapaññā paññāti. Uparivisesaṃ [P 1.0292] na jānanti. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ brāhmaṇassa uttarivisesabhūtaṃ maggasīlaṃ, phalasīlaṃ, maggapaññaṃ, phalapaññañca dassetvā arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhapeyya”nti. Atha naṃ kathetukamyatāya pucchanto – “katamaṃ pana taṃ, brāhmaṇa, sīlaṃ katamā sā paññā”ti āha. Atha brāhmaṇo – “mayā sakasamayavasena pañho vissajjito. Samaṇo pana maṃ gotamo puna nivattitvā pucchati, idānissāhaṃ cittaṃ paritosetvā vissajjituṃ [M 1.0261] sakkuṇeyyaṃ vā na vā? Sace na sakkhissaṃ paṭhamaṃ uppannāpi me lajjā bhijjissati. Asakkontassa pana na sakkomīti vacane doso natthī”ti puna nivattitvā bhagavatoyeva bhāraṃ karonto “ettakaparamāva maya”ntiādimāha. Tattha ettakaparamāti ettakaṃ sīlapaññāṇanti vacanameva paramaṃ amhākaṃ, te mayaṃ ettakaparamā, ito paraṃ etassa bhāsitassa atthaṃ na jānāmāti attho.

318. Why did he say, 'But what, brahmin, is that?' The Blessed One, it is said, considered thus: 'Brahmins, in their own tradition, designate the five precepts as 'virtue,' and the wisdom of grasping the three Vedas as 'wisdom.' They do not know a higher distinction. What if I were to show the brahmin the virtue of the path, the virtue of the fruit, the wisdom of the path, and the wisdom of the fruit, which are a higher distinction, and conclude the teaching with the summit of Arahantship.' Then, desiring to converse with him, he asked, 'But what, brahmin, is that virtue? What is that wisdom?' Then the brahmin thought: 'I have answered the question according to my own tradition. But the ascetic Gotama asks me again, turning back to the beginning. Now, will I be able to satisfy his mind and answer, or not? If I cannot, the shame that has already arisen in me will be shattered. But for one who is unable, there is no fault in saying, 'I cannot.'' So, turning back again and placing the burden on the Blessed One himself, he said, 'This is our limit,' and so on. Here, 'this is our limit' means: 'This much alone is the extent of our virtue and wisdom; we go this far. Beyond this, we do not understand the meaning of what is said.'

Athassa bhagavā sīlapaññāya mūlabhūtassa tathāgatassa uppādato pabhuti sīlapaññāṇaṃ dassetuṃ – “idha brāhmaṇa, tathāgato”tiādimāha. Tassattho sāmaññaphale vuttanayeneva veditabbo, ayaṃ pana viseso, idha tividhampi sīlaṃ – “idampissa hoti sīlasmi”nti evaṃ sīlamicceva niyyātitaṃ paṭhamajjhānādīni cattāri jhānāni atthato paññāsampadā. Evaṃ [V 1.0236] paññāvasena pana aniyyātetvā vipassanāpaññāya padaṭṭhānabhāvamattena dassetvā vipassanāpaññāto paṭṭhāya paññā niyyātitāti.

Then, to show him the virtue and wisdom beginning from the arising of the Tathāgata, who is the foundation of virtue and wisdom, the Blessed One said, 'Here, brahmin, a Tathāgata...' and so on. Its meaning should be understood in the same way as stated in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta. This, however, is the difference: here, the threefold virtue—'This, too, of his, is in respect to virtue'—is designated simply as virtue. The four jhānas, starting with the first jhāna, are in essence the accomplishment of wisdom. However, wisdom is not designated as such through the jhānas, but they are shown merely as the basis for insight-wisdom, and from insight-wisdom onwards, wisdom is designated.

Soṇadaṇḍaupāsakattapaṭivedanākathā

The Discourse on Soṇadaṇḍa's Declaration as a Lay Follower

319-322. Svātanāyāti padassa attho ajjatanāyāti ettha vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Tena maṃ sā parisā paribhaveyyāti tena tumhe dūratova disvā āsanā vuṭṭhitakāraṇena maṃ sā parisā – “ayaṃ soṇadaṇḍo pacchimavaye ṭhito mahallako, gotamo pana daharo yuvā nattāpissa nappahoti, so nāma attano nattumattabhāvampi appattassa āsanā vuṭṭhātī”ti paribhaveyya. Āsanā me taṃ bhavaṃ gotamo paccuṭṭhānanti mama agāravena avuṭṭhānaṃ [P 1.0293] nāma natthi, bhoganāsanabhayena pana na vuṭṭhahissāmi, taṃ tumhe hi ceva mayā ca ñātuṃ vaṭṭati. Tasmā āsanā me etaṃ bhavaṃ gotamo paccuṭṭhānaṃ dhāretūti, iminā kira sadiso kuhako dullabho, bhagavati panassa agāravaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā bhoganāsanabhayā kuhanavasena evaṃ vadati. Parapadesupi eseva nayo. Dhammiyā kathāyātiādīsu taṅkhaṇānurūpāya dhammiyā kathāya diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaṃ atthaṃ sandassetvā kusale dhamme samādapetvā gaṇhāpetvā. Tattha naṃ samuttejetvā saussāhaṃ katvā tāya ca saussāhatāya aññehi ca vijjamānaguṇehi sampahaṃsetvā dhammaratanavassaṃ vassitvā uṭṭhāyāsanā [M 1.0262] pakkāmi. Brāhmaṇo pana attano kuhakatāya evampi bhagavati dhammavassaṃ vassite visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhi. Kevalamassa āyatiṃ nibbānatthāya vāsanābhāgiyāya ca sabbā purimapacchimakathā ahosīti.

319-322. The meaning of the word `svātanāya` is to be understood by the same method as explained here for `ajjatanāya`. 'Lest that assembly should hold me in contempt': For that reason—that is, for the reason of rising from my seat upon seeing you from afar—that assembly might hold me in contempt, thinking: 'This Soṇadaṇḍa is established in his final years, an elder, whereas Gotama is young, a youth, not even fit to be his grandson. Yet that Soṇadaṇḍa rises from his seat for one who has not even attained the status of his grandson!' There is no such thing as not rising out of disrespect on my part; rather, I will not rise for fear of the loss of my wealth. It is proper that this be known by both you and me. Therefore, may the venerable Gotama regard this gesture of mine as rising from the seat. It is said that a trickster such as this is hard to find. However, there is no disrespect in him towards the Blessed One; therefore, he speaks thus deceitfully out of fear of the loss of his wealth. In other passages, too, this is the method. In the phrases beginning with `dhammiyā kathāya`: Having shown the benefit pertaining to the present life and the life to come with a Dhamma talk suitable for the occasion, having caused him to undertake and grasp wholesome states, and having incited him therein, made him zealous, and gladdened him with that zeal and with other existing virtues, and having rained down the rain of the Dhamma-gem, he rose from his seat and departed. The brahmin, however, due to his own trickery, was unable to bring forth any special attainment even when the Blessed One had thus rained down the rain of Dhamma. Merely, all his previous and subsequent talk came to be for the sake of Nibbāna in the future and for establishing a supportive disposition.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Thus, in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya,

Soṇadaṇḍasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta is concluded.

5. Kūṭadantasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Kūṭadanta Sutta

323. Evaṃ [P 1.0294][V 1.0237][M 1.0263] me sutaṃ…pe… magadhesūti kūṭadantasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ apubbapadavaṇṇanā. Magadhesūti magadhā nāma jānapadino rājakumārā, tesaṃ nivāso ekopi janapado rūḷhīsaddena magadhāti vuccati, tasmiṃ magadhesu janapade. Ito paraṃ purimasuttadvaye vuttanayameva. Ambalaṭṭhikā brahmajāle vuttasadisāva. Kūṭadantoti tassa brāhmaṇassa nāmaṃ. Upakkhaṭoti sajjito. Vacchatarasatānīti vacchasatāni. Urabbhāti taruṇameṇḍakā vuccanti. Ete tāva pāḷiyaṃ āgatāyeva. Pāḷiyaṃ pana anāgatānampi anekesaṃ migapakkhīnaṃ sattasattasatāni sampiṇḍitānevāti veditabbāni. Sabbasattasatikayāgaṃ kiresa yajitukāmo hoti. Thūṇūpanītānīti bandhitvā ṭhapanatthāya yūpasaṅkhātaṃ thūṇaṃ upanītāni.

5. “Thus have I heard… in Magadha”—this is the Kūṭadanta Sutta. Herein is the explanation of new words. `Magadhesu`: The princes who are lords of the country are called the Magadhas. Their dwelling place, even a single country, is called 'Magadha' by conventional usage; thus, 'in that country of the Magadhas'. From this point on, the method is the same as that stated in the previous two suttas. Ambalaṭṭhikā is just as it was described in the Brahmajāla Sutta. `Kūṭadanto`: This is the name of that brahmin. `Upakkhaṭo`: Prepared. `Vacchatarasatāni`: Hundreds of young bulls. `Urabbhā`: These are called young rams. These, for a start, are what are mentioned in the Pāḷi text. However, it should be understood that of the many other beasts and birds not mentioned in the Pāḷi, seven hundred of each are also included. It is said that he desired to perform a sacrifice involving seven hundred of each. `Thūṇūpanītāni`: Brought near to the post, known as a `yūpa` or sacrificial post, for the purpose of being tied and kept there.

328. Tividhanti ettha vidhā vuccati ṭhapanā, tiṭṭhapananti attho. Soḷasaparikkhāranti soḷasaparivāraṃ.

323. `Tividhaṃ`: Herein, `vidhā` is called `ṭhapanā` (establishment), which refers to the states of non-remorse that establish an uninterrupted stream of merit. The meaning is 'having three such establishments' (i.e., the three kinds of non-remorse). `Soḷasaparikkhāraṃ`: Having sixteen requisites, meaning, having sixteen attendants.

330-336. Paṭivasantīti yaññānubhavanatthāya paṭivasanti. Bhūtapubbanti idaṃ bhagavā pathavīgataṃ nidhiṃ uddharitvā purato rāsiṃ karonto viya bhavapaṭicchannaṃ pubbacaritaṃ dassento āha. Mahāvijitoti so kira sāgarapariyantaṃ mahantaṃ pathavīmaṇḍalaṃ [P 1.0295] vijini, iti mahantaṃ vijitamassāti mahāvijito tveva saṅkhyaṃ agamāsi. Aḍḍhotiādīsu yo koci attano santakena vibhavena aḍḍho hoti, ayaṃ pana na kevalaṃ aḍḍhoyeva, mahaddhano mahatā aparimāṇasaṅkhyena dhanena samannāgato. Pañcakāmaguṇavasena mahantā uḷārā bhogā assāti mahābhogo. Piṇḍapiṇḍavasena ceva suvaṇṇamāsakarajatamāsakādivasena ca jātarūparajatassa pahūtatāya pahūtajātarūparajato, anekakoṭisaṅkhyena jātarūparajatena samannāgatoti attho. Vittīti tuṭṭhi, vittiyā upakaraṇaṃ vittūpakaraṇaṃ tuṭṭhikāraṇanti attho. Pahūtaṃ nānāvidhālaṅkārasuvaṇṇarajatabhājanādibhedaṃ vittūpakaraṇamassāti pahūtavittūpakaraṇo. Sattaratanasaṅkhātassa [V 1.0238] nidahitvā ṭhapitadhanassa sabbapubbaṇṇāparaṇṇasaṅgahitassa dhaññassa ca pahūtatāya pahūtadhanadhañño[M 1.0264]. Athavā idamassa devasikaṃ paribbayadānaggahaṇādivasena parivattanadhanadhaññavasena vuttaṃ.

328. 330-336. `Paṭivasanti`: They dwell nearby for the purpose of partaking in the sacrifice. `Bhūtapubbaṃ`: The Blessed One said this, revealing a past deed that was concealed by another existence, just as one might unearth a treasure hidden in the ground and make a heap of it before them. `Mahāvijito`: It is said that he conquered the great circle of the earth, bounded by the ocean. Thus, because he had a great conquered territory, he came to be known as Mahāvijita. In the phrases beginning with `aḍḍho`: Anyone is wealthy by means of the prosperity that is their own possession. This king, however, was not merely wealthy; he was also `mahaddhano`, one of great wealth, endowed with great and immeasurably-numbered riches. `Mahābhogo`: Because he had great and splendid enjoyments by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure, he was one of great fortune. `Pahūtajātarūparajato`: Due to the abundance of gold and silver, both in the form of lumps and in the form of gold and silver `māsaka` coins and so on, he was one with abundant gold and silver. The meaning is that he was endowed with many crores of gold and silver. `Vitti`: This means satisfaction (`tuṭṭhi`). An instrument for satisfaction is `vittūpakaraṇaṃ`; the meaning is 'a cause of satisfaction'. `Pahūtavittūpakaraṇo`: Because he had abundant means of satisfaction, of various kinds such as diverse ornaments, gold and silver vessels, and so on, he was one with abundant means for satisfaction. `Pahūtadhanadhañño`: Due to the abundance of wealth that had been stored away, known as the seven treasures, and of grain, comprising all early and late crops, he was one with abundant wealth and grain. Alternatively, this was said with respect to his circulating wealth and grain, by way of daily expenditure, giving, receiving, and so on.

Paripuṇṇakosakoṭṭhāgāroti koso vuccati bhaṇḍāgāraṃ, nidahitvā ṭhapitena dhanena paripuṇṇakoso, dhaññena paripuṇṇakoṭṭhāgāro cāti attho. Athavā catubbidho koso – hatthī, assā, rathā, pattīti. Koṭṭhāgāraṃ tividhaṃ – dhanakoṭṭhāgāraṃ, vatthakoṭṭhāgāraṃ, dhaññakoṭṭhāgāranti, taṃ sabbampi paripuṇṇamassāti paripuṇṇakosakoṭṭhāgāro. Udapādīti uppajji. Ayaṃ kira rājā ekadivasaṃ ratanāvalokanacārikaṃ nāma nikkhanto. So bhaṇḍāgārikaṃ pucchi – “tāta, idaṃ evaṃ bahudhanaṃ kena saṅgharita”nti? Tumhākaṃ pitupitāmahādīhi yāva sattamā kulaparivaṭṭāti. Idaṃ pana dhanaṃ saṅgharitvā te kuhiṃ gatāti? Sabbeva te, deva, maraṇavasaṃ pattāti. Attano dhanaṃ agahetvāva gatā, tātāti? Deva, kiṃ vadetha, dhanaṃ nāmetaṃ pahāya gamanīyameva, no ādāya gamanīyanti. Atha rājā nivattitvā sirīgabbhe nisinno – ‘adhigatā kho me’tiādīni cintesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādī”ti.

Regarding 'Paripuṇṇakosakoṭṭhāgāro' (his treasury and storehouses were full): here, 'koso' is said to be a treasury. He has a treasury full of wealth that has been stored and kept, and a granary full of grain—this is the meaning. Alternatively, 'koso' is fourfold: elephants, horses, chariots, and foot soldiers. 'Koṭṭhāgāraṃ' is threefold: a treasury for wealth, a storehouse for cloth, and a granary for grain. All of this was completely full for him; hence, he is called 'paripuṇṇakosakoṭṭhāgāro'. 'Udapādi' (arose) means it came to be. It is said that this king one day went out for what is called an inspection tour of the jewels. He asked the treasurer, “My good man, by whom was this great wealth accumulated?” “By your father, grandfather, and so on, for as long as seven generations of the family lineage, sire.” “But having gathered this wealth, where have they gone?” “All of them, sire, have fallen under the sway of death.” “My good man, did they go without taking their wealth with them?” “Sire, what are you saying? This thing called wealth must indeed be left behind when one goes; it is not to be taken along.” Then the king, having returned and sat in his glorious inner chamber, thought, ‘I have indeed attained…’ and so on. Therefore, it was said: “Thus, this reflection arose in his mind.”

337. Brāhmaṇaṃ [P 1.0296] āmantetvāti kasmā āmantesi? Ayaṃ kirevaṃ cintesi – “dānaṃ dentena nāma ekena paṇḍitena saddhiṃ mantetvā dātuṃ vaṭṭati, anāmantetvā katakammañhi pacchānutāpaṃ karotī”ti. Tasmā āmantesi. Atha brāhmaṇo cintesi – “ayaṃ rājā mahādānaṃ dātukāmo, janapade cassa bahū corā, te avūpasametvā dānaṃ dentassa khīradadhitaṇḍulādike dānasambhāre āharantānaṃ nippurisāni gehāni corā vilumpissanti janapado corabhayeneva kolāhalo bhavissati, tato rañño dānaṃ na ciraṃ pavattissati, cittampissa ekaggaṃ na bhavissati, handa, naṃ etamatthaṃ saññāpemī”ti tato tamatthaṃ saññāpento “bhoto, kho rañño”tiādimāha.

337. Regarding 'Brāhmaṇaṃ āmantetvā' (having addressed the brahmin): why did he address him? It is said that he thought thus: “It is fitting for one who is giving a gift to consult with a wise person before giving, for a deed done without consultation causes later regret.” Therefore, he addressed him. Then the brahmin thought: “This king wishes to give a great gift, but there are many bandits in his country. If he gives the gift without having pacified them, bandits will plunder the houses, empty of men, of those who are bringing the requisites for the gift, such as milk, curds, and rice. The country will be in an uproar precisely because of the fear of bandits. Then the king’s gift-giving will not proceed for long, and his mind will not be concentrated. Come now, I should make him understand this matter.” Then, informing him of that matter, he said the words beginning with, “Indeed, Your Majesty’s…”

338. Tattha sakaṇṭakoti corakaṇṭakehi sakaṇṭako. Panthaduhanāti panthaduhā, panthaghātakāti attho. Akiccakārī assāti akattabbakārī [M 1.0265] adhammakārī bhaveyya. Dassukhīlanti corakhīlaṃ. Vadhena vāti māraṇena vā koṭṭanena vā. Bandhanenāti addubandhanādinā. Jāniyāti hāniyā; “sataṃ gaṇhatha, sahassaṃ gaṇhathā”ti evaṃ pavattitadaṇḍenāti attho. Garahāyāti pañcasikhamuṇḍakaraṇaṃ, gomayasiñcanaṃ, gīvāya kudaṇḍakabandhananti [V 1.0239] evamādīni katvā garahapāpanena. Pabbājanāyāti raṭṭhato nīharaṇena. Samūhanissāmīti sammā hetunā nayena kāraṇena ūhanissāmi. Hatāvasesakāti matāvasesakā. Ussahantīti ussāhaṃ karonti. Anuppadetūti dinne appahonte puna aññampi bījañca bhattañca kasiupakaraṇabhaṇḍañca sabbaṃ detūti attho. Pābhataṃ anuppadetūti sakkhiṃ akatvā paṇṇe anāropetvā mūlacchejjavasena bhaṇḍamūlaṃ detūti attho. Bhaṇḍamūlassa hi pābhatanti nāmaṃ. Yathāha –

338. Here, 'sakaṇṭako' (thorny) means thorny with the thorns of bandits. 'Panthaduhanā' (highway robbers) means those who harm the roads, that is, highway attackers. 'Akiccakārī assā' (one who would do wrong) means one who would do what should not be done, one who would act unrighteously. 'Dassukhīlaṃ' (a stake of bandits) refers to the thorn-stump of bandits. 'Vadena vā' (by killing) means by execution or by beating. 'Bandhanena' (by imprisonment) means by means of fetters, stocks, and so on. 'Jāniyā' (by fining) means by causing loss; the meaning is by a punishment enacted thus: “Take a hundred, take a thousand.” 'Garahāya' (by public humiliation) means by causing blame by doing things such as shaving the head into five tufts, pouring cow-dung water on the head, and tying a wooden collar around the neck. 'Pabbājanāya' (by banishment) means by expelling from the country. 'Samūhanissāmi' (I will uproot) means I will uproot them with a proper cause, with a right method, with a reason. 'Hatāvasesakā' (the survivors of the slain) means those remaining from the dead. 'Ussahanti' (they strive) means they make an effort. 'Anuppadetu' (let him supply) means: when what has been given is insufficient, let him again give other seed, food, and all the equipment for farming. 'Pābhataṃ anuppadetu' (let him supply capital) means: let him give the capital for goods by way of cutting off the principal, without making a witness or recording it on a leaf. For the capital for goods is named 'pābhataṃ'. As it is said:

“Appakenapi medhāvī, pābhatena vicakkhaṇo;

Samuṭṭhāpeti attānaṃ, aṇuṃ aggiṃva sandhama”nti. (jā. 1.1.4);

“A wise and discerning person, even with little capital, establishes themselves, just like one fanning a small fire.”

Bhattavetananti devasikaṃ bhattañceva māsikādiparibbayañca [P 1.0297] tassa tassa kusalakammasūrabhāvānurūpena ṭhānantaragāmanigamādidānena saddhiṃ detūti attho. Sakammapasutāti kasivāṇijjādīsu sakesu kammesu uyyuttā byāvaṭā. Rāsikoti dhanadhaññānaṃ rāsiko. Khemaṭṭhitāti khemena ṭhitā abhayā. Akaṇṭakāti corakaṇṭakarahitā. Mudā modamānāti modā modamānā. Ayameva vā pāṭho, aññamaññaṃ pamuditacittāti adhippāyo. Apārutagharāti corānaṃ abhāvena dvārāni asaṃvaritvā vivaṭadvārāti attho. Etadavocāti janapadassa sabbākārena iddhaphītabhāvaṃ ñatvā etaṃ avoca.

'Bhattavetanaṃ' (wages and food) means: let him give daily food and monthly and other allowances, together with the gift of official positions, villages, towns, and so on, in accordance with each person's lineage, work, and bravery. This is the meaning. 'Sakammapasutā' (devoted to their own work) means they are engaged and occupied in their own work, such as agriculture and trade. 'Rāsiko' (a heap) means a heap of wealth and grain. 'Khemaṭṭhitā' (established in security) means they are established in safety, without fear. 'Akaṇṭakā' (without thorns) means free from the thorns that are bandits. 'Mudā modamānā' (joyful and rejoicing) means some people rejoice, and others rejoice in return. Or this itself is the reading; the intention is that their minds are mutually delighted. 'Apārutagharā' (with unbarred houses) means: due to the absence of bandits, not having closed their doors, their doors are open. This is the meaning. 'Etadavoca' (he said this) means: having known the country's prosperity and abundance in every way, he said this.

Catuparikkhāravaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Four Requisites

339. Tena hi bhavaṃ rājāti brāhmaṇo kira cintesi – “ayaṃ rājā mahādānaṃ dātuṃ ativiya ussāhajāto. Sace pana attano anuyantā khattiyādayo anāmantetvā dassati. Nāssa te attamanā bhavissanti; yathā dānaṃ te attamanā honti, tathā karissāmī”ti. Tasmā “tena hi bhava”ntiādimāha. Tattha negamāti nigamavāsino. Jānapadāti janapadavāsino[M 1.0266]. Āmantayatanti āmantetu jānāpetu. Yaṃ mama assāti yaṃ tumhākaṃ anujānanaṃ mama bhaveyya. Amaccāti piyasahāyakā. Pārisajjāti sesā āṇattikārakā. Yajataṃ bhavaṃ rājāti yajatu bhavaṃ, te kira – ayaṃ rājā “ahaṃ issaro”ti pasayha dānaṃ adatvā amhe āmantesi, ahonena suṭṭhu kata”nti attamanā evamāhaṃsu. Anāmantite panassa yaññaṭṭhānaṃ dassanāyapi na gaccheyyuṃ. Yaññakālo mahārājāti deyyadhammasmiñhi asati mahallakakāle ca evarūpaṃ dānaṃ dātuṃ na sakkā, tvaṃ pana mahādhano ceva taruṇo ca, etena te [V 1.0240] yaññakāloti dassentā vadanti. Anumatipakkhāti anumatiyā pakkhā, anumatidāyakāti attho. Parikkhārā bhavantīti parivārā bhavanti. “Ratho sīlaparikkhāro, jhānakkho cakkavīriyo”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.4) ettha pana alaṅkāro parikkhāroti vutto.

339. “Then, indeed, Your Majesty,” (tena hi bhavaṃ rājā)—so the brahmin, it is said, thought: “This king is exceedingly eager to give a great gift. But if he gives without informing his own followers, the khattiyas and others, they will not be pleased with him. I will act in such a way that they are pleased with the gift.” Therefore, he said, “Then, indeed, Your Majesty,” and so on. Herein, ‘townspeople’ (negamā) means the inhabitants of the town. ‘Countryfolk’ (jānapadā) means the inhabitants of the countryside. ‘Let him summon’ (āmantayataṃ) means let him summon, let him make known. ‘That which would be for me’ (yaṃ mama assa) means: that your permission would be for me. ‘Ministers’ (amaccā) means dear companions. ‘Members of the assembly’ (pārisajjā) means the remaining officials who carry out orders. ‘May Your Majesty sacrifice’ (yajataṃ bhavaṃ rājā) means ‘May you, sir, sacrifice.’ They, it is said—thinking, “This king, instead of giving the gift by force with the thought ‘I am the ruler,’ has informed us. Oh, what he has done is excellent!”—were pleased and spoke thus. On the other hand, if they were not informed by him, they would not even go to see the place of sacrifice. ‘The time for sacrifice, great king’ (yaññakālo mahārāja)—for when there are no suitable gifts to be given and in old age, such a gift cannot be given. But you are both very wealthy and young; showing this, they say that this is your time for sacrifice. ‘Those on the side of consent’ (anumatipakkhā) means a faction of consent; the meaning is those who grant approval. ‘They become requisites’ (parikkhārā bhavanti) means they become attendants. But in the passage, “The chariot has virtue as its adornment, jhāna as its axle, and energy as its wheels” (Saṃ. ni. 5.4), ‘parikkhāra’ is said to mean ‘adornment’.

Aṭṭhaparikkhāravaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Eight Requisites

340. Aṭṭhahaṅgehīti [P 1.0298] ubhato sujātādīhi aṭṭhahi aṅgehi. Yasasāti āṇāṭhapanasamatthatāya. Saddhoti dānassa phalaṃ atthīti saddahati. Dāyakoti dānasūro. Na saddhāmattakeneva tiṭṭhati, pariccajitumpi sakkotīti attho. Dānapatīti yaṃ dānaṃ deti, tassa pati hutvā deti, na dāso, na sahāyo. Yo hi attanā madhuraṃ bhuñjati, paresaṃ amadhuraṃ deti, so dānasaṅkhātassa deyyadhammassa dāso hutvā deti. Yo yaṃ attanā bhuñjati, tadeva deti, so sahāyo hutvā deti. Yo pana attanā yena kenaci yāpeti, paresaṃ madhuraṃ deti, so pati jeṭṭhako sāmī hutvā deti, ayaṃ tādisoti attho. Samaṇabrāhmaṇakapaṇaddhikavaṇibbakayācakānanti ettha samitapāpā samaṇā, bāhitapāpā brāhmaṇā. Kapaṇāti duggatā daliddamanussā. Addhikāti pathāvino. Vaṇibbakāti ye – “iṭṭhaṃ dinnaṃ, kantaṃ, manāpaṃ, kālena anavajjaṃ dinnaṃ, dadaṃ cittaṃ pasādeyya, gacchatu bhavaṃ brahmaloka”ntiādinā nayena dānassa vaṇṇaṃ thomayamānā vicaranti. Yācakāti ye – “pasatamattaṃ detha, sarāvamattaṃ dethā”tiādīni vatvā yācamānā vicaranti. Opānabhūtoti udapānabhūto. Sabbesaṃ sādhāraṇaparibhogo, catumahāpathe khatapokkharaṇī [M 1.0267] viya hutvāti attho. Sutajātassāti ettha sutameva sutajātaṃ. Atītānāgatapaccuppanne atthe cintetunti ettha – “atīte puññassa katattāyeva me ayaṃ sampattī”ti, evaṃ cintento atītamatthaṃ cintetuṃ paṭibalo nāma hoti. “Idāni puññaṃ katvāva anāgate sakkā sampattiṃ pāpuṇitu”nti cintento anāgatamatthaṃ cintetuṃ paṭibalo nāma hoti. “Idaṃ puññakammaṃ nāma sappurisānaṃ āciṇṇaṃ, mayhañca bhogāpi saṃvijjanti, dāyakacittampi atthi; handāhaṃ puññāni karomī”ti [P 1.0299] cintento paccuppannamatthaṃ cintetuṃ paṭibalo nāma hotīti veditabbo. Iti imānīti evaṃ yathā vuttāni etāni. Etehi kira aṭṭhahaṅgehi samannāgatassa dānaṃ sabbadisāhi mahājano upasaṅkamati. “Ayaṃ dujjāto kittakaṃ kālaṃ dassati, idāni vippaṭisārī hutvā upacchindissatī”ti evamādīni cintetvā na koci upasaṅkamitabbaṃ maññati. Tasmā etāni aṭṭhaṅgāni parikkhārā bhavantīti vuttāni.

340. ‘With eight factors’ (aṭṭhahaṅgehi) means with the eight factors beginning with being well-born on both sides. ‘With fame’ (yasasā) means with the power that is the ability to establish authority. ‘Faithful’ (saddho) means one believes, “There is a result of giving.” ‘A giver’ (dāyako) means a hero in giving. The meaning is that he does not stand by faith alone, but is also able to relinquish. ‘A master of the gift’ (dānapati) means that whatever gift he gives, he gives it having become its master, not its servant, nor its friend. For one who eats sweet food himself but gives unsweet food to others, gives as a servant of the gift-object designated as ‘giving’. One who gives the very same thing that he himself eats, gives as a friend. But one who sustains himself with anything whatsoever, yet gives sweet food to others, gives as a master, a chief, a lord; the meaning is that this one is such a person. ‘To ascetics, brahmins, the poor, travelers, mendicants, and petitioners’ (samaṇabrāhmaṇakapaṇaddhikavaṇibbakayācakānaṃ)—herein, ascetics (samaṇā) are those who have pacified evil; brahmins (brāhmaṇā) are those who have cast off evil. ‘The poor’ (kapaṇā) are those in a difficult state, destitute people. ‘Travelers’ (addhikā) are wayfarers. ‘Mendicants’ (vaṇibbakā) are those who wander about praising the quality of the gift with such words as, “What is given is desirable, pleasing, agreeable, given at the right time, and blameless. May the giver’s mind be gladdened. May you go to the Brahma-world.” ‘Petitioners’ (yācakā) are those who wander about begging, saying such things as, “Give a handful, give a bowlful.” ‘Having become a public well’ (opānabhūto) means having become like a well. The meaning is that he has become for the common use of all, like a pond dug at a great crossroads. Herein, regarding ‘of one born of learning’ (sutajātassa), learning itself is what is meant by ‘born of learning’. Herein, regarding ‘to reflect on past, future, and present matters’ (atītānāgatapaccuppanne atthe cintetuṃ), it should be understood thus: one who reflects, “It is only because of merit having been done in the past that this prosperity is mine,” is called one who is capable of reflecting on a past matter. One who reflects, “Only by doing merit now is it possible to attain prosperity in the future,” is called one who is capable of reflecting on a future matter. One who reflects, “This deed of merit is the practice of good people; I, too, have wealth, and I have the mind of a giver; come now, I will do meritorious deeds,” is called one who is capable of reflecting on a present matter. ‘Thus, these’ (iti imāni) means these, as they have been stated. Indeed, the great populace from all directions approaches the gift of one who is endowed with these eight factors. Thinking such things as, “For how long will this low-born person give? Now, becoming regretful, he will cut it off,” no one considers it fit to approach. Therefore, these eight factors are said to be requisites.

Catuparikkhārādivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Four Requisites and so on.

341. Sujaṃ [V 1.0241] paggaṇhantānanti mahāyāgapaṭiggaṇhanaṭṭhāne dānakaṭacchuṃ paggaṇhantānaṃ. Imehi catūhīti etehi sujātādīhi. Etesu hi asati – “evaṃ dujjātassa saṃvidhānena pavattadānaṃ kittakaṃ kālaṃ pavattissatī”tiādīni vatvā upasaṅkamitāro na honti. Garahitabbābhāvato pana upasaṅkamantiyeva. Tasmā imānipi parikkhārā bhavantīti vuttāni.

341. ‘Of those who hold the sacrificial ladle’ (sujaṃ paggaṇhantānaṃ) means: of those who hold the giving-ladle in the place of receiving a great sacrifice. ‘By these four’ (imehi catūhi) means: by these qualities beginning with being well-born. For, when these four qualities are absent, there are no people who approach, having said such things as, “For how long will a gift that has come about through the arrangement of such a low-born person last?” However, due to the absence of anything blameworthy, they do indeed approach. Therefore, these four qualities also are said to be requisites.

342. Tisso vidhā desesīti tīṇi ṭhapanāni desesi. So kira cintesi – “dānaṃ dadamānā nāma tiṇṇaṃ ṭhānānaṃ aññatarasmiṃ calanti handāhaṃ imaṃ rājānaṃ tesu ṭhānesu paṭhamataraññeva niccalaṃ karomī”ti. Tenassa tisso vidhā desesīti. So bhoto raññoti idaṃ karaṇatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Bhotā raññāti vā pāṭho. Vippaṭisāro na karaṇīyoti “bhogānaṃ vigamahetuko pacchānutāpo na kattabbo, pubbacetanā pana acalā patiṭṭhapetabbā, evañhi dānaṃ mahapphalaṃ hotī”ti dasseti. Itaresupi dvīsu ṭhānesu eseva nayo. Muñcacetanāpi hi pacchāsamanussaraṇacetanā [M 1.0268] ca niccalāva kātabbā. Tathā akarontassa dānaṃ na mahapphalaṃ hoti, nāpi uḷāresu bhogesu cittaṃ namati, mahāroruvaṃ upapannassa seṭṭhigahapatino viya.

342. `Tisso vidhā desesi` means: he taught the three establishments. It is said that he thought: “Those who are called givers are wont to waver in one of the three stages. Come now, I shall make this king unwavering in those stages right at the very beginning before the sacrifice.” For that reason, it is said, he taught him the three ways. `So bhoto rañño`: this is a word in the genitive case in the sense of the unexpressed agent in the instrumental case. Or the reading is `bhotā raññā`. `Vippaṭisāro na karaṇīyo` shows that: “Remorse which has the loss of wealth as its cause should not be engaged in; but the prior volition should be established as unwavering, for thus the gift is of great fruit.” In the other two stages as well, this is the same method. Indeed, the volition at the time of giving and the volition of subsequent recollection should be made unwavering. For one who does not act thus, the gift is not of great fruit, nor does the mind incline towards excellent wealth, like that of the wealthy householder who had arisen in the Mahāroruva hell.

343. Dasahākārehīti dasahi kāraṇehi. Tassa kira evaṃ ahosi – sacāyaṃ rājā dussīle disvā – “nassati vata me dānaṃ, yassa me evarūpā dussīlā bhuñjantī”ti sīlavantesupi vippaṭisāraṃ uppādessati, dānaṃ na mahapphalaṃ bhavissati. Vippaṭisāro ca nāma dāyakānaṃ paṭiggāhakatova uppajjati[P 1.0300], handassa paṭhamameva taṃ vippaṭisāraṃ vinodemīti. Tasmā dasahākārehi upacchijjituṃ yuttaṃ paṭiggāhakesupi vippaṭisāraṃ vinodesīti. Tesaññeva tenāti tesaññeva tena pāpena aniṭṭho vipāko bhavissati, na aññesanti dasseti. Yajataṃ bhavanti detu bhavaṃ. Sajjatanti vissajjatu. Antaranti abbhantaraṃ.

343. `Dasahākārehi` means: by ten reasons. It is said that this thought occurred to him: “If this king, upon seeing immoral persons, thinks, ‘Alas, my gift is ruined, which such immoral ones as these enjoy,’ he will produce regret even in regard to the virtuous, and the gift will not be of great fruit. And regret, for donors, arises precisely because of the recipient. Come now, I shall dispel that regret of his right at the very beginning.” Therefore, he dispelled the regret concerning recipients, which ought to be cut off by ten reasons. `Tesaññeva tena` shows that: for them alone, because of that evil deed, there will be an undesirable result, not for others. `Yajataṃ bhavaṃ` means: may your majesty give. `Sajjataṃ` means: may he relinquish completely. `Antaraṃ` means: inside.

344. Soḷasahi ākārehi cittaṃ sandassesīti idha brāhmaṇo rañño mahādānānumodanaṃ nāma āraddho. Tattha sandassesīti – ‘idaṃ dānaṃ dātā evarūpaṃ sampattiṃ labhatī’ti dassetvā dassetvā kathesi. Samādapesīti tadatthaṃ samādapetvā kathesi. Samuttejesīti vippaṭisāravinodanenassa cittaṃ vodāpesi. Sampahaṃsesīti ‘sundaraṃ te kataṃ, mahārāja, dānaṃ dadamānenā’ti thutiṃ katvā kathesi. Vattā dhammato natthīti dhammena samena kāraṇena vattā natthi.

344. `Soḷasahi ākārehi cittaṃ sandassesi`: Here, the brahmin undertook what is called the rejoicing in the king's great gift. Therein, `sandassesi` means: showing again and again, “The giver of this gift obtains such-and-such an attainment,” he spoke. `Samādāpesi` means: causing him to grasp that meaning well, he spoke. `Samuttejesi` means: by dispelling regret, he purified his mind. `Sampahaṃsesi` means: having offered praise, saying, “A good deed has been done by you, O great king, in giving this gift,” he spoke. `Vattā dhammato natthi` means: there is no speaker [who can speak against it] in accordance with the true nature, with impartiality, and with suitable reason.

345. Na [V 1.0242] rukkhā chijjiṃsu yūpatthāya na dabbhā lūyiṃsu barihisatthāyāti ye yūpanāmake mahāthambhe ussāpetvā – “asukarājā asukāmacco asukabrāhmaṇo evarūpaṃ nāma mahāyāgaṃ yajatī”ti nāmaṃ likhitvā ṭhapenti. Yāni ca dabbhatiṇāni lāyitvā vanamālāsaṅkhepena yaññasālaṃ parikkhipanti, bhūmiyaṃ vā pattharanti, tepi na rukkhā chijjiṃsu, na dabbhā lūyiṃsu. Kiṃ pana gāvo vā ajādayo vā haññissantīti dasseti. Dāsāti antogehadāsādayo. Pessāti ye pubbameva dhanaṃ gahetvā kammaṃ karonti. Kammakarāti ye bhattavetanaṃ gahetvā karonti. Daṇḍatajjitā [P 1.0301] nāma daṇḍayaṭṭhimuggarādīni gahetvā – “kammaṃ karotha karothā”ti evaṃ [M 1.0269] tajjitā. Bhayatajjitā nāma – sace kammaṃ karosi, kusalaṃ. No ce karosi, chindissāma vā bandhissāma vā māressāma vāti evaṃ bhayena tajjitā. Ete pana na daṇḍatajjitā, na bhayatajjitā, na assumukhā rodamānā parikammāni akaṃsu. Atha kho piyasamudācāreneva samudācariyamānā akaṃsu. Na hi tattha dāsaṃ vā dāsāti, pessaṃ vā pessāti, kammakaraṃ vā kammakarāti ālapanti. Yathānāmavaseneva pana piyasamudācārena ālapitvā itthipurisabalavantadubbalānaṃ anurūpameva kammaṃ dassetvā – “idañcidañca karothā”ti vadanti. Tepi attano rucivaseneva karonti. Tena vuttaṃ – “ye icchiṃsu, te akaṃsu; ye na icchiṃsu, na te akaṃsu. Yaṃ icchiṃsu, taṃ akaṃsu; yaṃ na icchiṃsu, na taṃ akaṃsū”ti. Sappitelanavanītadadhimadhuphāṇitena ceva so yañño niṭṭhānamagamāsīti rājā kira bahinagarassa catūsu dvāresu antonagarassa ca majjheti pañcasu ṭhānesu mahādānasālāyo kārāpetvā ekekissāya sālāya satasahassaṃ satasahassaṃ katvā divase divase pañcasatasahassāni vissajjetvā sūriyuggamanato paṭṭhāya tassa tassa kālassa anurūpehi sahatthena suvaṇṇakaṭacchuṃ gahetvā paṇītehi sappitelādisammisseheva yāgukhajjakabhattabyañjanapānakādīhi mahājanaṃ santappesi. Bhājanāni pūretvā gaṇhitukāmānaṃ tatheva dāpesi. Sāyaṇhasamaye pana vatthagandhamālādīhi sampūjesi. Sappiādīnaṃ pana mahācāṭiyo pūrāpetvā – “yo yaṃ paribhuñjitukāmo, so taṃ paribhuñjatū”ti anekasatesu ṭhānesu ṭhapāpesi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “sappitelanavanītadadhimadhuphāṇitena ceva so yañño niṭṭhānamagamāsī”ti.

345. “No trees were cut for sacrificial posts, no dabbha grass was mown for the sacrificial ground-cover” means: The great pillars called sacrificial posts, which they set up after inscribing a name—such as, “Such-and-such a king, such-and-such a minister, or such-and-such a brahmin performs a great sacrifice of such-and-such a name”—and the dabbha grasses which they mow and use to encircle the sacrificial hall in the manner of a forest garland, or which they spread upon the ground—even those trees were not cut, and that dabbha grass was not mown. How then, it is shown, would cows or goats and the like be killed? “Dāsa” means household slaves and the like. “Pessa” means those who do work after having taken payment beforehand. “Kammakarā” means those who work after receiving food and wages. “Those threatened by punishment” (daṇḍatajjitā) means those who are threatened with sticks, rods, clubs, and the like, being told, “Do the work! Do the work!” “Those threatened by fear” (bhayatajjitā) means those threatened with fear, thus: “If you do the work, it is good. If you do not, we will cut you, or bind you, or kill you.” But these workers did not perform the preparations by being threatened by punishment, nor by being threatened by fear, nor with tear-stricken faces, weeping. Rather, they worked being addressed with pleasant speech. Indeed, there they do not address a slave as “slave,” nor a servant as “servant,” nor a worker as “worker.” Instead, having addressed them with pleasant speech according to their respective names and having shown them work appropriate for women, men, the strong, and the weak, they say, “Do this and this.” They too work according to their own wishes. Therefore it was said: “Those who wished, did; those who did not wish, did not. What they wished, they did; what they did not wish, they did not do.” “And that sacrifice was completed with ghee, oil, fresh butter, curd, honey, and molasses” means: The king, it is said, had great alms-halls built in five places—at the four gates outside the city and in the middle of the city within. Having allocated one hundred thousand for each alms-hall, he disbursed five hundred thousand each and every day. Starting from sunrise, at the appropriate times for each, he himself, taking a golden ladle, satisfied the great populace with exquisite gruel, snacks, rice, curries, drinks, and so on, all mixed with ghee, oil, and the like. For those who wished to take them, he had vessels filled and given just so. In the evening, he honored them well with cloth, perfumes, garlands, and the like. Furthermore, having had great jars filled with ghee and the like, he had them placed in many hundreds of locations, thinking, “Let whoever wishes to consume whatever, consume that.” It was in reference to this that it was said: “And that sacrifice was completed with ghee, oil, fresh butter, curd, honey, and molasses.”

346. Pahūtaṃ sāpateyyaṃ ādāyāti bahuṃ dhanaṃ gahetvā. Te kira cintesuṃ – “ayaṃ rājā sappitelādīni janapadato anāharāpetvā attano santakameva nīharitvā mahādānaṃ deti. Amhehi pana ‘rājā na kiñci āharāpetī’ti na yuttaṃ tuṇhī bhavituṃ. Na hi rañño ghare dhanaṃ akkhayadhammameva, amhesu ca adentesu ko añño rañño dassati, handassa dhanaṃ upasaṃharāmā”ti [V 1.0243] te gāmabhāgena ca nigamabhāgena [P 1.0302] ca nagarabhāgena ca sāpateyyaṃ saṃharitvā sakaṭāni pūretvā rañño upahariṃsu. Taṃ sandhāya – “pahūtaṃ sāpateyya”ntiādimāha.

346. “Taking abundant wealth” means taking much wealth. They, it is said, thought: “This king gives a great gift by bringing out his own property, not having ghee, oil, and the like brought from the countryside. It is not right for us to remain silent, thinking, ‘The king does not have us bring anything.’ Indeed, the wealth in the king’s house is not of an inexhaustible nature, and if we do not give, who else will give to the king? Come, let us bring wealth for him.” Thus, they collected wealth by village-share, by market-town-share, and by city-share, and having filled carts, they brought it to the king. It was in reference to this that the Blessed One said, “taking abundant wealth,” and so on.

347. Puratthimena [M 1.0270] yaññavāṭassāti puratthimato nagaradvāre dānasālāya puratthimabhāge. Yathā puratthimadisato āgacchantā khattiyānaṃ dānasālāya yāguṃ pivitvā rañño dānasālāya bhuñjitvā nagaraṃ pavisanti. Evarūpe ṭhāne paṭṭhapesuṃ. Dakkhiṇena yaññavāṭassāti dakkhiṇato nagaradvāre dānasālāya vuttanayeneva dakkhiṇabhāge paṭṭhapesuṃ. Pacchimuttaresupi eseva nayo.

347. “To the east of the sacrificial enclosure” means in the eastern part of the alms-hall at the eastern city gate. They established it in such a place that those coming from the eastern direction, having drunk gruel at the alms-hall of the khattiyas and having eaten at the alms-hall of the king, would enter the city. “To the south of the sacrificial enclosure” means they established it in the southern part of the alms-hall at the southern city gate, in the same way as described. In the west and north also, this is the method.

348. Aho yañño, aho yaññasampadāti brāhmaṇā sappiādīhi niṭṭhānagamanaṃ sutvā – “yaṃ loke madhuraṃ, tadeva samaṇo gotamo katheti, handassa yaññaṃ pasaṃsāmā”ti tuṭṭhacittā pasaṃsamānā evamāhaṃsu. Tuṇhībhūtova nisinno hotīti upari vattabbamatthaṃ cintayamāno nissaddova nisinno hoti. Abhijānāti pana bhavaṃ gotamoti idaṃ brāhmaṇo parihārena pucchanto āha. Itarathā hi – “kiṃ pana tvaṃ, bho gotama, tadā rājā ahosi, udāhu purohito brāhmaṇo”ti evaṃ ujukameva pucchayamāno agāravo viya hoti.

348. “Oh, the sacrifice! Oh, the success of the sacrifice!” means: The brahmins, having heard of the sacrifice’s completion with ghee and so on, thought, “Whatever is sweet in the world, that is what the ascetic Gotama speaks of. Come, let us praise his sacrifice!” With delighted minds and full of praise, they spoke thus. “He sat silent” means: Thinking of the matter to be spoken of next, he sat without a sound. “But does the venerable Gotama recall?”—this the brahmin said, asking indirectly to avoid disrespect. For otherwise, if he were asked directly, thus: “Indeed, good Gotama, were you the king at that time, or the brahmin chaplain?” it would be as if disrespectful.

Niccadānaanukulayaññavaṇṇanā

Explanation of Constant Alms and Ancestral Sacrifices

349. Atthi pana, bho gotamāti – idaṃ brāhmaṇo “sakalajambudīpavāsīnaṃ uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya dānaṃ nāma dātuṃ garukaṃ sakalajanapado ca attano kammāni akaronto nassissati, atthi nu kho amhākampi imamhā yaññā añño yañño appasamārambhataro ceva mahapphalataro cā”ti etamatthaṃ pucchanto āha. Niccadānānīti dhuvadānāni niccabhattāni. Anukulayaññānīti – “amhākaṃ pitupitāmahādīhi pavattitānī”ti katvā pacchā duggatapurisehipi vaṃsaparamparāya pavattetabbāni yāgāni, evarūpāni kira sīlavante uddissa nibaddhadānāni tasmiṃ kule daliddāpi na upacchindanti.

349. “But is there, good Gotama…”—this the brahmin said, wishing to ask this question: “For all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, to give what is called a gift, having arisen and exerted themselves, is burdensome, and the entire country will perish, not doing its work. Is there indeed for us another sacrifice, other than this sacrifice, that has fewer preparations and is more fruitful?” “Constant alms” means perpetual alms, constant alms-food. “Ancestral sacrifices” means sacrifices established by our fathers, grandfathers, and other ancestors, which should be continued in succession by lineage, even by poor men afterwards. Such constant gifts, dedicated to the virtuous, are not interrupted in that family, even by the poor.

Tatridaṃ [P 1.0303] vatthu – anāthapiṇḍikassa kira ghare pañca niccabhattasatāni dīyiṃsu. Dantamayasalākāni pañcasatāni ahesuṃ. Atha taṃ kulaṃ anukkamena dāliddiyena abhibhūtaṃ, ekā tasmiṃ kule dārikā ekasalākato uddhaṃ dātuṃ nāsakkhi. Sāpi pacchā setavāhanarajjaṃ gantvā khalaṃ sodhetvā laddhadhaññena taṃ salākaṃ adāsi. Eko thero rañño [M 1.0271] ārocesi. Rājā taṃ [V 1.0244] ānetvā aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Sā tato paṭṭhāya puna pañcapi salākabhattasatāni pavattesi.

Here is the story: In Anāthapiṇḍika’s house, it is said, five hundred constant alms-meals were given. There were five hundred ivory tokens. Then that family was gradually overwhelmed by poverty, and one girl in that family was unable to give more than one token. Later, she too went to the kingdom of Setavāhana, cleaned the threshing floor, and with the grain she had obtained, gave that token. An elder informed the king. The king brought her and established her in the position of chief queen. From then on, she again established five hundred token-meals.

Daṇḍappahārāti – “paṭipāṭiyā tiṭṭhatha tiṭṭhathā”ti ujuṃ gantvā gaṇhatha gaṇhathāti ca ādīni vatvā dīyamānā daṇḍappahārāpi galaggāhāpi dissanti. Ayaṃ kho, brāhmaṇa, hetu…pe… mahānisaṃsatarañcāti. Ettha yasmā mahāyaññe viya imasmiṃ salākabhatte na bahūhi veyyāvaccakarehi vā upakaraṇehi vā attho atthi, tasmā etaṃ appaṭṭhataraṃ. Yasmā cettha na bahūnaṃ kammacchedavasena pīḷāsaṅkhāto samārambho atthi, tasmā appasamārambhataraṃ. Yasmā cetaṃ saṅghassa yiṭṭhaṃ pariccattaṃ, tasmā yaññanti vuttaṃ, yasmā pana chaḷaṅgasamannāgatāya dakkhiṇāya mahāsamudde udakasseva na sukaraṃ puññābhisandassa pamāṇaṃ kātuṃ, idañca tathāvidhaṃ. Tasmā taṃ mahapphalatarañca mahānisaṃsatarañcāti veditabbaṃ. Idaṃ sutvā brāhmaṇo cintesi – idampi niccabhattaṃ uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya dadato divase divase ekassa kammaṃ nassati. Navanavo ussāho ca janetabbo hoti, atthi nu kho itopi añño yañño appaṭṭhataro ca appasamārambhataro cāti. Tasmā “atthi pana, bho gotamā”tiādimāha. Tattha yasmā salākabhatte kiccapariyosānaṃ natthi, ekena uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya aññaṃ kammaṃ akatvā saṃvidhātabbameva. Vihāradāne pana kiccapariyosānaṃ atthi. Paṇṇasālaṃ vā hi kāretuṃ koṭidhanaṃ vissajjetvā mahāvihāraṃ vā, ekavāraṃ dhanapariccāgaṃ katvā kāritaṃ sattaṭṭhavassānipi vassasatampi vassasahassampi gacchatiyeva. Kevalaṃ jiṇṇapatitaṭṭhāne paṭisaṅkharaṇamattameva kātabbaṃ [P 1.0304] hoti. Tasmā idaṃ vihāradānaṃ salākabhattato appaṭṭhataraṃ appasamārambhatarañca hoti.
