Yasmā panettha suttantapariyāyena yāvadeva sītassa paṭighātāyāti ādayo navānisaṃsā vuttā, khandhakapariyāyena.

“Striking with sticks”—when giving, after saying things like, “Stand in line, stand in line,” and “Go straight and take it, take it,” striking with sticks and seizing by the neck are seen. “This, brahmin, is the cause… and of greater benefit.” Here, because in this ticket-food, unlike in a great sacrifice, there is no need for many attendants or requisites, therefore it is less troublesome. And because here there is no great undertaking, described as oppression by means of interrupting the work of many people, therefore it has less undertaking. And because this is offered and relinquished to the Sangha, it is called a sacrifice. Furthermore, because for a gift endowed with six factors, it is not easy to measure the flow of merit, just as it is not easy to measure the water in the great ocean, and this gift is also of such a kind, therefore it should be known as more fruitful and of greater benefit. Hearing this, the brahmin thought: “For one who gives this constant alms-food, having arisen and prepared day after day, one person's work is destroyed. New effort must be generated again and again. Is there indeed another sacrifice that is less troublesome and has less undertaking than this?” Therefore, he asked, “But, good Gotama, is there…?” and so on. Here, in the ticket-food, there is no end to the task; one must rise and prepare, not doing any other work, but being engaged in just that. But in the case of giving a monastery, the task has an end. Whether one has a leaf-hut built, or having given up ten million in wealth, has a great monastery built, once the giving of wealth has been done and it is built, it lasts for seven or eight years, a hundred years, or even a thousand years. Only the mere act of repairing is to be done in worn-out and fallen places. Therefore, this gift of a monastery is less troublesome and has less undertaking than the ticket-food. Moreover, in the Suttanta method, nine benefits such as “just for the prevention of cold” are stated, while in the Khandhaka method…

“Sītaṃ uṇhaṃ paṭihanti, tato vāḷamigāni ca;

Siriṃsape ca makase ca, sisire cāpi vuṭṭhiyo.

It wards off cold and heat, and likewise wild animals; serpents and mosquitoes, and rains in the cold season.

Tato vātātapo ghoro, sañjāto paṭihaññati;

Leṇatthañca sukhatthañca, jhāyituñca vipassituṃ.

Then a harsh wind and heat arise and are warded off; for shelter and happiness, and to meditate and contemplate.

Vihāradānaṃ [V 1.0245] saṅghassa, aggaṃ buddhena vaṇṇitaṃ;

Tasmā hi paṇḍito poso, sampassaṃ atthamattano;

Vihāre kāraye ramme, vāsayettha bahussute.

The gift of a monastery to the Sangha is praised by the Buddha as supreme. Therefore, a wise person, seeing their own benefit, should have delightful monasteries built and have the learned dwell therein.

Tasmā annañca pānañca, vatthasenāsanāni ca;

Dadeya ujubhūtesu, vippasannena cetasā.

Therefore, with a clear and serene mind, one should give food and drink, clothing and lodging to those who are upright.

Te tassa dhammaṃ desenti, sabbadukkhāpanūdanaṃ;

Yaṃ so dhammaṃ idhaññāya, parinibbāti anāsavo”ti. (cūḷava. 295);

They teach him the Dhamma, which dispels all suffering; having understood that Dhamma here, he, without influxes, attains final Nibbāna.

Sattarasānisaṃsā vuttā. Tasmā etaṃ salākabhattato mahapphalatarañca mahānisaṃsatarañcāti veditabbaṃ. Saṅghassa pana pariccattattāva yaññoti vuccati. Idampi sutvā brāhmaṇo cintesi – “dhanapariccāgaṃ katvā vihāradānaṃ [M 1.0272] nāma dukkaraṃ, attano santakā hi kākaṇikāpi parassa duppariccajā, handāhaṃ itopi appaṭṭhatarañca appasamārambhatarañca yaññaṃ pucchāmī”ti. Tato taṃ pucchanto – “atthi pana bho”tiādimāha.

Seventeen benefits have been stated. Therefore, this should be known as more fruitful and of greater benefit than ticket-food. Furthermore, because it is relinquished to the Sangha, it is called a sacrifice. Hearing this too, the brahmin thought: “The gift of a monastery, which requires giving up wealth, is difficult to do. Indeed, even a small coin belonging to oneself is difficult to relinquish for another. Come now, let me ask about a sacrifice that is even less troublesome and has less undertaking than this.” Then, wishing to ask about that, he spoke the words beginning: “But is there, good sir…”

350-351. Tattha yasmā sakiṃ pariccattepi vihāre punappunaṃ chādanakhaṇḍaphullappaṭisaṅkharaṇādivasena kiccaṃ atthiyeva, saraṇaṃ pana ekabhikkhussa vā santike saṅghassa vā gaṇassa vā sakiṃ gahitaṃ gahitameva hoti, natthi tassa punappunaṃ kattabbatā, tasmā taṃ vihāradānato appaṭṭhatarañca appasamārambhatarañca hoti. Yasmā ca saraṇagamanaṃ nāma tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ jīvitapariccāgamayaṃ puññakammaṃ saggasampattiṃ deti, tasmā mahapphalatarañca mahānisaṃsatarañcāti veditabbaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ pana ratanānaṃ jīvitapariccāgavasena yaññoti vuccati.

Therein, because even when a monastery has been relinquished once, there is still work to be done again and again by way of repairing the roofing, breakages, and cracks, but refuge, whether taken once in the presence of a single monk, the Sangha, or a group, is simply taken. There is no need for it to be done again and again. Therefore, it is less troublesome and has less undertaking than the gift of a monastery. And because going for refuge is a meritorious act consisting of the dedication of one's life to the Three Jewels that yields heavenly attainment, it should be known as more fruitful and of greater benefit. Furthermore, on account of relinquishing one's life for the Three Jewels, it is called a sacrifice.

352. Idaṃ [P 1.0305] sutvā brāhmaṇo cintesi – “attano jīvitaṃ nāma parassa pariccajituṃ dukkaraṃ, atthi nu kho itopi appaṭṭhataro yañño”ti tato taṃ pucchanto puna “atthi pana, bho gotamā”tiādimāha. Tattha pāṇātipātā veramaṇītiādīsu veramaṇī nāma virati. Sā tividhā hoti – sampattavirati, samādānavirati setughātaviratīti. Tattha yo sikkhāpadāni agahetvāpi kevalaṃ attano jātigottakulāpadesādīni anussaritvā – “na me idaṃ patirūpa”nti [V 1.0246] pāṇātipātādīni na karoti, sampattavatthuṃ pariharati. Tato ārakā viramati. Tassa sā virati sampattaviratīti veditabbā.

352. Hearing this, the brahmin thought: “To give up one's own life for another is difficult to do. Is there, I wonder, a sacrifice with even less trouble than this?” Therefore, wishing to ask about it, he again spoke the words beginning, “But is there, good Gotama…”. Therein, regarding the words beginning “abstention from the destruction of life,” the word “abstention” (veramaṇī) means abstinence (virati). That abstinence is of three kinds: situational abstinence (sampattavirati), abstinence by undertaking (samādānavirati), and abstinence that destroys the bridge (setughātavirati). Among these, there is one who, even without having undertaken the training rules, simply by recollecting one's own birth, clan, family, and so forth, thinks, “This is not suitable for me,” and does not commit acts such as the destruction of life; one avoids the object that has come into one's presence. One abstains, keeping far from it. That abstinence of such a person is to be known as situational abstinence.

“Ajjatagge jīvitahetupi pāṇaṃ na hanāmī”ti vā “pāṇātipātā viramāmī”ti vā “veramaṇiṃ samādiyāmī”ti vā evaṃ sikkhāpadāni gaṇhantassa pana virati samādānaviratīti veditabbā.

Furthermore, the abstinence of one who undertakes the training rules, saying either, “From today onwards, even for the sake of my life, I will not kill a living being,” or, “I abstain from the destruction of life,” or, “I undertake the training rule of abstention,” is to be known as abstinence by undertaking.

Ariyasāvakānaṃ pana maggasampayuttā virati setughātavirati nāma. Tattha purimā dve viratiyo yaṃ voropanādivasena vītikkamitabbaṃ jīvitindriyādivatthu, taṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattanti. Pacchimā nibbānārammaṇāva. Ettha ca yo pañca sikkhāpadāni ekato gaṇhati, tassa ekasmiṃ bhinne sabbāni bhinnāni honti. Yo ekekaṃ gaṇhati, so yaṃ vītikkamati, tadeva [M 1.0273] bhijjati. Setughātaviratiyā pana bhedo nāma natthi, bhavantarepi hi ariyasāvako jīvitahetupi neva pāṇaṃ hanati na suraṃ pivati. Sacepissa surañca khīrañca missetvā mukhe pakkhipanti, khīrameva pavisati, na surā. Yathā kiṃ? Koñcasakuṇānaṃ khīramissake udake khīrameva pavisati? Na udakaṃ. Idaṃ yonisiddhanti ce, idaṃ dhammatāsiddhanti ca veditabbaṃ. Yasmā pana saraṇagamane diṭṭhiujukakaraṇaṃ nāma bhāriyaṃ. Sikkhāpadasamādāne pana viratimattakameva. Tasmā etaṃ yathā vā tathā vā gaṇhantassāpi sādhukaṃ gaṇhantassāpi appaṭṭhatarañca appasamārambhatarañca. Pañcasīlasadisassa pana dānassa abhāvato ettha mahapphalatā mahānisaṃsatā ca veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Furthermore, for noble disciples, the abstinence associated with the path is called abstinence that destroys the bridge. Therein, the former two kinds of abstinence arise by taking as their object that basis—such as the life-faculty—which is liable to be transgressed by way of killing, etc. The latter has only Nibbāna as its object. And herein, for one who undertakes the five training rules together, if one is broken, all are broken. For one who undertakes them one by one, only that which one transgresses is broken. But for the abstinence that destroys the bridge, there is no such thing as breaking. Indeed, even in another existence, a noble disciple will not kill a living being or drink intoxicants, even for the sake of their life. Even if one were to mix intoxicants and milk and place it in their mouth, only the milk enters, not the intoxicant. What is the simile? Just as for cranes, in water mixed with milk, only the milk enters, not the water. If it is said, “This is accomplished due to their species,” it should also be known, “This is accomplished due to the nature of the Dhamma.” Furthermore, because in going for refuge the matter of straightening one's view is burdensome, whereas in undertaking the training rules it is merely a matter of abstinence, this is therefore less troublesome and has less undertaking, whether one undertakes them in any way whatsoever or undertakes them well. However, due to the absence of a gift equal to the five precepts, it should be known that herein there is great fruit and great benefit. For this has been said:

“Pañcimāni[P 1.0306], bhikkhave, dānāni mahādānāni aggaññāni rattaññāni vaṃsaññāni porāṇāni asaṃkiṇṇāni asaṃkiṇṇapubbāni na saṅkiyanti na saṅkiyissanti appaṭikuṭṭhāni samaṇehi brāhmaṇehi viññūhi. Katamāni pañca? Idha, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hoti. Pāṇātipātā paṭivirato, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ abhayaṃ deti, averaṃ deti abyāpajjhaṃ deti. Aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ abhayaṃ datvā averaṃ datvā abyāpajjhaṃ datvā aparimāṇassa abhayassa averassa abyāpajjhassa bhāgī hoti. Idaṃ, bhikkhave, paṭhamaṃ dānaṃ mahādānaṃ…pe… viññūhīti.

“Bhikkhus, these five are great gifts—known as supreme, known for a long time, of noble lineage, ancient, unadulterated, unadulterated in the past, not being adulterated now, and they will not be adulterated in the future; they are unreproached by wise ascetics and brahmins. What five? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple, having abandoned the destruction of life, abstains from the destruction of life. By abstaining from the destruction of life, bhikkhus, a noble disciple gives to limitless beings freedom from fear, freedom from enmity, and freedom from affliction. Having given to limitless beings freedom from fear, freedom from enmity, and freedom from affliction, one becomes a partaker of limitless freedom from fear, freedom from enmity, and freedom from affliction. This, bhikkhus, is the first great gift… unreproached by the wise.”

Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako adinnādānaṃ pahāya…pe… kāmesumicchācāraṃ [V 1.0247] pahāya…pe… musāvādaṃ pahāya…pe… surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānaṃ pahāya…pe… imāni kho, bhikkhave, pañca dānāni mahādānāni aggaññāni…pe… viññūhī”ti (a. ni. 8.39).

“Furthermore, bhikkhus, a noble disciple, having abandoned taking what is not given… having abandoned sexual misconduct… having abandoned false speech… having abandoned the use of distilled and fermented intoxicants which are a basis for negligence… These, bhikkhus, are the five great gifts—known as supreme… unreproached by the wise.”

Idañca pana sīlapañcakaṃ – “attasinehañca jīvitasinehañca pariccajitvā rakkhissāmī”ti samādinnatāya yaññoti vuccati. Tattha kiñcāpi pañcasīlato saraṇagamanameva jeṭṭhakaṃ, idaṃ pana saraṇagamaneyeva patiṭṭhāya rakkhitasīlavasena mahapphalanti vuttaṃ.

Furthermore, this pentad of precepts is called a 'sacrifice' because it is undertaken with the thought, 'Having given up love for self and love for life, I will protect them.' Therein, although going for refuge is indeed superior to the five precepts, it is nevertheless said that these precepts are of great fruit by virtue of being virtue that is protected while established in the going for refuge itself.

353. Idampi [M 1.0274] sutvā brāhmaṇo cintesi – “pañcasīlaṃ nāma rakkhituṃ garukaṃ, atthi nu kho aññaṃ kiñci īdisameva hutvā ito appaṭṭhatarañca mahapphalatarañcā”ti. Tato taṃ pucchanto punapi – “atthi pana, bho gotamā”tiādimāha. Athassa bhagavā tividhasīlapāripūriyaṃ ṭhitassa paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ yaññānaṃ appaṭṭhatarañca mahapphalatarañca dassetukāmo buddhuppādato paṭṭhāya desanaṃ ārabhanto “idha brāhmaṇā”tiādimāha. Tattha yasmā heṭṭhā vuttehi guṇehi samannāgato paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ, paṭhamajjhānādīsu ṭhito dutiyajjhānādīni nibbattento na kilamati, tasmā tāni appaṭṭhāni appasamārambhāni. Yasmā panettha paṭhamajjhānaṃ ekaṃ kappaṃ brahmaloke āyuṃ deti. Dutiyaṃ aṭṭhakappe. Tatiyaṃ catusaṭṭhikappe. Catutthaṃ pañcakappasatāni. Tadeva ākāsānañcāyatanādisamāpattivasena [P 1.0307] bhāvitaṃ vīsati, cattālīsaṃ, saṭṭhi, caturāsīti ca kappasahassāni āyuṃ deti; tasmā mahapphalatarañca mahānisaṃsatarañca. Nīvaraṇādīnaṃ pana paccanīkānaṃ dhammānaṃ pariccattattā taṃ yaññanti veditabbaṃ.

353. Hearing this as well, the brahmin thought: 'The five precepts are burdensome to protect. Is there, I wonder, some other sacrifice that, being just like this, is less troublesome and more fruitful?' Therefore, wishing to ask about it, he again spoke the words beginning, 'But is there, good Gotama...'. Then the Blessed One, wishing to show him the sacrifices of the first jhāna and so on for one established in the fulfillment of the threefold virtue—which are less troublesome and more fruitful—began the discourse, starting from the appearance of a Buddha, saying, 'Here, brahmin...'. Therein, because one who is endowed with the qualities spoken of below is not fatigued when generating the first jhāna, and one established in the first jhāna and so on is not fatigued when generating the second jhāna and so on, they are less troublesome and involve less affliction for beings. Furthermore, because herein the first jhāna gives a lifespan of one incalculable eon in the Brahma world; the second, eight great eons; the third, sixty-four great eons; and the fourth, five hundred great eons. And that same fourth jhāna, when developed by way of the attainments beginning with the base of infinite space, gives a lifespan of twenty thousand, forty thousand, sixty thousand, and eighty-four thousand great eons. Therefore, they are more fruitful and of greater benefit. And because opposing states such as the hindrances are abandoned, this is to be known as a 'sacrifice'.

Vipassanāñāṇampi yasmā catutthajjhānapariyosānesu guṇesu patiṭṭhāya nibbattento na kilamati, tasmā appaṭṭhaṃ appasamārambhaṃ; vipassanāsukhasadisassa pana sukhassa abhāvā mahapphalaṃ. Paccanīkakilesapariccāgato yaññoti. Manomayiddhipi yasmā vipassanāñāṇe patiṭṭhāya nibbattento na kilamati, tasmā appaṭṭhā appasamārambhā; attano sadisarūpanimmānasamatthatāya mahapphalā. Attano paccanīkakilesapariccāgato yañño. Iddhividhañāṇādīnipi yasmā manomayañāṇādīsu patiṭṭhāya nibbattento na kilamati, tasmā appaṭṭhāni appasamārambhāni, attano attano paccanīkakilesappahānato yañño. Iddhividhaṃ panettha nānāvidhavikubbanadassanasamatthatāya. Dibbasotaṃ devamanussānaṃ saddasavanasamatthatāya; cetopariyañāṇaṃ [V 1.0248] paresaṃ soḷasavidhacittajānanasamatthatāya; pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ icchiticchitaṭṭhānasamanussaraṇasamatthatāya; dibbacakkhu icchiticchitarūpadassanasamatthatāya; āsavakkhayañāṇaṃ atipaṇītalokuttaramaggasukhanipphādanasamatthatāya mahapphalanti veditabbaṃ. Yasmā pana arahattato visiṭṭhataro añño yañño nāma natthi, tasmā arahattanikūṭeneva desanaṃ samāpento – “ayampi kho, brāhmaṇā”tiādimāha.

Insight knowledge also, because, being established in the qualities culminating in the fourth jhāna, it is brought into being without exertion, is therefore effortless and without striving. Moreover, because of the absence of a happiness similar to the happiness of insight, it is of great fruit. It is called a sacrifice because of the relinquishing of opposing defilements. The mind-made power also, because, being established in insight knowledge, it is brought into being without exertion, is therefore effortless and without striving; it is of great fruit due to its ability to create a form similar to oneself. It is a sacrifice because of the relinquishing of one's own opposing defilements. The knowledges of the kinds of psychic power and so on also, because, being established in the mind-made knowledge and so on, they are brought into being without exertion, are therefore effortless and without striving; each is a sacrifice because of the abandoning of its own opposing defilements. Herein, it should be understood that the following are of great fruit: the kinds of psychic power, due to the ability to display various transformations; the divine ear, due to the ability to hear the sounds of gods and humans; the knowledge of others’ minds, due to the ability to know the sixteen kinds of minds of others; the knowledge of recollecting past lives, due to the ability to recollect whatever place is wished for; the divine eye, due to the ability to see whatever visible form is wished for; and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, due to the ability to produce the supremely refined happiness of the supramundane path. Furthermore, because there is no other sacrifice more distinguished than Arahantship, therefore, concluding the discourse with the pinnacle of Arahantship, He said, “This too, O brahmin…” and so on.

Kūṭadantaupāsakattapaṭivedanāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of Kūṭadanta's Declaration as a Lay Follower

354-358. Evaṃ [M 1.0275] vutteti evaṃ bhagavatā vutte desanāya pasīditvā saraṇaṃ gantukāmo kūṭadanto brāhmaṇo – ‘etaṃ abhikkantaṃ bho, gotamā’tiādikaṃ vacanaṃ avoca. Upavāyatūti upagantvā sarīradarathaṃ nibbāpento tanusītalo vāto vāyatūti. Idañca pana vatvā brāhmaṇo purisaṃ pesesi – “gaccha, tāta, yaññavāṭaṃ pavisitvā sabbe te pāṇayo bandhanā mocehī”ti. So “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā tathā katvā āgantvā “muttā bho, te pāṇayo”ti ārocesi. Yāva [P 1.0308] brāhmaṇo taṃ pavattiṃ na suṇi, na tāva bhagavā dhammaṃ desesi. Kasmā? “Brāhmaṇassa citte ākulabhāvo atthī”ti. Sutvā panassa “bahū vata me pāṇā mocitā”ti cittacāro vippasīdati. Bhagavā tassa vippasannamanataṃ ñatvā dhammadesanaṃ ārabhi. Taṃ sandhāya – “atha kho bhagavā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Puna ‘kallacitta’ntiādi ānupubbikathānubhāvena vikkhambhitanīvaraṇataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

354-358. The phrase “When this was said” means that when the Blessed One had thus spoken, the brahmin Kūṭadanta, pleased with the teaching and wishing to go for refuge, spoke these words, beginning with “Excellent, Master Gotama.” The phrase “Let it blow” (upavāyatu) means “let a gentle, cool wind blow, assuaging the fever of the body.” And having said this, the brahmin sent a man, saying, “Go, my dear, enter the sacrificial enclosure and release all those creatures from their bonds.” He replied, “Very well,” and having done so, he returned and reported, “Sir, those creatures have been released.” As long as the brahmin had not heard that news, the Blessed One did not teach the Dhamma. Why? Because “there was agitation in the brahmin’s mind.” But upon hearing, “Indeed, many creatures have been freed by me,” his mental state became serene. Knowing his serene mind, the Blessed One began the Dhamma teaching. It is with reference to this that the passage beginning “Then the Blessed One…” was spoken. Again, the passage beginning “with a ready mind…” was spoken with reference to the suppression of the hindrances through the power of the gradual discourse. The rest is clear in meaning.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Thus in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya,

Kūṭadantasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the Kūṭadanta Sutta is concluded.

6. Mahālisuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Mahāli Sutta

Brāhmaṇadūtavatthuvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Story of the Brahmin Messenger

359. Evaṃ [P 1.0309][V 1.0249][M 1.0276] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā vesāliyanti mahālisuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ apubbapadavaṇṇanā. Vesāliyanti punappunaṃ visālabhāvūpagamanato vesālīti laddhanāmake nagare. Mahāvaneti bahinagare himavantena saddhiṃ ekābaddhaṃ hutvā ṭhitaṃ sayaṃ jātavanaṃ atthi, yaṃ mahantabhāveneva mahāvananti vuccati, tasmiṃ mahāvane. Kūṭāgārasālāyanti tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe saṅghārāmaṃ patiṭṭhapesuṃ. Tattha kaṇṇikaṃ yojetvā thambhānaṃ upari kūṭāgārasālāsaṅkhepena devavimānasadisaṃ pāsādaṃ akaṃsu, taṃ upādāya sakalopi saṅghārāmo “kūṭāgārasālā”ti paññāyittha. Bhagavā taṃ vesāliṃ upanissāya tasmiṃ saṅghārāme viharati. Tena vuttaṃ – “vesāliyaṃ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāya”nti. Kosalakāti kosalaraṭṭhavāsino. Māgadhakāti magadharaṭṭhavāsino. Karaṇīyenāti avassaṃ kattabbakammena. Yañhi akātumpi vaṭṭati, taṃ kiccanti vuccati, yaṃ avassaṃ kātabbameva, taṃ karaṇīyaṃ nāma.

359. The sutta beginning with the words 'Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was in Vesālī' is the Mahāli Sutta. Herein is the explanation of terms not previously explained. 'In Vesālī' means: in the city that obtained the name Vesālī because it repeatedly attained a state of vastness. 'In the Great Forest' means: there is a naturally grown forest outside the city, which stood connected with the Himavanta, and which is called the Great Forest simply because of its vastness; in that Great Forest. 'In the Hall with the Gabled Roof' means: in that forest grove, they established a monastery. There, by fitting a pinnacle on top of the pillars, they constructed a mansion resembling a celestial abode, in the form of a hall with a gabled peak; on account of that, the entire monastery came to be known as the 'Hall with the Gabled Roof.' The Blessed One, dwelling dependent on that Vesālī, resided in that monastery. Therefore it was said: “He was dwelling at Vesālī, in the Great Forest, in the Hall with the Gabled Roof.” 'Kosalans' means: residents of the Kosala country. 'Māgadhans' means: residents of the Magadha country. 'With a duty' means: by a task that must necessarily be done. For that which it is suitable even not to do is called a 'task' (kicca); that which must necessarily be done is called a 'duty' (karaṇīya).

360. Paṭisallīno bhagavāti nānārammaṇacārato paṭikkamma sallīno nilīno, ekībhāvaṃ upagamma ekattārammaṇe jhānaratiṃ anubhavatīti attho. Tatthevāti tasmiññeva vihāre. Ekamantanti [P 1.0310] tasmā ṭhānā apakkamma tāsu tāsu rukkhacchāyāsu nisīdiṃsu.

360. ‘The Blessed One was in seclusion’ means: having withdrawn from the movement of mind in various sense-objects, he was well secluded and withdrawn; having attained a state of solitude, he was experiencing the delight of jhāna in a single object; this is the meaning. ‘There’ means: in that very monastery. ‘To one side’ means: having departed from that place, they sat in the shade of various trees.

Oṭṭhaddhalicchavīvatthuvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Story of Oṭṭhaddha the Licchavi

361. Oṭṭhaddhoti addhoṭṭhatāya evaṃladdhanāmo. Mahatiyā licchavīparisāyāti purebhattaṃ buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa dānaṃ datvā bhagavato santike uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhahitvā gandhamālādīni gāhāpetvā ugghosanāya mahatiṃ licchavirājaparisaṃ sannipātāpetvā tāya nīlapītādivaṇṇavatthābharaṇavilepanapaṭimaṇḍitāya [V 1.0250] tāvatiṃsaparisasappaṭibhāgāya mahatiyā licchaviparisāya saddhiṃ upasaṅkami. Akālo kho mahālīti [M 1.0277] tassa oṭṭhaddhassa mahālīti mūlanāmaṃ, tena mūlanāmamattena naṃ thero mahālīti ālapati. Ekamantaṃ nisīdīti patirūpāsu rukkhacchāyāsu tāya licchaviparisāya saddhiṃ ratanattayassa vaṇṇaṃ kathayanto nisīdi.

361. ‘Oṭṭhaddha’ means: he obtained this name because he had a split upper lip. ‘With a great assembly of Licchavis’ means: having given alms to the Sangha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha before noon, and having undertaken the Uposatha precepts in the Blessed One’s presence, he then had perfumes, garlands, and so forth taken, and having assembled a great assembly of Licchavi princes by proclamation, he approached together with that great Licchavi assembly, which was adorned with clothes, ornaments, and unguents of blue, yellow, and other colors, and which was comparable to the assembly of the Tāvatiṃsa gods. ‘It is not the time, Mahāli’ means: Mahāli was the original name of that Oṭṭhaddha. Therefore, the elder addressed him simply by his original name, Mahāli. ‘He sat down to one side’ means: sitting in suitable tree-shades with that Licchavi assembly, he sat speaking of the qualities of the Triple Gem.

362. Sīho samaṇuddesoti āyasmato nāgitassa bhāgineyyo sattavassakāle pabbajitvā sāsane yuttapayutto “sīho”ti evaṃnāmako sāmaṇero, so kira taṃ mahāparisaṃ disvā – “ayaṃ parisā mahatī, sakalaṃ vihāraṃ pūretvā nisinnā, addhā bhagavā ajja imissā parisāya mahantena ussāhena dhammaṃ desessati, yaṃnūnāhaṃ upajjhāyassācikkhitvā bhagavato mahāparisāya sannipatitabhāvaṃ ārocāpeyya”nti cintetvā yenāyasmā nāgito tenupasaṅkami. Bhante kassapāti theraṃ gottena ālapati. Esā janatāti eso janasamūho.

362. ‘Sīha the novice’ means: a novice named Sīha, who was the nephew of the Venerable Nāgita, having gone forth at the age of seven, was diligently engaged in the Dispensation. It is said that, seeing that great assembly, he thought: “This assembly is vast, sitting and filling the entire monastery. Surely today the Blessed One will teach the Dhamma to this assembly with great effort. What if I were to inform my preceptor and have the fact that a great assembly has gathered announced to the Blessed One?” Thinking thus, he approached the Venerable Nāgita. ‘Venerable Kassapa’ means: he addresses the elder by his clan name. ‘This populace’ means: this multitude of people.

Tvaññeva bhagavato ārocehīti sīho kira bhagavato vissāsiko, ayañhi thero thūlasarīro, tenassa sarīragarutāya uṭṭhānanisajjādīsu ālasiyabhāvo īsakaṃ appahīno viya hoti. Athāyaṃ sāmaṇero bhagavato kālena kālaṃ vattaṃ karoti. Tena naṃ thero “tvampi dasabalassa vissāsiko”ti vatvā gaccha tvaññevārocehīti āha. Vihārapacchāyāyanti vihārachāyāyaṃ, kūṭāgāramahāgehacchāyāya pharitokāseti attho. Sā kira kūṭāgārasālā dakkhiṇuttarato [P 1.0311] dīghā pācīnamukhā, tenassā purato mahatī chāyā patthaṭā hoti, sīho tattha bhagavato āsanaṃ paññapesi.

Regarding ‘You yourself inform the Blessed One’: It is said that Sīha was intimate with the Blessed One. For this elder had a large body, and because of the heaviness of his body, a slight laziness in rising, sitting, and so forth, seemed not yet abandoned. Now, this novice performs his duties for the Blessed One from time to time. Therefore, the elder, saying to him, “You too are intimate with the One of Ten Powers,” said, “Go, you yourself inform him.” ‘In the shade of the monastery’ means: in the shade of the monastery; the meaning is, in the open space pervaded by the shade of the great gabled hall. It is said that that gabled hall was long from south to north and faced east. Therefore, a great shadow was spread out in front of it. There, Sīha prepared a seat for the Blessed One.

363. Atha kho bhagavā dvārantarehi ceva vātapānantarehi ca nikkhamitvā vidhāvantāhi vippharantīhi chabbaṇṇāhi buddharasmīhi saṃsūcitanikkhamano valāhakantarato puṇṇacando viya kūṭāgārasālato nikkhamitvā paññattavarabuddhāsane nisīdi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho bhagavā vihārā nikkhamma vihārapacchāyāya paññatte āsane nisīdī”ti.

363. Then the Blessed One, whose emergence was well indicated by the six-colored Buddha-rays that issued forth from between the doorways and windows, running about and spreading out, came out from the gabled hall like the full moon emerging from between the clouds and sat down on the prepared excellent Buddha-seat. Therefore it was said: “Then the Blessed One, having come out from the dwelling, sat down on the prepared seat in the shade of the dwelling.”

364-365. Purimāni[M 1.0278], bhante, divasāni purimatarānīti ettha hiyyo divasaṃ purimaṃ nāma, tato paraṃ purimataraṃ. Tato paṭṭhāya pana sabbāni purimāni ceva purimatarāni ca honti. Yadaggeti mūladivasato paṭṭhāya yaṃ divasaṃ aggaṃ parakoṭiṃ katvā viharāmīti attho, yāva vihāsinti vuttaṃ hoti. Idāni tassa parimāṇaṃ dassento “naciraṃ tīṇi vassānī”ti āha. Atha vā yadaggeti yaṃ divasaṃ aggaṃ katvā naciraṃ tīṇi vassāni viharāmītipi attho[V 1.0251]. Yaṃ divasaṃ ādiṃ katvā naciraṃ vihāsiṃ tīṇiyeva vassānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayaṃ kira bhagavato pattacīvaraṃ gaṇhanto tīṇi saṃvaccharāni bhagavantaṃ upaṭṭhāsi, taṃ sandhāya evaṃ vadati. Piyarūpānīti piyajātikāni sātajātikāni. Kāmūpasaṃhitānīti kāmassādayuttāni. Rajanīyānīti rāgajanakāni. No ca kho dibbāni saddānīti kasmā sunakkhatto tāni na suṇāti? So kira bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā dibbacakkhuparikammaṃ yāci, tassa bhagavā ācikkhi, so yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipanno dibbacakkhuṃ uppādetvā devatānaṃ rūpāni disvā cintesi “imasmiṃ sarīrasaṇṭhāne saddena madhurena bhavitabbaṃ, kathaṃ nu kho naṃ suṇeyya”nti bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā dibbasotaparikammaṃ pucchi. Ayañca atīte ekaṃ sīlavantaṃ bhikkhuṃ kaṇṇasakkhaliyaṃ paharitvā [P 1.0312] badhiramakāsi. Tasmā parikammaṃ karontopi abhabbo dibbasotādhigamāya. Tenassa na bhagavā parikammaṃ kathesi. So ettāvatā bhagavati āghātaṃ bandhitvā cintesi – “addhā samaṇassa gotamassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahampi khattiyo ayampi khattiyo, sacassa ñāṇaṃ vaḍḍhissati, ayampi sabbaññū bhavissatī’ti usūyāya mayhaṃ na kathesī”ti. So anukkamena gihibhāvaṃ patvā tamatthaṃ mahālilicchavino kathento evamāha.

364-365. Regarding the phrase “in the past days, Venerable sir, even earlier days”: here, yesterday is called “past” (purima), and the day before that is “even more past” (purimatara). From that point onward, all days are both “past” and “even more past.” The phrase “from which as the beginning” (yadagge) means: “starting from the root day, taking a certain day as the beginning, I dwelt.” This is to say, “for as long as I dwelt.” Now, indicating its duration, he said, “not long, three years.” Alternatively, “from which as the beginning” can also mean: “taking a certain day as the beginning, I dwelt for not long, three years.” This is to say, “Taking a certain day as the beginning, I dwelt for not long, only three years.” It is said that this one attended upon the Blessed One for three years while taking the Blessed One’s bowl and robe. It is with reference to this that he speaks thus. “Pleasing forms” (piyarūpāni) means forms that are of a dear nature, of a delightful nature. “Connected with sensual pleasures” (kāmūpasaṃhitāni) means associated with the enjoyment of sensual pleasure. “Provoking passion” (rajanīyāni) means productive of lust. Regarding “but not divine sounds”: why did Sunakkhatta not hear them? It is said that he approached the Blessed One and requested the preliminary practice for the divine eye. The Blessed One instructed him, and he, having practiced as instructed, developed the divine eye. Seeing the forms of deities, he thought: “In this bodily form, there must be a sweet sound. How, indeed, might I hear it?” He approached the Blessed One and asked about the preliminary practice for the divine ear. Moreover, in a past life, this one had struck a virtuous bhikkhu on the ear, making him deaf. Therefore, even while performing the preliminary practice, he was incapable of attaining the divine ear. For this reason, the Blessed One did not teach him the preliminary practice. On this account, he harbored resentment toward the Blessed One, thinking: “Surely, the ascetic Gotama thinks thus: ‘I am a khattiya and he is also a khattiya. If his knowledge increases, he too will become omniscient.’ Out of envy, he did not teach me.” He gradually returned to the lay life and, while explaining this matter to Mahāli the Licchavi, spoke thus.

366-371. Ekaṃsabhāvitoti ekaṃsāya ekakoṭṭhāsāya bhāvito, dibbānaṃ vā rūpānaṃ dassanatthāya dibbānaṃ vā saddānaṃ savanatthāya bhāvitoti attho. Tiriyanti anudisāya. Ubhayaṃsabhāvitoti ubhayaṃsāya ubhayakoṭṭhāsāya bhāvitoti attho. Ayaṃ kho mahāli hetūti ayaṃ dibbānaṃyeva rūpānaṃ dassanāya ekaṃsabhāvito samādhi hetu. Imamatthaṃ sutvā so licchavī cintesi – “idaṃ dibbasotena saddasuṇanaṃ imasmiṃ sāsane uttamatthabhūtaṃ maññe imassa nūna atthāya ete [M 1.0279] bhikkhū paññāsampi saṭṭhipi vassāni apaṇṇakaṃ brahmacariyaṃ caranti, yaṃnūnāhaṃ dasabalaṃ etamatthaṃ puccheyya”nti.

366-371. “Developed for one part” (ekaṃsabhāvito) means developed for one side, for one portion; that is, developed for the purpose of seeing divine forms or for the purpose of hearing divine sounds. “Across” (tiriyaṃ) means in an intermediate direction. “Developed for both parts” (ubhayaṃsabhāvito) means developed for both sides, for both portions. “This, Mahāli, is the cause” means: this concentration, developed for one part only for the seeing of divine forms, is the cause. Having heard this matter, that Licchavi thought: “I suppose this hearing of sounds with the divine ear is the highest purpose in this Dispensation. Surely it is for this purpose that these monks lead the flawless holy life for fifty or even sixty years. What if I were to ask the One with Ten Powers about this matter?”

372. Tato tamatthaṃ pucchanto “etāsaṃ nūna, bhante”tiādimāha. Samādhibhāvanānanti ettha samādhiyeva samādhibhāvanā, ubhayaṃsabhāvitānaṃ samādhīnanti attho. Atha yasmā sāsanato bāhirā etā samādhibhāvanā, na ajjhattikā. Tasmā tā paṭikkhipitvā yadatthaṃ bhikkhū brahmacariyaṃ caranti, taṃ dassento bhagavā “na kho mahālī”tiādimāha.

372. Then, wishing to ask about that matter, he said, “Surely, venerable sir, for the sake of these…” and so on. Regarding “of the developments of concentration” (samādhibhāvanānaṃ): here, concentration itself is the development of concentration. The meaning is “of concentrations developed for both purposes.” Then, because these developments of concentration are external to the Dispensation, not internal, the Blessed One, having rejected them, showed for what purpose the monks live the holy life, saying, “Not so, Mahāli,” and so on.

Catuariyaphalavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Four Noble Fruits

373. Tiṇṇaṃ [V 1.0252] saṃyojanānanti sakkāyadiṭṭhiādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ bandhanānaṃ. Tāni hi vaṭṭadukkhamaye rathe satte saṃyojenti, tasmā saṃyojanānīti vuccanti. Sotāpanno [P 1.0313] hotīti maggasotaṃ āpanno hoti. Avinipātadhammoti catūsu apāyesu apatanadhammo. Niyatoti dhammaniyāmena niyato. Sambodhiparāyaṇoti uparimaggattayasaṅkhātā sambodhi paraṃ ayanaṃ assa, anena vā pattabbāti sambodhiparāyaṇo.

373. “Of the three fetters” (tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ) means: of the three bonds, beginning with personality-view. They indeed bind beings in the danger of the suffering of the round of existence; therefore, they are called fetters. “Is a stream-enterer” (sotāpanno hoti) means: he has entered the stream of the path. “Of a nature not to fall” (avinipātadhammo) means: of a nature not to fall into the four states of deprivation. “Fixed” (niyato) means: fixed by the fixed nature of the Dhamma. “Destined for enlightenment” (sambodhiparāyaṇo) means: for him, enlightenment, reckoned as the three higher paths, is the further destination; or, it is to be attained by him, thus he is “destined for enlightenment.”

Tanuttāti pariyuṭṭhānamandatāya ca kadāci karahaci uppattiyā ca tanubhāvā. Orambhāgiyānanti heṭṭhābhāgiyānaṃ, ye hi baddho upari suddhāvāsabhūmiyaṃ nibbattituṃ na sakkoti. Opapātikoti sesayonipaṭikkhepavacanametaṃ. Tattha parinibbāyīti tasmiṃ uparibhaveyeva parinibbānadhammo. Anāvattidhammoti tato brahmalokā puna paṭisandhivasena anāvattanadhammo. Cetovimuttinti cittavisuddhiṃ, sabbakilesabandhanavimuttassa arahattaphalacittassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Paññāvimuttinti etthāpi sabbakilesabandhanavimuttā arahattaphalapaññāva paññāvimuttīti veditabbā. Diṭṭheva dhammeti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve. Sayanti sāmaṃ. Abhiññāti abhijānitvā. Sacchikatvāti paccakkhaṃ katvā. Atha vā abhiññā sacchikatvāti abhiññāya abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇena sacchikaritvātipi attho. Upasampajjāti patvā paṭilabhitvā. Idaṃ sutvā licchavirājā cintesi – “ayaṃ pana dhammo na sakuṇena viya uppatitvā, nāpi godhāya viya urena gantvā sakkā paṭivijjhituṃ[M 1.0280], addhā pana imaṃ paṭivijjhantassa pubbabhāgappaṭipadāya bhavitabbaṃ, pucchāmi tāva na”nti.

“Attenuation” (tanuttā) is due to the weakness of their manifestation and their arising only occasionally, thus their attenuated state. “Of those pertaining to the lower part” (orambhāgiyānaṃ) means: of those pertaining to the lower part. For one bound by these is unable to be reborn above in the Pure Abodes. “Spontaneously arisen” (opapātiko) is a term that excludes the remaining modes of birth. “Attaining final Nibbāna there” (tattha parinibbāyī) means: one who is of the nature to attain final Nibbāna in that very higher existence. “Of a nature not to return” (anāvattidhammo) means: one who is of the nature not to return from that brahma world by way of rebirth-linking. “Liberation of mind” (cetovimuttiṃ) means: the purity of mind. This is a designation for the mind of the fruit of arahantship, which is liberated from all bonds of defilements. Here too, “liberation by wisdom” (paññāvimuttiṃ) should be understood as the wisdom of the fruit of arahantship, which is liberated from all bonds of defilements. “In this very life” (diṭṭheva dhamme) means: in this very existence. “By oneself” (sayaṃ) means: on one’s own. “Through direct knowledge” (abhiññā) means: having known through higher knowledge. “Having realized” (sacchikatvā) means: having made it manifest. Alternatively, “having realized through direct knowledge” (abhiññā sacchikatvā) also means: having realized through direct knowledge, that is, through superior knowledge. “Having entered upon” (upasampajja) means: having reached, having obtained. Hearing this, the Licchavi king thought: “This Dhamma cannot be penetrated by flying up like a bird, nor can it be penetrated by going on one’s chest like an iguana. Surely, for one who is to penetrate this, there must be a preliminary practice. Let me first ask about it.”

Ariyaaṭṭhaṅgikamaggavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Noble Eightfold Path

374-375. Tato bhagavantaṃ pucchanto “atthi pana bhante”tiādimāha. Aṭṭhaṅgikoti pañcaṅgikaṃ turiyaṃ viya aṭṭhaṅgiko gāmo viya ca aṭṭhaṅgamattoyeva hutvā aṭṭhaṅgiko, na aṅgato añño maggo nāma atthi. Tenevāha – “seyyathidaṃ, sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhī”ti. Tattha [P 1.0314] sammādassanalakkhaṇā sammādiṭṭhi. Sammā abhiniropanalakkhaṇo sammāsaṅkappo. Sammā pariggahaṇalakkhaṇā sammāvācā. Sammā samuṭṭhāpanalakkhaṇo sammākammanto. Sammā vodāpanalakkhaṇo sammāājīvo. Sammā paggahalakkhaṇo sammāvāyāmo. Sammā upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇā sammāsati. Sammā samādhānalakkhaṇo sammāsamādhi. Etesu ekekassa tīṇi tīṇi [V 1.0253] kiccāni honti. Seyyathidaṃ, sammādiṭṭhi tāva aññehipi attano paccanīkakilesehi saddhiṃ micchādiṭṭhiṃ pajahati, nirodhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti, sampayuttadhamme ca passati tappaṭicchādakamohavidhamanavasena asammohato. Sammāsaṅkappādayopi tatheva micchāsaṅkappādīni pajahanti, nirodhañca ārammaṇaṃ karonti, visesato panettha sammāsaṅkappo sahajātadhamme abhiniropeti. Sammāvācā sammā pariggaṇhati. Sammākammanto sammā samuṭṭhāpeti. Sammāājīvo sammā vodāpeti. Sammāvāyāmo sammā paggaṇhati. Sammāsati sammā upaṭṭhāpeti. Sammāsamādhi sammā padahati.

Therefore, wishing to ask the Blessed One, he spoke the words beginning with, “But is there, venerable sir?” The term ‘eightfold’ is so called by being merely eight factors, like a five-limbed musical instrument or a village with eight parts, and there is no path other than its factors. Therefore, He said: “That is to say, Right View… up to… Right Concentration.” Therein, Right View has the characteristic of right seeing. Right Intention has the characteristic of right directing of the mind. Right Speech has the characteristic of right encompassing. Right Action has the characteristic of right arousing. Right Livelihood has the characteristic of right purifying. Right Effort has the characteristic of right uplifting. Right Mindfulness has the characteristic of right establishing. Right Concentration has the characteristic of right placing. Among these, each one has three functions. That is to say, Right View, for its part, abandons wrong view together with other opposing defilements, makes cessation its object, and by dispelling the delusion that conceals it, sees associated states without confusion. Right Intention and the others, in the same way, abandon wrong intention and so forth, and make cessation their object. Specifically, among these, Right Intention directs co-arisen states. Right Speech rightly encompasses. Right Action rightly arouses. Right Livelihood rightly purifies. Right Effort rightly uplifts. Right Mindfulness rightly establishes. Right Concentration rightly places.

Api cesā sammādiṭṭhi nāma pubbabhāge nānākkhaṇā nānārammaṇā hoti, maggakkhaṇe ekakkhaṇā ekārammaṇā. Kiccato pana “dukkhe ñāṇa”ntiādīni cattāri nāmāni labhati. Sammāsaṅkappādayopi pubbabhāge nānākkhaṇā nānārammaṇā honti. Maggakkhaṇe ekakkhaṇā ekārammaṇā. Tesu sammāsaṅkappo kiccato “nekkhammasaṅkappo”tiādīni tīṇi nāmāni labhati. Sammā vācādayo tisso viratiyopi honti, cetanādayopi honti, maggakkhaṇe pana viratiyeva. Sammāvāyāmo sammāsatīti idampi dvayaṃ kiccato sammappadhānasatipaṭṭhānavasena cattāri nāmāni labhati. Sammāsamādhi pana pubbabhāgepi maggakkhaṇepi sammāsamādhiyeva.

Furthermore, this Right View, so called, has diverse moments and diverse objects in the preliminary stage, but at the moment of the path it is of a single moment and a single object. Functionally, however, it obtains four names, such as “knowledge in suffering.” Right Intention and the others also have diverse moments and diverse objects in the preliminary stage; at the moment of the path they are of a single moment and a single object. Among these, Right Intention functionally obtains three names, such as “intention of renunciation.” The three beginning with Right Speech are both abstinences and volitions, but at the moment of the path, they are only abstinences. This pair, Right Effort and Right Mindfulness, functionally obtains four names each by way of the Right Exertions and the Foundations of Mindfulness. Right Concentration, however, is Right Concentration both in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the path.

Iti [M 1.0281] imesu aṭṭhasu dhammesu bhagavatā nibbānādhigamāya paṭipannassa yogino bahukārattā paṭhamaṃ sammādiṭṭhi desitā. Ayañhi “paññāpajjoto paññāsattha”nti (dha. sa. 20) ca vuttā. Tasmā etāya pubbabhāge vipassanāñāṇasaṅkhātāya sammādiṭṭhiyā avijjandhakāraṃ vidhamitvā kilesacore ghātento khemena [P 1.0315] yogāvacaro nibbānaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tena vuttaṃ – “nibbānādhigamāya paṭipannassa yogino bahukārattā paṭhamaṃ sammādiṭṭhi desitā”ti.

Thus, among these eight factors, the Blessed One first taught Right View to the yogī practicing for the attainment of Nibbāna, because it is of great benefit. For it has been called: “the light of wisdom, the sword of wisdom.” Therefore, with this Right View, which in the preliminary stage is designated insight-knowledge, the yogāvacara dispels the darkness of ignorance, slays the thieves that are the defilements, and safely attains Nibbāna. Hence it was said: “To the yogī practicing for the attainment of Nibbāna, Right View is first taught because it is of great benefit.”

Sammāsaṅkappo pana tassā bahukāro, tasmā tadanantaraṃ vutto. Yathā hi heraññiko hatthena parivaṭṭetvā parivaṭṭetvā cakkhunā kahāpaṇaṃ olokento – “ayaṃ cheko, ayaṃ kūṭo”ti jānāti. Evaṃ yogāvacaropi pubbabhāge vitakkena vitakketvā vipassanāpaññāya olokayamāno – “ime dhammā kāmāvacarā, ime dhammā rūpāvacarādayo”ti pajānāti. Yathā vā pana purisena koṭiyaṃ gahetvā parivaṭṭetvā parivaṭṭetvā dinnaṃ mahārukkhaṃ tacchako vāsiyā tacchetvā kamme upaneti, evaṃ vitakkena vitakketvā vitakketvā dinne dhamme yogāvacaro paññāya – “ime kāmāvacarā, ime rūpāvacarā”tiādinā nayena paricchinditvā kamme upaneti[V 1.0254]. Tena vuttaṃ – “sammāsaṅkappo pana tassā bahukāro, tasmā tadanantaraṃ vutto”ti. Svāyaṃ yathā sammādiṭṭhiyā evaṃ sammāvācāyapi upakārako. Yathāha – “pubbe kho, visākha, vitakketvā vicāretvā pacchā vācaṃ bhindatī”ti, (ma. ni. 1.463) tasmā tadanantaraṃ sammāvācā vuttā.

Right Intention, however, is of great help to that Right View; therefore, it is spoken of next. For just as a money-changer, turning a coin over and over with his hand and examining it with his eye, knows, “This is genuine; this is counterfeit,” so too the yogāvacara, in the preliminary stage, having reflected with thought and examined with insight-wisdom, discerns, “These states belong to the sense-sphere; these states belong to the form-sphere and so on.” Or, just as a carpenter planes with an adze a great log—given by a man who had taken it by the end and turned it over and over—and applies it to the work, so too the yogāvacara, with wisdom, defines the states given by thought that has reflected upon them over and over, in the manner beginning with, “These are of the sense-sphere; these are of the form-sphere,” and applies them to the work. Therefore, it was said: “Right Intention, however, is of great help to that; therefore, it is spoken of next.” Just as this is helpful to Right View, so too is it helpful to Right Speech. As it is said: “First, Visākha, having reflected and considered, one then breaks forth into speech.” Therefore, Right Speech is spoken of next.

Yasmā pana – “idañcidañca karissāmā”ti paṭhamaṃ vācāya saṃvidahitvā loke kammante payojenti; tasmā vācā kāyakammassa upakārikāti sammāvācāya anantaraṃ sammākammanto vutto. Catubbidhaṃ pana vacīduccaritaṃ, tividhañca kāyaduccaritaṃ pahāya ubhayaṃ sucaritaṃ pūrentasseva yasmā ājīvaṭṭhamakaṃ sīlaṃ pūreti, na itarassa, tasmā tadubhayānantaraṃ sammāājīvo vutto. Evaṃ visuddhājīvena pana “parisuddho me ājīvo”ti ettāvatā ca paritosaṃ katvā suttapamattena viharituṃ na yuttaṃ, atha kho “sabbiriyāpathesu idaṃ vīriyaṃ samārabhitabba”nti dassetuṃ tadanantaraṃ sammāvāyāmo vutto. Tato “āraddhavīriyenapi kāyādīsu catūsu vatthūsu [M 1.0282] sati sūpaṭṭhitā kātabbā”ti dassanatthaṃ tadanantaraṃ sammāsati [P 1.0316] desitā. Yasmā panevaṃ sūpaṭṭhitā sati samādhissupakārānupakārānaṃ dhammānaṃ gatiyo samannesitvā pahoti ekattārammaṇe cittaṃ samādhātuṃ, tasmā sammāsatiyā anantaraṃ sammāsamādhi desitoti veditabbo. Etesaṃ dhammānaṃ sacchikiriyāyāti etesaṃ sotāpattiphalādīnaṃ paccakkhakiriyatthāya.

Furthermore, because in the world people engage in actions after first arranging with speech, 'We will do this and that,' therefore, speech is serviceable to bodily action; for that reason, Right Action is spoken of immediately after Right Speech. Furthermore, because for one who fulfills both kinds of good conduct, having abandoned the fourfold verbal misconduct and the threefold bodily misconduct, the virtue with livelihood as the eighth is fulfilled—and not for another—therefore, Right Livelihood is spoken of immediately after those two. Moreover, for one with a purified livelihood, it is not fitting to dwell, having become sleepy and heedless, after finding contentment with just this much: 'My livelihood is purified.' Rather, to show that 'this effort should be well undertaken in all postures,' Right Effort is spoken of immediately after that. Then, for the purpose of showing that 'even by one with aroused energy, mindfulness should be made well-established in the four bases, beginning with the body,' Right Mindfulness is taught immediately after that. Furthermore, because mindfulness, thus well-established, is able to concentrate the mind on a single object after having thoroughly investigated the courses of phenomena that are helpful and unhelpful to concentration, therefore it should be understood that Right Concentration is taught immediately after Right Mindfulness. 'For the realization of these states' means for the purpose of directly realizing these states, beginning with the fruit of stream-entry.

Dve pabbajitavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of the Two Wanderers

376-377. Ekamidāhanti idaṃ kasmā āraddhaṃ? Ayaṃ kira rājā – “rūpaṃ attā”ti evaṃladdhiko, tenassa desanāya cittaṃ nādhimuccati. Atha bhagavatā tassa laddhiyā āvikaraṇatthaṃ ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ āharituṃ idamāraddhaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – “ahaṃ ekaṃ samayaṃ ghositārāme viharāmi, tatra vasantaṃ maṃ te dve pabbajitā evaṃ pucchiṃsu. Athāhaṃ tesaṃ buddhuppādaṃ dassetvā tantidhammaṃ nāma kathento idamavocaṃ – “āvuso, saddhāsampanno nāma kulaputto evarūpassa satthu sāsane pabbajito, evaṃ tividhaṃ sīlaṃ pūretvā paṭhamajjhānādīni patvā ṭhito ‘taṃ jīva’ntiādīni vadeyya, yuttaṃ nu kho etamassā”ti? Tato tehi “yutta”nti vutte “ahaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, evaṃ jānāmi, evaṃ passāmi, atha ca panāhaṃ na vadāmī”ti taṃ vādaṃ paṭikkhipitvā uttari khīṇāsavaṃ dassetvā “imassa evaṃ vattuṃ na yutta”nti avocaṃ. Te mama vacanaṃ sutvā attamanā ahesunti. Evaṃ vutte sopi attamano ahosi[V 1.0255]. Tenāha – “idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano oṭṭhaddho licchavī bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandī”ti.

376-377. Why was this 'Ekamidāhaṃ' begun? It is said this king was one who held the view 'form is self.' Because of that, his mind was not inclined towards the teaching. Then, this was begun by the Blessed One in order to bring forth a reason for the purpose of making his view manifest. Herein, this is the meaning in brief: 'I, at one time, was dwelling in the Ghositārāma. While I was dwelling there, those two wanderers questioned me thus. Then I, having shown them the arising of a Buddha, and while teaching the doctrine of the textual tradition, said this: "Friends, a clansman endowed with faith, having gone forth in the dispensation of such a Teacher, having fulfilled the threefold virtue and, having attained the first jhāna and so on, were established therein, should he say, ‘That is the soul,’ and so on—would that be fitting for him?" Then, when they said, "It is fitting," having rejected that view by saying, "But I, friends, know this thus, see this thus, and yet I do not say so," and having further shown the Arahant, I said, "It is not fitting for this one to speak thus." Having heard my words, they were delighted.' When this was said, he too was delighted. Therefore, it is said: 'The Blessed One said this. Delighted, the Licchavi Oṭṭhaddha rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.'

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Thus in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya.

Mahālisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mahāli Sutta is concluded.

7. Jāliyasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Jāliya Sutta

Dve pabbajitavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of the Two Who Went Forth

378. Evaṃ [P 1.0317][M 1.0283][V 1.0256] me sutaṃ…pe… kosambiyanti jāliyasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ apubbapadavaṇṇanā. Ghositārāmeti ghositena seṭṭhinā kate ārāme. Pubbe kira allakapparaṭṭhaṃ nāma ahosi. Tato kotūhaliko nāma daliddo chātakabhayena saputtadāro avantiraṭṭhaṃ gacchanto puttaṃ vahituṃ asakkonto chaḍḍetvā agamāsi, mātā nivattitvā taṃ gahetvā gatā, te ekaṃ gopālakagāmaṃ pavisiṃsu. Gopālakena ca tadā bahupāyāso paṭiyatto hoti, te tato pāyāsaṃ labhitvā bhuñjiṃsu. Atha so puriso balavapāyāsaṃ bhutto jīrāpetuṃ asakkonto rattibhāge kālaṃ katvā tattheva sunakhiyā kucchismiṃ paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā kukkuro jāto, so gopālakassa piyo ahosi. Gopālako ca paccekabuddhaṃ upaṭṭhahati. Paccekabuddhopi bhattakiccapariyosāne kukkurassa ekekaṃ piṇḍaṃ deti, so paccekabuddhe sinehaṃ uppādetvā gopālakena saddhiṃ paṇṇasālampi gacchati. Gopālake asannihite bhattavelāyaṃ sayameva gantvā kālārocanatthaṃ paṇṇasāladvāre bhussati, antarāmaggepi caṇḍamige disvā bhussitvā palāpeti. So paccekabuddhe mudukena cittena kālaṃkatvā devaloke nibbatti[P 1.0318]. Tatrassa ghosakadevaputto tveva nāmaṃ ahosi. So devalokato cavitvā kosambiyaṃ ekassa kulassa ghare nibbatti. Taṃ aputtako seṭṭhi tassa mātāpitūnaṃ dhanaṃ datvā puttaṃ katvā aggahesi. Atha attano putte jāte sattakkhattuṃ ghātāpetuṃ upakkami. So puññavantatāya sattasupi ṭhānesu maraṇaṃ appatvā avasāne ekāya seṭṭhidhītāya veyyattiyena laddhajīvito aparabhāge pituaccayena seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ patvā ghosakaseṭṭhi nāma jāto. Aññepi kosambiyaṃ kukkuṭaseṭṭhi[M 1.0284], pāvāriyaseṭṭhīti dve seṭṭhino atthi, iminā saddhiṃ tayo ahesuṃ.

378. Thus have I heard… etc.… at Kosambi is the Jāliya Sutta. Herein is the explanation of new terms. Ghositārāma means: in the park built by the merchant Ghosita. Formerly, it is said, there was a country named Allakappa. From there, a poor man named Kotūhalika, due to fear of starvation, while going to the country of Avanti with his wife and child, being unable to carry his son, abandoned him and went on. The mother, turning back, took the child and went. They entered a cowherds' village. And at that time, much milk-rice had been prepared by a cowherd. They, having received milk-rice from there, ate. Then that man, having eaten the rich milk-rice and being unable to digest it, died in the night. Right there, taking rebirth-linking in the womb of a bitch, he was born a dog. That dog became dear to the cowherd. And the cowherd attended upon a Paccekabuddha. The Paccekabuddha also, at the conclusion of the meal, would give a single morsel to the dog. The dog, having developed affection for the Paccekabuddha, would also go to the leaf-hut together with the cowherd. When the cowherd was not present at mealtime, it would go by itself and bark at the door of the leaf-hut to announce the time. Also on the path, seeing fierce beasts, it would bark and make them flee. That dog, having passed away with a tender mind towards the Paccekabuddha, was reborn in the deva-world. There, his name was indeed Ghosaka Devaputta. Having passed away from the deva-world, he was reborn in Kosambi in the house of a certain family. A childless merchant, having given wealth to his parents, took him, making him his son. Then, when his own son was born, the merchant endeavored seven times to have him killed. But he, due to his merit, did not meet death in any of the seven instances. In the end, his life was obtained through the cleverness of a merchant's daughter. Later, upon his father's passing, he attained the position of a merchant and became known as Ghosaka the merchant. In Kosambi there were also two other merchants: Kukkuṭa the merchant and Pāvāriya the merchant. Together with him, there were three.

Tena ca samayena himavantato pañcasatatāpasā sarīrasantappanatthaṃ antarantarākosambiṃ āgacchanti[V 1.0257], tesaṃ ete tayo seṭṭhī attano attano uyyānesu paṇṇakuṭiyo katvā upaṭṭhānaṃ karonti. Athekadivasaṃ te tāpasā himavantato āgacchantā mahākantāre tasitā kilantā ekaṃ mahantaṃ vaṭarukkhaṃ patvā tattha adhivatthāya devatāya santikā saṅgahaṃ paccāsisantā nisīdiṃsu. Devatā sabbālaṅkāravibhūsitaṃ hatthaṃ pasāretvā tesaṃ pānīyapānakādīni datvā kilamathaṃ paṭivinodesi, ete devatāyānubhāvena vimhitā pucchiṃsu – “kiṃ nu kho, devate, kammaṃ katvā tayā ayaṃ sampatti laddhā”ti? Devatā āha – “loke buddho nāma bhagavā uppanno, so etarahi sāvatthiyaṃ viharati, anāthapiṇḍiko gahapati taṃ upaṭṭhahati. So uposathadivasesu attano bhatakānaṃ pakatibhattavetanameva datvā uposathaṃ kārāpesi. Athāhaṃ ekadivasaṃ majjhanhike pātarāsatthāya āgato kañci bhatakakammaṃ akarontaṃ disvā – ‘ajja manussā kasmā kammaṃ na karontī’ti pucchiṃ. Tassa me tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Athāhaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘idāni upaḍḍhadivaso gato, sakkā nu kho upaḍḍhuposathaṃ kātu’nti. Tato seṭṭhissa paṭivedetvā “sakkā kātu”nti āha. Svāhaṃ upaḍḍhadivasaṃ upaḍḍhuposathaṃ samādiyitvā tadaheva kālaṃ katvā imaṃ sampattiṃ paṭilabhi”nti.

And at that time, five hundred ascetics from the Himālaya would come to Kosambi from time to time to refresh their bodies. These three merchants built leaf-huts for them in their own respective gardens and attended to them. Then one day, those ascetics, coming from the Himālaya, became thirsty and weary in a great wilderness. They came to a large banyan tree and sat down, hoping for hospitality from the deity dwelling there. The deity, stretching out a hand adorned with all ornaments, gave them drinking water, beverages, and so on, and dispelled their weariness. Astonished by the deity’s power, they asked: “O deity, what kamma did you perform to attain such fortune?” The deity replied: “In the world, the Blessed One named Buddha has arisen. He now dwells in Sāvatthī, and the householder Anāthapiṇḍika attends to him. On Uposatha days, he gives his hired workers their usual provisions of food and wages and has them undertake the Uposatha. Then one day, I arrived at midday for the morning meal and saw that none of the hired workers were working. I asked, ‘Why are the people not working today?’ They explained the matter to me. Then I said, ‘Now half the day has passed—is it possible to undertake a half-day Uposatha?’ Then, having informed the merchant, they replied, ‘It is possible to do so.’ So I, having undertaken the half-day Uposatha for half a day, passed away that very day and obtained this fortune.”

Atha te tāpasā “buddho kira uppanno”ti sañjātapītipāmojjā tatova sāvatthiṃ gantukāmā hutvāpi – “bahukārā no upaṭṭhākaseṭṭhino tesampi imamatthamārocessāmā”ti [P 1.0319] kosambiṃ gantvā seṭṭhīhi katasakkārabahumānā “tadaheva mayaṃ gacchāmā”ti āhaṃsu. “Kiṃ, bhante, turitāttha, nanu tumhe pubbe cattāro pañca māse vasitvā gacchathā”ti ca vutte taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesuṃ. “Tena hi, bhante, saheva gacchāmā”ti ca vutte “gacchāma mayaṃ, tumhe saṇikaṃ āgacchathā”ti sāvatthiṃ gantvā bhagavato santike pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Tepi seṭṭhino pañcasatapañcasatasakaṭaparivārā [M 1.0285] sāvatthiṃ gantvā dānādīni datvā kosambiṃ āgamanatthāya bhagavantaṃ yācitvā paccāgamma tayo vihāre kāresuṃ. Tesu kukkuṭaseṭṭhinā kato kukkuṭārāmo nāma, pāvāriyaseṭṭhinā kato pāvārikambavanaṃ nāma, ghositaseṭṭhinā kato ghositārāmo nāma ahosi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “kosambiyaṃ viharati ghositārāme”ti.

Then those ascetics, upon hearing, 'The Buddha, it is said, has arisen!', were filled with joy and delight. Although they wished to go to Sāvatthī right from there, they thought, 'Our attendant merchants are of great help to us; we shall also inform them of this matter.' So they went to Kosambi, and having been honored and shown great respect by the merchants, they said, 'We shall go this very day.' When the merchants asked, 'Why the haste, venerable sirs? Did you not formerly stay for four or five months before departing?', the ascetics explained the situation. And when the merchants said, 'In that case, venerable sirs, let us go together,' the ascetics replied, 'We are going; you may come slowly.' Then, having gone to Sāvatthī, they went forth in the presence of the Blessed One and attained Arahantship. Those merchants also, each with a retinue of five hundred carts, went to Sāvatthī. After performing giving and other meritorious deeds, they requested the Blessed One to come to Kosambi. Then they returned and had three monasteries built. Among them, the one built by the merchant Kukkuṭa was named Kukkuṭārāma; the one built by the merchant Pāvāriya was named Pāvārikambavana; and the one built by the merchant Ghosita was named Ghositārāma. With reference to that, it was said: '...he dwells at Kosambi, in the Ghositārāma.'

Muṇḍiyoti idaṃ tassa nāmaṃ. Jāliyoti idampi itarassa nāmameva. Yasmā panassa upajjhāyo dārumayena pattena piṇḍāya carati, tasmā dārupattikantevāsīti vuccati. Etadavocunti upārambhādhippāyena vādaṃ āropetukāmā hutvā etadavocuṃ. Iti kira nesaṃ ahosi, sace samaṇo gotamo “taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīra”nti vakkhati, athassa mayaṃ etaṃ vādaṃ āropessāma – “bho gotama, tumhākaṃ laddhiyā idheva satto bhijjati, tena vo vādo ucchedavādo [V 1.0258] hotī”ti. Sace pana “aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīra”nti vakkhati, athassetaṃ vādaṃ āropessāma “tumhākaṃ vāde rūpaṃ bhijjati, na satto bhijjati. Tena vo vāde satto sassato āpajjatī”ti. Atha bhagavā “ime vādāropanatthāya pañhaṃ pucchanti, mama sāsane ime dve ante anupagamma majjhimā paṭipadā atthīti na jānanti, handa nesaṃ pañhaṃ avissajjetvā tassāyeva paṭipadāya āvibhāvatthaṃ dhammaṃ desemī”ti cintetvā “tena hāvuso”tiādimāha.

"Muṇḍiya" is the name of that wanderer. "Jāliya" is also the name of the other. Furthermore, because his preceptor wanders for alms with a bowl made of wood, he is called 'the pupil of the one with the wooden bowl.' As for 'they spoke thus,' they spoke thus with the intention of censure, desiring to level an accusation. It seems this was their thought: "If the ascetic Gotama should say, 'The life-principle is the same as the body,' then we will level this accusation against him: 'Venerable Gotama, according to your doctrine, a being is destroyed in this very life; because of that, your view becomes annihilationism.' But if he should say, 'The life-principle is one thing, the body another,' then we will level this accusation against him: 'In your view, the physical body is destroyed, but the being is not destroyed. Because of that, in your view, the being becomes eternal.'" Then the Blessed One, having thought, "These ask a question for the purpose of leveling an accusation. They do not know that in my teaching there is a middle practice that does not approach these two extremes. Well now, without answering their question, I shall teach the Dhamma for the purpose of making that very practice clear," said, "Well then, friends," and so on.

379-380. Tattha kallaṃ nu kho tassetaṃ vacanāyāti tassetaṃ saddhāpabbajitassa tividhaṃ sīlaṃ paripūretvā paṭhamajjhānaṃ [P 1.0320] pattassa yuttaṃ nu kho etaṃ vattunti attho. Taṃ sutvā paribbājakā puthujjano nāma yasmā nibbicikiccho na hoti, tasmā kadāci evaṃ vadeyyāti maññamānā – “kallaṃ tassetaṃ vacanāyā”ti āhaṃsu. Atha ca panāhaṃ na vadāmīti ahaṃ etamevaṃ jānāmi, no ca evaṃ vadāmi, atha kho kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā bhāventassa paññābalena uppannaṃ mahaggatacittametanti saññaṃ ṭhapesiṃ. Na [M 1.0286] kallaṃ tassetanti idaṃ te paribbājakā – “yasmā khīṇāsavo vigatasammoho tiṇṇavicikiccho, tasmā na yuttaṃ tassetaṃ vattu”nti maññamānā vadanti. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

Therein, as for 'Is it proper for him to say this?': the meaning is, 'Is it indeed proper for one who has gone forth out of faith, having fulfilled the threefold virtue and attained the first jhāna, to say this?' Hearing that, the wanderers, thinking, 'Because a worldling is not without doubt, he might therefore sometimes speak thus,' said, 'It is proper for him to say this.' As for 'And yet I do not say so': 'Although I know this thus, I do not speak thus. Rather, I have established the perception that this is a sublime consciousness, arisen by the power of wisdom for one who develops it after doing the preliminary work on a kasiṇa.' As for 'It is not proper for him,' those wanderers say this thinking, 'Because one whose cankers are destroyed is free from bewilderment and has overcome doubt, it is therefore not proper for him to say this.' The rest herein has an obvious meaning.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Thus in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya.

Jāliyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition on the Jāliya Sutta is concluded.

8. Mahāsīhanādasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta

Acelakassapavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of Kassapa the Naked Ascetic

381. Evaṃ [P 2.0349][V 1.0259][M 1.0287] me sutaṃ…pe… uruññāyaṃ viharatīti mahāsīhanādasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ apubbapadavaṇṇanā. Uruññāyanti uruññāti tassa raṭṭhassapi nagarassapi etadeva nāmaṃ, bhagavā uruññānagaraṃ upanissāya viharati. Kaṇṇakatthale migadāyeti tassa nagarassa avidūre kaṇṇakatthalaṃ nāma eko ramaṇīyo bhūmibhāgo atthi. So migānaṃ abhayatthāya dinnattā “migadāyo”ti vuccati, tasmiṃ kaṇṇakatthale migadāye. Aceloti naggaparibbājako. Kassapoti tassa nāmaṃ. Tapassinti tapanissitakaṃ. Lūkhājīvinti acelakamuttācārādivasena lūkho ājīvo assāti lūkhājīvī, taṃ lūkhājīviṃ. Upakkosatīti upaṇḍeti. Upavadatīti hīḷeti vambheti. Dhammassa ca anudhammaṃ byākarontīti bhotā gotamena vuttakāraṇassa anukāraṇaṃ kathenti. Sahadhammiko vādānuvādoti parehi vuttakāraṇena sakāraṇo hutvā tumhākaṃ vādo vā anuvādo vā viññūhi garahitabbaṃ, kāraṇaṃ koci appamattakopi kiṃ na āgacchati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti, “kiṃ sabbākārenapi tava vāde gārayhaṃ kāraṇaṃ [P 2.0350] natthī”ti. Anabbhakkhātukāmāti na abhūtena vattukāmā.

381. The Mahāsīhanāda Sutta begins: “Thus have I heard…pe… he was dwelling at Uruññā.” Therein, this is the explanation of terms not previously explained. 'At Uruññā' means: Uruññā is the name of both that country and that city. The Blessed One dwells depending on the city of Uruññā. 'In the deer park at Kaṇṇakatthala' means: Not far from that city, there is a delightful plot of land named Kaṇṇakatthala. Because it was given for the safety of deer, it is called a 'deer park'. [The Blessed One was dwelling] in that deer park at Kaṇṇakatthala. 'Acela' means a naked wanderer. 'Kassapa' is his name. 'An ascetic' means one who depends on ascetic practices. 'Living a rough life' means: by way of the practice of a naked ascetic, conduct abandoned by men of good family, and so on, his livelihood is rough; therefore, he is one who lives a rough life. [The text refers to] him, the one living a rough life. 'He reproaches' means he derides. 'He finds fault' means he censures, he scorns. 'And they explain a teaching in conformity with the teaching' means: Do they state a reason that is in accordance with the reason spoken by the venerable Gotama? 'A debate and counter-debate in accordance with the teaching' means: Does your statement or counter-statement, being based on a reason in accordance with the reason stated by others, not lead to any ground, even the slightest, that is censurable by the wise? This is what is meant: 'Is there no censurable point in your doctrine in any way whatsoever?' 'Desiring not to slander' means: not wishing to speak what is untrue.

382. Ekaccaṃ tapassiṃ lūkhājīvintiādīsu idhekacco acelakapabbajjāditapanissitattā tapassī “lūkhena jīvitaṃ kappessāmī”ti tiṇagomayādibhakkhanādīhi nānappakārehi attānaṃ kilameti, appapuññatāya ca sukhena jīvitavuttimeva na labhati, so tīṇi duccaritāni pūretvā niraye nibbattati.

382. In the passage beginning 'a certain ascetic, living a rough life,' the meaning should be understood thus: Here, a certain person is an ascetic because he depends on ascetic practices such as the renunciation of a naked ascetic. Thinking, 'I will make my living in a rough way,' he torments himself in various ways, such as by eating grass, cow dung, and so on. And due to his lack of merit, he does not obtain even a comfortable means of livelihood. Having fulfilled the three kinds of misconduct, he is reborn in hell.

Aparo tādisaṃ tapanissitopi puññavā hoti, labhati lābhasakkāraṃ. So “na dāni mayā sadiso atthī”ti attānaṃ ucce ṭhāne sambhāvetvā “bhiyyosomattāya lābhaṃ uppādessāmī”ti [V 1.0260] anesanavasena tīṇi duccaritāni pūretvā niraye nibbattati. Ime dve sandhāya paṭhamanayo vutto.

Another, though depending on such asceticism, is meritorious; he obtains gain and honor. Thinking, 'Now there is no one equal to me,' he esteems himself in a high position and thinks, 'I will generate gain in great measure.' By means of improper seeking, he fulfills the three kinds of misconduct and is reborn in hell. With reference to these two, the first method was spoken.

Aparo tapanissitako lūkhājīvī appapuñño hoti, na labhati sukhena jīvitavuttiṃ. So “mayhaṃ pubbepi akatapuññatāya sukhajīvikā nuppajjati[M 1.0288], handadāni puññāni karomī”ti tīṇi sucaritāni pūretvā sagge nibbattati.

Another who depends on asceticism lives a rough life and has little merit; he does not obtain a comfortable livelihood. He thinks, 'For me, because of not having done merit in the past, a comfortable living does not arise. Well now, I shall perform meritorious deeds!' Having fulfilled the three kinds of good conduct, he is reborn in heaven.

Aparo lūkhājīvī puññavā hoti, labhati sukhena jīvitavuttiṃ. So – “mayhaṃ pubbepi katapuññatāya sukhajīvikā uppajjatī”ti cintetvā anesanaṃ pahāya tīṇi sucaritāni pūretvā sagge nibbattati. Ime dve sandhāya dutiyanayo vutto.

Another who lives a rough life is meritorious; he obtains a comfortable livelihood. Thinking, 'For me, because of having done merit in the past, a comfortable living arises,' he abandons improper seeking, fulfills the three kinds of good conduct, and is reborn in heaven. With reference to these two, the second method was spoken.

Eko pana tapassī appadukkhavihārī hoti bāhirakācārayutto tāpaso vā channaparibbājako vā, appapuññatāya ca manāpe paccaye na labhati. So anesanavasena tīṇi duccaritāni pūretvā attānaṃ sukhe ṭhapetvā niraye nibbattati.

Furthermore, a certain ascetic dwells with little suffering. He is endowed with external practices, being either an ascetic or a covered wanderer. And due to his lack of merit, he does not obtain pleasing requisites. By means of improper seeking, he fulfills the three kinds of misconduct and, having established himself in comfort, is reborn in hell.

Aparo [P 2.0351] puññavā hoti, so – “na dāni mayā sadiso atthī”ti mānaṃ uppādetvā anesanavasena lābhasakkāraṃ vā uppādento micchādiṭṭhivasena – “sukho imissā paribbājikāya daharāya mudukāya lomasāya samphasso”tiādīni cintetvā kāmesu pātabyataṃ vā āpajjanto tīṇi duccaritāni pūretvā niraye nibbattati. Ime dve sandhāya tatiyanayo vutto.

Another is meritorious. He gives rise to conceit, thinking, 'Now there is no one equal to me.' Either by generating gain and honor through improper seeking, or by way of wrong view, thinking such things as, 'The touch of this young, tender, fine-haired female wanderer is pleasant,' and falling into indulgence in sensual pleasures, he fulfills the three kinds of misconduct and is reborn in hell. With reference to these two, the third method was spoken.

Aparo pana appadukkhavihārī appapuñño hoti, so – “ahaṃ pubbepi akatapuññatāya sukhena jīvikaṃ na labhāmī”ti tīṇi sucaritāni pūretvā sagge nibbattati.

Furthermore, another who dwells with little suffering has little merit. He thinks, 'Because I did not make merit in the past, I do not obtain a livelihood with ease.' He fulfills the three kinds of good conduct and is reborn in heaven.

Aparo puññavā hoti, so – “pubbepāhaṃ katapuññatāya sukhaṃ labhāmi, idāni puññāni karissāmī”ti tīṇi sucaritāni pūretvā sagge nibbattati. Ime dve sandhāya catutthanayo vutto. Idaṃ titthiyavasena āgataṃ, sāsanepi pana labbhati.

Another is meritorious. He thinks, 'Because I made merit in the past, I obtain happiness. Now, too, I will make merit.' He fulfills the three kinds of good conduct and is reborn in heaven. With reference to these two, the fourth method was spoken. This has come by way of the sectarians, but it is also found in the Dispensation.

Ekacco hi dhutaṅgasamādānavasena lūkhājīvī hoti, appapuññatāya vā sakalampi gāmaṃ vicaritvā udarapūraṃ na labhati. So – “paccaye uppādessāmī”ti vejjakammādivasena vā anesanaṃ [V 1.0261] katvā, arahattaṃ vā paṭijānitvā, tīṇi vā kuhanavatthūni paṭisevitvā niraye nibbattati.

Indeed, a certain person lives a rough life by means of undertaking the ascetic practices, or due to lack of merit, he does not get his fill even after wandering through an entire village. Thinking, 'I will generate requisites,' he is reborn in hell, either by engaging in improper seeking by means of medical practice and so on, or by claiming arahantship, or by practicing the three bases of deceit.

Aparo [M 1.0289] ca tādisova puññavā hoti. So tāya puññasampattiyā mānaṃ janayitvā uppannaṃ lābhaṃ thāvaraṃ kattukāmo anesanavasena tīṇi duccaritāni pūretvā niraye uppajjati.

And another such person is meritorious. Because of that accomplishment of merit, he generates conceit. Desiring to make permanent the gain that has arisen, he fulfills the three kinds of misconduct by means of improper seeking and arises in hell.

Aparo samādinnadhutaṅgo appapuññova hoti, na labhati sukhena jīvitavuttiṃ. So – “pubbepāhaṃ akatapuññatāya kiñci na labhāmi, sace idāni anesanaṃ karissaṃ, āyatimpi dullabhasukho bhavissāmī”ti tīṇi sucaritāni pūretvā arahattaṃ pattuṃ asakkonto sagge nibbattati.

Another who has undertaken the ascetic practices has little merit; he does not obtain a comfortable livelihood. He thinks, 'Because I did not make merit in the past, I obtain nothing. If I now engage in improper seeking, in the future, too, I will be one for whom happiness is difficult to obtain.' Fulfilling the three kinds of good conduct, and being unable to attain arahantship, he is reborn in heaven.

Aparo puññavā hoti, so – “pubbepāhaṃ katapuññatāya etarahi sukhito, idānipi puññaṃ karissāmī”ti anesanaṃ pahāya tīṇi sucaritāni pūretvā arahattaṃ pattuṃ asakkonto sagge nibbattati.

Another is meritorious. He thinks, 'Because I made merit in the past, I am happy now. Now, too, I will make merit.' Abandoning improper seeking and fulfilling the three kinds of good conduct, being unable to attain arahantship, he is reborn in heaven.

383. Āgatiñcāti – “asukaṭṭhānato nāma ime āgatā”ti evaṃ āgatiñca. Gatiñcāti idāni gantabbaṭṭhānañca. Cutiñcāti tato cavanañca. Upapattiñcāti tato cutānaṃ puna upapattiñca. Kiṃ sabbaṃ tapaṃ garahissāmīti – “kena kāraṇena garahissāmi, garahitabbameva hi mayaṃ garahāma, pasaṃsitabbaṃ pasaṃsāma, na bhaṇḍikaṃ karonto mahārajako viya dhotañca adhotañca ekato karomā”ti dasseti. Idāni tamatthaṃ pakāsento – “santi kassapa eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā”tiādimāha.

383. “Āgatiñca” means: ‘These beings have come from such-and-such a place of existence’; thus, it means the place of existence from which one has come. “Gatiñca” means the place of existence to which one is now to go. “Cutiñca” means passing away from there. “Upapattiñca” means the rebirth of those who have passed away from there. “Why should I blame all asceticism?”—He shows the meaning: ‘For what reason should I blame it? Indeed, we blame only that which is blameworthy, and we praise that which is praiseworthy. We do not, like a great washerman making a bundle, put the washed and the unwashed together.’ Now, wishing to clarify that meaning, He said the words beginning with, “There are, Kassapa, some ascetics and brahmins...”

384. Yaṃ te ekaccanti pañcavidhaṃ sīlaṃ, tañhi loke na koci “na sādhū”ti vadati. Puna yaṃ te ekaccanti pañcavidhaṃ veraṃ, taṃ na [P 2.0352] koci “sādhū”ti vadati. Puna yaṃ te ekaccanti pañcadvāre asaṃvaraṃ, te kira – “cakkhu nāma na nirundhitabbaṃ, cakkhunā manāpaṃ rūpaṃ daṭṭhabba”nti vadanti, esa nayo sotādīsu. Puna yaṃ te ekaccanti pañcadvāre saṃvaraṃ.

384. “That which some of them...” refers to the fivefold virtue; indeed, no one in the world says of it, “It is not good.” Again, “that which some of them...” refers to the fivefold enmity; no one says of it, “It is good.” Again, “that which some of them...” refers to the lack of restraint at the five sense-doors. It is said that they declare: “The eye, it is said, should not be restrained; a pleasing form should be seen with the eye.” This is the method for the ear and the other senses. Again, “that which some of them...” refers to restraint at the five sense-doors.

Evaṃ paresaṃ vādena saha attano vādassa samānāsamānataṃ dassetvā idāni attano vādena [V 1.0262] saha paresaṃ vādassa samānāsamānataṃ dassento “yaṃ maya”ntiādimāha. Tatrāpi pañcasīlādivaseneva attho veditabbo.

Having thus shown the similarity and dissimilarity of His own view in relation to others' views, now, wishing to show the similarity and dissimilarity of others' views in relation to His own view, He said the words beginning with, “That which we...” Therein also, the meaning should be understood by way of the five precepts and so on.

Samanuyuñjāpanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Interrogation

385. Samanuyuñjantanti [M 1.0290] samanuyuñjantu, ettha ca laddhiṃ pucchanto samanuyuñjati nāma, kāraṇaṃ pucchanto samanugāhati nāma, ubhayaṃ pucchanto samanubhāsati nāma. Satthārā vā satthāranti satthārā vā saddhiṃ satthāraṃ upasaṃharitvā – “kiṃ te satthā te dhamme sabbaso pahāya vattati, udāhu samaṇo gotamo”ti. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo.

385. “Samanuyuñjanti” means “let them interrogate.” Herein, one who asks about a doctrine is called one who “interrogates” (samanuyuñjati); one who asks about the reason is called one who “investigates” (samanugāhati); one who asks about both is called one who “discusses” (samanubhāsati). “With the Teacher or the teacher” means by comparing one's teacher with the Teacher, asking: “Does your teacher practice having abandoned those things in every way, or does the ascetic Gotama?” This same method applies to the second phrase as well.

Idāni tamatthaṃ yojetvā dassento – “ye imesaṃ bhavata”ntiādimāha. Tattha akusalā akusalasaṅkhātāti akusalā ceva “akusalā”ti ca saṅkhātā ñātā koṭṭhāsaṃ vā katvā ṭhapitāti attho. Esa nayo sabbapadesu. Api cettha sāvajjāti sadosā. Na alamariyāti niddosaṭṭhena ariyā bhavituṃ nālaṃ asamatthā.

Now, connecting and showing that meaning, He said the words beginning with, “Those of these venerable ones...” Therein, “unwholesome and designated as unwholesome” means: they are unwholesome and are designated as ‘unwholesome,’ or are known as such, or are established by being classified into a category. This is the method in all instances. Furthermore, herein, “blameworthy” (sāvajja) means “with fault” (sadosa). “Not noble” (na alamariya) means they are not able, not capable of being noble (ariya) in the sense of being faultless.

386-392. Yaṃ viññū samanuyuñjantāti yena viññū amhe ca aññe ca pucchantā evaṃ vadeyyuṃ, taṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati, atthi taṃ kāraṇanti attho. Yaṃ vā pana bhonto pare gaṇācariyāti pare pana bhonto gaṇācariyā yaṃ vā taṃ vā appamattakaṃ pahāya vattantīti attho. Amheva tattha yebhuyyena pasaṃseyyunti idaṃ bhagavā satthārā satthāraṃ samanuyuñjanepi āha – saṅghena saṃghaṃ samanuyuñjanepi. Kasmā? Saṅghapasaṃsāyapi satthuyeva pasaṃsāsiddhito. Pasīdamānāpi hi buddhasampattiyā saṅghe, saṅghasampattiyā ca buddhe pasīdanti, tathā hi bhagavato sarīrasampattiṃ [P 2.0353] disvā, dhammadesanaṃ vā sutvā bhavanti vattāro – “lābhā vata bho sāvakānaṃ ye evarūpassa satthu santikāvacarā”ti, evaṃ buddhasampattiyā saṅghe pasīdanti. Bhikkhūnaṃ panācāragocaraṃ abhikkamapaṭikkamādīni ca disvā bhavanti vattāro – “santikāvacarānaṃ vata bho sāvakānaṃ ayañca upasamaguṇo satthu kīva rūpo bhavissatī”ti, evaṃ saṅghasampattiyā buddhe pasīdanti. Iti yā satthupasaṃsā, sā saṅghassa. Yā saṅghassa pasaṃsā, sā satthūti saṅghapasaṃsāyapi satthuyeva pasaṃsāsiddhito bhagavā dvīsupi nayesu – “amheva tattha yebhuyyena pasaṃseyyu”nti āha. Samaṇo gotamo ime dhamme anavasesaṃ pahāya vattati, yaṃ vā pana bhonto pare gaṇācariyātiādīsupi panettha ayamadhippāyo – sampattasamādānasetughātavasena [M 1.0291] hi tisso viratiyo. Tāsu sampattasamādāna viratimattameva aññesaṃ hoti, setughātavirati pana sabbena sabbaṃ [V 1.0263] natthi. Pañcasu pana tadaṅgavikkhambhanasamucchedapaṭipassaddhinissaraṇappahānesu aṭṭhasamāpattivasena ceva vipassanāmattavasena ca tadaṅgavikkhambhanappahānamattameva aññesaṃ hoti. Itarāni tīṇi pahānāni sabbena sabbaṃ natthi. Tathā sīlasaṃvaro, khantisaṃvaro, ñāṇasaṃvaro, satisaṃvaro, vīriyasaṃvaroti pañca saṃvarā, tesu pañcasīlamattameva adhivāsanakhantimattameva ca aññesaṃ hoti, sesaṃ sabbena sabbaṃ natthi.
