“That which the wise, interrogating...” means: the basis exists, the reason is present, for which the wise, questioning us and others, would speak thus. “Or these other venerable group-teachers...” means: other venerable group-teachers practice having abandoned some insignificant thing or other. “They would mostly praise us in that matter.” The Blessed One said this both in the case of interrogating a teacher by comparison with the Teacher, and in the case of interrogating a community by comparison with the Sangha. Why? Because praise of the Sangha culminates in praise of the Teacher himself. Indeed, those who are inspired are inspired in the Sangha because of the Buddha's accomplishment, and in the Buddha because of the Sangha's accomplishment. For instance, having seen the Blessed One's physical accomplishment or having heard his teaching of the Dhamma, they become speakers, saying: “Oh, it is a gain for the disciples who are followers in the presence of such a Teacher!” Thus, they are inspired in the Sangha because of the Buddha's accomplishment. On the other hand, having seen the monks' conduct and resort, their advancing and returning, and so on, they become speakers, saying: “Oh, if this quality of calm belongs to the disciples who are followers in his presence, of what kind must be the Teacher's quality of calm!” Thus, they are inspired in the Buddha because of the Sangha's accomplishment. In this way, the praise that is for the Teacher is for the Sangha, and the praise that is for the Sangha is for the Teacher. Therefore, because praise of the Sangha culminates in the praise of the Teacher himself, the Blessed One said in both cases, “They would mostly praise us in that matter.” As for the passage beginning, “The ascetic Gotama practices having abandoned these things without remainder, whereas these other venerable group-teachers...”, the intention here is this: There are three kinds of abstinence, namely, by way of occurrence, undertaking, and destroying the cause. Of these, others possess only abstinence by way of occurrence and undertaking; abstinence by destroying the cause is completely absent in them. Furthermore, among the five kinds of abandoning—by substitution of opposites, by suppression, by cutting off, by tranquillization, and by escape—others possess only abandoning by substitution of opposites (by way of mere insight) and abandoning by suppression (by way of the eight attainments). The other three kinds of abandoning are completely absent in them. Likewise, there are five kinds of restraint: restraint by virtue, by patience, by knowledge, by mindfulness, and by energy. Of these, others possess only the five precepts and only the patience of endurance; the rest are completely absent in them.

Pañca kho panime uposathuddesā, tesu pañcasīlamattameva aññesaṃ hoti. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ sabbena sabbaṃ natthi. Iti akusalappahāne ca kusalasamādāne ca, tīsu viratīsu, pañcasu pahānesu, pañcasu saṃvaresu, pañcasu uddesesu, – “ahameva ca mayhañca sāvakasaṅgho loke paññāyati, mayā hi sadiso satthā nāma, mayhaṃ sāvakasaṅghena sadiso saṅgho nāma natthī”ti bhagavā sīhanādaṃ nadati.

Furthermore, there are these five Uposatha recitations. Of these, others possess only the five precepts. The virtue of restraint of the Pātimokkha is completely absent in them. Thus, in the abandoning of the unwholesome and the undertaking of the wholesome, in the three abstinences, in the five kinds of abandoning, in the five kinds of restraint, and in the five recitations, the Blessed One utters a lion's roar: “It is I and my community of disciples who are renowned in the world. For there is no teacher like me, and no community of disciples like mine.”

Ariyaaṭṭhaṅgikamaggavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Noble Eightfold Path

393. Evaṃ sīhanādaṃ [P 2.0354] naditvā tassa sīhanādassa aviparītabhāvāvabodhanatthaṃ – “atthi, kassapa, maggo”tiādimāha. Tattha maggoti lokuttaramaggo. Paṭipadāti pubbabhāgapaṭipadā. Kālavādītiādīni brahmajāle vaṇṇitāni. Idāni taṃ duvidhaṃ maggañca paṭipadañca ekato katvā dassento – “ayameva ariyo”tiādimāha. Idaṃ pana sutvā acelo cintesi – “samaṇo gotamo mayhaṃyeva maggo ca paṭipadā ca atthi, aññesaṃ natthīti maññati, handassāhaṃ amhākampi maggaṃ kathemī”ti. Tato acelakapaṭipadaṃ kathesi. Tenāha – “evaṃ vutte acelo kassapo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca…pe… udakorohanānuyogamanuyutto viharatī”ti.

393. Having roared this lion’s roar, in order to make known the unperverted nature of that lion’s roar, the Blessed One said, “There is, Kassapa, a path,” and so forth. Herein, ‘path’ means the supramundane path. ‘Practice’ means the preliminary-stage practice. The terms beginning with ‘one who speaks in accordance with time’ have been explained in the Brahmajāla Sutta. Now, wishing to show that two-fold path and practice together, he said, “This very noble…” and so forth. Furthermore, upon hearing this, the naked ascetic thought: “The ascetic Gotama thinks, ‘Only I have a path and a practice; others do not.’ Come now, I shall also declare our path to him.” Then he spoke of the practice of the naked ascetics. Therefore, it is said: “When this was said, the naked ascetic Kassapa said this to the Blessed One… he dwells committed to the practice of descending into the water.”

Tapopakkamakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on the Undertaking of Austerities

394. Tattha tapopakkamāti tapārambhā, tapakammānīti attho. Sāmaññasaṅkhātāti samaṇakammasaṅkhātā. Brahmaññasaṅkhātāti brāhmaṇakammasaṅkhātā. Acelakoti niccolo, naggoti attho. Muttācāroti visaṭṭhācāro, uccārakammādīsu lokiyakulaputtācārena virahito [M 1.0292] ṭhitakova uccāraṃ karoti, passāvaṃ karoti, khādati, bhuñjati ca. Hatthāpalekhanoti hatthe piṇḍamhi ṭhite jivhāya hatthaṃ apalikhati, uccāraṃ vā katvā hatthasmiññeva daṇḍakasaññī hutvā hatthena apalikhati. “Bhikkhāgahaṇatthaṃ ehi, bhante”ti vutto na etīti na ehibhaddantiko. “Tena hi [V 1.0264] tiṭṭha, bhante”ti vuttopi na tiṭṭhatīti natiṭṭhabhaddantiko. Tadubhayampi kira so – “etassa vacanaṃ kataṃ bhavissatī”ti na karoti. Abhihaṭanti puretaraṃ gahetvā āhaṭaṃ bhikkhaṃ, uddissakatanti “imaṃ tumhe uddissa kata”nti evaṃ ārocitaṃ bhikkhaṃ. Na nimantananti “asukaṃ nāma kulaṃ vā vīthiṃ vā gāmaṃ vā paviseyyāthā”ti evaṃ nimantitabhikkhampi na sādiyati, na gaṇhati. Na [P 2.0355] kumbhimukhāti kumbhito uddharitvā diyyamānaṃ bhikkhaṃ na gaṇhati. Na kaḷopimukhāti kaḷopīti ukkhali vā pacchi vā, tatopi na gaṇhati. Kasmā? Kumbhikaḷopiyo maṃ nissāya kaṭacchunā pahāraṃ labhantīti. Na eḷakamantaranti ummāraṃ antaraṃ katvā diyyamānaṃ na gaṇhati. Kasmā? “Ayaṃ maṃ nissāya antarakaraṇaṃ labhatī”ti. Daṇḍamusalesupi eseva nayo.

394. Herein, ‘the undertaking of austerities’ (tapopakkama) means the commencement of austerities, that is, ascetic actions. ‘Considered as the practice of an ascetic’ (sāmaññasaṅkhāta) means regarded as the work of an ascetic. ‘Considered as the practice of a brahmin’ (brahmaññasaṅkhāta) means regarded as the work of a brahmin. ‘A naked ascetic’ (acelaka) means unclothed, that is, naked. ‘Of unrestrained conduct’ (muttācāra) means of abandoned behavior; in matters such as defecation, he is devoid of the conduct of worldly gentlemen and defecates, urinates, chews, and eats only while standing. ‘One who licks his hands’ (hatthāpalekhana) means when the food in his hand is finished, he licks his hand with his tongue; or after defecating, regarding his hand as a stick, he wipes with his hand. When told, “Come, venerable sir, to receive alms,” he does not come—thus, he is a ‘no-come-venerable-sir’ (na ehibhaddantika). Even when told, “Then stay, venerable sir,” he does not stay—thus, he is a ‘no-stay-venerable-sir’ (natiṭṭhabhaddantika). It is said he does neither of these, thinking, “I would be acting on this person’s word.” ‘Brought forward’ (abhihaṭa) means alms brought, having been taken beforehand. ‘Specially prepared’ (uddissakata) means alms announced as, “This was prepared with you in mind.” ‘Not accepting an invitation’ (na nimantana) means he does not accept alms even when invited with, “May you enter such-and-such a family, street, or village.” ‘Not from the mouth of a pot’ (na kumbhimukha) means he does not accept alms being given, having been taken out of a pot. ‘Not from the mouth of a cooking pot’ (na kaḷopimukha): a kaḷopī is a cooking pot or a basket, and he does not accept from that either. Why? Because he thinks, “On my account, the pots and cooking pots receive a blow from a ladle.” ‘Not with a threshold in between’ (na eḷakamantara) means he does not accept what is given with a threshold placed in between. Why? Because he thinks, “On my account, this is made into an interval.” For sticks and pestles, it is the same way.

Dvinnanti dvīsu bhuñjamānesu ekasmiṃ uṭṭhāya dente na gaṇhati. Kasmā? “Ekassa kabaḷantarāyo hotī”ti. Na gabbhiniyātiādīsu pana “gabbhiniyā kucchiyaṃ dārako kilamati. Pāyantiyā dārakassa khīrantarāyo hoti, purisantaragatāya ratiantarāyo hotī”ti na gaṇhati. Saṃkittīsūti saṃkittetvā katabhattesu, dubbhikkhasamaye kira acelakasāvakā acelakānaṃ atthāya tato tato taṇḍulādīni samādapetvā bhattaṃ pacanti. Ukkaṭṭho acelako tatopi na paṭiggaṇhati. Na yattha sāti yattha sunakho – “piṇḍaṃ labhissāmī”ti upaṭṭhito hoti, tattha tassa adatvā āhaṭaṃ na gaṇhati. Kasmā? Etassa piṇḍantarāyo hotīti. Saṇḍasaṇḍacārinīti samūhasamūhacārinī, sace hi acelakaṃ disvā – “imassa bhikkhaṃ dassāmā”ti manussā bhattagehaṃ pavisanti, tesu ca pavisantesu kaḷopimukhādīsu nilīnā makkhikā uppatitvā saṇḍasaṇḍā caranti, tato āhaṭaṃ bhikkhaṃ na gaṇhati. Kasmā? Maṃ nissāya makkhikānaṃ gocarantarāyo jātoti.

‘From two’ (dvinnaṃ) means if, when two are eating, one gets up to give, he does not accept it. Why? Because he thinks, “It causes an interruption to the other’s morsel.” Regarding ‘not from a pregnant woman,’ and so forth: he does not accept, thinking, “The child in the pregnant woman’s womb suffers. For a nursing woman, there is an interruption to the child’s milk. For a woman engaged with a man, there is an interruption to sexual pleasure.” ‘At subscription meals’ (saṃkittīsu) means meals prepared by collecting contributions. It is said that in times of famine, the disciples of the naked ascetics, for the sake of the naked ascetics, have rice and so forth collected from various places and cook a meal. The most eminent naked ascetic does not accept even from that. ‘Not where a dog is present’ (na yattha sā) means where a dog is present thinking, “I will get food,” he does not accept what is brought without first giving to it. Why? Because he thinks, “It causes an interruption to this dog’s food.” ‘Where flies swarm’ (saṇḍasaṇḍacārinī): this means moving in swarms. For if, upon seeing a naked ascetic, people think, “We will give alms to him,” and enter the kitchen, as they enter, flies that were resting at the mouth of the rice pot and so forth fly up and move about in swarms. He does not accept the alms brought from there. Why? Because he thinks, “On my account, an interruption to the flies’ feeding ground has occurred.”

Thusodakanti [M 1.0293] sabbasassasambhārehi kataṃ sovīrakaṃ. Ettha ca surāpānameva sāvajjaṃ, ayaṃ pana sabbesupi sāvajjasaññī. Ekāgārikoti yo ekasmiṃyeva gehe bhikkhaṃ labhitvā nivattati[P 2.0356]. Ekālopikoti yo ekeneva ālopena yāpeti. Dvāgārikādīsupi eseva nayo. Ekissāpi dattiyāti ekāya dattiyā. Datti nāma ekā khuddakapāti hoti, yattha aggabhikkhaṃ pakkhipitvā ṭhapenti. Ekāhikanti ekadivasantarikaṃ. Addhamāsikanti addhamāsantarikaṃ. Pariyāyabhattabhojananti vārabhattabhojanaṃ, ekāhavārena dvīhavārena sattāhavārena aḍḍhamāsavārenāti evaṃ divasavārena āgatabhattabhojanaṃ.

‘Sour gruel’ (thusodaka) means sovīraka, made with the components of all grains. And here, only the drinking of liquor is blameworthy, but this ascetic perceives blame in all of them. ‘One who goes to only one house’ (ekāgārika) is one who, having received alms in just one house, returns. ‘One who subsists on a single morsel’ (ekālopika) is one who sustains himself with just one morsel. For ‘one who goes to two houses’ and so forth, it is the same way. ‘One who subsists on a single portion’ (ekissāpi dattiyā): this means from one portion. A datti is a small bowl in which they place and keep the first portion of alms. ‘One who eats every other day’ (ekāhika) means with an interval of one day. ‘One who eats every half-month’ (addhamāsika) means with an interval of half a month. ‘Eating meals by turns’ (pariyāyabhattabhojana) means eating meals in rotation; that is, eating the meal that comes by the turn of days, whether by a rotation of one day, two days, seven days, or half a month.

395. Sākabhakkhoti [V 1.0265] allasākabhakkho. Sāmākabhakkhoti sāmākataṇḍulabhakkho. Nīvārādīsu nīvāro nāma araññe sayaṃjātā vīhijāti. Daddulanti cammakārehi cammaṃ likhitvā chaḍḍitakasaṭaṃ. Haṭaṃ vuccati silesopi sevālopi. Kaṇanti kuṇḍakaṃ. Ācāmoti bhattaukkhalikāya laggo jhāmakaodano, taṃ chaḍḍitaṭṭhānatova gahetvā khādati, “odanakañjiya”ntipi vadanti. Piññākādayo pākaṭā eva. Pavattaphalabhojīti patitaphalabhojī.

395. ‘One who eats greens’ (sākabhakkha) means one who eats fresh greens. ‘One who eats sāmāka’ (sāmākabhakkha) means one who eats sāmāka rice grains or millet. Among nīvāra and so forth, nīvāra is a type of wild paddy that grows by itself in the forest. ‘Scrapings’ (daddula) means the scrapings discarded by leatherworkers after scraping a hide. Both tree-resin and algae are called ‘haṭa’. ‘Broken rice’ (kaṇa) means broken rice. ‘Scum’ (ācāma) means the burnt rice crust stuck to the rice pot; he takes it only from the place where it was discarded and eats it. Some also say it is rice-water. Oil-cake (piññāka) and so forth are well-known. ‘One who eats fallen fruit’ (pavattaphalabhojī) means one who is accustomed to eating only fruit that has fallen.

396. Sāṇānīti sāṇavākacoḷāni. Masāṇānīti missakacoḷāni. Chavadussānīti matasarīrato chaḍḍitavatthāni, erakatiṇādīni vā ganthetvā katanivāsanāni. Paṃsukūlānīti pathaviyaṃ chaḍḍitanantakāni. Tirīṭānīti rukkhatacavatthāni. Ajinanti ajinamigacammaṃ. Ajinakkhipanti tadeva majjhe phālitakaṃ. Kusacīranti kusatiṇāni ganthetvā katacīraṃ. Vākacīraphalakacīresupi eseva nayo. Kesakambalanti manussakesehi katakambalaṃ. Yaṃ sandhāya [P 2.0357] vuttaṃ –

396. ‘Sāṇāni’ means garments woven from hemp fiber. ‘Masāṇāni’ means garments woven from mixed hemp. ‘Chavadussāni’ means cloths discarded from a corpse, or garments made by weaving together eraka grass and so forth. ‘Paṃsukūlāni’ means rags without fringes discarded on the ground. ‘Tirīṭāni’ means garments made of tree bark. ‘Ajina’ means the hide of an ajina-beast. ‘Ajinakkhipa’ means that very hide, split in the middle. ‘Kusacīra’ means a garment made by weaving kusa grass. The same method applies to garments made of bark fiber and wooden planks. ‘Kesakambala’ means a blanket made of human hair. Concerning which it was said:

“Seyyathāpi bhikkhave, yāni kānici tantāvutāni vatthāni, kesakambalo tesaṃ paṭikiṭṭho akkhāyati. Kesakambalo, bhikkhave, sīte sīto, uṇhe uṇho appaggho ca dubbaṇṇo ca duggandho dukkhasamphasso”ti.

“Just as, bhikkhus, of whatever woven fabrics there are, a hair blanket is said to be the most despised. A hair blanket, bhikkhus, is cold in the cold, hot in the heat, of little value, of bad color, of bad smell, and of unpleasant touch.”

Vāḷakambalanti [M 1.0294] assavālehi katakambalaṃ. Ulūkapakkhikanti ulūkapakkhāni ganthetvā katanivāsanaṃ. Ukkuṭikappadhānamanuyuttoti ukkuṭikavīriyaṃ anuyutto, gacchantopi ukkuṭikova hutvā uppatitvā uppatitvā gacchati. Kaṇṭakāpassayikoti ayakaṇṭake vā pakatikaṇṭake vā bhūmiyaṃ koṭṭetvā tattha cammaṃ attharitvā ṭhānacaṅkamādīni karoti. Seyyanti sayantopi tattheva seyyaṃ kappeti. Phalakaseyyanti rukkhaphalake seyyaṃ. Thaṇḍilaseyyanti thaṇḍile ucce bhūmiṭhāne seyyaṃ. Ekapassayikoti ekapasseneva sayati. Rajojalladharoti sarīraṃ telena makkhitvā rajuṭṭhānaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati, athassa sarīre rajojallaṃ laggati, taṃ dhāreti. Yathāsanthatikoti laddhaṃ āsanaṃ akopetvā yadeva labhati, tattheva nisīdanasīlo. Vekaṭikoti vikaṭakhādanasīlo. Vikaṭanti gūthaṃ vuccati. Apānakoti paṭikkhittasītudakapāno. Sāyaṃ tatiyamassāti sāyatatiyakaṃ. Pāto, majjhanhike, sāyanti divasassa tikkhattuṃ pāpaṃ pavāhessāmīti udakorohanānuyogaṃ anuyutto viharatīti.

'Vāḷakambala' means a blanket made from horse tails. 'Ulūkapakkhika' means a garment made by weaving together owl feathers. 'One devoted to the practice of squatting' means one devoted to the exertion of squatting; even when going, he goes by squatting, jumping up and up. 'One who lies on thorns' means one who, having driven iron thorns or natural thorns into the ground and having spread a hide on them, performs standing, walking, and so forth. Regarding sleeping: even when sleeping, he prepares his bed right there. 'Sleeping on a plank' means sleeping on a wooden plank. 'Sleeping on the bare ground' means sleeping on a high place on the ground. 'One who lies on one side' means one who sleeps on one side only. 'A wearer of dust and dirt' means one who, having anointed his body with oil, stands in a place where dust rises; then dust and grime cling to his body, and he wears it. 'One who accepts whatever seat is offered' means one who, not displacing a seat that has been received, is in the habit of sitting wherever he gets one. 'Vekaṭika' means one who is in the habit of eating what is repulsive; 'vikaṭa' is said to be excrement. 'Apānaka' means one who has rejected the drinking of cold water. 'One for whom the evening is the third time' is so called because for him the evening is the third time. Morning, midday, and evening, thinking 'I will wash away evil three times a day,' he lives devoted to the practice of descending into water.

Tapopakkamaniratthakatāvaṇṇanā

An Exposition on the Futility of Ascetic Practices

397. Atha [V 1.0266] bhagavā sīlasampadādīhi vinā tesaṃ tapopakkamānaṃ niratthakataṃ dassento – “acelako cepi kassapa hotī”tiādimāha. Tattha ārakā vāti dūreyeva. Averanti [P 2.0358] dosaveravirahitaṃ. Abyāpajjanti domanassabyāpajjarahitaṃ.

397. Then the Blessed One, wishing to show the futility of those ascetic practices without the accomplishment of virtue and so forth, said the words beginning with, 'Even if, Kassapa, one is a naked ascetic…' Therein, 'far away' means far away indeed. 'Free from enmity' means devoid of the enmity that is hatred. 'Free from ill will' means devoid of the ill will that is displeasure.

398. Dukkaraṃ, bho gotamāti idaṃ kassapo “mayaṃ pubbe ettakamattaṃ sāmaññañca brahmaññañcāti vicarāma, tumhe pana aññaṃyeva sāmaññañca brahmaññañca vadathā”ti dīpento āha. Pakati kho esāti pakatikathā esā. Imāya ca, kassapa, mattāyāti “kassapa yadi iminā pamāṇena evaṃ parittakena paṭipattikkamena sāmaññaṃ vā brahmaññaṃ vā dukkaraṃ sudukkaraṃ nāma abhavissa, tato netaṃ abhavissa kallaṃ vacanāya dukkaraṃ sāmañña”nti ayamettha padasambandhena saddhiṃ attho. Etena nayena sabbattha padasambandho veditabbo.

398. Kassapa said, 'It is difficult, Master Gotama,' wishing to clarify: 'Formerly, we wandered about considering just this much to be the ascetic life and the holy life, but you speak of a different ascetic life and holy life.' 'This is a conventional saying' means this is a common statement. 'And if, Kassapa, by this measure'—here, the meaning, together with the connection of the words, is: 'Kassapa, if by this measure, by such a limited course of practice, the ascetic life or the holy life were to be called difficult or very difficult, then it would not be fitting to say, “The ascetic life is difficult.”' The connection of the words should be understood in this way throughout.

399. Dujjānoti [M 1.0295] idampi so “mayaṃ pubbe ettakena samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā hotīti vicarāma, tumhe pana aññathā vadathā”ti idaṃ sandhāyāha. Athassa bhagavā taṃ pakativādaṃ paṭikkhipitvā sabhāvatova dujjānabhāvaṃ āvikaronto punapi – “pakati kho”tiādimāha. Tatrāpi vuttanayeneva padasambandhaṃ katvā attho veditabbo.

399. This too, 'It is hard to know,' he said, referring to this: 'We formerly wandered about thinking, “By this much one becomes an ascetic or a brahmin,” but you speak otherwise.' Then the Blessed One, rejecting that conventional statement and revealing the inherent nature of being difficult to know, again said the words beginning with, 'It is a conventional saying…' Therein also, the meaning should be understood by making the connection of the words in the way already stated.

Sīlasamādhipaññāsampadāvaṇṇanā

An Exposition on the Accomplishment of Virtue, Concentration, and Wisdom

400-401. Katamā pana sā, bho gotamāti kasmā pucchati. Ayaṃ kira paṇḍito bhagavato kathentasseva kathaṃ uggahesi, atha attano paṭipattiyā niratthakataṃ viditvā samaṇo gotamo – “tassa ‘cāyaṃ sīlasampadā, cittasampadā, paññāsampadā abhāvitā hoti asacchikatā, atha kho so ārakāva sāmaññā’tiādimāha. Handa dāni naṃ tā sampattiyo pucchāmī”ti sīlasampadādivijānanatthaṃ pucchati. Athassa bhagavā buddhuppādaṃ dassetvā tantidhammaṃ kathento tā sampattiyo dassetuṃ – “idha kassapā”tiādimāha. Imāya ca kassapa sīlasampadāyāti idaṃ arahattaphalameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Arahattaphalapariyosānañhi bhagavato sāsanaṃ. Tasmā arahattaphalasampayuttāhi sīlacittapaññāsampadāhi [P 2.0359] aññā uttaritarā vā paṇītatarā vā sīlādisampadā natthīti āha.

400-401. 'But what, Venerable Gotama, is that?' Why does he ask this? It is said that this wise one grasped the teaching even as the Blessed One was speaking; then, having realized the fruitlessness of his own practice, he thought: 'The ascetic Gotama said, "For him, this accomplishment of virtue, accomplishment of mind, and accomplishment of wisdom are undeveloped and unrealized, and so he is far from the ascetic life," and so on. Well now, I shall ask him about those accomplishments.' Thus, he asks for the purpose of understanding the accomplishment of virtue and so forth. Then the Blessed One, having shown the arising of a Buddha and teaching the traditional doctrine, in order to reveal those accomplishments, spoke the words beginning with, 'Here, Kassapa…' And this statement, 'Kassapa, by this accomplishment of virtue,' was spoken with reference only to the fruit of Arahantship. For the Blessed One's dispensation culminates in the fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, he said that there is no other accomplishment of virtue and so forth that is higher or more excellent than the accomplishments of virtue, mind, and wisdom associated with the fruit of Arahantship.

Sīhanādakathāvaṇṇanā

An Exposition of the Discourse on the Lion's Roar

402. Evañca [V 1.0267] pana vatvā idāni anuttaraṃ mahāsīhanādaṃ nadanto – “santi kassapa eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā”tiādimāha. Tattha ariyanti nirupakkilesaṃ paramavisuddhaṃ. Paramanti uttamaṃ, pañcasīlāni hiādiṃ katvā yāva pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlā sīlameva, lokuttaramaggaphalasampayuttaṃ pana paramasīlaṃ nāma. Nāhaṃ tatthāti tattha sīlepi paramasīlepi ahaṃ attano samasamaṃ mama sīlasamena sīlena mayā samaṃ puggalaṃ na passāmīti attho. Ahameva tattha bhiyyoti ahameva tasmiṃ sīle uttamo. Katamasmiṃ? Yadidaṃ adhisīlanti yaṃ etaṃ uttamaṃ sīlanti attho. Iti imaṃ paṭhamaṃ sīhanādaṃ nadati.

402. And having said this, now, roaring the unsurpassed great lion's roar, he spoke the words beginning with: 'There are, Kassapa, some ascetics and brahmins...' Here, 'noble' (ariya) means without defilement, supremely pure. 'Supreme' (parama) means highest. For, beginning with the five precepts up to the virtue of the Pātimokkha restraint, it is merely ordinary virtue. But that which is associated with the supramundane path and fruit is called supreme virtue. 'I am not there' means: 'In that ordinary virtue and in that supreme virtue, I do not see a person equal to myself by means of a virtue equal to my own.' 'I alone am superior there' means: 'I alone am supreme in that virtue.' In what? 'That is, in higher virtue' (yadidaṃ adhisīlaṃ) means 'that which is this supreme virtue.' Thus, he utters this first lion's roar.

Tapojigucchavādāti [M 1.0296] ye tapojigucchaṃ vadanti. Tattha tapatīti tapo, kilesasantāpakavīriyassetaṃ nāmaṃ, tadeva te kilese jigucchatīti jigucchā. Ariyā paramāti ettha niddosattā ariyā, aṭṭhaārambhavatthuvasenapi uppannā vipassanāvīriyasaṅkhātā tapojigucchā tapojigucchāva, maggaphalasampayuttā paramā nāma. Adhijegucchanti idha jigucchabhāvo jegucchaṃ, uttamaṃ jegucchaṃ adhijegucchaṃ, tasmā yadidaṃ adhijegucchaṃ, tattha ahameva bhiyyoti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Paññādhikārepi kammassakatāpaññā ca vipassanāpaññā ca paññā nāma, maggaphalasampayuttā paramā paññā nāma. Adhipaññanti ettha liṅgavipallāso veditabbo, ayaṃ panetthattho – yāyaṃ adhipaññā nāma ahameva tattha bhiyyoti vimuttādhikāre [P 2.0360] tadaṅgavikkhambhanavimuttiyo vimutti nāma, samucchedapaṭipassaddhinissaraṇavimuttiyo pana paramā vimuttīti veditabbā. Idhāpi ca yadidaṃ adhivimuttīti yā ayaṃ adhivimutti, ahameva tattha bhiyyoti attho.

‘Those who speak on austerity-and-disgust’ (tapojigucchavādā) are those who speak on austerity-and-disgust. Herein, ‘it burns’ (tapati), thus it is ‘austerity’ (tapo); this is a name for the energy that scorches the defilements. That very energy is disgusted by (jigucchati) those defilements, thus it is ‘disgust’ (jigucchā). In ‘noble and supreme’ (ariyā paramā), it is ‘noble’ because of being faultless. The austerity-and-disgust which has arisen through the eight bases for instigating energy and is known as the energy of insight is merely ordinary austerity-and-disgust; that which is associated with the path and fruit is called ‘supreme’. In ‘higher disgust’ (adhijegucchaṃ), the state of disgust is ‘disgust’ (jegucchaṃ), and the supreme disgust is ‘higher disgust’ (adhijegucchaṃ). Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: ‘In this, that is, higher disgust, I alone am superior.’ Also in the section on wisdom, the wisdom of ownership of kamma and the wisdom of insight are called ‘wisdom’; that which is associated with the path and fruit is called ‘supreme wisdom’. Here in ‘higher wisdom’ (adhipaññaṃ), a change of gender should be understood. And this is the meaning here: ‘In that which is called higher wisdom, I alone am superior.’ In the section on liberation, the liberations by substitution of opposites and by suppression are called ‘liberation’; but the liberations of eradication, tranquilization, and escape are to be known as ‘supreme liberation’. And here too, ‘that is, in higher liberation’ (yadidaṃ adhivimutti) means: ‘In that which is higher liberation, I alone am superior.’

403. Suññāgāreti suññe ghare, ekakova nisīditvāti adhippāyo. Parisāsu cāti aṭṭhasu parisāsu. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

403. ‘In an empty abode’ (suññāgāre) means in an empty house, having sat down all alone—this is the intention. ‘And in assemblies’ (parisāsu ca) means in the eight assemblies. And this has also been said:

“Cattārimāni, sāriputta, tathāgatassa vesārajjāni. Yehi vesārajjehi samannāgato tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.150) suttaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

‘These four, Sāriputta, are the Tathāgata's grounds of self-confidence. Endowed with these grounds of self-confidence, the Tathāgata claims the bull's place and roars the lion's roar in the assemblies.’ This sutta should be elaborated.

Pañhañca naṃ pucchantīti paṇḍitā devamanussā naṃ pañhaṃ abhisaṅkharitvā pucchanti. Byākarotīti [V 1.0268] taṅkhaṇaññeva vissajjesi. Cittaṃ ārādhetīti pañhāvissajjanena mahājanassa cittaṃ paritosetiyeva. No ca kho sotabbaṃ maññantīti cittaṃ ārādhetvā kathentassapissa vacanaṃ pare sotabbaṃ na maññantīti, evañca vadeyyunti attho. Sotabbañcassa maññantīti devāpi manussāpi mahanteneva ussāhena sotabbaṃ maññanti. Pasīdantīti supasannā kallacittā muducittā honti. Pasannākāraṃ karontīti na muddhappasannāva honti, paṇītāni cīvarādīni veḷuvanavihārādayo ca mahāvihāre pariccajantā pasannākāraṃ karonti. Tathattāyāti yaṃ so dhammaṃ deseti tathā bhāvāya, dhammānudhammapaṭipattipūraṇatthāya paṭipajjantīti attho. Tathattāya ca paṭipajjantīti tathabhāvāya paṭipajjanti, tassa hi [M 1.0297] bhagavato dhammaṃ sutvā keci saraṇesu keci pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhahanti, apare nikkhamitvā pabbajanti. Paṭipannā ca ārādhentīti tañca pana paṭipadaṃ paṭipannā pūretuṃ sakkonti, sabbākārena pana pūrenti, paṭipattipūraṇena [P 2.0361] tassa bhoto gotamassa cittaṃ ārādhentīti vattabbā.

‘And they ask him a question’ (pañhañca naṃ pucchanti) means: wise devas and humans, having prepared a question, ask him. ‘He answers’ (byākaroti) means: he replies at that very moment. ‘He pleases their minds’ (cittaṃ ārādheti) means: by answering the question, he certainly delights the minds of the great assembly. ‘And they do not think it should be listened to’ (no ca kho sotabbaṃ maññanti) means: even when he speaks after having pleased their minds, they do not think his speech should be listened to; ‘they would speak thus’ is the meaning. ‘And they think it should be listened to’ (sotabbañcassa maññanti) means: both devas and humans think it should be listened to with great enthusiasm. ‘They become confident’ (pasīdanti) means: they become very confident, with wholesome minds and tender minds. ‘They make a show of confidence’ (pasannākāraṃ karonti) means: they are not merely superficially confident; giving up fine robes and so forth, and great monasteries such as the Veḷuvana Vihāra, they make a show of confidence. ‘For the sake of that state’ (tathattāya) means: for the sake of the state of that Dhamma which he teaches, for the purpose of fulfilling the practice that accords with the Dhamma, they do not practice—this is the meaning. ‘And they practice for the sake of that state’ (tathattāya ca paṭipajjanti) means: they practice for the sake of that state. For, having heard the Dhamma of the Blessed One, some are established in the refuges, some in the five precepts, and others go forth from home life and become monastics. ‘And those who practice please him’ (paṭipannā ca ārādhenti) means: having undertaken that practice, they are able to fulfill it; indeed, they fulfill it in every way. By fulfilling the practice, they please the mind of the Venerable Gotama—this is what should be said.

Imasmiṃ panokāse ṭhatvā sīhanādā samodhānetabbā. Ekaccaṃ tapassiṃ niraye nibbattaṃ passāmīti hi bhagavato eko sīhanādo. Aparaṃ sagge nibbattaṃ passāmīti eko. Akusaladhammappahāne ahameva seṭṭhoti eko. Kusaladhammasamādānepi ahameva seṭṭhoti eko. Akusaladhammappahāne mayhameva sāvakasaṅgho seṭṭhoti eko. Kusaladhammasamādānepi mayhaṃyeva sāvakasaṅgho seṭṭhoti eko. Sīlena mayhaṃ sadiso natthīti eko. Vīriyena mayhaṃ sadiso natthīti eko. Paññāya…pe… vimuttiyā…pe… sīhanādaṃ nadanto parisamajjhe nisīditvā nadāmīti eko. Visārado hutvā nadāmīti eko. Pañhaṃ maṃ pucchantīti eko. Pañhaṃ puṭṭho vissajjemīti eko. Vissajjanena parassa cittaṃ ārādhemīti eko. Sutvā sotabbaṃ maññantīti eko. Sutvā me pasīdantīti eko. Pasannākāraṃ karontīti eko. Yaṃ paṭipattiṃ desemi, tathattāya paṭipajjantīti eko. Paṭipannā ca maṃ ārādhentīti eko. Iti purimānaṃ dasannaṃ ekekassa – “parisāsu ca nadatī”ti ādayo dasa dasa parivārā. Evaṃ te dasa purimānaṃ dasannaṃ parivāravasena sataṃ purimā ca dasāti dasādhikaṃ sīhanādasataṃ hoti. Ito aññasmiṃ pana sutte ettakā sīhanādā dullabhā, tenidaṃ suttaṃ mahāsīhanādanti vuccati. Iti bhagavā “sīhanādaṃ kho samaṇo gotamo nadati, tañca kho suññāgāre nadatī”ti evaṃ vādānu vādaṃ paṭisedhetvā idāni parisati naditapubbaṃ sīhanādaṃ dassento “ekamidāha”ntiādimāha.

However, standing in this context, the lion's roars should be combined. For, ‘I see a certain ascetic reborn in hell’ is one lion's roar of the Blessed One. Another is: ‘I see another ascetic reborn in heaven.’ Another is: ‘In the abandoning of unwholesome qualities, I alone am the best.’ Another is: ‘In the undertaking of wholesome qualities, I alone am the best.’ Another is: ‘In the abandoning of unwholesome qualities, my community of disciples alone is the best.’ Another is: ‘In the undertaking of wholesome qualities, my community of disciples alone is the best.’ Another is: ‘In virtue, there is none equal to me.’ Another is: ‘In energy, there is none equal to me.’ Another is: ‘…in wisdom… in liberation…’ Another is: ‘Roaring the lion's roar, I sit in the midst of the assembly and roar.’ Another is: ‘Being confident, I roar.’ Another is: ‘They ask me a question.’ Another is: ‘When asked a question, I answer.’ Another is: ‘By my answer, I please the mind of another.’ Another is: ‘Having heard, they consider it worth listening to.’ Another is: ‘Having heard me, they are inspired with faith.’ Another is: ‘They show the signs of one inspired with faith.’ Another is: ‘Whatever practice I teach, they practice for the attainment of that state.’ Another is: ‘And those who have practiced please me.’ Thus, for each of the first ten, there are ten associated statements beginning with ‘he roars in the assemblies.’ In this way, the retinue for the first ten amounts to one hundred, and with the first ten, it becomes one hundred and ten lion's roars. Furthermore, in another sutta apart from this one, so many lion's roars are difficult to find; for that reason, this sutta is called the Great Lion's Roar. Thus the Blessed One, having refuted the assertion, ‘The ascetic Gotama indeed roars a lion's roar, but he roars it in an empty dwelling,’ now, to show the lion's roar previously roared in an assembly, spoke the words beginning with ‘ekamidāhaṃ’.

Titthiyaparivāsakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on the Probation for Sectarians

404. Tattha [P 2.0362][V 1.0269] tatra maṃ aññataro tapabrahmacārīti tatra rājagahe gijjhakūṭe pabbate viharantaṃ maṃ aññataro tapabrahmacārī nigrodho nāma paribbājako[M 1.0298]. Adhijeguccheti vīriyena pāpajigucchanādhikāre pañhaṃ pucchi. Idaṃ yaṃ taṃ bhagavā gijjhakūṭe mahāvihāre nisinno udumbarikāya deviyā uyyāne nisinnassa nigrodhassa ca paribbājakassa sandhānassa ca upāsakassa dibbāya sotadhātuyā kathāsallāpaṃ sutvā ākāsenāgantvā tesaṃ santike paññatte āsane nisīditvā nigrodhena adhijegucche puṭṭhapañhaṃ vissajjesi, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Paraṃ viya mattāyāti paramāya mattāya, atimahanteneva pamāṇenāti attho. Ko hi, bhanteti ṭhapetvā andhabālaṃ diṭṭhigatikaṃ añño paṇḍitajātiko “ko nāma bhagavato dhammaṃ sutvā na attamano assā”ti vadati. Labheyyāhanti idaṃ so – “ciraṃ vata me aniyyānikapakkhe yojetvā attā kilamito, ‘sukkhanadītīre nhāyissāmī’ti samparivattentena viya thuse koṭṭentena viya na koci attho nipphādito. Handāhaṃ attānaṃ yoge yojessāmī”ti cintetvā āha. Atha bhagavā yo anena khandhake titthiyaparivāso paññatto, yo aññatitthiyapubbo sāmaṇerabhūmiyaṃ ṭhito – “ahaṃ bhante, itthannāmo aññatitthiyapubbo imasmiṃ dhammavinaye ākaṅkhāmi upasampadaṃ, svāhaṃ, bhante, saṃghaṃ cattāro māse parivāsaṃ yācāmī”tiādinā (mahāva. 86) nayena samādiyitvā parivasati, taṃ sandhāya – “yo kho, kassapa, aññatitthiyapubbo”tiādimāha.

404. Therein, tatra maṃ aññataro tapabrahmacārī means: there in Rājagaha, while I was dwelling on Vulture's Peak mountain, a certain ascetic who lives the holy life, the wanderer named Nigrodha. Adhijegucche means: he asked a question in the matter of higher disgust for evil through energy. This was said with reference to the following: The Blessed One, while seated in the great monastery on Vulture's Peak, heard with his divine ear-element the conversation of the wanderer Nigrodha and the lay follower Sandhāna, who were seated in the park of Queen Udumbarikā. Having come through the sky and taken a prepared seat near them, he answered the question on higher disgust that was asked by Nigrodha. Paraṃ viya mattāya means: by the highest measure, by an exceedingly great standard; this is the meaning. Ko hi, bhante means: setting aside a blind fool holding wrong views, what other wise person, having heard the Dhamma of the Blessed One, would not be delighted in mind? So he speaks. Labheyyāhaṃ: He spoke this having thought: 'Alas, for a long time I have wearied myself, having applied myself to the path that does not lead to release. Like one turning around on the bank of a dry river thinking, "I will bathe," or like one pounding chaff, no benefit has been achieved. Come now, I will apply myself to the proper method.' Then the Blessed One, with reference to the probation for sectarians that was laid down by him in the Khandhaka—which one who was formerly of another sect, standing in the stage of a novice, undertakes and observes according to the method beginning, 'Venerable sir, I, so-and-so, formerly of another sect, desire higher ordination in this Dhamma and Vinaya. I, venerable sir, ask the Saṅgha for four months' probation'—spoke the words beginning, 'Yo kho, Kassapa, aññatitthiyapubbo...'

405. Tattha pabbajjanti vacanasiliṭṭhatāvaseneva vuttaṃ, aparivasitvāyeva hi pabbajjaṃ labhati. Upasampadatthikena pana nātikālena gāmappavesanādīni aṭṭha vattāni pūrentena parivasitabbaṃ. Āraddhacittāti aṭṭhavattapūraṇena [P 2.0363] tuṭṭhacittā, ayamettha saṅkhepattho. Vitthārato panesa titthiyaparivāso samantapāsādikāya vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pabbajjakhandhakavaṇṇanāya vuttanayena veditabbo. Api ca metthāti api ca me ettha. Puggalavemattatā viditāti puggalanānattaṃ viditaṃ. “Ayaṃ puggalo parivāsāraho, ayaṃ na parivāsāraho”ti idaṃ mayhaṃ pākaṭanti dasseti. Tato kassapo cintesi – “aho acchariyaṃ buddhasāsanaṃ, yattha evaṃ ghaṃsitvā koṭṭetvā yuttameva gaṇhanti, ayuttaṃ chaḍḍentī”ti, tato suṭṭhutaraṃ pabbajjāya sañjātussāho – “sace bhante”tiādimāha.

405. Herein, pabbajjaṃ is said merely for the sake of euphony, for one obtains the going forth even without observing probation. But one who desires higher ordination must observe the probation while fulfilling the eight duties, beginning with not entering a village at an untimely hour. Āraddhacittā means: those whose minds are pleased by the fulfillment of the eight duties. This is the concise meaning here. In detail, however, this probation for sectarians should be understood according to the method stated in the explanation of the Pabbajjakkhandhaka in the Vinaya commentary, the Samantapāsādikā. Api ca metthā means api ca me ettha (and also for me here). Puggalavemattatā viditā means: the diversity among individuals is known. This shows: 'It is clear to me that this person is worthy of probation, and this one is not worthy of probation.' Then Kassapa thought: 'Oh, how wonderful is the Buddha's Dispensation, where, after rubbing and striking in this way, they accept only the suitable and discard the unsuitable.' Then, with even greater enthusiasm for the going forth, he spoke the words beginning, 'If, venerable sir...'

Atha [M 1.0299] kho bhagavā tassa tibbacchandataṃ viditvā – “na kassapo parivāsaṃ arahatī”ti aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantesi – “gaccha bhikkhu kassapaṃ nhāpetvā pabbājetvā ānehī”ti. So [V 1.0270] tathā katvā taṃ pabbājetvā bhagavato santikaṃ āgamāsi. Bhagavā taṃ gaṇamajjhe nisīdāpetvā upasampādesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “alattha kho acelo kassapo bhagavato santike pabbajjaṃ, alattha upasampada”nti. Acirūpasampannoti upasampanno hutvā nacirameva. Vūpakaṭṭhoti vatthukāmakilesakāmehi kāyena ceva cittena ca vūpakaṭṭho. Appamattoti kammaṭṭhāne satiṃ avijahanto. Ātāpīti kāyikacetasikasaṅkhātena vīriyātāpena ātāpī. Pahitattoti kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkhatāya pesitacitto vissaṭṭhaattabhāvo. Yassatthāyāti yassa atthāya. Kulaputtāti ācārakulaputtā. Sammadevāti hetunāva kāraṇeneva. Tadanuttaranti taṃ anuttaraṃ. Brahmacariyapariyosānanti maggabrahmacariyassa pariyosānabhūtaṃ arahattaphalaṃ. Tassa hi atthāya kulaputtā pabbajanti. Diṭṭheva dhammeti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve. Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvāti attanāyeva paññāya paccakkhaṃ [P 2.0364] katvā, aparappaccayaṃ katvāti attho. Upasampajja vihāsīti pāpuṇitvā sampādetvā vihāsi, evaṃ viharanto ca khīṇā jāti…pe… abbhaññāsīti.

Then the Blessed One, knowing his intense eagerness and recognizing that 'Kassapa does not deserve probation,' addressed a certain monk: 'Go, monk, have Kassapa bathed, give him the going forth, and bring him here.' That monk did so, gave him the going forth, and came to the Blessed One. The Blessed One had him sit in the midst of the assembly of monks and gave him the higher ordination. Therefore it was said: 'The naked ascetic Kassapa obtained the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he obtained the higher ordination.' Acirūpasampanno means: not long after having become fully ordained. Vūpakaṭṭho means: secluded in body and mind from objective sensual pleasures and defilemental sensual pleasures. Appamatto means: not abandoning mindfulness on the meditation subject. Ātāpī means: ardent with the ardor of energy, known as bodily and mental, that burns up defilements. Pahitatto means: with a mind dispatched and a relinquished state of being, due to having no concern for the body and life. Yassatthāya means: for the purpose of which. Kulaputtā means: sons of good families by way of conduct. Sammadeva means: only by a proper reason, only by a proper cause. Tadanuttaraṃ means: that which is unsurpassed. Brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ means: the fruit of Arahantship, which is the culmination of the holy life of the path. Indeed, it is for the sake of this that sons of good families go forth. Diṭṭheva dhamme means: in this very existence. Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā means: having made it directly perceived by one's own wisdom, not relying on another as a credible source; this is the meaning. Upasampajja vihāsi means: having reached and accomplished, he dwelt. And dwelling thus: 'Birth is destroyed… (etc.)' he profoundly knew.

Evamassa paccavekkhaṇabhūmiṃ dassetvā arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpetuṃ “aññataro kho panāyasmā kassapo arahataṃ ahosī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha aññataroti eko. Arahatanti arahantānaṃ, bhagavato sāvakānaṃ arahantānaṃ abbhantaro ahosīti ayamettha adhippāyo. Yaṃ yaṃ pana antarantarā na vuttaṃ, taṃ taṃ tattha tattha vuttattā pākaṭamevāti.

Having thus shown the ground for his reviewing knowledge, in order to conclude the discourse with the pinnacle of Arahantship, it was said: 'And the Venerable Kassapa became one among the Arahants.' Therein, aññataro means: he became one. Arahataṃ means: among the Arahants; he became included among the Arahants who were disciples of the Blessed One—this is the intention here. As for whatever word was not explained in between, that word is evident because it has been explained in those respective places.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Thus in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya,

Mahāsīhanādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta is concluded.

9. Poṭṭhapādasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta

Poṭṭhapādaparibbājakavatthuvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Account of the Wanderer Poṭṭhapāda

406. Evaṃ [P 2.0365][V 1.0271][M 1.0300] me suttaṃ…pe… sāvatthiyanti poṭṭhapādasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ apubbapadavaṇṇanā. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāmeti sāvatthiṃ upanissāya yo jetassa kumārassa vane anāthapiṇḍikena gahapatinā ārāmo kārito, tattha viharati. Poṭṭhapādo paribbājakoti nāmena poṭṭhapādo nāma channaparibbājako. So kira gihikāle brāhmaṇamahāsālo kāmesuādīnavaṃ disvā cattālīsakoṭiparimāṇaṃ bhogakkhandhaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā titthiyānaṃ gaṇācariyo jāto. Samayaṃ pavadanti etthāti samayappavādako, tasmiṃ kira ṭhāne caṅkītārukkhapokkharasātippabhutayo brāhmaṇā nigaṇṭhaacelakaparibbājakādayo ca pabbajitā sannipatitvā attano attano samayaṃ vadanti kathenti dīpenti, tasmā so ārāmo samayappavādakoti vuccati. Sveva ca tindukācīrasaṅkhātāya timbarūrukkhapantiyā parikkhittattā tindukācīro. Yasmā panettha paṭhamaṃ ekāva sālā ahosi, pacchā mahāpuññaṃ paribbājakaṃ nissāya bahū sālā katā. Tasmā tameva ekaṃ sālaṃ upādāya laddhanāmavasena ekasālakoti vuccati. Mallikāya pana pasenadirañño deviyā uyyānabhūto so pupphaphalasampanno ārāmoti katvā mallikāya ārāmoti saṅkhyaṃ gato. Tasmiṃ samayappavādake tindukācīre ekasālake mallikāya ārāme.

406. Thus have I heard… at Sāvatthī… is the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta. Therein, this is the explanation of terms not previously explained. 'He was dwelling at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery' means: dwelling near Sāvatthī, in the monastery which the householder Anāthapiṇḍika had built in the grove of Prince Jeta; there he dwelt. 'Poṭṭhapāda the wanderer' means: by name, Poṭṭhapāda, a wanderer who is covered. It is said that in his household life he was a brahmin of great wealth, but having seen the danger in sensual pleasures, he renounced a mass of wealth measuring forty koṭis and went forth. He became a teacher of a group of sectarians. 'They propound their views there'—thus it is a 'place for propounding views' (samayappavādaka). At that spot, it is said, brahmins like Caṅkī, Tārukkha, Pokkharasāti, and others, as well as ascetics such as Nigaṇṭhas, Acelakas, and wanderers, would gather to state, speak of, and explain their respective views. Therefore, that monastery was called a 'place for propounding views'. Moreover, it was enclosed by a row of Tinduka trees, hence it was called Tindukācīra. And because at first there was only one hall here, and later, on account of a wanderer of great merit, many halls were built, it is called Ekasālaka (the Single Hall) based on the name it acquired by reference to that one hall. Furthermore, as it was the park of Queen Mallikā, wife of King Pasenadi, a monastery complete with flowers and fruits, it came to be known as 'Mallikā’s Monastery'. In that monastery of Mallikā, the Samayappavādaka, the Tindukācīra, the Ekasālaka.

Paṭivasatīti nivāsaphāsutāya vasati. Athekadivasaṃ bhagavā paccūsasamaye sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ [P 2.0366] pattharitvā lokaṃ pariggaṇhanto ñāṇajālassa antogataṃ paribbājakaṃ disvā – “ayaṃ poṭṭhapādo mayhaṃ ñāṇajāle paññāyati, kinnu kho bhavissatī”ti upaparikkhanto addasa – “ahaṃ ajja tattha gamissāmi, atha maṃ poṭṭhapādo nirodhañca nirodhavuṭṭhānañca pucchissati, tassāhaṃ sabbabuddhānaṃ ñāṇena saṃsanditvā tadubhayaṃ kathessāmi, atha so katipāhaccayena [V 1.0272] cittaṃ hatthisāriputtaṃ gahetvā mama [M 1.0301] santikaṃ āgamissati, tesamahaṃ dhammaṃ desessāmi, desanāvasāne poṭṭhapādo maṃ saraṇaṃ gamissati, citto hatthisāriputto mama santike pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti. Tato pātova sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā surattadupaṭṭaṃ nivāsetvā vijjulatāsadisaṃ kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā yugandharapabbataṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhitamahāmeghaṃ viya meghavaṇṇaṃ paṃsukūlaṃ ekaṃsavaragataṃ katvā paccagghaṃ selamayapattaṃ vāmaaṃsakūṭe laggetvā sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pavisissāmīti sīho viya himavantapādā vihārā nikkhami. Imamatthaṃ sandhāya – “atha kho bhagavā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

'He dwells' means: he dwells because of the comfort for dwelling. Then one day, at dawn, the Blessed One, having spread out his knowledge of omniscience and surveyed the world, saw the wanderer who had entered into the net of his knowledge. Reflecting, 'This Poṭṭhapāda appears in my net of knowledge, what will become of him?' he saw: 'Today I will go there. Then Poṭṭhapāda will ask me about cessation and the emergence from cessation. I will explain both to him, having aligned it with the knowledge of all Buddhas. Then, after a few days have passed, he will take Citta, the elephant trainer's son, and come to my presence. I will teach them the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the teaching, Poṭṭhapāda will go for refuge to me. Citta, the elephant trainer's son, having gone forth in my presence, will attain Arahantship.' Therefore, early in the morning, having attended to his bodily needs, he put on a well-dyed lower garment of two layers, fastened a belt like a flash of lightning, put on a dust-heap robe the color of a cloud over one excellent shoulder like a great cloud that stands encircling Mount Yugandhara, hung a brand new bowl made of stone on the tip of his left shoulder, and, intending to enter Sāvatthī for alms, he departed from the monastery like a lion from the foothills of the Himalayas. It was with reference to this meaning that the Venerable Ānanda spoke the words 'Then the Blessed One...' and so on.

407. Etadahosīti nagaradvārasamīpaṃ gantvā attano rucivasena sūriyaṃ oloketvā atippagabhāvameva disvā etaṃ ahosi. Yaṃnūnāhanti saṃsayaparidīpano viya nipāto, buddhānañca saṃsayo nāma natthi – “idaṃ karissāma, idaṃ na karissāma, imassa dhammaṃ desessāma, imassa na desessāmā”ti evaṃ parivitakkapubbabhāgo panesa sabbabuddhānaṃ labbhati. Tenāha – “yaṃnūnāha”nti, yadi panāhanti attho.

407. 'This occurred to him' means: having gone near the city gate and, by his own inclination, having looked at the sun and seen that it was still very early, this thought occurred. The particle 'yannūna' is one that illuminates doubt. However, for the Buddhas, there is no such thing as doubt. But this preliminary stage of reflection—'We will do this, we will not do this; we will teach the Dhamma to this person, we will not teach it to this person'—is found in all Buddhas. Therefore, he said, 'Yannūnāhaṃ,' which has the meaning, 'What if I were to...'

408. Unnādiniyāti uccaṃ nadamānāya, evaṃ nadamānāya cassā uddhaṃ gamanavasena ucco, disāsu patthaṭavasena mahā saddoti uccāsaddamahāsaddāya, tesañhi paribbājakānaṃ pātova vuṭṭhāya kattabbaṃ nāma cetiyavattaṃ vā bodhivattaṃ vā ācariyupajjhāyavattaṃ [P 2.0367] vā yoniso manasikāro vā natthi. Tena te pātova vuṭṭhāya bālātape nisinnā – “imassa hattho sobhano, imassa pādo”ti evaṃ aññamaññassa hatthapādādīni vā ārabbha, itthipurisadārakadārikādīnaṃ vaṇṇe vā, aññaṃ vā kāmassādabhavassādādivatthuṃ ārabbha kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā anupubbena rājakathādianekavidhaṃ tiracchānakathaṃ kathenti. Tena vuttaṃ – “unnādiniyā uccāsaddamahāsaddāya anekavihitaṃ tiracchānakathaṃ kathentiyā”ti.

408. 'Unnādinī' means making a loud sound. Because the sound goes upwards, it is a high sound; because it spreads in the directions, it is a great sound. Thus, 'of high and great sound'. For those wanderers have no duties to perform upon rising early in the morning, such as duties at a shrine, duties at a Bodhi tree, duties towards teachers and preceptors, or proper attention. Therefore, rising early in the morning and sitting in the morning sun, they initiate conversation concerning each other's hands and feet—'This one's hand is beautiful,' 'This one's foot is beautiful'—or concerning the fine features of women, men, boys, and girls, or concerning other topics that are a basis for delight in sensual pleasures, delight in existence, and so on. In due course, they speak various kinds of worldly talk, such as talk about kings. Therefore it was said: 'making a high and great sound, speaking various kinds of worldly talk.'

Tato poṭṭhapādo paribbājako te paribbājake oloketvā – “ime paribbājakā ativiya aññamaññaṃ agāravā, mayañca samaṇassa gotamassa pātubhāvato paṭṭhāya sūriyuggamane khajjopanakūpamā jātā, lābhasakkāropi no parihīno. Sace panimaṃ ṭhānaṃ samaṇo gotamo vā gotamassa sāvako vā gihī upaṭṭhāko vā tassa āgaccheyya[M 1.0302], ativiya lajjanīyaṃ bhavissati, parisadoso kho pana parisajeṭṭhakasseva upari ārohatī”ti itocito ca vilokento bhagavantaṃ addasa. Tena vuttaṃ – “addasā kho poṭṭhapādo paribbājako…pe… tuṇhī ahesu”nti.

Then the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda, looking at those wanderers, thought: 'These wanderers are extremely disrespectful to one another. And we, since the appearance of the recluse Gotama, have become like fireflies at sunrise; our gain and honor have also declined. If the recluse Gotama, or a disciple of Gotama, or a lay attendant of his should come to this place, it would be extremely shameful. Indeed, the fault of the assembly falls upon the head of the assembly.' Looking from side to side, he saw the Blessed One. Therefore it was said: 'Poṭṭhapāda the wanderer saw... they became silent.'

409. Tattha [V 1.0273] saṇṭhapesīti sikkhāpesi, vajjamassā paṭicchādesi. Yathā susaṇṭhitā hoti, tathā naṃ ṭhapesi. Yathā nāma parisamajjhaṃ pavisanto puriso vajjapaṭicchādanatthaṃ nivāsanaṃ saṇṭhapeti, pārupanaṃ saṇṭhapeti, rajokiṇṇaṭṭhānaṃ puñchati; evamassā vajjapaṭicchādanatthaṃ – “appasaddā bhonto”ti sikkhāpento yathā susaṇṭhitā hoti, tathā naṃ ṭhapesīti attho. Appasaddakāmoti appasaddaṃ icchati, eko nisīdati, eko tiṭṭhati, na gaṇasaṅgaṇikāya yāpeti. Upasaṅkamitabbaṃ maññeyyāti idhāgantabbaṃ maññeyya. Kasmā panesa bhagavato upasaṅkamanaṃ paccāsīsatīti? Attano vuddhiṃ patthayamāno. Paribbājakā kira buddhesu vā buddhasāvakesu vā attano santikaṃ āgatesu – “ajja amhākaṃ santikaṃ samaṇo gotamo āgato[P 2.0368], sāriputto āgato, na kho pana te yassa vā tassa vā santikaṃ gacchanti, passatha amhākaṃ uttamabhāva”nti attano upaṭṭhākānaṃ santike attānaṃ ukkhipanti, ucce ṭhāne ṭhapenti, bhagavatopi upaṭṭhāke gaṇhituṃ vāyamanti. Te kira bhagavato upaṭṭhāke disvā evaṃ vadanti – “tumhākaṃ satthā bhavaṃ gotamopi gotamasāvakāpi amhākaṃ santikaṃ āgacchanti, mayaṃ aññamaññaṃ samaggā. Tumhe pana amhe akkhīhipi passituṃ na icchatha, sāmīcikammaṃ na karotha, kiṃ vo amhehi aparaddha”nti. Athekacce manussā – “buddhāpi etesaṃ santikaṃ gacchanti kiṃ amhāka”nti tato paṭṭhāya te disvā nappamajjanti. Tuṇhī ahesunti poṭṭhapādaṃ parivāretvā nissaddā nisīdiṃsu.

409. Herein, 'he settled the assembly' means he instructed it and concealed its faults. He established it in such a way that it was well-composed. Just as a man entering the midst of an assembly, in order to conceal his faults, arranges his lower garment, arranges his upper robe, and dusts a spot soiled with dirt; in the same way, to conceal the assembly's faults, instructing it with, 'Be quiet, sirs,' he established it in such a way that it was well-composed—this is the meaning. 'Desiring quiet' means he desires a low sound; he sits alone, he stands alone, he does not spend his time in company. 'He might think it fit to approach' means he might think it fit to come here. But why does this one hope for the Blessed One's approach? Because he desires his own advancement. It is said that when Buddhas or the disciples of a Buddha come to them, wanderers, in the presence of their own supporters, exalt themselves, saying: 'Today the ascetic Gotama has come to us, Sāriputta has come. Indeed, they do not go to just anyone. Behold our superior state!' They place themselves in a high position. They also strive to win over the Blessed One's supporters. It is said that upon seeing the Blessed One's supporters, they speak thus: 'Your teacher, the venerable Gotama, and Gotama's disciples come to us; we are in harmony with one another. But you do not wish to even look at us; you do not perform respectful duties. What wrong have we done you?' Then some people think, 'Even Buddhas go to them, what about us?' and from then on, seeing those wanderers, they are not negligent towards them. 'They became silent' means they surrounded Poṭṭhapāda and sat down without a sound.

410. Svāgataṃ, bhanteti suṭṭhu āgamanaṃ, bhante, bhagavato; bhagavati hi no āgate ānando hoti, gate sokoti dīpeti. Cirassaṃ kho, bhanteti kasmā āha? Kiṃ bhagavā pubbepi tattha gatapubboti, na gatapubbo. Manussānaṃ pana – “kuhiṃ gacchantā, kuto āgatattha, kiṃ maggamūḷhattha, cirassaṃ āgatatthā”ti evamādayo piyasamudācārā [M 1.0303] honti, tasmā evamāha. Evañca pana vatvā na mānathaddho hutvā nisīdi, uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavato paccuggamanamakāsi. Bhagavantañhi upagataṃ disvā āsanena animantento vā apacitiṃ akaronto vā dullabho. Kasmā? Uccākulīnatāya. Ayampi paribbājako attano nisinnāsanaṃ papphoṭetvā bhagavantaṃ āsanena nimantento – “nisīdatu, bhante, bhagavā idamāsanaṃ paññatta”nti āha. Antarākathā vippakatāti nisinnānaṃ vo ādito paṭṭhāya yāva mamāgamanaṃ, etasmiṃ antare kā nāma kathā vippakatā, mamāgamanapaccayā katamā kathā pariyantaṃ na gatā, vadatha, yāva naṃ pariyantaṃ netvā demīti sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ pavāresi. Atha paribbājako – “niratthakakathā esā nissārā vaṭṭasannissitā, na tumhākaṃ purato vattabbataṃ arahatī”ti dīpento “tiṭṭhatesā[P 2.0369], bhante”tiādimāha.

410. “Welcome, venerable sir,” indicates: “The Blessed One’s arrival is a good arrival, venerable sir; for when the Blessed One comes to us there is joy, and when he goes there is sorrow.” Why did he say, “It has been long, venerable sir”? Had the Blessed One gone there before? He had not gone there before. But among people, such pleasant social courtesies as, “Where are you going? From where have you come? Are you lost on the way? It has been a long time since you came,” are customary; therefore, he spoke thus. And having said this, he did not remain seated, stiff with pride, but rose from his seat and went to meet the Blessed One. For it is rare to find one who, seeing the Blessed One approaching, does not invite him with a seat or does not show respect. Why? Because of his high lineage. This wanderer, too, having dusted off the seat where he had been sitting, invited the Blessed One with a seat, saying: “May the Blessed One be seated, venerable sir, this seat is prepared.” “The conversation was left unfinished” means: “From the time you all sat down until my arrival, in this interval, what was the talk that was left unfinished? Due to my arrival, which talk did not reach its conclusion? Tell me, and I will bring it to its conclusion.” Thus he made the omniscient one’s invitation. Then the wanderer, indicating, “This talk is meaningless, without substance, connected to the round of rebirth, and is not worthy of being spoken before you,” said, “Let that be, venerable sir,” and so on.

Abhisaññānirodhakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Cessation of Higher Perception

411. Tiṭṭhatesā[V 1.0274], bhanteti sace bhagavā sotukāmo bhavissati, pacchāpesā kathā na dullabhā bhavissati, amhākaṃ panimāya kathāya attho natthi. Bhagavato panāgamanaṃ labhitvā mayaṃ aññadeva sukāraṇaṃ pucchāmāti dīpeti. Tato taṃ pucchanto – “purimāni, bhante”tiādimāha. Tattha kotūhalasālāyanti kotūhalasālā nāma paccekasālā natthi. Yattha pana nānātitthiyā samaṇabrāhmaṇā nānāvidhaṃ kathaṃ pavattenti, sā bahūnaṃ – “ayaṃ kiṃ vadati, ayaṃ kiṃ vadatī”ti kotūhaluppattiṭṭhānato kotūhalasālāti vuccati. Abhisaññānirodheti ettha abhīti upasaggamattaṃ. Saññānirodheti cittanirodhe, khaṇikanirodhe kathā uppannāti attho. Idaṃ pana tassā uppattikāraṇaṃ. Yadā kira bhagavā jātakaṃ vā katheti, sikkhāpadaṃ vā paññapeti tadā sakalajambudīpe bhagavato kittighoso pattharati, titthiyā taṃ sutvā – “bhavaṃ kira gotamo pubbacariyaṃ kathesi, mayaṃ kiṃ na sakkoma tādisaṃ kiñci kathetu”nti bhagavato paṭibhāgakiriyaṃ karontā ekaṃ bhavantarasamayaṃ kathenti – “bhavaṃ gotamo sikkhāpadaṃ paññapesi, mayaṃ kiṃ na sakkoma paññapetu”nti attano sāvakānaṃ kiñcideva sikkhāpadaṃ paññapenti. Tadā pana [M 1.0304] bhagavā aṭṭhavidhaparisamajjhe nisīditvā nirodhakathaṃ kathesi. Titthiyā taṃ sutvā – “bhavaṃ kira gotamo nirodhaṃ nāma kathesi, mayampi taṃ kathessāmā”ti sannipatitvā kathayiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “abhisaññānirodhe kathā udapādī”ti.

411. “Let that be, venerable sir,” indicates: “If the Blessed One wishes to hear it, this talk will not be difficult to have later. But for us, there is no benefit in this talk. Having the opportunity of the Blessed One’s arrival, we would rather ask about another, better matter.” Then, asking about that, he said, “In former times, venerable sir,” and so on. Therein, regarding ‘in the hall of curiosity’: there is no specific hall named the ‘hall of curiosity.’ Rather, any place where various ascetics and brahmins of different sects engage in diverse discussions is called the ‘hall of curiosity’ because it is a place for the arising of curiosity for many who wonder, “What is this one saying? What is that one saying?” Regarding ‘on the cessation of higher perception’: here, ‘abhi’ is merely a prefix. ‘On the cessation of perception’ means the discussion arose concerning the cessation of mind, or momentary cessation. This is the meaning. Now, this is the reason for its arising. It is said that when the Blessed One tells a Jātaka tale or lays down a training rule, his fame spreads throughout all of Jambudīpa. Hearing this, the sectarians, acting in imitation of the Blessed One, think, “The venerable Gotama, it seems, has told of a past life. Are we not able to tell something of that sort?” and they tell a story from some other existence. They think, “The venerable Gotama has laid down a training rule. Are we not able to lay one down?” and they lay down some training rule for their own disciples. At that time, the Blessed One, sitting in the midst of an eightfold assembly, taught a discourse on cessation. Hearing this, the sectarians conferred, “The venerable Gotama, it seems, has taught on what is called ‘cessation.’ We too shall teach on that,” and having gathered, they discussed it. Therefore, it was said by Poṭṭhapāda: “A discussion arose on the cessation of higher perception.”

Tatrekacceti tesu ekacce. Purimo cettha yvāyaṃ bāhire titthāyatane pabbajito cittappavattiyaṃ dosaṃ disvā acittakabhāvo santoti samāpattiṃ bhāvetvā ito cuto pañca kappasatāni asaññībhave ṭhatvā puna idha uppajjati. Tassa saññuppāde ca nirodhe ca hetuṃ apassanto – ahetū appaccayāti āha.

Among them, some say thus. The first one among these is one who, having gone forth in an external sectarian fold, saw a fault in the occurrence of thought and, thinking, ‘The state of no-thought is peaceful,’ developed that attainment. Having passed away from here, he remained in the realm of non-percipient beings for five hundred great eons and then was reborn here. Not seeing a cause for the arising and cessation of perception, he said: ‘It is without cause, without condition.’”

Dutiyo [P 2.0370] naṃ nisedhetvā migasiṅgatāpasassa asaññakabhāvaṃ gahetvā – “upetipi apetipī”ti āha. Migasiṅgatāpaso kira attantapo ghoratapo paramadhitindriyo ahosi. Tassa sīlatejena sakkavimānaṃ uṇhaṃ ahosi. Sakko devarājā “sakkaṭṭhānaṃ nu kho tāpaso patthetī”ti alambusaṃ nāma devakaññaṃ – ‘tāpasassa tapaṃ bhinditvā ehī’ti pesesi. Sā tattha gatā. Tāpaso paṭhamadivase taṃ disvāva palāyitvā paṇṇasālaṃ pāvisi. Dutiyadivase kāmacchandanīvaraṇena bhaggo taṃ hatthe aggahesi, so tena dibbaphassena phuṭṭho visaññī hutvā tiṇṇaṃ [V 1.0275] saṃvaccharānaṃ accayena saññaṃ paṭilabhi. Taṃ so diṭṭhigatiko – “tiṇṇaṃ saṃvaccharānaṃ accayena nirodhā vuṭṭhito”ti maññamāno evamāha.

The second one, having refuted him and taking the case of the non-percipient state of the ascetic Migasiṅga, said: ‘It comes and it goes.’ It is said that the ascetic Migasiṅga was one who mortified himself, practiced severe austerities, and had supremely restrained senses. Due to the power of his virtue, Sakka’s celestial palace grew hot. Sakka, the king of the gods, thinking, “Could this ascetic be aspiring to my position?” sent a celestial nymph named Alambusā, saying, “Go and break the ascetic’s austerity.” She went there. On the first day, upon seeing her, the ascetic fled and entered his leaf hut. On the second day, his wholesome disposition broken by the hindrance of sensual desire, he grasped her by the hand. Touched by that divine contact, he became unconscious and regained perception only after three years had passed. That person, holding a wrong view and thinking, “After three years, he has arisen from cessation,” spoke thus.

Tatiyo naṃ nisedhetvā āthabbaṇapayogaṃ sandhāya “upakaḍḍhantipi apakaḍḍhantipī”ti āha. Āthabbaṇikā kira āthabbaṇaṃ payojetvā sattaṃ sīsacchinnaṃ viya hatthacchinnaṃ viya mataṃ viya ca katvā dassenti. Tassa puna pākatikabhāvaṃ disvā so diṭṭhigatiko – “nirodhā vuṭṭhito aya”nti maññamāno evamāha.

The third one, having refuted him, said with reference to the application of Atharvaṇa spells: ‘They draw it forth and they draw it back.’ It is said that practitioners of the Atharvaṇa Veda, applying their spells, can make a being appear as if its head were cut off, as if its hands were cut off, or as if it were dead. Seeing that being return to its natural state, that person, holding a wrong view and thinking, “This one has arisen from cessation,” spoke thus.

Catuttho naṃ nisedhetvā yakkhadāsīnaṃ madaniddaṃ sandhāya “santi hi bho devatā”tiādimāha. Yakkhadāsiyo kira sabbarattiṃ devatūpahāraṃ kurumānā naccitvā gāyitvā aruṇodaye ekaṃ surāpātiṃ pivitvā [M 1.0305] parivattitvā supitvā divā vuṭṭhahanti. Taṃ disvā so diṭṭhigatiko – “suttakāle nirodhaṃ samāpannā, pabuddhakāle nirodhā vuṭṭhitā”ti maññamāno evamāha.

The fourth one, having refuted him, said with reference to the intoxicated sleep of the yakkhinī servants: ‘Indeed, venerable sirs, there are deities,’ and so on. It is said that the yakkhinī servants, after spending the whole night making offerings to the deities, dancing, and singing, drink a cup of liquor at dawn, roll over, and sleep, only rising when the sun is high. Seeing this, that person, holding a wrong view and thinking, “While asleep, they attained cessation; upon waking, they have arisen from cessation,” spoke thus.

Ayaṃ pana poṭṭhapādo paribbājako paṇḍitajātiko. Tenassa taṃ kathaṃ sutvā vippaṭisāro uppajji. “Imesaṃ kathā eḷamūgakathā viya cattāro hi nirodhe ete paññapenti, iminā ca nirodhena nāma ekena bhavitabbaṃ, na bahunā. Tenāpi ekena aññeneva bhavitabbaṃ, so pana aññena ñātuṃ na [P 2.0371] sakkā aññatra sabbaññunā. Sace bhagavā idha abhavissa ‘ayaṃ nirodho ayaṃ na nirodho’ti dīpasahassaṃ viya ujjāletvā ajjameva pākaṭaṃ akarissā”ti dasabalaññeva anussari. Tasmā “tassa mayhaṃ bhante”tiādimāha. Tattha aho nūnāti anussaraṇatthe nipātadvayaṃ, tena tassa bhagavantaṃ anussarantassa etadahosi “aho nūna bhagavā aho nūna sugato”ti. Yo imesanti yo etesaṃ nirodhadhammānaṃ sukusalo nipuṇo cheko, so bhagavā aho nūna katheyya, sugato aho nūna katheyyāti ayamettha adhippāyo. Pakataññūti ciṇṇavasitāya pakatiṃ sabhāvaṃ jānātīti pakataññū. Kathaṃ nu khoti idaṃ paribbājako “mayaṃ bhagavā na jānāma, tumhe jānātha, kathetha no”ti āyācanto vadati. Atha bhagavā kathento “tatra poṭṭhapādā”tiādimāha.

Now, this wanderer Poṭṭhapāda was of a wise nature. Therefore, upon hearing their talk, remorse arose in him: “The talk of these men is like the talk of the drivelling and dumb. For they declare four kinds of cessation, but this thing called cessation must be one, not many. And that one must be a different one altogether from what they describe. Furthermore, that one cannot be known by another, except by the All-Knowing One. If the Blessed One were here, he would, saying, ‘This is cessation, this is not cessation,’ illuminate it like a thousand lamps and make it plain this very day.” Thus, he repeatedly called to mind the One with Ten Powers. Therefore, he said, “For me, venerable sir…” and so on. Herein, ‘aho nūna’ is a pair of particles in the sense of repeated recollection. Thus, for him who was repeatedly recollecting the Blessed One, this occurred: “Oh, if only the Blessed One were here! Oh, if only the Sugata were here!” The intention here is this: “He who is highly skilled, subtle, and expert in these matters of cessation—oh, may that Blessed One explain! Oh, may that Sugata explain!” ‘One who knows the nature’ means one who knows the nature, the inherent characteristic, due to the mastery gained through practice. The wanderer says, “How might it be?” as a way of requesting: “Blessed One, we do not know; you know. Please explain it to us.” Then the Blessed One, intending to explain, said: “In that case, Poṭṭhapāda…” and so on.

Ahetukasaññuppādanirodhakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Arising and Ceasing of Perception without a Cause

412. Tattha tatrāti tesu samaṇabrāhmaṇesu. Āditova tesaṃ aparaddhanti tesaṃ ādimhiyeva [V 1.0276] viraddhaṃ, gharamajjheyeva pakkhalitāti dīpeti. Sahetū sappaccayāti ettha hetupi paccayopi kāraṇasseva nāmaṃ, sakāraṇāti attho. Taṃ pana kāraṇaṃ dassento “sikkhā ekā”ti āha. Tattha sikkhā ekā saññā uppajjantīti sikkhāya ekaccā saññā jāyantīti attho.

412. Therein, `tatrā` refers to 'among those ascetics and brahmins.' `Āditova tesaṃ aparaddhaṃ` shows that 'their error is right at the beginning'; they have stumbled right in the middle of the house. In the phrase `sahetū sappaccayā`, both `hetu` and `paccayo` are names for 'cause' (`kāraṇa`); the meaning is 'with a cause.' Then, showing that cause, He said, `sikkhā ekā`. Therein, `sikkhā ekā saññā uppajjanti` means that through training, certain perceptions arise; this is the meaning.

413. Kā ca sikkhāti bhagavā avocāti katamā ca sā sikkhāti bhagavā vitthāretukamyatāpucchāvasena avoca. Atha yasmā adhisīlasikkhā adhicittasikkhā adhipaññāsikkhāti tisso sikkhā honti. Tasmā tā dassento bhagavā saññāya sahetukaṃ uppādanirodhaṃ dīpetuṃ buddhuppādato pabhuti tantidhammaṃ ṭhapento “idha poṭṭhapāda, tathāgato loke”tiādimāha. Tattha adhisīlasikkhā [M 1.0306] adhicittasikkhāti dve eva sikkhā sarūpena āgatā, tatiyā pana “ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti kho poṭṭhapāda mayā ekaṃsiko dhammo desito”ti ettha sammādiṭṭhisammāsaṅkappavasena pariyāpannattā āgatāti veditabbā. Kāmasaññāti pañcakāmaguṇikarāgopi asamuppannakāmacāropi[P 2.0372]. Tattha pañcakāmaguṇikarāgo anāgāmimaggena samugghātaṃ gacchati, asamuppannakāmacāro pana imasmiṃ ṭhāne vaṭṭati. Tasmā tassa yā purimā kāmasaññāti tassa paṭhamajjhānasamaṅgino yā pubbe uppannapubbāya kāmasaññāya sadisattā purimā kāmasaññāti vucceyya, sā nirujjhati, anuppannāva nuppajjatīti attho.

413. Regarding `Kā ca sikkhāti bhagavā avoca`: this means the Blessed One spoke by way of a question, desiring to elaborate, saying, 'And what is that training?' Now, since there are three trainings—the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom—therefore, to show them, the Blessed One, in order to explain the arising and cessation of perception with its cause, and establishing the traditional teaching from the time of the Buddha's appearance, said, 'Here, Poṭṭhapāda, a Tathāgata appears in the world,' and so on. Therein, the two trainings, the training in higher virtue and the training in higher mind, are mentioned in their own form. The third, however, should be understood as being included by way of right view and right intention in the passage, 'This, Poṭṭhapāda, is the path leading to the cessation of suffering, a definitive teaching taught by me.' `Kāmasaññā` refers to both lust related to the five strands of sensual pleasure and unarisen sensual activity. Therein, lust related to the five strands of sensual pleasure is eradicated by the path of the non-returner, but unarisen sensual activity is applicable in this context. Therefore, regarding `tassa yā purimā kāmasaññā`: for that person endowed with the first jhāna, that which, due to its similarity to a previously arisen perception of sensual pleasure, would be called the 'former perception of sensual pleasure'—that ceases. The meaning is that, being unarisen, it does not arise.

Vivekajapītisukhasukhumasaccasaññīyeva tasmiṃ samaye hotīti tasmiṃ paṭhamajjhānasamaye vivekajapītisukhasaṅkhātā sukhumasaññā saccā hoti, bhūtā hotīti attho. Atha vā kāmacchandādioḷārikaṅgappahānavasena sukhumā ca sā bhūtatāya saccā ca saññāti sukhumasaccasaññā, vivekajehi pītisukhehi sampayuttā sukhumasaccasaññāti vivekajapītisukhasukhumasaccasaññā sā assa atthīti vivekajapītisukhasukhumasaccasaññīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Esa nayo sabbattha. Evampi sikkhāti ettha yasmā paṭhamajjhānaṃ samāpajjanto adhiṭṭhahanto, vuṭṭhahanto ca sikkhati, tasmā taṃ evaṃ sikkhitabbato sikkhāti vuccati. Tenapi sikkhāsaṅkhātena paṭhamajjhānena evaṃ ekā vivekajapītisukhasukhumasaccasaññā uppajjati. Evaṃ ekā kāmasaññā nirujjhatīti attho. Ayaṃ sikkhāti bhagavā avocāti ayaṃ paṭhamajjhānasaṅkhātā ekā sikkhāti, bhagavā āha. Etenupāyena sabbattha attho daṭṭhabbo.

Regarding vivekajapītisukhasukhumasaccasaññīyeva tasmiṃ samaye hoti: the meaning is that at the time of the first jhāna, the subtle perception designated as 'bliss and happiness born of seclusion' is true (saccā) and actual (bhūtā). Alternatively, because coarse factors such as sensual desire have been abandoned, the perception is subtle (sukhumā), and because it is actual, it is true (saccā); hence, it is a 'subtle, true perception' (sukhumasaccasaññā). The subtle, true perception associated with the bliss and happiness born of seclusion is vivekajapītisukhasukhumasaccasaññā. One possesses this, hence one is a vivekajapītisukhasukhumasaccasaññī. Thus should the meaning be understood here. This method applies everywhere. In Evampi sikkhā, since one who is entering, resolving upon, and emerging from the first jhāna trains, therefore, because it is to be trained in this way, it is called 'training' (sikkhā). The meaning is: through that first jhāna, designated as 'training', a certain subtle, true perception associated with the bliss and happiness born of seclusion arises. In this way, a certain perception of sensual pleasure ceases. Regarding Ayaṃ sikkhāti bhagavā avoca: the Blessed One said, 'This is the one training designated as the first jhāna.' By this method, the meaning should be understood everywhere.

Yasmā pana aṭṭhamasamāpattiyā aṅgato sammasanaṃ buddhānaṃyeva hoti, sāvakesu sāriputtasadisānampi [V 1.0277] natthi, kalāpato sammasanaṃyeva pana sāvakānaṃ hoti, idañca “saññā saññā”ti, evaṃ aṅgato sammasanaṃ uddhaṭaṃ. Tasmā [M 1.0307] ākiñcaññāyatanaparamaṃyeva saññaṃ dassetvā puna tadeva saññagganti dassetuṃ “yato kho poṭṭhapāda…pe… saññaggaṃ phusatī”ti āha.

Furthermore, since comprehension of the eighth attainment by way of its factors occurs only for Buddhas and does not exist even for disciples like Sāriputta—for disciples, there is only comprehension by way of aggregates—and this comprehension by way of factors, 'perception, perception,' has been set forth. Therefore, having shown perception as culminating in the base of nothingness, to show again that this very thing is the peak of perception, He said, 'When, Poṭṭhapāda... he touches the peak of perception.'

414. Tattha [P 2.0373] yato kho poṭṭhapāda bhikkhūti yo nāma poṭṭhapāda bhikkhu. Idha sakasaññī hotīti idha sāsane sakasaññī hoti, ayameva vā pāṭho, attano paṭhamajjhānasaññāya saññavā hotīti attho. So tato amutra tato amutrāti so bhikkhu tato paṭhamajjhānato amutra dutiyajjhāne, tatopi amutra tatiyajjhāneti evaṃ tāya tāya jhānasaññāya sakasaññī sakasaññī hutvā anupubbena saññaggaṃ phusati. Saññagganti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ vuccati. Kasmā? Lokiyānaṃ kiccakārakasamāpattīnaṃ aggattā. Ākiñcaññāyatanasamāpattiyañhi ṭhatvā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanampi nirodhampi samāpajjanti. Iti sā lokiyānaṃ kiccakārakasamāpattīnaṃ aggattā saññagganti vuccati, taṃ phusati pāpuṇātīti attho.

414. Therein, yato kho poṭṭhapāda bhikkhūti means 'whatever monk, Poṭṭhapāda...' Idha sakasaññī hotīti means 'here in this Dispensation, he is one with his own perception'; or this is the reading. The meaning is: he possesses perception by means of his own first jhāna perception. So tato amutra tato amutrāti means that monk, from that first jhāna to the next, the second jhāna, and from that to the next, the third jhāna—thus, possessing his own perception with each respective jhāna perception, he gradually touches the peak of perception. Saññagganti refers to the base of nothingness. Why? Because it is the highest of the mundane, functional attainments. For, being established in the attainment of the base of nothingness, they attain both the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the attainment of cessation. Thus, because it is the highest of the mundane, functional attainments, it is called the 'peak of perception.' The meaning of 'he touches it' (phusati) is 'he reaches it' (pāpuṇāti).

Idāni abhisaññānirodhaṃ dassetuṃ “tassa saññagge ṭhitassā”tiādimāha. Tattha ceteyyaṃ, abhisaṅkhareyyanti padadvaye ca jhānaṃ samāpajjanto ceteti nāma, punappunaṃ kappetīti attho. Uparisamāpattiatthāya nikantiṃ kurumāno abhisaṅkharoti nāma. Imā ca me saññā nirujjheyyunti imā ākiñcaññāyatanasaññā nirujjheyyuṃ. Aññā ca oḷārikāti aññā ca oḷārikā bhavaṅgasaññā uppajjeyyuṃ. So na ceva ceteti na abhisaṅkharotīti ettha kāmaṃ cesa cetentova na ceteti, abhisaṅkharontova nābhisaṅkharoti. Imassa bhikkhuno ākiñcaññāyatanato vuṭṭhāya nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samāpajjitvā “ekaṃ dve cittavāre ṭhassāmī”ti ābhogasamannāhāro natthi. Uparinirodhasamāpattatthāya eva pana ābhogasamannāhāro atthi, svāyamattho puttagharācikkhaṇena dīpetabbo.

Now, to show the cessation of higher perception, He said, tassa saññagge ṭhitassā’ti, and so on. Therein, in the two words ceteyyaṃ and abhisaṅkhareyyaṃ, one entering jhāna is said to 'intend' (ceteti); the meaning is 'he plans again and again.' One who generates desire for a higher attainment is said to 'fabricate' (abhisaṅkharoti). Imā ca me saññā nirujjheyyun’ti means 'may these perceptions of the base of nothingness cease.' Aññā ca oḷārikā’ti means 'and other gross life-continuum perceptions may arise.' Here, in so na ceva ceteti na abhisaṅkharoti, although he is indeed intending, he is not said to intend; although he is indeed fabricating, he is not said to fabricate. For this monk, having emerged from the base of nothingness and entered the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there is no application of mind with the thought, 'I will remain for one or two thought-processes.' But there is application of mind only for the purpose of the higher attainment of cessation. This meaning should be illustrated by the example of pointing out the son's house.

Pitugharamajjhena kira gantvā pacchābhāge puttassa gharaṃ hoti, tato paṇītaṃ bhojanaṃ ādāya āsanasālaṃ āgataṃ daharaṃ thero – “manāpo piṇḍapāto kuto ābhato”ti pucchi. So “asukassa gharato”ti laddhagharameva ācikkhi. Yena panassa pitugharamajjhena gatopi āgatopi [M 1.0308] tattha ābhogopi natthi. Tattha āsanasālā viya ākiñcaññāyatanasamāpatti [P 2.0374] daṭṭhabbā, pitugehaṃ viya nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpatti, puttagehaṃ viya nirodhasamāpatti, āsanasālāya ṭhatvā pitugharaṃ amanasikaritvā puttagharācikkhaṇaṃ viya ākiñcaññāyatanato vuṭṭhāya nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samāpajjitvā “ekaṃ dve cittavāre ṭhassāmī”ti pitugharaṃ amanasikaritvāva [V 1.0278] uparinirodhasamāpattatthāya manasikāro, evamesa cetentova na ceteti, abhisaṅkharontova nābhisaṅkharoti. Tā ceva saññāti tā jhānasaññā nirujjhanti. Aññā cāti aññā ca oḷārikā bhavaṅgasaññā nuppajjanti. So nirodhaṃ phusatīti so evaṃ paṭipanno bhikkhu saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ phusati vindati paṭilabhati.

It is said that having gone through the middle of the father's house, the son's house is in the rear part. An elder asked a young monk who had come to the sitting hall after taking excellent food from there, 'From where was this delightful almsfood brought?' He replied, 'From such-and-such a house,' indicating only the house from which it was obtained. But though he had gone and come through the middle of the father's house, he had no advertence to it. In this simile, the attainment of the base of nothingness should be seen as the sitting hall; the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the father's house; and the attainment of cessation as the son's house. Just as, while standing in the sitting hall, one indicates the son's house without attending to the father's house, so too, having emerged from the base of nothingness and entered the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, without attending to it with the thought, 'I will remain for one or two mind-moments,' the attention is solely for the purpose of the higher attainment of cessation. In this way, though he intends, he is not said to intend; though he fabricates, he is not said to fabricate. 'And those very perceptions' means those perceptions associated with the jhāna of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception cease. 'And others' means other, gross, life-continuum perceptions do not arise. 'He touches cessation' means that monk, having practiced thus, touches, finds, and obtains the cessation of perception and feeling.

Anupubbābhisaññānirodhasampajānasamāpattinti ettha abhīti upasaggamattaṃ, sampajānapadaṃ nirodhapadena antarikaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Anupaṭipāṭiyā sampajānasaññānirodhasamāpattīti ayaṃ panetthattho. Tatrāpi sampajānasaññānirodhasamāpattīti sampajānantassa ante saññā nirodhasamāpatti sampajānantassa vā paṇḍitassa bhikkhuno saññānirodhasamāpattīti ayaṃ visesattho.
