In the phrase anupubbābhisaññānirodhasampajānasamāpatti, the word abhi is merely a prefix. The word sampajāna is spoken with the word nirodha intervening. The meaning here, however, is 'the attainment of the cessation of perception of a clearly comprehending one, in sequence' (anupaṭipāṭiyā sampajānasaññānirodhasamāpatti). Even there, 'the attainment of the cessation of perception of a clearly comprehending one' means 'the attainment of the cessation of perception at the end of the practice of one who is clearly comprehending', or 'the attainment of the cessation of perception of a wise monk who is clearly comprehending'. This is the special meaning.

Idāni idha ṭhatvā nirodhasamāpattikathā kathetabbā. Sā panesā sabbākārena visuddhimagge paññābhāvanānisaṃsādhikāre kathitā, tasmā tattha kathitatova gahetabbā.

Now, at this point, the discourse on the attainment of cessation should be given. However, this has been explained by me in all its aspects in the Visuddhimagga, in the chapter on the benefits of the development of wisdom. Therefore, it should be understood from what was explained there.

Evaṃ bhagavā poṭṭhapādassa paribbājakassa nirodhakathaṃ kathetvā – atha naṃ tādisāya kathāya aññattha abhāvaṃ paṭijānāpetuṃ “taṃ kiṃ maññasī”tiādimāha. Paribbājakopi “bhagavā ajja tumhākaṃ kathaṃ ṭhapetvā na mayā evarūpā kathā sutapubbā”ti paṭijānanto, “no hetaṃ bhante”ti vatvā puna sakkaccaṃ bhagavato kathāya uggahitabhāvaṃ dassento “evaṃ kho ahaṃ bhante”tiādimāha. Athassa bhagavā “suuggahitaṃ tayā”ti anujānanto “evaṃ poṭṭhapādā”ti āha.

Thus, having given the discourse on cessation to the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda, the Blessed One then, in order to have him acknowledge the absence of such a discourse elsewhere, said, 'What do you think?' and so on. The wanderer, too, acknowledging, 'Venerable Sir, setting aside your discourse today, such a discourse has never been heard by me before,' said, 'That is not the case, venerable sir.' Then, showing that he had respectfully grasped the Blessed One's discourse, he said, 'So it is, venerable sir,' and so on. Then the Blessed One, approving, 'It has been well grasped by you,' said, 'So it is, Poṭṭhapāda.'

415. Atha paribbājako “bhagavatā ‘ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ saññagga’nti vuttaṃ. Etadeva nu kho saññaggaṃ, udāhu avasesasamāpattīsupi [P 2.0375] saññaggaṃ atthī”ti cintetvā tamatthaṃ pucchanto “ekaññeva nu kho”tiādimāha. Bhagavāpissa vissajjesi. Tattha puthūpīti bahūnipi. Yathā yathā kho, poṭṭhapāda, nirodhaṃ [M 1.0309] phusatīti pathavīkasiṇādīsu yena yena kasiṇena, paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ vā yena yena jhānena. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sace hi pathavīkasiṇena karaṇabhūtena pathavīkasiṇasamāpattiṃ ekavāraṃ samāpajjanto purimasaññānirodhaṃ phusati ekaṃ saññaggaṃ, atha dve vāre, tayo vāre, vārasataṃ, vārasahassaṃ, vārasatasahassaṃ vā samāpajjanto purimasaññānirodhaṃ phusati, satasahassaṃ, saññaggāni. Esa nayo sesakasiṇesu. Jhānesupi sace paṭhamajjhānena karaṇabhūtena ekavāraṃ purimasaññānirodhaṃ phusati ekaṃ saññaggaṃ. Atha dve vāre[V 1.0279], tayo vāre, vārasataṃ, vārasahassaṃ, vārasatasahassaṃ vā purimasaññānirodhaṃ phusati, satasahassaṃ saññaggāni. Esa nayo sesajjhānasamāpattīsupi. Iti ekavāraṃ samāpajjanavasena vā sabbampi sañjānanalakkhaṇena saṅgahetvā vā ekaṃ saññaggaṃ hoti, aparāparaṃ samāpajjanavasena bahūni.

415. Then the wanderer, thinking, 'The Blessed One said, "The base of nothingness is the peak of perception." Is this alone the peak of perception, or is there a peak of perception in the remaining attainments as well?' and asking about that matter, said, 'Is it only one?' and so on. The Blessed One also answered him. Therein, 'puthūpi' means 'many'. 'In whatever way, Poṭṭhapāda, one touches cessation' means by whichever kasiṇa among the earth kasiṇa and so on, or by whichever jhāna among the first jhāna and so on. This is what is meant: if, with the earth kasiṇa as the instrument, one who attains the earth kasiṇa attainment once touches the cessation of prior sense-sphere perception, that is one peak of perception. Then, if one who attains it twice, three times, a hundred times, a thousand times, or a hundred thousand times touches the cessation of prior sense-sphere perception, there are a hundred thousand peaks of perception. This is the method for the remaining kasiṇas. In the jhānas too, if, with the first jhāna as the instrument, one touches the cessation of prior sense-sphere perception once, that is one peak of perception. Then, if one touches the cessation of prior sense-sphere perception a hundred thousand times, there are a hundred thousand peaks of perception. This is the method for the remaining jhāna attainments as well. Thus, either by way of attaining once, or by comprehending all with the characteristic of perceiving, there is one peak of perception. By way of attaining again and again, there are many.

416. Saññā nu kho, bhanteti bhante nirodhasamāpajjanakassa bhikkhuno “saññā nu kho paṭhamaṃ uppajjatī”ti pucchati. Tassa bhagavā “saññā kho, poṭṭhapādā”ti byākāsi. Tattha saññāti jhānasaññā. Ñāṇanti vipassanāñāṇaṃ. Aparo nayo, saññāti vipassanā saññā. Ñāṇanti maggañāṇaṃ. Aparo nayo, saññāti maggasaññā. Ñāṇanti phalañāṇaṃ. Tipiṭakamahāsivatthero panāha –

416. 'Is it perception, venerable sir?' means he asks: 'Venerable sir, for a monk who is attaining cessation, does perception arise first?' To him, the Blessed One explained, 'It is perception, Poṭṭhapāda.' Therein, 'perception' means jhāna perception; 'knowledge' means insight knowledge. Another method: 'perception' means insight perception, which arises first; 'knowledge' means path knowledge, which arises later. Another method: 'perception' means path-associated perception, which arises first; 'knowledge' means fruition knowledge, which arises later. However, the Elder Tipiṭaka Mahāsiva said:

Kiṃ ime bhikkhū bhaṇanti, poṭṭhapādo heṭṭhā bhagavantaṃ nirodhaṃ pucchi. Idāni nirodhā vuṭṭhānaṃ pucchanto “bhagavā nirodhā vuṭṭhahantassa kiṃ paṭhamaṃ arahattaphalasaññā uppajjati, udāhu paccavekkhaṇañāṇa”nti vadati. Athassa bhagavā yasmā phalasaññā paṭhamaṃ uppajjati, pacchā paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ[P 2.0376]. Tasmā “saññā kho poṭṭhapādā”ti āha. Tattha saññuppādāti arahattaphalasaññāya uppādā, pacchā “idaṃ arahattaphala”nti evaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇuppādo hoti. Idappaccayā kira meti phalasamādhisaññāpaccayā kira mayhaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ uppannanti.

What are these monks saying? Poṭṭhapāda previously asked the Blessed One about cessation. Now, asking about emergence from cessation, he says, 'Venerable Sir, for one emerging from cessation, does the perception associated with the fruit of arahantship arise first, or does reviewing knowledge arise?' Then, because the perception of the fruit arises first and reviewing knowledge afterwards, the Blessed One said, 'It is perception, Poṭṭhapāda.' Therein, 'because of the arising of perception' means because of the arising of the perception of the fruit of arahantship, afterwards the arising of reviewing knowledge occurs with the thought, 'This is the fruit of arahantship.' 'Dependent on this, it seems, for me' means: 'Dependent on the perception associated with the fruition attainment, it seems, my reviewing knowledge has arisen.'

Saññāattakathāvaṇṇanā

An Explanation of the Discourse on Perception and Self

417. Idāni paribbājako yathā nāma gāmasūkaro gandhodakena nhāpetvā gandhehi anulimpitvā mālādāmaṃ piḷandhitvā sirisayane āropitopi [M 1.0310] sukhaṃ na vindati, vegena gūthaṭṭhānameva gantvā sukhaṃ vindati. Evameva bhagavatā saṇhasukhumatilakkhaṇabbhāhatāya desanāya nhāpitavilittamaṇḍitopi nirodhakathāsirisayanaṃ āropitopi tattha sukhaṃ na vindanto gūthaṭṭhānasadisaṃ attano laddhiṃ gahetvā tameva pucchanto “saññā nu kho, bhante, purisassa attā”tiādimāha. Athassānumatiṃ gahetvā byākātukāmo bhagavā – “kaṃ pana tva”ntiādimāha. Tato so “arūpī attā”ti evaṃ laddhiko samānopi “bhagavā desanāya sukusalo, so me āditova laddhiṃ mā viddhaṃsetū”ti cintetvā attano laddhiṃ pariharanto “oḷārikaṃ kho”tiādimāha. Athassa bhagavā tattha dosaṃ dassento “oḷāriko ca hi te”tiādimāha[V 1.0280]. Tattha evaṃ santanti evaṃ sante. Bhummatthe hi etaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Evaṃ santaṃ attānaṃ paccāgacchato tavāti ayaṃ vā ettha attho. Catunnaṃ khandhānaṃ ekuppādekanirodhattā kiñcāpi yā saññā uppajjati, sāva nirujjhati. Aparāparaṃ upādāya pana “aññā ca saññā uppajjanti, aññā ca saññā nirujjhantī”ti vuttaṃ.

417. Now, the wanderer... just as a village pig, though bathed with fragrant water, anointed with perfumes, adorned with a garland, and placed on a glorious bed, does not find happiness, but quickly goes only to a place of filth and finds happiness. In this very same way, though bathed, anointed, and adorned by the Blessed One’s teaching—which is subtle, refined, and sealed with the three characteristics—and placed on the glorious bed of the discourse on cessation, he does not find happiness there. Grasping his own view, which is like a place of filth, and asking about that very view, he said, “Venerable sir, is perception the self of a person?” and so on. Then, the Blessed One, having understood his inclination and wishing to explain, said, “But what do you [posit as the self]?” and so on. Thereupon, although he held the view, “The self is formless,” he thought, “The Blessed One is very skilled in teaching; may he not destroy my view right from the start.” Wishing to avoid his own view being refuted, he said, “The gross one…” and so on. Then the Blessed One, showing him the fault in that, said, “For your gross one…” and so on. Therein, `evaṃ santaṃ` means `evaṃ sante` (when it is thus). Indeed, this is a word in the accusative case used in the sense of the locative case. Alternatively, the meaning here is: “of you who returns to a self that is thus.” Because of the simultaneous arising and ceasing of the four mental aggregates, although whichever perception arises, that very one ceases, it is said, based on succession, “Other perceptions arise, and other perceptions cease.”

418-420. Idāni aññaṃ laddhiṃ dassento – “manomayaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhante”tiādiṃ vatvā tatrāpi dose dinne yathā nāma ummattako yāvassa saññā nappatiṭṭhāti, tāva aññaṃ gahetvā aññaṃ vissajjeti, saññāpatiṭṭhānakāle pana vattabbameva vadati, evameva [P 2.0377] aññaṃ gahetvā aññaṃ vissajjetvā idāni attano laddhiṃyeva vadanto “arūpī kho”tiādimāha. Tatrāpi yasmā so saññāya uppādanirodhaṃ icchati, attānaṃ pana sassataṃ maññati. Tasmā tathevassa dosaṃ dassento bhagavā “evaṃ santampī”tiādimāha. Tato paribbājako micchādassanena abhibhūtattā bhagavatā vuccamānampi taṃ nānattaṃ ajānanto “sakkā panetaṃ, bhante, mayā”tiādimāha. Athassa bhagavā yasmā so saññāya uppādanirodhaṃ passantopi saññāmayaṃ attānaṃ niccameva maññati. Tasmā “dujjānaṃ kho”tiādimāha.

Now, wishing to present another view, he said, “Venerable sir, I [hold that the self is] mind-made…” and so on. When the fault was pointed out in that as well, it is just as a madman, for as long as his perception is not yet established, grasps one thing and discards another, but when his perception is established, he says only what should be said. In this very same way, having grasped another view and discarded another, now wishing to state only his own view, he said, “The formless one…” and so on. Therein also, because he desires the arising and ceasing of perception, yet considers the self to be eternal, the Blessed One, wishing to show him the fault in the very same way as before, said, “Even being thus…” and so on. Then, because the wanderer was overwhelmed by wrong view, not knowing that difference between perception and self even when it was being spoken by the Blessed One, he said, “Venerable sir, is it possible for me…” and so on. Then, because he, although seeing the arising and ceasing of perception, still considers the self that is made of perception to be permanent, the Blessed One said, “It is difficult to know…” and so on.

Tatthāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – tava aññā diṭṭhi, aññā khanti, aññā ruci, aññathāyeva te dassanaṃ pavattaṃ, aññadeva ca te khamati ceva ruccati ca, aññatra [M 1.0311] ca te āyogo, aññissāyeva paṭipattiyā yuttapayuttatā, aññattha ca te ācariyakaṃ, aññasmiṃ titthāyatane ācariyabhāvo. Tena tayā evaṃ aññadiṭṭhikena aññakhantikena aññarucikena aññatrāyogena aññatrācariyakena dujjānaṃ etanti. Atha paribbājako – “saññā vā purisassa attā hotu, aññā vā saññā, taṃ sassatādi bhāvamassa pucchissa”nti puna “kiṃ pana bhante”tiādimāha.

Herein, this is the concise meaning: Your view is different, your acceptance is different, your preference is different; your seeing has occurred in a different way, and what you accept and prefer is something different. Your exertion is in another practice, your diligent application is in a different practice, and your teachership is elsewhere; your state of being a teacher is in another sectarian sphere. Therefore, for you—who has a different view, different acceptance, different preference, different exertion, and different teachership—this is difficult to know. Then the wanderer, thinking, “Let the self of a person be perception, or let it be other than perception; I will ask about its state of being eternal, etc.,” again said, “But what, venerable sir?” and so on.

Tattha lokoti attānaṃ sandhāya vadati. Na hetaṃ poṭṭhapāda atthasañhitanti poṭṭhapāda etaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ na idhalokaparalokaatthanissitaṃ, na attatthaparatthanissitaṃ. Na dhammasaṃhitanti na navalokuttaradhammanissitaṃ. Nādibrahmacariyakanti sikkhattayasaṅkhātassa sāsanabrahmacariyakassa na ādimattaṃ, adhisīlasikkhāmattampi na hoti. Na nibbidāyāti saṃsāravaṭṭe nibbindanatthāya na saṃvattati. Na [P 2.0378] virāgāyāti vaṭṭavirāgatthāya na saṃvattati. Na nirodhāyāti vaṭṭassa nirodhakaraṇatthāya na saṃvattati. Na upasamāyāti vaṭṭassa vūpasamanatthāya na saṃvattati. Na abhiññāyāti vaṭṭābhijānanāya paccakkhakiriyāya na saṃvattati. Na sambodhāyāti vaṭṭasambujjhanatthāya na [V 1.0281] saṃvattati. Na nibbānāyāti amatamahānibbānassa paccakkhakiriyāya na saṃvattati.

Herein, when he says “the world,” he speaks referring to the self. “This, Poṭṭhapāda, is not connected to benefit” means: Poṭṭhapāda, this wrong view is not based on benefit in this world and the next, nor is it based on one’s own benefit and the benefit of others. “It is not connected to the Dhamma” means: it is not based on the nine supramundane Dhammas. “It is not the beginning of the holy life” means: it is not the mere beginning of the holy life of the Dispensation, which is comprised of the threefold training; it is not even the mere training in higher virtue. “It does not lead to disenchantment” means: it does not conduce to disenchantment with the round of saṃsāra. “It does not lead to dispassion” means: it does not conduce to dispassion for the round. “It does not lead to cessation” means: it does not conduce to bringing about the cessation of the round. “It does not lead to peace” means: it does not conduce to the stilling of the round. “It does not lead to direct knowledge” means: it does not conduce to directly knowing and realizing the round. “It does not lead to enlightenment” means: it does not conduce to fully awakening to the round. “It does not lead to Nibbāna” means: it does not conduce to the realization of the deathless, great Nibbāna.

Idaṃ dukkhantiādīsu taṇhaṃ ṭhapetvā tebhūmakā pañcakkhandhā dukkhanti, tasseva dukkhassa pabhāvanato sappaccayā taṇhā dukkhasamudayoti. Ubhinnaṃ appavatti dukkhanirodhoti, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti mayā byākatanti attho. Evañca pana vatvā bhagavā “imassa paribbājakassa maggapātubhāvo vā phalasacchikiriyā vā natthi, mayhañca bhikkhācāravelā”ti cintetvā tuṇhī ahosi. Paribbājakopi taṃ ākāraṃ ñatvā bhagavato gamanakālaṃ ārocento viya “evameta”ntiādimāha.

In “This is suffering,” and so on: Setting aside craving, the five aggregates belonging to the three realms are the truth of suffering. Because it is the cause of that very suffering, craving, together with its conditions, is the truth of the origin of suffering. The non-occurrence of both is the truth of the cessation of suffering. The noble eightfold path is the practice, the way leading to the cessation of suffering. The meaning is: “Thus it has been declared by me.” And having said this, the Blessed One, thinking, “For this wanderer, there is no manifestation of the path or realization of the fruit, and for me, it is the time for the alms-round,” became silent. The wanderer, too, knowing that manner of his, as if announcing the Blessed One’s time of departure, said, “So it is…” and so on.

421. Vācāsannitodakenāti vacanapatodena. Sañjhabbharimakaṃsūti sañjhabbharitaṃ nirantaraṃ phuṭṭhaṃ akaṃsu, upari vijjhiṃsūti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhūtanti sabhāvato vijjamānaṃ. Tacchaṃ, tathanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Dhammaṭṭhitatanti navalokuttaradhammesu [M 1.0312] ṭhitasabhāvaṃ. Dhammaniyāmatanti lokuttaradhammaniyāmataṃ. Buddhānañhi catusaccavinimuttā kathā nāma natthi. Tasmā sā edisā hoti.

421. “With the goad that is speech” means: with the verbal goad. “They made it completely filled” means: they made it completely filled, pervaded without interval; it is said to mean, “they pierced from above.” “Real” means: existing by its own nature. “True” and “actual” are synonyms for that. “The state of being founded on the Dhamma” means: the state of being established in the nine supramundane Dhammas. “The fixed nature of the Dhamma” means: the fixed nature of the supramundane Dhamma. Indeed, for the Buddhas, there is no such thing as a discourse that is devoid of the Four Truths. Therefore, that teaching is of such a kind.

Cittahatthisāriputtapoṭṭhapādavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Account of Citta Hatthisāriputta and Poṭṭhapāda

422. Citto ca hatthisāriputtoti so kira sāvatthiyaṃ hatthiācariyassa putto bhagavato santike pabbajitvā tīṇi piṭakāni uggahetvā sukhumesu atthantaresu kusalo ahosi, pubbe katapāpakammavasena pana sattavāre vibbhamitvā gihi jāto. Kassapasammāsambuddhassa kira sāsane dve sahāyakā ahesuṃ, aññamaññaṃ samaggā ekatova sajjhāyanti. Tesu eko anabhirato gihibhāve cittaṃ uppādetvā itarassa ārocesi. So gihibhāve ādīnavaṃ pabbajjāya ānisaṃsaṃ [P 2.0379] dassetvā taṃ ovadi. So taṃ sutvā abhiramitvā punekadivasaṃ tādise citte uppanne taṃ etadavoca “mayhaṃ āvuso evarūpaṃ cittaṃ uppajjati – ‘imāhaṃ pattacīvaraṃ tuyhaṃ dassāmī’ti”. So pattacīvaralobhena tassa gihibhāve ānisaṃsaṃ dassetvā pabbajjāya ādīnavaṃ kathesi. Athassa taṃ sutvāva gihibhāvato cittaṃ virajjitvā pabbajjāyameva abhirami. Evamesa tadā sīlavantassa bhikkhuno gihibhāve ānisaṃsakathāya kathitattā idāni cha vāre vibbhamitvā sattame vāre pabbajito. Mahāmoggallānassa, mahākoṭṭhikattherassa ca abhidhammakathaṃ kathentānaṃ antarantarā kathaṃ opāteti. Atha naṃ mahākoṭṭhikatthero apasādeti. So [V 1.0282] mahāsāvakassa kathite patiṭṭhātuṃ asakkonto vibbhamitvā gihi jāto. Poṭṭhapādassa panāyaṃ gihisahāyako hoti. Tasmā vibbhamitvā dvīhatīhaccayena poṭṭhapādassa santikaṃ gato. Atha naṃ so disvā “samma kiṃ tayā kataṃ, evarūpassa nāma satthu sāsanā apasakkantosi, ehi pabbajituṃ idāni te vaṭṭatī”ti taṃ gahetvā bhagavato santikaṃ agamāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “citto ca hatthisāriputto poṭṭhapādo ca paribbājako”ti.

422. Citta Hatthisāriputta, it is said, was the son of an elephant trainer in Sāvatthī. After going forth in the presence of the Blessed One, he mastered the three Piṭakas and became skilled in subtle points of meaning. However, due to unwholesome kamma done previously, he disrobed seven times and became a householder. It is said that in the dispensation of Kassapa the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, there were two companions who were harmonious with each other and recited together. Among them, one, being discontent, conceived a thought for household life and informed the other. He, showing the drawback in household life and the benefit in the going forth, advised him. Hearing that, he took great delight, but one day, when such a thought arose again, he said to him: ‘Friend, such a thought arises in me: “I will give you this bowl and robe.”’ He, out of greed for the bowl and robe, then showed the benefit in household life and spoke of the drawback in the going forth. Then, as soon as he heard that, his mind became disenchanted with household life and he found delight only in the going forth. Thus, because he had then spoken of the benefit in household life to a virtuous bhikkhu, he now disrobed six times and went forth for the seventh time. While Mahāmoggallāna and Mahākoṭṭhita Thera were discussing the Abhidhamma, he occasionally interrupted their discussion. Then Mahākoṭṭhita Thera rebuked him. Unable to stand firm under the great disciple’s words, he disrobed and became a householder. Now, he was a householder friend of Poṭṭhapāda. Therefore, after disrobing, when two or three days had passed, he went to Poṭṭhapāda. Then, seeing him, Poṭṭhapāda said, ‘Friend, what have you done? You have withdrawn from the dispensation of such a Teacher. Come, it is proper for you to go forth now.’ Taking him, he went to the Blessed One. Hence it is said, ‘Citta Hatthisāriputta and Poṭṭhapāda the wanderer.’

423. Andhāti paññācakkhuno natthitāya andhā, tasseva abhāvena acakkhukā. Tvaṃyeva nesaṃ eko cakkhumāti subhāsitadubbhāsitajānanabhāvamattena paññācakkhunā cakkhumā. Ekaṃsikāti ekakoṭṭhāsā. Paññattāti [M 1.0313] ṭhapitā. Anekaṃsikāti na ekakoṭṭhāsā ekeneva koṭṭhāsena sassatāti vā asassatāti vā na vuttāti attho.

423. ‘Blind’ means blind due to the absence of the eye of wisdom; and due to the non-existence of that very thing, they are without eyes. ‘You alone are the one with the eye among them’ means one has the eye by means of the eye of wisdom, which is merely the state of knowing what is well-spoken and ill-spoken. ‘One-sided’ means having one part. ‘Declared’ means established. ‘Not one-sided’ means not having one part; the meaning is that it is not stated by a single part as ‘eternal’ or ‘not eternal’.

Ekaṃsikadhammavaṇṇanā

Explanation of One-Sided Teachings

424-425. Santi poṭṭhapādāti idaṃ bhagavā kasmā ārabhi? Bāhirakehi paññāpitaniṭṭhāya aniyyānikabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Sabbe hi titthiyā yathā bhagavā amataṃ nibbānaṃ, evaṃ attano attano samaye lokathupikādivasena niṭṭhaṃ paññapenti, sā ca na niyyānikā. Yathā paññattā [P 2.0380] hutvā na niyyāti na gacchati, aññadatthu paṇḍitehi paṭikkhittā nivattati, taṃ dassetuṃ bhagavā evamāha. Tattha ekantasukhaṃ lokaṃ jānaṃ passanti puratthimāya disāya ekantasukho loko pacchimādīnaṃ vā aññatarāyāti evaṃ jānantā evaṃ passantā viharatha. Diṭṭhapubbāni kho tasmiṃ loke manussānaṃ sarīrasaṇṭhānādīnīti. Appāṭihīrakatanti appāṭihīrakataṃ paṭiharaṇavirahitaṃ, aniyyānikanti vuttaṃ hoti.

Why did the Blessed One begin with, ‘There are, Poṭṭhapāda’? To show the non-leading-out nature of the final goal declared by outsiders. For all sectarians, just as the Blessed One declares the deathless Nibbāna, so too do they, in their own doctrines, declare a final goal by way of 'the world's peak' and so on; but that goal is not one that leads out. As it is declared, it does not lead out, it does not proceed; on the contrary, being rejected by the wise, it turns back. To show this, the Blessed One spoke thus. Therein, the passage beginning ‘knowing and seeing the world as exclusively happy’ refers to the question: ‘Do you dwell knowing thus and seeing thus: “In the eastern direction there is a world of exclusive happiness,” or in one of the other directions, such as the western? Have the bodily forms and so on of humans in that world been seen by you before?’ The term `appāṭihīrakataṃ` means it is unsubstantiated, indefensible; it is said to be non-leading-out.

426-427. Janapadakalyāṇīti janapade aññāhi itthīhi vaṇṇasaṇṭhānavilāsākappādīhi asadisā.

‘Janapadakalyāṇī’ means a woman in the country who is unmatched by other women in terms of complexion, figure, graceful deportment, attire, and so on.

Tayoattapaṭilābhavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Three Acquisitions of Self

428. Evaṃ bhagavā paresaṃ niṭṭhāya aniyyānikattaṃ dassetvā attano niṭṭhāya niyyānikabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “tayo kho me poṭṭhapādā”tiādimāha. Tattha attapaṭilābhoti attabhāvapaṭilābho, ettha ca bhagavā tīhi attabhāvapaṭilābhehi tayo bhave dassesi. Oḷārikattabhāvapaṭilābhena [V 1.0283] avīcito paṭṭhāya paranimmitavasavattipariyosānaṃ kāmabhavaṃ dassesi. Manomayaattabhāvapaṭilābhena paṭhamajjhānabhūmito paṭṭhāya akaniṭṭhabrahmalokapariyosānaṃ rūpabhavaṃ dassesi. Arūpaattabhāvapaṭilābhena ākāsānañcāyatanabrahmalokato paṭṭhāya nevasaññānāsaññāyatanabrahmalokapariyosānaṃ arūpabhavaṃ dassesi. Saṃkilesikā dhammā nāma dvādasa akusalacittuppādā. Vodāniyā dhammā nāma samathavipassanā.

428. Thus, having shown that the practice of other sectarians is not a means of escape, the Blessed One, in order to show that his own practice is a means of escape, said the words beginning with, “Poṭṭhapāda, there are these three acquisitions of self.” Herein, ‘acquisitions of self’ means acquisitions of individuality. And herein, the Blessed One showed three kinds of existence by means of three acquisitions of individuality. By the acquisition of a gross individuality, he showed the sense-sphere existence, beginning from Avīci and ending with the Paranimmitavasavattī realm. By the acquisition of a mind-made individuality, he showed the fine-material existence, beginning from the plane of the first jhāna and ending with the Akaniṭṭha brahma world. By the acquisition of a formless individuality, he showed the immaterial existence, beginning from the brahma world of the base of infinite space and ending with the brahma world of the base of neither perception nor non-perception. The twelve arisings of unwholesome consciousness are called ‘defiling states.’ Serenity and insight are called ‘purifying states.’

429. Paññāpāripūriṃ [M 1.0314] vepullattanti maggapaññāphalapaññānaṃ pāripūriñceva vipulabhāvañca. Pāmujjanti taruṇapīti. Pītīti balavatuṭṭhi. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yaṃ avocumha “sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihiratī”ti, tattha tassa evaṃ viharato taṃ pāmojjañceva bhavissati, pīti ca nāmakāyapassaddhi ca sati ca sūpaṭṭhitā uttamañāṇañca sukho ca vihāro. Sabbavihāresu ca ayameva vihāro “sukho”ti vattuṃ yutto “upasanto paramamadhuro”ti. Tattha [P 2.0381] paṭhamajjhāne pāmojjādayo chapi dhammā labbhanti, dutiyajjhāne dubbalapītisaṅkhātaṃ pāmojjaṃ nivattati, sesā pañca labbhanti. Tatiye pīti nivattati, sesā cattāro labbhanti. Tathā catutthe. Imesu catūsu jhānesu sampasādanasutte suddhavipassanā pādakajjhānameva kathitaṃ. Pāsādikasutte catūhi maggehi saddhiṃ vipassanā kathitā. Dasuttarasutte catutthajjhānikaphalasamāpatti kathitā. Imasmiṃ poṭṭhapādasutte pāmojjaṃ pītivevacanameva katvā dutiyajjhānikaphalasamāpattināma kathitāti veditabbā.

429. ‘The perfection and abundance of wisdom’ means the completeness and extensiveness of path-wisdom and fruition-wisdom. ‘Gladness’ is tender rapture. ‘Rapture’ is strong delight. What is meant by this? It was stated: ‘Having realized it for himself through direct knowledge, he abides having attained it.’ Therein, for one abiding thus, there will be that gladness, rapture, tranquility of the mental body, well-established mindfulness, supreme knowledge, and a pleasant abiding. And among all abidings, this very abiding is fit to be called ‘pleasant,’ ‘peaceful,’ and ‘supremely sweet.’ Herein, in the first jhāna, all six states beginning with gladness are obtained. In the second jhāna, gladness, which is described as weak rapture, ceases, and the remaining five are obtained. In the third, rapture ceases, and the remaining four are obtained. Likewise in the fourth. Among these four jhānas, in the Sampasādaniya Sutta, only the jhāna that is a basis for pure insight was taught. In the Pāsādika Sutta, insight together with the four paths was taught. In the Dasuttara Sutta, the attainment of fruition associated with the fourth jhāna was taught. In this Poṭṭhapāda Sutta, it should be known that by taking gladness simply as a synonym for rapture, what is called the attainment of fruition associated with the second jhāna was taught.

432-437. Ayaṃ vā soti ettha vā saddo vibhāvanattho hoti. Ayaṃ soti evaṃ vibhāvetvā pakāsetvā byākareyyāma. Yathāpare “ekantasukhaṃ attānaṃ sañjānāthā”ti puṭṭhā “no”ti vadanti, na evaṃ vadāmāti attho. Sappāṭihīrakatanti sappāṭiharaṇaṃ, niyyānikanti attho. Mogho hotīti tuccho hoti, natthi so tasmiṃ samayeti adhippāyo. Sacco hotīti bhūto hoti, sveva tasmiṃ samaye sacco hotīti attho. Ettha panāyaṃ citto attano asabbaññutāya tayo attapaṭilābhe kathetvā attapaṭilābho nāma paññattimattaṃ etanti uddharituṃ nāsakkhi, attapaṭilābho tveva niyyātesi. Athassa bhagavā rūpādayo cettha dhammā, attapaṭilābhoti pana nāmamattametaṃ, tesu tesu rūpādīsu sati evarūpā vohārā hontīti dassetukāmo tasseva kathaṃ gahetvā nāmapaññattivasena niyyātanatthaṃ “yasmiṃ citta samaye”tiādimāha.

In the phrase ‘This or that’ (`ayaṃ vā so`), the particle ‘or’ (`vā`) has the meaning of clarification. We would explain by distinguishing and clarifying thus: ‘This is that.’ The meaning is that we do not speak in the same way as others who, when asked, ‘Do you know a self that is exclusively happy?’, answer, ‘No.’ ‘Defensible’ (`sappāṭihīrakataṃ`) means with refutation; the meaning is ‘leading to escape’ (`niyyānikaṃ`). ‘It is void’ (`mogho hoti`) means it is empty; the intention is that it does not exist at that time. ‘It is true’ (`sacco hoti`) means it is real; the meaning is that at that time, it alone is true. But herein, this Citta, due to his own lack of omniscience, having spoken of the three acquisitions of self, was unable to deduce that ‘this thing called acquisition of self is a mere concept,’ and so he concluded it simply as ‘acquisition of self.’ Then the Blessed One, wishing to show that herein there are phenomena such as form, and ‘acquisition of self’ is but a mere name, and that when those respective phenomena like form exist, such conventional expressions arise, took up Citta’s very statement and, for the purpose of concluding it by way of name-and-concept, said the words beginning with, ‘At whatever time, Citta…’

438. Evañca pana vatvā paṭipucchitvā vinayanatthaṃ puna “sace taṃ, citta, evaṃ puccheyyu”ntiādimāha[V 1.0284]. Tattha yo me ahosi atīto attapaṭilābho[M 1.0315], sveva me attapaṭilābho, tasmiṃ samaye sacco ahosi, mogho anāgato mogho paccuppannoti [P 2.0382] ettha tāva imamatthaṃ dasseti – yasmā ye te atītā dhammā, te etarahi natthi, ahesunti pana saṅkhyaṃ gatā, tasmā sopi me attapaṭilābho tasmiṃyeva samaye sacco ahosi. Anāgatapaccuppannānaṃ pana dhammānaṃ tadā abhāvā tasmiṃ samaye “mogho anāgato, mogho paccuppanno”ti, evaṃ atthato nāmamattameva attapaṭilābhaṃ paṭijānāti. Anāgatapaccuppannesupi eseva nayo.

438. And having said this, questioning him in return for the purpose of instruction, he then said the words beginning with, ‘If, Citta, they were to ask you thus…’ Herein, regarding the statement, ‘Whatever past acquisition of self was mine, that very acquisition of self was mine; at that time it was true, the future was void, the present was void,’ he first shows this meaning: because those phenomena that are past do not exist now—though they have come to be reckoned as ‘they were’—therefore that acquisition of self of mine was true at that very time. But because future and present phenomena did not exist at that time, at that time ‘the future was void, the present was void.’ Thus, in terms of its meaning, he acknowledges the acquisition of self as a mere name. This same method applies also to the future and the present.

439-443. Atha bhagavā tassa byākaraṇena saddhiṃ attano byākaraṇaṃ saṃsandituṃ “evameva kho cittā”tiādīni vatvā puna opammato tamatthaṃ sādhento “seyyathāpi citta gavā khīra”ntiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho, yathā gavā khīraṃ, khīrādīhi ca dadhiādīni bhavanti, tattha yasmiṃ samaye khīraṃ hoti, na tasmiṃ samaye dadhīti vā navanītādīsu vā aññataranti saṅkhyaṃ niruttiṃ nāmaṃ vohāraṃ gacchati. Kasmā? Ye dhamme upādāya dadhītiādi vohārā honti, tesaṃ abhāvā. Atha kho khīraṃ tveva tasmiṃ samaye saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Kasmā? Ye dhamme upādāya khīranti saṅkhyā nirutti nāmaṃ vohāro hoti, tesaṃ bhāvāti. Esa nayo sabbattha. Imā kho cittāti oḷāriko attapaṭilābho iti ca manomayo attapaṭilābho iti ca arūpo attapaṭilābho iti ca imā kho citta lokasamaññā loke samaññāmattakāni samanujānanamattakāni etāni. Tathā lokaniruttimattakāni vacanapathamattakāni vohāramattakāni nāmapaṇṇattimattakāni etānīti. Evaṃ bhagavā heṭṭhā tayo attapaṭilābhe kathetvā idāni sabbametaṃ vohāramattakanti vadati. Kasmā? Yasmā paramatthato satto nāma natthi, suñño tuccho esa loko.

Then the Blessed One, in order to align his own explanation with Citta's explanation, having said, 'Just so, Citta,' and so on, and again, wishing to establish that meaning by way of a simile, said, 'Suppose, Citta, from a cow, milk...' and so on. Herein, this is the condensed meaning: Just as from a cow comes milk, and from milk and so on, curds and so on come to be, therein, at the time when it is milk, it does not come to be designated, termed, named, or called 'curds' or any other among butter and so on. Why? Because of the absence of those phenomena depending on which the conventions 'curds', etc., arise. But indeed, at that time, it is designated only as 'milk'. Why? Because of the presence of those phenomena depending on which the designation, term, name, and convention 'milk' arises. This is the method everywhere. 'These, Citta'—that is, the gross acquisition of self, the mind-made acquisition of self, and the formless acquisition of self—'these, Citta, are worldly conventions.' In the world, these are merely conventions, merely acknowledgements. Likewise, these are merely worldly expressions, merely paths of speech, merely usages, merely name-concepts. Thus the Blessed One, having previously spoken of the three acquisitions of self, now says, 'All this is merely usage.' Why? Because in the ultimate sense, there is no being. This world is empty, void.

Buddhānaṃ pana dve kathā sammutikathā ca paramatthakathā ca. Tattha “satto poso devo brahmā”tiādikā “sammutikathā” nāma. “Aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā khandhā dhātuyo āyatanāni satipaṭṭhānā sammappadhānā”tiādikā paramatthakathā nāma. Tattha yo sammutidesanāya “satto”ti [P 2.0383] vā “poso”ti vā “devo”ti vā “brahmā”ti vā vutte vijānituṃ paṭivijjhituṃ niyyātuṃ [M 1.0316] arahattajayaggāhaṃ gahetuṃ sakkoti, tassa bhagavā āditova “satto”ti vā “poso”ti vā “devo”ti vā “brahmā”ti vā katheti, yo paramatthadesanāya “anicca”nti vā “dukkha”nti vātiādīsu aññataraṃ sutvā vijānituṃ paṭivijjhituṃ niyyātuṃ arahattajayaggāhaṃ gahetuṃ sakkoti, tassa “anicca”nti vā “dukkha”nti vātiādīsu aññatarameva katheti. Tathā sammutikathāya [V 1.0285] bujjhanakasattassāpi na paṭhamaṃ paramatthakathaṃ katheti. Sammutikathāya pana bodhetvā pacchā paramatthakathaṃ katheti. Paramatthakathāya bujjhanakasattassāpi na paṭhamaṃ sammutikathaṃ katheti. Paramatthakathāya pana bodhetvā pacchā sammutikathaṃ katheti. Pakatiyā pana paṭhamameva paramatthakathaṃ kathentassa desanā lūkhākārā hoti, tasmā buddhā paṭhamaṃ sammutikathaṃ kathetvā pacchā paramatthakathaṃ kathenti. Sammutikathaṃ kathentāpi saccameva sabhāvameva amusāva kathenti. Paramatthakathaṃ kathentāpi saccameva sabhāvameva amusāva kathenti.

But the Buddhas have two discourses: conventional discourse and ultimate discourse. Therein, that which begins with 'a being, a person, a god, a brahmā' is named 'conventional discourse.' That which begins with 'impermanent, suffering, non-self, aggregates, elements, sense bases, foundations of mindfulness, right efforts' is named 'ultimate discourse.' Therein, for a person who is able to understand, to penetrate, to escape, and to grasp the banner of victory of Arahantship when 'a being,' or 'a person,' or 'a god,' or 'a brahmā' is spoken by means of the conventional teaching, the Blessed One speaks to them from the very beginning with 'a being,' or 'a person,' or 'a god,' or 'a brahmā.' For a person who is able to understand, to penetrate, to escape, and to grasp the banner of victory of Arahantship upon hearing one or another among 'impermanent,' 'suffering,' and so on, by means of the ultimate teaching, He speaks to them only of one or another among 'impermanent,' 'suffering,' and so on. Likewise, even to a being who is to be awakened by conventional discourse, He does not first teach the ultimate discourse. But having caused them to understand through conventional discourse, He afterwards teaches the ultimate discourse. Even to a being who is to be awakened by ultimate discourse, He does not first teach the conventional discourse. But having caused them to understand through ultimate discourse, He afterwards teaches the conventional discourse. But by nature, for one who teaches the ultimate discourse first, the teaching becomes harsh in character. Therefore, the Buddhas, having first taught the conventional discourse, afterwards teach the ultimate discourse. Even when teaching conventional discourse, they speak what is true, what is of its own nature, and what is not false. Even when teaching ultimate discourse, they speak what is true, what is of its own nature, and what is not false.

Duve saccāni akkhāsi, sambuddho vadataṃ varo;

Sammutiṃ paramatthañca, tatiyaṃ nūpalabbhati.

The Fully Enlightened One, the best of speakers, proclaimed two truths: conventional truth and ultimate truth. A third is not found.

Saṅketavacanaṃ saccaṃ, lokasammutikāraṇaṃ;

Paramatthavacanaṃ saccaṃ, dhammānaṃ bhūtalakkhaṇanti.

The speech of convention is true, being the reason for worldly convention; the speech of the ultimate is true, being the true characteristic of phenomena.

Yāhi tathāgato voharati aparāmasanti yāhi lokasamaññāhi lokaniruttīhi tathāgato taṇhāmānadiṭṭhiparāmāsānaṃ abhāvā aparāmasanto voharatīti desanaṃ vinivaṭṭetvā arahattanikūṭena niṭṭhāpesi. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

'By which the Tathāgata speaks without grasping' means: by whichever worldly conventions and worldly expressions the Tathāgata speaks, He does so without grasping, due to the absence of the misapprehensions of craving, conceit, and views. Thus, having turned the discourse back, He concluded it with the pinnacle of Arahantship. The remainder everywhere has a plain meaning.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Thus, in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya,

Poṭṭhapādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta is concluded.

10. Subhasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Subha Sutta

Subhamāṇavakavatthuvaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Story of the Young Man Subha

444. Evaṃ [P 2.0384][V 1.0286][M 1.0317] me sutaṃ…pe… sāvatthiyanti subhasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ anuttānapadavaṇṇanā. Aciraparinibbute bhagavatīti aciraṃ parinibbute bhagavati, parinibbānato uddhaṃ māsamatte kāle. Nidānavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva bhagavato pattacīvaraṃ ādāya āgantvā khīravirecanaṃ pivitvā vihāre nisinnadivasaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Todeyyaputtoti todeyyabrāhmaṇassa putto, so kira sāvatthiyā avidūre tudigāmo nāma atthi, tassa adhipatittā todeyyoti saṅkhyaṃ gato. Mahaddhano pana hoti pañcacattālīsakoṭivibhavo, paramamaccharī – “dadato bhogānaṃ aparikkhayo nāma natthī”ti cintetvā kassaci kiñci na deti, puttampi āha –

Thus have I heard… at Sāvatthī… is the Subha Sutta. Therein, this is the commentary on the terms that are not obvious. ‘Not long after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna’ means: when the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna not long ago, in the period of about a month after the Parinibbāna. In accordance with the method already stated in the commentary on the introduction, this was said referring to the day when, having taken the Blessed One’s bowl and robe and come, having drunk a milk purgative, he was sitting in the monastery. ‘The son of Todeyya’ means the son of the brahmin Todeyya. It is said that not far from Sāvatthī there is a village named Tudigāma. Because of being its chief, he came to be known as Todeyya. He was of great wealth, possessing a fortune of forty-five crores, and was extremely miserly. Thinking, ‘For one who gives, there is no such thing as the non-exhaustion of wealth,’ he gave nothing to anyone. He also instructed his son:

“Añjanānaṃ khayaṃ disvā, vammikānañca sañcayaṃ;

Madhūnañca samāhāraṃ, paṇḍito gharamāvase”ti.

444. “Seeing the depletion of collyrium, the accumulation of anthills, and the gathering of honey, a wise person should dwell at home.”

Evaṃ adānameva sikkhāpetvā kāyassa bhedā tasmiṃyeva ghare sunakho hutvā nibbatto. Subho taṃ sunakhaṃ ativiya piyāyati. Attano bhuñjanakabhattaṃyeva bhojeti, ukkhipitvā varasayane sayāpeti. Atha bhagavā ekadivasaṃ nikkhante māṇave taṃ gharaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Sunakho bhagavantaṃ disvā bhukkāraṃ karonto bhagavato samīpaṃ gato. Tato naṃ bhagavā avoca “todeyya tvaṃ pubbepi maṃ ‘bho, bho’ti paribhavitvā sunakho jāto, idānipi bhukkāraṃ katvā avīciṃ gamissasī”ti. Sunakho taṃ kathaṃ sutvā vippaṭisārī hutvā uddhanantare chārikāya nipanno, manussā naṃ ukkhipitvā sayane sayāpetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu[P 2.0385].

Having thus taught only non-giving, with the breakup of the body, he was reborn as a dog in that very house. Subha was extremely fond of that dog. He fed it his own meal and, lifting it up, had it sleep on an excellent bed. Then one day, when the young man had gone out, the Blessed One entered that house for alms-food. The dog, seeing the Blessed One, approached him, barking. Then the Blessed One said to it, “Todeyya, in a former time you disrespected me, saying ‘bho, bho,’ and were born a dog. Now also, by barking, you will go to Avīci.” Hearing these words, the dog became remorseful and lay down in the ashes of the hearth. The people were unable to lift it and make it sleep on the bed.

Subho āgantvā “kenāyaṃ sunakho sayanā oropito”ti āha. Manussā “na kenacī”ti [V 1.0287] vatvā taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesuṃ. Māṇavo sutvā “mama pitā brahmaloke nibbatto, samaṇo pana gotamo me pitaraṃ sunakhaṃ karoti yaṃ kiñci esa mukhārūḷhaṃ bhāsatī”ti kujjhitvā bhagavantaṃ musāvādena [M 1.0318] codetukāmo vihāraṃ gantvā taṃ pavattiṃ pucchi. Bhagavā tassa tatheva vatvā avisaṃvādanatthaṃ āha – “atthi pana te, māṇava, pitarā na akkhātaṃ dhana”nti. Atthi, bho gotama, satasahassagghanikā suvaṇṇamālā, satasahassagghanikā suvaṇṇapādukā, satasahassagghanikā suvaṇṇapāti, satasahassañca kahāpaṇanti. Gaccha taṃ sunakhaṃ appodakaṃ madhupāyāsaṃ bhojetvā sayanaṃ āropetvā īsakaṃ niddaṃ okkantakāle puccha, sabbaṃ te ācikkhissati, atha naṃ jāneyyāsi – “pitā me eso”ti. So tathā akāsi. Sunakho sabbaṃ ācikkhi, tadā naṃ – “pitā me”ti ñatvā bhagavati pasannacitto gantvā bhagavantaṃcuddasa pañhe pucchitvā vissajjanapariyosāne bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gato, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “subho māṇavo todeyyaputto”ti. Sāvatthiyaṃ paṭivasatīti attano bhogagāmato āgantvā vasati.

Subha, upon returning, asked, “By whom was this dog taken down from its bed?” The people, saying, “By no one,” related the incident. Hearing this, the young man became angry, thinking, “My father was reborn in the Brahma world, but the ascetic Gotama makes my father a dog. This one says whatever comes to his mouth.” Desiring to accuse the Blessed One of false speech, he went to the monastery and asked about the incident. The Blessed One, having spoken to him just as before, said for the purpose of demonstrating the infallibility of his words, “But, young man, is there any wealth not told of by your father?” “There is, Venerable Gotama: a golden garland worth a hundred thousand, golden sandals worth a hundred thousand, a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand, and one hundred thousand kahāpaṇas.” “Go, feed that dog honeyed milk-rice with little water, place it on the bed, and when it has slightly fallen asleep, ask. It will tell you everything. Then you will know of it, ‘This is my father.’” He did so. The dog told everything. Then, knowing of it, “This is my father,” he became one with a confident mind in the Blessed One. Having gone to the Blessed One and asked fourteen questions, at the conclusion of the answers, he went for refuge to the Blessed One. Referring to him, it was said, “Subha the young man, son of Todeyya.” ‘He resides in Sāvatthī’ means: having come from his village of enjoyment, he resides there.

445-446. Aññataraṃ māṇavakaṃ āmantesīti satthari parinibbute “ānandatthero kirassa pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā āgato, mahājano taṃ dassanatthāya upasaṅkamatī”ti sutvā “vihāraṃ kho pana gantvā mahājanamajjhe na sakkā sukhena paṭisanthāraṃ vā kātuṃ, dhammakathaṃ vā sotuṃ gehaṃ āgataṃyeva naṃ disvā sukhena paṭisanthāraṃ karissāmi, ekā ca me kaṅkhā atthi, tampi naṃ pucchissāmī”ti cintetvā aññataraṃ māṇavakaṃ āmantesi. Appābādhantiādīsu ābādhoti visabhāgavedanā vuccati, yā ekadese uppajjitvā cattāro iriyāpathe ayapaṭṭena ābandhitvā viya gaṇhati, tassā abhāvaṃ pucchāti vadati. Appātaṅkoti [P 2.0386] kicchajīvitakaro rogo vuccati, tassāpi abhāvaṃ pucchāti vadati. Gilānasseva ca uṭṭhānaṃ nāma garukaṃ hoti, kāye balaṃ na hoti, tasmā niggelaññabhāvañca balañca pucchāti vadati. Phāsuvihāranti gamanaṭhānanisajjasayanesu catūsu iriyāpathesu sukhavihāraṃ pucchāti vadati. Athassa pucchitabbākāraṃ dassento “subho”tiādimāha.

‘He addressed a certain young man’ means: When the Teacher had attained Parinibbāna, having heard, ‘It is said that the Elder Ānanda has come, having taken his bowl and robe; a great crowd of people is approaching to see him,’ he thought, ‘Having gone to the monastery, in the midst of a great crowd of people, it is not possible to make a pleasant exchange of greetings or to hear a Dhamma talk. Seeing him only when he has come to my house, I will be able to make a pleasant exchange of greetings. And I have a certain doubt; I will ask him about that doubt too.’ Thinking thus, he addressed a certain young man. In the phrases beginning with ‘with little illness,’ `ābādha` is said to be a disagreeable feeling, which, arising in one part of the body, seizes the four postures as if having bound them with an iron plate; he says, ‘Ask about its absence.’ `Ātaṅka` is said to be a disease that makes living difficult; he says, ‘Ask about its absence too.’ For one who is sick, getting up is heavy, and there is no strength in the body; therefore, he says, ‘Ask about the state of being without illness and about strength.’ `Phāsuvihāra` means: he says, ‘Ask about dwelling comfortably in the four postures: going, standing, sitting, and lying down.’ Then, showing him the manner in which to ask, he spoke the words beginning with ‘Subha…’.

447. Kālañca samayañca upādāyāti kālañca samayañca paññāya gahetvā upadhāretvāti attho. Sace amhākaṃ sve gamanakālo bhavissati, kāye balamattā ceva pharissati, gamanapaccayā ca añño aphāsuvihāro [M 1.0319] na bhavissati, athetaṃ kālañca gamanakāraṇasamavāyasaṅkhātaṃ samayañca upadhāretvā – “api eva nāma sve āgaccheyyāmā”ti vuttaṃ hoti.

447. ‘Taking into account the time and the occasion’ means: having grasped and considered with wisdom the time and the congruence of conditions. If tomorrow will be the time for us to go, and if a measure of strength will pervade the body, and if there will not be any other uncomfortable state on account of the journey, then, having considered that time and this occasion—reckoned as the combination of causes for going—it is said, ‘Perhaps we might come tomorrow.’

448. Cetakena [V 1.0288] bhikkhunāti cetiraṭṭhe jātattā cetakoti evaṃ laddhanāmena. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyanti bho, ānanda, dasabalassa ko nāma ābādho ahosi, kiṃ bhagavā paribhuñji. Api ca satthu parinibbānena tumhākaṃ soko udapādi, satthā nāma na kevalaṃ tumhākaṃyeva parinibbuto, sadevakassa lokassa mahājāni, ko dāni añño maraṇā muccissati, yatra so sadevakassa lokassa aggapuggalo parinibbuto, idāni kaṃ aññaṃ disvā maccurājā lajjissatīti evamādinā nayena maraṇapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā therassa hiyyo pītabhesajjānurūpaṃ āhāraṃ datvā bhattakiccāvasāne ekamantaṃ nisīdi.

448. ‘By the monk from Cetaka’: Because he was born in the Ceti country, he was thus known by the name Cetaka. ‘A friendly and memorable conversation’: ‘Venerable Ānanda, what was the illness of the One of Ten Powers? What did the Blessed One partake of? Moreover, did not grief arise in you due to the Teacher’s final Nibbāna? The one called the Teacher did not attain final Nibbāna only for you; it is a great loss for the world with its gods. When even that foremost individual in the world with its gods has attained final Nibbāna, who else now will be freed from death? Now, seeing what other person will the King of Death be ashamed?’ In this manner, after concluding a friendly and memorable conversation connected with death, having given the elder food suitable for the medicine taken the previous day, he sat down at one side at the conclusion of the meal duties.

Upaṭṭhāko santikāvacaroti upaṭṭhāko hutvā santikāvacaro, na randhagavesī. Na vīmaṃsanādhippāyo. Samīpacārīti idaṃ purimapadasseva vevacanaṃ. Yesaṃ so bhavaṃ gotamoti kasmā pucchati? Tassa kira evaṃ ahosi “yesu dhammesu bhavaṃ gotamo imaṃ lokaṃ patiṭṭhapesi, te tassa accayena naṭṭhā nu kho, dharanti nu kho, sace dharanti, ānando jānissati, handa naṃ pucchāmī”ti, tasmā pucchi.

‘An attendant who stays close’: one who, being an attendant, stays close; not one who seeks for faults, nor one with the intention to investigate. ‘One who stays nearby’ is a synonym for the previous term. Why does he ask the question beginning, ‘Of which [teachings] was the Venerable Gotama...’? It is said that this thought occurred to him: ‘Those teachings in which the Venerable Gotama established this world—have they been lost with his passing, or do they still exist? If they still exist, Ānanda will know. Well then, I shall ask him.’ Therefore, he asked.

449. Athassa [P 2.0387] thero tīṇi piṭakāni tīhi khandhehi saṅgahetvā dassento “tiṇṇaṃ kho”tiādimāha. Māṇavo saṅkhittena kathitaṃ asallakkhento – “vitthārato pucchissāmī”ti cintetvā “katamesaṃ tiṇṇa”ntiādimāha.

449. Then the elder, showing how the three Piṭakas were included in the three aggregates, said, ‘Of the three…’ and so on. The young man, not comprehending what was said in brief, thought, ‘I will ask in detail,’ and said, ‘Which three?’ and so on.

Sīlakkhandhavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Aggregate of Morality

450-453. Tato therena “ariyassa sīlakkhandhassā”ti tesu dassitesu puna “katamo pana so, bho ānanda, ariyo sīlakkhandho”ti ekekaṃ pucchi. Theropissa buddhuppādaṃ dassetvā tantidhammaṃ desento anukkamena bhagavatā vuttanayeneva sabbaṃ vissajjesi. Tattha atthi [M 1.0320] cevettha uttarikaraṇīyanti ettha bhagavato sāsane na sīlameva sāro, kevalañhetaṃ patiṭṭhāmattameva hoti. Ito uttari pana aññampi kattabbaṃ atthi yevāti dassesi. Ito bahiddhāti buddhasāsanato bahiddhā.

Then, when the elder had pointed out 'the noble aggregate of morality' among those teachings, he was again asked about each one: 'But what, Venerable Ānanda, is that noble aggregate of morality?' The elder, for his part, having shown the arising of a Buddha and teaching the Dhamma of the textual lineage, answered everything sequentially in the very manner spoken by the Blessed One. Therein, the phrase 'There is indeed something further to be done here' shows that in the Blessed One's dispensation, morality alone is not the essence; it is merely a foundation. Beyond this, there is indeed something more to be done—thus he showed. 'Outside of this' means outside of the Buddha's dispensation.

Samādhikkhandhavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Aggregate of Concentration

454. Kathañca[V 1.0289], māṇava, bhikkhu indriyesu guttadvāro hotīti idamāyasmā ānando “katamo pana so, bho ānanda, ariyo samādhikkhandho”ti evaṃ samādhikkhandhaṃ puṭṭhopi ye te “sīlasampanno indriyesu guttadvāro satisampajaññena samannāgato santuṭṭho”ti evaṃ sīlānantaraṃ indriyasaṃvarādayo sīlasamādhīnaṃ antare ubhinnampi upakārakadhammā uddiṭṭhā, te niddisitvā samādhikkhandhaṃ dassetukāmo ārabhi. Ettha ca rūpajjhānāneva āgatāni, na arūpajjhānāni, ānetvā pana dīpetabbāni. Catutthajjhānena hi asaṅgahitā arūpasamāpatti nāma natthiyeva.

454. Regarding the passage, 'And how, young man, is a monk one who has guarded doors in the sense faculties?', the Venerable Ānanda, although asked about the aggregate of concentration thus, 'But what, venerable Ānanda, is that noble aggregate of concentration?', desiring to show the aggregate of concentration, began by explaining in detail those supportive factors for both virtue and concentration that were pointed out in brief between virtue and concentration, immediately after virtue, such as sense-restraint and so forth, in the passage, 'accomplished in virtue, one who has guarded doors in the sense faculties, endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension, content'. And here, only the form-sphere absorptions have come directly, not the formless-sphere absorptions; however, they should be brought in and explained. Indeed, there is no such thing as a formless attainment that is not included by the fourth absorption.

471-480. Atthi cevettha uttarikaraṇīyanti ettha bhagavato sāsane na cittekaggatāmattakeneva pariyosānappatti nāma atthi, itopi uttari pana aññaṃ kattabbaṃ atthi yevāti dasseti. Natthi cevettha uttarikaraṇīyanti ettha bhagavato sāsane ito uttari kātabbaṃ nāma natthiyeva, arahattapariyosānañhi bhagavato sāsananti dasseti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

By the text, 'Here, there is indeed something further to be done,' he shows that in this Dispensation of the Blessed One, there is no such thing as reaching the culmination merely by one-pointedness of mind; beyond this, there is still another task to be done. By the text, 'Here, there is nothing further to be done,' he shows that in this Dispensation of the Blessed One, beyond this fruition of Arahantship, there is no further task to be done; indeed, the Dispensation of the Blessed One has the fruition of Arahantship as its culmination. In all instances, the remaining text has a plain meaning.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Thus in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya.

Subhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Subha Sutta is concluded.

11. Kevaṭṭasuttavaṇṇanā

11. Exposition of the Kevaṭṭa Sutta

Kevaṭṭagahapatiputtavatthuvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Story of Kevaṭṭa, the Householder's Son

481. Evaṃ [P 2.0388][V 1.0290][M 1.0321] me sutaṃ…pe… nāḷandāyanti kevaṭṭasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ apubbapadavaṇṇanā. Pāvārikambavaneti pāvārikassa ambavane. Kevaṭṭoti idaṃ tassa gahapatiputtassa nāmaṃ. So kira cattālīsakoṭidhano gahapatimahāsālo ativiya saddho pasanno ahosi. So saddhādhikattāyeva “sace eko bhikkhu aḍḍhamāsantarena vā māsantarena vā saṃvaccharena vā ākāse uppatitvā vividhāni pāṭihāriyāni dasseyya, sabbo jano ativiya pasīdeyya. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ bhagavantaṃ yācitvā pāṭihāriyakaraṇatthāya ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ anujānāpeyya”nti cintetvā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāha.

481. The sutta beginning 'Thus have I heard... at Nāḷandā' is the Kevaṭṭasutta. Therein, this is the exposition of words not previously explained. 'In Pāvārika's mango grove' means in the mango grove of Pāvārika. 'Kevaṭṭa' is the name of that householder's son. He, it is said, was a great householder of substantial wealth, possessing forty crores, and was exceedingly faithful and devoted. Precisely because of his excessive faith, he thought thus: 'If a certain monk, either after half a month, or after a month, or once a year, having flown up into the sky, were to display various miracles, all the people would become exceedingly devoted. It would be good if I, having requested the Blessed One, were to get him to permit a certain monk for the purpose of performing a miracle.' Having thought thus, he approached the Blessed One and spoke thus.

Tattha iddhāti samiddhā phītāti nānābhaṇḍaussannatāya vuddhippattā. Ākiṇṇamanussāti aṃsakūṭena aṃsakūṭaṃ paharitvā viya vicarantehi manussehi ākiṇṇā. Samādisatūti āṇāpetu ṭhānantare ṭhapetu. Uttarimanussadhammāti uttarimanussānaṃ dhammato, dasakusalasaṅkhātato vā manussadhammato uttari. Bhiyyosomattāyāti pakatiyāpi pajjalitapadīpo telasnehaṃ labhitvā viya atirekappamāṇena abhippasīdissati. Na kho ahanti bhagavā rājagahaseṭṭhivatthusmiṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññapesi, tasmā “na kho aha”ntiādimāha.

Therein, `iddhā` means prosperous. `Phītā` means developed due to an abundance of various goods. `Ākiṇṇamanussā` means crowded with people moving about as if striking one shoulder-tip with another. `Samādisatū` means 'may he command', 'may he appoint to a position'. `Uttarimanussadhammā` means 'from the state of superior humans (i.e., meditators and noble ones)', or 'superior to the human state which is reckoned as the ten wholesome actions'. `Bhiyyosomattāya` means 'they will become exceedingly devoted to an excessive degree', just as a lamp, already burning by its nature, burns even more brightly upon receiving oil-fuel. Regarding 'Not I...', the Blessed One laid down a training rule in the story of the Rājagaha merchant; therefore, he spoke the words beginning with 'Not I...'.

482. Na dhaṃsemīti na guṇavināsanena dhaṃsemi, sīlabhedaṃ pāpetvā anupubbena uccaṭṭhānato otārento nīcaṭṭhāne [P 2.0389] na ṭhapemi, atha kho ahaṃ buddhasāsanassa vuddhiṃ paccāsīsanto kathemīti dasseti. Tatiyampi khoti yāvatatiyaṃ buddhānaṃ kathaṃ paṭibāhitvā kathetuṃ visahanto nāma natthi. Ayaṃ pana bhagavatā saddhiṃ vissāsiko vissāsaṃ vaḍḍhetvā vallabho hutvā atthakāmosmīti tikkhattuṃ kathesi.

482. By 'I do not destroy,' he shows: 'I do not destroy by means of destroying virtue; having caused a breach of virtue, I do not, while gradually bringing one down from a high position, place them in a low position. Rather, I speak while hoping for the growth of the Buddha's Dispensation.' Regarding 'And for a third time...': There is no one who dares to speak up to a third time, having contradicted the words of the Buddhas. However, because this layman was intimate with the Blessed One, he, having increased his intimacy and become a favorite, spoke three times, thinking, 'I am one who desires the welfare (of the Dispensation).'

Iddhipāṭihāriyavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Miracle of Psychic Power

483-484. Atha [V 1.0291] bhagavā ayaṃ upāsako mayi paṭibāhantepi punappunaṃ yācatiyeva. “Handassa pāṭihāriyakaraṇe ādīnavaṃ dassemī”ti cintetvā [M 1.0322] “tīṇi kho”tiādimāha. Tattha amāhaṃ bhikkhunti amuṃ ahaṃ bhikkhuṃ. Gandhārīti gandhārena nāma isinā katā, gandhāraraṭṭhe vā uppannā vijjā. Tattha kira bahū isayo vasiṃsu, tesu ekena katā vijjāti adhippāyo. Aṭṭīyāmīti aṭṭo pīḷito viya homi. Harāyāmīti lajjāmi. Jigucchāmīti gūthaṃ disvā viya jigucchaṃ uppādemi.

Then the Blessed One, thinking, "This lay follower keeps requesting again and again despite my forbidding it. Come now, I shall show him the danger in performing a miracle," said the words beginning with, "There are three..." Therein, as for `amāhaṃ bhikkhuṃ`, it means: that monk, I. As for `gandhārī`, it is a science created by a sage named Gandhāra, or a science that arose in the Gandhāra country. It is said that many sages lived there; the meaning is that it is a science created by one of them. As for `aṭṭīyāmi`, it means: I am as if oppressed and afflicted. As for `harāyāmi`, it means: I am ashamed. As for `jigucchāmi`, it means: I produce revulsion, as if upon seeing excrement.

Ādesanāpāṭihāriyavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Miracle of Disclosure

485. Parasattānanti aññesaṃ sattānaṃ. Dutiyaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Ādisatīti katheti. Cetasikanti somanassadomanassaṃ adhippetaṃ. Evampi te manoti evaṃ tava mano somanassito vā domanassito vā kāmavitakkādisampayutto vā. Dutiyaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Itipi te cittanti iti tava cittaṃ, idañcidañca atthaṃ cintayamānaṃ pavattatīti attho. Maṇikā nāma vijjāti cintāmaṇīti evaṃ laddhanāmā loke ekā vijjā atthi. Tāya paresaṃ cittaṃ jānātīti dīpeti.

485. As for 'parasattānaṃ', it means: of other beings. The second term is a synonym for that very one. As for 'ādisati', it means: he tells. As for 'cetasikaṃ', joy and displeasure are intended. As for 'evampi te mano', it means: thus is your mind, either endowed with joy or endowed with displeasure, or associated with sensual thought, etc. The second phrase is a synonym for that very one. As for 'itipi te cittaṃ', it means: thus is your mind; the meaning is that it proceeds while thinking of this and that matter. As for 'maṇikā nāma vijjā', there is in the world a certain science that has obtained the name 'cintāmaṇi' (wish-fulfilling gem). It indicates that by that science one can know the minds of others.

Anusāsanīpāṭihāriyavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Miracle of Instruction

486. Evaṃ vitakkethāti nekkhammavitakkādayo evaṃ pavattentā vitakketha. Mā evaṃ vitakkayitthāti evaṃ kāmavitakkādayo pavattentā mā vitakkayittha. Evaṃ manasi karothāti evaṃ aniccasaññameva, dukkhasaññādīsu vā aññataraṃ manasi karotha. Mā [P 2.0390] evanti “nicca”ntiādinā nayena mā manasi karittha. Idanti idaṃ pañcakāmaguṇikarāgaṃ pajahatha. Idaṃ upasampajjāti idaṃ catumaggaphalappabhedaṃ lokuttaradhammameva upasampajja pāpuṇitvā nipphādetvā viharatha. Iti bhagavā iddhividhaṃ iddhipāṭihāriyanti dasseti, parassa cittaṃ ñatvā kathanaṃ ādesanāpāṭihāriyanti. Sāvakānañca buddhānañca satataṃ dhammadesanā anusāsanīpāṭihāriyanti.

486. 'Evaṃ vitakkethā' means: you should think thus, developing thoughts such as those of renunciation. 'Mā evaṃ vitakkayitthā' means: do not think thus, developing thoughts such as those of sensuality. 'Evaṃ manasi karothā' means: you should attend thus, to the perception of impermanence, or to one among the perceptions of suffering, etc. 'Mā evaṃ' means: do not attend thus, in the way of 'permanent,' etc. 'Idaṃ' means: abandon this lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Idaṃ upasampajjā' means: having attained this, dwell—that is, having reached, attained, and accomplished this supramundane Dhamma, differentiated as the four paths and fruits, you should dwell. Thus, the Blessed One shows the kinds of psychic power as the miracle of psychic power; the telling after knowing another's mind as the miracle of disclosure; and the constant teaching of the Dhamma by disciples and Buddhas as the miracle of instruction.

Tattha [V 1.0292] iddhipāṭihāriyena anusāsanīpāṭihāriyaṃ mahāmoggallānassa āciṇṇaṃ, ādesanāpāṭihāriyena anusāsanīpāṭihāriyaṃ dhammasenāpatissa. Devadatte saṃghaṃ bhinditvā pañca bhikkhusatāni gahetvā gayāsīse buddhalīḷāya tesaṃ dhammaṃ desante hi bhagavatā pesitesu dvīsu aggasāvakesu dhammasenāpati tesaṃ cittācāraṃ ñatvā dhammaṃ desesi[M 1.0323], therassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pañcasatā bhikkhū sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Atha nesaṃ mahāmoggallāno vikubbanaṃ dassetvā dassetvā dhammaṃ desesi, taṃ sutvā sabbe arahattaphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Atha dvepi mahānāgā pañca bhikkhusatāni gahetvā vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā veḷuvanamevāgamiṃsu. Anusāsanīpāṭihāriyaṃ pana buddhānaṃ satataṃ dhammadesanā, tesu iddhipāṭihāriyaādesanāpāṭihāriyāni saupārambhāni sadosāni, addhānaṃ na tiṭṭhanti, addhānaṃ atiṭṭhanato na niyyanti. Anusāsanīpāṭihāriyaṃ anupārambhaṃ niddosaṃ, addhānaṃ tiṭṭhati, addhānaṃ tiṭṭhanato niyyāti. Tasmā bhagavā iddhipāṭihāriyañca ādesanāpāṭihāriyañca garahati, anusāsanīpāṭihāriyaṃyeva pasaṃsati.

Therein, the miracle of instruction accompanied by the miracle of psychic power was the practiced habit of Mahāmoggallāna, and the miracle of instruction accompanied by the miracle of disclosure was that of the General of the Dhamma. Indeed, when Devadatta split the Saṅgha and took five hundred monks to Gayāsīsa, teaching them the Dhamma with the Buddha's graceful demeanor, the General of the Dhamma, among the two chief disciples sent by the Blessed One, knowing the disposition of their minds, taught them the Dhamma. Having heard the elder’s teaching, the five hundred monks were established in the fruit of stream-entry. Then Mahāmoggallāna, showing various transformations again and again, taught them the Dhamma. Having heard that, all were established in the fruit of arahantship. Then both great spiritual heroes, taking the five hundred monks, rose into the air and returned to the Veḷuvana monastery. The miracle of instruction, however, is the constant teaching of the Dhamma of the Buddhas. Among these, the miracles of psychic power and disclosure are subject to reproach and are faulty; they do not last for a long time, and because they do not last for a long time, they do not lead out from the round of suffering. The miracle of instruction is not subject to reproach and is faultless; it lasts for a long time, and because it lasts for a long time, it leads out from the round of suffering. Therefore, the Blessed One censures the miracles of psychic power and disclosure, but praises only the miracle of instruction.

Bhūtanirodhesakavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of the Monk Who Sought the Cessation of the Elements

487. Bhūtapubbanti idaṃ kasmā bhagavatā āraddhaṃ. Iddhipāṭihāriyaādesanāpāṭihāriyānaṃ aniyyānikabhāvadassanatthaṃ, anusāsanīpāṭihāriyasseva niyyānikabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Api ca sabbabuddhānaṃ mahābhūtapariyesako nāmeko bhikkhu hotiyeva. Yo mahābhūte pariyesanto yāva brahmalokā vicaritvā vissajjetāraṃ alabhitvā āgamma [P 2.0391] buddhameva pucchitvā nikkaṅkho hoti. Tasmā buddhānaṃ mahantabhāvappakāsanatthaṃ, idañca kāraṇaṃ paṭicchannaṃ, atha naṃ vivaṭaṃ katvā desentopi bhagavā “bhūtapubba”ntiādimāha.

487. Why did the Blessed One begin with “In the past”? To show that the miracle of psychic power and the miracle of disclosure are not conducive to liberation, while the miracle of instruction alone is conducive to liberation. Moreover, for all Buddhas, there is always one monk named the Seeker of the Great Elements. He, seeking the great elements, wandering as far as the Brahma-world, not finding anyone who could answer, returned and questioned the Buddha himself, thereby becoming free from doubt. Therefore, to reveal the greatness of the Buddhas, and because this reason was hidden, the Blessed One, revealing it and teaching it, spoke the words beginning with “In the past.”

Tattha kattha nu khoti kismiṃ ṭhāne kiṃ āgamma kiṃ pattassa te anavasesā appavattivasena nirujjhanti. Mahābhūtakathā panesā sabbākārena visuddhimagge vuttā, tasmā sā tatova gahetabbā.

Herein, 'where indeed?' means: In what place, on account of what, having attained what, do those great elements cease without remainder by way of non-reoccurrence? Moreover, this discourse on the great elements is explained in all its aspects in the Visuddhimagga; therefore, it should be taken from there.

488. Devayāniyo maggoti pāṭiyekko devalokagamanamaggo nāma natthi, iddhividhañāṇasseva panetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tena hesa yāva brahmalokāpi kāyena vasaṃ vattento devalokaṃ yāti. Tasmā “taṃ devayāniyo maggo”ti vuttaṃ. Yena cātumahārājikāti samīpe ṭhitampi bhagavantaṃ apucchitvā dhammatāya codito devatā mahānubhāvāti maññamāno upasaṅkami. Mayampi kho, bhikkhu, na jānāmāti buddhavisaye pañhaṃ [M 1.0324] pucchitā devatā na jānanti[V 1.0293], tenevamāhaṃsu. Atha kho so bhikkhu “mama imaṃ pañhaṃ na kathetuṃ na labbhā, sīghaṃ kathethā”ti tā devatā ajjhottharati, punappunaṃ pucchati, tā “ajjhottharati no ayaṃ bhikkhu, handa naṃ hatthato mocessāmā”ti cintetvā “atthi kho bhikkhu cattāro mahārājāno”tiādimāhaṃsu. Tattha abhikkantatarāti atikkamma kantatarā. Paṇītatarāti vaṇṇayasaissariyādīhi uttamatarā etena nayena sabbavāresu attho veditabbo.

488. 'The path leading to the devas' does not mean a separate path for going to the deva world; rather, it is a designation for the knowledge of the kinds of psychic power. For by this, making his will prevail with his body, he goes to the deva world, even as far as the Brahma-world. Therefore, it is called 'the path leading to the devas'. Wherefore he went to the Cātumahārājika devas: without asking the Blessed One who was staying nearby, urged by the natural order of things, he approached, thinking, "The devas are of great power." As for "We too, monk, do not know": the devas, being asked a question that was in the domain of the Buddha, did not know; therefore, they spoke thus. Then that monk overwhelms those devas, saying, "It is not permissible not to answer this question of mine. Answer quickly!" He asks again and again. Those devas, thinking, "This monk overwhelms us. Come, let us free him from our hands," spoke the words beginning with, "There are, monk, the Four Great Kings..." Therein, 'more excellent' means surpassing and more pleasing. 'More sublime' means more superior in appearance, retinue, sovereignty, and so on. By this method, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

491-493. Ayaṃ pana viseso – sakko kira devarājā cintesi “ayaṃ pañho buddhavisayo, na sakkā aññena vissajjituṃ, ayañca bhikkhu aggiṃ pahāya khajjopanakaṃ dhamanto viya, bheriṃ pahāya udaraṃ vādento viya ca, loke aggapuggalaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ pahāya devatā pucchanto vicarati, pesemi naṃ satthusantika”nti. Tato punadeva so cintesi “sudūrampi gantvā satthu santikeva nikkaṅkho bhavissati[P 2.0392]. Atthi ceva puggalo nāmesa, thokaṃ tāva āhiṇḍanto kilamatu pacchā jānissatī”ti. Tato taṃ “ahampi kho”tiādimāha. Brahmayāniyopi devayāniyasadisova. Devayāniyamaggoti vā brahmayāniyamaggoti vā dhammasetūti vā ekacittakkhaṇikaappanāti vā sanniṭṭhānikacetanāti vā mahaggatacittanti vā abhiññāñāṇanti vā sabbametaṃ iddhividhañāṇasseva nāmaṃ.

However, this is the distinction: Sakka, the king of the devas, it is said, thought: “This question is within the Buddha’s domain; it cannot be answered by another. And this monk, like one who, having abandoned a fire, blows on a firefly, or like one who, having abandoned a great drum, strikes his belly, wanders about questioning devas after abandoning the foremost person in the world, the Perfectly Enlightened One. I shall send him to the Teacher’s presence.” Then again he thought, “Even having gone very far, only in the Teacher’s presence will he become free from doubt. Such a person indeed exists. Let him wander a little and get tired for now; later he will know.” Then he said to him the words beginning with, “I too…” The path to the Brahma-world is also similar to the path to the deva world. Whether it is called 'the path leading to the devas', or 'the path leading to the Brahma-world', or 'the bridge of Dhamma', or 'absorption in a single moment of consciousness', or 'decisive intention', or 'sublime consciousness', or 'the knowledge of the higher powers'—all this is simply a name for the knowledge of the kinds of psychic power.

494. Pubbanimittanti āgamanapubbabhāge nimittaṃ sūriyassa udayato aruṇuggaṃ viya. Tasmā idāneva brahmā āgamissati, evaṃ mayaṃ jānāmāti dīpayiṃsu. Pāturahosīti pākaṭo ahosi. Atha kho so brahmā tena bhikkhunā puṭṭho attano avisayabhāvaṃ ñatvā sacāhaṃ “na jānāmī”ti vakkhāmi, ime maṃ paribhavissanti, atha jānanto viya yaṃ kiñci kathessāmi, ayaṃ me bhikkhu veyyākaraṇena anāraddhacitto vādaṃ āropessati. “Ahamasmi bhikkhu brahmā”tiādīni pana me bhaṇantassa na koci vacanaṃ saddahissati. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ vikkhepaṃ katvā imaṃ bhikkhuṃ satthusantikaṃyeva peseyyanti cintetvā “ahamasmi bhikkhu brahmā”tiādimāha.

494. 'Previous sign' refers to a sign in the preliminary stage of an arrival, like the dawn before the rising of the sun. Therefore, they indicated: "Just now Brahmā will come; thus we know." 'He appeared' means he became manifest. Then that Brahmā, being questioned by the monk and realizing it was not his domain, thought: "If I say, 'I do not know,' these Brahmās will look down on me. Or if, pretending to know, I say something, this monk, unpacified by my explanation, will bring up a point of contention. And when I say, 'I am Brahmā, monk,' my words will indeed be believed. What if I, having created a diversion, were to send this monk to the Teacher's presence?" Having thought thus, he spoke the words beginning with, "I am Brahmā, monk..."

495-496. Ekamantaṃ [M 1.0325] apanetvāti kasmā evamakāsi? Kuhakattā. Bahiddhā pariyeṭṭhinti telatthiko vālikaṃ nippīḷiyamāno viya yāva brahmalokā bahiddhā pariyesanaṃ āpajjati.

'Having led him to one side'—why did he do so? Because of being a deceiver. 'An external search'—like one who wants oil and squeezes sand, he undertakes an external search, apart from the Blessed One, as far as the Brahma-world.

497. Sakuṇanti kākaṃ vā kulalaṃ vā. Na kho eso, bhikkhu, pañho evaṃ pucchitabboti [V 1.0294] idaṃ bhagavā yasmā padesenesa pañho pucchitabbo, ayañca kho bhikkhu anupādinnakepi gahetvā nippadesato pucchati, tasmā paṭisedheti. Āciṇṇaṃ kiretaṃ buddhānaṃ, pucchāmūḷhassa janassa pucchāya dosaṃ dassetvā pucchaṃ sikkhāpetvā pucchāvissajjanaṃ. Kasmā? Pucchituṃ ajānitvā paripucchanto duviññāpayo hoti. Pañhaṃ sikkhāpento pana “kattha āpo cā”tiādimāha.

497. 'A bird' means a crow or a hawk. Regarding the statement, 'Indeed, monk, this question should not be asked thus,' the Blessed One forbids it. This is because this question should be asked partially, whereas this monk asks it without limitation, including even that which is unappropriated. Therefore, He forbids it. It is said to be the custom of the Buddhas to point out the fault in the question to a person who is confused about it, teach them how to ask, and then give the answer. Why? Because one who asks without knowing how to ask is difficult to make understand. Then, teaching the question, He spoke the words beginning, 'Where do water...'

498. Tattha na gādhatīti na patiṭṭhāti, ime cattāro [P 2.0393] mahābhūtā kiṃ āgamma appatiṭṭhā bhavantīti attho. Upādinnaṃyeva sandhāya pucchati. Dīghañca rassañcāti saṇṭhānavasena upādārūpaṃ vuttaṃ. Aṇuṃ thūlanti khuddakaṃ vā mahantaṃ vā, imināpi upādārūpe vaṇṇamattameva kathitaṃ. Subhāsubhanti subhañca asubhañca upādārūpameva kathitaṃ. Kiṃ pana upādārūpaṃ subhanti asubhanti atthi? Natthi. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhārammaṇaṃ paneva kathitaṃ. Nāmañca rūpañcāti nāmañca dīghādibhedaṃ rūpañca. Uparujjhatīti nirujjhati, kiṃ āgamma asesametaṃ nappavattatīti.

498. Therein, 'finds no footing' means 'is not established.' The meaning is: On what account do these four great elements become unestablished? He asks with reference only to that which is appropriated. 'Long and short' refers to derived matter spoken of by way of shape. 'Fine and coarse' means small or large; by this too, only appearance as derived matter is spoken of. 'Beautiful and ugly' speaks only of derived matter that is beautiful and ugly. But is there derived matter that is 'beautiful' or 'ugly'? There is not. Rather, agreeable and disagreeable objects are spoken of thus. 'Name and form' refers to name, and form with its divisions of long, etc. 'Is obstructed' means 'ceases.' On what account does this entirely not occur?

Evaṃ pucchitabbaṃ siyāti pucchaṃ dassetvā idāni vissajjanaṃ dassento tatra veyyākaraṇaṃ bhavatīti vatvā – “viññāṇa”ntiādimāha.

Having shown the question, 'Thus it should be asked,' and now, wishing to show the answer, having said, 'Therein is the explanation,' He spoke the words beginning with 'consciousness'.

499. Tattha viññātabbanti viññāṇaṃ nibbānassetaṃ nāmaṃ, tadetaṃ nidassanābhāvato anidassanaṃ. Uppādanto vā vayanto vā ṭhitassa aññathattanto vā etassa natthīti anantaṃ. Pabhanti panetaṃ kira titthassa nāmaṃ, tañhi papanti etthāti papaṃ, pakārassa pana bhakāro kato. Sabbato pabhamassāti sabbatopabhaṃ. Nibbānassa kira yathā mahāsamuddassa yato yato otaritukāmā honti, taṃ tadeva titthaṃ, atitthaṃ nāma natthi. Evameva aṭṭhatiṃsāya kammaṭṭhānesu yena yena mukhena nibbānaṃ otaritukāmā honti, taṃ tadeva titthaṃ, nibbānassa atitthaṃ nāma natthi. Tena vuttaṃ “sabbatopabha”nti. Ettha āpo cāti ettha [M 1.0326] nibbāne idaṃ nibbānaṃ āgamma sabbametaṃ āpotiādinā nayena vuttaṃ upādinnaka dhammajātaṃ nirujjhati, appavattaṃ hotīti.

499. Therein, 'because it is to be specially known,' it is called 'consciousness.' This is a name for Nibbāna. That Nibbāna, because it cannot be pointed out, is called 'non-manifest.' Because for this Nibbāna there is no limit of arising, nor a limit of ceasing, nor a limit of alteration for that which exists, it is called 'endless.' Furthermore, this word 'pabha' is indeed a name for a landing place. For, 'they drink variously here,' thus it is called 'papa.' Furthermore, for the letter 'p,' the letter 'bh' has been substituted. 'It has a landing place on all sides,' thus it is called 'luminous on all sides.' Indeed, for Nibbāna, it is like the great ocean: from whichever place one wishes to descend, that very place is a landing place; there is no place that is not a landing place. In the same way, among the thirty-eight meditation subjects, by whichever entrance one wishes to descend into Nibbāna, that very entrance is a landing place; for Nibbāna, there is no entrance that is not a landing place. Therefore, it was said, 'luminous on all sides.' As for 'Here, water...,' it means: in this Nibbāna, having reached this Nibbāna by taking it as an object, this whole mass of appropriated phenomena, spoken of in the manner beginning with 'water,' ceases and becomes non-recurrent.

Idānissa nirujjhanūpāyaṃ dassento “viññāṇassa nirodhena etthetaṃ uparujjhatī”ti āha. Tattha viññāṇanti carimakaviññāṇampi abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇampi[P 2.0394], carimakaviññāṇassāpi hi nirodhena etthetaṃ uparujjhati. Vijjhātadīpasikhā viya apaṇṇattikabhāvaṃ yāti. Abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassāpi anuppādanirodhena anuppādavasena uparujjhati. Yathāha “sotāpattimaggañāṇena abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa nirodhena ṭhapetvā sattabhave anamatagge saṃsāre ye [V 1.0295] uppajjeyyuṃ nāmañca rūpañca etthete nirujjhantī”ti sabbaṃ cūḷaniddese vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Now, wishing to show the means of its cessation, He said, 'With the cessation of consciousness, this ceases here.' Therein, 'consciousness' means both the final consciousness and the constructing consciousness. For with the cessation of the final consciousness, this ceases here. Like the flame of an extinguished lamp, it goes to a state beyond designation. The constructing consciousness also ceases through the cessation of non-arising, by way of non-arising. As it was said: 'By the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, with the cessation of the constructing consciousness, setting aside seven existences, whatever name and form would arise in the beginningless saṃsāra, they cease here.' All this should be understood in the very way spoken of in the Cūḷaniddesa. The remainder is clear everywhere.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Thus in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya,

Kevaṭṭasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Kevaṭṭa Sutta is concluded.

12. Lohiccasuttavaṇṇanā

12. The Explanation of the Lohicca Sutta

Lohiccabrāhmaṇavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Story of the Brahmin Lohicca

501. Evaṃ [P 2.0395][V 1.0296][M 1.0327] me sutaṃ…pe… kosalesūti lohiccasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ anuttānapadavaṇṇanā. Sālavatikāti tassa gāmassa nāmaṃ, so kira vatiyā viya samantato sālapantiyā parikkhitto. Tasmā sālavatikāti vuccati. Lohiccoti tassa brāhmaṇassa nāmaṃ.

501. Thus have I heard… and so on… in Kosala. This is the Lohicca Sutta. Herein is an exposition of the unelucidated terms. Sālavatikā is the name of that village; it was, it is said, surrounded on all sides by rows of sal trees, as if by a fence. Therefore, it is called Sālavatikā. Lohicca is the name of that brahmin.

502-503. Pāpakanti parānukampā virahitattā lāmakaṃ, na pana ucchedasassatānaṃ aññataraṃ. Uppannaṃ hotīti jātaṃ hoti, na kevalañca citte jātamattameva. So kira tassa vasena parisamajjhepi evaṃ bhāsatiyeva. Kiñhi paro parassāti paro yo anusāsīyati, so tassa anusāsakassa kiṃ karissati. Attanā paṭiladdhaṃ kusalaṃ dhammaṃ attanāva sakkatvā garuṃ katvā vihātabbanti vadati.

'Evil' means base because it is devoid of compassion for others, but it is not one of the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism. 'Arises' means it is born, and not merely arisen in the mind alone. It is said that because of that view, he spoke thus even in the midst of the assembly. 'What indeed can one do for another?' means: what can the one who is being instructed do for his instructor? He says that the wholesome Dhamma attained by oneself should be honored and respected by oneself, and one should abide thus.
