504-407. Rosikaṃ nhāpitaṃ āmantesīti rosikāti evaṃ itthiliṅgavasena laddhanāmaṃ nhāpitaṃ āmantesi. So kira bhagavato āgamanaṃ sutvā cintesi – “vihāraṃ gantvā diṭṭhaṃ nāmaṃ bhāro, gehaṃ pana āṇāpetvā passissāmi ceva yathāsatti ca āgantukabhikkhaṃ dassāmī”ti, tasmā evaṃ nhāpitaṃ āmantesi.

'He addressed the barber, Rosika': he addressed the barber who had acquired the name 'Rosikā' in the feminine gender. It is said that, hearing of the Blessed One’s arrival, he thought: 'Going to the monastery to see him would be a burden; however, by having him invited to my house, I can both see him and give alms to the visiting monks according to my ability.' Therefore, he addressed the barber thus.

508. Piṭṭhito piṭṭhitoti kathāphāsukatthaṃ pacchato pacchato anubandho hoti. Vivecetūti vimocetu, taṃ diṭṭhigataṃ vinodetūti vadati. Ayaṃ kira upāsako lohiccassa brāhmaṇassa piyasahāyako. Tasmā tassa atthakāmatāya evamāha. Appeva nāma siyāti ettha paṭhamavacanena bhagavā gajjati, dutiyavacanena anugajjati. Ayaṃ kirettha [P 2.0396] adhippāyo – rosike etadatthameva mayā cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni. Kappasatasahassañca vividhāni dukkarāni karontena pāramiyo pūritā[V 1.0297], etadatthameva sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭividdhaṃ, na me lohiccassa diṭṭhigataṃ bhindituṃ bhāroti, imamatthaṃ dassento paṭhamavacanena bhagavā gajjati. Kevalaṃ rosike [M 1.0328] lohiccassa mama santike āgamanaṃ vā nisajjā vā allāpasallāpo vā hotu, sacepi lohiccasadisānaṃ satasahassassa kaṅkhā hoti, paṭibalo ahaṃ vinodetuṃ lohiccassa pana ekassa diṭṭhivinodane mayhaṃ ko bhāroti imamatthaṃ dassento dutiyavacanena bhagavā anugajjatīti veditabbo.

508. ‘Following behind, following behind’ (piṭṭhito piṭṭhito) means following behind for the ease of conversation. ‘Let him dissuade’ (vivecetu) means he says: ‘Let him liberate him, let him remove that wrong view.’ It is said that this lay follower was a dear friend of the brahmin Lohicca. Therefore, wishing for his welfare, he spoke thus. ‘Perhaps it may be so’ (appeva nāma siyā): here, with the first utterance, the Blessed One roars; with the second utterance, he echoes the roar. The meaning here is this: ‘Rosika, for this very purpose I have fulfilled the perfections for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand kalpas, performing various difficult deeds. For this very purpose, I have penetrated the knowledge of omniscience. It is no burden for me to shatter Lohicca’s wrong view.’ Showing this meaning, the Blessed One roars with the first utterance. ‘Rosika, let there merely be Lohicca’s coming to me, sitting, or conversation. Even if there is the doubt of a hundred thousand like Lohicca, I am capable of dispelling it. What burden is it for me to remove the wrong view of just one Lohicca?’ Showing this meaning, the Blessed One echoes the roar with the second utterance—thus it should be understood.

Lohiccabrāhmaṇānuyogavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Interrogation of the Brahmin Lohicca

509. Samudayasañjātīti samudayassa sañjāti bhoguppādo, tato uṭṭhitaṃ dhanadhaññanti attho. Ye taṃ upajīvantīti ye ñātiparijanadāsakammakarādayo janā taṃ nissāya jīvanti. Antarāyakaroti lābhantarāyakaro. Hitānukampīti ettha hitanti vuḍḍhi. Anukampatīti anukampī, icchatīti attho, vuḍḍhiṃ icchati vā no vāti vuttaṃ hoti. Nirayaṃ vā tiracchānayoniṃ vāti sace sā micchādiṭṭhi sampajjati, niyatā hoti, ekaṃsena niraye nibbattati, no ce, tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattatīti attho.

509. ‘Born of revenue’ (samudayasañjāti) means the arising of revenue, the production of wealth; the meaning is the wealth and grain that arise from that. ‘Those who depend on it’ (ye taṃ upajīvanti) means those people—relatives, attendants, slaves, workers, and so on—who live relying on it. ‘Creating obstacles’ (antarāyakaroti) means one who creates an obstacle to gain. ‘Wishing for their welfare’ (hitānukampī): here, ‘welfare’ (hitaṃ) means increase (vuḍḍhi). ‘Compassionate’ (anukampī) means one is compassionate, meaning one desires; it is said, ‘Does one desire their increase or not?’ ‘To hell or the animal realm’ (nirayaṃ vā tiracchānayoniṃ vā): if that wrong view is accomplished and becomes fixed, one is certainly reborn in hell; if not, one is reborn in the animal realm—this is the meaning.

510-512. Idāni yasmā yathā attano lābhantarāyena sattā saṃvijjanti na tathā paresaṃ, tasmā suṭṭhutaraṃ brāhmaṇaṃ pavecetukāmo “taṃ kiṃ maññasī”ti dutiyaṃ upapattimāha. Ye cimeti ye ca ime tathāgatassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā ariyabhūmiṃ okkamituṃ asakkontā kulaputtā dibbā gabbhāti upayogatthe paccattavacanaṃ, dibbe gabbheti attho. Dibbā, gabbhāti ca channaṃ devalokānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Paripācentīti devalokagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pūrayamānā dānaṃ, dadamānā, sīlaṃ rakkhamānā, gandhamālādīhi, pūjaṃ kurumānā bhāvanaṃ bhāvayamānā pācenti vipācenti paripācenti pariṇāmaṃ gamenti. Dibbānaṃ bhavānaṃ abhinibbattiyāti dibbabhavā nāma devānaṃ vimānāni[P 2.0397], tesaṃ nibbattanatthāyāti attho. Atha vā dibbā gabbhāti dānādayo puññavisesā. Dibbā bhavāti devaloke vipākakkhandhā, tesaṃ nibbattanatthāya tāni puññāni karontīti attho. Tesaṃ antarāyakaroti tesaṃ maggasampattiphalasampattidibbabhavavisesānaṃ antarāyakaro. Iti bhagavā ettāvatā aniyamiteneva opammavidhinā yāva bhavaggā [M 1.0329] uggataṃ brāhmaṇassa mānaṃ bhinditvā idāni codanārahe tayo satthāre dassetuṃ “tayo kho me, lohiccā”tiādimāha.

510–512. Now, because beings are agitated by an obstacle to their own gain in a way they are not by that of others, therefore, wishing to make the brahmin desist more thoroughly, He stated the second suitable reason, beginning with ‘What do you think about this?’ (taṃ kiṃ maññasi). ‘And those’ (ye ca ime) refers to those sons of good families who, having heard the Tathāgata’s teaching, are unable to enter the noble ground. ‘Divine wombs’ (dibbā gabbhā) is a nominative expression used in the sense of the accusative; the meaning is ‘divine worlds’ (dibbe gabbhe). And ‘divine wombs’ (dibbā gabbhā) is a designation for the six celestial worlds. ‘They bring to maturity’ (paripācenti) means that, while fulfilling the practice that leads to the celestial world, giving gifts, observing virtue, making offerings with perfumes, garlands, and so on, and cultivating meditation, they cause it to ripen (pācenti), cause it to ripen especially (vipācenti), cause it to ripen all around (paripācenti), and bring it to a state of maturity (pariṇāmaṃ gamenti). ‘For the production of divine existences’ (dibbānaṃ bhavānaṃ abhinibbattiyā): ‘divine existences’ (dibbabhavā) refers to the mansions of the devas; the meaning is for the purpose of their arising. Alternatively, ‘divine wombs’ (dibbā gabbhā) refers to special meritorious deeds such as giving. ‘Divine existences’ (dibbā bhavā) refers to the resultant aggregates in the celestial world; the meaning is that they perform those meritorious deeds for the sake of their arising. ‘One who creates an obstacle for them’ (tesaṃ antarāyakaro) means one who creates an obstacle to their attainment of the path, attainment of the fruit, and special divine existences. Thus the Blessed One, having so far shattered the brahmin’s pride—which had risen as high as the peak of existence—by way of an unspecified simile, now, in order to point out the three teachers worthy of censure, said the words beginning with, ‘There are, Lohicca, three...’

Tayo codanārahavaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Three Worthy of Censure

513. Tattha [V 1.0298] sā codanāti tayo satthāre codentassa codanā. Na aññā cittaṃ upaṭṭhapentīti aññāya ājānanatthāya cittaṃ na upaṭṭhapenti. Vokkammāti nirantaraṃ tassa sāsanaṃ akatvā tato ukkamitvā vattantīti attho. Osakkantiyā vā ussakkeyyāti paṭikkamantiyā upagaccheyya, anicchantiyā iccheyya, ekāya sampayogaṃ anicchantiyā eko iccheyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Parammukhiṃ vā āliṅgeyyāti daṭṭhumpi anicchamānaṃ parammukhiṃ ṭhitaṃ pacchato gantvā āliṅgeyya. Evaṃsampadamidanti imassāpi satthuno “mama ime sāvakā”ti sāsanā vokkamma vattamānepi te lobhena anusāsato imaṃ lobhadhammaṃ evaṃsampadameva īdisameva vadāmi. Iti so evarūpo tava lobhadhammo yena tvaṃ osakkantiyā ussakkanto viya parammukhiṃ āliṅganto viya ahosītipi taṃ codanaṃ arahati. Kiñhi paro parassa karissatīti yena dhammena pare anusāsi, attānameva tāva tattha sampādehi, ujuṃ karohi. Kiñhi paro parassa karissatīti codanaṃ arahati.

513. Therein, ‘that censure’ (sā codanā) is the censure of one who censures the three teachers. ‘They do not apply their mind for the sake of knowledge’ (na aññā cittaṃ upaṭṭhapenti) means they do not apply their mind for the sake of knowing, for the purpose of knowing. ‘Having deviated’ (vokkamma) means not constantly practicing his teaching, they live having deviated from it; this is the meaning. ‘He would pursue one who is retreating’ (osakkantiyā ussakkeyya) means he would approach one who is moving back; he would desire one who is unwilling. It is said: when one woman is unwilling for union, one man would desire it. ‘Or he would embrace one who is turned away’ (parammukhiṃ vā āliṅgeyya) means he would go behind and embrace a woman who is standing with her face turned away, being unwilling even to be seen. ‘This is just so accomplished’ (evaṃsampadamidaṃ) means: Regarding this teacher also, even when his disciples are living having deviated from his teaching, if, thinking, ‘These are my disciples,’ he instructs them out of greed, I say that this quality of greed is just so accomplished, is just like this. Thus, that quality of greed of yours is of such a nature that you were like one pursuing a retreating woman or like one embracing a woman who is turned away; in this way too, one deserves that censure. ‘For what can another do for another?’ (kiñhi paro parassa karissati) means: In that Dhamma by which you instruct others, first accomplish it for yourself, make yourself upright. Indeed, what can the other (the disciple) do for the other (the teacher)? Thus, one deserves censure.

514. Niddāyitabbanti sassarūpakāni tiṇāni uppāṭetvā parisuddhaṃ kātabbaṃ.

514. ‘Should be weeded out’ (niddhāritabbaṃ) means that having pulled up the grasses that resemble the crop, it should be made pure.

515. Tatiyacodanāya kiñhi paro parassāti anusāsanaṃ asampaṭicchanakālato paṭṭhāya paro anusāsitabbo, parassa [P 2.0398] anusāsakassa kiṃ karissatīti nanu tattha appossukkataṃ āpajjitvā attanā paṭividdhadhammaṃ attanāva mānetvā pūjetvā vihātabbanti evaṃ codanaṃ arahatīti attho.

515. In the third censure, ‘For what can another do for another?’ (kiñhi paro parassāti) means: starting from the time of not accepting the instruction, what can the other who is to be instructed do for the other who is the instructor? Should one not then, having become unconcerned regarding that disciple, dwell honoring and revering for oneself the Dhamma that one has penetrated for oneself? In this way, one deserves censure; this is the meaning.

Na codanārahasatthuvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Teacher Unworthy of Reproach

516. Na [M 1.0330] codanārahoti ayañhi yasmā paṭhamameva attānaṃ patirūpe patiṭṭhāpetvā sāvakānaṃ dhammaṃ deseti. Sāvakā cassa assavā hutvā yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjanti, tāya ca paṭipattiyā mahantaṃ visesamadhigacchanti. Tasmā na codanārahoti.

516. He is not worthy of reproach, because, having first established himself in what is fitting, he teaches the Dhamma to his disciples. And his disciples, being obedient, practice as instructed, and by that practice they attain a great distinction. Therefore, he is not worthy of reproach.

517. Narakapapātaṃ papatantoti mayā gahitāya diṭṭhiyā ahaṃ narakapapātaṃ papatanto. Uddharitvā [V 1.0299] thale patiṭṭhāpitoti taṃ diṭṭhiṃ bhinditvā dhammadesanāhatthena apāyapatanato uddharitvā saggamaggathale ṭhapitomhīti vadati. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.

517. 'I was falling into the pit of hell' means: by the wrong view I had grasped, I was falling into the pit of hell. 'Having lifted me out, he set me on firm ground' means: having shattered that wrong view, with the hand of the Dhamma-teaching, having lifted me out from falling into the plane of misery, I have been established on the firm ground of the path to heaven. Thus he speaks. The rest here is clear indeed.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Thus, in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya,

Lohiccasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the Lohicca Sutta is concluded.

13. Tevijjasuttavaṇṇanā

13. The Exposition of the Tevijja Sutta

518. Evaṃ [P 2.0399][V 1.0300][M 1.0331] me sutaṃ…pe… kosalesūti tevijjasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ anuttānapadavaṇṇanā. Manasākaṭanti tassa gāmassa nāmaṃ. Uttarena manasākaṭassāti manasākaṭato avidūre uttarapasse. Ambavaneti taruṇaambarukkhasaṇḍe, ramaṇīyo kira so bhūmibhāgo, heṭṭhā rajatapaṭṭasadisā vālikā vippakiṇṇā, upari maṇivitānaṃ viya ghanasākhāpattaṃ ambavanaṃ. Tasmiṃ buddhānaṃ anucchavike pavivekasukhe ambavane viharatīti attho.

518. 'Thus have I heard...' and so on... 'in Kosala' is the Tevijja Sutta. Therein, this is the exposition of unclear terms. 'Manasākaṭa' is the name of that village. 'To the north of Manasākaṭa' means on the northern side, not far from Manasākaṭa. 'In the mango grove' means in a grove of young mango trees. It is said that plot of land was delightful. Below, sand like a silver plate was scattered about; above, the mango grove with its dense branches and leaves was like a jeweled canopy. The meaning is: he dwells in that mango grove, which is suitable for Buddhas and for the happiness of seclusion.

519. Abhiññātā abhiññātāti kulacārittādisampattiyā tattha tattha paññātā. Caṅkītiādīni tesaṃ nāmāni. Tattha caṅkī opāsādavāsiko. Tārukkho icchānaṅgalavāsiko. Pokkharasātī ukkaṭṭhavāsiko. Jāṇusoṇī sāvatthivāsiko. Todeyyo tudigāmavāsiko. Aññe cāti aññe ca bahujanā. Attano attano nivāsaṭṭhānehi āgantvā mantasajjhāyakaraṇatthaṃ tattha paṭivasanti. Manasākaṭassa kira ramaṇīyatāya te brāhmaṇā tattha nadītīre gehāni kāretvā parikkhipāpetvā aññesaṃ bahūnaṃ pavesanaṃ nivāretvā antarantarā tattha gantvā vasanti.

519. 'Well-known, well-known' means renowned in various places for their accomplishment in lineage, conduct, and so on. 'Caṅkī' and so on are their names. Among them, Caṅkī was a resident of Opāsāda. Tārukkha was a resident of Icchānaṅgala. Pokkharasāti was a resident of Ukkaṭṭhā. Jāṇussoṇi was a resident of Sāvatthī. Todeyya was a resident of Tudigāma. 'And others' means other brahmins of great wealth. Having come from their own respective residences, they reside there for the purpose of reciting mantras. It is said that due to the delightfulness of Manasākaṭa, those brahmins had houses built there on the riverbank, had them enclosed, prevented the entry of many others, and from time to time would go and dwell there.

520-521. Vāseṭṭhabhāradvājānanti vāseṭṭhassa ca pokkharasātino antevāsikassa, bhāradvājassa ca tārukkhantevāsikassa. Ete kira dve jātisampannā tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū ahesuṃ. Jaṅghavihāranti aticiranisajjapaccayā kilamathavinodanatthāya jaṅghacāraṃ. Te kira divasaṃ sajjhāyaṃ katvā sāyanhe vuṭṭhāya nhānīyasambhāragandhamālateladhotavatthāni gāhāpetvā attano parijanaparivutā nhāyitukāmā [P 2.0400] nadītīraṃ gantvā rajatapaṭṭavaṇṇe vālikāsaṇḍe aparāparaṃ caṅkamiṃsu. Ekaṃ caṅkamantaṃ itaro anucaṅkami, puna itaraṃ itaroti. Tena vuttaṃ “anucaṅkamantānaṃ anuvicarantāna”nti. Maggāmaggeti magge ca amagge ca. Katamaṃ nu kho paṭipadaṃ pūretvā katamena maggena sakkā sukhaṃ brahmalokaṃ gantunti evaṃ maggāmaggaṃ ārabbha kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesunti attho. Añjasāyanoti ujumaggassetaṃ vevacanaṃ, añjasā [M 1.0332] vā ujukameva etena āyanti āgacchantīti [V 1.0301] añjasāyano niyyāniko niyyātīti niyyāyanto niyyāti, gacchanto gacchatīti attho.

'Of Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja' means: of Vāseṭṭha, the pupil of Pokkharasāti, and of Bhāradvāja, the pupil of Tārukkha. It is said these two, accomplished in birth, were masters of the three Vedas. 'Walking for exercise' means walking about to dispel the weariness caused by sitting for a very long time. It is said that having recited their texts during the day, they would rise in the evening, have bathing requisites—perfumes, garlands, oil, and washed cloths—brought, and, surrounded by their retinue and desiring to bathe, they would go to the riverbank and walk back and forth on the sandbank that was the color of a silver sheet. One walking was followed by the other, and then again the other was followed by the first. Therefore it was said 'while they were walking up and down, while they were pacing about.' 'On the path and the non-path' means on the right path and the wrong path. The meaning is: they raised a conversation concerning the path and the non-path, thinking, 'Having fulfilled which practice, by which path might one be able to go with ease to the Brahma-world?' 'Añjasāyano' is a synonym for 'straight path.' Or, because by this path they 'come' (āyanti) 'straight' (añjasaṃ), 'directly' (ujukaṃ), it is called añjasāyano. 'Leading out, it leads out' (nīyyāniko niyyāti) means: going forth, one goes forth; proceeding, one proceeds.

Takkarassa brahmasahabyatāyāti yo taṃ maggaṃ karoti paṭipajjati, tassa brahmunā saddhiṃ sahabhāvāya, ekaṭṭhāne pātubhāvāya gacchatīti attho. Yvāyanti yo ayaṃ. Akkhātoti kathito dīpito. Brāhmaṇena pokkharasātināti attano ācariyaṃ apadisati. Iti vāseṭṭho sakameva ācariyavādaṃ thometvā paggaṇhitvā vicarati. Bhāradvājopi sakamevāti. Tena vuttaṃ “neva kho asakkhi vāseṭṭho”tiādi.

'For companionship with Brahmā for the doer of that' means: for one who undertakes and practices that path, it leads to a state of togetherness with Brahmā, to manifestation in the same place. This is the meaning. 'Yvāyaṃ' means 'yo ayaṃ' (this which). 'Akkhāto' means spoken, revealed. With the words 'by the brahmin Pokkharasāti,' he indicates his own teacher. Thus Vāseṭṭha goes about praising and upholding only his own teacher's doctrine. Bhāradvāja, too, goes about praising and upholding only his own teacher's doctrine. Therefore, 'Vāseṭṭha was not able...' and so on was said.

Tato vāseṭṭho “ubhinnampi amhākaṃ kathā aniyyānikāva, imasmiñca loke maggakusalo nāma bhotā gotamena sadiso natthi, bhavañca gotamo avidūre vasati, so no tulaṃ gahetvā nisinnavāṇijo viya kaṅkhaṃ chindissatī”ti cintetvā tamatthaṃ bhāradvājassa ārocetvā ubhopi gantvā attano kathaṃ bhagavato ārocesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “atha kho vāseṭṭho…pe… yvāyaṃ akkhāto brāhmaṇena tārukkhenā”ti.

Then Vāseṭṭha, thinking, 'The talk of both of us is inconclusive. In this world, there is no one named "skilled in the path" who is like the venerable Gotama, and the venerable Gotama dwells not far away. He will cut off our doubt like a merchant seated holding a scale,' informed Bhāradvāja of this matter. Then both of them went and reported their conversation to the Blessed One. Therefore it was said: 'Then Vāseṭṭha... and so on... which was declared by the brahmin Tārukkha.'

522. Ettha bho gotamāti etasmiṃ maggāmagge. Viggaho vivādotiādīsu pubbuppattiko viggaho. Aparabhāge vivādo. Duvidhopi eso nānāācariyānaṃ vādato nānāvādo.

522. 'In this, venerable Gotama' means in this matter of the path and the non-path. In 'contention, dispute,' and so on, the initial arising of opposition is 'contention' (viggaho). The taking up of opposition in the later stage is 'dispute' (vivādo). This, being of two kinds, is a 'difference of opinion' (nānāvādo) because of the doctrines of various teachers.

523. Atha kismiṃ pana voti tvampi ayameva maggoti attano ācariyavādameva paggayha tiṭṭhasi, bhāradvājopi attano ācariyavādameva, ekassāpi ekasmiṃ saṃsayo natthi. Evaṃ sati kismiṃ vo viggahoti pucchati.

523. 'Then in what, pray, is your contention?' means: You, saying, 'This alone is the path,' stand upholding only your own teacher's doctrine. Bhāradvāja, too, stands upholding only his own teacher's doctrine. Neither of you has any doubt about your own position. This being so, in what is your contention? Thus he asks.

524. Maggāmagge[P 2.0401], bho gotamāti magge bho gotama amagge ca, ujumagge ca anujumagge cāti attho. Esa kira ekabrāhmaṇassāpi maggaṃ “na maggo”ti na vadati. Yathā pana attano ācariyassa maggo ujumaggo, na [M 1.0333] evaṃ aññesaṃ anujānāti, tasmā tamevatthaṃ dīpento “kiñcāpi bho gotamā”tiādimāha.

524. 'In the matter of the path and the non-path, venerable Gotama' means: venerable Gotama, in the matter of the path and the non-path, the straight path and the crooked path. This is the meaning. It is said that this one does not say of any brahmin's path, 'That is not the path.' However, just as his own teacher's path is the straight path, he does not concede the same for the paths of others. Therefore, elucidating that very meaning, he said, 'Although, venerable Gotama...' and so on.

Sabbāni tānīti liṅgavipallāsena vadati, sabbe teti vuttaṃ hoti. Bahūnīti aṭṭha vā dasa [V 1.0302] vā. Nānāmaggānīti mahantāmahantajaṅghamaggasakaṭamaggādivasena nānāvidhāni sāmantā gāmanadītaḷākakhettādīhi āgantvā gāmaṃ pavisanamaggāni.

'Sabbāni tāni' (all those [neuter]): he says this with a change of gender; what is meant is 'sabbe te' (all of those [masculine]). 'Bahūni' (many) means eight or ten. 'Nānāmaggāni' (various paths) means paths for entering the village, of various kinds by way of great and large footpaths, cart-roads, and so on, which come from the surrounding villages, rivers, reservoirs, fields, and other places.

525-526. “Niyyantīti vāseṭṭha vadesī”ti bhagavā tikkhattuṃ vacībhedaṃ katvā paṭiññaṃ kārāpesi. Kasmā? Titthiyā hi paṭijānitvā pacchā niggayhamānā avajānanti. So tathā kātuṃ na sakkhissatīti.

“‘Do you say, Vāseṭṭha, that they lead out?’—thus the Blessed One, varying the utterance three times, caused him to make this affirmation. Why? Because sectarians, having made an affirmation, later deny it when being refuted. He (Vāseṭṭha) would not be able to do so.”

527-529. Teva tevijjāti te tevijjā. Vakāro āgamasandhimattaṃ. Andhaveṇīti andhapaveṇī, ekena cakkhumatā gahitayaṭṭhiyā koṭiṃ eko andho gaṇhati, taṃ andhaṃ añño taṃ aññoti evaṃ paṇṇāsasaṭṭhi andhā paṭipāṭiyā ghaṭitā andhaveṇīti vuccati. Paramparasaṃsattāti aññamaññaṃ laggā, yaṭṭhigāhakenapi cakkhumatā virahitāti attho. Eko kira dhutto andhagaṇaṃ disvā “asukasmiṃ nāma gāme khajjabhojjaṃ sulabha”nti ussāhetvā “tena hi tattha no sāmi nehi, idaṃ nāma te demā”ti vutte, lañjaṃ gahetvā antarāmagge maggā okkamma mahantaṃ gacchaṃ anuparigantvā purimassa hatthena pacchimassa kacchaṃ gaṇhāpetvā “kiñci kammaṃ atthi, gacchatha tāva tumhe”ti vatvā palāyi, te divasampi gantvā maggaṃ avindamānā “kuhiṃ no cakkhumā, kuhiṃ maggo”ti paridevitvā maggaṃ avindamānā tattheva mariṃsu. Te sandhāya vuttaṃ “paramparasaṃsattā”ti. Purimopīti purimesu dasasu brāhmaṇesu ekopi. Majjhimopīti [P 2.0402] majjhimesu ācariyapācariyesu ekopi. Pacchimopīti idāni tevijjesu brāhmaṇesu ekopi. Hassakaññevāti hasitabbameva. Nāmakaññevāti lāmakaṃyeva. Tadetaṃ atthābhāvena rittakaṃ, rittakattāyeva tucchakaṃ. Idāni brahmaloko tāva tiṭṭhatu, yo tevijjehi na diṭṭhapubbova. Yepi candimasūriye tevijjā passanti, tesampi sahabyatāya maggaṃ desetuṃ nappahontīti dassanatthaṃ “taṃ kiṃ maññasī”tiādimāha.

“‘Teva tevijjā’ means: those Brahmins who are knowers of the three Vedas. The letter ‘v’ is merely an augment for euphonic conjunction. ‘Andhaveṇī’ means a line of blind men (andhapaveṇī). Just as one blind man holds the end of a staff held by a sighted person, another blind man holds that blind man, and another holds him, and so on—thus, fifty or sixty blind men linked in succession are called a ‘blind line.’ ‘Paramparasaṃsattā’ means clinging to one another, devoid even of a sighted person to make them hold the staff; this is the meaning. It is said that a certain rogue, seeing a group of blind men, encouraged them, saying, ‘In such-and-such a village, food is easy to obtain.’ When it was said, ‘Then, master, lead us there; we will give you such-and-such,’ he took the bribe and, on the way, departed from the path. After circling a large thicket, he had the first blind man grasp the loincloth-end of the last one with his hand, and saying, ‘I have some business, you all go on ahead,’ he fled. Those blind men, having walked for a whole day and not finding the path, lamented, ‘Where is our sighted man? Where is the path?’ and, not finding the path, they died right there. With reference to them, it was said, ‘paramparasaṃsattā’ (linked in succession). ‘Purimopi’ means: not even one among the first ten Brahmin sages. ‘Majjhimopi’ means: not even one among the middle teachers and their teachers. ‘Pacchimopi’ means: not even one among the current Brahmins who know the three Vedas. ‘Hassakaññeva’ means: merely laughable. ‘Nāmakaññeva’ means: merely base. That statement, due to an absence of meaning, is void; and precisely because it is void, it is empty. For now, set aside the Brahma-world, which has never before been seen by those who know the three Vedas. To show that even with regard to the moon and sun, which the knowers of the three Vedas do see, they are unable to point out the path to companionship with them, he said, ‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi’ (‘What do you think of that?’), and so on.”

530. Tattha [M 1.0334] yato candimasūriyā uggacchantīti yasmiṃ kāle uggacchanti. Yattha ca oggacchantīti yasmiṃ kāle atthamenti, uggamanakāle ca atthaṅgamanakāle ca passantīti attho. Āyācantīti “udehi bhavaṃ canda, udehi bhavaṃ sūriyā”ti evaṃ āyācanti. Thomayantīti “sommo cando, parimaṇḍalo cando, sappabho cando”tiādīni vadantā pasaṃsanti. Pañjalikāti paggahitaañjalikā. Namassamānāti “namo namo”ti vadamānā.

530. “Therein, ‘yato candimasūriyā uggacchantī’ means ‘at which time they rise.’ ‘Yattha ca oggacchantī’ means ‘at which time they go to setting.’ The meaning is: they see them at the time of rising and at the time of setting. ‘Āyācanti’ means they request thus: ‘Rise, Lord Moon! Rise, Lord Sun!’ ‘Thomayanti’ means they praise, saying such things as: ‘The moon is cool; the moon is perfectly round; the moon is radiant.’ ‘Pañjalikā’ means having raised cupped hands. ‘Namassamānā’ means while saying, ‘Homage, homage.’”

531-532. Yaṃ passantīti ettha yanti nipātamattaṃ. Kiṃ pana na kirāti ettha idha pana [V 1.0303] kiṃ vattabbaṃ. Yattha kira tevijjehi brāhmaṇehi na brahmā sakkhidiṭṭhoti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

“In the phrase ‘yaṃ passati,’ the word ‘yaṃ’ is merely a particle. Regarding ‘kiṃ pana na kirā,’ the meaning should be understood thus: Wherein Brahmā has not been seen directly by the Brahmins who know the three Vedas, what is there to be said here in this matter?”

Aciravatīnadīupamākathā

The Discourse on the Simile of the Aciravatī River

542. Samatittikāti samabharitā. Kākapeyyāti yattha katthaci tīre ṭhitena kākena sakkā pātunti kākapeyyā. Pāraṃ taritukāmoti nadiṃ atikkamitvā paratīraṃ gantukāmo. Avheyyāti pakkoseyya. Ehi pārāpāranti ambho pāra apāraṃ ehi, atha maṃ sahasāva gahetvā gamissasi, atthi me accāyikakammanti attho.

542. “`Samatittikā` means evenly filled (`samabharitā`). `Kākapeyyā` means a river where a crow standing on any bank whatsoever is able to drink. `Pāraṃ taritukāmo` means one who, having crossed over the river, wishes to go to the other shore. `Avheyyā` means one should call (`pakkoseyya`). `Ehi pārāpāra`: The meaning is, 'O yonder shore, come to this shore! Then you shall take me and go quickly, for I have urgent business.'”

544. Ye dhammā brāhmaṇakārakāti ettha pañcasīladasakusalakammapathabhedā dhammā brāhmaṇakārakāti veditabbā[P 2.0403], tabbiparītā abrāhmaṇakārakā. Indamavhāyāmāti indaṃ avhāyāma pakkosāma. Evaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ avhāyanassa niratthakataṃ dassetvā punapi bhagavā aṇṇavakucchiyaṃ sūriyo viya jalamāno pañcasatabhikkhuparivuto aciravatiyā tīre nisinno aparampi nadīupamaṃyeva āharanto “seyyathāpī”tiādimāha.

544. “Here, regarding `ye dhammā brāhmaṇakārakā` (the qualities that make one a brahmin), it should be understood that the dhammas divided into the five precepts and the ten wholesome courses of action are what 'make one a brahmin'; their opposites are what 'do not make one a brahmin'. Regarding `indamavhāyāma`, it means: we call upon Indra, we summon him. Having thus shown the futility of the brahmins' calling, the Blessed One—shining like the sun in the belly of the ocean, surrounded by five hundred monks, and seated on the bank of the Aciravatī—wishing to bring forth yet another river simile, spoke the words beginning with 'Just as...'”

546. Kāmaguṇāti kāmayitabbaṭṭhena kāmā, bandhanaṭṭhena guṇā. “Anujānāmi bhikkhave, ahatānaṃ vatthānaṃ diguṇaṃ saṅghāṭi”nti (mahāva. 348) ettha hi paṭalaṭṭho guṇaṭṭho. “Accenti kālā tarayanti rattiyo, vayoguṇā anupubbaṃ jahantī”ti ettha rāsaṭṭho guṇaṭṭho. “Sataguṇā dakkhiṇā pāṭikaṅkhitabbā”ti [M 1.0335] (ma. ni. 3.379) ettha ānisaṃsaṭṭho guṇaṭṭho. “Antaṃ antaguṇaṃ (khu. pā. 3.1) kayirā mālāguṇe bahū”ti (dha. pa. 53) ca ettha bandhanaṭṭho guṇaṭṭho. Idhāpi eseva adhippeto. Tena vuttaṃ “bandhanaṭṭhena guṇā”ti. Cakkhuviññeyyāti cakkhuviññāṇena passitabbā. Etenupāyena sotaviññeyyādīsupi attho veditabbo. Iṭṭhāti pariyiṭṭhā vā hontu, mā vā, iṭṭhārammaṇabhūtāti attho. Kantāti kāmanīyā. Manāpāti manavaḍḍhanakā. Piyarūpāti piyajātikā. Kāmūpasañhitāti ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppajjamānena kāmena upasañhitā. Rajanīyāti rañjanīyā, rāguppattikāraṇabhūtāti attho.

546. “`Kāmaguṇā`: `kāmā` in the sense of 'that which is to be desired', and `guṇā` in the sense of 'that which binds'. For instance, in the passage, 'I allow, monks, a double-layered (`diguṇaṃ`) outer robe of new cloth,' `guṇa` has the meaning of 'layer' (`paṭalaṭṭho`). In, 'Times pass, nights fly by; the stages (`vayoguṇā`) of life are left behind in sequence,' `guṇa` has the meaning of 'group' or 'collection' (`rāsaṭṭho`). In, 'A gift of a hundredfold benefit (`sataguṇā`) is to be expected,' `guṇa` has the meaning of 'benefit' (`ānisaṃsaṭṭho`). And in, 'The small intestine (`antaguṇaṃ`) which binds the intestines (`antaṃ`)' and 'one should make many garlands (`mālāguṇe`)', `guṇa` has the meaning of 'binding' or 'string' (`bandhanaṭṭho`). Here too, this very meaning of 'binding' is intended. Therefore it was said, '`guṇā` in the sense of binding.' `Cakkhuviññeyyā` means 'to be seen by eye-consciousness.' By this method, the meaning of `sotaviññeyyā` (cognizable by the ear), etc., should also be understood. `Iṭṭhā` means: whether they are sought after or not, they are agreeable objects; this is the meaning. `Kantā` means desirable (`kāmanīyā`). `Manāpā` means they cause the mind to grow (`manavaḍḍhanakā`). `Piyarūpā` means they are of a dear nature (`piyajātikā`). `Kāmūpasañhitā` means they are connected with the sensual passion (`kāma`) that arises having taken them as an object. `Rajanīyā` means enticing (`rañjanīyā`); that is, they are a cause for the arising of passion; this is the meaning.”

Gadhitāti gedhena abhibhūtā hutvā. Mucchitāti mucchākārappattāya adhimattakāya taṇhāya abhibhūtā. Ajjhopannāti adhiopannā ogāḷhā “idaṃ sāra”nti pariniṭṭhānappattā hutvā. Anādīnavadassāvinoti [V 1.0304] ādīnavaṃ apassantā. Anissaraṇapaññāti idamettha nissaraṇanti, evaṃ parijānanapaññāvirahitā, paccavekkhaṇaparibhogavirahitāti attho.

“`Gadhitā` means being overcome by greed. `Mucchitā` means being overcome by excessive craving that has reached a state of delusion. `Ajjhopannā` means being overwhelmed, immersed, and having reached the final conclusion, 'This is the essence.' `Anādīnavadassāvino` means not seeing the danger. `Anissaraṇapaññā` means being devoid of the wisdom that discerns, 'This is the escape from it'; that is, being devoid of the practice of using things with reflection. This is the meaning.”

548. Āvaraṇātiādīsu [P 2.0404] āvarantīti āvaraṇā. Nivārentīti nīvaraṇā. Onandhantīti onāhanā. Pariyonandhantīti pariyonāhanā. Kāmacchandādīnaṃ vitthārakathā visuddhimaggato gahetabbā.

548. “Regarding `āvaraṇā` and so on: Because they obstruct (`āvaranti`), they are called obstructions (`āvaraṇā`). Because they prevent (`nivārenti`), they are called hindrances (`nīvaraṇā`). Because they descend upon and cover (`onandhanti`), they are called coverings (`onāhanā`). Because they completely descend upon and cover (`pariyonandhanti`), they are called complete coverings (`pariyonāhanā`). The detailed discourse on sensual desire and the other terms should be taken from the Visuddhimagga.”

549-550. Āvutā nivutā onaddhā pariyonaddhāti padāni āvaraṇādīnaṃ vasena vuttāni. Sapariggahoti itthipariggahena sapariggahoti pucchati. Apariggaho bho gotamātiādīsupi kāmacchandassa abhāvato itthipariggahena apariggaho. Byāpādassa abhāvato kenaci saddhiṃ veracittena avero. Thinamiddhassa abhāvato cittagelaññasaṅkhātena byāpajjena abyāpajjo. Uddhaccakukkuccābhāvato uddhaccakukkuccādīhi saṃkilesehi asaṃkiliṭṭhacitto suparisuddhamānaso. Vicikicchāya abhāvato cittaṃ vase vatteti. Yathā ca brāhmaṇā cittagatikā hontīti, cittassa vasena vattanti, na tādisoti vasavattī.

The words `āvutā`, `nivutā`, `onaddhā`, and `pariyonaddhā` are spoken in the sense of obstructions and so forth. `Sapariggaho`: He asks, 'Are you with possessions (`sapariggaho`)?' by way of possessing a woman. Regarding `Apariggaho, bho Gotama`, and so on, the meaning should be understood thus: Due to the absence of sensual desire, he is without possessions (`apariggaho`), that is, without the possession of a woman. Due to the absence of ill will, he is without enmity (`avero`) toward anyone, having no mind of enmity. Due to the absence of sloth and torpor, he is without mental affliction (`abyāpajjo`), which is known as sickness of the mind. Due to the absence of restlessness and remorse, his mind is unstained (`asaṃkiliṭṭhacitto`) by defilements such as restlessness and remorse, and his mind is perfectly pure (`suparisuddhamānaso`). Due to the absence of doubt, he wields mastery over his mind. And whereas brahmins are `cittagatikā`, that is, they act under the mind's power, he is not like that; therefore, he has mastery (`vasavattī`).

552. Idha [M 1.0336] kho panāti idha brahmalokamagge. Āsīditvāti amaggameva “maggo”ti upagantvā. Saṃsīdantīti “samatala”nti saññāya paṅkaṃ otiṇṇā viya anuppavisanti. Saṃsīditvā visāraṃ pāpuṇantīti evaṃ paṅke viya saṃsīditvā visāraṃ aṅgamaṅgasaṃbhañjanaṃ pāpuṇanti. Sukkhataraṃ maññe tarantīti marīcikāya vañcetvā “kākapeyyā nadī”ti saññāya “tarissāmā”ti hatthehi ca pādehi ca vāyamamānā sukkhataraṇaṃ maññe taranti. Tasmā yathā hatthapādādīnaṃ saṃbhañjanaṃ paribhañjanaṃ, evaṃ apāyesu saṃbhañjanaṃ paribhañjanaṃ pāpuṇanti. Idheva ca sukhaṃ vā sātaṃ vā na labhanti. Tasmā idaṃ tevijjānaṃ brāhmaṇānanti tasmā idaṃ brahmasahabyatāya maggadīpakaṃ tevijjakaṃ pāvacanaṃ tevijjānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ. Tevijjāiriṇanti tevijjāaraññaṃ iriṇanti hi agāmakaṃ mahāaraññaṃ vuccati. Tevijjāvivananti pupphaphalehi aparibhogarukkhehi sañchannaṃ nirudakaṃ araññaṃ[P 2.0405]. Yattha maggato ukkamitvā parivattitumpi na sakkā honti, taṃ sandhāyāha “tevijjāvivanantipi vuccatī”ti. Tevijjābyasananti tevijjānaṃ pañcavidhabyasanasadisametaṃ. Yathā hi ñātirogabhoga diṭṭhi sīlabyasanappattassa sukhaṃ nāma natthi, evaṃ tevijjānaṃ tevijjakaṃ pāvacanaṃ āgamma sukhaṃ nāma natthīti dasseti.

552. `Idha kho pana` means: here, on this path to the Brahmā world. `Āsīditvā` means: having approached what is not the path as if it were the path. `Saṃsīdanti` means: they sink down, like those who, with the perception that it is level ground, have entered into mud; they become submerged. `Saṃsīditvā visāraṃ pāpuṇanti` means: having thus sunk down as if in mud, they reach disintegration, the breaking of their major and minor limbs. `Sukkhataraṇaṃ maññe taranti` means: deceived by a mirage, with the perception that it is a `kākapeyyā` river, they think, 'We will cross,' and striving with hands and feet, it is as if they are making a dry crossing. Therefore, just as they would reach the breaking and shattering of their hands, feet, and other limbs, so too they reach breaking and shattering in the lower realms. And here in this present life, they obtain neither the bliss of jhāna (`sukhaṃ`) nor the pleasure of insight (`sātaṃ`). Therefore, `idaṃ tevijjānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ` means: this teaching of the Three-Veda-knowers, which is recognized as showing the path to companionship with Brahmā, belongs to the brahmins who know the Three Vedas. `Tevijjairiṇaṃ` means the wilderness of the Three-Veda-knowers; for a great, village-less forest is called an `iriṇa`. `Tevijjavivanaṃ` means a desolate forest, covered with trees whose flowers and fruits are of no use, and which is without water. Referring to a place where, having strayed from the path, one is not even able to turn about, the Blessed One said, 'It is also called the desolate forest of the Three-Veda-knowers.' `Tevijjabyasanaṃ` means: this teaching is similar to the five kinds of disaster for the Three-Veda-knowers. For just as there is no happiness for a person who has met with disaster concerning relatives, disease, wealth, views, or virtue, so too, this shows that for the Three-Veda-knowers, by relying on their teaching, there is no happiness.

554. Jātasaṃvaḍḍhoti jāto ca vaḍḍhito ca, yo hi kevalaṃ tattha jātova hoti, aññattha [V 1.0305] vaḍḍhito, tassa samantā gāmamaggā na sabbaso paccakkhā honti, tasmā jātasaṃvaḍḍhoti āha. Jātasaṃvaḍḍhopi yo ciranikkhanto, tassa na sabbaso paccakkhā honti. Tasmā “tāvadeva avasaṭa”nti āha, taṅkhaṇameva nikkhantanti attho. Dandhāyitattanti ayaṃ nu kho maggo, ayaṃ na nukhoti kaṅkhāvasena cirāyitattaṃ. Vitthāyitattanti yathā sukhumaṃ atthajātaṃ sahasā pucchitassa kassaci sarīraṃ thaddhabhāvaṃ gaṇhāti, evaṃ thaddhabhāvaggahaṇaṃ. Na tvevāti iminā sabbaññutaññāṇassa appaṭihatabhāvaṃ dasseti. Tassa hi purisassa mārāvaṭṭanādivasena siyā ñāṇassa [M 1.0337] paṭighāto. Tena so dandhāyeyya vā vitthāyeyya vā. Sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pana appaṭihataṃ, na sakkā tassa kenaci antarāyo kātunti dīpeti.

554. ‘Born and brought up’ means born and raised there. For one who is merely born there but raised elsewhere, the village paths all around are not entirely apparent; therefore, He said, ‘born and brought up.’ Even for one born and brought up who departed long ago, the paths are not entirely apparent. Therefore He said, 'who has just departed'; the meaning is, one who has departed at that very moment. ‘Slowness’ means the state of being slow due to doubt, wondering, ‘Is this the right path, or is this not the right path?’ ‘Stiffness’ means the grasping of a state of stiffness, just as when someone is suddenly asked about a subtle matter, their body becomes rigid. By ‘But not so,’ He shows the unobstructed nature of the knowledge of omniscience. For that man, there might be an obstruction to knowledge due to the influence of Māra and so on. Therefore, he might be slow or stiff. But the knowledge of omniscience is unobstructed; it is not possible for anyone to create an obstacle for it—this He clarifies.

555. Ullumpatu bhavaṃ gotamoti uddharatu bhavaṃ gotamo. Brāhmaṇiṃ pajanti brāhmaṇadārakaṃ, bhavaṃ gotamo mama brāhmaṇaputtaṃ apāyamaggato uddharitvā brahmalokamagge patiṭṭhapetūti attho. Athassa bhagavā buddhuppādaṃ dassetvā saddhiṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadāya mettāvihārādibrahmalokagāmimaggaṃ desetukāmo “tena hi vāseṭṭhā”tiādimāha. Tattha “idha tathāgato”tiādi sāmaññaphale vitthāritaṃ. Mettāsahagatenātiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ visuddhimagge brahmavihārakammaṭṭhānakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Seyyathāpi vāseṭṭha balavā saṅkhadhamotiādi pana idha apubbaṃ. Tattha balavāti balasampanno. Saṅkhadhamoti [P 2.0406] saṅkhadhamako. Appakasirenāti akicchena adukkhena. Dubbalo hi saṅkhadhamo saṅkhaṃ dhamantopi na sakkoti catasso disā sarena viññāpetuṃ, nāssa saṅkhasaddo sabbato pharati. Balavato pana vipphāriko hoti, tasmā “balavā”tiādimāha. Mettāya cetovimuttiyāti ettha mettāti vutte upacāropi appanāpi vaṭṭati, “cettovimuttī”ti vutte pana appanāva vaṭṭati. Yaṃ pamāṇakataṃ kammanti pamāṇakataṃ kammaṃ nāma kāmāvacaraṃ vuccati. Appamāṇakataṃ kammaṃ nāma rūpārūpāvacaraṃ. Tañhi pamāṇaṃ atikkamitvā odissakaanodissakadisāpharaṇavasena vaḍḍhetvā katattā appamāṇakatanti vuccati. Na taṃ tatrāvasissati na taṃ tatrāvatiṭṭhatīti taṃ kāmāvacarakammaṃ tasmiṃ rūpāvacarārūpāvacarakamme na ohīyati, na tiṭṭhati. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti – taṃ kāmāvacarakammaṃ tassa rūpārūpāvacarakammassa antarā laggituṃ vā ṭhātuṃ vā rūpārūpāvacarakammaṃ pharitvā pariyādiyitvā attano okāsaṃ gahetvā patiṭṭhātuṃ na sakkoti. Atha kho rūpāvacarārūpāvacarakammameva kāmāvacaraṃ mahogho viya parittaṃ udakaṃ pharitvā pariyādiyitvā attano okāsaṃ gahetvā tiṭṭhati. Tassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā sayameva brahmasahabyataṃ upanetīti. Evaṃvihārīti evaṃ mettādivihārī.

555. ‘May the Venerable Gotama lift up’ means ‘may the Venerable Gotama rescue.’ ‘The brahmin offspring’ means the brahmin boy; the meaning is: ‘May the Venerable Gotama, having rescued me, a brahmin's son, from the path to the plane of misery, establish me on the path to the Brahma-world.’ Then the Blessed One, wishing to show the arising of a Buddha and to teach the path leading to the Brahma-world together with the preliminary practice, beginning with the abiding in loving-kindness, said, ‘Then, Vāseṭṭha,’ and so on. Therein, ‘Here, a Tathāgata…’ and so on is explained in detail in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta. In ‘with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness,’ and so on, whatever should be said, all of that has been stated in the Visuddhimagga, in the section on the meditation subjects of the divine abidings. However, ‘Just as, Vāseṭṭha, a strong conch-blower,’ and so on, is new here. Therein, ‘strong’ means possessed of strength. ‘Conch-blower’ means a conch-blower. ‘With little effort’ means without trouble, without difficulty. For a weak conch-blower, even while blowing the conch, is not able to make it known to the four directions with the sound, nor does his conch sound spread everywhere. But for a strong one, it is pervasive; therefore, He said, ‘strong,’ and so on. In ‘by the liberation of mind through loving-kindness,’ when ‘loving-kindness’ is said, both access and absorption are appropriate. But when ‘liberation of mind’ is said, only absorption is appropriate. Regarding ‘whatever measured kamma,’ what is called ‘measured kamma’ is kamma of the sense-sphere. ‘Immeasurable kamma’ is the name for kamma of the form and formless spheres. For it is called ‘immeasurable’ because it is done having transcended measure and having been developed by way of pervading specified beings, unspecified beings, and the directions. ‘That does not remain there, that does not persist there’ means that sense-sphere kamma does not get left behind, does not persist, when that form-sphere and formless-sphere kamma is present. What is meant? That sense-sphere kamma is not able to attach itself or to stand in the midst of that form and formless-sphere kamma, nor is it able to pervade and overwhelm the form and formless-sphere kamma and, having taken its own opportunity, establish itself. Rather, it is the form and formless-sphere kamma itself that, like a great flood pervading and overwhelming a small amount of water, pervades and overwhelms the sense-sphere kamma and, having taken its own opportunity, stands firm. Having blocked the result of that sense-sphere kamma, it itself leads to companionship with Brahmā. ‘One who dwells thus’ means one who dwells thus with loving-kindness and so on.

559. Ete [V 1.0306][M 1.0338] mayaṃ bhavantaṃ gotamanti idaṃ tesaṃ dutiyaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ. Paṭhamameva hete majjhimapaṇṇāsake vāseṭṭhasuttaṃ sutvā saraṇaṃ gatā, imaṃ pana tevijjasuttaṃ sutvā dutiyampi saraṇaṃ gatā. Katipāhaccayena pabbajitvā aggaññasutte upasampadañceva arahattañca alatthuṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

559. ‘We, venerable Gotama…’—this is their second going for refuge. For indeed, at first they had already gone for refuge after hearing the Vāseṭṭha Sutta in the Majjhima Paṇṇāsaka. But having heard this Tevijja Sutta, they went for refuge a second time. After a few days, having gone forth, they attained both higher ordination and Arahantship during the Aggañña Sutta. The rest is clear everywhere.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Thus, in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya,

Tevijjasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the Tevijja Sutta is concluded.

Niṭṭhitā ca terasasuttapaṭimaṇḍitassa sīlakkhandhavaggassa

And concluded is that of the Sīlakkhandha Vagga, adorned with thirteen suttas:

Atthavaṇṇanāti.

The Explanation of the Meaning.

Sīlakkhandhavaggaṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sīlakkhandha Vagga is completed.
